When available, a centrifuge with a swinging bucket rotor is
ideal for the ﬂotation step (Fig. 5.2B). The strained feces-ﬂotation
solution mixture is poured into a 15-mL conical centrifuge tube,
and enough ﬂotation solution is added to form a reverse meniscus
at the top of the tube. A coverslip is then placed on top of the
meniscus and the tube spun with the coverslip in place. A second
tube of equal volume is needed to balance the centrifuge. Once
completed, the coverslip is removed and transferred along with
the adherent ﬂuid face down on a slide, and the slide is examined
(see Fig. 5.2B).
If only a ﬁxed-angle bucket rotor is available, the feces-ﬂotation
solution mixture can be poured into a 15-mL centrifuge tube to
the point at which it is almost full but does not spill when placed
into the centrifuge bucket (approximately 13 mL). The tube is then
spun without a coverslip. The top layer of the centrifuged material
can be collected by carefully touching the base of a small test tube
or a microbiologic loop to the surface and then transferring the
adherent ﬂuid to a slide. A coverslip is then applied and the
preparation examined using a microscope.
Slides should be completely examined using the 10× and, when
necessary, the 40× objective. Scanning a slide at low power (×4) is
not suﬃcient to allow detection of many nematode eggs and most
protozoan diagnostic stages. 1 Quantiﬁcation methods such as the
Wisconsin or modiﬁed McMaster egg counting techniques are not
used for routine canine and feline fecal ﬂotation. Some diagnostic
laboratories add a comment on the report about the relative
number of eggs, cysts, or oocysts detected. Nonetheless, it is
critical to start with an adequate amount of feces to optimize
sensitivity.
Fecal sedimentation
Sedimentation is used only for detection of helminths that shed
heavier eggs (see Table 5.1). Eggs of several trematodes, cestodes,
and even some nematodes (e.g., Physaloptera spp.) are not
routinely recovered on fecal ﬂotation. When these infections are
suspected, either simple or centrifugal sedimentation, as
described below, should be performed. Concentration is not as
great with sedimentation as it is with ﬂotation, but heavier eggs

vetexamprep.ir

are more likely to be detected with these methods than by direct
smear of feces alone.
For simple sedimentation, 100 mL of either tap water or saline is
combined in a beaker with approximately 10 g of feces, strained
through cheesecloth into a second beaker, and then allowed to
se le for 1 hour. The supernatant is then decanted, more water
added, and the se ling step repeated. A small amount of sediment
is then placed on a slide, a coverslip applied, and the slide
scanned using the 10× objective. Some protocols recommend use
of a smaller amount of feces and water combined in a test tube
rather than in a beaker. Centrifugation accelerates the separation,
but if mucus or fat are present, the fecal material should ﬁrst be
combined with Hemo-De (Scientiﬁc Safety Solvents, Keller, TX,
USA) to facilitate separation of eggs. For centrifugal
sedimentation, 1 g of feces is mixed with 10 mL of either 10%
formalin or water and poured into a glass or polypropylene
centrifuge tube and Hemo-De is added. The tube is capped and
vigorously shaken, then centrifuged for 5 minutes at 650 × g. An
applicator stick is used to break the top plug of debris so that both
the debris plug and the supernatant can be decanted. The
remaining sediment is placed on a slide, a coverslip applied, and
the slide examined using the 10× objective. 1
Baermann assay
The Baermann assay is used to recover motile nematode larvae,
such as lungworm larvae (see Chapter 117) and Strongyloides
stercoralis (see Chapter 116), from feces (see Table 5.1). The assay
should only be performed with fresh feces. Results will be
confounded by larvae from hatched hookworm eggs in specimens
even just a few days old, as well as by the presence of free-living
nematode larvae in feces collected from the ground.
Approximately 10 g of feces is placed in a double layer of
cheesecloth, secured by a rubber band, and suspended at the top
of a disposable wine glass with a hollow stem. The apparatus is
then ﬁlled with room temperature water to completely immerse
the feces and held at room temperature for 8 to 16 hours. Any
larvae present in the feces will migrate into the water and collect
at the base of the hollow stem. After resting, the feces is removed
and discarded and a small amount of ﬂuid removed from the base

vetexamprep.ir

of the stem with a pipe e, placed on a slide, a coverslip applied,
and examined for larvae using the 4× or 10× objective. 1
TABLE 5.2

+, useful or indicated; –, not used or recommended.

Preservation of Feces
No speciﬁc preservation or addition of ﬁxative is necessary before
routine fecal ﬂotation for common gastrointestinal parasites. If
submission will be delayed a few days, refrigeration is
recommended to prevent growth of mold and delay development
of nematode eggs. If examination is delayed for several days and
there is a desire to preserve protozoa, fresh feces can be mixed
with a preservative before shipment. Enough ﬁxative solution
should be added to the feces to ensure adequate ﬁxation. Some
commonly used solutions include polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and
10% formalin. 4 Ten percent formalin solution is an appropriate
ﬁxative for specimens suspected to contain Cryptosporidium,
because formalin ﬁxation, unlike ﬁxation with PVA, does not
interfere with immunodetection assays employed to detect
Cryptosporidium (e.g., direct ﬂuorescent antibody).
Potassium dichromate (1%) is the solution of choice for storing
specimens that contain oocysts of coccidia because it allows the
oocysts to sporulate, permi ing the precise measurements of
sporocysts and sporozoites and complete evaluation of oocyst
structure that are needed for identiﬁcation. 5 A 2% solution of
sulfuric acid is an acceptable alternative to 1% potassium
dichromate. Historically, PVA has been considered the best choice
for ﬁxing trophozoites because permanently stained slides can be
prepared from PVA-ﬁxed fecal material. However, both PVA,

vetexamprep.ir

which contains mercuric chloride, and potassium dichromate are
potent toxins and should be handled with great care. Less toxic,
more environmentally safe commercial substitutes for PVA have
become available, including Proto-Fix (AlphaTec Systems,
Vancouver, WA, USA) and ECOFIX (Meridian Diagnostics,
Cincinnati, OH, USA). 6

Microscopic Examination of Whole Blood
Diagnostic stages of parasites may be detected both in fresh blood
and in blood collected into anticoagulants. Microﬁlaria are often
detected in EDTA-anticoagulated blood by direct examination of a
saline wet mount of whole blood or by Kno test (see Chapter
111). In contrast, the most common method used to detect
protozoa in blood is by microscopic examination of a stained
blood smear. Bloodborne and systemic parasites that can be
detected in stained blood smears or in fresh wet mounts are listed
in Table 5.2.
Collection of Blood Specimens
Appropriate collection procedures for blood are dictated, in part,
by the parasites suspected to be the cause of disease. If diagnosis
requires blood smear examination, care should be taken during
blood collection and handling to avoid hemolysis that may
destroy parasites. Smears from fresh whole blood should be made
immediately after collection; blood collected into EDTA
anticoagulant can be submi ed for smears to be made at a later
time or for examining blood for microﬁlaria. 7 Some protozoa,
especially Babesia spp., are more easily found in the peripheral
circulation of microcapillary beds; detection of these parasites
may be enhanced by collecting from an ear margin or clipped
toenail.
Testing for Microfilaria
When present in high numbers, microﬁlaria may be found in
saline wet mounts of whole blood. However, the modiﬁed Kno
test, which concentrates any microﬁlaria present in 1 mL of blood,
allows more sensitive detection. To prepare a wet mount, a small
drop of anticoagulated whole blood is placed on a slide, a drop of
saline added, the specimen brieﬂy mixed, a coverslip applied, and

vetexamprep.ir

the material directly examined using the 10× objective for any
microﬁlaria present. Relative numbers and motility pa erns of
microﬁlaria present on a direct wet mount can support a
diagnosis of Diroﬁlaria immitis infection. However, accurate
measurement of microﬁlaria with an ocular micrometer is only
readily achieved using a Kno test.
To perform the modiﬁed Kno
test, 1 mL of EDTAanticoagulated whole blood is placed in a centrifuge tube and 9
mL of 2% formalin added. The specimen is capped and mixed
brieﬂy to lyse the red blood cells, then centrifuged at 650 × g for 5
minutes. The supernatant is discarded and a drop of 0.1%
methylene blue added to the sediment. Stained material is then
transferred to a microscope slide using a pipe e, a coverslip
applied, and the specimen examined using the 10× objective for
microﬁlaria. In the modiﬁed Kno test, microﬁlaria will be
immobilized, fully extended, and readily measured and examined
for key features that allow conﬁrmation of their identity as either
D. immitis or one of the other species that may be found in the
blood. The stain highlights microﬁlarial nuclei, aiding
identiﬁcation (see Chapter 111 for additional tests for heartworm
disease).
Preparation of Blood Films
Examination of dried blood ﬁlms is often useful for diagnosis of
protozoal infections. Thick ﬁlms allow examination of a larger
volume of blood, which increases sensitivity, but thin ﬁlms are
necessary for morphologic identiﬁcation. If possible, multiple
slides (at least two thick and two thin) should be prepared and
submi ed unstained. 3
Thin ﬁlms are prepared by placing a small drop of blood at one
end of a clean microscope slide and then using a second slide to
spread the blood. Blood should not be pushed across the slide
because this may rupture parasites. To prepare thick ﬁlms, two or
three drops of blood are placed on a clean microscope slide and
spread with the corner of another slide in a circular motion over a
2-cm area. Fresh blood should be stirred on the slide for an
additional 30 seconds to prevent formation of ﬁbrin strands.
EDTA-anticoagulated blood does not need to be stirred after
spreading. 3

vetexamprep.ir

Both thick and thin ﬁlms should be air dried at room
temperature on a ﬂat surface. The choice of stain will determine
the need for additional preparation and ﬁxation before staining.
Some stains require thick ﬁlms to be laked (immersed in distilled
water to lyse erythrocytes) before staining. Thin ﬁlms that are not
stained within 48 hours should be ﬁxed in 100% methanol. All
ﬁlms should be stored in a cool, dry, clean place in a sealed box. 3
Staining Blood Films
Giemsa, Wright, and Wright-Giemsa are the most commonly used
stains to detect and identify hemoprotozoa on blood smears. DiﬀQuik can be used, but both detection of the presence of protozoa
and subsequent morphologic identiﬁcation to species may be
more diﬃcult. 7 Giemsa-stained blood smears have the added
advantage of permanency; Wright-stained blood smears fade over
time.
Examination of Blood Films
Stained blood ﬁlms may be examined with or without a coverslip.
When a coverslip is not used, a drop of immersion oil can be
placed on the stained smear to reduce diﬀraction and facilitate
microscopic examination at low power and with the high-dry
objectives. Additional immersion oil should then be added and
the feathered edge of the stained smear examined closely using
the oil immersion objective. If preferred, a thin (#1) coverslip can
be applied with neutral mounting medium before examination.
The mounting medium prevents the coverslip from moving
around on the stained smear and also reduces diﬀraction in a
manner similar to immersion oil applied directly to the smear. 3
One advantage of using a coverslip is that it allows the slide to be
thoroughly cleaned with lens cleaner and reexamined at a later
date by another diagnostician; the surfaces of stained smears that
do not have a coverslip cannot be cleaned.

Examination of Intact Parasites
Intact metazoan parasites are often recovered from vomit, feces,
skin, or from other tissues collected at surgery or necropsy.
Whenever possible, all available specimens should be submi ed
for morphologic identiﬁcation to a diagnostic veterinary

vetexamprep.ir

parasitology laboratory. Helminths may be submi ed fresh in
saline or, if submission will be delayed, ﬁxed in dilute (5%)
formalin; the 10% formalin used for preservation of tissues can
destroy helminth structures needed for full identiﬁcation.
Arthropods should be submi ed in 70% ethanol. All specimens
from which nucleic acid will be collected for molecular
identiﬁcation or comparison should be placed in 70% ethanol.
Formalin-ﬁxed specimens are of limited value for molecular
evaluation.

Microscopic Examination of Other Specimens
Parasites may sometimes be found on histologic examination of
biopsy specimens, tissues collected at necropsy, or on cytology.
Ideally, intact helminths or arthropods will be submi ed directly
for identiﬁcation. Although intact stages of parasites may be
detected and identiﬁed on microscopic examination of aspirates
or impression smears and protozoa can be identiﬁed in histologic
sections (see Table 5.2), thin sections of only one portion of a large
metazoan parasite often precludes complete identiﬁcation.
Histopathology
Parasites may be found on histologic examination of tissues with
routine hematoxylin and eosin staining. Accurate identiﬁcation of
metazoan parasites in thin sections requires both advanced
training in histoparasitology and sections made in a location that
shows key features of the parasite. When tissue sections are
limited or when stages are small (such as microﬁlaria in skin
biopsies), deﬁnitive identiﬁcation to genus and species by
microscopy alone may not be possible. For protozoa, entire
organisms are usually present on sections and identiﬁcation is
more readily achieved. Special stains may be used to improve
detection or enhance morphologic characteristics of the stage of
parasite seen, allowing more conﬁdent identiﬁcation. Tissue
specimens to be examined by histology for protozoan parasites
should be collected and submi ed quickly for frozen section
evaluation when an immediate diagnosis is desired, or they
should be placed in 10% formalin if processing will be delayed.
Tissues on which electron microscopy will be performed should
be placed in a glutaraldehyde-based ﬁxative. 3

vetexamprep.ir

Cytologic Examination of Other Body Fluids
Parasites are only rarely found on direct microscopic examination
of aqueous humor, CSF, synovial ﬂuid, urine, transtracheal wash,
or bronchoalveolar lavage. Giardia trophozoites may occasionally
be seen in duodenal aspirates collected at endoscopy. To
determine if motile protozoa are present, all body ﬂuids should be
examined by direct smear immediately after collection; storage of
specimens for even a short time may result in lysis of organisms
and subsequent failure to detect infection. Specimens are
processed for examination by centrifuging collected ﬂuid at 2000 ×
g for 5 minutes and then making smears with the sediment and
adding a small amount of associated ﬂuid. After drying, smears
should be stained as described for blood smears and examined for
protozoa. Eggs of some nematodes (e.g., Pearsonema plica,
Dioctophyme renale) may be found in urine sediment and directly
identiﬁed (see Chapter 116). Similarly, larvae of some nematodes
will be present in specimens collected by transtracheal wash or
bronchoalveolar lavage; centrifugation of these specimens and
direct microscopic examination of sediment enhances likelihood
of detection.
Fine-Needle Aspirates
Parasites, especially protozoa, are occasionally found in ﬁneneedle aspirates of lymph node, spleen, liver, or bone marrow.
Dried smears of ﬁne-needle aspirates are stained with Giemsa,
Wright, or Wright-Giemsa and examined for protozoa as
described for blood smears. Occasionally, some stages of
metazoan parasites may also be found on lymph node aspirates
including microﬁlaria and Demodex spp. mites. 8 , 9
Impression Smears
Examination of stained impression smears of superﬁcial lesions or
of tissue collected at biopsy or necropsy may also reveal parasites,
usually protozoa (e.g., Leishmania spp.). For this reason,
impression smears should be made of all biopsy material when a
parasitic infection is suspected.
Collection of Parasites from Skin

vetexamprep.ir

Large arthropods such as ticks, ﬂeas, or lice should be placed in
70% ethanol and submi ed intact for identiﬁcation. A ﬁne-toothed
ﬂea comb will often facilitate recovery of larger arthropods.
However, mites are more readily recovered intact on skin scrapes,
by swabbing ears (e.g., Otodectes cynotis), or by collecting dander
and examining for superﬁcial mites (e.g., Cheyletiella yasguri).
Occasionally, larger arthropods (e.g., Cuterebra) or nematodes
(e.g., Dracunculus) may be present in subcutaneous cysts or found
emerging from dermal ulcers. Whenever possible, these
organisms should be removed and submi ed intact for
identiﬁcation.
To perform a skin scrape, a sterile scalpel blade is dipped in
mineral oil and then used to abrade the aﬀected area of skin; the
material adherent to the blade is then transferred to a microscope
slide. To enhance recovery of mites, collecting several scrapes
from diﬀerent areas of aﬀected skin is recommended. 10 When ear
mites are suspected, a swab with a small amount of mineral oil is
used to transfer aural exudate to a slide. A drop of mineral oil is
added if needed, a coverslip applied, and the material carefully
examined for mites. Whenever skin mites are suspected, a fecal
specimen should also be submi ed for ﬂotation. This is
particularly important in cats, as mites may be removed during
grooming and not detected on a skin scrape but will be found
intact and can be readily identiﬁed by fecal ﬂotation. 11

Culture, Animal Inoculation, and Xenodiagnosis
Culture and Animal Inoculation
Fecal Culture
Fecal culture for parasites is occasionally helpful in small animal
practice. Specialized diagnostic laboratories that perform fecal
culture for parasites should be identiﬁed before specimen
submission. The specimen should be fresh and sent by the most
rapid means available. Preservative should not be added. In
addition, a empts should be made to identify parasites present in
feces as speciﬁcally as possible based on their morphologic
appearance before submi ing specimens for culture.
Although fecal culture for diagnosis of parasites is not common,
speciﬁc media have been developed that support the growth of T.

vetexamprep.ir

blagburni . The InPouch TF test (BioMed Diagnostics, White City,
OR, USA) is a useful in-clinic culture technique for identiﬁcation
of T. blagburni in cat feces. The test consists of a sterile pouch that
contains liquid media. The media is inoculated with feces and
held at room temperature with contents examined every 48 hours
for evidence of motile trichomonads. Fecal specimens collected by
clients for culture or microscopic examination for T. blagburni
should be submi ed fresh, not frozen or placed in ﬁxative, kept
warm and moist, free of cat li er, and unrefrigerated before
testing in the clinic. 2 Pentatrichomonas spp., another ﬂagellate
occasionally found in diarrheic feces of dogs and cats, grows
slowly in medium in which T. blagburni readily replicates. 12
Therefore, it is not likely that Pentatrichomonas spp. would be
isolated in commercial pouch systems.
Blood Culture and Animal Inoculation
Although usually reserved for research projects, blood culture and
animal inoculation are occasionally performed to detect and
document the presence of protozoa. However, because these are
rarely performed for clinical diagnosis, arrangement should be
made with the laboratory before submission of specimens and
speciﬁc instructions obtained on specimen collection and
handling. In general, whole blood is collected aseptically into
EDTA and then submi ed to the laboratory as soon as possible.
Culture of Other Specimens
In some cases, culture of tissue aspirates, biopsy specimens, or
body ﬂuids other than blood may be desired. When indicated, an
aliquot of the specimen collected for cytologic evaluation is placed
in a sterile tube at the time of collection. Culture or animal
inoculation can then be performed with this specimen as
indicated. Rapid submission to an appropriate diagnostic
laboratory will increase the likelihood of successfully culturing
any protozoa present. To facilitate the process and receive exact
instructions on specimen handling and submission, the diagnostic
laboratory to be used should be contacted before collection of
specimens.

Xenodiagnosis

vetexamprep.ir

Xenodiagnosis is a rarely performed procedure for clinical
diagnosis. Laboratory-reared, parasite-free arthropods are
allowed to feed on suspected infected hosts, and then, after
appropriate time for development has elapsed, the arthropods are
examined for the presence of parasites. Xenodiagnosis has
historically been used for the diagnosis of trypanosomiasis but
may also be useful to detect other protozoa.

Antigen Detection
Parasite antigen present in clinical specimens may be detected by
ELISA, by staining via direct FA, or by immunohistochemistry
(see Chapter 2). Antigen may be excreted into blood or feces or, in
the case of some protozoa detected by FA microscopy, be present
on the surface of the parasite (Fig. 5.4). Although not a perfect
substitute for direct microscopic examination, these assays
enhance detection of parasites that are present in low numbers in
clinical specimens or that are not yet patent and thus not shedding
stages into blood or feces at all or in adequate numbers to allow
microscopic detection.

Commercial immunodiagnostic assays are available for
detection and identiﬁcation of several helminths and protozoa.
POC antigen tests are used on whole blood, serum, or plasma to
diagnose infection with D. immitis in practice (Fig. 5.5A), and in
diagnostic laboratories with microtiter plate assays. In some
specimens, antigen may be present but trapped in immune
complexes, which precludes detection. Treatment of the specimen
to disrupt these immune complexes can increase sensitivity of
detection. 13 Antigen tests are also available to detect
Angiostrongylus vasorum, the French heartworm, in endemic areas.
14 Fecal antigen tests that detect ascarids, hookworms, and
whipworms in the intestinal lumen are currently only available
through a single commercial reference laboratory (IDEXX
Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook, ME, USA). 15 , 16
The stages of several common intestinal protozoa, including
cysts of Giardia (Fig. 5.5B) and E. histolytica and oocysts of
Cryptosporidium spp., can be detected in fecal specimens using
antigen tests. Some of the assays used were originally developed
for diagnosis of human infections. Care should be taken to
optimize performance a ributes of any assay not approved for
use in veterinary specimens. At present, the Companion Animal
Parasite Council (www.capcvet.org) only recommends Giardia
antigen detection tests be used in clinically ill animals. Because
other parasites may be present and because false-negative results
can occur, these tests should always be performed along with
microscopic examination of feces after centrifugal concentration.
Parasite antigen can also sometimes be detected in ﬁne-needle
aspirates and biopsy specimens. Aliquots of specimens should be
placed in a separate sterile tube at the time of collection and
submi ed to appropriate laboratories for direct FA or
immunohistochemistry. Matching specimens should always be
submi ed for simultaneous cytologic or histologic examination
whenever direct FA or immunohistochemical detection is
pursued.

Molecular Detection
Detection of parasite-speciﬁc nucleic acid sequences in patient
specimens provides direct evidence of current or recent infection.
In addition, larger metazoan parasites can often be identiﬁed by

vetexamprep.ir

molecular methods when only damaged or partial specimens are
available, precluding morphologic identiﬁcation, provided the
nucleic acid has not been damaged by ﬁxation. A molecular
approach to metazoan identiﬁcation can prove particularly useful
when a empting to distinguish between morphologically similar
or identical organisms but should always be used as a
complementary approach rather than the sole means of parasite
identiﬁcation. The most commonly used molecular techniques to
detect or identify parasites in a diagnostic laboratory are PCR and
in situ hybridization (see Chapter 6).
PCR has been used extensively for detection of Giardia spp. and
Cryptosporidium spp. in feces from both dogs and cats, and for
detection of T. blagburni in cats. Some PCR assays can distinguish
between human-associated genotypes of Giardia spp. and those
found only in dogs or cats. 17 Molecular diagnostic assays for
intestinal protozoa are also available through diagnostic
laboratories to screen animals with diarrhea. Some laboratories
prefer fresh or frozen feces for PCR, whereas others suggest that a
small amount (approximately 100 mg) of feces should be placed
into a tube ﬁlled with 3 to 5 mL of 70% isopropyl alcohol and
shipped at room temperature to the diagnostic laboratory. 2 PCR
primers that amplify T. blagburni DNA can also amplify
Pentatrichomonas spp. DNA, necessitating additional steps in
identiﬁcation, such as restriction enzyme digestion or sequencing
of PCR products, to make a deﬁnitive diagnosis. 12
PCR is also useful to evaluate blood specimens for the presence
of hemoprotozoa; commercial diagnostic assays are available for
Babesia spp., Hepatozoon spp., and Cytauxzoon felis. Whole blood
specimens to be submi ed for PCR should be collected into new
blood tubes containing the anticoagulant speciﬁed by the
laboratory; EDTA is the most common anticoagulant used. PCR
can also be performed on specimens of other body ﬂuids, ﬁneneedle aspirates, and biopsy specimens. In situ hybridization is
only performed at specialized research laboratories for a few
protozoa.

Serologic Testing
Feline heartworm antibody assays are widely used to determine if
cats have been previously infected with D. immitis larvae (see

vetexamprep.ir

Chapter 111). Serologic assays that detect antibodies to protozoa
often are available through diagnostic laboratories. Indirect FA is
the
most

used
platform,
but
ELISA,
immunochromatographic strip (Fig. 5.6), and parasite
agglutination tests are also available.
Individual laboratories should be consulted before submi ing
specimens. Care should be taken to prevent hemolysis during
specimen collection or handling. Serum separated from the clot
may be frozen before testing.

Serologic testing for parasites has several advantages, including
ease of specimen collection and low cost of most procedures.
However, most of these assays are based on detection of IgG,
which develops often after clinical disease has begun and remains
elevated for months to years after initial infection, complicating
interpretation of a single titer in a clinically ill animal. Diagnosis
of active infection with an IgG-based test is supported by
demonstrating a fourfold change in titer in two paired serum
specimens collected 2 to 4 weeks apart. Some IgM-based tests are
available. However, the presence of IgM antibodies in the serum
does not correlate directly with clinical illness in all animals.
Many healthy animals have detectable antibodies to protozoa, and
immunosuppressed animals may not develop antibodies despite

vetexamprep.ir

infection and clinical disease. Diﬀerent assays vary in sensitivity
and speciﬁcity, and there is potential for serologic cross-reactivity
(e.g., among Babesia species). When necessary, the diagnostic
laboratory performing the assay should be consulted for
assistance in interpretation of results.

6: Molecular Diagnostic
Methods for Pathogen
Detection
Emir Hodzic, Jane E. Sykes, and Shelley C. Rankin

KEY POINTS
• Molecular diagnostic tests that detect nucleic acids, such as
PCR assays, are now widely available for diagnosis of
companion animal infectious diseases.
• Molecular diagnostic tests include tests that involve detection
and amplification of nucleic acids (nucleic acid amplification
tests [NAAT]), or probe-based assays that do not involve
nucleic acid amplification.
• Specimens for these assays should be collected using aseptic
technique in order to minimize contamination.
• Interpretation of molecular diagnostic test results requires
knowledge of the problems and pitfalls of each type of assay.
The results of testing at one laboratory may differ from those
at another because of variations in assay design.
• With increased automation, laboratory proficiency testing,
improved quality assurance, and standardization of reporting,
the availability and utility of molecular diagnostic tests for
companion animal infectious diseases continues to increase.

Introduction
One of Koch’s postulates states that a microorganism must be
isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture in
order to prove that it causes disease. This poses a problem, as

vetexamprep.ir

many microorganisms are particular and fastidious in their
growth requirements and cannot be cultivated on artiﬁcial media.
Two major reasons have emerged to explain why most microbial
agents cannot be cultured: (1) some only grow under speciﬁc
nutritional conditions oﬀered by the host, and (2) some
microorganisms only grow in the presence of other microbial
species. 1
Commonly used methods of pathogen detection include
microscopy, culture, biochemical methods, immunologic
methods, and molecular methods. 2–8 As none of these methods
are 100% sensitive and speciﬁc, it is recommended that multiple
types of diagnostic assays be applied, depending on specimen
type, clinical signs, and the suspected pathogen. 9 Traditional
bacteriology can be time consuming because organisms have to be
cultured, and usually a series of biochemical tests must be
completed for identiﬁcation. 10 Molecular diagnostic methods are
suited to the detection of organisms that are not easily found
using cytology or histopathology, are slow growing or diﬃcult to
culture, or when a rapid (<12 hours) diagnosis is required. Other
applications are shown in Box 6.1. 11 , 12
Although techniques for the ampliﬁcation of pathogen-speciﬁc
DNA sequences such as PCR are sensitive, there remain limits to
this sensitivity when working with clinical specimens. Impurities
within some specimens can inhibit PCR assays, and the use of
small volumes for DNA extraction means that cells often have to
be concentrated to increase sensitivity. 13

Essential Prerequisites for A Positive Outcome
with Molecular Diagnostic Tests
As for culture, the accuracy of molecular diagnostic tests depends
on the appropriate specimen selection, collection, and
transportation (Chapter 1).

Specimen Collection and Transport
When collecting specimens for molecular diagnostics, the timing
of collection relative to the course of disease and the best
specimen type must be considered. For acute diseases, molecular
assays are most useful early in the course of disease. For chronic

vetexamprep.ir

diseases, timing is less critical. Knowledge of organism shedding
pa erns can help to determine the most appropriate timing of
specimen collection. For example, Leptospira organisms are
primarily present in blood in the ﬁrst week of acute illness, after
which they may be shed in the urine. 14 Specimens should be
collected before administration of antimicrobial drugs, although
this is less critical than for specimens that are to be cultured.
Although specimen processing is usually well standardized in
the diagnostic laboratory, pre-analytical procedures that occur
before specimens arrive at the laboratory have considerable
variability. For example, false-negative results may occur due to
specimen degradation during transport. The main concerns
during specimen transport and storage include specimen
integrity, contamination, specimen identity, and the risk of
environmental hazards due to infectious material. Because
contamination can occur outside the PCR laboratory as well as
within the laboratory, collection of specimens for nucleic acid
testing should be performed aseptically to reduce the risk of falsepositive results. Gloves should be worn, and disposable
instruments should be used (e.g., disposable blades, punch biopsy
instruments). 15–17 The recommendations for specimen collection
and transport presented here are based on the guidelines
published by the CLSI. 18 These guidelines are updated on a
regular basis and ensure that detection of nucleic acids within
clinical specimens is optimal.
For detection of pathogens that contain DNA (i.e., all bacteria,
fungi, some viruses), either fresh or frozen specimens should be
submi ed. In general, DNA is stable in tissue for up to 24 hours at
2°C to 8°C, at least 2 weeks at –20°C, and at least 2 years at –70°C.
18 All specimens must be promptly transported to the diagnostic
laboratory, preferably within 2 hours. In general, specimens for
detection of bacterial agents should not be stored for more than 24
hours, and no more than 2 to 3 days at 4°C for viruses. 19
Specimens should not be stored in frost-free freezers, as these
undergo repeated freeze-thaw cycling, which can be associated
with DNA degradation. 20 Box 6.2 outlines recommendations
based on specimen type. 21

RNA is highly susceptible to degradation during storage and
transport. Swabs and body ﬂuids should be immediately sent to
the laboratory on wet ice. Tissue should ideally be snap-frozen at
–70°C within half an hour of collection and shipped on dry ice
without being thawed in the interim. RNA is stable for at least 2
years at or below –70°C. Naturally occurring ribonucleases can
continue to degrade RNA at –20°C.
The optimal amount of tissue specimen for molecular testing is
1 to 2 g, although more or less may be required depending on the
cellularity of the specimen. 18 Tissues stored in formalin,
especially for prolonged periods, are suboptimal for PCR because
the formalin cross-links the DNA in the specimen. Tissues ﬁxed
brieﬂy in formalin (less than 18 hours) and then embedded in
paraﬃn are preferable to tissues stored in formalin, because the
formalin is removed during the embedding process. Paraﬃnembedded specimens should only be used when no other
specimens are available. 18

Specimen Preparation in the Laboratory
Molecular detection methods depend more and more on proper
specimen preparation. Clinical specimens are very heterogeneous
(stool, plasma, CSF), so preparation must be a factor to consider in
order to achieve results within a reasonable amount of time. The
overall goals of specimen preparation are: (1) to concentrate the
target, because pathogens may be present at low concentrations
and molecular detection methods commonly use small volumes of
specimen for nucleic acid extraction; (2) to remove or reduce the
eﬀects of inhibitory substances; and (3) to reduce the
heterogeneity of specimens in order to ensure negligible
variations in serially collected specimens. If homogenized

vetexamprep.ir

thoroughly, pooling of specimens facilitates high-throughput
analysis in some cases. 8 , 13 , 22

Quality assurance and quality control in the diagnostic laboratory
must be taken into consideration. Components that are required
for validation and veriﬁcation of microbiologic diagnostic tests or
test systems should include: (1) internal and external controls in
each run; (2) participation in interlaboratory test results
comparison; (3) validation of employee competence; (4)
calibration and maintenance of instruments; and (5) correlation
with clinical ﬁndings. 23 , 24

Molecular Methods for Pathogen Detection
The ultimate goal of a molecular diagnostic test is rapid, sensitive,
and accurate pathogen detection. Molecular diagnostics oﬀer
many advantages over traditional microbiologic and immunologic
methods for pathogen detection. These include faster processing
time as well as the potential for more accurate species
identiﬁcation and strain typing, which has resulted in a vastly
improved understanding of infectious disease epidemiology.
Molecular diagnostics has also revolutionized pathogen detection,
evaluation of emerging novel infections, surveillance, early
detection of bio-threat agents, and antimicrobial resistance
proﬁling. 7 , 25

vetexamprep.ir

(A) Fluorescence in situ hybridization
(FISH). A nucleic acid probe that is
complementary to a segment of leptospiral
DNA that has been tagged with a fluorescent
label is incubated with a tissue section on a
slide. (B) Unbound probe is washed away and
the section is examined using fluorescence
microscopy. Leptospira FISH image courtesy Dr.
FIG. 6.1

Richard Goldstein.

Molecular assay types include endpoint (conventional) PCR,
RT-PCR, real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), isothermal
ampliﬁcation, 26 , 27 terminal restriction fragment length
polymorphism (T-RFLP), 28 nucleic acid sequencing, 29 highresolution melt analysis, 30 DNA microarrays, 31 tissue arrays, 32
and ﬂuorescent-labelled in situ hybridization (FISH). 33 , 34
Despite the development of this broad range of ampliﬁcation
technologies, qPCR remains the most widely used method in both
research and diagnostic laboratories for pathogen detection. 28 , 35
Specimens vary considerably in physical properties, chemical
composition, and microbial diversity, so molecular detection
methods are typically developed for complex specimen types. For
example, fecal ma er is a complex mixture of undigested or
partially digested food components as well as viable and
nonviable microbial cells, with many inhibitors. The use of
appropriate ampliﬁcation controls by the laboratory facilitates
detection of false negatives due to the presence of inhibitors.
Other special requirements of molecular detection technology in

vetexamprep.ir

order to ensure reliable results include proper establishment of
quality-assured procedures, laboratory set-up, and proper
training of staﬀ in order to minimize the chance of contamination
and false positives.

Direct Hybridization
Direct hybridization uses labeled oligonucleotide probes to detect
bacteria, which are usually directed to 16S rRNA sequences
speciﬁc to the species, genus, or other phylogenetic level of
interest (Fig. 6.1). The oligonucleotide probes are small DNA or
RNA segments that bind to complementary sequences within
DNA or RNA molecules. 33 One end of the probe is designated the
5-prime (5′) end, and the other is the 3-prime (3′) end. A variety of
oligonucleotide probes are available commercially as kits for
detection of human pathogens. Some of these can also be used to
detect the same pathogens in specimens from dogs or cats. Probes
are widely used in human clinical microbiology laboratories to
identify organisms that have been grown in culture (e.g., GenProbe Inc., San Diego, CA).
Probe hybridization can be performed on a nitrocellulose
membrane (solid-phase hybridization); on formalin-ﬁxed, paraﬃnembedded sections mounted on a microscope slide (in situ
hybridization); or in solution (liquid-phase hybridization). For solidphase hybridization, the probe is reacted with microorganism
DNA that has been immobilized on the membrane. Unbound
probe is washed away, and the bound probe is detected using
ﬂuorescence, chemiluminescence, radioactivity, or color
development (in the same way that bound antibody or antigen is
detected in an ELISA or IFA assay). For in situ hybridization,
formalin-ﬁxed, paraﬃn-embedded specimens are sectioned and
mounted on a special slide. The sections are deparaﬃnized, dried,
and incubated with a solution that contains the probe, so both the
presence and the location of the target pathogen within tissues
can be identiﬁed. In situ hybridization assays that include a
ﬂuorescent-labeled probe are referred to as ﬂuorescence in situ
hybridization (FISH) assays (see Fig. 6.1). 33 , 36 The optimum
specimen for FISH is a tissue that has been snap-frozen in liquid
nitrogen after being embedded in optimal cu ing temperature
(OCT) medium. 18 FISH has been increasingly used to identify

vetexamprep.ir

intralesional bacteria in companion animals, including: dogs with
bacterial endocarditis, 37 histiocytic ulcerative colitis, 38 hepatitis,
39 and Lyme nephritis 40 ; cats with small intestinal lymphoma; 41
and dogs and cats with gastric helicobacteriosis. 42
Because liquid-phase hybridization occurs in solution, unbound
probe cannot be washed away. To overcome this problem, a
chemiluminescent acridinium ester label is a ached to the probe.
A subsequent chemical hydrolysis step selectively degrades only
unbound probe. On addition of peroxides, the intact (hybridized)
probe then emits light. 43
Although not yet widely used for veterinary applications,
peptide nucleic acid (PNA ) probes are now increasingly available to
detect target DNA. PNA probes are uncharged peptides that
mimic DNA and bind to complementary DNA sequences just as a
nucleic acid probe would. 44 , 45 PNA probes lack the net negative
charge of nucleic acid probes; therefore, the electrostatic repulsion
that normally occurs when two negatively charged DNA strands
hybridize does not occur. The result is a more stable and speciﬁc
binding of the probe to its target, which in turn can be associated
with increased assay sensitivity and speciﬁcity.

vetexamprep.ir

are hybridized on either side of a specific
segment of a pathogen’s DNA. Also present in

rapidly and repeatedly heat and cool the tubes

DNA is repeatedly copied, with logarithmic

Branched DNA assays and hybrid capture assays are highly
sensitive hybridization methods that include steps to intensify the

vetexamprep.ir

signal generated from probe hybridization. 46 , 47 They are not yet
widely used in veterinary medicine.

Nucleic Acid Amplification
The general principles of all nucleic acid ampliﬁcation
technologies share common characteristics that fall into three
categories: (1) target ampliﬁcation systems, (2) probe
ampliﬁcation systems, and (3) signal ampliﬁcation. These all use
enzyme-mediated processes (a heat-stable DNA polymerase, such
as that derived from Thermophilus aquaticus, a bacterium that is
adapted to live in hot springs), two oligonucleotide primers, four
deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs; G, T, A, and C), reaction
buﬀer, and a target (a genomic or complementary DNA
fragment). A solution (mastermix) is created in the laboratory that
includes the polymerase, appropriate primers, dNTPs, and buﬀer,
and this is then divided into aliquots for addition of DNA that has
been extracted from the specimen. Once assembled, the reaction is
placed in a thermal cycler, an instrument that subjects the reaction
to a series of diﬀerent temperatures for set amounts of time. Each
round of temperature and time adjustments is referred to as one
cycle of ampliﬁcation. Each PCR cycle theoretically doubles the
number of target DNA segments (amplicon) in the reaction. The
end result is the production of millions to billions of copies of the
targeted sequence in a ma er of hours, and in each case, the
ampliﬁcation products (amplicons) can serve as templates for
subsequent rounds of ampliﬁcation.
Nucleic acid ampliﬁcation methods include not only PCR
methods (i.e., endpoint PCR, RT-PCR, nested PCR, multiplex
PCR, qPCR, digital PCR [dPCR]), but also alternative
technologies, such as such as strand-displacement ampliﬁcation,
loop-mediated isothermal ampliﬁcation, ligase chain reaction, and
nucleic acid sequence–based ampliﬁcation. 36 , 48
Types of PCR assays are broadly divided into three main
groups: (1) endpoint PCR, (2) qPCR, and (3) dPCR.
Endpoint PCR
Endpoint PCR assays (previously referred to as conventional PCR
assays) are the simplest PCR assays and although still widely for
research purposes, their use for diagnostic purposes has

vetexamprep.ir

decreased. In this method, nucleic acids (genomic DNA and/or
total RNA) are extracted from biological specimens using a
commercially available extraction kit. A pair of primers, roughly
20 nucleotides long, is then used to bracket a desired DNA
sequence, which is subsequently copied using a DNA polymerase
enzyme (Fig. 6.2). Initially the DNA is heated to 95°C, which
causes the paired strands of DNA to separate (denature). Next, the
tubes are cooled to a speciﬁc annealing temperature (usually 50°C
to 65°C), which allows the primers to bind to their respective
sequences. Finally, the tubes are heated to 72°C. This is the
temperature at which the DNA polymerase adds dNTPs to the
primers, extending the primers as it copies the sequence of the
template DNA. The three-step cycle is repeated 30 to 50 times,
which results in logarithmic accumulation of a PCR product that
is an exact copy of the segment of DNA between the two primers.
7 , 8 , 36 , 47

Products of PCR ampliﬁcation are separated using agarose gel
electrophoresis, stained with a dye that intercalates DNA (such as
ethidium bromide), and the resulting ﬂuorescent DNA bands are
visualized using ultraviolet transillumination. The longer the PCR
product, the more slowly it moves through the gel during
electrophoresis. When a series of molecular weight markers are
run alongside the end product of PCR, the size of the PCR
product can be estimated (Fig. 6.3). The true identity of the
product can then be conﬁrmed using sequencing or by
transferring it to a membrane and performing DNA hybridization
with a speciﬁc probe. The process of loading the PCR product in
agarose gels requires that the PCR tubes be opened, which can
lead to aerosolization of PCR amplicons. These amplicons can
then contaminate reagents, equipment, and tubes that are used for
running subsequent PCR assays. Unless proper controls are

vetexamprep.ir

included, false positives resulting from such contamination may
go unidentiﬁed and lead to erroneous reporting of results. 49
Real-Time Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
For diagnostic purposes, endpoint PCR assays have largely been
superseded by qPCR, which monitors the accumulation of PCR
product while the reaction takes place, usually through detection
of ﬂuorescence. 50 This provides quick, sensitive, quantitative
detection of PCR products in a closed-tube format, thereby
signiﬁcantly reducing the risk of contamination and false-positive
test results. 51 , 52 qPCR assays are amenable to automation, and
reactions are generally loaded onto covered 96- or 384-well plates.
Loading can be done robotically, further reducing the possibility
of contamination and manual loading errors. qPCR instruments
consist of a thermal cycler with an integrated excitation light
source, a ﬂuorescence detection system, and software. The
software performs the quantitative analysis of detected
ﬂuorescence during the assay (Fig. 6.4). These instruments can
simultaneously detect diﬀerent wavelengths of light. 53 , 54 Special
carousel thermocyclers are also available that rapidly heat and
cool the reactions, which are placed in specially designed glass
capillaries. As a result, some PCR assays can be completed in 45
minutes, instead of the 4 to 5 hours required for endpoint assays.
55

Detection chemistries used in real-time quantitative PCR
The choice of probe chemistry used to detect PCR products in
qPCR assays inﬂuences assay sensitivity and speciﬁcity, and so it
can be helpful for clinicians to have an awareness of the
approaches used. Fluorescent chemistries available that allow
detection of target sequences during ampliﬁcation can be
categorized into two types: (1) double-stranded DNA (dsDNA)
intercalating dyes (i.e., SYBR Green I, SYBR Gold, EvaGreen, LC
Green, BOXTO, ResoLight, BEBO, SYTO, YO-PRO-1), and (2)
ﬂuorophore-labeled, sequence-speciﬁc oligonucleotide probes,
which are designed to bind to the target sequence being
ampliﬁed. 53 , 54 , 56
When free in solution, dsDNA intercalating dyes exhibit li le
ﬂuorescence, but when in contact with dsDNA, the dye

vetexamprep.ir

intercalates between nucleic bases and assumes a conformation
that emits ﬂuorescence at a particular wavelength upon excitation.
The ﬂuorescent signal from a reaction is proportional to the
amount of dsDNA present, and will increase as the target is
ampliﬁed. Because there is no probe, carefully designed primers
are required to ensure high speciﬁcity for the pathogen of interest.
Intercalating dyes require melt-curve analysis to identify diﬀerent
reaction products. As a result, the presence of nonspeciﬁc
products in a qPCR reaction may contribute to the overall
ﬂuorescence and aﬀect the accuracy of quantiﬁcation. Also,
intercalating dyes cannot be used for multiplex reactions
(reactions that target multiple pathogens in the same tube). 7 , 53

FIG. 6.5

Scorpions probe-primer assay.

Fluorophore primer- and probe-based chemistries can diﬀer in
their sequence geometry and binding mechanism, but nearly all
share a ﬂuorescent reporter dye partnered with a quencher dye,

vetexamprep.ir

which are usually a ached to an oligonucleotide probe. The
quencher is a chromophore designed to absorb the ﬂuorescent
signal from the reporter dye when they are in close proximity,
taking advantage of Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), to
ensure speciﬁc ﬂuorescence detection only in presence of
ampliﬁed product. This can be accomplished by a aching a
quencher molecule to the nucleic acid probe, and devising some
mechanism by which the reporter and quencher become
separated from one another when the probe binds to its speciﬁc
target. 57 Fluorophore-labeled oligonucleotides used in the PCR
reaction have been divided into three subgroups 54 :
(1) Primer-probe assays (e.g., Scorpions, Ampliﬂuor, LUX,
Cyclicons, Angler). In this case, one of the two PCR
primers is connected to a probe by a quencher dye. The
probe has a hairpin loop conformation that brings the
quencher dye close to a ﬂuorescent reporter dye a ached
to the 5′ end of the probe. Fluorescence emi ed from
primer-probe is detected and measured during the
denaturation or extension phase of the qPCR. A commonly
used primer-probe assay is Scorpions, which improves
signals, has low background, and simple design. 58 During
the course of PCR, the hairpin loop unfolds and the loop
region of the probe hybridizes to the newly synthesized
target sequence, causing the reporter dye to separate from
the quencher dye and emit ﬂuorescence (Fig. 6.5).
(2) Probe assays use a linear oligonucleotide that is
complementary to the target nucleic acid sequence in
addition to the primers, which is expected to anneal
between the two primers. The oligonucleotide probe is
labeled with a reporter dye on the 5′ end and quencher dye
on the 3′ end ﬂuorophore, although the opposite
orientation can also be used. The close proximity of the
quencher dye to the reporter dye on the probe inhibits the
reporter dye from emi ing ﬂuorescence. There are two
types of probes used: (a) hydrolysis probes (e.g., TaqMan,
Minor Groove Binding [MGB]-TaqMan, Snake assay), and
(b) hybridization probes (e.g., Hybprobe or FRET, Molecular
Beacons, HyBeacon, MGB-Pleiades, MGB-Eclipse,
ResonSense, Yin-Yang or displacing). Hydrolysis probes

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
g
y
y p
rely on the 5′–3′ exonuclease activity of Taq polymerase.
When the Taq DNA polymerase copies the section of DNA
between the two primers, it encounters the probe and
chops it into pieces, because it has inherent exonuclease
activity. This causes the reporter dye to separate from the
quencher dye. The reporter dye then emits ﬂuorescence,
which can be measured using a spectrophotometer. 53 , 54 ,
59–61 The amount of ﬂuorescent signal detected is directly
proportional to the amount of the target ampliﬁed during
the PCR reaction. 7 , 54 Many veterinary laboratories that
oﬀer probe-based PCR assays use TaqMan probes. MGBTaqMan probes are designed to improve target DNAbinding speciﬁcity and sensitivity, and are becoming
widely used for diagnosis of microbial pathogens. An
example of a hybridization probe assay is the FRET probe
assay. FRET probe assays use two probes that are
predicted to lie adjacent to one another on the target
sequence. The ﬁrst probe is tagged at the 3′ end with one
ﬂuorophore, and the second probe contains a second
ﬂuorophore at the 5′ end, and a phosphate group a ached
to its 3′ end to prevent DNA ampliﬁcation. When the two
dyes come together during annealing, one ﬂuorophore
transfers its energy to the other, causing it to emit
ﬂuorescence, which can then be detected. 62 Currently
there are only rare reports of the use of this technology for
diagnosis in veterinary medicine.
(3) Probes that are analogues of nucleic acids (PNA, LNA, ZNA,
non-natural bases: Plexor primer, Tiny-Molecular Beacon)
are much shorter than nucleic acid probes due to the
higher binding aﬃnity of the analogue nucleic acid bases
to standard DNA, and they are more stable in biological
ﬂuids. An analogue may have alterations in its phosphate
backbone, pentose sugar (either ribose or deoxyribose) or
nucleobases. Such probes only need to be 8–9 bases long.
53 , 54

Primer and probe design
Primers are a critical component of PCR reactions. The primers
are extended by the polymerase upon binding to the pathogen

vetexamprep.ir

target DNA, and are designed to bind to the opposite strand to
facilitate exponential ampliﬁcation, which is the hallmark of PCR.
The DNA polymerase synthesizes the new DNA copy by moving
from the 5′ end toward the 3′ end. Both the sequence of the
primers and that of the target sequence can aﬀect the eﬃciency of
PCR. A number of free and commercially available software
programs are available for the purpose of designing primers. The
following are important considerations when primers are
designed:
• Primer speciﬁcity, as nonspeciﬁc ampliﬁcation of nontarget
DNA is one of the greatest challenges for successful target
ampliﬁcation. The speciﬁcity of primers and probes are
veriﬁed using commercial software programs.
• Primer length (typically 16 to 28 nucleotides long).
• Amplicon length (usually 100 to 250 base pairs).
• Primer G and C base pair content, which is maintained
between 35% and 65%.
• Primer 3′ end stability, which can contribute to nonspeciﬁc
primer extension by Taq DNA polymerase, especially if
the binding of the 3′ nucleotide bases is relatively tight to
the nontarget template. Primers with very high 3′ terminal
stability (as determined using a software program) are
usually rejected.
• Primer melting temperature (Tm). Most primer design
software programs can predict melting (annealing)
temperature based on the nucleotide composition of the
primers under evaluation. 7 , 54 , 63 The Tm of each primer
used must be similar so that they anneal at the same
temperature during PCR.
Validation and optimization of qPCR assays
In theory, the amount of ﬂuorescence emi ed during each PCR
cycle doubles, and it is proportional to the number of copies of
pathogen DNA in the clinical specimen. However, imperfections
that result from variable pre-assay conditions, assay design, and
improper data analysis can lead to inaccurate results and
erroneous diagnostic conclusions. Before being used for
diagnostic purposes, qPCR assays must be shown to be sensitive,

vetexamprep.ir

speciﬁc, reproducible, and eﬃcient through validation and
veriﬁcation. A number of factors can be altered to obtain optimum
assay performance, which will lead to higher molecular
sensitivity, speciﬁcity, and precision.
During validation of PCR assays, the laboratory uses the assay
to test serial dilutions of a known amount of target DNA. For
qPCR, the limit of detection is the lowest number of copies of the
target DNA or RNA sequence that the assay can detect (also
known as analytical sensitivity). The results are used to create a
graph known as a standard curve. This consists of the logarithm of
the initial starting quantity of DNA on the x-axis and the
quantiﬁcation cycle (Cq; also known as cycle threshold [CT]) values
obtained on the y-axis (see Fig. 6.4). Cq represents the number of
cycles that elapse before ﬂuorescence is detectable above a
threshold value set by the thermocycler manufacturer. A standard
curve is commonly generated using a 10-fold serial dilution series
of at least ﬁve template concentrations. The standard curve can
then be used to predict the amount of target DNA in a clinical
specimen based on the Cq value.
The standard curve should result in a slope that demonstrates
good eﬃciency, accuracy, and sensitivity. The eﬃciency of a qPCR
reaction is the degree to which the polymerase converts reagents
to produce target amplicons. Factors that aﬀect the eﬃciency of a
qPCR reaction include amplicon length and sequence, primer
sequence, impurities and inhibitors in the sample, and cycling
conditions. Once the standard curve is generated, the eﬃciency of
the reaction is calculated from the slope of the log-linear portion
of the standard curve (10-1/slope-1). A qPCR assay that has an
eﬃciency of 100% doubles the number of copies of template in
every PCR cycle. Eﬃciencies below 90% are unacceptable for
quantitative assays, and ideally eﬃciency should be greater than
95%. Ideally, this is compared with a similar curve that uses
dilutions of the standard DNA spiked into a clinical specimen, to
show that inhibitors within the specimen do not aﬀect eﬃciency.
64 , 65

From a diagnostic standpoint, a qPCR assay may lack
sensitivity (many false negatives) if the assay fails to detect all
possible strains of a target organism. This can occur if the probe or
primers are strain speciﬁc, rather than species speciﬁc, and many
strains of the target organism exist with variable sequences (as is

vetexamprep.ir

the case with RNA pathogens such as FCV). As part of the
validation process, the assay should be shown to be inclusive and
detect as many strains or variants as possible.
A qPCR assay has poor analytical speciﬁcity if false positives
occur as a result of contamination or because of manual loading
error. Speciﬁcity may also be poor if the primers bind to and
initiate ampliﬁcation of DNA from unrelated organisms or the
host animal (i.e., cat, dog, human DNA). Speciﬁcity is tested
during the validation process by showing that the qPCR assay
fails to amplify DNA from clinical specimens that contain
organisms that are genetically related to the target organism, as
well as organisms that may be expected to be contaminating
normal ﬂora. 64

The results of qPCR assays must also be repeatable. Repeatability
is determined for qPCR assays by determining whether the Cq

vetexamprep.ir

value varies signiﬁcantly for the same specimen when tested
multiple times. Usually intra-assay (within the same run) and
inter-assay (across diﬀerent runs) variations are measured. 66
Analysis of qPCR assay results
Data analysis includes an examination of the raw qPCR data, an
evaluation of their quality and reliability, and the generation of
reportable results. The output of a qPCR assay is an ampliﬁcation
curve, which is subject to background ﬂuorescence (see Fig. 6.4).
A range of factors aﬀect the degree of background ﬂuorescence,
including choice of plasticware, unquenched probe ﬂuorescence,
and signal carryover into the neighboring sample wells. In welldesigned assays, the background is low compared with the
ampliﬁed signal. However, variation in the background signal
may aﬀect quantiﬁcation comparisons between diﬀerent
specimens, so the laboratory must correct for baseline variations.
Most laboratories run approximately 40 cycles of ampliﬁcation,
and so specimens that generate Cq values less than 40 are
considered to be positive. Said another way, if PCR proceeds to 40
cycles without emission of ﬂuorescence (Cq = 40), then the target
DNA is not detectable in the specimen, and the result is reported
as negative. The lower the Cq value, the more target DNA (=
organism load) is present in the specimen, because fewer cycles
elapse before ﬂuorescence is detected. Because specimen size
varies, the Cq value may be normalized to the approximate
number of host cells present in the specimen. Knowledge of
organism load may have prognostic value for some infections, can
allow infection to be monitored over time with treatment, and
may be useful to diﬀerentiate low-level colonization from active
infection causing clinical signs (see Interpretation of Results,
later). At the time of writing, veterinary diagnostic laboratories
performing PCR assays variably report organism loads to the
clinician. 67

Prevention of PCR Contamination and Quality
Assurance
PCR contamination can be diﬃcult to eradicate once it occurs, so
prevention of contamination is critical (Box 6.3). Laboratories
should include negative controls in every run, and a positive

vetexamprep.ir

control should be included to ensure that the assay is working,
preferably one that is also subjected to the nucleic acid extraction
process. The positive control should contain a low concentration
of DNA, because abundant DNA used as a positive control may
serve as a source of contamination for other assays. Many
laboratories run two separate negative controls. One of the
negative controls contains mastermix and nuclease-free water in
place of nucleic acid that has been extracted from a specimen. The
other consists of water or a known negative specimen that is
subjected to the extraction process to ensure that contamination
does not occur during extraction (negative extraction control).
When 96- or 384-well plate formats are used, negative control
wells are interspersed among the test wells to monitor for plate
contamination. 67
In order to prevent contamination, some laboratories use
deoxyuracil triphosphate (dUTP) instead of deoxythymidine
triphosphate (dTTP) in the PCR mastermix. This substitution
results in generation of PCR products that contain uracil (U) in
place of thymidine (T). The enzyme uracil-N-glycosylase (UNG) is
also added to the mix. This enzyme destroys DNA amplicons that
contain deoxyuracil residues, and eliminates any contaminating
DNA amplicons from previous reactions before PCR ampliﬁcation
begins. When the reaction mix is heated in the initial denaturation
step, the UNG is destroyed. 68
Many biological specimens contain components that inhibit
PCR, such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, bile salts, humic acids,
urea, and collagen, 13 and require extensive puriﬁcation.
However, extensive puriﬁcation leads to losses and is expensive.
Complete removal of inhibitors may not be possible. Various
methods can be used to assess the presence of inhibitors within
clinical specimens, as follows:
1. Determine the PCR eﬃciency in a test sample by subjecting
serial dilutions of the sample to PCR. 69
2. Use a reference gene (formerly known as a housekeeping
gene). A reference gene is an endogenous ampliﬁcation
control gene that copuriﬁes with the target nucleic acid
and is ampliﬁed at the same time as the target pathogen
DNA using a separate set of primers and probes.

vetexamprep.ir

Ampliﬁcation of a reference gene is usually performed on
a separate aliquot of the extracted specimen at the same
time as the assay for the target pathogen. Reference genes
are typically host (dog or cat) genes that are expected to be
present in the sample, such as canine or feline
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH),
histone, or 18S DNA. A negative reference gene PCR assay
result (or a high Cq value for the assay, which is
equivalent to a weak positive result) suggests that
inhibitors may be present in the specimen, or that DNA in
the submi ed specimen may have degraded during
storage or transport. Some qPCR assays use an internal
reference gene control, in which a reference gene is ampliﬁed
within the same reaction mix (known as multiplexing, see
later in this chapter) with the qPCR assay for the target
microorganism.
3. Use an exogenous control, also known as a spike or SPUD gene.
The spikes typically consist of a chemically synthesized
nucleic acid template (RNA or DNA, depending on the
target) and two primers speciﬁc to the template and are
run in the presence of SYBR Green I dye or a speciﬁc
probe. The spike template is ampliﬁed in a separate
control reaction, resulting in a characteristic Cq. Alongside
this control reaction, the exogenous control is also spiked
into specimens and the ﬂuorescence emi ed from the
spike is compared with that emi ed from the control.
When inhibitors are not present, the Cq from the spiked
clinical specimen will remain the same as the control,
whereas in the presence of a contaminated specimen the
Cq is higher. 70 , 71

Variations of Polymerase Chain Reaction
Assays
Variations of polymerase chain reaction include
transcriptase qPCR, nested PCR, and multiplex PCR.

reverse-

Reverse-Transcriptase qPCR
Reverse-transcriptase qPCR (RT-qPCR) is used for detection of
pathogen RNA (such as RNA viruses) and gene expression

vetexamprep.ir

studies. After extraction of total RNA from clinical specimens
using a commercial kit or automated platform, the enzyme reverse
transcriptase is used together with dNTPs to transcribe RNA into
complementary DNA (cDNA). The RT step can be initiated with
oligo(dT) primers (primers that anneal to a poly-A tail), random
primers (a mixture of primers with randomly assigned bases), a
mixture of the two, or gene-speciﬁc primers. Subsequently, the
cDNA is then used as the template for qPCR ampliﬁcation. 72 , 73

Nested PCR. A second set of internal
primers are used in a second round of PCR to
increase the sensitivity and specificity of the
assay.
FIG. 6.6

Nested PCR
In nested PCR, a small amount of ampliﬁed PCR product is
subjected to a second round of PCR using another set of internal
primers (Fig. 6.6). Having an additional set of primers increases
the speciﬁcity of the PCR assay and also greatly increases its
sensitivity. 74 Unfortunately, the increased sensitivity means that
false positives due to contamination can be extremely problematic

vetexamprep.ir

with this method, and it has lost popularity for diagnostic
purposes.
Multiplex PCR
Multiplex PCR assays use multiple sets of primers in the same
reaction tube to simultaneously detect multiple organisms (or
multiple genes from the same organism). Duplex PCR assays can
detect two organisms, and triplex PCR assays can detect three
organisms. The potential downside of multiplex reactions is that if
one organism is present in higher abundance, this may reduce the
sensitivity of the assay for the other target organisms because
ampliﬁcation of the abundant pathogen DNA consumes reagents
that are then unavailable for ampliﬁcation of the other pathogen.
Successful multiplexing results from careful experimental design
and optimization of reaction conditions. 64 , 75 , 76
Isothermal PCR
Isothermal PCR is a process that ampliﬁes nucleic acids at a
constant temperature, and has been the basis for in-clinic PCR
assay development, because an expensive thermocycler is not
required. Dozens of complex diﬀerent isothermal ampliﬁcation
methods have been published, and some have reached the
practice environment in human medicine (e.g., Loopamp
MALARIA, Human Diagnostics Worldwide) and most recently in
veterinary medicine (e.g., PCRun, Biogal). Examples include
rolling-circle ampliﬁcation and loop-mediated isothermal
ampliﬁcation (LAMP). In-clinic assays involve a DNA extraction
step, followed by addition of reagents required for ampliﬁcation,
incubation in a heated block (e.g., 60°C for 1 hour), then detection
of the PCR product. Detection of the products of PCR either
involves the use of a lateral-ﬂow disposable nucleic acid detection
device (into which the tube containing the ampliﬁed DNA is
inserted), or a small benchtop bioilluminator device that can semiquantify the amount of DNA present in the reaction. 77 Isothermal
in-clinic assays have been marketed for Leptospira spp., Ehrlichia
canis, Anaplasma platys, Leishmania spp., Babesia canis, CPV, feline
panleukopenia virus, and Mycoplasma haemofelis, which allow
detection of a PCR product within 75 minutes. In one study, the
clinical sensitivity and speciﬁcity of one assay for M. haemofelis
(PCRun, Biogal) was compared with that of an endpoint PCR

vetexamprep.ir

assay. Using one extraction method, the sensitivity and speciﬁcity
was 94% and 96%, respectively; using a more crude extraction
method recommended by the manufacturer, the sensitivity and
speciﬁcity was 78% and 96%, respectively. 78 When compared
with a qPCR assay, a Leishmania POC PCR assay oﬀered in Europe
by the same manufacturer also had high clinical speciﬁcity (100%)
but low sensitivity (10% to 57%, depending on specimen type). 77
Sensitivity was also low (30%) and speciﬁcity high (100%) for an
E. canis POC assay when compared with qPCR in experimentally
infected dogs. 79 It was suggested that this may be because larger
quantities of DNA must be present within a specimen for
detection by the POC assays compared with detection by qPCR,
based on the specimen types that tested positive for Leishmania
and the stage of E. canis infection when positive results were
obtained using the POC assays. 77 An insulated isothermal PCR
(iiPCR) POC assay (POCKIT Nucleic Acid Analyzer, GeneReach
USA, Lexington, MA) for Babesia gibsoni was shown to have high
clinical sensitivity (90%) and speciﬁcity (99%) when compared
with a qPCR assay (IDEXX Laboratories Inc., Westbrook, ME,
USA), and generated results within 2 hours. 80
DNA Microarrays
One of the limitations of culture is the inability to detect a target
pathogen when it exists in a matrix that contains a large number
of additional organisms. With microarray technology, the
products of PCR ampliﬁcation of a universal bacterial gene (such
as bacterial 16S rRNA) can be hybridized onto a solid platform
that contains thousands to more than a million oligonucleotide
probes. These either hybridize to bacterial 16S rRNA genes;
genus-, species-, or strain-speciﬁc genes; genes that specify
resistance to antimicrobials; or toxin genes. The products of
ampliﬁcation are labeled with ﬂuorescent dyes and the ampliconprobe interactions are measured using a laser scanner and
analyzed by a computer. Examples are PhyloChip (Second
Generation Solutions), which has been widely used to analyze
microbial communities using 16S bacterial rRNA probes, and
Prove-It Sepsis (Mobidiag, Finland), which detects 60 species of
bacteria and 13 fungi, as well as the mecA resistance gene, in blood
specimens within a 3.5-hour time frame.

vetexamprep.ir

Digital PCR. (A-C) The PCR reaction
mixture is partitioned into droplets and the
presence or absence of fluorescence from
each droplet is measured. (D) The fraction of
fluorescing droplets can be used to determine
the number of target molecules present per
droplet using Poisson distribution statistics.
FIG. 6.7

Digital PCR (dPCR)
First described in 1992, 81 dPCR is a reﬁnement of PCR that can be
used to more accurately quantify nucleic acids (including DNA,
cDNA, methylated DNA, or RNA). In contrast to traditional PCR,
the assembled reaction mixture is separated into a large number
of individual portions (in microwell plates, capillaries, oil
emulsions, or other chambers) and the reaction is carried out on
each partition individually. After multiple cycles of PCR, the
samples are checked as to whether they ﬂuoresce or not. Poisson
statistics are then used to measure the quantity of DNA present,
and use of a calibration curve is not necessary; the fraction of
ﬂuorescing droplets predicts the number of target copies per
droplet (Fig. 6.7). This separation allows a more reliable collection
and sensitive measurement of nucleic acid amounts. It provides
absolute quantiﬁcation, because the number of droplets
ﬂuorescing due to proper ampliﬁcation are determined, rather
than DNA quantity being extrapolated using a calibration curve.
The interest in dPCR has grown over the last 10 years because
technologic progress makes it practical, with unparalleled
precision, absolute quantiﬁcation, ﬂexibility, and increasingly
aﬀordable. dPCR may also be more reproducible and less
susceptible to inhibition than qPCR. The method has been useful
for viral/pathogen detection and quantiﬁcation, gene expression

vetexamprep.ir

p
g
q
g
p
studies, food testing, detection of point mutations, and clonal
ampliﬁcation for next-generation sequencing. 82 , 83

Interpretation of PCR Assay Results
A properly designed and highly eﬃcient qPCR assay can detect
very few copies (one or two) of a targeted gene, but both viable
and nonviable organisms can be detected, which may be an
obstacle for the clinician when trying to determine the signiﬁcance
of a positive qPCR result in light of an animal’s disease. An
understanding of the pathogenesis of infectious diseases and
organism shedding pa erns is crucial when interpreting positive
qPCR results. Correct interpretation of the results relies on
knowledge of the methods used by a laboratory and their
advantage and disadvantages.

Factors that can lead to negative test results are shown in Box 6.4.
An example of the use of the wrong specimen type would be
submission of blood for a Borrelia burgdorferi qPCR test, when B.
burgdorferi is found predominantly in connective tissue, 84 and
only in blood for a short period of time during early infection. As
discussed in this chapter, assay inhibition and specimen
degradation can be identiﬁed by interpretation of reference gene
control assay results, which should be performed by the
laboratory; therefore, the clinician should use reliable laboratories
and ensure that they use quality controls.

vetexamprep.ir

Factors that must be considered when interpreting positive test
results are shown in Box 6.4. The most common reason for falsepositive test results for assays that involve DNA ampliﬁcation is
contamination. Loading errors, in which specimen extracts are
inadvertently loaded into the wrong wells on a microtiter plate,
may also lead to false-positive results and are reduced with the
use of automated methods. Because of the exquisite sensitivity of
qPCR, the signiﬁcance of a true positive result should be
interpreted with a caution. The organism may be part of the
normal ﬂora or carried subclinically (e.g., latent FHV-1 in a nasal
biopsy). Several US veterinary laboratories oﬀer qPCR “panels”
for diagnostic purposes, whereby qPCR assays for several
diﬀerent pathogens are performed in separate reaction wells (one
per pathogen) on nucleic acid extracted from a single clinical
specimen. This high-throughput panel format allows assays to be
oﬀered at a substantial discount over the cost of multiple
individual assays. This type of testing can occasionally result in
unexpected positive test results, such as a positive result for the
Clostridium perfringens toxin gene in a cat with diarrhea that is
suspected to have trichomoniasis. In this situation, the C.
perfringens may be an incidental ﬁnding and unrelated to the
clinical problem, because healthy cats can have such toxin genes
in their feces (see Chapter 64). As with any laboratory test,
positive results need to be interpreted in light of the clinical
history, clinical signs, and the pathogenesis of the disease in
question. A positive result can also occur if an a enuated live
vaccine for the target organism was recently administered.
Because qPCR detects both viable and nonviable organisms, qPCR
can be positive for days after antimicrobials have been
administered, when culture is negative. 85–87 The duration of
qPCR positivity after treatment depends on the sample type
tested and the target pathogen.

Challenges of Current Molecular Detection
Methods
The reliability of a molecular diagnostic test depends on its
detection limit. Some methods have limited ability to detect low
numbers of organisms without steps to amplify the population in
advance of PCR. Culture-based enrichment has been used reliably

vetexamprep.ir

to expand a pathogen’s population, but this technique is a timeconsuming step in the analysis. 88
Molecular techniques have limitations, such as those that relate
to inhibition of PCR, lack of sensitivity in chronic infections, and
diﬀerentiation of vaccine organisms from true pathogens. Often,
multiple diﬀerent types of diagnostic tests (culture, PCR,
serology) must be performed for successful pathogen detection,
and a correct diagnosis relies on interpretation of these results in
light of the total clinical picture.
Pathogens are most accurately identiﬁed by sequencing the
entire chromosome, or one or more genes of the unknown
organism, and comparing the sequences generated to others in an
identiﬁcation database such as Genbank. Sequences can be
generated using PCR-based technology. This technology, known
as whole genome sequencing, can be used to identify fungi, bacteria,
and viruses. It can be used to identify slow-growing organisms, or
even those that cannot be cultured. The major disadvantage of
whole genome sequencing is the high costs associated with it in
terms of dedicated facilities, personnel training, time, and
consumables.
