7: Clinical Epidemiology in
Infectious Diseases and
Interpretation of Diagnostic
Tests
Janet E. Foley, Rance K. Sellon, W. Zach Mills, James F. Evermann, Jane
E. Sykes, and Shelley C. Rankin

KEY POINTS
Epidemiology
• Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of healthrelated states or events in populations and the application of these
principles to control health outcomes.
• The epidemiologic triangle highlights how disease outcomes depend
upon: (1) pathogen factors, (2) host factors, and (3) environment.
• Endemic or enzootic disease refers to a disease that is established in a
population and occurs regularly in that population at a background level,
whereas an epidemic or outbreak occurs whenever cases are
widespread in the community and exceed this baseline level.
• Molecular typing methods that can be used to study the epidemiology of
an infectious disease include multilocus sequence typing, pulsed-field
gel electrophoresis, and whole genome sequencing.
• Spatial epidemiology involves use of modeling to determine factors that
influence the geographic distribution of an infectious disease.
• Multiple logistic regression analysis is often used to identify factors that
increase the risk of an infectious disease while controlling for
confounding.

Diagnostic Test Interpretation
• Diagnostic tests can be divided into organism detection tests and
antibody detection tests.
• Before requesting a diagnostic test, veterinarians need to have an
understanding of the clinical sensitivity and specificity of that test, what
the target of the test is (e.g., antigen, DNA, or antibody), and whether
the test is appropriate for the purpose it is being applied for. An

vetexamprep.ir

understanding of the pathogenesis of the infectious disease, including
shedding patterns and sites, and whether a carrier state or latency
occurs, is critical for interpretation of test results.

Clinical Epidemiology
Epidemiologic Concepts in Infectious
Disease
Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of
health-related states or events in speciﬁed populations and the
application of these principles to control health outcomes. 1
Clinical epidemiology can be used in medical practice to evaluate
diagnostic tests, determine causality, analyze risk factors
associated with the likelihood of acquiring a disease, and compile
prognostic factors that will determine the course of a particular
disease.
The concept of the epidemiologic triangle is useful in clinical
epidemiology of infectious disease. The epidemiologic triangle is
a model that highlights how disease outcomes are interdependent
of: (1) pathogen factors, (2) host factors, and (3) environment. 2–4
Pathogen factors include the ability to survive in the environment,
the propensity of the microorganism to spread, virulence factors
and the manner in which they are expressed, resistance to
antimicrobial drugs, and the ability to evade host immune
defenses. Numerous host factors have the potential to inﬂuence
infection and disease, including sex, breed, age, and immune
status. 5 Environmental factors include physical (e.g., local terrain
or climate), biological (e.g., insect vectors), and social (e.g.,
households vs. ca eries). The epidemiology of FIP is a good
example of the concept of the epidemiologic triangle. The
prevalence of the fatal disease, FIP, in ca eries can be as high as
5%, whereas the prevalence in one-cat or two-cat households is
0.02% (see Chapter 31). This increased prevalence in ca eries
reﬂects higher levels of low-virulence strains of FCoV in the
environment, increased viral replication from acquired immune
suppression caused by concurrent infections, pregnancy, stress of
crowding, and host cat genetic factors. 6 , 7 These factors are

vetexamprep.ir

thought to accelerate the accumulation of virus mutations that
allow the virus to infect macrophages and cause FIP.
The progression of an infectious disease is a continuum that
begins in a particular environment and a unique, susceptible (or
naïve) host. Once there is exposure to an infectious agent, the
timing of clinical signs (if any), and shedding of pathogens, vary
depending on the individual host and the type of pathogen
involved. There may then be an incubation period before the
onset of clinical signs, during which time an animal may shed
infectious organisms. Death or complete recovery may follow, or
the host may become a carrier in the absence of clinical signs.
Carrier hosts may either shed organisms (e.g., FCV infections), or
harbor persistent infections in the absence of shedding. Hosts that
are carriers of vector-borne pathogens do not shed organisms but
may act as reservoir hosts that transmit pathogens to vectors
when they feed. For example, Ehrlichia canis establishes a chronic,
subclinical infection in dogs that can last years, providing a
reservoir for infection of uninfected ticks. 8–10 Other pathogens can
establish regressive or latent infections (e.g., FeLV [as provirus] or
FHV-1 [in the trigeminal ganglia]), and later reactivation and
shedding of these pathogens can occur with immune suppression.
Typically, infected animals that show clinical signs are thought to
be the most highly infectious to other at-risk animals and humans
because they shed larger quantities of organisms and/or have
signs (such as sneezing) that facilitate transmission.
Analysis of contact pa erns within and among populations can
reveal targets for interventions that prevent spread of infectious
diseases. In order to persist, some pathogens require frequent
interhost transmission and constant exposure to susceptible hosts,
others chronically persist in their hosts, and others succeed as a
result of prolonged survival in the environment (e.g., CPV-2). It is
also important to consider the potential for interspecies spread of
infectious microorganisms, as for rabies, CPV-2, and inﬂuenza
viruses. 8 , 11–14
The potential for an infectious disease to occur in an “outbreak”
or epidemic/epizootic is a concern for infectious disease
epidemiologists. Endemic or enzootic disease refers to a disease that
is established in a population and occurs regularly in that
population at a background level. Hyperendemic refers to
persistent, high levels of disease. An epidemic occurs whenever

vetexamprep.ir

cases are widespread in the community and exceed this
background level, and a pandemic is an epidemic that occurs over
several countries or continents. An outbreak carries the same
meaning as an epidemic but is generally used to refer to the
occurrence of a greater-than-normal level of disease within a
speciﬁc geographic region. Epidemics or outbreaks occur when
there is an increase in the quantity or virulence of a pathogen,
when a pathogen is introduced into new regions with naïve hosts,
when the mode of transmission of a pathogen is enhanced, when
there is a change in host susceptibility, and/or when factors
increase host exposure or permit a change in the mode of
transmission. 15 Outbreaks can be common-source (when hosts are
all exposed to an infectious agent from the same source),
propagated (when there is transmission from one host to another),
mixed (comprising both common-source and propagated features),
or other (where disease occurs neither as a result of commonsource exposure or propagation; introduction of a vector-borne
infectious disease is one example). 15
To some extent, epidemics can be predicted using mathematical
tools such as compartment models, which are sets of inter-related
diﬀerential equations that model instantaneous changes in
numbers of individuals who are either: (1) susceptible (S) to
infection (not previously infected, or recovered but not immune);
(2) currently infected (I); or (3) recovered and immune (R). This
Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model is the simplest
version of a compartment model, but more elaborate models can
allow for many additional factors such as no immunity, an
exposed but not yet infectious state (E), arthropod vectors, and
other complexities.
A crucially important value that derives from an SIR model is
R0 (R naught; also known as basic reproductive rate or basic
reproduction number). 16 R0 is meant to be a measure of the
contagiousness of a disease that takes into account host behavior
and pathogen characteristics; it is the number of cases that are
expected to occur after the introduction of a single infectious
individual into a fully susceptible population. A value of R0 that
exceeds 1 predicts continuation of an epidemic. When R0 < 1, the
epidemic is expected to die out. The magnitude of R0 can correlate
with the potential size of an epidemic and can be used to

vetexamprep.ir

determine the proportion of the population that may need to be
vaccinated to prevent ongoing transmission. However, it is not a
measure of the severity of an infectious disease or the speed of a
pathogen’s spread through a population of hosts. The calculation
of R0 generally requires mathematical models that are developed
using assumptions about the mechanisms of disease transmission
in a population. It has been noted that R0 is readily susceptible to
misapplication and misinterpretation because many researchers
that use R0 lack suﬃcient training in the mathematical techniques
required to accurately calculate R0. For example, a simple R0 may
not be applicable to diseases where there is no recovered and
immune state, or once the population comprises a mix of naïve
and recovered individuals. Nevertheless, it remains a useful
benchmark by which to compare magnitudes of predicted
epidemics of diﬀerent diseases or disease in diﬀerent types of
populations (Box 7.1, Figs. 7.1–7.3).

BOX 7.1

Te r m s Use d i n C l i ni ca l E pi de m i o l o gy

Confounding: A spurious association between a risk factor
and dependent outcome, caused by a variable that
inﬂuences both the independent and dependent variable.
Etiologic (or A ributable) Fraction or Risk: The diﬀerence
between the incidence of disease in a group of individuals
exposed to a risk factor and in a group that are not
exposed.
Etiologic Predictive Value: A value that informs how well a
single test for a single pathogen predicts the true
underlying cause of clinical signs in the circumstances
where there is no single best test and when some
individuals may be infected with an agent but not show
signs (a carrier).
Fit-for-Purpose: An assay is “ﬁt for purpose” if test
methods and related procedures are appropriate for
speciﬁc diagnostic applications in order for the test
results to be of relevance. 17

vetexamprep.ir

Sensitivity: The number of truly infected, test-positive
individuals divided by the total number of infected
individuals. This indicates how well the test detects all
truly infected individuals (Fig. 7.1).
Speciﬁcity: The number of test-negative individuals who
are truly uninfected, divided by the total number of
uninfected individuals. This allows assessment of the
likelihood of a false-positive test result. 18
Positive Predictive Value: The positive predictive value
(PPV) is the probability that an animal that has tested
positive is infected with the pathogen of concern. 17
Negative Predictive Value: The negative predictive value
(NPV) is the probability that an animal that has tested
negative is not infected with the pathogen of concern. The
positive and negative predictive values depend on the
prevalence of the disease in the regional animal
population (Fig. 7.1). 17
Risk Factor: Any characteristic or exposure that may
modify the likelihood of developing a disease or being
test positive. Risk factors may be positive (increasing
probability of disease) or negative (protective).
Odds Ratio (OR ): The relative odds of an outcome
occurring (e.g., a positive test result) when there is a
particular exposure or risk factor, compared with the
odds of the outcome occurring in the absence of that
exposure. An OR signiﬁcantly greater than 1 implies that
a risk factor increases likelihood of the outcome; an OR <
1 means the risk factor is protective; and an OR = 1 means
that the risk factor has no eﬀect on the outcome (Fig. 7.2).
Relative Risk: The ratio of the rate of infection or disease in
animals exposed to a risk factor compared with those
animals not exposed to the risk factor. As with OR,
individuals with risk factors that impose a relative risk
greater than 1 have increased risk of disease (Fig. 7.2).
Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC ) Curve: Plots of
true-positive rates (sensitivity, y-axis) against falsepositive rates (1-speciﬁcity, x-axis) for a test at diﬀerent
cutoﬀ values used to deﬁne a positive test result. ROC
analysis is often used to help determine the cutoﬀ point
that optimizes sensitivity and speciﬁcity. As cutoﬀ values

vetexamprep.ir

decrease, sensitivity increases while speciﬁcity decreases,
and vice versa. The overall performance of a diagnostic
test can be measured by determining the area under the
ROC curve (AUC). The closer the AUC is to 1, the be er
the overall diagnostic performance of the test. The closer
the AUC is to 0.5 (straight line, or “chance diagonal”), the
closer the diagnostic test performance is to pure chance
for distinguishing positive from negative results (Fig. 7.3).

Molecular Epidemiology
Molecular epidemiology focuses on how nucleic acid–based data
can inform understanding of disease etiology, transmission, and
distribution. Nucleic acid–based approaches can be used to
understand pathogen transmission pathways, the evolution and
spread of virulence genes, and host-microbe interactions and
disease pathogenesis. Molecular epidemiology can reveal changes
in evolving and emerging pathogens, their spread in space and
emergence in new hosts, and their relationship with the
environment.

vetexamprep.ir

Receiver operating characteristic
(ROC) curves. Each curve represents
excellent, good, and worthless assays that
have been plotted on the same graph. Test
accuracy depends on the degree to which the
test separates those with and without the
infectious disease of interest. Accuracy is
represented by the area under the ROC curve
(AUC). The test is perfect if the AUC is 1; an
AUC of 0.5 represents a worthless test. An
AUC above 0.8 is considered to be a good
assay. From Interpreting Diagnostic Tests. Thomas G.
FIG. 7.3

Tape, MD. University of Nebraska Medical Center;
http://gim.unmc.edu/dxtests/roc3.htm

Some molecular techniques used to study epidemiology target a
small portion of a pathogen’s genetic material, such as a single

vetexamprep.ir

gene or intergenic region. Such assays can be used to document
the presence of a pathogen in a host population, or to describe
genetic relationships among multiple related strains and species
of pathogens. Targets for single-gene studies must be chosen with
care because DNA sequences that are relatively conserved among
diﬀerent strains are not as informative for epidemiologic studies
as sequences that are moderately variable. In contrast, highly
variable genes may not allow strains to be grouped at the level of
resolution intended. The epidemiologic analysis of some microbes
can be complicated by the diversity of evolutionary mechanisms
by which microbes mutate (e.g., horizontal gene transmission by
plasmids, transposons, viral vectors, homologous recombination,
and other processes) that create downstream impacts on genetic
lineages. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) is a commonly used
epidemiologic strain typing method that is referred to throughout
this book. In classical MLST, a series of DNA segments (typically
7) from diﬀerent parts of the genome (loci) are ampliﬁed using
PCR and sequenced. The sequences of the collection of loci from
diﬀerent strains are compared. For example, MLST has been used
to describe strains of Leptospira interrogans that might derive from
diﬀerent reservoir host species, 19 and an MLST protocol is a
standard typing method for comparing Cryptococcus isolates. 20
Another frequently used strain typing method for comparing
bacteria isolated from diﬀerent sources is pulsed-ﬁeld gel
electrophoresis (PFGE). With PFGE, the entire genome of an
organism is digested with one or more restriction enzymes which
recognize speciﬁc short sequences of DNA and cut the DNA into
fragments at these sequences (e.g., SmaI, which cuts in the center
of the sequence “CCCGGG”). A pulsing electrical ﬁeld is then
used to move the DNA fragments through an agarose gel such
that they are sorted by size. The sorted pa ern of fragments is
characteristic of each bacterial genotype and these “ﬁngerprints”
can be compared. Strains that have identical ﬁngerprints are
generally regarded to have originated from a common source.
Whole genome sequencing (WGS ) is now practical for the molecular
epidemiology of most viruses and bacteria and in some cases has
replaced techniques such as PFGE and classical MLST. A hybrid
approach that is increasingly being applied is core genome MLST
(cgMLST), whereby the sequences of hundreds of core genes are
compared among isolates following WGS. For example, a cgMLST

vetexamprep.ir

approach that uses 545 core genome sequences has been used to
type leptospiral strains. 21 This method has high discrimination
power and allows identiﬁcation of species, sequence types, and
most probable serogroups, allowing tracking of Leptospira strains
in diﬀerent hosts and over time. 22
Molecular typing methods have been used to recognize genetic
changes in pathogens that might correlate with increased or
reduced virulence (as might occur when a virus adapts to a host),
the emergence of viruses that have jumped a host-species barrier,
and to detect antimicrobial-resistant bacterial strains. 7 , 12–14 , 23 ,
24 An important cause for disease emergence is when a microbe
gains the ability to cross a host-species barrier, as occurred with
the emergence of CIV H3N8 (Fig. 7.4). Diagnosis requires
suspicion that this has occurred so that a test can be applied in the
new species. As pathogens spread, molecular tools help detect
changing pa erns of genetic relatedness and movement, a science
called phylogenetics. Phylogenetic approaches have been used, for
example, to monitor the northward spread of a particularly
aggressive but cryptic lineage of the brown dog tick, Rhipicephalus
sanguineus, in the United States. 25

Spatial Epidemiology
Spatial epidemiology is the study of the geographic distributions
of pathogens, vectors, diseases, and risk factors for these
distributions. It incorporates spatially implicit models, whereby
precise locations of geographic regions are not accounted for but
implied by a model, and spatially explicit work, such as risk
mapping of disease, whereby precise locations are known. 26
Spatially implicit models are often based on metapopulations,
which are dynamic groups of small “patches” (areas in space),
each with a small subpopulation, and each connected to other
patches. 27 For infectious disease modeling, the subpopulation
that resides in a patch would typically be a group of host
individuals. Use of metapopulations in small animal medicine is
uncommon, but interested readers are referred to the suggested
readings list for further information. 28
Spatial epidemiology uses maps and studies features of disease
and underlying factors, such as clustering of disease in space and
time, association of disease with spatially pa erned risk factors

vetexamprep.ir

p
y p
(such as soil type, weather conditions, location of water sources),
and changes in disease distributions. Mapping approaches
commonly use geographic information system (GIS), a computerbased system that employs widely used software applications
such as GRASS or ArcMap. These applications manage spatial
data, produce maps, and allow for spatial modeling and analysis.
Data are mapped and often color-coded to highlight degrees of
risk. Once data are mapped, clusters of risk factors or disease can
be assessed visually and analyzed using statistical approaches.
Merging spatial information about a disease with data on risk can
allow for hypothesis testing, such as whether disease is
signiﬁcantly associated with proximity of water sources or other
predictors. GIS has also been used to examine theory of disease
spread; this has been done for plague and rabies. 29 , 30

vetexamprep.ir

Integrating Clinical Epidemiology into Practice
Primary data on infections, diseases, results of diagnostic testing,
and risk factors are collected by veterinarians and diagnostic
laboratories. These data are routinely used in practice to diagnose
disease and inform medical management and preventative
strategies for pets. They have also been used to provide
information on human disease, such as when dogs act as sentinels
for human disease. Clear recommendations for the expectations
and limitations of diagnostic assays for diagnoses or screening are
increasingly available via online technical bulletins and assay kit
package inserts, and veterinarians interpreting these bulletins
must have an understanding of concepts such as analytical
sensitivity and speciﬁcity (how a test performs in the laboratory)
and how they might relate to clinical sensitivity and speciﬁcity
(how a test performs when applied to a population of animals
with and without infection). 31
Increased sensitivity and speciﬁcity of newer molecular and
serologic diagnostic assays has resulted in more rapid turnaround
and reduced costs. Commercial diagnostic laboratories, corporate
veterinary practices, and medical scientiﬁc literature make
valuable contributions to our knowledge of infectious disease
epidemiology because the results of testing large numbers of
specimens with the same assay are now available for analysis.
These data provide evidence to inform decisions regarding
vaccination frequency, which vaccines to use, what populations of
animals are at elevated risk, and how likely animals are to serve as
carriers and reservoirs of infection. Such data are needed for
biosecurity and are particularly helpful if reported back to the
clinicians and clients.

Risk Analysis
Through risk analysis, the relative importance of diﬀerent risk
factors associated with an animal’s susceptibility to infection and
disease can be assessed. Relative risk can be determined by

vetexamprep.ir

studying groups of animals with deﬁned risk factors (cohorts)
over deﬁned time periods for development of infection or disease.
For example, introduction of a tetravalent leptospira vaccine in
Swi erland was associated with a marked decrease in
leptospirosis and AKI among dogs. 32 Relative risk and odds
ratios do not provide information about the proportion of cases
resulting from exposure to a risk factor. These values are
determined by calculating the a ributable risk, which accounts for
the relative risk and the proportion of the population exposed to
the risk factor (see Fig. 7.2).
An understanding of associations between disease and risk
factors can inform decisions about targeted diagnostic testing,
preventive management and intervention, and prognostication.
Although a variety of statistical methods are applied depending
on the study design, one common statistical approach is logistic
regression analysis. Logistic regression analysis evaluates how a
dependent binary variable (binary meaning one thing or another—
diseased or not, test positive or test negative) is associated with
independent variables (e.g., sex, breed, species, outdoor access) or
risk factors. This highly ﬂexible tool allows multiple risk factors to
be assessed simultaneously, takes into account interactions among
risk factors, controls for confounding eﬀects, and can identify the
strength of an association with each risk factor. In contrast,
univariate analysis only allows the eﬀect of one risk factor to be
assessed at a time and does not take into account interactions or
control for confounding. The ability of logistic regression analysis
to control for confounding is particularly important. For example,
univariate analysis might reveal that an increased frequency of
leptospira vaccination increases the risk of adverse events such as
anaphylaxis. However, young animals are vaccinated more
frequently than older animals, and the increased rate of reactions
might be due to age rather than frequency of vaccination. Logistic
regression analysis controls for these eﬀects and typically
identiﬁes a smaller number of signiﬁcant risk factors when
compared with univariate analysis of all of the individual risk
factors included in the regression analysis.

Diagnostic Testing for Infectious Diseases
Diagnostic Versus Screening Assays

vetexamprep.ir

Veterinarians use diagnostic tests to diagnose acute or chronic
infectious disease. The same assay may be used to assess the
prevalence of disease, infection, or exposure in populations. A
single assay may be validated for one or more intended purposes
by optimizing its performance characteristics for each purpose.
An assay that is used as a screening assay (to rule out an infectious
disease agent) should have a high diagnostic sensitivity and a
high negative predictive value. Screening an animal to show that
it is free of a disease should be done with the assumption that the
animal is truly free of the disease because the disease prevalence
in the population represented by the animal is zero, or extremely
low (e.g., Brucella canis). Screening tests are generally associated
with a lower diagnostic speciﬁcity and positive results should be
conﬁrmed by a test with high speciﬁcity for the pathogen of
interest. Clinicians need to be aware of problems associated with
using tests that have been designed and validated as diagnostic
tests for screening purposes in animals that are unlikely to have
the disease of interest.

Types of Diagnostic Tests
Diagnostic tests for infectious diseases can be broadly divided
into: (1) organism detection tests, and (2) antibody detection tests.
Organism detection tests include culture/isolation, which detects
viable pathogens; tests that detect antigen(s) of a pathogen (e.g.,
direct IFA, IHC, antigen detection ELISA); and tests that detect
pathogen DNA or RNA such as PCR and isothermal ampliﬁcation
(collectively known as nucleic acid ampliﬁcation tests [NAAT]),
and ﬂuorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). Antibody detection
tests provide evidence of previous exposure to a pathogen and
include indirect IFA assays, HI, serum neutralization, antibody
detection ELISA, and colloidal gold immunochromatographic
assays (GICA). Tests may be available through diagnostic
laboratories or may be POC tests, which can be used in the clinic
or low-resource environments such as shelters.
Serologic tests are often assumed to be antibody detection tests,
but the term “serologic assay” (or immunoassay) can also refer to
an assay that detects antigen if the use of antibodies is employed
in test design. Clinicians need to consider whether they are trying
to make a diagnosis of an infectious disease (and that also includes

vetexamprep.ir

documenting exposure to an infectious agent) or show that the
animal is free of disease. Whenever the use of a diagnostic test is
considered, it is critical that clinicians understand whether the
assay detects viable pathogens (culture), components of a
pathogen that might be viable or nonviable (antigen or DNA), or
not replicating (proviral DNA in the case of a retrovirus infection),
or antibodies (exposure). The purpose of a particular test is
important when syndromic panels, which are designed to detect
multiple infectious agents and/or antibodies to those agents, are
requested. For example, diarrhea panels are available that include
culture for enteric pathogens, antigen ELISA assays for clostridial
organisms, and PCR for bacteria, viruses and parasites that
commonly cause diarrhea in particular animal hosts. There are
also immunoassays such as the IDEXX SNAP 4Dx Plus test
(IDEXX Laboratories Inc., USA) and the Antech AccuPlex 4 assay
(Antech Diagnostics, USA) that detect vector-borne pathogens
(Table 7.1). Use of such panels can occasionally produce
unexpected positive results that may be diﬃcult to interpret. 33 A
positive PCR test result is not always a marker for active shedding
or for disease status because pathogen nucleic acids may be
present in latent and subclinical infections; or when animals have
recovered but retain nonviable pathogens or free nucleic acids,
damaged cells, or debris. Positive PCR results can also occur when
specimens become contaminated with environmental DNA. 33
Positive test results must be assessed in light of the patient’s
history, clinical signs, physical examination ﬁndings, the reason
the test was performed, results of other diagnostic testing, and a
knowledge of the extent to which these organisms can be detected
in healthy animals as opposed to those that are diseased. 18

It is particularly important to understand whether panels consist
of organism detection tests, antibody detection tests, or both, and
the signiﬁcance of a positive result for each target in light of the
pathogenesis of disease.
Serology is the foundation for serodiagnosis, serosurveillance,
and studies of vaccine-induced immunity. Serodiagnosis can
assist in the diagnosis of current disease, such as the use of IgM
assays to detect acute infection, or the use of antigen ELISA
testing for detection of heartworm and FeLV infection.
Serodiagnostic assays that detect IgG can imply previous
infection, while a fourfold (two-step) rise in antibody titer over 1–
4 weeks (e.g., 1:4 to 1:16, 1:16 to 1:64) suggests recent, active
infection. For some diseases, determination of serum antibody
titers can also aid in assessment of vaccine-induced protection (see
Chapter 20). For example, dogs with speciﬁc CDV and CPV
antibody titers are generally considered protected against CDVand CPV-induced diseases. Antibody titers do not correlate with
protection for other diseases, such as leptospirosis. In addition,
factors such as degree of environmental exposure, and level of
natural and pharmacologic-induced immune suppression need to
be considered when antibody titers are used to determine the
need for booster vaccinations.
The limits of test sensitivity and timing of positive test results
over the course of infection are important considerations in
diagnosis. Early after exposure, during the acute phase of an

vetexamprep.ir

infection, the best options for diagnosis are tests which are
sensitive, detect the pathogen directly (e.g., antigen ELISA, PCR,
culture), and are performed on the appropriate target specimen.
Serology tests that detect antibodies can be negative early in the
course of illness if clinical signs appear after a short (< 10 days)
incubation period. Subsequently, IgM antibodies circulate, the
presence of which usually correlates with recent infection,
followed by longer lasting IgG which indicates exposure to a
given, or cross-reacting, pathogen. As the infection matures, direct
tests for antigen or nucleic acids reveal animals with acute clinical
infection as well as those with latent infection and those which are
carriers. For chronic diseases or diseases that occur after a long
incubation period (e.g., Lyme borreliosis, FIP), determination of
acute and convalescent phase titers over a 1- to 4-week period is
generally not appropriate because a signiﬁcant change in titer
does not occur. When diﬀerent test options are available, it is best
to choose a test with appropriate sensitivity and speciﬁcity for the
desired purpose, and to consider the prevalence of the disease in
the patient population. As an example, dogs with clinical CPVassociated enteritis are likely to be CPV fecal antigen ELISA
positive and PCR positive for CPV. Both tests are a good choice
for the diagnosis of CPV enteritis; however, the la er can conﬁrm
active infection and also detect dogs that are subclinically infected
or recently vaccinated with a enuated live vaccines (Fig. 7.5). 8
Some laboratories that perform real-time PCR results will report
cycle threshold values, or an estimate of nucleic acid target copy
number (see Chapter 6), with detection of nucleic acid in high
copy number being more likely to relate to clinically signiﬁcant
infection than detection of nucleic acid in low copy number (e.g.,
some assays for CDV or FeLV infections). Depending on the
pathogen, testing may lend itself to a diagnostic test hierarchy
(Fig. 7.6). Multiple tests may need to be applied in parallel or in
series to optimize diagnosis.

Summary

vetexamprep.ir

The interface between disease diagnosis and clinical epidemiology
has continued to be fortiﬁed by the ever-increasing knowledge of
the importance of animal populations and their interactions with
other animals and humans. With the development of molecular
diagnostic assays, the ﬁner details of how a pathogen sustains
itself in a population by establishing short- and long-term carrier
states have become more apparent. These assays have also shed
light on how the potential for interspecies transmission impacts
the nature of emerging infections. Although clinical epidemiology
involves the understanding of health and disease in populations,
it is fundamental in decision-making for the individual animal.
An understanding of the epidemiologic features of a particular
infectious disease facilitates the early identiﬁcation of an outbreak,
which in turn helps the clinician select the most appropriate
diagnostic test and interpret the results of subsequent diagnostic
testing. This early detection is essential for the development,
implementation, and monitoring of prevention and control
strategies.

Section 2

Anti-infective Drugs
Mark G. Papich

The majority of this book deals with diagnosis, pathology, and
management of speciﬁc infectious diseases in dogs and cats.
However, the book would not be complete without chapters on
the agents used to treat and manage these infections. In this
section, there are six chapters. The ﬁrst chapter is a review of
general principles of antimicrobial therapy. This chapter includes
the importance of identifying the organism, pharmacokinetic
properties of the agents, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD) issues, and antimicrobial drug resistance. This introductory
chapter sets the stage for the chapters that follow.
The remaining ﬁve chapters in Section 2 cover the major groups
of drugs that are used to treat infections in dogs and cats:
antiviral, antibacterial, antifungal, antiprotozoal, and antiparasitic
agents. Included with the antiviral chapter is a section on
immunomodulatory agents, which are often used to manage viral
infections, but have also been used for other infectious diseases.
Each of these chapters accompanies the speciﬁc sections on
diseases that are contained in the majority of the book.
These chapters on speciﬁc antimicrobial agents include drugs
that are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration
(FDA), or regulatory authorities in other countries, for treating
infections in dogs and cats. However, even with these approved
agents available, there are still many unmet needs. The
importance of these chapters lies in the realization that there are
not always drugs approved by regulatory authorities to treat all of
the infections encountered in dogs and cats. For example, there
are no antiviral drugs approved in the United States for dogs and

vetexamprep.ir

cats. Except for topical agents, there is only one antifungal agent
approved. The available antibacterial agents do not cover many of
the most important bacterial infections. Many antiprotozoal
agents are used extralabel. Therefore, extralabel (oﬀ-label) human
drugs or drugs approved for other animals are often used.
Because the uses, dosing information, pharmacokinetics, and
adverse eﬀects are not available for these drugs on an approved
drug label, these chapters are needed to provide veterinarians
with a resource for the important characteristics of these agents.
Each chapter includes state-of-the-art information available from
published papers and experts who have studied these
medications. The use of each drug listed is based on a consensus
opinion of experts consistent with good clinical practice. Each
chapter is referenced to original studies or the approved drug
label to support the use. The recommendations, including
dosages, listed in these chapters are based on the the best
available evidence at the time this book was prepared. The
authors cannot guarantee safety and eﬃcacy of all the treatments
discussed, and new information may emerge that was not known
at the time the book was prepared.

vetexamprep.ir

8: Principles of Anti-infective
Therapy
Jane E. Sykes, and Mark G. Papich

KEY POINTS
• Use of antimicrobial drugs (AMDs) selects for resistant
bacterial populations, both within the targeted bacterial
population and also commensal bacterial populations.
• Bacterial mechanisms of drug resistance include production of
enzymes that inactivate AMDs, drug exclusion through
membrane alterations and efflux pumps, protection of target
sites (e.g., ribosome), and modification of the site of action (or
target) of the AMD.
• Strategies that minimize selection for drug resistance include:
(1) confirmation of the presence of infection before AMD
treatment is commenced, (2) proper identification of the
infecting organism, (3) selection of agents with activity specific
to the pathogen present, (4) administration of an adequate
dose of AMD, and (5) administration of AMD for the proper
duration of time (often as short as possible).
• Selection of an appropriate AMD should be based on the
activity of the agent against the suspected pathogen;
knowledge of drug pharmacokinetics, which includes
bioavailability and tissue penetration; consideration of host
factors such as concurrent illness, medications, or
immunosuppression; and consideration of the agent’s
pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) properties. The
PK-PD properties include whether the drug exhibits
concentration- or time-dependent antibacterial effects, which
dictates the design of the dosage regimen.

vetexamprep.ir

Introduction
Antimicrobial drugs (AMDs; Box 8.1) have been considered one of
the greatest inventions of the 20th century. The modern era of
AMD treatment began with the discovery of sulfonamides in 1935.
1 In the 1940s, the therapeutic value of penicillin and streptomycin
was discovered, and by 1950, the “golden age” of AMD therapy
was underway. The increased use of AMDs in people, companion
animals, and livestock has been accompanied by increased rates of
antimicrobial resistance—in some instances, an alarming
transition to multidrug resistance that has severely limited the
available antimicrobial choices. Among 1,485 non-urinary
Escherichia coli isolates from dogs in the United States from 2004 to
2011, there was a signiﬁcant increase in the prevalence of
resistance to cefazolin, cefoxitin, cephalothin, enroﬂoxacin, and
tetracycline. 2 In the United Kingdom from 2003 to 2012, the
prevalence of resistance among 14,555 clinical isolates of
Staphylococcus
intermedius
group
organisms
(primarily
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius) increased signiﬁcantly. 3 Most of
the veterinary isolates of S. pseudintermedius are MDR, which
greatly limits the choices for treatment. 4 Clonal dissemination of
methicillin-resistant S. pseudintermedius 5 and ESBL enzyme
producing E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae 6 , 7 has been reported
among companion animals worldwide. This has been
compounded by a declining rate of development of new classes of
AMDs for veterinary use, and increased scrutiny of the use of
critically
important
human
antimicrobial
agents
for
administration to animals.
Antimicrobial resistance genes were present in microbes long
before antimicrobial agents were used in therapy. Microbe
populations generally consist of a mixture of genetically
susceptible and resistant organisms. The use of AMDs exerts
pressure that favors selection of the resistant microbes (“survival
of the ﬁ est”) within both the targeted bacterial population and
other commensal bacteria (which have the potential to become
pathogenic when host defenses are impaired).
The risk of emergence of resistant bacterial strains depends on
factors that include the size of the inoculum, ability of the bacteria
to acquire mutations, the ability of host defenses to eliminate
resistant bacteria, drug concentrations at the site of infection, and

vetexamprep.ir

the duration of exposure to AMDs. Selection pressures are highest
when bacteria are exposed to suboptimal dosage regimens (i.e.,
concentrations of drug below the level needed to kill or suppress
the growth of the bacteria). In this scenario, the most susceptible
strains are eliminated, but the more resistant strains ﬂourish
because of decreased competition. Resistant bacteria are not
necessarily more virulent than susceptible bacteria, but they may
require drugs not commonly used, or other measures not
commonly used for treatment of the susceptible strains of
bacteria.
According to the Infectious Disease Society of America,
antimicrobial stewardship refers to coordinated interventions
designed to improve and measure the appropriate use of
antimicrobials by promoting the selection of the optimal AMD
regimen, dose and duration of therapy, and route of
administration. 7 Guidelines for prudent antimicrobial use have
been published by several professional veterinary organizations
and societies with the intention of reducing selection for resistant
bacterial pathogens. 8–14 An AVMA taskforce on antimicrobial
stewardship in companion animal practice has developed an
antimicrobial stewardship program that includes client
educational handouts and a series of antimicrobial use “dos and
don’ts” for veterinary practitioners. 15

BOX 8.1

Ant i m i cr o bi a l , Ant i bi o t i c, Ant i ba ct e r i a l ,

W hi ch I s C o r r e ct ?

vetexamprep.ir

The terms “antibiotic,” “antimicrobial,” and “antibacterial”
are often used interchangeably. They have diﬀerent
meanings that are often overlooked. An antibiotic is a
natural chemical, produced by other organisms, that is
designed to suppress the growth of other organisms
(including bacteria, fungi, or protozoa). An antimicrobial is
any compound, natural or synthetic, that suppresses
microbial growth. An antibacterial is any compound that
suppresses bacterial growth. The term “antimicrobial
agent” is preferred by certain groups such as CLSI. Many
times, even in this chapter, the terms are used
interchangeably with the same meaning.
Speciﬁc guidelines regarding antimicrobial selection, dosing
and duration of treatment for infections of the urinary tract, skin,
and respiratory tract have been developed by consensus of the
Antimicrobial Guidelines Working Group of the International
Society
for
Companion
Animal
Infectious
Diseases
(www.iscaid.org). Veterinary hospitals are encouraged to adapt
these guidelines or develop their own hospital-speciﬁc
antimicrobial guidelines based on evaluation of the local
prevalence (antibiograms) of AMD resistance and local
prescribing practices. Strategies that may reduce the selection for
antimicrobial resistance include documentation of the presence of
infection; appropriate susceptibility testing; proper identiﬁcation
of the infecting organism; and the use of agents that are as speciﬁc
for the pathogen as possible, at the proper dose and for the proper
duration of time. There are older, outdated recommendations that
recommended treatment for longer than necessary, which has led
to a current trend to shorten the duration of antimicrobial therapy
whenever possible for companion animals.

Identification of The Infecting Organism
The detection of fever or leukocytosis does not imply bacterial
infection and the need for antibiotic treatment, especially given
the relatively high prevalence of sterile inﬂammatory and

vetexamprep.ir

immune-mediated diseases in dogs and viral infections in cats.
Selection of the most appropriate AMD relies on knowledge of: (1)
the presence of an infectious agent, (2) the type of infectious agent
present, and (3) the likelihood of susceptibility of the agent to the
AMD prescribed. In some cases, treatment with AMDs may not be
necessary even though the cause of disease is bacterial. Some
infections undergo spontaneous cures without the aid of an
antibiotic. For example, a cat bite abscess can often be drained and
resolved without the need to administer an antibiotic (see Chapter
75). Many transmissible respiratory infections, such as those
belonging to the canine infectious respiratory disease complex, are
self-limited and often spontaneously resolve without antibiotics.
In some situations, collection of a specimen for cytology or
histopathology permits a diagnosis of infection to be established.
Some diﬃcult to grow or fastidious infectious agents, such as
ricke sial and fungal pathogens, may be presumptively identiﬁed
to the genus or species level based on their morphology. If skin
cytology from a dog reveals cocci (a Gram stain is not necessary to
conﬁrm the presence of gram-positive cocci), then the presence of
S. pseudintermedius is highly probable. If, on the other hand,
cytology from an ear swab reveals rods, the possibility of
Pseudomonas aeruginosa must be considered. In either case, this
knowledge is valuable for selecting appropriate initial
antibacterial therapy. The use of molecular diagnostic techniques,
such as nucleic acid ampliﬁcation tests (NAATs), can also allow
rapid identiﬁcation of an infecting organism, which can help to
guide AMD selection. Many commercial laboratories now use
MALDI-TOF MS for rapid identiﬁcation and diagnosis of
pathogens (see Chapter 3).
For example, identiﬁcation of a vector-borne pathogen (e.g.,
Ricke sia spp., Ehrlichia canis) is helpful because doxycycline is
usually the ﬁrst drug of choice for the majority of these pathogens.
Once the pathogen is identiﬁed, or presumptively identiﬁed,
antibiotics can be administered that have a high probability of
success based on typical susceptibility pa erns for the wild-type
strains. Unfortunately, there is now greater likelihood of
encountering
drug-resistant
(non-wild-type)
organisms.
Therefore, in many instances, it has become important to collect
specimens for culture and susceptibility testing before treatment
with AMDs is commenced. Although there is an initial cost to the

vetexamprep.ir

client for culture and susceptibility testing, long-term costs to the
client may be reduced because prompt treatment with the most
appropriate agent will decrease prescription of unnecessary or
inappropriate AMDs, improved likelihood of rapid resolution of
the underlying disorder with early diagnosis and appropriate
treatment, and reduced need for more expensive, second- or thirdline AMDs. Early a ainment of therapeutic targets is important
for rapid clinical resolution and decreased emergence of resistant
bacteria. 16 Administration of AMDs without identiﬁcation of the
infectious agent can also decrease subsequent chances of
successful culture and proper diagnosis if the problem does not
resolve. Proper interpretation of culture and susceptibility panel
results is also imperative. Practitioners should examine a culture
report carefully and question whether a bacterial species isolated
is truly the cause of infection as opposed to a contaminant or
commensal. Among the agents listed as “susceptible” in a report,
the clinician will have to decide on the best choice based on drug
and patient characteristics. The reader is referred to Chapter 3 for
more information on bacterial culture and susceptibility testing.
The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) also
provides an excellent resource for the interpretation of culture and
susceptibility results for pathogens from animals. 17
In animals with life-threatening infections, institution of AMD
treatment is necessary before the results of culture and
susceptibility become available. The choice of treatment at this
stage can be based on cytology and knowledge of the type of
infections that most commonly occur at the anatomic site involved
(also known as bacteriologic statistics). Because of the lifethreatening nature of these infections, the practice of “deescalation” (as opposed to “escalation”) is employed. This is the
practice of initially selecting a highly active agent that has a high
probability of successful elimination of the pathogen and
initiating treatment quickly; then once the infectious agent has
been identiﬁed, the drug spectrum should be changed or
narrowed according to culture and susceptibility results. If the
infection is life threatening, highly active agents such as an
aminoglycoside or ﬂuoroquinolone, or extended-spectrum βlactam can be selected initially. Then, if culture and susceptibility
show susceptibility to other β-lactam agents, treatment should be
continued with these agents alone. Routine inclusion of an

vetexamprep.ir

“antimicrobial time-out” 48 to 72 hours after initiating AMD
therapy has been recommended when culture and susceptibility
data or other clinical information becomes available. During this
period, the clinician should reassess whether antimicrobial
therapy should be continued, discontinued or modiﬁed. 15
When available, use of regional or hospital-speciﬁc
antibiograms can also help guide appropriate empirical
antimicrobial therapy. A regional antibiogram lists commonly
isolated species of bacteria and the likelihood of susceptibility to
various AMDs based on cumulative culture and susceptibility
data from a practice or region. The practitioner can then select the
AMD based on the likelihood of a particular bacterial species
being present at the site of an infection and its predicted resistance
pa ern. The term “antibiogram” has also been used incorrectly to
describe an individual bacterial isolate’s susceptibility pa ern, so
“regional antibiogram” is the recommended term to describe
cumulative susceptibility data. Development of practice-speciﬁc
antibiograms is recommended because antibiograms can diﬀer
considerably from one practice to another even within the same
region, depending on factors such as clinician preference for AMD
choices, the types of cases seen, and whether the patient
population is primary or referral based.

Classification of Antimicrobial Drugs
AMDs may be classiﬁed based on their structure (e.g., β-lactams,
ﬂuoroquinolones), spectrum of activity (gram-positive versus
gram-negative bacteria), mechanism of action (Table 8.1; Fig. 8.1),
whether they are bacteriostatic (inhibit or slow growth) or
bactericidal drugs, and their pharmacodynamic properties (see
Pharmacodynamics of Antimicrobial Drugs, later).
The diﬀerence between bactericidal and bacteriostatic drugs has
become more blurred in recent years. Some drugs are diﬃcult to
deﬁne because they may have diﬀerent action on diﬀerent
bacterial species. The “static” versus “cidal” nature of many drugs
depends on the concentration achieved. At low concentrations
(e.g., 1 × MIC, 2 × MIC) they may be bacteriostatic, but at higher
concentrations (e.g., 4 × MIC, 8 × MIC) they can be bactericidal. In
reality, there are no examples where a bactericidal agent is
preferred over a bacteriostatic agent based on available evidence

vetexamprep.ir

and extensive evaluation from human clinical studies. 18 From a
clinical perspective, it is more useful to describe drugs as time
dependent versus concentration dependent rather than as
bactericidal or bacteriostatic. This allows the clinician to consider
the dosage regimen and dosing interval to optimize therapy.
Antibacterial drugs have also been classiﬁed for veterinary use
as ﬁrst-line, second-line, or third-line drugs 19 (in some guidelines,
the authors use “ﬁrst-choice,” “second-choice,” and so forth, and
in the ISCAID guidelines the authors use ﬁrst-tier, second-tier,
third-tier, for the same meaning). First-line drugs are those that
could be used for empirical selection in the absence of or pending
the results of culture and susceptibility testing, and include
amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalexin, doxycycline,
minocycline, and trimethoprim-sulfonamides. Second-line drugs
are those to be used on the basis of culture and susceptibility
testing and because of the lack of any appropriate ﬁrst-line
options. These include piperacillin-tazobactam, amikacin, and
third-generation cephalosporins. Some consensus documents
(e.g., ISCAID guidelines, BSAVA guidelines) have considered
some third-generation cephalosporins as appropriate ﬁrst-line
agents in special circumstances. Cefovecin may be considered
when compliance may be a problem. Cefpodoxime proxetil has
been considered by ISCAID to be either a “ﬁrst- or second-tier”
antibiotic because of its activity against staphylococci.
Fluoroquinolones are usually considered second-tier antibiotics
because ﬂuoroquinolone exposure has been associated with
emergence of antimicrobial resistance and treatment failures. 20
Fluoroquinolones could be considered as ﬁrst-line drugs for dogs
and cats suspected to have serious gram-negative bacterial
infections that require treatment pending the results of culture
and susceptibility testing.

Pharmacodynamics of Antimicrobial Drugs
Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters (PK-PD
exposure relationships) are important determinants of the eﬃcacy
of AMDs and serve as the basis for determination of clinically
eﬀective dosage regimens and susceptibility breakpoints and for
the development of guidelines for AMD use for speciﬁc types of
infections. 21
Antimicrobial activity is classiﬁed as concentration dependent or
time dependent. AMDs that exhibit concentration-dependent killing
are ﬂuoroquinolones and aminoglycosides. These drugs work
optimally when the peak concentration in the plasma (Cmax) or

vetexamprep.ir

the area under the curve (AUC) exceeds the MIC by a deﬁned
index factor (Fig. 8.2). These are typically bactericidal agents, and
the ability to kill bacteria increases as the AMD concentrations are
optimized. Target concentrations have been deﬁned for laboratory
animals and humans and have been extrapolated to veterinary
patients. For example, the Cmax to MIC ratio (Cmax/MIC) should
exceed 8 to 10 for optimum dosing of aminoglycosides. The AUC
for a 24-hour interval to MIC ratio (AUC24/MIC) should exceed
approximately 100 for ﬂuoroquinolones and exceed 90 for
aminoglycosides. For some infections, a ratio of 125 for
ﬂuoroquinolones is be er, and in some patients (e.g.,
immunocompromised patients with life-threatening infections), a
ratio of 250 may be desirable. Drugs that exhibit concentrationdependent killing also have postantibiotic eﬀect (PAE). The PAE is a
persistent antimicrobial eﬀect after drug concentrations at the site
of infection fall below the MIC. The exact cause of the PAE varies
with the drug, but it may result from irreversible binding of a
drug to the target site. The duration of the PAE is inﬂuenced by
the duration of antibiotic exposure, the drug concentration, the
bacterial species present, and the class of antibiotic. For
concentration-dependent antibiotics, administration of the total
daily dose as a single dose every 24 hours is preferred to a smaller
divided dose in order to maximize Cmax or AUC. For
aminoglycosides, this also reduces risk of kidney injury.

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 8.2 Antimicrobial pharmacodynamics. (A)
Antimicrobial drug (AMD) pharmacodynamics.
Concentration-dependent drugs are most active when
the peak concentration (Cmax) or the area under the

vetexamprep.ir

curve (AUC) in the plasma exceeds the MIC by a
defined factor. For time-dependent drugs, outcome is
correlated with the time that the AMD concentration at
the site of infection spends above the MIC. This is
usually expressed as the percent of time above the MIC
during a 24-hour interval (T > MIC). (B) As AMD
concentrations increase, the ability of concentrationdependent drugs such as fluoroquinolones (in this case,
ciprofloxacin) to kill bacteria increases. As
concentrations of time-dependent drugs such as βlactam drugs (in this case, ticarcillin) increase, bacterial
killing plateaus.

β-lactams (penicillins and cephalosporins) exhibit timedependent killing. The activity of these drugs is maximized by the
time above the MIC rather than the magnitude of the
concentration. This is usually expressed as the percent of time
above the MIC during a 24-hour interval (T > MIC). These drugs
are most eﬀective when administered multiple times a day or as
continuous-rate infusions, in order to maintain drug
concentrations at the site of infection. For some drugs (e.g., some
cephalosporins), a long T > MIC is achieved by virtue of a long
half-life. The required time above the MIC for an AMD varies
with the pathogen present, the drug, and the site of infection. For
a β-lactam antimicrobial (penicillin, cephalosporin), the desired
target is a plasma concentration greater than the MIC maintained
for at least 40% to 50% of the dosing interval. 21 Drug dosages that
achieve these target concentrations in excess of an MIC for these
periods can be calculated based on pharmacokinetic data. For
time-dependent AMD with long half-lives (such as macrolides,
clindamycin, vancomycin, and tetracyclines), eﬃcacy is
determined primarily by the extent to which the AUC exceeds the
MIC. The magnitude of the target varies with each drug class, but
in general an AUC/MIC ratio of the unbound drug > 25 is a
desired target.
These parameters and indices constitute the PK-PD properties
of the antimicrobial agent, also known as the PK-PD cutoﬀ. As the
MIC of an organism increases, it becomes more diﬃcult to achieve
these PK-PD targets (i.e., above the PK-PD cutoﬀ), and organisms
are regarded as resistant.

vetexamprep.ir

Site of Infection
In general, the concentration of an AMD at the site of infection
should at least equal the MIC for the infecting organism, but the
exact concentration and the duration of the concentration at the
site varies with the class of antimicrobial. For some AMDs, the
serum or plasma total (bound and unbound) drug concentrations
may not reﬂect the drug concentration in tissues. Examples are the
highly lipophilic macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin) for
which the tissue drug concentration is much higher than plasma
drug concentration because of sequestration inside cells. On the
other hand, tissue concentrations greatly underestimate the
plasma or serum drug concentration for poorly lipophilic agents
such as aminoglycosides or β-lactams. Antimicrobial selection for
diﬀerent body sites are suggested in Box 8.3.
The concentration of an AMD at the site of infection is aﬀected
by factors such as lipid solubility, protein binding, pH at the site
(or cell), and other factors reducing permeability, such as the
presence of large amounts of pus, scar tissue, foreign material,
devitalized tissue, and bone. Lipid-soluble drugs such as
chloramphenicol, rifampin, ﬂuoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and
trimethoprim are most adept at crossing membranes, including
the blood-brain, alveolar, and prostatic barriers. In contrast,
poorly lipophilic, polar drugs such as penicillins and
aminoglycosides do not cross lipid membranes and will not
achieve adequate concentrations in tissues in which there is a
barrier to penetration (e.g., prostate, brain, eye, or intracellular
sites). In human patients, aminoglycosides and amphotericin B
have been administered intrathecally to treat CNS infections, 22 , 23
but this is a rare treatment in veterinary medicine. In order to use
β-lactam antibiotics to treat these infections, high doses are
required because of a poorly penetrated blood-brain barrier. Even
in the face of inﬂammation, the brain/blood concentration ratio of
these drugs is low. Water-soluble AMDs are excreted in active
form by the liver and concentrated in bile, such as tetracyclines,
aminopenicillins, and cephalosporins; therefore, they are
acceptable choices for susceptible hepatobiliary infections (see
Chapter 126). Lower urinary tract infections can be successfully
treated with drugs such as amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate,
cephalosporins, and trimethoprim-sulfonamides, because these

vetexamprep.ir

agents are highly concentrated in the urine of animals with
healthy kidneys (see Chapter 127).

Other Host Factors
Other host factors that should be considered in AMD selection
and route of administration include the following:
1. History of adverse drug reactions. These are most
commonly gastrointestinal in dogs and cats, but may
include hypersensitivity reactions. Examples include
trimethoprim-sulfonamides and penicillins.
2. Age. The administration of systemic tetracyclines is
contraindicated in young animals because of the potential
for teeth discoloration (see Fig. 10.5). Doxycycline is less
likely to produce this reaction if administered for a short
course. Fluoroquinolones have the potential to cause
cartilage and joint toxicity in dogs aged between 7 and 28
weeks. 24 , 25
3. Species. Dogs and cats diﬀer in their susceptibility to
adverse drug reactions. For example, dogs can develop
severe cutaneous reactions to 5-ﬂucytosine. Dogs are the
species most susceptible to adverse reactions to
sulfonamides (see #4 below). Cats are susceptible to acute
retinal degeneration following treatment with enroﬂoxacin
doses above 5 mg/kg. Cats also are prone to esophageal
ulceration from oral doxycycline hyclate or clindamycin
hydrochloride. To avoid this eﬀect, these drugs can be
administered with a bolus of water or food to ensure
passage of the medication into the stomach.
4. Sulfonamides. Dogs are the species most susceptible to
reactions from sulfonamides (including trimethoprimsulfonamides) because of an inability to acetylate the
parent drug for elimination. Subsequently, some breeds of
dog convert the drug to a cytotoxic metabolite that
produces hypersensitivity-like reactions following
trimethoprim-sulfonamide administration. Doberman
pinschers may be at higher risk for this problem.
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye) is also a risk when
administering sulfonamides to dogs.
5. Gastric acidity. The absorption of some AMDs, such as
ketoconazole and itraconazole, is impaired by medications
that suppress gastric acid production.

vetexamprep.ir

6. Concurrent medications. Drug interactions, such as
concurrent use of drugs that require metabolism using
cytochrome P450 enzymes, can aﬀect the choice or dose of
AMD used. For example, chloramphenicol and
ketoconazole are well-known P450 enzyme inhibitors,
whereas rifampin is an enzyme inducer. Fluoroquinolone
and tetracycline antibiotics can chelate with divalent and
trivalent cations, which inhibits oral absorption. Therefore,
administration of these drugs with supplements
containing aluminum, iron, magnesium, or calcium can
diminish oral absorption.
7. Pregnancy. Penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides,
and macrolides are generally considered safe during
pregnancy. The volume of distribution in pregnancy is
greater, and so higher doses may be required to achieve
equivalent serum concentrations. On the other hand, azole
antifungals, griseofulvin, and trimethoprim-sulfonamides
carry risks during pregnancy.
8. Renal and hepatic function. The dose of AMDs that are
dependent on renal elimination may require reduction in
these animals with impaired renal function in order to
minimize toxicity. For example, ﬂuoroquinolones may be
more likely to cause seizures or retinal toxicity in animals
with kidney disease. The use of nephrotoxic drugs such as
amphotericin B or aminoglycosides may be more likely to
worsen kidney injury (and should be avoided) in animals
with kidney disease. 26 Adverse eﬀects may be more
common when drugs that require hepatic metabolism,
such as azole antifungals, metronidazole, rifampin,
sulfonamides, or chloramphenicol, are administered to
animals with impaired liver function.

Route of Administration
The most common routes of administration for AMDs in dogs and
cats are topical, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, and
oral. For localized infections of the skin, eye, or ear canal, topical
administration has the advantage of delivering a high
concentration of the AMD to the site, which may overcome
bacterial resistance mechanisms and minimize systemic exposure

vetexamprep.ir

to the drug. Parenteral administration, especially intravenous
administration, provides maximum bioavailability when there
may be questions regarding oral absorption or when oral
medications must be avoided. This route is recommended for: (1)
treatment
of
life-threatening
infections,
(2)
systemic
administration of antimicrobials with poor oral bioavailability
(such as aminoglycosides and some injectable β-lactam
antibiotics), and (3) when gastrointestinal signs or malabsorption
preclude eﬀective drug administration via the oral route. Because
parenteral AMDs are generally administered in hospital,
compliance with this mode of administration is also likely to be
greater. Absorption may be delayed after subcutaneous or
intramuscular administration when perfusion of these tissues is
impaired; therefore, these routes are avoided unless the patient is
well hydrated and tissues are well perfused. Peak plasma drug
concentrations are achieved immediately after intravenous bolus
administration. Therefore, bolus administration is an optimum
approach for a concentration-dependent antimicrobial provided
rapid injection does not produce toxicity (such as may occur with
ﬂuoroquinolones). For a time-dependent drug such as a β-lactam,
a slow infusion, or a constant rate infusion (CRI) optimizes the
time-dependent activity and can improve the outcomes in animals
with severe infection.
Provided gastrointestinal function is healthy, administration of
many oral AMDs results in acceptable bioavailability. For drugs
that have oral absorption less than 100%, the low absorption is
accounted for in the adjustment of the dosage regimen. However,
it should be remembered that when oral absorption is low, more
active drug remains in the intestine and may alter the intestinal
bacterial population. Drugs with the highest oral bioavailability in
dogs and cats are the ﬂuoroquinolones; β-lactams have low and
variable bioavailability depending on the drug. Nevertheless, once
the animal can tolerate oral medications and its clinical condition
becomes stable, a switch can be made from parenteral to oral
antimicrobials. Peak plasma concentrations are always lower with
oral administration than with intravenous administration, but for
time-dependent drugs or for drugs that achieve eﬃcacy on the
basis of an AUC/MIC exposure relationship, this route is
acceptable for a cure. Early switch from intravenous to oral
therapy in human patients has gained increased favor in recent

vetexamprep.ir

years because of reduced lengths of hospitalization, lowered costs,
fewer intravascular catheter-related infections, and decreased
selective pressure on nosocomial bacterial infections. 27–29 The oral
bioavailability of some drugs can be maximized if they are
administered with food (e.g., clavulanic acid-amoxicillin) or
without food (e.g., azithromycin, tetracyclines). Some drugs are
simply not absorbed orally and must be administered parenterally
or by the topical route. These drugs include penicillin G,
piperacillin, aminoglycosides, many cephalosporins (cefazolin,
cefotaxime, cefoxitin), meropenem, imipenem, and vancomycin.
Some drugs are not absorbed orally unless administered as a
prodrug. An example is cefpodoxime proxetil. The proxetil
portion of the molecule is cleaved oﬀ at the time of intestinal
absorption to allow for adequate systemic concentrations. 30

Antimicrobial Resistance
Infectious agents may be intrinsically resistant to an AMD, or
acquire resistance through genetic variations. Intrinsic resistance
refers to the innate ability of an organism to resist the eﬀects of an
AMD owing to structural or functional characteristics of that
organism. For example, enterococci are intrinsically resistant to
cephalosporins because they lack the PBPs that bind these
antibiotics. 31 Anaerobic bacteria are intrinsically resistant to
aminoglycosides because oxygen is required for entry of the drug
to the bacteria. Bacteria of the Enterobacterales (for example E. coli
and Enterobacter) are intrinsically resistant to macrolide
antibiotics. Mycoplasmas have intrinsic resistance to penicillins
because they lack a cell wall. A list of Intrinsic Resistance is
available in Appendix B of the CLSI VET01 document 32 and
laboratories may use this information to avoid testing some drugbacteria combinations.
Bacterial resistance should not be deﬁned by whether they are
wild-type or non-wild-type bacteria. Wild-type strains of bacteria are
those that have an absence of acquired and mutational resistance
mechanisms. Non-wild-type strains of bacteria are those that have
the presence of an acquired or mutational resistance mechanism
to the drug in question. Wild-type strains may include bacteria
that have inherent resistance to antimicrobials as described above.
However, clinical resistance, as deﬁned below, is a measure of the

vetexamprep.ir

bacteria to respond to clinically achievable drug concentrations.
Wild-type
bacteria
can
be
clinically
resistant
(e.g.,
Enterobacterales are resistant to aminopenicillins), and non-wildtype bacteria can be susceptible to some antibacterial agents.

FIG. 8.3

Genetic mechanisms of resistance in

bacteria.
The deﬁnition of resistance (or clinical resistance) used by CLSI
relies on PK-PD cutoﬀ targets, MIC distributions (wild-type
cutoﬀ), and clinical response (clinical cutoﬀ). If suﬃcient drug
concentrations can be achieved to a ain a clinical cure—even in
some cases when the bacteria are non-wild-type—the bacteria can
be considered “susceptible.” On the other hand, if drug
concentrations after a standard dose cannot meet the PK-PD
target deﬁned for that drug-bug combination, the bacteria are
reported as “resistant.” In other words, the pathogen is
considered resistant when standard dosage regimens cannot reach
the PK-PD target of a particular Cmax, AUC, or time above MIC.
Genetic resistance to an AMD may occur as a result of point
mutations, DNA rearrangements, or acquisition of foreign DNA.
Point mutations can result in alteration of the target site of an

vetexamprep.ir

AMD, such as the susceptibility of bacterial DNA gyrase to
ﬂuoroquinolones. 33 DNA rearrangements may include
inversions, deletions, duplications, insertions, or transpositions
(including chromosome to plasmid) of large segments of DNA.
The single most important mechanism of antibacterial resistance
is acquisition of foreign DNA by horizontal transfer, especially
that carried by plasmids and transposons. 34 Plasmids are circular,
double-stranded DNA molecules that are capable of independent
replication and can be transferred from one bacterial strain or
species to another through the process of bacterial conjugation.
Transposons are small, mobile segments of DNA that are ﬂanked
by inverted repeats and encode one or more resistance genes (Fig.
8.3). They depend on the chromosome or plasmids for replication.
Plasmid-associated genes that confer AMD resistance are
frequently on transposons and can move from the plasmid to the
bacterial chromosome. A single plasmid may contain resistance
genes for more than ﬁve diﬀerent AMDs and represents an
important mechanism for rapid spread of resistance genes among
bacterial populations, including from one bacterial species to
another.

Mechanisms of Antimicrobial Resistance
Antimicrobial Inactivation
Bacterial enzymes capable of inactivation of AMDs include βlactamase enzymes, enzymes that modify aminoglycoside
structure, chloramphenicol acetyltransferase, and macrolide
(erythromycin) esterase. β-lactamase production is ubiquitous
among Staphylococcus spp., and these enzymes hydrolyze
penicillins and aminopenicillins, but not cephalosporins. βlactamases are the most important mechanism of resistance to βlactam antibiotics among gram-negative bacteria. 34 A vast array
of β-lactamase enzymes have been discovered, which have been
extensively classiﬁed into groups. 35 , 36 ESBLs can hydrolyze not
only penicillins and ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins, but also
extended-spectrum cephalosporins such as cefotaxime and
ceftazidime (which contain an oximino group). To date, ESBLs
have only been described in gram-negative bacilli and are most
commonly produced by E. coli and K. pneumoniae. Some, but not
all, ESBLs can be inhibited by β-lactamase inhibitors such as

vetexamprep.ir

clavulanic acid. The ESBL with the most importance at the present
time for small animals are the CTX-M β-lactamases, which
hydrolyze cefotaxime and other third-generation cephalosporins.
Other types of β-lactamase enzymes include AmpC β-lactamases,
which are encoded by chromosomal genes, and metallo-βlactamases. 34 , 37 These types of β-lactamase enzymes are resistant
to clavulanic acid. The most recent and alarming development has
been the discovery of metallo-β-lactamases that can inactivate
carbapenems such as meropenem and imipenem. These
carbapenemases render the bacteria resistant to practically all
available antibiotics.
Membrane Alteration
Protein channels called porins facilitate the passage of hydrophilic
AMDs into gram-negative bacteria. Acquisition of porin
mutations can result in conformational changes of or reduced
expression of porins. The result is exclusion of AMDs such as βlactams and ﬂuoroquinolones. 38
Efflux Pump Induction
Expression of eﬄux pumps by bacteria allows them to exclude
certain AMDs. This is a major mechanism of resistance to
tetracyclines in gram-negative bacteria. A variety of eﬄux pumps
have been described. 39 Eﬄux pumps may not be speciﬁc for one
particular class of antimicrobial; in other words, one MDR
bacterial species can “pump” out diﬀerent classes of drugs.
Therefore, these have been termed “multidrug” eﬄux pumps and
mediate multidrug resistance. The acquisition of MDR
mechanisms greatly reduces the eﬀective options for therapy.
MDR organisms such as P. aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii
can utilize multidrug eﬄux pumps in concert with a variety of
other resistance mechanisms, including β-lactamase enzyme
production, drug target alterations, and AMD modiﬁcation
enzymes.
Target Modification
Methylation of ribosomal targets by bacterial methyltransferases
can lead to resistance to tetracyclines, lincosamides,
aminoglycosides, and especially macrolide antibiotics. Expression

vetexamprep.ir

of altered PBPs is an important mechanism of resistance to βlactam antimicrobials. Expression of PBP2a by staphylococci,
which is encoded by the mecA gene, confers resistance to all βlactam antimicrobials, including β-lactamase-resistant penicillins
such as methicillin and oxacillin (methicillin-resistant
staphylococci). Mutations of DNA gyrase can confer resistance to
ﬂuoroquinolones. 34 Resistance to trimethoprim-sulfonamides can
result from altered dihydropteroate synthetase and dihydrofolate
reductase enzymes. 40
Target Protection
Target protection 41 is another mechanism of conferring resistance
that serves a similar purpose as target modiﬁcation. Target
protection mechanisms are best known for tetracycline antibiotics;
they can confer resistance to chloramphenicol and related drugs,
oxazolidinones, ﬂuoroquinolones, and others. In target protection,
the target is not modiﬁed; instead, a target protection protein
binds to the target to prevent the antibiotic from inhibiting the
target mechanism.

Novel Approaches to Antimicrobial Drug
Resistance
With rapid spread of MDR bacterial pathogens, alternatives to
antibiotics have been investigated. 42 One approach is
bacteriophage therapy. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect
bacteria, and because of their speciﬁcity for certain bacterial
species, they can deliver targets to one type of organism without
harming others. 43 , 44 Bacteriophage infections may result in
bacterial lysis, or delivery of a gene to the bacterial cell that
increases its susceptibility to a given class of AMD. 42
Bacteriophage treatment may also be more successful than AMD
treatment in the presence of bioﬁlms, which impair antibiotic
penetration. Barriers to implementation of phage therapy include
the host immune response to the phage, bacterial resistance
mechanisms, and uncertainties relating to dosing and the impact
of other unidentiﬁed genes that might be present in
bacteriophages. Other approaches that are under investigation
include use of bacterial lysins, cationic antimicrobial peptides,

vetexamprep.ir

antisense antibiotics, and antibacterial antibodies. 42 Bacterial
lysins are derived from bacteriophages and are active only on
gram-positive bacteria. Cationic antimicrobial peptides are
derived from eukaryotic cells, have immunomodulatory
properties, and rapidly kill a variety of bacteria. 45 Although it is
diﬃcult for bacteria to develop resistance to these peptides,
multiple resistance mechanisms have been described. Antisense
antibiotics are oligonucleotides that bind to the DNA of
pathogenic microorganisms and inhibit gene expression. 46

Antimicrobial Drug Combinations
When an infectious agent is suspected but has not yet been
identiﬁed, the use of AMD combinations is tempting because of
the added broad spectrum of coverage that they provide.
However, use of AMD combinations does not necessarily reduce
the chance of selection for a resistant organism, adds expense, and
may predispose to drug toxicity. Theoretically, drug combinations
may have additive, synergistic, or antagonistic eﬀects (Fig. 8.4).
These properties are not as well established in clinical situations.
For example, antagonism between a bacteriostatic antibiotic (e.g.,
tetracycline) and a bactericidal antibiotic that requires bacterial
growth for eﬃcacy (e.g., a β-lactam) is also theoretically possible,
but there is only one clinical example of this occurrence,
published in the 1950s. 47 Such antagonism has not been
replicated since that time.

effects of antimicrobial drug combinations.
