FIG. 8.4

The use of antibiotic combinations may be justiﬁed in some
scenarios, such as:
1. Some drugs are administered in combination with other
drugs to prevent rapid development of resistance
compared with the use of a single agent. Examples are 5ﬂucytosine for antifungal treatment and rifampin in
combination with macrolides for treatment of
Mycobacterium spp. infections.
2. If a polymicrobial infection is present, combination drugs
broaden the spectrum of activity.
3. If the nature of an infection is not known and infection is
life threatening, it is reasonable to commence treatment
with a broad-spectrum combination (e.g., a
ﬂuoroquinolone and a β-lactam), based on knowledge of
the likely pathogen present and local prevalence of AMD
resistance, pending the results of culture and susceptibility
testing. Once the results of culture and susceptibility
testing are available, de-escalation should be performed.

vetexamprep.ir

4. Certain combinations of AMD are synergistic for treatment
of speciﬁc infections. For example, the combination of a βlactam and an aminoglycoside may be synergistic for
treatment of enterococcal infections, but not likely helpful
for other infections. The relatively slow bactericidal
activity of the β-lactam is enhanced by the addition of the
aminoglycoside, such that shorter durations of treatment
or extension of the dosing interval becomes possible
without aﬀecting outcome. 18 Combination therapy has
been recommended for treatment of resistant P. aeruginosa
infections, brucellosis, gastric helicobacteriosis, and some
mycobacterial infections..
5. Some drugs are not eﬀective against anaerobic bacteria
(e.g., aminoglycosides and ﬂuoroquinolones with the
exception of pradoﬂoxacin). They should be combined
with an agent active against anaerobes (e.g., clindamycin
or metronidazole) when a mixed infection with anaerobic
and aerobic bacteria is suspected.
6. When a vector-borne pathogen is suspected, doxycycline
may be administered until the results of further diagnostic
tests conﬁrm or eliminate this suspicion. In these cases,
patients are frequently administered doxycycline in
combination with another active agent to treat alternative
bacterial infections that have not yet been ruled out.

Monitoring The Response To Treatment
The response to antimicrobial treatment is best monitored based
on clinical assessment, which may include follow-up cytologic
examination or cultures. However, in some situations such as
bacterial cystitis, follow-up cultures are not recommended
because the aim of AMD therapy is clinical cure rather than
microbiological cure. Therapeutic drug monitoring can be used to
ensure adequate serum drug concentrations when treating with
aminoglycosides, vancomycin, and azole antifungal drugs, but
these assays are rarely available in commercial veterinary
diagnostic laboratories. Veterinary clinicians can check with local
laboratories (e.g., human laboratories) to locate the availability of
these assays in their area. It should be remembered that reference

vetexamprep.ir

ranges for these laboratories are established from the human use
of these drugs; veterinary therapeutic ranges are not established.

Prophylactic Antimicrobials
Prophylactic use of AMDs to prevent anticipated infections is
controversial because of the increased risk of selecting for
resistant microorganisms. In general, prophylactic AMD use is
discouraged, with the exception of perioperative AMD therapy to
prevent surgical infections when contamination is expected,
treatment of deep bite wounds, and following chemotherapy
when moderate to severe neutropenia develops (<1000
neutrophils/µL). 48 When used perioperatively to prevent surgical
infections (e.g., orthopedic surgery) the administration should be
as short as possible—rarely is there a need to extend the
administration beyond the duration of the surgical procedure. For
cancer chemotherapy prophylaxis, treatment for 3 to 7 days has
been recommended if severe neutropenia is identiﬁed. Although
more controversial, antimicrobial prophylaxis has also been
suggested following chemotherapy in patients with a high risk of
sepsis, including small breed dogs, those with hemic malignancy,
and those treated with vincristine or doxorubicin. 48 In one
prospective study, dogs administered trimethoprim-sulfadiazine
following treatment of osteosarcoma or lymphoma with
doxorubicin had signiﬁcantly reduced hospitalization rate,
nonhematologic toxicity, and gastrointestinal toxicity when
compared with dogs that did not receive prophylactic
antimicrobials. 49 Use of prophylactic antimicrobials for clean
surgeries, routine elective surgery, dental procedures (in the
absence of abscessation), and following placement of urinary
catheters is strongly discouraged.

9: Antiviral Chemotherapy and
Immunomodulatory Drugs
Katrin Hartmann, Jane E. Sykes, and Mark G. Papich

KEY POINTS
• Most antiviral drugs available for treatment of feline and canine viral
infections are nucleoside analogues with greatest activity against
retroviruses, herpesviruses, and coronaviruses.
• Antiviral drugs also affect the function of host cell machinery; therefore, they
have considerable potential for toxicity.
• Antiviral drugs are widely used in human medicine for treatment of HIV,
herpesvirus infection, and other viral infections. Much less is known about
these medications in cats and dogs, and there are only few diseases of cats
and dogs for which efficacy has been demonstrated.
• There are important differences between human and animal virus infections;
therefore, it should not be assumed that the use of an antiviral agent in
humans can be translated to a use in animals unless there is evidence of
safety and efficacy.
• The most common indication for antiviral drugs in animals is treatment of
FHV-1 infections with famciclovir and cidofovir. Zidovudine, an antiretroviral
drug, has been used to treat FIV and FeLV infections. In addition, new
antiviral drugs are now used to treat FIP.
• Antiviral drugs can act synergistically with immunomodulatory agents.
• Immunomodulators include microbial products, plant-derived
immunomodulators, naturally occurring mammalian proteins, and synthetic
drugs. The effect of many of these drugs on outcome in cats and dogs with
infectious diseases has not been fully evaluated with well-designed studies.
• The parenteral use of natural or recombinant human cytokines in cats and
dogs can produce neutralizing antibodies after 1 to 2 weeks of treatment,
which can cross-react with endogenous proteins.
• Antiviral treatments are intended to suppress viral entry, multiplication, or
transmission. Some of these antiviral agents can produce a remission or
assist the patient’s immune system to limit the course of the viral disease.

Introduction

vetexamprep.ir

This chapter describes the antiviral and immunomodulating agents used in cats
and dogs. Unfortunately, there are limited approvals of drugs for these
indications, and their use has relied on in vitro and in vivo studies, which have
produced variable success. Only those drugs currently approved in the United
States or Europe for use in animals or humans are discussed in this chapter with
few exceptions of promising experimental drugs.

Antiviral Drugs
Antiviral drug administration is still relatively uncommon in veterinary
medicine, and the number of controlled studies of the eﬃcacy of these drugs is
limited. In contrast to antibacterial, antifungal, or antiprotozoal therapy,
antiviral drugs are virustatic, that is, they do not inactivate viruses or achieve
elimination of the virus. The beneﬁt of these agents is to limit the spread of the
virus, shorten duration of clinical signs, or improve patient well-being.
Diagnosis of viral infections is often made after the viral replicative phase; thus,
antiviral drugs are commonly used to treat chronic viral infections and to
prevent reactivation of latent infections.
Antiviral drugs depend on host cell activity for their action. Subsequently,
adverse eﬀects in treated patients can be common, and many antiviral drugs
active in vitro are not commercially available for this reason. Many others can
only be given topically to avoid systemic toxicity. With the exception of feline
interferon (IFN)-ω (not available in the United States), no antiviral drugs are
speciﬁcally licensed for use in dogs and cats. Many human antiviral drugs were
developed to treat HIV infection. Some of these compounds have activity
against FIV, and sometimes FIV treatment studies were conducted to screen new
compounds before their use in HIV-infected patients. Feline herpesvirus-1
(FHV-1) infection can be treated with several topical antiviral drugs (Table 9.1)
and one promising oral compound. 1 , 2 New compounds for treatment of FIP
are promising and undergoing evaluation (see Chapter 31). 3–5
Some drugs used to treat FIP have been used investigationally or repurposed
for investigations to treat humans with COVID-19 caused by SARS-CoV-2. A list
of these agents are provided in Table 9.2. In dogs, treatment of viral infections is
mainly supportive, and antiviral drugs are rarely used.
Antiviral drugs can be assigned to diﬀerent drug classes based on the stage(s)
of virus replication they interfere with (Table 9.3). 6 , 7 Potential targets in the
retroviral replication process for antiviral drugs include binding of virus to
speciﬁc cell surface receptors, entry into the cell and uncoating of the virus,
reverse transcription of viral genome, integration of proviral DNA into host
genome, viral protein processing, virion assembly and maturation, and virion
release. 6 , 8 , 9 Combinations of antiviral drugs with diﬀerent mechanisms of
action and combinations that include immunomodulatory drugs are
increasingly used to treat human viral infections. For example, most HIV
infection protocols consist of a combination of drugs that allows for a decrease
in toxicity and reduction in selection for resistant mutants. Experience with
combination treatment in cats and dogs is limited.

Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
The retroviral enzyme reverse transcriptase transcribes viral RNA into proviral
DNA, which is subsequently integrated into the host cell’s genome. 10
Compounds that inhibit this step have become the cornerstone of successful
anti-HIV therapy. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors can be divided into three
categories: nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), nucleotide
reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NtRTIs), and non-nucleoside reverse
transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). Of these, NRTIs are the most commonly used
drugs in human medicine.
NRTIs are analogues of mammalian 2′-deoxynucleosides and inhibit the
polymerase function of the retroviral reverse transcriptase enzyme. Nucleosides
are building blocks for the formation of DNA or RNA that are composed of a
nitrogenous base and a ﬁve-carbon sugar (ribose or deoxyribose; Fig. 9.1). Like
natural nucleosides, NRTIs must ﬁrst be converted to a 5′-triphosphate form
(nucleotide) through phosphorylation. In this form, they compete with host
nucleotides and are incorporated into the elongating proviral DNA strand, thus
functioning as competitive substrate inhibitors. However, NRTIs lack a 3′hydroxyl group on the deoxyribose moiety, and this leads to strand termination
as the subsequent nucleotide cannot form the next 5′-3′ phosphodiester bond
necessary to extend the DNA strand. Latent viral infections are not aﬀected
because the replication of latent virus is suspended. However, reactivation of
these infections can be prevented or reduced in frequency. Many NTRIs have
documented in vitro activity not only against HIV but also against FIV, including
zidovudine, 11 , 12 stavudine, 12–15 didanosine, 12 , 14 and zalcitabine. 14 , 16 To
date, only zidovudine (AZT) has shown evidence of in vivo activity against
feline retroviral infections with acceptable toxicity. Fozivudine, didanosine,
stavudine, zalcitibine, lamivudine, decitabine, and gemcitabine might have
in vitro activity against FIV and FeLV, but have not been evaluated in cats, have
insuﬃcient in vivo eﬃcacy or are too toxic to administer to cats (Table 9.4).
Therefore, discussion is limited to zidovudine.

Zidovudine (AZT)
Zidovudine (3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine, AZT) is a thymidine analogue ﬁrst
synthesized in the 1960s as a potential anticancer agent. 11 In 1987, it was the ﬁrst

vetexamprep.ir

drug to be approved by the FDA for the treatment of HIV, and it remains an
important component of HIV treatment protocols. 17 , 18 Inside host cells, it is
converted to the active triphosphate form.
Zidovudine is available as a 10 mg/mL suspension and a 10 mg/mL injectable
formulation. It has good oral bioavailability in cats and high distribution in
tissues, including the CNS. It is metabolized to an inactive form by the liver and
excreted by the kidneys. Dosage reduction has been recommended for cats with
renal failure. Some cats treated with zidovudine develop dose-related
hematologic adverse eﬀects, most commonly nonregenerative anemia and
neutropenia; therefore, the CBC should be monitored during treatment. Adverse
eﬀects can be confused with retrovirus-induced cytopenias.
Zidovudine inhibits FIV replication in infected cats. It reduces plasma viral
load, improves the immunologic and clinical status of FIV-infected cats,
increases quality of life, and prolongs life expectancy. In placebo-controlled
trials, zidovudine improved stomatitis and increased the CD4:CD8 ratio in
naturally FIV-infected cats. 19–23 Viral load was signiﬁcantly lower in treated cats
after 6 months of therapy compared with pre-treatment, while untreated cats
showed a signiﬁcant increase in viral load. 23 Neurologic abnormalities can
improve with treatment, sometimes within days of therapy. 24 A decrease in
viral load was even more signiﬁcant when lamivudine was used in combination
with zidovudine. 24 Zidovudine-resistant FIV mutants can arise after only 6
months’ use as a result of a single-point mutation in the reverse transcriptase
enzyme. 25–29
Zidovudine is active against FeLV in vitro. 30–32 Activity against FeLV was also
documented in experimentally infected cats when treatment was initiated less
than 3 weeks after infection. When treated less than 1 week after experimental
infection, cats were protected from bone marrow infection and persistent
viremia. 32 , 33 In naturally infected cats, however, treatment for 6 weeks did not
lead to improvement of clinical, laboratory, immunologic, or virologic
parameters. 34 Thus, the eﬃcacy of zidovudine in FeLV-infected cats is less
promising than in FIV-infected cats. Nevertheless, improvement in stomatitis,
reduced antigenemia, and decreased incidence of lymphoma have been reported
in naturally and experimentally infected cats treated with AZT. 22 , 35

Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
NtRTIs also interact with the catalytic site of the viral reverse transcriptase and
are incorporated into the elongating proviral DNA strand, causing strand
termination. 36 , 37 They compete with the natural nucleotides and thus, also
function as competitive substrate inhibitors. However, in contrast to NRTIs,

vetexamprep.ir

NtRTIs contain a phosphate group and therefore need only two intracellular
phosphorylation steps to be converted into their active forms. 36 This
circumvents the ﬁrst and often rate-limiting phosphorylation step. 37 , 38
Compounds in this group with in vitro activity against FIV are adefovir and
tenofovir.

Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
Unlike NRTIs and NtRTIs, which bind to the catalytic site of reverse
transcriptase, NNRTIs interact with a single allosteric site of the enzyme 36 and
are not incorporated into the proviral DNA strand. 37 They do not require
intracellular activation. 9 , 37 The interaction with the allosteric site leads to
conformational changes within reverse transcriptase. 39 , 40 This causes a
decrease in the interaction between the DNA primer and the polymerase
domain of the enzyme and inhibition of virus replication. 39 , 40 Most NNRTIs
are highly speciﬁc for HIV. The only compound that has been used in veterinary
medicine is suramin.

Nucleoside Analogue DNA/RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
The nucleoside analogue DNA/RNA synthesis inhibitors act similarly to the
nucleotide analogues that inhibit reverse transcriptase, but mainly are used for
treatment of herpesvirus infections. Nucleoside analogues used in human
patients with herpesvirus infections are acyclovir and penciclovir, and their
prodrugs valacyclovir and famciclovir, respectively. These drugs are activated
by the herpesviral enzyme thymidine kinase (TK), which phosphorylates them
to a monophosphate form. Host cell enzymes then phosphorylate the drugs
further to triphosphate forms, which concentrate in virus-infected cells and
interfere with viral DNA replication by inhibition of the viral DNA polymerase
enzyme. The DNA polymerases of diﬀerent herpesviruses are inhibited to
varying degrees by each drug, and thus, not all herpesvirus infections are
equally susceptible. Drug resistance results from reduced viral TK activity,
altered TK, or altered viral DNA polymerase. The drugs cidofovir, idoxuridine,
triﬂuridine, and vidarabine are not dependent on TK for phosphorylation.
Therefore, they have greater host cell toxicity than other drugs that require
phosphorylation such as acyclovir. One of those agents regularly used in cats is
famciclovir. In small animal medicine, the drugs not depending on viral TK
have been mainly used as topical treatments for ocular FHV-1 infections (Table
9.5).
New drugs have recently been developed that have strong eﬃcacy against
coronaviruses, including feline coronavirus (FCoV). The nucleoside analogue
GS-441524 is the prodrug of remdesivir and thus closely related to remdesivir,
the antiviral drug used to treat COVID-19. GS-441524 has recently been
evaluated for treatment of FIP, and shows promise, but it is not yet
commercially available. 3 , 5 Ultimately remdesivir may also prove to be an
eﬀective treatment for FIP, and more widely available than GS-441524.
Acyclovir

vetexamprep.ir

Acyclovir (acycloguanosine, 9-[2-hydroxyethoxymethyl]guanine) is a synthetic
nucleoside analogue that is widely used to treat a variety of herpesvirus
infections. It interferes with actively replicating herpesviruses, but not when in a
latent stage. Acyclovir is given parenterally, orally, and topically in humans to
treat mucocutaneous and genital herpesvirus infections caused by herpes
simplex virus (HSV), varicella-zoster virus (e.g., shingles), and parenterally to
treat herpesvirus encephalitis. Resistance of human herpesviruses to acyclovir
occurs. Among the nucleoside analogues, acyclovir exhibits a particular
selectivity for herpesvirus over host DNA polymerases because it is only
activated in virus-infected cells, and the viral DNA polymerase is 10-fold more
sensitive to the activated drug than the host enzyme.
In cats, acyclovir has been used systemically or topically to treat ocular FHV-1
infections. Oral administration of 50 mg/kg acyclovir to cats results in low peak
plasma concentrations due to poor bioavailability. 41 Systemic administration
can cause bone marrow toxicity. 41 When given in higher doses, the parent drug
can precipitate in the renal tubules, causing obstructive nephropathy if diuresis
is inadequate. In these cases, needle-shaped acyclovir crystals can be detected in
the urine sediment. Urinalysis should be performed regularly in long-term
acyclovir treatment. Renal failure is reversible with adequate rehydration.
Table 9.5

CBC, complete blood (cell) count; PO, by mouth.

Acyclovir is about 1000-fold less active against FHV-1 in vitro than against
HSV, and is signiﬁcantly less active against FHV-1 than other antiherpesviral
drugs. 42–44 The main reason for poor eﬃcacy against FHV-1 versus HSV is
reduced phosphorylation by FHV-1 TK; the activity of this enzyme is markedly
lower in FHV-1 than in HSV. 45 It has been suggested that acyclovir could be
combined with human IFN-α or feline IFN-ω in cats because these drugs might
have synergistic activity with acyclovir, as demonstrated in vitro. 46 Application
of acyclovir as 0.5% ophthalmic ointment q5h in cats with ocular disease
a ributable to FHV-1 led to resolution of clinical signs after 10 days in a
nonmasked, nonplacebo-controlled study. 47 However, in cats treated q8h, it
took approximately twice as long. Therefore, frequent application (q4h) is
necessary, and this, combined with its low activity against FHV-1, limits its use.
Valacyclovir

vetexamprep.ir

Valacyclovir (2-[(2-amino-1,6-dihydro-6-oxo-9H-purin-9-yl) methoxy]ethyl Lvalinate hydrochloride) is a prodrug of acyclovir. It is the L-valine ester of
acyclovir and has the same antiviral spectrum but a threefold to ﬁvefold increase
in oral bioavailability when compared with acyclovir. In humans, it is mainly
used for treatment of herpes zoster, treatment of genital herpesvirus infection,
and cytomegalovirus prophylaxis in kidney transplant recipients. In humans, it
is rapidly absorbed orally and hydrolyzed to acyclovir and L-valine. Although
plasma concentrations of acyclovir exceeding the IC50 for FHV-1 can be achieved
after oral administration of this drug to cats, cats under treatment have
developed renal tubular epithelial and hepatocellular necrosis, and severe bone
marrow suppression. 48 Thus, valacyclovir should not be administered to cats.
Ganciclovir
Ganciclovir (2-amino-9-{[(1,3-dihydroxypropan-2-yl)oxy]methyl}-6,9-dihydro3H-purin-6-one) is used to treat human herpesvirus infections. 49 Ganciclovir is a
nucleoside analogue of 2′-deoxyguanosine and is phosphorylated to a
deoxyguanosine triphosphate analogue, which is the active form. Ganciclovir
resembles acyclovir except that it has an additional hydroxymethyl group on its
acyclic side chain (see Fig. 9.1). In humans, ganciclovir is widely used to treat
cytomegalovirus
infections,
which
can
be
life
threatening
in
immunocompromised individuals. Systemic administration of ganciclovir to
humans is associated with a high incidence of adverse reactions, especially
cytopenias and CNS signs; therefore, the use of ganciclovir is limited to humans
with life-threatening or sight-threatening infections. It is available for oral or
intravenous administration in humans, but is associated with more severe
neurologic toxicity, neutropenia, and bacterial infections than is acyclovir. 50 , 51
Additionally, an intravitreal sustained-release ganciclovir implant has been
developed for treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis in humans, 52 and a 0.15%
ophthalmic gel is commercially available for treatment of acute human herpetic
keratitis. 53 A prodrug form with improved oral bioavailability (valganciclovir)
also has been developed. 54 Ganciclovir is approximately 10-fold more active
against FHV-1 in vitro than acyclovir. 42 , 43 , 55 Anecdotal reports of its topical
administration to cats in Europe are very promising. However, safety, eﬃcacy,
and pharmacokinetics of ganciclovir or valganciclovir have not been reported in
cats.
Penciclovir
Penciclovir
(2-amino-9-[4-hydroxy-3-(hydroxymethyl)butyl]-6,9-dihydro-3Hpurin-6-one) is a nucleoside deoxyguanosine analogue with a similar
mechanism of action to acyclovir. Like acyclovir, it requires viral and cellular
phosphorylation. However, it is present at much higher concentrations and for
longer duration in cells than is acyclovir, which permits less frequent dosing.
Penciclovir is absorbed poorly when given orally, and it is used mainly as a
topical treatment (e.g., against HSV in herpes labialis). In a rabbit model of
human HSV-1 keratitis, a 3% penciclovir ointment administered one, two, or
four times daily decreased the severity of epithelial keratitis. Thus, a topical
ophthalmic penciclovir ointment might be eﬀective in cats with FHV-1 ocular

vetexamprep.ir

disease, but there are no commercially available preparations available for
56
ophthalmic
use.
While
2-amino-9-(3-acetoxymethyl-4isopropoxycarbonyloxybut-1-yl)- purine was not successful as an oral prodrug
for penciclovir, 57 famciclovir is an eﬀective prodrug of penciclovir with good
oral bioavailability.
Whereas acyclovir showed very poor ability to inhibit FHV-1 replication
in vitro, penciclovir and cidofovir were nearly equally highly eﬀective. When the
FHV-1 inoculation dose was raised, penciclovir was more active than cidofovir.
58 , 59 An implantable cylindrical device made from penciclovir-impregnated
silicone for long-term, steady-state delivery of this drug suppressed primary
infection of FHV-1 in a cell culture system. 60 Penciclovir-resistant mutants of
FHV-1 with altered TK have been described. 59
Famciclovir
Famciclovir is a prodrug of penciclovir with improved oral bioavailability. In
humans with HSV infections and herpes zoster, famciclovir is as eﬀective as
acyclovir. In cats, penciclovir (and thus famciclovir) are much more potent
inhibitors of FHV-1 replication than acyclovir.
In humans, famciclovir is well absorbed orally and rapidly metabolized to
penciclovir. 61 This requires di-deacetylation to BRL42359 in blood, liver, or
small intestine, with oxidation to penciclovir by hepatic aldehyde oxidase. 62–64
Most drug is eliminated unchanged in urine. In humans, concurrent food
administration decreases peak plasma concentrations without aﬀecting
bioavailability. Neither famciclovir nor BRL42359 are active against FHV-1, 65 so
metabolism to penciclovir is required. However, hepatic aldehyde oxidase
activity in cats is minimal. 66 Famciclovir pharmacokinetics in the cat are
complex and nonlinear (i.e., doubling of famciclovir dose does not lead to
doubling of plasma penciclovir concentration), presumably due to saturation of
the hepatic oxidase. 67 , 68 High plasma concentrations of BRL42359 accumulate,
67 but clinical responses occur in cats with both acute and chronic clinical signs
of FHV-1 infection with negligible adverse eﬀects. 69 , 70 Responses typically
occur within a week of treatment. However, a single dose of famciclovir (125 or
500mg) administered to cats at shelter intake was not eﬃcacious in reducing
clinical signs when 40% of the cats were already shedding FHV-1. 71
There is controversy about the optimum famciclovir dose in cats. Doses used
have ranged from 8 mg/kg q24h 70 to 140 mg/kg q8h. 72 , 73 In a masked, placebocontrolled trial, cats experimentally infected with FHV-1 and administered
famciclovir at 90 mg/kg q8h PO achieved a peak plasma penciclovir
concentration of 2100 ng/mL. 69 Compared with control cats, treated cats had
reduced clinical signs, serum globulin concentrations, histologic evidence of
conjunctivitis, viral shedding and serum FHV-1 titers, as well as increased
conjunctival goblet cell density. 69 However, administration of one dose of 40
mg/kg PO to healthy cats achieved nearly identical plasma penciclovir
concentrations to those achieved with a dose of 90 mg/kg. 74 Naturally infected
client-owned cats with spontaneous disease administered famciclovir at 40
mg/kg q8h had tear penciclovir concentrations likely to be eﬀective against
FHV-1 for at least 3 hours after a dose of 40 mg/kg q8h. 73 Based on a study of

vetexamprep.ir

healthy cats treated with famciclovir at 30, 40, or 90 mg/kg q12h or q8h, it was
recommended that cats receive a dose of 90 mg/kg q12h because this regimen
achieved comparable plasma and tear penciclovir concentrations to those
achieved with 90 mg/kg q8h. 67 Furthermore, when famciclovir was
administered to 59 client-owned cats, the median duration of therapy required
for clinical improvement was signiﬁcantly longer in cats administered 40 mg/kg
(33 cats) than in cats treated with 90 mg/kg (26 cats). 72 Costs of care were
estimated to be lower in the cats treated with the higher dose due to reduction in
treatment duration, and potentially the number of recheck examinations
required. Adverse events, which were mostly minor gastrointestinal signs, were
reported in 17% of cats receiving 40 or 90 mg/kg q8h, with no diﬀerence between
the two doses. 72 Although famciclovir is safer than acyclovir, cats administered
famciclovir should be closely monitored, and assessment of the CBC and serum
biochemistry panel should be considered in cats with known concurrent disease
or cats expected to receive famciclovir for long periods. As in humans, 75
reduction in dose frequency should be considered in cats with renal disease. 67 ,
72 Human famciclovir tablets are commonly too large for some cats and can be
diﬃcult to administer. Some veterinary compounding pharmacies have
prepared oral formulations of compounded famciclovir for cats. However,
testing of these formulations showed poor quality, inconsistency, and failure to
show that the concentrations in these compounded forms were as stated on the
label. These products made by veterinary compounding pharmacies failed to
meet the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) (www.usp.org) compendial
standards for compounded products and thus, cannot be recommended for cats.
Instead, veterinarians are encouraged to use a pharmacy that adheres to the USP
standard or modify the human-approved tablets.
Cidofovir
Cidofovir is a nucleotide analogue of deoxycytidine monophosphate. Thus,
cidofovir already contains a monophosphate group, 76 and its metabolism to the
active diphosphate form by host cellular enzymes is not dependent on viral TK.
Therefore, it can be used to treat acyclovir- and famciclovir-resistant infections.
Its safety arises from its relatively high aﬃnity for viral DNA polymerase
compared with human DNA polymerase. 77 In human patients, cidofovir is also
used to treat cytomegalovirus retinitis. Cidofovir has extremely low (<5%) oral
bioavailability, so it has to be administered intravenously, intravitreally, or
topically. Cidofovir has a prolonged intracellular half-life, which enables
infrequent parenteral dosing regimens in human patients (weekly, and then
every other week for maintenance). Cidofovir applied q12h as a 0.5% or 1.0%
ophthalmic solution in rabbit models of human herpetic keratoconjunctivitis
was as eﬀective as triﬂuridine q3–6h. 56 , 78 This makes it the topical treatment of
choice for ocular FHV-1 infections. Local irritation and scarring of the
nasolacrimal duct has been reported with topical administration in humans and
rabbits with keratoconjunctivitis, 79 , 80 so treated cats should be monitored for
nasolacrimal cicatrization. Cidofovir 0.5% retains eﬃcacy when compounded
with saline and refrigerated (4°C) or frozen (–20°C or –80°C) in plastic or glass
for up to 6 months. 81 Cidofovir is highly active against FHV-1 in vitro. 42 , 43 It

vetexamprep.ir

was also eﬀective in a feline whole corneal explant model supporting FHV-1
replication. 82 In cats with experimental FHV-1 infection, cidofovir
administration was associated with a signiﬁcant improvement in clinical scores
and ocular virus shedding when compared with placebo. 83
Cidofovir also has in vitro activity against canine herpesvirus-1 (CHV-1). 84
Cidofovir was used to treat dendritic ulcerative keratitis in a 4-year-old dog
associated with CHV-1 infection based on positive PCR results and rising serum
antibody titers. 85 In dogs with experimentally induced ocular CHV-1 infection,
application of topical 0.5% cidofovir ophthalmic solution q12h reduced duration
of viral shedding, but caused ocular irritation leading to higher ocular disease
scores and higher conjunctival and corneal leukocyte inﬁltration scores. 84
Idoxuridine and Trifluridine
Idoxuridine and triﬂuridine are halogenated thymidine analogues that are
phosphorylated by cellular enzymes to active triphosphate forms, which act as
pyrimidine antagonists. Both drugs cause myelosuppression when given
systemically, and so are only applied topically. 86 , 87 They are used in humans to
treat HSV keratitis and dermatitis. When not commercially available, topical
idoxuridine can be obtained from a compounding pharmacy as a 0.1%
ophthalmic solution. Triﬂuridine is available as a 1% ophthalmic solution.
Frequent application of both of these drugs is required (q4–6h). Local
application is generally well tolerated, but prolonged use can cause corneal
irritation or ulceration. 88 Triﬂuridine has be er corneal penetration than
idoxuridine, 89 but is more likely to cause ocular irritation in cats than
idoxuridine. 90
Idoxuridine and triﬂuridine are active against FHV-1 in vitro, 43 , 55 although
both are more active against HSV. 43 , 55 In cats with ocular disease a ributed to
FHV-1, 0.1% idoxuridine solution was used q4–6h with improvement of clinical
signs in three cats and no improvement or worsening in four cats. 87 Treatment
with 1% triﬂuridine solution q4–8h was associated with improvement in one cat
and no improvement or worsening in two cats. 87
Corneal ulcerations associated with a naturally occurring CHV-1 infection
appeared to respond to topical idoxuridine or triﬂuridine treatment. 91 Frequent
topical ocular application of 1% triﬂuridine ophthalmic solution was well
tolerated by dogs with experimentally induced recurrent ocular canine CHV-1
infection and reduced disease scores and viral shedding duration. 92
Vidarabine
Vidarabine (9-β-D-arabinofuranosyladenine monohydrate, adenine arabinoside)
is a purine nucleoside that is phosphorylated by host cellular enzymes to
vidarabine triphosphate. It was originally developed as a cancer
chemotherapeutic. Vidarabine triphosphate disrupts DNA synthesis by
interfering with DNA polymerase. It has activity against herpesviruses,
poxviruses, and retroviruses, as well as idoxuridine-resistant herpesvirus
strains. In humans, it is used to treat smallpox and HSV keratitis, dermatitis, and
encephalitis. 93 Systemic toxicity has restricted its use in veterinary practice to
topical treatment as a 3% ophthalmic ointment. Local application in cats is well

vetexamprep.ir

tolerated, but frequent application (q4–6h) is necessary. 90 Where not available
commercially, it can be obtained from a compounding pharmacist. 2
Vidarabine is active against FHV-1 in vitro 55 and has been used topically in
ocular FHV-1 infections, although cidofovir has largely replaced its use because
it can be applied less frequently. In a retrospective study of cats with ocular
disease a ributed to FHV-1, treatment with vidarabine was associated with
improvement in one cat and no improvement or worsening in two cats. 87
Vidarabine also has in vitro activity against FCoV, 94 but studies have not been
performed to demonstrate eﬃcacy in cats with FIP.
GS-441524
Treatment with the nucleoside analogue GS-441524, which is the prodrug of the
COVID-19 antiviral drug remdesivir, reversed disease in 10 research cats when
given subcutaneously once daily for 2 weeks. 3 Two of these cats required a
second course of treatment, but were disease-free 8 months later. In a ﬁeld
study, 31 naturally infected cats without neurological or ocular FIP were treated
with GS-441524 (2 mg/kg q24h SC, increasing to 4 mg/kg q24h SC). 5 Five of the
cats died or were euthanized within 26 days of starting treatment. The
remaining 26 cats received the full 12 weeks of treatment, and of these, 8 had
relapses in 3 to 84 days, and the remaining 18 were healthy at the time of
publication. In some of the cats that relapsed, remissions were obtained with
another course of treatment, and ultimately, at the time of publication, 25 cats
remained healthy. The time of diagnosis to the time of publication was 18 to 22
months. With increased availability of remdesivir following the COVID-19
pandemic, remdesivir might have the potential to be useful for treatment of FIP
although it is less potent than GS-441524.

Nucleotide Synthesis Inhibitors
There are two types of nucleotide synthesis inhibitors: (1) pyrophosphate
analogues that directly inhibit DNA and RNA polymerase (e.g., foscarnet) and
(2) inhibitors of triphosphate synthesis that inhibit inosine monophosphate
dehydrogenase, an essential enzyme for synthesis of nucleotides (e.g., ribavirin).
Nucleotide synthesis inhibitors usually have a broad antiviral spectrum but also
marked toxicity.
Foscarnet
Foscarnet (phosphonoformic acid, PFA) has in vitro activity against FIV, FeLV,
and FHV-1. 95 , 96 However, its short half-life, poor oral absorption, and adverse
eﬀects have limited its use in cats. No in vivo studies in cats with virus infections
have been published.
Ribavirin
Ribavirin (1-β-D-ribofuranosyl-1 H-1,2,4-triazole-3-carboxamide, RTCA) is active
against a signiﬁcant number of feline and canine viruses in vitro, including FIV,
FeLV, FHV-1, FCV, FCoV, Borna disease virus (BDV), as well as CDV and canine
parainﬂuenza virus. 97–99 However, its clinical usefulness is limited because of its
systemic toxicity, and it is not used in veterinary medicine. It is also no longer

vetexamprep.ir

recommended for treatment in humans. Still, ribavirin might have the potential
to be a promising drug for treating dogs with CDV. Further studies are required
for understanding pharmacokinetics and toxicity of ribavirin in dogs.

Protease Inhibitors
Protease inhibitors are widely used to treat HIV infection and hepatitis C in
humans. They prevent viral replication by selectively binding to viral proteases
and blocking proteolytic cleavage of protein precursors needed for the
production of infectious viral particles. Protease inhibitors currently on the
market are highly selective for HIV and are not active against FIV. However,
experimentally designed protease inhibitors had activity against FIV or FIV/HIV
chimeras. 100–102 In addition, commercially available protease inhibitors, such as
nelﬁnavir, have been evaluated for their activity against FCoV, and new
protease inhibitors with potential activity against FCoV have been engineered.
103 The use of nelﬁnavir was also reported in a few cats with FIP in the ﬁeld, 104 ,
105 but toxicity and pharmacokinetics of nelﬁnavir in cats and its eﬃcacy for
treatment of FIP in controlled studies remains unknown.

GS376
Inhibitors that target 3C-like protease with broad-spectrum activity against
important human and animal coronaviruses have recently been created. 106 One
protease inhibitor (GS376) was shown to have activity against FCoV in vitro 107
and was eﬀective to treat FIP in an experimental se ing, but is not yet
commercially available. Prolonged remissions were documented in some
naturally infected cats. In one ﬁeld study, 6 of 20 cats were in remission 18
months after 12 weeks of treatment, administered subcutaneously twice a day. 4
One of the challenges was treatment of neurologic FIP, likely because of failure
of drug penetration of the CNS. Further ﬁeld studies with this drug are
required, and the compound is not yet commercially available.

Receptor Blockers
Receptor blockers belong to a group of antiviral drugs known as entry inhibitors,
which also include fusion inhibitors. Receptor blockers are either homologs or
antagonists of cellular viral receptors or co-receptors. If receptor blockers bind to
the virus or to the cellular receptor, they inhibit a achment of the virus to the
cell surface. Most receptor blockers on the market or under development are
highly selective for HIV and not useful for veterinary medicine. One exception
are bicyclams (e.g., plerixafor), because of the similarity between HIV and FIV in
regards to chemokine receptor usage. 108–112 Plerixafor (1,1’-(1,4phenylenbismethylene)-bis(1,4,8,11-tetraazacyclotetradecane)-octachlo-ride
dehydrate, AMD3100) is the prototype bicyclam drug. It is used in humans for
stem cell mobilization. 113 Plerixafor is active against FIV in vitro. 114 In naturally
FIV-infected cats in a placebo-controlled double-blind clinical trial, treatment
with plerixafor resulted in a signiﬁcant decrease in provirus load, but also a
decrease in serum magnesium levels, which however was not clinically relevant.

vetexamprep.ir

115 It has been administered to cats at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg q12h. Magnesium and

calcium levels should be monitored during treatment. 115

Integrase Inhibitors
The retroviral enzyme integrase catalyzes strand transfer (3′-end joining), which
inserts both proviral DNA ends into a host cell chromosome. The high degree of
conservation of integrase active sites for many retroviruses suggests that FIV
and FeLV could be sensitive to integrase inhibitors. 116
Raltegravir
In human patients, raltegravir is approved for treatment of HIV infections and is
used in combination with other antiretroviral drugs. Raltegravir is highly active
in vitro against FeLV. 116 , 117 Concentrations in the eﬀective range were not toxic
to cell monolayers. However, raltegravir is partly eliminated as glucuronide.
Some (but not all) glucuronide pathways are deﬁcient in cats. This might
increase the risk of toxicity in cats. 113 The eﬃcacy and safety of raltegravir in a
noncontrolled study of seven cats with experimentally induced progressive
FeLV infection was investigated. 118 Raltegravir was administered at 40 mg q12h
PO for 6.5 weeks and then 80 mg q12h PO for 2.5 weeks. The treatment reduced
viremia in each cat, with up to 1 log10 reduction in viral RNA in four of seven
cats, and the drug a ained therapeutic plasma concentrations at both doses,
with no adverse eﬀects noted. However, viremia rebounded in all cats following
drug removal. Raltegravir also had activity against FHV-1 in cell culture as well
as in a feline whole corneal explant model. 82

Nucleocapsid Inhibitors
Nucleocapsid inhibitors interact with viral assembly and disassembly through
NCp7 zinc ﬁnger-targeted agents. 119 Such zinc ﬁnger inhibitors or zinc ejectors
are compounds that interact adversely with zinc and cause them to release their
zinc from its binding site, disrupting the conformation of the polypeptide chain
and rendering the zinc ﬁngers ineﬀective, thereby preventing them from
performing their associated cellular functions. Zinc ﬁngers are involved in
mRNA regulation, reverse transcription, protection of synthesized viral DNA,
transcription inhibition, and initial integration processes. Nucleocapsid
inhibitors are used to treat HIV, but many other human viruses, such as Ebola
virus, measles virus, and polio virus, have similar zinc ﬁnger motifs and could
potentially beneﬁt from zinc ﬁnger inhibitor technology. Several novel
nucleocapsid
inhibitors,
such
as
fused
tetrathiocines,
bis[1,2]dithiolo[1,4]thiazines and bis[1,2]dithiolopyrrole derivatives, and 5thieno-, 5-oxo-, and 5-imino-1,2,3-dithiazole derivatives, have been synthesized
and evaluated for activity against FIV. These new compounds display potent
nanomolar activity and low toxicity against FIV in vitro, 61 , 120 , 121 but they are
not yet available.

Neuraminidase Inhibitors

vetexamprep.ir

Neuraminidase inhibitors prevent release of virus from the host cell. They
inhibit virus replication by binding the viral enzyme neuraminidase, a viral
surface glycoprotein. Oseltamivir is the only agent from this class that has been
used in cats and dogs.
Oseltamivir
Oseltamivir, ethyl (3R,4R,5S)-5-amino-4-acetamido-3-(pentan-3-yloxy)-cyclohex1-ene-1-carboxylate, is the prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylate, a potent inhibitor
of inﬂuenza virus neuraminidase (Fig. 9.2). Oseltamivir is active against viruses
that have neuraminidase in their envelope, including inﬂuenza viruses,
parainﬂuenza viruses, and paramyxoviruses, and is used in the treatment and
prophylaxis of inﬂuenza virus A and inﬂuenza virus B infections in humans.
The viral neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues on the surface of infected
cells, which allows new virus particles to be released from host cells. It also
prevents aggregation of virus particles after they are released and facilitates
spread of virus through the mucus of the respiratory tract by cleaving sialic acid
residues in mucin.
Oseltamivir was the ﬁrst orally active neuraminidase inhibitor to be
commercially developed. It is a prodrug, which is hydrolyzed in the liver to an
active metabolite, the free carboxylate of oseltamivir. A lipophilic side chain of
the active drug binds to the viral neuraminidase, blocking its ability to cleave
sialic acid residues, resulting in an inability of cells to release progeny virions. In
humans and dogs, oseltamivir has high oral bioavailability. 122 Oseltamivir is
used early in the course of human inﬂuenza to shorten the duration of illness by
approximately 20 hours.

vetexamprep.ir

Structure of an influenza virus. The M2 protein,
which is only present in influenza A viruses, is inhibited by
tricyclic amines such as amantadine. Oseltamivir inhibits the

FIG. 9.2

Oseltamivir has been used to treat canine parvovirus enteritis in puppies,
with anecdotal reports of improved outcome. Although it does not have activity
against CPV, and CPV does not possess a neuraminidase, it was used in a
prospective, randomized, masked, placebo-controlled trial of 35 dogs with CPVinduced enteritis. Dogs treated with oseltamivir (2 mg/kg PO q12h) had no
signiﬁcant drop in their white blood cell count, whereas untreated dogs had
white blood cell count decrease in the ﬁrst 5 days of hospitalization. 123 Treated
dogs also gained weight during hospitalization, whereas untreated dogs lost
weight. However, there was no diﬀerence in hospitalization time, treatments
needed, clinical scores, morbidity, or mortality between the two groups, and the
number of dogs in each group was small. As CPV has no neuraminidase, it was
hypothesized that oseltamivir instead might act on the neuraminidases of
bacteria that are normally responsible for secondary bacterial infections in CPV
enteritis, which are primarily those of the gastrointestinal tract. The role of
bacterial neuraminidases in the pathogenesis of enteric bacterial infections and
bacterial translocation is unknown. Bacterial neuraminidase enzymes might
play a role in bioﬁlm formation and help bacteria to invade mucin layers of the
respiratory tract. 123 , 124 It has been suggested that gut bacteria might use
neuraminidase to cleave sialic acid residues on gastrointestinal epithelial cells,
which exposes receptor sites for bacterial adherence.

Ion Channel Blockers
The uncoating of viruses can be blocked by ion channel blockers that bind to
viral proteins, such as inﬂuenza A virus M2 proteins, which normally function

vetexamprep.ir

as ion channels for proton inﬂux into the virus. Blocking the M2 protein leads to
a pH change that inhibits viral fusion and internalization of the virus by
endocytosis. Cycloalkylamine derivatives are used for this purpose in human
medicine, mainly against inﬂuenza virus infections. Amantadine is the most
important example of a cycloalkylamine derivative, and the only one that has
been used in veterinary medicine. Related drugs include rimantadine, which has
equal or greater eﬃcacy to amantadine with reduced CNS adverse eﬀects but
more gastrointestinal irritation, and tromantadine, which is used topically to
treat human herpesvirus infection. New experimental compounds that inhibit
viroporins, viral proteins with ion channel activity that are possessed by several
viruses, including FCoV, have been investigated in vitro, 125 but are not
commercially available.
Amantadine
Amantadine
(tricyclo[3,3,1,13,7]dec-l-ylamine
hydrochloride,
Ladamantanamine) is a stable cyclic amine with activity against enveloped RNA
viruses. Amantadine was once applied as prophylaxis of human inﬂuenza, but it
is rarely used for this indication currently because there are newer more potent
agents available. As a dopaminergic drug, amantadine has been used to treat
Parkinson’s disease, cocaine dependence, and apathy in multiple sclerosis. It has
also been also used in cats and dogs to treat neuropathic pain and osteoarthritis.
126 Data on the usefulness of amantadine in dogs and cats as an antiviral drug
are limited. Amantadine was active against BDV in vitro in one study, 127 but in a
diﬀerent study, there was no in vitro activity in concentrations that were
eﬀective against inﬂuenza virus. 128 Anecdotal reports of successful outcomes
following amantadine treatment exist in cats with BDV infection in northern
Europe.

Antiviral Amino Acids
Amino acids and peptides can act as antivirals when they competitively inhibit
translation and virus assembly.
L-Lysine
Initial interest in L-lysine arose from in vitro data and clinical trials in humans.
129 Arginine is essential for FHV-1 130 and HSV 131 replication, and it has been
suggested that lysine antagonizes the availability or utilization of arginine by
these viruses during protein synthesis. Protein fraction-I of the histone layer
around the DNA of the eukaryotic or host cells is 28% L-lysine and 3% to 4%
arginine. In contrast, the capsid protein composition of herpesviruses has
approximately three times more arginine than lysine. 132 Thus, it was originally
hypothesized to preferentially aﬀect protein synthesis of the virus over that of
the host because viral proteins had a higher arginine-to-lysine content than did
human (and feline) proteins 132 ; however, recent analyses suggested that the
diﬀerence in feline and FHV-1 protein amino acid content is minimal. 133 Both
an excess arginine and an absence of arginine interferes with the replication of
HSV in vitro. 134 , 135 Excess L-lysine in the media has the same eﬀect, likely by
acting as an analogue of arginine, or by competing for cellular transport

vetexamprep.ir

mechanisms, or both. 131 , 136 Markedly elevated L-lysine concentrations in
combination with low arginine concentrations suppressed HSV-1 131 , 135 and
FHV-1 130 replication in vitro. However, this did not occur with physiologic
amino acid concentrations. 137 In a more recent study, various L-lysine
concentrations did not inhibit in vitro replication of FHV-1 at arginine
concentrations suﬃcient to maintain cell growth. 137 Thus, data on in vitro
activity of L-lysine are controversial.
L-lysine is inexpensive and well tolerated in cats, with only mild and
reversible gastrointestinal disturbances reported for some cats. 138 No adverse
eﬀects were seen in cats fed diets supplemented to up to 8.6% (dry ma er) with
L-lysine. 139 However, in vivo data regarding the eﬃcacy of L-lysine in cats with
FHV-1 infection are also contradictory. Although L-lysine is promoted by
sponsors of dietary supplements for cats (which are not FDA regulated), the
clinical results have not shown a beneﬁt in naturally occurring infections. A
recent meta-analysis, published by two biologists who owned cats with chronic
FHV-1 infection presented multiple levels of evidence that L-lysine
supplementation is not eﬀective for the prevention or treatment of FHV-1
infection in cats. 133 Lysine does not antagonize arginine in cats, and evidence
that low intracellular arginine concentrations would inhibit viral replication is
lacking. Furthermore, lowering arginine levels is undesirable since cats cannot
synthesize this amino acid themselves, and arginine deﬁciency might result in
hyperammonemia, which could be fatal. Contradictory to this meta-analysis,
administration of 500 mg L-lysine PO q12h beginning 6 hours before inoculation
of cats with FHV-1 was associated with less severe conjunctivitis without a
change in virus shedding when compared with placebo. 138 The eﬀects of Llysine administration on clinical signs and ocular shedding of FHV-1 were
studied after reactivation of latent infection. Treated cats had fewer viral
shedding episodes after stress of rehousing compared with the control group
cats. Fewer cats and eyes had conjunctivitis, and onset of clinical signs of
infection was delayed in cats receiving L-lysine. 140 In cats latently infected
following experimental inoculation but without clinical signs at the time of the
study, oral administration of 400 mg L-lysine q24h reduced viral shedding
compared with placebo-treated cats. 140 However, in the only study to assess
bolus administration of L-lysine in naturally infected cats, 144 shelter-housed
cats received 250 mg (ki ens) or 500 mg (adult cats) L-lysine q24h for their entire
shelter stay. Outcomes were compared with an untreated control group. No
signiﬁcant treatment eﬀect was detected for any parameter. 141 There was
concern that the stress of tablet administration actually contributed to disease in
these cats. Dietary supplementation with L-lysine also appears to have no
beneﬁcial impact on upper respiratory tract disease in shelters. 141–143 In fact, cats
that received a supplemented diet had more severe disease and more frequent
viral shedding than cats that received a nonsupplemented diet, despite a
detectable increase in plasma lysine concentrations. 143 The supplemented diet
did not aﬀect plasma arginine concentration; therefore, altered arginine levels
did not contribute to increased disease severity. 2 Thus, L-lysine has not
demonstrated clear beneﬁt in naturally occurring infections.

vetexamprep.ir

Immunostimulant Drugs
“Immunomodulator” is a nonspeciﬁc term that has also been referred to as
biologic response modiﬁers. These drugs include agents that suppress the
immune system (e.g., glucocorticoids) and those that stimulate the immune
system. In this chapter, only drugs that stimulate the immune system are
discussed. Some of these compounds not only aﬀect the immune system but also
possess antiviral activity (e.g., IFNs). Probiotics also have immunomodulatory
activity and have been used to treat viral infections (e.g., FHV-1). 83 , 144 These
compounds are discussed in Chapter 125. Speciﬁc neutralizing antibodies
(passive immunization), such as against FHV-1, FCV, FPV, CPV, CDV, and
infectious canine hepatitis virus, have also been used for treatment of virus
infections with variable results 145–147 but are not the subject of this chapter.
Vaccines, such as intranasal vaccines, also have been used as therapeutic
immunomodulators (see Chapter 20).
Categories of immunomodulators are shown in Table 9.6. Treatment of canine
and feline viral infections with immunostimulating drugs has commonly
produced disappointing results. Data from large, prospective, controlled clinical
trials are lacking, and many are used infrequently or are not widely available
(Table 9.7). Because of this, only those currently in use that appear to have some
clinical beneﬁt are discussed in detail. Doses of immunostimulants evaluated in
dogs and cats are shown in Table 9.8.

Naturally Occurring Cytokines
Interferons
Interferons are polypeptide molecules that mediate antiviral and antigrowth
responses and modulate the immune response. 148 A number of diﬀerent
interferons have been identiﬁed that are subdivided into type I, type II, and type
III interferons. 149 IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-ω, and IFN-γ have been used in veterinary
medicine. The ﬁrst three belong to type I IFNs, while IFN-γ is a type II IFN.
Type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β, and IFN-ω) are produced by virus-infected
cells, 88 , 150 whereas type II interferon (IFN-γ) is produced by activated T cells
and natural killer cells in response to recognition of infected cells. 151

Interferons bind to speciﬁc cell surface receptors and stimulate expression of
proteins that interfere with various stages of viral replication. 152 Viral protein
synthesis is not aﬀected, so the antiviral activity of interferons is thought to be
related to interference with later stages of viral replication, such as virion
assembly and release. 150 , 153 Interferons also trigger virus-infected cells to
undergo apoptosis. 151 , 153 Thus, interferons prevent the spread of virus from
infected cells and aid in the clearance of viral infection. 151 Recombinant
interferons that are commercially available, mostly used in cats and dogs, are
human IFN-α and feline IFN-ω. IFN-γ plays a critical role in the clearance of
intracellular pathogens by macrophages. Recombinant human IFN-γ has been

vetexamprep.ir

used to treat chronic granulomatous disease caused by intracellular bacteria and
fungi in humans, but few studies have been performed in cats and dogs. Lowdose feline IFN-γ and interleukin (IL)-12, experimentally prepared by a method
known as Sequential Kinetic Activated, have been used in cats experimentally
infected with FHV-1 with some success. 154 Recombinant adenoviruses
engineered to contain IFN-γ genes had antiviral activity against CPV.155
Human Interferon-α
Naturally occurring IFN-α represents a group of more than 20 molecules that
vary slightly in composition. They inhibit viral nucleic acid and protein
synthesis. A variety of recombinant and natural human IFN-α preparations are
available, including pegylated forms that have prolonged half-lives. IFN-α is
active against many DNA and RNA viruses. 152 There are two common
treatment regimens for use of IFN-α in cats, SC injection of high-dose (104 to 106
IU/kg q24h) IFN-α or oral application of low-dose (1 to 50 IU/kg q24h) IFN-α.
When given parenterally to cats, human IFN-α becomes ineﬀective after 3 to 7
weeks because of development of neutralizing antibodies. 33 IFN-α can be given
orally for a longer period, as no antibodies will develop during oral treatment.
Given orally, IFN-α is inactivated by gastric acid and destroyed by trypsin and
other proteolytic enzymes in the duodenum. 156 Therefore, immunomodulatory
activity is thought to result from stimulation of oropharyngeal lymphoid tissue,
which leads to cytokine release and a cascade of immunologic responses that
ultimately act systemically. 157 , 158
IFN-α is active against FIV in vitro. 159 Although it is sometimes used for
treatment of FIV-infected cats, no controlled studies that evaluated the eﬀect of
high-dose parenteral human IFN-α in FIV-infected cats have been conducted.
Use of low-dose oral human IFN-α in sick cats with natural FIV infections (50
IU/kg on the oral mucosa q24h for 7 days on alternating weeks for 6 months,
followed by a 2-month break, and then repetition of the 6-month treatment)
resulted in improvement of clinical signs in a placebo-controlled double-blind
study. 160
In vitro, FeLV replication is inhibited by human IFN-α. 161 Treatment of cats
that had persistently high FeLV antigenemia with high-dose SC human IFN-α
following experimental infection resulted in decreases in circulating FeLV
antigen beginning 2 weeks after initiation of therapy. 33 However, because of
anti-IFN-α antibody development, cats became refractory to therapy after
several weeks. 33 In a placebo-controlled double-blind study in naturally FeLVinfected cats, a similar high-dose treatment regimen with human IFN-α (1 × 105
IU/kg SC q24h for 6 weeks) did not lead to improvement of clinical, laboratory,
immunologic, or virologic parameters. 34 Low-dose oral IFN-α was used in a
placebo-controlled study in experimentally induced FeLV infection. 157 Eight
cats were treated with 0.5 IU/cat and ﬁve were treated with 5 IU/cat on 7
consecutive days on alternate weeks for a period of 1 month after challenge.
There was no diﬀerence in development of viremia between groups, but treated
cats had fewer clinical signs and longer survival times than the placebo group
(with a be er response in the cats given 0.5 IU). Uncontrolled ﬁeld studies have
reported apparent responses in a limited number of cats treated with low-dose

vetexamprep.ir

oral IFN-α. 162 , 163 Signiﬁcantly longer survival times were reported in 69
clinically aﬀected cats treated with low-dose oral IFN-α (30 IU/kg for 7
consecutive days on a 1-week-on 1-week-oﬀ schedule) when compared with
historical controls. 163 However, in a placebo-controlled study, treatment of sick
client-owned FeLV-infected cats with the same protocol did not result in a
signiﬁcant diﬀerence in FeLV status, survival time, clinical or hematologic
parameters, or subjective improvement in the owners’ impression when
compared with a placebo group. 164 Improvement in clinical signs and
laboratory abnormalities in FeLV-infected cats were noted with low-dose oral
IFN-α in other studies, 165 , 166 but concern was raised about evidence of a
rebound eﬀect after treatment was discontinued. These studies lacked a control
group.
In vitro studies with dosages of 1 × 105 to 5 × 105 IU/mL of IFN-α showed
reduced FHV-1 concentration and FHV-1-induced cytopathic eﬀects without
observable cytotoxicity to a feline corneal cell line 167 or Crandell-Rees feline
kidney (CRFK) cells. 168 Administration of 108 IU/kg IFN-α SC q12h for 2 days
(beginning a day before challenge) to 12 ki ens experimentally infected with
FHV-1 led to reduction of clinical signs over a 14-day period when compared
with placebo. 169 FCV replication is also inhibited when cell cultures are treated
with IFN-α. 170 When IFN-α was given SC (105 IU/kg q24h for 14 days) to seven
shelter cats with chronic upper respiratory tract disease that tested positive for
FHV-1 or FCV by PCR, there was some improvement of clinical signs, 171 but
further studies are needed to evaluate this approach in a larger cat population.
IFN-α also has been administered orally to FHV-1 infected cats, but no
controlled studies have been performed. 87 In cats with ocular disease, topical
IFN-α q4-6h for 1 week beyond clinical resolution has been recommended. In
cats with naturally occurring viral keratoconjunctivitis, ocular administration of
high doses of IFN-α q12h for 14 days did not improve clinical disease or virus
shedding when compared with saline. 172 With availability of famciclovir,
topical IFN-α is used less frequently, or it is being used in combination with
other drugs, based on observations of in vitro synergistic activity against FHV-1
or HSV-1 when combined with acyclovir. 46 , 173 Investigations of the eﬃcacy of
nucleoside analogues in combination with IFN-α in cats are warranted.

The antiviral activity of IFN-α against a FIP-causing FCoV strain was
demonstrated in vitro. 174 A combination of IFN-α with ribavirin resulted in
antiviral eﬀects that were greater than the sum of the eﬀects from either
ribavirin or IFN-α alone, 174 but the combination was not eﬀective in vivo. In one
study, 74 cats (52 treated, 22 controls) with experimentally induced FIP received
IFN-α, Cutibacterium acnes, a combination, or placebo. Prophylactic and
therapeutic administration of high-dose (104 or 106 IU/kg) IFN-α did not reduce
mortality in treated cats, but the mean survival time in cats treated with 106
IU/kg IFN-α with C. acnes was signiﬁcantly prolonged for 3 weeks. 175
IFN-α inhibits replication of CDV in vitro, with or without ribavirin, 176 but no
in vivo studies have been published. IFN-α has been used to treat dogs with viral
papillomatosis, but controlled studies are lacking. 177 In humans with
papillomatosis, IFN-α has been used at 106 IU/person parenterally until
regression occurred. A similar treatment regimen, intralesional injection or oral
low-dose treatment, might be eﬀective in dogs.
Feline Interferon-ω
Recombinant feline interferon-ω (IFN-ω) is licensed for use in cats and dogs in
Europe, Asia, and Australia. It is not available in the United States. It has been
used for treatment of viral infections in cats and dogs as well as for treatment of
some tumors (e.g., feline mammary tumors) 178 and canine atopic dermatitis. 179
In healthy dogs, IFN-ω enhances the activities of whole blood cells,
macrophages, and natural killer cells. 180 IFN-ω is produced in silkworms using
a recombinant baculovirus. It can be used in cats for long periods without

vetexamprep.ir

antibody development. 150 In FIV and FeLV infection, a dose of 106 IU/kg SC
q24h on 5 consecutive days is suggested. No severe adverse eﬀects have been
reported in cats, 181 but transient lethargy, fever, vomiting, mild diarrhea, and
anorexia have been documented in some treated cats, especially at higher doses
(2.5 × 106 U/kg). Mild neutropenia, eosinophilia, and reversible increases of
serum AST activity have also been described. 182 IFN-ω inhibits the replication
of FIV, 159 FeLV, 183 FCoV, 184 FHV-1 and FCV, 167 , 168 , 170 FPV and CPV, 184 and
CDV 185 in vitro.
When used in a placebo-controlled multicenter trial to treat 62 naturally FIVinfected cats (106 IU/kg SC q24h on 5 consecutive days), there were no changes
in survival in treated cats when compared with a placebo group, although some
clinical improvement was noted. 181 In naturally FIV-infected cats housed in a
shelter, clinical improvement was observed, but there was no control group
included. Oral administration of a lower dose of IFN-ω (105 U/cat PO q24h for
90 days) to clinically aﬀected, naturally FIV-infected cats was associated with
improvement of clinical scores. 186 The improvement was not diﬀerent from that
observed in a historical control group treated with 106 IU/kg SC IFN-ω, which
suggested that PO administration of the lower dose of IFN-ω could be used as
an alternative to the licensed protocol at reduced cost. In a follow-up study of
naturally FIV-infected cats treated either with PO or SC IFN-ω, there was no
change in viremia and most cytokine concentrations measured, 187 which raised
questions about the eﬃcacy noted in the previous trials that lacked placebotreated controls. It is possible that the clinical improvement observed resulted
from an eﬀect of IFN-ω on secondary infections rather than on the FIV infection
itself. 150 Indeed, 16 naturally FIV- and/or FeLV-infected cats that were followed
for 65 days during IFN-ω treatment had reduced excretion of co-infecting
viruses (FCV, FHV-1, FCoV, and FPV). 88 Additional randomized, placebocontrolled, and double-blind studies are required to fully determine the eﬃcacy
of IFN-ω for treatment of FIV infections.
In one study, 48 cats with naturally occurring FeLV infection were treated
with IFN-ω (106 IU/kg SC q24h SQ for 5 days). This treatment was applied three
times, separated by several treatment-free weeks. There was a signiﬁcant
diﬀerence in the survival time of treated versus placebo-treated cats in a 9month follow-up period, but not after 1 year. 181 Some clinical improvement was
noted with IFN-ω treatment of FeLV-infected cats housed in a shelter, but no
placebo group was included. 88 No studies have been published on the use of
PO low-dose IFN-ω in FeLV-infected cats.
In an uncontrolled study, 12 cats that were suspected to have FIP were treated
with IFN-ω in combination with glucocorticoids and supportive care. 188
Although most cats died, four cats with abdominal eﬀusion survived 2 years,
suggesting that treatment of cats with IFN-ω might increase survival time. In a
randomized double-blind treatment trial, 34 cats with FIP were treated with
glucocorticoids in conjunction with placebo or IFN-ω (106 IU/kg SC q48h until
clinical improvement, then once weekly). 189 In all cats, FIP was conﬁrmed by
histology and/or immunohistochemical or immunoﬂuorescent staining of FCoV
antigen in eﬀusion or tissue macrophages. Some cats in both groups survived
for weeks to months (longest survival 200 days). There was, however, no

vetexamprep.ir

signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the mean survival time or quality of life of cats treated
with IFN-ω when compared with placebo. 189
At higher concentrations, the eﬀect of IFN-ω on FHV-1 replication appears to
be greater than that of IFN-α. 168 However, when used topically to treat
experimentally infected cats with conjunctivitis, IFN-α had higher eﬃcacy than
IFN-ω, and cats treated with IFN-ω even had a worsened conjunctivitis score. 190
In cats with naturally occurring viral keratoconjunctivitis, ocular administration
of IFN-ω q12h for 14 days did not improve clinical disease or virus shedding
compared with treatment with saline solution. 172 In a noncontrolled ﬁeld study,
cats with suspected acute FCV infection showed improvement in clinical signs
(e.g., upper respiratory tract disease or stomatitis) following treatment with IFNω (2.5 × 106 IU/kg IV q48h, 3 times). 191 However, in a placebo-controlled study,
treatment with IFN-ω was not eﬀective in ameliorating clinical signs. 192 In a
prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial, 37 cats
with acute FCV- and/or FHV-1-induced clinical signs were treated with IFN-ω
(2.5× 106/kg SC once, followed by 0.5× 106 topically on the conjunctiva,
intranasally, and orally q8h for 21 days). Treatment with IFN-ω was not eﬀective
in ameliorating clinical signs when compared with placebo, but accelerated a
reduction in FCV load in infected cats. 192 Local injection of IFN-ω into oral
lesions in cats with chronic gingivostomatitis, some of which were infected with
FCV, was followed by some improvement, but the cats were also treated with
other drugs and dental procedures, and a control group was not included. 193 In
a controlled study, oromucosal administration of IFN-ω to cats with FCVassociated chronic gingivostomatitis had the same eﬃcacy as glucocorticoid
treatment, suggesting that IFN-ω might be an alternative to glucocorticoids. 194
In conclusion, data do not support the use of IFN-ω for treatment of FHV-1
infection, but there might be some eﬃcacy for treatment of FCV infections,
especially in cats with chronic gingivostomatitis.
In a case series that included ﬁve cats with cowpox virus pneumonia, two cats
survived, both of which were treated with IFN-ω. 195 However, controlled
studies are lacking.
When used to treat beagle puppies that were experimentally infected with
CPV, the number of dogs that developed clinical signs did not diﬀer
signiﬁcantly between the treated dogs and the placebo groups, but clinical signs
were less severe in dogs treated with IFN-ω. 196 In one double-blind trial, 10
beagle puppies with experimentally induced CPV disease were randomized to
two groups of ﬁve dogs each. Four days after challenge, one group was treated
with saline and the other with IFN-ω (2.5 × 106 IU/kg IV q24h for 3 consecutive
days). All ﬁve dogs in the placebo group died within 10 days. In the treated
group, one animal died on day 2 after treatment was started, whereas the other
four dogs recovered. 197 In a randomized, double-blind, multicenter ﬁeld study
in France, 92 dogs aged 1 to 28 months were treated with either IFN-ω (2.5 × 106
IU/kg IV q24h for 3 consecutive days) or placebo. Clinical signs in treated
animals improved signiﬁcantly in comparison with control animals, and in the
IFN-ω group, 3 dogs died compared with 14 in the placebo group. 198 In a
similar ﬁeld study in Japan, mortality was also reduced in the dogs treated with
IFN-ω (14/72) when compared with the control group (13/21). 199 These data

vetexamprep.ir

suggest that IFN-ω improves clinical signs and reduces mortality due to CPV.
There are no controlled studies of the use of IFN-ω to treat cats with
panleukopenia. IFN-ω was not eﬀective in preventing panleukopenia in cats
after entering a ca ery. 200
Lymphocyte T-cell Immunomodulator
Lymphocyte T-cell immunomodulator (LTCI) is a protein derived from thymus
epithelial cells. According to the product brochure, LTCI upregulates IL-2
production in vitro and regulates CD4 T-cell function. It was also reported to
stimulate platelet production in mice with chemotherapy-induced
thrombocytopenia. LTCI has been conditionally approved in the United States as
an aid for treatment of FIV and FeLV infections, and for the associated signs of
cytopenias and opportunistic infections, but controlled independent studies of
the eﬃcacy of LTCI in cats are required.

Naturally Occurring Biologic Response Modifiers
Lactoferrin
Commercial lactoferrin is a mammalian iron-binding glycoprotein of bovine
origin with immunomodulatory properties. Lactoferrin is produced by the
mucosal epithelial cells of all mammals and is present in secretions, especially in
milk. It has been used for its local immunomodulatory eﬀect in the oral cavity,
and it has been shown to increase cellular phagocytic activity. 201 It binds iron,
reducing its availability for bacteria, and thus has not only antibacterial but also
antifungal, antiprotozoal, and antiviral activity, and its antitumor activity has
also been investigated. 202 Lactoferrin inhibits inﬂuenza virus hemagglutination
and cell infection. 203 A protective eﬀect of lactoferrin during lethal bacteremia
has been reported in mice. 204 Long-term oral administration of bovine
lactoferrin to a dog with β2-integrin-related neutrophil dysfunction was
associated with increased neutrophil function and recovery from opportunistic
infections. 205 Lactoferrin was also administered long term to two canine
li ermates with familial neutrophil dysfunction and improved their clinical
signs. 206 Adverse eﬀects have not been reported.
Topical application of lactoferrin (40 mg/kg q24h for 14 days) to the mouth of
a small number of FIV-infected and noninfected cats with stomatitis was
associated with improved appetite and reduced oral inﬂammation, salivation,
and pain, and increased neutrophil phagocytic activity. 201 Treatment with
lactoferrin might also have the potential to improve functions of overactivated
lymphocytes by modulating the cell proliferation, cell cycle, and cytokine
expression in cats in the terminal stage of FIV infection. 207 Lactoferrin has
antiviral activity against FHV-1, CHV-1, and FCV in vitro. 208–210 No in vivo data
are available so far in cats infected with FHV-1. Lactoferrin appeared to reduce
the clinical signs in cats with chronic gingivostomatitis in one study, but it is
unknown whether the cats were infected with FCV. 211 One cat with stomatitis
and FCV infection was treated with lactoferrin powder (200 mg) that was
applied directly to lesions for 22 months. Clinical signs began to resolve after 11
months, and resolution of clinical signs coincided with the cessation of FCV

vetexamprep.ir

shedding. 212 However, the cat also received other medications, and because
spontaneous resolution of this condition can occur, further studies are necessary.
Plant-Derived Biologic Response Modifiers
A few plant-derived biologic response modiﬁers are on the market, such as
polyprenyl immunostimulant. Other plant extracts with antiviral activity have
undergone preliminary in vitro assessment, but safety or clinical eﬃcacy have
not been reported. 213 Polyprenyl immunostimulant is a plant-derived
veterinary biologic that is made of phosphorylated, linear polyisoprenols.
In vitro, it upregulates synthesis of Th1 cytokines and has antiviral and
antineoplastic properties. 214 , 215 Polyprenyl immunostimulant appeared to
have a beneﬁcial eﬀect in two cats with histologically conﬁrmed and one cat
with suspected FIP without eﬀusion. 216 One cat survived 14 months, and the
other two cats were still in clinical remission after 24 and 28 months,
respectively. In a ﬁeld study, treatment with polyprenyl immunostimulant was
evaluated in 60 cats that were suspected to have FIP by primary care and
specialist veterinarians, but FIP was not conﬁrmed. None of the cats had
eﬀusion. There was no control group. Of the 60 treated cats, 8/60 survived over
200days and of those, 4/60 survived over 300days. Veterinarians of treated cats
that survived over 30days reported improvements in clinical signs and behavior.
The survival times were signiﬁcantly longer in cats who were not treated with
corticosteroids concurrently. 217 Use of polyprenyl immunostimulant might hold
some promise for treatment of cats with FIP that have no eﬀusion, while its use
in cats with FIP with eﬀusions has been disappointing. However, controlled
studies in cats with conﬁrmed FIP would be very important.
According to the manufacturer, cats with experimentally induced FHV-1
infection had a decreased severity and duration of upper respiratory tract signs
when treated with polyprenyl immunostimulant in comparison with cats
receiving placebo, but independent controlled studies are lacking.

Synthetic Compounds
Antiparasitic and Antibacterial Compounds
Some antiparasitic compounds nonspeciﬁcally stimulate cell-mediated or
humoral immunity and thus have immunomodulatory activity. The antiparasitic
agent ivermectin has been investigated for treating human patients with SARSCoV-2 infection. Although ivermectin has theoretical potential for this use, 218
the concentrations achieved in patients with standard doses are not high enough
to produce antiviral eﬀects. 219 Some antibiotics also have immunomodulatory
properties, including the macrolides, doxycycline, and metronidazole, but there
are no prospective studies using these drugs in virus-infected cats and dogs.
Other Synthetic Compounds
Pentoxifylline and propentofylline are synthetic methylxanthines derived from
theobromine. Propentofylline is marketed in Europe as a veterinary product.
Both compounds are phosphodiesterase inhibitors with a variety of
immunomodulatory properties. In rodents and humans, they inhibit tumor
necrosis factor (TNF)-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-12 production, as well as activation of

vetexamprep.ir

T and B cells, and increase neutrophil mobility and chemotaxis. They also
increase erythrocyte cAMP levels, which results in increased erythrocyte
deformability, lowered blood viscosity, and improved microcirculation and
tissue perfusion. They decrease platelet aggregation and increase tissue
plasminogen activator in patients with hyperaggregable platelets; thus, they can
be useful for treatment of disorders that result in hypercoagulable states.
Pentoxifylline has been evaluated as a treatment for equine endotoxemia.
Despite decreases in TNF-α and IL-6 activity after incubation of equine
monocytes with pentoxifylline in vitro, these eﬀects did not occur in horses. 220
Beneﬁcial eﬀects of pentoxifylline are limited in horses when administered IV
after challenge with endotoxin. 221 In dogs, pentoxifylline has been used to treat
canine atopic dermatitis, dermatomyositis, and cutaneous vasculopathies, 222 ,
223 as well as cognitive dysfunction in geriatric dogs. 224 In dogs, pentoxifylline
has a low and unpredictable oral bioavailability and a short half-life, and q8h
administration has been recommended. Adverse eﬀects include vomiting and
inappetence, which are more likely to occur when the tablets are crushed.
Crushed tablets are also unpalatable to cats.
According to anecdotal reports, pentoxifylline has been used to treat some
cats with FIP, with apparent improvement in clinical signs and survival time.
However, when the closely related drug propentofylline was used in a doubleblind trial of 23 cats with naturally occurring FIP, there was no diﬀerence in
survival time, quality of life, amount of eﬀusion, or TNF-α concentration in cats
treated with propentofylline versus placebo. 225
