Transmission of FECV is by the fecal-oral route. Infectious
virions pass through the stomach intact, and there is evidence
from cell cultures suggesting that trypsin and possibly other
proteolytic enzymes may alter the surface spikes and play an
important role in subsequent enteric coronavirus infectivity and
cytopathicity. 73 FECV ultimately targets the mature apical
epithelium at the tips of intestinal epithelium (see Fig. 29.2).
Unlike TGEV of swine and BoCV infection of calves, which can
cause severe and often fatal enteritis, FECV infection of cats is
only a minimal pathogen and there is a weak statistical
association with diarrhea. Its clinical importance is related to its
propensity to mutate to the FIPV biotype. The comparative
importance of FECV in diarrhea has been studied in shelter cats. 74
Twelve enteric pathogens were identiﬁed, including coronavirus,
Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin A, Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia
spp., Cystoisospora spp., hookworms, ascarids, Salmonella spp.,
astrovirus, FPV, FCV, and Spirometra spp. Of fecal specimens
testing positive for one or more of these agents, FECV was the
most common. Only FCoV was signiﬁcantly (P = .03) more

vetexamprep.ir

prevalent in cats with diarrhea (58%) than cats with normal feces
(36%).
Virus is released when the apical epithelial cells undergo
natural- or virus-induced apoptosis, with spread to adjacent and
distant villi. FECV infection in 275 purebred cats from six ca eries
was studied by collection of fecal specimens for FECV RT-PCR
every 1–3 months. 65 A large proportion of these ca ery cats shed
virus at any given time, but most manifested cycles of shedding
and non-shedding. Similarly, all adult cats in an Abyssinian
ca ery shed virus in their feces at least once during the year and
4/15 cats were shedding greater than 75% of the time. 75 In a study
of the persistence and evolution of endemic FECV infection in a
closed cat-breeding facility, viral RNA was detected by RT-PCR in
the feces of 36/42 cats (86%) tested and 4/5 cats were still shedding
when tested 111 days later. 76 Two cats were then placed in strict
isolation and virus shedding lasted up to 7 months in one animal.
A viremic stage has not been conﬁrmed. In a study of 50 healthy
ki ens and cats from a shelter that had feces tested, 28 were found
to be FCoV shedders, but only two had detectable FCoV RNA in
buﬀy coat cells. 77
Experimental FECV infection studies were ﬁrst conducted on
SPF cats. 10 , 37 , 42 Clinical signs were frequently inapparent or
consisted of transient diarrhea, occasionally preceded by
vomiting. Fecal shedding, as determined by RT-PCR on rectal
swabs, appeared within as li le as 2 days 10 , 12 and was
signiﬁcantly higher in ki ens than in older cats. 42 FECV was
identiﬁed throughout the intestine through day 28, at which time
occasional virus-positive macrophages were seen in the sinuses of
reactive mesenteric lymph nodes. 12 The viral load was 10–100,000
times higher in the colon than in other sites in the intestine. FECV
shedding remained at high levels for 2–10 months before
eventually evolving into one of three excretion pa erns: 1)
persistent virus shedding at varying levels over 9–24 months; 2)
periods of virus shedding interlaced with periods of nonshedding; and 3) cessation of virus shedding after 5–19 months. 37
The colon appears to be the main site of FECV persistence. 12
Active infection is associated with the appearance and rise in
FCoV antibody titers and cessation of shedding with a marked
drop in titers. 37 Pregnancy, parturition, and lactation have no

vetexamprep.ir

inﬂuence on fecal shedding by queens, and methylprednisolone
acetate treatment does not appear to induce non-shedders to shed
and shedders to increase shedding. 37
Feline Infectious Peritonitis Virus (Feline Infectious
Peritonitis)
FIP is caused by speciﬁc mutants that occur during FECV
infection. 52 These mutant FECVs lose tropism for the intestinal
epithelium and gain tropism for monocyte/macrophages. This
drastic switch in tropism leads to an entirely diﬀerent disease,
which closely resembles other macrophage-associated diseases
such as tuberculosis, leprosy, the deep mycoses, and
leishmaniosis. The anatomic sites where mutations occur are not
clear, but one likely site is in the lymphoid tissues regional to the
primary persistent infection site in the cecum and colon. 36 In a
study of the eﬀect of FECV coinfection in FIV
immunocompromised laboratory cats, mutations capable of
causing FIP occurred in 11% of primary FECV infections. 78 Given
an incidence of around 1%, it is apparent that only about 1 in 100
FIPV mutations actually lead to FIP. FIPVs generated by internal
mutation are genetically unique to each cat and are contained
solely within infected macrophages in diseased tissues and
eﬀusions and have limited access to the outside. Therefore, cat-tocat transmission is an infrequent occurrence and when it occurs, it
presents as a self-limiting epizootic caused by the same virus.
Mutations in FECVs that lead to the switch in cell tropism occur
in at least three identical regions of the viral genome. The most
universal mutation site involves the putative fusion peptide on
the spike (S) gene and consists of a single nucleotide change at
either nucleotide 1058 or 1060. The M1058L mutation (methionine
to leucine) occurs in 91.6% of all FIPVs. The S1060A mutation
(serine to methionine) occurs in 4.3% of isolates. 79 Neither
mutation is found in FECVs. Unfortunately, 4% or more of FIPV
isolates do not have either mutation, which makes it diﬃcult to
identify their role in FIP pathogenesis. This site is most likely
involved in how FIPV and FECV enter their respective host cells.
One possibility is that subtle changes in the fusion domain
inhibits infection of intestinal epithelium through its normal

vetexamprep.ir

receptor and favors internalization of FIPV by peritoneal
macrophages through alternative Fc receptors.
The second most consistent mutation to be associated with the
FIPV biotype is in the accessory 3c gene. 52 Most FIPV isolates
have numerous mutations leading to signiﬁcant amino acid
changes in the 3′ region of the gene. 11 These mutations frequently
lead to truncation of the gene and a totally nonfunctional 3c gene
product, and are unique for each isolate. 11 , 52 , 79–82 The function
of the 3c protein is unknown. The loss of a functional 3c protein in
FIPVs appears to enhance viral replication in macrophage-like
cells. 83
A third site for FIPV mutations is in the S1/S2 cleavage region,
which is involved in two thirds of FIPV isolates. 84 The S1 protein
is cleaved from S2 in the Golgi network by the host protease furin.
Mutations at this site are again unique to each FIPV and alter the
eﬃciency of cleavage of the S protein by furin. Because the
eﬃciency of furin cleavage is increased in many FIPV isolates,
whereas in others it is decreased or unchanged, it is also diﬃcult
to ascribe a functional signiﬁcance to mutations at this region of
the FECV genome.
Bone marrow–derived monocytes are recruited into the sites of
peritoneal macrophage infection, most likely by the eﬀect of
macrophage-derived cytokines on nearby endothelial cell
adhesion proteins. The incoming monocytes evolve into M1
macrophages, again by the action of cytokines, evoking either a
protective innate and adaptive T-cell immunity and no disease, or
to a persistent infection, a ﬂamboyant cytokine storm, immunemediated inﬂammation, and disease. 24 The incubation period in
naïve cats is 14 to 21 days, which corresponds with the
appearance of ﬁrst antibodies. The epitope responsible for both
antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) and in vitro virus
neutralization is on the S protein of FIPV. 85 Complement is also
bound to virus and antibody, 86 which facilitates the uptake of
FIPV by macrophages 87 , 88 through Fc receptor binding. Immune
complex formation contributes to venulitis by evoking Arthus- or
immediate-type hypersensitivity reactions. Both neutrophils and
macrophages are involved in this reaction. 89 The resultant
vasculitis is manifested grossly by edema, hyperemia, microhemorrhage, thrombosis, and ﬁbrosis. The vasculitis associated

vetexamprep.ir

with eﬀusive FIP often leads to coagulation abnormalities
indicative of DIC. 90 However, clinical signs of DIC are
uncommon.
It has been postulated that FIP is a balance between Th1- and
Th2-mediated immunity. 24 In this scenario, non-eﬀusive FIP is
associated with a strong delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) and
weak immediate-type hypersensitivity reactions, whereas eﬀusive
FIP is a result of strong immediate hypersensitivity and weak
DTH reactions. This is reminiscent of cellular immune responses
in lepromatous compared with tuberculoid leprosy of humans.
Evidence for the role of T-cell immunity in FIP comes from
research with a coronavirus that infects mice, mouse hepatitis
virus (MHV). MHV, like FIPV, exists as two biotypes, enterotropic
and polytropic. Certain polytropic laboratory strains of MHV
cause a disease syndrome analogous to FIP of cats when they
infect IFN-γ–deﬁcient mice. 91 Infection with enterotropic MHV in
immunocompetent mice is limited to the small intestine for the
ﬁrst week and then to the cecum and colon for the next 2weeks. Bcell–deﬁcient mice exposed to enterotropic MHV develop chronic
subclinical infection restricted to the GI tract that lasts for 7–
8weeks. In contrast, T-cell–deﬁcient mice infected with the same
enterotropic MHV develop a multi-systemic, lethal, FIP-like
disease. These mouse studies indicate that the FIPV mutations are
preventing the T-cell immune responses normally associated with
FECVs.

Clinical Signs
FIP tends to occur in two distinct forms with transitions often
occurring between them. The classic wet, eﬀusive, or nonparenchymatous form of FIP is a diﬀuse peritonitis associated
with a large outpouring of inﬂammatory ﬂuid from diseased
venules on serosal surfaces, mesenteries, and omentum. Similar
disease may also involve the thorax. Non-eﬀusive (“dry”) FIP is
manifested by more focal and organized granulomatous lesions in
organs such as the mesentericlymph nodes, cecum, colon, kidney,
lungs, pericardium, eyes, brain, and spinal cord, and
miscellaneous sites. Disease signs may evolve over weeks,
months, and rarely a year or more. Wet FIP has been likened to
the lepromatous form of human leprosy.

vetexamprep.ir

The dry, non-eﬀusive, or parenchymatous form of FIP has been
compared to the tuberculoid form of human leprosy. Dry FIP
frequently begins as a brief episode of apparent or inapparent
eﬀusive disease, whereas non-eﬀusive FIP can morph into eﬀusive
disease. A mixture of the two forms can also be seen at necropsy.
There is ample evidence that infection may incubate for days,
weeks, months, and rarely years before either resolving or
clinically manifesting itself. This initial infection is most likely
contained to foci of infection in organs such as the cecum, ileum,
and colon, and associated lymph nodes. Clinical signs in this
latent period may be inapparent or associated with retardation of
growth, increased susceptibility to other common pathogens, or
other vague signs of ill health. Once disease becomes apparent, it
is usually progressive and fatal. However, there are reports of cats
that make an apparent recovery, only to have clinical signs recur
months and even years later. 56 , 92
Both the non-eﬀusive and eﬀusive forms of FIP share many of
the same initial clinical signs. The earliest overt signs include a
progressively worsening lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss.
Ki ens and adolescent cats may be smaller than normal, have
poor quality coats, may be less active, and suﬀer recurrent bouts
of vague illnesses compared with siblings or cats of the same age.
A ﬂuctuating antibiotic-unresponsive fever is common with FIP
and in one study, 22% of all cats presenting with a fever were
ultimately found to have FIP. 93 Additional clinical manifestations
vary greatly depending on the form and organ distribution of the
inﬂammation. The timing of the subsequent disease course is also
variable and ultimately fatal if untreated in almost all cases.
Although the disease course for FIP is generally assumed to be a
few days or weeks, some cats with either wet or dry FIP can
survive for many weeks, months, and occasionally a year or more
with just supportive care.

The eﬀusive form of FIP is more common in ki ens but also
observed in adolescent, adult, and aged cats (Table 31.1). Eﬀusions
are observed solely in the abdomen in about 75% of cats, solely
thoracic eﬀusions in 10%–15%, and a mixture of thoracic and
abdominal eﬀusions in less than 10% of cases (see Table 31.1). 61
Abdominal eﬀusions are manifested by abdominal distention and
may be one of the ﬁrst signs of FIP noted by the owners. Intact
male cats may manifest scrotal enlargement due to inﬂammation
of testicular tunics, whereas female cats with ascites may be
considered pregnant and the disease discovered on spaying.
Tachypnea may accompany thoracic eﬀusion. Involvement of the
CNS and eyes is seen in only about 10% of ki ens with abdominal

vetexamprep.ir

and/or thoracic eﬀusions (see Table 31.1). Pericardial eﬀusions are
uncommon, either as a primary clinical manifestation or in
combination with ﬂuid accumulation in other body cavities.
About one fourth of cats with FIP have non-eﬀusive or
predominantly non-eﬀusive FIP. 61 However, this proportion
appears to be rising, either because of improved diagnosis or to an
actual increase in incidence. The dry form also predominates in
certain popular breeds such as the Birman 71 and Burmese. 69 The
non-eﬀusive form is also more apt to be subclinical 56 , 92 , 94 and
may go unnoticed until host resistance is eventually overcome,
and the disease becomes either eﬀusive or involves the CNS and
eyes. Clinical signs vary according to the organs that are involved.
For instance, a disproportionate number of cats with non-eﬀusive
FIP develop neurologic and/or ocular disease (Table 31.2). A
colonic form of the disease was ﬁrst described in 1983 (Fig. 31.2).
95 FIP colitis is manifested by chronic diarrhea associated with
mucus, fresh blood, and straining to defecate. The thickened
colon, cecum, and ileocecocolic lymph nodes are readily palpated
or visualized on abdominal ultrasound. FIP colitis has also been
diagnosed at surgery for abdominal emergencies when a colonic
pyogranuloma causes intestinal obstruction.
Neurologic disease is the sole presenting sign in about 22% of
cats with non-eﬀusive FIP, while an additional 7% is accompanied
by detectable lesions in the peritoneal cavity (see Table 31.2).
Ocular disease occurs as the sole manifestation in 14% of noneﬀusive FIP cases (see Table 31.2), while ocular disease plus CNS
or other organ involvement occurs in 10% of cases. CNS
involvement in cats with non-eﬀusive FIP is varied in its clinical
expression. Meningitis, ependymitis, and choroiditis with
extension into adjacent tissues are common lesions in cats with
brain involvement (Fig. 31.3). CNS involvement can manifest in
early stages by spontaneous muscle twitches, atypical limb
extension and swallowing motions, and brief episodes of staring.
Signs will then progress slowly or rapidly to ataxia, usually worse
in the pelvic limbs. Cerebellar-vestibular signs including
nystagmus, head tilt or circling may be present. Hydrocephalus,
secondary to disease of the choroid and ependyma, has also been
documented 96–98 and can lead to dementia, personality changes
(aggression, rage, hiding/withdrawal, etc.), or seizures.

FIP is a major contributor to inﬂammatory/infectious disease of
the spine. 99 Spinal involvement with FIP often leads to severe
posterior paresis and urinary or fecal incontinence.
Once the virus enters the CNS or eyes, it is sheltered from the
normal bloodborne immune responses. However, the infection is
still capable of stimulating a systemic immune response as a result
of lymphatic connections between the brain and cervical lymph
nodes. 100 Such stimulation may explain why serum and
CSF/aqueous antibody titers are so high in this form of FIP. This
compartmentalization of infection and immune responses can

vetexamprep.ir

lead to a scenario where virus-infected macrophages outside
protected sites are eliminated, whereas infection in sites such as
the brain and eye persist. This may also explain why many cats
with CNS disease do not have noticeable extra-abdominal lesions
(see Table 31.2).
Ocular FIP is usually manifested by a varying degree of uveitis
and/or retinitis 101 that often starts in one and then progresses to
involve both eyes (Fig. 31.4A–C). The earliest signs of anterior
uveitis may be a discoloration of the iris, aqueous ﬂare, and
keratic precipitates. Although FIP is the major cause of uveitis in
young cats, it can be confused with idiopathic uveitis. In one
study, the duration of disease tended to be shorter in cats with FIP
than in cats with idiopathic uveitis. 102 In another study of 92 cats
with uveitis from the UK, cats with FIP uveitis had the youngest
age (median 1.4 years) whereas those with neoplasia (such as
lymphoma) had the oldest age (median 12.8 years), and cats with
FIP or lymphoma were more likely to be purebred than cats with
idiopathic uveitis. 103 Microbial nucleic acids, antigens, or
antibodies against a causative agent were seldom found in the
blood/serum of cats with idiopathic uveitis, whereas serum FCoV
titers ≥ 1:6400 were detected only in cats with FIP. Aqueous
humor contained predominantly neutrophils in cats with FIP and
large reactive lymphocytes and plasma cells more frequently in
cats with idiopathic uveitis. However, neither clinical nor
cytologic assessment of anterior chamber contents reliably
diﬀerentiated idiopathic uveitis from FIP.

Retinitis is manifested by congestion of retinal blood vessels
and hemorrhage that may be associated with retinal detachment
and degeneration of the tapetum and optic disc. It can be
unilateral or bilateral. Retinitis is often a sign of brain involvement
and associated neurologic signs. Uncommon sites for
extraperitoneal and extrapleural lesions, other than the CNS and
eyes, include the oral cavity, nasal passages, testicles, and skin.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of FIP is based ﬁrst and foremost on consideration
of signalment (age, sex, and breed), environmental origin, disease
history, abnormalities on physical examination (including
eﬀusions if present), and routine CBC and serum chemistry
ﬁndings. There is sometimes enough evidence at this point to
make a presumptive diagnosis of FIP, and whether more invasive
diagnostic tests are warranted can be discussed with the owner.

vetexamprep.ir

104 The next step, if needed, is to choose tests that will either

further increase the odds that the disease signs are due to FIP
using “indirect tests” or a empt to provide a deﬁnitive diagnosis
using “direct tests.” It must be remembered that no test is 100%
sensitive and speciﬁc and that diagnostic sensitivity and
speciﬁcity is strengthened by the inclusion of other supportive
clinical ﬁndings.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count and Serum Chemistry Profile
A CBC and serum chemistry panel that includes bilirubin, total
protein, globulin, and albumin are probably the simplest and
most informative indirect tests for FIP. 56 , 61 , 105 Common CBC
abnormalities include nonregenerative anemia (anemia of
inﬂammatory disease), leukocytosis with an absolute increase in
neutrophils and a relative or absolute decrease in lymphocytes,
and eosinopenia (Table 31.3). Occasionally, mild to moderate
bandemia is present. The degree of lymphopenia is a good
indicator of disease activity and severity, especially in cats with
eﬀusive FIP, whereas cats with non-eﬀusive FIP often have low
normal to normal lymphocyte counts. 106 Monocyte counts are
variable and usually in the normal range.
An increased plasma total protein concentration is frequent in
cats with FIP, especially in cats with non-eﬀusive disease. Serum
globulin concentration is frequently high and albumin

vetexamprep.ir

concentration may be low (Table 31.4). This results in albumin-toglobulin ratios (A:G) ratios that are frequently below normal
(<0.6). 61 Although the A:G ratio has been advocated as a useful
test for FIP, the predictive value of the A:G ratio is very much
dependent on the presence of other historical, clinical/physical, or
laboratory abnormalities associated with the disease. 107
FIP is perhaps the most common cause of hyperbilirubinemia in
young cats, especially those with eﬀusive FIP. 61
Hyperbilirubinemia is usually not associated with increased liver
enzyme activity, 108 as the liver parenchyma is often spared in cats
with FIP. Rather, bilirubin is a by-product of intravascular and
extravascular destruction of RBCs by macrophages and a species
deﬁciency in glucuronidation. 109
Serum Protein Electrophoresis
Analysis of 155 serum specimens from cats with increased serum
total protein or globulin concentration found that 136 (87.7%) had
abnormal serum electrophoresis proﬁles, most commonly from a
polyclonal increase in gamma globulins (Fig. 31.5). 110 Alpha and
beta globulins are also increased in many FIP sera due to
increased production of acute-phase reactants and complement
proteins. The most common disease classiﬁcation associated with
serum protein abnormalities in the 155 feline sera was
infectious/inﬂammatory disease (80/136; 58.8%), including 39 cats
with a diagnosis of FIP. Monoclonal gammopathy was observed
in four cats, including one with FIP, one with lymphoma, and two
with splenic plasmacytoma.
Analysis of Effusions
The presence of a characteristic type of ﬂuid in the peritoneal
cavity and/or pleural cavity is one of the most diagnostic clinical
features of FIP. Classic FIP eﬀusions are usually yellow tinged
(sometimes blue green), cloudy, high in protein (near or equal to
plasma levels), and have white cell counts of 3,000 cells/µL or
greater (Table 31.5). Red cells are often present but seldom in
numbers that grossly tinge the ﬂuid. The ﬂuid color is due to the
presence of bilirubin (yellow) or biliverdin (blue green). The
deeper colored the ﬂuid, the more red cell destruction is occurring
and the more severe the inﬂammatory process. Classic FIP

vetexamprep.ir

eﬀusions are often viscous with an egg-white consistency, contain
ﬁbrin tags, and frequently form partial clots when placed in a
serum tube.
Eﬀusions from cats with more chronic and ﬁbrotic disease may
be clear or pale yellow, have protein content as low as 2.0 g/L, and
cell counts nearer to 200 cells/µL. Such eﬀusions are frequently
and incorrectly called “modiﬁed transudates.” However, they
have their origin in inﬂammatory and not transudative processes
and do not meet the established physical or physiologic criteria
for a modiﬁed transudate. 111 A more appropriate term, if it
existed, would be “modiﬁed exudate.”
The exudate of FIP is unlike that seen in rare cases of bacterial
peritonitis or in cats with pyothorax. These are much more
purulent in appearance, with extremely high neutrophil counts
and not as viscous or yellow tinged. The neutrophils in bacterial
peritonitis are often toxic, whereas those in FIP ﬂuid are typically
mature. However, secondary bacterial infections have also been
identiﬁed on occasion in cats with eﬀusive FIP. Eﬀusions
associated with liver and heart disease, lymphatic duct rupture
(chylous eﬀusions), and neoplasia seldom have the same overall
physical and cellular characteristics as FIP eﬀusions.

Rivalta test
The Rivalta test has been long used for diagnosing FIP-associated
exudates. 105 The test involves placing a few drops of eﬀusion into
a weak acetic acid solution. The appearance of a ball (“jellyﬁsh”)
of white ﬂocculent material that moves through the solution
indicates a positive test (Fig. 31.6). In a study of 497 cats with
eﬀusions, 35% of which had conﬁrmed FIP, the Rivalta test had a
sensitivity of 91% and a speciﬁcity of 66%, with a positive
predictive value of 58% and a negative predictive value of 93%. 112
The diagnostic performance of the test increased when cats with
lymphoma or bacterial infections were excluded, or when only
cats of ≥ 2years of age were considered. Therefore, the value of the
Rivalta test for diagnosis of FIP increases as more diagnostic
features of FIP are included and signs of other disorders excluded.
Eﬀusions that have low protein and cell counts, and are less

vetexamprep.ir

inﬂammatory in origin, are unlikely to test positive and the
interface between positive and negative is not always clear.

Analysis of Cerebrospinal Fluid and Aqueous Humor
The results of CSF analysis were reported on cats with necropsyconﬁrmed FIP from ﬁve veterinary institutions from the United
Kingdom, Australia, and United States. 113 Total protein
concentration was increased (mean, 9.4 g/L; median, 3.6 g/L;
range, 0.85–28.8 g/L) as was total nucleated cell count (mean, 196/
µL; median, 171/µL; range, 15–479/µL). Neutrophils were the
dominant cell in most cats, whereas lymphocytes and a mixture of
neutrophils and lymphocytes were observed in a smaller
proportion (Table 31.6).

vetexamprep.ir

α1-Acid Glycoprotein
α1-Acid glycoprotein (AGP) has been used extensively,
particularly in parts of Europe, as an indicator test for FIP. AGP is
hyposialylated in cats with FIP, but not in healthy cats or in cats
with other diseases. 114 One study concluded that serum AGP
could be used as a discriminating marker for FIP, but only when
coupled with other risk factors or test results supportive of a
diagnosis of FIP. 115 AGP serum concentrations of 1.5–2µg/mL
add further support to the diagnosis when the index of suspicion
is high.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Plain thoracic radiography may reveal pleural eﬀusion,
enlargement of the cardiac silhoue e in cats with pericardial
eﬀusion, and pulmonary nodular or peribronchial inﬁltrates in
cats with pyogranulomatous pneumonia (Fig. 31.7). Abdominal
radiographs may show loss of peritoneal or retroperitoneal detail
due to peritoneal eﬀusion, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly,
renomegaly, or mass lesions associated with the GI tract or
abdominal lymph nodes.
Sonographic Findings
The diagnosis of FIP often depends on the ability to identify
abdominal or thoracic eﬀusions and to obtain a ﬂuid specimen for
analysis. Ultrasound can be helpful for identiﬁcation and
collection of small volumes of ﬂuid (Fig. 31.8). Ultrasound can
also locate lesions such as enlarged abdominal lymph nodes,
kidney masses, or inﬁltrative lesions of the colon or other organs.
Ultrasound-guided biopsies of such lesions may be required to
obtain tissues for microscopic, IHC, or PCR testing.
Ultrasonography may also be helpful for diagnosis of FIP in cats
with neurologic or ocular signs, as abdominal lesions such as
enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes are present in most of these cats
and are often not appreciated on palpation.
Ultrasonographic ﬁndings were reviewed retrospectively in 16
cats with strongly suspected eﬀusive or non-eﬀusive FIP. 116 The
liver was normal in echogenicity in 11 (69%) cats, diﬀusely

vetexamprep.ir

hypoechoic in 3 cats, focally hyperechoic in 1 cat and focally
hypoechoic in another. Five cats had a hypoechoic subcapsular
rim in one or both kidneys. Free ﬂuid was present in the
peritoneal cavity in seven cats and in the retroperitoneal space in
one cat. Abdominal lymphadenopathy was noted in nine cats. The
spleen had normal echogenicity in 14 cats and was hypoechoic in
2 cats. One cat had bilateral orchitis, with loss of normal testicular
architecture. The authors concluded that, while none of these
ultrasonographic ﬁndings were speciﬁc for FIP, their signiﬁcance
was greatly increased when included with other suggestive
ﬁndings.

Microbiologic Tests (Table 31.7)
Serologic Diagnosis
The accepted gold standard method for detection of antibodies to
FCoV is an IFA using cat cell lines with tissue culture–adapted
FIPV-79-1146 as the antigen. 59 , 64 TGEV grown on pig cells or
CCoV grown on dog cells can also be used. IFA serology is
accurate if properly done, but controversy still exists over its
diagnostic value as FECV and FIPV evoke identical type
antibodies. Although antibody titers tend to be higher in cats with
FIP, they also trend high among healthy cats in the same
environments that produce FIP. 43 , 59 Nonetheless, there is some

vetexamprep.ir

value in determination of FCoV antibody titers. Antibodies to
FCoV appear within 2weeks of FECV infection, typically to titers
of around 1:100 to 1:400 and then drop to levels of 1:25 or lower in
cats that develop immunity and cease shedding. 37 Cats with
antibody titers ≥ 1:400 are almost always FECV shedders, and cats
with titers of ≤ 1:25 are usually non-shedders.
Rising FCoV antibody titers can also indicate progression of
subclinical FIP, but the opportunity or rationale for such
sequential testing is limited. FCoV antibody titers were found to
rise above their baseline among a colony of cats with enzootic
FECV infection that were subsequently infected with FeLV that
appeared to reactivate FIP (Fig. 31.10). 59 Most healthy FECV
exposed cats have titers of 1:400 or less. Only a few healthy cats
have FCoV titers of 1:1600, while titers ≥ 1:3200 (provided the
assay is performed correctly) are highly suggestive of FIP 105 and
can be considered deﬁnitive if coupled with other signs of FIP.
However, there are some cats with FIP that have low or even
negative FCoV titers. 117 This means that very high titers from a
reliable laboratory support a diagnosis of FIP in combination with
suggestive clinical signs, but low or negative titers cannot be used
to rule out FIP. A progressive rise in titer over a period of several
months may also indicate that FIP is changing from a subclinical
to clinical form (see Fig. 31.10).
A 7b serum ELISA antibody test was developed on a faulty
premise that FECVs lack the 7b gene and hence do not produce
the 7b protein, whereas FIPVs have the 7b gene, produce the
protein, and therefore evoke a 7b antibody response. However,
virtually all ﬁeld isolates of FIPVs and FECVs possess an intact 7b
gene and therefore both evoke anti-7b antibodies. 118 The 7b
antibody test is essentially the same as other FCoV antibody tests.
However, there are no good studies on how to interpret 7b
antibody titers in context to disease status.

FCoV antibody tests have also been adapted to ELISA and rapid
immunochromatographic test formats. 119 , 120 All are 96% to 100%
sensitive in detecting antibody in blood or eﬀusions. Serology on
CSF has also been applied for diagnosis of neurologic FIP. In one
study, the most useful antemortem indicators of neurologic FIP
were positive IgG anti-CoV antibody titer in the CSF, increased
serum total protein concentration, and MRI ﬁndings suggesting
periventricular contrast enhancement, ventricular dilatation, and

vetexamprep.ir

hydrocephalus. 96 However, in another study, CSF antibody was
detected only in cats with serum titers of 1:4,096 to 1:16,384 and
the investigators concluded that CSF antibodies were passively

were measured to determine whether proteins in the CSF were of
blood or local origin. Neither the albumin quotient nor IgG index
identiﬁed a pa ern consistent with intrathecal IgG synthesis in

coronavirus antibodies enter the CSF at high levels when they are
also at very high levels in the serum. 123
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR testing of feces for FCoV shedding is of limited value. The
fecal virus is of the FECV biotype, even in cats with FIP.
Furthermore, cats with FIP often shed FECV at low or negligible
levels compared with healthy cats. 11 , 80 , 124 Routine testing of
healthy cats by breeders to predict FIP problems should also be
discouraged because the odds of healthy FECV shedders
developing FIP are very low. 14 , 77 There is evidence, however,
that the higher the proportion of cats in a ca ery that shed
coronavirus at a given time, and the higher the level of shedding,
the more likely FIP will occur in the population. 65 This is an
expensive and not a very accurate way of predicting future FIP
risk. Testing of feces for FECV shedding can be theoretically used
to eliminate FECV from a cat population such as was done in
conjunction with FCoV serology in an experimental cat breeding
facility. 14 However, such a use of RT-PCR must be coupled with
sequential testing and proper quarantine facilities and procedures,
as was done in this facility. A empts to isolate FECV-negative
ki ens and cats in conventional housing with inadequate
quarantine procedures are doomed to fail.
RT-PCR assays for replicating (mRNA) and non-replicating
forms of FCoV were also used to screen the blood buﬀy coat cells
and feces of 205 healthy shelter cats to predict whether they
would develop FIP later. 77 Of 205 buﬀy coats, 1 (0.5%) tested
positive for replicating forms of viral RNA (mRNA) and 9/205
(4.4%) for non-replicating RNA, whereas 28/50 (56%) fecal
specimens tested positive for mRNA. None of the 10 cats with

vetexamprep.ir

replicating or non-replicating forms of FCoV in their blood
developed FIP over the subsequent 6 months.
The 7b gene is often used as a target for FCoV PCR because it is
the most abundant viral transcript and most likely to be detected.
The M gene has also been targeted in some PCR assays, as it is
highly conserved across all isolates. 125 The use of the 7b RT-PCR
for diagnostic purposes is based on the premise that FECVs will
be only found in feces of healthy cats and FIPVs only in diseased
tissues and eﬀusions of cats with FIP. Although this test has
excellent sensitivity and speciﬁcity when used to detect FECV in
fecal specimens of healthy cats, test results for FIP tissues and
eﬀusions have been variable. In one study of 854 cats with ascites
that were suspected to have FIP based on clinical signs, 95% of
ascites specimens from purebred and 79% from random-bred cats
tested positive by RT-PCR. This decreased with each increasing
year of age, with 70% of eﬀusions from purebred and 42% from
random-bred cats of 12–24 months of age testing positive. 123 This
variation with breed or age can best be explained by the ﬁltering
eﬀect of known risk—pedigreed cats are more likely to develop
FIP than random-bred cats and younger cats are more likely to
have FIP than older cats. Therefore, the speciﬁcity and sensitivity
of PCR tests for FIP should always be considered along with other
risk factors. 126
The specimen type also inﬂuences the results of molecular
testing. PCR was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear
cells (PBMCs) of 21 cats with FIP, serum from 26 cats with FIP,
and cell-free abdominal or thoracic eﬀusions of 36 cats with FIP,
and results were compared to those from a control group with
other diseases. 127 PCR had a sensitivity of 29% and speciﬁcity of
100% in PBMCs, 15% sensitivity and 86%–100% speciﬁcity in
serum, and 89% sensitivity and 89%–100% speciﬁcity in cell-free
body cavity eﬀusions. When ﬂuid and cellular fractions of ascites
and blood were tested from cats with experimentally induced
eﬀusive abdominal FIP, most FCoV 7b RNA was found in the
cellular pellet of ascites ﬂuid rather than in supernatant, and
viremia was not reliably detected in serum or PBMCs. 128 Similar
observations were made in cats with naturally occurring FIP. 129
Viral RNA levels are too low in whole blood, plasma, or blood
cells to be reliably detected. When testing eﬀusions, a fresh cell

vetexamprep.ir

pellet is the preferred specimen to test. Tissues to be tested should
be only from lesions, and lesions from cats with non-eﬀusive FIP
would be expected to have lower viral RNA loads than lesions
from cats with eﬀusive FIP.
In one study, FCoV PCR on CSF from cats with neurologic signs
and other risk factors for FIP was highly sensitive and speciﬁc. 113
, 127 CSF was also a useful specimen when tested for both FCoV 7b
RNA and FCoV antibody by indirect IFA. 123 CSF antibody titers
of 1:640 or greater were found only in cats with FIP and were
always positive by RT-PCR.
There is now a more accurate understanding of the genetic
make-up of FECV and FIPV isolates and the mutations leading to
the FIPV biotype. Mutations in the ORF 3c and at the S1/S2 gene
cleavage site are unique to each FIPV and are therefore not good
candidates for a test that diﬀerentiates FECVs from FIPVs. 84 , 124
However, two SNP mutations in the fusion peptide of the S
protein occur in around 96% of FIPVs detected in diseased tissues
but never in true FECVs. 80 An RT-PCR test has been
commercialized that detects FIPV-speciﬁc mutations in the S gene.
In theory, the 7b RT-PCR assay should identify any FCoV RNA
in a specimen, whereas the FIPV-speciﬁc test would determine
whether the RNA belonged to the FECV or FIPV biotype.
However, the FIPV-speciﬁc assay has much lower sensitivity than
the FCoV-speciﬁc test. In specimens with high loads of FIPVspeciﬁc RNA, both tests will be positive and the presence of an
FIPV can be conﬁrmed. However, when the starting amount of
FIPV RNA is low, the more sensitive 7b FCoV test will be positive,
but the less sensitive FIPV S gene test may be negative. In a study
of 57 cats with proven FIP and 45 control cats without FIP,
identiﬁcation of S gene- mutated FCoVs as an additional step to
the detection of FCoV alone only moderately increased speciﬁcity
for tissue specimens (from 92.6% to 94.6%) and speciﬁcity was
unchanged for ﬂuid specimens (97.9%). 82 However, sensitivity
was signiﬁcantly decreased for the FIPV-speciﬁc tests for tissue
(from 89.8% to 80.9%) and ﬂuid specimens (from 78.4% to 60%). A
further complication of the S gene mutation test for FIPVs is that
these mutations are not found in all FIPV strains from the ﬁeld. 80 ,

Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
Abdominal and/or thoracic eﬀusions in cats with FIP range from a
few milliliters to over a liter, and the color from nearly clear to a
deep yellow (Fig. 31.11) The principal lesion is the pyogranuloma,
which appears grossly as focal whitish plaques ranging from
microscopic to several millimeters in diameter and most obvious
on serosal surfaces of abdominal or thoracic organs and
mesenteries (Fig. 31.12). The omentum and splenic mesentery are
usually thickened by varying degrees of edema and ﬁbrosis, the
intestinal mesenteries cloudy, and the visceral and parietal serosal
surfaces thickened with a ground-glass appearance. Focal
hemorrhages are often seen in the omentum and splenic
mesentery and the aﬀected tissues stained yellow from bilirubin.
Similar, but less deﬁned, gross lesions can occur on the parietal

vetexamprep.ir

and visceral surfaces of the chest, mediastinum, diaphragm,
pericardium, heart, and lungs.
Lesions of non-eﬀusive FIP can be classiﬁed as intraperitoneal/pleural, extra-peritoneal/pleural, or both. They are less
diﬀuse and more solitary than those of wet FIP, much larger, and
more typical of classic, sometimes tumor-like, granulomas. The
lesions are also more likely to extend down from the surface of
organs into the underlying parenchyma, hence the alternative
name of parenchymatous FIP. Almost 50% of cats with noneﬀusive FIP have disease localized to the peritoneal cavity and in
30% of cases solely abdominal lesions are present. Pleural cavity
lesions occur in only 10% of cats with non-eﬀusive FIP, usually in
association with peritoneal disease. Abdominal lymph node
involvement is often a primary manifestation of non-eﬀusive FIP,
especially in the subclinical form (Fig. 31.13). 56 , 92 , 94 The kidneys
are also a major target (Fig. 31.14). 47 Although eﬀusive and noneﬀusive FIP are considered distinct forms, they are in reality
creations of opposing immediate-type hypersensitivity and DTH
reactions to virus-infected macrophages and elements, and one or
both reactions may be observed in individual cats.
Histopathologic Findings
The microscopic lesions of eﬀusive FIP are characteristic, with the
hallmark lesion being a vasculitis targeted at venules in the
omentum, mesenteries and serosal surfaces of the abdomen, and
pleural surfaces, mediastinum, and pericardium of the heart (Fig.
31.15A). A second characteristic lesion is the pyogranuloma,
which consists of focal accumulations of macrophages and
neutrophils adjacent to blood vessels. FIPV can be detected by
IHC or immunoﬂuorescence within these macrophages (Fig.
31.15B). Pyogranulomas tend to be more diﬀuse in acute cases and
more deﬁned with chronicity. Hyperemia and edema associated
with more acute inﬂammation and loss of small vessel integrity is
also more pronounced in severe cases, while this tends to be
replaced by serous atrophy and ﬁbrosis in more chronic cases.

Lesions of non-eﬀusive FIP are centered around small
aggregates of macrophages resembling the pyogranuloma of
eﬀusive FIP, but with a large rim of lymphocytic/plasmocytic
inﬁltrate. Lesions tend to occur in the subcapsular parenchyma of
abdominal organs such as the kidney, liver, colon, cecum, spleen,
mesenteric lymph nodes, diaphragm, lungs, or pericardium rather
than on the peritoneal or parietal serosa. Lesions appear to be
remnants of an earlier serositis extending from the surface and
into the underlying parenchyma along blood vessels. The
ependyma and meninges are target tissues in the CNS and the
uveal tract and retina in the eyes. Lesions in the skin, testicles, and
nasal passages have also been described. The central
pyogranulomas in non-eﬀusive FIP are surrounded by dense
inﬁltrates of lymphocytes and plasma cells that invade the
surrounding parenchyma. The pyogranulomas contain fewer

vetexamprep.ir

infected macrophages than those in cats with eﬀusive FIP, which
suggests that the host is be er able to contain the infection in this
form of FIP. Intermediate forms of eﬀusive and non-eﬀusive FIP
may also be observed at necropsy. Intestinal 131 and renal lesions
47 of non-eﬀusive FIP may be mistaken for neoplasia. 132 In the
colonic form of the disease, foci of pyogranulomatous
inﬂammation in the submucosa and muscularis mucosa surround
pale pink-staining areas made up of collagen and sparse cells.
These foci are encapsulated in turn by dense layers of ﬁbrous
tissue. FIPV antigen is found in large macrophages within the
regions of active inﬂammation.

Immunohistochemistry
A deﬁnitive diagnosis of FIP cannot be made based solely on
gross and microscopic pathologic features and requires proof of
the presence of FIPV in tissues and in particular, macrophages
within lesions. IHC on tissues collected at biopsy or necropsy can

vetexamprep.ir

be as reliable as PCR, but accuracy is subject to many variables
and requires excellent quality controls. 133 , 134 The greatest causes
of false negatives and false positives include inadequate
specimens,
poor
reagents,
and
reading
errors.
Immunoﬂuorescence is more sensitive than immunoperoxidase
staining but requires fresh frozen tissue sections with or without
glycerol/resin protection medium. Immunoperoxidase staining
can be performed on formalin-ﬁxed tissues or cell pellets.
IHC of eﬀusions from cats suspected to have FIP is strongly
recommended, as eﬀusions contain numerous virus-positive
macrophages that can be concentrated onto slides. When the
results of direct immunoﬂuorescence on feline eﬀusions were
compared with histopathologic examination of tissues collected at
necropsy in 17 cats, histopathology supported a diagnosis of FIP
in 10/17 cases and ruled out FIP in 7/17 cases. 135 Antemortem
immunoﬂuorescence testing was positive in all 10 cases conﬁrmed
as FIP at necropsy. In the seven cats where FIP was ruled out at
necropsy, IHC was negative in ﬁve cases and falsely positive in
two cases. In another study, immunocytochemistry was 85%
sensitive and 72% speciﬁc for the diagnosis of FIP from eﬀusions.
136

IHC can also be used to detect FIPV-infected macrophages
within other specimens, such as CSF 137 or biopsy specimens.

Treatment
There is currently no approved, readily available, simple, or
inexpensive treatment for FIP and the default treatment consists
of drainage of ﬂuid when necessary, anti-inﬂammatory doses of
prednisolone, and reduction of stress. Numerous available drugs,
biologics, and nutritional supplements have been tried. 106
Antimicrobial drugs are seldom justiﬁed, as secondary bacterial
infections are usually absent. Claims of cures have been made
following many treatments, but these cures are uncommon and
anecdotal. The problem is that there are no accurate mortality
ﬁgures for FIP to evaluate any of these treatments. The only
certainties are that older cats tend to live longer than younger cats
and cats with non-eﬀusive disease tend to live longer than cats
with eﬀusive FIP. Cats that are severely ill are also more likely to
be euthanized upon diagnosis or shortly thereafter, whereas cats

vetexamprep.ir

with milder disease are often treated supportively and kept alive
longer, adding additional bias to mortality curves. Because of
these factors, it is essential that a control population be included
in studies of treatment eﬀects on the disease. Survival time for cats
with FIP also appear to be increasing over the last decade, which
may relate to owner persistence with diﬀerent treatments, or a
true change in disease expression (either as a result of host
genetics or virus factors).

Removal of abdominal eﬀusion, except in cases where it
interferes with breathing, is not recommended as it is rapidly
replaced from body stores. Unnecessary removal of eﬀusions can
lead to hypoproteinemia and electrolyte disorders. Removal of
thoracic eﬀusions is frequently required to relieve dyspnea and
can result in clinical improvement for several days or weeks.
Removal of enlarged abdominal lymph nodes, intestinal masses,
or single diseased kidney, is only indicated if life-threatening
complications exist (e.g., intestinal blockage), as infection is
almost always more widespread than clinically apparent. Other
supportive care measures such as ﬂuid therapy or placement of
feeding tubes also may be required.

a Monitor the complete blood count during treatment.

Anti-Inflammatory and Immunomodulating
Drugs
Prednisolone and alkylating drugs such as chlorambucil have
been used to reduce clinical signs in cats with FIP (Table 31.8), but
there is no evidence that they signiﬁcantly alter lifespan. Rather
than using this less speciﬁc therapeutic approach, a empts have
been made to inhibit the cytokine response. TNF inhibitors have
been used to alleviate some of the signs of FIP and may decrease
mortality when given in the initial stages of experimental FIPV
infection. 138 Pentoxifylline has been shown to inhibit TNF-α
production by macrophages and has been used to control
vasculitis in humans. However, a study of 23 cats with proven FIP
failed to detect an eﬀect of a related drug, propentoxifylline, on
the survival time, the quality of life, or any FIP-associated clinical
or laboratory parameters. 139

vetexamprep.ir

Nonspecific Immunostimulants
Anecdotal reports exist of cats presumed to be infected with FIP
being cured or having their lives prolonged with a variety of nonspeciﬁc immunomodulators (see Chapter 9). Polyprenyl
immunostimulant (PI) is a plant extract claimed to prolong the
lives, and possibly cure, some cats with mild forms of noneﬀusive FIP. 92 , 140 None of these biologics have been
demonstrated to stimulate normal immune processes in healthy
cats, and suﬃciently powered randomized, placebo-controlled,
double-masked studies of cats with conﬁrmed FIP are lacking. A
major problem is a lack of reliable survival statistics for cats
treated with supportive care alone. 140
Feline IFN-ω (Virbagen omega, Virbac) is a veterinary product
widely marketed in Europe and Asia for treatment of many
conditions of dogs and cats. It was proposed as a cure for cats
with FIP in a study from Japan. 141 Twelve clinically ill cats were
treated with a combination of a glucocorticoid and feline IFN-ω.
Complete remission was observed in four cats and temporary
remission in four cats. This study prompted widespread use of
feline IFN-ω for treatment of FIP, except in countries where it was
not approved for any veterinary use (including the United States).
A subsequent double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 37 clientowned cats with predominately eﬀusive FIP showed feline IFN-ω
to lack eﬃcacy. 142 Nonetheless, it continues to be used by some
veterinarians to treat FIP and there have been anecdotal reports of
occasional cats that have been cured. Human IFN-α given by
injection or orally has also been used to treat cats with FIP, but it
is immunogenic and is rendered ineﬀective after several weeks of
use (see Chapter 9).

Nonspecific Viral Inhibitors
No virus disease of animals has commanded as much a ention as
FIP, and many drugs and biologics with inhibitory activity against
FIPV in tissue culture have been studied. Many of the biologics
studied inhibit FIPV by suppressing normal cellular processes
that are usurped by the virus for its own replication, raising their
toxicity for the cat. Others work by reacting with surface proteins
and block infection in tissue culture but not in natural disease.

vetexamprep.ir

These include cyclosporine and related immunophilins, vioporin
inhibitors, pyridine N-oxide derivatives, chloroquine, plant lectins
(Hippeastrum hybrid agglutinin, Galanthus nivalis agglutinin),
ubiquitin inhibitors, and semisynthetic derivatives of
glycopeptide antibiotics (vancomycin, teicoplanin). 83 , 120 , 143–150
Only chloroquine has been tested for eﬃcacy in naturally
occurring disease in cats. The clinical scores of cats in groups
treated with chloroquine were only slightly be er than those of
cats in groups not treated with chloroquine and there was
evidence of hepatotoxicity. 120
Viral inhibitory peptides and silencing RNA molecules also
have been used to inhibit FIPV replication in tissue culture. In one
study, ﬁve overlapping peptides that span the heptad repeat (HR)
region of the S protein of a type II FIPV strain (NTU-156) were
used to inhibit virus replication by blocking the intercalation of
the HR1 and HR2 regions necessary for S protein-mediated
fusion. 151 One of the ﬁve peptides inhibited FIPV replication by
97%, and had a synergistic eﬀect with human IFN-α. In another
study, eight small synthetic interfering RNA (siRNA) that targeted
four regions of the genome were used to inhibit replication of the
serotype II FIPV strain 79-1146. 152 Two of the siRNAs (targeting
the 5’ leader sequence and the nucleocapsid gene) resulted in a >
95% reduction in virus replication in vitro. Similar results were
obtained by other investigators using ﬁve siRNAs that targeted
the 3′ leader sequence and nucleocapsid genes. 153 These
investigators then incorporated their siRNAs into infectious HIVderived replication competent plasmids, which were then used to
infect cultured feline hematopoietic stem cells. 154 The stem cells
then produced anti-CoV miRNA with a reduction in FCoV
replication, thus taking the application of siRNAs one step closer,
but still distant, from clinical application.

Targeted Antiviral Drug Therapy
The most successful antiviral therapies have involved drugs that
target viral genes that regulate key processes in virus a achment,
integration, or replication. Drugs used for related and unrelated
RNA virus infection of humans can target at least two FCoV
genes. One is the 3C-like protease 155 , 156 and the second is the

vetexamprep.ir

replicase gene responsible for RNA-dependent RNA transcription
of subgenomic RNA transcripts. 157
Viral Protease Inhibitors
GC376, a 3C-like protease inhibitor, was the ﬁrst speciﬁc antiviral
drug tested against both experimental 156 and naturally occurring
FIP. 155 GC376 is a prodrug which is broken down to the active
moiety, GC373. GC373 is virtually identical to nirmatrelvir, the
active component of Paxlovid (Pﬁzer) for treatment of COVID-19.
158 GC373 inhibits the 3C-like protease. Structural proteins of CoV
are ﬁrst transcribed from mRNAs as polyproteins, which are then
cleaved by 3C-like proteases into individual proteins used in
virion production. Preliminary in vitro tests showed that GC376
was eﬀective in inhibiting FIPV replication at levels not toxic to
cells. 156 Use of GC376 to treat cats with experimental FIPV
infection resulted in cures when treatment was started at the onset
of disease and continued for 2 to 4 weeks. 157 A ﬁeld trial using 20
cats with naturally occurring FIP and twice-daily SC injections
yielded mixed results. 155 There was dramatic clinical
improvement in cats without neurologic signs within a few days
of starting treatment, and 6 of 20 cats developed sustained
remissions after 12 weeks of continuous treatment. However,
relapses that occurred during treatment or after treatment led to
euthanasia of 14 of the 20 cats. Development of neurologic disease
during or after treatment was the major cause of failure. Adverse
drug eﬀects were manageable and consisted of injection site
reactions and impaired development of permanent teeth. 155 At
the time of writing, GC376 is under development for treatment of
FIP and simultaneously being evaluated as a treatment for
COVID-19 by Anivive Life Sciences. 159
Nucleoside Analogues (RNA Transcription Inhibitors)
Ribavarin is a guanosine nucleoside analogue used once in
combination with IFN for the treatment of hepatitis C. It is an in
vitro inhibitor of FIPV 160 but had no eﬀect on experimental FIPV
infection. 161
The adenosine nucleoside analogue GS-441524, the active form
of the prodrug remdesivir (Gilead Sciences) is the most promising
treatment for FIP tested to date. GS-441524 and related

vetexamprep.ir

compounds have been developed as a result of research into
possible treatments for human RNA viral diseases such as Ebola,
Marburg, SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2, and MERS. GS-441524 is
the parent nucleoside of remdesivir (i.e., the active metabolite of
remdesivir, a prodrug). Remdesivir was originally developed to
treat hepatitis C in humans and has now been used extensively
worldwide to treat COVID-19. GS-441524 is taken up by cells,
phosphorylated stepwise to mono-, di-, and tri-phosphate forms,
which then compete with cellular adenosine nucleotide for
incorporation into replicating FIPV RNA (see also Chapter 9). 162
GS-441524 given SC demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics in
laboratory cats and was eﬀective against experimental disease. 162
A ﬁeld trial of 31 cats was conducted with various non-neurologic
forms of FIP and drug given SC q24h for a minimum of 12 weeks.
163 Five of the 31 cats recruited to the trial had to be euthanized
during the ﬁrst few days of treatment due to the severity of their
disease and complications, but 26 went on to be treated for 12
weeks or longer. Of the 26 cats, 25 achieved sustained disease
remission following one or two cycles of treatment with no
systemic signs of toxicity. Apparent cures were described by
owners in over 50% of 393 cats treated at home with GS-441524,
with a mean cost of treatment of $4920 (USD). 164
There are several limitations of drugs like GC376 and GS441524. The passage of both drugs into the CSF and aqueous
humor is impeded by the blood/brain and blood/eye barriers,
respectively. 157 , 162 A empts to overcome this by increasing the
drug dosage have not been successful for GC376, although clinical
signs were greatly decreased. 155 Higher dosages of GS-441524 can
overcome the blood/brain barrier in cats with neurologic FIP. 165 A
second limitation has been cost. Treatment currently costs several
thousand dollars for drug alone, but this cost is expected to
decrease with time. 164 A ﬁnal, and more important limitation,
involves legal approval for veterinary use of closely related drugs
that have been developed for humans against COVID-19. These
drugs currently include the nucleoside analogues remdesivir 166
and molnupiravir, 167 and the viral protease inhibitor paxlovid. 158
These drugs have only conditional approval for in-hospital use
against COVID-19 at the time of writing. There is a concern
among large pharmaceutical companies that concurrent use of

vetexamprep.ir

these or closely related drugs in animals would complicate the full
approval process of drugs for human use. Without FDA approval,
veterinarians were initially unwilling to use drugs that were not
legally produced and sold. This led initially to a situation where a
cure was available for the ﬁrst time for FIP but no inclination to
apply it in the ﬁeld. However, the desperate need of cat owners
for a treatment for FIP and willingness of companies in China to
provide them the drugs quickly rendered these concerns moot.
People concerned about FIP, particularly those involved in
foster/rescue, were quick to embrace the treatment. 164 Their
eﬀorts resulted in tens of thousands of cats from around the world
being successfully cured of FIP from 2017 onward. This success
convinced some academic veterinarians to become involved. 164 ,
168 The legality of using unapproved antivirals for treatment of
diseases has also been overcome in some countries by allowing
veterinarians to use conditionally approved drugs like remdesivir.
169 Hopefully, such arrangements will be short-lived as drugs like
remdesivir, molnupiravir and paxlovid are given full approval for
coronavirus disease in people. Full approval by national entities
like the FDA will allow veterinarians to use them per label or
extra label fashion when no approved animal equivalent is
available, provided that they are compounded from federally
approved drugs. (AVMA)

Prognosis
The 1-year mortality for FIP is around 95% for cats treated with
various non-virus–speciﬁc medications. Younger cats, which tend
to have more acute and severe forms of FIP, have the shortest
survival times, whereas older cats with less severe and more
chronic forms of FIP tend to live longer. Marked pyrexia, lethargy,
inappetence, weight loss, and icterus are indications of a poor
prognosis. Lymphopenia is often associated with more fulminant
disease, whereas higher counts are associated with more localized
and less intense inﬂammation. Cats with pronounced abdominal
eﬀusions that are still active, eating, and maintaining weight are
more likely to manifest lower-grade fever, clearer ﬂuid, and less
likely to be icteric. Apparent long-term cures have now been
described for many cats treated with nucleoside analogues such as
GS-441524 and remdesivir.

vetexamprep.ir

Immunity
FECV immunity is mediated by humoral mucosal and systemic
responses. 170 Secretory antibody responses in the gut most likely
mirror IgG antibody levels in the blood. Antibodies measured by
indirect IFA appear in the blood within 10 to 14 days of infection
and rise to titers around 1:400 at the peak of shedding. 10 , 37
Serum antibody titers then fall to levels of 1:25 or less as virus
shedding becomes intermi ent and ﬁnally ceases. 37 Reinfections
are common and resemble primary infections in the pa ern of
fecal shedding and antibody responses. Reinfection has also been
observed in natural disease. 66 This pa ern of infection is typical,
as immunity to mucosal pathogens often requires a long period of
exposure or persistence to develop and does not evoke strong
memory. 171 Immunity to animal coronavirus vaccines is also
notoriously poor. 172
As noted earlier in this chapter, cellular immunity appears to be
important in determining the outcome of FIPV infection. Humoral
immunity is not thought to be nonprotective in FIP and
contributes to disease pathogenesis. In a study of experimentally
infected cats, investigators were unable to identify T-cell
responses that might predict disease outcome during early
infection with FIPV. However, on re-exposure to FIPV, antiviral Tcell responses appeared to be important in preventing disease. 173

Prevention
Minimizing Exposure
A empts have been made to eliminate FECV from cat
populations. One approach used has been to isolate pregnant
queens from all other cats and wean and isolate ki ens at 4–6
weeks of age. 174 Even if the queen is shedding FECV, most ki ens
have suﬃcient maternal-derived immunity to resist infection until
9–10 weeks of age. After early weaning, ki ens are strictly
quarantined and tested for fecal FECV shedding at monthly
intervals for several months to assure that they are free of the
virus. Once free from FECV, prevention of infection requires a
speciﬁc facility for noninfected cats and strict control of the
movement of people to avoid introduction of the virus on fomites.

vetexamprep.ir

It also precludes acquisition of new cats without strict testing and
quarantine and limits introduction of cats, all of which defeat the
purposes of pedigreed cat breeding.
FECV infection can also be allowed to burn itself out. In one
study of naturally infected cats, FECV shedding dramatically
decreased over 3 years, suggesting a type of herd immunity. 66 If a
ca ery or other multicat facility is closed to new susceptible cats,
either from outside or from within (i.e., ki ens bred in the
facility), the proportion of fecal shedders will slowly decline. This
can be facilitated through the testing of all the cats used to
produce a FCoV-free population by fecal PCR or serology. 14 Cats
that are negative by PCR and have low FCoV titers (≤1:25 by
indirect IFA) are segregated to one facility and quarantined. Cats
with strong positive PCR values and antibody titers ≥ 1:400 are
eliminated, and cats with intermediate values are segregated to a
second facility. This testing is repeated every month and within a
year or less the result will be two separate groups of cats that
should be free of infection with a minimum of loss of breeding
stock. These procedures have been used to eliminate FECV
infection from SPF experimental cat breeding colonies. 14
A direct relationship exists between the extent of fecal shedding
of FECV and FIP. 36 , 65 Cats over 3 years of age are also less apt to
be FECV carriers. Therefore, the severity of FECV exposure and
incidence of FIP can be diminished by reducing the numbers of
breeding cats to a minimum and by decreasing the proportion of
younger cats in a cat population. Breeding cats should be kept for
longer periods of time to reduce the numbers of young cats
introduced into the ca ery. Adult cats are also less likely to shed
other common pathogens, and when coupled with decreased
ki en density, this can also reduce the incidence of upper
respiratory and enteric infectious diseases. Ca eries that remain
free of FIP are often those that maintain six or less breeding
queens with one or two toms. Unnecessary cats should be
removed from the ca ery whenever possible. Ki en production
should be also minimized by more careful mate selection and
breeding for quality rather than quantity.

Vaccination

vetexamprep.ir

Several potential FIP vaccines have been described over the last
three decades. 56 , 57 These vaccines have had preventable
fractions that range from 0% to 75%, and results from the ﬁeld
have been mixed. 108 Only one vaccine, Primucell FIP (Zoetis,
Parsippany, NJ), has been successfully licensed and marketed in
the United States and several other countries. This is an intranasal
vaccine that contains a temperature-sensitive mutant of serotype
II FIPV-DF2, and initial vaccination consists of two doses of the
vaccine given 3 weeks apart. 175 Vaccination has not been shown
to be eﬀective when administered to cats less than 16 weeks of
age, suggesting that the immune system must reach a more
mature state of development than for other routinely used
vaccines. The vaccine has been shown to be safe with no signs of
ADE. 176 There are several aspects of the vaccine that limit its use
in the ﬁeld. It contains a serotype II strain of FIPV, while serotype
I strains predominate in the ﬁeld. Serotype I and II strains contain
diﬀerent virus-neutralizing epitopes. The vaccine is also without
eﬃcacy when administered to ki ens less than 16 weeks of age,
which is at least 6 weeks after ki ens from multi-cat environments
have been exposed to FECV. The vaccine may also lack eﬃcacy in
cats that have been previously exposed to FCoV. 108 In a placebocontrolled study of two high FIP–risk populations, 177 the vaccine
was safe and eﬃcacious in one population of cats that had low
antibody titers to FCoV at the time of vaccination. It was
concluded that vaccination could protect cats with no or low
FCoV antibody titer. However, ca eries with low CoV titers are at
low risk for FIP, and titers are generally high among ca ery,
rescue, and shelter cats. Therefore, the target group for this
vaccine would be cats exposed to uncommon serotype II strains of
FECV, with less than a 1% risk of developing FIP after such
exposure, and that are over 16 weeks of age and seronegative for
FCoV exposure when vaccinated. Furthermore, vaccination of
FCoV-naïve laboratory cats ≥ 16 weeks of age, was less than 70%
eﬀective against challenge exposure with a serotype II FIPV when
adjusted for the survival rate of nonvaccinates. 175 As a result of
these concerns, the AAFP has stated that, “at this time, there is
insuﬃcient evidence that the vaccine induces clinically relevant
protection, and use of the vaccine is not recommended.” 178

vetexamprep.ir

Genetic Selection
Susceptibility to FIP in pedigreed cats appears to be 50% heritable
in breeds studied. 70 A empts to use positive selection in a
laboratory se ing to enhance resistance among random-bred cats
failed, and the resultant inbreeding increased rather than
decreased FIP susceptibility. 72 Genetic susceptibility appears to
involve inheritance of numerous risk factors, some positive and
others negative. 71 , 72 Because inbreeding is a much greater
problem among pedigreed than random-bred cats, genetic factors
play a proportionately greater role in ca eries than in ki en
rescues or shelters. Other host and environmental co-factors are of
greater importance in random-bred populations. The fact that
some breeds and lines of pedigreed cats are at greater genetic risk
for FIP is a two-edged sword. Although inbreeding and artiﬁcial
genetic bo lenecks may increase FIP risk in pedigreed cats,
ca eries can control which toms and queens are bred and may be
able to associate certain breeding combinations with development
of FIP. The practice of not using cats that have produced ki ens
that have died of FIP or that are in closely related lines known to
have problems with FIP is widely accepted. Both toms and queens
contribute genetic risk factors, but because toms produce many
more ki ens, the culling of problem toms rather than queens can
be more eﬀective. 70 Tom cats from lines with no history of FIP
can overcome genetic deﬁciencies in queens, while breeding
genetically deﬁcient toms with deﬁcient queens can rapidly bring
FIP problems to the forefront.

Public Health Aspects
There is no evidence that humans can become infected with FCoV.
Most human coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 (the cause of
COVID-19), are beta- and not alpha-CoVs. SARS-CoV-2 can infect
and cause disease in cats (see Chapter 43). 179 Other coronaviruses
have been shown to cause FIP-like disease in ferrets and mice. If a
coronavirus emerged that could cause similar clinical
manifestations and outcomes in humans as FIPV can in cats, it
would clearly represent a major threat to humans, and would
without doubt be the subject of intense research.

vetexamprep.ir

Case Example
Signalment

“Ricky”, a 9-month-old male castrated domestic shorthair from
Sacramento, CA.

History

Ricky was obtained as a stray at 8 weeks of age by a local ki en
rescue group and adopted by the owner at 3 months of age. He
had experienced multiple upper respiratory tract infections
before being adopted but was healthy when placed in a new
home with one other cat. He was an indoor cat that was
sometimes walked brieﬂy outdoors.
Ricky was brought to a local veterinary clinic at 9 months of
age because of an acute onset of increased thirst and urination.
A serum chemistry panel showed hyperglobulinemia (7.7
mg/dL). The urine SpG was 1.025 with inactive sediment and
culture negative for aerobic bacteria. Ricky stopped eating over
the next 3 days and was returned to the clinic. Laboratory
abnormalities at that time included a mature neutrophilia
(11,904 cells/µL), lymphocytosis (5,104 cells/µL), eosinophilia
(1,536 cells/µL), hyperglobulinemia (6.9 mg/dL), and
hypoalbuminemia (2.4 mg/dL) with A:G ratio of 0.35. A FCoV
antibody titer was positive at 1:400. Serology for Toxoplasma
gondii was negative. Plain thoracic radiographs showed a mild
interstitial pa ern. Abdominal ultrasound showed a
moderately enlarged mesenteric lymph that was reactive on
aspiration. Ricky’s appetite recovered when cyproheptadine
was initiated for several weeks, after which treatment was
discontinued. Ricky remained outwardly normal over the next
3 weeks, although occasional soft feces were noticed in the li er
box. The owners were concerned about the possibility of FIP.
The owner suspected FIP and wanted a second opinion.

Physical Examination

Ricky was bright, alert, and active on presentation with a
weight of 4.2 kg, T = 103°F, HR = 200 beats/minute, and eupneic.
His eyes, ears, nose, and throat were normal, and his BCS was
5/9. Thoracic auscultation did not reveal any abnormalities, and
abdominal palpation was normal.

Laboratory Findings

vetexamprep.ir

A CBC demonstrated a slightly low HCT at 27.3%, a normal
MCV and MCHC, and a leukocytosis of 24,950 cells/µL with
neutrophilia (17,141 cells/µL), high normal lymphocytes (6,886
cells/µL), a monocyte count of 724 cells/µL, eosinophils of 200
cells/µL, and a slightly elevated platelet count (518,000/µL).
A serum chemistry proﬁle demonstrated a normal sodium,
potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphorous, calcium, BUN,
creatinine, and glucose. However, total protein concentration
was greatly elevated at 10.7 g/dL with a low normal albumin
(2.6 g/dL) and high globulin (8.1 g/dL) and A:G ratio of 0.32.
Serum liver enzyme activities (ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT) were
normal, as were the cholesterol and bilirubin concentrations. A
serum protein electrophoresis showed a polyclonal
gammopathy with a mild decrease in albumin and mild
increases in the α2 and β1 fractions consistent with the acutephase inﬂammatory response.

Imaging Findings

Ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated moderate
splenomegaly and a diﬀuse mesenteric lymphadenopathy. An
aspirate of a mesenteric lymph node showed a heterogenous
population of lymphocytes, predominated by small, mature
lymphocytes and low numbers of intermediate and large
reactive lymphocytes with sca ered plasma cells and
histiocytes. Immunocytochemistry using two diﬀerent
monoclonal antibodies to FCoV was negative.

Microbiologic Testing

FeLV antigen and FIV antibody serology were negative, as were
blood cultures for Bartonella clarridgeiae and Bartonella henselae.
Ricky was also seronegative for antibodies to Ehrlichia canis,
Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ricke sia spp., and whole blood
PCR-negative for A. phagocytophilum, Anaplasma platys,
Bartonella spp., E. canis, and Mycoplasma haemofelis. Aerobic and
anaerobic bacterial cultures of mesenteric lymph node aspirates
were negative; an FCoV 7b PCR on whole blood was also
negative. Serology for FCoV antibodies was positive at
1:102,400.

Diagnosis

A tentative diagnosis of FIP was made based on Ricky’s
background, the marked polyclonal gammopathy, and

vetexamprep.ir

extremely high CoV titer.

Treatment and Outcome

Ricky was treated with prednisolone (5 mg, PO, q12h for 7
days, followed by 5 mg, PO, q24h thereafter), and chlorambucil
(2 mg, PO, every 3 days). After 6 weeks of treatment, Ricky
appeared normal and CBC variables were within normal
reference ranges. However, his total protein was 8.5 g/dL with a
globulin of 4.5 g/dL and an abdominal ultrasound showed
persistent, but mild mesenteric lymphadenomegaly. A repeat
FCoV titer was 1:25,600 and treatment with feline IFN-ω was
commenced at 4.5 million units, SC, once weekly.
Ricky was next seen 3 months later, at which time he
appeared playful, his appetite was normal, and his body weight
had remained stable at 4.5 kg. A CBC showed mild anemia
(HCT 28.5%), with low normal WBC with neutrophils at 4,439
cells/µL and lymphopenia (468 cells/µL). A serum chemistry
panel and abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities,
which prompted discontinuation of the chlorambucil and IFNω and continuation of prednisolone.
Ricky was next seen 12 months after his illness, at which time
he was apparently healthy. CBC ﬁndings were unchanged from
the previous visit and his serum globulin concentration was 4.7
g/dL. The prednisolone dose was decreased to 5 mg q48h. One
month later, albumin and globulin concentrations were 3.3 and
5.1 g/dL, respectively, and the prednisolone dose was reduced
to 2.5 mg q48h. Two months later, a CBC was unremarkable,
but the globulin had increased to 5.7 g/dL, abdominal
ultrasound showed a mild enlargement of the mesenteric
lymph nodes, and the serum CoV antibody titer was 1:409,600.
The prednisolone dose was returned to 5 mg, PO, q24h, and 1
month later, the serum globulin concentration was 4.9 g/dL.
Ricky was still doing well clinically 1.5 months later, but a
mid-abdominal mass was palpated on physical examination
and the serum globulin concentration had increased again (5.6
g/dL). Abdominal ultrasound showed several moderately
enlarged and hypoechoic lymph nodes in the ileocolic region,
the largest of which measured 0.9 cm in diameter. The
surrounding mesentery was focally hyperechoic. There was also
focal hyperechoic retroperitoneal tissue surrounding the right
kidney with scant retroperitoneal ﬂuid. A empts to obtain

vetexamprep.ir

aspirates from the lymph nodes were unsuccessful. The
prednisolone dose was increased to 5 mg, PO, q12h, and
treatment with chlorambucil was reinstituted. Ricky became
lethargic and anorectic over the next week. A CBC showed
worsening anemia (HCT 24.3%) and persistent lymphopenia
(782 cells/µL). His globulin concentration was increased (5.8
g/dL) and albumin normal (3.3 g/dL). A fourth FCoV antibody
titer was 1:25,600. Treatment with cyproheptadine was initiated
and the chlorambucil and pentoxifylline discontinued. The
inappetence continued, he became persistently pyrexic (103.4°F
to 104°F), and hematochezia and tachypnea developed over the
next few days. HCT dropped to 16.5%, and hypokalemia,
hyponatremia, and hypochloremia developed. Ricky was
hospitalized and treated with 1 unit of packed RBCs, IV
crystalloids, and parenteral antimicrobial drugs. Thoracic
radiographs showed a severe, diﬀuse, patchy alveolar and
nodular interstitial pa ern with thickening of the bronchial
walls and mild pleural eﬀusion. A tracheobronchial lavage
showed marked mixed, predominantly pyogranulomatous
inﬂammation with moderate epithelial hyperplasia and some
degenerate neutrophils. Immunocytochemistry with an antiFCoV antibody was strongly positive (Fig. 31.16). Shortly
thereafter he began to seizure and was euthanized.

Necropsy Findings

A necropsy showed moderate to severe, multifocal to coalescing
pyogranulomatous inﬂammation involving the parietal and
visceral serosa of the spleen, liver, kidney, intestines,
diaphragm, thoracic and abdominal walls, and pericardium.
There was also multifocal pyogranulomatous splenitis,
hepatitis, nephritis, meningoencephalitis, and pneumonia with
pulmonary necrosis. Straw-colored eﬀusion was present in the
abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity, and pleural space. IHC was
strongly positive for FCoV antigen.

Comments

This case was typical of several cats that start out with dry FIP
localized primarily to the mesenteric lymph nodes. This has
been previously described as the mildest clinical form of FIP. In
this presentation, the host immune system can contain most of
the infection to the primary target organ (i.e., the mesenteric

vetexamprep.ir

lymph node), but the immune response is insuﬃcient to bring
about a complete cure and the disease becomes clinically
apparent. In other such cases, the disease has been known to
completely resolve or remain subclinical for many months and
possibly years. 56 , 92 Although Ricky appeared to respond on
several occasions to medications such as prednisolone and IFNω, there is reasonable evidence that none of these drugs are
eﬀective in altering the disease course, 160 , 163 and the ups and
downs in clinical condition during these earlier stages would be
as expected for this form of FIP. Ultimately, disease progressed
and
a
diagnosis
of
FIP
was
conﬁrmed
with
immunocytochemistry on a tracheobronchial lavage specimen.
The terminal development of eﬀusions is also more commonly
recognized and has been referred to as ‘dry-to-wet’ FIP. It is
often only when the disease becomes conspicuously eﬀusive
that the correct diagnosis is made. The PCR and
immunocytochemistry results early during illness were false
negatives, indicating that the level of virus in the samples at
these early stages was below the sensitivity of the assay
procedures or that sampling was inadequate. Drugs such as
GC376, GS-441524, and remdesivir have shown promise for
complete cure of disease in cases such as this, but were not
available at the time this cat was alive.
