32: Feline Leukemia Virus
Infection
Katrin Hartmann, Regina Hofmann-Lehmann, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: FeLV, a gammaretrovirus of domestic cats, is a
member of the Oncornavirus subfamily of retroviruses. It
contains a protein core with single-stranded RNA protected by
an envelope.
• First Described: FeLV was first described in 1964 by William
Jarrett and coworkers, when virus particles were seen
budding from the membrane of malignant lymphoblasts from a
cat with naturally occurring lymphoma. Although clusters of
lymphoma cases occurring in households had always been
observed, it was not until the discovery of FeLV that an
infectious etiology was finally proven.
• Affected Hosts: In nature, FeLV mainly infects domestic cats.
Some wild felids are also susceptible.
• Geographic Distribution: FeLV infection occurs worldwide. For
many years after its discovery, FeLV was considered to
account for most disease-related deaths in pet cats, and was
responsible for more clinical syndromes than any other single
agent.
• Route of Transmission: Prolonged close contact with salivary
secretions is the most common mode of transmission, and
less frequently FeLV is transmitted through biting,
transplacental transmission, transmission through milk, and
through blood transfusion.
• Major Clinical Signs: Most common clinical signs include
lethargy, pallor, signs of stomatitis, signs of underlying

vetexamprep.ir

lymphoma or leukemia, signs of immune-mediated disorders,
or signs of opportunistic infections.
• Differential Diagnoses: For cats with immunosuppression, FIV
infection is the primary differential diagnosis; for cats with
stomatitis, FCV infection or FIV infection are the differential
diagnoses; for cats with immune-mediated diseases and
cytopenias, primary immune-mediated disease and other
bone marrow diseases are the differential diagnoses.
• Human Health Significance: FeLV does not infect humans.

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
FeLV is a gammaretrovirus of domestic cats that belongs to the
Oncornavirus subfamily of retroviruses. It was ﬁrst described in
1964 by William Jarre and coworkers, when virus particles were
seen budding from the membrane of malignant lymphoblasts
from a cat with naturally occurring lymphoma. 1-4 FeLV contains a
protein core with single-stranded RNA protected by an envelope.
FeLV is an exogenous agent that replicates within many tissues,
including bone marrow, salivary glands, and respiratory
epithelium. If the immune response does not intervene after initial
infection, FeLV spreads to the bone marrow and infects
hematopoietic precursor cells. All retroviruses, including FeLV,
rely on a DNA intermediate for replication. The single-stranded
RNA genome is reversely transcribed into DNA, which is
integrated into the host’s cell genome as provirus with the help of
an integrase enzyme. After reverse transcription, synthesis of viral
proteins occurs with assembly of the virions near the cell
membrane and budding from the cell. Once the provirus is
integrated, cell division results in daughter cells that also contain
viral DNA. The ability of the virus to become part of the host’s
own DNA is crucial for the lifelong persistence of the virus after
bone marrow infection.
Both exogenous (foreign, “pathogenic”) and endogenous
(inherited, mostly “nonpathogenic”) retroviruses occur in cats. 5
Pathogenic exogenous viruses that can be transmi ed horizontally
from cat to cat include FeLV, FIV, and FFV (previously known as

vetexamprep.ir

syncytium-forming virus, see Chapter 36), which is widespread
but has a low pathogenicity.
On the basis of similarities in nucleotide sequences, it is likely
that FeLV evolved from a virus in an ancestor of the rat. It is
assumed that this event took place in the late Pleistocene up to 10
million years ago in the North African desert. Ancestral rats and
cats roamed freely, and the virus was transmi ed to cats through
ingestion or a rat bite. The initial spread of FeLV among cats
might have been inhibited by the aridity of the North African
desert. 6
FeLV is divided into several subgroups, but only subgroup
FeLV-A is infectious and transmi ed from cat to cat. The other
subgroups (e.g., FeLV-B and FeLV-C) are not transmi ed from cat
to cat under natural circumstances but can be generated de novo in
a FeLV-A-infected cat by mutation or recombination of the FeLVA genome with cellular genes or genes from endogenous
retroviruses in the cat’s genome. The feline sarcoma virus (FeSV)
also is a recombination of the FeLV-A genome with tumorassociated cellular genes (proto-oncogenes) and likewise is
generated de novo in a FeLV-A-infected cat.
The endogenous counterparts of exogenous FeLV, termed
enFeLVs, are integrated into the genome of domestic cats and
closely related wild felids. EnFeLV is thought to have originated
hundreds of thousands of years ago from cats that had eaten mice
viremic with a murine leukemia virus (MuLV) that was able to
incorporate its genome into the germline cells of the predator.
This MuLV was then inherited by the feline oﬀspring in a
Mendelian manner. EnFeLVs are present in every cat and every
feline cell. In contrast, more recently integrated endogenous
elements can display polymorphisms among cats. As enFeLV
elements are generally mutated and nonfunctional, they do not
form infectious virions, although expression of short transcripts
has been observed. 7 Recombination can occur between enFeLV
and exogenous FeLV-A following infection, which can give rise to
pathogenic viruses. Transduction of enFeLV env sequences
encoding for the viral envelope can lead to development of FeLVB or FeLV-D. 8-10 In addition, parts of, or the entire, gag genes of
enFeLV have been identiﬁed in FeLV isolates from naturally
infected cats. 11 Moreover, truncated envelope proteins encoded
by enFeLV (FeLIX) can facilitate infection with fusion-defective

vetexamprep.ir

exogenous FeLV by binding to the cellular receptor. 12 FeLIX
activity was detected at a functional level in sera from domestic
cats. 13 EnFeLV loads can vary among diﬀerent cat populations
and are inﬂuenced by the breed and gender of the cat. 14 An
association between enFeLV loads and FeLV-A replication but not
with outcome of FeLV infection was demonstrated. 15 Full-length
enFeLV elements with putative functional open reading frames
have been characterized. 16 These are present in only 9% to 15% of
domestic cats suggesting that they are relatively recent additions
to the feline genome. 17
Other endogenous retroviral elements are also found in cats,
such as RD-114, which is most closely related to an endogenous
baboon retrovirus. RD-114 elements and RD-114-related
sequences (RDRSs) likely entered the cat genome hundreds of
thousands of years ago as a result of predation of early primates
by ancestor cats, both before and after domestication. 18 , 19 No
loci that encode infectious RD-114 could be found in the feline
genome, but a virus nearly identical to RD-114 can be produced
by recombination between two defective RD-114 virus-related
proviruses. 20 , 21 Although there is no evidence of pathogenicity
of RD-114 in cats, or an immune response to the virus, it could
play a role in normal fetal diﬀerentiation. 22-24 Assays to screen for
RD-114 infection in cell culture, and a method to establish cell
lines with reduced risk of endogenous retroviruses have been
developed. 25 , 26
Various recombinations of RD-114, FeLV-related sequences, and
the baboon endogenous virus have been characterized, now
known as endogenous retroviruses of domestic cats (ERV-DCs).
Several proviral clones have been identiﬁed and numbered
according to their genomic insertions, for example, ERV-DC1, and
classiﬁed into genotypes I, II, and III by phylogenetic analysis.
Most contain deletions and mutations that render them
noninfectious, but there are several ERV-DCs that are infectious in
the domestic cat and can even infect human cell lines. Some of
these are ﬁxed in the cat genome, whereas others are mobile and
have the potential to eventually disappear. Approximately onethird of cats tested in Japan carried ERV-DC10 loci. 8 It is unclear
whether ERV-DCs are harmful or beneﬁcial to the host. Hosts

vetexamprep.ir

tend to tightly control their ERVs, particularly those with high
transcriptional activity, for example by promotor methylation. 27

FeLV Subgroups
FeLV subgroups are immunologically closely related but use
diﬀerent cellular receptors. 28-32 The three most established FeLV
subgroups are FeLV-A, FeLV-B, and FeLV-C (Table 32.1). The cell
surface entry receptor for FeLV-A is a putative thiamine
transporter (THTR1) which is widely expressed in cat tissues.
Therefore it was speculated that FeLV-A infection could disrupt
thiamine uptake with pathological consequences. 33 Thiamine
uptake was indeed blocked by FeLV-A; in feline ﬁbroblasts that
naturally express feline THTR1, this blockade resulted in a growth
arrest at physiological concentrations of extracellular thiamine.
THTR1 is highly conserved among diﬀerent feline species (Iberian
lynx, Asiatic and Indian lion, European wildcat, jaguarundi,
domestic cat) and thus variations in the THTR1 sequence do not
explain host species susceptibility diﬀerences. 34 FeLV-B uses Pit1
and Pit2 as receptors for virus entry; Pit1 and Pit2 normally
function as sodium-dependent phosphate transporters. 28 , 32 The
FeLV-C receptor (FLVCR) is a 12-transmembrane domain surface
protein that exports heme from cells. FLVCR is required for
erythroid maturation. 35-37 FLVCR is also important for
development and maturation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. 38
Only FeLV-A is transmi ed horizontally from cat to cat in
nature. The other subgroups evolve in FeLV-A-infected cats by
mutation and recombination between FeLV-A and cellular or
endogenous retroviral sequences contained in normal feline DNA.
Subgroup B originates from recombination of FeLV-A with
enFeLV. In one study of a closed colony of cats, multiple FeLV-B
variants were generated in more than half of the cats infected with
FeLV-A; horizontal transmission was also considered possible
because of a high degree of genetic similarity of the variants
among cats. 39 Subgroup C is less common and is the result of
mutations in the env gene. 2
Replication of FeLV-B and FeLV-C is usually only possible with
the help of FeLV-A, because important genomic sequences are
replaced in these recombinant viruses. Proposed FeLV-A helper

vetexamprep.ir

functions include enhanced replication eﬃciency, immune
evasion, and replication rescue for defective FeLV-B and FeLV-C
virions. However, in newborn SPF ki ens, experimental FeLV-B
or FeLV-C infection was established without the presence of FeLVA. 40 , 41 Moreover, by screening 300 ﬁeld isolates using
interference assays, two isolates, FeLV-2518 and FeLV-4314,
displayed the FeLV-B phenotype alone in the absence of a fully
functional helper FeLV-A virus. 42 Nevertheless, naturally infected
cats usually carry FeLV-A either alone or in combination with
FeLV-B, FeLV-C, or both. In consequence, if immunity to FeLV
subgroup A is present, the cat has immunity to infection by any
FeLV subtype.
In general, the pathogenicity of FeLV-B and FeLV-C, in
combination with FeLV-A, is higher than that of FeLV-A alone. 43
Envelope protein diﬀerences among subtypes have been shown to
be the major determinants of pathogenicity, but the mechanisms
by which these diﬀerences inﬂuence pathogenesis are not well
understood. FeLV-B infection is commonly associated with
malignancies, especially thymic lymphoma. FeLV-C is mainly
associated with nonregenerative anemia. 44
Other FeLV subgroups have been described more recently.
FeLV-D arises from recombination of FeLV-A and the env gene of
a feline endogenous gammaretrovirus (ERV-DC), genotype I. 8 , 45
FeLV-D was detected in the blood or tumor tissues of three of 283
FeLV-infected cats, but its infectivity and pathogenicity remain
unclear. Receptors for FeLV-D have not yet been identiﬁed. FeLVT is highly cytolytic for T lymphocytes and causes severe
immunosuppression 46-48 but is likely not important in the ﬁeld.
FeLV-T also uses Pit-1 as a receptor, like FeLV-B, but for reasons
that remain unclear, the host ranges of FeLV-B and FeLV-T are not
exactly the same. 32 FeLV-T is fusion-defective and requires the
cofactor FeLIX to infect cells. As described earlier, FeLIX is a
truncated envelope protein encoded by an endogenous FeLV,
which can function as either a transmembrane protein or a soluble
component to facilitate infection. 12 , 13 , 49 Another subgroup that
can
be
found
experimentally,
“FeLV
feline-acquired
immunodeﬁciency syndrome” (FeLV-FAIDS) virus, is composed
of FeLV-A and a highly immunopathogenic variant that infects
CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes and B lymphocytes in blood,

vetexamprep.ir

lymph nodes, and myeloid cells. 50 Widespread proliferation of
this virus greatly impairs the host immune response. In 2016, the
subgroup FeLV-TG35-2 was described, which originated from a
FeLV-infected cat, TG35, in Japan; 51 a folate transporter has been
identiﬁed as a possible receptor. 52

Virus Genome and Proteins
FeLV is a typical retrovirus (Fig. 32.1). It contains a singlestranded RNA molecule that is transcribed into proviral DNA by
the enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) and subsequently
integrated into the host cellular genome. The gene sequence
contains long terminal repeats (LTRs), which are repeated
sequences that have regulatory function and control expression of
the other viral genes but generally do not code for a protein
product. From the 5′ to the 3′ end, the gene order is LTR-gag-polenv-LTR (Table 32.2). LTR regions play a critical role in viral tissue
tropism and pathogenicity. Within the LTRs, recurrent enhancer
sequences (or upstream region enhancers [UREs]) are frequently
found in cats with myeloid leukemias and could play a role in
oncogenesis. 53 , 54 For example, the U3-LTR region has the ability
to upregulate the NFκB signaling pathway via activation of RasRaf-IκB kinase and degradation of IκB. 55 The gag (groupassociated antigen) gene encodes internal structural proteins,
including p15, p12, p27, and p10. The p27 protein is produced in
amounts that exceed that necessary for assembly of new virus
particles. Thus, p27 is abundant in the cytoplasm of individual
infected cells and also in the blood of infected cats, which is why
most available immunochromatographic tests, such as ELISA and
IFA assays, are designed to detect this protein, either free in

vetexamprep.ir

plasma or within neutrophils and platelets, respectively. Free p27
is also detectable in tears and saliva. The pol (polymerase) gene
encodes the viral enzymes RT, polymerase, and integrase. The env
(envelope) gene encodes the envelope components gp70 and
p15E. The envelope protein gp70 deﬁnes the virus subgroup and
appears to be important for inducing immunity. Antibodies to
gp70 result in neutralization of the virus and immunity to
reinfection. Thus, gp70 is important in natural resistance and
therefore as a target for vaccine production. The transmembrane
protein p15E is thought to interfere with host cell immune
responses, which facilitates viral persistence. 56

vetexamprep.ir

Structure of feline leukemia virus.
Gammaretroviruses contain two identical
strands of RNA and associated enzymes,
which include reverse transcriptase, integrase,
and protease, packaged into a core composed
of the capsid protein (p27) with a surrounding
matrix, all enclosed by a phospholipid
membrane envelope derived from the host cell.
The envelope contains a gp70 glycoprotein
and the transmembrane protein p15E.

Host Range
In nature, FeLV mainly infects domestic cats. Some wild felids are
also susceptible. In vitro, FeLV also can replicate in nonfelid cell
lines. FeLV-B replicates in cells derived from cats, dogs, cows,
pigs, hamsters, monkeys, and humans; and FeLV-C replicates in
cells of cats, dogs, guinea pigs, and humans. 1 , 57 , 58 Although
certain human cell lines can be infected by FeLV-A, FeLV is not
thought to pose a risk for humans; FeLV-A shed by cats carries
carbohydrates on the virus envelope (α-Gal epitope) that are
readily recognized by naturally occurring anti-αGal antibodies in
humans, and the virus is neutralized by complement. 59 However,

vetexamprep.ir

experimental FeLV infection with development of lymphoma
could be induced in young dogs and marmosets. 60 In
experimental infections with FeSV, ﬁbrosarcomas also could be
produced in nonfelids. 61 However, no reports exist on natural
transmission of FeLV to nonfelids.
FeLV infection is enzootic in some wild felid populations, such
as European wildcat populations. Introduction of FeLV into freeliving and captive wild felid populations such as Florida panthers
or the Iberian lynx has serious consequences for their health and
survival. In several instances of FeLV infection in wild felids,
contact with domestic cats was the source of infection. Within
felids from lineage 8 (to which the domestic cat belongs), FeLV
was isolated from the European wildcat (Felis silvestris silvestris). 62
FeLV-infected free-ranging European wildcats were reported in
Great Britain, Swi erland, France, Germany, Portugal, and Spain.
63-69 Up to 49% of wildcats tested FeLV antigen–positive, but no
evidence of FeLV-associated disease was found, although in one
study the FeLV antigen–positive wildcats had poorer body
condition than FeLV antigen–negative wildcats. 66 European
wildcats that tested provirus-positive using PCR were
signiﬁcantly more often coinfected with feline hemoplasmas than
FeLV provirus-negative wildcats. 70

Prevalence
FeLV infection exists in domestic cats worldwide. Studies report a
prevalence of 2.3% to 3.3% in the United States, 0% to 8.8% in
Europe, 0% to 24.5% in Asia, and 0.5% to 21% in Australia. 97-116
Only cats on some islands such as Grenada, the West Indies,
Isabela Island, and the Galapagos, have been found free of FeLV
infection. 117-119
The prevalence of FeLV infection varies depending on the
health status of the cat population sampled. 120 In healthy freeroaming cats, the prevalence typically ranges from 1% to 8%. 98 ,
101 , 103 , 120 , 121 In sick cats, the prevalence can be as high as 38%.

97 , 122 , 123

The overall prevalence of FeLV infection used to be decreasing
in many geographic areas. 97-99 , 101 , 103-105 , 123 , 124 The Tufts
Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, where approximately 2000
serum samples are tested yearly for FeLV antigen, reported a
decrease from 8% in 1989 to 4% in 1995. 125 In Germany, a steady
decrease in FeLV prevalence from 6% to 1% was observed when
investigating the FeLV infection rate from 1993 to 2002. 101 A
study from Swi erland found a decrease from 9% to 3% in FeLV
prevalence between 1990 and 2003. 126 The decrease in prevalence
is most likely the result of test and removal programs at breeding
facilities, the practice of testing cats at animal shelters before
adoption, and the widespread use of vaccination. However, in
more recent years, the prevalence of infection has plateaued. 101 ,
126 , 127

vetexamprep.ir

Models have been constructed to predict the dynamics of FeLV
infection in cat populations. These predicted that FeLV dynamics
depend on: (1) the size of the host population, and (2) the
relationship between host density and the pa ern of contacts of
individual cats. They found no threshold population size for virus
persistence in large populations but the possibility of FeLV
extinction in small populations. 128 A study that included a large
number of cats from the United States revealed a higher
prevalence of FIV infections in the southern and eastern United
States when compared to FeLV infection. In contrast, FeLV
infections were more prevalent in the western United States when
compared to FIV infections. 129 In a study of FeLV prevalence in 32
European countries, seven risk factors and three protective factors
were found. 110 Among the risk factors was the geographic origin
of the cat: FeLV prevalence was higher in southern countries
compared to northern and western parts of Europe. Other risk
factors included male intact sex, indoor and outdoor or outdooronly residence, living in large groups of ﬁve or more animals, and
being an ill cat. 110 Risk factors for FeLV and FIV infections are
only slightly diﬀerent. The prevalence of both infections is higher
in cats that roam outside 101 , 103 because direct contact is required
for transmission. Although ﬁghting, free-roaming, intact male cats
are still considered mainly at risk for acquiring FIV infection, the
same factors can facilitate FeLV infection. 101 , 110 , 130 However,
being male (neutered or not) and having access to the outdoors
has a stronger impact on FIV prevalence than on FeLV prevalence,
while presence of clinical illness is a stronger predictor for FeLV
infection. 129
Although FeLV transmission commonly occurs among infected
queens and ki ens and among cats living in prolonged close
contact, aggressive behavior plays a greater role than previously
reported. 131 Cats that exhibit aggressive behavior have a higher
risk of FeLV infection, 101 and more than 8% of cats examined by
veterinarians for ﬁghting injuries were FeLV antigen–positive in
one study, a prevalence considerably higher than in the clinically
healthy cat population. 131
Although no breeds are predisposed to being infected with
FeLV, infection is less commonly found in purebred cats, 110
possibly because they are more commonly kept indoors. In

vetexamprep.ir

addition, awareness in the cat-breeder community leads to
frequent testing. In older studies, young age was considered a risk
factor for FeLV infection. However, a study in the United States of
18,038 cats at 345 veterinary clinics and 145 animal shelters
revealed that adult cats were more likely to be FeLV-infected than
young cats. 103 In a study from Europe that included 6005 cats,
cats aged 1 to 6 years were at greatest risk. 110 In another study,
the median age of FeLV-infected cats was not lower than that of
uninfected cats. 101 This was unexpected because of the
phenomenon of age-related resistance to FeLV infection. 132 , 133
However, because of increased awareness, more cats are tested for
FeLV, FeLV infection is being recognized earlier, and medical care
is provided during the initial stage of the disease. In addition,
awareness among cat breeders and animal shelters has led to
routine testing of new pets entering the household or shelter.
A genetic predisposition might contribute to a susceptibility of
cats to FeLV infection. Analysis of single-nucleotide
polymorphisms (SNPs) in the APOBEC3H gene of domestic cats
showed that one of the SNPs was signiﬁcantly correlated with the
susceptibility to FIV and/or FeLV infections. 134
With few exceptions, FeLV prevalence studies are based on
detection of FeLV p27 antigen in blood. However, free antigen can
usually only be detected in the blood of viremic cats (in
progressively infected cats or in the early stage of regressive
infection, see Pathogenesis), because those with regressive
infections only harbor provirus, with no associated antigen
production. 135 In a study from Swi erland, 7% of cats had both
viral p27 antigen and provirus in blood, and 10% of cats had
negative results for p27 antigen and positive results for proviral
DNA in blood. 136 Comparable results were also found in a study
from Germany where the number of antigen-positive, proviruspositive cats was similar to the number of antigen-negative,
provirus-positive cats. 100

Transmission
FeLV spreads through close contact between virus-shedding cats
and susceptible cats. The transmission of FeLV occurs primarily
via saliva. Viremic cats constantly shed millions of virus particles

vetexamprep.ir

in saliva. 137 , 138 The concentration of virus in saliva and blood of
healthy viremic cats is as high as it is in sick cats. Fighting and
biting behavior, 101 , 131 as well as social behavior, such as sharing
food and water dishes, mutual grooming, and using common
li er areas, are the most eﬀective means of transmission of FeLV.
Although the virus can enter many tissues, body ﬂuids, and
secretions, urine and feces are less likely to be a source of infection
for other cats. However, FeLV is shed in small amounts in feces
and urine, 139 , 140 so fecal shedding of FeLV cannot fully be
excluded as a mode of transmission. 140 FeLV RNA has been
detected in ﬂeas and their feces, 141 , 142 but ﬂea transmission does
not seem to play a major role in nature. Iatrogenic transmission
can occur via contaminated needles, instruments, fomites, or
blood transfusions. 143 , 144
The viral envelope is lipid-soluble, and FeLV is readily
inactivated in the environment (usually within minutes, but
sometimes up to 48 hours). Therefore close contact among cats is
usually required for spread of infection. Single cats kept strictly
indoors are not at risk for acquiring infection. It is only because of
latency (in regressively infected cats) and reactivation that viremia
is occasionally detected in middle-aged to old cats that have lived
alone indoors since they were adopted as ki ens. A waiting
period is not needed before introducing a new cat into a
household after removal of an infected cat. FeLV transmission is
not a risk in a veterinary hospital or boarding kennel scenario as
long as cats are housed in separate cages, and routine cage
disinfection and hand washing are performed between handling
cats. 145
Vertical transmission from mother to ki ens occurs commonly.
Neonatal ki ens can be infected transplacentally or when the
queen has close contact with them. Transmission also can occur in
queens with regressive infection; FeLV transmission via milk to
oﬀspring from queens with FeLV antigen–negative test results has
been described. 146 If in utero infection occurs, fetal resorption,
abortion, and neonatal death can occur, although up to 20% of
vertically infected ki ens can survive the neonatal period to
become progressively infected adults. 123 Newborn ki ens from
infected queens can have negative FeLV antigen test results at
birth, but can test positive over subsequent weeks to months

vetexamprep.ir

when viral replication accelerates. Thus, if the queen or any ki en
in her li er is infected, the entire li er should be treated as if
infected and isolated from uninfected cats.
Susceptibility to progressive infection, which is associated with
persistent viremia and culminates in FeLV-associated disease, is
highest in young ki ens. It is more diﬃcult in adult cats to
achieve progressive infection after experimental infection, and
depending on the FeLV strain used, experimental infection does
not lead to progressive infection already in ki ens older than 16
weeks of age. 132 Age-related resistance to FeLV also exists in
nature. It has been suggested that age-related resistance might be
related to a decline in the number of cellular receptors (THTR1)
available for FeLV-A to enter target cells. Maturation of
macrophage function might also play a role. 147 Thus, the risk of
an adult cat becoming progressively infected after a brief
interaction with a FeLV-shedding cat is very low.

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
Although outcome of infection mainly depends on immune status
and age of the cat, it is also aﬀected by pathogenicity of the virus.
The outcome of FeLV infection thus also reﬂects genetic variation
both in the virus and the host population. Certain viral mutations
can increase the speed of disease onset, whereas others change
disease outcome entirely, and it has been suggested that LTR and
surface unit (SU) genes mediate a rapid pathogenesis with
distinctive clinical features and oncogenic mechanisms. 123
FeLV infection can have diﬀerent courses. Once integrated into
the cat genome, FeLV provirus can persist for years, and
recurrence of viremia and disease can occur in some cats. 148 , 149
However, integrated viral DNA can also elicit solid protection and
long-lasting maintenance of protective immunity. 150 The
currently accepted stages of FeLV infection are: (1) abortive
infection, (2) regressive infection, (3) progressive infection, and (4)
focal or atypical infection. 150-152
Although cats with only integrated proviral DNA without virus
replication do not shed infectious virus in saliva, proviral DNA
can be infectious via blood transfusion. 144 FeLV provirus and
plasma viral RNA are usually detectable by PCR within 1 week of
FeLV exposure, even if FeLV antigen is not. All cats with
progressive and regressive infection can undergo this phase and
develop similar proviral and plasma viral RNA loads in the
peripheral blood during early infection. 150 However, later in the
infection, proviral loads remain high in progressively infected cats
but decrease in regressively infected cats. 136
Abortive Infection
After initial infection, which most commonly occurs via oronasal
routes, virus replicates in the local lymphoid tissue in the
oropharyngeal area. In some immunocompetent cats, viral
replication is halted by an eﬀective humoral and cell-mediated
immune response, and viremia does not occur. 135 , 151 , 153-156
Abortive infection has been observed infrequently after
experimental FeLV inoculation with low inocula and is

vetexamprep.ir

characterized by negative test results for culturable virus, antigen,
viral RNA, and proviral DNA. 152 , 157 Thus, cats with abortive
infection have high levels of neutralizing antibody, but neither
FeLV antigen nor viral RNA or proviral DNA can be detected in
the blood. In these cats, virus never spreads systemically, and
infection usually remains undetected. Abortively infected cats
have the same life expectancy as cats that have never been
exposed to FeLV. 143 They have strong immunity and are
protected against new viral challenges, probably for several years
if not lifelong. Protective immunity is partly humoral and partly
cellular, and antibody production is not necessarily required for
protection; about 2% are protected without detectable antibodies.
Regressive Infection
Regressive infection follows an eﬀective immune response, with
containment of viremia before (or shortly after) the time of bone
marrow infection. After initial infection, FeLV spreads
systemically within lymphocytes and monocytes. 158 During this
period, cats have positive results on ELISA antigen tests and shed
virus. Cats can show lethargy, fever, or lymphadenomegaly
resulting from lymphocytic hyperplasia during this phase. The
virus spreads to target tissue, including thymus, spleen, lymph
nodes, and salivary glands. In most cats, viremia lasts only a few
weeks, but in some rare cases cats can overcome viremia even
after many months. 159 On the other hand, some regressively
infected cats are never antigen-positive.
In some cats, hematopoietic precursor cells in the bone marrow
then become infected and produce infected neutrophils and
platelets that circulate in the body. 158 , 160 A high level of viremia
develops, and lymphoid organs and salivary glands become
infected with up to 1 × 106 virus particles/mL of saliva. From this
time point on, viral antigen is also detectable intracellularly in
platelets and granulocytes by tests that detect large quantities of
intracellular antigen, such as IFA. Even if bone marrow becomes
infected, some cats can clear viremia (and develop regressive
infection); however, the longer the viremia lasts, the less likely it
will be contained. Once bone marrow cells are infected, cats will
remain provirus-positive because proviral DNA persists in bone
marrow stem cells. This has previously been referred to as “latent

vetexamprep.ir

infection” of the marrow, but is now considered a stage of
regressive infection. Once virus replication is contained, no intact
virus is actively produced, so cats with regressive infection have
negative results from routine tests (ELISA and IFA) that detect
FeLV antigen. Regressive infection can only be detected using
proviral PCR or culture of bone marrow samples in the presence
of high doses of glucocorticoids. Productive infection can be
reactivated spontaneously or with immune suppression with
viremia and therefore positive results on antigen tests. Regressive
infections can also reactivate in pregnancy, with reemergence of
FeLV infection in ki ens. Mammary glands of regressively
infected queens can produce infectious viral particles with onset
of lactation. 146
Reactivation is more likely the earlier the stress factor occurs
after the viremic phase. As time passes, regressive infections
become more diﬃcult to reactivate, even with high doses of
glucocorticoids. Nevertheless, regressively infected cats stay
provirus-positive and reactivation can take place many years after
infection. 148 , 154 In one SPF cat that had been experimentally
infected with FIV and FeLV, regressive FeLV infection occurred
and the cat remained aviremic for over 8 years. Subsequently, a
genetically altered FeLV virus reappeared with reactivation of
viremia. This coincided with the development of multicentric
lymphoma, likely because the immune system was by then,
severely depleted due to the FIV infection. 148
It is unclear how often regressive FeLV infection can result in
FeLV-related disease. One study found a high prevalence of
regressive infection in older cats at necropsy and suggested an
association with hematologic changes and inﬂammatory
processes. 161 In another study, two of 37 cats (5%) with
nonregenerative cytopenias and negative FeLV antigen test had
positive results with bone marrow provirus PCR. 162 FeLV
provirus can be detected occasionally in lymphomas of some
FeLV antigen–negative cats, 163-165 but a causative association has
not been made. Cats from FeLV cluster households had a 40-fold
higher incidence of FeLV antigen–negative lymphoma compared
to cats from the general population. Two studies reported that
regressive FeLV infections occurred in 50% to 52% of antigennegative lymphomas in older cats (> 7 years), 164 , 166 while other

vetexamprep.ir

groups found evidence of provirus in only 1 of 22, 167 in 1 of 10,166
and in 0 of 50 FeLV antigen–negative lymphomas 169 suggesting
that regressive infection is only rarely involved in tumor
development.
Integrated FeLV provirus has the potential to interrupt or
inactivate cellular genes in infected cells, or regulatory properties
of viral DNA can alter expression of neighboring genes. In
addition, because bone marrow microenvironment cells (e.g.,
myelomonocytic progenitor cells and stromal ﬁbroblasts) provide
a reservoir for regressive FeLV infections, provirus has the
potential to alter cellular functions and contribute to the
pathogenesis of myelosuppressive disorders. Finally, FeLV not
only contributes its genes to the host, but also has been shown to
appropriate (or “steal”) cellular genes, which could have the
potential to contribute to viral oncogenesis. 167 , 170 , 171
Replication-defective enFeLV can recombine with FeLV and thus
produce infectious oncogenic particles. However, using nextgeneration RNA-sequencing, no expression of FeLV has yet been
detected in feline tumor samples; in fact, there was even a
decreased expression of endogenous retrovirus genes in
lymphoma versus control specimens. 172
Progressive Infection
In cats with progressive FeLV infection, extensive virus replication
occurs, ﬁrst in the lymphoid tissues and then in the bone marrow
and in mucosal and glandular epithelial tissues in most infected
cats. 56 Mucosal and glandular infection is associated with viral
shedding, which persists for the life of the cat. Progressive
infection is characterized by insuﬃcient FeLV-speciﬁc immunity.
Progressively infected cats have low levels of detectable
neutralizing antibodies. 100 , 168 These cats usually develop FeLVassociated diseases that can be fatal.
Young and immunosuppressed cats are at higher risk for
developing progressive infection. In a cat with a ﬁrst-time single
contact with a FeLV-shedding cat, the risk of developing
progressive infection is less than 5%. However, if a shedding cat is
introduced into a naïve group of cats, and the cats are housed
together for an extended period, the risk increases to about 30%.
147

vetexamprep.ir

Regressive and progressive infections can be distinguished by
repeated testing for viral antigen in peripheral blood. 152 Many
infected cats initially have positive antigen test results within 2 to
3 weeks after virus exposure. In case of regressive infection, cats
will become negative in viral antigen tests 2 to 8 weeks later or, in
rare cases, months later. Both progressive and regressive
infections are almost always accompanied by persistent FeLV
proviral DNA in blood. However, FeLV proviral and viral RNA
loads in leukocytes, as analyzed by quantitative PCR, indicate that
FeLV progressive infection is associated with secondary viremia
of bone marrow origin, whereas regressive cats sustain only a
nonproductive viral infection in low numbers of lymphocytes. 173
During acute infection, blood proviral and viral RNA loads of cats
with progressive and regressive infections are not signiﬁcantly
diﬀerent, which, however, changes after weeks. 136 , 151 , 152
Subsequently, cats with progressive infections have higher virus
loads than cats with regressive infections, and virus loads within
speciﬁc leukocyte subsets diﬀer depending on the infection
outcome. 160
Focal or Atypical Infection
Focal infections or atypical infections have been reported as a rare
form of infection in both experimental and natural infections.
They are characterized by persistent atypical local viral replication
in certain tissues, such as the spleen, lymph nodes, small intestine,
or mammary glands. 146 , 174 This can lead to intermi ent or lowgrade production of p27 antigen. Therefore these cats can have
weakly positive or discordant results in antigen tests, or positive
and negative results can alternate. Queens with atypical infection
of their mammary glands can transmit the virus to their ki ens
via milk in the face of negative antigen test results. 146

Clinical Signs
Progressive infection with FeLV can result in tumors, hematologic
disorders, immunosuppression, immune-mediated diseases, and
other syndromes (including reproductive disorders, fading ki en
syndrome, and neuropathy). The death rate of progressively
infected cats in multicat households has been described as
approximately 50% in 2 years and 80% in 3 years. 23 , 123 However,

vetexamprep.ir

pp
y
y
y
survival time of progressively infected cats kept indoors in singlecat households with good veterinary care can be much higher.
Still, FeLV infection has the greatest impact on mortality in closed
households with mixed endemic viral infections. 100 , 175 A large
study in the United States compared the survival of more than
1000 FeLV-infected cats to more than 8000 age- and sex-matched
uninfected control cats 103 and found that in FeLV-infected cats,
median survival was 2.4 years compared to 6.0 years for control
cats.
Most cats with FeLV-associated disease are evaluated not for
tumors but for anemia or immunosuppression. Of 8642 FeLVinfected cats examined at US veterinary teaching hospitals,
coinfections (including FIP, FIV infection, upper respiratory
infection, hemotropic mycoplasmosis, and stomatitis) were the
most frequent ﬁndings (15%), followed by anemia (11%),
lymphoma (6%), leukopenia or thrombocytopenia (5%), and
leukemia or myeloproliferative disease (4%). 176
Disease expression can relate to virus factors, such as the FeLV
subgroup (e.g., FeLV-B is primarily associated with tumors, FeLVC is primarily associated with nonregenerative anemia), but
clinical outcome is also strongly inﬂuenced by the age of the cat at
the time of infection. 132 Neonatal ki ens can develop marked
thymic atrophy after infection (“fading ki en syndrome”),
resulting in severe immunosuppression, wasting, and early death.
As cats mature, they acquire resistance to infection. When older
cats become infected, they tend to have abortive or regressive
infections or, if they develop progressive infection, signs are
milder and they usually have a more protracted period of
apparent good health. 123
Tumors
FeLV infection is most commonly associated with lymphoma and
leukemia, and less commonly with other hematopoietic tumors. In
addition, unusual forms of lymphoma, such as feline
177
neurolymphomatosis
or
other

including
osteochondromas,

Feline oncornavirus cell membrane antigen (FOCMA) is an
antigen present on the surface of transformed cells. FOCMA can

vetexamprep.ir

be found on the surface of feline lymphoma and FeSV-induced
ﬁbrosarcoma cells but not on the surface of normal feline
lymphocytes. 178 , 179 Many cats with FeLV in cluster households
have antibodies against FOCMA. Those with the highest titers are
most likely to remain free of malignancies. However, some cats
that are viremic with a high FOCMA antibody titer can develop
lymphoma or leukemia months or years later after the titer
declined. 23 Currently, FOCMA is considered a nonhomogenous
group of viral antigens that can, although not always, be present
on the surface of FeLV-infected cells. At the least, FOCMA
antibodies indicate exposure to FeLV but since tests for the
detection of FOCMA are diﬃcult to establish and to standardize,
FOCMA is not considered to be of clinical value.
Lymphoma
Lymphomas and leukemias account for about 30% of all feline
tumors, the highest proportion recorded in any animal species. 180184 Progressively FeLV-infected cats have a 60-fold increased risk
of lymphoma. 185 Lymphoma can aﬀect up to 25% of cats with
progressive FeLV infection, usually within 2 years after diagnosis
of the infection. FeLV-induced lymphomas are mainly T-cell
lymphomas. 186 Mediastinal lymphoma is the most common form
(Fig. 32.2), followed by multicentric lymphoma, although spinal,
renal, ocular, and other forms of lymphoma are occasionally
reported in progressively FeLV-infected cats. 187 In the past,
young to middle-aged cats (median 7 years) were commonly
diagnosed with lymphoma, but lymphoma is now a disease of
mostly older cats with a median age of 11 years. 188 This also is
likely a result of the decreasing prevalence of progressive FeLV
infection as a contributing factor for development of lymphoma,
as cats with FeLV-associated lymphoma are usually younger than
cats with lymphoma without FeLV infection. 100 In addition, the
incidence of FeLV antigen–negative lymphomas increased from
approximately 18 cases per year before 1994 to approximately 32
cases per year from 1994 to 2003. 189

FIG. 32.2

In support of the association between FeLV infection and
lymphoma, lymphoma can be induced in ki ens by experimental
FeLV infection; 190-192 cats naturally infected with FeLV have a
higher risk of lymphoma than uninfected cats; 190 , 193 and in the
past, when the prevalence of FeLV infection was higher, most cats
with lymphoma had progressive FeLV infection. Previous studies
showed that up to 80% of feline lymphomas and leukemias were
FeLV-related. 194-197 A study conducted at a veterinary teaching
hospital in Germany showed that from 1980 to 1995, 59% of cats
with lymphoma were FeLV antigen–positive, but from 1996 to
1999, only 20% were positive. 188 In a study from the Netherlands,
only 4 of 71 cats with lymphoma were FeLV antigen–positive, and
22 of these cats had mediastinal lymphoma, which previously was
reported to be strongly associated with FeLV infection. 198
The most important mechanism for the development of
malignancy is insertion of the FeLV genome into the cellular
genome near a cellular oncogene (most commonly myc). This
results in activation and overexpression of that gene and
uncontrolled proliferation of these cells. FeLV can also incorporate

vetexamprep.ir

the oncogene to form a recombinant virus (e.g., FeLV-B, FeSV)
which contains cellular oncogene sequences that are then
rearranged and activated. When they enter a new cell, these
recombinant viruses are oncogenic. Thus, FeLV-induced
neoplasms are caused, at least in part, by somatically acquired
insertional mutagenesis in which the integrated provirus activates
a proto-oncogene or disrupts a tumor suppressor gene. In a study
of 119 cats with lymphoma, transduction (insertion into) the myc
locus had occurred in 38 cats (32%). 199 Transduction of the
NOTCH2 gene by FeLV was described in a naturally infected cat
with multicentric lymphoma. 200 Another study suggested that the
U3-LTR region of FeLV could transactivate cancer-related
signaling pathways through production of a noncoding 104-base
RNA transcript that activates NF-κ B. 201 Twelve common
integration sites for FeLV associated with lymphoma development
have been identiﬁed in six loci: c-myc, ﬂvi-1, ﬂvi-2 (contains bmi-1),
ﬁt-1, pim-1, and ﬂit-1. 202 C-myc is a proto-oncogene, bmi-1 and
pim-1 are myc-collaborators, ﬁt-1 appears to be closely linked to
myb, and ﬂit-1 insertion was associated with overexpression of
cellular genes, for example, activin-A receptor type II-like 1
(ACVRL1). 202 Flit-1 was identiﬁed as an important proviral
integration site. Of 35 FeLV-related tumors, 5 of 25 thymic
lymphomas had proviral insertion within the ﬂit-1 locus, whereas
none of four alimentary lymphomas, ﬁve of ﬁve multicentric
lymphomas, and one T-lymphoid leukemia had rearrangements
in this region. Some studies also show that variations in the FeLV
surface glycoprotein can determine the development of tumors.
203 In one study, oncogene-containing retroviruses were
experimentally generated by recombination events between viral
and cellular sequences, a phenomenon called “oncogene capture,”
and a novel FeLV virus “FeLV-AKT” was designed that captured
feline c-AKT1 in feline lymphoma. FeLV-AKT contains a gag-AKT
fusion gene that encodes a myristoylated Gag matrix protein and
the kinase domain of feline c-AKT1. It was therefore hypothesized
that AKT might be involved in FeLV-associated oncogenesis. 204
The predominant anatomical locations of lymphoma in cats in
general are alimentary (approximately 50%) and extranodal
(approximately 25%). 188 , 189 , 198 , 205 , 206 The majority of cats with
alimentary and extranodal lymphoma (mainly kidney and

vetexamprep.ir

nasopharyngeal) are now FeLV antigen–negative (96% and 89%,
respectively), 188 suggesting most cats have other underlying
etiologies, such as chronic inﬂammation or environmental and
genetic factors. Several decades ago, 25% to 31% of renal
lymphoma cases were associated with FeLV infection 195 , 206 , 207
compared with 0% to 6% in more recent studies. 163 , 188 , 198 , 208 A
similar situation is seen in multicentric lymphoma; in the 1980s
and 1990s, up to 69% of all lymphomas were multicentric, and
31% to 65% of these cats had progressive FeLV infection 164 , 195 ,
206 compared with 0% to 13% of cats in more recent studies. 163 ,
188 , 198 , 205 Mediastinal lymphoma is uncommon today (10%), 188
but many aﬀected cats still have progressive FeLV infection with a
prevalence ranging from 19% to 73%. 164 , 181 , 188 , 206 , 209 In a
study from the Netherlands, where the general prevalence of
FeLV was only 0.3%, 19% of cats with mediastinal lymphoma
were progressively FeLV-infected, but of cats with lymphoma, all
progressively infected cats had mediastinal lymphoma. 198 In a
UK study, 9% of cats with mediastinal lymphoma were
progressively FeLV-infected, which is higher than the general
prevalence. 210
The role of FeLV as a negative prognostic factor for lymphoma
patients with regard to remission and survival times is discussed
controversially, although more recent studies indicate a negative
impact of FeLV infection in cats with lymphoma. 198 , 206 , 207 , 211
FeLV antigen–negative cats with lymphoma had signiﬁcantly
longer remission times (472 days) than FeLV antigen–positive cats
(25 days) following treatment. 188 Median remission and survival
times for FeLV antigen–positive cats were 27 and 37 days,
respectively, and for FeLV antigen–negative cats, 146 and 170
days. 206 FeLV-associated lymphomas have a higher rate of
mitoses than those that are FeLV-negative, 212 possibly indicating
a more aggressive biological behavior that negatively aﬀects
outcome.
Leukemia
Leukemia in cats with FeLV infection most often involves
lymphocytes, but all other hematopoietic cell lines can be aﬀected,
including granulocytic, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lines,

vetexamprep.ir

resulting in myeloproliferative disease or MDS. The prognosis for
cats with myeloproliferative diseases in general is poor.
Diagnosis of acute leukemia is made by CBC and bone marrow
examination. Cytologic abnormalities of bone marrow include
increased cellularity, megaloblastic maturation, increased
myeloﬁbrosis, and immature blast cells. FeLV variants that bear
URE tandem repeats in their LTR can be associated with induction
of both MDS and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in cats. In one
study, experimental infection of cats with FeLV clone33
(originating from a cat with AML) resulted in MDS in 41% of the
cats, characterized by peripheral blood cytopenias and dysplastic
changes in the bone marrow. Some of the cats with MDS
eventually developed AML. 213
Chronic leukemias are rare in cats and sometimes associated
with FeLV. 214 , 215 They include well-diﬀerentiated chronic
lymphocytic
leukemia,
chronic
myelogenous
leukemia,
polycythemia vera, erythemic myelosis, and essential
thrombocythemia. Cats with erythemic myelosis have
nonregenerative or poorly regenerative anemia (12% to 15%) with
normal neutrophil counts and variable thrombocytopenia.
Abnormal erythrocyte stages are found in bone marrow and often
in peripheral blood. 216
Eosinophilic leukemia, polycythemia vera and essential
thrombocythemia in cats have also been reported in association
with FeLV infection. 217 , 218 Eosinophilic leukemia is diﬃcult to
distinguish from hypereosinophilic syndrome.
Fibrosarcoma
Fibrosarcomas that are associated with FeLV are caused by FeSV,
a recombinant virus that develops in FeLV-A-infected cats by
recombination of the FeLV-A genome with cellular oncogenes.
Through a process of genetic recombination, FeSV acquires one of
several oncogenes, such as fes, fms, or fgr. As a result, FeSV is an
acutely transforming virus, causing a polyclonal malignancy with
multifocal tumors arising simultaneously after a short incubation
period. With the decrease in FeLV prevalence, FeSV has become
very uncommon. FeSV-induced ﬁbrosarcomas usually occur in
young cats. Several strains of FeSV that have been identiﬁed from
naturally occurring tumors are defective. They are unable to
replicate without the presence of FeLV-A as a helper virus that

vetexamprep.ir

p
p
p
supplies proteins (such as those coded by the env gene) to FeSV.
The host range for FeSV depends on the helper FeLV-A.
Fibrosarcoma cells express FOCMA just as lymphoma cells do.
Experimental infection with FeSV causes tumors that progress in
some cats and regress in others. Those in which the tumors
regress have high FOCMA antibody titers. 219
Fibrosarcomas caused by various strains of FeSV tend to grow
rapidly, often with multiple cutaneous or subcutaneous nodules
that are locally invasive and metastasize to the lung and other
sites. Solitary ﬁbrosarcomas in old cats are typically injection-site
sarcomas and are not associated with FeSV or FeLV infection.
These tumors are slower growing, locally invasive, slower to
metastasize, and are occasionally curable by excision combined
with radiation and/or gene therapy.
Experimentally, FeSV has also been associated with melanoma
formation, showing that FeSV can transform cells of ectodermal
and of mesodermal origin. 22 Intradermal or intraocular
inoculation of FeSV into ki ens produced melanomas in the skin
or anterior chamber of the eye. 23 However, FeSV has not been
associated with naturally occurring melanomas of cats.
Other Tumors
A number of other tumors have been found in FeLV-infected cats,
but a link between FeLV infection and formation of these tumors
has not been clearly established. Iris melanomas, for example, are
not associated with FeLV infection as once was believed, as a
result of one study in which 3 of 18 eyes had positive test results
for FeLV-FeSV proviral DNA. 220 In a later study, however,
immunohistochemical staining and PCR did not reveal FeLV or
FeSV in the ocular tissues of any cats with iris melanomas. 221
One case report described a metastatic uterine adenocarcinoma
in a 2-year-old female Persian cat with progressive FeLV infection.
222 Osteochondromas (cartilaginous exostoses on ﬂat bones) have
also been described in FeLV-infected cats. Although histologically
benign, they can cause signiﬁcant morbidity if they put pressure
on adjacent tissues such as the spinal cord or nerve roots. 223-225
The pathogenesis of these osteochondromas is unknown.
Spontaneous feline olfactory neuroblastomas are aggressive,
histologically inhomogenous tumors of the nose and pharynx and

vetexamprep.ir

have high metastatic rates. Budding FeLV particles were found in
the primary tumors and lymph node metastases, and FeLV DNA
was found in tumor tissue. 226 Two of three cats described had
positive FeLV antigen test results. The exact role of FeLV in the
genesis of these tumors is uncertain. Cutaneous horns associated
with benign hyperplasia of keratinocytes have also been described
in FeLV-infected cats. 227
Hematologic Disorders
Hematologic disorders described in association with FeLV include
anemia (nonregenerative or regenerative); persistent, transient, or
cyclic neutropenia; panleukopenia-like syndrome; platelet
abnormalities
(thrombocytopenia
and
platelet
function
abnormalities); and aplastic anemia (pancytopenia) (Fig. 32.3).
Anemia
In older literature, it was estimated that more than two-thirds of
all nonregenerative anemias in cats were the result of FeLV
infection. This is no longer the case because of the decrease in
overall FeLV prevalence. In a 2009 study of 79 anemic cats, FeLV
was found in only two cats, both of which had hemolytic anemia.
228 Approximately 10% of FeLV-associated anemias are
regenerative. 229 Regardless of the cause, regenerative FeLVassociated anemias usually have a favorable response to
treatment. Most FeLV-associated anemias, however, are
nonregenerative and result from infection of hematopoietic stem
cells and supporting stroma cells. In addition to the direct eﬀect of
the virus on erythropoiesis, secondary disorders can cause
nonregenerative anemia in FeLV-infected cats.
Several mechanisms contribute to anemia in FeLV-infected cats
(Table 32.3). Hemolytic anemia caused by secondary infection
with hemotropic mycoplasmas can occur in FeLV-infected
immunosuppressed cats. FeLV-induced IMHA also has been
described. Aﬀected cats can have positive Coombs’ tests,
autoagglutination, and spherocytosis. In a study on IMHA in cats,
2 of 19 cats had positive FeLV antigen test results. 230 However, in
another study, Coombs’ positive results in cats with anemia were
not signiﬁcantly associated with retrovirus or hemoplasma
infection. 231 Regenerative anemia secondary to blood loss can

vetexamprep.ir

occasionally
occur
as
a
result
of
FeLV-associated
thrombocytopenia or platelet functional defects.
Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a severe, nonregenerative
anemia (hematocrit [HCT] < 15%). It can be caused by infection
with FeLV-C through interactions of FeLV-C with cell surface
receptors in the bone marrow. 232 , 233 Bone marrow examination
shows an almost complete lack of erythroid precursors with
normal myeloid and megakaryocytic precursors and an increased
myeloid-erythroid ratio. 23 , 123 These cats typically have
macrocytosis (rarely normocytosis) but no or few reticulocytes.
Whenever macrocytic anemia occurs in a cat in the absence of
reticulocytosis, FeLV infection should be suspected. The
macrocytosis results from skipped mitoses during erythropoiesis.
These cats do not have folate or vitamin B12 deﬁciencies. Iron is
present in macrophages but not erythrocyte precursors. Serum
erythropoietin (EPO) levels are markedly increased, indicating
that anemia is not caused by an EPO deﬁciency. 123 Treatment
with immunosuppressive drugs can result in resolution of anemia
within 3 to 5 weeks; however, relapse occurs when treatment is
discontinued. 234 An atypical presentation of PRCA in a 9-monthold, female, domestic longhair ki en with progressive FeLV
infection was reported. Histological examination of the bone
marrow revealed an almost complete absence of erythroid
precursor cells and mild to moderate myeloﬁbrosis. The cat also
had very unusual CNS defects. 235

Anemia of inﬂammatory disease can also contribute to anemia
in FeLV-infected cats, speciﬁcally in association with secondary
diseases. The HCT often increases spontaneously if the secondary
disease or comorbidity is treated successfully.
Hematopoietic tumors, including lymphoma or leukemia, as
well as opportunistic infectious agents, such as mycobacteria, can
cause anemia as a result of myelophthisis. Bone marrow
suppression with anemia can also result from MDS or
myeloﬁbrosis. Diagnosis of myeloﬁbrosis requires a bone marrow
core biopsy because aspiration is typically nondiagnostic.
Aplastic anemia can be present in FeLV-infected cats and is
characterized by aplasia of all cell lines with severe pancytopenia.
Bone marrow is usually hypocellular or can show necrosis
cytologically. 236 Cats with pancytopenia often had positive test
results for FeLV antigen in earlier times, but in a study of 13 cats
with aplastic anemia from 1996 to 2004, only two were FeLV
antigen–positive. 237 In FeLV-infected cats, cyclic hematopoiesis
with periodic ﬂuctuation in reticulocytes, granulocytes, and
platelets can be seen. FeLV can aﬀect bone marrow accessory cell
viability, growth, production, or all of these of hematopoietic

vetexamprep.ir

progenitor growth-regulating substances by altering cytokine
mRNA levels. 238-240 Cytologic examination of bone marrow
aspirates reveals few precursors, and core biopsy specimens
might be needed to obtain a diagnosis. Bone marrow
transplantation has not been successful in these cats, but some
respond to immunosuppressive drug therapy.

Platelet abnormalities
Thrombocytopenia can occur as a result of FeLV-induced bone
marrow suppression or hematopoietic tumors. Immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia can accompany IMHA in cats with underlying
FeLV infection. The life span of platelets is shortened in some
FeLV-infected cats. Giant platelets and thrombocytosis have been
observed in some progressively infected cats. 229
White blood cell abnormalities
FeLV can reduce leukocyte numbers and function. 241-243
Lymphopenia is seen in many cats with progressive FeLV
infection. Aﬀected cats can develop thymic atrophy and depletion
of lymph node paracortical zones. In some cats, lymphopenia is
characterized by preferential loss of CD4+ helper T cells, resulting
in an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio. 244 More commonly, substantial
losses of helper cells and cytotoxic suppressor cells (CD8+ cells)
occur, 245 and in long-term FeLV infection, a signiﬁcant decrease
in both CD4+ and, to a lesser degree, CD8+ lymphocytes was
demonstrated. 246
Neutropenia is common in FeLV-infected cats 247 and generally
occurs alone or in conjunction with other cytopenias. In some
cases, myeloid hypoplasia of all granulocytic stages is observed,
suggesting direct cytopathic infection of neutrophil precursors. In

vetexamprep.ir

some neutropenic FeLV-infected cats, bone marrow maturation
arrest can occur at the myelocyte and metamyelocyte stages. It has
been hypothesized that an immune-mediated mechanism might
be responsible in cases in which neutrophil counts recover with
glucocorticoid
treatment
(“glucocorticoid-responsive
neutropenia”). Glucocorticoid-responsive cyclic neutropenia also
has been reported. The cycles are usually regular, ranging from 8
to 14 days. Bone marrow cytology during the neutropenic phase
can indicate either granulocytic hyperplasia or hypoplasia, with a
disproportionate number of cells in the promyelocytic stage. Cats
with neutropenia commonly have recurrent fever or persistent
bacterial infections, and some cats have persistent gingivitis.
Neutrophils of progressively infected cats can also have decreased
chemotactic and phagocytic function. 241
Feline panleukopenia-like syndrome (FPLS) or FeLV-associated
enteritis (FAE) consists of severe leukopenia (fewer than 3000
cells/µL) and enteritis and destruction of intestinal crypt
epithelium that mimics feline panleukopenia caused by FPV. This
syndrome might actually not be caused by FeLV alone, as initially
thought, but by coinfection with FPV. 248 FAE is the preferred
term because clinical signs are usually enteric, and include
hemorrhagic diarrhea, vomiting, oral ulceration or gingivitis,
anorexia, and weight loss. 249 , 250
Immunosuppression and Secondary Infections
Diseases secondary to immunosuppression account for a large
portion of the morbidity and mortality of FeLV-infected cats. 251254 Progressively FeLV-infected cats are predisposed to secondary
infections primarily because of immunosuppression similar to
that in HIV infection, but immunosuppression is more severe than
that associated with FIV infection.
The exact mechanisms by which FeLV damages the immune
system
are
poorly
understood.
Speciﬁc
pathogenic
immunosuppressive variants, such as FeLV-T, have been
described that require a membrane-spanning receptor molecule
(Pit1) and a second co-receptor protein (FeLIX) to infect T
lymphocytes. 48 The la er protein is expressed from an
endogenous provirus arising from FeLV-A, which is similar to the
FeLV receptor-binding protein of FeLV-B. 46 Aﬀected cats can

vetexamprep.ir

develop thymic atrophy and depletion of lymph node paracortical
zones after infection.
Reduced leukocyte numbers and function associated with
infection also contribute to immunosuppression. Many immune
function tests of naturally FeLV-infected cats have been reported
to be abnormal, including poor response to T-cell mitogens,
prolonged
allograft
reaction,
reduced
immunoglobulin
production, depressed neutrophil function, and complement
depletion. Interleukin (IL)-2 and IL-4 are decreased in some cats,
123 , 239 but FeLV does not appear to suppress IL-1 production
from infected macrophages. Increased TNF-α levels have been
observed in serum of FeLV-infected cats as well as in FeLVinfected cells in culture. T cells of FeLV-infected cats produce
lower levels of B-cell stimulatory factors than do those of
noninfected cats, which becomes progressively more severe over
time. 251
Primary and secondary humoral antibody responses to speciﬁc
antigens are delayed and decreased in FeLV-infected cats.
Progressively FeLV-infected cats do not consistently mount an
adequate immune response to vaccines, such as rabies. 255
Therefore a need for more frequent vaccinations (e.g., yearly) has
been suggested for these cats.
There are many reports of FeLV-infected cats with concurrent
bacterial, viral, protozoal, and fungal infections (Fig. 32.4), but
there is li le evidence to demonstrate that FeLV-infected cats have
a higher prevalence of infections than cats without FeLV infection,
or that response to anti-infective therapies are less eﬀective in
FeLV-infected cats. Thus, although FeLV is capable of causing
immunosuppression, it should not be assumed that all concurrent
infections in FeLV-infected cats result from the underlying FeLV
infection. Secondary diseases that can be associated with FeLV
include FIP, coccidiosis, and feline upper respiratory tract disease.
256 , 257 A few studies have focused on the role and the inﬂuence of
FeLV infection on hemoplasma infection with controversial
results, because in some studies, FeLV infection was a risk factor
for hemoplasma infection, 258-261 whereas in other studies it was
not. 262-265 Cats that were naturally infected with FeLV were more
likely to develop and not eliminate Bartonella henselae infection;
however, the course and clinical outcome of Bartonella infection

vetexamprep.ir

was the same as in cats not coinfected with FeLV. 261 , 263 , 266 , 267
No association is generally found between FeLV infection and
feline leishmaniosis 268-270 with the exception of one study, where
the presence of Leishmania spp. antibodies and DNA was
signiﬁcantly associated with FeLV infection. 271 No association
was found with ricke sial infections 272 or sporotrichosis in cats in
Brazil. 273

Skin infections occur in some FeLV-infected cats. Progressively
FeLV-infected cats have a greater diversity of cutaneous and
mucosal microﬂora compared with uninfected cats, 274 and
infections associated with dermatologic conditions are usually
caused by immunosuppression. 275 Traumatic injuries can be
complicated by secondary bacterial infections or abscesses. Otitis
externa and miliary dermatitis can be initiated by ectoparasites or
allergies but persist because of secondary bacterial infections.
Most studies have not found an association between chronic
gingivostomatitis and progressive FeLV infection, 276 , 277 although
one study showed that cats with any oral inﬂammatory disease
were more likely to be infected with FeLV than cats with healthy
oral cavities. 278 One study investigated biopsy samples of oral
mucosal biopsies of 27 cats with chronic gingivostomatitis and
detected FeLV antigens by immunohistochemistry in the
epithelium and inﬂammatory inﬁltrate of 29.6% of cats. FIV
antigens were identiﬁed only in one, and FCV antigens in none of
the cats using immunohistochemistry. 279
Immune-Mediated Diseases
FeLV-infected cats can have immune-mediated diseases caused by
an overactive or dysregulated immune response to the virus.
Although humoral immunity to speciﬁc stimulation decreases in
FeLV-infected cats, nonspeciﬁc increases of IgG and IgM have
been noted. The loss of T-cell activity and the formation of
antigen-antibody complexes contribute to immune dysregulation.
280 Antigens that can form antigen-antibody complexes include
those associated with whole virus particles as well as free gp70,
p27, or p15E proteins. 281 , 282 Immune-mediated diseases
230
described in FeLV-infected cats include IMHA,

vetexamprep.ir

glomerulonephritis, 283 uveitis, 284 , 285 and polyarthritis. 227 A
chronic polyarthritis syndrome can also be caused by FFV, and
concurrent FIV infection can occur in either instance. 286 Although
hyperglobulinemia is often associated with immune-mediated
disorders, it does not appear to be more prevalent in progressively
infected cats when compared with FIV-infected cats. 287
Hyperproteinemia is not signiﬁcantly more prevalent in
progressively infected cats than in uninfected cats, whereas FIVinfected cats are more likely than uninfected cats to display
hyperglobulinemia. 280-282 , 287 , 288
Other Syndromes
Other syndromes directly associated with FeLV infection include
FeLV-associated neuropathy, reproductive disorders, and fading
ki en syndrome.
Neuropathies
Neurologic dysfunction has been described in FeLV-infected cats.
Most neurologic signs are associated with lymphoma and
lymphocytic inﬁltrations of the brain or spinal cord, or secondary
infectious diseases such as cryptococcosis, toxoplasmosis, FIP, or
unusual diseases such as encephalitozoonosis or listeriosis. 289
However, in some cases an underlying cause is not apparent, even
after necropsy. Anisocoria, mydriasis, central blindness, Horner’s
syndrome, or urinary incontinence caused by myelopathy 290 have
been described in progressively FeLV-infected cats without
morphologic changes. It is possible that FeLV has direct
neurotoxic properties. Envelope glycoproteins of retroviruses can
stimulate increased intracellular free calcium leading to neuronal
death, as described in HIV-infected humans. A polypeptide of the
FeLV envelope was found to cause dose-dependent neurotoxicity
associated with alterations in intracellular calcium ion
concentration, neuronal survival, and neurite outgrowth. The
polypeptide of a FeLV-C strain was signiﬁcantly more neurotoxic
than the same peptide derived from a FeLV-A strain. 291 , 292
Clinical signs in 16 cats with progressive FeLV infection and
neurologic signs consisted of abnormal vocalization,
hyperesthesia, and paresis progressing to paralysis. Some cats
develop anisocoria or urinary incontinence during the course of

vetexamprep.ir

their illness. Others have concurrent FeLV-related problems, such
as myelodysplastic disease. Microscopically, white-ma er
degeneration with dilation of myelin sheaths and swollen axons
has been identiﬁed in the spinal cord and brainstem of aﬀected
animals. 290 Immunohistochemical staining of aﬀected tissues
revealed consistent expression of FeLV p27 antigens in neurons,
endothelial cells, and glial cells, and proviral DNA was ampliﬁed
from multiple sections of the spinal cord. 290
Reproductive disorders
FeLV-infected queens can transmit the virus transplacentally.
Fetal resorption, abortion, and neonatal death can occur if in utero
FeLV infection occurs. Apparent infertility is likely caused by
early resorption of fetuses. Abortions usually occur late in
gestation, with expulsion of normal-appearing fetuses. Bacterial
endometritis can accompany abortions, particularly in cats with
neutropenia. 23
Fading kitten syndrome
Ki ens born to infected queens can become exposed to FeLV
transplacentally, but exposure also occurs at birth and throughout
the nursing period. Some ki ens become immune, but most
become progressively infected and die at an early age with fading
ki en syndrome, characterized by failure to nurse, dehydration,
hypothermia, thymic atrophy, and death usually within the ﬁrst 2
weeks of life. 123

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in cats with progressive FeLV
infection vary dramatically depending on the stage of infection
and the secondary disease process present. 293 , 294 There might be
no abnormalities, or cats can show signs of lethargy, fever,
mucosal pallor, petechial hemorrhages, dehydration, peripheral
lymphadenomegaly,
thin
body
condition,
stomatitis,
subcutaneous abscesses, or upper respiratory tract disease.
Anemic cats can have a hemodynamic heart murmur, tachypnea,
or tachycardia, or can be icteric. Cats with severe anemia can be
laterally recumbent or comatose and hypothermic. Cats with
thymic lymphoma can be tachypneic and have decreased lung

vetexamprep.ir

and cardiac sounds on thoracic auscultation as a result of pleural
eﬀusion, or heart sounds can be displaced caudally. Decreased
compressibility of the cranial thorax can also be detected.
Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, renomegaly, intestinal masses,
and/or abdominal lymph node enlargement can be detected on
abdominal palpation of cats with multicentric lymphoma.
Neurologic signs are detected infrequently when compared with
signs of anemia or thoracic or abdominal lymphoma and include
ataxia, anisocoria, and mydriasis. Although also relatively
uncommon, uveitis can be identiﬁed, or there might be other
ocular abnormalities as a result of intraocular lymphoma or
coinfections with other pathogens. 293-295

Diagnosis
General Statement about Diagnostic Tests
Testing for FeLV and consequently preventing exposure of healthy
cats to FeLV-infected cats is the most eﬀective way to prevent the
spread of infection. 296 , 297 FeLV vaccination should not be
considered a substitute for testing. The European Advisory Board
on Cat Diseases (ABCD) and AAFP have established guidelines
for testing cats for FeLV. 297 According to these guidelines, the
FeLV status of all cats should be known, because the infection has
serious health consequences that inﬂuence patient management,
both in illness and for wellness care. Failure to identify infected
cats can lead to inadvertent exposure and transmission to
uninfected cats. Misdiagnosis of infection in uninfected cats can
lead to unnecessary changes in lifestyle or even euthanasia. 297
When bringing a new cat into an established household, a followup antigen test should be performed at least 90 days after the
initial test or after a possible exposure to FeLV because cats could
be in the early stage of infection at the time of the ﬁrst test; and
this test should be performed before bringing the cat into the
home. 298
Cats can be tested at any age (Fig. 32.5), because screening tests
detect antigen and not antibodies, so neither maternal antibodies
nor antibodies from vaccination interfere with testing. However,
ki ens that are infected as a result of maternal transmission might
not test positive for weeks to months after birth. 299 It has been

vetexamprep.ir

suggested that blood collected immediately after vaccination
could contain detectable FeLV antigens from the vaccine itself, so
diagnostic samples should be collected before FeLV vaccine
administration. 300 It is not known how long this test interference
persists. Cats can require retrovirus testing at diﬀerent times in
their lives. 297

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
The CBC in progressively FeLV-infected cats can be normal or
show regenerative or nonregenerative anemia, neutropenia,
lymphopenia,
monocytopenia,
and/or
thrombocytopenia.
Evidence of agglutination can be present in cats with IMHA.
Moderate to marked leukocytosis due to neutrophilia and
bandemia can also be present. Large numbers of circulating blasts,
megakaryocytes, or dysplastic cells (such as erythrocytes with
giant Howell-Jolly bodies) can be found in cats with leukemia or
MDS. When compared to uninfected cats, progressively FeLV-

vetexamprep.ir

infected cats were nearly fourfold more likely to be anemic,
ﬁvefold more likely to be thrombocytopenic, fourfold more likely
to be neutropenic, and threefold more likely to have
lymphocytosis. 288
Serum Chemistry Profile
Findings on serum biochemistry analysis and urinalysis are
nonspeciﬁc and reﬂect underlying secondary disease processes.
Hyperbilirubinemia and bilirubinuria can be present in cats with
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia or hemoplasma infection. 288
Urinalysis
Cats with glomerulonephritis can be proteinuric. Bacteriuria may
be identiﬁed in cats with urinary tract infections secondary to
immunosuppression.
Bone Marrow Cytology and Histopathology
Both bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy specimens should be
obtained in cats with pancytopenia or severe nonregenerative
anemia. If aspirate results are not diagnostic, a core biopsy should
be collected, because bone marrow aspirates from cats with
aplastic anemia or myeloﬁbrosis are typically of low cellularity.
Bone marrow ﬁndings in cats with progressive FeLV infection can
include evidence of neoplastic lymphoid, erythroid, or myeloid
cells (which circulate in the peripheral blood of cats with
leukemia); myelodysplasia; hypoplasia or aplasia of erythroid,
myeloid, or megakaryocyte cell lines; erythroid, myeloid, and
megakaryocyte hyperplasia despite peripheral cytopenias; and
megakaryocyte hypoplasia. Cytochemical stains that identify cells
of the myeloid lineage (such as alkaline phosphatase, peroxidase,
Sudan black B, and nonspeciﬁc esterase), immunocytochemistry,
or ﬂow cytometry using antibodies that target cell surface cluster
of diﬀerentiation (CD) molecules might be needed to deﬁnitively
identify the cell type involved in some acute undiﬀerentiated
leukemias. 295

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiographs

vetexamprep.ir

Imaging ﬁndings in cats with FeLV infection can reﬂect a
secondary disease process and are extremely variable. Cats with
FeLV-associated thymic lymphoma have a mediastinal mass on
thoracic radiography that can be accompanied by mild to severe
pleural eﬀusion.
Sonographic Findings
Abdominal sonography in cats with multicentric lymphoma can
reveal hypoechoic and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes and
enlargement; or hypoechogenicity, or mo ling of the spleen, liver,
or kidneys. Increased hepatic echogenicity can occur with liver
lymphoma. Intestinal masses with loss of normal bowel wall
layering can be detected in cases of intestinal lymphoma.
Splenomegaly can sometimes be found in cats with immunemediated cytopenias.

Microbiologic Tests
For diagnosis of FeLV infection, usually direct organism detection
assays are preferred (Table 32.4). Routine tests are available that
detect free FeLV p27 antigen in blood. Free FeLV antigen can be
detected by ELISA or other immunochromatographic assays
(ICGAs). Cell-bound antigen can be detected by IFA. Nucleic acid
ampliﬁcation assays can be used to detect FeLV DNA (provirus)
or viral RNA, and virus isolation to demonstrate viable virus
particles can also be performed in specialized laboratories.
Detection of antibodies is necessary for demonstration of abortive
infection. The presence of antibodies also can indicate protection
against new infection. Table 32.5 shows the results of diﬀerent
diagnostic tests at diﬀerent stages of FeLV infection.
In practice, diagnosis of FeLV infection is usually based on
detection of FeLV p27 antigen. When also obtaining results for
proviral DNA, progressively and regressively infected cats are
detected, but not cats with abortive infections.
