Detection of FeLV Antigen
The mainstay of clinical testing for FeLV are ELISAs and other
immunochromatography or rapid immunomigration assays,
which are available for use as plate-based ELISAs or rapid POC
tests. Plate-based ELISAs are oﬀered by commercial veterinary
diagnostic laboratories. IFA testing for viral antigen is still in use

vetexamprep.ir

in some countries. 301 All of these assays detect free FeLV core
protein p27, but POC assays and plate-based ELISAs are more
sensitive than IFAs (the la er detects only intracellular antigen, so
becomes positive later than ELISA, once the bone marrow has
become infected). Cats with a positive POC test or plate-based
ELISA and a negative IFA result are more likely to later develop a
regressive infection than are cats with positive results on both
assays. In general, to distinguish between regressive and
progressive infection, cats should be retested for free p27 antigen
6 weeks after the ﬁrst positive test result. If the result is still
positive, the test should be repeated after another 6 weeks. If at
this time the cat remains positive, it is most likely progressively
infected and will develop FeLV-associated disease. To avoid the
need for serial retesting, cats positive for FeLV free p27 antigen
can be immediately retested using IFA. More than 90% of cats
with positive IFA results have progressive infection. 181 , 301-304 A
small number of cats with persistently positive ELISA and
negative IFA results can have focal or atypical infections that are
contained by the immune system. 303 A negative ELISA but
positive IFA always represents either a false-negative ELISA result
(which is rare) or a false-positive IFA result.
Plate-based ELISAs and POC assays
POC tests are the recommended screening tests for FeLV infection.
A positive whole blood, serum, or plasma POC test or plate-based
ELISA usually indicates that the cat is viremic. These assays
usually become positive within 28 days after exposure, in the ﬁrst
phase of viremia, before the bone marrow is aﬀected. Thus,
positive results can reﬂect transient viremia (in cats becoming
regressively infected) or persistent viremia (in progressively
infected cats). However, false-positive results are possible,
especially when whole blood is used on plate-based ELISAs and
some POC tests (that are based on an ELISA principle, such as the
SNAP [IDEXX Laboratories]), and particularly when samples are
hemolyzed. Thus, plasma or serum should be used with platebased ELISAs and the SNAP (IDEXX Laboratories).
Immunochromatography-based POC tests contain a ﬁltering
membrane, so whole blood and serum/plasma do not produce
diﬀerent results. 305 Membrane-based tests eliminate separate
washing steps and include positive and negative controls for each

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
p
g
test sample. Several comparisons of diﬀerent POC tests have been
performed. 305-310 It is diﬃcult to compare these studies because
gold standards diﬀer and tests with similar names can diﬀer
among countries or from one time period to the next. However, in
general, sensitivities and speciﬁcities of diﬀerent tests have been
similar. Positive predictive values of most tests in those
comparison studies were between 50% and 80%, whereas negative
predictive values were close to 100%. 308 False-positive results are
becoming more common because the decreasing prevalence of
FeLV infection is leading to lower positive predictive values. Thus,
in cat populations with a high prevalence of infection, for
example, cats with thymic lymphoma, a positive test result is
likely to be accurate, whereas in a lower-risk population, such as a
population of indoor cats from single-cat households, a positive
test should be viewed with more suspicion, and conﬁrmatory tests
should be performed, for example using a POC test from a
diﬀerent manufacturer or a provirus PCR assay. 123 Therefore in
general, negative test results are reliable because of the low
prevalence of infection in most populations, but positive results
have to be interpreted carefully. If a second conﬁrmatory test is
positive, this signiﬁcantly increases the predictive value. 305 POC
tests or plate-based ELISAs have been also used on tear and saliva
specimens; 311 however, this is not recommended because antigen
shedding with saliva and tears is intermi ent.
IFA
IFA on smears from blood or bone marrow detect cell-associated
p27 antigen within infected blood cells, primarily neutrophils, and
platelets. The earliest the test becomes positive after infection of
the bone marrow is at about 3 weeks of viremia. IFA is not
recommended as a screening test because cats in the ﬁrst weeks of
viremia that are already shedding virus and capable of
transmi ing infection are not detected. IFA can be used for
prognostic reasons or to conﬁrm positive and suspicious ELISA
results. IFA requires special processing and ﬂuorescent
microscopy and must be performed by a qualiﬁed reference
laboratory. Generally, two or more blood smears of good quality
should be air-dried and mailed, unﬁxed, to the laboratory. As
antigen is present at highest concentrations in neutrophils and

vetexamprep.ir

platelets, false-negative results can occur when these two cell lines
are deﬁcient. False-positive results occur when smears are too
thick, background ﬂuorescence is high, or the test is prepared and
interpreted by inexperienced personnel. Use of anticoagulated
blood rather than fresh blood for preparing smears can also cause
errors. 312 , 313 Variations in quality control among facilities have
been reported, and careful a ention should be paid to the
selection of the reference laboratory. 123
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR detects proviral DNA (integrated into the cellular genome of
the cat), while RT-PCR detects viral RNA (of free replicating
virus). PCR and RT-PCR can be performed on blood, saliva, bone
marrow, and tissues. When performed under optimal conditions,
PCR methods are the most sensitive tests for FeLV diagnosis and
can help resolve cases with discordant antigen test results.
However, they must be performed by experienced laboratories
and should be well validated. Minor alterations in sample
handling by laboratory personnel can destroy nucleic acid or
introduce contamination, leading to either false-negative or falsepositive results, respectively. There are no comparative studies of
the diagnostic accuracy of various commercial laboratories
oﬀering FeLV PCR. Assays usually target conserved regions of the
FeLV genome, but diﬀerent PCR assays can vary in their analytical
sensitivity and speciﬁcity. Minor strain variations can prevent
binding of the primers, a step necessary to amplify the viral
genome. Moreover, primers and probe must be designed to
distinguish endogenous FeLV-like sequences from exogenous
FeLV infection.
Quantitative real-time PCR and RT-PCR assays can be used to
quantify provirus and viral RNA loads, respectively. 15 , 136 , 158 ,
314-318 A clinically validated quantitative PCR assay is now
available commercially (IDEXX Laboratories) that can help to
ascertain whether a cat is progressively or regressively infected.
318

PCR for detection of FeLV DNA
An important indication for performing proviral PCR on whole
blood is to conﬁrm a positive ELISA result, especially in low-

vetexamprep.ir

prevalence populations. True-positive ELISA results are
accompanied by high proviral loads. 136 , 319 In early infection,
provirus PCR is positive earlier than antigen detection. Moreover,
provirus PCR is useful to detect regressively infected cats, and
prove absence of FeLV in a multicat environment, such as
breeding colonies and ca eries. Approximately 2% to 10% of cats
with negative antigen tests have been positive for FeLV provirus
by PCR. 100 , 136 , 137 Most of these cats remain antigen-negative, do
not shed virus, and are unlikely to ever develop FeLV-associated
diseases, but some can reactivate and then shed FeLV and develop
FeLV-associated disease. 149 In addition, these cats can transmit
infection if they act as blood donors. 144
RT-PCR for detection of FeLV RNA
Most commercially available PCR assays for FeLV are based on
detection of proviral DNA rather than viral RNA. If performed on
blood (or serum or plasma), RT-PCR should always be positive
when ELISAs are positive, thus indicating progressive infection.
Cats with regressive infection are provirus-positive but most do
not possess detectable viral RNA in the blood. If performed on
blood (or serum or plasma), RT-PCR should always be positive
when ELISA tests are positive. However, in some cats, plasma
viral RNA can be found in the absence of FeLV antigen. In
contrast, detection of viral RNA in saliva generally indicates
viremia. 137 , 138 RT-PCR results from plasma and saliva can also
be helpful in the very early phase of infection. Viral RNA can be
detected in plasma or saliva by RT-PCR as early as 1 week after
FeLV exposure—earlier than antigen testing by ELISA and even
earlier than provirus PCR from blood. 139 , 319 RT-PCR in saliva
has also been used to screen multicat households for FeLV
shedders. Active salivary shedding as detected using RT-PCR was
consistent in antigenemic cats, whereas non-antigenemic cats with
a low proviral load did not shed viral nucleic acid in saliva. FeLV
RNA is stable for more than 60 days in saliva specimens stored at
room temperature, and in naturally infected cats, RT-PCR on
saliva had a high sensitivity and speciﬁcity when compared to
tests for antigen in blood. 100 , 137 , 138 If the cost of testing is a
limitation in a multicat environment, pooled saliva specimens
could be used for RT-PCR, as the assay can be suﬃciently

vetexamprep.ir

sensitive to detect a single infected cat in a pool of up to 30
specimens. 138
Virus Isolation
Virus isolation is not practical for routine diagnosis because it is
diﬃcult and time-consuming to perform and requires special
facilities. Where available, it can be used to conﬁrm positive test
results or to be er understand a cat’s infection status if other
assays generate conﬂicting results.
Indirect Detection of Infection
FeLV-infected cats develop antibodies against several viral
proteins. Recently, antibodies against the p15E protein have been
demonstrated to be valuable predictors of FeLV exposure, 313 and
now a new POC test detecting p15E antibodies is available in
several European countries, but its usefulness under ﬁeld
conditions still has to be determined. In a study assessing the
status of FeLV infection in the cat population of southern
Germany, many cats that had never received FeLV vaccines had
FeLV antibodies despite negative antigen and PCR test results,
and thus were thought to be abortively infected. 100 FeLV lowdose exposure can result in antibody production during an
abortive infection, with cats having anti-FeLV antibodies but no
detectable FeLV antigen or DNA. 140 , 157
Detection of antibodies is the only way to diagnose abortive
FeLV infection. Cats with abortive FeLV infection do not get sick
and will not shed the virus, and infection will not be reactivated.
However, these cats are considered immune against new
infection, and thus vaccination might not be necessary. Therefore
to avoid overvaccination and injection-site sarcoma formation,
tests for FeLV antibodies ultimately might be useful as
prevaccination screening tests. The connection between the
presence of antibodies and immunity, however, is not absolute,
because some vaccinated cats will not develop antibodies, 100 and
there will be cats that are protected against FeLV infection despite
the absence of detectable antibodies. 319-323

Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Most of the pathologic ﬁndings in FeLV-infected cats reﬂect
secondary infections or tumors. FeLV itself can sometimes lead to
lymph node, CNS, or bone marrow changes.
Gross Pathologic Findings
Gross and histopathologic ﬁndings in cats with progressive FeLV
infection usually reﬂect secondary disease processes. Lymphoma
and evidence of myelodysplasia or leukemias are the most
common ﬁndings, but secondary infections also can be detected.
Histopathologic Findings
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia is a common ﬁnding in cats with
progressive FeLV infection. Histology of the bone marrow can
reveal lymphoma, leukemias, or myelodysplasia. The intestinal
tracts of cats with FAE can show crypt cell necrosis and
regeneration, lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates, and blunting and
fusion of villi. 324 CNS lesions can include loss of axons and
dilated myelin sheaths within the spinal cord. 290
Immunohistochemical stains can be applied to tissues, such as
bone marrow or tumor tissue, to conﬁrm the presence of FeLV
antigen. 161 , 162 , 169 , 325

Treatment
General Management of FeLV-Infected Cats
Disease in cats that test positive for FeLV antigen can be related or
unrelated to FeLV infection. Management protocols for FeLV
antigen–positive cats must include the housemates of the FeLVinfected cat (Box 32.1). 297 , 326 , 327

Multicat households

• FeLV is mainly transmi ed through social contact, but also

Individual cat households
• FeLV-infected cats should be kept indoors to avoid
transmission of FeLV to other cats and to reduce their risk

• Vaccinations should be administered to FeLV-infected cats
according to guidelines for immunocompromised cats.

• Surgery is well tolerated, but perioperative antibiotic

hospitalized patients, but in individual cages. They should
not be placed in isolation.
• If FeLV-infected cats become sick, prompt identiﬁcation of
the secondary illness is essential to allow early therapeutic
intervention. Most cats with FeLV infection respond as well

as uninfected cats to appropriate medications, although a
longer and more aggressive course of therapy might be
needed.
• In general, the use of glucocorticoids or other
immunosuppressive drugs should be avoided unless
speciﬁcally indicated, e.g., for neoplastic or immunemediated disease.

FeLV-Infected Households
In households with one or more progressively FeLV-infected cats,
all cats should be tested for FeLV antigen and provirus so that
their status is known. It is likely that all cats in that household
have been exposed and are progressively, regressively, or
abortively infected. Cats with regressive or abortive infection are
likely protected against new FeLV infection. Naïve cats should not
be introduced, even if vaccinated. Shedding of virus generally
occurs through salivary glands, and cat-to-cat transmission can
occur by allogrooming, sharing of food and water bowls and li er
boxes, and ﬁghting and biting behavior. Cats within the
household that have negative FeLV antigen test results will tend
to outlive progressively infected cats. Therefore after months or
years, all remaining cats will be antigen-negative and immune to
new infection.
Individual FeLV-Infected Cats
FeLV-infected cats should be conﬁned indoors to reduce the
likelihood of secondary infections, but also to prevent spread of
FeLV to other cats in the neighborhood. Good nutrition and
husbandry are essential to maintain good health. Raw meat, eggs,
and unpasteurized milk should be avoided because of the risk of
acquiring foodborne bacterial or parasitic infections. 298
In progressively infected cats, wellness visits to the veterinarian
should occur at least semiannually. Visits should include a
detailed history, a thorough physical examination including
accurate body weight determination, and an ophthalmic
examination. In addition, a CBC, biochemistry proﬁle, urinalysis,

vetexamprep.ir

yp

and centrifugal fecal ﬂotation should be performed at least yearly.
Intact males and females should be neutered to reduce stress
associated with estrus and mating behavior and to decrease the
desire to roam outside. Surgery is generally well tolerated by
subclinically infected cats. Perioperative antibiotic administration
should be considered during surgeries and dental procedures. 297 ,

and to determine necessity to revaccinate in adult cats. If an

with known progressive or regressive FeLV infections because
these vaccines have no eﬀect on viremia, carrier state or
elimination, or on development of FeLV-associated disease in an
already infected cat and do not prevent reactivation of regressive
infection. 329

Treatment of FeLV-Associated Diseases
In most cases, secondary diseases in progressively FeLV-infected
cats are treated as is for uninfected cats, and respond in a similar
manner. 330 Prompt and accurate identiﬁcation of FeLV-associated
disease aids early intervention and a more successful outcome
(Box 32.2). Nevertheless, the owner should be forewarned that
response to treatment can sometimes take longer than expected.
FeLV itself does not cause fever, so a search for a concurrent
infection must be made in persistently febrile cats.
Glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive drugs should be
avoided whenever possible in FeLV-infected cats, unless clearly
indicated. These drugs might compound the risk of secondary
infections. Also, cats with regressive FeLV infection should not
receive glucocorticoid treatment because it increases the risk of
reactivation. Myelosuppressive drugs should also be avoided

vetexamprep.ir

because they can potentiate the myelosuppressive syndromes
caused by FeLV.
Tumors
Although the prognosis is worse for FeLV-associated tumors
when compared with the same tumors in cats testing negative for
FeLV, 198 , 206 , 331 , 332 some patients greatly beneﬁt from antitumor
therapy. Antitumor therapy should be applied with identical
protocols used in non–FeLV-infected cats. In an older report of 38
cats with lymphoma treated with a COP (cyclophosphamide,
vincristine, and prednisolone) protocol, 75% achieved complete
remission with a median remission duration of 150 days and a 1year remission rate of 20%. 333 The most frequent tumor in these
cats was mediastinal lymphoma, and most cats were
progressively infected with FeLV. In a later report, cats from the
same geographic area were treated with the same protocol and
had a complete remission rate of only 47%, with a median
remission duration of 86 days. 334 In this group, few cats were
progressively FeLV-infected, and the alimentary form of
lymphoma was the most frequent. 334 Cats with acute leukemia
are diﬃcult to treat because the bone marrow becomes ﬁlled with
neoplastic blast cells, which must be destroyed before the normal
hematopoietic precursors can repopulate. This process can take 3
to 4 weeks. The remission rate in cats with acute lymphocytic
leukemia treated initially with vincristine and prednisone is
approximately 25%, whereas the rate in cats with AML treated
with doxorubicin or cytosine arabinoside is close to zero. 23 A cat
with suspected FeLV-associated chronic lymphocytic leukemia
was successfully treated with a combination of prednisone,
chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and lomustine. 214
Secondary infections are common and must be treated quickly
and aggressively, especially if they occur at the time of the
granulocyte nadir. Although prophylactic antibiotics are not given
routinely in the treatment of leukemia or lymphoma, broadspectrum bactericidal antibiotics should be given to progressively
FeLV-infected cats receiving tumor therapy, especially if fever or
other signs of secondary infection occur.

FeSV-induced feline sarcomas should be treated early, with

Hematologic Disorders
Although hematologic disorders are sometimes irreversible in
progressively FeLV-infected cats, the course can be cyclic and
there can be some improvement with time. Treatment with blood
transfusions or bone marrow–stimulating cytokines should be
considered. Of 29 anemic (HCT < 20%) FeLV-infected cats treated
with blood transfusions (over 2 weeks), the HCT returned to the
reference range in eight cats. Glucocorticoid treatment can
increase the lifespan of erythrocytes if the anemia is immunemediated, and antibodies are present against erythrocytes or
precursors, and some cats with FeLV-associated nonregenerative
anemia respond well to high-dose prednisolone. Occasionally,
secondary infections (e.g., hemoplasma infections) are responsible
for the anemia, and these can be treatable. Even though EPO
concentrations are often elevated in cats with FeLV-related
anemia, treatment with recombinant human erythropoietin
(rHuEPO) or darbepoetin can be helpful. RHuEPO treatment not
only increases erythrocyte counts but also can increase platelet
and megakaryocyte numbers. 335 In a study in FIV-infected cats,
all rHuEPO-treated cats had a gradual increase in erythrocyte
counts, hemoglobin concentrations, and HCT and increased white
blood cell counts. 336 The recommended dose is 100 IU/kg SC q48
hours until the desired HCT (usually 30%) is reached and then as
needed to maintain the HCT at 30%. A response might not be seen
for 3 to 4 weeks, and if it does not occur, iron supplementation
might be required. Iron should not be given to cats that have
received transfusions because whole blood contains 0.5 mg/mL of
iron, which increases risk of hepatic hemosiderosis. Anti-EPO
antibodies can develop in 25% to 30% of rHuEPO-treated animals
after 6 to 12 months. Binding of these antibodies to native EPO
can result in bone marrow failure and refractory anemia.
However, anti-EPO antibodies dissipate after discontinuation of
treatment. Darbepoetin alpha is a synthetic EPO that possesses an
additional two N-linked oligosaccharide chains, and seems to be

vetexamprep.ir

less likely to induce production of anti-EPO antibodies in cats
than EPO.
Neutropenia can lead to severe immunosuppression, and
antibiotics can be necessary in some neutropenic cats to prevent
secondary bacterial translocation and development of sepsis.
Treatment with ﬁlgrastim (5 µg/kg SC q24h for up to 21 days) has
caused transient responses. Potential adverse eﬀects include bone
discomfort, splenomegaly, allergic reactions, and fever. 336 , 337
Short-term increases in neutrophil counts can be followed by
neutropenia with continued use of ﬁlgrastim because of
development of dose-dependent neutralizing antibodies to this
heterologous product after 10 days to 7 weeks. Thus, treatment
should not be used for more than 3 weeks. 336 , 337 Another risk is
development of persistent antibodies against endogenous feline
granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (at higher dosages), with
rebound neutropenia. One study suggested that ﬁlgrastim is
contraindicated in FIV-infected cats because it led to increased
viral load. 336 In a pilot study, a small number of naturally FeLVinfected cats were treated with ﬁlgrastim; however, treatment did
not result in signiﬁcant changes in neutrophil counts. 338 Other
authors reported that ﬁlgrastim has been used in FeLV-infected
cats with cyclic neutropenia with some success. 123 In some FeLVinfected cats, neutropenia is immune-mediated, and responds to
immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids. In animals with
myeloid hypoplasia and in the absence of myeloid precursors,
direct eﬀects of FeLV are suspected, and glucocorticoids should
not be used. Thus, bone marrow aspiration and cytology should
be performed before glucocorticoids are considered.

large controlled studies have been conducted in naturally infected
cats, and most of them have shown unclear or no beneﬁt. 339-342

series, other experimental studies, and dramatic results from uncontrolled
studies.
EBM grade IV = Expert opinion, case reports, studies in other species,
pathophysiological justification.
(Including EBM grades for judgment of the available efficacy data including
expert opinion of the authors.)

In general, human antiviral drugs used to treat cats have been
less active against FeLV when compared to FIV. Most human
antiviral drugs were developed for treatment of HIV infection,
which is more closely related to FIV infection. Many drugs
developed for humans, such as ribavirin, 343 , 344 have caused
unacceptable toxicity in cats. Drugs that have been used in cats
that were experimentally or naturally infected with FeLV include
zidovudine (AZT), zalcitabine, adefovir, and suramin. Zidovudine
has been administered to FeLV-infected cats with acceptable
toxicity, but there has been no clear beneﬁt on clinical outcomes.
The same was true for adefovir. Some drugs, such as gemcitabine
and tenofovir, have activity against FeLV in vitro, but their eﬃcacy
in vivo and toxicity in cats are so far unknown. The integrase
inhibitor raltegravir was highly active against FeLV in vitro. 344 ,
345 Raltegravir was administered at 40 mg q12h PO for 6.5 weeks,
and then 80 mg q12h PO for 2.5 weeks. The treatment reduced
viremia in each cat, with up to 1 log10 reduction in viral RNA in
four of seven cats, and the drug a ained therapeutic plasma
concentrations at both doses, with no adverse eﬀects noted.
However, viremia rebounded in all cats following drug removal.
347

Immunomodulators used to treat FeLV-infected cats have
included human IFN-α, feline IFN-ω, staphylococcal protein A,
Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), Serratia
marcescens extract, poxvirus preparations, acemannan,
levamisole, and diethylcarbamazine. Beneﬁts of most of these
drugs have not been clearly demonstrated (see Chapter 9), and
some, such as levamisole, are too toxic for routine use.

Prognosis
Survival times for cats with FeLV infection vary considerably
depending on the stage of infection, host immunity, and the strain
of FeLV involved. Some older studies suggested that FeLVinfected cats live a maximum of 3 years after diagnosis, but these
studies involved group-housed cats in multiple-cat FeLV-endemic
environments. With proper care, FeLV-infected cats can live much
longer than 3 years and, in fact, die at an older age from causes
unrelated to their retroviral infection. 348 Most cats that are
progressively infected with FeLV go on to develop FeLV-

vetexamprep.ir

associated disease within 5 years of diagnosis. 175 A comparison of
more than 800 progressively FeLV-infected cats and 8000 controls
revealed a median survival time of 2.4 years for progressively
FeLV-infected cats versus 6.3 years for controls. 300 Still, many
progressively infected cats, especially adult cats, can live for
several years with a good quality of life, and so euthanasia is not
recommended solely on the basis of a persistently positive FeLV
antigen test. Some cats with FeLV-associated lymphoma can have
long-term remissions when treated with standard chemotherapy
protocols. Proviral DNA load and p27 antigen concentration
correlated with survival in one longitudinal study, with cats
having both proviral DNA load and p27 antigen concentration
above cutoﬀ values of 4 × 105 copies/mL and 37.5 ng/mL,
respectively (“high positive” cats) having a median survival time
of 1.37 years from time of enrollment; in contrast, over 90% of
“low positive” cats were still alive at the end of the 4-year study.
318 In another study, cats with regressive infections also had
evidence of a stronger immune response to the FeLV SU
glycoprotein compared with cats in other outcome groups, as well
as having evidence of virus-neutralizing antibodies. 349 These
assays have the potential to be increasingly used in the future to
predict outcome in cats that test positive for FeLV.

Immunity
The majority of cats naturally exposed to FeLV will become
immune to reinfection. This diﬀers for other retrovirus infections,
such as in FIV or HIV infection. As a result, although the
mechanism of protection against FeLV and the role of neutralizing
antibodies and cell-mediated immunity are still not completely
understood, eﬃcacious FeLV vaccines are commercially available.
Antibodies are at least partially protective. Experimentally,
susceptible ki ens can be protected from FeLV infection after
passive immunization with sera containing high antibody
concentrations against FeLV. 350 However, once persistent viremia
is established, treatment with virus-neutralizing monoclonal
antibodies is ineﬀective. 351 Most cats that overcome viremia
exhibit high antibody titers to the virus, 352-354 and cats with
regressive infection have higher antibody titers than cats with

vetexamprep.ir

progressive infection. 136 Antibodies are directed against diﬀerent
components of the virus. 352
Not all immune cats develop high antibody levels, and thus,
cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are also important. 352 Use of the
recombinant FeLV canarypox vaccine did not induce antibodies to
FeLV but cats were nonetheless protected from progressive
infection. 319 , 322 CTLs speciﬁc for FeLV appear before virusneutralizing antibodies, and the virus load in progressively FeLVinfected cats can be lowered after passive transfer of FeLV-speciﬁc
CTLs stimulated in vitro, which suggests an important role of
CTLs in FeLV immunity. 353 , 355

Vaccination
Vaccine Development and Efficacy
Cats with abortive and regressive FeLV infection mount an
eﬀective immune response and prevent or contain virus
replication. This is a unique feature of FeLV infection and
supports the idea that immune protection can be achieved
through vaccination. Live a enuated vaccines produce a strong
humoral immune response 356 but have the potential to establish
infection or integrate into the host genome and later result in FeLV
antigen–negative lymphomas. Most early inactivated FeLV
vaccines were either poor immunogens, ineﬀective in preventing
progressive FeLV infection, or enhanced tumor development.
With reﬁnement in cell culture conditions, large amounts of
soluble FeLV antigens could be harvested in cell culture
supernatants. 357 FeLV envelope antigen preparations alone were
shown to provide protection if used in conjunction with potent
adjuvants. 358 With such preparations, no viral genes could be
introduced into host cells, circumventing the oncogenic potential
of FeLV. The ﬁrst vaccine based on soluble FeLV antigens was
licensed in 1985, and then underwent further modiﬁcations to
improve eﬃcacy.
Although most FeLV vaccines eﬀectively protect cats from
progressive infection, there is controversy surrounding the degree
of eﬃcacy and which type of vaccine is most eﬃcacious. 323 Few
independent studies exist that compare the eﬃcacy of vaccines.
Testing protocols vary widely among studies, with diﬀerences in

vetexamprep.ir

time periods assessed between vaccination and challenge,
challenge strains, challenge doses, cats, and diﬀerent methods of
virus detection following challenge. Therefore meaningful
comparison of studies is diﬃcult if not impossible. To overcome
age-related resistance, some studies used glucocorticoids for
immunosuppression before intranasal challenge or performed
parenteral FeLV exposure. These challenges produce a much
higher proportion of infected control cats, reducing the overall
number of cats needed for eﬃcacy studies. The comparability of
these challenges to natural exposure has been questioned. 147 , 359362 However, some FeLV vaccines proved eﬃcacious even under
these severe challenge conditions, suggesting that the vaccines
could also protect cats against FeLV infection under natural
conditions. Some studies involved natural challenge, in which
vaccinated and control cats were housed together with FeLVshedding cats. 362 , 363 Although more comparable to a ﬁeld
situation, such natural challenge situations often fail to result in a
high rate of progressive infection in unvaccinated control cats,
leading to a low calculated eﬃcacy of the vaccine and unsuitable
data for vaccine approval. For example, for inactivated FeLV
vaccines, European licensing authorities require that less than 20%
of the vaccinated cats and more than 80% of the unvaccinated
controls develop progressive infection.
There are three types of FeLV vaccines licensed: (1) classical
inactivated whole virus vaccines; (2) genetically engineered
recombinant subunit vaccines based on the FeLV envelope protein
p45 (a nonglycosylated form of gp70 produced in bacteria); 364
and (3) infectious recombinant canarypox virus engineered to
express the env and gag/part of pol genes of FeLV. 365 The
recombinant FeLV p45 subunit vaccine was the ﬁrst commercial
recombinant vaccine for small animals and was demonstrated to
be highly eﬃcacious in protecting cats from progressive FeLV
infection. Later, a recombinant canarypox vaccine became
available in Europe, which is a diﬀerent product than that
licensed for use in the United States. An independent comparison
of FeLV whole virus vaccines available in the United States
revealed a very high eﬃcacy for two of four vaccines tested. 366
There was absence of provirus integration and viral RNA in most
cats vaccinated with the two whole virus vaccines, thus indicating

vetexamprep.ir

sterile immunity (complete absence of viral RNA, proviral DNA,
antigen, and culturable virus after challenge). These results
contradicted with those from an earlier study that showed that
neither one of the two whole virus vaccines nor the recombinant
canarypox vaccine led to sterilizing immunity. 319 FeLV provirus
was found to persist for years even after challenge in vaccinated
cats, and recurrence of viremia and disease development was
observed in some cats. 150 Thus, vaccination does not appear to
consistently protect against development of regressive infection.
While inactivated whole virus and recombinant protein
vaccines require adjuvants, the recombinant canarypox vaccine is
a replication-defective live virus vaccine that does not require an
adjuvant to induce protective immunity. 319 , 322 Cats protected by
the recombinant canarypox vaccine have a higher ratio of FeLVspeciﬁc IFN-γ- to IL-10-producing cells than susceptible cats, in
accordance with the known importance of CMI induced by this
vaccine. 367 An improved version of the recombinant canarypox
vaccine was produced by a target mutation within the FeLV
envelope protein to delete the immunosuppressive domain p15E;
this led to induction of a more pronounced cell-mediated immune
response and to slightly increased vaccine eﬃcacy. 367 Two studies
that compared the recombinant vaccine to an inactivated vaccine
have been the subject of controversial discussion. The ﬁrst study
claimed that an inactivated whole virus vaccine was superior in
protecting cats from FeLV challenge (90% protection from
progressive infection) compared to the recombinant canarypox
vaccine (20% protection from progressive infection). 368 The
validity of this study was debated, in part because an intercurrent
parvovirus infection was probably introduced by a contaminated
challenge
virus
preparation,
which
likely
created
immunosuppression. The challenge and parvovirus infection
occurred within 3 weeks after the second vaccination, so likely
impacted immunity to vaccination. 369 In the second study,
immunosuppression was created using high doses of
glucocorticoids during challenge, which occurred 3 months after
the second vaccination. 370 Under these circumstances, the whole
virus vaccine performed be er (preventable fraction 100%) than
the recombinant canarypox vaccine (preventable fraction 45%).
Concerns were raised in response to this study because the severe

vetexamprep.ir

immunosuppression during challenge likely speciﬁcally impacted
CMI, which is critical for responses to recombinant canarypox
vaccines. 371 In reaction to this, it was suggested that cats at risk
for FeLV infection in the ﬁeld might also be immunosuppressed.
372

These debates aside, the administration of FeLV vaccines
prolongs the life expectancy of FeLV-exposed cats. 151 FeLV
vaccines are considered noncore vaccines, so are recommended
for all cats with a potential FeLV exposure risk, such as cats
permi ed to roam outdoors or cats brought to or living in
multicat environments with other cats of uncertain FeLV status.
Cats kept strictly indoors are at risk if kept in multicat households
in which some cats have outdoor access. In areas with high FeLV
prevalence, vaccination of all ki ens and juvenile cats up to 1 year
of age should be considered, since the environment into which a
ki en enters can rarely be predicted with certainty. 373 , 374
Additionally, ki ens also have a particularly high risk of
developing progressive infection after FeLV exposure.
Recommendations for most vaccines are for two subcutaneous
doses 3 to 4 weeks apart for initial protection followed by a
vaccination 1 year later. FeLV vaccines should be given in the left
pelvic limb as distally as possible. 374 Results of several studies
indicate that FeLV vaccine-induced immunity persists for at least
12 months following vaccination, but likely much longer. Some
vaccines are licensed for yearly boosters, some for up to 3-year
boosters. Recommendations by diﬀerent expert panels vary
concerning the booster intervals of adult cats. In adult cats that
have received appropriate initial two-dose immunization and a
booster after 1 year, the need for subsequent vaccination and the
booster interval is best determined by analysis of risk. 374 At-risk
adult cats should continue to be vaccinated for FeLV annually, but
cats at low risk of FeLV exposure can be vaccinated every 3 years.
374 In a study that addressed the duration of immunity in cats
vaccinated with an adjuvanted inactivated whole virus vaccine, 10
of 12 cats vaccinated 2 years before FeLV exposure were protected
from progressive infection, while all 11 controls were unprotected
(preventable fraction 83%). 375 In another study using an
inactivated whole virus vaccine, cats were exposed 8, 20, and 36
months after vaccination to FeLV. The outcome of the study was

vetexamprep.ir

hampered by the age-related resistance, which meant that only 10
of the 32 control cats demonstrated progressive infection. 376
Nonetheless, only one of 44 vaccinated cats became progressively
infected.
It is not necessary to administer vaccines from the same
manufacturer for boosters. 377 Not all cats respond equally to
FeLV vaccination, and immunosuppressed cats can fail to develop
immunity. 378 In a 5-year ﬁeld study of a colony of 30 domestic
adult cats naturally exposed to FeLV infection, FeLV vaccination
was eﬀective in cats not infected with FIV, but failed to protect
FIV-infected cats. 98 In contrast, in an experimental study using a
recombinant FeLV p45 subunit vaccine, FIV-infected cats were
successfully immunized and protected from FeLV challenge
exposure in the early phase of infection. 379 No beneﬁt of FeLV
vaccination was observed in cats with progressive but subclinical
FeLV infection on virus load or life expectancy. 329 Therefore FeLV
vaccination is not recommended in progressively FeLV-infected
cats. Vaccination of cats with a history of regressive or abortive
infections should also not be necessary, since these cats most
likely have protective immune response against FeLV. As
described in the Diagnosis section, new antibody tests might be
useful to detect immune cats, but their validity still has to be
evaluated in the ﬁeld.

FeLV Vaccination and Injection-Site Sarcomas
In early studies, a statistical association was demonstrated
between FeLV and rabies vaccinations and later development of
feline injection-site sarcomas (FISS) (see Chapter 20). However, in
a subsequent multicenter case-control study in the United States
and Canada, no single vaccine brand or manufacturer within
antigen class could be identiﬁed as a risk factor for FISS
development. 380 One study compared the subcutaneous tissue
response to diﬀerent FeLV vaccines. Three groups of 15 cats were
injected with one of three FeLV multicomponent vaccines, a
recombinant canarypox vaccine, a vaccine with a lipid-based
adjuvant, and a vaccine adjuvanted with an alum-Quil A mixture.
On days 7, 21, and 62 post vaccination, signiﬁcantly less
inﬂammation was associated with administration of the
recombinant
canarypox
multicomponent
vaccine.
The

vetexamprep.ir

inﬂammation was most severe in cats receiving the
multicomponent vaccine containing FeLV p45 and an aluminumbased adjuvant. 381 Not only adjuvanted FeLV and rabies vaccines,
but also other vaccines and injections of long-acting drugs, such as
glucocorticoids, or injuries, such as through foreign bodies, and
microchip implants were associated with the development of FISS
in some case reports (see Chapter 20).
Some studies examined a possible role of FeLV and FeSV in the
development of FISS, but could not detect either FeLV or FeSV in
the tumors. 186 Furthermore, no other viruses, including FIV, FFV,
polyomaviruses, or papillomaviruses were detected in tumor
tissues. 382-385 No evidence was found for the replication or
expression of endogenous retroviruses in FISS. 383 , 385 In addition,
feline primary cutaneous lymphomas were described in
association with vaccination. A total of 17 cutaneous lymphomas
with a history of vaccine injection at the site of tumor
development were evaluated. Postinjection time of development
ranged from 15 days to approximately 9 years in ﬁve cats. FeLV
gp70 and/or p27 proteins were expressed in 10 of the 17 tumors. It
was suggested that persistent inﬂammation induced by the
injection and reactivation of FeLV expression might have
contributed to the development of these tumors. 386 Chapter 20
describes recommendations to minimize the risk of FISS. Along
these lines, no FeLV vaccinations should be administered to
indoor-only cats or already immune cats, 387 and, thus, FeLV
prevaccination testing is recommended.

Prevention
Preventative methods, including general precautions, testing and
removal strategies, and vaccination, have been successful in
signiﬁcantly decreasing the prevalence of FeLV infection. 110
FeLV is very fragile, surviving only minutes at most outside the
host animal. Thus, direct contact among cats and immediate
fomite transfer are the major risk factors, but transmission
requires prolonged, close contact. Progressively infected cats
should be physically separated from other cats in the
environment. In a veterinary hospital, FeLV-shedding cats can be
housed in the same ward with other hospitalized patients as long
as they are housed in separate cages and certain precautionary

vetexamprep.ir

measures are taken. Simple precautions (e.g., hand washing) and
routine cleaning procedures prevent transmission in the hospital
se ing.
Cats with progressive FeLV infection should be housed in
individual cages and conﬁned to them throughout their
hospitalization. They should never be placed in isolation with cats
that have other infections, such as viral respiratory infections,
because FeLV-infected cats may be immunosuppressed. Routine
hospital infection-control precautions will prevent transmission of
FeLV.
FeLV can be transmi ed hematogenously; therefore all feline
blood donors should be screened and conﬁrmed to be free of
infection before donating blood. 297 , 298 , 388 Pre–blood transfusion
screening should include not only ELISA to detect FeLV antigen,
but also provirus PCR testing because regressively infected cats
(antigen-negative, provirus-positive) also transmit the virus, and
blood product recipients can become regressively or even
progressively FeLV-infected. 144 FeLV was also detected in the
corneal tissues of cats by PCR and immunohistochemistry; 389
therefore screening potential corneal donors for FeLV infection is
also generally warranted.
In the mid-1970s, test and removal programs were extremely
eﬀective for eliminating the virus from ca eries. When testing was
ﬁrst implemented, the prevalence of FeLV in purebred ca eries
was 11%. Within 4 years, the rate was reduced to less than 2%.
Today, FeLV infection should be considered an abnormality in a
well-run ca ery. Many stray-cat shelters also implement testing in
their conditioning protocols, thus further reducing the rate of
FeLV infection. 123 , 390

Public Health Aspects
Although FeLV can replicate in human cell lines, 391 no conclusive
evidence of natural human infection with FeLV has been detected.
Concerns that relate to the possibility of zoonotic transmission of
FeLV infection have arisen from several observations. Firstly,
some FeLV strains grow in human cell cultures. 392 Secondly,
lymphoma has been induced by injection of large doses of virus
into neonates of nonfeline species, such as pups and marmosets. 60
Thirdly, contact of humans with sick cats was linked to

vetexamprep.ir

development of childhood leukemia, and the degree of contact
between FeLV-infected cats and children with leukemia was
double that of contact between healthy children and healthy cats.
393 , 394 Fourth, veterinarians were shown to have a higher death
rate from leukemia than a control population of physicians and
dentists. 22 , 359 , 395-397
Despite these facts, FeLV does not appear to be a risk to
humans. Some investigators have detected antibodies to FeLV in
humans with leukemia and owners of progressively FeLVinfected cats. 398-401 On the other hand, studies using more speciﬁc
radioimmunoassays obtained negative results. No human has
ever been found to be viremic with FeLV. PCR was used without
success to ﬁnd FeLV sequences in blood and bone marrow of
young and adult humans with leukemia. 402
One study found that human blood cells are uniquely resistant
to infection with FeLV due to the activity of cellular enzymes that
mutate the viral genome. A second blockade to infection was
identiﬁed that appears to suppress viral gene expression after the
viral genome has integrated into the host cell genome. As cells
derived from other normal human cell types are fully supportive
of FeLV replication, innate resistance of blood cells could be
critical in protecting against cross-species infection. 403 In
conclusion, there is no evidence that FeLV is transmi ed from cats
to humans. Still, if immunosuppressed people live in close contact
with FeLV-infected cats, there is a certain risk, not for FeLV
infection but for infection by secondary pathogens that have the
potential to be zoonotic.

Case Example
Signalment

“Mausi,” a 6-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair from
Munich, Germany.

History

Mausi was presented to the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitaet
Munich, Germany, Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital, for
lethargy and anorexia of 3 days’ duration. Mausi had not eaten

vetexamprep.ir

and not defecated during this time. There had been no change
in urination.
At a local veterinary clinic on the ﬁrst day of illness, a
physical examination revealed fever (105.1°F or 40.6°C).
Treatment with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid did not lead to
clinical improvement. Mausi tested positive for FeLV antigen 2
years previously, after which time the cat had been housed
exclusively indoors. There were three other cats in the
household that were also indoor-only since Mausi was found to
be infected with FeLV. A FeLV test had revealed that one other
cat was FeLV antigen–positive, the other two cats were FeLV
antigen–negative. None of the other three cats were ill. Mausi
had not had any known toxin exposure, there were no recent
changes in the environment, and the cat was fed a commercial
dry cat food.

Current Medications

Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid PO.

Other Medical History
None.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 6.9 kg
General: Quiet, alert, responsive, well hydrated, T = 104.4°F
(40.2°C), HR = 220 beats/min, RR = 36 breaths/min, mucous
membranes pink, CRT = 1 s, haircoat unkempt.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat (including dilated fundoscopic
examination): Mild gingivitis.
Musculoskeletal: Body condition score 7/9. Normal
ambulation.
Cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary,
and lymph nodes: Mausi resented palpation of her cranial
abdomen. No other clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were
detected.

CBC: HCT 24.6% (30%–50%),
MCV 48.4 fL (42–53 fL),
reticulocytes 7800 cells/µL,
WBC 12,470 cells/µL (4500–14,000 cells/µL),
neutrophils 10,438 cells/µL (2000–9000 cells/µL),

vetexamprep.ir

lymphocytes 344 cells/µL (1000–7000 cells/µL),
monocytes 229 cells/µL (0–1000 cells/µL),
platelets 192,000 platelets/µL (180,000–500,000 platelets/
µL),
On blood smear, the neutrophils showed mild toxicity.

mmol/L),

Imaging Findings

Plain abdominal radiographs: The intestines were relatively
empty. No masses were identiﬁed. Abdominal serosal detail
appeared normal.
Abdominal sonography: The left kidney measured 4.2 cm in
length and showed a mildly enlarged renal pelvis. The
remainder of the abdomen was unremarkable.

Microbiologic and Virologic Testing

Aerobic bacterial urine culture: growth of Escherichia coli
(sensitivity testing revealed that the E. coli was sensitive to
pradoﬂoxacin, but resistant to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid)

vetexamprep.ir

POC ELISA for FeLV antigen and FIV antibodies: positive for
FeLV antigen, negative for FIV antibodies

Diagnosis

Progressive FeLV infection and acute pyelonephritis
(characterized by fever, bacteriuria, and mild neutrophilia with
left shift). Right renal agenesis (likely congenital).

Treatment

Mausi was hospitalized and treated with intravenous ﬂuids,
and initially, while awaiting the culture and susceptibility
results, treated with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (20 mg/kg, IV,
q12h) and pradoﬂoxacin (oral suspension 5 mg/kg, PO q24h).
Rectal temperature normalized within 24 hours, and the cat
started eating again. After 48 hours, hematocrit was 27.6%,
neutrophil count was 5759 cells/µL with no bands or toxicity,
and lymphocyte count was 917 cells/µL. As culture and
susceptibility testing revealed an E. coli that was resistant to
amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, but susceptible to pradoﬂoxacin,
amoxicillin/clavulanic acid treatment was discontinued, and
Mausi was discharged from the hospital with instructions to
continue pradoﬂoxacin treatment for 1 month. Two weeks after
the antibiotics had been discontinued, Mausi appeared healthy.
A physical examination, CBC, kidney panel, urinalysis, and
aerobic bacterial urine culture showed no abnormalities. Her
hematocrit was 38.9%, and white blood cell count was 4620
cells/µL. One year later, Mausi remained clinically healthy, and
a CBC showed a hematocrit of 38.2%, white blood cell count of
4500 cells/µL, neutrophil count of 3362 cells/µL, and a
lymphocyte count of 905 cells/µL. Mausi remained alive and
well with a normal CBC 4 years after she was initially seen for
the pyelonephritis. Mausi died 2 years later, 7.5 years after ﬁrst
testing positive for progressive FeLV infection.

Comments

Even though this cat was initially seen for moderately severe
illness in association with progressive FeLV infection, there was
full clinical recovery with treatment and the cat remained alive
and well for 6 additional years. Fever, bacteriuria, and
neutrophilia with left shift were likely associated with
pyelonephritis. The nonregenerative anemia likely represented

vetexamprep.ir

an anemia of inﬂammatory disease, and the lymphopenia and
the hyperglycemia were likely stress-induced.
The two FeLV antigen–negative cats most likely had been
exposed to FeLV and had regressive or abortive FeLV infection,
in which case they would be protected against new FeLV
infection.
This case clearly demonstrates that other treatable diseases
can be present in progressively FeLV-infected cats, long-term
survival is possible, and that a search for the underlying cause
of clinical signs and adequate treatment is always
recommended.

33: Feline Immunodeﬁciency
Virus Infection
Julia A. Bea y, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: FIV (family Retroviridae, subfamily Orthoretrovirinae,
genus Lentivirus).
• First Described: California, 1986; 1 serologic evidence of
infection dates back to the 1960s. 2 , 3
• Affected Hosts: Domestic and wild cats; hyenas.
• Geographic Distribution: Endemic worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Primarily biting. Queen-to-kitten
transmission uncommon. Horizontal between housemates
rare. Iatrogenic via blood transfusion possible.
• Major Clinical Signs: Most FIV-infected cats are subclinically
infected for most or all of their lifetime. Signs include lethargy
and fever, stomatitis, chronic GI signs, wasting, neurologic
signs, high-grade lymphoma, immune-mediated diseases, and
opportunistic infections.
• Differential Diagnoses: Variable depending on clinical signs.
• Human Health Significance: FIV does not infect humans.
Immunosuppressed owners should be counseled regarding
the risk of opportunistic pathogen exposure from any
immunosuppressed pet.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
FIV is an enveloped, RNA virus that belongs to the Lentivirus
genus of the Retroviridae. It infects domestic and wild cats

vetexamprep.ir

worldwide, as well as hyenas. 4 FIV strains are highly hostspeciﬁc. Cross-species transmission, even among carnivore hosts,
is rare. 5 Like HIV, FIV establishes a chronic, persistent infection
that, in some cats, ultimately culminates in immunodeﬁciency.
Because of its similarities to HIV, FIV infection in cats has been
used as a research model for HIV infection in the past. 6 Thus,
relative to other viral infections of companion animals, much is
known about FIV pathogenesis.
Familiarity with retroviral structure and replication assists in
understanding diagnostic, treatment, and prevention strategies
for these infections. Like other retroviruses, FIV has a threelayered structure that is composed of an innermost genomenucleocapsid complex with helical symmetry, an icosahedral
capsid, and an envelope with glycoprotein spikes (Fig. 33.1). Each
virion contains a duplicate, single-stranded RNA genome. The
FIV genome contains three major genes: gag, which encodes the
virion core proteins (capsid [p24], nucleocapsid [p10], and matrix
[p15]); pol, which encodes the reverse transcriptase, protease, and
integrase enzymes; and env, which encodes surface (gp120) and
transmembrane (gp40) envelope glycoproteins. 7 Several accessory
and regulatory genes are also encoded. FIV Env binds to CD134,
the primary cell surface receptor, to initiate infection. 8 CD134 is
expressed on feline CD4+ T cells, B cells, and activated
macrophages. A conformational change in Env exposes the
binding site for the co-receptor CXCR4, a chemokine receptor,
triggering cell entry. 8 The viral envelope fuses with the cell
membrane, and the capsid is released into the cytoplasm where
reverse transcription occurs and a double-stranded DNA
(dsDNA) copy of the retroviral genome is made. Additional
sequences, known as long terminal repeats (LTRs), are added to
either end of the viral genome. The virus then passes into the
nucleus where the dsDNA copy integrates into the host genome;
at this point, the integrated dsDNA becomes a provirus.
Transcription of this proviral DNA, which is controlled by the
LTRs, leads to synthesis of new virion components, and virus
assembly and budding occur at the cell surface (Fig. 33.2).
Depending on the cellular environment, proviral DNA may either
be latent, whereby transcription does not occur, or be
transcriptionally active. Latency is one mechanism by which

vetexamprep.ir

retroviruses can evade the host immune system. Within an
infected cat, FIV mutates frequently to create a pool of variant
viruses. Point mutations introduced during reverse transcription
and recombination between viruses that co-infect a single cell are
the major mechanisms involved. Variable regions in env form the
basis for the phylogenetic classiﬁcation of FIV into major subtypes
or clades, A to F. Regional variation in the prevalence of subtypes
exists with subtypes A, B, and C being most common. 9 , 10
Classiﬁcation of FIV subtypes has become complex because
sequences used for subtyping do not detect all env recombinants.
Additionally, recombinant subtypes, such as A/B, B/E, and A/B/C,
are now recognized, 11 , 12 and the existence of additional
subtypes likely. The heterogeneity of the virus complicates the
design of molecular diagnostic tests and vaccines for FIV. The
clinical relevance of subtype classiﬁcation is not yet clear since
subtype does not consistently predict clinical manifestations or
vaccine protection. 13 , 14
FIV is transmi ed by direct inoculation of saliva or blood
during ﬁghting. 15 , 16 Other routes of transmission are of minor
epidemiologic signiﬁcance. Horizontal transmission of FIV
between cats in stable households is rare. 17 Queen-to-ki en
(prenatal, natal, and postnatal) transmission of FIV is documented
infrequently, although primary infection of the queen during
pregnancy may increase the risk of transmission. 18 Diagnosis of
FIV infection in one ki en does not imply that the whole li er is
infected. 19 Natural sexual transmission of FIV is not reported,
although experimentally, FIV can be recovered from semen, and
intravaginal exposure results in transmission. 20
Detection of circulating antibodies has been used as a marker of
infection in epidemiologic studies because FIV infection is
lifelong. Seroprevalence varies from <5% to >20% depending on
the region and the population tested (Table 33.1). FIV infection
rates are particularly high in Australia and Japan. Two studies in
Australia found that 14.6% and 15% of client-owned cats tested at
veterinary clinics were seropositive. 21 , 22 In Japan, the overall
seroprevalence was 23.2%, with up to one third of male cats
testing positive. 23 Risk factors for FIV infection are shown in
Table 33.2. The mean age at diagnosis is 6 to 8 years, and 80% to
90% of cats are more than 2 years of age. 24 Male cats are up to 4.7

vetexamprep.ir

times more likely to be seropositive than female cats. 25 In a North
American study, the prevalence of FIV infection in sick, feral cats
was 18.2%, whereas that in healthy indoor cats was only 0.7%. 25
Occasionally, co-infections with FeLV occur, and results of some
studies suggest that infection with one retrovirus is a risk factor
for infection with the other. 26 , 27

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
FIV infection is characterized by a progressive immune
dysfunction which, in some infected cats, results in clinical signs
suggestive of immune deﬁciency or inﬂammatory, immunemediated or neoplastic disease. 1 , 28 , 29 The immunopathogenesis
of FIV infection has been studied extensively in experimental
infections of young cats housed in minimal disease environments.
The immunologic changes documented in experimentally infected
cats are rarely accompanied by clinical signs. 30 An improved
understanding of the clinical course of FIV infection in naturally
infected cats, which are typically infected in adulthood and
exposed to infectious and environmental cofactors, awaits
longitudinal ﬁeld studies of FIV-infected cats and controls.
FIV infection can be broadly considered to progress in three
stages: a transient primary stage, a chronic subclinical stage, and
an advanced, clinical stage that is eventually terminal (Fig. 33.3).
During the primary stage, which lasts for several weeks, the virus
replicates rapidly and viremia is detectable by virus isolation and
PCR. 31 Immune dysfunction begins soon after FIV infection.
CD4+ T-cell numbers decline rapidly during the ﬁrst weeks of
infection. An early rise in an activated subpopulation of
lymphocytes that expresses low levels of the CD8 molecule,
CD8low, exacerbates a reduced CD4:CD8 ratio. 32 Lymphocyte
function is negatively impacted, for example, T-cell priming to
novel antigens is disrupted within 5 weeks of experimental
infection. 33 Dissemination of virus to lymphoid tissues occurs
and virus can be detected in saliva within 3 weeks of experimental
infection. 34 A strong immune response comprising CD8+,
cytotoxic T cells, and antibodies to viral proteins is detectable
from 2 to 6 weeks after experimental infection. 35 Virus replication
is contained but, crucially, not cleared by the host immune
system. Transient clinical signs sometimes accompany the
primary stage. These include lethargy, anorexia, waxing and
waning fever, neutropenia, and a lymphadenopathy due to
reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (Fig. 33.4), which can persist for
months.

vetexamprep.ir

The subclinical stage lasts for years and, often, for a cat’s
lifetime. Virus replication proceeds in peripheral lymph nodes, 36
but viremia is almost or completely absent. Hence, antigen testing
is not used for FIV diagnosis. CD4+-cell numbers in the periphery
rebound initially, then decline progressively. 37 , 38 Dysregulation
of cytokine production contributes to impaired immunity to
opportunistic pathogens. For example, primary challenge of
clinically normal FIV-infected cats with Toxoplasma gondii can
result in severe, systemic toxoplasmosis compared with only mild,
transient signs in FIV-uninfected cats. 39 Cats chronically infected
with FIV produce less IL-2 and IL-12, and more IL-10 in response
to T. gondii infection than control cats. 40 Innate as well as adaptive
immunity is aﬀected; defective natural killer (NK)-cell function
delayed clearance of Listeria monocytogenes in experimental FIV
infection. 41 Immune hyperactivation as well as suppression
contributes to immune dysfunction in FIV infection. Polyclonal Bcell stimulation results in hypergammaglobulinemia. 42 Chronic
antigenemia activates T-cell subpopulations which function as
immune suppressors. These include CD4+ and CD8+ cells that
express B7 and CTLA4, which contribute to immune anergy and
apoptosis in lymph nodes, as well as CD4+CD25+ T-regulatory
cells which function as nonspeciﬁc suppressors, thereby
impacting immunity to FIV and to opportunistic pathogens. 43 , 44

In some cats, clinical signs of advanced FIV infection eventually
ensue. The advanced stage of FIV infection is characterized by
profound lymphoid depletion, escape of virus from immunologic

vetexamprep.ir

control, and clinical signs including opportunistic infections,
neoplastic disease, myelosuppression, and neurologic disease
(Table 33.3). 45–48 Immune dysfunction can manifest clinically as
atypical and refractory bacterial, viral, or parasitic infections (Fig.
33.5). Respiratory infections, bacterial pyoderma, generalized
demodicosis, mycobacterial infection, disseminated cowpox,
pulmonary cryptococcosis, sporotrichosis, and lungworm
infections are reported. 28 , 49–51 Persistent cytopenias, particularly
neutropenia or lymphopenia, are described in advanced FIV
infection. 21 , 52 These infections are often more severe and less
responsive to treatment than the same infections in
immunocompetent cats. FIV infection has been linked to feline
chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS), a painful and debilitating
condition that can greatly impact quality of life (Fig. 33.6). 53 The
etiology of FCGS is ill-deﬁned, and it is likely to be multifactorial.
Epidemiologic evidence identiﬁes FIV as a risk factor in some
studies and, while FIV is clearly not causal, a role for the virus in
disease manifestation and severity in infected cats seems likely. 54
Immune stimulation triggered by FIV may contribute to chronic
oral inﬂammation, while immune suppression may delay
clearance of other pathogens, such as FCV or secondary bacterial
invaders. Signiﬁcant diﬀerences in the oral microbiota of FIVinfected cats compared with uninfected cats, including higher
relative abundance of fusobacteria and actinobacteria in FIV
infection, have been demonstrated. The clinical signiﬁcance of
these ﬁndings awaits clariﬁcation. 55

vetexamprep.ir

Changes in virus load and CD4+ Tcell numbers over the course of infection with
feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV). Viremia is
detected early after infection and may be
accompanied by systemic signs (primary
stage). Plasma viremia then falls to very low
levels and remains this way for many years
(subclinical stage). Although this period is
referred to as “clinical latency,” the virus itself
is not latent; there is ongoing production of
virus and a steady decline in CD4+ T-cell
counts. The rate of progression of the
subclinical stage depends on factors such as
the virus strain, co-infections with other agents
that activate virus transcription, and host
immunity. Some cats progress to the advanced
stage of infection where signs of
immunodeficiency develop, and plasma
viremia increases. Advanced FIV infection is
eventually terminal. Antibody production
declines, and antibody tests may be negative
in cats with advanced-stage disease, but
polymerase chain reaction assays are usually
positive.

The risk of lymphoma is increased in FIV-infected cats by
ﬁvefold to sixfold. 56 FIV-associated lymphomas are typically
high-grade, extranodal, B-cell tumors, similar to HIV-associated
diﬀuse large B-cell lymphoma. 57 Direct oncogenesis by FIV is
rare. Integration site mapping demonstrated truncation of a gene
on chromosome B3 and downregulation of the unaﬀected allele,
consistent with a loss-of-function mutation, in a single case. 58
FIV-induced immune dysfunction may play a role in
lymphomagenesis. Reduced CD4-cell counts, a known risk factor
for HIV-associated lymphoma, have been demonstrated in cats
developing FIV-associated lymphoma. 59 In HIV-associated
lymphomas, co-infecting gammaherpesviruses are causal in 20%–
100% of cases depending on the lymphoma subtype. 60 Whether
Felis
catus
gammaherpesvirus
1,
the
lymphotropic
gammaherpesvirus of domestic cats, is an infectious co-factor in
61
FIV-associated
lymphoma
is
under
investigation.
Hyperstimulation of the B-cell compartment in FIV infection
might also contribute to oncogenesis, with ampliﬁcation of normal
somatic mutations predisposing to B-cell tumors. Increased
numbers of circulating B cells, plasma immunoglobulin, and IL-1
and IL-6, which stimulate B-cell proliferation and diﬀerentiation,
have been documented in FIV-infected cats that develop
lymphoma. 62 Many other neoplasms are described in FIVinfected cats, but the role of FIV, if any, in these cancers is
unknown.
Severe unexplained weight loss can occur in advanced FIV
infection. This resembles wasting syndrome, an AIDS-deﬁning
condition in HIV infection, described as weight loss of 10% or
more over 30 days with no identiﬁable cause other than HIV
infection. Wasting syndrome is multifactorial with changes in
protein and lipid metabolism, altered energy requirements,

vetexamprep.ir

anorexia,
cytokine
derangements,
malabsorption,
endocrinopathies, and myopathies all contributing. An increased
risk for renal diseases in FIV infection is suspected, but a causal
association has been diﬃcult to prove. Renal proteinuria but not
renal azotemia has been associated with natural FIV infection. 63
FIV-associated neuropathology has been studied extensively as
an experimental model for neurodegenerative diseases in HIV
infection. The incidence of neurologic signs that accompany
natural FIV infection is unknown. Following experimental
infection, FIV provirus can be detected in the CNS from 2 to 4
weeks. The virus targets non-neuronal cells, primarily
macrophages and microglia, resulting in a progressive
encephalitis. 64 Histopathologic lesions are generally less severe in
FIV infection than in HIV infection. This may, in part, be
explained by the reduced macrophage tropism exhibited by FIV in
comparison with HIV, since macrophages carry virus across the
blood-brain and blood-CSF barriers. However, some FIV isolates
induce severe neuropathology. Lesions may be clinically silent or
induce progressive neurologic deﬁcits including behavioral
changes, stereotypic motor behaviors, increased aggression,
delayed placing reactions, and reduced pupillary light reﬂexes. 65
In natural FIV infection, compulsive roaming, changes in sleeping
pa erns, aggression, seizures, ataxia, tremors, movement
disorders, and paraparesis have been reported, but the extent to
which other etiologies were excluded is unclear. Some deﬁcits that
accompany HIV-associated neurodegeneration (such as reduced
concentration, memory or learning, and psychological problems)
66 cannot be routinely assessed in cats.
Perinatal FIV infection, although rare, has been associated with
an accelerated disease course, abortion, stillbirth, low birth
weights, reduced survival, and T-cell–deﬁcient ki ens. 67

Physical Examination Findings
Cats infected with FIV are often clinically normal or display
clinical signs that are unrelated to FIV infection. In the primary
stage of FIV infection, cats may be febrile or show generalized
peripheral lymphadenopathy. Common physical examination
ﬁndings in cats with advanced disease include FCGS, chronic
upper respiratory tract signs, otitis externa, pyoderma, and

vetexamprep.ir

abscesses as well as a diverse spectrum of disease manifestations
that relate to underlying opportunistic infections or neoplasia.
Behavioral abnormalities such as obtundation, aggression, and
cognitive impairment have been reported. Other neurologic
abnormalities include ataxia, anisocoria, and abnormal segmental
reﬂexes. Ocular abnormalities may result from the FIV infection
itself, opportunistic infections, or lymphoma, and include anterior
uveitis, hyphema, pars planitis, chorioretinitis, and/or glaucoma.

Diagnosis
FIV-infected cats should be identiﬁed to optimize individual
healthcare and to prevent infection of other cats. Indications for
testing, modiﬁed from recommendations by the AAFP, are shown
in Box 33.1. 68 Assessment of the clinical signiﬁcance of FIV
infection in a sick cat is challenging because the virus may, or may
not, be contributing to the current clinical signs. Surrogate
markers used to stage HIV infection in people, such as CD4+ Tcell counts and viral load, have not been extensively validated for
use in cats. 48 It is reasonable to assume that FIV may be playing a
role in infected cats with refractory or recurrent infections,
infections with intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria,
opportunistic pathogens, and cases of high-grade B-cell
lymphoma.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Laboratory abnormalities are not helpful for the diagnosis of FIV
infection. If abnormalities are identiﬁed, they may be associated
with intercurrent disease or may be a consequence of FIV
infection itself. Abnormalities that are commonly reported in FIV
infection are mild anemia, lymphopenia, neutropenia, and
hyperglobulinemia. 52 Such changes should be interpreted
cautiously in older sick cats where they are common regardless of
FIV status. 21 Mild prolongations in APTT, thrombin time, and
ﬁbrinogen concentrations compared with controls have been
reported in FIV-infected cats, although PT and platelet function
are generally normal.

Microbiologic Tests
Commercial FIV tests detect either anti-FIV antibodies using
immunoassays, or viral nucleic acid using PCR. Virus isolation
from PBMCs is not commercially available.
Serologic Diagnosis
Serology is the ﬁrst line for FIV testing. POC tests utilizing lateralﬂow ELISA or immunochromatography technologies and
diagnostic laboratory-based ELISA assays are in widespread use,

vetexamprep.ir

have rapid turnaround times, and high sensitivities and
speciﬁcities for antibody detection. 25 , 69 , 70 In cats over 6 months
of age that have not been vaccinated against FIV, anti-FIV
antibodies are a marker for FIV infection because the virus
establishes a persistent infection.
In countries where commercial FIV vaccines are available, or in
cats with a history of having been vaccinated for FIV, POC test
selection is important. This is because vaccination with inactivated
whole virus vaccines induce antibodies to a broad range of FIV
proteins, and POC kits vary in their ability to distinguish vaccineinduced from infection-associated anti-FIV antibodies. This means
that an uninfected cat that has been vaccinated for FIV can test
positive on POC tests in some circumstances. The antigens used in
POC kits vary among manufacturers but include p15, p24, and
gp40. In a study of FIV-vaccinated (n = 119) and unvaccinated (n =
239) owned cats, two POC assays, Witness FeLV/FIV (Zoetis
Animal Health, USA) and Anigen Rapid FIV/FeLV (BioNote,
Korea), performed well in their ability to detect antibodies
induced by natural FIV infection regardless of the cat’s FIV
vaccination status (PPV 70% and 100% and NPV 100% and 100%,
respectively). 71 The high speciﬁcity of these kits for identifying
FIV infection (98.1%) was conﬁrmed in an independent study of
104 FIV-uninfected speciﬁc pathogen free (SPF) cats that had been
vaccinated against FIV. 72 However, prospective studies of FIVuninfected ki ens and young cats vaccinated with the inactivated
FIV vaccine have reported that both the Witness and Anigen POC
kits may detect transient, vaccine-induced antibodies in up to 66%
of vaccinates. 73 , 74 Some evidence suggests that interference with
the results of Witness and Anigen assays by vaccination is more
likely in young cats, and within several months of vaccination. 73 ,
74 The SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo POC assay (IDEXX Corporation,
Maine, USA) has high (94%–100%) sensitivity and speciﬁcity for
detection of anti-FIV antibodies but does not distinguish between
the antibody response induced by vaccination and that induced
by natural infection. Of 119 FIV-vaccinated cats, of which only 5
were infected with FIV, all 119 tested positive using SNAP
FIV/FeLV Combo compared with 11 using the Witness assay and 5
(all conﬁrmed as infected using PCR) using the Anigen assay. 71
Clariﬁcation of the utility of POC kits from diﬀerent

vetexamprep.ir

manufacturers for determination of FIV infection status in cats
that may have been vaccinated for FIV is expected. The reliability
of a negative serologic test result is unchanged by a history of
vaccination.
Other serologic assays, including IFA assays and Western
blo ing, have limited availability. Both are technically
demanding, subject to interoperator variability in interpretation,
and Western blo ing may be less sensitive than ELISA assays
when performed by some laboratories. 75
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Molecular tests target integrated DNA provirus and some also
detect viral RNA by qPCR. Variability in performance among
laboratories has been demonstrated. 76 Commercial PCR assays
have diagnostic sensitivity that is 5%–15% lower than that of
serology, and diagnostic speciﬁcity that is similar to serology. 77–79
Sequence variability among isolates, low provirus or virus load,
poor sample quality, and technical issues may all impact the
sensitivity of PCR (see Chapter 6). FIV PCR should not be used to
screen for FIV infection. Rather, FIV PCR can be used as an
adjunct to serology to determine the true infection status of cats in
certain circumstances, including seropositive cats that may have
been vaccinated for FIV, seropositive cats less than 6 months of
age, seronegative cats that may have been recently exposed to FIV,
and seronegative cats where advanced-stage FIV is suspected.
After experimental FIV challenge, PCR can detect viral RNA
within 1 to 2 weeks and DNA within 3 weeks, but diﬀerences in
virus strain, dose, and assay sensitivities mean that it is hard to
predict how long after natural exposure PCR can be used to detect
FIV infection. 31 Positive PCR test results indicate that the cat is
almost certainly infected, whereas negative PCR results are
inconclusive.
Interpretation and Confirmation of Serologic Test Results
Interpretation of the results of serologic screening requires the
integration of clinical ﬁndings from the individual cat to guide
whether repeat serology or PCR is indicated and what the timing
of any repeat testing should be. 68 The time to seroconversion
following natural infection is variable and can be prolonged. 68 If

vetexamprep.ir

possible, a seronegative cat that may have been recently exposed
should be isolated from FIV-infected cats or cats of unknown FIV
status and retested after 60 days. Some cats in the terminal stage
of FIV infection have impaired antibody production. These cats
often have high plasma viral loads but are seronegative. 80 Thus, if
advanced FIV infection is suspected, negative test results should
be followed by PCR.
