35: Feline Calicivirus Infections
Alan Radford, Maria Afonso, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: 1957 (New Zealand, Fastier). 1
• Causes: FCV, family Caliciviridae, genus Vesivirus.
• Affected Hosts: Domestic cat and many other Felidae. Similar
viruses also isolated occasionally from dogs.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Oronasal, fomite spread.
• Major Clinical Signs: Oral ulceration, oculonasal discharges,
lethargy. Less commonly lameness, lower respiratory tract
infection, and signs of enteritis. Rare virulent forms may also
cause edema, icterus, skin necrosis, and death.
• Differential Diagnosis: Differential diagnoses for FCV infection
are other respiratory viral infections (FCV, influenza viruses),
infections with bacteria such as Bordetella bronchiseptica,
Mycoplasma spp., Streptococcus spp., or Chlamydia felis;
other causes of rhinitis such as cryptococcosis, aspergillosis,
neoplasia, foreign bodies, chronic idiopathic feline
rhinosinusitis, nasopharyngeal stenosis, or nasopharyngeal
polyps; feline chronic airway disease. For cats with oral
ulcerations, exposure to caustic substances may be
suspected.
• Human Health Significance: None known.

Etiology And Epidemiology
FCV is a small, unenveloped, single-stranded RNA virus, a
member of the Vesivirus genus of the Calicivirus family (Fig. 35.1

vetexamprep.ir

and Table 35.1). Both domestic cats and other members of the
Felidae family can be infected. 2–5 Although dogs have their own
genetically distinct calicivirus, 6 , 7 viruses antigenically and
genetically related to FCV have also been detected in dogs with
diarrhea (see Chapter 29), 8–10 and some epidemiologic evidence
suggests a link between the two. 11 The role of FCV strains in
canine disease and the signiﬁcance of dogs as a reservoir of feline
infection are not known. Other caliciviruses have been identiﬁed
in cats, notably feline norovirus, but the role of this virus in
disease is unknown. 12
A large number of diﬀerent strains of FCV exist, which vary
slightly in antigenicity and pathogenicity, although they are all
suﬃciently cross-reactive to be classiﬁed as one serotype. 13
Although in general antigenicity is not associated with
pathogenicity, some evidence suggests that FCV isolates collected
from chronic stomatitis cases may show minor antigenic
diﬀerences. 14 , 15 Genetically, FCV strains appear to represent one
large diverse group, with li le evidence of within-group clusters.
16–19 However, several studies have identiﬁed potential separate
genotypes in Asia and Europe using longer genomic sequences
which may provide for greater resolution. 20–24 Enteric strains
appear to diﬀer genetically from strains that cause respiratory
disease, and appear more likely to resist trypsin, and bile
treatment. 25 , 26 Considerable variability may be seen between
individual isolates, particularly in immunogenic regions of the
viral capsid gene. 22–28 This genetic diversity is useful
epidemiologically in that it allows diﬀerentiation among FCV
strains. 17 , 29–31
Most strains of FCV are suﬃciently related antigenically to
induce some degree of cross-protective immunity, but cats can
still be sequentially infected with diﬀerent strains of virus and
show varying degrees of clinical illness. Some isolates appear to
be more immunogenic and cross-reactive than others. The most
commonly used strains in vaccine products have been F9 and 255,
but other strains have also been used, some in bivalent or trivalent
FCV vaccines. 32–34 There is continued discussion over the degree
of cross-protection aﬀorded by such vaccines, particularly the
original monovalent FCV vaccines. Some evidence indicates that
they are still cross-reactive against the majority of ﬁeld isolates,

vetexamprep.ir

whereas other studies suggest that the percentage of isolates 17 , 35
neutralized by such vaccine strains may be decreasing, possibly as
a result of immune selection pressures from widespread vaccine
use. 17 , 36–38 Direct comparison between studies, however, can be
diﬃcult because results may vary according to factors such as the
population tested (including perhaps whether sick or healthy cats
are sampled), and the methodology used for testing. Nevertheless,
structured, routine monitoring of vaccine eﬃcacy against current
ﬁeld isolates would be useful. 17
The ability to readily grow FCV in cell culture has led to its
frequent use as a surrogate for calicivirus inactivation in
disinfection studies, as well as more general studies of calicivirus
structure and biology. FCV is moderately resistant in the external
environment for days to several weeks on dried surfaces at room
temperature, and longer in colder we er conditions. 13 The virus
is not as susceptible to the eﬀects of disinfectants as other
respiratory viruses such as FHV-1, 39 but useful disinfectants for
both viruses are accelerated hydrogen peroxide or household
bleach (5.25% sodium hypochlorite) diluted 1 part in 30 in water
(1750 ppm) with added detergent. 40 The use of 5% sodium
bicarbonate has also been shown to be eﬀective and has been
recommended by the ABCD. 41
FCV infections are fairly widespread in the general cat
population, with a generally higher prevalence in multicat
households, shelters, and also in younger animals. 11 , 17 , 42–44 The
virus is mainly shed in ocular, nasal, and oral secretions, and
spread is largely by direct contact with an infected cat. Acutely
infected animals are clearly one of the most important sources of
virus, but infection also commonly occurs from clinically
recovered carrier cats. 13 In some situations, particularly within a
ca ery, indirect transmission may occur. Contaminated secretions
may be present on cages, on feeding and cleaning utensils, and on
personnel. Some evidence suggests that feces from ﬂeas fed on
artiﬁcially FCV-infected blood may infect ki ens oronasally, 45 but
this is unlikely to be a signiﬁcant source of infection. Aerosols are
not thought to be of major importance for the spread of FCV; cats
do not appear to be able to produce an infectious aerosol for this
virus during normal respiration, although sneezed macrodroplets
may transmit infection over a distance of 1 to 2 m (3 to 6 ft).

vetexamprep.ir

Despite vaccination, carriers are widespread in the population
and are probably the main reason why FCV is so successful. An
understanding of the FCV carrier state is important to help
determine strategies for control. The carrier state is widespread in
the cat population, with approximately 10% of household pets
and 25% to 75% of shelter or colony cats testing positive for FCV
shedding (Fig. 35.2). 17 , 43 , 46–48 As with other pathogens, FCV is
likely to be common in situations of cat hoarding. 49 The virus
persists in carriers in tonsillar and other oropharyngeal tissues.
Although the precise mechanism of persistence is unclear, it is
likely to include immune selection pressure driving antigenic
variation in the viral capsid protein, which then allows the virus
to evade the host immune response. 22 , 24 , 28 However other host,
viral, and environmental factors also undoubtedly play a role.
In situations such as boarding and rescue facilities, many
diﬀerent FCV strains tend to be present, probably reﬂecting the
relatively rapid turnover of carrier cats bringing in their own
strains from diﬀerent sources. 28 , 30 In contrast, in colonies of cats
where FCV is endemic, in general only one or two distinct strains
circulate. 28 , 30 , 50 Longitudinal studies of these endemically
infected colonies have shown that although many cats appear to
be long-term carriers, only a small minority (approximately 10%)
are persistently infected, the remainder undergoing cycles of
reinfection from within the colony. 50 Those with true persistent
infection continuously evolve their own viral strain over time.
Unlike FHV-1, there appears to be no latent phase for FCV
carriers; FCV carriers shed virus more or less continuously. 51 The
remainder of long-term carriers appear to undergo cycles of
reinfection, either with a variant of the same strain, or in some
cases, a diﬀerent strain circulating within the colony.
Interestingly, some cats within these endemic situations appeared
to be resistant to infection, suggesting either age-related or
genetically determined resistance. 51 These ﬁndings help explain:
(1) the lower carriage rate of approximately 10% in household
pets, where opportunity for reinfection is less likely to occur; and
(2) the inability in some previous experimental studies to induce a
carrier state in small groups of cats.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The natural routes of infection for FCV are nasal, oral, and
conjunctival. Viral replication mainly occurs in the oral and
respiratory tissues, although some diﬀerences between strains can
be found. Some strains have a predilection for the lung, and
others have been found in synovial ﬂuid macrophages. 52 , 53 Virus
may also be found in visceral tissues, feces, and occasionally in
the urine. Oral ulcers are the most prominent pathologic feature of
FCV infection. 13 These ulcers begin as vesicles, which
subsequently rupture, with necrosis of the overlying epithelium
and inﬁltration of neutrophils at the periphery and the base.
Healing takes place over 2 to 3 weeks.
Lower respiratory complications are dominated by multifocal
desquamation of activated alveolar macrophages and less
frequently occasional type II pneumocytes with ﬁbrin exudation,
consistent with diﬀuse alveolar damage. FCV has also been
shown to infect and replicate in alveolar macrophages and, to a
lesser extent, type II pneumocytes. 54 Although primary

vetexamprep.ir

interstitial pneumonia can occur in FCV infection, particularly
with more virulent strains, it has probably been overemphasized
in the past as a result of experimental studies using aerosol
challenge rather than the more natural oronasal routes. More
recently it has been suggested that FHV-1 infection may facilitate
secondary FCV infection of type II pneumocytes and alveolar
macrophages. 54
Lesions seen in FCV-infected joints consist of an acute synovitis
with thickening of the synovial membrane and an increased
amount of synovial ﬂuid within the joint. In cases of FCVassociated virulent systemic disease (VSD), virus gains access to
cellular compartments not normally associated with FCV
infection. 55 Lesions are widespread and include subcutaneous
edema, oral ulceration, and variable levels of cutaneous
ulceration, particularly on the pinnae, paw pads, and nares. 51 , 56–
58 Other lesions are more variable and include bronchointerstitial
pneumonia and necrosis in the liver, spleen, and pancreas. Viral
antigens have been detected in the skin, nasal mucosa, lung,
pancreas, liver, and endothelial cells of the dermis associated with
necrosis. 51 , 59
TABLE 35.1

vetexamprep.ir

state.
Strains of FCV can diﬀer in tropism and virulence. Therefore, a
wide range of clinical signs may be seen. Most strains induce a
fairly characteristic, mild syndrome characterized by pyrexia, oral
ulceration, and mild respiratory and conjunctival signs. Signs of
enteritis have been associated with some strains. 25 , 26 Some
strains of FCV, however, are nonpathogenic; others are more
virulent and may induce more severe systemic disease. Rarely,
ki ens may develop a fatal pneumonia. 54 Several outbreaks of a
severe acute systemic febrile disease with high mortality have
been described worldwide caused by particularly virulent strains
of FCV (FCV-associated VSD [FCV-VSD]). 57 , 60 , 61
In a typical case of FCV infection, early signs include lethargy
and pyrexia. Oral ulceration is the most characteristic feature and
may be the only clinical sign present, and it is possible that many
cases go unreported (Fig. 35.3). Ulceration is usually on the
tongue but can occur elsewhere in the mouth, on the lips, and on
the nose. Skin ulceration on other parts of the body occurs rarely.
Sneezing, conjunctivitis, and ocular and nasal discharges typically

vetexamprep.ir

occur but are generally relatively mild. 62 , 63 Cats with oral ulcers
may show hypersalivation. Some strains can cause pneumonia
with associated dyspnea, and others have been associated with
diarrhea. 25 , 26
Other FCV isolates produce a febrile disease with lameness and
pyrexia. 64 The lameness may or may not be associated with oral
and respiratory signs, and it is likely that considerable overlap
exists between the conditions. Aﬀected cats are often dull and
anorexic. In most cases, full recovery occurs within 24 to 48 hours.
Acute lameness has also been observed after vaccination, and in
some of these cases, viruses originating from live vaccines may be
involved; this was particularly associated with one vaccine no
longer licensed, and lameness following vaccination is now rare.
60

vetexamprep.ir

Lingual ulceration and mucopurulent
nasal discharge in a cat infected with FCV.
FIG. 35.3

Many of the described outbreaks of FCV-VSD are nosocomial
infections, and each outbreak appears to have been caused by a
diﬀerent FCV strain. 55 , 57 , 58 , 65 Although highly contagious
within a group of cats, all outbreaks have been contained, and the
disease has not spread into the general population. Possible
reasons for the appearance of such strains and for their
subsequent disappearance are not understood but have been
discussed elsewhere. 13 , 66 High mortality among aﬀected cats
and disease containment may be two important factors that limit
spread of these outbreaks, though other factors may play a role. 66
Cats with FCV-VSD variably show facial and paw edema,
pyrexia, classic signs of oral ulceration and upper respiratory
infection, icterus, epistaxis and hematochezia, and high mortality.
Necropsy ﬁndings are again somewhat variable in individual
cases but include pneumonia, hepatomegaly, pancreatitis, and

vetexamprep.ir

pericarditis. 56 , 57 , 59 , 65 , 67 , 68 Many aﬀected cats are fully
vaccinated, suggesting that, as can occur with more typical strains
of FCV, vaccines may not completely protect against these VSDproducing isolates. Although the outbreaks have been relatively
well controlled with strict quarantine and isolation, given that
FCV is an inherently variable pathogen, clinicians must remain
vigilant for further outbreaks of this disease.
The chronic oral disease feline chronic gingivostomatitis
complex has also been associated with FCV infection (see also
Chapter 125). 69 The prevalence of this condition has been
estimated at 0.7% of consultations in ﬁrst opinion practice in the
United Kingdom 70 and can be a particular problem because of the
diﬃculty in treating this condition. In a number of studies, more
than 80% of cats with chronic oral disease have been found to
shed FCV compared with approximately 20% of controls, 66 but
these ﬁgures may vary depending on the criteria used to select
clinical cases and the diagnostic assays used. 71 Recent work has
shown no correlation between FCV load and disease severity or
outcome. 72 FCV infection has been associated with acute faucitis,
73 and in one colony of cats, chronic stomatitis developed after the
accidental introduction of FCV. 74 However, other agents, in
particular FIV, and various host factors are likely to be involved in
the condition, and the pathogenesis is not yet fully understood.

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in cats with FCV infections vary
from mild serous ocular discharge and conjunctivitis through to
fever, severe mucopurulent ocular and nasal discharges,
dehydration, stertorous respiration, tachypnea and/or respiratory
diﬃculty, increased breath sounds on thoracic auscultation,
hypersalivation, and ulceration of the nasal planum, tongue, and
lips (Fig. 35.4). Because ulcerative lesions can occur at the base of
the tongue near the larynx, examination of the entire tongue
should be performed in cats that are febrile and inappetent, which
may require sedation. Cats with VSD can have edema of the face
and lips, icterus, cutaneous ulceration, evidence of petechial
hemorrhages, and abdominal pain. Cats with feline chronic
gingivostomatitis complex frequently test FCV positive. These
animals may have ulceroproliferative caudal stomatitis or
buccal/alveolar mucositis and exhibit pain on examination of the
oral cavity (Fig. 35.5).

Diagnosis
A range of pathogens other than FCV are associated with upper
respiratory tract disease in the cat, notably FHV-1, but also
Bordetella bronchiseptica and to a lesser extent Chlamydia felis
(primarily ocular). Generally, FCV remains the most commonly
detected pathogen in diseased cats, either alone or less frequently
in mixed infections. 75 While clinical signs can be suggestive of
one pathogen over another, they are rarely pathognomonic.
Speciﬁc diagnostic testing for FCV is not always necessary,
particularly in individual cases of relatively mild upper
respiratory tract disease. However, identifying a causative agent
may be helpful when disease is severe, warranting speciﬁc
therapy, where multiple cats are involved, and where disease
occurs in vaccinated cats.

vetexamprep.ir

Severe lymphoplasmacytic caudal
stomatitis in a cat infected with FCV.
FIG. 35.5

Laboratory Abnormalities
There are no speciﬁc CBC, biochemistry proﬁle, or urinalysis
abnormalities that aid in a diagnosis of FCV infection. The CBC
may be normal or show a mild to moderate neutrophilia,
sometimes with band neutrophils or neutrophil toxicity, and
lymphopenia in severely aﬀected cats with secondary bacterial
pneumonia. Hematological abnormalities in cats with VSD have
included mild to severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutrophilia,
and lymphopenia. Serum biochemistry ﬁndings in cats with viral
respiratory disease are usually unremarkable unless disease is
severe or chronic. Cats with VSD may have hypoalbuminemia,
hyperbilirubinemia, mildly increased serum activities of ALT and
AST, and mild to moderately increased serum CK activities.
Serum CK activities up to 11,000 U/L can occur. 56 Cats with
chronic stomatitis may have hyperglobulinemia due to a
polyclonal gammopathy.

vetexamprep.ir

Tracheobronchial lavage specimens from cats with pneumonia
may show a suppurative or mixed exudate, sometimes with
evidence of sepsis. Aerobic bacterial culture with mycoplasma
culture if possible is indicated on wash specimens, and
antimicrobial susceptibilities should be obtained for any aerobic
bacteria isolated. Organisms such as Pasteurella spp.,
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, Streptococcus spp., Escherichia coli,
Klebsiella pneumoniae, and some Mycoplasma spp. infect the airways
as opportunists and are not considered to be primary pathogens.
Bacterial culture of nasal swabs is generally not recommended
because it often leads to growth of normal ﬂora, which has no
clinical relevance.

Diagnostic Imaging
In uncomplicated infections, plain thoracic radiographs may be
unremarkable or show a mild diﬀuse interstitial to
bronchointerstitial pa ern. Alveolar pa erns or lung lobe
consolidation may occur with secondary bacterial pneumonia.

Microbiologic Tests
A presumptive diagnosis may be a empted based on clinical
signs alone. For example, predominantly oral ulceration might
indicate FCV infection, whereas marked sneezing with more
severe respiratory and conjunctival signs might suggest infection
by FHV-1 (Table 35.2). With Chlamydia infection, the main clinical
sign is marked persistent conjunctivitis (see Chapter 49).
Conﬁrmatory diagnosis of FCV is typically made by collection
of oropharyngeal swabs for testing, and is generally suﬃcient
(Table 35.3). However, addition of conjunctival or other specimens
may modestly increase sensitivity of respiratory pathogen
diagnosis. 76 Traditionally, viral isolation in feline cell cultures has
been used to detect FCV. 77 Several RT-PCR assays have now been
described, using various approaches including targeting diﬀerent

vetexamprep.ir

regions of the genome 78–80 and such molecular testing for FCV is
now being widely used commercially. PCR and sequencing,
particularly of the hypervariable region of the capsid gene, are
useful for distinguishing between FCV isolates and have been
extensively used to be er understand the epidemiology of the
disease. 17 , 66 Serology is generally not helpful in the diagnosis of
FCV infection because of the high prevalence of seroreactivity
from vaccination.
When an organism is detected in an animal with respiratory
disease, it is reasonable to assume that the agent is involved in the
disease process. However, especially for FCV and Bordetella, a
relatively large number of clinically healthy cats will also be
shedding the organisms. Therefore interpretation of a positive
result may be problematic unless taken in conjunction with other
factors, such as the characteristic clinical signs. Similarly for FHV1, latently infected cats may also shed reactivated virus, and thus
a positive result may also be unrelated to the observed clinical
signs. In an epidemiologic context, however, a positive result
indicates the cat has been infected with FHV-1 and thus has the
potential to infect other cats. For FHV-1, quantitative PCR can
provide additional information with respect to viral load and
stage of infection, especially if consecutive samples are taken. In
countries where intranasal vaccines are available, a positive result
may be indicative of FHV-1 or FCV vaccine virus rather than
wild-type viruses. FCV can be also detected in fecal specimens,
although the signiﬁcance of this is unknown. 2 , 81

vetexamprep.ir

TABLE 35.3

VSD, virulent systemic disease.

Pathologic Findings
Gross lesions in cats with FCV infections include cutaneous and
lingual ulcerations, submandibular or retropharyngeal lymph
node enlargement, mucosal hyperemia, and mucopurulent
exudate within the nasal cavity and trachea. The oral ulcers most
typical of FCV infection begin as vesicles, which subsequently
rupture, with necrosis of the overlying epithelium and inﬁltration
of neutrophils at the periphery and the base. Healing takes place
over 2 to 3 weeks. Rarer lower respiratory complications are
dominated by multifocal desquamation of activated alveolar
macrophages and occasional type II pneumocytes with ﬁbrin
exudation, consistent with diﬀuse alveolar damage; FCV has been
shown to infect and replicate in these cell types. Lesions seen in
FCV-infected joints consist of an acute synovitis with thickening
of the synovial membrane and an increased amount of synovial
ﬂuid within the joint; viral antigen in synovial macrophages
suggests these cells may be permissive as seen in the lung.
Necropsy ﬁndings in cats with VSD have been variable. Gross
lesions are widespread and include subcutaneous edema,
ulceration of the mouth, and variable levels of ulceration of the
skin particularly on the pinnae, pawpads, and nares. Frequently

vetexamprep.ir

reported ﬁndings include individual hepatocellular necrosis and
dissociation with minimal inﬂammation, acute interstitial
pneumonia, and free pleural and abdominal ﬂuid. 56 , 57 , 65 , 67
Acute necrotizing vasculitis of subcutaneous and oral submucosal
vessels has been reported. 82 Intestinal crypt necrosis and
pancreatitis have been reported in experimentally infected cats.
Viral antigens have been detected in the skin, nasal mucosa, lung,
pancreas, liver, and endothelial cells of the dermis associated with
necrosis.

Treatment and Prognosis
Good nursing care is essential in cases of feline respiratory
disease, and in milder cases is generally best given at home by the
owner. Many cats will not eat because of an impaired sense of
smell or oral ulceration, and thus they should be encouraged to
eat by oﬀering highly palatable, aromatic foods. Warm, freshly
prepared food may have more appealing ﬂavor and odor.
Appetite stimulants may be eﬀective in some cats. If eating is
painful, baby foods or specialized proprietary or blended food
may be helpful. Cats with severe illness may require
hospitalization and ﬂuid therapy, and when anorexia is
prolonged, placement of a feeding tube may be indicated. Nasal
discharges should be wiped away with saline. Mucolytic drugs
(e.g., bromhexine hydrochloride) have been suggested to help
clear airways in the more chronic phase, but conventional steam
inhalation (e.g., placing the cat in a steamy room) or nebulizing
saline also may be useful. Administration of pain medications and
chlorhexidine mouthwashes may improve appetite for cats with
painful oral ulcerations.
In most cases of viral respiratory disease, antibacterial
treatment may not be required. Current guidelines suggest that
antibacterials are only indicated when clinical signs persist for
over 10 days and/or when the cat is systemically unwell; in such
cases, doxycycline or amoxicillin/clavulanate are preferred. 83
Because swallowing solid tablets may be painful for cats,
antibiotics may need to be given as syrups or long-acting
injections, or through a feeding tube.
No speciﬁc antiviral drugs are available for treatment of FCV
infections. Ribavirin is active in cell culture but was too toxic for

vetexamprep.ir

in vivo use. 84 , 85 FCV strains show varying susceptibility to IFN
in vitro. 86 Some authors advocate the use of IFN to treat feline
chronic gingivostomatitis complex. 13 , 87 A synthetic antisense
nucleotide sequence, phosphorodiaminate morpholino oligomer,
which speciﬁcally binds to FCV, was trialed in ki ens during
natural outbreaks of FCV-VSD. The results suggested an
increased survival in treated cats compared to untreated animals.
88 However, this was a small-scale study and such therapies are
not commercially available.

Immunity and Vaccination
For FCV, immunity has generally been measured by serum virusneutralizing (VN) antibody levels. Systemic antibodies measured
by VN have always been considered the hallmark of immunity for
FCV and are certainly important in protection, as studies using
mouse-cat chimeric antibodies have also shown. 89 , 90 However,
some cats with no detectable FCV-VN antibody have
demonstrated immunity to re-challenge with a heterologous
strain, and several types of cell-mediated immune responses have
been reported. 91 In a 2021 study, a enuated live vaccination of
research cats induced cellular but not humoral cross-protective
immune responses, highlighting the importance of non-humoral
mechanisms of immunity against FCV. 92 For both FCV and FHV1, local immune responses are also likely to be important.
Nevertheless, for both viruses, a reasonable correlation has been
shown with serologic (VN and ELISA) tests to predict resistance
or susceptibility to disease after challenge. 32 , 93 The ultimate test
of immunity is, of course, response to challenge.
With FCV infection, homologous VN antibody titers are
generally higher than those in FHV-1 and are be er correlated to
protection, 32 and immunity is also longer lived. However, some
variation exists, depending on the viral strain involved and
whether homologous or heterologous protection is being
considered. Reinfection with a second strain will generally boost
responses to both strains. After vaccination against FCV,
reasonable protection has been reported to last for at least 3 years,
and moderate levels of antibody for at least 4 years. 93–96 However,

vetexamprep.ir

this will likely depend on vaccine and challenge strain
combinations evaluated.
For FCV, in most ki ens, MDAs persist for 10 to 14 weeks. 13
However, there is considerable variation for both viruses. In one
study, 20% to 26% of ki ens had no detectable antibodies at 6
weeks of age. 97 In contrast, in some animals, levels of MDA that
interfere with vaccination may persist until 12 to 14 weeks of age.
97–99 Low levels of MDA do not necessarily protect against
subclinical infection.
Vaccines for FCV have been available for many years and
vaccination has been relatively successful in controlling disease.
However, disease can still be a problem, especially when cats are
kept grouped together and when ki ens lose their MDA before
vaccination. FCV is very widespread in the cat population and
carriers are common, ensuring plenty of exposure for naïve cats.
Prevention and control, therefore, often require a combined
approach of vaccination and management.
Three types of FCV vaccines are commercially available:
a enuated live virus vaccines administered parenterally or IN,
and inactivated virus vaccines given parenterally. The la er are
generally adjuvanted, but products are available in some parts of
the world where the inactivated FCV component is without
adjuvant.
In previously unexposed cats, all vaccines induce reasonable
protection against disease. There is increasing evidence that
vaccinated animals shed less virus following subsequent
challenge. 47 , 95 However, vaccination does not completely protect
against infection or the development of the carrier state, and as a
result, vaccinated animals can still act as an important reservoir of
FCV infection in the population.
Several FCV strains are used in commercial vaccines, including
strains F9 and 255. In addition, bivalent (G1/431) and trivalent
vaccines have been developed and in some cases marketed,
containing additional strains of FCV including those associated
with VSD. 32 , 34 , 95 , 100 , 101 Most of these strains seem to protect
against the majority of FCV isolates. 17 , 102 A 2021 study showed
reduction in viral RNA loads, duration of RNAemia, and severity
of clinical signs in cats vaccinated with a single a enuated live
FCV strain (F9) and challenged at 46 and 99 weeks with

vetexamprep.ir

heterologous strains. 103 However, for all vaccines, the antigenic
diversity of FCV means that strains will probably vary in the
degree of protection oﬀered by diﬀerent vaccines. Multivalent
vaccines may increase the proportion of strains against which the
vaccines are eﬀective when compared to the individual antigens
that they contain, 32 , 34 , 100 , 101 , 104 , 105 but more studies are
needed to validate this.
FCV vaccines are only licensed to control acute upper
respiratory tract disease. There is no evidence that vaccines aﬀect
the onset, development, or course of chronic stomatitis. For VSD,
many outbreaks have been reported in vaccinated animals.
Evidence for protection against VSD is perhaps conﬂicting. It is
clear that several outbreaks have been reported in vaccinated
animals. However, experimental challenge studies for some FCV
vaccines have shown protection against individual VSD strains. 32
, 100 Taken together, it is likely that other potentially virulent
strains exist in the ﬁeld but remain undetected because they
happen to be suﬃciently neutralized by vaccination. However, all
VSD outbreaks have so far been caused by distinct strains, and
there is no evidence to suggest the virulent viruses have a unique
antigenic proﬁle, distinct from more typical strains. 55 , 66
Therefore it is likely that no vaccine will protect against all VSD
strains. The priority for vaccine eﬃcacy should be to demonstrate
broad general cross reactivity against a wide range of strains of
varying pathogenicity that remains stable over time.
Parenteral a enuated live vaccines should be administered
carefully because clinical signs can be induced if the vaccine virus
reaches the oral-respiratory mucosa (i.e., if the cat licks the
injection site or if an aerosol is made with the syringe). Vaccine
virus should not become systemic; however, replication of FCV
vaccine virus after parenteral inoculation may sometimes occur,
with the potential for disease in the vaccinated cat and spread to
other cats. 13 , 106 However, genetic typing of FCV isolates from
vaccine reactions has shown that the majority are associated with
coincidental ﬁeld virus infection, with vaccine-like viruses only
being isolated rarely from either vaccine reactions or the general
cat population. 28 , 29 , 50 , 60 , 107
Intranasal vaccines induce strong protection, but mild to
moderate adverse eﬀects may develop, such as sneezing and

vetexamprep.ir

oculonasal discharges. Intranasal vaccines, however, are useful for
rapid (2 to 4 days) onset of protection. 108–110 Intranasal vaccines
used in conjunction with parenteral vaccine on entry have
reduced the severity of upper respiratory disease in cats
introduced or maintained at contaminated shelters for 3 or more
days. 111
Inactivated adjuvanted FCV vaccines are also eﬀective, and
modern adjuvants have led to improvements in immunogenicity.
Concerns about an association between adjuvanted vaccines and
injection site sarcomas have led to marketing of a nonadjuvanted
vaccine containing inactivated FCV antigens in some parts of the
world, although the FHV-1 and feline panleukopenia fractions
remain a enuated. Vaccination with an inactivated vaccine during
pregnancy can help protect ki ens by prolonging the duration of
MDA. However, product information supplied by the
manufacturer should be consulted to determine whether this is
approved.
There is a general agreement that FCV vaccination is a core
requirement for all cats, such that all cats should beneﬁt from
vaccine protection. However, the timing of such vaccines are
complicated as local and national guideline groups—including
the AAFP, the ABCD, and the WSAVA—seek to balance the desire
to reduce injections (and hence sarcoma risk) with the need to
ensure high levels of protection in the face of uncertain MDA
levels and duration of immunity. In most cases, product data
sheets advocate a primary ki en course with parenteral vaccines
at approximately 9 and 12 weeks of age. A third vaccination may
be considered 3 to 4 weeks later when MDA levels are believed to
be high enough to interfere with the ﬁrst two vaccines. 97–99 , 112
For example, a third ki en vaccine may be rationally introduced
in populations of cats where MDA levels are unknown but where
disease has occurred previously in young cats before the ﬁrst
booster (at 6 months or 1 year of age). Similarly, annual booster
vaccines would be reserved for those adult cats perceived to be
exposed to high-risk situations (e.g., boarding ca eries and rescue
shelters), with triennial vaccination being suﬃcient for cats at low
risk (e.g., indoor cats; those living in areas of low cat densities
where cat populations are generally stable). Such a tailored
approach clearly requires an individual risk-beneﬁt assessment to
determine the most appropriate vaccination strategy for a

vetexamprep.ir

particular cat. The diﬀerent approaches to vaccination are
reﬂected in practice where it seems a variable approach to
vaccination is taken. The reader is referred to Chapter 20 for more
information on immunization and the appendix for vaccination
interval recommendations.

Prevention
Household Cats
After the ﬁrst booster, pets should be vaccinated regularly against
FCV and FHV-1 (1 to 3 years), the frequency depending on the
individual cat’s perceived risk, and also the speciﬁc vaccine being
used and its duration of immunity claim. In general, however, for
cats at low risk (e.g., indoor cats; those living in areas of low cat
densities where cat populations are generally stable), triennial
vaccination is likely to be suﬃcient, whereas cats exposed to highrisk situations (e.g., boarding ca eries and rescue shelters) should
be vaccinated annually. Ideally, to minimize the possibility of
infectious disease, a friend or neighbor should feed the cat while
the owner is on vacation, rather than boarding the cat in a ca ery.
Individual cats should be protected from stress and high-risk
social contact as much as possible to avoid exposure.

Boarding Catteries
All cats entering a ca ery should have an up-to-date vaccination
record for FHV-1 and FCV. 46 In boarding ca eries, where animals
may be stressed and exposure to carriers is likely, annual boosters
may be advisable. When rapid protection is required, the
intranasal vaccine may be advisable. Clients should be aware that
such vaccines themselves may induce mild clinical signs.
Ca ery owners should not rely on vaccination alone for disease
control because pathogens will inevitably be present either from
the occasional cat incubating disease or from carriers. Thus,
measures should be taken to prevent spread of infection and
reduce the concentration of infectious agents in the environment
(Box 35.1).

Shelter Facilities

vetexamprep.ir

In general, the same management measures apply as those with
boarding ca eries. Although this practice may be more diﬃcult to
achieve, molecular typing studies have demonstrated that limiting
the spread of individual FCV isolates within a shelter is possible if
good hygiene measures are used. 30 , 50 Because the immune
status of cats in a rescue shelter is often unknown, incoming
animals should ideally be quarantined from existing residents.
Unless animals can be isolated on arrival for 3 to 4 weeks,
parenteral vaccines may not have time to become eﬀective. 95
Those with clinical signs should also be isolated. In these
circumstances, use of intranasal vaccines may be advisable if
available. Stress plays an important role in predisposing to
infection and disease for a range of feline pathogens, and it is
good practice to reduce stress levels where possible. 113 The reader
is referred to Chapter 16 for more information on prevention of
infectious diseases in shelter environments.

Breeding Catteries
If any ca ery has contact, whether direct or indirect, with other
cats, it is safest to assume that most will have some level of FCV
infection unless proven otherwise by repeat diagnostic testing. In
closed colonies trying to stay virus free, use of inactivated
vaccines is preferable. Care should be taken to avoid bringing
virus into the colony; any cat with a history of, or contact with,
oral or respiratory disease may be a carrier. Vaccinated cats can
also be carriers, and ki ens can be infected subclinically because
of MDA. This, in part, explains the risk of infection from cat
shows, where many cats are FCV positive. However, the greatest
risk of infection to disease-free households is likely to be from
stud cats and new breeding stock when exposure is prolonged;
introduction of such animals should ideally be from respiratory
disease-free colonies.
Cats entering a disease-free colony should be quarantined for 3
weeks to identify animals incubating the disease. Cats should be
tested for virus shedding at least twice a week during this time.
This practice increases the probability of detecting FHV-1 (as virus
may reactivate after a change of housing) and some FCV carriers
that may be shedding only low levels of virus. Even so, the risk
still exists of importing a latent FHV-1 carrier or a low-level FCV

vetexamprep.ir

carrier that may be a source of infection. For most situations, the
only reasonable course is to a empt disease control (Box 35.2).

Public Health Aspects
Feline calicivirus is generally considered species-speciﬁc and
poses no known human health risk. However, FCV has been used
as a surrogate virus for the study of human norovirus because of
shared biochemical and genomic properties between the two
viruses. It was also used to develop a mask decontamination
method to assess the ability to reuse N95 masks in the COVID-19
pandemic. 114

Case Example 1
Signalment

“Sam,” a 1-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat from
Orangevale, CA.

History

Sam’s owner, a veterinary technician, reported a 4-day history
of illness that began with ptyalism and progressed to
inappetence and diﬃculty prehending both canned and dry
food. The owner also noted that Sam’s mouth had a foul odor.
There had been no diarrhea, vomiting, coughing, or sneezing.
He was an indoor-outdoor cat and was obtained as a ki en,
with no previous health problems. There was one other 2-yearold cat in the household that was apparently healthy. Sam was
up to date on vaccinations, which included vaccines for FCV,
FHV-1, FPV, FeLV, and rabies.

Current Medications
None.

vetexamprep.ir

Physical Examination
Body weight: 5.6 kg
General: Quiet, alert, responsive, hydrated. Ambulatory
on all four limbs. Temperature = 102.9°F (39.4°C), heart
rate = 180 beats/min, respiratory rate = 48 breaths/min,
mucous membranes pink, CRT = 1 s.
Integument: A normal haircoat was present and there was
no evidence of ectoparasites.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No signiﬁcant abnormalities
of the eyes, nose, or ears were noted. There was moderate
ptyalism, and examination of the oral cavity revealed
multiple ulcerations along the right lip and a 1-cm ulcer
on the rostral aspect of the tongue.
Musculoskeletal: A body condition score of 6/9 was noted.
No visible lameness or musculoskeletal abnormalities
were noted.
Cardiovascular: Strong femoral pulses were noted. No
murmurs or arrhythmias were detected on thoracic
auscultation.
Respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary: No
abnormalities detected.
Lymph nodes: There was mild enlargement of the right
mandibular lymph node.

Laboratory Findings

Sam was anesthetized and a swab specimen was collected from
the oropharynx. The specimen tested strongly positive for FCV
using real-time PCR.

Diagnosis

FCV infection.

Treatment

While under anesthesia, an esophagostomy tube for
administration of food and water was placed without
complication. In addition, Sam was prescribed buprenorphine
(1.5 mg PO q12h) for pain and oral sucralfate suspension in an
a empt to coat the lingual ulcerations (1 mL PO q8h, at least 1

vetexamprep.ir

hour before buprenorphine). The feeding tube was removed 2
weeks later.

Comments

This case was interesting because of the sole ﬁnding of lingual
ulcerations, without any other evidence of respiratory disease,
which was so dramatic that a caustic cause of oral ulceration
was suspected by the clinician on the case. The positive PCR
test result does not prove that the cause of the oral ulcerations
was FCV, because of the carrier state, but the strong positive
test result in association with typical clinical signs in a young
cat owned by a veterinary technician was strongly suggestive.
The cat may have acquired infection from contact with other
outdoor cats, or it is possible that the owner introduced the
virus on her clothing or other fomites because she was
unwi ingly in contact with a carrier cat at her workplace.
Although she was instructed to do her best to separate this cat
from her other cat and disinfect her household with
disinfectants that have activity against FCV, it is likely that her
other cat had already been exposed. Fortunately, no clinical
signs appeared in this cat. This case also illustrates the
occurrence of disease in the face of proper vaccination, possibly
because of lack of strain cross-protection.

Case Example 2

You provide veterinary care to a breeding colony of some ﬁve
queens. On the 15th February, four 12-week-old ki ens received
their second a enuated live core FVRCP vaccine. One week
later (22nd February), the four ki ens developed lingual ulcers
and fever.
The owners were extremely disappointed as they were not
aware of previous infections in their colony. Because of the
history of recent vaccination, the similarity of the signs to FCV
infection, and the fact that an a enuated live vaccine was used,
you submit plain oropharyngeal swabs in virus transport
medium for diagnostic testing. Four days later, the results
conﬁrm that three of the ki ens are infected with FCV.

vetexamprep.ir

Oropharyngeal swabs were also submi ed for Bordetella
bronchiseptica isolation but were negative.
As a result of the positive tests for FCV, you discuss this case
with the vaccine manufacturer as a potential adverse event. It is
agreed that one of the ki en FCV isolates be typed and
compared to the sequence of the virus in the vaccine. This
sequence strongly suggested that the FCV infection in the
breeding household did not originate from the vaccine, rather
that the cats were infected with a distinct ﬁeld strain of virus.
Several questions should be considered in regard to why the
ki ens were infected with FCV ﬁeld viruses so soon after
vaccination.
1. Is FCV causing the disease? It is possible the disease in the
ki ens was not caused by FCV. The prevalence of FCV
carriers is high and therefore the FCV infection of these
cats may have been incidental. However, the clinical
signs were quite suggestive of FCV infection, so it seems
reasonable to assume that the virus caused the disease.
2. Why did these ki ens develop clinical disease if they have
already received vaccines? The incubation period for FCV is
generally approximately 2 to 7 days, although it may be
longer in some cases. Therefore it seems likely that the
ki ens were infected approximately between the 15th
and 20th February, 0 to 5 days after their second
vaccination on the 13th February. At this stage, the ki ens
were not completely protected by the anamnestic
response of vaccination. Therefore this case cannot be
considered a failure of the vaccine to protect. This only
becomes a concern when fully vaccinated animals
develop clinical disease.
3. Where did the virus isolated from the ki ens come from? The
most likely origin of this ﬁeld virus is other cats within
the breeding household. The prevalence of FCV in
households can be very high (up to 90%), unless there is
strict isolation of the cats in the colony. Infection can
remain clinically silent in fully vaccinated adult cats in
such households. Clinical disease may only occur when
ki ens become infected in the immunity gap between the
decline of MDA and onset of vaccine immunity. It can be

vetexamprep.ir

useful to determine the extent of FCV (and FHV-1)
infection in such colonies by testing some of the other
cats, especially if clinical disease in ki ens is a regular
occurrence. Owners are sometimes surprised to learn that
their adult cats have FCV (or FHV-1) infection when they
have no clinical disease and have been regularly
vaccinated. This is because FCV (and FHV-1) vaccines do
not protect against the establishment of the carrier state.

36: Feline Foamy (SyncytiumForming) Virus Infection
Chrissy Eckstrand

KEY POINTS
• Cause: FFV, family Retroviridae, subfamily Spumaretrovirinae.
• First Described: 1969, United States. 1
• Affected Hosts: Domestic cat and many other Felidae.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Route of Transmission: Unknown, but vertical transmission (in
utero and/or mammary) and salivary transmission through
close contact are hypothesized.
• Major Clinical Signs: An association between FFV infection
and clinical disease remains unproven, but the virus has been
detected in cats with idiopathic polyarthritis.
• Differential Diagnosis: Primary immune-mediated polyarthritis,
polyarthritis secondary to other infections such as FeLV, FCV,
Chlamydia felis, Mycoplasma spp. infection.
• Human Health Significance: Although foamy viruses can infect
multiple cell lines, no known transmission from cats to
humans has been documented.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
FFV, previously known as “feline syncytium-forming virus,” is a
retrovirus in the family Retroviridae, subfamily Spumaretrovirinae. 2
Host-speciﬁc viruses of this genus have also been isolated from
various mammalian species including ca le and nonhuman
primates and often have no, or low, pathogenic potential. 3 , 4

vetexamprep.ir

Foamy viruses are atypical retroviruses in that viral particles bud
from the endoplasmic reticulum, can contain DNA or RNA, and
are highly cell-associated. Additionally, reverse transcription can
occur late in the cell infection cycle. 2 , 5 Proviral DNA is
integrated into the host cell chromosome, and persistent infection,
with or without viral production, can result. The prevalence of
FFV infection is high in both clinically healthy and diseased cats.
At least two genotypes and serotypes have been identiﬁed, which
share broad serologic cross-reactivity even to the serotype-speciﬁc
ectodomain of the FFV Env-SU glycoprotein. 6–8 Virus has been
isolated from primary cultures of tissue and body secretions in up
to 90% of a population of cats. 9 More typically, the prevalence of
infection in a cat population varies between 25% and 50%,
depending on the age, geographic location, and local environment
of the cats. 10–16 Furthermore, 50% or more of ki ens born to FFVinfected queens are infected at birth, 15 and 15% of cultures from
fetal cats are positive for the virus, suggesting that it can be
transmi ed vertically. 17 In utero infection probably occurs by the
transfer of infected maternal leukocytes across the placenta, but
infection may also be transmi ed through milk of lactating
animals. 15
The highest prevalence of FFV infection is in roaming or
outdoor cats, suggesting possible transmission through bite
wounds (like FIV); however, epidemiologic evidence suggests that
FFV is more likely transmi ed by intimate social contact (like
FeLV). 18 This is also supported by serologic evidence that male
and female cats, with or without neutering, have an equal rate of
seroreactivity. 14 Some wild cat species (Felis silvestris, Felis
iriomotensis, and Felis bengalensis) also have a relatively high
prevalence rate of seroreactivity to FFV; however, extensive
surveys are not available. 13 , 19 , 20
FFV is a nuisance to virologists and manufacturers of feline
therapeutics like vaccines and mesenchymal stem cells because it
often only becomes apparent in feline tissues and cell cultures
after multiple passages. 21–23 In vitro, FFV is not highly host
speciﬁc; in addition to cat cells, it infects cells of dogs, chickens,
humans, and bats. 20 This is supported by evidence that foamy
viruses utilize heparan sulfate, a ubiquitous cellular
polysaccharide, as an a achment factor. 24 When FFV is produced,

vetexamprep.ir

it is enveloped and has long glycoprotein spikes (Fig. 36.1A). Viral
particles may accumulate in the host cell cytoplasm within
membrane-bound vesicles, giving the cell a foamy appearance. In
cell culture, it produces multinucleated syncytia within 1 to 2
weeks of growth in certain rapidly multiplying tissue cultures
(Fig. 36.1B). Cell lysis is a late event because large syncytia are not
viable. Syncytium formation in cell culture is not unique to FFV; it
also has been associated with a variant of FeLV where an insertion
into the FeLV envelope glycoprotein gene is responsible for this
CPE. 25 FFV can be distinguished from FeLV, which is visualized
only as it buds from the cell, whereas FFV often forms
recognizable intracytoplasmic inclusions and preassembled
nucleocapsids within the cytoplasm before budding (see Fig.
36.1A).
FFV has been considered an a ractive retroviral vector for the
delivery of feline vaccine antigens and heterologous genes
because of its lack of apparent pathogenicity, and its suitability as
such has been demonstrated. 26–30 The complete genome of FFV
proviral DNA has been cloned, manipulated to be replicationcompetent or replication-deﬁcient depending on the therapeutic
purpose, 31 , 32 and explored for use in cats. 31–34

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
FFV has never been unambiguously associated with disease.
Many cats have been infected naturally and experimentally and
had no clinical illness, a scenario that may reﬂect a very close
virus-host co-adaptation. 35 , 36 Virus replication in the cat is a
complex interplay between host immunity, host antiviral
restriction factors such as APOBEC3 proteins, and virus accessory
proteins, such as Bet, which counteracts APOBEC3. 37–40

vetexamprep.ir

Reports about FFV pathogenicity are controversial and
conﬂicting. Investigations into the presence of the virus in cats
with chronic polyarthritis are quite variable with 100% of cats
aﬀected with chronic progressive polyarthritis in one study and
15% in another. 41 , 42 Concurrent FeLV infection was found in 70%
of cats in the former study mentioned. The prevalence of infection

vetexamprep.ir

with both viruses was 2 to 10 times greater than that in agematched cats not having chronic progressive polyarthritis. By
altering the host immune system, FeLV may potentiate the ability
of FFV to produce disease. Combined infections with FFV and FIV
are also frequently found. 42 , 43 However, co-infection with FFV
and FIV did not increase the severity of FIV-induced illness in the
early stages of the disease. 32 A combined infection is most likely a
result of a common mode of transmission rather than a mutual
pathogenic mechanism. FFV strains infect lymphoblastoid cells
in vitro, producing altered replication, syncytia formation, and
fragmentation of cellular DNA. 44 These features of apoptosis may
be responsible for independent immune alterations in infected
cats.
Immune-mediated polyarthritis is hypothesized to result from
chronic antigenic stimulation and immune complex deposition.
Arthritis that occurs in conjunction with FFV infection is
characterized histologically in the acute stage as ﬁbrinopurulent
synovitis, and chronically as lymphoplasmacytic synovitis with
synovial hyperplasia, loss of articular cartilage, pannus, and
periosteal and subchondral bone remodeling. 45 An inherent
genetic tendency may explain why certain male cats are more
prone to developing disease despite the high prevalence of these
viral infections in the general population. It is currently not clear
whether FFV or any persisting feline virus contributes to arthritis
or related immunopathologic disease of cats. Using PCR, FFV
DNA was not detected in tissue from vaccine site-associated
sarcomas from cats. 28
Most FFV-infected cats show no clinical signs. Chronic
progressive polyarthritis of cats generally aﬀects naturally
infected males between 1½ and 6 years of age. 41 , 46–49 Two forms
of the disease have been described: one with osteoporosis and
periarticular periosteal proliferation, the other with periarticular
erosions, collapse of the joint space, and joint deformities.
Lymphadenomegaly and arthralgias are caused by both types. In
experimentally FFV-infected cats that were monitored for a 6month period PI, histopathologic changes of mild
glomerulonephritis and moderate interstitial pneumonia were
observed 50 ; however, no corresponding co-housed uninfected

vetexamprep.ir

control cats were evaluated to substantiate the association of the
virus infection with these mild lesions.

Diagnosis
Microbiologic Tests
Serologic Diagnosis
FFV infections are associated with the production of virus-speciﬁc
antibodies by the infected hosts. Therefore, assays based on
immunodiﬀusion methods, IFA, immunoblo ing, and ELISA are
used to test for virus-speciﬁc antibodies. 16 , 41 , 42 , 51 , 52 Infected
ki ens can be detected at birth by culturing buﬀy coat cells from
their peripheral blood. Animals are infected for life and develop
persistent, nonprotective antibody titers to the virus. 53 For this
reason, cats showing a serologic response toward FFV are
presumed to be infected. Neonatal ki ens born to infected queens
lose their maternal antibody by 6 to 8 weeks of age if they are not
infected. Serum antibody titers increase after this time if they
become infected. 17
Virus Isolation
In addition to serology, virus cultures to screen cats for infection
by the detection of FFV-speciﬁc antigens and CPEs (syncytia) can
be performed. Virus can be isolated from most tissues but requires
one to four passages in vitro. IHC has been developed to detect the
FFV Bet protein, and is predominantly present in cells of
lymphoid organs such as the lymph nodes, tonsils, thymus, and
spleen. 54 Additionally, FFV has been demonstrated in saliva. 53 It
appears that FFV replication in peripheral blood leukocytes is
suppressed by the host. This latent virus can be reactivated by cocultivating buﬀy-coat leukocytes with permissive feline cells. 53
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR can also be used directly to detect virus in blood leukocytes
or cells of body ﬂuids or tissues. There is a 100% correlation
between seropositive results in cats and detection of proviral
DNA in leukocytes. 52

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment And Prevention
FFV infection is lifelong and eradication therapies do not
currently exist. Additionally, speciﬁc antiviral therapies have not
been thoroughly investigated for use as infection is generally
considered nonpathogenic. The antiviral drug tenofovir can
salvage FFV-infected mesenchymal stem cells from CPEs when
cultured in vitro for autologous mesenchymal stem cell therapy. 21
Chronic progressive polyarthritis has no known cure, and the
clinical and pathologic changes it causes usually are temporarily
responsive for weeks to months to immunosuppressive therapy
such as prednisolone (10–15 mg/day per cat) and
cyclophosphamide (2.5 mg/day per cat, PO, for 4 days each week).
Cats identiﬁed as having polyarthritis should be eliminated from
research projects and removed from donating stem cells, vaccine
production, and SPF colonies because an infectious or contagious
etiology cannot be excluded.

Public Health Aspects
All nonhuman primate species harbor distinct host-species
speciﬁc strains of simian foamy viruses that are genetically
diﬀerent from FFV. 52 No data are available to document the
existence of an authentic human foamy virus; however, people
who are occupationally exposed to nonhuman primates have the
highest rate of exposure and zoonotic infection to the diﬀerent
simian foamy viruses. 55 Other foamy viruses of domestic animals,
including FFV, can infect a variety of cell types from diﬀerent
species in vitro. No transmission of these other viruses to people
has been documented. 3 , 52 Furthermore, data from studies of
seroreactivity
among
veterinarians
and
other
people
occupationally exposed to cats did not support an increased risk
of infection. 56

37: Paramyxovirus Infections
Hans Lu , Claire R. Sharp, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Viruses of the family Paramyxoviridae; genera
Morbillivirus (feline morbillivirus [FeMV], canine distemper
virus [CDV]), Henipavirus (including Hendra virus [HeV] and
Nipah virus], and the newly named Rubulavirus (previously
paramyxovirus; mumps virus [MuV]).
• First Described: FeMV was first described in China in 2012. 1
CDV was first described in France in 1905. 2 HeV was first
isolated in Queensland, Australia in 1994. 3 Nipah virus was
first identified in humans in Malaysia in 1999. MuV was first
described in 410 BC (Hippocrates).
• Affected Hosts: Domestic cats (FeMV); large wild Felidae,
dogs and other Canidae, Procyonidae (raccoons, pandas),
Mustelidae (ferrets, mink, skunks, otters), nonhuman primates
(CDV); horses, humans, flying foxes (reservoirs), domestic
cats (experimental infection only), guinea pigs (experimental),
dogs (HeV); pigs, humans, fruit bats (reservoirs), domestic
cats, dogs (Nipah virus); humans, dogs, cats (MuV).
• Geographic Distribution: Asia, Europe, North and South
America (FeMV); northeastern Australia (HeV); Malaysia,
Singapore, Bangladesh, India (Nipah virus); worldwide (MuV).
• Route of Transmission: Oronasal contact with virus in
secretions or excretions, droplet nuclei, and large particle
aerosol transmission.
• Major Clinical Signs: Paramyxoviruses cause infections of the
CNS, and respiratory and urinary tracts. FeMV has been
implicated in chronic kidney disease in cats, but its clinical
significance remains unclear. Natural infections of dogs with

vetexamprep.ir

HeV have been rare and subclinical. Natural infections of
dogs and cats with Nipah virus are also rare, but death and
severe respiratory signs have been described. MuV can
cause parotitis with salivary gland enlargement.
• Differential Diagnoses: These include other causes of
infectious respiratory disease; parasitic respiratory disease;
toxins such as lead and ethylene glycol; other causes of
infectious meningoencephalitis. Differential diagnosis for
mumps include other causes of parotitis such as immunemediated disease.
• Human Health Significance: FeMV is not known to infect
humans. HeV and Nipah viruses cause serious infections of
humans with high mortality. Mumps is a serious infection of
humans but largely controlled by vaccination; periodic
outbreaks still occur. Dogs and cats do not appear to be
important in transmission of these viruses to humans.

Introduction
The Paramyxoviridae family includes, among others, feline
morbillivirus (FeMV), canine distemper virus (CDV), Henipavirus
(including Hendra virus [HeV] and Nipah virus), and Rubulavirus
(including mumps virus [MuV]). These viruses aﬀect domestic
and wild felids, canids, procyonids, mustelids, and many more
mammalian species. Transmission is by close contact, droplets,
and aerosols. These infections, of which many occur around the
world, can cause mild to serious diseases of the CNS, and
respiratory and urinary tracts, but many infections are associated
with no symptoms. Henipavirus infections in Asia and Australia
are zoonotic diseases and can be very serious in humans, but are
hardly transmi ed to humans by cats and dogs.
Paramyxoviruses have been associated with emerging
infectious diseases in a variety of species in recent decades, and as
such are important viruses to both human and veterinary
medicine. 4 This chapter focuses on paramyxovirus infections in
cats, although infections of both dogs and cats with HeV, Nipah
virus, and MuV are also described. Diagnostic testing for these

vetexamprep.ir

la er three virus infections requires coordination with local public
health authorities given their signiﬁcance for human health.

Feline Morbillivirus Infection
Until recently, the genus Morbillivirus was recognized to contain
six species: CDV, measles virus, rinderpest virus (now
eradicated), peste des petits ruminants virus, phocine distemper
virus, and cetacean morbillivirus. Of these, only CDV had been
known to aﬀect felids, causing clinical signs in some large exotic
felids, but not in domestic cats. In 2012 however, a novel FeMV
was isolated from cats in Hong Kong and mainland China. 1
This virus was oﬃcially recognized as the seventh species of the
genus Morbillivirus in 2016. Early reports of FeMV infection were
only in domestic cats, however in 2020 the virus was identiﬁed by
RT-PCR in urine and homogenized kidney tissue from two black
leopards (Panthera pardus) in Thailand. 5
In 2012, FeMV RNA was identiﬁed by RT-PCR in 56 of 457
(12.3%) stray cats from Hong Kong. 1 Of the specimen types
collected, urine was most commonly PCR positive for FeMV
(53/56 cat specimens). Subsequently, many of these cats were
shown to have antibodies to the FeMV N protein (54/56 RT-PCR
positive cats were antibody positive). Additionally, 78/401 (19.5%)
RT-PCR-negative cats were antibody positive, suggesting
previous exposure. Concurrently, 1/16 diseased cats from
mainland China was RT-PCR positive to FeMV in oral and rectal
swabs. 1 To identify possible disease associations, necropsies were
performed in two stray cats that were RT-PCR positive for FeMV.
1 Histology revealed renal tubular degeneration and necrosis in
both cats, consistent with tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN), the
histologic correlate of CKD in cats. In a small case-control study of
a further 27 stray cats, TIN was documented in 7/12 cats that were
positive for FeMV using RT-PCR, but only 2/15 FeMV-negative
cats (P < .05), suggesting an association between FeMV and TIN. 1
This ﬁrst report suggesting an association between FeMV and TIN
generated signiﬁcant interest in the ﬁeld, given the large disease
burden of CKD in cats. 6
Since its discovery, epidemiologic studies have now
documented FeMV in domestic cats in Japan, 7–9 Europe, 10–14 the

vetexamprep.ir

United States, 15 Brazil, 16 Malaysia, 17 and additional cases in
China. 18
To identify infected cats, most investigators have tested urine or
kidney tissue specimens, reporting a prevalence of FeMV infection
using RT-PCR that has ranged from 3%, in the northeastern
United States, 15 to 52.9% (9/17 cats) in a multicat house that had
close contact with a stray cat colony in Brazil. 16 While the mode
of FeMV transmission is unknown, its higher prevalence in the
aforementioned multicat household, as well as in colony cats, 19
suggests that close cat contact may be involved. Male
predominance has also been reported in some molecular
epidemiologic studies. 17 , 20
The seroprevalence of FeMV has also varied widely, although
fewer studies report the results of antibody testing.
Seroprevalence of anti-FeMV antibodies has ranged from 21.2% in
Japan 9 , 20 to 66.7% in the United Kingdom. 13 However, none of
the FeMV serosurveys have employed virus neutralization (VN),
the gold standard for diagnostic serology, and thus methodologic
limitations may have resulted in inaccuracies in serologic data.
Development of VN assays is needed to be er understand the
epidemiology of, and immune response to, FeMV.
Studies that have reported concurrent molecular and serological
data identify four populations of cats: (1) those that have never
been exposed to the virus (both RT-PCR and seronegative), (2)
those that have been exposed, developed antibodies, and likely
cleared the virus from their urine (RT-PCR negative, and
seropositive), (3) those likely to be in the early stage of infection
but without antibodies (RT-PCR positive but seronegative), and
(4) those both RT-PCR and seropositive, suggesting both the
presence of active viral shedding and circulating antibodies. At
least some cats in the fourth group appear to be chronically
infected. 14 , 15 , 19
Several studies have a empted to investigate the role of FeMV
infection in CKD in cats. Some have suggested an association, 10 ,
20 , 21 while others have found no association. 9 , 13 , 16 , 17 , 19
Undoubtedly FeMV can be identiﬁed in cat urine, both by RTPCR and virus isolation, and will grow after inoculation of CRFK
cells. Additionally, some authors have identiﬁed FeMV in renal
tubular epithelial cells by IHC. 1 , 13 , 22 Nonetheless, associations

vetexamprep.ir

documented in some of these studies do not prove causation, and
pathogenesis studies are needed. Of note, other morbilliviruses
are not known to cause kidney disease, despite infecting epithelial
cells of the urogenital tract.
Given that morbilliviruses are signiﬁcant pathogens in a variety
of host species, it is tempting to hypothesize that FeMV may cause
pathology in cats. Morbilliviruses are classically lymphotropic
and epitheliotropic, resulting in clinical signs aﬀecting the skin,
respiratory tract, GI tract, and CNS. Additionally, morbilliviruses
classically result in immunosuppression. Whether or not FeMV
results in a similar spectrum of disease in cats remains to be
determined. Only two studies speciﬁcally evaluating in vitro
FeMV cell tropism have been published, documenting FeMV
replication in cat ﬁbroblasts, lymphoid cells, and glial cells as well
as in renal, pulmonary epithelial and primary brain cells. Feline
morbillivirus genotype 2 (FeMV-GT2) also replicates readily in
several types of lymphocytes. 23 , 24
Evidence that FeMV can infect glial cells in vitro, in addition to
occasional clinical reports of FeMV RT-PCR positivity of cat brain
tissue, 19 suggest the potential for the virus to be neurotrophic, as
is seen with other morbilliviruses. It remains unknown to what
degree FeMV infection may explain historic evidence of a
paramyxovirus-like agent in the CNS of stray and pet cats with
subclinical focal demyelinating encephalitis. 25 , 26 Unfortunately
at the time, while paramyxovirus-like nucleocapsids were
observed using electron microscopy in ﬁxed cat brain and optic
nerve tissues, as well as explant cultures of CNS tissue cocultivated with CRFK cells, the virus could not be deﬁnitively
identiﬁed. 26
Future FeMV research should focus on acute and chronic
pathogenesis studies using experimental infections to understand
the route of infection, transmission, viral receptor usage, and cell
tropism of FeMV, in addition to the immune response to the virus,
and the pathology it causes. Ultimately, if FeMV is identiﬁed as a
pathogen, there will be a need for commercially available
diagnostic tests, the development of eﬀective vaccines, and even
investigation of the role of antivirals for the treatment of active
infection. Currently, testing for FeMV is being done on a research
basis and not oﬀered on a commercial basis, given the unclear role
of FeMV in disease.

vetexamprep.ir

Canine Distemper Virus Infection in Cats
CDV, which also belongs to the genus Morbillivirus, infects a wide
variety of terrestrial carnivores. Information on CDV infection in
dogs is covered in depth in Chapter 22. Domestic cats can be
infected through experimental inoculation, but clinical signs do
not develop. Virus-neutralizing antibodies to CDV have been
detected in domestic cats housed in close proximity to dogs, but
again, clinical illness has not been documented. 27 , 28 In contrast
to domestic cats, large exotic Felidae are more susceptible to
infection with CDV. CDV isolates from exotic felids are similar to
virulent isolates from other carnivores, and infection likely
originates from wildlife and/or domestic dogs in close proximity
to exotic cats (Fig. 37.1). 29–39 Noncanid carnivores, such as
raccoons and skunks, may also act as vectors of CDV for exotic
cats in zoological gardens. 40
There are several case reports implicating CDV in progressive
neurologic disease, with or without respiratory signs, in exotic
cats around the world, including an African lioness (Panthera leo),
41 Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris tigris), 42 both captive and freeranging adult Siberian tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), 38 , 43 and two
snow leopards (Uncia uncia). 44 Although isolation of CDV was
not performed in many of these cases, the presence of consistent
histologic
lesions
(non-suppurative
encephalitis
or
meningoencephalitis), characteristic intranuclear inclusions, IHC,
and serologic documentation of CDV antibodies provide strong
support for CDV as the etiologic agent. The aforementioned snow
leopards were co-infected with feline panleukopenia virus (FPV),
44 suggesting the possibility of FPV-induced immunosuppression.
CDV was also implicated as the cause of death in an Iberian lynx
(Lynx pardinus) in the Donana National Park in South-Western
Andalusia, Spain. 45 The Iberian lynx is at present the most
critically endangered felid, and the virus was closely related to
that isolated from a stone marten (Martes foina) found close by.
Thus, CDV represents a constant threat to free-ranging wild
felids.
CDV has caused large outbreaks of disease in free-ranging wild
felid populations. 46–48 The ﬁrst such outbreak occurred in 1994,
resulting in the death of a considerable proportion of lions in the

vetexamprep.ir

Serengeti in Tanzania. 46 , 49–51 Clinical signs were primarily
neurologic. Pathologic ﬁndings were encephalitis and pneumonia.
Inclusion bodies immunologically cross-reacting with CDV
proteins were identiﬁed in 14/19 lion specimens that were
available for examination. A total of 71/83 serum samples were
found to be positive for anti-CDV antibodies. 46 Phylogenetic
analysis suggested that the lion CDV isolate was closely related to
the Onderstepoort strain of CDV, and may have originated from
domestic dogs living around the Serengeti parks. 46 Purported
contributors to the epizootic included hyenas transmi ing the
disease to local domestic dogs and lions, and loss of crossimmunization of lions by consumption of rinderpest-infected
buﬀaloes when the closely related rinderpest virus was eradicated
in the 1980s. To reduce the probability of further outbreaks of
CDV in lions, a program to vaccinate the domestic dogs living
around the parks was initiated.

CDV outbreaks have also occurred in captive lions, tigers, and
leopards. 41 , 52 , 53 Aﬀected cats developed anorexia, GI and/or
respiratory signs, followed by CNS signs of ataxia, myoclonus,
seizures, coma, and death. Vaccination has been recommended to
protect captive large exotic Felidae, however vaccine eﬃcacy
remains incompletely documented. 54 , 55 A multi-institutional
study of 812 captive large felids documented that canarypoxvectored CDV vaccines were used most commonly in tigers, lions,
snow leopards, leopards, and jaguars (96.3%) compared with
a enuated live CDV vaccines (3.7%). Both vaccine types were
associated with low rates of adverse eﬀects (0.5% for the
canarypox-vectored vaccine, and 2.9% for the a enuated live
vaccine). However, only 66% of animals with serologic data
available experienced seroconversion at some point postvaccination. 54

Hendra Virus Infection
In September 1994, an outbreak of acute respiratory disease in
horses occurred in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, Queensland,
Australia. 3 , 56 , 57 The horses developed anorexia, lethargy,
pyrexia, tachypnea, and ataxia. Terminally, head pressing and
nasal discharge were described. A stable hand and horse trainer
became ill with an inﬂuenza-like illness. The stable hand was ill
for 6 weeks, and the trainer died. A novel virus, HeV (genus
Henipavirus), that was closely related to a Morbillivirus was
isolated from the horses and humans. Histologically, the horses
had interstitial pneumonia with pneumocyte and capillary
degeneration. 58 Virus was detected in endothelial cells using

vetexamprep.ir

immunoﬂuorescence, as well as in CSF, brain tissue, and serum
using PCR. 59 Necrotizing lymphadenitis is also common, and
syncytial cells can be found in a variety of diﬀerent organs. AntiNipah virus antibody can be used for IHC due to cross-reactivity
(Fig. 37.2).
Since its ﬁrst isolation, over 90 HeV-associated fatalities in
horses and 4 human fatalities have been documented. 60 HeV is
transmi ed by excretions (saliva, feces, nasal discharge) of
pteropid bats (ﬂying foxes) 61 of which some species are now
known to be reservoirs. A large number of laboratory animal
species, including dogs and cats, were experimentally inoculated
subcutaneously with the virus. 3 , 58 The dogs and cats had been
vaccinated for common viral diseases but notably the dogs for
CDV. The dogs did not become ill, but the cats developed
inappetence and tachypnea by day 5 PI and died 1–2 days later.
The cats developed pulmonary edema, hilar lymphadenomegaly,
pneumonia, and pleural eﬀusion, but neurologic signs were
absent. Histologic lesions of vasculitis resembled those in aﬀected
horses. The virus was isolated from the lungs, spleen, kidney, and
brain. Of all laboratory species inoculated, cats were most
susceptible.
A limited serosurvey of cats in the metropolitan Brisbane area
did not reveal detectable antibody to the virus. 3 Subsequent
studies in cats have shown that they can be experimentally
infected by nonparenteral routes and that the virus can spread
naturally among cats. 62 However, no ﬁeld infections have been
described in cats to date. Transmission from bats to another
species, such as the horse, may be required for human exposure.
Although the case fatality rate is > 60% in horses and humans,
transmission studies have shown that the virus is not highly
contagious. Horses in direct contact with experimentally infected
cats and infected horses in contact with other horses or cats did
not transmit infection. 63 Similarly experimentally infected cats
did not transmit the infection to horses. In experimentally infected
animals, regardless of species, virus was most prevalent in the
kidney and urine, which suggests urinary transmission as the
means of spread. Additionally, HeV was isolated for up to 3
weeks after infection of a horse and 14 months in a human

vetexamprep.ir

developing infection, suggesting viral persistence and a carrier
state.
