Natural infections with HeV have been reported in at least two
dogs, and additional subclinical infections that were undetected
may also have occurred. In 2013, HeV was detected by RT-PCR in
the serum of a dog on the same farm as an infected horse in New
South Wales, Australia. 64 This dog had been in close contact with
the aﬀected horse and was apparently exposed to the horse’s
blood after the horse was euthanized 14 days prior. The dog was
apparently healthy and testing had been done as a surveillance
eﬀort. The dog also had virus neutralizing antibodies at a titer of
1:8. Because of concerns surrounding transmission risk, the dog
was euthanized 2 days later. At necropsy, necrotizing vasculitis
was detected in the dog’s kidney, brain, lymph nodes, spleen,
liver, intestine, and lungs. Small amounts of viral antigen were
detected in the kidney, and many tissues were positive for HeV

vetexamprep.ir

using RT-PCR; serum collected at necropsy had an antibody titer
of 1:128.
The risk of transmission of HeV from dogs to horses or humans
remains unknown, but it has been recommended that dogs be
kept away from infected horses. 64 Experimentally infected dogs
were shown to shed virus in nasal secretions at levels similar to
those detected in horses. 65

Nipah Virus Infection
An outbreak of fatal human encephalitis during 1998 and 1999 in
Malaysia was a ributed to Nipah virus (genus Henipavirus), at
that time a novel paramyxovirus acquired from swine. 66 , 67 Pigs,
humans (primarily pig farmers), dogs, and cats were infected. As
with HeV, fruit bats are reservoirs, which have a worldwide
distribution, with spillover to other mammalian hosts. Although
illness was reported in the other species, the disease in pigs was
self-limiting and, in some cases, subclinical. Human infection was
a ributed to close contact with pigs. The role of dogs or cats as
secondary sources of infection could not be excluded.
Since its emergence, over 700 cases of Nipah virus infection
have occurred in humans in South and Southeast Asia, with a
mortality rate of 40% to 70%. 66 Only one naturally infected cat
has been described. 58 Results of serosurveys of feral cats in
endemic areas suggest that transmission among bats and cats may
be uncommon. 68 In experimentally infected cats, Nipah virus was
similar in its behavior to that of the closely related HeV. Two cats
were experimentally infected by the oronasal route with Nipah
virus from an outbreak associated with respiratory and neurologic
signs in pigs. 69 Respiratory and neurologic disease was observed
in the cats, and virus was found in secretions of the oropharynx
and excreted in urine. The virus causes widespread systemic
vasculitis, especially the respiratory tract and CNS. Pulmonary
lesions are giant cell pneumonia, and the secretions and tissues
contain large amounts of virus. Transplacental infection also
occurs in experimentally infected pregnant cats with resultant
infection of ki ens. 70 , 71 Experimental subunit vaccines
containing soluble glycoprotein G of either HeV or Nipah virus

vetexamprep.ir

protected cats against subsequent challenge with virulent Nipah
virus. 72 , 73
Dogs were suspected of being reservoirs of infection during the
initial epidemic in humans. 74 Virus was identiﬁed by
immunohistochemical staining of tissues in two dogs that died. 58
One of the dogs was found dead, and the other had fever,
respiratory distress, conjunctivitis, and mucopurulent ocular and
nasal discharge. Interstitial pneumonia, renal tubular necrosis,
and nonsuppurative meningitis were described at necropsy. 58
Pigs were readily infected from fruit bats. Dogs were examined
because they lived communally with pigs and humans and could
have served as secondary reservoir hosts. Despite the high
prevalence of seroreactivity among dogs at the time of the initial
outbreak, 75 it was very low in dogs outside the immediate
disease-endemic area. 76 Thus, infected dogs acted as dead-end
hosts; infection did not spread in the absence of the infected pigs
that had been depopulated.

Mumps Virus Infection
MuV is a paramyxovirus causing parotitis and less frequently
deafness, orchitis, and other clinical signs, with a high incidence
in children aged between 5 and 9 years. 77 There are rare reports
of the transmission of MuV to dogs with signs of lethargy and
parotitis 78 and serologic evidence of exposure of cats. 79 After the
introduction of vaccines in 1965, and routine vaccination of
children, the incidence of disease in humans has decreased by
99%, but periodic outbreaks of disease still occur as a result of lack
of vaccination or vaccine failure. 80 , 81 Dogs and cats do not play a
signiﬁcant role in transmission of MuV to humans.

Avian Newcastle Disease Virus Infection
Avian Newcastle disease virus (genus Paramyxovirus) has not been
reported to naturally infect cats, but has been experimentally
inoculated into the CNS of domestic adult cats and ki ens,
producing disseminated encephalomyelitis. 82 , 83 Neonatal ki ens
can also be infected by intraocular or intranasal exposure to large
quantities of virus. The incubation period following oculonasal
administration of virus was relatively long (11 to 17 days) when

vetexamprep.ir

compared with that after direct CNS inoculation (3 to 4 days).
Clinical signs were seizures, head tilt, myoclonus, and progressive
lower motor neuron paralysis. In some aﬀected animals,
behavioral
alterations
were
present.
A
disseminated
nonsuppurative meningoencephalitis was found histologically;
virus appeared to spread throughout the nervous system along
the descending and ascending neuronal pathways.

38: Feline Poxvirus Infections
Conor O’Halloran

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Feline poxvirus infection was first described in
the United Kingdom in 1978. 1–3
• Causes: Poxviruses (family Poxviridae, genus Orthopoxvirus).
Cowpox virus infection is by far the most frequently reported
poxviral infection of both cats and dogs. Other poxvirus
infections have also rarely been described in pets. 4 , 5
• Affected Hosts: Cats, less often dogs, and a variety of other
mammalian host species.
• Geographic Distribution: Cowpox virus is limited to Europe
and Asia; infections with other poxviruses have been
described in North America.
• Mode of Transmission: Entry through a break in the skin.
• Major Clinical Signs: Single or multiple, papular, and crusted
skin lesions with fever, lethargy, hyporexia, and signs of
pneumonia can also occur in affected cats.
• Differential Diagnoses: Allergic dermatitis, facial dermatitis
caused by FHV-1, nocardiosis, mycobacteriosis, cutaneous
lymphoma, autoimmune dermatoses such as pemphigus
foliaceus, cutaneous drug reactions.
• Human Health Significance: Many poxviruses, including
cowpox and orf viruses, are zoonotic, and owners of affected
animals need to be advised of the threat to their health.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

Cowpox virus is a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus within the
family Poxviridae, which are large, enveloped, double-stranded
DNA viruses. Other orthopoxviruses include smallpox virus (now
eradicated), vaccinia virus (the smallpox vaccine virus),
monkeypox virus (which is endemic to central Africa but was
recently introduced to, and has since been eradicated from, North
America), and a range of other mammalian orthopoxviruses. 1 , 2 ,
4–9 All orthopoxviruses are closely related genetically and
antigenically; therefore, vaccinia virus can be used to immunize
against all orthopoxvirus infections. Cowpox virus has the largest
genome of all the orthopoxviruses. Diﬀerent strains of cowpox
virus exist, as determined by both biologic characteristics and
nucleotide sequence. 8 , 10–12 Whether these relate to geographic
variation in the virus (and therefore its main hosts and
pathogenicity) or a range of independent virus species is still to be
determined. For the purpose of this chapter, they are regarded as
a single viral species.
Despite its name and its original isolation from cows, cowpox is
rarely described in ca le; rather, cowpox virus circulates
primarily in wild rodents. 13 , 14 Cowpox virus has a wide
incidental host range that includes not only rodents, cats, dogs,
ca le, and humans but also a variety of captive wildlife mammals.
1 , 2 , 4 , 13 , 14 The main route of transmission among rodents is not
known, although, as for many orthopoxviruses, the respiratory
route is probably important. 1 , 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 In most incidental hosts,
which include domestic animals and humans, the most frequent
route of infection is through a break in the skin which gives rise to
the “primary” lesion. The main reservoirs of cowpox virus are
believed to be bank voles (Myodes glareolus), ﬁeld voles (Microtus
agrestis) and, to a slightly lesser extent, wood mice (Apodemus
sylvaticus). 1 , 14 As these rodent species undergo annual
population cycles, breeding mainly in the summer and fall
months, viral transmission and prevalence has strong seasonality.
Therefore, transmission to accidental hosts such as cats, dogs,
people, and zoo animals also occurs mainly (but not exclusively)
in the late summer, fall, and early winter. 4
Cats probably become infected directly from rodent hunting,
whereas infection in other species is often acquired from an
amplifying intermediate host. 1 , 2 These are incidental hosts in

vetexamprep.ir

which the virus replicates to higher titers than in the reservoir
rodent hosts; thus, they bridge the epidemiologic gap between the
reservoir and the host of interest. The main amplifying hosts for
human cases of cowpox virus infection are the domestic cat (and,
in the past, possibly ca le), followed by peri-domestic rodent
species such as rats. 1 , 2 , 4 , 7 Rats can also be a source of infection
for captive wildlife species. The virus is very hardy and survives
in scabs for weeks or months, including in the environment,
where it may be a source of human infection.
Reports of natural orthopoxvirus infection in wild or domestic
dogs are rare. A natural orthopoxvirus infection, characterized by
ulcerative dermatitis at the site of a suspected rat bite, was
identiﬁed in a domestic dog in the United Kingdom. 15 This
infection was likely caused by cowpox, because this has been the
only orthopoxvirus in the United Kingdom since smallpox was
eradicated. 8 Speciﬁc antibodies were found in 6% to 20% of foxes
in Germany. 16 , 17 Intradermal inoculation of 2 × 105 plaqueforming units of cowpox virus into red foxes (Vulpes vulpes)
produced mild skin lesions with minimal viral replication, and no
lesions were found after oral dose administration of virus. 16 , 17
Another orthopoxvirus, murine ectromelia, has caused congenital
disease in farm-raised silver foxes (Vulpes winter coat), blue foxes
(Alopex lagopus winter coat), and mink (Mustela vison) in the Czech
Republic. 18 A novel orthopoxvirus was described in 2018 in a 6month-old cat from Italy with severe and rapidly progressing
cutaneous disease that appeared to be more closely related to this
virus than to cowpox virus. 5

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The outcome of feline infection is likely to depend on the viral
strain, route and site of infection, dose of inoculated virus, and the
concurrent presence of systemic immunosuppression, such as
infection with exogenous retrovirus infections (FIV or FeLV) or,
critically, the administration of systemic glucocorticoids. 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 ,
19 In many hosts, such as humans, dogs, and ca le, the primary
lesion of cowpox virus infection, plus perhaps some limited virus
replication in draining lymph nodes, may be as far as disease

vetexamprep.ir

progresses. In cats and many captive wild mammalian species,
however, the virus replicates in monocytes and macrophages and
spreads to multiple organs, particularly the lungs and the spleen.
Here, the virus replicates further, giving rise to a secondary
viremia, which is often associated with pyrexia and mild or
occasionally severe systemic signs. In all species, infection most
commonly presents externally as focal cutaneous lesions, which
heal spontaneously, with no systemic signs. During the viremic
period, virus can be isolated from the respiratory tract. Fatal
necrotizing pneumonia has been described. 10
The strain of the virus may also inﬂuence the clinical severity of
disease. 20 For example, some cats within the United Kingdom
were seen with large areas of focal dermal necrosis (eschars) with
extensive erythema and edema, which may represent infection
with a particularly virulent strain.
In many captive wild Felidae, pneumonia is more common than
in domestic cats, and mortality is high. 21–23 Similarly, elephants
and rhinoceroses in central European zoos develop severe
systemic disease and often die—this can be such a severe disease
that elephants are vaccinated in many European zoological parks.
Reports of fatal cowpox in captive primates are rare, but high
rates of subclinical seroconversion in other primate populations
have been reported. 21–23 In wild rodent reservoir hosts, clinical
signs are absent or, at least, subtle. 13 , 14 Population-level studies
of naturally infected voles and mice show that infection may be
associated with decreased fecundity and decreased survival.
When lesions are seen in rodents, they are often in incidental
rodent hosts such as rats.

Physical Examination Findings
The skin lesions ﬁrst develop as papules, which become ulcers up
to 1 cm in diameter that crust over and heal over 4 to 6 weeks (Fig.
38.1A and B). This leaves small patches of alopecia until the hair
regrows. Lesions are most often found on the head, neck, or
forelimbs. In cats such as Siamese breeds, the haircoat may grow
back a darker color, and scars are often visible for years in cats if
they are clipped. Although unproven, it has been suggested that
some strains of cowpox virus may have increased pathogenicity,

vetexamprep.ir

with infection culminating in large areas of cellulitis, cutaneous
ulceration, and/or necrosis (Fig. 38.1C). 10 , 20

Diagnosis
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of poxvirus infections requires laboratory
identiﬁcation of the causative virus. 13 , 20 , 24 , 25 In Europe, where
cowpox virus is endemic, clinical signs combined with
identiﬁcation of an orthopoxvirus frequently suﬃce to make a
diagnosis. Elsewhere, however, more extensive laboratory tests,
including sequence analysis, may be required to speciﬁcally
identify the causative virus. Histopathology of biopsy specimens
also yields characteristic ﬁndings that can raise strong suspicion
for poxvirus infection. 10 Diagnostic test options are summarized
in Table 38.1.

Microbiologic Tests
Cell Culture
The best specimens to collect for virus isolation are fresh skin
lesions, although virus can be found in crusts from healing lesions
for several weeks. No special transport media are required and
specimens can be transported in any sterile container at room
temperature. 24 The virus replicates in a variety of both feline and
non-feline cell lines generating an obvious CPE, usually within 24
to 76 hours. Identiﬁcation of the virus can then be performed
using immunostaining or PCR assay and sequencing.

Electron microscopy can identify virus particles within skin
lesions, is a more rapid approach to diagnosis than cell culture
and is fairly sensitive (Fig. 38.2). 24 Negative-stained suspensions
of skin lesion material allow typical orthopoxvirus particles to be
seen in most cases.

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Some diagnostic laboratories oﬀer PCR assays for diagnosis of
poxvirus infection, which can be both sensitive and, if combined
with sequencing, speciﬁc. Orthopoxviruses are so similar
genetically that PCR assays targeted at many orthopoxvirus genes
only identify orthopoxviruses to the genus level. 24 PCR assays
that diﬀerentiate between orthopoxvirus species have been
described, but such assays tend to be available through research
or other specialist laboratories. Of course, in much of Europe,
cowpox virus is the only orthopoxvirus known to infect cats and
dogs, so identiﬁcation to the species level is often not necessary.
Serologic Diagnosis
Serum assays including virus neutralization, HI, complement
ﬁxation, and ELISA can detect antibody to orthopoxvirus, but a
rising titer is required to prove active infection. 24 However, the
prevalence of orthopoxvirus antibodies in domestic cats in Europe

vetexamprep.ir

is usually only 1% to 2%, so a consistent clinical history combined
with an antibody titer is reasonably speciﬁc. 8

Pathologic Findings
Histopathologic Findings
Characteristic histopathologic ﬁndings include suppurative
dermatitis with evidence of necrosis and ulceration. 10 Epithelial
hyperplasia, ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes and large,
cytoplasmic eosinophilic viral inclusion bodies within
keratinocytes are present (Fig. 38.3). IHC has been used to identify
intracellular orthopoxvirus antigen in epidermal and follicular
cells. 10

Treatment
Treatment is generally supportive as there are no antiviral drugs
licensed to treat cowpox infections. Broad-spectrum antibacterials
are recommended to treat secondary bacterial infections, if
identiﬁed, and additional nonspeciﬁc therapy, including ﬂuids,
may be necessary. Glucocorticoids are considered contraindicated
because they may exacerbate the condition. There appears to be
an association between administration of glucocorticoids and
progression of disease from limited skin lesions to pulmonary
disease, which may be severe and even fatal.

Historically, most cats with cowpox-induced pneumonia died
despite supportive treatment. In a recent case series, recombinant
feline interferon-omega (rfIFN-ω, Virbagen Omega, Virbac,
France) was used in four cats at a dose of 1 million international
units (IU) given either IV or SC for 3 to 5 days (see Chapter 9). 26 ,
27 Two of the cats with severe pneumonia survived. As this drug
has been shown to be safe to use in cats, it could be considered for
treatment of more severe cases. Other antiviral drugs could also
be considered. The most promising antiviral in cats is famciclovir
for the treatment of FHV-1 infections, but its eﬃcacy against
cowpox virus is unknown. 28 Vidarabine has activity against
poxviruses in vitro, and cidofovir has broad-spectrum activity
against poxviruses in humans, and cowpoxvirus in particular
in vitro (see Chapter 9). 29 , 30 Cidofovir was also shown to protect
mice from a lethal cowpox challenge. However, more research in
cats is needed as this drug has been shown to be nephrotoxic in
humans.

Public Health Aspects
Human cowpox is rare (with one or two cases occurring each year
in the United Kingdom), but cats are thought to be the source of
more than 50% of these cases. 7 , 9 The risk of cat-to-human
transmission is small if basic hygiene precautions are taken, and

vetexamprep.ir

so this illness does not warrant euthanasia of the cat on public
health grounds.

Case Example
Signalment

“Yogi,” a 9-year-old entire male domestic shorthaired cat from
Lancaster, Lancashire, United Kingdom.

History

Yogi was examined in September following the development of
a swollen lateral digit of the left thoracic limb noted by owner
over the last 3 days. The cat was in good general health, up to
date with all routine parasite prevention and core vaccinations,
and was an avid rodent hunter.

Physical Examination

The digit was swollen and erythematous but was not associated
with lameness. The associated superﬁcial cervical lymph node
was mildly enlarged. Multiple, nonpainful, haired crusts were
present over the dorsum, but no other clinical abnormalities
were detected. The patient was discharged with oral meloxicam
for 7 days.
At the week recheck appointment, a number of crusts had
fallen away and the alopecic areas oozed a serous to purulent
discharge. Histopathology of punch biopsies revealed severe
multifocal follicular dermatitis. The inﬂammatory cells present
mainly consisted of neutrophils, macrophages, and fewer
lymphocytes and plasma cells. There was multifocal ulceration
of the overlying epidermis adjacent to moderately hyperplastic
areas. Large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies
were seen in the epidermal and follicular epithelial cells
characteristic of poxvirus infection.

Diagnosis

Poxvirus infection.

Treatment

Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was initially prescribed to treat
secondary bacterial pyoderma, but this was switched to
cefovecin because the cat could not be medicated orally. IFN-ω
(1 million U/kg IV q24h for 3 days) was also administered. The

vetexamprep.ir

cat was monitored as an outpatient over 6 weeks, during which
time there was complete resolution of the clinical signs.

39: Pseudorabies
Diana Henke, and Marc Vandevelde

KEY POINTS
• First Described: 1902 (Hungary, Aujeszky). 1
• Cause: Suid (porcine) herpesvirus-1 (family Herpesviridae,
subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae, genus Varicellovirus).
• Affected Hosts: Domestic and feral swine, cattle, horses,
sheep, goats, dogs, cats, bears, raccoons, foxes, hedgehogs,
opossums, deer, Florida panther, jackals, coyotes, some
nonhuman primates (macaques, marmosets), chickens,
pigeons, geese, ducks, buzzards, sparrow hawks, rabbits,
guinea pigs, rats and mice.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: Fever, lethargy, hypersalivation, muscle
stiffness, variable facial pruritis, ataxia, behavioral changes,
vomiting, diarrhea, respiratory distress.
• Differential Diagnoses: Rabies, canine distemper, toxicoses
(e.g., organophosphates, heavy metals, ethylene glycol,
strychnine).
• Human Health Significance: Some cases of pseudorabies
virus-induced encephalitis have been reported in humans.

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Pseudorabies virus (PRV), also known as Aujeszky’s disease virus
or suid (porcine) herpesvirus-1 (SuHV-1), is an enveloped DNA
virus, which belongs to the family Herpesviridae, subfamily
Alphaherpesviridae, and genus Varicellovirus. 2 As with other
herpesviruses, PRV can cause latent infection, with viral DNA

vetexamprep.ir

being incorporated into the host cell genome. The virus is
relatively resistant to environmental factors and can survive
outside the host for several months under favorable climatic
conditions. Survival of PRV depends on temperature (10 days at
37°C, 40 days at 25°C) and pH (optimum, 7), and it is quickly
inactivated by drying and exposure to ultraviolet light. 3 The
molecular biology of PRV has been extensively studied because
PRV is probably one of the most used viruses in experimental
neuroscience. 4
Pseudorabies, the disease caused by PRV (also known as
Aujeszky’s disease, mad itch, and infectious bulbar paralysis) occurs in
most countries of the world, except Australia, and has been
responsible for massive economic losses to the swine industry. 5 , 6
The name pseudorabies was applied because the clinical signs
caused by the virus in rabbits resembled those of rabies. In swine,
clinical signs depend on the age at exposure and virus strain.
Subclinical infections and shedding occur commonly. When they
do develop signs, older pigs typically develop respiratory disease.
Encephalitis occurs in adult pigs infected with virulent strains or
in piglets; reproductive disease and fetal loss occurs in pregnant
sows. Recovered pigs develop latent infection of neuronal tissues
with reactivation and shedding of virus in nasal secretions
following stress. In the past, clinical disease outbreaks have been
reported in several European, South American, and Asian
countries. Restricted endemic areas are in the United States,
Mexico, Brazil, and China. However, a PRV surveillance scheme is
lacking in many countries. Continuous large-scale vaccination,
removal of wild-type infected animals, followed by elimination of
all PRV antibody-positive animals resulted in the eradication of
the disease from domestic pigs in large parts of continental
Europe (including Finland, Sweden, Norway, the Netherlands,
Denmark, Austria, Swi erland, Germany, Hungary, Slovakia), the
United Kingdom, Mexico, Canada, the United States, and New
Zealand. 7–10
Although many mammalian species are susceptible to infection
with PRV, it is predominantly a problem in pigs, the main
reservoir of the virus. 5 , 6 However, ca le, goats, sheep, dogs, and
cats are sporadically aﬀected. 11–18 It does not appear to aﬀect
humans; most reports of possible human infection have been

vetexamprep.ir

circumstantial and not documented. Infection frequently is
subclinical in pigs because they have become well adapted to the
virus. The disease is spread by commercial movement of infected
pigs or contaminated pork products. Venereal transmission occurs
when infected boars shed PRV in semen. Although wild animals
such as Iberian lynx, raccoons, panthers, 19–21 and rodents may act
as transient reservoirs, they are not important in maintaining the
disease in nature. Their role is limited to temporary local spread
of virus within enzootic areas. However, in many European
countries, the United States, Brazil, and Japan, PRV infection is
endemic in wild boars with strongly varying seroprevalences
ranging from 0 to 100%, creating a reservoir for the virus. 22–26
PRV infection in dogs and cats is thought to occur only in areas
where the disease is enzootic in pigs. Such interaction has been
documented by molecular biologic studies on viral isolates. 27 , 28
In fact, the occurrence of typical pseudorabies signs in companion
animals can be the ﬁrst indication that the disease is enzootic in
the local pig population. Companion animals almost invariably
are infected as a result of consuming contaminated raw pork. 12 ,
29 Dogs also have developed pseudorabies after having bi en
infected pigs. 30 Direct dog-to-dog spread has not been shown to
occur. 31 However, one report described an outbreak in animals
without direct contact with swine. Isolated strains of PRV showed
considerable diﬀerences in DNA pa erns to vaccine and isolated
strains obtained from pigs in the same region. 11 Feline and canine
cases have been reported in Poland, Italy, Austria, Argentina,
Germany, Northern Ireland, China, Japan, and the southern
United States (Florida, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Alabama). 11 , 12 , 14 ,
15 , 28 , 30 , 32–34 These are primarily hunting dogs that contact wild
swine, 35–39 which has followed global expansion in wild swine
populations; disease in dogs may be more likely to occur in
regions that have dense populations of wild swine, such as
southern parts of the United States (Fig. 39.1) and regions of
Europe such as Germany, France, Spain, Poland, and the Czech
Republic. 37 Dogs that reside on swine farms may also become
infected. 40 In some reports, packs of dogs have become infected
after consumption of uncooked oﬀal from infected pigs or pig
carcasses. 41 , 42 Dogs of any age, sex, and breed can be aﬀected,
and dog-to-dog transmission does not occur, presumably because

vetexamprep.ir

dogs do not shed suﬃcient virus to infect other hosts. Cats have
the potential to be infected after ingestion of pork waste or
infected rodents, but reports of naturally occurring Aujeszky’s
disease are extremely rare. 43 Because subclinical infections and
nonspeciﬁc signs of disease are common in swine, identiﬁcation of
pseudorabies in dogs may be the ﬁrst indication that disease is
present in a swine herd or wild swine populations.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
SuHV-1 is shed in the saliva and nasal discharges of swine, and
transmission can occur by direct contact with these discharges,
contact with aerosols from swine, and ingestion of infected swine
carcasses or other infected animals, especially wild animals. The
virus can survive on fomites and in carcasses for several weeks.
Naturally acquired infection in dogs and cats occurs after

vetexamprep.ir

ingestion of the virus, although a similar sequence of events
occurs after parenteral inoculation of virus. PRV enters the nerve
endings at the inoculation site and travels in retrograde fashion
via the axoplasm of the nerve ﬁbers to the brain, which results in
ganglioneuritis and encephalitis. Infection can also lead to
ganglioneuritis of the cardiac autonomic plexuses with associated
myocardial degeneration 44 and degeneration of intestinal
myenteric ganglia. 42 Clinical signs appear rapidly after a short
incubation period that typically ranges from 1 to 6 days, but
incubation periods up to 10 days have been reported. 41
Experimental studies in orally infected cats have shown that PRV
replicates in the tonsils and travels from the oral mucosa via the
sensory branches of the 9th and 10th cranial nerves to the nucleus
tractus solitarius and area postrema in the medulla oblongata. 45
The 5th cranial nerve has been less frequently involved.
Experimental infections in rats have shown that PRV spreads in a
highly speciﬁc manner through synaptic connections. 46 , 47 Viral–
cellular interactions have been studied in great detail in
experimental models. 4
The majority of dogs and cats that become infected develop
severe clinical signs. The onset of clinical illness is hyperacute,
and signs progress rapidly until death occurs (possibly as a result
of acute myocarditis); the total course rarely lasts longer than 48
hours. With very few exceptions, pseudorabies is always fatal in
dogs. Cats may be somewhat more resistant but have rarely
recovered from the disease. The initial sign often noted by the
owner is a change in behavior, such as inactivity, lethargy, and
indiﬀerence, although some animals become aggressive or
restless. Dyspnea; diarrhea, which may be hemorrhagic (e.g.,
hematemesis or melena); and vomiting are occasionally seen
(Table 39.1). The dyspnea is often caused by severe pulmonary
edema. Body temperature may be normal or abnormal, and
hypersalivation is common. However, the most characteristic sign
is intense pruritus, which usually occurs in the head region and
rarely occurs in other areas such as the neck and shoulders.
Aﬀected dogs violently scratch their faces and ears and rub their
heads against the ﬂoor or walls. One side of the head and neck
may become swollen. Self-mutilation results in erythema,
excoriation, and ulceration of the skin and underlying tissues (Fig.

vetexamprep.ir

39.2A and B ). The scratching becomes increasingly frantic and
may end in generalized seizures. Most of the other neurologic
signs observed in PRV infection refer to lesions in the lower
brainstem and consist of one or several deﬁcits in cranial nerve
function. These deﬁcits are usually unilateral and include
anisocoria, mydriasis, lack of direct or consensual pupillary light
reﬂexes, trismus, paresis and paralysis of the facial muscles, head
tilt, inability to swallow, and vocal changes. 28 Anisocoria and a
hoarse voice are considered to be highly consistent signs in the
cat. Less commonly observed neurologic signs include behavioral
abnormalities such as aggression, generalized hyperesthesia, head
pressing, and generalized seizures. The la er often occur as
sequelae to frantic scratching. Paresis and paralysis of the limbs
are sometimes noted shortly before death. Although less common,
in some cats, death has been preceded predominantly by acute GI
signs. Arrhythmias may occur as a result of myocarditis. 14 , 48 , 49
A variety of cardiac arrhythmias have been reported in
experimentally infected dogs, which have included ventricular
premature complexes, ventricular tachycardia, sinus arrest, atrial
tachycardia, atrial ﬁbrillation, wandering pacemaker, seconddegree heart block, T- and P-wave abnormalities, and
atrioventricular dissociation.
An atypical course of the disease has also been observed in cats
that died suddenly without developing neurologic signs. 50
Pruritus has been absent in some cases of spontaneous PRV
infection in dogs 15 , 51 and in experimental oral infection in cats. 45
In one case series, only 18% of dogs exhibited facial pruritis. 52 GI
signs have been the predominant feature of some infected dogs.

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings include lethargy, hypersalivation,
dehydration, muscle stiﬀness, tachypnea or respiratory diﬃculty,
and facial pruritis, excoriations, and edema due to self-trauma
(see Fig. 39.2). Other neurologic signs that may be detected
include ataxia, head tilt, circling, hyperesthesia, behavioral
abnormalities, anisocoria, mydriasis, nystagmus, slow or absent
pupillary light responses, recumbency, and coma. Fever may be
identiﬁed early in the course of infection (up to 108°F), 53 but
terminally, hypothermia may occur. A variety of cardiac
arrhythmias may also be identiﬁed on physical examination.

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of pseudorabies in dogs and cats is based on a
compatible history (i.e., exposure to domestic or wild swine in
regions where the virus is present), suggestive clinical signs, and
histopathology and/or virus detection methods such as IFA
staining, virus isolation, or PCR on tissues collected at necropsy
(Table 39.2). Antemortem diagnosis of pseudorabies in dogs and
cats using virus detection methods has not yet been described.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Hematologic or biochemical abnormalities are not found in
pseudorabies. Electrocardiographic ﬁndings may include cardiac
arrhythmias. 54 CSF may show increased protein concentration
and mononuclear pleocytosis. This ﬁnding is strongly indicative
of viral encephalitis but is not speciﬁc for pseudorabies.

Microbiologic Tests
Serologic Diagnosis
Virus neutralization, immunodiﬀusion, latex agglutination test,
and ELISA methods commonly are used to detect serum antibody
to PRV in pigs. Serologic studies have been valuable in
determining the prevalence of disease in pig populations. 22
Serology has not been useful for antemortem diagnosis in dogs
and cats. This likely reﬂects the rapid course of disease and
insuﬃcient time for antibody responses to develop.

Virus Isolation
Virus can be isolated in tissue culture from the lung and spleen
and especially from brain and tonsils of animals with

vetexamprep.ir

pseudorabies (Fig. 39.3). Although many cell lines have been
used, most laboratories use pig kidney epithelial cells. A deﬁnite
CPE consisting of syncytial formation is visible after 12 to 24
hours (Fig. 39.4). Virus isolation is not always easy in dogs, even
in well-substantiated cases. 55 Pharyngeal washings, tonsillar
swabs, and saliva are unsuitable for viral isolation in dogs. 56
Haired skin from regions of pruritis could be considered for
testing.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR for diﬀerent viral genes is the method of choice to detect the
presence of PRV in the porcine population. 57–59 In dogs and cats,
besides IHC, rabbit inoculation test, and virus isolation, PCR has
been used successfully to detect the virus at necropsy. 14 , 28
Whether these assays are useful for antemortem diagnosis is not
known, but PCR could be a empted on specimens such as
biopsies of pruritic regions or tonsillar swabs.

Pathologic Findings
No gross lesions are diagnostic of pseudorabies, with the
exception of the skin lesions that result from intense pruritus.
Gross pathologic abnormalities include evidence of facial
dermatitis, tonsillar enlargement, and GI mucosal hyperemia and
ulceration. In some cases, abnormal stomach contents have been
noted because of pica. Pulmonary edema and congestion have
been consistent ﬁndings. Focal myocarditis and ecchymosis have
been found in dogs and cats. Histopathology of the tonsils reveals
suppurative tonsillar inﬂammation, sometimes with necrosis.
Lesions in the CNS are almost exclusively located in the brainstem
and primarily involve cranial nerve nuclei. 14 , 60 They may be
unilateral and consist of perivascular cuﬃng with mononuclear
cells and pronounced proliferation of astrocytes and microglial
cells (Fig. 39.5A and B ). The areas of focal gliosis often show
degeneration (karyorrhexis) in the center and may progress to the
formation of microabscesses. Severe changes occur in neurons,
with chromatolysis and disintegration of the nucleus (Fig. 39.5C).
The most deﬁnitive ﬁnding is the presence of weak eosinophilic
viral inclusion bodies in the nuclei of astrocytes and neurons.
Viral-speciﬁc antigen or nucleic acid can be demonstrated in

Diagnostic methods include IHC, immunoﬂuorescence, or in
situ hybridization on smears or frozen sections of various tissues.
The brain and tonsils are the tissues of choice in such studies.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of pseudorabies is generally futile because the disease
is almost always fatal. Heavy sedation and anesthesia may lessen
or relieve the itching and convulsions; however, nothing can alter
the outcome of the disease. Treatment with anti-PRV serum did
not improve the condition of a dog with Aujeszky’s disease 51 and
is considered to be ineﬀective in the prevention of infection. 31

Immunity and Vaccination
Although vaccines are used in swine to reduce losses in
geographic locations where the disease is enzootic, vaccines are
not available for dogs and cats because of the sporadic incidence
of the disease. It is possible to vaccinate small animals against
PRV, although this would be indicated only in endemic areas
where exposure to infected domestic pigs and wild boars may
occur. Natural infection with PRV has not been observed in
vaccinated dogs and cats. 65 However, experimental vaccination
challenge studies showed that it may be diﬃcult to protect dogs
with an inactivated vaccine, although most animals develop
serum neutralizing antibodies to PRV. 31 A enuated PRV vaccines
may cause postvaccinal reactions that may be as lethal as the
natural infection. PRV deletion mutants have been developed for
vaccination of pigs. 10 Such “deletion” vaccines are safe and useful
for controlling the disease because serologic surveys can
distinguish between vaccine-induced and natural anti-PRV
antibodies. Deletion vaccines have been tested in raccoons, albeit
with limited success. 66 DNA vaccines have also been developed.
45 Human adenoviruses have been used as vectors for
experimental immunization of cats against PRV antigens. 67 To the
authors’ knowledge, none of these modern vaccines have been
systematically tested or applied in dogs and cats. Considerable
progress has been made in the eradication of PRV infection in
swine in many areas of the world. 10 As a result, Aujeszky’s
disease has become a very rare condition in dogs and cats, and the

vetexamprep.ir

development and application of PRV vaccines in small animals
have remained insigniﬁcant. In view of the extremely low
frequency of the disease in dogs and cats, further developments
are unlikely.

Prevention
Prevention is the most important means of control of PRV
infection in dogs and cats. Pseudorabies can be eﬀectively
prevented by feeding only cooked food to dogs and cats, control
of rodents, and prevention of contact between domestic swine (in
regions where the disease is enzootic) and wild swine and dogs.

Public Health Aspects
In general, humans appear to be refractory to infection with
SuHV-1. However, cases of PRV-induced encephalitis, as
determined by PCR in CSF samples have been discovered in
humans working with pigs in China. 68

40: Papillomavirus Infections
Jennifer A. Luﬀ, and John S. Munday

KEY POINTS
• First Described: The transmissibility of canine
papillomaviruses was described in the late 1800s; electron
microscopic descriptions occurred in the late 1960s. 1 , 2
Papillomavirus infections of cats were not recognized until
1990. 3
• Cause: Papillomaviruses (family Papillomaviridae).
• Affected Hosts: With the notable exception of bovine
deltapapillomaviruses, papillomaviruses appear to have high
species specificity.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Cutaneous or mucosal inoculation,
probably through microtrauma.
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs: oral or cutaneous exophytic or
endophytic papillomas, cutaneous pigmented plaques,
possibly cutaneous and oral SCCs. Cats: cutaneous viral
plaques, cutaneous Bowenoid in situ carcinomas, possibly
cutaneous SCCs, oral papillomas, and feline sarcoids.
• Human Health Significance: Canine and feline papillomavirus
do not infect humans.

Etiologic Agents And Epidemiology
Papillomaviruses are small (30 to 60 nm), nonenveloped,
icosahedral viruses with a circular double-stranded DNA genome
(Fig. 40.1). They lack a lipid envelope, are resistant in the
environment, and survive detergents and high temperatures. With

vetexamprep.ir

rare exceptions, papillomaviruses are strictly host speciﬁc and
have been identiﬁed in most mammalian species. 4
Papillomaviruses infect keratinocytes at mucosal and cutaneous
sites, most likely through microabrasions. Most papillomavirus
infections are subclinical. 5 However, due to the ability of
papillomaviruses to inﬂuence cell growth and regulation,
infection by some papillomavirus types can result in marked
proliferation of epithelial cells. This proliferation results in
thickening and folding of the epidermis and the development of a
hyperplastic, self-resolving papilloma (also referred to as a wart).
5 Less commonly, infection by papillomaviruses can inﬂuence the
development of neoplasia (Box 40.1). In humans, whether
infection remains asymptomatic, results in a papilloma, or
promotes neoplasia is largely determined by the papillomavirus
type 5 and the immune status of the host. 6 It is likely that the
same is true for papillomavirus infections of dogs and cats, with
both viral and host factors important in determining the
manifestation of disease.
Due to the routine use of molecular testing, the number of
diﬀerent papillomavirus types identiﬁed in dogs and cats has
expanded dramatically in recent years. 4 Papillomaviruses are
classiﬁed on the basis of the L1 capsid gene nucleotide sequence. 7
At least 23 diﬀerent types have been identiﬁed in dogs so far, with
several additional novel types that have not been fully sequenced
(Table 40.1). 8–24 These viruses have been classiﬁed into three
distinct genera: Lambdapapillomavirus, Taupapillomavirus, and
Chipapillomavirus. 10 , 25 , 26 In cats, six Felis catus papillomavirus
(FcaPV) types have been fully sequenced with FcaPV1 classiﬁed
within the Lambdapapillomavirus genus, FcaPV2 classiﬁed within
the Dyothetapapillomavirus genus, and FcaPV3, 4, 5, and 6 likely to
be classiﬁed within the Taupapillomavirus genus. 27–32 As with
dogs, it appears likely that additional FcaPV types will be
identiﬁed in the future.
The canine lambdapapillomaviruses include Canis familiaris
papillomavirus (canine papillomavirus, CPV † ) types 1 and 6. 8 ,
10 CPV1 was the ﬁrst CPV identiﬁed. This virus commonly infects
young dogs, often resulting in numerous oral papillomas that
spontaneously regress. This CPV has also rarely been associated
with cutaneous endophytic (inverted) papillomas and invasive

vetexamprep.ir

cutaneous SCCs. 33–37 CPV6 was identiﬁed from a single
cutaneous papilloma that regressed spontaneously. 10 CPV19 was
identiﬁed from a single oral papilloma. 22
Taupapillomaviruses that have been identiﬁed in dogs include
CPV types 2, 7, 13, 17, 21, 22, and 23. CPV2 has been identiﬁed
within cutaneous papillomas and is only rarely associated with
SCC. 18 However, in a research colony of dogs with X-linked
severe combined immunodeﬁciency, CPV2 caused cutaneous
papillomas that progressed to invasive and metastatic SCC. 38
CPV7 has thus far only been reported from a single cutaneous
papilloma/in situ SCC. 10 CPV13 was identiﬁed from oral
cytobrush specimens from a dog with oral papillomatosis. 9
CPV17 was identiﬁed as the likely cause of multiple oral SCCs in a
dog. 39 , 40 CPV21, CPV22, and CPV23 were identiﬁed using viral
metagenomics from nasal swabs and the association with clinical
disease is currently unknown. 24
Chipapillomaviruses include CPV types 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12,
14, 15, and 16. All of these chipapillomaviruses are associated
with cutaneous pigmented plaques. CPV3 has been reported in
multiple dogs, including a dog that developed numerous
pigmented plaques and in situ SCC, 16 one dog with pigmented
plaques, 41 one dog with pigmented plaques, basal cell
carcinomas, SCCs, and trichoblastomas, 42 and one dog with a
pigmented viral plaque that progressed to SCC. 36 CPV4 has been
most commonly associated with pigmented plaques in pug dogs,
17 , 43–45 but other dog breeds can be aﬀected. 41 CPV9 has been
identiﬁed in several dogs with pigmented plaques, 12 , 19 , 41 , 46
including one dog that developed multicentric invasive SCC in
association with its persistent pigmented plaques. 47 CPV12 has
been identiﬁed in two dogs with pigmented plaques 20 , 41 and
two additional related Basenji dogs. 15 In one Basenji dog, the
lesions progressed to invasive and metastatic SCC. The other
Basenji dog developed metastatic SCC associated with pigmented
plaques due to CPV16. 13 , 15 CPV16 has also been identiﬁed in
two additional dogs with pigmented plaques that progressed to
SCC. 36 , 48 CPV5 and CPV15 have been identiﬁed in small
numbers of dogs with pigmented plaques, 10 , 41 while CPV types
8, 10, 11, and 14 have thus far only been identiﬁed from single

vetexamprep.ir

cases of pigmented plaques. 11 , 12 , 14 , 21 CPV18 was originally
identiﬁed within a pigmented plaque from a pug dog, 23 and has
been identiﬁed in one additional pug dog with a pigmented
plaque and basal cell tumor. 45 CPV20 is most likely a
Chipapillomavirus based upon its sequence, but there is currently
no reported information for this virus.

There have been several reports of pigmented plaques
progressing to SCC. The associated CPV type, however, has only
rarely been identiﬁed; therefore, it remains unknown whether
pigmented plaques caused by a particular CPV type are at greater
risk of progressing to SCC. Thus far, only CPV3, CPV9, CPV12,
and CPV16 have been associated with malignant progression of
pigmented plaques to invasive and metastatic SCC. 13 , 15 , 47
Overall, these are rare cases and there is currently no evidence to
suggest that CPVs are a signiﬁcant cause of either cutaneous or
oral SCCs. 49–51

Many of these CPV types have been identiﬁed in small numbers
of dogs, and often from a single lesion or a single animal.
Therefore, it is diﬃcult to determine their prevalence, geographic
distribution, biologic characteristics, or clinical behavior.
In general, lesions due to papillomavirus infection are more
frequently recognized in dogs than in cats. In cats, infections by
papillomaviruses are believed to cause feline viral plaques and
Bowenoid in situ carcinomas (BISCs). As viral plaques can
progress into BISCs, 52 these two lesions probably represent a
continuum of papillomavirus-induced hyperplasia and dysplasia
of the epidermis. BISCs have been previously referred to as
multicentric SCCs in situ. However, as BISCs can develop as single
lesions, and as BISCs contain histologic features not observed in
sun-induced in situ SCCs, this term is not favored. In cats,
papillomaviruses are also recognized to cause feline sarcoids
(previously known as ﬁbropapillomas) and oral papillomas. In
cats, there is increasing evidence that papillomaviruses may
inﬂuence the development of a proportion of cutaneous SCCs.
While papillomaviral DNA has been occasionally detected in
feline oral SCCs, 53–56 there is currently no evidence that feline oral
SCCs are caused by papillomaviruses. 57
Felis catus papillomavirus type 1. This Lambdapapillomavirus was
initially identiﬁed in a feline viral plaque from a cat that was
suspected to be immunosuppressed. 30 Subsequent research
suggests that FcaPV1 is a rare cause of feline viral plaques.
However, this papillomavirus was identiﬁed in two feline oral

vetexamprep.ir

papillomas 58 and, as FcaPV1 is closely related to the
papillomaviruses that cause oral papillomas in lions and snow
leopards, this virus is the likely cause of oral papillomas in
domestic cats.
Felis catus papillomavirus type 2. This Dyothetapapillomavirus
currently appears to be the most common cause of
papillomavirus-induced disease in cats. The majority of feline
viral plaques and BISCs appear to be caused by infection with this
papillomavirus type. 59 However, as FcaPV2 can be detected on
the skin of most cats 60 and yet only a small proportion develop
disease, host factors appear to be important for disease
development. The importance of host factors is demonstrated by
the observation that Devon Rex, and the closely related Sphinx,
cats develop an unusually severe manifestation of FcaPV2induced disease early in life. 61 , 62 The host factors that are
important in disease development are currently uncertain. Initial
studies suggested immunosuppression predisposed to disease;
however, both viral plaques and BISCs can develop without any
detectible loss of immune function. This suggests that
immunosuppression is not essential for disease development.

In addition to viral plaques and BISCs, there is increasing
evidence that FcaPV2 is a signiﬁcant cause of feline cutaneous
SCCs. FcaPV2 DNA has been detected more frequently in SCCs
than in non-SCC skin specimens, 59 papillomavirus-induced
changes in cell regulatory proteins have been detected in SCCs

vetexamprep.ir

that contain FcaPV2 DNA, 63 diﬀerences in biological behavior
have been observed between SCCs with evidence of
papillomavirus infection and those without, 64 and FcaPV2
oncogene RNA has been detected within a proportion of feline
cutaneous SCCs. 65–67 Overall, FcaPV2 could inﬂuence the
development of 30%–50% of feline cutaneous SCCs. SCCs from
haired skin are most likely to contain evidence of a papillomaviral
etiology. However, some evidence also suggests that FcaPV2 can
act as a co-factor with sun exposure to promote SCC
development. 68
Felis catus papillomavirus types 3, 4, 5, and 6. These
papillomaviruses will probably all be classiﬁed within the
Taupapillomavirus genus. These types have been detected in
association with pre-neoplastic or neoplastic skin lesions in cats.
However, these seem to be less common causes of feline viral
plaques, BISCs, and SCCs than FcaPV2. 27 , 31 , 32 , 69 Currently, it
is uncertain whether lesions caused by these four papillomavirus
types have a diﬀerent clinical behavior to lesions caused by
FcaPV2. However, these types may be more likely to result in the
development of basal cell carcinomas. 70
Feline sarcoids. Evidence suggests that these mesenchymal
neoplasms are caused by cross-species infection with bovine
papillomavirus (BPV) type 14. 71 BPV14 is a Deltapapillomavirus
like BPV1 and BPV2, which are thought to cause equine sarcoids.
It is interesting to note that BPV14 has not been detected in an
equine sarcoid, and neither BPV1 nor BPV2 has been detected in a
feline sarcoid. Evidence of viral replication is not present within
feline sarcoids, and these are considered to be dead-end
infections. 72 How the papillomavirus is transferred from cow to
cat is currently unknown.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical
Examination Findings
Infection with papillomaviruses follows inoculation of the virus
through microabrasions in the skin and mucous membranes
caused by physical trauma. Initial infection and viral
ampliﬁcation occurs within keratinocytes of the stratum basale. 73

vetexamprep.ir

p

y
As basal keratinocytes undergo diﬀerentiation, early viral
proteins (E proteins) are expressed and associate with regulators
of the cell cycle to stimulate cell cycle progression. 73 This can lead
to enhanced proliferation of cells in the stratum spinosum and
stratum granulosum, with accumulation of infected cells and
papilloma formation (Fig. 40.2). With the exception of feline
sarcoids, which remain as latent (or nonproductive) infections,
late viral products, including the virus capsid proteins (L1 and
L2), are ﬁrst expressed in cells of the stratum spinosum.
Papillomaviruses are nonlytic viruses, and mature virions are
shed with cells that exfoliate from the stratum corneum or the
nonkeratinized cells of the mucous membranes. Infected cells
develop a characteristic CPE, which consists of cytoplasmic
vacuolization. Tens of thousands of virus particles are produced
by each infected cell. Papillomaviruses can predispose to the
neoplastic transformation of infected cells because their viral E6
and E7 proteins (also known as oncoproteins) alter normal cell
cycle regulation and/or apoptosis. 74 For example, human “highrisk” papillomavirus types produce proteins that degrade p53 and
retinoblastoma protein (pRb), which are important tumor
suppressors. 75 Accidental integration of the DNA of human
“high-risk” papillomavirus types into host cell DNA can result in
a marked increase in papillomavirus oncogene expression. The
resultant population of rapidly dividing and genetically unstable
cells is greatly predisposed to neoplastic transformation. 74
Canine Oral Papillomatosis
Canine oral papillomas most commonly occur in young dogs and
often regress spontaneously over a 4- to 8-week period. 26 They
can also occur as a result of immunosuppression, such as after
treatment
with
cyclosporine,
less
commonly
chronic
glucocorticoid treatment, or chronic infection with Ehrlichia canis.
Rarely, papillomas in the caudal oropharynx obstruct respiration.
Oral papillomas can occur on the lips, mucocutaneous junctions,
tongue, pharynx, eyelids, and infrequently haired skin 26 (Fig.
40.3). They may cause halitosis, ptyalism, and oral discomfort.
Early lesions are smooth and raised, but as they enlarge they may
become cauliﬂower-like. They may be pigmented or
nonpigmented.

vetexamprep.ir

Canine Cutaneous Papillomas
Cutaneous exophytic and endophytic papillomas usually occur as
solitary masses. 26 Exophytic papillomas are proliferative nodules,
whereas endophytic papillomas are cup-shaped cutaneous
nodules that range in size from 2 mm to 2 cm in diameter with a
central keratin-ﬁlled depression. Cutaneous exophytic papillomas
are wart-like projections that appear anywhere on the body, but
especially the lower limbs and footpads. Single or multiple lesions
can occur anywhere on the body (Fig. 40.4). They have also been
described in the interdigital space. 38 Rarely, papillomas can form
along sites of previous surgery. 76
Canine Pigmented Plaques
Pigmented plaques can develop as single or multiple lesions on
the skin and have variable degrees of pigmentation. The lesions
usually range in size from 1 mm to 1 cm, but can become larger.
They appear as dark (although this can be variable),
hyperkeratotic ﬂat lesions that are typically present on the
ventrum or medial aspects of the limbs 48 (Fig. 40.5). Pugs and
miniature schnauzers are considered to be predisposed, but many
other breeds can be aﬀected. The lesions can regress
spontaneously over the course of a few months, but may persist in
some dogs. These are generally not of clinical signiﬁcance,
although rarely they can progress to SCCs. 15 , 48 , 77
Canine Squamous Cell Carcinomas
These neoplasms are often ulcerated, nodular masses that may be
found alongside pigmented plaques or cutaneous papillomas
when malignant transformation occurs. However, transformation
of oral and cutaneous papillomas is rare, and most cases of canine
SCCs are not associated with papillomavirus infection. 49–51
Feline Viral Plaques
Plaques typically develop on older cats and often present as
multiple, less than 1 cm in diameter, sessile, hairless, pigmented
lesions. They tend to develop most frequently around the face,
although they can develop anywhere on the body.
Bowenoid In Situ Carcinoma (BISC)

vetexamprep.ir

BISCs also typically develop on older animals, although have been
reported in Devon Rex cats as young as 3 years of age. 61 Most cats
with BISCs will develop multiple lesions, although the
development of a single lesion does not exclude BISC as a
diagnosis. 78 BISCs most commonly involve the head and dorsum
of cats (Fig. 40.6). They typically appear as roughly spherical
hairless masses that can either be ulcerated or covered by
orthokeratosis. They can be pigmented. Diﬀerentiation between a
feline viral plaque and a BISC may not be possible clinically, but
as a general rule, the larger the lesion is, the greater the likelihood
of a BISC.

Feline Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinomas
These appear as ulcerated masses. Feline cutaneous SCCs can be
subdivided into those that are caused by sun exposure and
develop as a progression from actinic keratosis and those that are
caused by papillomavirus infection and develop as a progression
from a BISC. As sunlight appears to be the most common cause of
feline cutaneous SCCs, these neoplasms most often occur in
lightly pigmented and lightly haired areas of the body. SCCs that
develop on the pinnae are the least likely to contain evidence of
papillomavirus infection, while SCCs from haired, pigmented
skin are most likely to have a putative papillomaviral etiology.
Feline Oral Papillomas
These lesions are rarely reported in middle-aged to older cats.
However, as the papillomas do not cause clinical signs and are
only discovered as an incidental ﬁnding, the true prevalence of
oral papillomas in cats is unknown. Oral papillomas appear as
multiple < 5-mm diameter pale raised lesions on the ventral
surface of the tongue. 58
Feline Sarcoids
Feline sarcoids have been described in cats from North America,
New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Australia. They
are thought to be caused by BPV14, and contact with ca le
appears necessary for disease development. Aﬀected cats are
often young (<5 years), male, outdoor cats from rural
environments. 79 Sarcoids typically appear as hairless, solitary,
ﬁrm, exophytic masses. Although they most commonly develop
around the mouth and nose, especially the nasal philtrum (Fig.
40.7), they have also been reported at other locations such as in
digits, tail tip, eyelids, and pinnae. 79 , 80

Diagnosis
The history and gross appearance of oral papillomas in dogs is
generally suﬃcient for diagnosis. For other papillomas and

vetexamprep.ir

plaques, the diagnosis can be conﬁrmed with biopsy and
histopathology. A full-thickness biopsy that includes adjacent
normal skin should be collected. The presence of
papillomaviruses can be investigated using PCR, IHC, in situ
hybridization, or electron microscopy, although these techniques
are primarily used on a research basis. Caution should be used
when interpreting the results of PCR assays because
papillomaviruses can be detected on normal skin, 60 , 81 so results
should be interpreted in association with clinical signs. While
DNA in situ hybridization is considered less sensitive than PCR,
this technique can conﬁrm the location of papillomavirus DNA
within the lesion. However, the presence of DNA within a lesion
does not necessarily prove causality. Assays to detect
papillomaviral oncogene RNA in a lesion have been used to
further investigate whether the papillomavirus is likely to be
inﬂuencing cell behavior or simply present within the lesion as an
“innocent bystander.” 15 , 65
IHC and electron microscopy can be used to detect viral antigen
and viral particles, respectively. These techniques can only detect
papillomaviruses in lesions that contain viral replication.
Typically, li le or no viral replication is present in SCCs and
sarcoids, which makes these techniques of reduced value to
investigate a papillomavirus etiology of these lesions. In the
authors’ experience, few papillomavirus-induced lesions contain
antipapillomavirus immunostaining in the absence of
histologically detectible papillomavirus-induced cell changes.
Canine and feline papillomavirus-speciﬁc reagents are not widely
available, and care has to be taken to ensure cross-reactivity
between the available antipapillomavirus antibodies and canine
and feline papillomaviruses.
IHC to detect p16CDKN2A protein (p16) can also be used to
investigate a possible papillomaviral etiology of a lesion.
Papillomaviruses consistently alter normal cell regulation by
degrading pRb. Loss of normal pRb function in a cell increases
p16. Therefore, the detection of intense nuclear and cytoplasmic
p16 immunostaining in a human oral SCC is considered consistent
with a papillomaviral etiology. 82 Similarly, intense p16
immunostaining has been observed in association with loss of pRb
in feline viral plaques, BISCs, and papillomavirus-associated
SCCs. 75 Additionally, increased p16 immunostaining was

vetexamprep.ir

y
p
g
observed in a feline oral papilloma and in a canine oral SCC that
was associated with CPV17 infection. 40 , 58 The advantage of p16
immunostaining over papillomavirus immunostaining is that p16
immunostaining is not dependent on active viral replication. In
addition, the presence of increased p16 within a lesion that
contains papillomavirus DNA provides evidence that the
papillomavirus was altering cell regulation rather than being
present as an incidental infection. However, a disadvantage of p16
immunostaining is that any cause of reduced pRb function will
increase cell p16 and the speciﬁcity of this test for the detection of
a papillomavirus etiology in dogs and cats has not been
determined.

Microbiologic Tests
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR assays can be used to detect papillomaviruses within biopsy
or cytobrush specimens from dogs and cats. Consensus primers
are available to detect multiple diﬀerent papillomavirus types. If
unﬁxed tissue is available, either rolling circle ampliﬁcation or
next generation sequencing can be used to amplify whole circular
genomic DNA. 26 , 29

Pathologic Findings
Productive infection of an epithelial cell by a papillomavirus can
result in papillomavirus-induced cell changes. Recognition of
these changes is good evidence that the lesion was caused by

vetexamprep.ir

g
g
y
papillomavirus infection. Furthermore, each papillomavirus
genus appears to result in subtly diﬀerent cell changes and so
detection of these changes can be valuable to suggest the likely
etiologic agent. 69 Papillomavirus infection can result in koilocytosis
—cells with a dark shrunken nucleus surrounded by a clear
cytoplasmic halo. Papillomavirus infection can also result in the
development of large cells that have increased quantities of bluegray ﬁbrillar cytoplasm (see Fig. 40.4C). Less frequently,
papillomaviruses can result in the development of prominent
intracytoplasmic bodies, likely due to aggregates of keratin.
Papillomaviruses can also be visible as amphophilic to basophilic
intranuclear inclusions in the upper layers of the epidermis,
although these inclusions tend to be transient and can sometimes
be hard to diﬀerentiate from nucleoli (see Fig. 40.4C).
Histopathology of canine exophytic papillomas generally
reveals exophytic projections of epidermal hyperplasia
(acanthosis) with extensive hyperkeratosis and clumped
keratohyalin granules in the stratum spinosum (see Fig. 40.3C).
Endophytic papillomas are cup-shaped masses of epithelial
hyperplasia that occur below the level of the surrounding normal
skin (see Fig. 40.4B). Koilocytosis and intranuclear inclusions are
often prominent (see Fig. 40.4C).
Histopathology of canine pigmented plaques reveals locally
extensive
epidermal
hyperplasia,
hyperkeratosis,
hyperpigmentation, and clumped keratohyalin granules;
koilocytes and viral inclusions are generally not observed. 26
Feline viral plaques appear as focal well-demarcated areas of
epidermal thickening. They frequently contain koilocytes and
often contain cells that have increased quantities of blue-gray
ﬁbrillar cytoplasm.
BISCs also appear as well-demarcated foci of epidermal
thickening; however, in contrast to a viral plaque, the thickened
epidermis contains evidence of dysplasia (see Fig. 40.6). The cells
within the basal cell layers typically become crowded and groups
of cells can develop dorsoventrally aligned nuclei resulting in a
“windblown” appearance. Papillomavirus-induced cell changes
can be present within BISCs; however, they tend to be less
frequent in advanced lesions. The presence of invasion of cells
through the basement membrane prompts a classiﬁcation of SCC.

vetexamprep.ir

SCCs that are associated with papillomavirus infection rarely
have evidence of papillomavirus infection and histology cannot be
used to predict which SCCs contain papillomaviral DNA.
Feline oral papillomas appear as a focus of thickened
epithelium that is arranged as exophytic folds supported by a
ﬁbrovascular stalk. Papillomavirus-induced cell changes are
present including the presence of prominent eosinophilic
cytoplasmic bodies. 58
Feline sarcoids appear as dermal ﬁbroplastic proliferations. The
overlying epidermis is mildly hyperplastic and includes long, thin
rete ridges that extend into the tumor. 79 The characteristic
epidermal changes allow diﬀerentiation from a ﬁbrosarcoma.
Papillomaviral replication does not occur in feline sarcoids, and
these lesions do not contain papillomavirus-induced cell changes.

Treatment and Prognosis
The outcome of a papillomavirus infection depends on the
papillomavirus type and as more information becomes available,
certain papillomavirus types may be found to be more likely to
result in neoplastic transformation, which may aid
prognostication. The prognosis also appears to be inﬂuenced by
host factors. The overwhelming majority of oral and cutaneous
papillomas in young dogs regress spontaneously 4 to 16 weeks
after onset of clinical signs. However, they may persist in older
dogs, or when there is underlying immune compromise, and
occasionally progress to malignancy. 36 , 37 If possible, underlying
immunosuppression should be treated (for example, through
removal or tapering of immunosuppressive drug treatment).
Lesions can be removed surgically if they cause physical
obstruction or for cosmetic reasons, but surgical treatment may be
followed by recurrence. As in human medicine, cryotherapy
appears to be a useful technique to treat canine papillomas that
persist. As seen in humans with warts, repeated treatments may
be required for some canine papillomas. 83 Numerous other
treatments have been proposed to accelerate resolution of a
papilloma. However, because a high proportion of papillomas
eventually spontaneously regress, deﬁnitively proving that a
treatment inﬂuences resolution is diﬃcult. Treatment with
azithromycin (10 mg/kg PO q24h for 10 days) appeared to be

vetexamprep.ir

eﬀective in a prospective, randomized, double-blinded placebocontrolled clinical trial that included 12 dogs with oral
papillomatosis and 5 dogs with cutaneous papillomatosis. 84
However, azithromycin has been subsequently reported to have
been used without showing beneﬁcial clinical eﬀects. The use of
topical or intralesional immunomodulators (such as imiquimod
cream) and antiviral drugs (such as cidofovir) has shown promise
for treatment of persistent papillomas in humans, but these
treatments have not been evaluated for papillomas in dogs.
Papilloma regression is dependent on CMI and there is no
evidence that stimulating a humoral antibody response by
autogenous vaccination inﬂuences resolution of a papilloma.
Canine pigmented plaques can persist, but transformation to
invasive SCC is rare. 15 , 47 There are single case reports
demonstrating successful treatment of extensive cutaneous
pigmented plaques with carbon dioxide laser treatments 85 and
the antineoplastic agent tigilanol tiglate. 86
The behavior of feline viral plaques and BISCs is poorly
understood. It appears that spontaneous regression is possible,
although some lesions remain stable over a long period of time,
and others progress to SCC. 87 Progression to SCC appears to be
especially frequent and rapid in Devon Rex and Sphinx cats with
subsequent metastases reported. 61 , 62 In a study of 12 cats with
BISCs that were treated using topical imiquimod cream, partial
resolution of a treated lesion was noted in all cats with 5 cats
reported to have complete remission of at least one BISC lesion. 78
However, ﬁve cats developed erythema at the site of treatment
and two cats showed signs of systemic toxicity. While this study
showed some promise, no untreated cats with BISCs were
included and whether or not imiquimod signiﬁcantly alters the
disease course in cats with BISCs remains unknown. It should also
be noted that imiquimod does not have any speciﬁc action against
papillomaviruses. Due to the surface location of BISCs, it appears
likely that cryotherapy may be a potential treatment option,
although there are no published studies using this as a treatment
for BISCs in cats. As in humans, papillomavirus-associated feline
cutaneous SCCs appear to have a more favorable prognosis than
nonpapillomavirus-associated SCCs. 64

vetexamprep.ir

Most feline oral papillomas probably spontaneously resolve
and there is no evidence that they progress to oral SCCs in cats. 50
, 58

Feline sarcoids often recur locally after surgical removal, but
metastasis does not occur. Topical imiquimod cream did not
appear to slow the disease progression in a cat with a feline
sarcoid. 71

Immunity and Vaccination
Regression of a papilloma is associated with papillomavirus typespeciﬁc resistance to reinfection. Immunity to papillomaviruses
comprises: (1) the host immune response to the virus and (2) a
cell-mediated immune response to the tumor, which is ultimately
responsible for tumor regression. This explains why new tumors
may not occur, but old tumors persist and continue to grow in the
face of an immune response to the virus, and immunization with
the virus does not induce tumor regression. Papillomaviruses can
evade the host immune response because infection is limited to
the skin, and the immunogenic capsid protein is not expressed
until the virus reaches the terminally diﬀerentiated outer layer. A
variety of other mechanisms of immune evasion have been
identiﬁed in human papillomavirus infections, including
downregulation of the antiviral interferon response by
papillomavirus proteins. 88

Prevention
No vaccines are available for prevention of papillomavirusinduced disease in dogs and cats. While vaccination against CPV1
would be expected to prevent oral papillomas and a proportion of
cutaneous papillomas, it appears unlikely that clients would pay
for a vaccine to prevent a benign disease that almost always
spontaneously resolves. An experimental vaccine against FcaPV2
was recently developed and shown to induce antibodies against
this virus. However, the vaccine did not decrease the viral load on
the skin of cats. 89 This suggests that any vaccine has to be given
prior to ﬁrst infection by the virus. As cats seem to be infected
immediately after birth, 90 it appears to be hard to use vaccines to
prevent FcaPV2-induced BISCs or SCCs in cats. Prevention of

vetexamprep.ir

immunosuppressive conditions, such as retrovirus infections in
cats, and cautious use of potent immunosuppressive drugs, such
as cyclosporine, may reduce the chance of papillomavirusinduced disease.

Public Health Aspects
More than 250 papillomavirus types infect humans.
Papillomaviruses are relatively species speciﬁc, and there is no
evidence that either CPV or feline papillomavirus infect humans.

Case Example
Signalment

“Oscar,” an adult male neutered Ro weiler mix (Fig. 40.8).

History

Oscar was brought to the University of California-Davis,
Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital for examination after
adoption by a veterinary student as a stray from an American
Indian reservation in Arizona. The student was concerned
about the possibility of malnourishment, a painful mouth, and
pruritic skin disease. Since his rescue 5 days previously, the
student had been feeding him four times daily with
maintenance commercial wet and dry dog foods. His appetite
had been ravenous and tapeworm segments had been observed
in his feces. He had been isolated from other pets in the
household.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 25.5 kg.
General: Bright and alert with normal mentation, nervous.
T = 100.8°F (38.2°C), HR = 90 beats/minute, RR = 18
breaths/minute, mucous membranes pink, CRT = 1
second.

Rottweiler with a high antibody titer to
Ehrlichia canis, malnutrition,
gastrointestinal parasitism, and sarcoptic
mange. (B) Oral papillomatosis was
present on oral examination and
involved the hard and soft palates,
buccal mucosa, and lips.

Integument: A dull haircoat was present. Patchy
generalized alopecia with severe scaling, crusting,
hyperpigmentation, ulceration, and licheniﬁcation was
present on the face, pinnae and pinnal margins,
shoulders, trunk, and extremities.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Moderate mucoid discharge
was present from both eyes. The incisor teeth were
severely worn. Oral examination also revealed pain on
opening the mouth and multiple pink to gray
pedunculated masses that ranged from a few millimeters
to over 1 cm in diameter on the buccal mucosa and
gingiva, lateral aspect of the tongue, and on the hard and
soft palates (see Fig. 40.8B). These were consistent with
oral papillomatosis.
Musculoskeletal: BCS 1/9. Normal gait. No other
musculoskeletal abnormalities were noted.
Cardiovascular and respiratory: No clinically signiﬁcant
abnormalities were detected.
GI and genitourinary: Abdominal palpation was within
normal limits. Intact male with soft, symmetrical testes.
Soft feces were noted on rectal examination.
Lymph nodes: Mandibular and superﬁcial cervical nodes
were enlarged (approximately 3 cm); the popliteal nodes
were sized within normal limits.

Lateral and dorsoventral thoracic radiographs were

of the abdominal structures was within normal limits.

Microbiologic Testing

Lateral ﬂow ELISA assay for antibodies to E. canis,
Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Borrelia burgdorferi and
Diroﬁlaria immitis antigen (SNAP 4Dx Plus, IDEXX
Laboratories, ME, USA): Positive for antibodies to
Ehrlichia spp.

phagocytophilum, E. canis, Ricke sia spp. IFA): Positive for
antibodies to E. canis (1:655,360) and Ricke sia spp.
(1:40,960).
Fecal ﬂotation: Giardia spp. cysts (<1 per 40× ﬁeld),
Sarcoptes mites (1 to 10 per 10× ﬁeld).

Diagnosis

Canine oral papillomatosis; malnutrition; sarcoptic mange;
suspected chronic canine monocytic ehrlichiosis; previous
exposure to SFG ricke sias; giardiasis; cestodiasis.

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment

Oscar was treated with doxycycline (5 mg/kg PO q12h for 6
weeks) for ehrlichiosis, topical selamectin (every 2 weeks for a
total of 6 weeks) for sarcoptic mange, praziquantel (5 mg/kg,
once) for cestodiasis, cephalexin (22 mg/kg q12h for 4 weeks)
for secondary bacterial pyoderma, and fenbendazole (50 mg/kg
PO q24h for 3 days) for giardiasis. The owner was instructed to
bathe him with an oatmeal shampoo twice weekly. At a recheck
appointment 4 weeks later, Oscar weighed 31.5 kg. The skin
lesions had improved, and new hair growth was noted. Pruritus
was still present. More oral papillomas were present, and the
owner described worsened halitosis. Mandibular lymph nodes
remained enlarged. Treatment with cephalexin and doxycycline
was continued for an additional 3 weeks. After 3 weeks, Oscar’s
bodyweight was 33.4 kg, the oral papillomas and mandibular
lymphadenomegaly had resolved, and Oscar was vaccinated
with CDV, canine parvovirus, CAdV, CPIV, and rabies virus
vaccines and neutered.

Comments

The gross appearance of the oral lesions in this dog was
suﬃcient to make a diagnosis of oral papillomatosis.
Papillomatosis has been reported in other dogs with chronic E.
canis infection, but the extent to which ehrlichiosis contributed
to papillomatosis in this dog is unknown. The
immunosuppression associated with malnutrition may also
have played a role. Resolution of lesions occurred within 7
weeks after treatment of the immunosuppressive disorders, but
papillomatosis can also resolve spontaneously over the same
time period.

41: Arthropod-Borne Viral
Infections
Jane E. Sykes, and Andrea Tipold

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Eastern equine encephalitis, 1831 (horses,
Massachusetts) 1 ; West Nile virus infection, 1937 (human,
Uganda) 2 ; tick-borne encephalitis virus, 1931 (humans,
Austria); 3 African horse sickness virus, 1569 (horses, Africa).
4

• Causes: RNA viruses that belong to the families Togaviridae
(genus Alphavirus), such as eastern equine encephalitis virus;
Bunyaviridae, such as La Crosse virus; Reoviridae, such as
African horse sickness virus, and Flaviviridae, such as West
Nile virus and tick-borne encephalitis virus.
• Affected Hosts: A variety of animal species including horses,
humans, and dogs.
• Geographic Distribution: Follows that of the vector host.
Eastern equine encephalitis virus is found in the eastern and
southeastern United States, as well as Central and South
America; West Nile virus is found in Africa, Asia, Middle East,
Europe, and the United States; African horse sickness virus is
found in Africa and the Middle East; tick-borne encephalitis
virus is found in continental Europe and Asia.
• Mode of Transmission: Primarily mosquitoes, and for tickborne encephalitis virus, Ixodes ticks. Dogs can be infected
with African horse sickness virus by ingestion of horse meat,
but Culicoides midges in addition to mosquitoes may also be
involved in transmission of the virus to dogs.

vetexamprep.ir

• Major Clinical Signs: Fever (sometimes >105°F [40.6°C]),
lethargy, neurologic signs, and sometimes systemic signs
such as anorexia and diarrhea. African horse sickness virus
also causes respiratory signs due to pulmonary edema.
• Differential Diagnoses: Rabies, distemper, pseudorabies;
bacterial, protozoal, or fungal meningitis; meningoencephalitis
of unknown origin (MUO); hemic neoplasia with CNS
involvement. Differential diagnosis for African horse sickness
virus infection also includes severe viral or bacterial
respiratory tract diseases (e.g., influenza virus infection or
Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus infection).
• Human Health Significance: Humans are susceptible to
disease caused by many arboviruses. Dogs and cats are
dead-end hosts and do not serve as reservoirs for human
infection. Blood and tissues of affected dogs and cats should
be handled with caution.

Etiology, Epidemiology, and Clinical Features
A large number of viruses that are spread by arthropod vectors
(sometimes referred to as arboviruses, for arthropod-borne viruses)
can infect dogs and cats, often causing encephalitis (Box 41.1 and
Table 41.1). These viruses are enveloped RNA viruses that are
unstable in the environment and readily inactivated with routine
disinfectants. Disease is sporadic, and for many arboviruses, only
subclinical infections have been documented in dogs and cats.
Arboviruses are maintained in vectors and often small rodent
and/or avian reservoir hosts, and some of these reservoir hosts
can develop illness in association with infection. The geographic
distribution is dependent on that of the vectors and reservoir
hosts. Dogs and cats, as well as other domestic animal and human
hosts, are generally considered “dead-end” hosts that do not
maintain suﬃcient viremia to infect arthropods (Fig. 41.1).
Arboviruses replicate within the arthropod vector and are
transmi ed to vertebrate hosts when the vector feeds; this is
followed by viremia and, in some cases, viral spread to the CNS
and neuroinvasion, with subsequent neuronal necrosis and
inﬂammation. When neurologic disease occurs, it has important

vetexamprep.ir

public health signiﬁcance, because the clinical signs can mimic
those of rabies. Because humans have the potential to be infected
with these viruses, serologic evidence of infection of dogs and cats
in a region where disease in humans is not widely recognized can
also have public health signiﬁcance.
