Alphavirus Infections (Family Togaviridae)
Alphaviruses are enveloped, single-stranded RNA mosquitoborne viruses that belong to the family Togaviridae. Members of
this group that are of importance to human and animal health
include Eastern, Western, and Venezuelan encephalitis viruses,
which cause disease in humans and horses in the Americas; and

vetexamprep.ir

Ross River virus, which causes disease in humans in Australia and
the Paciﬁc islands. Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV)
primarily causes outbreaks of disease in horses and humans in
Central and the northern parts of South America, although an
outbreak occurred in Texas in 1971, and there is the potential for
additional outbreaks in the United States. 5 Experimental infection
of dogs with VEEV resulted in fever, leukopenia, and neurologic
signs. 6 Although there is one possible report of encephalitis in a
puppy due to a VEEV, 7 only eastern equine encephalitis virus
(EEEV) is a signiﬁcant cause of naturally occurring disease in
dogs. Dogs have been used as sentinels for the presence of VEEV
variants (such as Everglades virus) in epidemiologic serosurveys.
8 Western equine encephalitis virus causes encephalitis in dogs
after experimental parenteral or intracerebral inoculation, but
naturally occurring disease has not been described. 9

Other alphaviruses cause subclinical seroconversion when they
infect dogs under natural conditions. Ross River and Barmah
Forest viruses are endemic in Australia, aﬀecting kangaroos and
wallabies as major mammalian reservoirs. Serum neutralizing
antibodies are widespread in human and mammalian
populations, and have been detected in dogs and cats. Dogs and
cats that were experimentally fed infected mosquitoes were
relatively resistant to both viral infections. 10 A few animals
seroconverted, but none developed viremia or clinical signs.
Therefore they are unlikely to be important reservoirs of these
viruses.
EEEV is endemic in swampy areas of the southeastern United
States, 11 where it is maintained in a variety of avian reservoir
hosts. It causes disease in humans, horses, dogs, and other
domestic animal species. Diﬀerent viral lineages vary in
pathogenicity for humans and horses. Human cases occur in the
southeastern, eastern, and Great Lakes regions of the United
States, but especially Florida, Georgia, Massachuse s, and New
Jersey; there has been most recent expansion of the virus’
geographic range in the New England region (Fig. 41.2A). 12–15
Most aﬀected dogs have been reported from Georgia; dogs from
New York state and Michigan have also been aﬀected, as well as
captive wolf pups in Michigan in 2019. 13 , 16 , 17 Dogs with signs
of encephalitis have always been young (<7 months of age).

vetexamprep.ir

Disease usually occurs in late spring or summer. Clinical signs
include fever, lethargy, inappetence, and diarrhea, with rapid
progression (within 1 to 2 days) to recumbency, tachypnea,
miosis, nystagmus, tremors, seizures, and death. 11 , 16

Bunyavirus Infections
Like togaviruses, bunyaviruses are enveloped, single-stranded
RNA viruses. Clinically important bunyaviruses for animal and
human health are the mosquito-borne viruses Rift Valley fever
(genus Phlebovirus) and La Crosse (genus Bunyavirus) viruses; the
tick-borne virus Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (genus
Nairovirus); and members of the genus Hantavirus, which are not
transmi ed by vectors and cause hemorrhagic febrile and
respiratory illness in humans (see Chapter 43, Emerging and
Miscellaneous Viral Infections). Serologic evidence of infection
with some vector-borne bunyaviruses has been documented in
dogs and cats.
Tensaw Virus
Tensaw virus is a bunyavirus found in the southeastern United
States. It infects a variety of mammalian species, and although not
considered a signiﬁcant disease threat to humans, there is
widespread human exposure to the virus, and it has rarely caused
human encephalitis. 18 When inoculated into dogs and cats, it
produced
subclinical
viremia,
and
mosquito-mediated
transmission from infected dogs was demonstrated. 19
Rift Valley Fever Virus
Rift Valley fever virus (genus Phlebovirus, family Bunyaviridae)
causes widespread outbreaks of abortion and death in livestock in
parts of Africa and the Arabian peninsula, often after heavy
rainfall, which facilitates emergence of infected mosquitoes.
Humans can also be infected, either as a result of mosquito-borne
transmission, or contact with infected livestock tissues, ﬂuids, or
aborted material. 20 Disease in humans tends to be self-limiting,
but 1% to 2% of infected humans can develop clinically signiﬁcant
hepatitis, retinitis, delayed-onset encephalitis, or hemorrhagic
disease, the la er with high mortality. Because it threatens both

vetexamprep.ir

livestock and human health, Rift Valley fever virus is of signiﬁcant
public health concern.
When experimentally inoculated subcutaneously into newborn
puppies and ki ens, Rift Valley fever virus can cause viremia with
fever then neurologic signs (ataxia and seizures), terminal
hypothermia, and death. 21–24 In contrast, older puppies and adult
dogs show no clinical signs, but the virus can cause abortions and
stillbirths in experimentally infected pregnant bitches. 21 Puppies
were shown to transmit the virus to their mother and to other
puppies, raising concern for the possible role of dogs in
transmission of the virus to livestock or humans. Under natural
conditions, it has been suggested that dogs might become infected
through inhalation or ingestion of the virus from infected
carcasses. Given that only neonatal puppies and ki ens are
capable of transmi ing infection following experimental infection,
the role of dogs and cats in the epidemiology of this disease seems
to be of limited signiﬁcance.
La Crosse Virus
La Crosse virus rarely causes naturally occurring disease in dogs.
25 , 26 La Crosse virus was named after La Crosse in Wisconsin,
where it was ﬁrst identiﬁed as a human pathogen, and is mostly
found in the eastern and midwestern United States (Fig. 41.2B).
The virus is maintained in rodents, especially Eastern gray
squirrels and chipmunks. Vector infection can be lifelong, with
transovarial transmission to subsequent generations of
mosquitoes. La Crosse virus is a major cause of human pediatric
encephalitis in North America, although mortality is low. Aﬀected
dogs have included an adult dog from Florida and three puppies
from southern Georgia. 25 , 26 Mild fever, lethargy, ataxia,
vestibular signs, and ultimately seizures occurred in the adult
dog, and sudden death was reported in the puppies.

Reovirus Infections
Reoviruses are icosahedral, nonenveloped viruses. The major
reovirus of signiﬁcance to dogs and cats is African horse sickness
virus (genus Orbivirus). As its name implies, African horse
sickness virus causes outbreaks of disease in horses in Africa with
high (90%) mortality. Infection occurs throughout sub-Saharan

vetexamprep.ir

Africa, extending from Senegal to Somalia and South Africa. The
disease also occurs sporadically in the Middle East, India, and
Pakistan, and spread to Spain in 1966 and again in 1987, which
resulted in signiﬁcant equine mortality. 27 It is spread by biting
Culicoides imicola midges; other biting insects may play a lesser
role in transmission. 27 In horses, disease results from damage to
the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, and has been divided
into a mild febrile form; a peracute pulmonary form, with rapid
death due to pulmonary edema; a subacute cardiac form
characterized by fever and subcutaneous edema; and a mixed
cardiopulmonary form. 4 Dogs are the only other animals capable
of developing the severe form of disease. Dogs can be naturally
infected, most commonly when they ingest infected horse meat,
but there have also been reports of infection of dogs from South
Africa without this history, suggesting the possibility of vectorborne transmission. 27 , 28 In further support of vector-borne
transmission, most of these cases were seen during peak seasonal
Culicoides midge activity (late summer). Many dogs show no
clinical signs, but severe disease can occur. The incubation period
is 1 to 2 weeks, followed by variable fever, lethargy, inappetence,
and signs of pulmonary edema, including tachypnea, cough, and
foamy nasal discharge. This can be followed by diarrhea and
seizures, with high mortality. 27–29
A reovirus with historical signiﬁcance for dogs is bluetongue
virus, which causes disease in sheep and to a lesser extent in ca le
in Australia, the United States, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and
Europe. Natural disease caused by this virus in dogs is unlikely
based on the observed low prevalence of seropositivity in dogs in
endemic areas. 30 Abortion in pregnant bitches and their
subsequent death occurred 7 to 9 days after vaccination with a
bluetongue virus-contaminated, a enuated live virus combination
canine vaccine in the early 1990s. 31 , 32 Lesions in the dam
consisted of interstitial pneumonia, myocardial degeneration,
hepatic vasculitis, and renal glomerulitis. 32

Flavivirus Infections
Flaviviruses are small, icosahedral, enveloped viruses with a
single-stranded RNA genome. Vector-borne ﬂaviviruses (ﬂavi =
“yellow,” Latin) of importance to human and animal health are
the mosquito-borne viruses Japanese encephalitis virus, yellow
fever virus, Murray Valley encephalitis virus, St. Louis
encephalitis virus, Wesselsbron virus, Dengue viruses, and West
Nile virus (WNV), as well as the tick-borne viruses inducing tickborne encephalitis (TBE) virus, Louping-ill virus, and Powassan
virus. Japanese encephalitis virus, Murray Valley encephalitis

vetexamprep.ir

virus, and St. Louis encephalitis virus all belong to the Japanese
encephalitis complex. Antibodies to some of these viruses have been
detected in dogs and to a lesser extent, cats in serosurveys, 33–37
but serologic cross-reactivity among ﬂaviviruses can occur.
Although uncommon, WNV in the United States and TBE virus in
Europe have been reported to cause disease in dogs on more than
one occasion. One dog from Africa with fatal encephalitis was
initially thought to be infected with Wesselsbron disease virus, 38
but the isolate was later conﬁrmed to be WNV. 39
West Nile Virus Infection
WNV was ﬁrst isolated in 1937 from a woman in the West Nile
region of Uganda. 2 In the 1950s, the virus was recognized in
Israel as a cause of human neurologic disease in the elderly, 40 and
subsequently was identiﬁed in other parts of Europe and South
Africa. In 1999, it appeared in New York state, possibly by
transport of infected humans, birds, or mosquitoes. 41 WNV then
spread explosively westward across the United States, and by
2003, disease was detected across the United States to California
(Fig. 41.2C). WNV also spread into Canada, Mexico, the
Caribbean, and Central and South America, and is now one of the
most broadly distributed arboviruses. 41 , 42 Several diﬀerent
variants of the virus exist, which diﬀer in virulence. Strains
circulating within the Western hemisphere, Europe, the Middle
East, India, Africa, and Australia belong to WNV lineage 1;
lineage 2 strains circulate in South Africa, Madagascar, and, now
also Europe. Other lineages have also been reported, but these are
not associated with outbreaks of human disease.
Although most of the natural transmission of WNV in the
United States has been associated with three Culex subspecies
(pipiens, quinquefasciatus, and tarsalis), WNV has been isolated
from at least 65 mosquito species. 43–72 Transmission of WNV by
mosquitoes increases in the warmer months, with peak activity in
the northern hemisphere between July and October. Birds
(especially passerines such as crows, jays, brown sparrows, and
the American robin; shorebirds; owls; and hawks) are important
reservoir hosts (see Fig. 41.1). Some avian species, such as brown
sparrows, maintain high viremia in the absence of clinical signs,
whereas crows develop high viremias and near-uniform

vetexamprep.ir

mortality. Other modes of transmission include ingestion through
predation of infected birds or rodents, blood transfusion, needlestick injuries, and transplacental transmission. Increased ambient
temperature is associated with increased eﬃciency of
transmission from mosquitoes to birds. Disease primarily occurs
in birds, humans, and horses, but disease has been reported in
several other vertebrate species, including farmed alligators. 44
Most mammalian species develop a viremia of insuﬃcient
magnitude to infect feeding mosquitoes, but some exceptions
occur, including among some rodent and lagomorph species. 45
Dogs develop low-titer viremia and are considered incompetent
as amplifying hosts, but treatment of dogs with glucocorticoids
before infection resulted in levels of viremia roughly 50 times that
in untreated dogs. 46
After inoculation, the virus replicates in keratinocytes, dendritic
cells, and Langerhans cells. This is followed by spread to draining
lymph nodes, further replication in lymph node macrophages,
cell-associated viremia, and dissemination to peripheral organs. 43
The vast majority of infected humans experience no clinical signs.
When signs occur in humans they follow an incubation period of
2 to as long as 21 days (usually 2 to 6 days). They are often mild
and self-limiting and include fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, GI
symptoms, and a transient rash. 43 , 47 Rarely, hepatitis,
pancreatitis, myocarditis, rhabdomyolysis, orchitis, uveitis, and
chorioretinitis can occur. Severe neuroinvasive disease occurs in
fewer than 1% of cases, is most common in the elderly, those with
advanced immunosuppression, or people with chronic medical
conditions. Severe disease is characterized by high fever, cervical
rigidity, muscle weakness, seizures, and ﬂaccid paralysis, and
neurological signs may persist for over a year in those that
recover. Fatality rates in humans with encephalitis are reported to
be 3% to 19%. 45 Neurologic signs result from viral invasion of
neurons in the brainstem, deep nuclei, and anterior horns within
the spinal cord. Neuroinvasion appears to occur by both
anterograde and retrograde axonal transport. 43 , 48 The innate
immune system plays a critical role in control of WNV replication.
Cellular immunity, mediated by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, is
essential for clearance of virus from the CNS, but in some cases,

vetexamprep.ir

cellular immune responses appear to contribute to
immunopathogenetic lesions in the CNS. 49
Clinical signs in horses result from polioencephalomyelitis and
include fever and neurologic signs such as ataxia, weakness, and
muscle tremors. 50 Approximately two-thirds of horses recover.
Infected wild birds can exhibit neurologic disease but are usually
found dead. Myocarditis and meningoencephalitis are common
necropsy ﬁndings in these birds. 51
In dogs, there is widespread serologic evidence of infection, but
disease is rare. Dogs have been widely used as sentinels for
evidence of WNV in diﬀerent geographic locations. Serologic
surveys have revealed prevalences of 27% in Senegal in 2014, 62%
in working dogs in Morocco in 2012, 52 28% in Saskatchewan,
Canada in 2008–2010, 53 5% in New York City in 1999, 4.6% in
China in 2011, 54 18% in Harris County, Texas in 2005, 55 and 56%
in Louisiana after Hurricane Katrina. 56 Cats also can become
infected and seroconvert, but illness has not been described. Dogs
that were experimentally infected with WNV using mosquitoes
developed viremia of low magnitude and short duration, and
failed to show clinical manifestations of illness, except for
transient pyrexia in one dog. 57 Cats infected experimentally by
feeding them infected mice remained healthy, and cats infected
using mosquitoes developed transient fever, inappetence, and
lethargy, with viremia that was more sustained than that in dogs.
Five clinically aﬀected dogs have been described following
natural infection. All, apart from a dog from Africa, resided in
various parts of the United States (Missouri, Mississippi,
California, and Illinois). 58–61 All of the dogs showed signs of fever
and progressive neurologic disease. Neurologic signs included
generalized tremors, ataxia, a head tilt, bobbing movements,
altered mentation, cervical pain, abnormal placing reactions, and
tetraparesis. Diarrhea, serous oculonasal discharge, conjunctivitis,
abdominal pain, cardiac arrhythmias due to myocarditis,
tachypnea, tachycardia, and a stiﬀ gait associated with mild
neutrophilic polyarthritis have been reported (Fig. 41.3). For all
dogs, diagnosis was made at necropsy. In Europe, WNV infection
was suspected at necropsy of dogs with encephalitis of unknown
origin after detection of immunohistological precipitates using

vetexamprep.ir

virus-speciﬁc antibodies; however,
conﬁrmed using other techniques. 62

Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus
TBE virus is a notiﬁable disease that causes potentially fatal
neurologic disease in humans in Europe and Asia, where it is the
most important tick-borne viral disease of humans. 63 The virus is
transmi ed transstadially and to a lesser extent transovarially
within infected ticks, and ticks can transmit the disease to each
other while co-feeding, independent of systemic viremia in
vertebrate hosts. 64 The primary reservoirs for the virus are small
rodents such as mice and voles. Consumption of raw milk from
infected ruminants (especially goats) is a lesser mode of
transmission to humans (Fig. 41.4). TBE has been reported not
only in humans, but also in dogs, horses, monkeys, and wild
ruminants, but not in cats.
At least three subtypes of TBE virus exist, which vary in
virulence and geographic distribution. The three predominant
subtypes are designated the European, Siberian, and far-eastern
subtypes, 65 , 66 although as of 2019 two additional subtypes have
been proposed—the Baikalian and Himalayan subtypes. 66 The
far-eastern subtype occurs in far-eastern Russia, Japan, Korea, and
China and is the most virulent subtype, with mortality rates in
humans that may exceed 20%. In much of Europe, Ixodes ricinus
ticks spread the European subtype (Western and Central
European TBE). Ixodes persulcatus ticks transmit the other viral
subtypes in northeastern Europe, Russia, and far-east Asia
(Eastern European TBE) (Fig. 41.2D). 67 Both Siberian and
European subtypes may be found in eastern Europe. The disease
was originally detected in 1937 in Austria (Central European TBE),
but its geographic distribution has expanded rapidly so that the
European subtype now occurs throughout Europe as far west as
France and now possibly Belgium, the Netherlands, Northern
Germany, and the United Kingdom. 37 , 66 , 68 , 69 Until very
recently, TBE had not been reported in the United Kingdom and
Ireland, but a related tick-borne ﬂavivirus, Louping-ill virus, was
known to be present. However, a recent surveillance eﬀort in the
United Kingdom detected TBE virus in ticks from the

vetexamprep.ir

Norfolk/Suﬀolk (Thetford Forest) area, where the seroprevalence
of ﬂavivirus infection was highest. 66 No human or canine cases of
TBE have yet been reported in the United Kingdom. An
astonishing ﬁnding suggests that a speciﬁc adaptation of the tick
populations to their respective TBE virus isolates occurs. 70
In Europe, some of the highest incidence rates have occurred in
central European countries, especially the Czech Republic. 71
Disease seasonality correlates with the activity of the tick in
various parts of Europe.
In humans, signs of TBE occur in approximately one-third of
infected individuals 4 to 28 days (and usually 7 to 14 days) after a
tick bite and are usually biphasic. 66 In the ﬁrst, viremic phase,
fever, malaise, headache, myalgia, and vomiting occur, which
resolve within 1 week. In some individuals, after an asymptomatic
period that lasts 2 to 10 days, clinical signs return and are
accompanied by signs of meningitis, meningoencephalitis,
meningoencephalomyelitis,
or
meningoencephaloradiculitis.
About 4 to 14% of cases are fatal, most often in the elderly, 72 but
neurologic signs can persist for months or longer than a year. Coinfections with Borrelia (Borreliella) burgdorferi can occur. Vaccines
are currently recommended for prevention of TBE in humans, and
national vaccination programs have greatly reduced the incidence
of disease. 73
Subclinical infection of dogs with TBE virus is widespread, and
so dogs have been important sentinels for the presence of the
virus in new regions of Europe. Rarely, illness that resembles that
in humans can occur in dogs. Aﬀected dogs have been described
from Sweden, Norway, Greece, Swi erland, Austria, Germany,
the Czech Republic, and Italy. 63 , 74–77 Several reports have
described disease in ro weilers, but it is not clear whether this
represents a true breed predisposition. Signs in dogs include high
fever (over 39°C [102.5°F]), lethargy, anorexia, and neurologic
signs such as decreased mentation, behavioral changes such as
aggression, delayed placing reactions, ataxia, ﬂaccid paralysis,
reduced segmental reﬂexes, neck pain, vestibular signs, tremors,
tetraparesis, miosis, anisocoria, and generalized seizures. 63 , 67
These signs progress rapidly over several days to a week,
sometimes culminating in death or euthanasia. In a 2021 longterm follow-up study of 54 dogs with TBE, the disease was

vetexamprep.ir

clinically biphasic, with initial non-speciﬁc clinical signs followed
by onset of neurologic deﬁcits. The case fatality rate in that study
was 33%. 77 Of the dogs that died, all died within 4 months, and of
those that survived, 17% had residual neurologic signs.
Neurologic sequelae were more often detected in older dogs and
dogs with seizures at the time of initial evaluation. Because of the
rapid progression of neurologic signs, the disease is sometimes
mistaken for rabies. Recovery has been described rarely.
Louping-Ill Virus
Louping-ill virus is transmi ed by I. ricinus ticks, which are the
most abundant ticks in the United Kingdom, and mainly causes
neurologic disease in sheep (especially weaned lambs) and red
grouse, an economically important gamebird. This is in contrast to
TBE virus, which does not cause disease in sheep. Several
diﬀerent molecular types of the virus have been described that
circulate in distinct geographic regions, and although the virus
has been detected in Europe, disease predominantly occurs in
rough pastures and upland heather moorland of Scotland,
Cumbria, Wales, Devon, North Yorkshire, and Ireland (Fig. 41.5).
78 , 79 Red grouse and sheep, together with mountain hares, are
considered to be important reservoir hosts, another important
diﬀerence from TBE virus, which is maintained in small rodents.
Red grouse are most often infected as a result of ingestion of
infected ticks. The virus rarely causes encephalitis in other
species, such as ca le, humans, horses, pigs, goats, farm-raised
deer, and dogs. 79–82 Fewer than 50 cases have been reported in
humans, but when disease caused by Louping-ill virus occurs in
people it is typically a febrile illness that may be followed by
neurological signs, and most often occurs in aba oir workers,
farm workers, and laboratory staﬀ. 79 Disease in cats has not been
described. In sheep, mixed infections with Anaplasma
phagocytophilum and Louping-ill virus can be associated with high
mortality. Much of the eﬀorts to prevent the disease have been to
protect red grouse for hunting. 78

vetexamprep.ir

Transmission cycle for tick-borne
encephalitis virus. From Sykes JE. Canine and
FIG. 41.4

Feline Infectious Diseases. Elsevier; 2014.

Working sheepdogs and gun dogs are at increased risk of
exposure. A virus that was genetically very similar to sheepderived Louping-ill virus strains was identiﬁed in one infected
dog. 82 The risk of infection is also highest in the spring and fall,
when tick activity is greatest. Most dogs are probably
subclinically infected. When clinical signs develop, initial signs
are primarily caused by cerebellar dysfunction and include mild
paresis, ataxia, and tremors. Within 24 hours, severe
incoordination, tetraplegia, and opisthotonos may develop. In
surviving dogs, recovery has been slow, and neurological signs
may persist for months to years.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities and Diagnostic
Imaging
Laboratory abnormalities in dogs with vector-borne viral
encephalitis are nonspeciﬁc. No or minimal abnormalities may be

vetexamprep.ir

detected in some dogs. Mild anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia, or
leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia (sometimes with a left shift)
may occur. The CSF may also be unremarkable, or there may be
increased protein concentration and mononuclear pleocytosis.
MRI ﬁndings described in a puppy with EEEV infection consisted
of changes consistent with multifocal meningoencephalitis with
transtentorial and foramen magnum herniation. 83

Microbiologic Tests
Serologic Diagnosis

vetexamprep.ir

Serologic assays such as serum neutralization or ELISAs are
available for detection of antibodies to arboviruses through
specialized veterinary diagnostic or research laboratories, and
have primarily been used for epidemiologic serosurveys of dogs
and cats. Serologic assays have, in general, not been very useful
for diagnosis of acute viral encephalitis in dogs and cats. First,
because disease is rare, arbovirus infections are often not
suspected before death or euthanasia, and euthanasia is often
performed early because of suspicion for rabies. Second,
incubation periods are often short and disease in dogs progresses
rapidly with a high mortality rate, so there is usually insuﬃcient
time for an antibody response to develop. The possibility of
previous exposure confounds interpretation of single titers.
Serologic assays have mainly been used to detect IgG and IgM in
serum and CSF of dogs with TBE from Europe. 34 Demonstration
of serum antiviral IgM is the standard diagnostic test for equine
WNV disease, and in any species, a fourfold or greater rise in
neutralization titer is evidence of an infection.
Virus Isolation
Arboviruses can be isolated in a variety of cell lines, and virus
isolation has been used to detect WNV, TBE virus, La Crosse
virus, and African horse sickness virus in naturally infected dogs.
25 , 59 , 84 , 85 Fresh or fresh-frozen brain or spinal cord
homogenates from dogs with encephalitis are suitable specimens.
Because viremia occurs, blood, CSF, lung, spleen, and liver might
also be useful specimens for isolation. 59 , 63 Immunoﬂuorescent
antibody staining and RT-PCR assays can be used to conﬁrm the
presence of the virus in cell cultures. 11 , 59 Because many of these
viruses can infect humans, specialized biosafety level 3 facilities
are generally required. This limits the availability and practicality
of virus isolation for routine diagnostic purposes.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
End point (conventional) and real-time RT-PCR assays have been
described for many diﬀerent arboviral pathogens. Specialized
veterinary diagnostic and research laboratories generally perform
these assays. In dogs, RT-PCR assays have been used to detect

vetexamprep.ir

EEEV, African horse sickness virus, TBE (CSF), and WNV in
clinical specimens. 11 , 27 , 28 , 59 , 83

Pathologic Findings
In general, histopathology of the CNS in dogs with vector-borne
viral infections reveals nonsuppurative meningoencephalitis or
meningoencephalomyelitis, with multifocal mild to moderate
gliosis, neuronal necrosis, and perivascular cuﬃng with
lymphocytes, histiocytes, and plasma cells within Virchow-Robin
spaces. 25 , 59 , 63 Neutrophils predominate within the meninges of
dogs infected with EEEV. 11 Within brain tissue, inﬂammatory
inﬁltrates in dogs infected with EEEV have been most prominent
in the gray ma er of the cerebral cortices and midbrains. Gray
ma er has also been preferentially infected in dogs with WNV
encephalitis. 59 Pathologic changes in dogs with TBE are most
severe in the gray ma er of the brainstem and the cerebellum; 86–
88 meningitis and spinal cord involvement have also been
described. 63 In animals with Louping-ill virus infection, lesions
have been concentrated in the spinal cord and cerebellum.
Immunohistochemical reagents are available for detection of most
arboviruses that can infect dogs, and have been used to detect
antigen of WNV, La Crosse virus, African horse sickness virus,
and TBE virus in CNS and other tissues of dogs. 26 , 27 , 59 , 73 , 88 In
dogs with advanced TBE virus infection, viral antigen is not easily
found, suggesting rapid clearance of the virus occurs early in the
course of infection.
Extraneural lesions have mainly been reported in dogs infected
with WNV and young puppies that were experimentally infected
with Rift Valley fever virus, although foci of myocardial
degeneration have been noted in dogs with naturally occurring
EEEV. Dogs with African horse sickness virus infection had acute
interstitial pneumonia and pleuritis (Fig. 41.6). 27 Multifocal to
diﬀuse hepatocellular necrosis has been the most consistent
ﬁnding in neonatal puppies and ki ens infected with Rift Valley
fever virus. Lesions in experimentally infected puppies and
ki ens showed poorly deﬁned intrahepatic eosinophilic
intranuclear inclusions and Councilmanlike bodies, which are
more prominent in other hosts. 24 Lymphocytic and necrotizing

vetexamprep.ir

myocarditis was present in some puppies and a ki en
experimentally infected with Rift Valley fever virus, and several
dogs naturally infected with WNV (Fig. 41.7). Other ﬁndings in
dogs with WNV infection have included evidence of hepatic and
renal tubular epithelial cell necrosis, adrenal gland cortical
necrosis and lymphoid aggregates, neutrophilic pancreatitis, and
mild plasmacytic synovitis. 58–61

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of dogs with vector-borne viral encephalitis is
supportive only. The prognosis appears to be poor, but because
only a handful of infected dogs have been reported, the true
prognosis is poorly understood. In virtually all dogs with
neurologic signs, diagnosis has been made at necropsy. Some
dogs with TBE recover with supportive care. 34 In the 2021 study
of 54 dogs from Swi erland, the case fatality rate was 33%, and
long-term neurological deﬁcits occurred in 17% of the dogs. 77
Glucocorticoids have been used to treat some dogs and cats with
viral encephalitides, but their use is controversial because of
immunosuppression, and controlled studies are not available.

Immunity and Vaccination
Exposure to vector-borne viruses appears to confer immunity to
future infections with the same virus. Vaccines are not available
for dogs because disease is uncommon to rare. However, vaccines
are available and used widely in endemic areas to prevent
ﬂavivirus infections in humans (such as TBE, yellow fever, and
Japanese encephalitis); WNV encephalitis in horses; and Loupingill virus infection in sheep, ca le, and goats. Human vaccines have
been used to prevent TBE in dogs, but there is limited evidence of
the eﬃcacy of these vaccines in dogs. Use of inactivated Loupingill virus vaccines for sheep in dogs has resulted in ﬂuid-ﬁlled
swellings at the site of injection that may require surgical
drainage, and dogs appear to require at least two injections to
elicit a detectable serum antibody response. 89

Prevention
The risk of arboviral infections in dogs and cats can be reduced
through control of mosquito and tick vectors. Keeping pets
indoors, especially at dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most
active, can also reduce exposure, provided mosquitoes are
excluded through the use of proper screens and windows. For

vetexamprep.ir

g
p p
WNV, prevention of predation on dead birds or rodents may also
reduce the risk of infection, and for African horse sickness, dogs
should be prevented from consuming carcasses from dead horses
in endemic areas. Drainage of standing water and removal of
containers (tin cans, old tires, ﬂower pots, clogged gu ers,
bunched tarpaulins) that act as breeding sites are important for
mosquito control. Water in birdbaths should be changed at least
weekly. Weeds and brush should be reduced. Human mosquito
repellents that contain DEET (N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide) are
not recommended for pets, because they can be toxic. 53 Some
products labeled for tick prevention in dogs and cats may help to
repel mosquitoes but are not likely to completely protect against
mosquito bites. More information on tick prevention can be found
in Chapter 13. Only products speciﬁcally labeled for cats should
be used on cats or on dogs that are in contact with cats, because of
the sensitivity of cats to permethrin toxicosis. 54

Public Health Aspects
Many arboviruses that cause disease in humans also infect dogs
and cats. Dogs and cats are generally not considered reservoirs for
transmission of virus to humans because they do not develop
high-level or sustained viremia. As noted previously, dogs have
been used as sentinels for the presence of these viruses in
epidemiologic studies.

Case Example
Signalment

“Paloma,” a 13-year-old female spayed golden retriever–Irish
se er mix from Vacaville in northern California.

History

Paloma was evaluated at the University of California, Davis,
VMTH in September for a 3-day history of inappetence and
lethargy. Two days before, physical examination by the

vetexamprep.ir

referring veterinarian had revealed tachycardia (96 beats/min)
and pyrexia (103.1°F or 39.5°C). Results of routine CBC,
biochemistry tests, and a urinalysis did not reveal clinically
signiﬁcant abnormalities. The dog was treated with amoxicillin
(20 mg/kg PO q12h) and enroﬂoxacin (10 mg/kg PO q12h),
without improvement.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 28.6 kg.
General: Obtunded, 5% dehydrated. T = 106°F (41.1°C),
HR = 140 beats/min, RR = 92 breaths/min, mucous
membranes pink, CRT = 1 s.
Integument: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Bilateral enophthalmos, mild
serous ocular discharge, conjunctivitis, and nuclear
sclerosis were present. Moderate to severe dental disease
was present. Examination of the ocular fundus showed no
abnormalities.
Musculoskeletal: Body condition score 4/9. Ambulatory
on all four limbs, but generalized weakness was noted.
Moderate atrophy of the temporalis, quadriceps, and
gastrocnemius muscles was present.
Cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, urogenital, and lymphoid
systems: Tachypnea and tachycardia were identiﬁed.
There was mild cranial abdominal discomfort on
palpation. All peripheral lymph nodes were normal sized.
Neurologic examination: Decreased placing reactions
were noted in all four limbs, and there was pain on
manipulation of the neck.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 37.5% (40%–55%), MCV 67.3 fL (65–75 fL),
MCHC 34.4 g/dL (33–36 g/dL), WBC 6050 cells/µL (6000–
13,000 cells/µL), neutrophils 5627 cells/µL (3000–10,500
cells/µL), lymphocytes 363 cells/µL (1000–4000 cells/µL),
monocytes 61 cells/µL (150–1200 cells/µL), adequate
platelet numbers (clumped on smear).

vetexamprep.ir

Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 144 mmol/L (145–154
mmol/L), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.6–5.3 mmol/L),
chloride 110 mmol/L (108–118 mmol/L), bicarbonate 16
mmol/L (16–26 mmol/L), phosphorus 3.1 mg/dL (3.0–6.2
mg/dL), calcium 9.1 mg/dL (9.7–11.5 mg/dL), BUN 8
mg/dL (5–21 mg/dL), creatinine 0.6 mg/dL (0.3–1.2
mg/dL), glucose 86 mg/dL (64–123 mg/dL), total protein
5.7 g/dL (5.4–7.6 g/dL), albumin 2.3 g/dL (3.0–4.4 g/dL),
globulin 3.4 g/dL (1.8–3.9 g/dL), ALT 25 U/L (19–67 U/L),
AST 34 U/L (19–42 U/L), ALP 53 U/L (21–170 U/L), GGT 3
U/L (0–6 U/L), cholesterol 236 mg/dL (135–361 mg/dL),
total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL (0–0.2 mg/dL).

Imaging Findings

Thoracic, abdominal, spinal, and joint radiographs: No
signiﬁcant abnormalities were noted.
Abdominal ultrasound: Mild mesenteric and moderate
sublumbar lymphadenomegaly was identiﬁed. The dog
exhibited pain on ultrasound of the right cranial abdomen, but
no abnormalities in this region were identiﬁed. Impressions:
mesenteric and sublumbar lymphadenomegaly.

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures (ﬁve sequentially
collected specimens): negative.
Serology for Ehrlichia canis, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and
Borrelia burgdorferi antibodies (POC assay, IDEXX Laboratories,
ME, USA): negative.

Treatment

Paloma was treated with lactated Ringer’s solution (3 mL/kg/h
IV) with potassium chloride supplementation (20 mEq/L),
amoxicillin (22 mg/kg PO q8h), enroﬂoxacin (10 mg/kg PO
q24h), and doxycycline (5 mg/kg PO q12h). Physical
examination on day 2 revealed persistent pyrexia (105.6°F),
tachycardia (108 beats/min), and a stiﬀ gait, but there was no
evidence of joint pain or swelling on palpation. Cytologic
analysis of synovial ﬂuid collected from both carpal and
tibiotarsal joints using arthrocentesis revealed mild suppurative
and mononuclear inﬂammation.

vetexamprep.ir

On day 3, the dog became tetraparetic and was unable to
stand for longer than a few seconds. Pyrexia (104.5°F) persisted,
and treatment with dexamethasone sodium phosphate (0.2
mg/kg IV once) and hydromorphone (0.05 mg/kg IV once) was
initiated. Neurologic examination disclosed mental dullness,
decreased placing reactions in all four limbs, and normal
segmental reﬂexes. Further evaluation for neurologic disease,
such as imaging of the brain, CSF analysis, or both, was oﬀered,
but declined by the owner because of ﬁnancial limitations. On
day 4, the dog was normothermic, and sternally recumbent.
Prednisone (1 mg/kg PO q12h) and metronidazole (10 mg/kg
PO q8h) were added to the treatment regimen. Despite this
treatment, by day 5, Paloma was laterally recumbent and
obtunded. The owner elected euthanasia.

Necropsy Findings

Histopathologic ﬁndings at necropsy consisted of severe acute
multifocal necrotizing perivascular and random neutrophilic
pancreatitis; severe lymphocytic and neutrophilic myocarditis
and vasculitis with myonecrosis; and mild, multifocal gliosis
and perivascular to random lymphoplasmacytic and
neutrophilic polioencephalomyelitis. The cervical spinal cord
was the most severely aﬀected. Mild perivascular plasmacytic
synovitis was also present. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures of
the liver, spleen, lung, and synovial ﬂuid were negative. West
Nile
virus
(WNV)
antigen
was
detected
with
immunohistochemical stains within foci of encephalomyelitis
and myocarditis. The virus was isolated from fresh-frozen lung
tissue, and WNV RNA was detected using RT-PCR in the
synovium, synovial ﬂuid, spinal cord, heart, and kidney tissue.

Diagnosis

Encephalitis, myocarditis, and polyarthritis associated with
WNV infection.

Comments

This was a rare case of encephalitis and myocarditis associated
with WNV infection in a dog. Disease occurred in September,
the time of peak activity for virus transmission by mosquitoes
(July to October).

42: Bornavirus Infection
Jonas Johansson Wensman, Mikael Berg, and Karin Hultin Jäderlund

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Staggering disease was first described in the
1970s in Sweden (Kronevi et al., 1974). It was linked to BoDV
infection in 1995 in Sweden (Lundgren et al., 1995).
• Causes: Borna disease virus (BoDV) (species Mammalian 1
orthobornavirus), family Bornaviridae.
• Affected Hosts: Mammalian 1 orthobornavirus mainly affects
horses and sheep, but also cats, dogs, other equids, and
ungulates.
• Geographic Distribution: Europe (endemic in horses and
sheep in Central Europe; in cats mainly reported in Sweden),
worldwide serologic evidence of exposure in various species.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Not entirely known. Reservoirs
(small mammals) have been suggested.
• Major Clinical Signs: Gait disturbances and behavioral
changes.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other feline encephalitides and
neoplastic diseases affecting the CNS.
• Human Health Significance: A variant bornavirus has been
associated with three cases of fatal encephalitis in breeders of
variegated squirrels. Also, at least eight cases of BoDV-1 in
humans have been described further emphasizing the
zoonotic potential for BoDV-1, especially in endemic regions.
The suggested association of BoDV and neuropsychiatric
disorders in humans is however still highly controversial.

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Naturally occurring clinical feline bornavirus infection,
characterized by behavioral and motor dysfunction (“staggering
disease”), was ﬁrst described in Sweden. 1 Although BoDV
infection has been reported in cats with ataxia and other
neurologic signs in the United Kingdom, Japan, and Belgium, 2 a
direct etiologic role of BoDV has not been established in these
cases. One case of feline Borna disease (BD), veriﬁed by IHC, was
reported from Swi erland. 3 Two dogs have been reported with
BD, one from Austria 4 and the other from Japan. 5 BoDV has been
detected in dogs in China, associated with importation of infected
sheep from Germany. 6 A wild cat (Lynx lynx) in Sweden was also
diagnosed with classic BD. 7 Feline BoDV isolates have however
only been rarely reported.
BoDV is an enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-stranded RNA
virus of the family Bornaviridae in the order Mononegavirales. 8 The
genus Orthobornavirus consists of a number of new species such as
Mammalian 1 orthobornavirus, Elapid 1 orthobornavirus, Passeriform 1
and 2 orthobornavirus, Psi aciform 1 and 2 orthobornavirus, and
Waterbird 1 orthobornavirus. This chapter will only deal with
Mammalian 1 orthobornavirus viruses. These viruses seem to be
rather stable genetically, whereas the genetic variation within
other virus species is considerably greater.
BoDV persistently resides within the CNS after natural and
experimental infection of various animal species, ranging from
birds to primates. 9 Historically, BoDV infected military horses in
the endemic area around the city of Borna in Germany. 10 Cases of
“classic BoDV encephalomyelitis”, or “BD,” in horses, sheep, and
ca le seem to be restricted to endemic regions in Germany,
Swi erland, and Austria. However, numerous other species may
also be infected naturally, possibly including humans. Special
concern was raised after fatal transmission of a bornavirus variant
to three humans who were breeding variegated squirrels (Sciurus
variegatoides), 11 indicating that some bornaviruses may be
zoonotic.
Speciﬁc BoDV antibodies have been detected in horses and cats
in various regions of the world. The disease in horses may be
largely subclinical because the prevalence of antibodies in sera is

vetexamprep.ir

much greater than the prevalence of clinical illness. 12 Based on
serologic and nucleic acid screening, many feline infections are
also subclinical. Serologic studies indicate that in addition to
Europe, cats have been subclinically exposed in the Philippines,
Indonesia, Turkey, Japan, and Australia. 13 BoDV antibodies have
also been detected in cats with a wide variety of clinical signs.
Although the clinical manifestations may not be directly caused
by BoDV, it is possible that the virus is an opportunistic pathogen.
Serologic results from two studies suggest that cats infected with
FIV are more prone to BoDV infection. 14 , 15
Disease associated with BoDV occurs most frequently in spring
and summer, 13 and thus arthropod transmission has been
suspected. A deﬁnitive reservoir host has not been documented,
but rodents, insectivores, and birds are suspected. There are a
number of recent reports of BoDV in various small mammals such
as white-toothed shrews 16 and bank voles, 17 which indicate that
diﬀerent hosts exist in various geographical regions.
Viral RNA has been detected in feces and urine of naturally
infected cats, 18 and in salivary, nasal, and conjunctival secretions
of horses and sheep 12 , 19 ; animals may become infected by direct
contact with these secretions or with fomites, such as
contaminated food or water. Infection does not appear to spread
readily among cats. Epidemiologic studies suggest that risk
factors for infection in cats are highest for intact males that hunt
mice in rural woodland environments. 20

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
BoDV is highly neurotropic and probably gains access to the CNS
by transmucosal entry into nerve endings terminating in the
olfactory, oropharyngeal, or GI mucosae. 21 Similar to the spread
of rabies virus, BoDV spreads into and throughout the CNS by
intra-axonal transport and from there spreads centrifugally into
the peripheral nerves. 22 Unlike rabies virus, the replication rate of
BoDV is slow. The immune response to viral antigens is not
protective but incites an immunopathologic response. 23
Neutralizing antibodies appear in the serum and CSF. This
response fails to clear the infection; the inﬂammation subsides,

vetexamprep.ir

and BoDV persists at low levels in the CNS of the host. In the
CNS, BoDV infects neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and
ependymal cells. Experimental infection of feline astrocytes has
been shown to impair their glutamate uptake function, a
proposed mechanism for additional neuronal injury. 24
Interactions between BoDV and host proteins likely contribute to
the development of clinical signs. 21 , 25 , 26
In experimentally infected rats, acute-phase immunity is
cellular, with T cells as the predominant cell inﬁltrate. With
chronic infection, plasma cell inﬁltrates and antibody titers
increase and may magnify the inﬂammatory reaction. 27 These
ﬁndings are similar to those found with naturally infected cats
with staggering disease, in which T cells predominate in the CNS
and peripheral circulation, 28 with an intense IFN-γ gene
expression in the CNS. 29 Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells are thought to
induce this immune response against the virus. Antibody titers
increase with persistent infection of the CNS.
Experimentally and naturally infected cats develop humoral
immune responses to the BoDV proteins p24 and p40. 30 Serum
antibodies to another BoDV protein, p10, have also been found in
cats with ataxia. 31 In addition to the systemic humoral response,
BoDV-speciﬁc antibodies are produced intracerebrally in
naturally and experimentally infected cats. 30 Intracerebral
inoculation of BoDV produces high antibody titers against the
immunodominant proteins in CSF; however, natural infections
induce a weak humoral immune response in cats, primarily
directed against BoDV p24. 30

Clinical signs
Aﬀected cats are typically presented with a history of gait
disturbances mixed with behavioral changes. 18 , 32 The gait is
most often described as unsteady, predominantly in the pelvic
limbs, with stiﬀ and slow movements, as well as falling. At the
same time, aﬀected cats often become more social and
aﬀectionate, vocalize more frequently, with absent-minded
behavior. Besides these overt neurological signs, > 40% of the cats
are inappetent and approximately every fourth case exhibits

vetexamprep.ir

constipation. 18 , 32 Otherwise, aﬀected cats are apparently
healthy.

Physical Examination Findings
On physical examination, almost half of aﬀected cats are febrile
(≥39.3°C). 18 , 32 About as many have an inability to retract the
claws, predominantly of the pelvic limbs, and show signs of
lumbosacral pain on palpation. 18 , 32 On neurologic examination,
aﬀected cats display varying degrees of proprioceptive ataxia with
a stiﬀ, stilted gait, sometimes with an abnormally stiﬀ tail. As a
rule, postural reactions and menace responses are absent or
decreased. A majority of the aﬀected cats is mildly obtunded and
a similar proportion of cats exhibit increased vocalization
throughout the whole examination. 18 , 32 In one study, 86% of
aﬀected cats behaved abnormally during a nociception test; their
pupils dilated and their muscles ﬂexed in response to a perceived
painful stimulus, but they showed a reduced inclination to
physically retreat from the painful stimulus. 18 Spinal reﬂexes are
normal to exaggerated. Neurological deﬁcits are bilateral and
mainly symmetrical. Some clinical signs previously associated
with other feline neurologic diseases, such as epileptic seizures,
compulsive walking, lateralized vestibular syndrome, or facial
paresis, are seldom included in the plethora of neurologic signs in
cats with staggering disease. 18

Diagnosis
Laboratory abnormalities
Complete Blood Count and Serum Chemistry Profiles
Leukopenia, or a WBC count in the low-normal range, has been
the only hematologic abnormality present in aﬀected cats.
Approximately 50% of the aﬀected cats have had WBC counts
below the reference range. Both neutrophil and lymphocyte
counts have been at the lower end of the reference range. A few
aﬀected cats have had a slight increase in the activity of serum
ALT. 18 , 32
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis

vetexamprep.ir

On CSF analysis, a mononuclear pleocytosis is found in about one
third of cats with staggering disease. The CSF protein content is
increased (> 0.36 g/L) in approximately 50% of aﬀected cats. 18 , 32
In a few cases, there has been evidence of previous intrathecal
hemorrhage in the form of xanthochromia.

Microbiologic Tests
Because BoDV causes a persistent infection of the CNS,
associating infection with clinical disease can be challenging.
Therefore, positive test results using serologic and molecular
methods support staggering disease as a tentative diagnosis when
other explanations for clinical signs have been ruled out.
Antibodies are most often detected using indirect IFA testing. 17
This method is considered to be speciﬁc, but insensitive. In one
study, antibodies were found in 81% of cats with staggering
disease compared with 16% in a control group. 18 Nested RT-PCR
has been frequently used in research se ings to detect BoDV RNA
in peripheral blood monocytes or brain tissue. 33 , 34 This method
is highly sensitive, but because of its inherent high risk of
laboratory contamination, the results have been questioned. 35 To
overcome this drawback, real-time RT-PCR assays have been
developed and used to detect BoDV RNA in brain tissue, though
its use as an antemortem clinical diagnostic tool has not yet been
demonstrated. 36 , 37 Virus RNA has been detected mainly in
blood in a few clinical cases in cats. 18
Detection in the CNS of BoDV antigen by IHC, of BoDV RNA
by in situ hybridization, or both in combination with
neurohistopathologic alterations is considered the most reliable
method of conﬁrming active CNS disease. BoDV can be isolated
from CNS tissue by inoculation of cell cultures or rats. 38
Although lesions of feline BD resemble those of feline
poliomyelitis, no evidence suggests that these disorders are
related. The histologic and clinical features of BD should be
contrasted with feline poliomyelitis, which predominantly aﬀects
the spinal cord, causing progressive lower motor neuron
dysfunction with milder brainstem involvement (see Chapter
129).

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic Findings
The inﬂammatory reaction in the CNS is characterized by a
lymphohistiocytic or lymphoplasmacytic meningoencephalitis in
the gray ma er of the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex,
hippocampus, basal ganglia, and brainstem. 18 , 32 The spinal cord
is aﬀected to a lesser degree. Perivascular mononuclear cell
inﬁltrates mainly consist of lymphocytes. The surrounding brain
parenchyma is also aﬀected, sometimes with neuronophagia and
neuronal degeneration (Fig. 42.1). Inﬂammation of intraabdominal ganglions may also be observed. BoDV antigen and
nucleic acid persist in brain tissue of cats, particularly within
astrocytes, causing chronic inﬂammatory lesions (Fig. 42.2). In one
cat, large amounts of virus but no inﬂammation were found
within neurons, presumably from viral persistence by infection at
an early age. 39

vetexamprep.ir

BD in dogs has been characterized by a rapid onset of
progressive intracranial CNS deﬁcits that are similar to those in
canine distemper. 4 , 5 Histopathologic lesions, which
predominated in the forebrain and midbrain, have been
characterized by a nonsuppurative meningoencephalitis with
perivascular cuﬃng and diﬀuse mononuclear cell inﬁltrates of
adjacent neuropil. Inﬂammatory cells in the cuﬀs largely comprise
CD3+ T cells. Viral antigen and RNA can be detected in neurons
using IHC and in situ hybridization.

Treatment And Prognosis
In the initial stage of staggering disease, supportive care such as
IV ﬂuids should be considered. In addition, antibacterial drugs,
glucocorticoids, and/or the antiviral drug amantadine
hydrochloride have been used in many cats. In a retrospective
study of 54 aﬀected cats, broad-spectrum antimicrobial drugs and
glucocorticoids, as well as combinations of such medications, had
a beneﬁcial eﬀect on survival time. Treatment with amantadine
hydrochloride did not signiﬁcantly increase survival time. 40
Treatment with glucocorticoids, especially at an early stage of
disease, also has shown promise. 41 However, in the absence of
controlled treatment trials, the eﬀect of any therapy is anecdotal.
Clinical signs progress within 1 to 4 weeks until the clinical
condition either deteriorates, resulting in euthanasia, 18 or
stabilizes and might improve slightly with time, still leaving most
cats permanently aﬄicted with motor dysfunction, personality
changes, or both (Fig. 42.3). In surviving cats, neurologic signs
often eventually relapse. However, survival times for up to 7 years
have been described. 40

Immunity And Vaccination
There is currently no available vaccine for BoDV infection.

Prevention
Because the mechanism of BoDV transmission is currently not
completely understood, it is diﬃcult to provide adequate advice
on preventive measures. BoDV is inactivated by common
decontamination methods, such as heat, detergents, and chlorine.

Public Health Aspects
BoDV has been studied as a cause of human neuropsychiatric
illnesses. 42 , 43 Antibodies to the virus have been detected in sera
of patients with psychiatric disorders in various countries. The

vetexamprep.ir

prevalence of BoDV-speciﬁc antibodies is fourfold higher in
patients with HIV infection than in control patients. 44
As in animals, controversy surrounds the signiﬁcance of BoDV
infection in humans. 45–47 The most deﬁnitive evidence of a link
between infection and disease has been the detection of BDVspeciﬁc antigen and RNA in the brains of humans with
hippocampal sclerosis and schizophrenia. 48–50 Also, a number of
human fatal cases of encephalitis were described in association to
BoDV-1 infection. 51 Thus, BoDV shall be considered to be a
potential lethal zoonotic virus for both immunocompromised as
well as fully healthy individuals. However, it is unclear how these
patients were infected in the ﬁrst place.
A variant bornavirus was associated with fatal encephalitis in
breeders of variegated squirrels. In one squirrel, the same virus as
detected in aﬀected humans was found, suggesting direct
transmission from apparently healthy squirrels to humans. 11

Case Example
Signalment

“Teddy,” a 4-year-old male, neutered, European shorthair cat
from Alunda in the Uppsala area, Sweden.

History

Teddy was described to be ataxic 4 weeks before initial
examination. Treatment with oral prednisolone and amoxicillin
was initiated for a tentative diagnosis of staggering disease.

vetexamprep.ir

Teddy improved somewhat initially, but ataxia then worsened.
Over the 2 weeks leading up to initial examination, pelvic limb
ataxia, “knuckling” of the thoracic limbs, and changes in
behavior (abnormal degree of aﬀection and increased
vocalization) were noted. Although his appetite was unaﬀected,
a 1-kg weight loss over the last month had occurred. He was up
to date on vaccinations. Teddy was an outdoor cat from rural
surroundings. There were three other cats in the household,
and all were healthy.

Current Medications

Prednisolone 2.5 mg q24h PO.

Physical Examination

Body temperature = 38.5°C; body weight = 3.5 kg; BCS = 3/9; HR
= 130 beats/minute; mucous membranes moist and pink. No
signiﬁcant abnormalities were noted during examination of
lymph nodes, integument, eyes, ears, nose and throat,
cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, or genitourinary organs.

Neurologic Examination

Mental status: Slightly obtunded. Behavior: Aﬀectionate and
meowing. Posture: Stiﬀ limbs. Extension of the claws were
noted in both thoracic and pelvic limbs. Gait: Teddy was
ambulatory, with paraparesis and a severe ataxia, more
pronounced in the pelvic limbs. The gait was stiﬀ and stilted.
Cranial nerves: Menace reactions were reduced, otherwise no

In this case, a diagnosis of staggering disease was strongly

43: Emerging and
Miscellaneous Viral Infections
Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• The infectious diseases described in this chapter are either:
(1) diseases of humans or other animals generally transmitted
through contact with the secretions or excretions of rodents
(hantaviruses, arenaviruses, and encephalomyocarditis virus),
swine (hepatitis E virus), monkeys (Ebola virus), or bats
(systemic coronaviruses); (2) common diseases of humans
where the role of companion animals in transmission has
been investigated (enteroviruses, SARS-CoV-2); (3) diseases
of significant importance to the agricultural industry (foot-andmouth disease virus, vesicular exanthema,
encephalomyocarditis virus); or (4) significant diseases of
potential prey of dogs and cats (rabbit hemorrhagic disease
virus).
• Clinical illness has not always been confirmed in dogs and
cats with these infections, but evidence of seroconversion to
these viruses exists.
• In some cases, concern has been raised in the possible role
of dogs and cats in zoonotic transmission; this has been
heightened by the COVID-19 pandemic.
• In general, research suggests that dogs and cats do not play a
major role in transmission of these viruses, but the potential
exists should new viral variants emerge.

Hantavirus Infection

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic Agents and Epidemiology
Hantaviruses are enveloped RNA viruses that belong to the
family Bunyaviridae, which contains four other genera (Nairovirus,
Orthobunyavirus, Phlebovirus, and Tospovirus), and are named after
the Hantan River area in South Korea where the disease was ﬁrst
observed. Hantaviruses are the only members of the Bunyaviridae
that are not transmi ed by arthropod vectors (for comparison, see
Bunyaviridae in Chapter 41, Arthropod-Borne Viral Infections).
Each hantavirus strain of is uniquely adapted to a subclinically
infected rodent, shrew, or bat reservoir, and humans usually
become infected through contact with rodent feces, urine, or
saliva. Direct physical contact with the rodents is not required, so
aerosolized virus is the likely means of spread of infection
between rodents and humans. Rodent bites have also been
documented as a means of transmission. 1 Although humans are
generally considered dead-end hosts, some strains (Andes virus in
South America) can be directly transmi ed between humans.
Species diﬀerences exist among rodents as to the length of
salivary excretion, with times ranging up to 1 year. Infected
rodents are thought to harbor the virus in their lungs and kidneys
for life.
Over 50 diﬀerent hantavirus strains have been identiﬁed
worldwide. Those that are pathogenic for humans cause two
clinically distinct syndromes. Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with
renal syndrome (HFRS ) is the vastly more common syndrome, and
is caused by Hantan River, Seoul, Dobrava-Belgrade, and
Saaremaa viruses in Europe, Asia, and Africa. Hantavirus
pulmonary syndrome (HPS; also known as hantavirus
cardiopulmonary syndrome), a pulmonary disease with 40%–50%
mortality, occurs in North, Central, and South America. It is
primarily caused by Sin Nombre virus in North America, which is
carried by deer mice. In the United States, most human infections
have occurred in the Four Corners states (Arizona, Colorado, New
Mexico, and Utah), although only a few dozen cases are reported
in North America annually (Fig. 43.1). 2 Monongahela, New York,
Bayou, and Black Creek Canal viruses also cause HPS in North
America and are found in eastern Canada and the eastern and
southeastern regions of the United States. In South and Central
America, a number of other viruses can cause HPS, including

vetexamprep.ir

Andes virus in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile; Laguna Negra virus
in Bolivia and Paraguay; and Choclo virus in Panama. 3
The disease is more prevalent during seasons and years when
population densities of rodents are highest. The greatest incidence
of infection in humans occurs when their work or recreational
activities expose them to rodents. Infections occur on farms, in
suburbs, and in residential areas. In laboratory rats in the United
States, infection by the Seoul virus has been controlled by
serologic testing and by producing rodents from cesarean-derived
stock maintained under strict barrier conditions.
Although human infections receive the most a ention, dogs and
cats have the potential to become infected following contact with
rodents and rodent excreta. The possibility of hantavirus infection
in cats was initially raised in a study from China that indicated
that cat ownership was a risk factor for hantavirus infection in
humans. 4 Several studies conducted worldwide have identiﬁed
hantavirus antibodies in domestic cats, with seroprevalences of
5% in Austria, 5 9.6% in Great Britain, 6 16.9% in Belgium, 7 2.9% in
rural cats from the southwestern Canadian prairie, 8 and 2.8% in
New Mexico and northeastern Arizona. 9 Cats that are allowed to
roam or hunt outdoors have the highest seroprevalence, and in
the Belgian study, cats and dogs living in forested areas had
higher seroprevalence. 7 Hantavirus antigen was detected in the
lungs of 2 of 100 cats that had a history of rodent hunting at
necropsy. 10 The seroprevalence in dogs has been low, 4.9% in
Belgium, 7 0% in the Canadian prairie, 8 and 3.5% in New Mexico
and Arizona. 9 At this time, it seems that neither coyotes nor dogs
or cats appear to play a major role in the maintenance and
transmission of Sin Nombre virus.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
In cats and dogs, clinical hantavirus infection has never been
documented, and so most or all infections are probably
subclinical. Both hantaviral syndromes result from vascular
leakage, although the pathogenesis of this remains unclear. 1 In
humans, hantavirus infection resembles leptospirosis, which is an
important diﬀerential diagnosis. 11 The clinical manifestations

vetexamprep.ir

depend on viral strain, but in general, HFRS is associated with
fever, headache, abdominal pain, signs of renal dysfunction,
thrombocytopenia, hemorrhagic diathesis, and sometimes
neurologic signs. HPS is characterized by fever, myalgia,
vomiting, abdominal pain, respiratory signs resulting from acute
pulmonary edema, and circulatory collapse. 12 Some humans also
develop renal insuﬃciency, although this is less common when
compared with HFRS. Radiographs reveal acute bilateral
pulmonary interstitial inﬁltrates. Most deaths associated with
HPS are related to cardiogenic shock rather than pulmonary
failure; therefore, the term “hantavirus cardiopulmonary
syndrome” is more appropriate than “hantaviral pulmonary
syndrome.” 3

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of hantavirus infection in humans is made using
serologic and molecular methods. Early in the course of illness,
virus can be detected using RT-PCR in whole blood. 12 A serologic
diagnosis can be made using a variety of serologic methods (most
commonly ELISA) through detection of serum IgM, a fourfold
increase in serum IgG, or detection of IgG or IgM against the N
protein.

Treatment
In human patients, treatment includes cautious IV crystalloid
ﬂuid administration, colloids, electrolyte replacement, oxygen
supplementation, blood pressure support, and dialysis. 12
Intravenous ribavirin has also been eﬀective in the treatment of
HFRS when used early in the course of illness. Excessive ﬂuid
administration must be avoided because it may increase the
severity of pulmonary edema.

Public Health Aspects
Avoidance of contact with rodents and their excreta is the most
eﬀective way to reduce the prevalence of disease. Masks, and in
some cases respirators, should always be worn by people cleaning
rodent-infested buildings. Areas to be cleaned should be
thoroughly soaked with disinfectants such as dilute sodium
hypochlorite before they are mopped. Vacuuming and sweeping
should be avoided to minimize aerosolization.

Arenavirus Infection
The arenaviruses are enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses that
generally infect rodents (genus Mammarenavirus, family
Arenaviridae). At least eight diﬀerent arenaviruses cause disease in
humans, which range in severity. Each arenavirus species is
usually associated with a particular rodent reservoir host. One of
the most signiﬁcant arenaviruses is lymphocytic choriomeningitis
virus (LCV), an arenavirus of house mice (Mus musculus) that is
found worldwide. Hamsters are also competent reservoirs. LCV is
transmi ed in utero or at birth and persists for the life of the

vetexamprep.ir

rodent in high concentrations in tissues. Humans can become
infected as a result of contact of mucous membranes or abraded
skin with aerosols from infected rodents. Immunocompromised
people are most susceptible; postnatal infections cause acute
aseptic meningoencephalitis, whereas congenital infections
produce CNS and ocular malformations. 13 Outbreaks in humans
resulted from contact with pet or laboratory hamsters, including
accidental transmission of the infection in organ recipients. 14–16
Other arenaviruses have more restricted geographic distributions
(e.g., Lassa virus in West Africa and Whitewater Arroyo virus in
the southwestern United States) and cause febrile or febrile
hemorrhagic diseases in humans.
Outbreaks of rodent lymphocytic choriomeningitis infections
have raised concern that domestic dogs or cats might serve as
reservoirs or vectors of the virus for human exposure. Although
puppies did not develop clinical illness after parenteral or cerebral
inoculation, 17 they developed neutralizing antibody titers to the
virus, and infection was transmi ed from infected to noninfected
puppies. Except for intranuclear inclusions in the adrenal cortex,
pathologic changes were not observed. It is unlikely that dogs or
cats become infected or spread the virus by natural exposure,
because most human infections result from direct contact with
rodents.

Encephalomyocarditis Virus Infection
Encephalomyocarditis virus (also known as Cardiovirus A) is a
small, nonenveloped RNA virus that belongs to the genus
Cardiovirus in the family Picornaviridae. It infects a variety of
domestic and wild animals worldwide, with rodents as
subclinically infected reservoir hosts. Humans may also be
infected. Most human infections are thought to be subclinical. 18
Rodents shed virus for up to 29 days after infection. Transmission
is by the fecal-oral route, and infections typically occur through
ingestion of contaminated food, water, or carcasses. Pigs are most
susceptible and can develop myocarditis or transplacental
infection with fetal death at various time periods of gestation.
Disease in humans is rarely described, and can range from a mild
febrile illness to meningoencephalitis. 18

vetexamprep.ir

The extent to which encephalomyocarditis virus can cause
disease in dogs and cats is unclear. In Austria, 0.5% of 200 cats
19
were
seropositive
to
encephalomyocarditis
virus.
Encephalomyocarditis virus antigen was found in the brains of
four
dogs
and

with

20
meningoencephalitis. In China, an encephalomyocarditis virus
(EMCV-C15) was detected in 4 of 69 serum specimens from dogs
with fever and variable GI and respiratory signs using real-time
PCR. 21 These four dogs were co-infected with canine parvovirus.
The virus was subsequently propagated in cell culture, and
experimental infection of 4-week-old puppies with the isolate was
followed by development of pulmonary edema, myocarditis,
pelvic limb paralysis and encephalitis. The virus was then
detected in a variety of tissues, but especially the heart and brain,
using RT-PCR. However, whether the experimentally infected
dogs were tested for CPV infection was not reported.

Enterovirus Infections
Enteroviruses are tiny, nonenveloped, single-stranded RNA
viruses that belong to the genus Enterovirus (family Picornaviridae).
Viruses in this genus commonly infect humans worldwide and
were previously separated into polioviruses, coxsackieviruses
(types A and B), echoviruses, and as yet unclassiﬁed enteric
viruses. However, because of recognized overlap in these viral
groups, newer members of the genus are called enteroviruses
(EVs), which are designated by a sequential numbering system
(e.g., EV70). The genus also includes the human rhinoviruses
(which cause the common cold) and poliovirus. EVs are
environmentally resistant and infect humans primarily via the
fecal-oral route, but are also shed in respiratory secretions and can
contaminate fomites. After replication in submucosal lymphoid
tissues, the viruses can spread systemically to various other
tissues.
Dogs have been tested to determine whether they harbor a
variety of human EVs because of the possible zoonotic potential
(Table 43.1). 22–27 Similar information is not available for cats. Dogs
are exposed to and can shed human EVs. Although dogs appear
to become infected with these viruses, clinical signs have not been
apparent. The viruses can be found in canine feces for a period of

vetexamprep.ir

months, but whether the extended shedding results from
persistence or reinfection is uncertain. EVs recovered from
nasopharyngeal or fecal cultures of dogs have been grown in
tissue culture and cause cytopathogenic eﬀects, primarily in
monkey kidney but not canine cell lines, supporting the fact that
they are human viruses. Neutralization tests have shown them to
be closely related to human isolates. 28 , 29 In some instances, EVs
in canine feces were believed to be simply passing through the GI
tract of dogs, rather than causing infection. Alternatively, they
may be canine EVs antigenically related to human EVs, such as the
recently discovered canine picornavirus. 30 Newer techniques to
determine viral homogeneity by genetic analysis should shed
light on this in the future.
TABLE 43.1

Oral inoculation of dogs with echovirus 6 or coxsackievirus B1
produced minimal signs of enteric disease. Although virus could
be isolated from the feces, seroconversion did not occur. 31 , 32
Although dogs shed these viruses in low amounts, viral spread to
susceptible dogs has resulted in infection. 32 Whether infected
dogs can be a source of human infection is uncertain. In one
study, dog and cat ownership had a protective eﬀect on EV
infection in infants. 33

Ebola Virus Infection
Ebola virus is a ﬁlamentous, enveloped, single-stranded RNA
virus that belongs to the genus Ebolavirus and family Filoviridae
(Fig. 43.2). The virus causes vascular injury, leading to a fulminant
hemorrhagic fever in human and nonhuman primates with a 40%

vetexamprep.ir

to 80% mortality rate. Clinical signs in humans include fever,
fatigue, abdominal pain, severe headache, vomiting, diarrhea,
myalgia, arthralgia, weakness, and hemorrhages. 34 Death
generally results from hypovolemic shock and multiorgan
dysfunction. The ﬁrst recorded description of the disease was in
1976 in Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo), and the
virus is named after the Ebola River where the ﬁrst outbreak
occurred. Various species of fruit bats act as reservoir hosts. 35
Humans become infected by contact with body ﬂuids of other
infected humans, or contact with other infected animals,
especially bats. Infections have occurred as a result of handling
meat of bats, nonhuman primates, or duikers (a species of
antelope) (Fig. 43.3). 35 Healthcare workers have also been
infected. Transmission is more likely later in the course of
infection than in the ﬁrst few days of clinical signs, and the
incubation period is 2 to 21 days (average 8 to 10 days). Diagnosis
of infection in humans is based on cell culture, serologic detection
of antibodies or antigen, and/or detection of viral RNA with realtime RT-PCR assays. 36 Treatment is with aggressive supportive
care, as no antiviral drugs have yet proven to be eﬀective. 34 The
virus can persist weeks to months in some recovered humans, and
chronic infection of semen has led to sexual transmission. The
possibility of development of an eﬀective vaccine holds promise.

The most signiﬁcant outbreak began in Guinea in December
2013 and spread rapidly throughout West Africa. The outbreak
continued to early 2016, aﬀecting approximately 30,000 people
and resulting in over 11,000 deaths. 34 , 38 During the outbreak, the
virus underwent mutation that increased its tropism for human
cells, and decreased its tropism for bat cells, which was thought to
contribute to the size of the outbreak. 39 In August 2014, the WHO
declared the outbreak was an international public health
emergency. Human-to-human transmission occurred outside
Africa in Madrid, Spain, and Dallas, Texas. In Spain, a nurse was
infected when she cared for a patient with Ebola virus infection
that was transferred from West Africa to Spain. She subsequently
recovered. In Texas, a man contracted the disease after ﬂying from
Liberia to Dallas. Subsequently, two nurses that cared for him
became infected. The man died, but the nurses recovered with
supportive care.
Antibodies to Ebola virus have been detected in the serum of
dogs, 38 , 40 raising concerns about the role of feral and domestic
dogs in the transmission of Ebola virus. During the 2001-2002
outbreak of Ebola virus in Gabon, Africa, dogs were observed
feeding on animal carcasses. The seroprevalence in dogs in the
virus-epidemic area (25.2%) was higher than the seroprevalence in
nonepidemic areas of Gabon (15.2%) or France (2%). 40 In another
study that aimed to investigate the role of dogs as sentinels for
human exposure to ﬁloviruses, 47 (73%) of 64 dog serum
specimens had evidence of exposure to ﬁloviruses, and up to
100% of dog serum specimens from some regions where Ebola
had occurred in humans had evidence of possible exposure to
Ebola virus. 38 Neither Ebola virus antigens nor nucleotide

vetexamprep.ir

sequences or cultivated virus were detected in any seropositive or
seronegative dog blood specimens. Clinical signs have not been
observed in exposed dogs, and whether they can serve as a source
of infection for people remains uncertain. In 2014, the Spanish
government ordered the pet dog of the nurse in Spain,
“Excalibur,” to be euthanized, and “Bentley,” a Cavalier King
Charles spaniel owned by one of the nurses in Dallas was
quarantined under BSL-4 precautions for 3 weeks. Such
precautions require considerable resources, including people
trained in how to use and remove appropriate personal protective
equipment (PPE). Suitable quarantine facilities were not available
in Spain. 41 Although Excalibur was not tested for Ebola virus
infection, no evidence of Ebola virus infection was detected in
Bentley despite repeated testing over the course of the quarantine
period. As a result of concerns about the role of companion
animals in transmission of Ebola virus infection, the AVMA and
CDC issued guidance statements for public health oﬃcials on pets
of Ebola virus disease contacts and on quarantine of dogs and cats
after exposure to a human with conﬁrmed Ebola virus disease. 42
Quarantine is required for a minimum of 3 weeks after the pet
was last exposed to a person with Ebola. In order to avoid
quarantine, it is recommended that animals in contact with a
person being monitored for development of symptoms be moved
to another household, so that in the event symptoms do occur,
those animals are not exposed.

Hepatitis E Virus Infection
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) generally causes an acute self-limiting
hepatitis in humans. Although previously considered a disease
primarily occurring in developing tropical and subtropical
countries, it has recently emerged as the most common cause of
acute hepatitis in the United Kingdom. 43 Chronic infections that
can culminate in cirrhosis can occur in immunosuppressed
individuals such as transplant recipients. 44 The virus is
icosahedral and nonenveloped, with a single-stranded positivesense RNA genome, and belongs to the family Hepeviridae, genus
Orthohepevirus. Strains that infect humans are classiﬁed into four
genotypes; genotypes 1 and 2 exclusively infect humans, but
genotypes 3 and 4 infect humans and other animal species, with

vetexamprep.ir

pigs considered the predominant reservoir (Table 43.2). 44–46
Additional strains of HEV have been detected in other animal
species, including chickens, rats, ferrets, and moose, but these are
genetically distinct from those that infect humans. 45 All
genotypes are shed in feces with fecal-oral contact as the means of
transmission. Genotype 1 infection is the most common form of
acute hepatitis in people in Asia, with most infections resulting
from ingestion of water that has been contaminated with feces.
Outbreaks of genotype 1 infection occur in developing countries
in southeast and central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa,
especially after heavy rainfall and monsoons. Sporadic outbreaks
caused by genotype 2 occur in Mexico and West Africa. Genotype
3 causes disease in developed countries and genotype 4 in China,
Taiwan, and Japan. Foodborne transmission through consumption
of undercooked pork, deer, and boar meat predominates for
genotypes 3 and 4, and outbreaks are uncommon. Genotype 3
strains have also been detected in wild and farmed rabbits. 45
Contamination of water with pig feces can result in contamination
of other foodstuﬀs, including shellﬁsh and fruit.
Antibodies to HEV have been detected in cats and dogs
worldwide, and an epidemiologic connection between pet
ownership and human HEV infection has been implied because of
the number of infected humans that have reported dog or cat
contact. 47–49 Seroprevalences have been reported of
approximately 20% in dogs and 6% in cats from China, 50 , 51 0%
in dogs and 8% in cats from Korea, 52 28% of 287 dogs from South
Korea, 38 0.9% of 212 dogs in the United States, 53 0.8% in dogs
from the United Kingdom, 54 less than 1% in dogs and 2% in cats
from Japan, 55 , 56 7% in dogs from Brazil, 57 and 23% of 44 dogs
from India. 58 In China, dogs and cats were more likely to be
seropositive if they shared kitchen scraps with humans, as
opposed to being fed a commercial pet food. 51 However, a empts
to detect HEV RNA in serum, liver, and feces from dogs and cats
have consistently yielded negative results. 54 , 55 , 59 , 60 This
included one a empt that used broadly reactive primers expected
to detect strains divergent from those that infect humans. 54
Furthermore, pet veterinarians a ending a conference in Portugal
were not found to have an increased risk of seropositivity when
compared with the general population, 61 whereas in the United

vetexamprep.ir

States, swine veterinarians were much more likely to be
seropositive than those who did not have contact with swine. 62
Currently, the evidence suggests that dogs and cats do not play an
important role in transmission of HEVs to humans. Prevention of
HEV infection involves general sanitation.
