Foot-And-Mouth Disease
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious febrile
vesicular disease of wild and domestic cloven-hoofed animals. It
is caused by various strains of FMD virus, a nonenveloped RNA
virus (genus Aphthovirus, family Picornaviridae). It occurs
worldwide and has signiﬁcant economic impact on the
agricultural industry. Seven serotypes are recognized, named
following their recognition in France, Germany, South Africa, and

vetexamprep.ir

Pakistan (O, A, C, SAT1, SAT2, SAT3, Asia-1). Eradication has
been variably successful in Australia, New Zealand, Japan,
Europe, and North America, with the last outbreak in the United
States occurring in 1929. 63 Many countries in South America are
considered disease-free (Fig. 43.4). 64 The disease continues to be a
problem in the Middle East, Africa, and parts of Asia, and
reappearance of the disease in places it has been eradicated,
usually as a result of accidental importation of contaminated meat
(or pigs fed contaminated meat products) from countries where
FMD persists, results in major economic losses. For example, the
2001 outbreak in the United Kingdom was estimated to cost US
$12.3 to 13.8 billion. 63 Culling, restriction of movement,
disinfection, monitoring, and vaccination are used to control the
disease. Vaccines do not cross-protect among diﬀerent strains, so
they must be designed to target a particular outbreak strain.
Dogs and cats are resistant to infection and do not play a major
role in spreading or harboring the disease under conditions of
natural exposure. Dogs and cats can be experimentally infected, 65
but naturally occurring disease has not been recognized.
Carnivores have the potential to become incidentally infected
during outbreaks in herbivores by contacting these animals or
their oﬀal, but are only considered to play a role in transmission
by acting as fomites. Dogs can also contribute to the spread of
FMD by carrying remains of animals from one location to another.
Guidelines have been established for dog owners in areas
known to have infected animals. Dogs in areas with infected
animals must be leashed or enclosed to a conﬁned space at all
times. Dogs must not be walked across farmland and contact with
livestock and wild animals should be prevented. Certain sporting
activities involving dogs should not be allowed in quarantined
areas. In the United Kingdom, concerns about the spread of FMD
during the 2001 outbreak resulted in postponement of the Crufts
Dog Show. Similarly, cats should be kept indoors as much as
possible. Disinfectants suitable for inactivating the virus are 4%
sodium carbonate, 0.5% citric acid, 4%–5% acetic acid, 1%
potassium peroxymonosulfate, 3% sodium hypochlorite (2:3 ratio
of gallons of household bleach to 3 gallons of water), or 2%
sodium hydroxide. 66 Phenolic disinfectants, quaternary
ammonium compounds, and biguanides are not eﬀective.

vetexamprep.ir

Halogens such as sodium hypochlorite or iodine are less eﬀective
because of inactivation by organic ma er.

Vesicular Exanthema and Other Caliciviruses
Vesicular exanthema of swine is caused by a calicivirus that causes
lesions on the mouth, lips, snout, and feet of pigs. It has only been
reported in the United States, and not since 1959, but is of historic
importance because it can be confused with FMD. Dogs have
developed clinical signs of illness characterized by vesicular
eruptions when outbreaks of vesicular exanthema virus infection
have occurred in swine. 67 Virus was not deﬁnitely isolated in
these cases. Experimentally infected dogs developed fever within
24 hours after inoculation and vesicular eruptions on their
tongues and in their oral cavities. 67 These lesions healed within a
few days. Virus was isolated from the spleen of a dog that became
febrile after inoculation.
In 2018, several additional caliciviruses were isolated from
military working dogs in the United States. 68 These were closely
related to canine calicivirus. Further work will be required to
determine their pathogenicity. A calicivirus (canine vesivirus) was
isolated from dogs that died in 2015 during a focal outbreak of
hemorrhagic gastroenteritis in a pet housing facility in Virginia,
USA. Virus nucleic acid was found in association with areas of
necrosis and hemorrhage in the intestinal tract, but also in the
brain of a dog that had nonsuppurative meningoencephalitis. 69

Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease
Rabbit hemorrhagic disease (RHD), also known as rabbit calicivirus
disease, is an acute, highly contagious, and often fatal disease of
rabbits caused by rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus (RHDV, genus
Lagovirus, family Caliciviridae). Transmission of the virus is by
direct contact with secretions from infected rabbits or with
infected fomites. The disease was ﬁrst identiﬁed in China in 1984,
spread rapidly to Europe, where it killed millions of domesticated
rabbits in less than a year, and has now also been reported in
other parts of Asia, Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and the
Americas. In 2010, a new variant of the virus, RHDV2, emerged in
France. The virus was introduced into Australia and held under

vetexamprep.ir

quarantine to investigate its utility to control rabbit
overpopulation, but escaped quarantine in 1995 and killed over 10
million rabbits within a 2-month period. Subsequently, it was
deliberately and illegally introduced into New Zealand. In 2019
and 2020, it appeared in wild and domestic lagamorphs in the
northwestern and southwestern United States, respectively. 70 , 71
By March of 2022, the virus had been identiﬁed in lagomorphs
from 19 diﬀerent US states. 72 Aﬀected rabbits develop a febrile
hemorrhagic disease, sometimes accompanied by icterus,
neurologic signs, and cutaneous ulceration.
Only rabbits are susceptible to disease caused by RHDV. Feral
cats in New Zealand have antibodies to RHDV, and the virus was
detected using nested RT-PCR in the liver of one seropositive cat.
73 Cats fed rabbit livers infected with RHDV developed serologic
titers to the virus, and RHDV RNA was detected in the tonsils,
mesenteric lymph nodes, spleen, and liver. Even though large
amounts of virus were found, clinical disease was not observed.
Active replication of RHDV was not demonstrated.

Severe Acute Respiratory Coronavirus
Infections
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronaviruses are
betacoronaviruses most closely related to betacoronaviruses
isolated from bats. Other betacoronaviruses include OC43 and
HKU1, the cause of common colds in humans; Middle Eastern
Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) virus; canine respiratory
coronavirus (CRCoV); and bovine coronavirus (BoCV) (Table
43.3). While also a betacoronavirus, CRCoV is more closely related
to BoCV and OC43 than SARS-CoVs (Fig. 43.5). 74 The original
SARS-CoV, which caused disease in humans from 2002 to 2004,
was thought to be transmi ed to farmed civets after
recombination in bats. 75 When Himalayan palm civets were
transported to Guangdong market in China, the virus spread
among market civets; spillover to humans likely occurred in 2002,
with spread of the virus that extended over the course of 2003.
Civet cats are not true cats but small mammals that resemble
weasels; they are more closely related to mongoose. The virus was
also found in raccoon dogs at street markets. However, civets

vetexamprep.ir

seemed like a more likely conduit than raccoon dogs because the
virus was able to persist in infected animals for up to 2 weeks, and
many infections were associated with restaurants where civet
meat was prepared and served. Extensive culling of palm civets
followed. SARS-CoV-1 causes respiratory illness in humans with
pneumonia and lymphopenia after an incubation period of 2 to 10
days, with a case fatality rate of 9.6%. 76 The SARS outbreak
ended by 2004, with no more cases resulting from person-toperson transmission since then. In total, there were about 8,000
cases in 30 countries, including North America, South America,
Europe, and Asia. 77 It was the search for other human
coronaviruses at this time that led to the discovery of the common
cold coronaviruses NL63 and HKU1. 78 It is generally believed
that civets and raccoon dogs do not represent ongoing reservoirs
of SARS-CoV-1. A small number of pet cats tested positive and
seroconverted in a large outbreak of SARS that occurred in an
apartment complex in Hong Kong. 79 In that outbreak, which
involved over 300 people, there was evidence that airborne
transmission of the virus was occurring as a result of hydraulic
action of sewerage drainage pipes, so the situation was unusual. 80
Experimental infection of six ferrets and six cats was also
accomplished. 79 None of the cats in that study had clinical signs,
whereas several ferrets developed lethargy and one died.
Infection was transmi ed to a limited number of in-contact
animals, and only ferrets developed clinical illness. However,
pulmonary pathology was detected in the cats that was similar to
that in humans.

MERS-CoV was ﬁrst isolated from the lungs of a 60-year-old
person who died from severe respiratory illness in Saudi Arabia
in 2012. 81 Clinical manifestations range from none to severe
pneumonia, acute renal failure, and septic shock. Since then, 2,984
conﬁrmed cases have been reported with 858 deaths in 27
countries. 82 Three-quarters of patients had co-morbidities. All
human cases have been associated with travel to the Arabian
Peninsula. Only two infected humans have been reported in the
United States. 83 Dromedary camels have been implicated as
amplifying hosts based on the detection of antibodies in these
camels as well as sequences resembling MERS-CoV in camels
from the Arabian Peninsula. In addition, most people with the
disease have a history of interactions with dromedary camels.
However, the precise role that dromedaries play in the
transmission of MERS remains unknown. 84 No sustained humanto-human transmission has been documented anywhere in the
world.

SARS-CoV-2 infection emerged in late 2019 in Wuhan, China, as
the cause of COVID-19, a highly contagious systemic viral disease
that at the time of writing has infected nearly 500 million people
worldwide and contributed to the death of over 6.1 million
people. 85 COVID-19 occurs after an incubation period of 2 to 14
days, and consists of fever, myalgia and fatigue, respiratory signs
(primarily cough and shortness of breath), GI signs, and anosmia
and ageusia (loss of taste). Less frequently, stroke-like neurologic
signs, cardiac arrhythmias due to myocarditis, and acute kidney
injury have been described. Severe outcomes and death are more
likely in older people and those with chronic conditions such as
diabetes mellitus, chronic lung disease, and cardiovascular
disease. Early in the pandemic, a case fatality rate of 10%–27%
was reported in people over 85 years of age, 3% to 11% in those

vetexamprep.ir

aged 65–84 years, 1% to 3% in those aged 55–64 years, <1% in
those aged 20–54 years, and 0% in those aged less than 19 years. 86
The precise origin of SARS-CoV-2 is not known (Fig. 43.6). The
overwhelming majority of CoVs have been identiﬁed only in bats,
and so bats are considered the major natural CoV reservoirs.
However, two of the human common cold CoVs likely originated
in rodents. Importantly, domestic animals are important
intermediate hosts for transmission of CoVs to humans, and
camelids, ca le, civet cats, dromedary camels, and pigs have all
been implicated in this role. 87 Pangolins have been most closely
studied as a possible amplifying host for SARS-CoV-2, because
they have been shown to harbor genetically very similar CoV
strains (albeit more diﬀerent than those found in bats),
coronavirus strains capable of infecting human cells, and are sold
in Chinese food markets. 88 Considered the world’s most
traﬃcked mammal, pangolins have been traﬃcked for their scales,
which are used in traditional Chinese medicine, and they are also
a luxury food item. It has been suggested that the African swine
fever outbreak in China may have contributed to emergence of
SARS-CoV-2 because shortage of pork products drove an
increased trade of farmed susceptible animals and wildlife as a
source of food. 89 Accidental or deliberate release of an engineered
virus from a laboratory (the “lab-leak theory”) has also been
suggested as a possible origin of the virus, but has been disputed
on the basis of epidemiological studies or studies of the
composition of the virus. 90 , 91
The host receptor for SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 is the
angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, whereas MERS
binds to the dipeptidyl peptidase 4 receptor. A receptor-binding
domain (RBD) on the viral spike (S) protein interacts with the
ACE2 receptor, which is followed by viral entry into host cells.
The S protein must be activated before the virus can enter cells.
This requires the synergistic action of host furin enzymes, which
cleave the S protein into S1 and S2 components, and a cell surface
serine protease enzyme known as serine 2 (TMPRSS2). 92
Although the amino acid sequence of the ACE2 receptor can
inﬂuence whether a host species can be infected, other factors,
such as the distribution and density of ACE2 receptor expression
in tissues, host and virus factors inﬂuencing spike protein

vetexamprep.ir

cleavage, the use of co-receptors (such as neuropilin 1), and the
host immune response to infection, also inﬂuence species
susceptibility and expression of clinical disease. 93
Experimental infection studies have shown that cats and ferrets
are capable of transmi ing SARS-CoV-2 infection to other cats
and ferrets, whereas dogs did not transmit infection to a small
number of in-contact dogs. 94–97 Hamsters, rabbits, deer, American
minks, raccoon dogs, deer mice, fruit bats, o ers, and nonhuman
primates are also susceptible to experimental infection. 98 At the
time of writing, more than 200 pet dogs and cats worldwide have
tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, with reports documented by the
OIE and the USDA. 99 , 100 Most dogs and cats have been
subclinically infected, or if signs are present, it has not been
possible to determine whether they are associated with infection
or due to an unrelated comorbidity. 100 , 101 , 102 , 103 A small
number of animals died shortly after they tested positive, but comorbidities explained the reason for death. However, one 4month-old ki en from the United Kingdom was euthanized and
viral pneumonia was conﬁrmed at necropsy, with FA showing
intralesional SARS-CoV-2 antigen. 104 Of 10 dogs and cats that
tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and then died or were euthanized
in the United States, it was concluded that infection was an
incidental ﬁnding in 8 animals, but was the cause of disease in one
dog and one cat. 105 In a necropsy surveillance study of 5 animals
in contact with infected humans, infection was conﬁrmed in 3 cats
and a tiger, but infection was not thought to be the cause of death
in any of the cases. The remaining animal was a dog that died of
bronchopneumonia, but this dog tested negative for SARS-CoV-2.
106 A small number of infected dogs and cats have been reported
to have cardiac disease at the time of death, 103 , 105 including the
ﬁrst dog reported to be infected with SARS-CoV-2. Suspected
myocarditis was described in association with natural infection in
8 cats and 3 dogs in the United Kingdom. 107 However, cardiac
disease and exposure to SARS-CoV-2 in pet dogs and cats is likely
widespread, and no convincing evidence for an association
between these and disease exists at the time of writing. The
possibility remains that new variants of SARS-CoV-2 could arise
that are more virulent in dogs and cats or more transmissible, so
ongoing monitoring is critical.Animals with positive test results

vetexamprep.ir

have typically been in contact with infected owners. Evidence of
transmission of infection from dogs or cats back to owners has not
been documented, but remains theoretically possible. Mink on
mink farms appear to be the most susceptible to infection and
disease, with fatal infections reported. There has been evidence of
mink-to-mink, mink-to-human, and mink-to-dog and cat
transmission on mink farms worldwide. In addition, an outbreak
of the delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 in Syrian hamsters in a pet
shop in Hong Kong was followed by zoonotic transmission and
then human-to-human transmission. 98 Extensive culling eﬀorts
associated with these zoonotic transmission events have drawn
considerable media a ention. Recently, likely transmission from
white-tailed deer to humans was described. 108 Concern has been
raised that evolution of the virus in wildlife with subsequent
“spillback” to humans could lead to additional pandemic waves,
potentially with higher mortality. One study provided evidence
that the highly transmissible Omicron variant may have evolved
in mice, with subsequent spillback to humans, 109 , 110 although
the true origin of the Omicron variant at the time of writing
remains unknown.

In early April of 2020, a report was released of an infected tiger
at the Bronx zoo in New York. 111 The tiger was tested because it
developed a cough and inappetence and was in contact with a
caregiver that was subclinically shedding SARS-CoV-2. In
addition, the tiger’s sister, two Siberian tigers, and three lions at
the zoo were reported to also have clinical signs of respiratory
illness. It was later published that there were two separate
transmission events that involved the tigers and the lions, with the
lions being infected with a slightly diﬀerent variant than the
tigers. Infected animals shed infectious virus in their respiratory
secretions and feces. 112 Since then, there have been reports of
other clinical infections in captive wild felids worldwide (puma,
snow leopards, lions, and tigers) 113 , 114 Widespread vaccination
of captive wildlife species and mink has been introduced to
reduce morbidity and mortality in these species. The vaccine
being used for this purpose in the United States at the time of

vetexamprep.ir

writing is an experimental recombinant subunit vaccine (Zoetis,
NJ, USA). 115
Since the start of the pandemic, evidence has been accumulating
in regard to the extent of infection of pet dogs and cats. One
commercial veterinary diagnostic laboratory (IDEXX Laboratories,
ME, USA) reported no positive PCR tests in 4,617 dogs and cats
from Asia, Europe, and North America for which specimens were
submi ed for respiratory viral PCR testing from mid-February
2020 to mid-April 2020. 116 Instead, assays were positive for
common respiratory pathogens such as FCV, Bordetella
bronchiseptica, and Mycoplasma cynos. The seroprevalence has
ranged from 0% to 40% in dogs and 0% to 44% in cats (Tables 43.4
and 43.5). The prevalence of positive PCR results has ranged from
0% to 13% in dogs and 0% to 25% in cats. Virus has been more
often detected in respiratory swab specimens than in rectal swabs
or feces, and shedding in cats has been documented in respiratory
secretions for up to 25 days. 117 In many cases, full-length SARSCoV-2 genome sequence has been obtained using next-generation
sequencing platforms, and shown to match that of the animal’s
owner. 117–119 In a Texas study, SARS-CoV-2 infection was
identiﬁed using PCR and sequencing in 3 of 17 (17.6%) cats and 1
of 59 (10.3%) dogs from 4 of 39 separate households. All PCRpositive animals were subclinically infected. In a study from
Idaho and Washington, USA, signs of illness that could be
consistent with COVID-19 were reported in 20% of dogs and 39%
of cats that had been in contact with people with COVID-19. 120
Diﬀerences in prevalence may reﬂect variations in assay
performance, the time of year, as well as the degree of contact
between positive owners and sampled animals. Behaviors that
promote close contact between humans and pets, such as sharing
of food dishes and beds may increase risk of transmission. 120 , 121
In general, the results of studies to date suggest that subclinical
infection of dogs and cats with SARS-CoV-2 occurs commonly,
although shedding of virus is relatively uncommon. Cats appear
to be more susceptible to infection than dogs and may be able to
show signs of respiratory illness and shed virus for over a week.
Although domestic cats can transmit infection to other cats
following experimental infection, the extent to which this occurs
in the ﬁeld remains unknown. However, veterinarians working in

vetexamprep.ir

small animal practice have not been identiﬁed as at increased risk
of infection and contact with other humans continues to represent
the main risk factor for human infection. Over time, it is possible
that the virus could develop a greater propensity to cause illness
in, or be shed by dogs and cats through further mutation, a
situation that requires close monitoring. If this should occur,
SARS-CoV-2 vaccines for companion animals may be needed.
According to CDC recommendations, humans that test positive
for SARS-CoV-2 should quarantine themselves with their pets,
and limit contact with their pets in the household until the
quarantine period is over (including distancing, wearing a mask
in the house, hand washing, and if possible separating the pets
and having others perform activities that require contact). 3 If their
pet becomes sick, someone else in the household should take the
pet to the veterinarian, and if possible, an initial telemedicine
consultation should be organized. Veterinary clinics should
question people that plan to bring animals in for care about
potential infection by, or exposure to, SARS-CoV-2, as is done in
human healthcare institutions. Updated guidance for
veterinarians on appropriate prevention practices for diﬀerent
exposure situations is provided by the CDC, together with a
variety of other resources. 122 Testing for SARS-CoV-2 may need
to be done in conjunction with local public health authorities. 123

B, body; ELISA, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; F, feces; LIPS,
luciferase immunoprecipitation system; N, nasal; NP, nasopharyngeal; O, oral;
OP, oropharyngeal; PR, pooled respiratory; R, rectal; VN, virus neutralization.
a Virus sequence obtained.

Should a pet test positive for the virus, owners should interact
with them as if there were a positive human in the household
(although the pet should not be made to wear a mask). Owners
can be referred to guidance from the CDC 3 and the AVMA 124 on
SARS-CoV-2 and animals. The virus is readily susceptible to
disinfectants, and temperatures that exceed 55°F can inactivate the
virus in well under an hour. 125 At the time of writing, the risk of
fomite transmission is considered low, generally less than 1 in
10,000 (see Suggested Readings), so the primary mode by which
people are infected with SARS-CoV-2 is through respiratory
droplet exposure. 126

Section 2

Bacterial Diseases
Jane E. Sykes

This section covers a number of important vector-borne and
zoonotic diseases including ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, and
ricke sioses; Q fever; leptospirosis and borreliosis; bartonellosis;
brucellosis; plague; and tularemia. Although previously thought
to be transmi ed by ﬂeas, evidence has accumulated that feline
hemotropic mycoplasmas are most likely transmi ed primarily
through aggressive interactions among cats and that vectors are
not involved (Chapter 58). With the increasing use of more potent
immunosuppressive drugs, especially in dogs, there is also more
recognition of atypical bacterial diseases such as nocardiosis and
mycobacteriosis; these are covered in Chapters 60 and 61.
The modern era of antimicrobial therapy began with the
discovery of sulfonamides in 1936. This was followed in the 1940s
by the discovery of the therapeutic value of penicillin and
streptomycin, and by 1950, the “golden age” of antimicrobial
therapy was underway, and well-intentioned academic leaders
predicted the demise of bacterial infections. But after only a few
decades, antimicrobials are now facing an uncertain future. By the
late 1980s, methicillin-resistant staphylococci were widespread,
and gram-negative rods emerged as important nosocomial
pathogens in hospitals. Veterinarians face major challenges with
the increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant pathogens, such
as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (Chapter
51), Bordetella bronchiseptica (Chapter 55), and other gram-negative
bacteria (Chapter 53), and few new drugs in the antibiotic
pipeline. Some strains of drug-resistant bacteria that have the
potential to cause disease in humans have been identiﬁed with

vetexamprep.ir

increasing prevalence in dogs and cats, such as Clostridioides
diﬃcile (Chapter 64) and pathogenic Escherichia coli (Chapter 63). It
is critical that we model good antibacterial stewardship if we are
to preserve critical weapons against life-threatening bacterial
infections.

44: Ehrlichiosis
Shimon Harrus, Trevor Waner, Mathios E. Mylonakis, Jane
E. Sykes, and Barbara Qurollo

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Ehrlichia canis was first described in 1935
(Algeria). 1 Ehrlichia ewingii was described in 1992 (United
States). 2 Ehrlichia chaffeensis was described in 1991 (United
States). 3 The first report of naturally occurring ehrlichiosis in a
cat occurred in France in 1986. 4
• Cause: The most important species causing disease in dogs
are E. canis (canine monocytic ehrlichiosis) and E. ewingii
(canine granulocytic ehrlichiosis).
• Affected Hosts: Ehrlichia canis causes disease in dogs,
humans, and cats. Ehrlichia ewingii causes disease in dogs,
humans, and goats and has been detected in a clinically ill
cat. Ehrlichia chaffeensis causes disease in humans, possibly
dogs and goats, and has been detected in a clinically healthy
cat. Ehrlichia muris subsp. eauclairensis causes disease in
humans and possibly dogs. Panola Mountain Ehrlichia causes
disease in dogs, goats, and humans in the United States.
• Geographic Distribution: Ehrlichia canis is distributed
worldwide, but is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical
regions. Ehrlichia ewingii is primarily found in the southcentral and southeastern United States. Most reports of E.
chaffeensis infection are from the southern and south-central
United States, but it has also been identified in Africa.
Ehrlichia muris subsp. eauclairensis has been found in the
Upper Midwest of the USA. Panola Mountain Ehrlichia has
been found in the southeastern United States.

vetexamprep.ir

• Mode of Transmission: Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks (E.
canis); Amblyomma americanum ticks (E. ewingii and E.
chaffeensis), Ixodes scapularis ticks (E. muris subsp.
eauclairensis), and A. americanum and Amblyomma
maculatum ticks (Panola Mountain Ehrlichia).
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs—typical clinical signs of E. canis
infection are fever, lethargy, inappetence, weight loss,
cutaneous and mucosal petechial and/or ecchymotic
hemorrhages, lymphadenomegaly, splenomegaly, and uveitis.
Ehrlichia ewingii primarily causes fever, lethargy, inappetence,
and signs of polyarthritis. Cats—typical clinical signs of
Ehrlichia canis infection are fever, lethargy, inappetence,
weight loss, hyperesthesia, and joint pain. E. ewingii was
detected in a clinically ill cat with thrombocytopenia and
anemia.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other tick-borne diseases (e.g.,
granulocytic anaplasmosis, Lyme borreliosis, babesiosis, and
cytauxzoonosis [cats]), bartonellosis, hemotropic
mycoplasmosis, leptospirosis, and other systemic non-vectorborne diseases such as lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and
systemic primary immune-mediated disease.
• Public Health Aspects: All four Ehrlichia species can infect
and cause disease in humans. The most virulent human
pathogen is E. chaffeensis and results in the highest
percentage of hospitalizations and death compared with the
other North American Ehrlichia species.

Ehrlichioses are a group of tick-transmi ed diseases caused by
intracellular, gram-negative bacteria that include Ehrlichia canis,
Ehrlichia ewingii, and Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis. An organism related to
Ehrlichia ruminantium, the cause of heartwater disease in ca le, has
also been detected in ill dogs from South Africa. 5 Ehrlichia muris
eauclairensis has been detected in an ill dog and humans from
Upper Midwest of the United States (formerly E. muris-like). 6
Panola Mountain Ehrlichia was detected in a dog with atypical
lymphocytosis and clonal T-cell expansion. 7 These organisms
form morulae (Latin for “mulberry”), clusters of bacteria, within

vetexamprep.ir

phagosomes of circulating leukocytes. E. canis infects monocytes,
macrophages, and less frequently lymphocytes (Fig. 44.1A–C),
and causes canine monocytic ehrlichiosis (CME), one of the most
important infectious diseases of domestic dogs that are exposed to
ticks, worldwide. Ehrlichia ewingii infects granulocytes and causes
canine granulocytic ehrlichiosis; the organism is very diﬃcult to
culture and only short-term maintenance in cultured cells has
been documented to date. 8 Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis causes human
monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME); dogs are a proposed reservoir for
this organism. The geographic distribution of each pathogen is
generally restricted to that of their vectors and mammalian
reservoir hosts. According to one large study, the prevalence of
exposure to Ehrlichia spp. in the United States in dogs has been
increasing in both endemic and nonendemic areas. 9
Organisms in the genus Ehrlichia are grouped within the family
Anaplasmataceae. Also within this family are the bacteria
Anaplasma platys and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, which cause
canine thrombocytic and granulocytic anaplasmosis, respectively
(see Chapter 45); and organisms belonging to the genera
Neoricke sia (see Chapter 47). Ricke sia ricke sii, the cause of
Rocky Mountain Spo ed Fever (RMSF), and other spo ed fever
group ricke siae belong to a separate family, the Ricke siaceae
(see
Chapter
46).
The
families
Ricke siaceae
and
Anaplasmataceae are phylogenetically related through the order
Ricke siales (Table 44.1).
The severity of clinical signs in animals with ehrlichial
infections depends on factors such as the organism species and
strain, inoculum size, host immunity, and genetic factors. Because
of shared arthropod vectors and/or concurrent exposure to
multiple tick species, co-infections with more than one ricke sial
pathogen, as well as other arthropod-borne pathogens (such as
Babesia and Bartonella spp.) occur and may obscure the clinical
picture.

Ehrlichia canis
Shimon Harrus, Trevor Waner, Mathios E. Mylonakis

Etiology and Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

Ehrlichia canis is transmi ed primarily by the brown dog tick,
Rhipicephalus sanguineus sensu lato (Fig. 44.2), one of the most
widely distributed tick species, worldwide. In a transmission
study, when E. canis-infected ticks were placed on naïve dogs, E.
canis DNA could be detected in the dogs as early as 3 hours
postexposure to the ticks. 10 Infection has been reported in dogs
from Asia, Africa, Europe, the Americas, and most recently in
Australia. 11 New Zealand appears to be free of E. canis infection.
The DNA of E. canis has been detected in other tick species, which
include other Rhipicephalus species (e.g., Rhipicephalus turanicus
and Rhipicephalus bursa), 12 , 13 Ixodes ricinus, 14 and Haemaphysalis
15 and Dermacentor spp. 15 , 16 In one study, experimental
transmission was accomplished with Dermacentor variabilis ticks. 17
Diﬀerent strains of E. canis exist in diﬀerent geographic regions
and may vary in virulence. Although Rh. sanguineus is found
throughout the United States (Fig. 44.3), it prefers warm climates,
and so CME is diagnosed most frequently in dogs living in the
southeastern and southwestern states. In Europe, Rh. sanguineus is
primarily found in the Mediterranean basin, but its distribution
appears to be moving northward, and CME has been reported in
dogs that lack travel history as far north as the Netherlands. 18
Dogs can be persistent subclinical carriers for years. 19 Such dogs
may be transported to nonendemic regions and subsequently
develop the disease months or years later. Tick larvae or nymphs
acquire infection when they feed on infected dogs and transmit
the disease as nymphs or adults when feeding on naïve dogs.
Jackals, foxes, and possibly coyotes may also act as reservoir
hosts. Ehrlichia canis is transmi ed transstadially (i.e., from larva
to nymph to the adult tick) (Fig. 44.4). 20 , 21 Male ticks can also
transmit the pathogen intrastadially. 22 No clear age or sex
predilection for CME exists, but German shepherd dogs are
reportedly more susceptible, and prognosis may be poorer in this
breed. Cross-bred dogs may be less likely to develop CME. 23

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Ehrlichia canis multiplies by binary ﬁssion within vacuoles of
mononuclear phagocytes (see Fig. 44.1A–C); rupture of infected
host cells leads to infection of additional cells. Immune-mediated
mechanisms are important in the pathogenesis of the disease, and
the presence of the spleen appears to contribute to disease
severity. 24
Stages in the invasion and pathogenesis of Ehrlichia include
adhesion, internalization, proliferation, and spreading. Outer
membrane glycoproteins (e.g., gp19, gp36, and gp140kDa) are
associated with adhesion and internalization. 25 The movement of
E. canis through cells is dependent on polymerization of actin
cytoskeleton and lysosomal evasion, and requires inﬂux of iron
and calcium ions. 26 The course of CME has been divided into
acute, subclinical, and chronic phases. Clinical signs occur 8 to 20
days after infection. The clinical manifestations vary considerably
among dogs, which may reﬂect factors such as E. canis strain
variation, host immune response, stage of disease, and concurrent
infections. Lethargy, inappetence, fever, and weight loss are the
most common signs of the acute disease. Replication of the
organism in reticuloendothelial tissues is associated with
generalized lymphadenomegaly and splenomegaly. Ocular and
nasal discharge and uveitis are common ﬁndings and are

vetexamprep.ir

associated with lymphocytic-plasmacytic inﬂammation in these
tissues. Retinal detachment may occur in rare cases due to serum
hyperviscosity and subretinal hemorrhage. Bleeding tendencies
occur in some dogs and may result from thrombocytopenia and
platelet dysfunction. 24 Platelet dysfunction may at least in part be
the result of immune-mediated platelet damage. 27 Experimentally
infected dogs developed low platelet counts, activated platelets,
and antiplatelet antibodies. 28 , 29 The results of
thromboelastography in one study revealed evidence of a
hypercoagulable, hypoﬁbrinolytic state. 28

Neurologic signs may result from meningeal inﬂammation or
hemorrhage. Dogs can recover spontaneously from the acute
phase within 2 to 4 weeks, after which time they may eliminate
the infection or remain subclinically infected. Sequestration of
organisms within the spleen or other tissues may occur, and the
organisms may evade the host immune system through
modulation of the host immune response and by decreasing its
antiehrlichial activities (i.e., decreased presentation by
downregulation of MHC class II receptors, evasion of phagosome-

vetexamprep.ir

lysosome fusion, decreased host cell apoptosis, recombination,
and antigenic variation). 25 , 26 The subclinical phase of CME may
persist for months to years. 19
Chronic CME develops in only some infected dogs. Factors that
inﬂuence the development of the chronic disease are unclear, but
the pathogen, the host genetics, and the interrelations between
them probably play their role. The presence of severe
pancytopenia characterizes the severe chronic form of ehrlichiosis,
and results from hypoplasia of all bone marrow cell lines. 30
Clinical signs at this stage are usually severe and include lethargy,
inappetence, bleeding tendencies, mucosal pallor, fever or
hypothermia, weight loss, lymphadenomegaly, splenomegaly,
dyspnea, anterior uveitis, retinal hemorrhage, and edema. 23 , 31–33
Secondary opportunistic infections such as protozoal infections,
viral papillomatosis, and bacterial UTIs can also develop. Marked
granular lymphocytosis and bone marrow plasmacytosis may
occur in all phases, sometimes accompanied by a monoclonal
gammopathy, which may lead to misdiagnosis of lymphocytic
leukemia or multiple myeloma. This has led to the
recommendation that all dogs with well-diﬀerentiated
lymphocytosis
or
otherwise
unexplained
monoclonal
34
gammopathy be tested for E. canis infection.
Common physical examination ﬁndings in dogs with CME
include
lethargy,
fever,
generalized
peripheral
lymphadenomegaly, and splenomegaly. Ocular and nasal
discharge, cutaneous and mucosal petechial hemorrhages (Fig.
44.5A–C), peripheral edema, and/or neurologic signs may be
evident. Ocular abnormalities include anterior uveitis, hyphema,
scleral, conjunctival or retinal hemorrhage, retinal detachment,
and optic neuritis, with anterior uveitis being most commonly
reported (Fig. 44.6A and B). 32 , 33 Neurologic signs include
twitching, ataxia, seizures, vestibular signs, hyperesthesia, and
cranial nerve deﬁcits. Dogs with chronic ehrlichiosis may have
thin body condition or diﬀuse muscle atrophy and mucosal pallor
in addition to the aforementioned signs.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities

vetexamprep.ir

Complete Blood Count
Thrombocytopenia is the most common hematologic abnormality
of CME, occurring 1 to 4 weeks following infection with E. canis,
in more than 90% of acutely infected dogs. Occasionally, mild
leukopenia due to neutropenia, monocytopenia, and lymphopenia
may occur, together with a mild left shift. 35 Nonregenerative
anemia is usually present. During the subsequent subclinical
phase, mild thrombocytopenia, with increased mean platelet
volume, may persist. 36 Typically, dogs in the severe chronic
phase of CME are profoundly pancytopenic. 30 Moderate to
marked granular lymphocytosis may also occur in subclinically or
chronically infected dogs.
In some acutely infected dogs, morulae are visualized within
the circulating monocytes and less frequently in lymphocytes (see
Fig. 44.1A). Examination of buﬀy coat smears, or lymph node or
splenic aspirates increases the sensitivity for detection of morulae.
37 Cytology is notoriously insensitive for the detection of morulae
in the subclinical and especially chronic infection, and it does not
distinguish between E. canis and E. chaﬀeensis infection. In one
study, morulae were found in only 2 of 19 dogs with chronic CME
after careful screening. 30 Dogs with acute CME may have
evidence of reactive lymphocytes, activated monocytes, mild left
shift,
erythrophagocytosis,
metarubricytosis,
thrombophagocytosis, phagocytosis of nuclear material, and
megaplatelets in their blood smears. 12 , 35

Serum Biochemical Tests
Serum chemistry abnormalities are seen during the acute and
chronic
phases
and
include
hypoalbuminemia,
hyperglobulinemia, hypergammaglobulinemia and elevated
activities of serum ALT and ALP. Most often, hyperglobulinemia
is due to polyclonal gammopathy. 23 Monoclonal gammopathy
can also develop but is uncommon. Less frequently, increases in
serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations are present. 29
Urinalysis
Transient proteinuria has been reported in dogs with acute CME.
38 Dogs with chronic CME may also have evidence of proteinuria.

vetexamprep.ir

Coagulation Profile
In addition to thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities in
dogs with CME include prolongation of the buccal mucosal
bleeding time (BMBT), decreased platelet aggregation
(thrombocytopathy), and prolongation of APTT. 29 , 39
Thromboelastography may reveal evidence of hypercoagulability
and hypoﬁbrinolysis. 28
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
Dogs with CNS involvement may have increased CSF protein
concentrations and lymphocytic pleocytosis. Although rarely
found, morulae may be detected in cells within the CSF. 40–42
Bone Marrow Analysis
Bone marrow is commonly hypercellular in the acute phase but
with chronic disease becomes hypoplastic and pale, which is the
result of fa y inﬁltration, decrease of all bone marrow elements,
decreased iron stores, and marrow plasmacytosis (Fig. 44.7). Bone
marrow mastocytosis has also been described. 43 Myeloﬁbrosis
does not typically develop in chronic CME. 44
Diagnostic Imaging
Sonographic Findings
Findings on abdominal ultrasonography in dogs with CME
include splenomegaly, alterations in splenic echotexture,
enlargement and hypoechogenicity of the abdominal lymph
nodes, and scant peritoneal eﬀusion.
Microbiologic Tests
Available diagnostic assays for ehrlichiosis in dogs are listed in
Table 44.2.
Serologic Diagnosis
Most often, the diagnosis of CME is made using serology, which
may be performed either by IFA testing, ELISA, or Western
immunoblo ing. 45 Using IFA testing, which is considered the
gold standard serologic test, antibodies can be detected between 7
and 28 days after initial infection. Dogs with acute ehrlichiosis

vetexamprep.ir

may have false-negative test results if suﬃcient time has not
elapsed for antibody production to occur. PCR assays may be
helpful for diagnosis in this situation. Use of a combination of
serology with PCR is highly recommended as it allows be er
interpretation of the results and the animal health status. A
positive initial serum antibody titer may reﬂect previous exposure
and not necessarily active infection. Retesting should be
performed 2 to 3 weeks later to demonstrate seroconversion
and/or the possibility of an increase in the E. canis antibody titer.
Serologic test results should be interpreted in light of a dog’s
clinical signs and the results of testing for other potential causes of
the dog’s illness. Dogs with subclinical and chronic E. canis
infection frequently have very high IFA titers (≥1:3,200), and these
antibodies may persist in the face of treatment, suggesting
persistence of the organism. 19 Antibody titers may decline in
some dogs with treatment. High titers do not correlate with the
severity of hyperglobulinemia, severity of disease, or duration of
illness. A titer of 1:100 or greater is suggestive of exposure.
Serologic cross-reactivity with other Ehrlichia species can occur,
which includes E. chaﬀeensis and, less frequently, E. ewingii. 46
Variable cross-reactivity to A. phagocytophilum antigens can also
occur. 45 In areas where other ricke sial agents are endemic,
Western immunoblo ing can be used to conﬁrm that positive IFA
antibody titers are truly reactive to E. canis antigens. However,
Western blo ing is laborious to perform and interpret, and not
routinely available. As a result, Western immunoblo ing has
predominantly been used on a research basis. When E. canis
antigens are used as target antigens, it may be diﬃcult to
distinguish between E. canis and E. chaﬀeensis infections. 47
Species-speciﬁc peptides in microtiter plate-based ELISA assays
are highly speciﬁc for the detection of antibodies speciﬁc to E.
canis, E. ewingii, and E. chaﬀeensis in experimentally and naturally
infected dogs. 48 , 49

51 Practitioners should be aware that a positive result on these
tests could reﬂect active infection or previous exposure, as is the
case with IFA assays. If a positive result is obtained,
determination of a quantitative titer using IFA may be helpful;
high titers (e.g., greater than 1:800) may support chronic CME,
and a fourfold rise in titer may support recent infection.
Molecular Diagnosis
Whole-blood PCR assays for detection of E. canis DNA are more
sensitive than IFA or ELISA for early diagnosis of CME. PCR
assays, targeting diﬀerent genetic loci (16S rRNA, p28, p30,
disulﬁde oxidoreductase, gp19, gp36, gp140), are widely available
for routine diagnosis of E. canis infection. 12 Several laboratories
oﬀer panels that include real-time PCR assays for a variety of
diﬀerent vector-borne pathogens. The results of these assays
should be interpreted in light of a dog’s anamnesis (e.g., presence
of ticks, trip to an endemic area), clinical signs, and the results of
appropriate serologic assays; the la er should be performed to
support the results of PCR testing. PCR assays for E. canis may be
performed on blood, splenic aspirates, lymph nodes, or bone
marrow specimens. IFA or ELISA testing is more sensitive than
PCR assays for diagnosis of chronic CME. 30 , 52 , 53 The sensitivity
of PCR assays for diagnosis of CME when performed on bone
marrow in dogs with chronic ehrlichiosis has ranged from 25% to
68%, depending on the laboratory. 30 The use of PCR assays in the
absence of serology is currently not suitable for screening
potential blood donors for infection because of the lack of
sensitivity of PCR. PCR assays may be useful to conﬁrm infection
in the ﬁrst week of illness, when serologic assays are often
negative. Real-time PCR assays are widely available which can
distinguish E. canis from other Ehrlichia species. Clinicians should

vetexamprep.ir

consult their diagnostic laboratory to ensure this is the case,
especially in regions where multiple Ehrlichia species are present.
LAMP assays also have been developed for detection of E. canis.
54 These assays allow ampliﬁcation under constant temperature
(60°C to 65°C), allowing them to be performed in the clinic se ing,
as well as in a commercial diagnostic laboratory (see Chapter 6).
LAMP assays are highly speciﬁc, eﬃcient, and rapid (result
available in less than an hour). In one study, the results of a
LAMP-based POC assay for Ehrlichia spp. (PCRun, Biogal, Galed
Laboratories, Israel) were equivalent to that of a TaqMan assay. 55
The study included 33 samples from dogs in the United Kingdom
and 100 samples from dogs in Israel with a prevalence of infection
as determined using TaqMan of 42% and 21%, respectively. The
PCRun assay was shown to detect multiple species of Ehrlichia as
well as A. phagocytophilum and A. platys without being able to
distinguish among them, so more speciﬁc assays are required for
an accurate diagnosis of CME.
Isolation in Culture
Ehrlichia canis can be cultured (e.g., from blood samples) in certain
cell lines, such as DH82 and J774.A1 cells. Isolation is timeconsuming and generally performed only on a research basis. 12
Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in CME include widespread petechial
and ecchymotic hemorrhages, generalized pallor, edema,
lymphadenomegaly, and splenomegaly. 56 , 57 On histopathology,
lymphoid and plasma cell hyperplasia and lymphoplasmacytic
inﬁltrates may be present in numerous organs, such as the brain,
eyes, spinal cord, spleen, liver, kidneys, lymph nodes, bone
marrow, and lungs. Histiocytic inﬁltrates may be found in the
lymph nodes. With chronicity, the proportion of plasma cells
increases. Nonsuppurative meningitis and perivascular cuﬃng
within the CNS can also occur. 56 , 57 Glomerulonephritis is rare in
dogs with CME. 57 Interstitial renal plasmacytosis may occur in
dogs with ehrlichiosis and may account for the proteinuria in
some cases. Minimal histologic changes were noticed in the
kidneys of dogs experimentally infected with E. canis.

vetexamprep.ir

Ultrastructural examination showed fusion of podocyte processes
that coincided with the development of proteinuria. 38

Treatment and Prognosis
Antimicrobial Treatment
The treatment of choice for CME consists of antibacterial agents
and supportive care (Table 44.3). Generally, the earlier the
treatment of acutely infected dogs is initiated, the more favorable
the prognosis and outcome. Dogs in the chronic phase that have
severe myelosuppressive disease may be unresponsive to
treatment. 58 Doxycycline (see Chapter 10) is considered the drug
of choice for CME. It is readily absorbed to produce high blood,
tissue, and intracellular concentrations. Given that Ehrlichia spp.
can persist intracellularly, drug penetration into the cell is
essential in eliminating infection. Doxycycline has the added
advantages of a longer half-life and a higher CNS penetration
when compared with other tetracyclines. A consensus statement
of the ACVIM Infectious Disease Study Group suggested that
dogs with CME should be treated with doxycycline (10 mg/kg
daily) for a minimum of 28 days. 34 However, several studies have
shown that shorter periods may be suﬃcient. 58 One study found
that doxycycline (5 mg/kg twice daily) used for 14 days
completely eliminated experimentally induced E. canis infection,
as detected by PCR or blood cultures, from eight acutely infected
dogs. 59 Other studies have shown that either 16 to 23 days or 21
to 28 days of treatment with doxycycline was suﬃcient to clear
the organisms from all infected dogs. 28 , 60 , 61 However, in
another study, a 6-week course of doxycycline (10 mg/kg, PO,
daily) was not suﬃcient to clear E. canis bacteria from all
subclinically experimentally infected dogs. 62 It is therefore
currently recommended to treat acutely infected dogs with
doxycycline (10 mg/kg, PO, daily) for 21 to 28 days. 58
Minocycline (10 mg/kg, PO, q12h) was also shown to clear
infection as determined using whole-blood PCR in ﬁve naturally
infected dogs, although the time to clearance (28 days) was longer
than that for ﬁve dogs treated with doxycycline (10 mg/kg, PO,
q24h) (21 days), with all dogs remaining PCR negative 7 days
after discontinuing treatment. 63

The eﬃcacy of the “consensus doxycycline regimen” was
investigated following experimental E. canis infection in the dog.
64 Despite clinical and hematologic recovery of the dogs and
negative blood PCR results, Rh. sanguineus ticks fed on the dogs
after doxycycline treatment became PCR positive for E. canis
DNA, regardless of the phase during which the treatment was
initiated. These results may imply that a very low level of
infection, not detectable in whole blood using PCR, may persist in
some cases following doxycycline treatment. Overall, noteworthy
clinical improvement generally occurs within 24 to 48 hours after

vetexamprep.ir

initiation of doxycycline therapy in dogs with acute-phase
disease, as well as many dogs with mild chronic disease. The
platelet count correspondingly begins to increase during this time
and is usually in the reference range by 10 to 14 days after
treatment initiation. Administration of glucocorticoids at standard
immunosuppressive doses to a small number of dogs that had
been experimentally infected with E. canis and treated with
doxycycline was not found to be associated with recrudescence of
infection. 65
Rifampicin, an inhibitor of the B subunit of DNA-dependent
RNA polymerase, has been assessed as a potential alternative
drug to doxycycline for treatment of CME. In a recent
experimental study, rifampicin (10 mg/kg, PO, q24h, for 21 days)
hastened hematologic recovery in E. canis acutely infected dogs
compared with untreated dogs, but achieved E. canis clearance in
only two out of ﬁve dogs. 66
Recovery is not equated with permanent immunity, and dogs
can be reinfected with E. canis after a previously eﬀective
treatment. Moreover, experimental reinfection with heterologous
strains has caused more severe disease manifestations than those
with homologous strains. 59
There is currently limited evidence-based justiﬁcation for using
other tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, oxytetracycline), or other
drugs such as chloramphenicol, enroﬂoxacin, or imidocarb
dipropionate in the treatment of CME. Ehrlichia canis appears to
have intrinsic gyrase-mediated resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones, 67
so although their use may be associated with clinical
improvement, 68 they are not recommended. Imidocarb
dipropionate, an antiprotozoal drug, has been used in the past in
treating E. canis infections. In vitro and in vivo studies have shown
that imidocarb (6.6 mg/kg, IM, two injections given 2 weeks apart)
was not eﬀective in clearing E. canis infection in dogs. 69 Because
co-infection with Babesia canis and/or Hepatozoon canis (organisms
transmi ed by the same vector as for E. canis) may occur,
imidocarb dipropionate may be used in conjunction with
doxycycline when co-infections are identiﬁed.
Risk factors for mortality from CME in one study were severe
leukopenia (WBC < 930 cells/µL), severe anemia (HCT < 11.5%),
hypokalemia (<3.7 mmol/L), and prolonged APTT (>18.25 second).

Supportive Care
For dogs with CME that are dehydrated or anemic, intravenous
ﬂuids or blood products, respectively, may be required. In a
nonseverely pancytopenic dog, if thrombocytopenia fails to
resolve with doxycycline administration, a short course of therapy
with immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids could be
considered in addition to doxycycline. In one case report, use of
high-dose ﬁlgrastim (50 µg/kg, SC, q48h for 4 days) together with
glucocorticoids was followed by bone marrow recovery. 71

Immunity and Vaccination
A commercial vaccine for E. canis infection is currently not
available, but in one study vaccination of dogs with an a enuated
strain extensively reduced disease manifestations in dogs
challenged with a virulent strain of E. canis. 72 The immune
response to E. canis infection is not well understood. Because E.
canis is an intracellular pathogen, cell-mediated immune response
is required for pathogen elimination. In one study, dogs with
acute infection developed CD8+ lymphocytosis that subsided after
several weeks, despite organism persistence. 73 Cytokine studies
suggest that the immune response may vary according to the
strain of E. canis involved. 74 , 75 Genetic factors of the host are also
likely to be important determinants of the immune response and
outcome of infection.

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
Avoidance of tick-infested areas and routine inspection of dogs
for ticks after outdoor activities, especially in endemic areas, can
help to prevent ehrlichiosis. Clients should be instructed to
remove ticks properly and avoid handling ticks with bare hands
or crushing them, to prevent exposure to infected hemolymph. A
variety of devices are available to assist tick removal, which are
placed around the area where the mouthparts enter the skin to
avoid crushing or squeezing the tick and leaving the mouthparts
behind (see Fig. 44.2). Fine-tipped tweezers can be used to grasp
the tick as close to the skin as possible, followed by steady
retraction to remove the tick. The bite wound should then be
thoroughly cleaned with a suitable antiseptic solution (such as
iodine or chlorhexidine-based antiseptics) or soap and water.
Ticks can be disposed of in alcohol or tested for vector-borne
pathogens using PCR assays.
The use of topical ectoparasiticides with activity against ticks
also prevent tick-borne infectious diseases (see Chapter 13).
Examples of eﬀective canine products include those that contain
amitraz, ﬁpronil, pyrethroids (permethrin, etofenprox, pyrethrin,
deltamethrin, ﬂumethrin), sarolaner, afoxolaner, lotilaner, and
ﬂuralaner. Products that contain pyrethroids and amitraz have the
most potent activity against ticks. In one ﬁeld study, the use of
monthly imidacloprid 10% and permethrin 50% eﬀectively
prevented infection with E. canis in kennel dogs. 76 In another
study, the use of monthly (days 0, 28, and 56) topical imidacloprid
10% and permethrin 50% prevented tick transmission of E. canis to
experimentally infected dogs, whereas use of monthly afoxolaner
or a single dose of ﬂuralaner did not completely prevent infection.
77 It was suggested that failure of isoxazolines to prevent
transmission resulted from the slower speed of kill for these
products, which was signiﬁcantly lower than that for the
imidacloprid/permethrin combination. Amitraz, a monoamine
oxidase inhibitor, should not be used in dogs treated with
selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as ﬂuoxetine,
and pet owners who are receiving SSRIs should also use
alternative preventatives for their dogs. Prophylactics should be
applied consistently at the recommended interval for optimum
activity. No preventatives completely protect dogs or cats from

vetexamprep.ir

tick a achment, especially where tick infestation rates are high.
Unfortunately, acaricide-resistant strains of Rh. sanguineus have
been reported following the indiscriminate use of these drugs. 76
Low-dose doxycycline (6.6 mg/kg, PO, q24h) has also been used
to prevent infection in working dogs or those residing in kennels
in which E. canis infection is a substantial problem. Resistance to
doxycycline remains a theoretical concern in this situation.
Because of the potential persistent subclinical carrier state,
blood donor dogs should be screened with serology and PCR for
evidence of E. canis exposure or infection. All seropositive/PCRpositive dogs should be excluded as donors. Transport of
persistent carrier dogs to nonendemic regions has the potential to
introduce the infection or new strains of E. canis to these regions if
the appropriate tick vectors are present.

Public Health Aspects
Ehrlichia canis DNA has been detected in some human patients
from Venezuela with clinical signs compatible with HME, 78 and
in samples from blood bank donors in Costa Rica, 79 , 80
suggesting that strains closely related to E. canis might be a cause
of monocytic ehrlichiosis in people in Central and South America.
Appropriate precautions should be taken to prevent transmission
when handling engorged ticks as well as blood and tissue
specimens from infected dogs, and care should be taken to
prevent needle-stick injuries.

Ehrlichia chaffeensis
Shimon Harrus, Trevor Waner, Mathios E. Mylonakis

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis, the cause of HME, can naturally infect dogs,
based on molecular detection of the organism in southeastern
Virginia, Oklahoma, North Carolina, Venezuela, and South Korea.
81–87 White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) serve as the
principal reservoir host that sustains the enzootic cycle of Ehrlichia
chaﬀeensis in North America. 88 E. chaﬀeensis is transstadially
transmi ed primarily by the lone star tick, Amblyomma

vetexamprep.ir

americanum, but can also be transmi ed by the gulf coast tick,
Amblyomma maculatum. Dermacentor variabilis and possibly Rh.
sanguineus and other tick species may also play a minor role in the
transmission of this agent. 88–90

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Experimentally infected dogs develop mild and inconsistent
clinical and clinicopathologic abnormalities, including fever,
thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. 82 , 91–94 Overall, the intensity
of thrombocytopenia and histopathologic lesions in several organs
tended to be less severe in dogs experimentally infected with E.
chaﬀeensis compared with dogs inoculated at the same time with
E. canis. 82 , 91 Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis DNA could be PCR ampliﬁed
and antibody titers detected for up to 117 days and 180 days
postinoculation, respectively, 93 while ticks could acquire the
infection for up to 566 days following intradermal inoculation of a
dog. 92 Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis infection in dogs may lead to a
persistent carrier state, with localization in several tissues (e.g.,
bone marrow, spleen, liver, lymph nodes, lungs, kidneys, and
brain). 91 , 92
Physical Examination Findings
In naturally infected dogs, E. chaﬀeensis infection has been
associated with lymphadenomegaly, anterior uveitis, and
epistaxis, 82 but the clinical implications of this infection in dogs
are still unclear.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count and Serum Chemistry Profile
Anemia,
thrombocytopenia,
moderate
pancytopenia,
hyperproteinemia, and hypoalbuminemia have been reported in a
limited number of naturally infected dogs. 81 , 86 , 87 However, as
coinfections are common in naturally infected dogs, these ﬁndings
should be interpreted with caution.

vetexamprep.ir

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
The diagnostic sensitivity of cytology for the conﬁrmation of the
E. chaﬀeensis infection has yet to be evaluated and to the best of the
authors’ knowledge, no microscopic visualization of E. chaﬀeensis
morulae has been reported in experimentally or naturally infected
dogs. Of note, the cytologic diﬀerentiation between E. canis and E.
chaﬀeensis morulae in host cells is not possible. 95
Serologic Diagnosis
Dogs experimentally infected with E. chaﬀeensis develop IgG
antibody titres 7 to 23 days postinoculation, which remain
detectable for at least 6 months postinoculation. 81 , 91 , 93 In the
clinical se ing, serologic diagnosis is complicated by strong crossreactivity of E. chaﬀeensis antibodies with antigens of other
Ehrlichia species. 12 , 81 , 83 , 84 , 96 Recently, species-speciﬁc
peptides in microtiter plate-based ELISA assays have been shown
to demonstrate very high speciﬁcity in the detection of antibodies
speciﬁc to E. ewingii, E. canis, and E. chaﬀeensis in experimentally
and naturally infected dogs. 46 , 49 , 81 , 83 , 84 , 96
Molecular Detection Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Real-time PCR assays for detection of E. chaﬀeensis have been
applied mostly to whole blood and occasionally other tissues
specimens. 85 , 91–93 Some commercial veterinary diagnostic
laboratories oﬀer vector-borne PCR panels that include an assay
that speciﬁcally detects E. chaﬀeensis, with separate assays for E.
canis and E. ewingii. The 16S rRNA gene has been the major
molecular target, but other genes including the p28, gp120, homp,
and disulﬁde oxidoreductase have also been targeted. 81 , 83 , 85 , 92

, 93

Treatment
In vitro susceptibility testing has indicated that doxycycline and
rifampicin are the most active drugs against E. chaﬀeensis
infection, but clinical trials are lacking for both antibiotic agents. 97

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
In endemic areas, the risk of acquiring E. chaﬀeensis infection can
be lowered by implementing strict tick control programmes for
dogs and premises. No vaccines are currently available for the
protection of dogs against E. chaﬀeensis infection. However,
vaccination with a live, a enuated E. chaﬀeensis mutant (Ech_0660)
may have induced a pathogen-speciﬁc humoral and cellular
immunity conferring protection in vaccinated dogs against ticktransmi ed E. chaﬀeensis infection but not against a heterologous
challenge with E. canis. 94

Public Health Aspects
In south-central and southeastern United States, E. chaﬀeensis is
considered the major causative agent for HME, which is exhibited
as an acute inﬂuenza-like illness characterized by fever, headache,
malaise, and occasionally death in severely aﬀected humans. 98
Dogs may be carriers of E. chaﬀeensis in endemic geographic
regions and may be involved in transporting infected ticks to
humans.

Ehrlichia ruminantium
Shimon Harrus, Trevor Waner, Mathios E. Mylonakis
Ehrlichia ruminantium, the cause of heartwater in ca le, has been
detected using PCR in the blood of dogs presenting with clinical
signs suggestive of ehrlichiosis and also in clinically healthy dogs
from countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including South Africa,
Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and Mali. 5 , 99 The organism
has not been isolated from the blood of dogs in culture or tested
for its infectivity to dogs; therefore, its virulence, potential vectors,
and deﬁnitive classiﬁcation are uncertain. Whether the clinical
signs, which were similar to those of E. canis infection, were
caused by or were incidental to the infection with this organism is
uncertain.

Ehrlichia muris subspecies eauclairensis
Shimon Harrus, Trevor Waner, Mathios E. Mylonakis, Jane E.
Sykes

vetexamprep.ir

Ehrlichia muris was originally isolated from a wild mouse in
Japan, 100 and later PCR ampliﬁed and sequenced. 101 Ehrlichia
muris or a closely related organism was detected using molecular
techniques in a febrile person in Russia, 102 and then in four
people with febrile disease from Minnesota and Wisconsin. 103
The people from Minnesota and Wisconsin had clinical signs and
laboratory abnormalities resembling those of human ehrlichiosis
or granulocytic anaplasmosis, but no morulae were visualized in
blood smears. They were seronegative to A. phagocytophilum and
showed variable seroreactivity to E. chaﬀeensis. 103 The DNA of
this organism was also detected in Peromyscus leucopus mice as
well as Ixodes scapularis ticks from Minnesota and Wisconsin. 104
Subsequently, additional human cases were identiﬁed in the
United States (at the time of writing, more than 100 cases
according to the CDC), and multilocus sequence analysis led to
the proposal that the organism from the United States be classiﬁed
as a novel species, E. muris subsp. eauclairensis. 105
Dogs experimentally infected with E. muris did not show
clinical or hematologic abnormalities, did not seroconvert, and
their PCR was negative for the duration of the follow-up period.
101 In 2012, the DNA of E. muris subsp. eauclairensis was identiﬁed
in an ill dog from northern Minnesota that was seronegative for E.
canis and seroreactive to Anaplasma spp., although the extent to
which this organism contributed to the dog’s clinical signs was
unclear. 6 The extent to which E. muris subsp. eauclairensis can
cause disease in dogs requires further investigation.

Panola Mountain Ehrlichia
Jane E. Sykes
Panola Mountain Ehrlichia is a novel species of Ehrlichia that was
identiﬁed in a goat in Georgia in the USA in 2006 106 and
subsequently detected in a human from Atlanta with doxycyclineresponsive neck pain. The person had been hiking 3 weeks
previously in the Panola Mountain State Park in Georgia and had
removed an A. americanum nymphal tick from his upper arm. 107
The organism is closely related to E. ruminantium and was
subsequently detected in A. americanum ticks from all over the
southeastern United States, 108 as well as A. maculatum ticks in the

vetexamprep.ir

United States and Amblyomma variegatum ticks from the Caribbean
and Africa. 109 Infections have been detected in white-tailed deer,
which were also shown to be susceptible to experimental infection
using infected Amblyomma ticks and may be reservoirs for the
organism. 110 Panola Mountain Ehrlichia was also detected in a
dog from Raleigh, North Carolina, with reactive lymphocytosis
and clonal expansion of T cells, which appeared to respond to
treatment with doxycycline. 7 The extent to which this organism
causes disease in dogs and humans requires further study.

Ehrlichia ewingii
Barbara Qurollo

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Ehrlichia ewingii, a gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium
is the causative agent of canine and human granulocytic
ehrlichiosis. To date, the organism has only been transiently
cultured in vitro. Ehrlichia ewingii has been detected in dogs from
North America, Cameroon, and Brazil. 2 , 79 , 111 In the southcentral and southeastern states of the United States, E. ewingii may
be the primary agent of canine ehrlichiosis. Of mostly healthy
dogs from Oklahoma and Arkansas, 45% were seropositive for E.
ewingii. 112 Furthermore, in two large-scale studies addressing
healthy and sick dogs, the overall seroprevalence was 14.5% in the
central states (Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri, and Kansas) and
5.9% in the southeastern states, 113 while seroprevalences of 5.7%,
5.2%, 3.4%, 1.2%, and 0.4% were reported in mid-Atlantic, south,
northeast, midwest, and west, respectively. 49 The PCR-based
prevalence of Ehrlichia ewingii infection ranges from 6% to 30% in
ill or apparently healthy dogs. 83 , 84 , 112 , 114 The median age of 41
infected dogs in one study was 9 years, with most cases occurring
in summer (39%), fall (27%), and winter (24%). 115 E. ewingii is
transmi ed transstadially by the lone star tick, A. americanum,
which is the only proven vector, but the DNA of E. ewingii has
also been detected in D. variabilis, Rh. sanguineus, and rarely A.
maculatum ticks. 84 , 88 , 116 Infection and associated disease was
identiﬁed for the ﬁrst time in Texas in 2019, suggesting the

vetexamprep.ir

presence of infected Amblyomma ticks in this region, and possibly
an under-recognized disease. 117
The white-tailed deer and possibly dogs are the major reservoir
hosts of E. ewingii in nature. 114 , 118 One case report described
evidence of vertical transmission of Mycoplasma haemocanis but not
E. ewingii from an infected pregnant beagle. 119

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Dogs experimentally or naturally infected with E. ewingii can
maintain the infection for at least 5 months or 2 years,
respectively, possibly serving as reservoir hosts. 118 , 120–122 Like A.
phagocytophilum, E. ewingii replicates in neutrophils and delays
neutrophil apoptosis thus prolonging the life span of the host
cells. 123 The course of infection is usually subclinical, or after an
incubation period of 2–3 weeks may culminate in an acute disease
with intermi ent fever, lethargy, anorexia, lameness due to
neutrophilic polyarthritis, and possibly neurologic manifestations.
122 , 124

Physical Examination Findings
The most common clinical ﬁndings include fever and
musculoskeletal signs. In dogs that are naturally infected with E.
ewingii, physical examination may indicate a thin body condition,
fever, lethargy, peripheral lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or
hepatomegaly, reluctance to move, lameness or stilted gait, joint
swelling or pain on palpation, peripheral edema, and occasionally
vomiting or diarrhea. 115 , 125 Joint pain was the most commonly
reported sign in one study of 41 naturally infected dogs, and was
present in over one third of the dogs. 115 Dogs that tested PCR
positive for other vector-borne pathogens were excluded from this
study, but other concurrent disorders were present in many of the
dogs tested. Reported neurologic signs include proprioceptive
deﬁcits, paraparesis, ataxia, neck pain, anisocoria, tremors, and
head tilt. 124 Importantly, an unknown proportion of dogs with
spontaneous infection do not develop any clinical manifestations.
115 , 118

vetexamprep.ir

the study of 41 infected dogs, morulae were reported in 6 (16%) of
37 dogs where CBC ﬁndings were available. 115
Common hematologic abnormalities in dogs naturally infected
with E. ewingii include thrombocytopenia (43% of dogs in one
study), anemia, and mild to moderate neutrophilic leukocytosis
with a left shift or rarely leukopenia. 111 , 115 , 124 , 125 Reactive
lymphocytosis and mild neutrophil toxic changes may also occur.
115 , 124 Serum biochemistry may be unremarkable or show mild
abnormalities such as hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, and
mildly elevated activities of serum ALP and ALT. 115 , 124 , 125
Increased serum urea nitrogen and symmetric dimethylarginine
(SDMA) concentrations were detected in approximately one third
of 41 infected dogs, and signiﬁcant proteinuria in the face of
inactive urine sediments was also frequently detected, suggesting
the possibility of glomerulonephritis. 115 Synovial ﬂuid analysis
reveals neutrophilic polyarthritis (nucleated cell counts may range
16,000–125,000/µL).
Microbiologic Tests
Serologic Diagnosis
In experimentally infected dogs, antibodies appear approximately
1 month PI. 122 Serologic diagnosis of E. ewingii infection is
currently limited to a POC ELISA assay that detects the presence
of antibodies to a speciﬁc peptide of E. ewingii (SNAP 4Dx Plus,
IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME, USA). Because this peptide
is combined on a spot with a peptide that detects antibodies to E.
canis, the antibody response to these pathogens cannot be
distinguished from one another. Cross-reactions may also occur to
other Ehrlichia species such as E. chaﬀeensis. Recently, species-

vetexamprep.ir

speciﬁc peptides in microtiter plate-based ELISA assays have been
shown to demonstrate very high speciﬁcity for the detection of
antibodies speciﬁc to E. ewingii, E. canis, and E. chaﬀeensis in
experimentally and naturally infected dogs. 46 , 48 , 49 , 112 , 113 , 118
Dogs with acute illness may initially test negative with serologic
assays, and positive test results may reﬂect the presence of
antibodies from previous exposure or subclinical infection. 48 , 122
A total of 83% of 41 infected dogs had antibodies to Ehrlichia
species antigens using the SNAP 4Dx Plus assay. 115
Seroconversion from a negative to a positive result over a 2- to 4week time period in paired serum samples may support a
diagnosis of current active E. ewingii infection in endemic areas.
