Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing

vetexamprep.ir

Whole-blood PCR assays with variable sensitivities have been
developed for the speciﬁc detection of E. ewingii DNA. 115 , 118 , 124
, 125 Taking into account the low speciﬁcity of serologic tests, E.
ewingii-speciﬁc PCR assays are currently the only means to
conﬁrm active infection with this pathogen and to diﬀerentiate it
from A. phagocytophilum infection. In experimental studies, PCR
was shown to become positive as early as 4 days after inoculation.
122

Treatment
Treatment with doxycycline results in rapid clinical improvement
within 24 to 48 hours. 85 , 124 Subclinically infected dogs may
spontaneously clear the infection within weeks to months. 118 , 121

Prevention
In the endemic areas, the risk of acquiring E. ewingii infection can
be lowered by implementing strict tick control programs for dogs
and premises. Potential blood donor dogs should be screened for
infection with E. ewingii-speciﬁc ELISA and PCR assays.

Public Health Aspects
Human infection with E. ewingii has been rarely described in
endemic regions of the United States. 85 , 126 , 127 In one study of
4,177 human patients that were tested using real-time PCR for
Ehrlichia across 41 US states, 10 (9.2%) of 109 Ehrlichia infections
were E. ewingii, with 2 patients from New Jersey and Indiana,
where cases had previously not been described. 128 The remaining
infections were caused by E. chaﬀeensis (99 cases) and none tested
positive for E. muris subsp. eauclairensis. Aﬀected humans show
headache, nausea, fever, myalgia, and thrombocytopenia, with or
without leukopenia, and respond to doxycycline treatment. Both
immunocompetent and immunocompromised humans have
reportedly been aﬀected. 126 Although direct dog-to-human
transmission does not occur, blood from aﬀected dogs should be
handled with caution.

Feline Ehrlichioses

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
The species of Ehrlichia that infect cats after natural exposure have
not been fully determined. Reports of Ehrlichia-like bodies or
morulae have been detected in peripheral lymphocytes or
monocytes of naturally exposed cats in the United States 129 (Fig.
44.8), Kenya, 130 , 131 France, 4 , 132–136 Brazil, 137 and Thailand. 138
Electron microscopic assessment of an isolate from feline
mononuclear cells revealed organisms from 0.54 to 1.3 µm,
intermediate in size between E. canis and Neoricke sia sennetsu. 130
Conﬁrmation of feline ehrlichiosis on a molecular basis using PCR
has improved our understanding of which species of Ehrlichia
infect cats. Many recent studies in cats document PCR-ampliﬁed
DNA from Ehrlichia spp. with similar, and in some cases identical,
DNA sequence from those Ehrlichia spp. commonly detected in
dogs. 139 , 139–151 In one North American report, 143 DNA most
consistent with E. canis was documented in the blood of three
clinically ill cats, and a second retrospective study 146 described
Ehrlichia DNA in 6 of 331 (1.8%) feline whole blood samples that
had been submi ed for vector-borne disease testing. Of those six
cats, sequence analysis identiﬁed one cat with E. canis, two cats
with E. chaﬀeensis and three cats with E. ewingii infections.
Prevalence studies of vector-borne pathogens in cats in Brazil
have often yielded positive PCR results for Ehrlichia, whereas
many studies from North America and Europe have been
negative for Ehrlichia DNA, instead amplifying the DNA of
Anaplasma or Bartonella species, or hemoplasmas. Ehrlichia canis
DNA segments ampliﬁed from three cats in Brazil were 99%
identical with each other and 100% identical with reported
sequences from dogs in the area, suggesting that the same strain
was infecting dogs and cats. 144 Furthermore, molecular studies
from Brazil described ampliﬁed regions of the 16S rDNA and dsb
gene from infected cats as 100% identical to E. canis. 139–141 , 149 , 151
In a Brazilian study of cats from Rio de Janeiro, investigators
ampliﬁed 16S rRNA gene sequences with 100% identity to E.
canis, but obtained negative dsb gene PCR results. 150 However,
another study from Brazil identiﬁed 16S rDNA from Ehrlichia spp.
that was 98% identical to E. canis in one cat and 97% identical to E.
chaﬀeensis in another cat indicating the potential for a diﬀerent
species of Ehrlichia that infect cats. 142 In a French report, 132 the

vetexamprep.ir

16S rDNA Ehrlichia sequences obtained from two cats were 100%
identical to those obtained from North American cats, and in two
recent reports from Europe, Ehrlichia spp. DNA was ampliﬁed
from 14 (5.4%) of 260 cats in Italy 148 and 35 (5.4%) of 649 domestic
and stray cats in Portugal. 147 Sequence analysis was reported for
one of the Portugal cats, which conﬁrmed the presence of E. canis
DNA. Ehrlichia canis DNA was ampliﬁed from blood of one cat in
Trinidad, West Indies. 145 These reports support a conclusion that
cats can be infected with the same or similar species of Ehrlichia
commonly diagnosed in dogs and that veterinarians should
consider molecular testing modalities in cats with clinical signs of
ehrlichiosis. Most cats for which signalment was reported were
domestic short-haired cats and 1 year or older. Both male and
female cats were aﬀected.
To the knowledge of the authors, only one experimental
inoculation study of cats with E. canis has been conducted. 152
When cats were inoculated subcutaneously with an E. canis strain
(North Carolina State University canine isolate) maintained in cell
culture, E. canis DNA or antibodies that reacted to E. canis
morulae were not detected in an 8-week follow-up period. 152 It is
possible that: (1) subcutaneous inoculation is not an eﬀective
method for infecting cats with E. canis; (2) natural transmission via
a tick species is necessary for infection; (3) the E. canis strain
maintained after many passages through cell culture lost its
natural virulence in a host animal; or (4) Ehrlichia species that
replicate in cats are not identical to those infecting dogs. 143
Additional experimental infection studies in cats using diﬀerent
Ehrlichia spp. and transmission methods are warranted. In
addition, whether E. muris can be transmi ed to cats that ingest
infected rodents requires further study. 100 , 101
Sera from cats have been assessed for Ehrlichia spp. antibodies
using IFA, ELISA, or Western immunoblot. By the use of IFA,
serum antibodies that react with E. canis morulae have been
detected in cats from multiple states of the United States, 129 , 146 ,
153 France, 135 , 136 Italy, 154 , 155 Spain, 156–160 Kenya, 161 and Brazil.
140–142 , 150 , 162 In a neighborhood in Colorado from which a cat
infected with a monocytic Ehrlichia was identiﬁed, 14 of 17 cats
(82.4%) and 9 of 17 cats (52.9%) had serum antibodies detected by
IFA against E. canis and Neoricke sia risticii, respectively. 129 Cats

vetexamprep.ir

with antibodies against both species generally had higher titers to
E. canis antigens. A recent serologic survey of 715 archived feline
serum samples from client-owned cats in North America
documented a low Ehrlichia seroprevalence. 146 The samples were
screened with a qualitative ELISA with Ehrlichia-genus and
species-speciﬁc peptides, and a subset of those were further
analyzed by whole cell E. canis and E. chaﬀeensis IFA. Ehrlichia spp.
antibodies to peptides were detected in 12 of 715 cats (0.14%),
with species-speciﬁc seroreactivity to E. canis, E. chaﬀeensis, and E.
ewingii documented in 5, 1, and 2 cats, respectively. Of the 59 cats
screened by IFA, 5 cats had serum antibodies to E. chaﬀeensis, 1 of
which was also seroreactive to E. canis, and 2 cats were
seroreactive to E. canis. 146 Serosurveys performed in other
countries using E. canis IFA documented E. canis antibodies in 67
of 680 client-owned and stray cats (9.9%) from Spain, 57 of 216
client-owned cats (26.4%) from Brazil, and 88 of 212 client-owned
and stray cats (41.5%) from Brazil. 140 , 150 , 157 Recent serosurveys
using E. canis or Ehrlichia spp. peptide ELISAs measured Ehrlichia
antibodies in 73 of 624 (11.7%) client-owned cats from Germany
and 2 of 100 (2%) stray cats from Bulgaria. 163 , 164 Overall,
seroprevalence of Ehrlichia spp. in client-owned cats in North
America was low, with potential epizootic areas such as the area
in Colorado, while feline Ehrlichia seroprevalence was higher in
Europe and South America. The diﬀerences in prevalence may be
due to serologic testing modalities, lifestyle of the cats tested, and
prevalence of Ehrlichia spp.
Many healthy cats have serum antibodies from exposure to
other pathogens (e.g., Bartonella henselae) 160 that may cross-react
with E. canis antigens, as observed for dogs. 153 Additionally,
variable serologic cross-reactivity occurs among Ehrlichia,
Neoricke sia, and Anaplasma spp.; therefore, seroreactivity to a
speciﬁc test antigen does not deﬁnitely document exposure to the
Ehrlichia spp. morulae or peptides used for testing. 34 , 152 , 165 , 166
Serologic cross-reactivity has been suspected in epidemiologic
investigations in domestic or exotic cats, which likely
overestimates infection prevalence. 146 , 156 , 159 , 160 , 162 , 167–169 For
example, one study documented a cat with A. phagocytophilum
DNA in blood that had serum antibodies to E. chaﬀeensis by IFA,
and another cat with E. chaﬀeensis DNA in blood that did not have

vetexamprep.ir

serum antibodies to E. chaﬀeensis by IFA but had antibodies to E.
canis by IFA. 146 Standardization of Ehrlichia spp. serologic
methodologies between laboratories has not been performed, and
the most appropriate cutoﬀ values have not been determined.
Results of serologic tests performed by diﬀerent laboratories have
not shown 100% concordance. 143 Thus, results of antibody-based
surveys should be interpreted with caution until such time as
laboratories can be er correlate serologic results with feline
Ehrlichia spp. isolates or PCR assay ﬁndings.
The way in which the clinically ill, naturally exposed cats with
ehrlichiosis described in the literature were infected remains
unknown. Documentation of arthropod exposure in proven cases
has been variable. A study in Brazil documented Rh. sanguineus
sensu lato ticks parasitizing three cats infected with E. canis,
where one of the a ached ticks was also PCR positive for E. canis.
151 Haemaphysalis leachi was found on each of four cats with
clinical ehrlichiosis in Kenya. 130 , 131 Amblyomma aureolatum was
found on an infected cat in Brazil. 149 Ctenocephalides felis taken
from cats in the United States and Australia were negative for
Ehrlichia and Anaplasma spp. DNA. 170 , 171

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs and Physical Examination
Findings
The pathogenesis of disease associated with ehrlichiosis in cats is
unknown. Based on clinical, laboratory, and radiographic
ﬁndings, pathogenesis of disease may be similar to that for
Ehrlichia infection of dogs. In the three cats with E. canis-like DNA
in blood, antinuclear antibodies were detected along with
cytopenias, similar to results reported for infected dogs. 143 In one
cat infected with E. ewingii, clinical signs were also similar to those
seen in infected dogs, and consisted of anemia and
thrombocytopenia.146 Additional studies monitoring cats
naturally or experimentally infected with Ehrlichia spp. are
needed to be er understand the pathogenesis of feline
ehrlichiosis.
Clinical manifestations of ehrlichiosis have been described in 22
cats with suspected morulae in mononuclear cells, 4 , 129–131 , 134 ,

vetexamprep.ir

135 , 137 , 172 and in 4 cats with Ehrlichia spp. DNA in blood (see

Table 44.1). 143 , 146 Ehrlichiosis has also been suspected in 34
reported feline cases in which the diagnosis was presumptively
based on the combination of positive E. canis or N. risticii serology
results, clinical or laboratory ﬁndings consistent with ehrlichial
infection, and response to known antiehrlichial drugs. 129 , 135 , 136 ,
172–175 Furthermore, several studies that evaluated clinical signs in
cats that were seropositive and/or PCR positive for Ehrlichia
documented abnormalities consistent with ehrlichiosis, but results
of treatment were not reported. 141 , 148 , 158 Some cats that tested
positive for Ehrlichia using PCR have been apparently healthy. In
other cats, co-morbidities such as lymphoma or concurrent
infection with Mycoplasma haemofelis, Cryptococcus neoformans,
FeLV, or FIV infections were detected.
When clinical signs are present, fever and nonspeciﬁc signs of
lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss are common
manifestations. Hyperesthesia, joint pain, dyspnea, vomiting, and
diarrhea have also been described. Reported physical examination
abnormalities include splenomegaly, lymphadenomegaly,
dyspnea, petechiae, retinal detachments, vitreous hemorrhages,
epistaxis, and pale mucous membranes.

Diagnosis
Diagnostic tests used to detect Ehrlichia infections in cats are
similar to those used in dogs (see Table 44.2). Assessment of
regional and tick exposure, clinical signs, and characteristic
laboratory abnormalities should prompt clinicians to proceed
with diagnostic modalities such as PCR, IFA, ELISA, and cytologic
examination of blood smears. Use of a combination of molecular
and serologic modalities can improve evidence of infection or
exposure to Ehrlichia spp. 176 Cytologic examination of blood, joint
ﬂuid, CSF, and tissue aspirates can identify active infections but is
generally less sensitive than molecular techniques.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Anemia is most commonly nonregenerative and has been noted in
cats with chronic disease histories. One cat with regenerative
anemia was co-infected with a hemotropic Mycoplasma species. 4

leukocytosis,
neutrophilia,
neutropenia,

lymphopenia,
lymphocytosis,

and
thrombocytopenia occur in some cats, alone or in combination. A
Brazilian study documented thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia
as the most common CBC abnormalities in eight cats with E. canis
DNA in their blood 141 ; the same study evaluated 42 cats
seropositive to E. canis by IFA and documented anemia,
leukocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, and
monocytosis. A recent study of 57 cats from Brazil, either
seropositive or PCR positive for E. canis reported anemia,
thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, left-shift neutrophilia, and
hyperproteinemia as the most common abnormalites. 150 In
contrast, 14 cats from Italy with Ehrlichia spp. in their blood, 148 3
cats with E. canis in their blood,151 and 1 cat in the southern
United States with E. chaﬀeensis DNA in its blood had no CBC
abnormalities. 146 Bone marrow evaluation of cats with cytopenias
has revealed primarily hypoplasia of the aﬀected cell line.
However, one cat had bone marrow cytologic characteristics
consistent with myeloid leukemia. 143 In regions where ticks are
abundant, ehrlichiosis should be considered on the diﬀerential list
for cats with unexplained leukocytosis or cytopenias.
Biochemical abnormalities have been infrequently reported in
cats with suspected clinical ehrlichiosis and are nonspeciﬁc.
Hyperproteinemia was the most consistent abnormality and
polyclonal gammopathy was detected in ﬁve of the cats assayed
by protein electrophoresis. 133 , 143 , 150 , 172 In a separate study, an
epidemiologic association was made between monoclonal
gammopathy and cats seropositive for E. canis antibodies. 153
Based on these results, in tick endemic regions, ehrlichiosis should
be on the diﬀerential list for cats with hyperglobulinemia.
Cytologic Examination
Microscopic examination of stained blood smears may reveal
Ehrlichia morulae in mononuclear cells or granulocytes. However,
this method of diagnosis is not sensitive and cannot identify the
Ehrlichia spp. present.
Organism Cultivation
Infection by Ehrlichia spp. can be conﬁrmed by cell culture, but
this is not routinely used in a clinical se ing. Furthermore, not all

vetexamprep.ir

Ehrlichia spp. can be grown in cell culture. A empts to culture an
Ehrlichia spp. from cats seropositive to E. canis were unsuccessful.
158 An Ehrlichia-like organism was isolated from whole blood from
domestic cats on monocyte cultures 130 but not from a lioness
from Kenya. 131 Although results of PCR assays will likely be used
to help further deﬁne feline ehrlichiosis, clinicians should assist
research laboratories in eﬀorts to obtain feline Ehrlichia spp.
isolates for comparative microbiologic studies.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR assays have been used to successfully diagnose Ehrlichia
infections in cats through the ampliﬁcation of a variety of gene
targets and comparison of DNA sequences with known Ehrlichia
species. 132 , 139–149 The same assays used for dogs can be applied
to cat blood and tissue specimens.
Serologic Testing
When antibodies are present, most cats with morulae in
mononuclear cells have had antibodies in sera to E. canis, as
detected using IFA. However, some cats with ehrlichiosis have
been seronegative, and thus clinicians may have to obtain
convalescent samples to document seroconversion. There has
been poor correlation between the detection of E. canis DNA and
seroreactivity. Of three cats with E. canis-like DNA in blood in one
study, none had detectable antibodies to E. canis by IFA in two
diﬀerent laboratories, even though chronic disease existed. 143
Subsequent studies have examined the combination of serologic
and molecular test results for detection of Ehrlichia spp. infection
in cats. 140–142 , 146 , 156 Of eight cats from Brazil that were PCR
positive for E. canis, six had serum antibodies to E. canis by IFA.
141 In another study, 12 of 20 cats that were PCR positive for E.
canis had antibodies. 140 These results suggest that not all cats
seroconvert when infected with Ehrlichia spp., that another E.
canis-like organism that does not induce cross-reacting antibodies
is present, or the sensitivity of currently available serologic assays
is poor. In another study, ﬁve cats with presumed ehrlichiosis had
serum antibodies that reacted with N. risticii but not to E. canis. 175
POC ELISAs designed to detect antibodies reactive to speciﬁc
Ehrlichia spp. peptides are available for testing dog sera. Because

vetexamprep.ir

these tests do not apply host species-speciﬁc conjugate, use of
feline sera has been reported. 146 , 163 , 177 However, cats’
immunologic reactivity to diagnostic peptides may diﬀer from
that of dogs. For example, one study reported that ﬁve cats
seroreactive to the E. canis p16 peptide were not seroreactive to E.
canis p30/p31-1 peptides or whole cell antigen from E. chaﬀeensis
or E. canis. 146 Hence, a diagnosis of feline ehrlichiosis should
never be based on positive serologic test results alone. Clinicians
should always exclude other potential causes of the clinical
syndrome.
Other Testing
Antinuclear antibody test results are positive in some cats with
Ehrlichia spp. infection. 143 Coombs’ test results have generally
been negative. Neutrophilic polyarthritis and increased CSF
protein concentrations were present in one cat. 143 Lymph node
aspirates, when performed, show lymphoid or plasma cell
hyperplasia.
Diagnostic Imaging
Of cats with ehrlichiosis that had historical or physical
examination ﬁndings consistent with respiratory disease,
interstitial lung pa erns were the only abnormalities reported.
Cardiomegaly was reported in two cats with E. canis-like DNA in
their blood; however, most thoracic and abdominal radiographs
were within normal limits.
Pathologic Findings
Before treatment, pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis was detected
in a mesenteric lymph node from a cat from Colorado with
antibodies against E. canis and N. risticii. 129 Perivascular plasma
cell and lymphocyte inﬁltrates were detected in the lungs,
kidneys, and liver of an untreated lioness in Kenya. 131 After
doxycycline treatment in one cat, ARDS developed that was
followed by death. 143 Neutrophilic and histiocytic myocarditis
and pneumonia, multifocal lymphoplasmacytic nephritis, and
multifocal lymphoplasmacytic pancreatitis were the predominant
ﬁndings. However, Ehrlichia spp. or other infectious causes were
not identiﬁed after death.

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of cats with monocytic ehrlichiosis is as recommended
for dogs (see Table 44.3). Resolution of illness was seen in three
cats following administration of doxycycline at 5 mg/kg, q12hr for
21 days and in one cat after treatment at 10 mg/kg, q24hr for 21
days. 129 , 173 One cat was seropositive 180 days after discharge but
seronegative 1365 days after discharge, and another cat was
seronegative 180 days after completing doxycycline therapy.
Serologic follow-up was available for multiple presumptive cases
in France, 135 , 136 where most cats became seronegative with time.
However, increasing or persistently positive titers can occur as
reported for the dog. 178 Imidocarb dipropionate administered at 5
mg/kg, intramuscularly, and repeated in 14 days was followed by
resolution of disease in two cats in Kenya. 130 Although not
eﬀective in clearing E. canis, imidocarb diproprionate has been
used for the treatment of infected dogs 161 and has been shown to
be safe when administered to cats. 179 Enroﬂoxacin was used to
treat two cats with suspected mononuclear ehrlichiosis 136 ;
however, this drug is considered to be inferior to tetracyclines for
the treatment of ehrlichiosis in dogs. 34 , 69 The Infectious Disease
Study Group of the ACVIM currently recommends treating cats
with suspected clinical ehrlichiosis with doxycycline at 10 mg/kg,
PO, q24h for a minimum of 28 days. 34 Whether the treatment
protocols used to date eliminate the organism is currently
unknown. 180 , 181
Two cats with morulae in mononuclear cells were euthanized
because of treatment failures with tetracycline 4 or doxycycline, 134
and death occurred in another. 143 Thrombocytopenia did not
resolve until 7 months after doxycycline treatment in a cat
infected with E. ewingii. 146

Immunity and Vaccination
Epidemiologic studies of tick-borne diseases in cats document a
lower prevalence of Ehrlichia infections in cats than in dogs, and
fewer tick-borne diseases are diagnosed in cats than in dogs. This
may be due to environmental factors (many cats are strictly
indoors), shorter periods of tick a achment in cats due to
fastidious grooming, decreased testing of cats for vector-borne

vetexamprep.ir

g
g
g
pathogens by veterinarians, and/or potential diﬀerences in canine
and feline immune function. 184 Vaccines for feline ehrlichiosis are
not available.

Prevention
Because routes of transmission for naturally infected cats are
unknown, deﬁnitive statements concerning prevention cannot be
made. Exposure of cats to potential arthropod vectors and
ingestion of rodents should be avoided. Several topical
ectoparasiticides with activity against ticks are available for cats.
However, those with permethrin, deltamethrin, and amitraz
cannot generally be used in cats (see Chapter 13), and use of these
products should also be avoided on dogs that co-habitate with
cats. Isoxazolines have been developed as oral ectoparasiticides
and some formulations have been approved for use in cats. 185
Ehrlichia spp. can be transmi ed by blood transfer, so cats used as
blood donors that are in tick-endemic areas should be screened
using both serology and PCR and excluded if positive. 184–186

Public Health Aspects
Human infection with E. canis has never been reported in
association with cat contact. If cats are housed indoors and
arthropod control is maintained, the risk to humans should be
minimal. Appropriate precautions should be taken to prevent
transmission when handling engorged ticks as well as blood and
tissue specimens from infected cats.

On physical examination, no abnormalities were noted. CBC
revealed no hematologic and biochemistry abnormalities. The
spleen had returned to a sonographically normal appearance,
and the abdominal lymph nodes were markedly reduced in
size. Additional serology or follow-up PCR was not performed.
He was subsequently lost to follow-up.

Feline Ehrlichiosis 129
Signalment

“Squirrel,” a 10-year old female spayed domestic short-hair cat
from Colorado.

History

“Squirrel” was brought to the College of Veterinary Medicine at
Colorado State University because of a 2-week history of
intermi ent fever, anorexia, lethargy, and pain in the lumbar
area. The referring veterinarian completed a CBC and serum
biochemical analysis and reported abnormalities which
included hyperproteinemia (8.9 g/dL; reference range, 5.4–8.4
g/dL), hyperglobulinemia (5.9 g/dL; reference range, 2.9–4.4
g/dL) and hypercholesteremia (263 mg/dL; reference range, 53–
217 mg/dL). Serum antibodies for FeLV, FIV, Toxoplasma gondii,
and FCoV were undetectable. The cat was treated with oral
amoxicillin for 7 days with no improvement and then
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and subcutaneous ﬂuids prior to
presentation.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 3.1 kg.
General: Listless. T = 102°F (38.9°C), HR = 195
beats/minute, RR = 46 breaths/minute. Approximately 7%
dehydrated.
Integument: No clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No clinically signiﬁcant
ﬁndings.
Musculoskeletal: Signs of pain upon palpation of the
lumbar area.
Neurologic examination: No clinically signiﬁcant
ﬁndings.

vetexamprep.ir

Cardiovascular and respiratory systems: No clinically
signiﬁcant ﬁndings.
GI and urogenital systems: No clinically signiﬁcant
ﬁndings.
Lymph nodes: All peripheral lymph nodes were of
normal size.

Laboratory Findings

CBC
abnormalities:
Normocytic,
normochromic
nonregenerative anemia: PCV 25%, MCV 43 fL, MCHC 32 g/dL.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis: 23,700 nucleated cells/µL and 21,330
neutrophils/µL.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Hyperglobulinemia 4.6 g/dL
(reference range, 2.9–4.4 g/dL)
Serum protein electrophoresis: Increased in β1 fraction 0.9
g/dL (reference range, 0.23–0.84 g/dL)
Urinalysis: No clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings.

Cytologic Findings

Paracentesis was performed based on previous ﬁndings of fever
and nonspeciﬁc hyperesthesia and showed a small amount of
ﬂuid with a large number of nondegenerate neutrophils,
moderate numbers of large mononuclear cells, few eosinophils,
and rare small mononuclear cells and basophils.
Exploratory laparotomy
Exploratory laparotomy was performed because of concern for
peritonitis. A 2- to 4-cm, irregular, raised mass was identiﬁed at
the ileocecal junction. The liver was a mo led yellow, nutmeg
color.
Postsurgical Histology and Cytology
Histopathology of the excised ileocecal mass was reported as
inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration of a lymph node. The cells were
primarily neutrophils and macrophages and a diagnosis of
severe pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis was assigned. Liver
tissue showed mild multifocal inﬁltration of bile ducts by
neutrophils and lymphocytes and a diagnosis of mild
cholangitis was assigned. Impression smears of mesenteric
lymph nodes revealed clumps of intracellular gram-negative
organisms in mononuclear cells, morphologically similar to E.
canis.

vetexamprep.ir

Microbiologic Testing

All specimens were negative for routine aerobic bacterial
culture.
No antibodies to Chlamydia spp. were detected (see Chapter
49).
Vector-borne disease serology (IFA): Positive for antibodies to
E. canis at 1:80 and 1:160, 180 days following discharge. Positive
for antibodies to N. risticii at 1:40, 180 days following discharge.

Diagnostic Imaging

Abdominal and thoracic radiographs were within normal
limits.

Diagnosis

Suspected feline monocytic ehrlichiosis.

Treatment

At the referral hospital, Squirrel was initially treated with with
cefoxitin (22 mg/kg, IV, q8h), crystalloids (lactated Ringer’s
solution), cat food puree administered via a gastrostomy tube.
The antibiotic was changed to amoxicillin (22 mg/kg, PO, q12h)
4 days after surgery, upon release to the owner. At
reexamination 4 days after release, Squirrel was lethargic and
febrile (rectal temperature of 103.6°F). Doxycycline (5 mg/kg,
PO, q12h) was administered via the gastrostomy tube. Two
days later, the cat’s a itude improved and fever was absent;
treatment was continued for 21 days. The gastrotomy tube was
removed 14 days following discharge and at that time the cat
was clinically normal. E. canis and N. risticii antibody titers were
negative 1,365 days after discharge.

Comments

In this cat, while organisms cytologically similar to E. canis were
visualized and antibodies to E. canis detected by IFA, active
infection with E. canis was not conﬁrmed through culture or
molecular testing. Where the cat became infected was unclear,
but vector-borne disease testing performed on 17 cats living
within a 2 mile radius of the infected cats identiﬁed 14 and 9
cats with antibodies to E. canis and N. risticii, respectively. The
rationales for paracentesis and exploratory laparotomy were
not completely clear. Two of the seropositive cats had a 2- to 4month history of malaise and one cat lost weight during this

vetexamprep.ir

time. All cats were apparently healthy at the time of blood
collection and no abnormalities were detected by CBC, serum
biochemistry panel, buﬀy coat ﬁlms, urinalysis, or serology
testing for other infectious agents. The two cats with malaise
were treated with doxycycline (5 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 21 days)
which was followed by resolution of illness within days after
initiation of treatment.

45: Anaplasmosis
Jennifer Granick, Michael
R. Lappin, Trevor Waner, Shimon Harrus, and Mathios E. Mylonakis

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Anaplasma phagocytophilum (granulocytic
anaplasmosis), Anaplasma platys (thrombocytotropic
anaplasmosis).
• First Described: First reports of A. phagocytophilum infection
came from sheep in 1951 (Scotland). 1–3 Canine infection was
first reported in the United States (California) in 1982 4 and in
domestic cats in 1999. 5 Anaplasma platys was first reported
in the United States in dogs (Florida) in 1978 6 and in cats in
Brazil in 2010. 7
• Affected Hosts: Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes disease
in dogs, cats, humans, ruminants (European strains), horses,
and camelids. Anaplasma platys causes thrombocytopenia in
dogs and cats.
• Geographic Distribution: In the United States, A.
phagocytophilum is most prevalent in the upper midwestern,
northeastern, and western states. Infection also occurs
throughout continental Europe and the United Kingdom, Asia,
and Russia. The organism has been detected in dogs from
Africa and South America. Anaplasma platys occurs
throughout the Americas, Europe, Asia, Australia, the Middle
East, and Africa.
• Mode of Transmission: Tick vectors, primarily Ixodes ricinuspersulcatus complex ticks transmit A. phagocytophilum.
Rhipicephalus sanguineus is suspected to be the major vector
of A. platys, though this remains unconfirmed.

vetexamprep.ir

• Major Clinical Signs: The major clinical signs of A.
phagocytophilum infection are fever, lethargy, inappetence,
and lameness due to polyarthritis. Vomiting, diarrhea, cough,
and neck pain may occur. Infection by A. platys is usually
associated with no signs, but fever and lethargy are possible.
• Differential Diagnoses: Major differential diagnoses include
other tick-borne diseases (such as ehrlichioses, rickettsioses,
Lyme borreliosis, and babesiosis), bartonellosis, leptospirosis,
primary immune-mediated disease, and lymphoma.
• Human Health Significance: Anaplasma phagocytophilum
causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis. Dogs act as
sentinels for human infection and may carry unfed ticks to
humans on their coats.

Anaplasma Phagocytophilum Infection
Jennifer Granick, Michael Lappin

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Canine and feline granulocytic anaplasmosis are caused by
Anaplasma phagocytophilum, a tick-borne, obligately intracellular
bacterium belonging to the family Anaplasmataceae. Based on
DNA sequencing, the causative agent formerly called Ehrlichia
equi, Ehrlichia phagocytophila, and, in humans, the human
granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE) agent, was removed from the
genus Ehrlichia in 2001 and placed into the genus Anaplasma. 8
Anaplasma phagocytophilum is tropic for granulocytes, primarily
infecting neutrophils, where it forms host membrane-enclosed
morulae. Ticks that belong to the Ixodes ricinus-persulcatus
complex are the major vectors for A. phagocytophilum.
Ricke siae of the family Anaplasmataceae are gram-negative,
nonmotile, pleomorphic bacteria. They are obligate aerobes and
obligate intracellular parasites. 9 All species in the genus
Anaplasma inhabit cell membrane–derived vacuoles in immature
or mature hematopoietic cells of mammalian hosts. 8 Anaplasma
phagocytophilum preferentially infects cells of the myeloid lineage,
predominantly neutrophils and rarely eosinophils. 8 Unlike other

vetexamprep.ir

gram-negative bacteria, members of the family Anaplasmataceae
lack a cell wall, and the absence of a peptidoglycan layer or LPS
makes them dependent upon host cholesterol for survival but
allows them to closely associate inside cellular inclusions. 9
Replication inside vacuoles results in the formation of morulae,
which are basophilic structures detectable by light microscopy
typically 1.5 to 2.5 µm (but up to 6 µm) in diameter, within the
cytoplasm of granulocytes (Fig. 45.1). 10
Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes granulocytic anaplasmosis in
dogs, humans, horses, and, in Europe, domestic ruminants that
include sheep, ca le, goats, and deer. Cats and camelids may also
be aﬀected. A variety of wild animal species, which include
rodents and deer, act as reservoir hosts. For the midwestern and
eastern United States, white-footed mice, the woodland deer
mouse, and eastern chipmunks may act as reservoirs.
Seroreactivity to A. phagocytophilum in white-footed mice in
endemic areas of North America ranges from 10.1% to 85%. 11–14
In the western states, dusky-footed woodrats, gray squirrels, and
chipmunks have all been implicated as reservoirs, but the duskyfooted woodrat is one of the most extensively exposed species
(seroprevalence ranging from 17% to 80%), 15 , 16 followed by the
western gray squirrel (70.7% seroprevalence and 12.1% PCR
prevalence). 17 In Europe, bank voles, wood mice, yellow-necked
mice, shrews, and roe and red deer are likely reservoirs. 18 , 19 In
addition to mammals, birds likely play a role in the spread of
infected ticks. Migratory birds in Europe and North America can
be infected with A. phagocytophilum and evidence suggests that, in
addition to spreading infection, they also can act as reservoirs by
transmi ing infection to tick larvae that co-feed with infected
nymphs. 20 , 21 Dogs, cats, and humans are accidental hosts and
are not important in the transmission of infection to other host
species.
The geographic distribution of granulocytic anaplasmosis
follows that of the Ixodes tick vectors and is expanding as vector
ranges change, likely due to climate change (Fig. 45.2). Because
Ixodes ticks are three-host ticks, and tick-to-tick transmission of A.
phagocytophilum only occurs transstadially, nymph and adult
stages are potential vectors. 8 In the northeastern and upper
midwestern United States, the tick vector of A. phagocytophilum is

vetexamprep.ir

Ixodes scapularis, though recent extension into Ontario, Canada,
has been reported. 22 Dispersal of I. scapularis ticks by ovenbirds
and wood thrushes are responsible for the expanding range of
these ticks both west and south. 23 Ixodes paciﬁcus is the vector in
the western United States. In Europe, the primary vector is I.
ricinus, and the disease has been described in dogs throughout
continental Europe and in the United Kingdom. Ixodes persulcatus
and Dermacentor silvarum ticks transmit the organism in Asia and
Russia. Other Ixodes spp. ticks have also been implicated in
transmission. Ixodes inopinatus has been shown to carry A.
phagocytophilum in Germany, though transmission has not been
veriﬁed. 24 Evidence of A. phagocytophilum infection has been
found in dogs from Brazil and Tunisia, and a closely related
organism was found in dogs from South Africa. 25–27

Many strains of A. phagocytophilum exist that diﬀer in DNA
sequence, geographic distribution, pathogenicity, and host
tropism. For example, strains that infect domestic ruminants in
Europe and white-tailed deer in the United States appear to be
distinct from those that infect horses, humans, and dogs.
Phylogenetic analyses have grouped strains into North American
and European lineages, 28 though there is heterogeneity among
lineages. Further analyses have separated the North American

vetexamprep.ir

lineage into two clades, upper Midwest and Northeast, 29 , 30 and
the European lineage into three other clades. 25 , 29 These
diﬀerences likely have clinical implications. In the Netherlands
and Belgium alone, four distinct and geographically separated
ecotypes were identiﬁed, and only one of these was linked to
human disease. 31 Higher morbidity and mortality rates in
humans seem to be associated with American strains of A.
phagocytophilum compared with those in Europe. 2 , 3 Conversely,
in ruminants, A. phagocytophilum causes signiﬁcant mortality in
Europe but is considerably less pathogenic in North America. 32–35
There is a signiﬁcant mismatch at the spatial scale between clinical
cases in humans, dogs, and horses in the western United States
and infection in the supposed reservoirs. 36 Similarly, the
prevalence of strains causing disease in domestic animals and
humans is decreased in eastern European locales in which roe
deer are present versus those in which red deer predominate. 37
Taken together, these data suggest that multiple distinct A.
phagocytophilum strains, which diﬀerentially infect various
mammalian species, could circulate in endemic ecosystems.

Many seroprevalence studies of dogs and cats have been
reported worldwide. 38 , 39 The seroprevalence varies with
geographic location and whether the animals studied were
clinically ill or healthy. The prevalence of positive antibody titers
in dogs from some regions of Europe and North America exceeds
50%. A study that used a commercially available ELISA assay to
determine the prevalence of seroreactivity to A. phagocytophilum in
more than 400,000 dogs from the United States revealed wide
variation in seroprevalence rates, with some counties in the upper

vetexamprep.ir

midwestern
and
northeastern
United
States
having
40
seroprevalence rates that exceeded 40%.
A 2014 study found
that the overall seroprevalence in these regions were 7.1% and
3.9%, respectively. 41 Interestingly, prevalence of seroreactivity to
A. phagocytophilum in dogs appears to be increasing in some states
and decreasing in others, which may reﬂect changes in
ecosystems, testing, or tick prevention. 42 Less data exists for cats,
though one study found that 3.7% of healthy cats and 21.7% of
clinically ill cats presenting to one practice in Maine were
seropositive for A. phagocytophilum. 43 In feral cats in the
northeastern United States, A. phagocytophilum serum antibodies
were detected in 17 of 175 cats (9.7%) and speciﬁc DNA was
ampliﬁed from blood of 12 of 175 cats (6.9%). 44 Serologic crossreactivity with A. platys may also inﬂuence these data in both dogs
and cats, particularly in areas where Rhipicephalus sanguineus is
endemic.
The seasonal pa ern of disease reﬂects times of peak nymphal
and adult tick activities, as well as periods when humans and
their dogs are active outdoors. In the western United States, A.
phagocytophilum infection occurs most frequently in dogs between
April and July, when nymphal ticks are abundant. Some
infections occur in October, during early questing of adult ticks. In
Minnesota and Wisconsin, most cases are diagnosed in late spring
(May, June) and fall (October, November). 45–47 In a study from
Berlin, most cases occurred between May and September. 48 The
median age of clinically aﬀected dogs is 6 to 8 years (range, 6
months to 14 years). 46 , 47 , 49 , 50 In the upper Midwest of the
United States, a bimodal age distribution has been recognized,
with 25% of dogs 1 year of age or less, and 50% of dogs at least 8
years of age. 46 Aﬀected cats in the northeastern United States
have ranged from 4 months to 13 years of age (mean, 3.7 years). 51
Although no breed predispositions are recognized, in one study,
golden retrievers comprised almost half of aﬀected dogs; this may
reﬂect the popularity of these dogs for outdoor activities. 52
Infection with other tick-borne pathogens is a risk factor for A.
phagocytophilum infection. Evidence for co-infection with Borrelia
burgdorferi is common because B. burgdorferi is transmi ed by the
same Ixodes tick species. 40 , 45 , 46 When a population of 731
naturally exposed dogs from one veterinary practice in Minnesota

vetexamprep.ir

was evaluated, seroreactivity to both A. phagocytophilum and B.
burgdorferi was detected more frequently in dogs with clinical
signs compatible with tick-borne illness than in healthy dogs. 45 In
northern California, dogs seroreactive to A. phagocytophilum were
18 times more likely to be seropositive for Bartonella vinsonii
subsp. berkhoﬃi than dogs that were seronegative. 53 In cats,
seroreactivity to both A. phagocytophilum and B. burgdorferi is also
common. 43 , 44

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Anaplasma phagocytophilum is transmi ed transstadially within the
tick (i.e., from larva to nymph to adult), and not transovarially
(from adult to egg). Dogs and cats thus become infected after
exposure to infected nymphs or adult ticks, which acquire
infection when they feed on wild animal reservoir hosts as larvae
or nymphs (Fig. 45.3). Ticks must a ach for 24 to 48 hours for
transmission to occur. 54 Transmission could potentially occur
more quickly, as A. phagocytophilum can reside in the salivary
glands of unfed Ixodes spp. ticks. 55 Though the mechanisms of A.
phagocytophilum entry into the bloodstream are unclear, in vitro
infection of endothelial cells results in upregulation of cell
adhesion molecules and inﬂammatory mediators that recruit and
promote adhesion of neutrophils to the endothelial surface. 56 This
may serve as a way for the bacteria to disseminate into the
bloodstream. Furthermore, endothelial cells may serve as a
reservoir for persistent infection, though this is controversial and
may be strain dependent.

vetexamprep.ir

Life cycle of Ixodes scapularis ticks
and Anaplasma phagocytophilum infection.
Uninfected larvae (top right) hatch in the late
spring and acquire infection from small rodents
in the summer. They then over-winter (often in
protected mouse burrows) and then molt into
nymphs the following spring. The nymphs feed
in the late spring or early summer on a variety
of animal species including rodents, humans,
deer, and dogs. Nymphs molt into adults in the
late summer to fall, which subsequently feed
on large mammals such as deer, where they
mate and drop off. The females then lay eggs
and die. Dogs, cats, and humans become
infected by nymphs or adult ticks.
FIG. 45.3

Once A. phagocytophilum enters the bloodstream, it a aches to
the sialylated ligands on the surface of neutrophils, such as Pselectin glycoprotein ligand-1. 38 The organism then enters the
neutrophil through caveolae-mediated endocytosis. Anaplasma
phagocytophilum survives in the harsh neutrophil environment

vetexamprep.ir

through dysregulation of neutrophil function and by bypassing
phagolysosomal pathways. It inhibits neutrophil superoxide
production and can reduce neutrophil motility and phagocytosis.
Anaplasma phagocytophilum also reduces the adherence of infected
neutrophils
to
endothelium
and
inhibits
neutrophil
transmigration into tissues, possibly through downregulation of
selectin molecule expression. 38 This may promote its survival in
peripheral blood. Normally, neutrophils circulate for 10 to 12
hours before they enter tissues and undergo death through
apoptosis. Anaplasma phagocytophilum delays neutrophil apoptosis,
which allows it to survive longer periods of time within the
neutrophil. 38 Anaplasma phagocytophilum may also infect other
cell types, such as bone marrow cells, endothelial cells, and
megakaryocytes, although the importance of these cells in the
pathogenesis of infection is not clear.
The clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities that occur in
dogs and cats with granulocytic anaplasmosis probably vary
somewhat in diﬀerent geographic locations as a result of local
strain variation. The vast majority of dogs and cats infected with
A. phagocytophilum show no clinical signs. Some dogs and cats
develop a self-limiting febrile illness, which in dogs occurs after
an incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks. Lethargy occurs in almost all
clinically aﬀected cats and dogs. Fever and inappetence are also
common ﬁndings. Lameness, reluctance to move, polydipsia,
vomiting, diarrhea, and a soft cough can also occur. Generalized
lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly develop as a result of
reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and, in the spleen, concurrent
extramedullary hematopoiesis. 57 Uncommonly, hemorrhage,
manifested as mucosal petechiae, melena, or epistaxis, has been
reported in naturally infected dogs, but co-infections with other
tick-borne pathogens may contribute to these signs in some dogs.
47 , 49 , 50 , 58 Neurologic signs such as seizures, circling, cervical
pain, and decreased placing reactions have been described in a
few dogs from the upper Midwest with granulocytic
anaplasmosis, but one dog with seizures had a history of
idiopathic epilepsy. 47 , 58 Neurologic signs and detection of the
organism in the CSF have been uncommonly reported in humans.
59 , 60

vetexamprep.ir

Infection with A. phagocytophilum results in mild to moderate,
and occasionally severe, thrombocytopenia, although other
cytopenias may also occur (Table 45.1). The mechanism(s) of these
hematologic abnormalities remain unclear. Though A.
phagocytophilum are able to infect megakaryocytes, platelet
production is not aﬀected. 61 Antiplatelet antibodies occur in
serum from humans and dogs with granulocytic anaplasmosis, 49 ,
62 suggesting the possibility of immune-mediated mechanisms of
thrombocytopenia. However, thrombocytopenia occurs in acute
disease, before antibodies are noted, so other mechanisms may be
important. Platelet destruction or consumption might be involved
in the observed thrombocytopenia, as the bone marrow of infected
dogs shows megakaryocyte hyperplasia.
Impaired neutrophil function as a result of A. phagocytophilum
infection may predispose to development of secondary
opportunistic infections or inﬂuence the outcome of co-infections
with other tick-borne pathogens such as B. burgdorferi. Although
uncommon, opportunistic infections have been occasionally
documented in humans and dogs with granulocytic anaplasmosis
and are well recognized in small ruminants. 63
Infection with A. phagocytophilum appears to be self-limiting in
many infected dogs and cats, with minimal fatality. Whether
persistence of infection and chronic disease manifestations exist is
controversial and may be dependent on the infecting strain and
host immune response to infection. In one study, prednisolone
treatment of three dogs that were experimentally inoculated with
a Swedish strain of A. phagocytophilum, up to 6 months after
infection was followed by the development of positive PCR results
for the organism and, in some dogs, thrombocytopenia and
reappearance of morulae on blood smears. 64 None of these dogs
were treated with doxycycline. In another study, six dogs were
inoculated with A. phagocytophilum via ticks harvested in the
northeastern United States. 65 Prednisolone administration did not
result in reactivation of infection regardless of whether or not the
dogs were treated with doxycycline prior to immunosuppression.
However, one dog’s blood was positive for A. phagocytophilum via
PCR 24 weeks after inoculation. Persistent infection is not
recognized in humans, 66 and there is li le evidence for persistent

vetexamprep.ir

infection in naturally infected dogs; thus, the clinical signiﬁcance
of these experimental ﬁndings remains unclear.
Physical Examination Findings
The most common ﬁndings on physical examination in dogs
include lethargy, fever (up to 106.7°F [41.5°C]), dehydration,
tachypnea, mild peripheral lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
38 , 61 Scleral injection in dogs and conjunctivitis in cats may be
noted. Lameness, reluctance to move, swollen joints, and pain on
joint manipulation may also be detected in some dogs. Increased
lung sounds, abdominal pain, diarrhea, epistaxis, petechial
hemorrhages, and neurologic signs such as circling, cervical pain,
and decreased placing reactions occur uncommonly.
Physical examination ﬁndings reported in cats have been
similar to those described in dogs, and include fever, lethargy,
tachypnea, increased lung sounds, mild abdominal pain,
hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, vomiting, ataxia, hyperesthesia,
muscle and joint pain, lameness, conjunctivitis, and ocular
discharge. 39 , 51 , 67–69

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Granulocytic anaplasmosis should be suspected in dogs and cats
with acute febrile illness and thrombocytopenia that reside in
endemic areas, regardless of tick exposure history. Diagnosis
relies on detection of morulae within granulocytes, results of
acute and convalescent serology, or molecular testing using PCR
assays. The diagnostic criteria for conﬁrmed human granulocytic
anaplasmosis are clinical signs and laboratory ﬁndings suggestive
of granulocytic anaplasmosis together with: (1) a fourfold rise in
antibody titer to A. phagocytophilum; (2) presence of A.
phagocytophilum antigen in tissue via immunoﬂuorescence; (3) a
positive PCR test result using speciﬁc A. phagocytophilum primers;
or (4) isolation of A. phagocytophilum from blood. 66 Consistent
clinical signs along with either detection of morulae in the blood
or a single positive antibody titer of ≥ 640 is considered supportive
of, but not diagnostic for, infection. 66 These criteria could also be
applied to dogs. The use of multiple diagnostic modalities may be

vetexamprep.ir

needed to conﬁrm the diagnosis of granulocytic anaplasmosis in
some dogs and cats.

Complete Blood Count
Thrombocytopenia occurs in approximately 90% of dogs with
granulocytic anaplasmosis. 46 , 47 , 49 , 50 , 70 The platelet count in
thrombocytopenic dogs is often mild to moderately decreased,
though can occasionally be as low as 5,000 platelets/µL (see Table
45.1). 46 , 47 , 49 , 50 , 70 In one study of 54 thrombocytopenic dogs
with PCR-conﬁrmed granulocytic anaplasmosis, 39% had severe
thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts below 30,000/µL. 70 The
majority of aﬀected dogs are lymphopenic, but lymphocytosis can
occur. 47 , 49 , 50 Circulating reactive lymphocytes may be present.
Anemia is common and typically mild and nonregenerative. In
one study, a direct Coombs test was positive in 17% of dogs
tested, suggesting a possible immune-mediated component to
anemia in some dogs. 70 Both neutrophilia and neutropenia occur,
but most dogs have neutrophil counts that lie in the lower half of
the reference range. Low numbers of band neutrophils, as well as
mild neutrophil toxicity, are often present. Monocytopenia or
monocytosis can occur. 47 , 49 , 50 Cytologic examination of blood
smears often reveals morulae within granulocytes (Fig. 45.4).
Morulae were detected in neutrophils from 36%, 56%, 67%, and
100% of dogs in four respective case series. 47 , 49 , 50 , 52 Morulae
appear as early as 4 days after experimental inoculation of dogs,
well before seroconversion, and persist for 4 to 8 days. 57 The

vetexamprep.ir

morulae are indistinguishable from those of Ehrlichia ewingii, so
serology or PCR assays are needed to conﬁrm A. phagocytophilum
infection.
Presence of thrombocytopenia in cats with PCR-conﬁrmed
granulocytic anaplasmosis is variable and moderate in severity
when it occurs. In two reports from the northeastern United
States, 2 of 5 cats and 7 of 16 cats had thrombocytopenia at the
time A. phagocytophilum DNA was ampliﬁed from blood. 69 , 71 In
cats infected with A. phagocytophilum and B. burgdorferi after
infestation with I. scapularis wild caught ticks from Rhode Island,
lymphopenia was the only signiﬁcant CBC ﬁnding. In one study
of 16 cats, lymphopenia was detected in 7 of 11 cats with CBC
results available for review. 71 In the same 11 cats, morulae were
detected in neutrophils of three cats.
Serum Biochemical Tests
The most frequent serum biochemistry ﬁnding in dogs with
granulocytic anaplasmosis is mild to moderate hypoalbuminemia
(Table 45.2). Mild hyperglobulinemia, mild electrolyte
abnormalities (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic
acidosis), and a mild increase in the activities of serum ALP and to
a lesser extent ALT may occur. 47 , 50 , 52 , 61 , 70 Abnormalities in
serum biochemical panel results from experimentally or naturally
infected cats are uncommon. 39 , 69 , 71 , 72
Urinalysis
Urinalysis in dogs with granulocytic anaplasmosis may reveal
isosthenuria, hyposthenuria, and proteinuria. Increased urine
protein-to-creatinine ratios were reported in two aﬀected dogs
from the United States (1.5 and 2.2), 61 but there is no evidence
that A. phagocytophilum infection causes severe glomerulonephritis
in dogs. Proteinuria was detected by dipstick in 2 of the 4
naturally infected cats tested in one report of 16 cases. 71
Synovial Fluid Analysis
Dogs with granulocytic anaplasmosis can develop neutrophilic
polyarthritis. In one study, 13 of 63 dogs had clinical signs and
physical examination ﬁndings of lameness and 3 had synovial
ﬂuid cytologic ﬁndings consistent with immune-mediated

vetexamprep.ir

polyarthritis. 70 Cytologic examination of synovial ﬂuid in these
dogs revealed increased numbers of nondegenerate neutrophils.
In some aﬀected dogs, morulae are found within these cells and
the synovial ﬂuid can be PCR positive (Fig. 45.4C). 70
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Thoracic radiographs are usually normal in dogs with
granulocytic anaplasmosis but may show a mild interstitial
inﬁltrate. Focal alveolar inﬁltrates occur as well. 73
Sonographic Findings
Abdominal ultrasound may reveal splenomegaly, with a
hypoechoic spleen, or mild abdominal lymphadenomegaly.

Serologic Diagnosis
Diagnosis of granulocytic anaplasmosis can be accomplished with
acute and convalescent serology. Many veterinary laboratories
perform serologic testing using IFA techniques. IgG antibodies are
ﬁrst detectable approximately 8 days after exposure, 2 to 5 days
after morulae appear. As a result, early in the course of illness,
antibodies may be undetectable. PCR assays may be more useful
for diagnosis of acute infection in the absence of detectable
morulae. Because positive titers can reﬂect previous exposure,
demonstration of a fourfold rise in titer is required. Antibody
titers may persist for many months. 52 , 64 In some human patients,
antibody titers have persisted as long as 3 years. 63 In the United
States, a silicon disc-based ELISA assay is available commercially
for detection of antibodies to A. phagocytophilum (Accuplex 4,
Antech Diagnostics, Irvine, CA, USA). The performance of this
assay when compared with IFA requires further study. An inclinic lateral-ﬂow ELISA device (SNAP 4Dx Plus, IDEXX
Laboratories, ME, USA), which uses a recombinant Msp2/p44
protein, is also available for the detection of antibodies to
Anaplasma species in dog serum. Positive results obtained with
these ELISA assays do not imply that A. phagocytophilum is the
cause of illness, and as with IFA testing, negative results can occur
in dogs with acute illness due to the lag in antibody production
relative to the onset of clinical signs.
Serologic cross-reactivity between Anaplasma species occurs.
Dogs infected with A. platys also seroreact to A. phagocytophilum

vetexamprep.ir

antigen; this includes the recombinant Msp2 assay. 40 Serologic
cross-reactivity between A. phagocytophilum and Ehrlichia canis also
occurs, but is relatively uncommon and minor. 50 , 73 , 74 Dogs
diagnosed with granulocytic anaplasmosis that have antibodies to
A. phagocytophilum generally lack antibodies to E. canis using IFA
testing. 38 , 40
While not approved by the USDA for use with feline serum, one
commercially available device (SNAP 4Dx Plus, IDEXX
Laboratories, ME, USA) has been shown to detect A.
phagocytophilum and B. burgdorferi antibodies in sera from
naturally exposed and experimentally infected cats. 43 , 72
Antibodies against A. phagocytophilum in feline sera can also be
detected by IFA.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Several endpoint and real-time PCR assays for A. phagocytophilum
exist for detection of A. phagocytophilum DNA in peripheral blood,
buﬀy coat, bone marrow, or splenic tissue. These can be useful for
early diagnosis of granulocytic anaplasmosis in dogs and cats. The
sensitivity and speciﬁcity of PCR assays may vary depending on
the assay design and the laboratory used. Most, but not all, assays
detect either the 16S rRNA gene or the outer surface protein gene
msp2 (p44). Assays that detect the msp2 gene are usually speciﬁc
for A. phagocytophilum, whereas assays that detect the 16S rRNA
gene may detect other Anaplasma species, and even other bacteria.
Anaplasma phagocytophilum DNA has occasionally been ampliﬁed
from healthy dogs, so results must be interpreted in light of the
clinical signs. 45 In experimentally infected dogs, whole-blood
PCR becomes positive several days before and after morulae
appear on blood smears. 57 , 64
In cats that are experimentally infected with A. phagocytophilum
and B. burgdorferi following I. scapularis infestation, DNA can be
ampliﬁed from blood up to 2 weeks before detection of antibodies.
72 This has also been documented in some ﬁeld cases. 69
Culture
Anaplasma phagocytophilum can be isolated in human
promyelocytic leukemia cell lines (HL-60) and tick embryo cell
lines. Culture is highly sensitive for diagnosis of acute infection in

vetexamprep.ir

human patients, 75 but it is not routinely used in dogs for
diagnostic purposes because it requires special facilities, technical
expertise, and prolonged incubation.
Pathologic Findings
Li le information is available regarding the pathology of
granulocytic anaplasmosis in dogs or cats. Tissue injury appears
to result from the host inﬂammatory response, rather than the
bacterial infection itself. 76 In humans, splenic lymphoid
depletion, macrophage aggregates and apoptosis within the liver,
paracortical lymphoid hyperplasia, and hemophagocytic cells
within reticuloendothelial tissues have been described. 77

Treatment and Prognosis
The treatment of choice for granulocytic anaplasmosis in dogs and
cats is doxycycline (5 mg/kg, PO, q12h). 39 , 78 In 16 naturally
infected dogs, doxycycline therapy for 28 days resulted in clinical
resolution in all dogs, and all dogs were negative by molecular
testing of blood 1 and 2 months after initiation of therapy. 78 The
optimum duration of therapy is unknown, but 2 weeks appears to
be suﬃcient. The prognosis is excellent. Most dogs show clinical
improvement within 24 to 48 hours of treatment, although some
dogs require more than 1 week of treatment before clinical signs
resolve. 46 , 50 , 78 Platelet counts often normalize 2 to 14 days after
treatment is initiated, though in one study 4/16 dogs remained
thrombocytopenic after a 4-week course of doxycycline. 46 , 78 In
one study, 30% of 23 owners reported that their dog returned to
normal activities in 1 to 2 days after treatment was initiated, 30%
reported this took 3 to 5 days, 21% reported this took 1 to 3 weeks,
and 17% reported that it took 1 month or longer for their dogs to
return to normal activity. 46 Death due to granulocytic
anaplasmosis has not been described in dogs or cats. Intravenous
crystalloid ﬂuids and antiemetics may be required for supportive
care until clinical signs improve.

Immunity and Prevention
The immune response to A. phagocytophilum infection is not fully
characterized. Both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses
appear to be important in clearance of infection. Host cytokines
such as IFN-γ may play a role in the initial control of A.
phagocytophilum infection 79 , 80 but may also contribute to the
inﬂammatory process associated with disease. 81 In lambs, A.
phagocytophilum evades the host immune response through
diﬀerential expression of MSP2, an outer surface protein involved
in immune recognition. 82 Variation in MSP2 also occurs in
chronically infected woodrats. 83 Further research is required to
document whether persistence occurs through similar
mechanisms in other host species. It is possible that recovery from
natural infection confers long-term protection against
development of disease. Reinfection has not been reported in
dogs, but was described in one human patient. 84
A vaccine for granulocytic anaplasmosis is not available for
companion animals. There is one study of cats experimentally
infested with A. phagocytophilum and B. burgdorferi containing ticks
from Rhode Island, twice, 6 months apart. 85 In that study,
repeated infection was documented in one of the four cats with

vetexamprep.ir

primary A. phagocytophilum infection, suggesting that immunity
against the agent was not permanent.
Infection may be prevented by avoidance of tick exposure,
prompt tick removal, and use of topical ectoparasiticides (see
Chapter 13). Although not a guaranteed protection, combinations
of topical imidacloprid and permethrin; or ﬁpronil, amitraz, and
(S)-methoprene; and imidacloprid and ﬂumetrin prevent
transmission of A. phagocytophilum to dogs from infected ticks. 86–
88

Public Health Aspects
Anaplasma phagocytophilum infection was ﬁrst recognized in
humans in the upper Midwest of the United States in the early
1990s and has since been increasingly recognized in humans from
the United States, Europe, and Asia. Men are aﬀected slightly
more frequently than women. In Europe, the disease is most
commonly reported in Sweden and Slovenia, where it was ﬁrst
reported in 1997, and those involved in forestry, hunting, farming,
and veterinary care are at most risk. 89 , 90 Morulae are observed
less often in humans with granulocytic anaplasmosis in Europe,
and the disease may be milder than that described in humans
from the United States.
Human granulocytic anaplasmosis closely resembles the
disease in dogs, which has been described as an “inﬂuenza-like
illness after a tick bite.” 91 The most common clinical signs
reported in human patients are myalgia, headache (which is often
severe), malaise, and chills. Anorexia, nausea, arthralgias, and
cough may also occur. 66 , 91 , 92 The disease typically resolves
within 2 months in the absence of appropriate antibiotic
treatment. Occasionally, more severe disease may occur. In one
study, up to 17% of aﬀected humans required admission to an
intensive care unit. 91 Death occurs in 1% or fewer clinically
aﬀected humans, usually as a result of complications such as a
septic or toxic shock–like syndrome, respiratory insuﬃciency,
opportunistic fungal or viral infections, rhabdomyolysis, acute
renal failure, hemorrhage, or neurologic disease. 66 Severe illness
tends to occur in humans of advanced age or with concurrent
immunosuppressive illness or drug therapy. Peripheral blood
neutrophils containing morulae are present in 80% of cases,

vetexamprep.ir

though only a low number of neutrophils may be infected. 91
Laboratory testing of peripheral blood typically reveals normal or
slightly decreased white blood cell and platelet counts, sometimes
with a neutrophilic left shift, and mild to moderate elevation of
hepatic transaminase activities. In the United States, the disease is
reportable to the CDC. Dogs act as sentinels for human exposure
and may be a source of infection through mechanical carriage of
infected ticks to humans. 93 , 94 Blood from aﬀected dogs should
be handled with caution, needle-stick injuries should be avoided,
and precautions should always be taken when performing
necropsies on an animal with suspected A. phagocytophilum
infection.

Anaplasma Platys Infection
Trevor Waner, Shimon Harrus, Mathios Mylonakis

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Anaplasma platys (previously Ehrlichia platys), is the cause of
infectious canine cyclic thrombocytopenia (ICCT). The disease
was ﬁrst described by Harvey et al. in the United States in 1978 6
and since then it has been reported worldwide. 95 Anaplasma
platys is an obligatory intracellular ricke sial organism which has
a tropism for platelets (Figs. 45.5 and 45.6). To date, the organism
has not been cultivated in vitro. The reclassiﬁcation of the
organism in 2001 as Anaplasma was based on nucleotide sequences
of the heat shock protein gene (groEL), the heat shock operon
(groESL), and the citrate synthase gene (gltA). 8
Based on the identiﬁcation of A. platys DNA in Rh. sanguineus
(the brown dog tick) from diﬀerent regions of the world, and the
molecular evidence for transstadial transmission by Rh. sanguineus
sensu lato, it is most likely that A. platys is transmi ed by this tick
species. 96 , 97 One study from Thailand identiﬁed A. platys DNA
in Dermacentor auratus ticks from dogs. 98 Notwithstanding, no
evidence was present that this tick species could potentially
transmit the organism to dogs. The possibility that D. auratus ticks
may have passively ingested A. platys while feeding on infected
dogs is more likely.

vetexamprep.ir

Recent studies have suggested that vertical transmission of A.
platys from pregnant bitches to their oﬀspring (maternal
transmission), during the ﬁrst half of gestation, might occur. 99 ,

100

Although the disease has been identiﬁed as a disease of dogs,
there is growing evidence that A. platys can infect a number of
other animal species. Molecular evidence has identiﬁed the
possibility of infection of cats with A. platys. 7 , 101 In both reports,
the cats were thrombocytopenic. One of the cats had anorexia and
inclusion bodies were observed in platelets. 7 In Portugal, A. platys
has been reported in dogs, ticks, and red foxes, and recently in red
deer and wild boars. 102 Other animals reported to be infected
with A. platys include Bactrian camels in Xinjiang, China 103 ;
Arabian camels (Camelus dromedarius) in Tunisia 104 ; and ca le in
Algeria. 105 The ability of A. platys to cause disease in these host
species has not been established. The importance of these ﬁndings
lies in the possibility that these animals may serve as a reservoir
for A. platys.

Clinical features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
There is some evidence that a variation in the virulence and
pathogenesis of diﬀerent A. platys strains exists between the
United States and Australia compared with countries bordering
the Mediterranean basin, suggesting that A. platys strains from the
la er geographic locations are more pathogenic. 106 Co-infection
with other vector-borne pathogens, which can modify or even
exacerbate clinical signs, may also inﬂuence disease severity. 107
Increased intraoperative hemorrhage was described in dogs coinfected with A. platys and E. canis, 107 but this more likely reﬂects
the inﬂuence of E. canis, which is the more pathogenic ricke sial
species.

Dogs with milder forms of infection may show minimal clinical
signs such as fever and hematochezia; rarely more severe clinical
signs have been recognized. 108 These include anorexia, fever,
cutaneous petechiae, ecchymoses, hyphema, hematuria,
hematochezia, and epistaxis. Cutaneous signs including
hyperkeratosis, alopecia, and erythema have been described in a
study of 32 naturally infected dogs from the Mediterranean basin
region. 109 However, the authors noted that although the
prevalence of cutaneous signs was high (31.3% of dogs), the

vetexamprep.ir

results should be interpreted carefully as other vector-borne
diseases that cause cutaneous lesions are endemic in the area.
Lethargy and musculoskeletal disorders were observed less often,
and splenomegaly, ocular lesions, and dehydration were
infrequently observed. 109

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Thrombocytopenia is the hallmark of A. platys infection. Mild
nonregenerative anemia may also occur. Blood smear evaluation
may reveal reactive lymphocytes and monocytes. 109 Morulae in
the platelets have been documented to be present in dogs
artiﬁcially infected IV with A. platys after 7 to 19 days. 110 Cycles
of thrombocytopenia may occur at intervals of 1 to 2 weeks. 95
Microscopic Detection in Blood Smears
Diagnosis can be made when the morulae are observed within
platelets on blood smears (see Fig. 45.5); however, this is
insensitive. The cyclic nature of the thrombocytopenia severely
limits this diagnostic technique due to the low levels of
bacteremia during thrombocytopenic episodes (Fig. 45.7);
therefore, additional tests are recommended in order to conﬁrm a
diagnosis. Moreover, platelet inclusions such as dense bodies and
alpha granules can be mistaken for morulae.
Serologic Testing
Serologic cross-reactivity exists between A. platys and A.
phagocytophilum 111 ; however, cross-reactivity between A. platys
and E. canis is negligible. 112 Seroconversion of experimentally
infected dogs occurs shortly after the ﬁrst episode of bacteremia.
113 An immunoblot analysis based on recombinant A. platys major
outer membrane proteins, P44 and Omp-1X, has been developed
as a simple tool for the detection of antibodies against A. platys. 114
However, such assays require laboratory expertise.
Point-of-care (POC) ELISA test kits that detect Anaplasma
antibodies are available commercially (e.g., SNAP 4Dx Plus Test,
IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME, USA). 115 , 116 Due to the
cross-reaction between A. platys and A. phagocytophilum

vetexamprep.ir

antibodies, it is not possible to distinguish between the two, which
can be problematic when both agents exist in the same geographic
region. A positive result indicates exposure to either or both of the
agents. It should also be taken into account that antibodies to A.
platys only develop 1 to 2 weeks after infection; therefore, a
recently infected dog might be seronegative to A. platys. A
continuingly rising titer (paired titers) would indicate an active
infection with either agent.
Molecular Detection
Considering the limitations of microscopy and serology in the
diagnosis of A. platys infection, molecular detection is considered
the most sensitive and speciﬁc diagnostic test. A number of PCRbased assays have been developed to detect A. platys in infected
dogs and are oﬀered by commercial veterinary diagnostic
laboratories, often as part of vector-borne pathogen panels. A
POC loop-mediated isothermal ampliﬁcation (LAMP)-based assay
has been developed. 117 Such assays may assist in rapid diagnosis,
although further assessment of their clinical performance is
required.

Treatment and Prognosis
Although the optimal doxycycline dose and period of treatment of
dogs with ICCT is unknown, a similar treatment protocol as
recommended for E. canis (10 mg/kg doxycycline, PO, q24h) for 21
days is currently recommended. 118 , 119 However, some dogs with

vetexamprep.ir

the more severe Mediterranean form of ICCT may not respond to
28 days of doxycycline at this dose. 109
Infection with A. platys has also been documented to be a
potential causative agent of secondary IMHA. 120 This should be
considered in the course of the treatment and may aﬀect the
prognosis and the outcome of treatment.
As ticks are responsible for the natural transmission of A. platys,
vector control prophylaxis is recommended to prevent the spread
of ICCT (see Chapters 13 and 109).

Public Health Aspects
Infection with A. platys was documented in two women from
Venezuela. 121 In one case, A. platys morulae were identiﬁed
ultrastructurally and in the second case A. platys DNA was
ampliﬁed. In another report, a veterinarian with extensive animal
and vector exposure in Grenada, Ireland, and South Africa was
diagnosed with a co-infection of A. platys, Bartonella henselae, and a
Mycoplasma species. 122 Furthermore, emphasizing the zoonotic
potential of A. platys, sequential PCR testing has provided
molecular evidence supporting intravascular persistence of A.
platys and Ehrlichia spp. in two humans and their dog. 123

Case Example
Signalment

“Loki,” a 2-year-old male neutered Siberian Husky dog from
Minneapolis, MN.

History

Loki’s owner reported a 3-day history of inappetence and
lethargy and a 2-day history of vomiting. Diarrhea was not
observed. Loki continued to drink normally. Loki’s owner also
noted that he had been displaying some reluctance to lie down.
The owner removed a tick from Loki about 1 week before
presentation. He was up to date on core vaccines. Loki had no
travel history outside of Minnesota.

Physical Examination

vetexamprep.ir

Body weight: 29.0 kg.
General: Quiet, alert, and responsive. Temperature =
104.3°F (40.2°C), HR = 130 beats/minute, RR = 32
breaths/minute, mucous membranes pink, CRT = 1
second.
Integument: Healthy haircoat was present. No
ectoparasites observed. No evidence of petechiation or
ecchymoses.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No signiﬁcant abnormalities
were noted. Mild dental plaque and calculus of canine
teeth, maxillary fourth premolars, and mandibular ﬁrst
molars. Mild amount of ceruminous debris was present
within both ear canals.
Musculoskeletal: Normal gait and range of motion of
joints in all limbs. Repeatedly painful on palpation of
thoracolumbar spine. No pain on palpation of hips,
stiﬂes, tarsi, elbows, or carpi. No joint eﬀusion detected.
Cardiovascular: Normal heart rhythm. Femoral pulses
strong and synchronous. No murmurs detected.
Respiratory: Normal rate and eﬀort. Normal
bronchovesicular sounds. No crackles or wheezes on
auscultation.
GI and genitourinary: Painful on palpation of mid to
caudal abdomen (possibly referred back pain). No
obvious masses, organomegaly, or ﬂuid waves detected.
Lymph nodes: Peripheral lymph nodes small and
symmetrical.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 37.0% (37.5%–60.3%), MCV 68.1 fL (63–75.3 fL),
MCHC 34.7 g/dL (33.6–37.4 g/dL), WBC 6920 cells/µL
(3,880–14,570 cells/µL), neutrophils 6,570 cells/µL (2,100–
11,200 cells/µL), lymphocytes 280 cells/µL (780–3,360
cells/µL), monocytes 70 cells/µL (0–1200 cells/µL),
platelets 65,000 platelets/µL (129,000–395,000 platelets/
µL).
Blood smear ﬁndings: 1+ echinocytes, 1+ reactive
lymphocytes, 1+ large platelets, few morulae present

vetexamprep.ir

within neutrophils.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 137 mmol/L (145–153
mmol/L), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.6–5.3 mmol/L),
chloride 105 mmol/L (109–118 mmol/L), bicarbonate 17.4
mmol/L (15–25 mmol/L), phosphorus 3.8 mg/dL (3.3–6.8
mg/dL), calcium 10.1 mg/dL (9.3–11.5 mg/dL), BUN 8
mg/dL ( 9–31 mg/dL), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.6–1.6
mg/dL), glucose 107 mg/dL (75–117 mg/dL), total protein
6.6 g/dL (5.0–6.9 g/dL), albumin 3.0 g/dL (2.7–3.7 g/dL),
globulin 3.6 g/dL (1.7–3.5 g/dL), ALT 48 U/L (22–92 U/L),
AST 39 U/L (16–44 U/L), ALP 132 U/L (8–139 U/L),
creatine kinase 115 U/L (36–348 U/L), GGT 3 U/L (0–6
U/L), cholesterol 440 mg/dL (143–373 mg/dL), total
bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL (0–0.3 mg/dL), magnesium 2.2 mg/dL
(1.7–2.4 mg/dL).
Urinalysis: SPG 1.007; pH 7.5, no protein (SSA), no
bilirubin, no hemoprotein, no glucose, 0–1 WBC/HPF,
occasional RBC/HPF, no crystals, 5–20 lipid droplets/HPF.

Imaging Findings

Abdominal radiographs: Serosal margin detail was good
throughout the abdomen. The stomach was mildly distended
with gas. Small intestinal size was diﬀusely normal, and the gas
content of the small intestine was appropriate. No fecal material
was identiﬁed in the colon, but there was no colonic distention.
The liver, spleen, and kidneys appeared normal. The urinary
bladder was moderately to markedly distended with ﬂuid.
Fluid was persistently present in the caudal portion of the
intrathoracic esophagus. The caudal vena cava was mildly
small. No musculoskeletal abnormalities were seen.

Serology

Negative for heartworm antigen, negative for antibodies to
Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, and Borrelia (SNAP 4Dx Plus Assay,
IDEXX Laboratories, ME, USA).

Diagnosis

Canine granulocytic anaplasmosis.

Treatment

Doxycycline, 5 mg/kg PO q12h for 14 days; maropitant 2 mg/kg
PO q24hr for 3 days; carprofen 1.9 mg/kg PO q12hr for 5 days.

vetexamprep.ir

Fever resolved and appetite improved within 24 hours after
initiation of treatment. Loki was back to normal within 3 days.

Comments

This dog was diagnosed with granulocytic anaplasmosis based
on the presence of characteristic cytologic ﬁndings of morulae
within neutrophils on blood smear evaluation. The morulae
were presumed to be due to A. phagocytophilum and not E.
ewingii, which can have an identical cytologic appearance, due
to the restricted geography of these infections. The
thoracolumbar pain present in this dog was unusual, but could
have been associated with polyarthritis, despite no obvious
eﬀusion of limb joints. The timing of clinical signs
approximately 1 week after tick exposure is consistent with the
acute nature of this infection. Loki was seronegative using the
SNAP 4Dx Plus test (IDEXX Laboratories) as it was too early in
the course of disease for seroconversion. This highlights the
need for additional testing for diagnosis. In this case, morulae
were present within granulocytes on blood smear evaluation,
though this is not always the case. Additional testing could
have included PCR of whole blood.
