46: Spo ed Fever Ricke sioses,
Flea-Borne Ricke sioses, and
Typhus
Linda Kidd, and Edward B. Breitschwerdt

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Rickettsia rickettsii was first described in
Montana, United States, 1909 1 (Ricketts).
• Cause: Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative, obligately
intracellular bacteria. Other spotted fever group (SFG)
Rickettsia spp., typhus group (TG) Rickettsia spp., and
Rickettsia felis (a separate lineage designated ancestral
group) are important causes of emerging infectious disease in
people. Rickettsia conorii, a SFG Rickettsia spp., causes
Mediterranean spotted fever (MSF) in people and a
doxycycline-responsive disease in dogs that is similar to
Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF). A novel Rickettsia
species causing a febrile illness similar to R. rickettsii and R.
conorii has been more recently reported in dogs in the United
States.
• Affected Hosts: Humans and dogs (R. rickettsii).
• Geographic Distribution: North, Central, and South America.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Ticks (Dermacentor spp.,
Rhipicephalus sanguineus, Amblyomma spp.). Most affected
dogs lack a history of a tick bite. Rickettsia conorii is
transmitted by Rh. sanguineus in the Mediterranean basin.
• Major Clinical Signs: RMSF is generally an acute, febrile
illness. Clinical signs are consistent with a vasculitis because
R. rickettsii infects endothelial cells. Major clinical signs
include fever, vomiting, ocular signs (retinal hemorrhage,

vetexamprep.ir

uveitis, episcleral injection), lymphadenomegaly,
splenomegaly, peripheral edema, cutaneous hyperemia and
necrosis, polyarthritis, and neurologic signs. Signs may be
complicated by prior or simultaneous infection with other tickborne pathogens. The degree to which other SFG Rickettsia,
TG Rickettsia, and R. felis cause illness in dogs and cats is
being investigated.
• Differential Diagnoses: Infection with other tick-borne agents
such as Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia spp.,
Bartonella spp., Babesia spp., and Borrelia burgdorferi should
be considered. Other causes of severe systemic
decompensation and vasculitis such as sepsis and SIRS due
to other causes may mimic RMSF. Leptospirosis and other
causes of vasculitis and thrombocytopenia may also mimic
RMSF. Other differential diagnoses for the neurologic signs
seen in RMSF must also be considered. Appropriate
antimicrobial treatment with doxycycline must begin before the
diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory testing. Misdiagnosis and
delayed or inappropriate antimicrobial drug therapy increase
morbidity and mortality.
• Human Health Significance: Owners and their physicians
should be contacted whenever RMSF is diagnosed in any
canine patient, because illness in dogs can coincide with or
precede illness in humans. Dogs also are sentinels for MSF in
people. Control of flea and tick vectors on dogs and cats is
important to prevent rickettsioses in people.

Etiologic Agents And Epidemiology
Ricke sial diseases are important causes of morbidity and
mortality in dogs and humans worldwide. The terms “ricke sial
disease,” “ricke sioses,” and even the term “Ricke sia” have been
used to refer to several obligately intracellular organisms
including Ricke sia, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Coxiella, and
Neoricke sia. Previously, all of these organisms belonged to the
order Ricke siales and most were in the family Ricke siaceae,
based on their fastidious or intracellular nature and other
characteristics. Therefore, members of these diverse genera were

vetexamprep.ir

collectively referred to as “ricke sial organisms.” 2 , 3 Advances in
molecular biologic techniques have resulted in the reclassiﬁcation
of several of these organisms. Many have been moved out of the
family Ricke siaceae, and others have been moved out of the
order Ricke siales. Currently the order Ricke siales includes only
two families, the family Anaplasmataceae, which contains the
genera Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Neoehrlichia, Wolbachia, and
Neoricke sia; and the family Ricke siaceae, which includes the
genera Ricke sia and Orientia. 3–6 The term “ricke sial” refers to
diseases caused by organisms in the order Ricke siales,
“ricke sioses” refers to diseases caused by organisms in the
family Ricke siaceae (Ricke sia and Orientia), and “Ricke sia”
refers speciﬁcally to members of the genus Ricke sia. 2 , 3 , 5
The genus Ricke sia is divided into the SFG and the typhus
group (TG) and an ancestral group based on phenotypic and,
more recently, genotypic characteristics. 3 , 5–7 There is some
evidence that Ricke sia felis and Ricke sia akari (currently classiﬁed
as SFG Ricke sia) may have separate lineages. 6 , 8 Phenotypic
characteristics that have historically been used to group the
organisms into TG or SFG include the types of vectors that
transmit them, their pathophysiologic manifestations of the
disease, and serologic diﬀerences. Therefore, the division of
Ricke sia into SFG and TG has clinical relevance.
SFG ricke sia species are transmi ed by arthropod (primarily
tick) vectors and infect endothelial cells in mammalian hosts. 3 , 6 ,
7 The two most pathogenic and well-studied SFG ricke siae that
cause disease in humans and dogs are Ricke sia ricke sii, the cause
of Rocky Mountain Spo ed Fever (RMSF) in North, Central, and
South America, and Ricke sia conorii, the cause of Mediterranean
spo ed fever (MSF) in Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.
The ﬁrst human case of RMSF was described in the late 1800s, and
the ﬁrst case of MSF was described in the 1920s. 9 Therefore, these
organisms and their associated diseases are the most well
characterized among the SFG ricke siae. 5 Currently, there more
than 20 species of tick-borne ricke siae. 5 , 7 Some species appear
to be nonpathogenic endosymbionts of ticks. 7 However, some
SFG ricke siae previously thought to be nonpathogenic, such as
Ricke sia parkeri and Ricke sia massiliae, have more recently been
associated with disease in humans. 10–12 Previously thought to

vetexamprep.ir

have rather limited geographic boundaries, many SFG ricke siae
have also been detected in expanding geographic locales around
the world. 7 Increasing travel and the eﬀects of climate change on
tick populations and habitat are thought to be partly responsible
for this phenomenon. 13 , 14
Dogs are sentinels for SFG ricke sioses in humans. Both R.
ricke sii and R. conorii infect and cause disease in dogs. 15–21
Ricke sia ricke sii infection in dogs can occur before, or coincide
with, outbreaks of RMSF in people in the same household or
community. 22–26 Similarly, several serosurveys in endemic areas
have shown an increased risk of MSF in people who live near
dogs that are seropositive for SFG ricke siae. 27–29 Other SFG
ricke sial species infect dogs, but the extent to which they cause
clinical disease has not yet been deﬁnitively established. Species
implicated in natural infection in dogs include R. massiliae, R.
parkeri, R. felis, R. akari, Ricke sia amblyommii, Ricke sia
montanensis, Ricke sia japonica, and Ricke sia australis. 30–37 These
ricke sial infections along with ﬂea-borne ricke sioses are
discussed further below. The DNA from SFG ricke siae R.
massiliae and R. conorii has been ampliﬁed from naturally infected
cats, and cats in regions endemic to pathogenic and
nonpathogenic SFG Ricke sia are seropositive to SFG ricke siae.
38–41 The degree to which SFG ricke siae cause illness in cats has
yet to be deﬁned. 38 , 39 Typhus group ricke siae are a
phenotypically and genotypically distinct group of ricke siae that
are described at the end of this chapter.

Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
Young and purebred dogs are overrepresented in some but not
other studies of RMSF in dogs. 18 , 19 Although some studies
suggest that male dogs are at increased risk, no sex predilection
has been deﬁnitively documented. 18 , 19 , 42 Severe disease has
been
reported
in
English
springer
spaniels
with
phosphofructokinase (PFK) deﬁciency and in German shepherd
dogs. 19 , 42 Dogs that live outdoors, particularly those with access
to shrubs and high grass, are at increased risk for RMSF. 18
Ricke sia ricke sii is transmi ed by several hard (ixodid) ticks
including Dermacentor variabilis (the American dog tick) (Fig.

vetexamprep.ir

46.1A), Dermacentor andersoni (the Rocky Mountain wood tick)
(Fig. 46.1B), Amblyomma americanum (the lone star tick),
Amblyomma cajennense sensu lato (the Cayenne tick), Amblyomma
aureolatum (the yellow dog tick), and Rhipicephalus sanguineus (the
brown dog tick). 7 , 43–47 The primary vectors for R. ricke sii in the
south-central and southeastern United States are Dermacentor
ticks, whereas Rh. sanguineus is the primary vector in the
southwest United States and Mexico. Tick species other than D.
variabilis, D. andersoni, and Rh. sanguineus are also associated with
R. ricke sii in the United States. For example, A. americanum
transmi ed RMSF to a person in North Carolina, and the
organism has been isolated from Dermacentor occidentalis in
California. 45 , 48 Amblyomma cajennense sensu lato species and to a
lesser extent, A. aureolatum transmit this ricke sia in Brazil. 49
Ticks that transmit R. ricke sii feed once during each life stage
(Fig. 46.2). Both transstadial and transovarial transmission occurs
in Dermacentor spp. infected with R. ricke sii, making them a
reservoir as well as a vector of infection. 50 , 51 Dermacentor spp.
and Amblyomma spp. are three-host ticks. Infection is transmi ed
among mammalian hosts and ticks when the tick feeds on
diﬀerent hosts during each stage of molting. The sylvatic cycle for
Dermacentor ticks involves small mammals, such as chipmunks,
pine voles, mice, and ground squirrels. After organisms are
ingested by the tick, SFG ricke siae initially replicate in the
epithelial cells of the tick midgut, enter the hemolymph and
hemocytes, and then multiply in tissues. 51 Once in the salivary
glands, the organism is transmi ed to a naïve mammalian host on
feeding. Transmission can occur within hours of a achment.
However, transmission may be prolonged (up to 48 hours) when
changes in virulence occur under conditions such as starvation of
the tick. These “dormant” ricke siae undergo a process called
reactivation after the tick begins feeding. 52 Therefore, rapid tick
removal can decrease the risk of transmission in many, but not all,
circumstances.

Rhipicephalus sanguineus is a one-host tick, with dogs being the
preferred host. 53 It can adapt to hot environments and commonly
resides in walls of housing structures in close proximity to
humans. 53 Increases in global temperature have been implicated
in association with increased feeding on humans. 13 , 53 The role of
this tick as a reservoir for R. ricke sii in nature has yet to be
elucidated.
The role of dogs as a natural reservoir of infection for R. ricke sii
is also unknown. Dogs are thought to act as incidental hosts when
Dermacentor ticks are the vectors, because ticks rarely acquire the
organism from ricke semic dogs. 54 In contrast, all stages of Rh.
sanguineus acquired infection at a high rate from experimentally
infected dogs in one study, but this may have been related to the
virulence of the ricke sial strain used. 47 A relatively high
infection rate with SFG ricke siae in naturally infected Rh.
sanguineus has also been described. 7 , 46 , 48 Therefore, dogs may
play a role in maintenance of a reservoir of R. ricke sii infection in
endemic foci where Rh. sanguineus is the primary vector.
Direct transmission of R. ricke sii to humans has been described
in laboratory se ings through aerosolization. Direct transmission
from tick blood or other contaminated biologic products also has
the potential to occur. For example, in Portugal, a SFG ricke sia
was directly transmi ed to a human through conjunctival
inoculation after a Rh. sanguineus tick removed from a dog was
crushed. 55 Therefore, care should be taken when handling
laboratory specimens and removing ticks.
RMSF occurs in North, Central, and South America (where it is
known as Brazilian spo ed fever). In North America, most cases
of RMSF occur in the southeastern and south-central states. North
Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Missouri
consistently have the highest reported number of human cases in
the United States (Fig. 46.3). Disease distribution in the United
States primarily follows the distribution of D. variabilis, the
primary vector in this region; however, over the last decade the
importance of D. variabilis as vectors in endemic areas has been
questioned. 56 Although disease can occur at any time of the year,
most cases of canine and human RMSF in the United States are
reported from April through October, months of peak Dermacentor
tick activity. 18 , 57–59 Interestingly, in contrast to the southern

vetexamprep.ir

regions of the United States, a 2016 study showed no seasonality
for the occurrence of human SFG ricke sioses in the western
United States. The authors speculated that moderate temperatures
and year-round activity of Rh. sanguineus, the vector for R.
ricke sii in the southwest, might explain this ﬁnding. 58
This tick also helps explain why the geographic distribution of
RMSF in people in the United States has expanded beyond the
distribution of D. variabilis and D. andersoni. Novel vectors,
including Rh. sanguineus, have played a role in this phenomenon.
This tick was associated with an outbreak of fatal human RMSF in
a previously nonendemic area of Arizona. 24 , 60 Infection existed
in the dog population before the fatal outbreak in people. 25 , 26
Rhipicephalus sanguineus is found throughout the United States,
southern Canada, Mexico, and South America. Notably, Rh.
sanguineus is the main vector for R. ricke sii in some parts of the
Western Hemisphere. 7 Over the last decade, an outbreak in
Mexicali, Mexico, just across the border from California and
Arizona, was also a ributed to R. ricke sii transmi ed by Rh.
sanguineus ticks associated with dogs. 61 This prompted ongoing
surveillance eﬀorts in ticks, dogs, and humans in southern
California, a nonendemic area for RMSF. Ricke sia ricke sii was
not found in Rh. sanguineus ticks removed from dogs residing in
animal shelters located just across the United States border from
the Mexican outbreak. 62 , 63 In addition, a 2020 study found
increased exposure to SFG ricke siae in dogs living in a California
county that borders Mexico that had a history of traveling into
Mexico, compared with dogs living in the same region that had
not crossed the border. 64 These regional discrepancies in
exposure risk may be due to subtle diﬀerences in
microenvironment or other factors that aﬀect regional infection
rates in ticks and further emphasize the need for ongoing
vigilance and surveillance for RMSF. 65
Over the last decade, the incidence of SFG ricke sioses in
people in the United States has increased. 58 There was a
signiﬁcant increase in the number of conﬁrmed or suspected cases
of SFG ricke sioses reported to the CDC in 2010–2014 as
compared with 2005–2009 (Wilcoxon matched pairs signed-rank
test P = .0058;) (Fig. 46.4). Some of the increase may be due to
disease caused by species of SFG ricke siae other than R. ricke sii.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs

vetexamprep.ir

The endotheliotropism of Ricke sia spp. infection results in the
characteristic clinical sign of infection, which is disseminated
vasculitis. In humans, cutaneous macules, papules, and
petechiation that occur in association with vasculitis form a rash
that looks like “spots,” hence the name “spo ed fever.” 9 The
clinical signs, time course of illness, and response to therapy for
RMSF in dogs are very similar, if not identical, to those associated
with RMSF in humans. 18–21 However, cutaneous lesions are not
always present in dogs or humans (“RMSF”). In humans, SFR
caused by organisms other than R. ricke sii are often associated
with an eschar (an area of cutaneous necrosis) formation. 4 , 7 , 14
Clinicians should keep in mind that dogs from nonendemic areas
that have classic signs of RMSF, or those that develop atypical
clinical signs, may be infected with R. ricke sii or other SFG
ricke sial species.
Once the organism is inoculated, it spreads through lymphatics
or directly into the bloodstream to the small capillaries. Ricke sia
ricke sii primarily infects endothelial cells, although smooth
muscles and monocytes may also be infected. 4 , 68 The bacterial
autotransporter outer membrane protein A (OmpA) and outer
membrane protein B (OmpB), are important for a achment,
adhesion, and virulence. 69–71 These proteins also account for
diﬀerences in serotype, and antibodies to OmpB and OmpA
contribute to immunity to reinfection. Other autotransporter
proteins such as Sca1 and Sca2 are important for adhesion. 72
Phagocytosis is likely triggered by adhesion proteins interacting
with host cell receptors. 72 Enzymes such as phospholipase D and
hemolysin C facilitate the release of the organisms into the host
cell cytoplasm. 70 , 71 SFG Ricke sia live in both the cytoplasm and
the nucleus, deriving nutrients and energy from the host cell. 4 , 6 ,
69 They spread from cell to cell by inducing actin to polymerize,
which transports the bacteria directly into adjacent cells. 70 , 73
This helps the bacteria to evade the immune response and to
disseminate without rupturing the cell. They are also released into
circulation when they exit the luminal surface of the cell
membrane or when endothelial cell death or detachment occurs.
70 SFG ricke siae activate the transcription factor NF-κB, which
inhibits apoptosis, fosters further growth of the organism, and
promotes inﬂammation. 69 , 70

vetexamprep.ir

Damage to endothelial cells leads to vasculitis and an increase
in microvascular permeability. Mechanisms of cellular damage
include oxidative injury through the production of reactive
oxygen species, cellular necrosis, and induction of endothelial
apoptosis by CD8+ T cells. 68–70 , 72 , 74 Activation of PFK may be
important in maintaining vascular integrity and energy
metabolism in endothelial cells under hypoxic or oxidative stress,
75 , 76 which may explain the predisposition of English springer
spaniels with PFK deﬁciency to severe disease. Vasculitis
associated with R. ricke sii infection manifests as disordered
primary hemostasis, tissue edema, hypovolemia, and
microthrombosis.
Increased vascular permeability and the associated edema and
hypovolemia results from disruption of adherens junctions,
endothelial cell death, expression of inﬂammatory cytokines, such
as IL1-β, IFN-γ, and TNF-α, and induction of COX-2 with
subsequent prostaglandin production. 68 , 72 Microthrombosis
results from altered platelet adherence to endothelium, increased
tissue factor expression, increased plasminogen activator
inhibitor, and thrombomodulin expression and the release of von
Willebrand’s factor. 68 , 72
Low numbers of organisms circulate in blood for approximately
13 days after infection, which includes the time that clinical signs
are observed. 20 , 77 , 78 Organisms are free and also contained
within circulating endothelial cells, which are thought to be
released from the vessels because of decreased adhesion after
ricke sial invasion. 70 Thus, RMSF is primarily an acute disease.
However, a 2014 study demonstrated a recurrence of clinical signs
44 days and circulating ricke sial organisms 60 days after
experimental infection via D. variabilis ticks in a beagle. 79 Chronic
infection has not been documented in naturally infected dogs or
humans. Co-infection with other vector-borne agents is common.
A 2014 serological survey involving dogs in the United States
showed R. ricke sii and Ehrlichia spp. co-exposure to be the most
common among vector-borne disease agents nationally. 59 Coinfection should be considered if the clinical signs are atypical, if
there is an incomplete response to doxycycline therapy, or if
clinical signs have been present chronically. 18 , 80

vetexamprep.ir

Because of variation in the extent and severity of vascular injury
among dogs, a range of signs can occur, and importantly, disease
manifestations are initially mild and nonspeciﬁc. 16 , 18 , 19 Often,
there is no known history of a tick bite. Therefore, the clinician
(physician or veterinarian) must have a high index of suspicion in
order to correctly diagnose and treat this disease. A delay in
diagnosis and appropriate antimicrobial therapy dramatically
increases morbidity and mortality in humans and dogs. 18 , 57
Lethargy and anorexia are common and may be the only clinical
signs. Vomiting and diarrhea occur frequently in dogs and
humans with RMSF. Melena may be observed, as may a variety of
CNS abnormalities including vestibular disease and seizures. 18 ,
19 , 21 Dramatic and rapid weight loss has been described. 21

Physical Examination Findings
Fever is present in approximately 80% of naturally infected dogs.
Ocular signs are also frequently observed and may include a
mucopurulent discharge, scleral and conjunctival injection and
hemorrhage, conjunctivitis, uveitis, retinal hemorrhage, and
retinitis (Fig. 46.5). Lymphadenomegaly and splenomegaly also
occur. Respiratory abnormalities include nasal discharge,
epistaxis, and tachypnea. Mucocutaneous and cutaneous
abnormalities include petechiae, ecchymosis, peripheral edema
(which can be localized over a joint, the prepuce, or the mammary
chain), hyperemia, and necrosis. Gangrenous necrosis can be so
severe as to require reconstructive surgery after successful
treatment of the acute febrile illness. 16–19 , 21 , 42 , 81 Orchitis and
scrotal edema, hyperemia, and epididymal pain are common in
intact male dogs and should prompt consideration of RMSF when
present. Generalized myalgia and arthralgia can be observed.
Arrhythmias may also be detected. CNS abnormalities can be
focal or generalized and include paraparesis, tetraparesis, ataxia,
hyperesthesia, ataxia, central or peripheral vestibular signs,
stupor, seizures, and/or coma. Neurologic signs are more common
in dogs with a high R. ricke sii antibody titer, which suggests a
longer duration of illness or a delay in diagnosis. 18 Residual
neurologic deﬁcits may occur after infection in severely aﬀected
individuals. Microvascular hemorrhage, thrombosis, hypotension,

vetexamprep.ir

oliguric renal failure, cardiovascular collapse, and coma can occur
terminally.

Diagnosis
Application of a combination of diagnostic tests is often necessary
to conﬁrm infection by SFG ricke siae. Active infection is
conﬁrmed in a patient with compatible acute clinical signs and
demonstration of the organism using PCR assays or IHC, or
documentation of seroconversion (Fig. 46.6). Importantly, a high
index of suspicion based on clinical signs is necessary because
treatment must be instituted before the results of diagnostic tests
(including rapid PCR assays) conﬁrm infection. 18 , 21 Co-infection
with other vector-borne disease agents or alternate causes of
illness should be considered in patients who fail to respond
rapidly to treatment (within the ﬁrst 24 to 48 hours after initiation
of doxycycline treatment). 80 Because direct inoculation into blood
or aerosolization can cause infection, all specimens should be
handled with care and marked clearly as biohazards. Needle-stick
injuries, contact with cuts in the skin, and aerosolization of
ricke semic blood should be avoided.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count

vetexamprep.ir

Thrombocytopenia is common in RMSF and occurs due to
vasculitis and immune-mediated platelet destruction. 82 However,
thrombocytopenia does not occur in all dogs with RMSF. 18 , 21
The white blood cell count may initially decrease and then tends
to increase with duration of illness. 19–21 Neutrophils may have
toxic change. 18 Despite the acute nature of this severe illness, a
nonregenerative anemia may be present and persist until the dog
is treated appropriately and begins to recover. 16 , 18 , 21
Serum Biochemical Tests
Serum biochemical abnormalities can include hypoalbuminemia
(due to vasculitis or protein-losing nephropathy), increased serum
ALP activity, hyponatremia, and mild hyperbilirubinemia. 16 , 18 ,
21 , 83 Hyponatremia is thought to occur secondary to antidiuretic
hormone secretion in response to hypovolemia in people with
RMSF. 57
Urinalysis
Urinalysis results in dogs with RMSF are variable and may
include proteinuria, hematuria and bilirubinuria, and pyuria.
Granular casts can be observed. 18 , 19
Coagulation Profile
Coagulation abnormalities include prolonged APTT and
increased serum ﬁbrinogen concentration. Less commonly,
prolonged PT and increased ﬁbrin degradation products are
observed. Although a prothrombotic state can occur during
fulminant disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation is
uncommon. 16 , 18

Cytologic Examination of Tissue Aspirates and
Body Fluids
Cytologic examination of aspirates from enlarged lymph nodes in
dogs with RMSF is consistent with reactive lymphoid hyperplasia.
18 , 19 Arthrocentesis may reveal neutrophilic polyarthritis. 18 , 19
CSF analysis in dogs with neurologic signs may reveal a mixed
cellular, neutrophilic, or lymphocytic pleocytosis. 18 , 19 , 21 , 84

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnostic Imaging
Thoracic radiographs in dogs with RMSF may show an
unstructured interstitial pa ern. 19 , 85 Testicular ultrasound
ﬁndings may be consistent with orchitis in intact males. 81

Microbiologic Tests
Diagnostic assays available for RMSF in dogs are shown in Table
46.1. Because of the pathogenesis of the infection, laboratory
diagnostics (including serology and PCR assays) may not indicate
that infection is present at the time that clinical signs manifest (see
Fig. 46.6). In addition, most diagnostic tests do not diﬀerentiate
among species of SFG ricke siae.
Culture
Because of the obligately intracellular and extremely pathogenic
nature of R. ricke sii, cell culture is diﬃcult to perform and
processing of specimens for isolation is limited to BSL-3 facilities
(see Table 46.1). Therefore, culture is not commonly used for
routine diagnosis.
Serologic Diagnosis
Indirect microimmunoﬂuorescence (MIF) assays that detect IgM
and IgG antibodies are most commonly used to document
seroconversion in dogs infected with R. ricke sii. 18 Because of a
lack of speciﬁcity, assays that detect IgM alone cannot be used to
accurately diagnose acute RMSF. 86 There is extensive serologic
cross-reactivity among SFG ricke siae, and thus a positive titer
only indicates exposure to SFG ricke sial species. In general, the
infecting species is presumed based on geographic locale, so
RMSF is the presumptive diagnosis in dogs that seroconvert in the
southeastern United States. However, other species of SFG
ricke siae may also be present and potentially induce disease. 30 ,
87 Seropositivity that indicates exposure to SFG Ricke sia is
common in dogs in the United States. Exposure to nonpathogenic
SFG ricke siae, some of which are common endosymbionts in
ticks, may be a common cause of positive titers, particularly low
and persistent titers, to R. ricke sii in healthy people and dogs. 67 ,
88 Serologic cross-reactivity with SFG ricke siae does not appear

vetexamprep.ir

to occur in dogs infected with Bartonella spp. 89–91 In addition,
previous infection with R. ricke sii may result in persistent
antibody titers. 86 Thus, infection with R. ricke sii cannot be
deﬁnitively diagnosed based on a single positive titer. However, a
single high titer in the context of acute and compatible clinical
signs and an appropriate response to therapy suggests infection.
18 Titers are commonly negative early in the course of infection,
because clinical signs often occur before seroconversion in
naturally and experimentally infected dogs. 21 , 86 , 92 Thus, acute
and convalescent serology (run in the same laboratory and ideally
in the same batch) and documentation of a fourfold change in titer
is necessary to conﬁrm acute SFG ricke siae infection. The
convalescent serum specimen should be drawn 2 to 3 weeks after
the acute specimen.

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR testing of whole blood can be used to conﬁrm infection in
seronegative dogs during the acute phase of disease. 77 , 78 , 92 A
sensitive PCR assay that detects and diﬀerentiates among SFG
ricke siae that infect dog blood has been described, and a variety
of PCR assays are available through commercial veterinary
diagnostic laboratories. 92 However, because R. ricke sii circulates

vetexamprep.ir

g
in blood in low numbers and only transiently, the sensitivity of
any diagnostic assay to detect infection in the bloodstream is
limited. One real-time PCR assay, which could detect as few as
ﬁve copies of organism DNA, had a sensitivity of only 53% for
detection of R. ricke sii in acute samples from naturally infected
dogs with signs of RMSF. 92 The sensitivity of another R. ricke sii
PCR assay for detection of R. ricke sii in experimentally infected
dogs ranged from 33% to 100% depending on the day of sample
collection. 78 Furthermore, false negatives can occur after initiation
of appropriate antimicrobial treatment. Therefore, although a
positive PCR assay result conﬁrms infection, a negative result
does not exclude the diagnosis. Some PCR assays can diﬀerentiate
among infecting Ricke sia species, whereas others only amplify
conserved ricke sial DNA targets. 77 , 92 Clinicians should consult
with laboratories to determine the in vitro (analytical) and in vivo
(clinical) sensitivity of a PCR assay and its ability to diﬀerentiate
among infecting Ricke sia species. Whenever possible, it is
important for veterinary and human clinicians to submit
specimens to laboratories that use PCR assays that diﬀerentiate
among Ricke sia species. 58 Samples should be obtained before
antiricke sial antibiotic therapy is administered. Combining PCR
with serologic testing, repeating PCR assays on samples taken
before treatment, and serologic testing of convalescent samples
facilitates diagnosis. 92

Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in dogs with RMSF are consistent with
vasculitis and may include edema, particularly of the ears,
muzzle, and scrotum; and ecchymosis, petechiae, and/or focal
hemorrhages of the skin, mucous membranes, and viscera
(including the brain). Lymphadenomegaly and splenomegaly are
also common ﬁndings. 16 , 17 , 21 , 23
Histopathologic Findings
Microscopically, the predominant lesion is vasculitis. Neutrophils,
monocytes, and/or lymphoreticular cells predominate in the
inﬂammatory lesions. Inﬂammatory cells may surround and

vetexamprep.ir

invade large-, small-, and medium-size vessels of multiple organs
and tissues and this is frequently accompanied by focal necrosis
and hemorrhage. Meningoencephalitis, splenitis, myocardial
necrosis, glomerulonephritis, and renal vasculitis have been
described. 16 , 21 , 23
Direct IFA can be used to detect organisms in skin and other
organs. Identiﬁcation of abundant SFG ricke siae within and
around small- to medium-size vessels and vascular endothelial
cells can conﬁrm infection. 21 In experimentally infected dogs, the
sensitivity of IHC was 78.3%, and organisms could be visualized
between days 7 and 12 of infection (days 3 to 8 of fever). 93 In that
study, specimens collected from areas other than the central focus
of vasculitis were negative. However, in naturally infected dogs,
the sensitivity was 80% for skin specimens collected from the
inguinal region. Half of those specimens lacked gross lesions. 19
Thus, the diagnostic sensitivity of IHC is most likely enhanced by
obtaining lesional biopsies, but may not be decreased when a
lesion is not biopsied. The sensitivity of direct IHC is decreased by
antibiotic therapy. IHC does not diﬀerentiate between SFG
ricke sial species. Gimenez stain can also be used to visualize
ricke sial organisms in tissues or tissue culture isolation a empts,
but this stain is not ricke sia speciﬁc and does not allow for
diﬀerentiation among species.

Treatment
Antimicrobial Treatment

vetexamprep.ir

Appropriate antibiotic therapy must be immediately instituted
based on clinical suspicion for SFG ricke siosis, and before
diagnostic tests conﬁrm infection. Inappropriate or delayed
antibiotic therapy may increase morbidity and mortality. 18 , 57
Some antimicrobial drugs such as trimethoprim-sulfonamides
may worsen disease progression of RMSF in human patients. 57
Doxycycline is the treatment of choice (Table 46.2). It eﬀectively
eliminates infection with R. ricke sii and also has activity against
A. phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia spp., and B. burgdorferi, which may be
present in co-infections or cause disease that resembles RMSF. In
most cases, 7 days of treatment is adequate for RMSF. Treatment
for a few days beyond defervescence is recommended. A longer
course of treatment is recommended for dogs that are co-infected
with Ehrlichia spp. or B. burgdorferi (see Chapters 44 and 69). Tooth
discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, which are permanent
adverse eﬀects of tetracycline use in pediatric patients, has not
been observed with short-term (7–10 days), low-dose
(approximately 2.2 mg/kg q12h) doxycycline therapy in children
less than 8 years of age. 57 , 94 Therefore, as is the case for adults,
doxycycline is the treatment of choice for RMSF in children. 57
Chloramphenicol was eﬀective for RMSF in experimentally
infected dogs. 95 However, it may be less eﬀective than
doxycycline for treating RMSF in humans and has less activity
in vitro against Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis and A. phagocytophilum. 57 , 96
Enroﬂoxacin was eﬀective for treatment of RMSF in
experimentally infected dogs. 95 However, enroﬂoxacin is not
eﬀective for treatment of Ehrlichia canis infections. 97 Use of
parenteral antimicrobial drugs may be necessary in severely
debilitated or vomiting patients.

Supportive Care
Many dogs with RMSF require hospitalization. 21 Aggressive
supportive care for complications such as thrombosis, CNS
deﬁcits, and GI signs may be necessary. Because of the loss of
vascular integrity, ﬂuids should be administered with caution,
and colloids may be warranted in some cases. The clinician should
avoid exacerbation of interstitial edema, which can contribute to
cerebral edema and death. The use of glucocorticoids in dogs with

vetexamprep.ir

RMSF is controversial. Treatment with anti-inﬂammatory and
immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids did not aﬀect overall
outcome in experimentally infected dogs, but ricke semia was
prolonged in dogs concurrently treated with immunosuppressive
doses of glucocorticoids and doxycycline. 98 Anti-inﬂammatory
doses of glucocorticoids have been used in dogs with severe CNS
manifestations and may be necessary topically or systemically for
treatment of ocular abnormalities. 84 , 99

Prognosis
The response to appropriate antibiotic therapy in dogs with RMSF
is rapid (24 to 48 hours). Co-infection with B. burgdorferi, Ehrlichia
spp., Babesia spp., and Bartonella spp. should be considered in
dogs with severe or prolonged clinical signs or dogs that fail to
respond to doxycycline. Residual CNS and other deﬁcits may
occur in severely aﬀected patients. 18 The prognosis is good to
excellent if the disease is diagnosed and treated with appropriate
antibiotics and supportive care early in the course of illness. 18 , 84
Due to the potential clinical severity of RMSF, reactivation of
occult Bartonella spp. infection is possible. 89 In contrast to most
other canine vector-borne infections, doxycycline is not
recommended as a sole treatment for bartonellosis. 100

Immunity And Vaccination
Innate and adaptive (primarily CMI) immunity are important in
the clearance of SFG Ricke sia infections. Dendritic cells (DCs)
serve as a bridge between innate and adaptive immunity. Binding
of ricke sial LPS to DC TLR-4 causes DC activation and
production of inﬂammatory cytokines; recruitment, activation,
and expansion of NK cells and NK IFN-γ production; and DCmediated induction of T-helper 1 and T-helper 17 adaptive
immune responses. 72 CD4+ and CD8+ cells, along with
macrophages and DCs, are believed to be sources of inﬂammatory
cytokines such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β, and RANTES (CCL5).
These cytokines increase the production of nitric oxide synthetase
and hydrogen peroxide by the endothelial cell, which helps to
eliminate the organisms. 69 , 70 The endothelial cells themselves
also produce cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 (CCL2) that

vetexamprep.ir

recruit immune cells and combat infection. It is thought that
endothelial cells present antigen to CD8+ T cells in the context of
MHC I. 72 CD8+ cells appear to be particularly important in
clearance of ricke siae from the endothelium. 101 Antibodies are
not thought to be important initially for clearance of infection
because they form after the fulminant stages of disease. 70 , 72
However, antibodies are long-lived and together with CMI may
prevent subsequent infection. Immunity to reinfection is thought
to be lifelong in people, and experimentally infected dogs did not
develop illness following rechallenge at 6 months and 3 years
after the initial infection. Vaccination is not available for dogs or
humans currently, but may be in the future. 102 , 103

Prevention
The use of acaricides, avoidance of tick-infested areas, and routine
inspection of dogs for ticks after outdoor activities can help to
prevent RMSF. The reader is referred to Chapters 13 and 109 for
information on tick prevention and safe tick removal. Safe tick
removal is especially critical when exposure to R. ricke sii is a
possibility. In cases where Rh. sanguineus is the vector,
environmental control of ticks is particularly important. 104

Public Health Aspects
A “One Health” approach to the management of canine and
human RMSF is important. It has been well established that
people living near dogs and with dogs in endemic areas are at
increased risk for acquiring RMSF. This results from increased
human contact with ticks through interaction with tick-infested
dogs. Interestingly, one 2019 study of personnel working in
veterinary clinics showed that exposure risk was highest in
groomers. 105 Dogs and humans can also independently acquire
the infection from diﬀerent ticks questing in the same
environment, particularly as R. ricke sii is transmi ed
transovarially to oﬀspring. Because dogs have higher exposure to
ticks than their human counterparts, they serve as excellent
environmental sentinels for RMSF. 22 , 23 , 25 , 87 In the United
States, the diagnosis of SFG ricke sioses in humans is notiﬁable to
public health authorities. Some counties in certain states also

vetexamprep.ir

require reporting for dogs, particularly during suspected
outbreaks. 106 From a public health standpoint, it is important for
veterinarians to conﬁrm a diagnosis of RMSF in a dog whenever
possible, and to warn the family of the increased risk of acquiring
a R. ricke sii–infected tick in the same location as the dog acquired
the disease. Veterinarians must communicate with owners and
physicians that infection in a dog may precede tick-transmi ed
infection to owners or neighbors. Clients should be instructed to
remove ticks properly. Education of owners with regard to the
importance of tick control and prevention for both people and
pets and the environment is critical. Novel and well-characterized
species of SFG ricke siae are important causes of emerging
infectious disease in humans. Because dogs are sentinels for
infection, veterinarians play an important role in detection,
deﬁnition, and prevention of illness in their canine patients and
their human companions.

Mediterranean Spotted Fever
Ricke sia conorii subsp. conorii is the cause of an endemic tickborne ricke sial illness of people in the Mediterranean basin and
Africa known as MSF (or boutonneuse spo ed fever). Several
other subspecies of R. conorii (indica, caspia, and israelensis) are
responsible for clinical or subclinical infections in people in India,
Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, respectively. 7 In humans,
the clinical appearance of MSF is similar to RMSF, except that the
presence of an eschar at the site of tick bite is common.
MSF is transmi ed by Rh. sanguineus. It is suspected that this
tick serves as a reservoir for the disease. 7 Whether dogs or other
vertebrate hosts are also reservoirs is uncertain, but
experimentally, dogs are able to transmit the organism to Rh.
sanguineus ticks. 7 , 107 Serologic studies indicate a high rate of
exposure among clinically healthy dogs 29 , 108 and cats in endemic
areas. 108 However, seroconversion was associated with fever in a
2015 study of ill dogs in Italy. 35 Host immunity is likely
important in determining if clinical illness develops in dogs with
MSF. Like RMSF, dogs serve as sentinels for MSF in humans. 7
Interestingly, one study found that R. conorii survived 35 days in

vetexamprep.ir

stored canine whole blood, suggesting that iatrogenic infection
from transfused blood products is potentially possible. 109
Male Yorkshire terriers were the only aﬀected breed in the ﬁrst
clinical report of naturally occurring MSF in dogs. 15 This breed
also had the highest rate of infection with R. conorii in another
study testing for SFG ricke semia in large numbers of dogs in
Italy. 110 An inherent susceptibility to MSF in Yorkshire terriers is
suspected, but uncertain.
Findings of clinical and pathologic studies in experimentally
and naturally infected dogs with MSF are analogous to those
described in RMSF. Clinical signs include lethargy and, less
commonly, vomiting and diarrhea. 35 Physical examination
abnormalities include elevated rectal temperature (generally
40.1°C to 41°C [104.2°F to 105.8°F]), hyperesthesia, peripheral
edema, orchitis, erythema, stiﬀ gait, lymphadenomegaly,
splenomegaly, tachycardia, lameness, conjunctival swelling, and
dehydration. 15 , 35 , 111
Laboratory abnormalities associated with MSF in dogs include
neutrophilic leukocytosis with a variable left shift,
thrombocytopenia,
hypoproteinemia
and
concurrent
hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, and increased serum urea
nitrogen concentration, C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration,
and hepatic aminotransferase activities. Although αhyperglobulinemia is observed in RMSF in dogs as an acute-phase
reaction, the additional observation of increased β- and γglobulins in natural cases of MSF would suggest a longerstanding infection with R. conorii before the onset of clinical illness
or co-infection with other vector-borne pathogens.
Diagnosis is made either by demonstrating seroconversion, or a
positive PCR test, and a corresponding clinical improvement after
antiricke sial therapy. Serologic cross-reactivity with other SFG
Ricke sia preclude deﬁnitive speciation if diagnosis is based on
serologic testing. Because of the high seroprevalance in dogs in
endemic areas, a single positive titer does not conﬁrm active
infection.
Antimicrobial treatment is the same as for RMSF, and response
to doxycycline appears to be rapid. 15 The public health risk of
tick-infested dogs infected with R. conorii would be presumably
high because Rh. sanguineus can become domiciled indoors in

vetexamprep.ir

homes or kennels. This been demonstrated with Rh. sanguineusassociated RMSF in the United States and Mexico. 46 , 112 A higher
association of MSF in people with dog ownership supports this
contention. 113 Inadvertent tick bites and direct inoculation and
subsequent infection sustained during removal of ticks from dogs
have been associated with transmission to humans. 55 , 114 Tick
control in dogs and the environment would have a likely
beneﬁcial eﬀect of reducing the prevalence of this disease in both
humans and dogs. Interestingly, a 2016 serosurvey showed a
decrease of exposure to R. conorii in humans in an endemic area. It
was suggested that widespread tick control in dogs contributed to
the decline in human exposure. 115

Other Tick-Borne Spotted Fever Group
Rickettsiae
Although RMSF and MSF are the most well-characterized SFR in
the world, serologically, genetically, and pathogenically distinct
SFG ricke siae have also been described as important diseasecausing agents in humans. 7 Many closely related SFG ricke sial
species of unknown pathogenicity have been detected in or
isolated from ticks in the United States. Other than R. ricke sii,
SFG species isolated from ticks associated with dogs in the United
States include R. parkeri, R. amblyommii, R. montanensis (formerly
R. montana), Ricke sia rhipicephali, Ricke sia bellii, Ricke sia
andeanae, and R. massiliae. 30 , 83 , 116
Ricke sia parkeri was previously considered to be a
nonpathogenic SFG ricke sia. Its vector is Amblyomma maculatum
(the Gulf Coast tick). Ricke sia parkeri has now been shown to
cause clinical illness in humans in the United States. 117 It is
suspected that many cases of human RMSF that are diagnosed in
areas where A. maculatum is endemic are caused by R. parkeri
rather than R. ricke sii. 58 Ricke sia parkeri also was associated
with a spo ed fever type of illness in hikers in Arizona.
Amblyomma triste was the suspected vector. 118 Human disease
associated with R. parkeri infection appears to be milder and is
characterized by the presence of eschar and lymphadenomegaly,
signs not commonly seen with RMSF. 14 In 2011, R. parkeri was

vetexamprep.ir

ampliﬁed using PCR from overtly healthy shelter dogs in
Louisiana. 34
Ricke sia amblyommii, R. montanensis, R. rhipicephali, and R. bellii
are thought to be of low pathogenicity or nonpathogenic in
humans. 7 However, like R. parkeri, evidence suggests that R.
amblyommii and R. montanensis may cause illness in people in the
United States, and account for some of the reported SFR in areas
endemic for RMSF. 119 , 120 In the last decade, DNA from R.
amblyommii and R. montanensis has been ampliﬁed from the blood
of naturally exposed, apparently healthy dogs. 37 The ricke semia
was short-lived. Ricke sia rhipicephali, R. bellii, and R. andeanae
have not been shown to cause disease in dogs or humans to date.
Ricke sia massiliae has been characterized as a human pathogen
in Europe, and was implicated as a cause of febrile illness in dogs
and people living in a Rh. sanguineus-infested home in Los
Angeles. 30 , 121 Ricke sia massiliae DNA has also been ampliﬁed
from the blood of naturally infected cats and from the blood of a
naturally infected dog. 38 , 122 Ricke sia phillipii (SFG Ricke sia
strain 364D) is the cause of an emerging tick-borne disease known
as Paciﬁc Coast Fever. Paciﬁc Coast Fever is transmi ed by D.
occidentalis ticks. 123 Although cases have been reported in
California, cases could occur within the entire geographic range of
this tick, which includes Oregon to Baja California, Mexico.
Whether it causes disease in dogs has not been determined.
In a 2020 report, a novel, genetically well-characterized
ricke sia species with 95% homology to both R. massiliae and
Ricke sia heilongjiangensis was ampliﬁed from the blood of three
diﬀerent dogs in three diﬀerent regions of the United States. 124
Clinical signs resembled RMSF and the dogs were seroreactive to
R. ricke sii.
Diseases similar to MSF have also been described in people in
the Eastern Hemisphere. Queensland tick typhus (R. australis),
Flinders Island spo ed fever (Ricke sia honei), Australian spo ed
fever (Ricke sia marmionii), African tick bite fever (Ricke sia
africae), Astrakhan fever (R. conorii sub sp. caspia), Japanese
spo ed fever (R. japonica), Far Eastern spo ed fever (R.
heilongjiangensis), North Asian tick typhus (Ricke sia sibirica), and
European tick-borne lymphadenopathy (Ricke sia helvetica,
“Ricke sia sibirica sub sp. mongolotimonae,” Ricke sia slovaca,

vetexamprep.ir

Ricke sia aeschlimannii, R. massiliae) are analogous diseases of
humans caused by other SFG ricke siae and transmi ed by
arthropods in geographically distinct regions. 7 Ricke sia helvetica
is found in Ixodes spp. ticks and has a wide distribution in Europe
and the Far East. Ricke sia helvetica DNA, along with that from R.
japonica, has been identiﬁed by PCR in ticks removed from dogs
and cats in Japan. 125 Dogs and cats have had positive serologic
reactions to this Ricke sia, indicating exposure, and DNA of R.
japonica has been ampliﬁed from dog blood. 126 , 127 Ricke sia
japonica causes transient clinical signs including fever, anorexia,
and depression in immunosuppressed but not healthy
experimentally infected dogs. 33 Antibodies to R. australis have
been documented in dogs in southeastern Australia. Antibodies to
SFG ricke siae have been detected in the blood of dogs and cats in
the Tasmanian region of Australia; however, there was no
correlation between seroreactivity and the animal’s health. 128
Experimental infection in dogs was subclinical, and although
seroconversion occurred, R. australis could not be reisolated. 31
Taken together, these studies suggest that SFG ricke siae other
than R. ricke sii may cause milder disease in dogs, as is the case in
humans, and that novel ricke siosis should be considered in dogs
with atypical clinical signs or those presenting in endemic or
nonendemic areas. Some PCR assays and other molecular
biological techniques may be used to diﬀerentiate among species
in clinical cases. Whenever possible, it is important for veterinary
and human clinicians to submit to laboratories that use PCR that
can diﬀerentiate among SFG species. 58 Among other examples,
determination of the infecting species resulted in the recognition
of the novel Ricke sia sp. in dogs in the United States. 124
Antibodies to SFG ricke siae that are nonpathogenic (or of low
pathogenicity) cross-react with pathogenic SFG ricke siae and
therefore may make determining the meaning of a positive titer in
an ill patient challenging.

Rickettsialpox
Ricke sialpox is a nonfatal febrile zoonotic illness caused by R.
akari, a SFG ricke sia that predominantly aﬀects people in urban
areas. Serum antibodies to R. akari were found in dogs examined

vetexamprep.ir

during routine veterinary care in New York City. 129 The only
possible source of exposure for a person in North Carolina who
developed ricke sialpox was captured mice brought in by a pet
cat. 130 An 8-month-old dog from Mexico was infected with R.
akari and had hyporexia, fever, vomiting, and melena. 131 Physical
examination abnormalities were weight loss, abdominal
discomfort, suspected myalgia, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Hematologic and biochemical abnormalities included neutrophilic
leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, increased hepatic
aminotransferase
activity,
hypoalbuminemia,
and
hypoglobulinemia. Treatment was instituted with oral
doxycycline for 7 days, and remission occurred in 48 hours. The
organism was also detected by PCR in two Rh. sanguineus ticks
found on the dog. The maintenance of R. akari involves horizontal
transmission between the house mouse (Mus musculus) and its
mite (Liponyssoides sanguineus). Transovarial and transstadial
transmission occurs in the mite. Seropositivity in dogs indicates
that an alternative form of this transmission cycle might exist. It is
presumed that mites feed on dogs; however, a tick such as Rh.
sanguineus, or another tick vector as-yet unknown may be
responsible for exposing dogs.

Flea-borne spotted fever (Rickettsia Felis
infection)
A ﬂea-borne typhus-like illness caused by R. felis has been
reported in people from many countries worldwide. 132 Ricke sia
felis shares some phenotypic characteristics with the TG Ricke sia.
For example, R. felis is primarily ﬂea-borne rather than tick-borne,
and it is ultrastructurally indistinguishable from, and has
extensive serologic cross-reactivity with, Ricke sia typhi. However,
genotypic studies show that it is more closely related to SFG
Ricke sia, or may be a part of a separate phylogenetic lineage. 8 ,
133

The cat ﬂea (Ctenocephalides felis) is the primary vector for R.
felis, although R. felis has been detected in other arthropod vectors
including other ﬂea species, ticks, and mites. 132 More than 90% of
ﬂeas purchased commercially for research purposes are infected,
whereas the percentage in naturally infected ﬂeas is much lower

vetexamprep.ir

and depends on the geographic area. In the United States, the
disease is endemic in southern Texas and California and overlaps
that of human murine typhus caused by R. typhi. 134 Opossums
and ﬂeas have been found to be co-infected with both ricke siae,
and cat ﬂea infection with R. felis is more common than with R.
typhi in these regions. 134–139 Given the presence of both agents in
ﬂeas, some reports of murine typhus based on serology may have
been caused by R. felis. 132 Indeed, PCR and restriction fragment
length polymorphism identiﬁed R. typhi in four of ﬁve people
from Texas who had typhus, and R. felis was found in the
remaining person. 138 However, the importance of R. felis as a
predominant cause of typhus-like illness in southern California
has been questioned. 140 An infection cycle in people with R. felis
and C. felis has been found in France, Germany, and Brazil. 141 , 142
The infection probably exists worldwide in areas where cat ﬂeas
are prevalent. In Africa, there is some evidence that additional
vectors may play a role in human cases. 132
Ricke sia felis is transmi ed vertically through transovarial
transmission and possibly through consumption of infected feces
by larvae to successive generations of C. felis. 132 , 143 , 144 Infection
can be maintained in cat ﬂeas for up to 12 generations without the
ﬂeas having fed on an infected host. Therefore, it is also likely
serves as a reservoir. 132 Horizontal transmission from vector to
vector by a shared meal occurs, but whether mammalian blood or
tissues serve as a source of infection for ﬂeas has been questioned.
132 Infection with R. felis has been transmi ed among cats by
infected ﬂeas, and cats are seropositive to R. typhi antigen in
endemic areas. 137 , 145 , 146 Experimental infection of cats with R.
felis produced subclinical infection with seroconversion between 2
and 4 months. 145 Fever was not associated with natural exposure
to R. felis in one study. 39 Another study suggested that
lymphadenopathy and polycythemia may be associated with
infection. 147 In one study, neither the organism nor its nucleic
acid was identiﬁed from blood of cats naturally infested with
infected C. felis. 148 However, a 2018 study described ampliﬁcation
of R. felis DNA from the blood of a community cat in southern
California. 135 Two additional cats in the California study had
circulating DNA from the R. felis-like agent “Candidatus Ricke sia
senegalensis.” Out of 64 ﬂea pools collected from community cats

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
y
in that study, 12 were PCR positive for R. felis, 5 were PCR
positive for “Candidatus R. senegalensis,” and none were PCR
positive for R. typhi.
Ricke sia felis was detected using PCR from dogs sampled in
northern Cambodia and Queensland, Australia, and dogs have
been shown to be seropositive in endemic areas in some but not
other studies. 137 , 146 , 149–151 A recent study using PCR and cell
culture demonstrated sustained R. felis ricke semia in
experimentally infected 14-week-old puppies. 152 Transmission of
R. felis between infected and uninfected C. felis ﬂeas also occurred.
No changes in RBC or platelet count were documented in infected
puppies, although some puppies developed transient
leukocytosis, self-limiting diarrhea, and decreased appetite. One
puppy demonstrated petechial hemorrhages. Whether clinical
disease may occur in naturally infected puppies or adult dogs
with or without co-morbidities is not known.
In the United States, R. felis has been detected in cat ﬂeas taken
from cats or dogs from states where sampling has been done. 135 ,
144 , 148 , 153 Cats, dogs, and opossums may be likely hosts that
transport infected ﬂeas into human habitats. 154 Infection in
humans is transferred by ﬂea bites; however, ﬂea feces contain
viable organisms that might be inoculated into cutaneous bites or
scratches similar to the suspected transmission of Bartonella
henselae. 132 Clinical signs in humans include fever, headache, and
rash. Fatigue, myalgia, photophobia, conjunctivitis, abdominal
discomfort, vomiting, and diarrhea are also observed. 155
Doxycycline is the preferred treatment in humans, but many of
the other drugs used to treat SFG ricke sial infections are also
eﬀective. Clearing of infection in cats or dogs by use of
antimicrobials has not been determined. Flea control is essential to
reduce the public health risk in endemic areas.

Typhus Group Rickettsiae
Typhus refers to diseases caused by TG ricke siae. The TG
Ricke sia spp. include Ricke sia prowazekii and R. typhi. TG
ricke siae are phenotypically and genotypically diﬀerent than
SFG ricke siae. For example, they are serologically distinct, they
reside in cytoplasm and not the nucleus, and they do not spread
between cells through actin polymerization, but instead replicate

vetexamprep.ir

until the cell bursts. 6 , 72 Humans are the primary reservoirs of
louse-borne typhus, or epidemic typhus, a sporadic illness caused by
R. prowazekii. It occurs when events favor proliferation and spread
of the human body louse, such as unsanitary conditions and
natural disasters. The organism infects the louse’s alimentary tract
and is excreted in its feces. Irritation from biting lice causes the
person to scratch, thereby contaminating the abraded site with
infected louse feces. Infection can also occur after rubbing
contaminated hands on mucosal surfaces. Lice infected by R.
prowazekii die within 1 to 3 weeks after ingestion of infected blood.
Lice do not transmit the infection transovarially to their progeny.
Another reservoir for this infection in humans in the United States
appears to be the southern ﬂying squirrel. The disease is referred
to as “sylvatic epidemic typhus.” The clinical signs in humans are
generally similar to those of RMSF. Interestingly, in apparent
contrast to infection with R. ricke sii, R. prowazekii can recrudesce
years after initial infection in the same person. 156 This is referred
to as “Brill-Zinsser disease” or recrudescent typhus. Antibody
reactivity to TG ricke siae has been observed in the sera of dogs
suspected of having ricke sial disease. 157 Ricke sia prowazekii
caused no illness or sustained infection in experimentally
inoculated immunocompetent dogs. 157 No information clariﬁes
whether this organism infects dogs or cats in nature.
Murine typhus, or endemic typhus, has a more worldwide
distribution than louse-borne typhus. It is caused by R. typhi,
which is transmi ed by ﬂeas. It is most prevalent in the temperate
and subtropical climates where the reservoir rodent hosts and
their ﬂeas are found. The disease is transmi ed by scratching of
infected ﬂea feces into a pruritic bite wound. Some transovarial
transmission occurs, so direct bites from ﬂeas can also produce
illness in people. The clinical signs in people are very similar to
those of RMSF. In the continental United States, murine typhus is
endemic in southern California and South Texas. In this region,
the natural host and vector system is the opossum and cat ﬂea. It
has also been isolated from cat ﬂeas infesting dogs in Oklahoma.
153 In one study, dog and cat owners were no more likely to be
seropositive than nonowners. 158 However, in another study,
owning a dog was a signiﬁcant risk factor for human exposure. 159
Because it is ﬂea-transmi ed, ﬂea control on pets is important to

vetexamprep.ir

help prevent human infection. Ricke sia typhi has been ampliﬁed
from the blood of dogs 160 and from Rh. sanguineus ticks, 161
suggesting other vectors may play a role in transmission.
Scrub typhus is a ricke sial disease of humans caused by
Orientia (previously Ricke sia) tsutsugamushi in southeastern Asia,
the South Paciﬁc, and Australia. It is transmi ed by the chigger
mite, and wild rodents and birds are reservoir hosts. Clinical signs
are similar to those of RMSF. However, dogs have been
experimentally infected with O. tsutsugamushi without signs of
clinical illness. Orentia tsutsugamushi was ampliﬁed from the
blood of a dog in Japan with clinical signs of ricke sial disease
that responded to minocycline. Blood samples taken from 10 dogs
fed in the same area as the ill dog were also PCR positive. 162 An
O. tsutsugamushi-like organism has also been ampliﬁed from the
blood of a naturally infected dog in South Africa. 163 The role of
this organism as a disease-causing agent in dogs and cats requires
further study.

Case Examples
Rocky Mountain Spo ed Fever In A
DogSignalment

A 5-year-old MC Australian shepherd from North Carolina.

History

The dog was examined by the North Carolina State University
veterinary emergency service on April 11 because of recent
onset of lethargy, fever, tachypnea, and a stiﬀ gait when
walking. Historically the dog had been healthy, had received
routine vaccinations, heartworm preventative, and a ﬂea
preventative, and ran approximately 3 miles each evening with
the owner, who was a veterinarian. On the day of examination
and several hours after the evening run, the dog became
lethargic, refused to eat dog food or treats, and seemed painful
upon manipulation. The owner noticed that the dog’s HR,
which was normally 50 to 60 beats/minute, was 120
beats/minute at rest. Rectal temperature at home just prior to
presentation was 104.4°F (40.2°C). Three days before the dog

vetexamprep.ir

was evaluated, the owner had removed a nonengorged tick
from the dog.

Physical Examination

Physical examination ﬁndings included a body weight of 21.3
kg, 3%–5% dehydration, pain score of 1 out of 4, rectal
temperature of 103.7°F (39.8°C), HR 130 beats/minute,
tachypnea (42 breaths/minute), and a normal CRT. The BCS was
5/9. The dog stood in a hunched position and had a stiﬀ gait,
but localizing pain was not elicited on palpation of the spine,
joints, or long bones. There was no nasal or ocular discharge, no
petechiae or rash, and no obvious swelling or joint eﬀusion.
Popliteal lymph nodes were prominent, but there were no other
abnormalities noted on physical examination. Systolic blood
pressure was 153 mmHg, and diastolic and mean blood
pressures were 93 and 111 mmHg, respectively.

Laboratory Findings

The hematocrit was 42%, total plasma protein was 6.2 mg/dL,
and the platelet count was 120,000/µL. A serum biochemical
proﬁle showed only hypoglobulinemia (1.7 g/dL).

Microbiologic Testing

A SNAP 4Dx Plus (IDEXX Laboratories, Portland, ME, USA) inhouse ELISA assay was negative. Indirect IFA assays for Babesia
canis, B. henselae, Bartonella vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi, and E. canis
were negative (no detectable antibodies at a 1:16 screening
dilution). The dog was seroreactive to R. ricke sii at a titer of
1:64. A PCR panel capable of detecting Anaplasma spp., Babesia
spp., Ehrlichia spp., and Ricke sia spp. was negative on whole
blood. A convalescent R. ricke sii antibody titer was 1:256,
which supported a diagnosis of SFG ricke siosis, most likely
RMSF.

Treatment

Because of the acute onset of lethargy and fever, the history of
recent
tick
a achment,
the
documentation
of
thrombocytopenia, and the relatively high frequency of RMSF
in dogs and people in North Carolina, doxycycline (4.8 mg/kg,
PO, q12h) was prescribed for 3 weeks before the results of
microbiologic testing became available. The dog responded
rapidly after doxycycline treatment, with appetite and behavior
normalizing within 24 to 48 hours after the ﬁrst dose.

vetexamprep.ir

Comment

Although the clinical signs in this dog were relatively
nonspeciﬁc, the clinical presentation was very typical of RMSF.
Because R. ricke sii causes generalized vascular injury resulting
in increased vascular permeability, ﬂuid and protein leakage
out of the intravascular space, and an acute neutrophilic
inﬂammatory response throughout tissue sites within the body,
pain that appears to shift in location (back pain, joint pain,
abdominal pain, and neck pain) is a typical disease
manifestation. Also, the hunched appearance reported in this
dog is commonly observed in dogs with RMSF. As this dog was
owned by veterinarian and a tick had been removed a few days
earlier, a clinical diagnosis and appropriate treatment were
initiated earlier in the course of illness than is typical of most
dogs with RMSF. The rapid initiation of doxycycline may have
blunted the humoral antibody response and decreased the
convalescent antibody titer to a level that is lower than expected
in most cases of RMSF in dogs. It is important to note that PCR
assay is insensitive in the early stages of RMSF, as there are
often inadequate numbers of organisms in the blood to achieve
successful ampliﬁcation of ricke sial DNA. A very rapid
response to doxycycline is expected, unless there has been a
delay in diagnosis, accompanied by the onset of neurologic
abnormalities. Dogs that develop neurologic complications
experience a more prolonged recovery and can have residual
neurologic deﬁcits.

Rocky Mountain Spo ed Fever In A Human
Patient

On May 9, a 61-year-old man, who resided on a farm in Wake
County, North Carolina, removed an embedded tick from the
hairy portion of his right armpit. Although the duration of
a achment was unknown, it was likely that the tick was
acquired 2 to 3 days earlier while pulling weeds from a hay
ﬁeld. Using a tick identiﬁcation key, an experienced research
technician classiﬁed the tick as a male A. americanum and stored
the tick in a vial containing alcohol. On May 16, while working
on the farm, the patient experienced mild nausea after drinking
water and became transiently dizzy. The next morning chills
developed, and by the mid-afternoon the patient became febrile

vetexamprep.ir

(101.2°F [38.4°C]), developed muscle pain, a mild headache, and
remained in bed until the next morning. These symptoms
became progressively more severe during the day and the tick
a achment site had developed into an erythematous, circular
lesion with induration and a necrotic center, consistent with a
ricke sial eschar. Due to the history of tick a achment and
fever (maximum temperature 102.9°F [39.4°C]), a SFR, such as
RMSF, or neutrophilic or monocytic ehrlichiosis, caused by
Ehrlichia ewingii or E. chaﬀeensis, respectively, was suspected.
Neutropenia (2,553 cells/µL) was accompanied by a left shift
(5% band neutrophils) and thrombocytopenia (148,000/µL).
Doxycycline was dispensed with instructions to take 100 mg
q12h for 7 days. That evening, after sleeping for 6 hours, the
patient ate a small quantity of food, after which he became
severely nauseated and fainted, and impact with the ﬂoor was
associated with a severe blow to the back of the head. The next
day (May 19) a maculopapular rash appeared that
predominantly involved the inferior portions of the arms and
legs. Throughout the day the distribution of the rash spread
and the severity progressed from barely visible to obvious over
most of the body. At no time did the rash involve the palms or
plantar surface of the feet. Fever resolved within 36 hours after
the initiation of doxycycline, and the rash began to fade
gradually after 48 hours of treatment. Within a week after
starting doxycycline, the patient was experiencing no
symptoms and had no sequelae as a result of the infection or
the fall. A repeat CBC (May 25) identiﬁed a normal neutrophil
count (4,378 cells/µL), no band neutrophils, and a normal
platelet count (320,000/µL). Acute-phase serum was collected
and stored until the convalescent sample was obtained.
Ricke sia and Ehrlichia spp. PCR was performed immediately.
PCR amplicons, obtained from the patient’s blood and from the
tick, were sequenced, conﬁrming the presence of R. ricke sii
DNA. PCR for Ehrlichia spp. DNA was negative from both the
tick and the patient. Subsequently, seroconversion to R. ricke sii
antigens was identiﬁed (1:64 acute titer, convalescent titer 1:512
after 4 weeks). The patient did not seroconvert to Ehrlichia spp.
antigens.

Comment

vetexamprep.ir

Historically, transmission of R. ricke sii in North America was
a ributed solely to D. variabilis in the eastern United States and
to D. andersoni in the western United States. However, between
2002 and 2004, researchers at the CDC documented Rh.
sanguineus transmission of R. ricke sii to people residing in
Arizona. Although this is most likely an infrequent occurrence,
this patient was infected with R. ricke sii by A. americanum. It is
important to note the similarities between the historical,
physical examination, and laboratory ﬁndings for the dog
discussed previously and the human patient. In several
published case reports, dogs develop RMSF before a family
member contracts the infection from a tick. Thus, it is important
for veterinarians to recognize and conﬁrm a diagnosis of RMSF
in dogs and to educate the client as to the risk of tick exposure
within their local environment.

47: Neoricke siosis
Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Neorickettsia helminthoeca, the Stellantchasmus
falcatus (SF) agent/Elokomin fluke fever (EFF) agent (salmon
poisoning disease [SPD]) and Neorickettsia risticii. All are
gram-negative, obligately intracellular bacteria that belong to
the family Anaplasmataceae. A related organism,
Neorickettsia sennetsu, causes febrile illness in humans who
ingest raw fish in Asia (Sennetsu fever).
• First Described: The first reports of SPD were from
northwestern Oregon, United States, in 1814 (Astoria). 1
Reports of natural infection of dogs with N. risticii first
appeared from the United States in 1994. 2
• Affected Hosts: Neorickettsia helminthoeca infects dogs,
foxes, coyotes, raccoons, and captive bears. The SF agent
infects dogs. Neorickettsia risticii infects horses (causing
Potomac horse fever or equine neorickettsiosis), bats, and
dogs. In addition, experimental transmission to dogs and cats
has resulted in disease.
• Intermediate Hosts: The intermediate hosts for N.
helminthoeca and probably the SF agent are aquatic snails
(Oxytrema silicula) and fish (especially salmonids). For N.
risticii, they are aquatic snails (Juga and Elimia spp.) and
aquatic insects (caddisflies and mayflies).
• Geographic Distribution: The distribution of SPD is limited to
the coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, northern California,
British Columbia, and Brazil (2004). Infections with N. risticii
have been documented in horses from the United States,
Canada, and South America, including Uruguay and Brazil.

vetexamprep.ir

• Route of Transmission: SPD is transmitted to dogs by
ingestion of the infected trematode vector Nanophyetus
salmincola, most often in salmonid fish. Neorickettsia risticii is
transmitted to horses by ingestion of the trematode vector
Acanthatrium oregonense within aquatic insects. The mode of
transmission of N. risticii to dogs is unknown, but they also
may become infected through ingestion of infected aquatic
snails or insects.
• Major Clinical Signs: SPD is often associated with fever,
lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, and
lymphadenomegaly. In the rare reports of N. risticii infection,
dogs and cats have shown signs of lethargy, vomiting,
hematemesis, petechial hemorrhages, fever, and polyarthritis.
• Differential Diagnoses: These include lymphoma, CPV
infection, CDV infection, granulocytic anaplasmosis,
ehrlichiosis, leptospirosis, septic shock, disseminated fungal
disease (especially cryptococcosis), hemorrhagic
gastroenteritis, dietary indiscretion, GI foreign body,
pancreatitis, hypoadrenocorticism, and inflammatory bowel
disease. For SPD, appropriate antimicrobial treatment with
doxycycline must begin before the diagnosis is confirmed by
laboratory testing. Misdiagnosis and delayed or inappropriate
antimicrobial drug therapy increase morbidity and mortality.
• Human Health Significance: Nanophyetus salmincola can
cause GI disturbances and eosinophilia in humans, but N.
helminthoeca does not cause human disease. Similarly, N.
risticii has not been reported to cause human disease.
Neorickettsia sennetsu is a related pathogen that causes
febrile illness in humans consuming raw fish in Asia.

Salmon Poisoning Disease
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Salmon poisoning disease (SPD) is primarily caused by the gramnegative, obligately intracellular ricke sial pathogen Neoricke sia
helminthoeca, which, like other Neoricke sia spp., resides within a
trematode (ﬂuke) vector for the course of the trematode’s life cycle

vetexamprep.ir

from egg to adult. The complete genome of N. helminthoeca has
been sequenced. 3
The trematode vector of N. helminthoeca is Nanophyetus
salmincola, thought to be the most common trematode species
endemic to the United States. The disease occurs in dogs, foxes,
and coyotes. In addition, two captive polar bears receiving longterm glucocorticoid therapy for skin conditions succumbed to an
SPD-like disease after eating inadequately frozen salmon, 4 an
SPD-like disease was also reported in two captive Malayan sun
bears after they were fed live trout from a northern California
reservoir, 5 and SPD was conﬁrmed using molecular methods in a
captive African lion (Panthera leo krugeri) from Oregon after it was
fed raw salmon. 6 Domestic cats are not susceptible to SPD, but
trematodes develop when infected ﬁsh are ingested. 7
SPD is geographically restricted to coastal regions of northern
California, Oregon, and Washington in the United States, and
southern British Columbia in Canada. This reﬂects the
distribution of an aquatic snail, Oxytrema silicula (also known as
Juga silicula), which is an intermediate host of the trematode (Fig.
47.1). The snail is prevalent in coastal streams. A similar disease
has been described in dogs from southern Brazil, 8–10 and infection
with N. helminthoeca was detected in several dead coatis (Nasua
nasua) from a wildlife sanctuary in Foz do Iguaçu (southern
Brazil). 11 It was not clear whether the infection in the coatis was
clinical or subclinical; two of the coatis had died as a result of
vehicle trauma. The trematode host and intermediate hosts
involved in southern Brazil remain unclear. 8
Another related, yet antigenically distinct organism is capable
of causing SPD in dogs, the Elokomin ﬂuke fever (EFF) agent. 12–16
Discovered during a empts to understand the role of black bears
as reservoirs for SPD, it was initially thought to be a less
pathogenic strain of N. helminthoeca, because experimental
infection of dogs with the agent resulted in only mild disease. 14
The EFF agent has never been sequenced. In 2020, an organism
known as the Stellantchasmus falcatus (SF) agent was detected in
three dogs from the Paciﬁc Northwest with severe clinical signs of
SPD. 17 This organism is so named because it was ﬁrst detected in
the metacercariae of the trematode SF in grey mullet ﬁsh in Japan.
18 , 19 Inoculation of the SF agent into a dog resulted in mild

vetexamprep.ir

disease. 19 The 16S rRNA gene sequence of the SF agent was
published in 1996, 20 and in 2016, an organism with the same 16S
rRNA gene sequence was detected in N. salmincola metacercariae
in Chinook salmon in the Willame e valley in Oregon. 21 It was
then suggested that the EFF agent and the SF agent might be the
same organism. The SF agent has also been detected in an adult
ﬂuke (Metagonimoides oregonensis) in Florida, 22 so there is the
possibility that as-yet unrecognized disease occurs in dogs in
Florida. The intermediate hosts for this ﬂuke on the east coast are
thought to be aquatic snails (Pleurocerca spp.) and the salamander
(rather than salmonid ﬁsh), and so disease may be unrecognized
on the east coast because intermediate hosts are infrequently
consumed by domestic dogs. Raccoons are the primary deﬁnitive
host for the ﬂuke.

vetexamprep.ir

Geographic distribution of salmon
poisoning disease in dogs from the United
States. The distribution also extends into the
southern portion of British Columbia.
FIG. 47.1

Dogs usually become infected with N. helminthoeca when they
ingest encysted trematode metacercariae within uncooked or
undercooked freshwater ﬁsh, most commonly salmonid ﬁsh. The
Paciﬁc giant salamander is also a competent second intermediate
host. Ingestion of encysted metacercariae is followed by
maturation of the trematode over a 6-day period, which feeds on
the intestinal mucosa and inoculates the ricke sia into the host.
The ﬂuke has an oral sucker and a ventral sucker, which are used
to grasp host intestinal tissue, although the ﬂuke itself does not

vetexamprep.ir

cause extensive damage to the intestinal wall. 23 Infected
trematode ova are shed in the stool for 60 to 250 days. 24 After
several months, miracidia develop within the eggs, hatch, swim
away, and penetrate the snail. They then develop into rediae, each
of which give rise to many free-swimming cercariae. Thousands
of cercariae are released intermi ently from the snail. These
rapidly penetrate the skin of a ﬁsh (or are ingested by the ﬁsh),
and encyst throughout the ﬁsh as metacercariae (Figs. 47.2 and
47.3). The metacercariae usually localize in the kidneys of ﬁsh, but
can be found in any tissue, as well as slime on the skin of ﬁsh.
Infected ﬁsh may contain more than 1,000 metacercariae. Infected
ﬁsh may have visible damage to their skin, and the infection may
also interfere with their swimming activity. 25 Fish are infected in
freshwater and retain the trematode and the ricke sial infection
throughout their ocean migration before returning to fresh water
up to 3 years later. 26 Dog-to-dog transmission of N. helminthoeca
has been demonstrated experimentally by mechanical
aerosolization or rectal administration of lymph node suspensions
or homogenates of rectal mucosa. 27 SPD also has been
transmi ed by parenteral injection of infected blood, spleen and
lymph suspensions, adult ﬂukes, helminth-infected snail livers,
and helminth eggs. Partial transmission success was obtained by
allowing ticks (Haemaphysalis leachi and Rhipicephalus sanguineus)
that had fed on infected dogs to subsequently feed on susceptible
dogs and by parenteral injection of suspensions of Rh. sanguineus
into dogs. 28
