Intact male dogs and Labrador retrievers appear to be
overrepresented among dogs with SPD, 29 possibly because they
are popular with individuals engaged in ﬁshing activities,
although dogs of any sex and breed can be aﬀected. Dogs of any
age are aﬀected; the median age in one study was 3 years. 29 Dogs
develop SPD at any time of year. Occasionally, dogs from areas
not endemic for SPD develop disease after they ingest ﬁsh that is
exported from endemic areas. 30
Most but not all infected dogs have a history of access to or
consumption of raw or improperly cooked ﬁsh. 29 , 31
Consumption of any part of the ﬁsh, including the entrails and
skin, may result in SPD. Supermarket-bought salmon may also be
infected. 29 Infection has also been reported after swimming
activity, without apparent exposure to ﬁsh. 29

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Neoricke sia helminthoeca replicates within macrophages.
Ricke siae enter the blood early in the course of the disease and
spread to the lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, thymus, liver, lungs,
and brain. 32 This results in a granulomatous inﬂammatory
response that is most profound in the stomach, intestines, lymph
nodes, and spleen. Granulomatous meningitis has also been
detected in dogs with SPD. 33 , 34 Aﬀected dogs in southern Brazil
have also had evidence of chronic interstitial pneumonia and
choroid plexitis. 8
The incubation period ranges from 2 to 14 days (median, 7
days), but may be as long as 33 days. 35 The severity of illness
varies considerably (Box 47.1). Dogs with peracute infection may
be found dead. 29 A marked febrile response is commonly
detected (>70% of cases) (Box 47.2) and may reach 42°C (107.6°F).
29 A median rectal temperature of 40.6°C (105°F) was reported in
one series of naturally infected dogs. 29 Rectal temperature
gradually decreases to normal or below normal over the
subsequent 4 to 8 days. Terminally ill dogs may be hypothermic.
Some animals show only a mild increase in temperature or a brief
period of fever; they may still die if left untreated. Virtually all

vetexamprep.ir

dogs develop inappetence or anorexia, and lethargy is also
common. Vomiting occurs in more than 80% of dogs, and rarely,
hematemesis. 29 Diarrhea is also common (>70% of dogs) and may
be semiformed to liquid in consistency, sometimes containing
frank blood, melena, and, less commonly, mucus. Occasionally, a
history of diarrhea and vomiting is absent. Other signs include
serous nasal discharge, weight loss, and increased thirst and
urination. Neurologic signs including mental obtundation,
myoclonic twitching, seizures, and apparent neck pain have been
reported in fewer than 20% of aﬀected dogs, a primary diﬀerential
diagnosis being CDV infection. 29 Dogs from southern Brazil have
also shown neurologic signs and evidence of respiratory distress. 8
Physical Examination Findings
Dehydration is frequently noted on physical examination and
may be severe. More than 70% of dogs have peripheral
lymphadenomegaly, which may be generalized or involve only
some peripheral lymph nodes (see Box 47.2). Lymph nodes may
be up to 4 cm in diameter and ﬁrm on palpation. Lack of
lymphadenomegaly may be present occasionally, sometimes as a
result of lymph node necrosis. Abdominal palpation may reveal
pain, and splenomegaly may also be detected. Other
abnormalities include tachypnea or labored respirations,
tachycardia, scleral or conjunctival injection, serous nasal
discharge, and edema that involves the limbs, face, or cervical
region. 29 Mucosal pallor, tachycardia, and weak pulses may be
present in dogs with hypovolemic shock. Cardiac arrhythmias
such as ventricular premature contractions have also been noted,
and signs of hemorrhage such as epistaxis and hyphema may also
be present. Rectal examination may indicate the presence of liquid
stool, sometimes accompanied by fresh blood or melena.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
Thrombocytopenia is present in 90% of aﬀected dogs. Anemia is
present in up to 40% of dogs with SPD and generally occurs as a
result of GI hemorrhage. More commonly, the CBC shows
evidence of lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutrophilia,

vetexamprep.ir

frequently with bandemia (Table 47.1). Uncommonly, neutropenia
occurs. 29 Toxic changes may be present within neutrophils, and
immature monocytes may occasionally be found in the peripheral
blood. Despite the association with helminthiasis, eosinophilia is
often not present.
Serum Chemistry Profile
Hyponatremia and hypokalemia are the most common electrolyte
abnormalities in dogs with SPD and result from GI losses that
occur with vomiting and diarrhea (Table 47.2). Low
concentrations of ionized calcium may be detected in some dogs,
possibly as a result of decreased intestinal absorption.
Hypoalbuminemia is present in most (>80%) dogs.
Hypoglobulinemia and hypocholesterolemia occur in fewer than
25% of dogs with SPD. Abnormal liver enzyme activities may be
present, the most common of which is increased ALP activity, 29 ,
34 but increases in the activity of ALT and AST may also occur,
and hyperbilirubinemia is present in fewer than 20% of dogs.
Azotemia can be evident in dogs with severe dehydration.

Urinalysis
Bilirubinuria and proteinuria are frequently detected on urinalysis
in dogs with SPD. 29 Uncommonly, cylindruria and glucosuria are
present, perhaps as a result of renal injury secondary to impaired
renal perfusion. Microscopic hematuria occurs in some dogs,
possibly reﬂecting underlying coagulopathies that can occur in
dogs with SPD.
Clotting Function
Evaluation of clo ing function in some dogs may show evidence
of DIC. Abnormalities include increased PT or APTT, increased
ﬁbrin degradation products, and decreased antithrombin activity.
29

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Abdominal radiographs may be unremarkable or reveal ﬂuidﬁlled small intestines; focal areas of decreased serosal detail; and

vetexamprep.ir

less frequently, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Thoracic
radiographs are typically unremarkable or show reduction in size
of the intrathoracic vasculature, consistent with hypovolemia.
Sonographic Findings
Abdominal ultrasound examination of dogs with SPD often
shows mild or moderate generalized abdominal or mesenteric
lymphadenomegaly, as well as splenomegaly with a mo led
splenic echotexture. Some dogs that lack peripheral
lymphadenomegaly have abdominal lymphadenomegaly on
ultrasound examination, 29 and ultrasound-guided aspiration of
enlarged abdominal lymph nodes can be helpful for diagnosis in
dogs that lack peripheral lymphadenomegaly. Lymph nodes
develop a rounded appearance with a hypoechoic or hypoechoic
mo led echogenicity (Fig. 47.4). Fluid-distended intestinal loops,
sometimes with wall thickening, corrugation, hypermotility, or
hypomotility, may be documented. Uncommonly, hepatomegaly
or a small amount of free peritoneal ﬂuid is identiﬁed.
Microbiologic Tests (Table 47.3)
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
SPD can be conﬁrmed when operculated trematode eggs are
found in fecal samples of dogs with consistent clinical signs,
which appear within 5 to 8 days after the ingestion of infected
ﬁsh. The light brown eggs are approximately 87 to 97 µm long
and 35 to 55 µm wide, with a small, blunt point on the end
opposite the indistinct operculum (Fig. 47.5). Although the
sensitivity of centrifugal zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation for detection of
N. salmincola ova in dogs with SPD is similar to that of fecal
sedimentation, some dogs that test negative by one method test
positive using the other, so the sensitivity of fecal examination for
diagnosis is maximized by performing both centrifugal zinc
sulfate fecal ﬂotations and fecal sedimentation together. In one
study, 93% of dogs with SPD tested positive for N. salmincola ova
using a combination of fecal ﬂotation and fecal sedimentation. 29
False negatives may occur when the duration of illness is shorter
than the prepatent period of N. salmincola or when light ﬂuke
burdens are present. The ﬁnding of ﬂuke ova on fecal examination
may not be diagnostic of SPD, because dogs may be infected with

vetexamprep.ir

trematodes that do not harbor the ricke sia, and ova may be shed
for months after recovery. Nevertheless, N. salmincola ova were
detected in only 0.2% of more than 1,800 fecal ﬂotations in dogs
seen at a teaching hospital in an endemic area, and all positive test
results were in dogs suspected to have SPD. Thus, the speciﬁcity
of fecal examination for a diagnosis of SPD appears to be
extremely high. 29

Enlarged and hypoechoic abdominal
(medial iliac) lymph nodes as detected using
abdominal sonographic examination in a 9year-old male German shepherd dog with
salmon poisoning disease.
FIG. 47.4

Centrifugal zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation may reveal co-infections
with other GI parasites, which can complicate the clinical picture.
Co-infections with Dipylidium caninum and Trichuris vulpis have
been reported in dogs with SPD. 29
Cytologic Diagnosis
In addition to fecal examination for trematode ova, SPD can be
diagnosed following cytologic examination of peripheral lymph
node aspirates, or ultrasound-guided aspirates of abdominal
lymph nodes or the spleen. Cytologic ﬁndings consist of

vetexamprep.ir

histiocytic hyperplasia and lymphoid reactivity. Ricke sial
organisms are 0.3-µm cocci or coccobacilli and may be seen in
large numbers within the cytoplasm of macrophages.
Pleomorphic rods up to 2 µm long, sometimes forming rings or
crescents, have also been observed. The organisms resemble
granular to amorphous material of a uniform blue color using
Wright stain, occasionally forming loose clusters of organisms
(morulae) (Fig. 47.6). 29 , 35 , 36 Similar ﬁndings were described in
dogs infected with the SF agent. 17 Extracellular organisms are not
easily separated from artifacts and should not be considered
diagnostic for SPD. In as many as one quarter to one third of dogs,
ricke sial organisms are not identiﬁed. The presence of histiocytic
hyperplasia should alert the clinician to the possibility of SPD.
Organisms may also be absent in dogs with a recent history of
antimicrobial therapy.

Serologic Diagnosis
Serologic tests for N. helminthoeca antibodies or antigen are not
available on a commercial basis for veterinary practitioners.
Antibodies to N. helminthoeca can cross-react serologically with
those of Ehrlichia spp., so it is possible that dogs with SPD might
test positive using serologic tests for Ehrlichia spp. (provided
enough time had elapsed for antibody formation to occur). 37 In
one study, most dogs with SPD that were tested for antibodies
against other ricke sial pathogens did not seroreact to Ehrlichia
canis or Anaplasma phagocytophilum. 29 Serologic cross-reactivity
occurs among N. helminthoeca, the SF agent, Neoricke sia risticii,
and Neoricke sia sennetsu. 38
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Real-time PCR assays have been used to detect the DNA of N.
helminthoeca in clinical specimens from aﬀected dogs. 29 Real-time
PCR assays for N. helminthoeca are available from some veterinary
molecular diagnostic laboratories and can be performed on blood,
lymph node or splenic aspirates, and possibly fecal samples from
dogs with SPD in order to conﬁrm the diagnosis. More research is
required to understand the sensitivity and speciﬁcity of PCR
assays for diagnosing SPD in dogs, including the optimum
specimen type for testing. A broad-spectrum Neoricke sia spp.
PCR assay was used to detect the SF agent in dogs. 17 Some realtime PCR assays designed to detect N. helminthoeca have the
potential to also detect the SF agent and other Neoricke sia spp. 29
However, genetic diﬀerences between the SF agent and N.
helminthoeca have been identiﬁed that would allow development
of species-speciﬁc assays. 38 Clinicians should contact their
laboratory to determine the speciﬁcity of the PCR assays oﬀered.
Cell Culture
Neoricke sia helminthoeca has been grown in canine monocytes, 16
canine leukocytes and sarcoma cells, mouse lymphoblasts, and a
macrophage cell line. 39 , 40 However, cell culture is not used for
routine diagnosis.
Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Gross Pathologic Findings
Gross necropsy ﬁndings in dogs with SPD consist of enlargement
of lymphoid tissues, including the tonsils, thymus, lymph nodes,
and spleen. Lymph nodes may be yellowish and edematous and
may contain white foci that represent foci of granulomatous
inﬂammation. Petechial hemorrhages may be noted on the lymph
nodes, GI tract, pancreas, gallbladder, and urinary bladder. The
GI tract may be thickened and contain white foci. The lumen of
the intestinal tract may contain free blood (Fig. 47.7A). Intestinal
intussusception has also been described in association with SPD. 4
Flukes are only 0.8 to 1.1 mm long and 0.3 to 0.5 mm wide 41 and
may not always be visible grossly.
Histopathologic Findings
Lymphoid tissues show marked depletion of lymphoid follicles,
and subcapsular and medullary sinuses are ﬁlled with histiocytes,
the cytoplasm of which can contain numerous ricke sial
organisms, which occasionally form clusters within vacuoles.
Organisms are readily appreciated using Giemsa stain (Fig.
47.7C). Lymph node and splenic necrosis may also be present. 4 ,
29 Inﬂammatory nodules that contain lymphocytes, plasma cells,
and infected histiocytes expand the lamina propria of the GI tract
and extend into the submucosa. Parasites consistent with N.
salmincola may be found embedded in the mucosa, primarily
within the duodenum (Fig. 47.7B). 27 , 33 Nevertheless, ﬂukes are
not always found using histopathology in dogs that die from SPD,
even in the absence of anthelmintic therapy.
One dog that died of SPD had widespread and multiple
thromboses involving numerous organs with associated tissue
infarction. Granulomatous meningitis has been described at
necropsy in dogs that were experimentally infected with N.
helminthoeca. 34 In addition to having characteristic GI and
lymphoid lesions described in dogs from the United States, dogs
from southern Brazil have had evidence of choroid plexitis as well
as chronic interstitial pneumonia, with marked accumulations of
alveolar macrophages and thickening of alveolar septa due to
hyperplasia of type II pneumocytes. 8 IHC was used to
demonstrate intralesional Neoricke sia antigen within aﬀected
tissues.

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Prognosis
The treatment of choice for SPD is doxycycline, tetracycline, or
oxytetracycline, which should be given for a minimum of 7 days.
Administration of tetracyclines is generally associated with
clinical improvement within 24 hours, and signs resolve within 1
to 4 days. 29 Dogs that are vomiting may require treatment with
parenteral tetracyclines. Clinical improvement has also been
reported following treatment with enroﬂoxacin and parenteral
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Antimicrobials that do not
appear to be eﬀective include ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins,
penicillins,
aminoglycosides,
chloramphenicol,
and
29
metronidazole. Although complete clinical recovery may occur
without anthelmintic treatment, the ﬂuke infection should be
treated with praziquantel after initial recovery from SPD (Table
47.4). 42 Elimination of N. salmincola from infected animals
minimizes the diarrhea associated with ﬂuke infections alone and
minimizes or eliminates ﬂuke eggs from feces. Dogs should also
be treated and evaluated for concurrent parasite infections of the
GI tract.
Dogs with mild signs or infrequent vomiting may respond well
to treatment with oral tetracyclines alone, whereas those with
more severe disease often require hospitalization for IV
antimicrobial and crystalloid ﬂuid therapy (Table 47.4). Oral
antimicrobial therapy can be continued once vomiting ceases. The
presence of severe hypovolemia or hypoalbuminemia may
necessitate treatment with colloids such as fresh frozen plasma,
dextrans, or hetastarch. Packed RBCs or whole blood may be
required for dogs with severe anemia. Treatment with central or
partial parenteral nutrition may also be required if vomiting is
persistent and does not respond to antiemetics such as
metoclopramide, maropitant, or ondansetron. Close monitoring of
HCT, albumin, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal parameters,
and coagulation parameters may be required in some severely
aﬀected dogs. Blood cultures should be considered in dogs with
severe hemorrhagic diarrhea and abnormal perfusion parameters,
after which treatment with broad-spectrum parenteral
antimicrobial drugs should be commenced.

Prolonged hospitalization may be required for dogs that
develop
complications
such
as
cardiac
arrhythmias,
intussusceptions, adverse reactions to tetracyclines, DIC, or
bacteremia. 29 , 31 In a study of dogs evaluated at a tertiary referral
hospital, death or euthanasia occurred in 14% of 29 dogs with
SPD. 29 The mortality rate may be lower in dogs seen in primary
care practice, so long as appropriate treatment can be
administered. In general, early treatment is associated with an
excellent prognosis. Without treatment, death can occur within 5
to 10 days. The exact cause of death in SPD is unknown. Bacterial
sepsis may result from translocation of bacteria across the
damaged intestinal wall. Severe hypoalbuminemia and anemia
secondary to GI hemorrhage and ﬂuid losses may contribute.

Immunity and Vaccination
Animals that recover from SPD are immune to reinfection with
the same strain of N. helminthoeca, 4 , 43 , 44 but challenge with an
alternate strain (then the EFF agent) results in disease, and
antibodies fail to cross-react with the alternate strain. Reinfection

vetexamprep.ir

with the EFF/SF agent may explain why SPD has been reported to
occur more than once in some dogs. 4 , 21 , 29 In an unpublished
survey of 331 practitioners in endemic areas, 35% reported that
they had diagnosed SPD in dogs that had been treated previously
for SPD. 4 No vaccine is available.

Prevention
Nanophyetus salmincola metacercariae are eﬀectively destroyed by
proper cooking or freezing of infected ﬁsh at –20°C for 24 hours. 30
Ingestion of raw ﬁsh by dogs in endemic areas should be
discouraged, and dog owners in endemic areas should be
educated about the disease. Dogs that have eaten raw ﬁsh from an
endemic area, or those swimming in rivers or lakes in these areas,
should be watched carefully for signs of lethargy, vomiting, or
decreased appetite that occur within 2 weeks of exposure. If
multiple dogs are simultaneously exposed to a source of N.
helminthoeca, and one dog develops SPD, treatment of the other
dogs in the group with 7 days of doxycycline should be
considered. Medical equipment used in the treatment of dogs
with SPD should not be reused on other patients without proper
sterilization.

Public Health Aspects
Human infection with N. helminthoeca has not been reported.
However, humans may become infected with the ﬂuke, N.
salmincola, after consumption of poorly cooked ﬁsh. Most humans
are subclinically infected, although abdominal discomfort,
diarrhea, vomiting, weight loss, nausea, and peripheral
eosinophilia may occur. 45 The SF agent was discovered during a
search for the cause of “Hyuga” fever, which was thought to be
caused by N. sennetsu. However, only the SF agent, and not N.
sennetsu, was discovered in metacercariae from grey mullet ﬁsh
ingested raw by most people that developed the disease. 19
Therefore, it is possible that the SF agent may be able to cause
febrile disease in people, but this requires further study.

Neorickettsia Risticii Infection
Rarely, dogs have been reported to develop disease in association
with infection by N. risticii, the cause of equine neoricke siosis
(“Potomac horse fever”), or a closely related organism. 2 The life
cycle of this organism involves a trematode vector, which in the
eastern United States is Acanthatrium oregonense. 46 The ﬂuke
miracidia infect aquatic snails (Elimia virginica and likely other
species) and metacercariae can be found in aquatic insects
(caddisﬂies and mayﬂies). 47 Adult trematodes also lay eggs in the
intestinal tract of insectivorous bats. 46 Potomac horse fever has
been reported from the United States, eastern Canada, and South
America, with reports from Uruguay and southern Brazil. 48
Horses are often infected in summer following ingestion of
infected aquatic insects and develop a severe systemic illness with
fever, lethargy, anorexia, dehydration, diarrhea, laminitis, or
abortion. In one report, N. risticii or a closely related organism was
detected using culture and PCR in a small number of dogs from
the western and southwestern United States with signs of fever,
lethargy, vomiting, hematemesis, petechial hemorrhages, edema,
or polyarthritis. 2 These dogs were seroreactive to N. risticii
antigens using IFA. Serologic evidence of exposure to Neoricke sia
spp. has also been documented in dogs from Thailand and Spain.
49 , 50 Experimental infection of dogs did not result in
development of clinical signs. 51 There is some evidence that N.
risticii can cause disease in cats. Clinical signs reported in a study
of experimentally infected cats included lethargy, fever, anorexia,
diarrhea, and lethargy, and infected cats seroconverted between

vetexamprep.ir

10 and 23 days after infection. 52 There were no clearly deﬁned
hematologic abnormalities associated with the infection. To date,
N. risticii has not been detected in naturally infected cats using
culture or molecular methods, but serologic evidence of
Neoricke sia spp. infection has been reported in cat populations
from the United States 53 and Spain 54 , 55 and in a small number
of cats with signs of anorexia, lethargy, fever, vomiting, diarrhea,
polyarthritis, and ocular discharge. 56 Laboratory ﬁndings in these
cats included anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.
Because of the possibility of serologic cross-reactivity with other
organisms, further studies are required to determine the
signiﬁcance of this organism in dogs and also in cats. In the
meantime, screening of blood donors using PCR assays for N.
risticii has been recommended given the potential for transmission
by blood transfusion. 57
Should infection by N. risticii be strongly suspected or
conﬁrmed in dogs or cats, treatment with doxycycline (5 mg/kg,
PO, q12h for 2–3 weeks) is recommended.

Case Example
Signalment

“Herman,” 9-year-old male German shepherd dog from
Sacramento, CA (Fig. 47.8).

History

Herman’s owner reported a 2-day history of inappetence,
lethargy, and one episode of vomiting. The dog had been
drinking normally. There had been no diarrhea, coughing,
sneezing, or increased thirst and urination. The owner also
reported that Herman ate turkey and chicken that contained
bones 3 days before the onset of illness. He was normally fed a
strict diet of rabbit- and potato-based prescription dog food and
grilled salmon because of atopic dermatitis. Herman was
sometimes fed salmon scraps from the local supermarket,
which the owner grilled brieﬂy. He had not traveled out of his
local area. He was up to date on vaccinations, which included
vaccines for distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus, and rabies.

Current Medications

vetexamprep.ir

Lincomycin 29 mg/kg PO q12h; trimeprazine tartrate 0.2 mg/kg
PO q48h; and prednisolone 0.1 mg/kg q48h for atopic
dermatitis.

Other Medical History

Herman had been diagnosed with hip osteoarthritis using
pelvic radiography 8 months earlier. Controlled weight loss
was the recommended treatment. He was cryptorchid, and the
abdominal testicle had been removed when he was a young
dog. The descended testicle was still present.

Treatment

Doxycycline, 5 mg/kg PO q12h for 14 days. This was associated

Comments

This dog was diagnosed with SPD based on the presence of
characteristic cytologic ﬁndings on examination of a lymph
node aspirate, together with the detection of N. salmincola ova in
the stool. The case was unusual because the dog was infected
after ingestion of incompletely cooked supermarket-bought
salmon, which the dog had been fed for years without
developing illness. Although the splenic aspirate contained
inﬂammatory cells typical of those seen in SPD, organisms
could not be convincingly documented.

48: Coxiellosis and Q Fever
Jane E. Sykes, and Jacqueline M. Norris

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Mid 1930s, Queensland, Australia, in
slaughterhouse workers (Derrick). 1
• Cause: Coxiella burnetii, an obligately intracellular gramnegative bacterial species that belongs to the family
Coxiellaceae.
• Affected Hosts: Humans are most susceptible; reproductive
disease can occur in farm animal species such as sheep,
goats, and cattle, but the evidence for disease in cats and
dogs is inconclusive.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide, with the exception of New
Zealand and Antarctica.
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs and cats are usually subclinically
infected. Abortion, premature birth, and stillbirth have been
reported in infected cats or dogs at the center of Q fever
outbreaks in humans, but the role of C. burnetii in disease in
cats and dogs is uncertain.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other infectious causes of reproductive
disorders or pregnancy loss such as brucellosis, herpesviral
infections, leptospirosis, neosporosis, CDV, and CPV
infection. Noninfectious causes of pregnancy loss, such as
endocrinopathies, genetic disorders, and nutritional deficiency,
should also be considered.
• Human Health Significance: Q fever in humans results
primarily from contact with infected sheep, goats, and cattle,
or indirect contact with surfaces contaminated with secretions
or excretions of these animals. However, contact with infected
periparturient companion animals can also lead to

vetexamprep.ir

transmission. Q fever in humans is most commonly an acute
febrile illness, but pneumonia and chronic complications such
as endocarditis, granulomatous hepatitis, and chronic fatigue
can occur.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Coxiella burnetii is a gram-negative, obligately intracellular, small,
pleomorphic rod that causes Q fever in humans, a signiﬁcant
zoonosis worldwide. Sheep, ca le, and goats are the most
commonly reported reservoirs for the organism, but infected cats
and less commonly dogs have also been implicated in
transmission to humans. 2–7 Animals other than humans are often
subclinically infected, although reproductive complications such
as premature birth, abortion, and stillbirth may occur. In avian
species, systemic illness has been associated with infection by
other Coxiella-like organisms. 8–10 Reservoir hosts shed organisms
in vaginal secretions and the products of parturition due to
recrudescence of infection during pregnancy, with shedding in
the urine, feces, saliva, and/or milk in some species. The placentas
of infected animals are heavily infected (up to 109 organisms per
gram of tissue). At parturition, aerosols are created, which are
subsequently inhaled by other animals and humans (Fig. 48.1).
Ingestion of unpasteurized contaminated milk is a less common
and more controversial mode of transmission. 11 , 12 The term Q
fever stands for query fever, the name it was given when it ﬁrst
emerged in Queensland, Australia, before the underlying cause
had been identiﬁed. In humans, acute Q fever is characterized by
a febrile “ﬂu-like” illness, with headaches and profound fatigue,
and sometimes pulmonary and hepatic involvement. However,
infection is initially asymptomatic in 60% of those infected. 13
Persistent focal Q fever (previously known as chronic Q fever) can
follow acute Q fever or asymptomatic infection and can be
characterized by cardiac disease (endocarditis, pericarditis,
myocarditis), fatigue syndromes, skin rash, and neurologic,
pulmonary, and hepatic disease.
Unlike other obligate intracellular pathogens, C. burnetii
survives prolonged periods in the environment, where it resists

vetexamprep.ir

high temperature, a variety of disinfectants, and ultraviolet light.
The organism exists in two forms: a small cell variant, which is a
nonreplicating form that survives in the environment, and a large
cell variant, which replicates within mononuclear phagocytes,
especially alveolar macrophages (lung) and Kupﬀer cells (liver).
Survival of the organism for up to 10 months on wool at 15°C to
20°C (59°F to 68°F) has been reported, and it can also survive in
tissues that have been stored in formalin for several months. It is
inactivated by 1% Lysol or 5% hydrogen peroxide. 14 Although
originally classiﬁed within the order Ricke siales, the availability
of sequence information led to its reclassiﬁcation as a
gammaproteobacterium in the order Legionellales, which also
includes Legionella species. Coxiella burnetii undergoes phase
variation, which is associated with alterations in its cell wall
components. The variants have nominally been called phase I and
phase II. 15 The changes in cell surface antigens and the creation of
phase variants have clinical implications for serologic testing in
humans due to the production of phase I and phase II antibodies
to the bacterium at diﬀerent stages of natural infection (see
Diagnosis, later). The whole genome of C. burnetii has been
sequenced. 16
Coxiella burnetii is extremely contagious, and only small
numbers of organisms are required to cause disease in humans.
The epidemiology of Q fever varies geographically. Because of its
predilection for domestic ruminant species, Q fever is most
commonly reported from rural areas although the potential role of
wildlife continues to be explored. Coxiella burnetii has been
detected within a huge variety of diﬀerent tick and other
arthropod species. Within ticks, it replicates in the midgut and it is
shed in large quantities in tick feces. Although ticks have the
potential to transmit the organism to domestic animal species, the
most signiﬁcant role of ticks appears to be in transmission to
wildlife, 17 and molecular investigations question whether C.
burnetii or other Coxiella spp. are involved. 18 Nevertheless,
transstadial transmission of C. burnetii in Ixodes ricinis ticks has
been accomplished under experimental conditions, supporting the
role of I. ricinus as a vector. 19 Coxiella burnetii has been identiﬁed
in ﬁsh, wild birds, rodents, marsupials, horses, swine, camels,
marine mammals, ducks, turkeys, geese, cats, dogs, and rabbits.

vetexamprep.ir

Although the mechanism is not clearly deﬁned or established, cats
and dogs could potentially become infected through exposure to
infected sheep, ca le, and goats—possibly through ingestion of
products from these species—and through contact with, or
ingestion of, infected wildlife reservoir hosts such as rodents,
birds, macropods, and rabbits.

vetexamprep.ir

Transmission of Coxiella burnetii.
The organism is most often transmitted to
humans when animals give birth. People
become infected by inhalation when they
directly contact the products of parturition or as
a result of indirect contact with organisms that
survive in the environment. Sheep, cattle, and
goats are the most common reservoirs of the
organism for human infection, but infected cats
and less commonly dogs can also transmit the
infection to humans. Although not a major
mode of transmission, ticks can also harbor
the organism and are thought to maintain
transmission to wildlife species, especially
rodents (such as small mice) and rabbits, and
also birds. Dogs, cats, and humans can also
become infected when they contact (or ingest)
wildlife species. Ingestion of infected milk also
may be a lesser mode of transmission.

identiﬁed three positive samples, two of which were from cats
with normal reproductive systems. 21 In the Netherlands,
following the largest Q fever outbreak in humans ever
documented (2007 to 2010, approximately 4,000 cases), C. burnetii
DNA was not detected in the placentas from 15 cats but was
found in 4 of 54 (7%) dog placentas from veterinary clinical
practices that focus their expertise on breeding animals. Some
seroprevalence studies suggest that infection is more common in
stray cats and dogs than in client-owned animals, while others
suggest an increased prevalence in breeding cats or dogs from
remote communities. 22–24 Further research is required to
determine risk factors for exposure in dogs and cats including the
role of ingestion of raw meat. 25–27 In one study from Australia, C.
burnetii DNA was detected in 43% of 58 raw meat packages sold
for companion animal consumption. 25 All of the positive samples
contained meat of kangaroo origin amongst other things, whereas
all the negative samples contained no kangaroo. No association
has been found between prevalence of Q fever in humans and cat
or dog ownership. 28 Laboratory-acquired infections have been
described in humans, and infection can occur as a result of
exposure to straw, manure, or dust, such as that from
contaminated farm vehicles and contaminated clothing. Q fever
has emerged as a disease of United States combat arms military
personnel deployed to Iraq. 29 Studies of a large, 2-year outbreak
in the Netherlands showed that dust-accumulating surfaces
contained higher levels of C. burnetii DNA than vaginal swabs
from sheep and goats. 30 The organism can travel for miles as a
result of windborne transmission.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
After inhalation (and to a lesser extent, ingestion), C. burnetii
enters mononuclear phagocytes and survives within the harsh
environment of the phagolysosome. 31 Remarkably, the acidic
conditions of the lysosome appear to be a requirement for the

vetexamprep.ir

metabolic functions of C. burnetii. Replication is prolonged, and
minimal CPEs occur in infected cells. The organism appears to
modulate apoptosis in order to inhibit cell death and promote its
own replication. 31 , 32 Subsequently, infected cells enter the
bloodstream. After experimental infection, bacteremia may be
prolonged (up to 1 month) in cats. 33 The organism can persist in a
variety of tissues, and in human patients, this contributes to
chronic disease manifestations, such as prolonged fever,
endocarditis, vasculitis, chronic fatigue, and immune-mediated
consequences such as demyelinating polyradiculoneuritis. 34
Appropriate diagnosis and treatment at the acute stage of clinical
illness is important in reducing the risk of postacute Q fever
sequelae and development of chronic disease. Reactivation of
shedding has been described during pregnancy in humans. 14
Infected cats and dogs usually show no clinical signs of infection,
but stillbirth, abortion, and prolonged vaginal bleeding for 3
weeks before delivery have been reported in cats. 7 , 35 The
organism replicates in trophoblasts, and in experimentally
infected goats, massive bacterial replication occurs in the placenta
just before abortion. 36 An infected rabbit hound dog that
transmi ed C. burnetii to a family in Nova Scotia gave birth to four
puppies, all of which died within 24 hours of birth. 2 The
importance of C. burnetii in reproductive tract disease and chronic
disease manifestations such as endocarditis in cats and dogs
requires further investigation.

Diagnosis
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnostic assays available for Q fever are listed in Table 48.1. In
humans, a combination of serologic testing and molecular testing
using PCR is recommended, especially in acute infections when
serologic test results are often negative. 37
Culture
Coxiella burnetii can be isolated in a variety of diﬀerent cell lines. It
has also been isolated in a cell-free medium that mimics the
phagolysosome environment. 38 Because it is highly infectious to
humans, most laboratories do not have the special facilities
required to isolate C. burnetii. Thus, diagnosis of infection is
usually performed using serology, PCR, or IHC.
Serologic Diagnosis
The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) reference test
for serologic diagnosis of C. burnetii infection in animals is ELISA.
39 A variety of serologic assays have been used to detect
antibodies to phase I or phase II C. burnetii antigens in humans
and other animals, including IFA assays, ELISA, and CFT. CFT is
considered the least sensitive and speciﬁc method, but is still used

vetexamprep.ir

for diagnosis. 40 In human patients, anti–phase II antibodies (IgG
and IgM) are present in acute Q fever, whereas anti–phase I IgG
antibodies predominate in chronic infection. 17 , 41 In humans, the
use of IFA assays has been recommended for diagnosis of Q fever.
14 , 37 , 42 Acute and convalescent serology is required for
diagnosis of acute Q fever in humans. It can take at least a month
before seroconversion occurs; titers peak around 8 weeks after
infection. 17 Diagnosis of focal persistent Q fever in humans is
based on detection of an increased phase I IgG antibody titer
(≥1:1024) and an identiﬁable persistent clinical manifestation, such
as endocarditis. 37 Because infection is usually not clinically
detected in dogs and cats, serologic assays have primarily been
used in dogs and cats for epidemiologic studies or as part of
import requirements to Q fever–free countries such as New
Zealand. An IFA assay has been optimized for use in feline and
canine serum and species-speciﬁc cutoﬀ values have now been
established that replace the less sensitive CFT used previously. 23 ,

24

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Both conventional and real-time PCR assays have been described
for detection of C. burnetii DNA. PCR assays are the diagnostic
test of choice for organism detection and have revolutionized
knowledge of the epidemiology of C. burnetii infections. In
animals, PCR assays have primarily been used on a research basis.
In humans, PCR is typically performed on whole blood (acute
infections) or heart valve tissue (endocarditis), and is almost
always positive in acute infections before antibodies develop. 37
Negative results can occur with PCR assays in chronic infections
or even as early as 2 weeks after onset of acute illness in humans,
because of undetectable levels of the infection or absence of
bacteremia. Because C. burnetii is highly infectious to humans,
special handling (BSL-3) conditions are required for fresh
specimens that are submi ed for C. burnetii PCR assays. When
infection by C. burnetii is suspected (such as in placentas or
aborted material), the laboratory should be contacted in advance,
and specimens should be labeled and transported appropriately.

Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Li le information is available about the pathology of C. burnetii
infection in dogs and cats. In aﬀected livestock, C. burnetii causes a
necrotizing placentitis with mixed inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrate and
nonsuppurative vasculitis. In some cases, small, basophilic
intracytoplasmic organisms can be seen (Fig. 48.2). The organisms
stain with Gimenez, Giemsa, and modiﬁed acid-fast stains, but
not Gram, silver, or periodic acid–Schiﬀ stains. 43 IHC and FISH 44
can be used to identify C. burnetii antigen within lesions.

Treatment
Many acute infections in humans are self-limiting (or even
subclinical), and symptoms respond to nonspeciﬁc therapy such
as antipyretics and rehydration. However, because of concerns
related to the development of focal persistent Q fever, speciﬁc
antimicrobial therapy is recommended regardless of the severity
of acute Q fever. When antimicrobial agents are required,
doxycycline for at least 14 days or quinolones have been used
successfully to treat pneumonia and hepatitis in human patients
with C. burnetii infection. Combination therapy, such as
doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine (which alkalinizes
phagolysosomes) (as recommended by the CDC) 37 or
doxycycline, ciproﬂoxacin, and rifampin for prolonged periods
(e.g., 2 years), has been required for treatment of Q fever
endocarditis, and valve replacement is frequently needed. 14 , 17
Antibody titers decrease with successful treatment. Q fever
during pregnancy, which may result in abortion when infection
occurs in the ﬁrst trimester, is treated with trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole for the duration of the pregnancy. 45 Treatment
of an infected sheep herd with oxytetracycline on days 100 and
120 of gestation did not prevent shedding of C. burnetii in milk,
vaginal swabs, or feces as assessed with PCR, nor did it aﬀect the
duration of shedding. 46

Public Health Aspects
In humans, asymptomatic infections with C. burnetii are probably
widespread. When it occurs, Q fever is most often a systemic
febrile illness. Because it mimics a variety of other illnesses, and
conﬁrmatory diagnostic tests require a speciﬁc index of suspicion
by the medical clinician, Q fever is most likely under recognized.
Veterinarians involved in mixed or farm animal practice,
slaughterhouse workers, and workers in the livestock industry
(farmers, shearers, transporters of animals) are most likely to
develop Q fever as a result of direct contact with infected
livestock. Person-to-person spread of Q fever is rarely reported,
but humans can shed organisms during parturition, and infection
of an obstetrician during delivery has been described. 47 Infection
during pregnancy may also be associated with reproductive

vetexamprep.ir

complications such as fetal death. 48 , 49 Transmission during
necropsy examinations has also been reported. Between 2014 and
2017, approximately 160 to 190 cases of Q fever were reported to
the CDC each year. 50 Approximately 80% of cases were acute and
20% were chronic, and more than one third of cases were from
three states—California, Iowa, and Texas (Fig. 48.3). Peak months
are in the spring and early summer, which correlates with the
peak of the birthing season for ca le, sheep, and goats. In
Australia where the disease is also notiﬁable, 300 to 500 cases are
reported annually with most cases occurring in two states—
Queensland and New South Wales. 51

Annual reported incidence (per
million persons) for Q fever in the United
States in 2017. Cases are most frequently
reported from western and plains states where
ranching and rearing of livestock are
common. From CDC,
FIG. 48.3

https://www.cdc.gov/qfever/stats/index.html

In humans, acute Q fever occurs after an incubation period that
ranges from 9 to 39 days, although shorter incubation periods are

vetexamprep.ir

possible with exposure to high doses of the agent. 14 The
incubation period after exposure to an infected cat has ranged
from 9 days to 4 weeks. 4 , 14 Males are predisposed, which relates
to an increased likelihood of exposure to ruminants, the more
common mode of exposure, and older men are more susceptible
to disease. 37 Patients who develop pneumonia may also develop
severe headache, as well as sweats, chills, fatigue, and myalgia.
Other signs include cough, chest pain, nausea and vomiting, sore
throat, diarrhea, a rash, and abdominal pain and hematuria. 14
Myocarditis and pericarditis can occur rarely. Blood work often
shows a normal white cell count, and thrombocytopenia or
marked thrombocytosis can occur. Serum biochemistry testing
reveals mild to moderate increases in the activity of hepatic
transaminases in almost all patients. 14 Pulmonary inﬁltrates are
present on thoracic radiographs (Fig. 48.4), and in some cases,
pleural eﬀusion. 14 , 17 Q fever pneumonia is rarely fatal. Focal
persistent Q fever may manifest as endocarditis, optic neuritis,
osteomyelitis, granulomatous hepatitis, interstitial pulmonary
ﬁbrosis, and prolonged fever. In addition, a chronic fatigue
syndrome, has been described in up to 10–15% of patients who
develop acute infection with C. burnetii. 52 This syndrome appears
to be due to cytokine dysregulation and may be characterized by
incapacitating fatigue, nausea, headache, night sweats, myalgia,
muscle fasciculations, lymphadenomegaly, disturbed sleep,
irrational anger, and inability to concentrate. Endocarditis follows
acute Q fever in fewer than 1% of cases, 41 and it may not become
apparent for several years after acute illness. Approximately 3% to
5% of human endocarditis cases have been a ributed to C.
burnetii. Host factors seem to be important in whether chronic
manifestations of Q fever occur. Cellular immunity and the
production of IFN-γ appear to be required for resolution of
infection. 41
Because treatment with tetracyclines does not seem to reduce
shedding by reservoir hosts, an emphasis has been placed on the
development of eﬀective vaccines for public health purposes. A
phase I inactivated vaccine (Coxevac, Ceva, France) is
commercially available in some parts of Europe to prevent
shedding by reservoir livestock species, such as sheep and goats.
Vaccination of sheep ﬂocks led to a reduced number of abortions

vetexamprep.ir

and decreased shedding, but did not completely prevent infection.
41 Vaccination was ineﬀective in previously infected ca le or naïve
pregnant ca le. 53 Another phase I whole cell vaccine (Q-VAX,
Commonwealth Serum Laboratories, Parkville, Australia) has also
been used to protect naïve but at-risk humans, such as livestock
workers (farmers, shearers, slaughterhouse workers, animal
transporters), veterinarians, veterinary nurses, cat and dog
breeders, wildlife carers, and laboratory workers, from infection.
A Q-VAX skin test as well as serologic assays are performed as a
prescreening of potential vaccine recipients for prior sensitization
to Q fever antigens to minimize adverse vaccine reactions;
humans with previous exposure to C. burnetii should never be
vaccinated. It has been recommended that humans should not
drink raw milk from infected farms. Aborted material and
placentas can be buried with lime or incinerated. 41

Q fever has occurred in people exposed to periparturient cats.
An outbreak in an Australian small animal veterinary hospital

vetexamprep.ir

recent infection (see case example). 3 The most severely aﬀected

appropriate PPE when around birth products and avoiding
mouth-to-mouth and mouth-to-nose resuscitation of neonates. In
mixed or large animal practices where veterinarians are exposed
to periparturient sheep and goats, the use of proper PPE,
including protective clothing (boots, coveralls) and eye protection
and N95 masks, is recommended. 50

Case Example
Signalment

A 50-year-old female veterinarian and a 23-year-old female
veterinary technician from southeastern Australia.

History

A 3-year-old female British short-hair cat with dystocia was
brought to a veterinary clinic by the breeder/owner at 8 o’clock
in the morning. One ki en was stillborn in the home
environment overnight. Safe delivery of the two remaining
ki ens required a cesarean section. Surgery was performed
immediately, and the ki ens were delivered and revived by
vigorous rubbing with dry towels. The ki ens were discolored
by yellow-green placental material and were slow to revive.
They were able to successfully suckle once the queen had
recovered from general anesthesia. The queen and ki ens were
returned to the breeder’s ca ery the same afternoon.
Two weeks after the surgery, the veterinarian and the
veterinary technician who had been involved in the cesarean
section developed fever, severe headache, neck pain, chills,
night sweats, myalgia, and stiﬀness. The veterinarian sought
medical a ention. Psi acosis was considered the most likely
diagnosis by the a ending physician, because psi acine birds
were frequently treated in the clinic. A serologic test for
chlamydiosis was negative, but nevertheless treatment with
doxycycline was commenced. The veterinary technician’s

vetexamprep.ir

clinical signs were more severe and included cough, chest pain,
nausea, and vomiting. As a result, she was hospitalized for 3
weeks for further diagnostic testing, treatment, and
convalescence. When the technician tested positive by PCR
assay for C. burnetii DNA on day 10 after the onset of illness,
serial diagnostic tests for Q fever were also performed on the
veterinarian. However, the veterinarian did not test positive
until over a month after the day of the cesarean (Table 48.2).

Comments

Determination of the date of onset of illness is essential in any
diagnostic investigation of Q fever in people for correct
interpretation of diagnostic test results. In the ﬁrst 8 to 10 days
after the onset of illness, patients are frequently (80%)
bacteremic (and therefore PCR positive) but still antibody
negative. IgM class antibody to phase II antigens, as measured
via IFA or ELISA assays, appear as early as 10 to 12 days after
the onset of illness, but this may also be delayed, as occurred in
the veterinarian in this example. IgM class antibody to phase I
and IgG class antibody to phase II antigens often appear on day
15 to 20, but again this can be delayed. Small animal
veterinarians and veterinary technicians or nurses who are
exposed to ki ens and placental secretions and subsequently
develop illness should inform their practitioner of the
possibility of exposure to C. burnetii because diagnosis requires
a high index of suspicion and speciﬁc diagnostic assays. Fatigue
often persists in patients for months after the onset of illness (as
was the case for the veterinary technician in this example) and
does not necessarily mean that focal persistent Q fever has
developed.

49: Chlamydial Infections
Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described in Cats: In 1944, United States. 1
• Causes: Chlamydia felis (and possibly other chlamydiae such
as Chlamydia pneumoniae) causes ocular disease in cats;
Chlamydia psittaci and Chlamydia abortus have both rarely
been detected in association with ocular and respiratory
disease in cats and dogs.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Direct contact with respiratory
secretions and possibly also vaginal secretions and feces.
• Major Clinical Signs (Cats): Acute and chronic conjunctivitis,
chemosis, serous to mucopurulent ocular discharge,
blepharospasm, with or without sneezing and nasal discharge.
• Differential Diagnoses (Cats): FHV-1, FCV, Mycoplasma spp.,
Bordetella bronchiseptica infections.
• Human Health Significance: Chlamydia felis has rarely been
documented as a cause of human conjunctivitis. The
importance of cats and dogs as a source of other human
chlamydial infections requires further investigation. Chlamydia
psittaci is generally acquired from avian species and not from
dogs and cats.

Etiology Agent and Epidemiology
Chlamydiae are obligately intracellular bacteria that belong to the
order Chlamydiales and primarily cause conjunctivitis in cats, but
may also play a role in other systemic and reproductive disorders

vetexamprep.ir

in dogs and cats that remain poorly characterized. Most
knowledge of chlamydial infections results from research on
human chlamydial infections, such as Chlamydia trachomatis,
Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia psi aci, which have
signiﬁcant clinical and public health importance (see Public
Health Signiﬁcance). Chlamydiae structurally resemble gramnegative bacteria, lack peptidoglycan, and have extremely small
genomes; they depend on the host cell for many amino acids and
nucleotides. They exist in two forms: an infectious elementary
body (EB), which is 0.2 to 0.6 µm in diameter and exists outside
the cell, and the reticulate body (RB), which is larger (0.5 to 1.5
µm), noninfectious, and replicates within the cytoplasm of host
cells, before it matures and forms EBs (Fig. 49.1). The EBs survive
only a few days in the environment at room temperature and are
readily inactivated by most disinfectants. Transmission occurs via
direct contact or, to a lesser extent, aerosols. Fomites are also
likely to be an important means of transmission among grouphoused cats in heavily contaminated environments. In one study
of stray and pet cats from Swi erland, rectal shedding was
documented using real-time PCR in 25% of infected cats; 22% of
infected cats had both positive conjunctival and rectal swabs.
Therefore, rectal shedding may also contribute to environmental
contamination. 2 Although the chlamydiae at one time separated
into two genera, Chlamydia and Chlamydophila, based on sequence
analysis of the 16S rRNA and 23S rRNA genes, there has been
disagreement in the ﬁeld regarding this classiﬁcation, and
reversion to the single genus Chlamydia has since been
recommended based on the availability of complete genome
sequence information. 3 , 4
Chlamydiae persistently infect epithelial cells of the ocular,
respiratory, GI, and genitourinary systems; chlamydial infections
of the synovium have also been reported in a number of diﬀerent
host species. Diﬀerent chlamydial species tend to cause disease in
certain hosts, although evidence has accumulated that some
chlamydial species may be capable of causing disease in more
than one host species (Table 49.1). Some disease manifestations in
a single host species may be caused by more than one chlamydial
species. For example, whilst the human ocular disease trachoma is
caused primarily by C. trachomatis, it has now also been associated
with infection by C. pneumoniae and C. psi aci. 5 Chlamydia felis is

vetexamprep.ir

an important cause of conjunctivitis and possibly reproductive
disease in domestic cats, but recently DNA that resembles that of
the human pathogen C. pneumoniae has now also been detected in
ocular swabs from cats with conjunctivitis from Europe. 6
Chlamydia abortus DNA was also detected in 4.3% of 69
Chlamydiaceae-infected cats from Swi erland 2 and was detected
in histopathology specimens from 1 of 13 cats with
arteriosclerosis. 7 There are rare reports of chlamydial infections in
dogs, in association with ocular and respiratory disease,
polyarthritis, and atherosclerosis. 8–13 However, chlamydiae were
not detected with PCR in canine atherosclerotic lesions from 16
dogs in one study. 7 Respiratory disease associated with C. psi aci
infection has been reported most frequently among dogs.
The most signiﬁcant pathogen of cats is C. felis, which causes
acute and chronic conjunctivitis in cats worldwide. Conjunctivitis
due to C. felis infection has also been reported in a free-ranging
Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx). 14 Based on sequence information from
outer membrane protein genes, all feline isolates appear to be
genetically similar. However, the results of serologic methods and
random
ampliﬁcation
of
polymorphic
DNA
(RAPD)
ﬁngerprinting suggest that more than one strain of C. felis might
exist. The prevalence of infection varies from one group of cats to
another, geographic location, age of the cat population sampled,
and presence or absence of clinical illness. Infection is most
commonly detected in multiple cat households, especially
breeding ca eries. Chlamydia felis DNA is uncommonly detected
in conjunctival swabs from healthy cats. For example, in
household cats, clinically healthy cats, those with a history of past
conjunctivitis, and those with active conjunctivitis, positive PCR
results were 0%, 4.6% and 7.3%, respectively. 15 Isolation rates of
up to 30% of household cats have been reported. 16 In shelter cats,
the prevalence of C. felis infection has ranged from 0% to 15%. 17–20
In cats from 218 European rescue shelters, breeding estab
lishments, and private households, the prevalence of infection in
cats without respiratory disease was 3% versus 10% in those with
evidence of respiratory disease. 21 In this study, infection with C.
felis was associated with suboptimal hygiene. Infection with C.
felis is more commonly detected in young cats, especially those
aged 2 to 12 months; ki ens less than 2 months of age may be

vetexamprep.ir

protected by maternal antibody, although neonatal infections
have been described. Cats older than 5 years of age are very
unlikely to be infected with C. felis. Co-infections with other
respiratory pathogens, such as FHV-1 and FCV, are common and
may contribute to increased severity of clinical signs.

(A) The binding of elementary bodies
(EBs) to host cells is initiated by the formation
of a trimolecular bridge between bacterial
adhesins, host receptors, and host heparan
sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs). Next, presynthesized type III secretion system (T3SS)
effectors are injected into the host cell, some of
which initiate cytoskeletal rearrangements to
facilitate internalization and creation of an antiapoptotic state. The EB is endocytosed into a
membrane-bound compartment (inclusion),
which dissociates from the endolysosomal
pathway. EBs convert to reticulate bodies
(RBs) and newly secreted inclusion membrane
proteins (Incs) promote nutrient acquisition by
redirecting exocytic vesicles that are in transit
from the Golgi apparatus to the plasma
membrane. The RBs then replicate
exponentially and secrete effectors that
modulate processes in the host cell. Under
stress, RBs enter a persistent state and
transition to enlarged aberrant bodies. The
bacteria can be reactivated upon removal of
the stress. In late stages of infection, RBs
synthesize EB-specific effectors before
differentiating back to EBs. The EBs exit the
host through lysis or extrusion. Modified from

and pathogenesis. Nat Rev Microbiol. 2016;14:385–
400.

The DNA of organisms that belong to the family
Parachlamydiaceae has also been detected in cats with ocular
disease. These organisms are Chlamydia-like organisms that reside
symbiotically within amoebae. Parachlamydial species include
Neochlamydia, Parachlamydia, Protochlamydia, Rhabdochlamydia,
Criblamydia, Simkania, and Waddlia. DNA that closely resembles
that of Neochlamydia hartmanellae has been detected in feline

vetexamprep.ir

conjunctival specimens. 22 This organism is an endosymbiont of
the amoeba Hartmannella vermiformis, which has been identiﬁed as
a cause of ocular surface infection in humans and may play some
role in feline ocular infections. The DNA of Parachlamydia
acanthamoebae has also been detected with PCR in cats with
keratitis and conjunctivitis. 23 As yet, amoebic co-infections have
not been detected in cats. Further studies are required to
determine the prevalence and clinical signiﬁcance of these
organisms.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Chlamydia felis infection is acquired by cats primarily through
close contact, fomite, or, to a lesser extent, aerosol transmission.
Ki ens may be infected from the mother at birth. Whether
venereal transmission occurs, as reported for other chlamydial
species, is unknown, but in some infected cats, the organism is
shed in vaginal discharges and from the rectum as well as in
ocular discharges. After uptake of EBs, the EB transitions into the
RB, which replicates by binary ﬁssion in a membrane-enclosed
vacuole called an inclusion, and avoids lysosomal fusion. The RBs
then transition back to the EB form, which is released into the
extracellular milieu after cell lysis occurs and subsequently infect
other host cells. The entire replication cycle takes about 2 days to
complete (see Fig. 49.1). 24
Chlamydiae primarily infect columnar epithelial cells, but they
can also infect a variety of other cell types including endothelial
cells, smooth muscle cells, lymphocytes, monocytes, and
macrophages. Chlamydia felis replicates in the cytoplasm of
conjunctival epithelial cells, and also spreads via the bloodstream
to a variety of other tissues, such as the tonsil, lung, liver, spleen,
GI tract, and kidney. Infection is typically followed 2 to 5 days
later by the development of acute, chronic, or recurrent
conjunctivitis, with or without signs of rhinitis, such as nasal
discharge and sneezing. Most cats remain otherwise well and
appetent. Lower respiratory tract signs such as cough and
dyspnea rarely, if ever, occur. Corneal disease such as keratitis or
corneal ulceration is rare, and if present, is likely caused by other

vetexamprep.ir

or co-infecting pathogens such as FHV-1 or bacteria. Experimental
inoculations have also been associated with fever, lethargy,
lameness and joint pain (possibly due to polyarthritis), and weight
loss. 25 There are also rare reports of gastritis and peritonitis in
association with the detection of Chlamydia-like organisms in cats.

a Infection may occasionally extend to other host species.

After the initial episode of acute conjunctivitis, infection may
persist for many months, and this may be accompanied by mild
signs of conjunctivitis, or in some cases, no clinical signs of
disease. Organisms have been isolated from the conjunctiva for up
to 215 days after experimental infection. 28 , 29 Whether chronic
disease is the result of repeated reinfection or the presence of
persistent chlamydiae is unclear. Co-infections with other agents
such as FCV, FHV-1, Bordetella, or Mycoplasma may increase the
clinical severity of infection and duration of shedding. Other
bacteria, including those that normally colonize the healthy
conjunctival sac, can also act as secondary invaders and worsen
the disease.
Whether C. felis can cause reproductive disease in cats remains
unclear. The stage of pregnancy at which infection occurs, coinfection with other organisms such as FHV-1, concurrent
immunosuppression, route of infection, and the strain involved
may be important in determining the ability of C. felis to cause
reproductive dysfunction, if this indeed occurs in cats.
Chlamydial infections are infrequently described in dogs.
Chlamydia psi aci has been detected in dogs with respiratory
disease, such as pneumonia and pleural eﬀusion, and/or
keratoconjunctivitis. 8–10 One group of bitches that had ocular and
lower respiratory signs as well as stillbirths and low li er signs
had nasal, conjunctival, and pharyngeal swab specimens that
tested positive for C. psi aci infection with a nested PCR assay. 8
Chlamydia abortus was detected in a dog with keratoconjunctivitis.
11 The DNA of C. pneumoniae was detected in atherosclerotic

vetexamprep.ir

lesions from dogs in Japan, 12 and Chlamydia-like organisms were
found in a dog from South Africa with polyarthritis. 13

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in cats with chlamydiosis include
conjunctivitis, chemosis, serous to mucopurulent ocular
discharge, and blepharospasm (Fig. 49.2). Signs of nasal
involvement, such as stertorous respiration, serous or
mucopurulent nasal discharge, and sneezing, may accompany
conjunctivitis. Mucopurulent vaginal discharge has been reported
in some cats that were experimentally infected by ocular
inoculation.
Physical examination ﬁndings described in dogs with
chlamydiosis have included fever, tachypnea, keratoconjunctivitis
with mucopurulent ocular discharge, shifting leg lameness, and
lymphadenopathy. 8–11 , 13

Diagnosis
There are no clinically signiﬁcant laboratory abnormalities in cats
with chlamydiosis, and there is insuﬃcient information on
laboratory abnormalities that might occur in aﬀected dogs.
Diagnosis of chlamydiosis is most often based on the results of
molecular testing using PCR. For all diagnostic tests that detect
chlamydial organisms, an a empt to collect suﬃcient numbers of
infected epithelial cells should be made. This generally involves
vigorous swabbing of infected mucosal sites such as the
conjunctiva using a co on swab (Table 49.2).

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination for Inclusions
Using light microscopy, chlamydial intracytoplasmic inclusions
may be seen in epithelial cells that are present in smears of
conjunctival scrapings. Inclusions comprise clusters of coccoid
bacteria, and are usually 10 µm in diameter and stain basophilic
(Fig. 49.3). Large inclusions adjacent to the nucleus can have a
“cloak-like” appearance (hence the name Chlamydia which is
derived from the Greek word meaning “cloak”). Giemsa is the
preferred staining method. Inclusions are generally visible only
early, if at all, during the course of infection, so this method is
insensitive. Also, melanin granules in the cytoplasm of
conjunctival epithelial cells can yield false-positive results. The
use of direct FA staining or immunocytochemistry with antibodies
directed to chlamydial antigens increases sensitivity and
speciﬁcity.
ELISA Antigen Detection
A variety of commercial antigen detection enzyme immunoassay
kits have been developed and marketed for diagnosis of human
chlamydial infections in the past (e.g., Chlamydiazyme, Abbo
Labs, Chicago, IL, USA). Nucleic acid ampliﬁcation tests have now
largely replaced the use of these assays for diagnosis of human
infections. Reagents in ELISA used to detect the antigen of human
chlamydial pathogens in swab specimens (such as conjunctival
swabs) cross-react with C. felis antigen, so have also been used for
diagnosis of feline chlamydiosis. Unfortunately, the kits vary

vetexamprep.ir

considerably in their sensitivity and speciﬁcity. In general, ELISA
methods that detect chlamydial antigen have lower sensitivity and
speciﬁcity than cell culture, direct FA methods, and PCR for
detecting feline infections.
Cell Culture
Culture of chlamydiae has traditionally been considered the gold
standard for chlamydial diagnosis, but is now mostly performed
on a research basis. Isolations from cats are usually highest from
conjunctival swabs, although nasal and pharyngeal swab
specimens may also contain infectious organisms. To enhance
organism survival, swabs can be placed immediately in a
chlamydial transport medium such as 2SP (0.2 M sucrose and 0.02
M phosphate). Routine viral transport medium contains
antibiotics which will inactivate the organisms. The sample
should be refrigerated (4°C) if it is not immediately sent to the
laboratory and ideally should reach the laboratory within 24
hours of specimen collection. In the laboratory, organisms can
readily be grown in the yolk sac of embryonating eggs or in cell
lines such as McCoy or HeLa cells. Incubation times are in the
order of 2 to 3 days. Chlamydial inclusions within the infected cell
culture are then identiﬁed using FA (Fig. 49.4).

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
The use of molecular assays such as PCR has revolutionized the
diagnosis of chlamydial infections in animals and humans,
because these assays are rapid, sensitive, speciﬁc, and do not
require special transport conditions. Sequence analysis of PCR

vetexamprep.ir

products can be used to diﬀerentiate among species of
chlamydiaceae. Both endpoint (conventional) and real-time PCR
assays have been used to detect C. felis in conjunctival swab
specimens from cats, 30–32 and real-time PCR assays that detect C.
felis are oﬀered by several commercial veterinary diagnostic
laboratories
worldwide.
Unfortunately,
considerable
interlaboratory variation in assay performance can exist. 33 In
addition, PCR assays for C. felis may not detect other chlamydial
species, such as C. pneumoniae. Genus- or family-speciﬁc
chlamydial PCR assays must be used to detect these organisms.
The use of a DNA microarray assay for detection and
identiﬁcation of chlamydiae in cats was also reported. 7 The
microarray assay consists of a chip that carries species- and genusspeciﬁc probes for identiﬁcation purposes. DNA within the
specimen is ﬁrst ampliﬁed and biotin labeled with PCR, then
reacted with the microarray probes. 34
PCR assays for C. felis are usually more sensitive than culture in
which comparisons have been made in naturally infected cats (see
Table 49.2). 30 During antimicrobial treatment of infected cats,
PCR results may continue to be positive for several days. 30 , 31 In
one study, topical ophthalmic solutions such as proxymetacaine
and ﬂuorescein did not interfere with the ability of real-time PCR
to detect C. felis, although there was a slight inhibitory eﬀect when
fusidic acid was used. 35 Because cats without signs of
conjunctivitis have occasionally tested PCR positive for C. felis, the
results of PCR must be interpreted in light of the history, clinical
signs present, and response to appropriate treatment.
Serologic Testing
Serologic tests are not widely available for routine diagnosis of
chlamydial infections. Assays for serum antibodies to chlamydiae,
such as IFA or ELISA, have been of limited beneﬁt for detection of
active infection because the IgG antibody titer increase is variable
or prolonged, and IgM antibody titers are inconsistently
increased. However, very high antibody titers (≥ 1:512) have been
associated with clinical illness and/or chlamydial shedding, and
high antibody titers among group-housed cats with conjunctivitis
can suggest a role for C. felis in disease. 16 , 36 , 37 Chlamydial
infections persist in the presence of high serum antibody levels, so

vetexamprep.ir

serologic testing cannot be used to evaluate vaccine-induced
protection. Serial titers may be needed to document active
infections, and recent vaccination may interfere with
interpretation of positive titer results. An ELISA that
discriminates between the antibody response from vaccination
and that from natural infection has been described. 38

a Doxycycline is the treatment of choice. For cats that fail to tolerate

enrofloxacin and pradofloxacin are an option for cats that do not tolerate either
doxycycline or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Treatment and Prognosis
Chlamydial infections are generally treated with tetracycline
antibiotics. Oral administration of doxycycline at 5 to 10 mg/kg
q12h, for 3 to 4 weeks results in clinical resolution in most cats. A
dose of 10 mg/kg q24h can also be used. 37 Clinical improvement
occurs within 24 to 48 hours after treatment is initiated. Treatment
of all cats in a colony for 4 weeks is recommended, because in one
study that used real-time PCR to detect infection, a 3-week course
of treatment was insuﬃcient to clear infection in some cats, but
treatment for 28 days subsequently cleared infection in all cats. 31
Treatment may have to be continued for up to 6 to 8 weeks to
ensure that all cats have been successfully treated. Regardless,
treatment should continue for at least 2 weeks after the resolution
of clinical signs.
Failure to respond completely may reﬂect the concurrent
presence of viral causes of feline URTD. Because doxycycline
hyclate administration can result in esophagitis and esophageal
stricture formation, the administration of tablets should be
followed by a bolus of water or food (see Chapter 10 for
additional information on doxycycline). Ocular infections may
initially respond to tetracycline eye ointment applied two or three

vetexamprep.ir

times daily, 39 but recurrent infections have been documented, 40
possibly because systemic infection with chlamydiae can occur in
cats with conjunctivitis.
For cats that do not tolerate doxycycline, 4 weeks of amoxicillinclavulanate is a suitable alternative. 41 In experimentally infected
cats, the eﬃcacy of enroﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg, PO, q24h, for 14 days)
was similar to that of doxycycline as determined with direct FA on
conjunctival swabs, although a few cats in both the doxycycline
and enroﬂoxacin groups had evidence of persistent infection at
the end of the treatment period. 42 Doxycycline is the preferred
antimicrobial drug because of concerns that relate to the
possibility of retinal toxicity in cats treated with enroﬂoxacin.
Doxycycline was more eﬃcacious than pradoﬂoxacin in
experimentally infected cats that were monitored with PCR. 43
Sulfonamides or chloramphenicol are ineﬀective, and in vitro,
penicillin is only inhibitory at higher doses. Treatment with
azithromycin is also incompletely eﬀective when compared with
doxycycline (Table 49.3). 44

Immunity and Vaccination
Ki ens acquire maternal antibodies to C. felis that usually protect
them from infection until 7 to 9 weeks of age. Both humoral and
cell-mediated mechanisms are important for protective immunity
in chlamydial infections of other host species. Natural infection
seems to confer li le protection against reinfection, and this
protection appears to be short-lived. However, given the low
prevalence of chlamydiosis in older cats, an age-related resistance
to chlamydiosis appears to exist in cats. Both inactivated and
a enuated live vaccines are available to protect cats from
chlamydial respiratory disease. These vaccines do not entirely
prevent infection and shedding of chlamydiae after challenge, but
they minimize the replication of the organism and hence reduce
the severity of clinical signs. Transient fever, anorexia, lethargy,
and lameness have been described 1 to 3 weeks after use of
combined vaccines containing a enuated live C. felis in a low
percentage of cats. Chlamydial vaccines are noncore vaccines that
are recommended for cats with a high risk of acquiring infection,
such as those introduced to or that reside in ca eries with
documented endemic chlamydiosis. These cats should be

vetexamprep.ir

vaccinated after treatment
antimicrobial drugs.

all

cats

with

Prevention
Given that chlamydiae survive poorly in the environment and the
major route of transmission is close contact, transmission can be
minimized by good hygiene, quarantine, single housing, and
disinfection practices in ca ery situations. Chlamydiae are readily
inactivated by detergent solutions and common disinfectants.

Public Health Aspects
The most signiﬁcant chlamydial pathogens of humans are C.
trachomatis, C. pneumoniae, and C. psi aci. Chlamydia trachomatis
causes trachoma, the leading cause of infectious blindness
worldwide, and it also is the most common bacterial cause of
sexually transmi ed diseases in humans. Chlamydia pneumoniae is
extremely widespread, may infect nearly all humans, and is an
important cause of community-acquired pneumonia worldwide.
It has also been implicated in atherosclerotic cardiovascular
disease, although its role in this condition remains unclear.
Chlamydia psi aci is the cause of psi acosis in birds and humans, a
potentially life-threatening zoonosis.
Chlamydia felis has long been suspected as a cause of
conjunctivitis in humans. However, many of the reports of human
infection with C. felis before the advent of genetic detection
methods remain unconﬁrmed, because diagnosis was either based
on culture without identiﬁcation to the species level, or on
serologic testing, which has the potential to cross-react with other
chlamydiae and organisms such as Bartonella. Molecular assays
have since been used to conﬁrm the diagnosis of C. felis infection
in humans. Chlamydia felis has rarely been detected in the
conjunctiva of humans with conjunctivitis. 45 , 46 In these reports,
the organism found in the humans was genetically
indistinguishable from isolates recovered from the patients’ cats.
Although these associations have been diﬃcult to document,
routine precautions should be taken when handling cats with
conjunctivitis, especially young cats with chronic conjunctivitis.

vetexamprep.ir

Proper handwashing and routine cleaning and disinfection are
likely to be suﬃcient to prevent transmission.
The identiﬁcation of C. psi aci in dogs with respiratory disease
and C. pneumoniae in cats with ocular disease suggests that dogs
and cats may have the potential to be a source of these pathogens
for humans, although avian species and other infected humans,
respectively, are likely to be much more signiﬁcant sources of
infection.

Case Example
Signalment

“Sam,” a 3-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat from
Davis, CA.

History

Sam was brought to the University of California, Davis, by a
veterinary student for evaluation of fever, right thoracic limb
lameness, and bilateral conjunctivitis with mucopurulent ocular
discharge of 2 days’ duration. There had been no cough,
sneezing, vomiting, diarrhea, or abnormal thirst or urination
noted. Sam lived indoors with ﬁve other cats, three of which
also had severe conjunctivitis, ocular discharge, fever, lethargy,
and lameness for the last week. These three cats ranged in age
from 8 months to 2.5 years. All of the cats had been vaccinated
regularly for FHV-1, FCV, and FPV and tested negative for
FeLV and FIV as ki ens. They were all fed a commercial dry cat
food.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 6.7 kg.
General: Bright, alert, responsive, and hydrated. T =
103.6°F, HR = 240 beats/minute, RR = 66 breaths/minute,
mucous membranes pink, CRT = 1 second.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No evidence of ocular
discharge, mild conjunctival hyperemia; nasal planum
clean and moist with no discharge; no oral erosions or
ulcerations.

vetexamprep.ir

Musculoskeletal: BCS 7/9, decreased weight bearing on
left thoracic limb, sometimes holds left thoracic limb up
when si ing; possible mild eﬀusion in the left elbow;
resents ﬂexion of the left carpus and left and right elbows.
Cardiovascular: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities
detected.
Respiratory: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities.
GI and genitourinary: Nonpainful abdomen, no masses
palpated, small-sized bladder.
Lymph nodes: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities
detected.

CBC: HCT 46.3% (30%–50%), MCV 46.9 fL (42–53 fL),

9,000 cells/µL), lymphocytes 2,310 cells/µL (1,000–7,000
cells/µL), monocytes 525 cells/µL (50–600 cells/µL),

cells/µL (0–50 cells/µL), platelets 174,000/µL (180,000–
500,000 platelets/µL), with moderate macroplatelets.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 152 mmol/L (151–158
mmol/L), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.6–4.9 mmol/L),

hemoprotein, glucose, ketones, or bilirubin, 0–1
WBC/HPF, 0–2 RBC/HPF, few lipid droplets.
Synovial ﬂuid cytology: Synovial ﬂuid from the right
stiﬂe, right carpus, left carpus, and right tarsus was

vetexamprep.ir

examined. All specimens apart from that from the left
carpus were markedly blood contaminated and so could
not be properly evaluated. The cell counts in these
specimens ranged from 2,000 to 4,000 nucleated cells/µL,
and consisted predominantly of neutrophils (66%–80%)
and small mononuclear cells (7%–18%). The specimen
from the left carpus had 2,000 nucleated cells/µL, of
which 14% were neutrophils, 85% large mononuclear
cells, and 1% small mononuclear cells. There were
moderate numbers of erythrocytes and blood-associated

Conjunctival smear cytology: Chlamydial inclusions
visualized within several epithelial cells.

Imaging Findings

Radiographs of the left radius and ulna, including carpus and
elbow joints: No radiographic abnormalities.

Microbiologic Testing

FeLV antigen and FIV antibody serology: Negative
PCR for FCV (oropharyngeal swab specimens): Negative
Mycoplasma culture (conjunctival swab specimen):
Negative

Diagnosis

A tentative diagnosis of chlamydial conjunctivitis and arthritis
was made.

Treatment and Outcome

Treatment of all cats in the household with doxycycline (10
mg/kg, PO, q24h) was initiated. This was associated with rapid
resolution of fever, ocular signs, and lameness.

Comments

The cats in this household may have had conjunctivitis and
arthritis related to a chlamydial infection. The major diﬀerential
diagnosis was FCV infection, which is more widespread than

vetexamprep.ir

chlamydiosis and for which an association between lameness
and infection has been widely documented. Infection with
Mycoplasma spp. has also been associated with conjunctivitis as
well as synovitis in cats (see Chapter 57). Infection with C. felis
has been associated with development of lameness in
experimentally infected cats, but there are no reports of
lameness in association with natural infection. The negative
PCR and culture results for FCV and Mycoplasma spp.,
respectively, could not deﬁnitively rule out infection with these
agents. The presence of chlamydial inclusions in the
conjunctival smear supported a diagnosis of chlamydiosis, but
false positives can occur and unfortunately PCR was not
performed to conﬁrm the presence of a chlamydial agent.
Nevertheless, the rapid response to doxycycline supported the
possibility of a bacterial cause of the arthritis.
