50: Streptococcal and
Enterococcal Infections
John F. Presco , Jane E. Sykes, and Joshua B. Daniels

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Streptococci were first described in Germany
in 1868 by Billroth. 1 Enterococci were separated from the
genus Streptococcus in 1984. 2
• Major Causes: In dogs and cats, the most common causes
are Streptococcus canis, Streptococcus equi subsp.
zooepidemicus, Enterococcus faecium, and Enterococcus
faecalis, which are gram-positive coccoid bacteria.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Direct contact usually; hospital
environments can become contaminated with resistant
enterococci. Organisms are usually commensals that invade
opportunistically.
• Major Clinical Signs: Clinically highly variable opportunistic
infection; includes arthritis, bacteremia and endocarditis,
bronchopneumonia, cervical lymphadenitis,
cholangiohepatitis, discospondylitis, keratitis, mastitis,
meningoencephalitis, necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock
syndrome (primarily S. canis), neonatal bacteremia,
osteomyelitis, otitis externa, peritonitis, pharyngitis,
postoperative incision or wound infections, pyometra or
metritis, pyothorax, rhinitis and necrotizing sinusitis, and UTIs.
Inflammation associated with these infections tends to be very
pyogenic. In the lungs, these organisms are frequent
components of polymicrobial aspiration pneumonia.
• Differential Diagnoses: Primarily other gram-positive and
gram-negative bacterial infections.

vetexamprep.ir

• Human Health Significance: The role of dogs and cats in the
transmission of Streptococcus pyogenes, a major human
pathogen, (Lancefield group A) is commonly exaggerated.
Streptococcal species that infect dogs and cats occasionally
infect human patients. Dogs and cats, or their contaminated
environments, may also have the potential to serve as
sources of MDR enterococcal infections for humans.

Etiology, Epidemiology, and Clinical Features
Streptococci are catalase-negative, gram-positive, nonmotile cocci
that divide along a single axis, forming pairs and chains of
organisms (Figs. 50.1 and 50.2). They are facultative-to-strict
aerobes that require complex media for growth, preferably
supplemented with blood for the β-hemolytic types. They cause
localized to widespread pyogenic infections in animals and
humans. Although numerous species are pathogenic, many are
commensal microﬂora of the oral cavity, nasopharynx, skin, and
genital and GI tracts. More than 115 species of streptococci have
been described. Species of streptococci vary in host tropism and
virulence properties, and so are discussed separately. There has
been conﬂicting literature as to whether one of the most important
streptococcal pathogens of humans, Streptococcus pyogenes, which
causes human streptococcal pharyngitis (“strep throat”), can
infect dogs and cats. Reports in the medical literature that pets
may be a reservoir of infection for humans have frequently been
based on erroneous identiﬁcation studies (see Public Health
Aspects). However, interspecies transmission has been reported
for some pathogenic streptococci such as Streptococcus pneumoniae,
Streptococcus canis, and Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus. As
is the case in humans, streptococci that infect dogs and cats range
from commensals of low virulence to highly virulent organisms
that can cause severe disease manifestations and death.
Several classiﬁcation systems exist for streptococci based on
cultural characteristics, antigenic composition, and biochemical
features. Streptococci have been classiﬁed based on their in vitro
hemolytic properties as: β-hemolytic streptococci, which cause
complete hemolysis when they grow on blood agar; α-hemolytic
streptococci, which reduce hemoglobin to cause a greenish

vetexamprep.ir

discoloration of the agar around bacterial colonies; and, rather
strangely, “γ-hemolytic,” which are actually nonhemolytic
streptococci. The β-hemolytic strains tend to be most pathogenic.
Organisms in the α-hemolytic and nonhemolytic (γ-hemolytic)
categories are found on mucous membranes and skin of clinically
healthy animals. If present in an infectious process, they are
usually regarded as contaminants or unimportant invaders. When
they do cause illness, it may take the form of valvular endocarditis
or embolic abscess. The precise species classiﬁcation of
streptococci in numerous disease processes described next is in
doubt, especially in the older literature. The lack of harmonization
of methods used to speciate streptococci among veterinary
diagnostic laboratories unfortunately perpetuates this uncertainty.
Streptococci are also classiﬁed from A through W based on their
surface antigens (Lanceﬁeld classiﬁcation system) and further
classiﬁed based on phenotypic characteristics. The Lanceﬁeld
classiﬁcation system tends to correlate with pathogenicity.
Lanceﬁeld groups A, B, C, E, G, L, and M are usually β-hemolytic.
Major pathogenic streptococci of dogs and cats belong to
Lanceﬁeld groups B, C, D, or G (Table 50.1). “Pyogenic
streptococci” are β-hemolytic streptococci that belong to
Lanceﬁeld groups A (S. pyogenes), B (Streptococcus agalactiae), C
(includes Streptococcus dysgalactiae and S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus), and G (includes S. canis). “Viridans streptococci” is
an archaic term for catalase-negative gram-positive aerobic cocci
that are either nonhemolytic or α-hemolytic (viridis = Latin for
green) that tend to be commensals, have low virulence, and rarely
invade tissues opportunistically. Many of these streptococci,
which are also Lanceﬁeld group D, have now been classiﬁed as
enterococci. Molecular typing schemes have revealed that
hemolytic reactions, Lanceﬁeld antigens, and phenotypic
characteristics do not necessarily predict genetic relatedness
among streptococcal strains. Although these traditional
classiﬁcation methods are still in use by laboratory staﬀ,
microbiologists, and clinicians, most modern laboratories now use
MALDI-TOF or possibly kit biochemical systems to identify these
bacteria to their correct genus (Enterococcus, Streptococcus) and
species.

Streptococci invade tissues opportunistically when there is a
breach in normal host barriers. This leads to a wide variety of
clinical disease manifestations, such as arthritis, cellulitis,
endocarditis, meningoencephalitis, pyoderma, pneumonia,
osteomyelitis,
and
UTIs.
Severe
and
life-threatening
manifestations of streptococcal infection include necrotizing
fasciitis/myositis (NFM) and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
(STSS). The past decade has had a resurgence of severe invasive
group A human streptococcal infections characterized by septic
shock associated with multiple organ failure and with or without
NFM.
Predisposing conditions for streptococcal infections in dogs and
cats may include atopic dermatitis, wounds, foreign bodies (such
as migrating grass awns), immunosuppressive drug treatment,
and young age (especially neonates). 3 The most common clinical
manifestation among fetuses and neonates is streptococcal

vetexamprep.ir

bacteremia and sepsis, which can result in abortion and death.
Streptococcal pneumonia may occur in association with infections
with other respiratory pathogens, such as respiratory viruses, or
occur secondary to bronchitis, hematogenous spread, or
aspiration. In one study, streptococci were isolated from sick dogs
more frequently in summer months. 3

Streptococcus canis
Streptococcus canis is the streptococcal species most frequently
isolated from dogs and cats. 3 It is a β-hemolytic, group G
(pyogenic) streptococcus that colonizes the pharynx, GI tracts
(especially the mouth), genital mucosa, and skin of healthy dogs
and cats. It has also been isolated from other animal species, such
as foxes, mice, mink, rabbits, and rats. Infection with S. canis may
be associated arthritis, bacteremia, bronchopneumonia, cervical
lymphadenitis, cholangiohepatitis, discospondylitis, endocarditis,
ulcerative keratitis, mastitis, meningoencephalitis, NFM and STSS,
neonatal bacteremia/sepsis, osteomyelitis, otitis externa,
peritonitis, pharyngitis, postoperative incision or wound
infections, pyometra or metritis, pyothorax, rhinitis and
necrotizing sinusitis, and UTIs. Neonatal infections can occur
when organisms are transmi ed from the vaginal tract during
parturition; they can also occur if organism accesses the systemic
circulation via the umbilical vein. In juvenile ki ens (3 to 7
months old), cervical lymphadenitis may follow a subclinical
episode of pharyngitis and tonsillitis. Streptococcal meningitis
results from direct extension from the sinuses or middle ear, or
from bacteremia. Other embolic complications may accompany
bacteremia with S. canis. Although opportunistic infections with S.
canis occur sporadically, outbreaks of group G streptococcal
infection have been reported in group-housed animals, which
suggested spread of a virulent strain. 4–6

TABLE 50.1

Severe manifestations of S. canis infection, such as STSS and
NFM, have been increasingly recognized in dogs and cats years,
sometimes in the absence of obvious immunosuppressive
underlying conditions or wounds. 7–10 In most cases, aﬀected
animals were previously healthy adult dogs or cats younger than
1 year of age. Although toxic shock syndrome can also be caused
by staphylococci, STSS is deﬁned as any streptococcal infection
associated with the sudden onset of shock and organ failure.
Mechanisms of shock and organ failure identiﬁed in human group
A streptococcal infections include elaboration of pyrogenic
exotoxins by streptococci, which act as superantigens.
Superantigens stimulate T-cell responses through their ability to
bind to, and cross-link, the MHC class II complex of antigenpresenting cells, and the T-cell receptor, which bypasses normal
MHC-restricted antigen processing (Fig. 50.3). This leads to
sudden and massive cascade of cytokine release, which in turn
causes signs of fever, vomiting, and hypotension, together with
tissue damage, DIC, and multiple organ dysfunction. 11 Cats with
STSS had bacterial embolic localization with lesions in the lungs,
heart, and liver. 12 Other streptococcal virulence factors also
contribute to proinﬂammatory cytokine release and the
development of hypotension. Laboratory abnormalities include
thrombocytopenia, azotemia, hypoalbuminemia, and metabolic
acidosis. Death can occur within 48 hours after the onset of illness.
Speciﬁc criteria are used for diagnosis of STSS in human patients,
and similar deﬁnitions could be used for diagnosis of STSS in
dogs and cats (Box 50.1). Because relatively few dogs and cats
with STSS have been described, predisposing factors have not
been fully identiﬁed but in dogs include bites and use of antiinﬂammatory drugs. 7 , 9 Importantly, there is also evidence that
use of ﬂuoroquinolones can predispose dogs with initially minor

However as in dogs, predisposing factors are not always
identiﬁed.
NFM is a bacterial infection of the deep subcutaneous tissues
and fascia, characterized by extensive necrosis and gangrene of
the skin and underlying tissues. It often begins as a minor wound
and progresses rapidly over 24 to 72 hours, and it may be
accompanied by STSS (Fig. 50.4). The popular term “ﬂesh-eating
bacteria” has been used to describe the organisms involved in
“ﬂesh-eating disease.” Streptococcal NFM has been described in
both dogs and cats. Bacteria at the inoculation site synthesize
proteolytic enzymes and other products that facilitate the
organism’s spread via fascial planes and into muscles. Periosteal
involvement, adjacent to involved muscle, has also been reported.
13 Lesions usually involve a limb (although have been described in
one dog on the ventral thorax) and are intensely painful, with
localized heat and swelling and accumulation of exudate along
the fascial planes that requires drainage and debridement. In
some dogs, extensive sloughing of necrotic skin occurs. 7
Bacteremia and complications that result from septic emboli may
accompany NFM. 8 Outbreaks of NFM, arthritis, sinusitis, and
meningitis caused by S. canis have been reported in cats in
shelters, 4 breeding colonies, 14 and hoarding facilities. 6 In a
spectacular report described in a grossly unhygienic and
overcrowded institutional hoarding facility, the range of multiple
syndromes in numerous aﬀected cats included acute rhinitis,
cervical lymph node abscessation, severe septic arthritis,
meningitis, otitis, STSS, and NFM. 6 Molecular typing (by pulsedﬁeld gel electrophoresis) of isolates from one outbreak revealed
that isolates were clonally related, which indicated spread of a
virulent strain, 15 but another study of unrelated cases has not
identiﬁed clonal spread 16 so that strain virulence may be less
important than host predisposition.

Pathophysiology of toxic shock
syndrome. Streptococcus superantigens bind
first to MHC class II molecules on antigenpresenting cells, which stimulates cytokine
expression and release, as well as expression
of costimulatory molecules that promote T-cell
receptor binding and activation. Subsequently,
T-cell receptor binding occurs through the
variable region on the receptor’s beta chain
(Vβ). Because superantigens can bind to
multiple types of Vβ regions, a large proportion
of the T-cell population can be simultaneously
activated. For example, conventional antigens
might activate < 0.1% of the T-cell population,
whereas superantigens might activate > 20%
of the population.

Despite the recognition of severe disease manifestations in some
dogs and cats, relatively li le is known about virulence factors of
S. canis. A protein analogous to M protein, a major virulence
factor of S. pyogenes with important antiphagocytic properties, has
been identiﬁed in S. canis and was shown to bind plasminogen
and degrade thrombi. 17 This M protein, named SCM, has also
been shown to bind IgG. 18 Genes that encode other virulence
factors identiﬁed in S. pyogenes, such as pyrogenic exotoxins (Spe
genes), streptococcal superantigen (SSA), streptokinase (Ska), and
C5a peptidase (Scp, which cleaves the ﬁfth component of
complement), have not been detected. 19 However, one important
study showed that exposure of S. canis to the ﬂuoroquinolone
antibiotic enroﬂoxacin caused bacterial cell lysis through inducing
bacteriophage development, as a result of induction of the “SOS”
response in strains containing these bacterial viruses, and the
associated release of a bacteriophage-encoded lymphocyte
mitogen related to pokeweed mitogen. 20 The presence of this
mitogen gene on enroﬂoxacin-induced bacteriophages may
explain the frequently noted association between ﬂuoroquinolone
treatment and the occurrence of STSS/NFM in dogs 7 because of a
superantigen-like response of lymphocytes. Many of the dogs
reported with STSS/NFM had received enroﬂoxacin in the early
stages of disease, but the drug was not eﬀective in halting the
progression of the disease despite marginal in vitro susceptibility
in some cases. 7 In fact, as suggested, enroﬂoxacin may have
triggered the pathologic events caused by these virulent
streptococci. 7 , 20 Fluoroquinolones are thus contraindicated in
the treatment of dogs with S. canis infections.

Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus
Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus is a β-hemolytic, group C
streptococcus that is a commensal of the upper respiratory and
lower genital tracts, and mouth, of many species including cats,
dogs, guinea-pigs, horses, rabbits, seals, sheep, and swine. It is
best known as the major opportunist pathogen of horses in which
it causes wound infections, respiratory disease, endometritis, and
abortion, among many other manifestations. Infections have also
been reported in a variety of other animal species noted above but
also less frequently in ca le, monkeys, seals, and humans.
Diﬀerent strains of S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus exist that may vary
in pathogenicity and host tropism, and severe infections have

vetexamprep.ir

p
g
y
p
been identiﬁed in several diﬀerent host species, including the dog
and cat. Infected horses can be a source of infection for dogs in
some situations 21 but in most cases, there is no history of horse
contact.
Several outbreaks of hemorrhagic, ﬁbrinosuppurative, and
necrotizing pneumonia associated with S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus infection have been described in group-housed
dogs, such as those in kennels, research colonies, and shelter
environments, from a variety of geographic locations worldwide
and with an apparently increasing frequency (Fig. 50.5). 22–25 The
pneumonia progresses rapidly in some dogs and may be
accompanied by signs suggestive of STSS, such as fever and
systemic hypovolemia. In some dogs, severe tachypnea and death
occur within 24 to 48 hours of the ﬁrst signs of respiratory disease,
or dogs may be found dead without any preceding clinical signs.
Other infected dogs show only mild signs of respiratory disease.
Outbreaks of pneumonia, purulent rhinosinusitis, and
meningoencephalitis have also been described in cats. 26–28
Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus meningoencephalitis
occurred in a cat as a result of extension of otitis media/interna. 29
The pathogenesis of infection with S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
in dogs and cats is unclear, but there is no doubt that this virulent
organism can cause very severe disease, as it can in other species,
including humans. Diﬀerent strains are involved in outbreaks of
severe disease in dogs and cats, so increasing reports cannot be
a ributed to clonal expansion of virulent clones. There is no
evidence that there are diﬀerences in protective immunogenicity
among these strains. 23 Co-infection with other contagious
respiratory pathogens may initiate infection and can contribute to
the severity of disease. Co-infections with CDV, CAdV-2, CHV-1,
CIV, Bordetella bronchiseptica, or Mycoplasma cynos have been
documented in some, but not all, aﬀected dogs with S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus pneumonia. 22 Experimentally, co-infection of dogs
with both CIV and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus was associated
with more severe clinical manifestations of disease than when
either organism is inoculated alone. 30 Other environmental
factors such as overcrowding may predispose to disease and its
severity; in large prevalence surveys of respiratory pathogens in
dogs with CIRD, S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus is rarely detected

vetexamprep.ir

when compared with other pathogens in the complex. 31 , 32
Superantigen genes have been detected in some isolates of S. equi
subsp. zooepidemicus from dogs, 33 but there has been no
correlation between the presence of these genes and the severity
of
histopathologic
lesions.
However,
expression
of
proinﬂammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8 in the
lungs of aﬀected dogs suggests that a potent inﬂammatory
response is involved in the pathogenesis of disease. 24

Other Streptococcal Species
Streptococci other than S. canis and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus are
of relatively minor signiﬁcance in dogs and cats. Streptococcus equi
subsp. equi, the etiologic agent of strangles, was isolated from a
dog with tonsillar and submandibular lymphadenomegaly caused
by pharyngeal foreign body penetration. 34 Genetic
characterization conﬁrmed the isolate as this usually highly
equine-speciﬁc pathogen. The dog lived on premises where horses
were kept; unexpectedly, no clinical cases of strangles had been
identiﬁed in the horses in the local environment.
Group B streptococci (S. agalactiae) have been associated mainly
with neonatal bacteremia and postpartum metritis in humans and
mastitis in cows. Factors at the time of delivery, such as low birth
weight or diﬃcult delivery, precipitate the development of clinical
illness. Skin, pharyngeal, and wound infections can occur.
Immunosuppressed people can develop bacteremia, meningitis,
and endocarditis as a result of infection. Group B streptococci are
more frequently isolated than group G from people with these
syndromes. Streptococcus agalactiae infections are rare in dogs and
cats, although there are reports of involvement in bacteremia in a
dog, in endocarditis, endometritis, and neonatal sepsis (“fading
puppy syndrome”). Peritonitis with bacteremia and parturient
endometritis and placentitis have been described in cats. Whether
canine and feline strains are indigenous or of human or other
animal origin is uncertain.
Streptococcus dysgalactiae is a β-hemolytic, group C
streptococcus, like S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus. There are two
subspecies, S. dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis and S. dysgalactiae
subsp. dysgalactiae. After S. canis and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus,
S. dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis was the third most common β- or

vetexamprep.ir

γ-hemolytic streptococcal species isolated from dogs at a
veterinary teaching hospital in the United States, but was detected
in only 13 of 393 dogs with streptococcal infections. Aﬀected dogs
had bacteremia and sepsis, dermatitis, or pneumonia. 3
Streptococcus dysgalactiae subsp. dysgalactiae has been reported in
association with systemic neonatal infections and death in a li er
of great Dane puppies. 35
The porcine streptococcus, Streptococcus suis, has occasionally
been isolated from cats with meningoencephalitis, pyothorax, or
dermatitis. 36 , 37 Streptococcus suis was also isolated from the
urine of a systemically unwell dog that had fever and bacteriuria
in Canada. 38 The dog had no known exposure to swine; however,
it had been allowed to chew on pig ear treats. It can be isolated
from the anus, tonsils, and skin of healthy dogs and cats. 39
Streptococcus suis has been classiﬁed into serotypes, which have
epidemiologic importance. Human infections are usually
serotypes 2 and 14. The cases reported in dogs and cats have not
belonged to these serotypes.
Other streptococcal species isolated from dogs and cats include
the human pathogen Streptococcus constellatus (a Streptococcus
anginosus group organism), which was isolated from a dog with
pyoderma. 40 Streptococcus bovis group organisms are α- or
nonhemolytic and usually possess Lanceﬁeld group D antigens.
Biotypes that belong to this group, which diﬀer in their
biochemical characteristics, were reclassiﬁed as distinct species,
Streptococcus gallolyticus and Streptococcus infantarius. 41
Streptococcus bovis group organisms are commensals of the GI
tracts of humans and other animals, especially ruminants, and are
important causes of bacteremia and endocarditis in humans,
accounting for 11% to 17% of all endocarditis cases. They
frequently aﬀect multiple valves and are associated with embolic
complications. For unknown reasons, fecal carriage of S. bovis
group organisms by humans has been strongly associated with
colorectal cancer. This especially seems to be true for S. gallolyticus
subsp. gallolyticus. 42 Rarely, S. bovis group organisms are isolated
from dogs and cats with UTIs. They have also been isolated from
the blood of dogs with mitral valve endocarditis, one of which
also had sternebral osteomyelitis. 43 , 44

vetexamprep.ir

Enterococcus spp
Enterococci are α- or nonhemolytic gram-positive bacteria that
usually possess Lanceﬁeld group D antigens, and are commensals
of the GI tracts of humans and other animals. In humans and pets,
they have predominantly caused infections in hospitalized
patients as nosocomial complications and are problematic in
veterinary hospital se ings because of their ability to persist in the
environment as well as develop multiple antibacterial resistance.
Enterococci form pairs or short chains of organisms that cannot
morphologically be discriminated from streptococci. Enterococci
can survive harsh environmental conditions, and are more likely
than streptococci, especially β-hemolytic species, to survive in
clinic and hospital se ings. They are able to proliferate in medium
that contains 6.5% NaCl, at temperatures that range from 10°C to
45°C (50°F to 113°F), and can be metabolically active in the
presence of 40% bile salts, which in turn explains their improved
ability to grow in the intestine when compared with the less
robust genus Streptococcus. The genus Enterococcus, which contains
55 species, was separated from Streptococcus in the mid-1980s. 2
Not only are enterococci environmentally hardy but they are
often resistant to a wide variety of diﬀerent antimicrobial drug
classes. MDR enterococcal infections, especially those that are also
resistant to vancomycin (vancomycin-resistant enterococci [VRE]),
are a signiﬁcant problem in human medicine. Of great clinical
importance, resistance among enterococci occurs as a result of
both intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms. Intrinsic
resistance to low levels of most β-lactam antimicrobials occurs
because enterococci possess low-aﬃnity PBPs, making penicillins
generally bacteriostatic, not bactericidal, against enterococci.
Enterococci also have low-level intrinsic resistance to
aminoglycosides, which results from decreased drug uptake.
However, uptake of aminoglycosides is enhanced when
enterococci are exposed to β-lactams, explaining the synergistic
activity of this combination that is sometimes taken advantage of
in treatment. Enterococci are resistant to trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole because they utilize exogenously produced
folate. Thus, even if the organisms appear susceptible to
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in vitro (when exogenous folate is
lacking), the drug is not eﬀective in vivo. Many laboratories

vetexamprep.ir

therefore will not report MICs for this organism-drug
combination. Enterococcal resistance to other antimicrobials, such
as macrolides and vancomycin, results from acquired resistance
mechanisms. Extensive multidrug resistance has been well
documented in enterococci isolated from dogs and cats, but there
are few reports of enterococci with acquired vancomycin
resistance from dogs in the literature. These have been reports
from the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and the United States.
45–47 All other isolates examined have been vancomycin
susceptible. In contrast, in humans from Europe and North
America, VRE account for up to 30% of enterococcal infections,
notably in hospital-associated infections. 48
Clinical microbiology laboratories should identify and
distinguish between Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium,
the most prevalent species in humans. These two species diﬀer in
their epidemiology, antimicrobial susceptibility, and virulence
properties. Since these are often hospital-associated infections,
their identiﬁcation to species may be a clue to their presence as
contaminants in the environment, which may further be
suggested if they have a common resistance proﬁle. Enterococcus
faecium is more likely to show high-level resistance (HLR) to
penicillins, and to show multidrug resistance, than E. faecalis, and
as a result, in humans, the prognosis for serious E. faecium
infections may be worse than that for E. faecalis infections. 49
However, E. faecalis is more likely to produce bioﬁlms than E.
faecium and therefore are more likely to colonize catheters. 50
Although most infections in humans have been E. faecalis, an
increase in the prevalence of MDR E. faecium infections has
occurred, especially in hospitals. In particular, ampicillin- and
ﬂuoroquinolone-resistant E. faecium strains that belong to
hospital-adapted strains of the clonal complex 17 (CC17) have
emerged. 51 Strains belonging to this clade are a deﬁned, globally
disseminated population that is associated with hospitalized
human patients but only rarely found in the community; it might
be concluded that they have adapted to human hospitals. CC17
isolates have been found in dogs but belong to a diﬀerent clade
from those found in hospitalized humans. Their virulence gene
proﬁle and antimicrobial susceptibility proﬁles have diﬀered from
those of human isolates. 51–53 In contrast to E. faecium, clones of E.

vetexamprep.ir

faecalis are not found only in hospitals but are also present in
healthy humans and animals, and animals may therefore
represent a source of infection for humans. 51 , 53 As in humans,
the two most common species of Enterococcus associated with
disease in dogs and cats are E. faecalis and E. faecium. 54
In healthy dogs and cats, enterococci can be found on the skin
and within the oral cavity, nasal cavity, and GI tract. In the United
States, the most prevalent species in dogs appears to be E. faecalis,
which comprised 68% of 155 isolates. 54 In the cat, in one study it
was Enterococcus hirae, which comprised 52% of 121 isolates, 54 but
in a more recent study it was E. faecalis (77%) followed by E.
faecium (13%). 55 Other species isolated from sick dogs and cats
include Enterococcus casseliﬂavus, Enterococcus durans, and
Enterococcus gallinarum; Enterococcus canintestini has been isolated
from healthy dogs. 56–58
Although less pathogenic than many β-hemolytic streptococci,
important virulence factors have been identiﬁed in enterococci
that enable them to invade tissues and cause disease. These
include a cytolysin, gelatinase, and a serine protease, as well as
several surface proteins (e.g., the Ace protein, which allows the
organism to adhere to connective tissue components, such as
collagen). Enterococci also possess pili that play an important role
in adherence. The ability of many enterococci to form bioﬁlms
means they can colonize catheters or other surfaces and be very
diﬃcult to eradicate, because in bioﬁlms they are more likely to
resist phagocytosis and antimicrobial drugs. 50 In addition,
because enterococci are intrinsically resistant to a number of
antimicrobials, treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics (which
destroy competing bacteria) selects for mucosal, including
intestinal, colonization by enterococci. The development of
enterococcal UTIs may be promoted by repeated use of
antimicrobial drugs to treat recurrent UTIs if the underlying cause
of infection is not identiﬁed or cannot be resolved. Because of
these features and their robust nature, enterococci can
contaminate the hospital environment and survive for long
periods on fomites (door knobs, stethoscopes, monitoring
devices), as well as be transmi ed via the hands, gloves, and
clothing of hospital personnel. Inoculation may occur via urinary,

vetexamprep.ir

IV, or other invasive devices, or organisms may enter the body
from a damaged GI tract.
Severe concurrent illness and immunosuppression may
predispose to infection but is compounded by the resistance of
these bacteria to antibiotics and their ability to proliferate in the
large intestine and be shed in feces when the competing
microﬂora has been removed by antibiotics. In addition to UTIs,
enterococci may be isolated from dogs and cats with bacteremia
and endocarditis, cholangiohepatitis, discospondylitis, hepatic
abscesses, mastitis, pancreatitis, peritonitis, pyoderma, otitis
externa, and wound infections. There have been rare reports of GI
illness in association with enterococcal infection of the GI tract in
dogs and cats. In aﬀected cats, an association with diarrhea was
supported by the presence of large mats of enterococci in
association with the GI mucosa. 59 , 60 Frequently, enterococci are
isolated from lesions in mixed infections with other GI
microorganisms.
There is some evidence that E. hirae, a commensal species, plays
a protective role in ki ens infected with atypical enteropathogenic
Escherichia coli (aEPEC). 61 Preparations that contain E. faecium
strains have been investigated as probiotics in dogs and cats, with
mixed results. 62–66

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in dogs and cats with Streptococcus
or Enterococcus infections vary with the anatomic site(s) of
infection. Streptococcal infections are an important diﬀerential
diagnosis in “fading” neonates; dogs with physical examination
ﬁndings suggestive of endocarditis; dogs and cats with severe
pneumonia and pyothorax; STSS and NF; rapid onset of systemic
illness in association with a wound; or outbreaks of severe
purulent upper respiratory disease, hemorrhagic pneumonia, and
systemic illness in group-housed animals.
Findings suggestive of streptococcal or enterococcal
endocarditis include fever, lethargy, tachycardia, joint pain and
swelling, systolic heart murmurs, and signs of embolic
complications such as lameness, limb edema, weak or absent
pulses, or neurologic signs (see Chapter 122). Animals with
streptococcal pneumonia may have a fever (up to 106.3°F or

vetexamprep.ir

41.3°C), cough, tonsillar enlargement and hyperemia,
mucopurulent nasal discharge, and/or tachypnea with increased
lung sounds. Lung sounds may be decreased if pleural eﬀusion is
present. Animals with NFM have variable extents of regional
cutaneous erythema, sometimes in association with a wound;
cutaneous ulceration, swelling, edema, intense pain, and warmth
on palpation of the aﬀected area. In human patients, the “ﬁnger
test” has been used to assist recognition of NFM, whereby the
area of suspected involvement is inﬁltrated with a local anesthetic,
and a 2-cm incision is made in the skin and extended into the
deep fascia. A lack of bleeding is a sign of NFM. A sterile doublegloved ﬁnger is then used to probe the incision, and the test is
considered positive if tissues separate with li le resistance. 67 In
some animals, extensive skin sloughing can occur. In two dogs,
acute onset of posterior paresis with lower motor neuron deﬁcits
developed because of the presence of septic emboli in blood
vessels of the gray ma er of the spinal cord and extension of
infection into the surrounding connective tissue, muscle, and
peripheral nerves.
Animals with STSS may be obtunded, with weak pulses,
tachycardia, tachypnea, and prolonged CRT. Rectal temperatures
may exceed 106°F (41.1°C), although the presence of fever is
variable. Icterus may be present in animals that develop multiple
organ dysfunction syndrome in association with STSS.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Biochemistry, and Urinalysis
Findings
Dogs and cats with severe manifestations of streptococcal
infections (such as endocarditis, pneumonia, NF, and STSS)
usually have a neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift, toxic
neutrophils, lymphopenia, and monocytosis. A degenerative left
shift or circulating metamyelocytes may be present. STSS may be
accompanied by thrombocytopenia as a result of DIC, azotemia
and/or increased liver enzyme activities, hypoalbuminemia, and
hypoglycemia. Serum creatine kinase activity may be increased
with muscle involvement. The urinalysis of dogs and cats with

vetexamprep.ir

streptococcal or enterococcal UTIs may reveal pyuria, proteinuria,
or hematuria, and cocci in pairs or chains may sometimes be
evident on sediment examination.
Clotting Function
Dogs and cats with STSS that develop DIC may have clo ing
function abnormalities including prolonged coagulation times,
increased ﬁbrin degradation product and D-dimer concentrations,
and decreased antithrombin concentrations.
Cytologic Abnormalities
Cytologic examination of specimens (respiratory lavage ﬂuid,
aspirates of aﬀected tissues, or pus) from dogs and cats with
streptococcal or enterococcal infections typically reveals large
numbers of degenerate and nondegenerate neutrophils. Coccoid
bacteria in pairs or characteristically in chains may also be seen.
Cytologic examination of ﬁne-needle aspirates from swollen areas
in dogs and cats with NFM is essential to speed conﬁrmation of
infection and institute early appropriate antimicrobial therapy,
because virulent strains of gram-negative bacteria can also cause
this syndrome.

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Streptococci and enterococci that infect dogs and cats are readily
isolated on routine bacteriologic media from aspirates, tissue
biopsies, body ﬂuids, and lavage specimens. Inoculation of
complex solid media that contain blood is recommended and is
the usual practice in laboratories. Streptococci may grow well in
anaerobic incubation conditions, but these are not required
because of their facultative nature. The laboratory may use
selective media for specimens that are heavily contaminated with
other bacteria. Species are identiﬁed based on their phenotypic
characteristics (such as colony morphology and hemolytic
properties), biochemical reactions, grouping with Lanceﬁeld
antisera, and most frequently now by MALDI-TOF (see Chapter
3). Molecular typing methods such as pulsed-ﬁeld gel
electrophoresis or multilocus sequence typing may sometimes be

vetexamprep.ir

done to investigate outbreaks in group-housed animals or hospital
environments, largely for research purposes.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing for β-hemolytic streptococci
is often not performed by veterinary diagnostic laboratories,
because virtually all such strains are penicillin (and amoxicillin)
susceptible. This is also true for group A β-hemolytic streptococci
(GAS, S. pyogenes) that infect humans. However, an increased
prevalence of penicillin resistance, which occurs as a result of
altered PBPs, has been detected in S. pneumoniae, which is
primarily a human pathogen. 56 Streptococcus pneumoniae may
also be resistant to other β-lactam drugs and macrolides.
Acquired resistance may occur in non-β-hemolytic streptococci in
dogs and cats, and so susceptibility testing is recommended for
these bacteria. Some laboratories may falsely report β-hemolytic
streptococci as resistant to trimethroprim-sulfamethazine because
of the antagonistic eﬀect of thymidine in bacteriologic media
containing blood. Laboratory assessment of antimicrobial
susceptibility is of critical importance for enterococci because of
the high prevalence of resistance in this group, particularly among
E. faecium isolates. Isolates with a consistent antibiotype (pa ern
of antimicrobial susceptibility) may indicate that a clinic or
hospital has an Enterococcus contamination problem.

Pathologic Findings
Pathologic ﬁndings in Streptococcus infections vary depending on
the organ system aﬀected. Gross ﬁndings in S. canis sinusitis
include accumulation of purulent material within the frontal sinus
with osteolysis, and distortion of the nasal bridge in cats. 4 When
meningitis is present, purulent material may be found in
association with the meninges (Fig. 50.6). Lesions of NF in dogs
and cats consist of edema, ecchymoses, and necrosis that extend
within the fascia and subcutis in association with ulcerative skin
lesions (see Fig. 50.4). An accumulation of pus may be found
between fascial planes. Congestion of a variety of organs may be
present in animals that have accompanying STSS. When S. canis or
Enterococcus endocarditis is present, adherent and friable mass
lesions may be seen in association with the mitral and/or, less
commonly, the aortic valves. Dogs with streptococcal endocarditis
are more likely to have concurrent polyarthritis than dogs with

vetexamprep.ir

other bacterial causes of endocarditis. 43 On histopathology, valve
lesions generally contain large numbers of degenerate and
nondegenerate neutrophils, hemorrhage, necrosis, ﬁbrin thrombi,
and abundant gram-positive cocci (Fig. 50.7). Septic
thromboemboli may be present in a variety of organs.
Histopathologic lesions in neonates that die of sepsis include
severe inﬂammation and necrosis, as well as septic emboli in a
variety of tissues (see Fig. 50.1).
Grossly, the lungs of dogs with S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
pneumonia may be red, consolidated, and fail to collapse (see Fig.
50.5). There may be variable quantities of hemorrhagic pleural
eﬀusion, petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages on pleural
surfaces, and bloody exudate within the airways and nasal cavity.
24 Typical histopathologic changes include ﬁbrinous, necrotizing,
and/or suppurative pneumonia or bronchopneumonia; ﬁbrin
thrombi; and intralesional clusters or chains of coccoid bacteria.
Within lymph nodes, marked lymphoid depletion may be present,
but lymphoid hyperplasia has also been reported. Occasionally,
septic thromboemboli may be present in tissues or organs such as
the lymph nodes, renal glomeruli, adrenal glands, brain, and
splenic sinusoids. 68 , 69

Treatment and Prognosis
In general, streptococcal infections should be treated with a βlactam drug, preferably an aminopenicillin such as amoxicillin or
a ﬁrst-generation cephalosporin (Table 50.2). Early diagnosis and
prompt treatment with appropriate antimicrobial drugs are
essential to prevent more severe complications such as NF or
STSS. In animals that present with severe signs such as septic
shock or life-threatening pneumonia, initial treatment should be
with a broad-spectrum antimicrobial drug combination, such as a
β-lactam including amoxicillin and an aminoglycoside, which
together commonly also has synergistic activity against
streptococci, namely group C streptococci (S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus).

vetexamprep.ir

Prompt surgical exploration and debridement is of critical
importance in NF, because shock and organ failure will continue
to progress in the face of antimicrobial treatment when necrotic
tissue persists. Use of negative pressure wound therapy was
associated with successful outcomes in three dogs. 10 Surviving
animals often must have extensive skin grafting or dermoplasty to
close open wounds created by the necrotic process. Imaging
techniques such as ultrasound may be useful to help characterize
the extent of lesions before surgery. Extremely aggressive ﬂuid
resuscitation with crystalloids and blood products may also be
required, while blood pressure is monitored. STSS is a clinical
emergency and requires IV benzyl penicillin as the drug of choice
because of its exquisite activity. 70 In human patients, deep-seated
streptococcal infections (NF and STSS) are often treated with both
high-dose penicillin and clindamycin. This is because clindamycin
suppresses exotoxin production by GAS, is more active than
penicillin in experimental NF, and has a longer half-life than
penicillin. 70 , 71 However, a low prevalence of clindamycin
resistance exists in GAS, whereas all GAS are susceptible to
penicillin. 70 , 71 Approximately 10% to 15% of contemporary S.
canis isolates from dogs in Europe and nearly 18% of isolates from
dogs in Japan have demonstrated clindamycin resistance. 72–74
Given this ﬁnding, the same combination could be used to treat
NF in dogs and cats. In humans, IV immunoglobulin treatment is
also recommended on the basis of clinical trials. 70 As noted
earlier, ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotics should be avoided in
treatment of S. canis infections because they promote an
endogenous bacterial mitogen production. 20 In addition, they are
not of value in streptococcal infections because of their low
activity.

Meningitis/Meningoencephalitis
High-dose penicillin or amoxicillin was the drug of choice for
treatment of streptococcal meningitis in human patients caused by
S. pneumoniae before the emergence of penicillin resistance in this
species. It is the drug of choice for meningitis caused by βhemolytic streptococci despite the relatively limited penetration of
the CSF in uninﬂamed meninges; this is because of the strong
susceptibility of these streptococci to penicillin and the greater

vetexamprep.ir

penetration of penicillin in inﬂamed meninges. Trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole has been used with apparent success to treat
some dogs and cats with streptococcal meningitis. 27 , 75 See
Chapter 129 for additional information on treatment of bacterial
meningitis. Ceftriaxone has been used as an alternative to
benzylpenicillin for treatment of human streptococcal meningitis
and a ains higher concentrations in the CSF with the advantage
that its spectrum of activity covers gram-negative bacteria.

Enterococcal Infections
Suggested antimicrobial treatments for treatment of enterococcal
infections in dogs and cats are shown in Table 50.3. Successful
treatment of enterococcal infections requires awareness of the
intrinsic resistance of enterococci to low levels of β-lactams and
aminoglycosides, the synergistic eﬀect of high doses of these
drugs, the lack of eﬃcacy of trimethoprim-sulfonamide
combinations in vivo, and the ability of enterococci to acquire
resistance genes to a large number of other antimicrobial
compounds. Susceptibility testing is, therefore, always
recommended when isolates are believed to be clinically relevant.
Aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin generally have more activity
against enterococci than penicillin or the carbapenems.
Bactericidal regimens, which consist of a β-lactam and
gentamicin, are used in human patients to treat systemic
infections such as endocarditis or bacteremia. Enterococci are

vetexamprep.ir

usually resistant to aminoglycosides at dilutions used in routine
broth microdilution methods (low-level resistance). When the
synergistic combination is indicated, but low-level resistance is
present, isolates should be tested for HLR to aminoglycosides.
Aminoglycoside HLR results from production of an
aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme by enterococci. It emerged in
the 1980s and has been a growing problem in both E. faecium and
E. faecalis isolates from human patients. Aminoglycoside HLR has
also been reported in E. faecium and E. faecalis isolated from dogs
and cats, 45 , 46 , 76 but most isolates are susceptible to high
concentrations of gentamicin. In human patients, a combination of
ceftriaxone and ampicillin has been recommended to treat
endocarditis caused by aminoglycoside HLR enterococci. 49 When
enterococci show penicillin resistance, vancomycin can be
substituted for penicillin, but this requires prolonged
hospitalization for IV administration and is best avoided unless
there is no alternative therapy, because vancomycin is a critical
antimicrobial for treatment of resistant bacterial infections in
humans. Single-agent treatment with linezolid (see Chapter 10) is
an oral alternative for treatment of serious penicillin-resistant
enterococcal infections, but in human patients it is recommended
that this only be used when combinations of β-lactams and
gentamicin cannot be used because of resistance, toxicity, or
treatment failure. 48 Although most strains of enterococci isolated
from humans are susceptible to linezolid, resistant strains have
appeared. 77 Of concern, linezolid- and multidrug-resistant
enterococci were described in raw commercial dog food in Europe
in 2019 and 2020. 78 Use of linezolid may also be associated with
adverse eﬀects of anemia and gastrointestinal signs in dogs and
cats. 79 Chloramphenicol may be successful for treatment of
resistant enterococcal bloodstream infections when administered
orally, but it is bacteriostatic, and concerns regarding adverse
eﬀects in humans exist (see Chapter 10).
Treatment of enterococcal UTIs with β-lactams such as
ampicillin or amoxicillin may be successful even when resistance
is documented in the susceptibility panel, because of the high
concentrations that these drugs achieve in the urine. 48
Nitrofurantoin has also been useful for treatment of resistant
enterococcal UTIs in humans, but routine treatment of subclinical

vetexamprep.ir

bacteriuria caused by MDR enterococci is not recommended (see
Chapter 127). 80 When enterococci are present with other bacteria,
especially in the urinary tract, treatment of the nonenterococcal
pathogen may be suﬃcient to resolve the infection.

Prevention
Because outbreaks of streptococcal infections in dogs and cats
have been associated with overcrowding, co-infections, and other
stressors, appropriate shelter and kennel management and
hygiene, as well as vaccination against other respiratory
pathogens, may help to prevent streptococcal infections. The
predisposing factors may however not be clear. Proper wound
care may prevent serious streptococcal infections such as
bacteremia, endocarditis, NF, and STSS. Methods to reduce
nosocomial infections by enterococci are outlined in Chapter 15.
Resistant enterococcal infections may be prevented through
restricted and appropriate use of antimicrobial drugs and proper
management of underlying disorders that predispose to bacterial
infections.

Public Health Aspects
Streptococci include some of the most important bacterial
pathogens of humans. The β-hemolytic GAS S. pyogenes causes
streptococcal pharyngitis (“strep throat”) and scarlet fever, as well
as poststreptococcal rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease, and
glomerulonephritis. In 2005, it was estimated that globally, GAS
cause more than 616 million new cases of pharyngitis each year. 81
GAS have also been associated with other disease manifestations,
which include NF, STSS, myositis, vaginitis, and bacteremia. As a
result, S. pyogenes is the most extensively studied of all
streptococci. There are more than 100 diﬀerent serotypes, which
are classiﬁed based on the sequence of the M protein gene (known
as emm typing). M protein, a ﬁlamentous macromolecule that
traverses the cell wall (see Fig. 50.2), is a key virulence factor of
GAS. Chronic subclinical carriage of infection in the oropharynx
occurs in some individuals. GAS can survive extremes in
environmental temperature and humidity; however, most
infections are associated with direct or close contact among

vetexamprep.ir

susceptible individuals. Prevalence rates for GAS are higher in
young children, especially those in daycare or classroom
situations. The prevalence of positive throat culture ﬁndings in
such circumstances may approach 50%, even in the absence of an
obvious epidemic. Symptomatic, rather than carrier children, are
most likely to bring infection into the home. Under such
circumstances, the isolation rate in other people in the household
approaches 25% to 50%. If the child is asymptomatic, the rate is
only 9%. Although family pets have been implicated as a reservoir
in households with recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis, 82–84
colonization or infection of dogs and cats with GAS appears to be
rare or nonexistent when accurate streptococcal identiﬁcation
methods have been performed, although the idea that pets can be
reservoirs seems to remain an enduring and unfortunate myth.
One study found no evidence of oropharyngeal colonization by
GAS in pets that were in contact with children with acute
pharyngitis. 1 When domestic pets come into close contact with
infected individuals, some pets may apparently develop
pharyngeal colonization with GAS. Infected pets show no clinical
illness or tonsillar enlargement and usually eliminate their
infection within 2 to 3 weeks after they are removed from the
household. Treatment of infected humans is generally limited to
only those that are symptomatic, so it is not rational to screen pets
for evidence of colonization.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is an important commensal of the
human respiratory tract that causes a variety of diseases including
bacteremia, meningitis, and pneumonia, otitis media, and
sinusitis. Children are regarded as the most important reservoir.

Reports of human infection with S. canis and S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus exist, and represent a more genuine threat than the
potential for zoonotic transmission of S. pyogenes or S. pneumoniae
from companion animals discussed above. Streptococcus canis has
increasingly been recognized as a cause of soft tissue infections in
dog owners and has been isolated from humans with bacteremia,

vetexamprep.ir

endocarditis, UTIs, osteomyelitis, and pneumonia. 88–92 Population
genetic studies suggest that S. canis is a single population that can
infect multiple animal species including humans, suggesting that
the potential for human infection from dogs and cats is always
present. 92 The situation can be complicated because human
group G streptococci can be confused with S. canis, which is also
Lanceﬁeld group G. Rarely, S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus has been
isolated from humans with bacteremia, endocarditis, meningitis,
acute nephritis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, or
STSS. Most human infections with S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
have been traced to an animal source, such as contact with horses,
or consumption of inadequately pasteurized milk products or
pork. However, apparent transmission of S. equi subsp.
zooepidemicus from a dog with S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
pneumonia to a handler, who developed severe systemic illness,
has been described. 93 The sometimes very serious nature of S.
canis and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus infections in humans means
that dogs or cats with severe streptococcal infections should be
handled with appropriate precautions by anyone in contact with
them. The risk can probably be contained by wearing gloves and
protective clothing when handling dogs with STSS or NFM.
Dogs and cats are also a potential source for human infection by
MDR enterococci. In one study, dogs that left a veterinary
intensive care unit (ICU) were colonized with MDR enterococci
with the capacity for bioﬁlm formation and horizontal transfer of
antimicrobial resistance genes. 94 Enterococcal infections in
humans usually require signiﬁcant host predisposition, although
this is less the case for S. canis and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
infections. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci with the same
genotype as those found in people have been recovered from the
feces of pet dogs and cats, and the discovery of linezolid- and
multidrug-resistant enterococci in raw commercial dog food in
Europe has signiﬁcant public health implications. 79
Because of the potential for transmission of streptococci and
enterococci between dogs, cats, and humans, preventative
measures such as hand washing after pets are handled, household
disinfection, and avoidance of close contact (such as allowing pets
to lick wounds or mucous membranes) should be considered,
especially for immunocompromised pet owners. Dogs and cats
should not be fed raw diets, even if commercially available as

vetexamprep.ir

y
frozen raw food for pets. Veterinarians should also recognize the
potential for clinics and hospital environments to become
contaminated with E. faecalis and E. faecium, and take appropriate
hygiene steps if this is recognized to have occurred.

Case Example 1
Signalment

“Rigby,” an 8-year-old neutered Boston terrier from Central
Ohio.

History

Rigby was evaluated by the emergency service of the Ohio State
University Veterinary Medical Center for acute swelling of the
entire left pelvic limb distal to the stiﬂe. Two days prior to
examination, he had been hospitalized in another facility where
he was treated with activated charcoal, crystalloids, and GI
protectants after ingestion of an unknown amount of deracoxib.
Upon discharge from the other facility, the owner noticed a
small swelling on the left hock which progressed rapidly
towards the stiﬂe during that day. The owner reported that
Rigby had decreased energy and inappetence.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 10.9 kg.
General, cardiovascular, and respiratory: Bright, alert, and
responsive. Hydrated. T = 103.5°F (39.7°C), HR = 112
beats/minute, II/VI left apical systolic murmur, strong
femoral pulses, panting, BCS = 3/5, mucous membranes =
pink, CRT < 2 seconds, BP = 195 mmHg (Doppler) right
thoracic limb.
Integumentary and musculoskeletal: Ambulatory and
weight-bearing on all limbs. The left pelvic limb was
warm and erythematous with pi ing edema that
extended from the tarsus to the proximal tibia. The dog
was able to fully ﬂex the tarsal joint, however he was
painful upon deep palpation.
Peripheral lymph nodes, external genital, neurologic, and
ear/nose/throat examinations were all within normal

vetexamprep.ir

limits.

Laboratory Findings

CBC, serum chemistries, and urinalysis were within normal
limits.
Cytologic evaluation of an aspirate from a ﬂuid pocket on the
left tarsus revealed marked neutrophilic inﬂammation with
both intracellular and extracellular cocci that occasionally
formed chains.

Case Progression

Rigby was admi ed to the ICU and managed with IV
crystalloids and ampicillin/sulbactam with a diﬀerential
diagnosis of severe cellulitis or NFM. Over the next several
hours, the proximal left pelvic limb also became edematous and
amputation was performed without complication (Fig. 50.8).
The amputated limb revealed a positive ﬁnger test, 65 and
subsequent histopathologic characterization of the tissue
revealed extensive acute, diﬀuse, severe ﬁbrinosuppurative
cellulitis and dermatitis with hemorrhage and edema,
compatible with NFM. The next morning, aerobic culture of the
ﬂuid aspirate yielded a pure, heavy growth of S. canis. Rigby’s
management in the ICU was continued for 2 additional days,
and he was discharged on oral amoxicillin, tramadol,
gabapentin, and douxo wipes for his amputation site. The heart
murmur, which was appreciated on presentation and may have
indicated concern for streptococcal endocarditis, was not
recognized subsequently.

Case Example 2
Signalment

“Jazz,” a 6-year-old female spayed miniature pinscher from
Fairﬁeld in northern California.

History

Jazz was brought to the University of California, Davis,
Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital, for evaluation of
anorexia, lethargy, and diarrhea. Two days previously, the dog
had been seen by the dermatology service for a focal area of
alopecia and scaling on the dorsal midline in the thoracolumbar
region that ﬁrst appeared 7 months previously, enlarged to 6 ×
4 cm in diameter over 2 months, and then remained static in
size for the subsequent 5 months. Skin scrapings and fungal
culture were performed, and four skin biopsies were obtained.
An underlying vasculitis was suspected, and treatment with
vitamin E (200 U, PO, q12h) and an oral fa y acid supplement
was recommended pending the results of the diagnostic tests.
The following day the owner noted edema of the right pelvic
limb and discontinued the medications. Over the next 24 hours,
Jazz became lethargic, inappetent, and developed liquid
diarrhea and polydipsia. Jazz had been vaccinated regularly for
canine distemper, adenovirus, and parvovirus infections and
rabies and normally ate a commercial dry dog food. She was
last vaccinated just after the skin lesion ﬁrst appeared. The dog
was mostly indoors, going outside on leash walks only, and
there were no other pets in the household.

Other Medical History

vetexamprep.ir

Jazz had been spayed 5 weeks previously, at which time
pyometra was an incidental ﬁnding and was treated with a 7day course of amoxicillin.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 3.3 kg.
General: Lethargic, alert and ambulatory, but weak.
Vocalized on palpation of the thorax and abdomen. T =
102.2°F (39.0°C), HR = 120 beats/minute, RR = 60
breaths/minute, mucous membranes pink, CRT = 1
second.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mild conjunctival hyperemia
and bilateral serous ocular discharge were present.
Integument: There was mild subcutaneous edema and a
small amount of serosanguinous ﬂuid in the region of the
skin biopsies, but sutures remained intact. There was a
single, raised erythematous lesion adjacent to the skin
biopsies that measured 0.5 × 0.5 cm in diameter. Severe
edema was noted in the cranioventral thoracic region,
which extended over an area that was 9 × 5 cm in
diameter.
Other systems, including peripheral lymph nodes: No
clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 53.1% (40%–55%), MCV 71.2 fL (65–75 fL),
MCHC 36.7 g/dL (33–36 g/dL), nucleated RBC 24/100
WBC, WBC 2,200 cells/µL (6,000–13,000 cells/µL),
neutrophils 792 cells/µL (3,000–10,500 cells/µL), band
neutrophils 748 cells/µL, metamyelocytes 88 cells/µL,
myelocytes 44 cells/µL, lymphocytes 308 cells/µL (1,000–
4,000 cells/µL), monocytes 220 cells/µL (150–1,200 cells/
µL), platelets 97,000/µL (150,000–400,000 platelets/µL).
Markedly toxic band neutrophils, metamyelocytes, and
myelocytes; moderately toxic neutrophils; and rare
reactive lymphocytes were present.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 128 mmol/L (145–154
mmol/L), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.6–5.3 mmol/L),

vetexamprep.ir

chloride 90 mmol/L (108–118 mmol/L), bicarbonate 21
mmol/L (16–26 mmol/L), phosphorus 8.7 mg/dL (3.0–6.2
mg/dL), calcium 10.0 mg/dL (9.7–11.5 mg/dL), BUN 63
mg/dL ( 5–21 mg/dL), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.3–1.2
mg/dL), glucose 75 mg/dL (64–123 mg/dL), total protein
5.6 g/dL (5.4–7.6 g/dL), albumin 2.2 g/dL (3.0–4.4 g/dL),
globulin 3.4 g/dL (1.8–3.9 g/dL), ALT 185 U/L (19–67 U/L),
AST 128 U/L (19–42 U/L), ALP 539 U/L (21–170 U/L),
cholesterol 526 mg/dL (135–361 mg/dL), total bilirubin 0.5
mg/dL (0–0.2 mg/dL).
Urinalysis: SpG 1.021; pH 5.0, 1+ protein (SSA), 1+
bilirubin, 4+ hemoprotein, no glucose, no ketones, rare
WBC/HPF, 0–2 RBC/HPF, few amorphous crystals, no
bacteria seen.

Imaging Findings

Abdominal ultrasound: Enlargement of the uterine stump was
present dorsal to the bladder. There were no cystic structures
within the stump and no evidence of ﬂuid in this region or
lymphadenopathy.

Cytologic Findings

Needle aspiration of edema ﬂuid from a region adjacent to the
right axilla revealed large numbers of cocci, some in pairs, in
the absence of signiﬁcant numbers of leukocytes.

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic bacterial culture (aspirate of edema ﬂuid): Large
numbers of S. canis colonies were isolated after overnight
culture, and identiﬁed by MALDI-TOF the same day. A
subsequent blood culture failed to yield any bacteria.

Treatment and Outcome

Treatment with IV ﬂuids (0.9% NaCl with 20 mEq KCl/L) was
initiated before the culture results were obtained. Ampicillin (20
mg/kg, IV, q6h), enroﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg, IV, q24h), and
butorphanol were administered. The dog’s body temperature
subsequently dropped to 98.0°F (36.7°C) and blood glucose
concentration dropped to 30 mg/dL. Fluids were supplemented
with dextrose and a warming pad was used, and the dog’s
temperature returned to normal limits. Within hours, the edema
had spread to the abdomen, and evidence of bruising appeared

vetexamprep.ir

on the right thorax and ventrum. The raised erythematous
lesion on the dorsum ulcerated, and dehiscence of the biopsy
site adjacent to this region became apparent. Blood work
showed a hematocrit of 39%, 2,700 WBCs/µL, 1,323 band
neutrophils/µL, 702 neutrophils/µL, 162 lymphocytes/µL, 513
monocytes/µL, and 37,000 platelets/µL; serum sodium
concentration was 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L,
creatinine 0.4 mg/dL, BUN 23 mg/dL, albumin 1.2 g/dL,
globulin 3.1 g/dL, cholesterol 221 mg/dL, and total bilirubin 2.3
mg/dL. The activities of ALT, AST, and ALP were 79 U/L, 136
U/L, and 292 U/L, respectively. Treatment with dextran and
plasma was initiated, but systolic blood pressure dropped to 80
mmHg, and the region adjacent to the biopsy sites became ﬁrm
and painful and tore when palpated. Ampicillin was replaced
by penicillin G (40,000 U/kg, IV, q6h), and enroﬂoxacin
treatment was stopped. Forty-eight hours after admission, the
dog was anesthetized and a large portion of necrotic skin was
surgically debrided from the dog’s dorsum. The debrided
region was covered with a stent. During recovery, the dog was
tachypneic, had increased lung sounds, and systolic blood
pressure dropped to 50 mmHg. The dog developed respiratory
arrest, and an endotracheal tube was placed, from which
bloody ﬂuid emanated. Cardiac arrest then ensued, and there
was no response to closed cardiopulmonary resuscitation
eﬀorts.

Necropsy Findings

At necropsy, necrosis extended through the intercostal
musculature of the right thoracic wall. Histopathologic lesions
included severe, focally extensive, hemorrhagic and necrotizing
panniculitis and fasciitis with intralesional bacteria and
multifocal thrombi; diﬀuse necrotizing myositis of the right
thoracic wall with intralesional bacteria; severe congestion and
mild, multifocal hemorrhage and thrombosis within the
kidneys; centrilobular congestion and severe bile stasis within
the liver; congestion and hemorrhage within the lung; and
generalized lymphoid depletion and sinusoidal histiocytosis
within lymph nodes. Around the uterine stump, there was focal
ﬁbrosis and mild granulomatous serositis, but very few S. canis
were cultured from the uterine stump. Histopathology of the
biopsy specimens that had been collected before the onset of

vetexamprep.ir

systemic illness showed severe, diﬀuse adnexal atrophy; mild,
chronic,
lymphoplasmacytic
mural
folliculitis;
focal
granulomatous furunculosis with hyperkeratosis; and mild,
multifocal,
perivascular
neutrophilic
dermatitis.
No
microorganisms were seen, although only special staining with
PAS and Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) was performed.

Diagnosis

NF, myositis, and STSS associated with S. canis infection.

Comments

This rare detailed case description illustrates how rapidly NF
can progress and the ineﬀectiveness of antibiotic treatment in
the presence of devitalized tissue. Clinical ﬁndings more than
satisﬁed the criteria for diagnosis of STSS and NF in Box 50.1.
The source of infection and the role that the uterine stump
infection played was unclear. The eﬀect of treatment of Jazz
with the ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic, enroﬂoxacin, on
development of STSS/NF is unclear, but this class of antibiotics
is contraindicated in cases of S. canis infection since they may
exacerbate disease as discussed earlier. 19
