51: Staphylococcal Infections
J. Sco Weese, and John F. Presco

KEY POINTS
• First Described: 1882, Scotland (Alexander Ogsten).
• Causes: In dogs and cats, the most common staphylococcal
pathogens are Staphylococcus pseudintermedius,
Staphylococcus aureus, and Staphylococcus schleiferi.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Transmission is primarily through
direct contact. Indirect transmission via fomites or the
environment can occur.
• Major Clinical Signs: Pyoderma, otitis externa, surgical site
infections, osteomyelitis, bacteremia and endocarditis,
bronchopneumonia, urinary tract infections, ocular surface
infections, rarely necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock
syndrome, pyothorax and peritonitis, discospondylitis, arthritis.
• Differential Diagnoses: Clinical signs are indistinguishable
from infections caused by other opportunistic bacterial
pathogens.
• Human Health Significance: Humans can become colonized
or infected with staphylococcal isolates that colonize or infect
dogs and cats. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus, which can
persistently colonize humans, is of greatest concern, although
human-pet transmission is probably much more common than
pet-human transmission. Staphylococcus pseudintermedius,
which can persistently colonize dogs, has occasionally been
isolated from sick and healthy people who are in contact with
dogs, and is of possible concern because of its tendency to
show a high degree of MDR.

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic AgentS and Epidemiology
The genus Staphylococcus contains a diverse genus of facultatively
anaerobic bacteria that are widespread to ubiquitous commensals
and opportunistic pathogens. They are gram-positive, catalasepositive cocci that tend to occur in clusters. As colonizers of
mucous membranes and the skin, various Staphylococcus species
can be found in or on most healthy animals. Widespread in
healthy animals, staphylococci are classic opportunistic pathogens
that can cause mild to life-threatening infections.
The clinical relevance of diﬀerent staphylococcal species varies
greatly. While virtually any species can cause disease, just a few
species account for the vast majority of clinical infections.
Staphylococcal species are divided into two main groups based on
the production of the enzyme coagulase. Coagulase-positive
staphylococci are the most virulent group and are most often
associated with disease. The most important coagulase-positive
species in dogs and cats are Staphylococcus pseudintermedius,
Staphylococcus aureus, and Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. coagulans.
All can be found in healthy animals, but they account for a large
percentage of opportunistic infections, including skin, ear, soft
tissue, and urinary tract infections, and are leading causes of
surgical site infections (SSIs). 1–5 Staphylococcus intermedius was
previously considered the main Staphylococcus in dogs and cats,
but it is now known that what was previously identiﬁed as S.
intermedius is truly the closely related species S. pseudintermedius. 6

,7

Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) are common
commensals that are often isolated as contaminants, but they can
cause disease in certain situations. This group includes
Staphylococcus
epidermidis,
Staphylococcus
haemolyticus,
Staphylococcus xylosus, Staphylococcus sciuri, Staphylococcus schleiferi
subsp. schleiferi, and Staphylococcus felis, among others. Typically,
CoNS infections involve compromised hosts and sites that have
been injured by foreign bodies and invasive devices (e.g., IV
catheters). Primary infections are uncommon, with the possible
exception of S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi pyoderma 8 and otitis and
S. felis UTI. 9 Interpretation of the clinical relevance of CoNS is
often complicated by their common presence at skin and mucosal

vetexamprep.ir

surfaces and the corresponding potential for contamination
during specimen collection.
There are diﬀerences in the epidemiology of staphylococcal
colonization and infection between diﬀerent staphylococcal
species and between dogs and cats. Staphylococci have often been
referred to as host-adapted species, but it is clear that dogs and
cats can be infected by many diﬀerent staphylococcal species.
Regular transmission of staphylococci between species (e.g.,
human-pet) likely occurs and staphylococcal status is dynamic.
While the term “colonization” is widely used to refer to the
presence of staphylococci in or on healthy individuals, it is clear
that there is no consistent “colonization” state. After exposure to a
Staphylococcus, multiple outcomes may occur. The organism may
be rapidly eliminated, reside in or on the haircoat or mucous
membranes
transiently
(sometimes
referred
to
as
“contamination”), multiply and live on the host for a short period
of time (“transient colonization”), or live on the host for
prolonged periods of time. The degree of host adaptation of the
Staphylococcus species and possibly the strain, and patient factors
(e.g., immune status, commensal microbiota), presumably
inﬂuence the outcome, although other factors such as genetics
could also be involved. As a host-adapted Staphylococcus, S.
pseudintermedius appears to be able to cause prolonged
colonization in at least some dogs, 10 whereas, in contrast, S.
aureus colonization in dogs appears to be more transient. 11 , 12
The incidence of staphylococcal disease is poorly described, but
staphylococci account for a large percentage of skin and soft tissue
infections encountered in dogs and cats, along with a variety of
less common conditions. Most, if not all, staphylococcal infections
are secondary to an underlying cause (e.g. skin disease, wounds)
and the constituents or basis of those underlying causes are the
main factors associated with risk of staphylococcal infection.

Staphylococcus pseudintermedius
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is a true canine commensal and is
found on the skin or mucosal surfaces of a large percentage of
dogs. Isolation rates of 31% to 68% have been reported in healthy
dogs, 13–16 with higher rates (up to 100%) in puppies. 17 It is likely
that the vast majority of dogs, if not all, harbor this species at least

vetexamprep.ir

periodically. Colonization starts early in life, with puppies
acquiring S. pseudintermedius from the dam within 8 hours after
birth. 17 Various body sites can be colonized, particularly the nasal
passages, oral cavity, skin, and perineal mucosa, although the
pharyngeal mucosa seems to be a main colonization site. 18
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is less prevalent in cats, being
reported in 6.8% to 22% of healthy cats. 15 , 19–21 As with dogs,
opportunistic infections can develop, but the inﬂuence of longterm or transient colonization on risk of disease is unknown. In
parallel with colonization rates, S. pseudintermedius infections are
less common in cats than in dogs. 4
Methicillin-resistant S. pseudintermedius (MRSP) has emerged as
an important pathogen in veterinary medicine.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is a well-recognized pathogen and common
commensal, although it is less commonly found in dogs than S.
pseudintermedius. It can be isolated from up to 12% to 14% of
clinically healthy dogs and 4.3% to 20% of clinically healthy cats,
but it may not truly be a commensal organism (at least in dogs) as
carriage tends to be transient. Colonization may be highly human
inﬂuenced, since the S. aureus strains found in dogs are often
indistinguishable from those found in their human contacts. 15 It
is possible that isolation of S. aureus often represents transient
colonization or contamination acquired from humans. This
appears to be particularly true with dogs. A study of dogs and
their owners reported that in 50% of households where S. aureus
was isolated from both a dog and family member, the S. aureus
strains were indistinguishable, strongly suggesting interspecies
transmission. 15 The situation with cats is less clear. Given the
higher apparent prevalence of S. aureus colonization in cats in
some studies and the lack of another predominant coagulasepositive Staphylococcus species commensal in cats, it is possible
that S. aureus is a true feline commensal. Regardless, it can clearly
be isolated from a small but still appreciable percentage of
clinically healthy dogs and cats and can also cause disease in
certain situations. The highest isolation rates are from skin and ear
infections. 22 Risk factors for colonization have not been

vetexamprep.ir

adequately investigated and may relate to the amount or degree
of human contact.

Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. coagulans
Staphylococcus schleiferi contains two subspecies; the coagulasepositive S. schleiferi subsp. coagulans and the coagulase-negative S.
schleiferi subsp. schleiferi. Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. coagulans is
less commonly identiﬁed than S. pseudintermedius and S. aureus,
but can be found in 0.8% to 4% of healthy dogs and 0% to 2% of
healthy cats. 1 , 15 , 19 , 23 , 24 It is most commonly implicated in
otitis externa and pyoderma, 8 , 19 , 25 , 26 but is rarely identiﬁed in
other types of infections. 27 There appears to be prominent
geographic variation in reports of this pathogen. Whether this is a
result of true geographic variation or diﬀerences in laboratory
identiﬁcation is unknown. This species may be misidentiﬁed as S.
pseudintermedius or S. intermedius group if methods aimed at
diﬀerentiating it from those similar species are not used. This may
be of li le clinical consequence given the identical approach to
management of infections caused by these species.

Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci
The coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp. group contains a large
number of species that are commonly found in healthy dogs and
cats, along with virtually all other mammalian species. They are
essentially ubiquitous inhabitants of the skin, nasal and oral
cavities, pharynx, perineal mucosa, GI tract, and conjunctiva of
dogs, cats, and other species. Commonly reported species from
dogs include S. epidermidis, S. xylosus, S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi,
and S. sciuri, with S. epidermidis, S. felis, S. haemolyticus,
Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and Staphylococcus simulans often
reported in cats. 9 , 17 , 28–38 However, a broad range of other
species can be encountered. As diagnostic laboratories rapidly
move to methods such as MALDI-TOF MS that provide more
accurate speciation (as opposed to the common generic
identiﬁcation of isolates as CoNS), the range of CoNS that are
encountered will probably increase. Genus-level identiﬁcation of
CoNS has predominated in the past because of the eﬀort required
to speciate isolates, particularly when speciation would have li le

vetexamprep.ir

to no impact on diagnosis or management of cases. However, as
more information about diﬀerent species becomes available, it is
likely that diﬀerences in the epidemiology and clinical relevance
of diﬀerent CoNS will be identiﬁed.
Despite widespread colonization, CoNS infections are
uncommon. While most, if not all, CoNS are opportunistic
pathogens with the potential to cause disease, virulence tends to
be limited and CoNS are most often isolated as commensals or
contaminants, not pathogens. In human medicine, CoNS are
primarily a concern in hospitalized individuals, where skin, soft
tissue, bloodstream, and invasive device infections predominate.
39–41 The role of CoNS in disease in dogs and cats is poorly
investigated and complicated by studies that report any isolation
of CoNS as “infection.” Diﬀerentiation of infection versus
contamination is a challenge, with most CoNS being of minimal
concern, but some species (i.e., S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi,
Staphylococcus lugdunensis, and S. felis) are potentially important
causes of community-onset disease. While rare, invasive S.
lugdunensis infections have been reported in dogs, 42 , 43 and this
may be a more virulent CoNS.

Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococci
While staphylococci are inherently susceptible to most
antimicrobials, acquired resistance emerged as a concern shortly
after the start of the “antibiotic era.” Staphylococci have
demonstrated an impressive ability to acquire new resistance
genes in response to continued antimicrobial development, and
resistant staphylococci have serious impacts on the health and
welfare of both humans and animals.
Methicillin resistance is of particular concern. While methicillin
is not used clinically in animals, the mechanism that confers
resistance to methicillin (mecA) renders staphylococci resistant to
virtually
all
beta-lactam
antimicrobials—penicillins,
cephalosporins, and carbapenems. This encompasses a large
percentage of the antimicrobials that are used, particularly
empirically. Additionally, methicillin-resistant staphylococci
(MRS) commonly possess other resistance genes, further limiting
eﬀective antimicrobial options. Methicillin resistance has emerged
in all clinically relevant staphylococci, and MRS have been

vetexamprep.ir

isolated from a wide range of companion animal, food animal,
exotic, and wildlife species.
As with methicillin-susceptible staphylococci, MRS can be
found as part of the commensal microbiota of healthy individuals.
Indeed, the majority of humans and animals that harbor MRS do
so without any evidence of disease. Methicillin resistance is not,
itself, a virulence factor, since it simply confers resistance to
antimicrobials. Infections caused by MRS are the same as those
caused by susceptible staphylococci, and occur in situations where
secondary infections can develop. However, they are harder to
treat because of the limited options and failure of empirical
therapy can have a negative impact on outcome.
Much of the a ention regarding MRS in dogs and cats initially
focused on methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). 44–51 The
emergence of MRSA in dogs and cats appears to be a direct
reﬂection of the spread of MRSA in the human population; MRSA
infections in pets were noted after MRSA emerged as an
important cause of disease in the general human population and
with MRSA strains from animals usually reﬂecting predominant
human strains. 48 , 51–54 Whether MRSA is truly established in the
dog and cat population, or whether colonization and infection of
those species is a result of direct infection from humans is unclear.
Regardless, MRSA can be isolated from a small percentage (e.g.,
0% to 4%) of clinically healthy dogs cats. 48 , 55–63 Higher rates can
be encountered periodically in animals in veterinary facilities;
however, most instances of MRSA isolation are not associated
with veterinary hospitals. Ownership by a human health care
worker and participation in hospital visitation programs are risk
factors for MRSA colonization in dogs, 11 as might be expected
based on the increased likelihood of exposure to colonized people.
Other risk factors for MRSA infection or colonization have been
identiﬁed, with varying strength of evidence, particularly
antimicrobial exposure and hospitalization. 22 , 59 , 64–66 Contact
with children has also been identiﬁed as a risk factor. 11 Although
these, and potentially other, risk factors should be considered,
MRSA can be identiﬁed in any animal, and absence of known risk
factors should not lead to excluding MRSA from consideration. In
humans and horses, MRSA colonization is a risk factor for clinical
MRSA infection in certain circumstances (e.g., after admission to

vetexamprep.ir

the hospital). 67 , 68 It is reasonable to assume that this also applies
to dogs and cats, yet this is not proven. Although MRSA
colonization has zoonotic concerns (see below), the animal health
implications of MRSA colonization in clinically healthy animals
are likely minimal.
While MRSA was the ﬁrst prominent methicillin-resistant
Staphylococcus sp. in animals, MRSP has surpassed MRSA in its
impact on dogs and cats. As with methicillin-susceptible strains,
MRSP can be found in or on clinically healthy dogs and cats, with
a wide range of reported prevalence (e.g., 0% to 17%). 29 , 61 , 63 ,
69–76 MRSP is an opportunistic pathogen, and colonization does
not necessarily lead to disease. Carriage of MRSP prior to tibial
plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) was shown to be a risk factor
for MRSP SSI, 77 but whether this applies to other surgical
procedures or other diseases is unknown. It is reasonable to
assume that colonization poses some degree of risk of subsequent
infection in many situations, albeit presumably rather low and
dependent on the presence of factors that predispose to
development of an opportunistic infection. Reported risk factors
for MRSP colonization or infection include antimicrobial exposure
(particularly beta-lactams, immunosuppressive therapy, and
hospitalization). 75 , 78–80 MRSP infections are not distinguishable
clinically from those caused by susceptible strains, but are
increasingly problematic because of the limited treatment options,
particularly since MRSP isolates in many regions are commonly
resistant to most available antimicrobials.
Methicillin resistance is not uncommon in commensal CoNS.
Studies have reported prevalence ranging from 5% to 13% in
clinically healthy dogs, and 5% in clinically healthy cats. 34 , 55 , 81
Methicillin-resistant strains are no more pathogenic than
methicillin-susceptible strains, and the implications of
colonization with methicillin-resistant CoNS are typically
inconsequential although these strains are likely sources of
acquired methicillin resistance for more virulent staphylococcal
species.

Clinical Features

vetexamprep.ir

Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical
Examination Findings
Staphylococci can possess a wide array of potential virulence
factors; however, the role that many of these play in the actual
development of disease is variable. Some virulence factors
facilitate adhesion to, and colonization of host tissues. Others
encode secreted enzymes and toxins that are responsible for
invasion as well as local and distant disease. The pathophysiology
of disease is complex and only superﬁcially understood, reﬂecting
the variable presence of numerous staphylococcal virulence
determinants in diﬀerent strains of the more pathogenic species.
Interactions between various virulence factors are presumably
critical, because no single virulence factor has been shown to be
suﬃcient to establish an infection.
The ability to colonize body sites is a critical component of
virulence, because it allows staphylococci to remain on or in the
body waiting for an opportunity to cause an infection, particularly
after an underlying insult such as a break in the body’s physical or
immunologic barriers. Important among these factors are surface
adhesins, which do not directly result in damage to host tissues,
but create an environment where staphylococci can persist.
Adhesins may also facilitate evasion of the immune system. For S.
aureus, the most important is probably protein A, which binds to
the Fc portion of IgG. 82 Other surface proteins that include
clumping factors, ﬁbronectin-binding proteins, coagulase, and
collagen-binding protein are important, since they each give
pathogenic staphylococci the ability to readily colonize breaks in
the skin or mucosal surfaces as the ﬁrst part of the infection
process. Once the organism reaches a suﬃcient density at this
local site of infection, release of a peptide signal through the Agr
quorum-sensing system activates many of the toxins and
degradative enzymes while downregulating the numerous
adhesion molecules. Various hemolysin toxins can lyse
erythrocytes and other body cells. Proteases can cleave antibodies,
play a role in protection against neutrophil defensins and platelet
microbicidal peptides, contribute to destruction of tissue protein,
and potentiate invasion. 83 Hyaluronidase and hyaluronate lysate
may further contribute to virulence through digestion of
hyaluronic acid in connective tissue and promoting degradation

vetexamprep.ir

of tissues. 84 , 85 Lipase has a negative eﬀect on the host’s immune
function and may help the bacterium harvest nutrients from the
local environment. Alpha toxin is a potent membrane-damaging
toxin that can produce local cell damage. Leukocidins damage
leukocytes and lipid membranes. One, the Panton-Valentine
leukocidin, has received much a ention because of its apparent
role in severe MRSA skin and soft tissue infections, as well as
necrotizing fasciitis and necrotizing pneumonia in humans. 86–89
This leukocidin has been found in MRSA from dogs and cats, 90 ,
91 but its role in disease is still unclear. Enterotoxin production is
mediated by several staphylococcal enterotoxin genes, many of
which can be found in S. aureus from dogs. 92 , 93 However, it is
unclear whether staphylococcal enteric disease is of relevance in
dogs and cats. Other toxins of note include exfoliative toxins A
and B, which cause staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, and
toxic shock syndrome toxins, which cause toxic shock syndrome.
Less is known about S. pseudintermedius, but evidence indicates
that this species has numerous virulence factors similar to those of
S. aureus, such as protein A, leukocidins, exfoliative toxins, other
exotoxins, ﬁbronectin-binding protein, and bioﬁlm-producing
factors. 94 , 95 The exfoliative toxin of S. intermedius can be found in
S. pseudintermedius isolates from a large percentage of dogs and
cats, 96–100 and it may play a role in pyoderma and otitis, but that
has not yet been proven.
Another potentially important aspect of staphylococcal
virulence is the ability to form bioﬁlms (see Chapter 121) (Fig.
51.1). Bioﬁlm may be most relevant for infections of implants and
invasive devices (e.g., IV catheters). Bioﬁlm formation has been
demonstrated for various staphylococci, including S.
pseudintermedius and S. aureus. 95 , 101–103 The role of bioﬁlm
formation in disease is not well understood, but it probably plays
an important role in development of chronic disease and
resistance to treatment in certain situations, particularly surgical
implant and invasive device infections.

vetexamprep.ir

Model of agr expression in
staphylococcal biofilms. After initial
colonization by individual cells (a),
microcolonies reach sufficient cell density for
agr-dependent gene expression (b) and
perhaps signaling between microcolonies (c,
arrows). Portions of the biofilm detach (d) as
either large aggregates or individual cells.
Simultaneously, parts of the biofilm population
become metabolically inactive and lose
membrane integrity. This is followed by new
growth in the voids left by detached cells (e),
and the cycle is repeated. The microcolony
finally reaches a relatively quiescent state
where growth is slow and agr expression is
undetectable (f). Green = metabolically active
bacteria that are producing virulence factors.
Red = bacteria with states of relative inactivity.

Staphylococci cause a wide range of opportunistic infections,
particularly acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (also
referred to as skin and soft tissue infections). Clinically, these can
range from mild pyoderma to rapidly fatal necrotizing fasciitis.
Any body system can be aﬀected, including otherwise sterile sites
(invasive infections). Severe manifestations of staphylococcal
infection include staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome,
bacteremia/sepsis, and necrotizing fasciitis (see Chapter 50). There
is li le to no diﬀerence in the clinical appearance of infections
caused by diﬀerent staphylococcal species, and no diﬀerence
between
methicillin-resistant
and
methicillin-susceptible
infections. Additionally, staphylococcal infections cannot be

vetexamprep.ir

diﬀerentiated from infections caused by other opportunistic
pathogens without diagnostic testing.
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius accounts for the vast majority of
staphylococcal infections (and probably overall opportunistic
infection) in dogs, and a lesser percentage in cats. The most
common clinical manifestation of infection is pyoderma, including
superﬁcial and deep disease. S. pseudintermedius also causes a
range of other infections including, in general order of occurrence,
wound infections, SSIs, abscesses, UTIs, septic arthritis,
osteomyelitis, discospondylitis, endocarditis, peritonitis, and
ocular infections. The severity of disease is highly variable.
Serious invasive infections including fatal toxic shock and
cellulitis have been reported, 104 , 105 but these are rare. Most
infections are mild to moderate in severity.
Staphylococcus aureus
A similar range of infections as produced by S. pseudintermedius
can be produced by S. aureus. The main diﬀerence between S.
pseudintermedius and S. aureus is the lower incidence of disease
caused by the la er rather than disease location or severity. S.
aureus infections may be more common in cats than in dogs,
which probably relates to a lower prevalence of S.
pseudintermedius colonization in cats. It is possible that infections
more commonly associated with human contact (i.e., wound and
SSIs contaminated by hands of owners or veterinary personnel)
are more likely to be caused by S. aureus (including MRSA), but
objective data are lacking.
Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. coagulans
The main apparent diﬀerence in clinical expression of disease
between S. schleiferi subsp. coagulans and other coagulase-positive
staphylococcal infections is the rarity of infections beyond the skin
and ears. However, the role of this staphylococcal species in
disease may be underestimated because of the failure of many
diagnostic laboratories to diﬀerentiate it from S. pseudintermedius.
It has been suggested that S. schleiferi subsp. coagulans may tend to
produce more superﬁcial skin disease than S. pseudintermedius and
S. aureus, 4 but supporting evidence is limited.

vetexamprep.ir

pp
g
Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci
Interpretation of the role of CoNS in disease is diﬃcult because
they are often found in cultures as contaminants. Since most
species are of limited virulence and often found at mucosal and
skin sites, interpretation of the relevance of isolation of CoNS and
the potential role in disease is a challenge. Further, as discussed
above, while CoNS are generally considered as a group, it is
possible that there are diﬀerences in clinical expression of disease
among CoNS species. In particular, S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi has
been implicated as a cause of pyoderma and otitis. 8 , 19 , 27 A
primary role of S. felis as an important cause of UTIs in cats has
been suggested, 9 but remains unclear. Staphylococcus lugdunensis
may also be a more pathogenic species. CoNS likely pose a greater
risk for infections of invasive devices, surgical incisions, and other
compromised sites.

Diagnosis
There are no clinical, clinicopathologic, or diagnostic imaging
results that are pathognomonic or even highly suggestive of
staphylococcal infection.

vetexamprep.ir

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
Evaluation of smears or aspirates can indicate the presence of
bacterial sepsis, and the presence of cocci, particularly clusters of
gram-positive cocci, is suggestive of staphylococcal infection (Fig.
51.2). Cytologic evidence of an infectious inﬂammatory response,
particularly an abundance of neutrophils and intracellular
bacteria, is particularly suggestive.
Culture and Susceptibility Testing
Isolation of staphylococci from an infected site is the standard for
diagnosis; however, whereas isolation of staphylococci tends to be
relatively easy, interpretation of results can be challenging.
Because staphylococci are common commensals, contamination of
specimens, particularly those from skin and soft tissue infections,
is a major problem in diagnosis. Care should, therefore, be taken
to avoid contamination when collecting culture specimens.
Particular care must be taken in diagnosing infections caused by
CoNS, since they are common contaminants and are uncommonly

vetexamprep.ir

pathogenic. This includes methicillin-resistant CoNS, which are
not uncommonly isolated from healthy animals. Isolation of CoNS
from a superﬁcial site should be interpreted with caution. If a
CoNS and another potential pathogen are identiﬁed concurrently,
the CoNS is typically considered a contaminant. Isolation of CoNS
from sterile sites (e.g., blood, pleural cavity) is more indicative of
disease as long as samples were collected and handled properly;
however, in human medicine, a single blood culture of CoNS is
often dismissed as a likely contaminant. 106 If quantitative or
semiquantitative culture results are provided, low growth (1+) of
CoNS is of questionable relevance and quite possibly
contamination, not infection.
Speciation of staphylococci is variably handled among
diagnostic laboratories. Some laboratories provide only superﬁcial
identiﬁcations. However, speciation is required for proper
antimicrobial susceptibility testing, as interpretive breakpoints
diﬀer among diﬀerent species of Staphylococcus (see Chapter 3). 107
, 108 Speciation can also be useful for infection control purposes to
help assess likely sources of infection and potential public health
concerns, particularly when MRS are involved. It is also useful
when trying to determine whether multiple culture results could
indicate a cluster of hospital-associated infections, because
infections with diﬀerent species would rule out a common source
exposure. It has often been considered that there is less need for
speciation of CoNS because they are, in general, less pathogenic,
with limited diﬀerence between species. However, if certain CoNS
are potentially important primary pathogens (e.g., S. schleiferi
subsp. schleiferi in pyoderma or S. felis in UTIs in cats), then
speciation could be important for interpreting the relevance of
isolation of CoNS.
Given the variability in susceptibility pa erns among
staphylococci and the emergence of MDR MRSP and MRSA, it is
important that proper susceptibility testing be performed to guide
treatment. Veterinarians should ensure that the diagnostic
laboratory they use follow standard Clinical and Laboratory
Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines for performance and
interpretation of susceptibility testing results. 109 In general,
methods to detect antimicrobial susceptibility among
staphylococci are well developed and validated. Problems with
identiﬁcation of methicillin resistance in S. pseudintermedius have

vetexamprep.ir

been previously encountered, 107 , 108 , 110 although changes in
CLSI guidelines for susceptibility testing of S. pseudintermedius
have improved this situation. Problems with assessment of
doxycycline susceptibility have also been identiﬁed, with use of
human interpretative breakpoints leading to false reporting of
doxycycline susceptibility in some S. pseudintermedius isolates. 111 ,
112 Revised breakpoints have been recommended, 113 but these are
not necessarily used by all diagnostic laboratories. Another area of
concern is determination of clindamycin resistance because of
inducible resistance, as is discussed under Systemic
Antimicrobials.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
While the movement to rapid diagnostic testing will continue,
there are currently no validated rapid tests for diagnosis of
staphylococcal infections in dogs and cats. Although molecular
assays based on PCR oﬀer the potential for a rapid result,
adequate test development and validation is required to ensure
sensitivity and speciﬁcity. Of greater interest are assays that will
rapidly identify MRSA or MRSP to guide initial treatment
decisions. There are commercial assays for rapid detection of
MRSA in humans; however, these have not been validated in
animals, and investigation of one test in horses demonstrated
poor performance. 114 A similar test for MRSP is not available, and
clinicians must be aware that commercial veterinary “MRSA” PCR
assays may simply be tests to detect mecA, the resistance gene that
can be found in any MRS species, including CoNS.

Treatment and Prognosis
Management of staphylococcal infections is highly variable
because of the diverse nature of disease. The general approach to
treatment varies li le between diﬀerent staphylococcal species,
and indeed between infections caused by staphylococci versus
other opportunistic pathogens. Infection site and severity are key
determinants of the required approach. Factors such as surgical
intervention and supportive care may be required, and are
sometimes the most important measures, but are not covered
here.

vetexamprep.ir

Antimicrobials are not always needed for staphylococcal
infections. In some situations, local approaches using biocides
such as chlorhexidine or other antibacterial substances may be
eﬀective. The best example of this is superﬁcial folliculitis, where
topical therapy with chlorhexidine has been shown to be eﬀective
in the absence of concurrent systemic antimicrobials 115 , 116 and
where topical therapy alone is the recommended ﬁrst-line
approach. 117 Other common situations may be amenable to
nonantimicrobial approaches. Biocides as well as other substances
with antibacterial activity (e.g., honey) can also be useful sole or
adjunctive approaches to wound infections. Incision and drainage
is the preferred approach for treatment of abscesses that are not
associated with evidence of systemic infection or signiﬁcant
localized cellulitis. Similarly, mild superﬁcial SSIs may be
eﬀectively managed through removal of skin sutures and cleaning
of the site. Thus, while systemic antimicrobials are often required
for the treatment of staphylococcal infections, there are many
instances where other treatment approaches may be eﬀective.

Systemic Antimicrobials
Treatment with systemic antimicrobials is ideally based on the
results of culture and susceptibility testing. This has become
particularly true as the prevalence of MDR staphylococci has
increased. The prevalence of resistance to diﬀerent antimicrobials
varies between (and even within) regions, so knowledge of local
susceptibility pa erns is useful. Knowledge of typical clinical
response to empirical antimicrobials can be useful to guide
decisions, particularly in situations where culture specimens are
uncommonly submi ed. Published data from research papers or
laboratory data compilations can provide interesting information
but are potentially biased since, in most regions, culture
specimens are disproportionately submi ed from infections that
are recurrent or have not responded to initial antimicrobial
therapy. Therefore, these can be expected to over-represent
(sometimes profoundly) the prevalence of antimicrobial
resistance. Databases from referral institutions can have similar
biases. Thus, care should be taken when making clinical decisions
from such data sets, and thought must be given to how well the
dataset represents the individual clinical case. Knowledge of

vetexamprep.ir

resistance trends in the practice is more useful to guide empiric
therapy and treatment while awaiting culture results, but nothing
takes the place of culture and susceptibility data from an
individual patient.
Drug options and dosages for treatment of staphylococcal
infections are listed in Table 51.1. In general, resistance is
uncommon to ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins (e.g., cephalexin) or
β-lactamase-resistant
penicillins
or
penicillin/β-lactamase
inhibitor combinations (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate), and these
drugs are widely used as ﬁrst-line treatments, although the
increase in methicillin resistance in many regions has impacted
the use of beta-lactams. In most situations, the prevalence of
methicillin resistance is still suﬃciently low that betalactams/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations or cephalosporins
can be used as initial or empirical therapy.
Clindamycin is another excellent option if the isolate is
susceptible in vitro, and has been recommended as a ﬁrst-line
treatment for superﬁcial folliculitis. 117 However, inducible
clindamycin resistance must be considered, particularly in S.
aureus. 118–120 With this phenomenon, isolates appear to be
susceptible to clindamycin in vitro; however, resistance is induced
on exposure in vivo, and treatment failure is expected. One study
reported inducible resistance in 71% of MRSA strains from
animals, 119 whereas another study reported that 55% of
erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible MRSA from dogs
were inducibly resistant. 118 Inducible resistance can be detected
in the laboratory using a “D-test” and it is important to know
what testing methods are used when diagnostic laboratories
report clindamycin susceptibility. S. aureus isolates that are
reported as erythromycin resistant but clindamycin susceptible
should be considered resistant to clindamycin unless the D-test
(or equivalent) has indicated the absence of inducible resistance.
Inducible resistance is not a concern if erythromycin susceptibility
is reported. Inducible resistance appears to be rare in S.
pseudintermedius but, because it has been reported, 118 , 121 it is
prudent to avoid clindamycin for the treatment of serious
infections caused by erythromycin-resistant S. pseudintermedius
without demonstration of absence of inducible clindamycin
resistance. The same likely applies to other staphylococci as
limited information is available.

Tetracyclines can be useful antistaphylococcal drugs, but
resistance is not uncommon. Doxycycline is the most commonly
used tetracycline and can be an eﬀective treatment for various
staphylococcal infections. Potential problems with the use of older
doxycycline breakpoints for S. pseudintermedius, as discussed in
more detail above, must be considered. If laboratories are using
currently recommended breakpoints (susceptible if MICs are <
0.125 µg/mL or > 25 mm zone diameter), 113 doxycycline is a
reasonable choice when in vitro susceptibility is reported.
Minocycline has a somewhat broader spectrum of activity since
some doxycycline-resistant staphylococci remain susceptible to

vetexamprep.ir

minocycline. 111 , 112 , 122 This depends on the genetic mechanism
of resistance, and the prevalence of minocycline susceptibility
among doxycycline-resistant staphylococci varies depending on
the S. pseudintermedius strain and the geographic region. Speciﬁc
testing for minocycline is required when doxycycline-resistant
isolates are encountered.
While most often used to target gram-negative pathogens,
aminoglycosides can be excellent antistaphylococcal drugs,
although the parenteral route of administration can be
problematic and nephrotoxicity is a concern. Despite these
concerns, amikacin has become a common treatment for MRSP
infections because of the very limited options. Clinically relevant
nephrotoxicity appears to be uncommon in systemically stable
patients and is typically reversible if amikacin administration is
stopped. Gentamicin can also be considered but is somewhat
more toxic than amikacin, and lack of availability of amikacin
would be the main reason to consider gentamicin.
Fluoroquinolones can have excellent intrinsic activity against
staphylococci. Given their in vitro activity, their ability to
penetrate the skin, the availability of oral formulations, and oncedaily dosing requirement, ﬂuoroquinolones have been popular
choices for staphylococcal infections. They can be highly eﬀective
clinically, but concerns about ﬂuoroquinolone resistance, in terms
of both clinical treatment failure and public health consequences,
have led to recommendations that they be reserved as second-line
choices for many types of infections (e.g., bacterial cystitis,
superﬁcial folliculitis) 117 , 123 and be used only when resistance to
other antimicrobials is present or likely. In humans,
ﬂuoroquinolones are not generally recommended as monotherapy
for MRSA because of poor clinical response and rapid
development of resistance. 124 This has not been objectively
investigated in dogs and cats but there is no reason to suspect that
it would be diﬀerent in these species, so ﬂuoroquinolones
probably should be avoided whenever possible as treatments of
resistant staphylococcal infections such as MRSA and MRSP when
other viable alternatives exist. There has been less discussion
about their indication in methicillin-susceptible infections. These
should perhaps be approached with caution as well, because the
presence or absence of methicillin resistance should be of limited
relevance to the likelihood of treatment failure or emergence of

vetexamprep.ir

resistance with quinolone treatment and because ﬂuoroquinolone
exposure is a well-documented risk factor for MRS infections in
humans and dogs. 22 , 124 , 125 It is reasonable, therefore, to
recommend prudent use of this drug class for any staphylococcal
infection and to avoid empirical use of ﬂuoroquinolones in any
serious or life-threatening staphylococcal infection if possible.
Trimethoprim-sulfonamide is commonly active against MRS
in vitro. Safety concerns exist, including keratoconjunctivitis sicca,
arthropathy, and other idiosyncratic eﬀects. These are most
relevant with long durations of treatment but can occur with
short-term therapy. Trimethoprim-sulfonamide can be used safely
in most patients and is appropriate in situations with few other
viable options. It should be avoided in animals with a history
of/risk factors for keratoconjunctivitis sicca.
Chloramphenicol is also often active against staphylococci
in vitro and anecdotally in vivo. There are human health concerns
relating to fatal aplastic anemia from exposure to
chloramphenicol, although this is an exceptionally rare
idiosyncratic reaction. Careful drug handling instructions and
client education as to its risks must be given. Chloramphenicol
can also cause bone marrow suppression (particularly in cats) and
is contraindicated in animals being treated with other
myelosuppressive drugs. If chloramphenicol is to be used for a
prolonged period of time, periodic (every 14 to 28 days)
monitoring of a CBC count is advisable. Florfenicol might be a
potential alternative to chloramphenicol, because it is not a health
risk to humans. It can be administered orally, although it may be
refused because of its taste. Although ﬂorfenicol has been used
with anecdotal success in the treatment of MRSP and MRSA
infections in dogs, treatment failure and development of
resistance during treatment have been reported, and objective
evaluation of eﬃcacy is lacking.
Fosfomycin is uncommonly used in dogs, mainly as a treatment
for resistant bacterial cystitis, but is a consideration for other
staphylococcal infections. Fosfomycin resistance is currently
uncommon in staphylococci 126 and fosfomycin represents a
potential oral treatment option of MDR staphylococci. Clinical
data are lacking and adverse GI eﬀects are not uncommon. This
drug should not be used in cats because of nephrotoxicity. 127

vetexamprep.ir

Nitrofurantoin is a potential option for treatment of
staphylococcal cystitis. While ineﬀective for infections other than
cystitis (including pyelonephritis), nitrofurantoin is an option for
some MDR staphylococcal cystitis cases. Resistance to
nitrofurantoin is uncommon, but can occur.
As MRS become more prevalent and some strains become
highly drug resistant, isolates that are resistant to almost all
available drugs are being encountered in some regions. This has
led to the consideration for use of antimicrobials that are critically
important in human medicine, such as vancomycin and linezolid.
Vancomycin, linezolid, tigecycline, and quinupristin-dalfopristin
are drugs that are important for treatment of serious MDR
infections in humans. Their use in animals raises many ethical
questions that are diﬃcult to answer. Concerns include increased
pressure toward resistance of animal-harbored staphylococci and
their subsequent transmission to humans. The concerns of public
health risk are often opposed with concerns about animal health
and welfare if proper treatment is not provided, and the fact that
animal use makes up a minuscule percentage of overall use of
these drugs. There is currently no consensus on the topic, but use
of these drugs in animals is banned in some countries (e.g., The
Netherlands, Sweden). At a minimum, these drugs should be
reserved for situations where there are no other viable treatment
alternatives, where the infection is not amenable to other (e.g.,
local) therapy, and where the infection is life threatening but
potentially treatable. Before considering drugs such as these, all
other therapeutic options should be considered and experts in
infectious diseases should be consulted if possible. Currently, it is
rare to require drugs such as these because there is almost always
another treatment option.

Local Antimicrobial Therapies
Local or regional administration of antimicrobials can deliver high
antimicrobial concentrations that can result in clinical eﬃcacy
even in the face of in vitro resistance. This is dependent on the
amount of drug that reaches the site, the duration that those levels
are achieved, and the MIC of the speciﬁc bacterial isolate. Various
approaches can be used, most commonly involving concentrationdependent drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides). Intra-articular injection

vetexamprep.ir

of antimicrobials (e.g., amikacin) can be considered in cases of
septic arthritis to achieve high local concentrations. This approach
is most commonly used in horses but is practical in many small
animal patients, especially surgery-associated stiﬂe infections in
large-breed dogs. Local administration of antimicrobialimpregnated materials such as beads or collagen sponges 128–131
can sometimes produce sustained high drug levels (see Chapter
121). This approach can be particularly useful in implantassociated infections or infections of poorly vascularized sites
such as bone. Other methods to deliver high drug levels to a site
of infection are under investigation or development, and new
options will likely be available in coming years.

Topical Antimicrobials
Topical antimicrobial therapy may be a useful adjunctive or sole
therapy. The ability to deliver high concentrations of antimicrobial
directly to the site of infection, with minimal systemic exposure, is
a desirable approach. Clinically relevant resistance of
staphylococci to topical antimicrobials such as mupirocin and
fusidic acid is uncommon, 132–136 and the high local antimicrobial
levels that can be achieved may largely oﬀset acquired resistance.
The main limitations to topical therapy are potential diﬃculties
ge ing topically applied antimicrobials to the infection site and
providing an adequate duration of contact. Thus, topical therapy
is best reserved as a sole method for treatment of very focal
superﬁcial infections, such as superﬁcial wound infection and
focal surface pyoderma, including otitis externa. Systemic therapy
or a combination of systemic and topical therapy should be used
for deeper infections or infections that do not respond completely
to topical monotherapy. Whether topical antimicrobials oﬀer any
advantage over topical application of biocides (e.g., chlorhexidine)
is unclear.

Other Topical Treatments
Direct topical application of biocides is a potential option for some
skin and skin structure infections and is a preferred approach for
the treatment of superﬁcial pyoderma. 117 The potential eﬃcacy of
biocides involves a balance between the bactericidal activity of the

vetexamprep.ir

compound and the tissue damage from biocide application. Some
compounds have profound antibacterial properties but are not
useful because of the degree of tissue damage that can ensue. For
some biocides, the costs versus beneﬁts of antibacterial properties
and tissue damage are not well understood. 137
As with topical antimicrobials, the ability of the biocide to reach
the infection site and limited contact time are the main limitations.
Biocides may be eﬀective as the sole treatment of superﬁcial
infections, or as adjunctive therapy for deeper infections.
Available options include chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, and
benzoyl peroxide gel. Topical use of chlorhexidine can be as
eﬀective as antimicrobials in resolving skin lesions in dogs with
pyoderma, including infectious caused by MRSP, 115 , 116 , 138 and
this is a recommended ﬁrst-line approach for superﬁcial
folliculitis. 117 Other compounds such as accelerated hydrogen
peroxide have also been proposed as topical therapies, but there is
currently li le information about their use. Silver-coated dressings
may be useful for treatment of skin and wound infections.
Essential oils are gaining popularity as topical therapies, although
clinical eﬃcacy data are limited. Various essential oils, including
tea tree oil, geranium oil, lavender oil, and grapefruit seed extract,
have been shown to possess antibacterial properties, including
activity against MRSA and MRSP. 137 , 139 , 140 They may have an
added eﬀect whereby the vapor generated by their oils within
bandage materials can penetrate more deeply into infected sites
than the liquid form. 139 , 141 However, an overlooked aspect is the
potential for tissue damage, because essential oils can have
cytotoxic eﬀects on mammalian cells. 142 Concerns about
cytotoxicity have led to a recommendation that tea tree oil not be
used in the treatment of burns. 141 Ingestion of a small volume of
tea tree oil has caused neurologic disease in children, 143 , 144 and
the risk to pets from licking topically applied oil or ingestion of
treated bandage material is unclear. Further study of eﬃcacy and
safety are required.
Topical application of honey is another appealing alternative to
antibiotic treatment that is safe. Honey has bactericidal eﬀects
against various bacteria, including staphylococci, in vitro and
in vivo. 145–148 There are diﬀerences in bactericidal activity among
diﬀerent types of honey, and the best investigated honey has been

vetexamprep.ir

Manuka honey, produced from the blossoms of Leptospermum
scoparium (Manuka). Basic use of honey in dogs and cats simply
involves direct application of food-grade honey to an infected site,
covered by a bandage. A preferred method of application involves
the use of dressings impregnated with Manuka honey because of
the enhanced and more predictable bactericidal activity of this
type of honey and pre-sterilization of the honey and dressing.
There are theoretical concerns about bacterial contamination of
honey, particularly with Clostridium botulinum. Although C.
botulinum can be found in honey, honey-associated botulism in
humans is almost invariably from ingestion of contaminated
honey by infants. Tissue infection would require clostridial spores
in honey reaching a deep, anaerobic site, something that is
unlikely, and the authors are unaware of any infections linked to
topical application of honey.

Other Considerations
Both S. aureus and S. pseudintermedius are important causes of
surgical implant–associated infections. 5 , 149–152 These infections
can be very diﬃcult to treat because of the implant and its
associated bioﬁlm. 95 , 103 , 153 Antimicrobial therapy can often
result in amelioration of clinical signs or initially apparent clinical
cure; however, relapse is very common after cessation of
antimicrobials. Elimination of infection can be diﬃcult to
impossible with implants in place, and removal of implants
should be considered as soon as possible.

Prevention
Prevention of staphylococcal infections largely involves
prevention or control of underlying risk factors (e.g., management
of allergic skin disease), since staphylococcal infections are
virtually always secondary, opportunistic infections. Measures to
reduce SSIs and other hospital-associated infections are discussed
further below and in Chapters 15 and 76.

Perioperative Prophylaxis
Staphylococci are leading causes of SSIs and perioperative
antimicrobial prophylaxis, when indicated, should include

vetexamprep.ir

excellent staphylococcal coverage. Most often, the ﬁrst-generation
cephalosporin cephazolin is used. Other options include
clindamycin or ampicillin; however, the commonness of betalactamase–producing staphylococci may preclude use of
ampicillin in many regions. When broad gram-negative coverage
is needed, a second-generation (e.g., cefoxitin) or third-generation
(e.g., cefotaxime) cephalosporin can be used, or a drug with be er
eﬃcacy against gram-negative bacteria (e.g., aminoglycoside,
ﬂuoroquinolone) can be added. Routine use of third-generation
cephalosporins and ﬂuoroquinolones should be minimized
because of the importance of those drug classes in human
medicine. While MRS, particularly MRSP, are important causes of
SSIs, routine prophylaxis targeting MRS is discouraged because of
the limited treatment options and concerns that routinely using
the few drugs available for therapy (e.g., amikacin) will increase
the risk of resistance and even further treatment challenges. There
may be limited situations where targeting MRS is indicated, such
as when the patient has a concurrent or recent MRS infection,
since MRSP colonization has been identiﬁed as predisposing to
MRSP SSI. 77 More information on perioperative and
postoperative prophylaxis for SSIs can be found in Chapter 76.

Public Health Aspects
Staphylococcus aureus
Public health concerns regarding pets and S. aureus have almost
exclusively involved MRSA, even though pet-to-human
methicillin-susceptible S. aureus infections probably occur.
Colonization of humans in contact with infected or colonized dogs
and cats has been widely reported, 48 , 57 , 90 , 154–158 although the
direction of transmission is usually unclear and it is likely that
most pet-human pairs with MRSA reﬂect human-to-pet
transmission since S. aureus seems to be more adapted to
colonization of humans than colonization of dogs and cats. MRSA
isolates from pets tend to reﬂect strains that predominate in
people in any given geographic region, likely a testament to the
human origin of MRSA in pets. Pets have been implicated as
sources of infection for humans in households 15 , 159 ; however,
this has been based on circumstantial evidence. MRSA should be

vetexamprep.ir

considered a potentially zoonotic pathogen and infection control
measures should be instituted, as is discussed below. However, it
should be realized that the incidence of pets being a source of
human disease is probably low, and most instances of MRSA
infection or colonization in pets are probably a result of the pet
acquiring MRSA from a human source.
Notwithstanding the predominant association of MRSA with
humans, there may be occupational health risks for veterinary
personnel. Numerous studies of MRSA colonization in veterinary
personnel have been performed, generally reporting colonization
rates of up to 18% in small animal veterinary personnel. 160–166 It
cannot be determined with certainty that these colonization rates
reﬂect acquisition of MRSA from animals; however, identiﬁcation
of higher rates than present in the general population and
similarity between human and animal strains support the
possibility of occupational origin.
Infection Control Precautions in Veterinary Clinics
MRSA and MRSP pose challenges in veterinary clinics as they can
be associated with clusters of infections in animals, as well as
potential transmission to veterinary personnel. Infection control
eﬀorts need to be directed both at controlling the endemic level of
disease and preventing outbreaks. The risks posed by MRSA and
MRSP are poorly deﬁned, as is the eﬃcacy of diﬀerent control
measures. The response to MRSA and MRSP can vary among
facilities based on the facility design, risk status of the patient
population for MRSA/MRSP colonization, risk status of the
patient population from MRSA/MRSP acquisition, risk adversity,
and other aspects. While there is no standard approach, some
basic concepts can be applied to all facilities and both MRSA and
MRSP. These include the use of good general hygiene practices
(especially handwashing), use of enhanced barriers (e.g., gown or
dedicated protective outerwear, gloves) with animals that are
known to be infected or colonized, routine and enhanced cleaning
and disinfection, and the use of a variety of other standard
infection control practices such as surgical asepsis (see Chapter
15).
When MRSA or MRSP infections are identiﬁed, a plan should
be in place regarding how to handle that animal in the clinic and
during subsequent examinations. All infected or colonized

vetexamprep.ir

animals should be considered carriers until proven otherwise, and
handled with contact precautions (gloves, dedicated protective
outerwear). In clinics, they should be housed in isolation (or miniisolation, with posted precautions and limited handlers)
whenever possible and have no direct or indirect contact with
other patients. Although there is li le risk of aerosol transmission,
housing infected animals in isolation decreases the likelihood of
transmission via personnel or fomites. Infected or colonized
outpatients should be admi ed directly to an isolation area or
examination room, rather than allowing them to remain in a
waiting area. The practicality and impact of these approaches will
vary between facilities. For example, in a dermatology practice, a
large percentage of patients may be MRSP or MRSA carriers. Use
of these measures on such a large number of animals may be
impossible and the implications of MRSP/MRSA exposure of
patients may not be as great as in a facility with a large elective
orthopedic surgery caseload, where MRSP SSIs can be highly
problematic. However, the higher likely MRSA and MRSP
burdens in the patient population could pose increased risk to
clinic personnel. Therefore, concurrent increases in hygiene and
personal protective equipment use (e.g., handwashing and proper
use of dedicated outerwear and gloves) may be more important
than a empting to isolate potential animals infected and
colonized with MRSA or MRSP. In contrast, in facilities with a
greater population of patients with greater risk or implications of
MRSA or MRSP infections (e.g., orthopedic surgery,
immunosuppressed or critically ill patients), there may be more
indication for isolation of known or high-risk patients infected or
colonized with MRS.
MRSA in Clinic Personnel
MRSA exposure, colonization, or infection of veterinary hospital
personnel can be a diﬃcult area to address because of the general
lack of understanding of the issues and the high-proﬁle nature of
MRSA. Concerns are often present when people realize that they
have had contact with an MRSA-infected or -colonized animal,
and the potential for occupational exposure is certainly present
based on the high rates of MRSA colonization in veterinary
personnel. Sometimes, people express a desire to have themselves
or their staﬀ tested for MRSA colonization. However, this is rarely

vetexamprep.ir

indicated and is associated with many potential problems. Given
the reported colonization rates of veterinarians and the
presumably frequent exposure to colonized animals, routine
infection control practices should be established to reduce the risk
of MRSA transmission from unknown carriers (staﬀ or pets).
Testing of staﬀ for MRSA colonization is not recommended.
MRSA rates are high in veterinary personnel and it would not be
surprising to ﬁnd positive individuals in the absence of known
MRSA transmission. Exclusion of colonized personnel from work
is not reasonable considering the high MRSA colonization rates
that have been identiﬁed and ongoing risk of exposure. Treatment
directed at MRSA decolonization of involved humans is unlikely
to be recommended by physicians, because it is uncommonly
used in people in the general population in most regions.
Furthermore, even with successful decolonization, there would be
a continued risk of occupational exposure.
Veterinary personnel who become aware that they are
colonized with MRSA should be especially diligent in following
all hand hygiene protocols in the clinic and avoidance of hand-tonose contact (because the nares are the most common site of
colonization in humans, and hands are the prime source of
transmission). There is no indication to remove a colonized
individual from patient care duties, although restriction of contact
with very high-risk patients (e.g., some surgical patients) could be
considered. However, because the vast majority of veterinary
personnel are not aware of their MRSA status, clinic personnel
should assume that both they and their patients could be
colonized. Employees who are concerned about MRSA
colonization (e.g., those who have been working with an MRSApositive animal) should be encouraged to see their physicians.
Veterinary personnel should also be aware of their likely
increased risk of MRSA infection and ensure that their physician
knows that they may be at higher risk than the general
population, something that might be important to consider when
empirically treating infections or deciding whether preoperative
MRSA screening is indicated.
Infection Control in Households
The principles of MRSA control for households are the same as
those for veterinary clinics. Infected sites on pets should be

vetexamprep.ir

covered with an impermeable barrier whenever possible. A key
point is recognition of additional high-risk body sites (nose,
mouth, and perineum) and avoidance of direct and indirect
contact with those sites. Owners should be counselled on good
household infection control practices, particularly regular hand
hygiene. Infected or colonized pets should be prevented from
having contact with pets outside the household until they are no
longer infected or colonized. Although MRSA can be transmi ed
in households, the incidence is unclear, as are risk factors. Owners
who have concerns, particularly if the concerns relate to the
presence of high-risk people in the household (very young or very
old, immunocompromised individuals), should be encouraged to
seek advice from their physicians. Routine testing of clinically
healthy pets whose owners have MRSA infection or of clinically
healthy owners whose pets have MRSA is not indicated.
Pet Owners Diagnosed with MRSA Infection
Infected or colonized owners can be a source of infection for their
pets, although the incidence of transmission from infected owners
to pets is unknown. Owners diagnosed with MRSA infection
should be told to wash their hands thoroughly before and after
handling their pet, in order to prevent transmission of MRSA to
the pet, and transmission from the pet should it subsequently
become colonized. Owners should not kiss their pets or allow
their pets to lick their faces or any broken skin. Screening of pets
for MRSA carriage is rarely indicated, and should only be done if
there is a clear plan to act on the results. Testing animals in the
absence of testing all human contacts is illogical, and testing of
animals can result in much confusion and the potential for poor
decision-making if is it not conducted as part of a comprehensive
household investigation with a plan of action in place to deal with
the results. Pet screening may rarely be indicated as part of a
whole-household intervention, which includes simultaneous
screening and MRSA decolonization of all people.

Staphylococcus pseudintermedius
While S. pseudintermedius can cause infection in humans, the
incidence of this appears to be very low. When one considers the
high prevalence of S. pseudintermedius carriage by healthy dogs

vetexamprep.ir

and the millions of dog-human contacts that occur on a daily
basis, it is apparent that the risk posed by this bacterium is
limited.
Colonization of humans with S. pseudintermedius occurs more
often than overt clinical infection but is still uncommon, with
reported rates of 1% to 4% in veterinary personnel and pet
owners. 66 , 167 , 168 Presumably, this low rate of S. pseudintermedius
carriage reﬂects pet-human transmission, as indistinguishable pet
and human isolates are common in households where concurrent
carriage is identiﬁed. 168 Like methicillin-susceptible strains,
MRSP can be found in a small percentage of pet owners and
veterinary personnel 66 , 167 , 169 and MRSP infections have been
reported in humans. 170–172 The risk posed by MRSP should be
considered low; however, given the highly drug-resistant nature
(and associated treatment diﬃculty), care should be taken to use
good infection control practices around infected animals in
households and veterinary clinics. Good hygiene in households
and veterinary clinics should greatly minimize the risk of MRSP
transmission from colonized animals.

Other Staphylococci
Public health concerns regarding other staphylococci are currently
limited. Since CoNS (including methicillin-resistant CoNS) are
common in both animals and humans and tend to be of limited
pathogenicity, they are not considered a relevant public health
concern. Although many of the same CoNS species can cause
disease in both humans and pets, it is unclear whether animals are
a potential source of infection. Most human infections occur in
hospitalized individuals, and there is currently no evidence
suggesting that isolation or other enhanced infection control
practices are required for pets with CoNS infections. Good general
hygiene practices should be more than adequate in most, if not all,
situations. This is probably most important as an act of prudence
for infected pets that will potentially have contact with high-risk
(very young, elderly, immunocompromised) individuals.

Screening for Methicillin-Resistant
Staphylococci and Decolonization

vetexamprep.ir

Carriage of MRSA or MRSP at colonization sites such as the nose,
pharynx, GI tract, or skin may be found in a small percentage of
healthy animals. Carriage is very common in animals with clinical
MRS infections and may persist for some time after resolution of
infection. MRSA carriage tends to be transient and self-limiting,
but prolonged carriage of MRSP can occur in some dogs. 10
Because of the potential for transmission of these important
staphylococci to other individuals and the role of these organisms
in disease, measures to detect and eliminate screening would be
desirable. In humans, MRSA screening is a key component of
MRSA control in hospitals, but not the general population. Active
decolonization, often using topical antimicrobials such as
mupirocin or fusidic acid, sometimes with concurrent oral
antimicrobial therapy, is used as a means of MRSA control in
some situations in some regions, such as in individuals
undergoing certain surgical procedures. 68 , 173 Even though longterm MRSA colonization can occur, the need for decolonization
therapy in otherwise healthy individuals in the community is
controversial and not universally performed because of variable
eﬃcacy, 174 questionable need, and concerns about development
of further antibacterial resistance. Decolonization is most
commonly used in speciﬁc populations, such as healthcare
workers, patients undergoing surgical procedures, patients in
intensive care units, or individuals in households with recurrent
MRSA infections, and even in those situations, it is not universally
applied and is not always eﬀective when it is performed.
While active elimination of MRSP or MRSA colonization in
dogs and cats could be desirable to reduce the risk of
development of clinical infection or transmission to other
individuals, there is no evidence that therapy to eliminate
colonization is indicated or even potentially eﬃcacious in dogs
and cats. Adequate topical application of an antimicrobial to the
entire nasal passages and pharynx of a dog or cat is not realistic,
and incomplete treatment could lead to further antibacterial
resistance. Because MRSA colonization appears to be transient in
most if not all dogs and cats, and the use of good general hygiene
measures to reduce reinfection almost invariably results in
spontaneous decolonization, it is questionable whether active
decolonization is even indicated. An active approach to MRSP
decolonization would be more appealing because of the potential

vetexamprep.ir

for long-term shedding in dogs. However, eﬀective decolonization
regimens have not been described.

Case Example
Signalment

“Meg,” an 8-year-old FS Labrador retriever in southern Ontario,
Canada.

History

This overweight but otherwise healthy dog was examined
because of acute onset of left pelvic limb lameness. After being
let out at night, Meg was heard barking and ran away, and was
thought to be chasing a raccoon. Upon returning, she was nonweight bearing on the left pelvic limb. The next morning, the
lameness was improved although still present. The dog would
bear limited weight on the leg.
Upon initial examination, Meg was bright, alert, and
responsive. She was overweight, with a BCS of 7/9. Grade 4/6
left pelvic limb lameness was present. Otherwise, physical
examination was unremarkable. She resented manipulation of
the left pelvic limb. A mild pain response was noted on
palpation of the stiﬂe. Moderate stiﬂe eﬀusion was noted. A
positive cranial drawer sign and tibial thrust were noted.
Radiographs of the stiﬂe revealed moderate increase in soft
tissue opacity within the joint, most consistent with joint
eﬀusion, and mild to moderate degenerative joint disease.
Cranial cruciate ligament rupture was diagnosed and the dog
underwent a TPLO procedure the following day. Cephazolin
was administered approximately 30 minutes prior to incision,
with one intraoperative dose 120 minutes after the initial dose
and two postoperative doses (22 mg/kg, IV, q12h). A CBC,
serum biochemistry proﬁle, and urinalysis were performed for
preoperative health screening, and no abnormalities were
present. Surgery was without complication, and postoperative
radiographs indicated appropriate tibial plateau leveling and
appropriate positioning of the implant. The dog experienced a
normal postoperative recovery and was treated with cephalexin
(22 mg/kg, PO, q12h) for 48 hours after surgery. However, 14

vetexamprep.ir

days after surgery, the dog developed worsened lameness, with
reluctance to bear weight on the surgically corrected limb.

Physical Examination Findings

On examination, Meg was bright, alert, and responsive. She
would stand on the aﬀected limb but exhibited grade 3-4/6
lameness. The surgical site was red and inﬂamed. It was
noticeably warm on palpation and a mild amount of pus was
extruded when the incision site was manipulated. The joint
appeared stable.

Laboratory Findings

None were performed initially upon re-presentation.

Imaging Findings

Radiographic ﬁndings were consistent with those normally
identiﬁed 2 weeks after a TPLO procedure.

Cytologic Findings

Using aseptic technique, an aspirate was collected from the soft
tissue overlying the surgical implant site. Marked suppurative
inﬂammation was noted, with abundant cocci within
neutrophils.

Microbiologic Testing

Culture of the aspirate ultimately yielded MRSP. Beyond betalactams, the isolate was resistant to doxycycline, clindamycin,
enroﬂoxacin, marboﬂoxacin, and trimethoprim sulfa. It was
susceptible to amikacin and chloramphenicol. Minocycline MIC
testing was requested, and the MIC was 0.125 µg/mL
(susceptible).

Diagnosis

Results were consistent with a deep SSI caused by MRSP.

Treatment

The dog was anesthetized, and skin sutures were removed.
Upon removal of the skin suture, it was apparent that there was
substantial infection of the subcutaneous tissues (Fig. 51.3). In
addition, the deep fascia overlying the implant had dehisced.
The infected site was thoroughly lavaged and treatment with
minocycline (5 mg/kg, PO, q12h) was started. Clinical signs
improved over the next 3 days and the amount of discharge
rapidly decreased. Antimicrobials were stopped after 28 days,
at which point the dog was clinically normal with evidence of

vetexamprep.ir

appropriate wound healing. However, 21 days after cessation of
antimicrobials, mild (grade 1-2/6) lameness was noted. Mild
stiﬂe eﬀusion was identiﬁed upon palpation. The surgical site
looked unremarkable grossly. An aspirate from over the plate
was collected and moderate suppurative inﬂammation was
evident cytologically. Culture of the specimen yielded an MRSP
isolate with an indistinguishable susceptibility pa ern from
that isolated previously. Radiographs were taken and complete
healing of the osteotomy was evident. After discussion with the
client, it was decided to remove the implant as it was suspected
to be colonized with bioﬁlm-embedded MRSP, with a poor
prognosis for elimination of the infection with the implant left
in situ. Amikacin (20 mg/kg IV) was administered
preoperatively and implant removal was unremarkable.
Amikacin was continued for 3 days (20 mg/kg, SQ, q24h)
postoperatively. No subsequent problems were encountered
with the limb.

Comments

MRSP is a leading cause of TPLO SSI, and TPLO infection rates
can be high. MRSP isolates are often strong bioﬁlm producers,
and elimination of implant-associated infections can be diﬃcult
because of the ability of MRSP to elude the eﬀects of
antimicrobials and the immune system while embedded within
bioﬁlm on a surgical implant. While some infections are
treatable with systemic antimicrobials, sometimes with
adjunctive approaches such as antimicrobial-impregnated
beads or gels, long-term cure is often not achieved. Removal of
the implant is typically required for full resolution of the
infection. In implant-associated infections, antimicrobials are
sometimes required systemically until the time that bone
healing permits implant removal. In this case, infection of the
bone seemed to be limited and there was li le apparent impact
on bone healing. It is debatable whether antimicrobials are
required after implant removal, but a short course (as was used
here) is often administered.
