52: Miscellaneous GramPositive Bacterial Infections
Joshua B. Daniels, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Uncommon to rare gram-positive bacterial infections in
dogs and cats include those caused by Rhodococcus equi
(synonym Rhodococcus hoagii), Corynebacterium spp.,
Listeria monocytogenes, Erysipelothrix spp., and Bacillus
anthracis.
• First Described: Rhodococcus equi: 1923, Sweden, in horses
(Magnusson) 1 ; Corynebacterium urealyticum: 1947, Spain, in
humans (Cifuentes and Soriano) 2 ; L. monocytogenes: 1927,
England, in laboratory rabbits and guinea pigs (Murray) 3 ;
Erysipelothrix spp.: 1876, in mice (Koch) 4 ; B. anthracis:
1850s, France, in sheep and cattle (Rayer, Devaine,
Pollender). 5
• Affected Hosts: Rhodococcus equi (horses, pigs, cattle, dogs,
cats, humans), C. urealyticum (dogs, cats, humans), L.
monocytogenes (many domestic mammals, poultry, humans),
Erysipelothrix spp. (especially pigs, turkeys, and laying hens;
but also other mammals including humans, dogs and cats;
birds, fish and reptiles), and B. anthracis (primarily
herbivorous mammals such as cattle, sheep and goats; but
also humans and rarely dogs and possibly cats).
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide; anthrax is most prevalent
in Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America.
• Route of Transmission: Inhalation, inoculation, or ingestion (R.
equi); invasion of normal microflora (Corynebacterium spp.);
ingestion (L. monocytogenes); inoculation and possibly

vetexamprep.ir

ingestion (Erysipelothrix spp.). Anthrax can be acquired
through ingestion, inoculation, or inhalation; most cases in
dogs result from ingestion, whereas humans are most
commonly infected through cutaneous inoculation.
• Major Clinical Signs: Rhodococcus equi: cutaneous
abscesses (cats), signs that depend on systemic organ
involvement; Corynebacterium spp.: lower urinary tract signs
(C. urealyticum), respiratory signs (Corynebacterium
ulcerans), otitis externa (Corynebacterium auriscanis); L.
monocytogenes: febrile gastroenteritis, neurologic signs,
abortion, cholecystitis, abdominal lymphadenitis (L.
monocytogenes); Erysipelothrix: fever, lameness, cardiac
murmurs, spinal pain, erythematous cutaneous lesions
(erysipelas); B. anthracis: fever, inappetence, edema of
tissues surrounding the upper GI tract.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other gram-positive and gramnegative bacterial infections.
• Human Health Significance: All of these organisms are
capable of causing disease in humans, and many infections in
humans result from exposure to animals or animal products.
Humans are not usually exposed as a result of contact with
dogs and cats, but care should be taken when handling
infected companion animals to avoid exposure through
needle-stick injuries or ingestion (i.e., hand hygiene after
handling infected animals). Isolation is not required.
Companion animals exposed to B. anthracis should be
decontaminated by thorough bathing.

Rhodococcus Equi (Synonym Rhodococcus
Hoagii) Infection
Rhodococcus equi is a pleomorphic, facultatively intracellular,
gram-positive bacillus that has been primarily associated with
pyogranulomatous
pneumonia
in
foals,
suppurative
lymphadenitis in pigs, and granulomatous lymphadenitis in
ca le. Although a revised name, Rhodococcus hoagii, has been
proposed for this organism, this name has been disputed in the
taxonomic literature, so the name Rhodococcus equi will continue to

vetexamprep.ir

be used from this point forward. 6 It belongs to the Nocardiaceae
family
which
also
includes
Nocardia,
Mycobacterium,
Corynebacterium, and Gordonia. Infection is acquired by inhalation
from soil, inoculation into wounds or mucous membranes, or
ingestion. Reports of infections in dogs and cats are rare, and are
usually associated with immunosuppression such as that caused
by chronic glucocorticoid administration 7 or retrovirus infection.
Rhodococcus equi has rarely been cultured from the mucosal
surfaces and skin of healthy dogs, as well as from dogs with
myositis, hepatitis, osteomyelitis, dermatitis, endocarditis,
pulmonary abscessation and pyothorax, endophthalmitis, and
lymphadenitis. 7–9 Rhodococcus equi pneumonia was described in a
dog from Brazil that was co-infected with Toxoplasma gondii and
CDV. 9 Infection with CDV was thought to have led to
immunocompromise and opportunistic infections with T. gondii
and R. equi.
Rhodococcus equi is commonly recovered from soil that is
enriched with herbivore manure and directly from feces of
herbivores. The organism may enter the body through a
contaminated penetrating wound and subsequently spread via
lymphatics to regional lymph nodes and hematogenously to the
liver, spleen, and visceral lymph nodes. Aﬀected foals are
typically infected through inhalation of dust. The organism then
invades macrophages and inhibits phagolysosomal fusion by
means of a complex cell wall, which results in pyogranulomatous
to granulomatous inﬂammation. Dissemination occurs as a result
of underlying immunosuppression. The virulence of R. equi has
been related to plasmids that encode a virulence-associated
protein (Vap), which allows it to persist in macrophages.
Pathogenic strains of R. equi have been described as virulent or
intermediately virulent based on carriage of host-adapted circular
VAP plasmid types. The VAPA and VAPB plasmids have been
associated with equine and porcine strains, respectively. The
VAPA plasmid was detected in a cat with cutaneous
rhodococcosis; the cat had a history of contact with horses. 10 A
linear plasmid type, pVAPN, been associated with bovine and
caprine strains. This plasmid type has been detected in R. equi
isolates from two dogs, 7 , 9 as well as in immunocompromised
humans. 11 A conserved conjugal transfer protein gene, traA, is

vetexamprep.ir

present in all strains that carry plasmids. Strains that lack VapA or
VapB genes (and are traA–) are considered avirulent, but have
been associated with disease in immunocompromised animals. 7
Most cats have abscesses or pyogranulomatous cellulitis that
involve an extremity, 12–14 although a 2020 case series of 40 cats
from Malaysia described pulmonary disease in 36 cats; 4 cats had
only cutaneous lesions. Most of the cats in this study (25/40) were
under 10 months of age. 15 Localized swelling with ulcerations or
ﬁstulas and purulent drainage have been found. Unlike typical
bite wound abscesses, the lesions are generally not painful, and
systemic signs of fever and anorexia are usually absent. Pyothorax
and mediastinal lymphadenitis may be associated with anorexia,
weight loss, and dyspnea.
Clinical ﬁndings in dogs and cats vary considerably depending
on sites of dissemination, and have included abdominal distention
with a palpable ﬂuid wave, hepatomegaly, and mesenteric
lymphadenomegaly;
corneal
ulceration;
endophthalmitis;
abscesses; cutaneous ulceration; cough, tachypnea and dyspnea
(Fig. 52.1). 7 In one infected dog, generalized hyperesthesia was
present. 8 Dissemination to many organs was associated with
necrotizing pyogranulomatous hepatitis, osteomyelitis, and
polymyositis.
Hematologic abnormalities may consist of leukocytosis with a
15
left
shift,
monocytosis,
and
thrombocytopenia.
Hypoalbuminemia (22%) and hyperproteinemia (64%) were
frequent ﬁndings in cats with rhodococcosis from Malaysia. 15
Radiographs have revealed soft tissue swelling; osteolytic and
osteoproliferative changes in bones; thoracic lymphadenopathy;
hepatomegaly; lung masses with pleural pneumothorax; eﬀusion;
and pulmonary interstitial or alveolar-interstitial pa erns. 7 , 15
Gram staining of aspirates or smear preparations of purulent
discharge may reveal large, pleomorphic, gram-positive bacilli,
which may be found inside macrophages. Thoracic or abdominal
eﬀusions are typically exudates with high protein (more than 3.5
g/dL) and nucleated cell counts (above 10,000 cells/µL); the
majority of cells are lymphocytes or nondegenerate neutrophils.
Organisms may not be apparent. Gross pathologic ﬁndings
include peripheral abscesses, often with sinus tracts and purulent
drainage; and enlarged and necrotic lymph nodes with a similar

vetexamprep.ir

discharge on sectioning. Histologic examination reveals
pyogranulomatous or granulomatous lesions with necrotic foci. 7
Macrophages contain phagocytized gram-positive bacteria. The
organisms also stain positive with Fite’s acid-fast stain.
Pyogranulomatous to granulomatous lesions containing bacteria
may be observed in a variety of parenchymal organs such as the
liver, lung, and heart valves in animals with disseminated disease.

Right eye of a 5-year-old female
spayed domestic shorthair with dyscoria
secondary to a retrobulbar abscess associated
with Rhodococcus equi infection. The cat

In the laboratory, R. equi grows readily in an aerobic
environment and has distinctive colonial characteristics, but
laboratories not familiar with equine isolates may fail to identify it
correctly. The use of MALDI-TOF MS is likely to improve
identiﬁcation. Clinicians should communicate any suspicion for R.
equi infection to the laboratory to ensure that proper microbiologic
techniques are used to enhance colony growth. Culture of

vetexamprep.ir

macerated tissue specimens appears to be more sensitive than
culture of swabs of exudates or infected tissues. 14
Surgical removal of extremity lesions is only temporarily
eﬀective, and new lesions commonly develop even after limb
amputation. Surgical drainage of abscesses is an essential
adjunctive procedure. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing should
always be performed because resistant strains have been
identiﬁed. In general, in vitro susceptibility is greatest to
erythromycin, ﬂuoroquinolones, rifampin, aminoglycosides,
glycopeptides, and carbapenems. 16 In cats, treatment with
lincomycin and gentamicin has been eﬀective, and results with
erythromycin have varied. Cats with disseminated lesions also
respond poorly. Treatment with amoxicillin-clavulanate has been
eﬀective in reducing the size of lesions when used for a minimum
of 14 to 16 days 13 but is a poor choice of antibacterials because of
poor penetration of macrophages and common resistance to betalactams. In humans with pneumonia, only long-term treatment
with erythromycin, combined with either rifampin or
vancomycin, has been eﬀective. 17 Monotherapy is not
recommended. 18 As with treatment of other persistently
intracellular organisms, combination treatment of lipophilic drugs
that penetrate cells well is superior. The standard, highly eﬀective
treatment in foals is prolonged oral administration of
erythromycin and rifampin. This combination can be
recommended for cats, although greater toxicity may occur.
However, the combination of clarithromycin-rifampin was
superior to erythromycin-rifampin or azithromycin-rifampin in
clinical improvement and radiographic resolution of pneumonia
in infected foals. 19 Cats have been successfully treated with
rifampin in combination with either clarithromycin, azithromycin,
or a ﬂuoroquinolone. 15 , 20 In humans, two- or three-drug
combinations are recommended that include a macrolide,
rifampin,
carbapenem,
ﬂuoroquinolones,
and/or
an
18
aminoglycoside. Several months of treatment may be required,
and in some cases, long-term treatment may be required to
prevent relapse (Table 52.1).
Infections with R. equi are recognized in immunocompromised
humans, including those infected with HIV (80% of cases),
diabetics, organ transplant recipients, hemic neoplasia, lung

vetexamprep.ir

cancer, and those with alcoholism. Infections in humans with HIV
infection appear to be declining in incidence as a result of highly
active antiretroviral therapy. 18 Pulmonary lobar inﬁltration with
cavitation, similar to that observed with tuberculosis, has been the
most frequently observed syndrome in human patients with AIDS
18 ; R. equi was the most common microbiologically conﬁrmed
cause of pulmonary cavitation in HIV-infected humans in one
study, accounting for 9% of cases. 17 , 18 , 21 Extrapulmonary
lesions occur in about 20% of people with pulmonary infection.
Infected cats or dogs have not been considered a major source of
infection for people, who usually acquire the infection from
environmental exposure. Nevertheless, infected pets with
draining lesions could pose a minor theoretical risk to
immunocompromised owners.

Corynebacterium Infections
Corynebacteria are club-shaped, aerobic, gram-positive rods that
are widely distributed in soil and water, and may contaminate the
hospital environment. Numerous seemingly nonpathogenic
corynebacteria have been isolated as microﬂora of dogs and cats.
Some have been reported as causing otic infections or UTIs. 22 , 23
Many veterinary diagnostic laboratories do not speciate
Corynebacterium spp. isolated from dogs and only report them at
the genus level. As molecular diagnostic instrumentation (e.g.,
MALDI-TOF) becomes more common in service laboratories,
associations between members of Corynebacterium spp. and
clinical syndromes will become more known to veterinarians.

75 mg every 24 hours.

Corynebacterium urealyticum has been occasionally associated
with lower UTIs in dogs and cats with compromised urinary
defense mechanisms, 24 including urinary retention secondary to
compressive myelopathy, urethral obstruction, catheterization,
and urologic surgery. 24–28 Anatomic defects, extensive
antimicrobial use for other causes of UTI, immunosuppressive
drugs, and foreign bodies have all been implicated as
predisposing causes. The infection is uniquely characterized by
the concurrent presence of alkaline urine, struvite, and calcium

vetexamprep.ir

phosphate crystals that may precipitate to form calculi with or
without encrusting urocystitis, which may be severe. Urinalysis
typically reveals alkaline urine, struvite crystalluria, pyuria,
hematuria, and variable bacteriuria. 24 Ultrasound examination of
the urinary bladder may reveal thickening of the bladder wall,
echogenic debris, and hyperechogenicity of the urinary bladder
wall (encrusting cystitis) (Fig. 52.2). Urolithiasis may also be
observed. 24 Findings suggestive of encrusting pyelitis have also
been described. A cat with a Corynebacterium jeikeium UTI has
been described with similar lesions. 29 Treatment involves
appropriate antimicrobial therapy and thorough mechanical
debridement of plaques associated with the bladder wall, which is
essential for resolution. Cystoscopic debridement has been
described as a minimally invasive treatment in veterinary
patients. 30 In addition to these treatments, oral administration of
urinary acidiﬁers has been used to treat human infections and
may be beneﬁcial. Many isolates are resistant to multiple
antimicrobial drug classes, and so susceptibility testing is essential
to guide therapy. In human patients, vancomycin is the treatment
of choice. In order to preserve the use of vancomycin for serious
human infections, doxycycline has been used in veterinary
patients as an alternative. Doxycycline achieves concentrations in
canine urine that exceed plasma concentrations and is likely
appropriate for multiple uropathogens. 31 Susceptibility to
chloramphenicol has been described in many isolates, and this
also may represent an eﬀective treatment. 24
Corynebacterium ulcerans is capable of expressing diptheria
toxins and has been associated with an exudative pharyngitis in
humans that is indistinguishable from that caused by
Corynebacterium diphtheriae. 18 Toxigenic strains of C. ulcerans have
been isolated from clinically healthy dogs, which may serve as a
source of infection for other dogs and animals. 32 Corynebacterium
ulcerans was isolated, along with other bacteria, from transtracheal
washings of a dog with suppurative bronchopneumonia. 33 It was
also isolated from nasal swabs from two cats with nasal discharge.
34 These isolates were found to contain the bacteriophage that
codes for diphtheria toxin and may have been responsible for the
clinical illness in these cats. Isolates from cats and dogs are
genetically similar to those from humans, and have been

vetexamprep.ir

incriminated in zoonotic spread of infection to humans. 35–37 In
one report, an immunocompromised person developed a
diphtheria-like illness, and the organism was isolated from the
throat and the tonsils, nose, and labial area of the person’s dog
that had chronic rhinorrhea. 36 However, consumption of raw
milk or its unpasteurized products or close association with
horses or cows is thought to be a more common source of
infection for humans than exposure to dogs or cats.
Corynebacterium auriscanis has been implicated in polymicrobial
otitis externa in the dog, usually as a mixed infection with
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius. 22 Infection with C. auriscanis has
also been associated with superﬁcial pyoderma 38 (usually also
polymicrobial) and has been reported in one human dog-bite case.
39 From the limited antimicrobial susceptibility data that have
been published about C. auriscanis, chloramphenicol, tetracyclines,
macrolides, and amikacin are the most eﬀective in vitro. However,
because these infections are almost always polymicrobial, it is
unclear how clinically relevant targeted antimicrobial therapy is
for this organism when more virulent components of infections
(e.g., coagulase-positive staphylococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are
adequately addressed by antibiosis.

Listeriosis
Listeria monocytogenes is a pathogenic, partially β-hemolytic, grampositive, rod-shaped facultative anaerobe that is morphologically
indistinguishable from diphtheroids and may be mistaken for a
contaminant in tissues, or misidentiﬁed as a diphtheroid,
streptococcus, or enterococcus. It is motile as a result of
possession of one to six polar ﬂagellae. It is capable of growing in
a wide range of temperatures, including refrigerator temperatures
(4°C to 10°C), which have been used to select for its growth in the
presence of contaminants. Although at least 16 serotypes of the
organism exist based on H or O antigens, most disease is caused
by types 4b, 1/2a, and 1/2b. 40 Isolates from companion animals,
when typed, have also been 4b, 41 1/2a, 42 or 1/2b. 43 As a
ubiquitous saprophyte, L. monocytogenes can be isolated from soil,
water, sewage, dust, and decaying vegetation. Pathogenic strains
of L. monocytogenes can also be recovered from the stool of healthy
animals, including humans. A study of fecal specimens from
animals in Japan found a prevalence of 0.9% in dogs, but no
bacteria were isolated from cats. 44 Commonly, L. monocytogenes
can be found in farm animal feed and silage and in food products
made from these animals. Recovery rates of 15 to 70% have been
reported from raw vegetables, raw milk, cheese, and meats,
including processed meats from delicatessen counters. Outbreaks
of disease in humans have been associated with poor hygiene
practices in the food production industry. Signiﬁcant outbreaks
have been associated with contaminated coleslaw, 45 turkey
delicatessen meat (which resulted in the largest recall of meat ever
in the United States), 46 chocolate milk, 47 , 48 and canteloupes. 49
Approximately one third of sporadic cases have been linked to
ingestion of soft cheeses or delicatessen meats. Most humans that
develop invasive disease are women in their third trimester of
pregnancy (which may result in spontaneous abortion, stillbirth,
premature labor, and neonatal infections), those over age 60, or
those immunosuppressed due to hematologic malignancy, organ
transplantation, HIV/AIDS, or glucocorticoid therapy. However,

vetexamprep.ir

immunocompetent
individuals
may
develop
febrile
gastroenteritis. A localized cutaneous infection was described in a
veterinarian after contact with an aborted calf. 50 Listeria
monocytogenes has also been isolated from raw pet foods,
including those that include beef or chicken. 51 In one study from
the Netherlands, 54% of raw food products for pets were
contaminated with L. monocytogenes. 52 In a study from the United
States, 12% of 576 raw pet food products tested positive. 53 In
general, the source of infection in companion animals is not
identiﬁed, but some cats have had a history of being fed raw food
diets. 54 Underlying immunosuppressive illnesses identiﬁed in
dogs have included endocrinopathies (diabetes mellitus and
42
hyperadrenocorticism),
hemic
neoplasia,
and
42
,
43
immunosuppressive drug therapy
; one aﬀected cat tested
positive for FeLV.
Natural infection usually results from ingestion of
contaminated food; damage to the intestinal mucosal integrity is
not necessary. More than 109 organisms are needed to infect
healthy mammals. Alkalinization of the stomach by antacids may
promote infection. Listeriosis in dogs and cats is uncommon;
when it occurs, it is usually associated with ingestion of
contaminated meat or meat by-products. The incubation period in
humans ranges from 11 to 70 days. Reports of bacteremia due to
L. monocytogenes in dogs and cats after oral ingestion of
contaminated food have been rare. After penetration of the
intestinal mucosa, L. monocytogenes localizes in mononuclear
phagocytes. Resultant bacteremia may be associated with
formation of septic emboli of many organs. The organism has a
particular predilection for the CNS (especially the brainstem
[rhombencephalitis] and meninges [meningitis]) and placenta.
Listeria endocarditis has also been described in humans.
Vaccines have been developed that use a enuated strains of L.
monocytogenes as a vector for expression of tumor antigens, which
concurrently activate cytotoxic T cells. There are rare reports of
such vaccines causing listeriosis in vaccinated humans. A
conditionally licensed canine osteosarcoma vaccine with a live
Listeria vector (COV-LLV, Aratana Therapeutics, Inc., KS, USA; at
time of writing now owned by Elanco Animal Health) was shown
in preliminary studies to signiﬁcantly improve survival time

vetexamprep.ir

when used in addition to standard-of-care amputation and
chemotherapy. 55 One dog developed a cavitary rib mass
following vaccination. The vaccine strain of L. monocytogenes was
isolated from aspirates of the mass, and histopathology of the
mass revealed metastatic osteoblastic osteosarcoma. 56 The dog
remained alive over a year after removal of the mass with no
further disease progression. A subsequent study described Listeria
infections in 4 of 49 vaccinated dogs with osteosarcoma, and
concerns were raised about the possibility of zoonotic
transmission.57
Listeria monocytogenes can persist indeﬁnitely in macrophages
and escape humoral immune responses. A cell surface protein,
internalin, interacts with E-cadherin on epithelial cells and
macrophages, inducing phagocytosis (Fig. 52.3). The main
virulence factor possessed by L. monocytogenes is listeriolysin O,
which is a porin that induces T-cell unresponsiveness. This porin,
together with phospholipases, enables the organism to escape
phagosomes. In the cytoplasm, the organism pushes pseudopodlike projections outward (known as ﬁlopods), which are ingested
by adjacent macrophages, enterocytes, or hepatocytes. The
bacterial surface protein ActA is responsible for actin
polymerization that promotes intercellular spread and evasion of
the host immune response. 58

and spleen. In immunocompromised
individuals, L. monocytogenes can cross the

cause meningitis, sepsis, premature birth, or

nonphagocytic cells, such as epithelial cells,
through receptor-mediated endocytosis, and in
most cases, it escapes from the vacuole. In

(SLAPs). Upon vacuolar escape, L.

spread from cell to cell. Listeriolysin O (LLO),

Clinical signs are caused by the degree of intestinal
inﬂammation and the sites of embolic microabscess formation.
Fever, diarrhea, and vomiting have been most frequently
reported. Neurologic signs, abortion, subclinical bacteriuria, and
bacteremia have been apparent in some cases. 41 , 42 , 59 Localized
infections can also occur. 42 , 60 Cholecystitis was described in one
dog; L. monocytogenes was isolated from bile collected using
cholecystocentesis. 43 Listerial myocarditis with congestive heart
failure was reported in a 14-week old puppy from southeastern
Australia that was evaluated for dyspnea, lethargy, and
inappetence. 61 Cytologic evaluation of bone marrow from one
dog with bacteremia revealed coccobacilli within macrophages
and neutrophils. 62 In cats, peritonitis, pneumonia, hepatic
involvement, encephalitis, and cutaneous abscesses have been
described. 63–65 Systemic listeriosis in association with pleural
mesothelioma was identiﬁed in one stray cat in the southern US at
necropsy. 66 In a case series of three cats with abdominal
lymphadenitis secondary to L. monocytogenes infection, two of
three aﬀected cats had a history of being fed raw food diets. 54 All
of the aﬀected cats were oriental breeds (Siamese, Tonkinese,

vetexamprep.ir

Burmese), and a genetic predisposition for infection was
speculated.
Diagnosis of infection may be made antemortem or at necropsy,
because infected animals often succumb to bacteremia. Cytologic
examination of aﬀected tissues may reveal pyogranulomatous
inﬂammation; organisms appear as short, intracellular and
extracellular gram-positive bacilli to coccobacilli. Microabscess
formations and focal necrotic lesions may be grossly or
microscopically visible in many organs, especially the liver and
spleen.
Listeria monocytogenes can be cultured and identiﬁed within 36
hours using routine media. Because the organism can be
commonly isolated from the GI tracts of healthy animals, stool
cultures may not be meaningful. Strain characterization can then
be performed using serotyping, multilocus sequence typing, or
whole genome sequencing. 67
Antimicrobial agents that are active against Listeria are
penicillin and ampicillin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol,
rifampin,
tetracycline,
trimethoprim-sulfonamide,
and
aminoglycosides. First-choice treatments in humans with CNS
infections are a combination of ampicillin and gentamicin, or
ampicillin and a trimethoprim-sulfonamide; the la er
combination has been associated with the lowest failure rate and
fewer neurologic sequelae. 40 Treatment with cephalosporins or
chloramphenicol has been associated with failure and relapse in
treated people. Quinolones are ineﬀective. Treatment of Listeria
gastroenteritis with antimicrobials is not recommended as the
disease is self-limited.
Listeria infection in animals has not always been considered a
public health risk because animals and people are exposed to the
same source of environmental contamination. Nevertheless, an
association has been made between human outbreaks and contact
with food-producing animals or their products. Direct
transmission from animals has occurred in veterinarians and farm
workers through contact of unprotected skin or mucous
membranes with infected animal tissues. 64 , 68 Most outbreaks
occur in urban areas, where foodborne contamination is
suspected. Infants, older adults, and pregnant women are most
commonly aﬀected. Recommendations for practices that prevent
foodborne listeriosis have been developed, 40 including avoidance

vetexamprep.ir

of certain foods (soft cheeses, delicatessen meats, smoked seafood)
for people at higher risk. In a case of reverse zoonosis, listerial
gastroenteritis was suspected in a li er of puppies and a newborn
infant who received Listeria-infected milk discarded from the
human mother’s mammary gland. 69

Erysipelothrix Infections
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae and Erysipelothrix tonsillarum are small,
gram-positive,
nonmotile,
nonsporulating
pleomorphic
facultatively anaerobic rods. These organisms, which are found
worldwide, are associated with swine production. Erysipelothrix
rhusiopathiae is the causative agent of swine erysipelas and other
diseases in animals such as joint-ill in sheep and ca le and
bacteremia in turkeys, ducks, and laboratory mice. The organism
can be cultured from the tonsils of clinically healthy swine, the
skin of freshwater and saltwater ﬁsh, and the decomposing plant
and animal ma er in their environments. Occupational exposure
to these sources of bacteria may cause localized cutaneous or
systemic infections in humans.
Initially, the genus Erysipelothrix was thought to have a single
species—rhusiopathiae—but biochemical and genetic analyses have
identiﬁed E. tonsillarum, a nonpathogenic commensal of the
tonsils of swine. 70 In dogs, endocarditis, diskospondylitis,
arthritis, and bacteremia were initially thought to be caused by E.
rhusiopathiae after natural 71 and experimental 72 inoculation.
However, all available isolates from these conditions reported in
dogs have been now reclassiﬁed as serovar 7 of E. tonsillarum,
which is nonpathogenic for swine. 70 , 73 , 74 DNA hybridization
studies have conﬁrmed this relationship. 75 There are rare reports
of dogs with bacteremia and cutaneous lesions (erysipeloid
lesions/erysipelas) associated with conﬁrmed E. rhusiopathiae
infection (Fig. 52.4). 76 Some aﬀected dogs had been treated with
immunosuppressive drug therapy before recognition of infection.
77 , 78

Clinical signs of fever, lameness due to septic/embolic arthritis,
spinal pain, with or without recent-onset heart murmur are
typically present in dogs infected with E. tonsillarum (see Chapters
121 and 122). The dogs infected with E. rhusiopathiae had fever,
lethargy, inappetence, and cutaneous lesions that consisted of

vetexamprep.ir

alopecia and erythematous macules in one dog; and welldemarcated, diamond-shaped, erythematous and indurated
lesions in another; evidence of endocarditis was not evident,
although echocardiography was only performed in one dog. 76 , 77
One of the dogs had GI signs. Laboratory abnormalities include
leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia, bandemia, thrombocytopenia,
and serum biochemistry ﬁndings that reﬂect bacterial
thromboembolic complications. The organism is readily cultured
from blood, and PCR assays have been used to identify the
organism and diﬀerentiate E. tonsillarum from E. rhusiopathiae. 76 ,

79

Erysipelothrix isolates have been susceptible to penicillin,
ampicillin, cephalosporins, clindamycin, carbapenems, and
quinolones in vitro but resistant to aminoglycosides, vancomycin,
and sulfonamides. 70 , 80 The treatment of choice for serious
infections in humans is penicillin G; ampicillin and ceftriaxone
have also been used with success. Many cases of Erysipelothrix
bacteremia in dogs are associated with endocarditis; therefore,
high doses of antimicrobials are recommended for at least 6 to 8
weeks. Relapses are often reported in infected animals and
humans. Most human infections are acquired through
occupational exposure; infections are found in slaughterhouse
workers, food handlers, and animal trappers. 68 Infected dogs do
not seem to pose a public health hazard.

Anthrax
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Anthrax, a disease found in mammals worldwide, is caused by
Bacillus anthracis, a large (1 to 1.2 µm × 3–6 µm), gram-positive,
aerobic, spore-forming bacillus. The disease and species name is
derived from the black, charcoal-appearing cutaneous lesion it
causes in humans (Greek anthrakis, meaning “coal”).
Microscopically, the organisms may appear as long chains of
gram-positive, square-ended bacteria, similar to a string of
boxcars; shorter chains of two to three cells may be seen (Fig.
52.5). Vegetative B. anthracis cells produce a polypeptide capsule
visible when the organism is stained with polychrome methylene
blue or Giemsa stains. Encapsulated anthrax organisms are

vetexamprep.ir

refractory to phagocytosis, which enhances their ability to
produce disease. Exotoxin production and capsule synthesis by
the bacteria are mediated by plasmids pX01 and pX02,
respectively.

vetexamprep.ir

and septic polyarthritis. No evidence of

Bacillus anthracis begins to sporulate at the end of the growth
phase in its life cycle, an adaptation crucial to the perpetuation of
the organism in nature. Spores are not seen on direct staining of
specimens; however, they appear in culture when nutrients are
depleted. Atmospheric oxygen is considered necessary for

vetexamprep.ir

sporulation because sporulation does not occur in the unopened
carcass of an animal succumbing to anthrax. Anthrax spores are
very resistant to heat, radiation, disinfectants, and desiccation,
resulting in their persistence for more than 40 years in certain soils
and environments. However, in most soils, the organism has to
compete with other soil bacteria, so survival is generally for
months and rarely more than 4 years. 81
Anthrax is most prevalent in Africa, the Middle East, and Latin
America. Anthrax has been sporadically reported in livestock in
the United States, most commonly in the central and the
Mississippi Delta regions, from Texas and Louisiana north to the
Dakotas and Minnesota (Fig. 52.6). Warm temperatures (above
18°C [60°F]), moisture, and alkaline soils with high nitrogen
content allow vegetative growth and proliferation of spores that
have been released into the soil from carcasses of animals that
died of anthrax. 82 Epizootics tend to occur in summer or fall after
heavy rainfall or ﬂooding preceded by drought conditions.
Livestock usually become infected by ingesting spores while
grazing or by eating contaminated feed (Fig. 52.7). Isolated
infections in dogs have been recorded during major anthrax
outbreaks in farm animals. Based on evidence from natural and
experimental infections, dogs and cats are considered relatively
resistant, 83 humans have intermediate resistance, and ruminants
and horses are most susceptible to infection. Many dogs and cats
may experience subclinical infections. Domestic dogs have been
used as a sentinel for surveillance eﬀorts based on serologic
surveys with ELISA assays. 84 , 85
Naturally occurring anthrax in dogs is extremely rare and most
commonly caused by ingestion of meat or hides from infected
carcasses, or possibly ingestion of spores from grooming
contaminated fur. There are no contemporary reports of anthrax
in domestic cats, and older reports are poorly documented. 86
Infections in captive wild canids and felids have also been
recorded after feeding on raw meat from contaminated carcasses.
In 2001 in the United States, there was documented terrorist
dissemination of anthrax spores to induce inhalation anthrax in
humans (the anthrax a acks, or “Amerithrax” from its FBI case
name). 87 Increased risk for inhalation anthrax may therefore exist
for police, guide, or search-and-rescue dogs.

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical Examination
Findings
Infection occurs after inert B. anthracis spores enter the host body
by ingestion (typical route for dogs), by inhalation, or through a
break in the skin. The incubation period is usually 3 to 7 days. At
the point of entry in the GI mucosa, a primary focal hemorrhagic
lesion is produced. Bacteria migrate to regional lymph nodes and
the spleen. In experimentally infected dogs, lesions have been
restricted to local foci in the lungs because the organisms are
generally contained by ﬁbrin and cellular inﬁltrations. 82 After
spores contact the pulmonary alveoli, they are phagocytized by
macrophages that migrate through the alveolar membrane and
enter pulmonary lymphatics, eventually reaching hilar lymph
nodes. Within host cells, the spores quickly germinate into fully
encapsulated vegetative cells that release toxins. Vegetative cells
respond to the host factors of high body temperature and carbon
dioxide levels, resulting in transcriptional activation of capsule
and toxin genes. The capsule is thought to be an antiphagocytic
factor, and the toxin induces large-scale generation of cytokines
such as IL-1 that result in septic shock. 88 Anthrax lethal toxin may
also contribute to shock by inhibitory eﬀects on glucocorticoid
receptor function. 89 Bacterial replication results in death of the
phagocytes, with release of organisms into the bloodstream.
Although most Bacillus species are nonpathogenic to animals and
humans, B. anthracis, through its pXO1 plasmid, expresses three
proteins: protective antigen (PA), edema factor (EF), and lethal
factor (LF). The three components are serologically distinct and
cause no lesions when injected separately, but in binary
combinations they produce edema toxin (PA and EF) and lethal
toxin (PA and LF). PA mediates the entry of either EF or LF into
the cytosol of host cells. EF is an adenylyl cyclase that inhibits
TNF-α synthesis and impairs host defenses. LF, a metalloprotease,
inhibits mitogen-activated protein kinases and induces
macrophage lysis.

The clinical expression of anthrax may be peracute, acute, or
subacute/chronic. In one report, the only clinical sign was
anorexia. 90 After oral exposure, the infection in dogs and cats is
usually manifest as fever (39.4°C to 40.5°C [103°F to 105°F]);
anorexia; and local inﬂammation, necrosis, and edema of the
upper GI tract—the ﬁrst tissues to contact ingested bacteria.
Swelling of head and neck tissues is usually apparent. Subsequent
spread to the local and mesenteric lymph nodes, spleen, and liver
typically occurs, causing enlargement of these organs. Acute
gastroenteritis, which is often hemorrhagic, can occur, as may
sudden death, particularly in younger animals. Signs in younger
or immunocompromised dogs and cats may resemble systemic
anthrax in more susceptible species, described as fulminating

vetexamprep.ir

bacteremia in which the principal lesions are edema, hemorrhage,
and necrosis.

Epidemiology of anthrax. Humans
(and dogs and cats) become infected through
ingestion of contaminated food products or

Cutaneous anthrax, the most common manifestation in humans
worldwide, is rarely the primary clinical form in canids or felids.
The initial cutaneous lesion at the site of inoculation appears ﬁrst
as a papule, progresses to a vesicle, ruptures, and develops into a
black eschar secondary to focal necrosis. Experimental exposure
of dogs to aerosolized anthrax spores did not reliably produce
clinical disease other than short-term fever and anorexia. 82 In
more susceptible species with suspected natural inhalational
exposures, clinical signs include fever, lethargy, cough, and
dyspnea, as well as signs that relate to bacteremia.

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnosis
Anthrax is usually suspected based on history and clinical signs.
Mild pulmonary inﬁltrates and pleural eﬀusion may be detected
radiographically in animals with inhalation anthrax.
Pus or tissue specimens from animals suspected of infection
should be Gram stained to show gram-positive bacilli (which have
the “boxcar” appearance) and stained with polychrome
methylene blue to show the polypeptide capsule (which has the
“string of pearls” appearance) (Fig. 52.8). Examination of stained
smears of blood from a peripheral vein or of ﬁne-needle aspirates
is the most eﬀective and safest means of making a diagnosis.
Serologic testing using ELISA to detect IgG to B. anthracis PA
and capsular antigen in people is highly sensitive and speciﬁc, 91 ,
92 although some people with prior exposure to herbivorous
animals or their by-products have seropositive test results. A
fourfold changing titer is needed to conﬁrm active infection or
recent exposure. Use of this test has been recommended because
some cutaneous cases have been culture- or PCR-negative. 93 Few
other antemortem tests are recommended. A skin test for
diagnosis of anthrax in humans was used in the former Soviet
Union. This anthrax skin test, which detects heightened CMI
against the organism, was usually positive after 3 days of illness
in 97% of those aﬀected. 94
Necropsy of aﬀected carcasses is not advisable because
sporulation occurs, releasing the resistant spores into the
environment. Bacillus anthracis can be isolated from clinical
specimens on routine culture media if the materials are fresh.
Colonies are gray-white to white and nonhemolytic. The isolates
are nonmotile and have a capsule. Vegetative cells may be isolated
from blood, sputum, CSF, eschar, and feces (in gastrointestinal
anthrax cases). In cases of suspected inhalation exposure, B.
anthracis spores may be collected for culture using sterile water–
moistened swabs taken from the nares and haired muzzle or face
within 24 to 48 hours of exposure to aerosolized spores. 95
Immunocytochemical direct FA examination of nasal swab
specimens, pleural ﬂuid smears, or pulmonary biopsy specimens
using antibodies to B. anthracis cell wall and capsule has been
used to diagnose inhalation anthrax in humans. 96 When
available, PCR of sterile body ﬂuids (blood or pleural eﬀusion)

vetexamprep.ir

can rapidly conﬁrm a diagnosis. Diagnostic pathology
laboratories and shippers should always be alerted before
receiving shipments of materials suspected of containing B.
anthracis. Specimens or intact carcasses should be shipped using a
biosecure procedure; they should be wrapped in plastic and kept
refrigerated during transit.

Pathologic Findings
Carcasses of animals that have died of anthrax generally show
li le or no rigor mortis, and dark, nonclo ing blood is usually
seen oozing from the oral and nasal cavities and anus. The carcass
often is bloated and decomposes rapidly. If necropsy is
inadvertently performed on an infected animal, characteristic
lesions will be observed. Extensive gelatinous edema with focal
areas of hemorrhage and necrosis is commonly seen at the site of
GI entry, and may be present around lymph nodes and elsewhere
in the GI tract. Diphtheritic membranes and ulceration may be
present on tonsillar surfaces. Splenomegaly and a friable liver are
often observed. Petechial hemorrhages may be noted on serosal
surfaces. On histopathology, extensive areas of necrosis in
submucosal tissues are accompanied by neutrophilic inﬁltrates.
Gram-positive bacterial colonies may be identiﬁed in mucosal
ﬁbrinous exudates.

vetexamprep.ir

Vegetative Bacillus anthracis with
edema and hemorrhage in the lung of
inhalation anthrax laboratory model (Brown
and Hopps, ×400). Courtesy Armed Forces Institute

Studies of inhalation anthrax lesions in dogs describe discrete,
dark, ﬁrm pulmonary lesions, consisting of a hemorrhagic core
surrounded by dense masses of ﬁbrin and a highly cellular
periphery formed from dense accumulation of neutrophils,
plasma cells, monocytes, and large macrophages. 82 This intense
ﬁbrinous and cellular local response has been interpreted as a
restrictive reaction by the resistant canine host to contain the B.
anthracis invasion. Intrathoracic lymph nodes were enlarged
because of reactive hyperplasia, but bacilli were not observed
during histologic examination. In humans, lymph node

vetexamprep.ir

enlargement causes mediastinal widening, a pathognomonic
radiographic sign in the diagnosis of inhalation anthrax.
In pathologic specimens, anthrax can be conﬁrmed by speciﬁc
immunohistochemical staining with an antibody conjugate that
speciﬁcally identiﬁes the galactose-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine
polysaccharide unique to B. anthracis. 97

Treatment and Prognosis
Information regarding the recommended treatment of dogs or
cats with suspected or conﬁrmed clinical anthrax is extrapolated
from literature reports of other species. Bacillus anthracis is
susceptible to a wide range of antimicrobials, including penicillin,
ﬂuoroquinolones, and tetracyclines (see Table 52.1). Other
antimicrobials that are active in vitro but that have not been
clinically evaluated are chloramphenicol, erythromycin,
aminoglycosides, and sulfonamides. Because of bacterial
production of a cephalosporinase, B. anthracis isolates are typically
resistant to cephalosporin antibacterials; potentiated sulfonamides
are also ineﬀective. Initial doses of antimicrobials should be
administered intravenously. The recommended treatment for
people with systemic anthrax is a combination of a quinolone and
a beta-lactam, such as meropenem; penicillin G could be used in
dogs. 81 Although tissue cultures become negative within 24 hours
after treatment is started, antibacterials are usually administered
for 7 to 14 days. Although cutaneous infection usually resolves
without medical treatment, antibacterials are recommended
because cases may progress to systemic involvement (the fatality
rate is 10% to 20% without treatment). 93 Humans with cutaneous
anthrax are treated with doxycycline or ciproﬂoxacin
monotherapy.
Additional supportive care may also be indicated. Animals with
respiratory compromise from cervical edema may need treatment
with glucocorticoids or tracheostomy. Pleural eﬀusion may
require drainage. Dressings with drainage from lesions should be
incinerated, autoclaved, or disposed of as biohazardous waste. A
dog or cat with suspected coat or skin exposure to anthrax aerosol
should be thoroughly bathed with soap and water, as
disinfectants that inactivate Bacillus spores are generally too
caustic to use on skin. Use of accelerated hydrogen peroxide

vetexamprep.ir

shampoos could also be considered. Persons decontaminating the
haircoat of a pet should wear disposable gloves, mask, and gown.
Isolation of aﬀected animals is not required because anthrax is not
transmissible after animals have been decontaminated.

Immunity and Vaccination
If not superseded by bacteremia and death, the host response
involves speciﬁc IgG antibodies against PA, with antibodies
functioning to inhibit spore germination and stimulate
phagocytosis by macrophages. Although livestock at risk should
receive annual vaccinations, currently marketed, these have not
been tested in companion animals, nor are they licensed or
recommended for use in these species. Animal vaccines approved
for large animals in endemic regions commonly use an avirulent
nonencapsulated (pXO2-deﬁcient) spore strain (Sterne strain). In
contrast, an anthrax vaccine licensed in the United States for use
in people is a cell-free ﬁltrate containing protective antigen and
alum. Five intramuscular injections (at 0 and 4 weeks and 6, 12,
and 18 months) are required for immunity, and annual booster
injections are recommended for maintenance. 93 An a enuated
live vaccine for people, which was developed in the former Soviet
Union, has been eﬀective; however, it is not available in other
countries.

Prevention
In endemic areas or during an outbreak, all meat fed to dogs and
cats should be thoroughly cooked to eliminate the risk of
exposure. To minimize environmental contamination by anthrax
spores, carcasses of animals dying from anthrax should be
destroyed by incineration or buried deep with a covering of
quicklime (anhydrous calcium oxide). Decontamination involves a
sporicidal solution of lye because ordinary disinfectants are
ineﬀective (5% NaOH for 1.5 hours at 27.8°C or 3.6 hours at 21.1°C
kills 99% of spores). 98 Soaking impervious articles in 10%
formaldehyde or 4% glutaraldehyde for a minimum of 2 hours is
sporicidal. 99 In the laboratory, surfaces can be decontaminated
with 5% hypochlorite. Instruments used should be autoclaved or
boiled at 100°C for 10 minutes. 98 All areas, equipment, and

vetexamprep.ir

buildings that may have contacted infected animals should be
cleaned and disinfected. Control of ﬂying insects and scavenging
insects and animals should be implemented. Personnel who are
cleaning up after an outbreak or terrorist a ack that kills livestock
must wear protective clothing and respirators.
Postexposure prophylaxis protocols for people recommend at
least 60 days of antibacterial administration because of concerns
about environmental and pulmonary spore persistence. 100
Tetracyclines are preferred for postexposure prophylaxis,
although amoxicillin or ampicillin may be substituted when the
treatment course is prolonged or when contraindicated in
pregnancy or lactation. The American Academy of Veterinary
Pharmacology and Therapeutics and the American College of
Veterinary Clinical Pharmacology have recommended that
exposed working dogs be treated with doxycycline (5 mg/kg, PO,
q24h) for 45 to 60 days. 101 Postexposure vaccination is also done
for people using a CDC investigational drug protocol, at 0, 2, and
4 weeks SC.

Public Health Aspects
Anthrax is a notiﬁable disease and should be reported to state and
federal agencies. Care must be taken when handling infected
tissues or carcasses because the organism can penetrate cuts in the
skin, resulting in localized infection with subsequent
dissemination. It has been estimated that between 2,000 and
20,000 cases occur worldwide each year. 93 In developed
countries, 95% of naturally occurring cases in humans are
cutaneous. They generally result from exposure to infected
animals or contaminated animal products (wool, hair, bone,
horns, hides). 93 Lesions are painless, pruritic papules, sometimes
surrounded by vesicles, with an ulcerated, circular, black necrotic
scab (Fig. 52.9). Although less common, inhalation or ingestion
can result in either a highly fatal bacteremia caused by
hemorrhagic
pneumonitis
or
an
oropharyngitis
and
gastroenteritis, respectively. Anthrax has been developed as a
biologic warfare agent by Japan, the United Kingdom, the United
States, Iraq, and the former Soviet Union. One millionth of a gram
of inhaled anthrax spores is a lethal dose to a person. Apart from

vetexamprep.ir

terrorist events, infection in people is almost always transmi ed
from infected animals or their by-products.

Case Example
Signalment

“Jimmy,” a 4-year-old male neutered German shepherd (Fig.
52.10).

History

Jimmy was evaluated by the University of California-Davis
VMTH Internal Medicine service for chronic weight loss,
inappetence, and diarrhea that was refractory to medical
therapy for inﬂammatory bowel disease. The clinical signs had
been present for 13 months, and were ﬁrst noticed shortly after
Jimmy’s owners moved from Hawaii to a 5-acre farm in

vetexamprep.ir

northern California. The local veterinarian suspected
inﬂammatory bowel disease or antibiotic-responsive diarrhea.
Fecal ﬂotations and a Giardia ELISA assay performed at that
time were negative for parasites. Jimmy was treated with
tylosin and a therapeutic diet trial with a prescription
hydrolyzed protein diet. This was associated with moderate
clinical improvement. Laboratory testing performed over the
next 6 months revealed persistent mild hypoalbuminemia and
severe hypocobalaminemia, which was treated with parenteral
cyanocobalamin.
A year after the signs were ﬁrst noted, the diarrhea recurred
and weight loss was noted with mildly decreased appetite. The
diarrhea was characterized by soft to liquid stool with increased
frequency of defecation (3–4 times a day), some mucus and
occasional mild hematochezia and tenesmus. Full thickness
intestinal biopsies were obtained via exploratory laparotomy.
Histopathology revealed chronic inﬂammatory gastroenteritis
with a prominent eosinophilic component and mild lacteal
dilation (suggestive of possible lymphangiectasia). Treatment
with methylprednisolone (0.5 mg/kg, PO, q12h) and
cyclosporine (5 mg/kg, PO, q24h) was not associated with
clinical improvement. Around the same time, oral and nasal
planum ulcerations were noted. Biopsy of these lesions was
consistent with a diagnosis of cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
Based on recommendations from a veterinary dermatologist,
cyclosporine was substituted with leﬂunomide (5 mg/kg, PO,
q24h), and the methylprednisolone dose was reduced (0.5
mg/kg, q24h). This was followed by improvement in the
cutaneous lesions but the diarrhea continued. A second diet
trial with a diﬀerent commercial hydrolyzed diet was
commenced.
From that point on, there was progressive weight loss,
variable appetite, occasional urinary accidents in the house, and
intermi ent mixed large and small bowel-type diarrhea with
hematochezia. The week before the dog was evaluated, the
owner noted a marked decrease in Jimmy’s energy and
appetite.

Current Medications

Methylprednisone 0.5 mg/kg, PO, q24h and leﬂunomide 5
mg/kg, PO, q24h.

trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, chloramphenicol.
Blood culture (aerobic and anaerobic): Blood samples were
collected at times 0, 20, and 60 minutes. Large numbers of
gram-positive rods were seen on a Gram-stained smear after
incubation, which were also identiﬁed as L. monocytogenes.

Diagnosis

Listeria monocytogenes bacteremia.
Chronic enteropathy associated with inﬂammatory bowel
disease.
Cutaneous lupus of German shepherd dogs.

Treatment

Leﬂunomide was discontinued and treatment with ampicillin
(20 mg/kg, IV, q6h) and gentamicin (10 mg/kg, SC, q24h) was
initiated. Methylprednisolone was continued. Magnesium
citrate was also administered (5 mg/kg, q24h) for
hypomagnesemia that likely resulted from chronic
malabsorption. At a recheck 1 week later, Jimmy’s owners
reported signiﬁcant improvement in his activity level and
appetite. His temperature had been normal at home and he was
playing with the other dogs. He ate almost all of his food but
did not ever seem very hungry, but his body weight increased
by 0.6 kg. No urinary accidents in the house had occurred.
Blood and urine cultures were negative. Although bandemia
had resolved on the CBC, there was a persistent mature
neutrophilia (27,245 cells/µL) and serum chemistry

vetexamprep.ir

p
(
µ )
y
abnormalities persisted, with further increase in the serum ALT
(1925 U/L). On physical examination, a new cardiac murmur
was detected (grade II/VI systolic left apical). An
echocardiogram revealed mild mitral valve regurgitation,
reduced systolic function, and a 1-cm circular echogenic lesion
that was adherent to the caudal apical surface of the left
ventricular endomyocardium (Fig. 52.11A and B). This was
suspected to be a mural thrombus. Serum troponin I
concentration was increased (0.97 ng/mL, reference range: 0.09–
0.17). Treatment with amoxicillin (20 mg/kg, PO, q8h) was
continued and gentamicin was discontinued. Treatment with
clopidogrel was considered, but withheld because of concerns
that it might lead to dislodgement of a clot. However,
approximately 1 week later, Jimmy developed acute onset of
left thoracic limb lameness. On physical examination, his entire
limb distal to the carpus was cool to the touch. No murmur was
detected. A repeat echocardiogram showed that the mural mass
was half the size it had previously been, with ragged edges.
Abdominal ultrasound examination showed lesions consistent
with multiple venous thrombi in the caudal vena cava, common
iliac, hepatic, and renal veins. Wedge-shaped hypoechoic
lesions were identiﬁed in the renal parenchyma and diﬀuse
mixed echogenic regions were in the liver, suggestive of infarcts
secondary to thromboemboli. Jimmy was treated with
clopidogrel (1.5 mg/kg, PO, q24h), enoxaparin (1 mg/kg, SC,
q8h), enalapril (0.5 mg/kg, PO, q12h) and pimobendan (0.3
mg/kg, PO, q12h). Amoxicillin was also continued.
One month later the lameness had resolved, there had been a
5-kg weight gain, and Jimmy’s appetite and energy level were
normal. Bloodwork showed resolution of laboratory
abnormalities, including serum troponin I concentration, and
echocardiography showed resolution of the mural lesion,
persistent mild mitral regurgitation, and improved systolic
function. Abdominal ultrasound examination showed
resolution of thrombi within the major veins and static chronic
renal changes consistent with infarcts. All medications except
the clopidogrel and methylprednisolone were discontinued; at a
recheck 2 months later, clopidogrel was discontinued and
methylprednisolone dose was halved, and vitamin B12
supplementation was commenced (1500 µg, SC, q2weeks)

vetexamprep.ir

because serum B12 concentration was low (219 ng/L, reference
range 271–875 ng/L). Six months later, there was worsening of
cutaneous lupus lesions, with appearance of multiple severe
oral ulcerations (Fig. 52.11C). The inﬂammatory bowel disease
was relatively well controlled with only mild intermi ent
diarrhea. Treatment with cyclosporine was commenced (5
mg/kg, PO, q24h), which was associated with resolution of the
ulcers. However, 6 months later, Jimmy became hyporexic and
weight loss was noted. The most signiﬁcant ﬁnding on an
extensive work-up that included bloodwork, blood cultures,
echocardiography, and abdominal ultrasound was moderate
thrombocytopenia (59,000 platelets/µL). Vector-borne disease
serology was negative. Four months later (2 years after the
diagnosis of listeriosis) he was brought to the UC Davis
veterinary emergency service and was in cardiopulmonary
arrest. A necropsy revealed disseminated, intravascular B-cell
lymphoma in the lung, brain, kidney, pancreas, liver, small and
large intestine, stomach, omentum, adrenal gland, heart, and
periocular haired skin as well as moderate, chronic, diﬀuse,
lymphoplasmacytic enteritis.

Comments

This dog likely developed L. monocytogenes bacteremia and
mural endomyocarditis with thromboembolic complications
secondary to immunosuppressive drug therapy and exposure
to farm animal species. Although the listeriosis was treated
successfully, ultimately persistence of immune-mediated
disease necessitated ongoing immunosuppression with
cyclosporine. It is possible that the use of cyclosporine
predisposed to the ultimate cause of death, disseminated B-cell
lymphoma. 102

53: Gram-Negative Bacterial
Infections
Virginia Sinno -Stu man, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Gram-negative bacteria were first described
in Berlin by the Danish scientist Hans Christian Gram in 1884
when he used Gram stain to visualize Klebsiella pneumoniae
in the lungs of people who died of pneumonia. 1
• Causes: Examples include Escherichia coli, Salmonella,
Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Klebsiella, Campylobacter,
Pseudomonas, and Acinetobacter.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Direct contact or contact with
contaminated fomites; the bacteria often invade
opportunistically.
• Major Clinical Signs: Affected sites include UTIs, wound
infections, pneumonia, pyothorax, peritonitis, pyometra, ocular
surface infections, otitis externa, pyoderma, bacteremia, and
endocarditis, but virtually any body system can be affected.
• Differential Diagnoses: Infections with gram-positive bacteria
such as Staphylococcus spp. and Streptococcus spp.; to a
lesser extent, infections with nonbacterial pathogens such as
fungi.
• Human Health Significance: Gram-negative bacteria shed by
dogs and cats have the potential to colonize humans,
especially those with impaired host defenses. They may also
be responsible for infections of dog or cat bites. Infections
caused by gram-negative pathogens resistant to all available
antibiotics have resulted in the death of human patients. 2

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic Agents, Epidemiology, and Clinical
Features
Gram-negative bacteria are ubiquitous agents of opportunistic
infections in dogs and cats and primarily cause disease when host
defenses are impaired. They are important causes of nosocomial
disease; several species belong to the ESKAPE group of bacteria
(Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae,
Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter
spp.), a term that was developed to reﬂect the ability of these
organisms to escape antimicrobial activity through resistance and
highlight their importance as signiﬁcant causes of morbidity and
mortality in human healthcare facilities. Distinguishing the gramnegative species in this group from gram-positive bacteria is a
complex outer membrane that contains LPS, as well as structures
known as porins that regulate transport of molecules in and out of
the cell including antimicrobial drugs. Between this outer
membrane and the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane is a periplasmic
space, which contains the structural polymer peptidoglycan (or
murein) (Fig. 53.1). The peptidoglycan layer of gram-negative
bacteria is much thinner than that of gram-positive bacteria,
approximately one layer, or 7 to 8 nm thick (compared with many
layers, or 20 to 80 nm thick for gram-positive bacteria). The inner
cytoplasmic membrane contains many diﬀerent proteins that are
lipoproteins anchored into the outer lipid bilayer leaﬂet,
transmembrane proteins, or peripheral membrane proteins that lie
adjacent to the bilayer leaﬂets. Of particular clinical relevance are
eﬄux pumps which can allow an organism to become resistant to
multiple antibiotic classes. The pump type that most commonly
causes such resistance is called the resistance-nodulation-cell
division (RND) pump. This pump system, when active, can
extrude a variety of molecules from gram-negative bacteria,
including antimicrobial agents of various classes, conferring
multidrug resistance to gram-negative organisms of several
genera including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas
species. 3
LPS is a large molecule that varies in composition from one
bacterial species and strain to another. It contributes to the
structural integrity of gram-negative bacteria and is a potent
virulence factor. It consists of the lipid A backbone, a core

vetexamprep.ir

oligosaccharide, and the O antigen side chain. Lipid A is a
phosphorylated disaccharide to which long, hydrophobic fa y
acid chains are a ached, which anchor the LPS into the outer
membrane (Figs. 53.1 and 53.2). The lipid A component is also
known as endotoxin because it is the biologically active portion of
the molecule, in that it stimulates a potent host inﬂammatory
response (see Chapter 123). The core oligosaccharide connects
lipid A to the O antigen side chain. Its composition diﬀers
between bacterial species. The O antigen is a repeating
polysaccharide that projects from the surface of the bacterial cell
and varies in length from 1 to 60 repeats. It is the antigenic portion
of the molecule and is responsible for serogroup classiﬁcation of
gram-negative bacteria.
Gram-negative cocci, such as Moraxella or Neisseria, are not
widely recognized as signiﬁcant pathogens of dogs and cats.
However, as commensals of the canine and feline oral cavity, they
can cause bite wound infections in humans, 4 and Neisseria canis
was isolated in pure culture from a deep mandibular abscess from
one dog. 5 Gram-negative rods are classiﬁed into Enterobacterales
(previously Enterobacteriaceae) and non-Enterobacterales species.
Enterobacterales that cause disease in dogs and cats include E.
coli, Proteus, Salmonella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia, Klebsiella,
and Providencia. Non-Enterobacterales species include the
Pasteurellaceae (Pasteurella multocida), as well as P. aeruginosa,
Acinetobacter, and Ralstonia. Other gram-negative bacteria are
coccobacilli or spiral-shaped organisms and include Bartonella,
Bordetella, Campylobacter, Francisella, Helicobacter, and Brucella.
Like gram-positive cocci, some gram-negative bacteria have
tremendous ability to form bioﬁlms, or bacterial aggregates that
are embedded in a matrix of exopolysaccharide (bacterial slime),
which form on living or nonliving surfaces. These protect the
bacteria, and organisms in bioﬁlms can resist the eﬀect of
antimicrobial drugs and disinfectants. In addition, expression of
eﬄux pumps has been shown to be a key component of bioﬁlm
formation in gram-negative organisms. 6

Virulence Factors
While the majority of gram-negative infections are caused by
opportunistic pathogens that take advantage of weakened host
immune systems, some gram-negative organisms have virulence
factors which allow them to: (1) persist in host tissues that they do
not normally colonize; (2) evade immune responses, and/or (3)
adhere to, invade, or damage host cells. Diﬀerent serotypes of the
same species may vary greatly in their potential to cause disease.
For example, E. coli O157:H7 is often isolated from cases of
hemolytic uremic syndrome because it expresses two powerful
virulence factors, Shiga toxin (Stx-2) and verocytotoxins (Shigalike toxins). These induce necrosis of endothelial cells, which
results in widespread thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, and often
death. In contrast, E. coli strain VR50 is associated with

vetexamprep.ir

asymptomatic bacteriuria in humans, and is currently being
investigated as a therapeutic inoculum to prevent recurrent
symptomatic UTIs in women. 7
As whole genome sequencing is becoming an increasingly
commonplace aspect of microbiology, hundreds of individual
virulence factor genes across several genera of gram-negative
organisms have been identiﬁed. These can be divided into several
categories based on how they contribute to establishing infections
and causing disease.
Adhesion Molecules
Adhesion mechanisms among gram-negative bacteria vary
widely, but the general motif involves the interaction between
bacterial surface organelles and either epithelium or an abiotic
surface (i.e., surgical implant). Surface organelles include
ﬁmbriae, pili, and ﬂagella. In most cases, genes involved in
adhesion are regulated alongside genes that are involved with
bioﬁlm development. The virulence factor that allows E. coli VR50
to adhere to the mucosa of human bladders has been identiﬁed as
the gene for aﬁmbrial adhesion (afa). 8
Invasion
Organisms that can cross epithelial barriers and/or invade host
cells must possess enzymes that can break down membranes and
connective tissue. As such, the host of invasion virulence factors
include genes coding for various isoenzymes of phospholipase,
collagenase, hyaluronidase, and lecithinase. In contrast to factors
that mediate adhesion, invasion virulence factors generally cause
some level of damage to target tissues. Genes that encode
phospholipase D (pld) are key virulence factors that allow A.
baumannii to penetrate the pulmonary epithelial barrier. 9
Competition for Iron and Nutrients
Iron is tightly bound to proteins (such as hemoglobin) in
mammals; free iron concentration in the host environment is
minute. To facilitate survival, gram-negative bacteria express iron
acquisition systems that are not required in iron-rich
environments. Iron-sequestering proteins produced by gramnegative bacteria are among the most eﬃcient iron chelators in the

vetexamprep.ir

natural world. Examples of eﬃcient bacterial iron chelators are
enterobactin in E. coli and pyoverdine in P. aeruginosa. 10
Resistance to Host Immunity
Microorganisms can evade host immunity in myriad ways. While
most gram-negative organisms are not innately pathogenic and
thus have li le genome space dedicated to this task, pathogenic
strains of E. coli modulate the host’s response to endotoxin by
inserting tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs into cell membranes
which dampen the production of proinﬂammatory cytokines in
response to the presence of endotoxin and other pathogenassociated molecular pa erns. Additionally, E. coli can bind the Fc
receptor of macrophages directly (without antibody present) and
induce an inhibitory response, blocking phagocytosis. 11
Toxin Secretion
Gram-negative pathogens can express genes which interrupt
normal metabolic functions of host cells. In general, far greater
numbers of gram-negative organisms possess these genes than
express them, likely because there is a “ﬁtness cost” (ATP cost)
associated with their expression. These toxins are sometimes used
to create a more favorable environment for bacterial replication.
For example, in microanaerobic conditions, P. aeruginosa can
produce exotoxin A, which inhibits protein synthesis by host cells,
presumably so that competition for oxygen is reduced. 12

vetexamprep.ir
