Bacterial Motility
Gram-negative bacteria that possess ﬂagella are not necessarily
able to demonstrate coordinated motion. Motility pa erns such as
twitching, swimming, and swarming (which involves
communication between organisms and activation of “quorum
sensing” genes) are associated with ascending UTIs and medical
device–related infections. Twitching is more commonly found in
Proteus isolated from catheter-associated UTIs than in Proteus
isolated from the feces of healthy individuals. 13
Virulence Plasmids
Plasmids are packets of genetic material which bacteria can trade
among one another. Many plasmids confer groups of potent
virulence factors, often genes for cytotoxins, as well as
antimicrobial resistance genes. In this way, an otherwise
innocuous bacterial clone can quickly acquire both pathogenicity
and antimicrobial resistance. Toxins associated with E. coli
O157:H7 are largely encoded for on a virulence plasmid, pO157,
and include enterohemolysin, serine protease, and catalaseperoxidase. Each of these enzymes alone is capable of interrupting
cellular metabolism, initiating coagulation, or inducing apoptosis
under certain conditions. Expression of all three as well as Shiga
toxin can result in devastating diarrheal illness and hemolytic
uremic syndrome. 14

Enterobacterales
Many Enterobacterales contribute to the normal gastrointestinal
ﬂora of animals. Enterobacterales are non-spore forming, non-acid
fast, facultative, anaerobic, gram-negative rods. They possess a
capsule (K antigen) and may be motile via ﬂagella (H antigen).
Highly encapsulated species, such as Klebsiella and Enterobacter,
have a mucoid appearance when they grow in culture. The
ﬂagella project from the bacterial cell and contain the ﬁlamentforming protein ﬂagellin, which (with LPS) can stimulate the host
inﬂammatory
response.
An
internationally
recognized

vetexamprep.ir

classiﬁcation system for Enterobacterales has been established
based on diﬀerences in the antigen surface molecules, O (LPS), K
(capsular), H (ﬂagellar), with serotypes identiﬁed by a numerical
assignment to each antigen they possess listed after the genus and
species name (i.e., E. coli O157:H7). Additionally clonal strains of
species of speciﬁc microbiologic or pathologic interest can be
identiﬁed by serial alphanumeric designation (i.e., E.coli 83972
and E. coli VR50, two strains causing asymptomatic bacteriuria in
women). The Enterobacterales also possess ﬁmbriae or pili, which
are thinner than ﬂagella and play a role in adhesion and
sometimes bacterial aggregation. Finally, they possess a variety of
complex secretion systems (type I, II, III secretion systems). These
facilitate export of toxins such as hemolysins, and molecules that
are inserted into, and form pores in, host cell membranes.
Escherichia coli
More than any other species of Enterobacterales, E. coli possess the
potential to be true pathogens, capable of causing communicable
disease in otherwise healthy individuals. Diarrheagenic E. coli are
a leading cause of human diarrheal disease in the developing
world and a source of outbreaks in the developed world.
Outbreaks of foodborne illness occur when produce becomes
contaminated with animal (usually ca le) feces. Based on the
virulence factors they express, enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) are
classiﬁed into six major pathovars (i.e., groups deﬁned by the
speciﬁc pathologic lesions they produce). The reader is referred to
Chapter 63 for more complete information on intestinal E. coli
infections; however, those pathovars known to cause illness in
dogs and cats are discussed below.
Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli
Organisms collectively called EPEC may comprise several
serovars of E. coli. The group is deﬁned by its pathogenesis, which
is characterized by the distinctive lesions they create on the
surface of intestinal epithelial cells. Termed “a aching and
eﬀacing,” all EPEC express the eae gene for intimin, an adhesion
protein partially responsible for the denuding of microvilli, but
they do not express genes encoding for Shiga toxin. EPEC has
been isolated from cats with and without diarrhea. 15 Dogs have
long been implicated as carriers of EPEC, and healthy dogs

vetexamprep.ir

without diarrhea can harbor EPEC. 16 This complicates the
question of whether EPEC causes diarrhea in dogs. EPEC has
been detected in dogs with diarrhea, but many of these dogs were
also infected or colonized with other enteropathogens, so it was
unclear if EPEC was a secondary pathogen or a primary cause of
diarrhea. 17 In a case series in which a reasonable a empt was
made to exclude other pathogens, EPEC were detected based on
PCR analysis of E. coli isolated from all of seven dogs with
hematemesis and/or hemorrhagic diarrhea. 18 Given the
infrequency with which molecular diagnostics are performed in
veterinary cases of diarrheal illness, EPEC may be underreported
as a cause of diarrhea. EPEC should be among the diﬀerential
diagnoses in cases where multiple members of a household or
community of dogs are aﬀected by diarrhea, keeping in mind the
zoonotic potential of this pathogen.
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) produces either heat-stable toxin
(ST), heat-labile toxin (LT), or both. There is li le genomic
homology among strains of ETEC and conserved genes do not
encode proteins associated with pathogenesis. Instead, it is
thought that the acquisition of plasmids that encode for
colonization factors (to allow adhesion to intestinal epithelium)
and ST, LT, or both deﬁne ETEC. 19 Diarrhea is induced by ST and
LT, which stimulate secondary messenger systems that in turn
open the cystic ﬁbrosis transmembrane conductance regulator
(CFTR) of enterocytes. The end result is bulk chloride loss into the
intestinal lumen. As water and sodium follow, voluminous
watery diarrhea results. ETEC has been identiﬁed in dogs with
diarrhea. 20 , 21
Adherent invasive Escherichia coli
Unlike most other pathovars of E. coli, adherent invasive E. coli
(AIEC) is still deﬁned by its phenotype because virulence genes
associated with invasiveness have yet to be identiﬁed in this
pathovar. An E. coli is deﬁned as AIEC if it can invade and
replicate within cell cultures eﬃciently enough to escape
inactivation by gentamicin. 22 Adherent and invasive E. coli induce
disease through a combination of host genetic predisposition and

vetexamprep.ir

immune stimulation. These organisms adhere to and invade ileal
cells (humans) and ileal and colonic cells (dogs), which is
associated with Crohn’s disease and granulomatous colitis,
respectively. The microorganisms replicate within epithelial cells
as well as macrophages, with inhibition of macrophage apoptosis.
This results in high levels of TNF-α with associated intestinal
inﬂammation and granuloma formation in patients with Crohn’s
disease. 19 , 23 Boxer dogs and French bulldogs with
granulomatous colitis have AIEC associated with their lesions.
Remission associated with ﬂuoroquinolone administration
suggests a similar pathogenesis. 24 , 25 Given the emergence of
resistance and the microbiologically catastrophic eﬀect of
antibiotics on the gut microbiome, alternate therapies are being
investigated in humans with Crohn’s disease. Nonantibiotic
therapies targeted at blocking AIEC adhesion and colonization are
under investigation. 26
Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli
Following the same nomenclature system used for EPEC,
organisms that cause disease outside of the intestinal tract are
often designated as extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC). An
important subset of ExPEC, serovars or clones with virulence
a ributes that allow for urinary tract invasion, are often referred
to as uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC). Escherichia coli is the most
common cause of UTIs in dogs and cats and can also be isolated
from dogs and cats with pyometra, prostatitis, peritonitis,
cholangitis,
cholecystitis,
bacteremia
and
endocarditis,
bronchopneumonia (such as that secondary to aspiration), and
pyothorax. 27 There are two reports of severe soft tissue infections
(necrotizing fasciitis) in dogs associated with E. coli infection. 28 , 29
Antimicrobial resistance in E. coli isolates from dogs and cats is an
increasing problem; 51% of 376 isolates collected from sick dogs
and cats in the United States in 2005 showed resistance to at least
one drug, and 29% of the 376 isolates were MDR (deﬁned as
resistant to three or more classes of antimicrobial drugs). 30
Another investigation similarly found an increasing trend for
resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins
for nonurinary tract E. coli infections from 2002 to 2011. 31 A
European investigation found that beta-lactamase production

vetexamprep.ir

among E. coli respiratory infections in dogs was high, with only
37% of isolates sensitive to ampicillin but 83% susceptible to
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. 32 The prevalence of resistance in 395
isolates from healthy dogs and cats from Canada was lower (19%).
33 In a prevalence study in the United Kingdom, 1.9% of dogs
visiting veterinary clinics had E. coli that expressed extendedspectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) genes in their feces, and recent
antibiotic use and being fed raw poultry were identiﬁed as risk
factors for carrying resistant E.coli. 34 ESBL enzyme production
has also been identiﬁed in E. coli isolates from dogs and cats in the
United States, 35 and a few isolates were found to express New
Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM-1), which hydrolyses
carbapenems. 36 Nosocomial infections with MDR E. coli have also
been described in dogs and cats.
In humans, strains of UPEC that cause UTIs diﬀer from those
that cause diarrhea, and there is some evidence that this may also
be true for strains that cause UTIs versus pyometra in dogs and
cats. 37–39 These strains possess a number of virulence factors, such
as siderophores, type 1 and P ﬁmbriae, hemolysin, and cytotoxic
necrotizing factor. Speciﬁc virulence factors, as well as bioﬁlmforming capacity, have been associated with persistent or
relapsing UTIs, 40 , 41 and UPEC can invade and persist within
bladder epithelial cells. In a recent study of 194 UPEC specimens
obtained from clinical human UTI cases, the most commonly
expressed virulence genes (expressed in 58%–68% of strains) were
two genes that permit adhesion to bladder epithelium (ﬁm, iha), a
gene coding for a capsule which may allow the organism to evade
the immune system (kpsMT), and a gene for a toxin which is
associated with the development of pyelonephritis (usp). 42 In one
study, canine E. coli UTIs were more likely to be recurrent than
those associated with other uropathogens. 43 Another
investigation revealed that recurrent E. coli UTIs are more likely to
be increasingly resistant to antibiotics. 31 There has been concern
that dogs may act as a source of E. coli strains that are pathogenic
for humans. 39 , 44 In other extraintestinal E. coli infections, E. coli
more closely resemble commensal strains, and host factors may be
more important than bacterial virulence factors. 45
Proteus

vetexamprep.ir

Proteus mirabilis is a common cause of upper and lower UTIs in
dogs as well as otitis externa and uncommonly pyoderma. It
produces a potent urease and can contribute to development of
struvite urolithiasis. Uroliths harbor bacteria that can emerge as
the uroliths dissolve. Proteus has a characteristic swarming
motility and may obscure the growth of other co-infecting
microorganisms when grown in the laboratory on agar. Recently,
highly resistant P. mirabilis isolates sharing some homology with
human isolates have been identiﬁed in canine patients in France.
46 Proteus penneri, an uncommon cause of nosocomial infections
and bacteremia in humans, has rarely been isolated from wound
infections in dogs seen at the editor’s hospital. 47
Klebsiella
The most common species of Klebsiella that infects dogs and cats is
K. pneumoniae. Klebsiella oxytoca is a nosocomial pathogen in
humans and has been reported in association with IV catheter
colonization in puppies with parvoviral enteritis. 48 Klebsiella
oxytoca has also been isolated from clinical veterinary specimens
(either cultures from patients or pathology specimens) in both
Italy (n = 24) and Japan (n = 14, 7 of which were from urine). 49 , 50
Klebsiella pneumoniae primarily causes upper and lower UTIs in
dogs and cats, but can also cause pneumonia, sometimes with
abscessation (Figs. 53.3 and 53.4). It has been isolated from dogs
with hepatic abscesses. 51 Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important
cause of nosocomial infections and may be associated with
bacteremia, endocarditis, and postoperative skin and soft tissue
infections. The capsule of K. pneumoniae is a major virulence
factor. It inhibits phagocytosis and is responsible for the mucoid
appearance of the organism in culture (Fig. 53.5A).
All strains of K. pneumoniae are resistant to ampicillin because
they possess a chromosomal gene that encodes a penicillin βlactamase. Some isolates, such as nosocomial isolates or those
from persistent UTIs, possess plasmids that contain resistance
genes for multiple antimicrobial drugs. Of greatest concern are
Klebsiella isolates that express ESBL enzymes, which hydrolyze
third-generation cephalosporins. The genes that encode ESBLs are
often located on plasmids that also contain genes for
aminoglycoside resistance. Although MDR K. pneumoniae are not

vetexamprep.ir

uncommonly isolated from dogs and cats, ESBL-producing K.
pneumoniae isolates are rarely encountered but have recently been
isolated from veterinary specimens in Swi erland. 52 Treatment
options for MDR K. pneumoniae may be limited to
aminoglycosides, carbapenems, and sometimes trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole.

Serratia marcescens
Serratia marcescens is an important cause of nosocomial infections
in both human and veterinary medicine. In human patients,
infections with S. marcescens are often linked to IV drug use. The
organism has a tremendous ability to survive in the environment
and may contaminate and remain viable in disinfectant solutions.
53 It has been isolated from saline vials used in a multiple-dose
fashion to dilute drugs in a veterinary hospital. 54 It sometimes
grows as a contaminant, such as in blood cultures. Some, but not
all, strains of S. marcescens produce a red pigment when grown in
culture. 55
In dogs, S. marcescens infection has been associated with UTIs,
bacteremia and aortic valve endocarditis, 56 catheter-related
infections in canine parvoviral enteritis, 43 and necrotizing
fasciitis. 57 Contamination of blood products was linked to an

vetexamprep.ir

outbreak of bacteremia in cats. 58 It has also caused severe
necrosuppurative myositis in a young cat. 59 Serratia is resistant to
ampicillin and ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins as a result of a
chromosomal β-lactamase. It may also acquire plasmid-mediated
resistance to other antimicrobial drugs.
Enterobacter
Enterobacter cloacae and, to a lesser extent, Enterobacter aerogenes
represent the majority of Enterobacter species isolated from clinical
specimens from dogs and cats. 60 Enterobacter spp. are mainly
isolated from dogs and cats with UTIs but occasionally cause
wound or catheter-related infections and have been isolated from
samples from the ear, skin, and eye. 60 They generally are
intrinsically resistant to ampicillin and ﬁrst-generation
cephalosporins and may also be resistant to multiple other
antimicrobial drug classes.
Citrobacter
Citrobacter species are named for their ability to use citrate as a
sole carbon source. Citrobacter freundii is most commonly isolated
from dogs and cats with UTIs but can also cause catheter-related
infections, bacteremia, and endocarditis. 61 , 62 Citrobacter koseri
was isolated from puppies with myocarditis. 63 Like Enterobacter
and Serratia, Citrobacter are usually resistant to ampicillin and
ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins and may acquire a number of
plasmid-mediated resistance genes, including those that encode
ESBLs and resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones.

Non-Enterobacterales
Pasteurella
Pasteurellaceae are small, fastidious, nonmotile bacilli or
coccobacilli that are commensals of the oral cavities and upper
respiratory tracts of dogs and especially cats. The most common
species of Pasteurella associated with disease in dogs and
especially cats is P. multocida. Other species include Pasteurella
canis, Pasteurella dagmatis, and Pasteurella stomatis. Pasteurella spp.
have been associated with a wide variety of disease
manifestations that include pyothorax, upper respiratory tract

vetexamprep.ir

infections (usually secondary to viral infections or chronic
rhinosinusitis), bronchopneumonia, UTIs, ocular surface
infections, wound infections, cutaneous abscesses, otitis externa,
bacteremia, and, rarely, infective endocarditis. They may be found
in mixed infections with other bacteria, such as Streptococcus canis,
other gram-negative bacteria, or anaerobes. In humans, they are
an important cause of animal bite wound infections. 4 , 64
Pasteurella spp. are usually broadly susceptible to antimicrobial
drugs, and the treatment of choice is a penicillin such as penicillin
G, ampicillin, or amoxicillin.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the main pathogenic species in the
family Pseudomonadaceae. It is known for its ability to produce a
variety of pigments when grown in culture, such as pyocyanin
(blue), pyorubin (red), pyomelanin (black), and pyoverdin
(yellow-green to yellow-brown and ﬂuorescent), and for its
characteristic “corn taco” or “grape”-like odor (Fig. 53.5B and C).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa has one polar ﬂagellum and is covered in
thin, hair-like pili (Fig. 53.6). It can also produce an extracellular
polysaccharide known as alginate, which results in a mucoid
colony appearance.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is widespread in the environment and
can grow in a huge variety of diﬀerent conditions, reﬂecting its
importance as a nosocomial pathogen. It is commonly found on
plants, water, and soil. It can survive in disinfectants and grow in

vetexamprep.ir

diesel and jet fuel. It is occasionally isolated from the skin,
mucous membranes, and feces of healthy animals and humans.
Almost any site of the body that is subject to injury can become
colonized and subsequently infected. In humans, communityacquired infections can occur as a result of exposure to
contaminated hot tubs, swimming pools, and contact lens
solutions. In the hospital environment, P. aeruginosa often
colonizes moist environments such as sinks, endotracheal tubes,
and ventilator equipment. It also colonizes damp, macerated
tissues such as the ear canals, damaged cornea, traumatized skin
(such as wounds and burns), and the interdigital space. Because
the organism can be resistant to a large number of diﬀerent
antimicrobial drugs, repeated treatment of secondary bacterial
infections in sites where impaired host defenses exist with a
variety of antimicrobials can select for MDR P. aeruginosa infection
at these sites. Examples of such conditions in dogs and cats
include recurrent aspiration pneumonia and/or bronchiectasis,
cystitis, prostatitis, chronic feline rhinosinusitis, and otitis
externa/media.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa possesses virtually every type of
bacterial virulence factor, including exotoxins, a type III secretion
system, LPS, pili, ﬂagella, several proteases, phospholipases, ironscavenging mechanisms such as pyoverdin production, and the
ability to form extensive bioﬁlms. Alginate protects the organism
from phagocytosis, and the pigment pyocyanin produces reactive
oxygen species, which in turn damage host cells. Multidrug
resistance results from the production of speciﬁc β-lactamase
enzymes (which can include ESBLs), antibiotic eﬄux pumps,
enzymes that modify aminoglycosides or alter antibiotic-binding
sites (such as DNA gyrase for ﬂuoroquinolones), and decreased
bacterial permeability.
Infections with broadly susceptible P. aeruginosa isolates could
be treated with an antipseudomonal β-lactam (e.g., piperacillin, a
carbapenem, cefepime, ceftazidime) alone or in combination with
an aminoglycoside or a ﬂuoroquinolone. As the MIC of most P.
aeruginosa isolates is often closer to the breakpoint for
ﬂuoroquinolones than it is for other gram-negative organisms, it is
wise to use the higher end of the dose range for ﬂuoroquinolones
with ﬂexible dosing options. 65 The combination of an
aminoglycoside and an antipseudomonal penicillin has

vetexamprep.ir

synergistic activity against some P. aeruginosa infections.
Currently, most MDR P. aeruginosa isolates from dogs and cats
remain susceptible to carbapenems (such as meropenem) and
aminoglycosides (especially amikacin), and so the usual treatment
of choice is: (1) a combination of these two drugs, (2) removal of
any foreign or necrotic material and, (3) if possible, resolution or
management of any other underlying cause for impaired host
defenses. Because parenterally administered aminoglycosides do
not eﬀectively penetrate airway mucus, nebulized tobramycin has
been used to treat resistant P. aeruginosa infections of the airways
in human patients, but these may not adequately penetrate
consolidated lung tissue and the use of inhaled aminoglycosides
is not recommended in the most recent guidelines for
antimicrobial use in respiratory infections due to lack of evidence.
66 Eﬀective treatment of MDR P. aeruginosa infections when they
occur in locations such as the feline nasal cavity may be extremely
diﬃcult, if not impossible, because of irreversible turbinate loss,
the requirement for injectable antimicrobial drugs, poor
penetration of aminoglycosides to the site of infection, and an
inadequate ability to eﬀectively treat all surfaces of the nasal
cavity with topical aminoglycosides.
Investigation of suspected nosocomial outbreaks of P. aeruginosa
infection generally requires typing of isolates from aﬀected
animals and the environment with molecular methods such as
pulsed-ﬁeld gel electrophoresis or multilocus sequence typing.
Use of antibiograms alone does not adequately discriminate
between strains.
Acinetobacter
Like P. aeruginosa, Acinetobacter is an important nosocomial
opportunistic pathogen. Acinetobacter is present in soil and water
and can be found in frozen foods, pasteurized milk, and an
enormous array of inert objects in the hospital environment,
where it may persist for months. It colonizes the skin and mucous
membranes of healthy humans as well as those of dogs and cats.
67 , 68 The main species that cause disease in animals are A.
baumannii and, to a lesser extent, Acinetobacter lwoﬃi and
Acinetobacter calcoaceticus. MDR isolates of A. baumannii have been
responsible for outbreaks of nosocomial infections in veterinary
hospitals 69 , 70 and, like MDR P. aeruginosa, may be resistant to a

vetexamprep.ir

wide variety of antimicrobial drug classes. Carbapenem-resistant
A. baumannii have been isolated from humans as well as animals.
70 , 71 Clinical manifestations of Acinetobacter infections in dogs
and cats include nosocomial UTIs (e.g., after invasive urinary
procedures such as catheterization), surgical wound infections,
pneumonia, catheter-related bacteremia, and, rarely, endocarditis.
Necrotizing fasciitis associated with A. baumannii infection was
described in a cat. 72 When Acinetobacter is grown from a
specimen, care should be taken to diﬀerentiate infection from
contamination. Most veterinary isolates are susceptible to
aminoglycosides and carbapenems; some are susceptible to
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ﬂuoroquinolones. 69

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Biochemistry, and Urinalysis
Findings
Dogs and cats with superﬁcial gram-negative infections of sites
that drain to the exterior, such as wounds, the external ear canal,
the nasal cavity, and the lower urinary tract, often have no
clinically signiﬁcant laboratory abnormalities. Deep tissue or
systemic infections with gram-negative bacteria may be associated
with marked neutrophilia and a left shift, toxic neutrophils, or a
degenerative
left
shift,
sometimes
with
circulating
metamyelocytes. Thrombocytopenia may be present in dogs and
cats that develop disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Anemia of inﬂammatory disease, lymphopenia, and monocytosis
may be present. The urinalysis of dogs and cats with gramnegative bacterial UTIs may reveal pyuria, proteinuria, hematuria,
and sometimes bacterial rods on sediment examination.

Clotting Function
Systemic gram-negative bacterial infections may be associated
with evidence of DIC due to activation of the coagulation cascade
by endotoxin. Elevations in PT, APTT, D-dimers, and reduced or
falling platelet counts are common in DIC. Viscoelastic
coagulometry (thromboelastography or thromboelastometry) in
animals with sepsis often reveals a hypercoagulable state most
noticeable in the maximum amplitude or maximum clot
formation value, although in dogs with septic peritonitis (which

vetexamprep.ir

commonly involves gram-negative infections), it was found that
nonsurvivors were less likely to be hypercoagulable. 73

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
The presence of rod-shaped bacteria on cytologic examination of
Wright-Giemsa or Diﬀ-Quik-stained smears of aﬀected tissue
aspirates, lavage ﬂuid or purulent exudate suggests presence of a
gram-negative organism in most cases of infection in the dog and
cat, with Gram stain being conﬁrmatory (Fig. 53.7). Large
numbers of degenerate and/or nondegenerate neutrophils and
lilac debris that suggests necrosis may be observed.
Isolation and Identification
Gram-negative bacteria are readily isolated from aspirates, tissue
biopsies, body ﬂuids, blood, and lavage specimens. MacConkey
and blood agar are usually used to isolate gram-negative bacteria,
which usually grow within 24 to 48 hours. Pasteurella spp. are
more fastidious, and species that infect dogs and cats do not grow
on MacConkey agar. Isolated organisms are traditionally then
identiﬁed based on colony morphology and biochemical
reactions. MALDI-TOF permits identiﬁcation of rapid
identiﬁcation of organisms at the ﬁrst sign of growth to the
species level, and has the potential to rapidly identify genetic
elements conferring resistance and thus informing antibiotic
selection 24 to 48 hours before susceptibility results are available.
Evaluation of antimicrobial susceptibility is important for all
Enterobacterales, P. aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter spp., given their
propensity to develop resistance to many antimicrobial drug
classes.

Treatment and Prognosis
The approach to treatment of gram-negative infections depends
on patient history, the site of infection, and the severity of disease
(Table 53.1). Identiﬁcation and management of the underlying
cause are also important to minimize selection for resistant
organisms. Any foreign material (such as catheters or implants)
must be removed, and necrotic tissue debrided. Bioﬁlmproducing bacteria are more likely to be associated with deep
tissue and bone infections, and higher doses and longer duration
of therapy should be considered if bioﬁlm is suspected. 74 When
systemic antimicrobial drug treatment is required, it should
preferably be based on the results of susceptibility testing. In cases
of life-threatening infection, it is impractical to wait until such
results return to commence therapy. Previous antibiotic therapy
may select for resistant organisms and, given the ability of gramnegative organisms to rapidly acquire both multidrug resistance
and virulence, a thorough consideration of the expectation of
resistance is warranted prior to antibiotic selection. First, a

vetexamprep.ir

thorough history which includes all antibiotics the patient has
received in the last 6 months should be obtained, and inquiry into
antibiotic use in co-habitating animals and humans is also
reasonable. Avoidance of drugs of the same class as used
previously is reasonable, especially in life-threatening infections.
Second, consideration of whether the infection could be hospital
acquired is indicated. A hospital-acquired infection should be
considered if the patient shows signs of infection after admission
to the hospital or within 2 to 3 days after discharge form the
hospital. Additionally, if the region of infection was associated
with a procedure or invasive device (i.e., signs of UTI after urinary
catheterization), hospital-acquired organisms should be
suspected. In such cases, treatment should also be based on
knowledge of local resistance pa erns among gram-negative
bacteria, which may vary from region to region and practice to
practice.
Pasteurella spp. are generally susceptible to penicillin or
aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin. Because gram-negative
bacteria have higher MICs to penicillins than do gram-positive
bacteria, the high end of the dose range and more frequent
administration may be necessary. In cases of severe infections, for
time-dependent drugs of short half-life, a continuous infusion
may be indicated at least for the ﬁrst 2 to 3 days to allow drug
concentrations to remain above the target MIC for 100% of the
dosing interval. Some Enterobacterales are intrinsically resistant
to ampicillin and ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins, and initial
treatment of serious infections while awaiting the results of
susceptibility testing should include an aminoglycoside, a thirdgeneration cephalosporin, or a ﬂuoroquinolone. Trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, or clavulanic acid–amoxicillin are
reasonable initial choices for treatment of UTIs associated with
bacterial rods. 75

Prevention
Prevention of gram-negative infections involves resolution of
impairment in host defenses and strict hospital infection control
practices (see Chapter 15).

Public Health Aspects

vetexamprep.ir

Strains of E. coli and other MDR gram-negative bacteria harbored
by dogs resemble pathogenic strains isolated from humans. 44 , 71
As a result, concern has been raised that companion animals may
be a source of organisms for human infection, especially those that
reside with humans with compromised host defenses. It has been
suggested through genomic sequencing of phylogenetic group B2
infections in humans and companion animals that cats and dogs
may be a spillover host for MDR E. coli (meaning pets are exposed
to these strains by their owners but then the organism persists in
the companion animal). 76 , 77
Pasteurella multocida is the most commonly isolated organism
from human dog and cat bite wounds. 4 Pasteurella spp. can also
colonize the respiratory tracts of humans with underlying
respiratory disease such as bronchiectasis or chronic sinusitis, and
they occasionally have been reported in association with
peritonitis, bacteremia, and endocarditis. Most of these humans
have had contact with domestic animals in the household, and
isolates from aﬀected humans have been shown by molecular
methods to be identical to those colonizing animals in the
household. 78
Thus, immunocompromised owners or those with impaired
anatomic barriers should be instructed to wash their hands after
handling their pet and perform regular household cleaning and
disinfection. Companion animals should not be allowed to lick
open wounds, the region that surrounds healing surgical
incisions, or the owner’s face.

Case Example
Signalment

“Lo ie,” a middle-aged, female spayed domestic shorthair from
northern California.

History

Lo ie was evaluated for chronic nasal discharge. Since her
rescue as a stray 2.5 years earlier, intermi ent sneezing and
bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge had been noted, and the
discharge sometimes contained blood. Ten months before the
evaluation, Lo ie had been anesthetized for a nasal ﬂush at a

vetexamprep.ir

local veterinary clinic, but developed respiratory distress on
recovery and was hospitalized with oxygen supplementation
for 24 hours. She was ataxic, leaned to one side, and did not eat
well for days, but over the subsequent months the ataxia and
leaning gradually resolved. For the 2 weeks before the
evaluation, Lo ie had stertorous respiration and intermi ent
episodes of open-mouth breathing. For the past 9 months,
Lo ie had been treated with marboﬂoxacin and prednisolone.
Before that, treatments for the nasal discharge included
clavulanic acid–amoxicillin, doxycycline, or azithromycin, as
well as L-lysine supplementation. Lo ie lived with six other
cats, all of which had access to the outdoors, and she was fed
commercial canned and dry cat food. The FeLV and FIV status
of these cats was unknown.
Current medications: marboﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg PO q24h)
and prednisolone (1 mg/kg PO q24h).

Physical Examination
Body weight: 4 kg.
General: Bright, alert and responsive, hydrated. T =
100.3°F (37.9°C), HR = 220 beats/minute, purring, BCS 7/9.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mucopurulent nasal
discharge was present that was most profuse on the left
side. Nasal airﬂow was absent on the left side. Mild
dental calculus was present, but there were no oral
masses or ulceration.
Respiratory: An inspiratory stertor was present, and
referred upper airway noises were detected on
auscultation of the thorax.
Cardiovascular, GI and genitourinary, and lymph nodes:
No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected. It
was diﬃcult to palpate abdominal structures due to the
presence of abdominal fat.
Neurologic examination: There was a mild, intermi ent, leftsided head tilt. No other abnormalities were detected on full
neurologic examination.

cells/µL), WBCs 21,210 cells/µL (4,500–14,000 cells/µL),

Imaging Findings
Thoracic radiographs:

Cardiovascular structures were within normal limits. There was
a small amount of air in the cervical esophagus (likely due to
aerophagia) and a mild diﬀuse bronchointerstitial pa ern that
was a ributed to an obese body condition.

Contiguous transverse 0.6-mm collimated images of the skull
were available for review without contrast administration.
There was moderate turbinate destruction of both right and left

Rhinoscopy:

Severe turbinate destruction with diﬀuse hyperemia and large

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic bacterial culture and Mycoplasma culture (nasal brush
specimen): a direct smear showed moderate numbers of
neutrophils, but no organisms were seen. Moderate numbers of
P. aeruginosa were isolated. The P. aeruginosa was resistant to
amoxicillin–clavulanic acid, ampicillin, cefazolin, cefovecin,
cefoxitin, cefpodoxime, ceftiofur, chloramphenicol, doxycycline,

vetexamprep.ir

enroﬂoxacin, marboﬂoxacin, ticarcillin, ticarcillin–clavulanic
acid, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. It was susceptible
only to amikacin (≤4 µg/mL), gentamicin (2 µg/mL), and
imipenem (≤1 µg/mL).

Histopathology of Nasal Biopsy Specimens

The submucosa was markedly expanded and multifocally
eﬀaced by sheets of lymphocytes and plasma cells, with
neutrophils and fewer numbers of mast cells surrounding
irregular spicules of woven bone extending from primary
turbinates. Less aﬀected sections contained similar,
predominately lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates that separated
submucosal glands and elevated the superﬁcial epithelium.
Pathologic diagnosis: severe, chronic, and extensive
lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic rhinitis with turbinate
remodeling.

Diagnosis

Feline chronic rhinosinusitis with suspected opportunistic MDR
P. aeruginosa infection.

Treatment and Outcome

The nasal cavity was lavaged. The prednisolone was tapered
over 1 week, then discontinued, and 7 days later, treatment
with piroxicam was commenced (0.3 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 7
days, then q48h thereafter). Other medications discussed with
the owner were N-acetylcysteine and intranasal gentamicin
drops, but the prognosis given for disease resolution was poor.

Comments

The underlying cause of feline chronic rhinosinusitis is poorly
deﬁned, but infection of ki ens with respiratory viruses such as
FHV-1 is suspected to play a role. Severe turbinate destruction
predisposes to secondary opportunistic infections with a variety
of bacteria, which include staphylococci, Bordetella
bronchiseptica, S. canis, Mycoplasma spp., E. coli, P. multocida, and
P. aeruginosa. In this cat, selection for MDR P. aeruginosa likely
resulted from repeated and chronic use of a variety of
antimicrobial drugs. The reticulocytosis and increased serum
BUN concentration likely was secondary to chronic epistaxis
and swallowed blood. The cat’s neurologic signs and head tilt
were thought to be due to peripheral vestibular disease,

vetexamprep.ir

possibly due to otitis media, but there was no evidence of
middle ear disease on the CT scan.

54: Anaerobic Bacterial
Infections
Dubraska Diaz-Campos, Jenessa A. Winston, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: 1860s (Louis Pasteur). 1
• Causes: Bacteroides, Prevotella, Porphyromonas,
Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Clostridium,
Actinomyces, Propionibacterium, other species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: Abscess formation in a variety of tissues,
pyothorax, peritonitis, pyometra, periodontal disease,
osteomyelitis, bacteremia.
• Differential Diagnoses: Bacterial infections caused by grampositive and gram-negative aerobes.
• Human Health Significance: Anaerobes of the oral cavity of
dogs and cats are an important component of animal bite
wound infections in humans.

Etiologic Agents and Epidemiology
Anaerobic infections are of great importance in human and
veterinary medicine. Although anaerobic bacteria were discovered
in the middle of the nineteenth century, the identiﬁcation and
isolation of these microorganisms were, and still are, a challenge.
Obligate anaerobes are deﬁned as microorganisms that require a
reduced oxygen tension for growth and fail to form colonies on
the surface of solid media in 10% CO2, in air (18% oxygen). 2 They
cannot grow in the presence of molecular oxygen because

vetexamprep.ir

anaerobes do not make superoxide dismutase, and most do not
produce catalase. These enzymes are necessary for the breakdown
of reactive oxygen intermediates (e.g., superoxide anion,
hydrogen peroxide) that are normally generated when bacteria
grow in the presence of oxygen. 3 Species of obligate anaerobic
bacteria and their morphology on Gram-stained smears are
described in Table 54.1.
Normal host microbiota is responsible for a signiﬁcant portion
of innate immunity; however, some of these microorganisms also
have the potential to become important opportunistic pathogens. 4
, 5 Anaerobes exist in the environment and make up a signiﬁcant
portion of the normal microbiota of dogs and cats. 6–9 The
predominant microorganisms that colonize most mucosal surfaces
are anaerobes, and metabolic by-products produced by this group
are important in the regulation of the numbers of aerobic species
(facultative and obligate) that also make up the normal
microbiota. Thus, anaerobic bacteria play an important role in
protection of mucosal surfaces from interactions involving other
microorganisms with pathogenic potential. 7 For example,
approximately 1 million salmonellae are needed to produce
disease in animals with intact anaerobic gut microbiota, whereas
fewer than 10 salmonellae are needed to produce disease in
animals with few anaerobes. The importance of this observation is
seen clinically; dogs are more susceptible to salmonellosis when
they are medicated with antimicrobials, especially those eﬀective
in reducing the anaerobic component of the normal gut
microbiota (e.g., ampicillin). 10
Compromise of a mucosal surface or an adjacent area by
perforation or other trauma may provide a portal of entry for the
normal anaerobic microbiota into a normally sterile site. At this
point, anaerobes and other members of the normal microbiota
become opportunistic pathogens. These are important
considerations because, to eﬀectively prevent anaerobic infection,
antibacterial therapy is commonly started before results of
microbiologic analysis of collected clinical specimens are received.
Knowledge of the normal microbiota at a speciﬁc site helps in
making an educated guess about the microorganisms likely to be
causing the infection. If anaerobic bacteria are involved in an
infectious process, on average, two diﬀerent species are almost

vetexamprep.ir

always present with aerobic bacteria. The most commonly
associated aerobic bacteria are enterics (mainly Escherichia coli),
and members of the genus Pasteurella, Staphylococcus spp. and
Enterococcus spp. 11
If anaerobic bacteria possess appropriate virulence factors, they
may also cause mucosal disease. In addition to periodontal
disease, anaerobes are associated with disease in other regions of
the GI tract; the most important of these anaerobes within the
intestine are Clostridioides diﬃcile (previously Clostridium diﬃcile)
and Clostridium perfringens (see Chapter 64). 12 , 13 Both of these
species may be a part of the normal gut microbiota of dogs and
cats, although evidence suggests that both may be passed to
previously uncolonized animals. 14–16
In human patients, infectious processes involving structures
above the diaphragm are more likely to contain anaerobes
originating in the mouth, whereas disease below the diaphragm
usually involves anaerobes from the intestinal tract. 17 In dogs and
cats, anaerobic bacteria are indigenous in diﬀerent body sites.
Actinomyces spp., Porphyromonas spp., and Fusobacterium spp. are
the most prevalent genera of anaerobic bacteria in the oral
microbiota of dogs. 6 , 9 In humans and in animals, bite wounds
are frequently associated with polymicrobial infections with a
component of anaerobic bacteria. 6 , 18
The GI tract is loaded with a myriad of microorganisms,
including anaerobic bacteria. Members of the order Clostridiales
such as C. perfringens and C. diﬃcile are also considered normal
gut microbiota in dogs and cats. Bacteroides spp. and Fusobacterium
spp. among other anaerobes are also found in the GI tract. 6 , 15 , 16

, 19–21

Disease produced by C. diﬃcile is the result of its proliferation in
the enteric tract of the host after a trigger event (e.g., certain
antimicrobial and chemotherapeutic agents). Epidemiologic
evidence from human hospitals suggests that the agent can be
spread from patient to patient, which results in outbreaks of C.
diﬃcile–associated disease. 22 Such observations imply that the
organism either is, or has the potential to be, contagious.
Determining whether C. diﬃcile is truly a contagious pathogen is
diﬃcult because it is so prevalent in the enteric tract of clinically
healthy animals. 12 , 15 , 16 There is evidence that the canine claw

vetexamprep.ir

bed and nasal cavity can be colonized by toxigenic C. diﬃcile; thus,
they could disseminate this microorganism or its spores between
households and environment and potentially contribute to
community-relevant sources for C. diﬃcile infection in humans. 15 ,

23–25

TABLE 54.1

Although C. perfringens is commonly associated with GI
infections, it has also been implicated in other clinical conditions
in dogs and cats. 26 , 27 It is unclear whether toxigenic C.
perfringens is contagious. It likely causes disease when it
proliferates in the intestinal tract and produces enterotoxin. Novel
pore-forming toxin genes (netE and netF) were identiﬁed in a C.
perfringens type A strain associated with acute hemorrhagic
diarrhea in dogs and foals. 28–30 Factors that stimulate
proliferation of C. perfringens are unknown. It must also be
determined whether the source of the agent is endogenous,
acquired from another infected animal, or acquired from the
environment. The report of outbreaks of C. perfringens–associated
diarrhea in small animal hospital se ings suggests that it may be
contagious, although it is important to remember that some C.

vetexamprep.ir

perfringens are present in the enteric tract of clinically healthy
dogs. 13 , 31 , 32 Detectable levels of C. perfringens enterotoxin are
not often found in the feces of clinically healthy animals. 33
Bacteroides spp. represent an important component of the
microbiome in dogs and cats. 34 In particular, Bacteroides fragilis
frequently cause anaerobic infections in dogs and cats, often
associated with the GI tract and abdominal ﬂuid, body organs
(lung, liver, kidney), abscesses, and subcutaneous tissues. 26 , 27 , 34
The genus Fusobacterium is also an important component of the
oral mucosal and GI normal microbiota. 34 , 35 Fusobacterium
canifelium is common in the oral cavity of dogs and cats and has
been isolated from dog and cat bite wounds in humans. 36
Unfortunately, this organism is typically resistant to quinolones,
unlike human isolates. Data compiled from 4,333 anaerobic
cultures submi ed to 10 institutions showed that Clostridium,
Bacteroides, and Peptostreptococcus spp. were the three most
frequently isolated species of obligate anaerobes from dogs and
cats (Table 54.2).

Pathogenesis
Most commonly, obligate anaerobic bacteria cannot live in healthy
tissue. On certain mucosal surfaces (e.g., intestinal tract, gingival
crevices, genital tract), they live with other microorganisms
(facultative anaerobes) that scavenge molecular oxygen, which
generates a local environment with very low redox potential (E h ,
a measure of oxygen tension). Likewise, in compromised tissue,
inﬂammatory cells and co-inoculated aerobic microorganisms
lower E h suﬃciently for anaerobes to grow. Factors that
predispose to anaerobic infections are shown in Box 54.1.
Components of anaerobic bacteria elicit potent inﬂammatory
responses. Gram-negative anaerobes possess LPS with endotoxic
activity. The peptidoglycan of gram-positive anaerobes incites the
same inﬂammatory response as gram-positive aerobic
microorganisms. Some anaerobic bacteria have capsular antigens
(e.g., B. fragilis, pigmented Prevotella spp., and Porphyromonas
spp.), which incite inﬂammatory responses that result in abscess
formation; capsules without viable bacteria can also induce
abscess formation. 17 , 19 , 37 Some evidence suggests that co-

vetexamprep.ir

inoculated aerobic microorganisms induce anaerobe capsule
formation. Capsules also play a more traditional role by inhibiting
phagocytosis. 38

Aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms have a synergistic
relationship. 38 , 39 Anaerobes act with facultative aerobes such as
E. coli to induce abscess formation more rapidly than either
bacterial group alone. Actinomyces, a facultative anaerobe, is
commonly found in association with foreign body migrations,
pyothorax, or peritonitis. 40 , 41 Facultative bacteria lower the
oxidation-reduction potential of the tissue environment,
facilitating anaerobic bacterial proliferation. Necrotic and
abscessed tissue protect facultative organisms and anaerobic

vetexamprep.ir

bacteria from antimicrobials, as well as body defenses such as
phagocytosis. Aerobic organisms also scavenge oxygen and
curtail phagocytosis of anaerobes (and vice versa). 42 Enzymes
such as β-lactamase produced by one member of the aerobicanaerobic partnership protect susceptible microorganisms in the
vicinity from being inactivated by β-lactam antibacterials. These
synergistic interactions are important to keep in mind when
designing therapeutic regimens, because antibacterial therapy
should be directed at both populations for optimal resolution of
the infection.
Some anaerobes produce toxins. Fusobacterium necrophorum
produces a toxin that forms pores in leukocyte membranes. 43
Clostridioides diﬃcile produces toxins (A and B) that disrupt the
cytoskeletal elements of the intestinal epithelial cell, resulting in
cell death. 15 , 22 , 31 Clostridium perfringens produces an
enterotoxin that interacts with the target cell membrane, resulting
in the formation of pores that are made partly by the enterotoxin
and partly by the target cell. Electrolytes are lost through these
pores, resulting in reversal of ion and water ﬂow (diarrhea) and,
ﬁnally, death of the cell. 32 , 33 A pore-forming toxin within the
leukocidin/hemolysin superfamily family, NetF, has been
associated with canine hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and foal
necrotizing enteritis (see Chapters 64 and 125). 28 Other studies
have also suggested that C. perfringens strains that possess netE
and netF genes may play a role in dogs with acute hemorrhagic
disease syndrome. 29 , 30
Some species of anaerobes produce adhesins (pili or ﬁmbriae),
which have been associated with virulence. 44 However, adhesins
probably do not play a major role in pathogenesis other than by
way of their association with speciﬁc locations on mucosal
surfaces. For example, blood or abscess isolates of B. fragilis are
rarely piliated, whereas those found on mucosal surfaces almost
always have pili. 38

Clinical Features
Anaerobic bacteria stimulate pyonecrotic inﬂammation in a
variety of organs. This process stems primarily from the
inﬂammatory response triggered by anaerobic capsule material,
cell wall constituents of microorganisms, and thwarted a empts

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
at phagocytosis (which leads to deposition of lysosomal contents
into surrounding tissue). The prevalence of anaerobic bacterial
infections varies depending on the anatomic site of infection. Most
anaerobic bacteria cultured from dogs and cats are associated
with GI tract disorders, followed by pleural or abdominal ﬂuids,
abscesses, or respiratory tract infections (Table 54.3). 45
Clinical ﬁndings in anaerobic infections also depend on the
aﬀected body site (Table 54.4). Exudates from infectious processes
that contain anaerobes often are malodorous and may be darkly
discolored. Fever, leukocytosis, hypoglycemia, increased serum
ALP activity, and hypoalbuminemia reﬂect the systemic
manifestations of an acute-phase reaction to the anaerobic
infection. Hypoalbuminemia may be compounded by loss of
serum proteins into eﬀusions or from draining wounds. 41
Anaerobes of the oral cavity are important contributors to
periodontal disease; tooth root abscessation and mandibular
osteomyelitis; retrobulbar abscesses; and bite wound infections.
Along with other bacteria, anaerobes may be isolated from the
lungs and pleural cavity of dogs or cats with aspiration
pneumonia and pyothorax, respectively. Intestinal anaerobes may
be isolated from the abdominal cavity of animals with septic
peritonitis that has resulted from intestinal or cecal rupture. The
female genital tract is also heavily colonized with anaerobic
bacteria, and pyometra may sometimes be associated with mixed
aerobic and anaerobic infections that include the anaerobic species
Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, and Peptostreptococcus.

Plant awn migration in dogs and cats may lead to abscess
formation in a variety of tissues, including retroperitoneal tissues
and the brain. These abscesses usually contain a mixed population
of aerobes and anaerobes, especially Fusobacterium, Actinomyces,
and Bacteroides spp. Brain abscessation can follow direct extension
of anaerobic bacterial infection from otitis, or tooth root infection.
Alternatively, spread may occur via the hematogenous route (Fig.
54.1).

Periodontal Disease
Periodontal disease is one of the most common disorders seen in
veterinary medicine and may result in chronic pain, decreased
appetite, and loss of teeth. Periodontal disease begins with
formation of dental plaque, a bacterial bioﬁlm comprised
primarily of gram-positive facultative aerobes, which occurs as a
result of poor oral hygiene and other host factors. Subsequently
there is proliferation of pathogenic bacteria, which include gramnegative rods and especially anaerobes, which secrete toxins and
incite an inﬂammatory response. Anaerobes implicated in canine
and feline periodontal disease (such as Porphyromonas gulae)
appear to diﬀer than those isolated from human periodontal
disease (Porphyromonas gingivalis). 46–49 Periodontal disease is
manifested as gingival erythema, edema, gingival bleeding, and
halitosis, with accumulation of calculus, gingival recession,
alveolar bone loss, and sometimes the presence of purulent
exudate (Fig. 54.2).

Retrobulbar Abscesses
Retrobulbar or orbital abscesses may result from tooth root
abscessation, penetrating foreign bodies such as grass awns, or
penetrating trauma to the orbit. They are characterized by

vetexamprep.ir

unilateral exophthalmos, protrusion of the third eyelid,
conjunctival hyperemia, serous to mucopurulent ocular discharge,
inappetence, fever, and pain on opening the mouth (Fig. 54.3). A
ﬂuctuant swelling or draining tract posterior to the last ipsilateral
molar may be present on examination of the oral cavity. In one
study, Bacteroides spp. and Clostridium spp. were the most
frequent anaerobes isolated from 34 dogs with retrobulbar
abscesses; other frequently isolated bacteria were Staphylococcus,
E. coli, and Pasteurella spp. In cats, the most frequent anaerobe was
Bacteroides vulgatus, and the most common non-anaerobe was
Pasteurella spp. 50

Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
Cat bite abscesses may be one of the most common reasons that
cats are brought to veterinary clinics. Clinical signs include fever,
lethargy, inappetence, pain, and ﬁrm or ﬂuctuant subcutaneous
swellings, which may rupture and drain purulent material. In
addition to Pasteurella multocida, oral anaerobes are frequently
isolated from these abscesses. 51 Anaerobic species involved
include Peptostreptococcus anaerobius, Porphyromonas spp.,
Clostridium spp. (e.g., Clostridium villosum), Fusobacterium spp.,
Bacteroides spp. (especially Bacteroides tectum), and Prevotella spp.

52

Other skin and soft tissue infections associated with a variety of
anaerobes include foreign body penetrating wounds and dog bite
wounds (see Chapter 75). Necrotizing fasciitis has generally been
associated with toxigenic microaerophilic gram-positive bacterial
infections in dogs and cats (Chapter 50), although gram-negative
organisms may also be involved. Necrosis and spread of infection
can be associated with co-infecting anaerobic bacteria that
contaminate the site of infection. In some cases, anaerobic bacteria
are isolated as the predominant organisms. 53

vetexamprep.ir

TABLE 54.4

Pneumonia and Pyothorax
Anaerobic bacteria such as Fusobacterium spp., Peptostreptococcus
anaerobium, Prevotella spp., and Porphyromonas spp. can be isolated
from dogs and cats with aspiration pneumonia, foreign body
pneumonia (especially that due to plant awn migration), and
pyothorax. 54 Dogs with plant awn migration develop multifocal
necrotizing pneumonia with abscess formation. Anaerobic
bacterial pneumonia can also result from aspiration of anaerobes
within the oral cavity. This usually occurs in animals with
underlying esophageal or laryngeal defects, neurologic disorders,
altered consciousness, or dysphagia. In some cases, aspiration
pneumonia may be followed by lung abscess formation (Fig. 54.4).
In human patients, a period of 6 to 7 days after aspiration is

vetexamprep.ir

required for necrosis and abscess formation to occur, and so
aspiration pneumonia with lung abscess formation is generally a
chronic disease process.
Clinical signs of pulmonary infections include fever, lethargy,
inappetence, cough, and tachypnea. The reader is referred to
Chapter 124 for more detailed descriptions of bacterial pneumonia
and pyothorax.

Peritonitis
Septic peritonitis that involves anaerobes may result from rupture
of the intestinal tract, especially the cecum or colon. Anaerobes
such as Bacteroides spp. and Clostridium spp. may be more likely to
be isolated from these infections. Other anaerobes that may be
present in dogs and cats with septic peritonitis include
Fusobacterium spp. and Propionibacterium spp. 55 Disease that
results from bowel perforation often contains a population of
organisms that reﬂect the bowel microbiota at the site of
perforation, which may include anaerobes, aerobic gram-positive
bacteria (such as Enterococcus spp.), Candida spp., and gramnegative aerobes such as E. coli. Rupture of the female genital tract
secondary to pyometra may also be associated with peritonitis
that involves anaerobes.

Bacteremia
Anaerobic bacteremia in dogs and cats can be associated with
seemingly localized anaerobic infections, such as peritonitis or
pyothorax, although it is not often recognized. 56 , 57 When
anaerobes are occasionally isolated from dogs and cats with
bloodstream infections, they are usually polymicrobial infections
together with aerobic bacteria. In a European study of 66
bacteremic cats, 12% of bacterial isolates from the bloodstream
were obligate anaerobes. 56 In a study of 140 dogs with
bacteremia, anaerobes comprised 9% of the isolates. 57 Of 39 dogs
and 10 cats with critical illness and bacteremia from Colorado,
anaerobes were isolated from 31% of the dogs and 40% (4 of 10) of
the cats. The most common anaerobic bacterial species isolated
from the dogs was C. perfringens (nine dogs), followed by
Bacteroides species (two dogs). 58 The cats were infected with

vetexamprep.ir

Bacteroides or Fusobacterium species. The possibility of bacteremia
due to a mixed population of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria
should be considered in dogs with systemic grass awn migration.
Anaerobic bacteria appear to be a very rare cause of endocarditis
in dogs (see Chapter 122). 59

Diagnosis
Abnormalities that suggest an anaerobic bacterial infection
include a putrid odor, discolored purulent discharge, gas
production within tissues (especially with C. perfringens
infections) (Fig. 54.5), a bite or puncture wound, penetrating
foreign bodies, abscessation, pyothorax, aspiration pneumonia,
damage to mucosal surfaces with which anaerobes are usually
associated, and/or necrotic or gangrenous tissue (Box 54.2).
However, absence of these features does not rule out infection
with anaerobes, and some of these abnormalities can occur in
association with isolated aerobic bacterial infections. For example,
although anaerobes such as Clostridium spp. may be involved in
emphysematous cystitis in humans and dogs, the most common
cause of emphysematous cystitis are gram-negative aerobes,
especially E. coli.

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
In addition to clinical features, cytologic analysis of specimens can
help to determine whether an anaerobic infection is present.
Abundant degenerative neutrophils are usually found with
multiple and often morphologically diverse forms of intracellular
and extracellular bacteria. Large and ﬁlamentous morphology is
often typical of anaerobes (Fig. 54.6). 60 , 61 Some gram-negative
anaerobic rods are pale-staining and they are often thin, can be
sometimes misshapen, and occasionally have pointed ends.
Extracellular bacteria may result from bacterial contamination
of a specimen or contamination of the staining solution.
Microscopic evaluation for morphologic shape and Gram staining
should be performed when the specimen is collected so that the
results can be compared with culture results or the type of
organism can be predicted by its shape and staining properties
(see Table 54.1). The prediction of an anaerobic infection based on
cytologic (Gram stain) ﬁndings may guide the empiric use of
therapeutic agents targeted for this class of microorganisms. 26 , 61

Culture
Anaerobes are diﬃcult to isolate in clinical practice unless
precautions are taken. Errors in specimen collection, handling,
and submission are the primary reasons anaerobes are not
routinely isolated. Therefore, a ention to collection practices,
minimizing transport time, optimizing transport temperature, and
use of appropriate transport media are fundamental if anaerobic
culture is performed (see Chapter 3) (Table 54.5). 19 , 60 , 62 , 63
Anaerobes are sensitive to oxygen and because they grow slowly,
they are also easily overgrown in specimens that contain aerobes;
greater than 70% of cultures are mixed. In addition, multiple
anaerobes are often found in the same specimen (Table 54.6).
Because swabs tend to dry out and become oxygenated, their use
is discouraged. If swabs are used, the tip should be moistened
with a pre-reduced medium such as brain-heart infusion broth
and maintained in anaerobic conditions. Refrigeration has been
shown to be detrimental to the isolation of anaerobic bacteria;
thus, specimens should not be held at temperatures lower than
4°C (see Table 54.5). In comparison, aerobes multiply at 25°C and
in some cases overgrow the anaerobic component. At 15°C,
aerobes do not multiply to any signiﬁcant extent, and anaerobes
remain viable. Acceptable time periods between specimen

vetexamprep.ir

collection and culture depend on specimen type, volume, and
whether transport medium is used. Anaerobic microorganisms in
large pieces of tissue or quantities of ﬂuid (greater than 2 mL) are
relatively protected from toxic interaction with oxygen and can
survive for up to 24 hours before culture, whereas anaerobes in
smaller specimens or swabs usually cannot. Anaerobic transport
media greatly increase the survival of anaerobes and discourage
the growth of aerobes. Anaerobic media are available for transport
of aspirated material, tissue or biopsy material, and material
collected on swabs. 62 , 64 Culture of anaerobic bacteria is
laborious, expensive, and time consuming. At the laboratory,
media must be inoculated with specimens as soon as they are
received. Use of pre-reduced, anaerobically sterilized media
improves the success of isolation. After inoculation, media is
placed in an anaerobic chamber with an atmosphere of 5% carbon
dioxide, 5% hydrogen, and 90% nitrogen, or in an oxygen-free
carbon dioxide until it can be put in the chamber. During culture
follow-up, culture plates must always be handled in an anaerobic
hood or a chamber that has been ﬂushed with anaerobic gas mix.
Commonly, the isolation and identiﬁcation of an anaerobe in a
sample containing only one species takes 2–4 days. 60 , 62 , 63

Anaerobic culture is costly and most infectious processes
contain an average of two diﬀerent species of anaerobes and at
least one aerobe. This signiﬁcantly increases the eﬀort and cost
associated with anaerobe isolation. Use of phenotypical and
biochemical methods for identiﬁcation is laborious and requires
well-trained personnel. The adoption of MALDI-TOF MS has
allowed laboratories to more accurately and rapidly identify new
anaerobes (see Chapter 3). 65–67 However, the acquisition of this
technology is cost prohibitive for small laboratories.

vetexamprep.ir

Mucosal disease produced by anaerobes is somewhat more
diﬃcult to diagnose. Isolation from sites where obligate anaerobes
are part of the resident microbiota, such as the oral or pharyngeal
cavity, vagina, external auditory meatus, conjunctiva, or skin, can
be diﬃcult to associate with pathogenicity. Diagnosis of GI
disease caused by C. diﬃcile and C. perfringens requires the use of
specialized agar for isolation, immunologic tests to determine the
presence of microorganism or toxin in feces or in broth culture, or
molecular assays that detect toxin genes in feces or the isolates
themselves. 60 , 68
Few veterinary laboratories perform susceptibility testing for
anaerobes because it is diﬃcult and expensive. Guidelines for
testing have been established by the CLSI. 69 The agar dilution
assay has been considered the only validated and recommended
method for all anaerobic organisms; however, this method can be
labor intensive and the assay results have not always been
repeatable or consistent for all anaerobic species. 63 , 69 , 70 The
CLSI recommends broth microdilution method only for testing
Bacteroides spp. and Parabacteroides spp. 69 Some laboratories use
commercial gradient strips (E-testing) because these are more
convenient for routine testing (see Chapter 3). 26 However, a lack
of agreement when using this method has also been described. 63 ,

71

A disc test can be performed to determine whether an isolate
produces β-lactamase (Nitroceﬁn Disc, B.D. Sparks, MD, USA).
For this test, a portion of an isolated colony is smeared onto a disc
that contains a substrate that changes color when a β-lactamase is
present. The most common anaerobic β-lactamases are encoded
by the cepA gene, and more than 97% of B. fragilis carry this gene.
72 , 73 These strains are resistant to penicillin, ampicillin,
amoxicillin, and most of the cephalosporins, except cefoxitin.
Clavulanate irreversibly binds to these enzymes. Cefoxitin
resistance is most commonly due to a β-lactamase encoded by the
cfxA gene. Cefoxitin resistance rates in B. fragilis group organisms
range from 3.7% to 19% by species in the United States and 9.6%
to 75% internationally. 72 The presence of cepA and cfxA have been
reported in Bacteroides spp. isolated from domestic animals. 27
Table 54.7 summarizes the prevalence of β-lactamase production

found among various anaerobes isolated from dogs and cats in
one study.
Because of the cost and diﬃculties of culture and low sensitivity
especially when specimens cannot reach the laboratory within
hours, presumptive diagnoses of anaerobic infections are often
made based on history, anatomic site, characteristics of the
exudate (e.g., odor and sometimes color), and results of cytologic
examination (see Box 54.2, Table 54.1, and Fig. 54.6). Antimicrobial
treatment of a suspected anaerobic component is usually empiric.

Treatment and Prognosis
Successful treatment of anaerobic infections may require medical
and, on many occasions, surgical interventions combined with
appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Antimicrobial therapy without
surgical drainage is usually unsuccessful. Abscesses or pus-ﬁlled
cavities have poor blood supply, and drainage allows for entrance
of newly exuded ﬂuids containing the antimicrobial agent.
Furthermore, few antibacterial drugs work eﬀectively in the
presence of accumulated pus. Because anaerobic infections are
often polymicrobial, antimicrobial therapy of infectious processes

vetexamprep.ir

with an anaerobic component should focus on the anaerobic and
the presumed aerobic components. In dogs and cats, the most
commonly isolated aerobes are enterics (E. coli), Pasteurella, and
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius. 5 , 26
Anaerobic bacteria are inherently resistant to certain
antibacterials (e.g., the aminoglycosides and the secondgeneration quinolones), although extended-spectrum (third- and
fourth-generation) quinolones, such as pradoﬂoxacin, have a
reasonable activity against anaerobes at generally used
therapeutic dosages. 74 , 75 Although there are reports of an
increase in the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in anaerobes
isolated from humans, the use of empiric agents in veterinary
medicine is still recommended. 26 The prevalence of resistance to
β-lactams and ﬂuoroquinolones is high among Bacteroides spp.,
but it is also observed in other anaerobes of the gram-negative
group. 27 , 72 , 74
The most active antimicrobials against anaerobes are
metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate, chloramphenicol, and
clindamycin (Table 54.8). Numerous β-lactamase inhibitor
combinations such as ampicillin-sulbactam, ticarcillin-clavulanate
(if available), and piperacillin-tazobactam have been shown to be
very active against human anaerobic isolates but have not been
tested on veterinary isolates. 26 , 27 , 70 Factors such as tissue
penetration should be considered when selecting antimicrobial
drugs, and the concurrent presence of aerobic bacteria must also
be taken into account. A combination of a β-lactam/β-lactamase
inhibitor drug or clindamycin and a drug with activity against
gram-negative bacteria, such as a ﬂuoroquinolone or an
aminoglycoside, could be a reasonable choice for initial treatment
of serious infections whilst awaiting the results of susceptibility
testing for aerobic bacteria when mixed aerobic-anaerobic
infections are suspected.

Prevention
Prevention of anaerobic bacterial infections involves management
or prevention of underlying conditions that predispose to these
infections (see Clinical Features). Vaccines for prevention of
anaerobic bacterial infections are not available. An inactivated,
whole cell vaccine preparation Porphyromonas denticanis, P. gulae,
and Porphyromonas salivosa was available for several years for
prevention of periodontal disease in dogs, but was withdrawn
from the market due to apparent lack of eﬃcacy when its
conditional license expired.

Public Health Aspects
It is estimated that 250,000 human bites, 400,000 cat bites, and 4.5
million dog bites occur in the United States each year in both
adults and children. 18 Although most of the wounds resulting
from animal bites contain aerobic microorganisms, approximately
one third contain anaerobes. All are thought to be members of the
normal oral cavity microbiota of dogs and cats. The most common
anaerobes belong to the same genera as the anaerobes found in
disease processes in dogs and cats. 18 , 78 Some members of the
oral microbiota of dogs and cats produce serious disease in
immunocompromised individuals and those that are asplenic or
have liver disease (see Chapter 75).
Clostridioides diﬃcile is an important cause of disease in humans
and it has been found in food-producing animals and retail meats.
Clostridioides diﬃcile ribotypes in animals are associated with
human infections; however, prevalence and spore numbers were
low. 79–82 No association between C. diﬃcile fecal carriage and raw
meat consumption was noted in dogs 81 ; however, other enteric
pathogens such as Salmonella were detected. 83 Clostridium
perfringens can be transmi ed to people on contaminated foods
from production animals. No data exist concerning the
communicability of C. perfringens from dogs and cats to people.

vetexamprep.ir

However, because it appears that this microorganism can be
acquired from contaminated environments, it seems likely, but
unproven, that C. perfringens from any source can infect dogs, cats,
or people. Whether resulting disease depends on a trigger event
remains undetermined (see Chapter 64).

Case Example
Signalment

“Cocoa,” a 4-month-old intact female Labrador retriever from
Gonzales, CA.

History

Cocoa was brought to the University of California, Davis,
William R. Pritchard Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital for
evaluation of a history of seizures. Approximately 6 weeks
before referral, the dog was seen for redness and protrusion of
the left eye (exophthalmos). She was treated with amoxicillinclavulanic acid for 1 week, and the left ocular exophthalmos
resolved, but subsequently protrusion of the right eye was
noted. A second 1-week course of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
was instituted, and the exophthalmos again resolved. One
month later, Cocoa appeared painful on opening her mouth.
She was treated with cephalexin and meloxicam with no
apparent improvement. Two days later she was inappetent.
When the owners oﬀered her food by hand, she ate, became
ataxic, fell over, her thoracic limbs stiﬀened, and foamy saliva
was noted around her mouth. She was taken to an emergency
clinic and she vomited in the car. At the emergency clinic, she
had three generalized seizures that were treated with
diazepam. She was also treated with enroﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg, IV,
once).
Cocoa’s diet normally consisted of commercial dog food and
she had been vaccinated for distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus at
8 and 12 weeks of age. There had been no coughing, sneezing,
diarrhea, exposure to ticks or toxins, trauma, or travel outside
California.

Physical Examination
Body weight: 15.3 kg.

vetexamprep.ir

General: Quiet but alert and responsive. Hydrated. T =
102.8°F (39.3°C), pulse = 110 beats/minute, panting, mucous
membranes pink, CRT = 1 second.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No clinically signiﬁcant
abnormalities were noted. No evidence of pain on opening the
mouth provided neck movement was prevented.
Integument: No abnormalities detected.
Musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary systems,
and peripheral lymph nodes: No clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings.
Neurologic examination: Mild obtundation noted. The dog
held her head down and was reluctant to move her neck. There
was moderate to marked ataxia that involved all four limbs,
with the pelvic limbs most severely aﬀected, and the right
pelvic and thoracic limbs more severely aﬀected than the left.
Cranial nerve examination revealed only a decreased corneal
reﬂex on the right side. Conscious proprioceptive deﬁcits were
noted in all four limbs, with the right limbs more severely
aﬀected. There was severe pain on palpation of the cervical
spine and moderate pain on palpation of the lumbosacral spine.
Based on the neurologic examination, multifocal CNS lesions
were suspected.

Laboratory Findings

CBC: HCT 34.4% (40%–55%), MCV 64.9 fL (65–75 fL), MCHC
34.9 g/dL (33–36 g/dL), reticulocytes 22,000 cells/µL (7,000–
65,000 cells/µL), WBC 17,780 cells/µL (6,000–13,000 cells/µL),
neutrophils 12,979 cells/µL (3,000–10,500 cells/µL), band
neutrophils 533 cells/µL, lymphocytes 3,023 cells/µL (1,000–
4,000 cells/µL), monocytes 1,245 cells/µL (150–1,200 cells/µL),
platelets 392,000 platelets/µL (150,000–400,000 platelets/µL).

Imaging Findings

Thoracic radiographs: Cardiopulmonary structures were within
normal limits.
Abdominal ultrasound: The gastric wall was mildly
thickened with bright, echogenic speckles within the muscularis
layer. The submucosa of the stomach was echogenic.
Impressions: Changes associated with the stomach were
suggestive of gastritis. The remainder of the abdominal
ultrasound was unremarkable.
Spinal radiographs: Open physes were present within the
vertebral column. No abnormalities were identiﬁed.
Brain MRI: In the pre-contrast brain study, a ﬂa ened,
fusiform structure was identiﬁed in the dorsal part of the
foramen magnum that caused moderate dorsoventral
compression of the spinal cord (Fig. 54.7). This structure was
hypointense to brain but hyperintense to CSF on the T1weighted images and moderately hyperintense on dual echo
and ﬂuid-a enuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images. The
post-contrast brain study showed diﬀuse meningeal
enhancement that involved the spinal cord and brain with the
most prominent enhancement noted along the ventral
brainstem and left cerebral hemisphere. The contrast
enhancement pa ern was consistent with meningitis. There was
a discrete rim of enhancement surrounding the aforementioned
fusiform structure, which gave it a cystic appearance. This
structure appeared to be extradural in location. The structure in
the foramen magnum had partial ﬂuid characteristics, but was
not consistent with pure ﬂuid, and in light of the meningeal
enhancement, was thought to most likely represent an abscess.

Analysis of CSF (Lumbar CSF)

CSF protein: 726 mg/dL (reference range, < 25 mg/dL)
Total RBCs: 5 cells/µL (reference range, 0 cells/µL)
Total nucleated cells: 7,500 cells/µL (reference range, < 2
cells/µL)

vetexamprep.ir

Diﬀerential: 88% neutrophils, 12% large mononuclear
cells
Microscopic evaluation: The specimen was highly cellular
and contained a large number of nondegenerate
neutrophils. A few pyknotic forms were noted. Lower
numbers of monocytoid cells, large reactive lymphocytes,
and rare eosinophils also were observed. Interpretation:
Marked neutrophilic pleocytosis (purulent inﬂammation).

Cytologic Analysis of CSF (Cisternal)

A direct smear of cisternal CSF was examined and found to
contain disrupted cells and mildly to moderately degenerate
neutrophils. These were admixed with low numbers of
monocytoid cells and intermediate-sized reactive lymphocytes.
Rare neutrophils were observed with intracellular rod-shaped
bacteria. Few free rod-shaped bacteria were noted in the
background.

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic urine culture: No growth was detected.
Aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures: No growth was
detected.
Aerobic and anaerobic CSF culture: Small numbers of B.
fragilis, positive for β-lactamase production.

Diagnosis

Bacteroides fragilis meningitis with extradural abscess formation.

Treatment and Outcome

Cocoa was treated with ticarcillin (50 mg/kg, IV, q6h),
metronidazole (10 mg/kg, IV, q8h), and IV crystalloids (LRS
with 20 mEq/L KCl at 50 mL/h, IV). The following day her
mentation improved and she became more willing to move. On
day 3 after starting antibiotics, treatment was changed to
clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (16 mg/kg, PO, q8h) and
metronidazole (16 mg/kg, PO, q12h). On day 4, Cocoa was less
ataxic and had normal conscious proprioception, but had a

vetexamprep.ir

seizure while on a walk outside. The seizure lasted 45 seconds
and was manifested by jaw chomping and defecation, but
Cocoa did not fall over or lose consciousness. Potassium
bromide (40 mg/kg, PO, q8h for 4 days, then 40 mg/kg, PO,
q24h) was added to the treatment regimen and Cocoa was
discharged from the hospital.
At a recheck 3 weeks later, Cocoa’s owners reported that she
had shown steady clinical improvement and for the last week
she had been acting like a normal puppy. There had been no
seizures. She received her ﬁnal series of vaccines 1 week ago.
No abnormalities could be detected on full neurologic
examination. A CBC showed persistent mild nonregenerative
anemia (HCT 34.8%), 5,253 neutrophils/µL, and 228 band
neutrophils/µL. A repeat MRI showed a marked decrease in the
diﬀuse meningeal enhancement and marked reduction in the
size of the cystic structure, although there was persistent mild
spinal cord compression. Analysis of CSF revealed a CSF
protein concentration of 37 mg/dL, < 1 RBC/µL, 24 nucleated
cells/µL, with 12% neutrophils, 51% small mononuclear cells,
and 37% large mononuclear cells. Microscopic examination
revealed a heterogenous population of lymphocytes that
included small mature lymphocytes, larger reactive
lymphocytes, and many plasmacytoid lymphocytes along with
mature plasma cells and moderately vacuolated macrophages.
A few nondegenerate neutrophils were present. Antimicrobial
drug treatment was continued and a recheck was recommended
in 3 months, but the dog was subsequently lost to follow-up.

Comments

The history of exophthalmos increased suspicion for an
anaerobic bacterial infection of the CNS in this dog; therefore,
anaerobic culture of the CSF and blood was performed. Given
the young age of this dog, a migrating foreign body was
suspected. The history, together with the distribution of lesions
in the CNS and the lack of lesions elsewhere, suggested direct
extension of the infection from the retrobulbar location to the
meninges, rather than hematogenous spread of infection.
Because the dog was treated with antibiotics before culture was
performed, the concurrent presence of other facultative
organisms or other anaerobic species may have been obscured.
The identiﬁcation of β-lactamase production by the B. fragilis

vetexamprep.ir

isolate was not surprising because of the high (> 90%)
prevalence of β-lactamase production by this species. B. fragilis
is also known for its propensity to form abscesses.
