patients. In other situations, nonspeciﬁc clinical signs are present
and it has been impossible to clearly assign a disease causation
role to Bartonella in an individual patient. Establishing a clear
understanding of the role of Bartonella in disease causation has
also been hindered primarily by limitations in diagnostic tests.
Clinical Manifestations in Cats
Experimental infections of speciﬁc pathogen free (SPF) cats with
Bartonella have shed light on disease processes that can follow
natural infection of cats with Bartonella. Cats inoculated
intradermally with plate-grown B. henselae developed a small
papule or abscess at the site of inoculation (Fig. 70.4), with
concurrent transient fever and accompanying lethargy and
inappetence. Lymphadenomegaly of the nodes draining the
inoculation site lasted up to 6 weeks. 16–19 Transient mild
neurologic signs (including nystagmus, whole body tremors, focal
motor seizures, decreased or exaggerated responses to stimuli,
and mild behavioral abnormalities) occurred in some cats. 16–19 , 45
Reproductive disorders, such as failed conception and fetal
resorption, were also reported in multiple studies. 17 , 21 , 46 Most
cats infected with B. henselae and/or B. clarridgeiae show no clinical
signs, and gross lesions are lacking at necropsy. Cats infected with
culture-grown B. koehlerae, B. bovis, B. quintana, B. vinsonii subsp.
berkhoﬃi, or B. rochalimae also showed no clinical signs. 47
However, histopathology of cats infected by blood transfusion or
culture-grown B. henselae or B. clarridgeiae showed peripheral or
generalized lymph node hyperplasia, splenic follicular
hyperplasia, and focal splenic microabscesses, lymphocytic
cholangitis/pericholangitis,
lymphocytic
hepatitis,
lymphoplasmacytic myocarditis, and/or interstitial lymphocytic
nephritis. 16 , 18 Myocarditis was also reported in an
experimentally infected cat. 48 Collectively, results from
experimental infection studies involving cats suggest that the
source of inoculum, the route of inoculation, and the virulence
characteristics of the Bartonella species/strain can inﬂuence
clinical, hematological, and pathological ﬁndings.
Bartonella also causes endocarditis or myocarditis in naturally
infected cats, and was associated with feline endomyocarditis-left
ventricular endocardial ﬁbrosis complex in 18 of 36 cats evaluated.

vetexamprep.ir

49

Bartonella henselae DNA was ampliﬁed from aortic valvular
vegetative lesions of cats, with visualization of the organism in
lesions using silver stains. 20 , 50 Pyogranulomatous myocarditis
and diaphragmatic myositis were associated with B. henselae
infection in two cats, and organisms were detected in lesions with
silver stains and IHC (Fig. 70.5). 51 Bartonella vinsonii subsp.
berkhoﬃi DNA was detected in blood and bone lesions of a cat
with carpal and metacarpal osteomyelitis (Fig. 70.6). 52 Bartonella
vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi and B. henselae DNA was also PCR
ampliﬁed and sequenced from cardiac tissues of several cats with
systemic reactive angioendotheliomatosis, a vasculoproliferative
disorder. 53
The potential for Bartonella to be a contributor to chronic
diseases seems likely given the prolonged bacteremia reported,
and ﬁndings of inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrate in many tissues of
experimentally infected cats. As a result, Bartonella has been
investigated for a potential role in several idiopathic conditions of
cats (see Table 70.1). 50–52 , 54–62 These include uveitis, 54–56
gingivostomatitis, 56–59 , 61 , 62 fever of unknown origin, 60 lower
urinary tract disease, 56 , 59 , 63 hyperglobulinemia, anemia,
inﬂammatory polyps, chronic kidney disease, 56 , 59 high serum
pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity, 64 lymphadenopathy, 62
neurologic disease, 56 , 65 , 66 plasmacytic pododermatitis, 67 and
chronic idiopathic rhinosinusitis. 68 There is currently no
convincing and repeatable scientiﬁc evidence that Bartonella
infection causes any of these conditions. Studies have varied in the
methodology used to detect infection (serology, culture, and/or
PCR assays). The utility of serology for establishing disease
associations is limited, and studies that rely on Bartonella
seroreactivity to evaluate disease association should be
interpreted with caution. Finding Bartonella in tissues via PCR or
culture should be evaluated carefully, as high proportions of cats
may be infected with Bartonella species, and there may be other
etiologies for clinical conditions being investigated. Because of the
high prevalence of Bartonella exposure in domestic cats, an
understanding of the signiﬁcance of Bartonella in these conditions
will require carefully controlled, long-term prospective study of
large numbers of cats with clearly deﬁned clinical conditions
using Bartonella culture and/or PCR assays, along with

vetexamprep.ir

investigation for other etiologies. It is important to consider that
many of the conditions investigated likely have multifactorial
etiologies, and cats exposed to Bartonella are likely exposed to
other arthropod-vectored pathogens.

Clinical Manifestations in Dogs
Bartonella spp. are important causes of blood culture–negative
endocarditis in dogs, but they have also been detected within
lesions from many other pathologies using culture or PCR (see
Table 70.1). Infection with Bartonella was identiﬁed from 19% to
28% of dogs with culture-negative endocarditis. 45 , 69 In United
States military working dogs, 13 of 18 dogs with histologic
diagnoses of culture-negative endocarditis, 3 of 5 dogs with
endomyocarditis, and 3 of 3 dogs with endocardiosis tested
positive for Bartonella using PCR; in contrast, only 1 of 28 control
dogs without histologic evidence of cardiac lesions tested positive.
70 Worldwide, the DNA of several Bartonella species has been
detected in the heart valves of dogs with endocarditis. The most
common species identiﬁed has been B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi. In
dogs, Bartonella endocarditis usually involves the aortic valve,
although the mitral valve is occasionally aﬀected, so the

vetexamprep.ir

possibility of bartonellosis should not be ruled out in dogs with
mitral valve endocarditis. Dogs with Bartonella endocarditis are
more likely to be afebrile and more likely to have congestive heart
failure than dogs with other causes of endocarditis, and their
median survival time is shorter (Fig. 70.7). 45 Complications of
Bartonella endocarditis include murmur, lameness, weakness,
thromboembolic disease, neutrophilic polyarthritis, and collapse.

Bartonella isolates or Bartonella DNA have been detected in
lesions from dogs with a variety of chronic pyogranulomatous or
granulomatous inﬂammatory and vasculoproliferative diseases
(Fig. 70.8). Consequently, the clinical manifestations vary over the
time course of illness and in severity according to the organ or
tissue most severely aﬀected. Bartonella henselae was detected in a
dog with peliosis hepatis and B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi in a dog
with bacillary angiomatosis, both of which are rare conditions that
are strongly associated with Bartonella infection in humans. 71–73
Peliosis
hepatis
and
bacillary
angiomatosis
are
vasculoproliferative diseases characterized by the presence of
blood-ﬁlled proliferation of vascular tissue in the liver and skin,
respectively. Bartonella henselae was also detected in an SPF beagle
research dog that had aural vasculitis, with conﬁrmation of
intralesional infection using PCR ampliﬁcation, DNA sequencing,
and confocal immunostaining. 74 Based on case reports and
seroprevalence studies, Bartonella has been associated with
polyarthritis, epistaxis, and thrombocytopenia in dogs. 40
However, these associations could also reﬂect the presence of
other detected or undetected diseases, including co-transmi ed
vector-borne pathogens that cause these disorders. Bartonella has
been investigated for its potential role in lymphoma, 75 neurologic
diseases, 76 idiopathic cavitary eﬀusion, 77 , 78 idiopathic rhinitis, 79
and in splenic disorders including lymphoid nodular hyperplasia,
hemangiosarcoma, 80 and ﬁbrohistiocytic nodules. 81 Bartonella
spp. DNA was ampliﬁed and sequenced from fresh frozen tissues
from 73% of dogs diagnosed with hemangiosarcoma. 80 The
clinical relevance of ﬁnding Bartonella infection in association with
a neoplasm requires additional study.

Physical Examination Findings
Among 47 dogs conﬁrmed to be infected with one or more
Bartonella spp. in the United States, the most frequent signs were
fever (40%), lethargy (40%), weight loss (34%), anorexia (32%),
lymphadenopathy (30%), diarrhea (23%), neurological signs
(21%), heart murmurs (21%), respiratory signs (21%),
polyuria/polydipsia (21%), lameness (19%), vomiting (15%), and
splenomegaly (13%). 82 When compared to dogs suspected of
other tick-borne diseases, the presence of weight loss was more

vetexamprep.ir

frequent in dogs infected with Bartonella species. 83 In dogs with
Bartonella endocarditis, physical examination ﬁndings include
lethargy, inappetence, and thin body condition; lameness or
recumbency due to thromboembolic complications, weakness, or
polyarthritis; joint eﬀusion; and, uncommonly, fever (as high as
104.9°F [41°C]). Evidence of cardiac disease and congestive heart
failure is often present, including respiratory distress, cough,
increased lung sounds, and systolic and/or diastolic heart
murmurs, cardiac arrhythmias, and pulse deﬁcits. Neurologic
signs such as anisocoria and obtundation can occur in dogs with

evidence of ﬂea or tick infestations in some dogs. Other physical

cavitary eﬀusions; peripheral edema; epistaxis; or nodular skin

Diagnosis
Most clinical signs or clinical pathologic abnormalities proposed
to be a ributable to bartonellosis are shared by conditions
resulting from many other etiologies. Therefore determining
which animals likely have clinical signs resulting from Bartonella
infection can be diﬃcult. Diagnostic testing should not be focused
on Bartonella alone but should include evaluation for other
potential causes of the clinical condition(s) being evaluated.
Diagnosis of bartonellosis is based on the presence of consistent
clinical abnormalities (especially endocarditis or myocarditis, but
also other systemic inﬂammatory or vasculoproliferative
diseases), a history of exposure to arthropod vectors,
histopathologic ﬁndings, and positive culture or PCR assay results
on blood or aﬀected tissues (Table 70.2). It may be impossible to
identify Bartonella as the cause of disease if the organism is not
detected in the blood by PCR or enrichment blood culture/PCR
and if aﬀected tissues (e.g., valvular vegetations) cannot be
obtained for analysis. Also, because healthy cats and dogs can be
bacteremic, documentation of bacteremia must be viewed in the
clinical context of the animal’s illness. Similarly, visualizing
organisms (or amplifying organism-speciﬁc DNA sequences) in
tissue may not always conﬁrm causation due to Bartonella, as this
is distributed throughout many tissues because it is a blood-borne
pathogen. Other possible causes of disease must also be
investigated, and a response to antibiotic treatment could be
evaluated (see Case Example). Finally, disease resolution in
association with antibiotic administration may not indicate
Bartonella as a cause, since other undocumented bacterial

vetexamprep.ir

pathogens may be treated as a result of antibiotic therapy. Some
antibiotics have anti-inﬂammatory and/or immune-modulating
properties that make it diﬃcult to diﬀerentiate whether a positive
change in patient status is a result of antimicrobial properties of
the drug, other properties of the drug, the host immune response
having more time to address the pathogen, or a combination of
factors. 88 Documentation of seroconversion and seroreversion in
conjunction with antibiotic administration can be used to support
a diagnosis of bartonellosis. 89 Increased documentation of
seroconversion in dogs with an acute-onset illness will be
important to be er understand the extent to which acute versus
chronic infections occur in dogs. In contrast, when dealing with a
long-standing illness, serology (if positive) can only be used to
implicate Bartonella exposure. As Bartonella seroprevalence is
much lower in dogs compared to cats, positive serology is
perhaps more diagnostically useful when evaluating a sick dog. 38
More speciﬁcally (and as occurs in humans), dogs with Bartonella
endocarditis usually have high antibody titers to Bartonella spp.
Conventional organism detection tests (blood culture and PCR)
are insensitive because dogs tend to have very low levels of
bacteremia when compared with cats. The sensitivity of Bartonella
spp. detection has improved with the use of enrichment culture
coupled with a highly sensitive PCR, which is the current
recommended approach for conﬁrming bacteremia in dogs. 85 , 90 ,
91 Improved detection of Bartonella bacteremia in cats has also
been demonstrated using methods combining enrichment culture
and PCR assays. 92 Nonetheless, the prevalence rates of Bartonella
spp. in cats and dogs do not correspond with the low number of
reported clinical cases potentially because Bartonella infections are
underdiagnosed in dogs and cats. 93

Laboratory Abnormalities
Hematologic and biochemistry abnormalities in dogs and cats
with Bartonella endocarditis are nonspeciﬁc and often mild. Most
infected cats have no clinical pathologic abnormalities.
Chronically infected dogs may also be hematologically
unremarkable or have only mild nonregenerative anemia,
neutrophilia, neutropenia, or thrombocytopenia. A few dogs have
low to moderate numbers of circulating band neutrophils,
lymphocytosis, and/or monocytosis. 94–96 Serum biochemical
abnormalities can include azotemia, hypoalbuminemia,
hypoglobulinemia,
and
hyperglobulinemia.
Isosthenuria,
proteinuria, cylindruria, and slightly increased urine protein-tocreatinine ratios have been present in the urine of some aﬀected
dogs. Dogs with hepatic involvement have had moderately
increased serum ALT and/or ALP activities. 71 , 97 In one study

vetexamprep.ir

from the United States, the most common laboratory

proteinuria (40%), anemia (38%), leukocytosis (36%),
thrombocytopenia (34%), elevated liver enzymes (32%),
hyperbilirubinemia
(30%),
hyperglobulinemia
(26%),

abnormal coagulation panel (PT/PTT) (13%), leukopenia (11%),

diagnosed in a dog that failed immunosuppressive drug therapy,
but had resolution of the anemia after documentation of B.
henselae bacteremia, in association with antibiotic administration.
98 A 2022 study found no clinically relevant laboratory

Cardiac biomarkers such as troponin I and natriuretic peptide
(Nt-ProBNP) may be elevated in sick dogs with Bartonella
endocarditis or myocarditis. Cardiac troponin I is a highly
sensitive marker for myocardial damage, and was elevated (0.28
to 3.05 ng/mL, reference ≤0.11 ng/mL) in three out of eight
Bartonella spp. infected or exposed dogs, lacking diagnostic
indications of endocarditis. 100 Natriuretic peptides are a
biomarker for stress or stretching of the myocardium, and are
frequently elevated in patients with congestive heart failure,
which can be caused by endocarditis or myocarditis. 101

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Thoracic radiographs in dogs with Bartonella endocarditis often
show evidence of congestive heart failure, with venous
engorgement and pulmonary edema (Fig. 70.10). Lung lobe
consolidation and hilar lymphadenopathy were described in a
dog with systemic granulomatous disease and sialometaplasia. 102
Bilateral mandibular pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis and

vetexamprep.ir

pulmonary nodules were found in a dog with B. henselae
bacteremia. 103
Abdominal Ultrasound
Ultrasound examination of dogs with systemic granulomatous or
pyogranulomatous disease may reveal lymphadenomegaly and
organomegaly, 104 and mixed echogenic pa erns within the liver.
97 In two distinct reports, dogs with peliosis hepatis had
ascites/hemoperitoneum and multiple, small nodular masses and
hypoechoic cystic lesions within the liver (Fig. 70.11). 71 , 73
Electrocardiography
Arrhythmias and conduction disturbances have been more
frequently reported in patients with endocarditis or myocarditis,
but occur in dogs without echocardiographic evidence of these
disease processes. ECG ﬁndings are nonspeciﬁc and can vary from
atrial, nodal, or ventricular conduction disturbances, including
atrioventricular blocks and/or bundle branch blocks. In addition,
supraventricular and/or ventricular premature complexes may be
observed (Fig. 70.12).
Echocardiography
Echocardiography in dogs and cats with Bartonella endocarditis
reveals oscillating valvular vegetations or thickened and
hyperechoic valve leaﬂets, which usually involve the aortic valve
(Fig. 70.13). There may be evidence of aortic regurgitation or
insuﬃciency and eccentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle or
decreased cardiac output.

Microbiologic Tests
Culture
Despite the limitations described earlier, culture of blood or other
tissues for Bartonella facilitates a deﬁnitive diagnosis of infection.
However, blood culture requires special techniques and can be
insensitive because of the relapsing nature of bacteremia (see Fig.
70.3). Sensitivity can be improved by collecting serial blood
samples (e.g., three blood draws within 7 days). Culture has
especially low sensitivity in most dog populations because of the

vetexamprep.ir

low level of bacteremia (especially when dogs are incidental hosts
and develop the disease). Blood for culture should be obtained
using aseptic collection and placed in EDTA-containing tubes, and
then chilled or frozen during shipment. The collection of blood
into plastic EDTA tubes allows the tubes to be frozen directly,
which releases organisms from erythrocytes after which they are
inoculated into optimized liquid growth media. Blood should be
sent to laboratories familiar with the culture of these fastidious
organisms, and the laboratories should be contacted for
instructions regarding specimen collection and submission.
Special media (such as fresh chocolate agar, or brain-heart
infusion agar enriched with 5% to 10% blood) and culture
conditions (5% CO2, temperatures of 35°C to 37°C) are used to
enhance the likelihood of isolation of Bartonella. 75 Extended
incubation times of up to 6 to 8 weeks can be required for
successful isolation. The use of an insect growth medium
(Bartonella alpha Proteobacteria growth medium, or BAPGM) that
contains multiple micronutrients and deﬁbrinated sheep blood for
enrichment culture of blood, cerebrospinal and joint ﬂuid,
pathological eﬀusions, and potentially other tissues, followed by
PCR testing of the liquid culture at deﬁned time points, in
conjunction with sub-inoculation of the liquid culture medium
onto agar plates, has enhanced culture sensitivity, compared to
conventional microbiological approaches. It also has the potential
to yield other fastidious organisms not cultured under routine
conditions that may play a role in endocarditis. 105 Liquid culture
did not signiﬁcantly improve the isolation of Bartonella spp. in
cats. 106

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Many PCR-based assays have been developed for the rapid
detection of Bartonella DNA in blood or other tissues. 100 , 107 , 108
Some veterinary diagnostic laboratories oﬀer real-time PCR
assays for the detection of Bartonella species as a component of
vector-borne PCR panels. Some assays are designed to detect all
Bartonella spp., whereas other assays are designed to be speciesspeciﬁc. Genetic analysis of PCR products by DNA sequencing or
other modalities can be performed to identify the infecting
Bartonella species. Diagnostic utilization of droplet digital PCR
(ddPCR) has substantially improved the detection of Bartonella
DNA while maintaining exceptional speciﬁcity. 109 The clinical
performance of many of these assays, when compared among
laboratories or compared with culture, has not been well studied.
When used directly on blood specimens, PCR assays may be no

vetexamprep.ir

more sensitive than conventional culture for the detection of
Bartonella, and detection of DNA does not necessarily equate to
the documentation of living organisms. However, the turnaround
time for PCR assay results is typically much faster than for
culture. False-positive PCR assay results due to laboratory
contamination or sample contamination at the time of collection
(of particular concern with tissues collected at necropsy) have the
potential to occur. False-negative PCR results may occur due to
DNA degradation or cross-linking secondary to formalin ﬁxation
or other factors. Whenever possible, clinicians should
simultaneously collect and freeze tissues for PCR testing at the
same time tissues are collected for histopathology. Reputable
laboratories with experience in molecular diagnostics are
recommended to achieve optimal sensitivity and speciﬁcity.
Laboratories should be contacted before specimen submission for
guidelines for specimen collection and shipment.
Serologic Testing
Immunoﬂuorescent antibody (IFA), ELISA, and Western
immunoblot assays are available for the detection of Bartonella
spp. antibodies. Some degree of cross-reactivity occurs among
Bartonella species, but multiple species-speciﬁc assays still should
be performed to increase the chance of antibody detection. Crossreactivity can be observed for endocarditis cases, where antibody
titers can be quite high. 20 , 94 Experimentally, dogs generated a
speciﬁc antibody response by IFA testing to each Bartonella
species, without the development of cross-reactivity. 110 Bartonella
henselae Western immunoblot was more sensitive than B. henselae
IFA, but there were still infected dogs (PCR+) that were negative
by both testing modalities. 111 In addition to the possibility of
Bartonella spp. transmission by other arthropods, such as ticks,
clinicians should be aware that dogs with ﬂea infestations may be
exposed to multiple Bartonella spp. as a result of a single or
sequential ﬂea exposures. Acute and convalescent titers can be
used to assess a patient with an acute-onset illness, whereas
paired titers are less likely to be valuable for patients with chronic
and persistent infection. If serologic testing is performed in dogs,
a panel that includes testing for B. henselae, B. vinsonii subsp.
berkhoﬃi, B. rochalimae, B. koehlerae, and B. clarridgeiae would be
optimal. 112 In cats, a serologic panel including B. henselae, B.

vetexamprep.ir

p
g p
g
koehlerae, and B. clarridgeiae should be considered. In the authors’
experience, variability in the antigen of Bartonella species or strain
used for testing may result in diﬀerent results among laboratories.
Measurement of Bartonella serum antibodies has a limited ability
to help determine whether a sick animal has an active Bartonella
infection. In both cats and dogs, bacteremia can occur in the
absence of detectable antibodies, and seropositive cats and dogs
are not always bacteremic. Some dogs that are chronically ill and
Bartonella spp. nonseroreactive seroconvert after administration of
antibiotics, potentially reﬂecting enhanced antigenic recognition.
For example, in one study with 61 naturally infected and sick
dogs, only 7 of 19 (36.8%) B. henselae and 4 of 10 (40%) B. vinsonii
subsp. berkhoﬃi infected dogs for which sera were available were
seroreactive to B. henselae and B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi antigens,
respectively. Because of this, serology is not recommended as the
sole diagnostic test for canine or feline bartonellosis and should be
used and interpreted in conjunction with PCR testing or
enrichment culture/PCR. 38

Pathologic Findings
Gross necropsy of dogs and cats with Bartonella endocarditis may
reveal evidence of congestive heart failure, with lung congestion
and edema. Single or multiple nodules, variably sized, are
typically present on the periphery of valvular leaﬂets, which may
be small and ﬁrm or large, granular, and friable (Fig. 70.14). White
plaques may be found adherent to the adjacent endocardial
surfaces. Histopathology reveals chronic inﬂammation, with
ﬁbrous tissue and extensive mineral deposits. The presence of
valvular mineralization should raise suspicion for Bartonella
endocarditis because mineralization is uncommonly associated
with endocarditis caused by other bacteria. 45 Small bacilli may be
seen within lesions with silver stains or immunohistochemical
stains for B. henselae. 50 , 51 , 72 Silver stains must be interpreted

vetexamprep.ir

with caution because necrotic debris and nuclear material can
mimic positive staining. Gross lesions in the dog with peliosis
hepatis consisted of multiple, 0.1- to 0.3-cm cysts in the liver that
were ﬁlled with cloudy, serosanguineous ﬂuid (Fig. 70.15). 71 , 72
Nodular granulomatous or pyogranulomatous lesions in the
myocardium, kidneys, lymphoid, or other tissues have also been
described in animals with bartonellosis (Figs. 70.16 and 70.17), 97 ,
113 , 114 and nodular pyogranulomatous inﬂammatory lesions with
intralesional bacteria were described in the myocardium and
diaphragm of cats with Bartonella myocarditis and diaphragmatic
myositis (see Fig. 70.5). 51 , 115
Cats with acute or chronic experimental B. henselae or B.
clarridgeiae infections had hyperplasia of lymphoid organs, splenic
microabscesses, necrotizing granulomatous lesions in lymph
nodes, and small foci of pyogranulomatous, neutrophilic, or
lymphocytic inﬂammation in many tissues (including lung, liver,
kidney, heart, and spleen) (Figs. 70.18 and 70.19). 16 , 22

Treatment and Prognosis
Eﬃcacy has not been established for any antimicrobial for the
elimination of Bartonella infections in cats or dogs. In humans, the
2015 American and European guidelines for the management of
infective endocarditis recommend the use of doxycycline
combined with gentamicin for treatment of Bartonella infection, 116
, 117 but clinical improvement has been reported after the use of
other antibiotics. A recommendation has been made to avoid the
use of ﬂuoroquinolones alone for treatment in humans. 118 Valve
replacement is often indicated. Overall, treatment protocols for
human Bartonella infections vary with clinical presentation and
patient immune status. 107 , 119

The prognosis for Bartonella endocarditis in dogs and cats is
generally poor. Only a single case of successful treatment of
suspected B. henselae endocarditis in a cat has been reported at the
time of writing, where marboﬂoxacin and azithromycin were used
for 6 weeks. 120 Supportive care and medications to manage
congestive heart failure are often required. Bartonella spp.
antibiotic resistance or treatment failures have been reported in
association with the single use of azithromycin, doxycycline, and
ﬂuoroquinolones in dogs, 77 , 85 , 118 therefore monotherapy with
these antimicrobials is no longer recommended. As bacterial
isolation of Bartonella spp. is extremely diﬃcult to achieve,
determining antibiotic resistance pa erns is often not possible.
This greatly limits our ability to determine the mechanism(s) that
are responsible for treatment failures. Oral antimicrobial
alternatives for stable animals include high-dose doxycycline in
combination with rifampin or ﬂuoroquinolones, alone or in
combination with amoxicillin (Table 70.3). 121 To avoid a shocklike reaction (Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction) caused by the sudden
release of bacterial endotoxins/antigens during the ﬁrst days of
antimicrobial treatment, it is recommended that antibiotics are not
started concomitantly. Instead, the second antibiotic should be
introduced at least 5 to 7 days after the ﬁrst one. 121 Dogs with
CNS signs have been empirically treated with doxycycline and

vetexamprep.ir

rifampin; however, the use of rifampin in cats should be avoided
if other alternatives are available.

Data from experimentally or naturally infected cats indicate
that a high dose of doxycycline may be necessary to treat
Bartonella infection in cats. There is no consensus regarding the
best treatment for ill, infected cats, and data from randomized
clinical trials are lacking. Initial treatment with doxycycline may
be appropriate, with the addition of another antibiotic if this
treatment does not appear to be eﬀective. Antibiotic treatment
may induce resistant strains of Bartonella and other resident
microﬂora, therefore treatment should be reserved for use only in
Bartonella-positive cats showing clinical signs. While antibiotic
treatment reportedly decreases the level of bacteremia in cats,
there is no evidence that treatment will decrease the probability of
transmission of Bartonella to arthropod vectors, other cats, or
humans. Care should be taken to avoid scratches or bites when
administering drugs to bacteremic cats. Client education is
necessary regarding the uncertainty of treatment eﬃcacy, the
advisability of long-term follow-up, and the chance for reinfection
following treatment. The importance of ﬂea control and other

vetexamprep.ir

means of preventing transmission (see Prevention) should be
strongly emphasized.

Immunity and Vaccination
There are no vaccines available for the prevention of bartonellosis
in cats or dogs. Bartonella evades the host immune system and
establishes a persistent intracellular infection. Dogs and cats can
be co-infected with multiple diﬀerent Bartonella species, strains, or
genotypes. Developing a vaccine is challenging because
vaccination and challenge with the same or diﬀerent Bartonella
species/strains result in variable protection, and protection is
generally speciﬁc to the infecting species or even the genotype.
122–124

Prevention
Prevention of Bartonella infections in cats and dogs is best
accomplished by avoiding exposure to arthropod vectors and
infected animals. Vector control measures, such as the use of
ectoparasiticides, can interrupt transmission of B. henselae among
cats and should be maintained year-round for cats and dogs. 48 , 88
Housing cats indoors may also reduce exposure to ﬂeas. To the
extent possible, animal-to-animal contact should be restricted in
shows and other group events. 125 Bartonella spp. can be
transmi ed by blood inoculation to cats and dogs, therefore blood
donors should be screened for infection. The 2016 ACVIM
guidelines on canine and feline blood donor screening
recommend the optimal standard as to use dogs and cats that are
seronegative and PCR assay or culture negative (Table 70.4).
Because of the poor correlation between positive serology and
bacteremia, and the high seroprevalence rates in cats, the minimal
standard recommended by the ACVIM panel is to use a Bartonella
spp. PCR-negative donor, regardless of the serology results. 10
However, because Bartonella spp. may reside within a healthy
animal without evidence of bacteremia, it is important to
remember that no currently available screening test can rule out
Bartonella infection. It is not known how many Bartonella
seropositive cats that have negative culture as well as PCR test
results may be harboring Bartonella species. Therefore the most

vetexamprep.ir

conservative protocol would be to avoid the use of any
seropositive animal as a blood donor, even if PCR or BAPGM
results are negative.

Public Health Aspects
Dogs and cats are reservoirs for several zoonotic Bartonella
species. Cats are a major reservoir for B. henselae, the principal
cause of CSD in immunocompetent humans, and also serve as a
vector for transmission. The average annual incidence of CSD in
the United States is 4.5 outpatient diagnoses/100,000 population,
with a higher incidence in the southern United States (Fig. 70.20).
126 CSD is characterized by the formation of a papule at the site of
inoculation (a cat scratch) within 14 days, followed by the
development of local lymphadenopathy (Fig. 70.21) and malaise 1
to 3 weeks after the scratch (or bite), which can persist for weeks
to months. Most cases of CSD are self-limiting after several
months and respond minimally to antimicrobial drug treatment.

vetexamprep.ir

Occasionally, CSD is complicated by other disorders such as
encephalopathy,
relapsing
bacteremia,
osteomyelitis,
neuroretinitis, endocarditis, glomerulonephritis, and other
conditions, some of which require antimicrobial drug treatment. 29
, 116 , 127–132 Vasculoproliferative diseases such as bacillary peliosis
(e.g., peliosis hepatis) and bacillary angiomatosis (Fig. 70.22) are
among the most common complications in immunocompromised
humans. 15 , 133 Children from 5 to 9 years of age have the highest
incidence for outpatients and inpatients in the US. 126 Young cats
are most often implicated in transmission to humans because
young cats are more likely to be highly bacteremic than older cats.
Dogs are less likely to act as vectors for Bartonella spp. when
compared with cats, because the prevalence of Bartonella infection
and the magnitude of bacteremia in dogs are lower than that in
cats. Nevertheless, dogs have occasionally been suspected as the
source of transmission of Bartonella to humans through bite
wounds or scratches, and to date, all Bartonella species identiﬁed
in sick dogs are also pathogenic or potentially pathogenic in
humans. Immunocompromised people should preferably choose
healthy adult, well-socialized cats and dogs that have known
health histories as pets over ki ens and puppies, and should be
properly educated in regard to the need for vector control. Cats’
claws should be trimmed regularly, but there is no evidence that
declawing prevents transmission. Animal scratches or bites
should be avoided, and if they occur, the wounds should be
washed thoroughly with soap and water, after which prompt
medical a ention should be sought. Children should be closely
supervised when interacting with pet animals (see Chapter 75).
The 2022 guidelines for preventing opportunistic infections
among HIV-infected persons from the CDC, National Institutes of
Health, and Infectious Diseases Society of America state: “No
evidence indicates any beneﬁts to cats or their owners from
routine culture or serologic testing of the pet for Bartonella
infection or from antibiotic treatment of healthy, serologically
positive cats.” 134 Because there is no antimicrobial drug treatment
that is proven to reliably eliminate Bartonella infections from cats
or dogs, treatment of healthy infected animals is not
recommended. The administration of antimicrobial drugs to pets
may cause a false sense of security and result in unnecessary bites
or scratches. Owners should wear gloves when medicating sick

vetexamprep.ir

g
g
pets. The pros and cons of the testing of healthy cats for Bartonella
infection are shown in Box 70.1. 88

Advantages

Cats with positive Bartonella test results can be eliminated as
blood donors or breeding animals.
Compliance with client physician orders.

Disadvantages

Bartonella serology and PCR can be falsely positive or negative.
Some cats with positive serologic test results may have
eliminated the infection.
Cats with negative test results may still be bacteremic, or
become bacteremic within the near future.
Detection of positive Bartonella spp. test results in some
situations may lead to needless administration of antibiotics or
euthanasia.
A focus on testing may lead to lesser use of eﬀective
prevention methods such as ﬂea control.
No treatment reliably eliminates bacteremia in healthy cats.
Antimicrobial drug treatment of cats has not been shown to
prevent human infection or beneﬁt healthy infected animals.
Treatment of positive cats may lead to unnecessary lifethreatening adverse drug reactions, esophageal strictures
(doxycycline), or blindness (ﬂuoroquinolones).
The use of antimicrobials to treat healthy positive cats is
likely to lead to increased antimicrobial resistance not just of
Bartonella, but other microbes exposed to the administered
antibiotics.
Although cats and dogs are important reservoirs of Bartonella,
humans can also develop bartonellosis through other routes of
transmission, such as via other arthropods and possibly through
blood transfusions. 13 Human body lice primarily transmit B.

vetexamprep.ir

quintana among humans (especially the homeless), which causes
relapsing fever (trench fever) and endocarditis. 15

Case Example
Signalment

“Piper,” a 4-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat from
north-central Indiana.

History

Piper was evaluated at the Purdue University Veterinary
Teaching Hospital for ocular abnormalities, lethargy, decreased
appetite, and occasional cough and sneezing over 1 week. Piper
was obtained one year previously and had been a speciﬁc
pathogen-free cat prior to adoption. Piper had shown signs of
intermi ent idiopathic cystitis and two instances of lower
urinary tract obstruction/struvite crystalluria, for which he had
been treated with catheterization to relieve the lower urethral
obstruction, and was fed a prescription diet. Between episodes,
he appeared healthy with no other clinical abnormalities. Piper
had been housed indoors since adoption. He was neutered at 3
years of age without complication, just before adoption. Five
weeks before evaluation, the family had acquired another cat
from a pet store; this cat had ﬂeas at the time of acquisition, but
was otherwise healthy (Fig. 70.23). Piper was up to date on
vaccinations for respiratory viruses, panleukopenia virus, and
rabies. He was receiving heartworm preventative monthly and
no other medications.

Because of the history of the onset of the febrile illness closely
following the introduction of a new cat with ﬂeas into the
household, and the recurrence of fever following resolution of
the ophthalmologic clinical signs, blood was collected for
Bartonella culture, PCR, and serology, and doxycycline (5 mg/kg
PO q12h, immediately followed by a bolus of water) was
prescribed. Infection with B. henselae was conﬁrmed by blood
culture and PCR of blood. Piper was also seroreactive to B.
henselae.

Outcome

Piper was evaluated again 2 weeks later and had improved, was
no longer febrile or lethargic, and was eating well. Treatment
was continued for 6 weeks, and a follow-up CBC showed all
results within reference ranges.

Diagnosis

B. henselae bacteremia, likely a result of exposure to ﬂeas from
the newly introduced cat, was suspected to be the cause of the
recurrent fever and peripheral lymphadenomegaly following
resolution of the upper respiratory signs. The upper respiratory
signs were suspected to be a result of feline upper respiratory
disease, and could have been associated with pathogens such as
FCV, FHV-1, Mycoplasma, and/or Chlamydia, but speciﬁc testing
was not done for these infectious agents.

Comments

Bartonella infection in this cat was suspected because of fever
and lethargy that occurred after the introduction of a new cat
that had ﬂeas. Whether the treatment with doxycycline
contributed to the resolution of clinical signs cannot be
determined. Cats that are experimentally infected with
Bartonella show fever with lethargy approximately 2 to 4 weeks
after inoculation, and this resolves without any treatment.
The owner was educated about the transmission of Bartonella,
including the zoonotic potential, and the importance of treating
ﬂea infestations. Both cats were treated for ﬂeas including
preventive medications. The owners were advised to continue
to keep the cats indoors, and to use ﬂea preventative
medications in the future if the cats’ lifestyle changed.

71: Canine Brucellosis
Autumn P. Davidson, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Brucella canis was first isolated from dogs by
Leland Carmichael in 1966 (United States). 1
• Causes: Most commonly Brucella canis; rarely Brucella
abortus, Brucella suis, or Brucella melitensis. Brucella
organisms are small (1.0 to 1.5 μm), gram-negative, non–
spore-forming aerobic coccobacilli.
• Affected Hosts: The Brucella genus is composed of 12
classical species based on host preference, phenotypic
characteristics, and genetic analysis: B. abortus (cattle), B.
canis (dogs), B. melitensis (goats, sheep), Brucella neotomae
(rodents), Brucella ovis (sheep), Brucella pinnipedialis (seals),
Brucella ceti (porpoises, dolphins, whale), Brucella microti
(voles), Brucella inopinata (unknown host), Brucella papionis
(baboons), Brucella vulpis (foxes), and B. suis and its biovars
(pigs, cattle, hares, rodents, and wild ungulates). Although
most Brucella, with the exception of the biovars of B. suis,
show host preference, they can also infect other host species.
Brucella canis has a limited host range; only dogs and wild
Canidae have been found to be susceptible. Rural dogs are
susceptible to clinical infection with B. abortus, B. suis, and B.
melitensis.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide, but infections are most
often reported from the southwestern United States, Central
and South America, China, and Japan. Sporadic reports have
occurred in Canada and throughout Europe. Australia and
New Zealand appear to be free of the disease.
• Route of Transmission: Direct mucosal exposure (oral, nasal,
conjunctival, venereal) to contaminated body fluids (semen,

vetexamprep.ir

vaginal discharge, urine, aborted fetuses, and their
placentas).
• Major Clinical Signs: Most commonly infertility, abortion,
scrotal enlargement secondary to epididymitis/orchitis, scrotal
dermatitis, eventual testicular atrophy, lymphadenomegaly,
splenomegaly, signs related to discospondylitis (spinal pain,
pelvic limb paresis, or paralysis), uveitis, chorioretinitis, rarely
osteomyelitis and meningoencephalitis. No signs may be
present.
• Differential Diagnoses: Herpesvirus infection, bartonellosis,
mycobacterial infections, chronic vector-borne diseases
associated with splenomegaly such as ehrlichiosis and
babesiosis, coxiellosis, other bacterial and fungal causes of
metritis, orchitis/epididymitis, and discospondylitis,
intervertebral disc disease, hemic neoplasia (such as
lymphoma or multiple myeloma). Additional differential
diagnoses for dogs with ophthalmitis include deep mycoses,
rickettsial diseases, leptospirosis, and toxoplasmosis.
• Human Health Significance: Brucella canis can be transmitted
to humans and most often causes mild, influenza-like illness.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Canine brucellosis is most commonly caused by Brucella canis, a
small, gram-negative, non–spore-forming aerobic coccobacillus.
The genus Brucella is named after Major General Sir David Bruce
(1855–1931), an Australian-born British microbiologist. David
Bruce discovered Trypanosoma brucei and worked in the Army
Medical Service and the Royal Army Medical Corps. The Brucella
genus is composed of 12 classical species based on host
preference, virulence, phenotypic characteristics, and genetic
analysis: Brucella abortus (ca le), B. canis (dogs), Brucella melitensis
(goats, sheep), Brucella neotomae (rodents), Brucella ovis (sheep),
Brucella pinnipedialis (seals), Brucella ceti (porpoises, dolphins,
whale), Brucella microti (voles), Brucella inopinata (unknown host),
Brucella papionis (baboons), Brucella vulpis (foxes), and Brucella suis
and its biovars (pigs, ca le, hares, rodents, and wild ungulates). 2 ,

vetexamprep.ir

3

Factors that deﬁne host preference are unknown despite
remarkable (∼97%) similarity at the genome level.
Members of the Canidae family are the natural hosts of B. canis.
Brucella abortus, B. suis, and B. melitensis occasionally cause canine
infections but are comparatively rare. 4–7 Even an a enuated
vaccine strain of B. melitensis or B. abortus 8 can infect dogs. Cats
can be infected experimentally with B. canis, with transient
bacteremia, but are relatively resistant. Rabbits and nonhuman
primates also have been found to be susceptible to experimental
infections. No other animal species has developed signiﬁcant
agglutination titers. 9 Natural infection with non–B. canis species
is thought to occur after ingestion of contaminated placentas and
aborted fetuses from livestock; farm dogs may be predisposed. 10
In recent years, infection of dogs with B. suis has been associated
with hunting activity and the feeding of raw meat diets 11–13 ; a
dog in the Netherlands became infected after being fed raw hare
meat imported from Argentina. Dogs usually harbor the
organisms in the lymph nodes of their GI tracts for extended
periods. Dogs are not believed to be as important in the spread
and maintenance of these non–B. canis infections as their
respective farm animal or wildlife reservoirs. However, testing
and removal of aﬀected dogs from infected farms, in addition to
aﬀected livestock, have been considered the optimal preventive
measures for eradication. Brucella canis infections are zoonotic, but
other species of Brucella usually present a greater risk to human
health (see Public Health Aspects). 2 , 14
Brucellosis caused by B. canis is the primary contagious
infectious venereal disease of concern in canine reproduction.
Brucella canis causes reproductive failure in both male and female
dogs. Screening for B. canis infection is an important part of the
pre-breeding and pre-purchase evaluation of any dog (male or
female) and should be included in the initial diagnostics in any
case of canine abortion, orchitis, epididymitis, and apparent
infertility in dogs (failure to conceive, change in semen quality).
Because the incidence of canine brucellosis is low in many
geographic locations, breeder compliance with regular screening
can wane, which makes continued veterinarian vigilance
important. 15 Notably, neutered and maiden or virgin dogs can
also be infected. Interstate and international shipment of semen as

vetexamprep.ir

well as dogs can result in brucellosis outside of its endemic
regions. 16 , 17
Brucella canis can cause systemic disease (often manifested as
discospondylitis) in dogs not used for reproduction due to age or
neutering status. Dogs with B. canis discospondylitis are typically
medium- to large-breed dogs, with body weights that range from
14 to 64 kg; dogs have ranged in age from 1 to 8 years, with a
median of 4 years in one study. 18 , 19 Of 22 dogs with B. canis
discospondylitis known to the authors, 18 (82%) were intact male
dogs, 3 (14%) were female spayed, and 1 (4%) was male neutered.
20 Three dogs described in the literature with B. canis ophthalmitis
did not ﬁt this signalment; one dog was a Pomeranian and none
were intact males. 21
Natural transmission of canine brucellosis occurs by several
routes. Transmission of B. canis occurs through direct exposure to
body ﬂuids that contain suﬃcient numbers of the bacteria to cause
infection (the minimum oral infectious dose for dogs is
approximately 106 organisms, and the conjunctival dose is 104 to
105 organisms), most often in semen, lochia, aborted
fetuses/placentas, urine, and, to a lesser extent, milk. 9 Mucosal
transmission is therefore primarily oral, nasal, or conjunctival and
secondarily venereal. Oronasal and conjunctival exposure follows
the ingestion or aerosolization of infectious materials. The aerosol
route is especially important in crowded kennel or benched dog
show conditions. 22
Infected bitches transmit B. canis during proestrus and estrus, at
breeding, or after abortion through oronasal contact with vaginal
discharges. Transmission is most common by oronasal contact
with aborted materials because they contain up to 1010
organisms/mL. Shedding of B. canis may occur for periods up to 6
weeks after an abortion. Seminal ﬂuid and urine have been
incriminated as sources of infection from males that harbor
organisms in the prostate and epididymides. The rate of isolation
of B. canis from the semen of infected dogs is usually high for the
ﬁrst 6 to 8 weeks post inoculation (PI). Intermi ent shedding of
the organism in low numbers has been noted for up to 60 weeks
PI and may continue for at least 2 years. Urinary excretion begins
between 4 to 8 weeks after the onset of bacteremia and continues
for at least 3 months. Concentrations of 103 to 106 organisms/mL

vetexamprep.ir

of urine have been found in males, with lesser numbers of bacteria
in the urine of females. 9 At one time, urine of infected males was
thought to contain too few organisms to be infectious by the
oronasal route; however, studies have demonstrated that B. canis
can be transmi ed from infected to uninfected mature male dogs
after several weeks or months of close contact with infected dogs.
23 , 24 The propensity of males to shed the organism in the urine is
probably related to the localization of Brucella in the prostate and
epididymis, which are in close association with the urinary
bladder. Neutering helps reduce this risk to a large extent but
does not prevent shedding. Alternative means of transmission
occur less frequently under natural circumstances; low numbers
of organisms have been found in feces, nasal, and ocular
secretions. Brucellae are stable in the environment for up to 2
months in the presence of cooler temperatures and organic debris.
9

Transplacental transmission and direct cutaneous inoculation
can also occur. 25 Although fomite-associated transmission can
occur under appropriate circumstances (transmission has been
reported after vaginoscopy), B. canis is short-lived outside the host
and is readily inactivated by common disinfectants, including
quaternary ammonium compounds, 1% sodium hypochlorite,
70% ethanol, iodine/alcohol solutions, and accelerated hydrogen
peroxide. 9
Canine brucellosis occurs most commonly as outbreaks in large
commercial kennels, and less commonly in privately owned and
housed dogs, although exceptions exist. 26–28 Determination of
seroprevalence is strongly inﬂuenced by the method of testing
used and its interpretation. The disease is endemic in the
Americas, Africa, and Asia. Although the geographic distribution
of canine brucellosis is not fully understood, increased incidence
has been seen in the southern-most United States and commonly
in Mexico, Central and South America, the People’s Republic of
China, and Japan. 29 , 30 These pa erns may be associated with an
increase in free-roaming, intact dogs. Among breeds in this
region, beagles and Labrador retrievers have a higher prevalence
of infection, as do feral dogs. Seroprevalence in an Indian
reservation in South Dakota was 6.8%, with a gradual decrease in
the prevalence over time. 31 Older dogs were more likely to be

vetexamprep.ir

seropositive than younger dogs. Of 943 dogs entering a Minnesota
shelter, 3.5% of owner-surrendered and 3.1% of strays were
positive using the 2-mercaptoethanol rapid slide agglutination
test (ME-RSAT) assay, 32 but only one positive dog, a dog from
Texas, was also positive on AGID. Among Mississippi shelters, the
seroprevalence using RSAT followed by ME-RSAT ranged from
0% to 8.6%. 33 In Michigan, prevalence of infection was low in
dogs from noncommercial breeders, but infection appeared to be
endemic in dogs being produced for pet ownership by
commercial facilities. 34 Using a multilocus variable number of
tandem repeats (VNTR) analysis (MLVA-13Bc method), 229
isolates of B. canis from the United States were grouped into three
major clusters and 10 genotype groups. 35 Cluster A mainly
contained genotype groups 1 and 2, with some 3 isolates; Cluster
B contained group 6 isolates; and the remaining isolates were in
Cluster C. Molecular typing methods such as VNTR and MLST
are increasingly being applied to investigations of B. canis
infections in dogs worldwide. 36 , 37
There are sporadic reports of canine brucellosis in Canada and
throughout continental Europe and the United Kingdom. 17 , 37–45
Australia and New Zealand appear to be free of the disease and
have strict importation requirements in hopes of avoiding
establishment of the disease. 46 Evidence of exposure to B. suis
was detected in one in 10 eastern Australian dogs that had
cointact with feral swine. 47 However, because infection with B.
canis is chronic and subclinical, the organism can readily be
imported into regions where the prevalence of disease is low
through the movement of subclinically infected dogs. The
increased practice and success of canine semen processing for
exportation (chilling and cryopreservation) for the purpose of
artiﬁcial insemination now makes canine brucellosis a concern
worldwide, as direct mucosal contact among dogs is no longer
necessary for transmission. 16

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The general sequence of events after infection by Brucella is
summarized in Fig. 71.1. Brucella organisms a ach to and

vetexamprep.ir

penetrate mucous membranes; the severity of disease resulting is
proportional to the infectious dose. Because they contain the
highest concentration of organisms, vaginal discharge and semen
of infected dogs are the most likely sources for infection by
mucosal contamination. Brucella organisms have the ability to
replicate intracellularly and be transmi ed to new individuals,
maintaining infection within the population of their respective
reservoir host. Bacteria are phagocytized at contaminated mucosal
sites by tissue macrophages and other phagocytic cells and
transported to lymphatic and genital tract tissues where they
multiply. After replication in regional lymph nodes, bacteremia
occurs within 7 to 30 days after exposure and can persist up to 64
months. Brucella canis has a predilection for steroid-dependent
(reproductive)
tissues;
subsequent
dissemination
to
reticuloendothelial cells, the prostate, gravid uterus, testes,
epididymides, and placenta occurs. The organism survives
facultatively within monocytes and macrophages of the
reticuloendothelial system, avoiding or suppressing host
bactericidal mechanisms. Brucella organisms survive and multiply
in reticuloendothelial cells because they inhibit the bactericidal
myeloperoxidase-peroxide-halide system through the release of
5′-guanosine and adenine. The organism inhibits TNF-α,
disrupting the bactericidal activity of natural killer cells and
macrophages. 48 Early in infection, polymorphonuclear cells and
macrophages kill intracellular B. canis relatively ineﬀectually.
Generalized lymphoreticular hyperplasia (Fig. 71.2A) and
hyperglobulinemia occur during the course of infection. As with
other intracellular parasites, CMI is probably the most important
defense mechanism against B. canis. Persistent, nonprotective
antibody titers are characteristic of such infections and appear to
have li le inﬂuence on the level of bacteremia or number of
organisms in tissues. The greatest numbers of B. canis organisms
are found in the lymph nodes, spleen, and tissues of gonadal
steroid dependency. Although usually conﬁned to mononuclear
phagocytes, they may enter other cells such as placental
epithelium.

vetexamprep.ir

Sequential pathogenesis of canine
brucellosis. MPS, mononuclear phagocyte
system.
FIG. 71.1

Brucella organisms can be found in the rough endoplasmic
reticulum of placental trophoblastic giant cells in an infected
dam’s gravid uterus. Severe necrotizing placentitis with infarction
of the labyrinth region, coagulation necrosis of the chorionic villi,
and necrotizing arteritis result in fetal death. Embryonic death
may occur as early as 20 days after mating. The organism can be
found in the gastric contents of aborted fetuses. The uterus is not a
favored site of growth in the nongravid or diestrual female.
The primary target of Brucella in the male dog are the portions
of the reproductive tract that participate in the maturation,
transport, and storage of spermatozoa. Pyospermia develops 3 to
4 months post infection. Necrotizing vasculitis and
granulomatous inﬂammation results in epididymal and
subsequent testicular pathology. 49 , 50 Microscopic epididymal
inﬂammation usually develops beginning 5 weeks after infection
(Fig. 71.2B). Granulomatous inﬂammation of the epididymides
and testes in males causes sperm leakage, which provokes the
immune system to produce a complex of anti-sperm agglutinating
antibodies and DTH reactions against sperm that are unrelated to
the antibodies against B. canis. The immune responses produced

vetexamprep.ir

against spermatozoa further contribute to the epididymitis and
orchitis resulting in eventual spermatogenic arrest and testicular
atrophy seen in most infected males. Epididymitis and orchitis
usually progress despite treatment because of their
immunodestructive pathogenesis. The organism can be found in
the prostate gland and urethra and is shed intermi ently in the
urine. The prostate gland may be a site of Brucella persistence in
intact males for months to years.
Brucella canis, similar to other bloodborne bacteria, may localize
in nonreproductive tissues such as the end-arterial circulation of
the intervertebral disc, causing discospondylitis (see Chapter 121).
Concurrent sacroiliitis was described in one dog. 51 Other tissues
that ﬁlter bloodborne organisms or immune complexes may
become involved, including the eye (anterior uveitis), kidney
(glomerulopathy), and meninges (meningoencephalitis).
Spontaneous recovery from infection may occur within 1 to
more than 5 years post infection; however, dogs with
intervertebral disc or ocular infections, both sequestered from the
immune system, usually develop progression of the disease unless
it is treated. Antibacterial therapy may accelerate the clinical
recovery of all dogs. Some dogs may have persistent bacteremia
throughout this time, whereas others can harbor bacteria in
tissues for several months after the bacteremia ceases. Despite
tissue persistence, when B. canis is no longer detected in the blood,
serum agglutination titers decrease (see Diagnosis). 52 Dogs that
recover naturally have low or negative agglutination titers and yet
are immune to reinfection, suggesting that protective immunity is
cell mediated. Recovered dogs that were challenged orally or IV
as long as 4 years after spontaneous recovery from experimental
infection were immune. 53 However, chronically infected dogs
that were successfully treated with antibacterials were susceptible
to oronasal challenge 12 weeks after treatment had been halted.
Immunosuppression with glucocorticoids and antilymphocyte
serum appears to increase the susceptibility of dogs to initial
infection, but it does not augment the severity of the disease or
alter the course of infection in experimentally infected dogs. 9

Despite generalized systemic infection with B. canis, adult dogs
rarely are seriously ill. The clinical systemic signs are often subtle
or absent. Owners of working dogs have occasionally reported
dry, lusterless coats, loss of vigor, and suboptimal athletic
performance. Nongravid females show no signs of disease other
than lymphadenomegaly (pharyngeal if orally acquired, inguinal
and pelvic if venereally acquired), which occurs in both sexes.
Ocular abnormalities and discospondylitis are frequently present
in the absence of other systemic signs of illness. For unknown
reasons, ocular abnormalities are often unilateral and include
uveitis and multifocal granulomatous chorioretinitis. The most
common ﬁnding in dogs with discospondylitis is episodic spinal
pain
resulting
in
gait
abnormalities
and
lethargy.
Meningoencephalitis may result in behavioral changes and
neurologic deﬁcits. Chronic multifocal pyogranulomatous
dermatitis that resembled lick granuloma lesions has also been
reported in an infected dog, but a direct causal relationship was
not established. 54 Osteomyelitis or polyarthritis of the
appendicular skeleton causes lameness of the aﬀected limb.
Infection of the bone that surrounded a total hip replacement was
described in two dogs, 9 and 12 months after surgery.

canis–affected bitch. Note the variation in fetal
development indicating that death occurred at
different stages. Courtesy of Patricia Olson, DVM,
FIG. 71.3

PhD, DACT.

Overt clinical signs usually involve reproductive disturbances
in sexually mature animals. The primary clinical sign of canine
brucellosis in the breeding bitch is pregnancy loss. Bitches usually
abort dead pups between 45 and 60 days of gestation but show no
other clinical signs. Pups are usually partially autolyzed, with
subcutaneous edema and congestion and hemorrhage of the
abdominal subcutaneous region. Moderate quantities of
serosanguinous peritoneal eﬀusions are found. Their appearance
suggests fetal death in utero some time before abortion (Fig. 71.3).
Decomposed fetuses are not usually found because the bitch
ingests them. Abortion is typically followed by a brown or

vetexamprep.ir

greenish-gray vaginal discharge that lasts for 1 to 6 weeks.
Brucellosis should be suspected under any circumstance when
apparently healthy bitches abort 2 weeks before term. Less
commonly, bitches may carry infected puppies to term and whelp
both live and dead puppies within a single li er. Most pups that
are born alive will die within a few hours or days, but those that
survive or that are infected as neonates usually have generalized
peripheral lymphadenomegaly as the primary clinical
manifestation of disease until they reach sexual maturity. Such
puppies usually have persistent hyperglobulinemia, and some
may have transient fever, leukocytosis, or seizures as the systemic
manifestations of their infections. 9
Although abortion of dead puppies is the primary clinical sign
of reproductive failure reported with brucellosis, conception
failures can occur at any time after breeding. Embryonic death
may occur as early as 20 days after mating. Bitches with
pregnancy loss early in gestation (resorption) can appear to be
infertile (failure to conceive) unless early ultrasonographic
pregnancy evaluation was performed to identify pregnancy. As
with brucellosis in other species, infections with B. canis do not
interfere with normal estrous cycles. A high proportion of bitches
that abort may have normal li ers subsequently. However, even
after having normal li ers, some infected bitches experience
intermi ent reproductive failures and remain infectious to their
oﬀspring. 55 , 56

chorioretinal lesions (arrows) from a dog with

In male dogs, a variable degree of subfertility progressing to
infertility exists in all cases. Small li er size or failure to produce
pregnancy can be reported. Libido can be reduced and pain can be
associated with ejaculation. A decreased volume of ejaculate is
usually present. Clients are often unaware of the physical
abnormalities of the epididymides or testes; in contrast, scrotal
dermatitis is usually recognized because it causes self-excoriation.

Physical Examination Findings
Fever is uncommon and, with the exception of males, which
commonly have physical changes to the external genitalia, most
infections will not be diagnosed by routine history or physical
examination. Generalized peripheral lymphadenomegaly can be
present and splenomegaly may be detected on abdominal
palpation. Dogs with meningoencephalitis can exhibit behavioral
changes, anisocoria, ataxia, hyperesthesia, head tilt, and circling.
Dogs with discospondylitis initially exhibit spinal pain and later
paresis and ataxia if spinal cord compression develops. Delayed
placing reactions, pelvic limb hyperreﬂexia, and, uncommonly,
pelvic limb paresis or tetraparesis can occur. The presence of
splenomegaly or abdominal lymphadenomegaly in dogs with
discospondylitis should raise suspicion for B. canis infection.

vetexamprep.ir

Signs of ocular involvement include blepharospasm,
conjunctival hyperemia, evidence of uveitis such as aqueous ﬂare,
iris hyperpigmentation, loss of the normal contour of the iris
surface, hypopyon, posterior synechiae, and secondary glaucoma.
Corneal edema, vitreous opacities, swelling and hyperemia of the
optic disc, and evidence of multifocal granulomatous
chorioretinitis have also been described (Fig. 71.4). 21 , 57
Polyarthritis secondary to immune stimulation can be evidenced
by joint pain on palpation, decreased range of motion, or
lameness.
Aﬀected bitches in diestrus or anestrus can have normal
physical examination ﬁndings. Because of the prominent
testicular abnormalities, male dogs are presented for examination
more often than are females. Males otherwise appear to be in
good health. Aﬀected dogs commonly have scrotal enlargement
early in the course of disease due to epididymitis with or without
orchitis (Fig. 71.5). Serosanguinous scrotal edema can be present,
as well as scrotal erythema secondary to dermatitis from
excoriation or a secondary bacterial dermatopathy (Fig. 71.6).
Testicular atrophy and asymmetry are common chronic sequelae.

The urinalysis is generally within normal limits, even when B.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Abdominal radiographs can show splenomegaly in dogs with
systemic brucellosis. Plain radiography of the spine can show
evidence of either multifocal or focal discospondylitis (Fig. 71.7).
Advanced imaging (CT or MRI) may be more sensitive than plain

vetexamprep.ir

radiography for detection of endplate lucency (Fig. 71.8); see also
Chapter 121).
Sonographic Findings
Abdominal ultrasound examination of dogs with brucellosis can
show no abnormalities, or abdominal lymphadenomegaly and
splenomegaly can be present (Fig. 71.9A and B). Ultrasound of the
prostate may reveal prostatic irregularity, hyperechogenicity, and
parenchymal cysts typical of intact males. Ultrasound of the
scrotum and scrotal contents can conﬁrm the presence of edema
of the tunics, epididymal enlargement with hyperechogenicity,
testicular enlargement and hyperechogenicity, or atrophy and loss
of parenchymal detail (Fig. 71.10). 59

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
Aspirates of the spleen or lymph nodes of dogs with brucellosis
reveal lymphoid reactivity on cytologic examination, sometimes
with plasmacytosis. Scrotal edema is serosanguinous. Prostatic
aspirates in one dog with prostatitis showed granulomatous
inﬂammation with intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli. 42
CSF analysis in dogs with Brucella discospondylitis is usually
unremarkable. Pleocytosis, primarily consisting of neutrophils,
and increased protein concentration can occur with
meningoencephalitis, but they are unremarkable when
discospondylitis alone is present. 8 Aspirates of ocular ﬂuids
(aqueous or vitreous humor) from a dog with panophthalmitis
revealed pyogranulomatous inﬂammation with extracellular and
intracellular small gram-negative cocci. 25
Semen Examination
Sperm morphology should always be evaluated in dogs with
infertility because of the obvious abnormalities that occur with
brucellosis. Clinicians should keep in mind the potential
infectious nature of semen during collection and evaluation.
Semen abnormalities, evident by 5 weeks post infection, become
pronounced by 8 weeks. Diminished sperm counts (oligospermia),
poor motility (asthenospermia), and increased morphologic

vetexamprep.ir

abnormalities (teratospermia) are characteristic of semen in dogs
infected with Brucella, but are not speciﬁc for the disease.
Detached sperm heads, proximal and distal cytoplasmic droplets,
and acrosomal deformities are the most common morphologic
abnormalities (Fig. 71.11). By week 15 post infection, sperm headto-head agglutination suggests the presence of anti-sperm
antibodies. Large aggregates of inﬂammatory cells, usually
consisting of neutrophils, surround adherent macrophages
containing phagocytized sperm. More than 90% of the sperm are
abnormal by 20 weeks post infection. A lack of sperm cells
(azoopermia) without inﬂammatory cells corresponds with the
development of bilateral testicular atrophy.
Bacterial Isolation and Identification
Despite improvements in serologic diagnostic methods, blood
cultures are still indicated to conﬁrm infection if possible when
brucellosis is suspected. 52 A positive B. canis culture has been
advocated as the best diagnostic test in the ﬁrst 2 months of the
disease; however, dogs can be abacteremic 27 to 64 months after
disease onset despite active infection. Isolation of B. canis is time
consuming but not diﬃcult because the organism grows well
aerobically on conventional media used for other Brucella spp..
Only a positive result is deﬁnitive, because there are numerous
reasons for isolation failure. Of the Brucella spp. that infect dogs or
humans, B. canis is the only one with a consistent mucoid (rough)
colonial morphology because its cell wall contains truncated LPS
moieties. Isolation of the organism from blood, the most practical
ﬂuid for isolating the organism, is the most deﬁnitive diagnostic
procedure. Blood culture should not be the sole test used to
diagnose infection because bacteremia, although generally
sustained, may be absent or intermi ent in more chronically
infected animals. Antibacterial administration may interfere with
successful isolation of the organism. Blood culture can be helpful
if serologic tests are ambiguous. Whole blood must be taken for
culture because the organisms are associated with the leukocyte
fraction. Bacteremia is detected 2 to 4 weeks after oronasal
infection and, if untreated, persists for long periods (1 to 2 years
or more). Urine culture is positive in some dogs, especially males,
when blood culture is negative; however, unless cystocentesis is
performed, urinary isolation of B. canis may be diﬃcult because of

vetexamprep.ir

overgrowth by urethral contaminants. However, urine collected
via the urethra may have greater levels of semen, which is a
predominant source of B. canis organisms. Collection of semen by
ejaculation is valuable for culture during the ﬁrst 3 months of
infection, when the concentration of organisms is greatest. With
discospondylitis, culture of disc or bone specimens removed at
surgery, or material from needle aspiration of the disc space, may
also be cultured. Of dogs with Brucella discospondylitis or
ophthalmitis, 6 of 15 dogs tested positive by blood culture, 3 of 13
by urine culture, and 4 of 6 by culture of disc material or bone
chips from the intervertebral disc space obtained at surgery. 19 , 49
Brucella canis can be isolated from tissue specimens collected at
surgery or necropsy. The lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone
marrow, and male reproductive organs are the most common
sources even though gross lesions are seldom present in these
organs. In the dam, post-abortion uterus, fetuses, placentas, and
vaginal or uterine ﬂuids most consistently yield positive cultures.
False-negative results may occur in chronically infected animals
because of extremely low numbers of organisms present.
Centrifugation lysis methods may be advantageous under these
circumstances because they increase the ability to culture
intracellular pathogens. 39 Growth of Brucella can be identiﬁed on
the basis of rough (as opposed to smooth) colony morphology,
staining characteristics, and slide agglutination with anti-Brucella
serum. Identiﬁcation to the species level is best done by an
experienced laboratory. Diﬀerentiation between B. canis and B.
suis can be diﬃcult. Recently, MALDI-TOF MS has been useful in
assisting with rapid identiﬁcation of B. canis. 60 In the United
States, the New York State Diagnostic Laboratory at Cornell
University, the Tifton Veterinary Diagnostic and Investigational
Laboratory in Georgia, and the University of Florida are
recognized to be reliable for deﬁnitive testing made necessary by
positive B. canis screening tests in dogs intended for breeding, or
for clinically aﬀected dogs undergoing evaluation for infertility or
abortion, or when outbreaks are being managed. Susceptibility
testing can be performed, but in vitro test results may not correlate
well with the in vivo treatment response.

Serologic Diagnosis
Serologic testing is the most frequently used diagnostic method
for detecting canine brucellosis. There are two reasons to perform
serologic tests for brucellosis in dogs: (1) as part of a routine
screening program in breeding kennels, whereby healthy dogs are
screened for infection, and (2) for the initial diagnostics in sick
dogs that are suspected to have brucellosis because of infertility,
pregnancy
loss,
epididymitis/orchitis,
discospondylitis,
ophthalmitis or unexplained lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly.
Assays used for screening purposes are usually rapid and
inexpensive, but can suﬀer from low speciﬁcity due to strong
cross-reactivity between surface LPS antigens of B. canis and those
of other less or nonpathogenic infectious agents. Up to 50% to 60%
of dogs can have false-positive test results because of crossreacting antibodies to microorganisms such as Bordetella,
Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli, and Moraxella spp. All sera should be

vetexamprep.ir

pp
free of hemolysis because hemoglobin causes false-positive
agglutination of the tube test antigen.
Even when antibodies detected truly represent anti-Brucella
antibodies, the presence of these antibodies does not indicate
active infection with Brucella because dogs can remain
seropositive for months after they clear the infection. Antibodies
to Brucella do not become detectable until 2 to 12 weeks after
infection despite the presence of bacteremia at 2 weeks, so a
window of time exists in which an infected dog eludes serologic
diagnosis with any assay used. For this reason, newly acquired
animals should be tested sequentially at least twice at 30-day
intervals before introduction into a breeding kennel. Low or
intermediate titers may reﬂect previous or very recent infection,
and testing should be repeated, or a empts made to detect the
organism by blood culutre or PCR. 60 Males may harbor the
organism in the prostate glands and epididymides for extended
periods after bacteremia ceases. In such instances, agglutination
titers may decline naturally or as a result of treatment, yielding
false-negative test results. Beyond the ﬁrst 3 months of infection,
the sensitivity of screening assays is generally believed to be high.

Examples of screening assays include the RSAT; the
semiquantitative
ME-RSAT;
the
semiquantitative
tube
agglutination test (TAT); AGID assays; and indirect IFA or ELISA
assays. Veterinarians need to understand the limitations of the
assays available to them through local veterinary diagnostic
laboratories or in-house test kits. The RSAT uses B. ovis as the
antigen, whereas the ME-RSAT uses B. canis antigen, which may
improve speciﬁcity. However, in one study, the sensitivity of the
ME-RSAT was only 32%, when compared with 71% for the RSAT,
so the RSAT may be preferable for screening. 61 In the TAT, a titer
of more than 1:200 correlates well with positive blood cultures,
but lower titers are more diﬃcult to interpret. The performance of
AGID assays requires trained laboratory personnel and special
media. Two AGID assays are available: an assay that uses cell wall
antigens as the substrate (cell wall AGID assay) and an assay that
uses cytoplasmic antigens of Brucella as the substrate (cytoplasmic
AGID assay). The cell wall assay has the same low speciﬁcity as
other assays that detect antibodies to Brucella LPS, and the
sensitivity may be lower than that of the RSAT. 62 In contrast, the
cytoplasmic assay is speciﬁc for antibodies to Brucella, so, when
available, it is a useful conﬁrmatory assay for dogs that test
positive with other rapid serologic assays (Fig. 71.12). 63 Indirect
IFA has lower sensitivity than many other serologic assays. A
number of ELISA assays have been developed to overcome
diﬃculties that relate to the low speciﬁcity of serologic assays for
B. canis and the limited availability of other assays. The
performance of these ELISA assays has varied, but sensitive and
speciﬁc ELISA assays and a lateral ﬂow immunoassay have been
developed that may prove useful for rapid serologic testing in the
future. 64

In practice, for screening purposes, healthy bitches are tested at
least 1 month before a planned breeding with a serologic assay of
low speciﬁcity such as the RSAT because these assays are rapid,
readily available, and inexpensive. Healthy, fertile stud dogs
should be tested at least annually with the RSAT (and require that
all bitches be screened and negative before contact breedings). A
single high agglutination titer to B. canis usually indicates active
infection, but this should be substantiated by additional tests.
Dogs that are subclinical but have positive results on
agglutination procedures should never be condemned as infected
until blood culture results or the more speciﬁc cytoplasmic
