In cases of subfertility or if recent exposure is suspected and the
RSAT result is negative, a second test is performed a month later
to assess for seroconversion (which would be expected if the dog
was early in the course of infection when ﬁrst tested); the dog
should not be used for breeding in the interim. If the test result is
then positive, a conﬁrmatory assay should be performed. This
could include the TAT or a more speciﬁc assay, such as the
cytoplasmic AGID assay, a speciﬁc ELISA assay, blood or semen
culture (although blood culture can lack sensitivity), or a nucleic
acid-detection assay. The use of multiple assays may be required
to conﬁrm the diagnosis.
Chronically infected dams may have diagnostically equivocal
antibody titers and negative blood cultures. In females,

vetexamprep.ir

recrudescence of bacteremia and increased antibody titers develop
during proestrus, estrus, pregnancy, or abortion. These are the
most reliable times to screen subfertile or infertile dams for
infection.
Serologic tests should be evaluated in light of clinical ﬁndings
in the dog being evaluated (Fig. 71.13). Antibacterial therapy may
suppress bacteremia and the associated serologic response,
possibly contributing to false-negative serologic test results and
failure to isolate the organism from infected dogs. Antibacterials
should not be given until diagnostic testing has been completed.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
A variety of PCR assays have been developed for detection of B.
canis DNA in clinical specimens. In one study, PCR on whole
blood was more sensitive than blood culture or serology for
detection of canine infection. 61 PCR assays have been used to
successfully identify B. canis in semen from dogs with negative
culture results, which suggests that this may ultimately be the
most sensitive method of testing as part of the male dog prebreeding evaluation, especially in cases where management of an
outbreak is the concern. PCR testing of vaginal swab specimens
was more sensitive than blood culture or blood PCR in dams
suspected to be infected with B. canis. 62 PCR assays were also
used to detect B. canis in the aqueous humor of dogs with
endophthalmitis, and in lymph node aspirates. 21 , 58 Brucella canis
DNA has also been detected in multiple tissues from stillborn
fetuses and neonates at necropsy. Assays have been designed that
diﬀerentiate among Brucella species. 57 A real-time PCR assay was
used to detect B. canis in tissue specimens, urine, buﬀy coat, and
intervertebral disc material of a dog with discospondylitis when
culture of intervertebral disc material, blood, and urine was
negative. 9
Positive serologic test results in dogs with discospondylitis or
other disease manifestations suggestive of brucellosis should be
conﬁrmed using culture or a NAAT whenever possible. Although
uncommon, false-negative serologic test results can occur in dogs
with discospondylitis, so a empts should also be made to detect
the organism with culture or NAATs. Of various dogs with B.
canis discospondylitis or ophthalmitis, 15 of 18 were positive with

vetexamprep.ir

the RSAT, 16 of 16 were positive with the TAT, and 6 of 7 were
positive with AGID assays. The three dogs that were negative
with the RSAT had discospondylitis. One was positive by blood
culture, and the other two dogs tested positive with the TAT at a
later date. 19 , 21
Further studies are needed in dogs to determine if PCR
methods can be used as a predictor of successful eradication of the
organism. Several veterinary diagnostic laboratories in the United
States as well as veterinary academic laboratories now oﬀer realtime PCR assays for detection of B. canis on a commercial basis.

Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
Macroscopic changes in adults or surviving pups are usually
conﬁned to lymphadenomegaly and splenomegaly.
Histopathologic Findings
Lymph node enlargement is the result of diﬀuse lymphoreticular
hyperplasia. In dogs with chronic bacteremia, lymph node
sinusoids and the spleen are ﬁlled with plasma cells and
macrophages containing phagocytized bacteria. Diﬀuse
submucosal lymphocytic inﬁltration occurs in all genitourinary
organs. A necrotizing vasculitis occurs in the target tissues of
gonadal steroids, including the prostate, scrotum, sheath, or
vulva. Lesions are most prominent in the prostate, epididymides,
and uterus, whereas milder changes are observed in the renal
pelvis, testes, ductus deferens, urinary bladder, and ureters.
Extensive necrosis of the prostatic parenchyma and seminiferous
tubules is caused by inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration, which
eventually results in atrophy or ﬁbrosis. A chronic to subacute
endometritis can be seen in the uterus, with glandular hyperplasia
and reticular cell nodules (Fig. 71.14). Focal hepatic necrosis,
myocarditis, and meningoencephalitis also have been described.
Vertebral osteomyelitis and discospondylitis may be present in
dogs with discospondylitis. Renal abnormalities occur in some
dogs and consist of hyaline thickening of the basement membrane
of glomeruli with minimal cellular inﬁltration or proliferation. A
mild interstitial nephritis has been noted. Ocular disease includes
granulomatous iridocyclitis and exudative retinitis, with diﬀuse

vetexamprep.ir

inﬁltration by lymphocytes, plasmacytes, and neutrophils.
Corneal endothelium has vacuolated cytoplasm with variable
plasma cell inﬁltration; exudates with leukocytes are present in
the anterior chamber. Placental trophoblasts can contain large
numbers of gram-negative bacteria, and coagulative necrosis may
be present. In male dogs, lesions are more likely to be restricted to
the reproductive system. Special stains (e.g., Brown-Brenn stain)
must be used to detect intracellular organisms. IHC has been used
to conﬁrm the presence of Brucella spp. in placental tissues (Fig.
71.15).

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

In certain jurisdictions, brucellosis is a reportable disease in dogs
or in humans; once a diagnosis is conﬁrmed, proper authorities
should be notiﬁed. Any dog in contact with the conﬁrmed case
should be quarantined and carefully evaluated for infection over a
60-day period. Infected dogs should be isolated from further
contact with other dogs until they are less likely to be contagious.
In breeding kennels, the infected dog should never be used for
breeding again and should be removed from the breeding
program. Infected males are very unlikely ever to regain fertility
and should be neutered to reduce shedding. Infected females can
regain fertility, but infection can persist. This means that they
represent a source of infection for other dogs and that they are at
risk for future loss of oﬀspring; they also should be neutered.
Eradication of the disease in breeding kennel situations has not
been successful without removal of all current or historically
infected dogs. Carrier dogs are important in maintaining B. canis
infection in the dog population because its survival outside the
host is short lived. Application of routine hospital disinfectants
can inactivate the bacterium. The risk of infecting males when
breeding with previously infected females can be minimized by
judicious artiﬁcial insemination. Breeding of such animals should
be done only under exceptional circumstances when it is
considered essential (e.g., to prevent the loss of a valuable blood
line) and after the risk is explained to an owner.
Because of the zoonotic potential of the disease and diﬃculty in
eradicating the infection, euthanasia of aﬀected dogs has been
recommended; this is an unacceptable decision for many private
breeders/hobby kennels or pet owners, leading to requests for
therapy. Neutering is always indicated. Neutering decreases the
number of organisms shed in semen, urine, and vaginal discharge,
but does not eradicate infection.
Antibiotic therapy for treatment of brucellosis has historically
not been rewarding, likely because the organism is intracellular
and bacteremia is periodic. Antimicrobial drug treatment can
reduce antibody titers without clearing infection. Relapses are
common. Bacteremia often recurs days to months after treatment
is discontinued, making follow-up evaluation essential because
animals can still sequester infection in tissues. Antibody titers can
persist when infection has been cleared, making interpretation
diﬃcult. The organism is susceptible to several antibacterials, but

vetexamprep.ir

the ineﬀectiveness of in vivo therapy commonly leads to failures
or relapses. None of the treatment regimens is 100% successful.
For greatest eﬃcacy, dogs with brucellosis should not be treated
with a single antibacterial regimen; in all cases, combination
therapy should be used.

aUse in combination with one of the other drugs listed. Combinations of drugs
are preferred for treatment where possible.

Combination therapy should be used whenever possible,
preferably with tetracyclines (high-dose doxycycline or
minocycline) for at least 1 to 2 months and an aminoglycoside
(streptomycin or gentamicin) for the ﬁrst 1 to 2 weeks of treatment
(Table 71.2). Some also advocate use of two 1-week courses of
aminoglycoside treatment spaced 1 month apart, or treatment
with streptomycin every other week for 4–8 weeks. Combination
therapy with tetracyclines and streptomycin is thought to be the
most successful treatment, but unavailability of streptomycin,
nephrotoxicity, parenteral therapy requirements, and expense
may be problematic. 38 , 42 , 44 In addition, aminoglycosides do not
provide adequate ocular or CNS penetration for dogs with
ophthalmitis or meningitis. A combination of doxycycline and
rifampin has been used to treat human brucellosis but may not be
well tolerated by dogs because of GI adverse eﬀects. The use of
three or four drugs in combination (e.g., streptomycin,
enroﬂoxacin, doxycycline with or without rifampin) was
eﬃcacious for treatment of ophthalmitis in dogs. Topical 1%
prednisolone acetate and atropine ointment may be required for
management of uveitis. 65–67
One study reported a possible beneﬁt of therapy with
enroﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg, q12h, PO for 4 weeks, often for multiple
courses) in a small group of infected dogs. Enroﬂoxacin did not
completely eliminate B. canis, but it maintained fertility and
avoided the recurrence of abortions, transmission of the disease to

vetexamprep.ir

subsequently whelped puppies, and dissemination of
microorganisms during parturition. Ultimately, however, most
treated dogs remained culture positive. Clinical reproductive
illness may have been prevented; however, conﬁrmation of
eradication of the organism could not be conﬁrmed. 28
Combinations of enroﬂoxacin and doxycycline may be a more
eﬀective alternative for dogs unable to tolerate aminoglycoside or
rifampin treatment and for dogs that have ocular or CNS
involvement, but studies are lacking. Localized infections in hardto-reach areas such as in the intervertebral disc should be treated
with at least two or more sequential or intermi ent 4-week
courses of antimicrobial therapy after neutering. Treatment for 6
weeks or longer may be necessary and should be based on
clinical, radiographic, and serologic monitoring. 22 Doxycycline
and aminoglycoside combination is recommended for this
treatment. Surgical intervention is rarely needed unless the
diagnostic workup requires obtaining intervertebral tissues for
culture. Decompressive surgery should be avoided in paraparetic
dogs when possible by ﬁrst evaluating the clinical response to
antimicrobial therapy. Sequential radiography and titers at 3- to 6month intervals are used to monitor progress. Serologic
monitoring should be done with quantitative methods so that
relative changes can be detected. Endophthalmitis with B. canis
has been exceedingly diﬃcult to treat and requires long courses of
therapy with potent three- or four-drug combinations. There are
few reports of successful elimination of ocular infection in dogs.
The organism enters the eye, 68 and the ocular tissues are diﬃcult
to penetrate, especially with aminoglycosides. Enucleation is
required if the eye has been severely damaged, because vision will
never return and the eye acts as a persistent nidus for the
organism. Even use of two antimicrobials is associated with
relapse rates of ocular inﬂammation of 6% to 21%. Multiple-drug
combination therapy with doxycycline, gentamicin, enroﬂoxacin,
and subsequent addition of rifampin was successful in eliminating
the ocular inﬂammation in one infected dog. 69 As with other CNS
infections, therapy with antimicrobials must be at maximal levels
to obtain reasonable drug concentrations at the site of infection.
Furthermore, as the blood–CNS barrier heals, concentrations will
be much more diﬃcult to achieve. Aminoglycosides are of li le
use in clearing infections from the CNS.

vetexamprep.ir

Follow-up is always required after any course of antimicrobial
therapy. Antimicrobial regimens must be repeated should the
results indicate that infection has not been eliminated. Cures of
brucellosis must not be assumed because bacteremia may recur
weeks or months after antibacterials are discontinued. A empted
culture of bacteria or serologic testing immediately after treatment
is halted is deceiving. Reports of successful cures should be
viewed with caution unless subsequent cultures and serology and
PCR have been performed for at least 6 months. Use of
quantitative ME-TAT titers is the best means of monitoring
successful elimination of the organism. Testing should be
performed at 6- to 9-month intervals after a treatment regimen.
Titer values should decrease if therapy is eﬀective. Titers below
100 should be reached or else additional courses of treatment are
indicated. Corresponding AGID titers results should also become
negative. Persistence of increased (greater than 100) titers should
evoke suspicion that the infection still exists.
Large commercial kennels (puppy mills) present the most
challenging scenario. Owners are usually willing to euthanize
conﬁrmed positive cases but less willing to go through the
expense and time required to eradicate the disease from the
facility. Diﬃculties are compounded if antibacterial therapy is
instituted when brucellosis is suspected but not conﬁrmed,
because isolation of B. canis becomes uncertain and serologic tests
results are questionable. A kennel should be quarantined as soon
as the diagnosis of B. canis is ascertained, and infected animals
should be promptly eliminated. Appropriate disinfection
procedures should be implemented to arrest the spread of
infection via fomites. Persons working with infected dogs and
their discharges or secretions should wear gloves until serotesting
can be done to determine the extent of the infection. Animals
should not be admi ed to or released from the kennel until the
disease is eradicated. Movement of dogs within a colony also
should be restricted to removal of proven and suspect cases to
isolation quarters. New additions are at high risk for infection,
especially if dogs are not individually penned, which also
increases the number of animals requiring repeated testing during
the eradication process. Animals must not be released for sale or
any other purpose because they may spread the disease. All dogs
in an infected kennel should be serotested for at least 3 months

vetexamprep.ir

after seronegative status is achieved, especially before each
breeding, even if artiﬁcial insemination is used. If animals are
retained as pets or working dogs, or if treatment is contemplated,
they should be neutered and moved to separate housing.
Although determining the origin of infections is important, this
has proved diﬃcult because of the reluctance of owners to reveal
actual or suspected sources.
Preventive measures are particularly important in large
breeding kennels or wherever a large number of dogs are kept,
but no legally mandated control measures exist, and in the United
States, canine brucellosis is not a reportable disease in most states.
Prevention is accomplished by quarantine of all new acquisitions
until two serotest results at a 1-month interval are negative.
Animals from kennels known to have had breeding problems
should be rejected unless test results are negative. 70 Animals with
any clinical sign of canine brucellosis should be rejected. Animals
used for breeding should be tested 3 to 4 weeks before each
mating to allow time for test results to be reported. Dams should
not be mated to stud dogs unless they have been tested and
certiﬁed negative. If dogs leave a colony, they should be tested
before readmission. All canine blood donors should be screened
for brucellosis using serology because of the potential for
transmission through transfusion of contaminated blood
products. 71

Immunity And Vaccination
Serum agglutinating antibodies do not protect against infection in
the dog as immunity likely depends on CMI. Presently, the
development of a vaccine is considered undesirable because
Brucella vaccines evaluated have oﬀered only moderate protection,
and immunized dogs develop antibodies that confound
serodiagnosis. A promising vaccine candidate based on a B. ovis
mutant was able to protect dogs against challenge with B. canis;
dogs developed antibodies to rough Brucella spp. 72 Such a vaccine
may be useful if the serologic response can be diﬀerentiated from
that to B. canis through diagnostic test design.

Prevention

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention of infection and elimination of infected dogs should be
the principal control strategy in kennels. Prevention requires at
least yearly testing of all breeding stock and testing of all dogs to
be introduced into a kennel. Ideally, two negative screening tests
performed at least a month apart should occur before a dog or
bitch is introduced into a breeding facility. Conﬁrmed positive
dogs should be isolated (euthanasia is advised by some),
neutered, treated, and tested monthly (AGID, blood culture, or
PCR assay on blood) until two consecutive negative tests occur,
although occult infection can still be present.
Private breeders should require serologic screening of all female
dogs oﬀered for breeding. Should positive test results occur on
screening, breeders should not accept dogs unless follow-up
testing with conﬁrmatory assays is negative. Artiﬁcial
insemination without dog-to-dam contact should be used if any
concern exists. Stud dogs should be screened at least annually.
Because of the potential for non-venereal transmission, screening
of maiden dogs and bitches before breeding is also recommended.
15 , 22

Prevention of brucellosis in dogs caused by other species of
Brucella involves avoidance of raw meat diets, hunting activities,
and consumption of products of livestock parturition on farms. 11–

13

Public Health Aspects
Humans can become infected with B. canis, 73 , 74 although they
are relatively resistant to infection and other Brucella species
account for the majority of human disease, especially B. melitensis
(Fig. 71.16). The majority of human brucellosis cases in the United
States caused by all species of Brucella are reported from
California, Texas, Arizona, and Florida (Fig. 71.17).
Approximately 40 cases of human infection with B. canis have
been reported worldwide; however, the actual number is
unknown, and the close contact that exists between humans and
dogs increases the signiﬁcance of the zoonotic risk posed.
Brucellosis is the most commonly reported laboratory-acquired
infection. 75 Serologic assays used for diagnosis of brucellosis in
humans often do not detect antibodies to B. canis, so the disease
may be overlooked. Transmission to humans most commonly

vetexamprep.ir

occurs through contact with an infected dog’s semen, vulvar
discharge from an infected bitch, aborted fetuses or placentas, or
through direct, accidental laboratory exposure. Thus, disease is
more likely to occur in people who are in contact with breeding
dogs, but disease occasionally occurs in the owners of pet dogs
with discospondylitis. Immunocompromised humans, children,
and those who are pregnant may be at greater risk for
development of disease. Infection of humans with B. canis
typically results in nonspeciﬁc, persistent clinical signs of fever,
muscle aches, night sweats, and general malaise. Rarely,
granulomatous hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis,
pulmonary disease, and endocarditis have been reported. In one
case report, disease occurred in an HIV-infected dachshund dog
breeder who reported infertility in one of the dogs, which had
been tested by a veterinarian and was seropositive with a
screening assay. Conﬁrmatory testing with AGID performed at a
university veterinary diagnostic laboratory yielded a negative
result, so brucellosis was not thought to be present. However,
subsequent blood culture of all the dogs in the household was
positive in one other dog. 48 , 76 Aﬀected humans are typically
treated successfully with combinations of doxycycline and either
aminoglycosides (for the ﬁrst week) or rifampin, but monotherapy
has been associated with unacceptable rates of relapse.

Prevention of human disease involves eradication of the disease
in dog kennels; precautions such as the wearing of gloves and
protective clothing when in contact with aborted material; and
hand washing after handling dogs and before eating. Although it
is preferable that immunocompromised individuals do not
participate in dog breeding activities, if necessary, these
individuals should take special care if they interact with breeding
dogs. Contact with dogs with reproductive problems or their
secretions should be avoided whenever possible, and if aborted
material must be handled, gloves, gowns, and face protection
should be worn, all protective wear should be disposed of
properly, and hands should be washed thoroughly. 75 , 77 , 78–80

Case Example
Signalment

vetexamprep.ir

“Sadie,” a 6-year-old female spayed border collie mix from
northern California (Fig. 71.18).

History

Sadie was brought to her local veterinarian for listlessness and
reluctance to jump noted during the previous 48 hours. She had
been adopted from a local humane shelter and had been
ovariohysterectomized at 11 months of age. She lived in a rural
agricultural area in northern California and was the only dog in
the household; however, she was used for sheep herding with
several other dogs.

Current Medications

Sadie was not on any medications.

Physical Examination

Sadie’s vital signs were within normal limits, mucous
membrane color was pink, and she was quiet and alert on
physical examination. Body weight was 25 kg. Mild dental
tartar was evident. Thoracic auscultation and abdominal
palpation were unremarkable, pulses were synchronous, and
no peripheral lymphadenomegaly was evident. Palpable dorsal
thoracolumbar pain was demonstrated. She was reluctant to
rise but was ambulatory. The neurologic examination including
a funduscopic examination was normal.

Six-year-old female spayed
border collie mix with brucellosis.

FIG. 71.18

vetexamprep.ir

Laboratory Findings

A CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis with aerobic culture
were performed. Mild neutropenia (2,958 cells/µL; reference
range, 3,000–11,500 cells/µL) was found; the chemistries and
urinalysis were within normal limits with no proteinuria.

Imaging Findings

Radiographs of the spine revealed evidence of disc space
collapse, spondylosis, and probable discospondylitis at the T7T8 disc space (see Fig. 71.7).

Microbiologic Testing

A SNAP 4Dx Plus test (IDEXX Laboratories) for antigen of
Diroﬁlaria immitis and antibodies to Ehrlichia canis, Anaplasma
phagocytophilum, and Borrelia (Borreliella [incertae sedis])
burgdorferi was negative. Aerobic bacterial urine culture was
negative. Serum was submi ed for a B. canis IFA, which was
positive at a titer of 1:200. A B. canis AGID was submi ed and
was also positive.

Treatment

Sadie was treated with tramadol (1–2 mg/kg, PO, q8h) and
carprofen (3 mg/kg, PO, q12h). Once the serologic test results
were available, a tentative diagnosis of B. canis discospondylitis
was made, and she was treated with enroﬂoxacin (5.5 mg/kg,
PO, q12h). Clinical improvement was reported in 2 weeks, and
repeat radiographs were performed in 1 and 5 months.
Equivocal change was reported in the appearance of T7-T8 at 1
month, but the 5-month radiograph showed no progression,
suggesting the lesion was no longer active. The owners were
advised of the zoonotic potential of this disease and the
potential hazard of transmission to other dogs. The potential
need for lifelong intermi ent antibiotic therapy with risk of
relapses was also discussed. Repeat AGID testing post therapy
was advised. It was also advised that dogs in contact with Sadie
be screened for brucellosis.

Comments

Dogs with Brucella discospondylitis frequently are brought to
their veterinarian for clinical signs of spinal pain or lameness
that resemble common musculoskeletal injuries such as
intervertebral disc disease or rupture of the cranial cruciate

vetexamprep.ir

ligament. Although not typical, this case illustrates the fact that
B. canis disease can occur in a neutered female dog without any
breeding history, and often occurs in the absence of fever or
signiﬁcant abnormalities on routine laboratory testing. A
diagnosis of Brucella discospondylitis was strongly suspected
based on positive serologic test results with multiple assays.
Blood culture was not performed, but a urine culture was
negative. Monotherapy with ﬂuoroquinolones has been
associated with high rates of relapse in human patients once
antimicrobial drug treatment has been discontinued, so it is
generally not recommended. Nevertheless, it can occasionally
be successful.

72: Tetanus and Botulism
Jane E. Sykes, and Jamie M. Burki Creedon

KEY POINTS
• First Described: The etiology of tetanus was identified in the
late 1800s in Germany (Nicolaier). 1 Clostridium botulinum
and its toxin were first described in Belgium in 1897 (van
Ermengem). 2 Prior to that, descriptions of both tetanus and
botulism had been recorded; tetanus was described by
Hippocrates more than 2000 years ago.
• Causes: Tetanospasmin neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani
(tetanus); and botulinal neurotoxin of C. botulinum,
Clostridium baratii, or Clostridium butyricum (botulism).
• Affected Hosts: Both diseases affect humans and domestic
animals, including dogs and cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Both are ubiquitous organisms that
affect the worldwide population.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Inoculation of spores into a
wound (tetanus) or ingestion of preformed toxin (botulism).
• Major Clinical Signs: Spastic rigidity (tetanus) or flaccid
paralysis (botulism).
• Differential Diagnoses: Differential diagnoses for tetanus
include strychnine toxicosis, hypocalcemia, and masticatory
muscle myositis. Differential diagnoses for botulism include
causes of acute lower motor neuron disease such as
idiopathic polyradiculoneuritis (coonhound paralysis), tick
paralysis, coral snake envenomation, myasthenia gravis,
ionophore toxicosis, and paralytic rabies.
• Human Health Significance: Botulism and tetanus are not
directly transmissible from animals to humans, but care

vetexamprep.ir

should be taken when handling specimens from animals with
botulism.

Etiology: Tetanus and Botulism
Tetanus and botulism are neurologic diseases caused by the toxins
of Clostridium tetani and Clostridium botulinum, respectively. These
environmentally ubiquitous organisms are gram-positive,
anaerobic, spore-forming, rod-shaped bacteria, with worldwide
distributions. The spores of C. tetani and C. botulinum are
extremely hardy in the environment and resist boiling and
disinfection with alcohol or formalin.
The vegetative form of C. tetani produces the two toxins
tetanospasmin and tetanolysin. Botulism is caused by botulinal
neurotoxins (BoNTs), which comprise a family of seven
antigenically distinct toxins produced by C. botulinum (which
produces all seven BoNT types A–G), Clostridium butyricum (type
E only), and Clostridium baratii (type F only). Although these seven
neurotoxins are produced by a variety of clostridial organisms
and are themselves diﬀerent, they have identical toxicologic
eﬀects, and are thus considered together. BoNT is produced by
the sporulated or vegetative clostridial organism under anaerobic
conditions. Species susceptibility to BoNT serotypes varies. For
instance, most human cases of botulism are caused by BoNT types
A, B, or E. All reported clinical feline 3 and most canine 4–10 cases
of botulism have been caused by BoNT type C. Rare cases of
botulism caused by BoNT type D, 11 one likely caused by type A, 7
and one caused by type B 12 have been reported in dogs.
Tetanospasmin and BoNT have similar structures and
mechanisms of action even though they cause diseases that
contrast sharply with one another. Both toxins are among the
most potent toxins known with an LD50 of ≤ 1–5 ng/kg. 13 , 14 The
toxins consist of two polypeptide chains, a heavy (H) chain and a
light (L) chain, joined by a disulﬁde bond (Fig. 72.1). The H chain
a aches to presynaptic nerve terminal membrane receptors,
although the precise receptors have not been identiﬁed because of
the extremely low concentrations at which these toxins act.
Variation in receptor binding aﬃnities may explain diﬀerences in

vetexamprep.ir

species susceptibility to clostridial neurotoxins. The toxin is then
internalized via receptor-mediated endocytosis into the
presynaptic nerve terminal, where it has a local impact on nerve
cell function (BoNT) or travels by retrograde axonal transport to
the nerve cell body and diﬀuses into inhibitory interneurons,
where it impacts CNS inhibitory interneuron function
(tetanospasmin). The L chain, a zinc-dependent matrix
metalloproteinase, is released from the vesicle and subsequently
cleaves one or more docking proteins. These proteins are critical for
the release of neurotransmi ers from synaptic vesicles into the
synaptic cleft and are located on the membrane of synaptic
vesicles (synaptobrevin) or the presynaptic cell membrane (syntaxin
and SNAP-25). Synaptobrevin binds to the docking proteins
located on the presynaptic membrane. The resulting complex (the
SNARE complex) docks the synaptic vesicle at the proper location
for fusion and exocytosis of neurotransmi er molecules into the
synaptic space (Fig. 72.2). Tetanospasmin cleaves synaptobrevin,
whereas botulinum neurotoxin C cleaves syntaxin; other
botulinum neurotoxins cleave synaptobrevin or SNAP-25. The
process of recovery involves the sprouting of new presynaptic
terminals, followed by recovery of the original synapse, after
which new terminal outgrowths retract. 15

Tetanus
Epidemiology
Humans and horses are most susceptible to tetanus, and so
widespread vaccination against the disease is performed in these
species. Disease occurs occasionally in dogs and is rare in cats.
The development of tetanus in dogs and cats usually follows
introduction of environmental spores into a penetrating wound,
but more than one third of aﬀected dogs have no known wound
history (cryptogenic tetanus) 16 ; a similar prevalence of cryptogenic
tetanus has been reported in humans. 17 Traumatic wounds of the
feet, claws, or head; draining tracts associated with grass awn
migration; animal bite wounds; tick bite wounds; bleeding claw
trim wounds; wounds that result from chronic protozoal or fungal
infections of the skin; teething wounds in dogs; and surgical
wounds (particularly ovariohysterectomy and castration) have all

vetexamprep.ir

been implicated. 16 , 18–20 One study in dogs suggests that tetanus
occurs seasonally in the winter in England, though seasonality
was not found in dogs in California. 21 , 22 Although dogs of any
age, breed, or sex can develop tetanus, disease occurs most often
in young, large-breed, active, intact male dogs. 16 , 18 , 19 Disease is
seen in puppies as young as 8 weeks of age. Some studies describe
a signiﬁcant proportion of aﬀected dogs as less than 1 year of age.
Disease may be more severe in young than in mature dogs 16 ;
high mortality rates have been reported in the youngest people as
well. 23 Cats are often young animals with outdoor access, 24 but
cats of any age have been aﬀected. 25

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Clostridium tetani spores are introduced into tissues where they
germinate, replicate locally, and produce tetanospasmin toxin in
anaerobic conditions. Ingestion is not a route of transmission
because tetanospasmin is destroyed by GI secretions. Tetanolysin
appears to promote local tissue degradation at the site of
inoculation, which may optimize the tissue environment for

vetexamprep.ir

organism growth. The toxin is produced as a single polyprotein
that is cleaved extracellularly by a bacterial protease into the L
and H chains, which remain connected by the disulﬁde bond. It
then binds to presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons and is
internalized, travels up axons by retrograde axonal ﬂow, and
enters inhibitory interneurons in the brain and spinal cord, where
it interferes with the release of inhibitory neurotransmi ers aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glycine (see Fig. 72.2). Toxin can
also spread hematogenously to the CNS from the wound site. The
result is unhindered excitation of motor neurons, spastic rigidity,
and dysfunction of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous
systems. Clinical signs occur 3 days to 3 weeks after a wound in
both dogs and cats. Shorter incubation periods occur when the
inoculation site is nearer the CNS and when a large amount of
toxin is present. Paralysis may initially be localized to the wound
site but can then generalize. Involvement of the head is common
in dogs, and often owners of dogs with tetanus ﬁrst notice an
unusual appearance to their dog’s eyes, a “swollen” face, or
evidence of dysphagia. 16 Regurgitation or vomiting of food
occurs in less than 20% of aﬀected dogs, and a voice change or
dysuria may be noted. Abnormal activity during sleep (twitching,
running, vocalization) was documented in at least 46% of 50
surviving dogs with tetanus in the United Kingdom; these signs
resolved in approximately half of these dogs within 6 months. 26
Death occurs in severely aﬀected dogs due to paralysis of
respiratory muscles; infectious complications such as pneumonia;
upper airway obstruction; the development of severe
hyperthermia with DIC, multiple organ failure, and/or pulmonary
thromboembolism; and cardiac arrhythmias. 16 , 18 , 19 Hiatal
hernia and coxofemoral joint luxations have also been described
as complications of tetanus in dogs. 16 , 18 , 27 , 28 Disease in cats is
usually localized to the limbs, but generalized tetanus can occur.
24 , 25 , 29–35 Many aﬀected cats have an initial history of
disappearance or a recognized wound, after which rigid lameness
is noted.

Physical Examination Findings
Tetanus causes spastic muscle rigidity. Generalized tetanus involves
spastic rigidity of all four limbs in addition to muscles of the head.

vetexamprep.ir

Localized tetanus involves spasm in a single limb or region of the
body. Like humans, dogs more often experience generalized
tetanus; cats more often have localized tetanus, probably due to
the feline species’ relative resistance to tetanospasmin. Both
species can experience either type. The cephalic form of tetanus is
localized to the head secondary to a head wound; cephalic tetanus
is seen in humans and involves ﬂaccid facial paralysis that usually
precedes generalized tetanus with spastic rigidity 36 ; cephalic
tetanus has not been described in dogs or cats.
Dogs and cats with generalized tetanus experience rigidly
extended limbs. The tail is often held erect, or curved dorsally.
Dogs that are ambulatory walk slowly with a stiﬀ, stilted gait and
can have a wide-based or “sawhorse” stance; voluntary
movement of the head may occur slowly or appear diﬃcult.
Reﬂexes may be exaggerated or diﬃcult to elicit due to excessive
extensor tone. When muscles of the head are involved, tetanus
causes globe retraction and thus third eyelid elevation, a wrinkled
forehead and erect pinnae, retracted lips (risus sardonicus), and
trismus—spasms of masticatory muscles that make it diﬃcult to
open the mouth (Fig. 72.3A). Cats with generalized tetanus may
not have increased jaw tone. 33–35 Miosis may be present.
Laryngeal spasm and hypersalivation occur in approximately half
of aﬀected dogs. 18 , 19
Severely aﬀected dogs are anxious and hypersensitive, develop
opisthotonus, vocalize, or tremble, or can experience generalized
seizures when stimulated. Patients are often hyperthermic due to
increased muscle activity (up to 111°F [43.9°C]). 34 Moderate to
severe obtundation can result. Abdominal palpation may reveal
an enlarged bladder that is diﬃcult to express, or palpation may
be diﬃcult because of abdominal muscle spasm. Tetanic spasms
can lead to dyspnea and hypoventilation. 16 , 18 At least a third of
dogs with generalized tetanus in a referral environment are
bradycardic or have bradyarrhythmias (which include
atrioventricular block or sinus arrest), with heart rates that range
from 40 to 60 beats/minute; another one third of dogs are
tachycardic (>150 beats/minute) or have variable heart rates,
which may reﬂect autonomic dysfunction or pain. 16 The inciting
wound that allowed introduction of C. tetani may or may not be
found, particularly in dogs. In cats with tetanus, a wound is often

vetexamprep.ir

identiﬁed. 29–33 , 37 , 38 Animals with generalized tetanus usually
have a prolonged clinical course and require hospitalization for 1–
2 weeks or more; median hospital stay for dogs has been reported
to be 13–17 days. 18 , 19
Localized tetanus usually involves rigid extension of the limb
nearest or aﬀected by the inoculating wound. Dogs with localized
thoracic limb tetanus have caudal retraction of the limb with
extension of both the elbow and carpus. 25 When a cat’s thoracic
limb is aﬀected, spasm of the triceps muscle results in caudal
extension of the limb with carpal ﬂexion (in contrast to dogs) and
elbow extension (Fig. 72.3B). 24 , 30 The head and neck may deviate
toward the aﬀected limb. 25 Localized tetanus can progress to
generalized disease.

Diagnosis
Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis in all species. That is, there is no
clinicopathologic, microbiologic, serologic, imaging, or other
diagnostic test that is deﬁnitive for the disease; diagnosis is based
on history and physical examination, and the exclusion of other

vetexamprep.ir

y
p y
rule-outs for the problem. The main rule-outs for generalized
tetanus are hypocalcemic tetany, which is ruled out by a normal
serum ionized calcium concentration, and strychnine toxicosis.
Strychnine was historically used as a pesticide to kill small
mammals, but has largely been replaced in the western world by
other toxins. Thus, strychnine toxicosis is probably a less common
clinical problem today than tetanus. The primary diﬀerential
diagnosis for the facial signs of tetanus is masticatory muscle
myositis, which is ruled out if nonfacial musculature is involved
and by serologic testing for type 2M antibodies. A history of a
traumatic event, surgical procedure, or other wound in the
preceding 3 weeks, or of a period of disappearance, should raise
suspicion for tetanus.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Biochemical Tests, and
Urinalysis
Routine laboratory test results in animals with tetanus are often
normal, but stress hyperglycemia, mild to severe increases in the
activity of serum creatine kinase (usually < 20,000 U/L but
sometimes > 200,000 U/L, reference range: 46–320 U/L), mildly
increased AST activity, and myoglobinuria may be present. 16 , 18
Dehydration may result in hemoconcentration or prerenal
azotemia. Animals with wounds or aspiration pneumonia may
have an inﬂammatory leukogram. Severe hyperthermia in dogs
with tetanus may lead to laboratory evidence of multiple organ
dysfunction, with azotemia, increased liver enzyme activities, or
hyperbilirubinemia. Thrombocytopenia and coagulation test
abnormalities consistent with DIC may also be present in these
dogs.

Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
CSF analysis in dogs and cats with tetanus is typically normal.

Diagnostic Imaging
Thoracic radiographs in animals with tetanus may reveal
aspiration pneumonia. 16 , 18 , 19 Occasionally, dogs with
generalized tetanus have evidence of a hiatal hernia on thoracic
radiography, 16 , 27 , 39 , 40 which appears as a soft tissue mass in
the caudal thorax (Fig. 72.4A). Abdominal ultrasound and
advanced imaging modalities are generally noncontributory.

Electrodiagnostic Tests
Electrodiagnostic testing is not usually performed in animals with
tetanus since the diagnosis can generally be made without it, and
because electrodiagnostic ﬁndings in the disease are nonspeciﬁc.
Electromyography (EMG) evaluates the electrical activity in
muscle while nerve conduction studies evaluate the quality and
speed of nerve responses following stimulation. Animals with
tetanus have had normal electrodiagnostic measurements 18 in

vetexamprep.ir

some cases, and persistent electrical motor unit discharges in
others. 24 , 41

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
A empts to culture C. tetani from wounds are not recommended
because the presence of C. tetani in a wound does not necessarily
imply toxin production. In addition, culture for this organism is
insensitive. 17
Serologic Diagnosis
Serologic testing is not performed in cases of tetanus because it is
a clinical diagnosis with so few rule-outs that it is a nearly
pathognomonic presentation. Antibodies are produced to the
toxin during natural infection, 42 but serology is generally neither
available nor necessary for diagnosis.

Pathologic Findings
There are no speciﬁc gross or histopathologic ﬁndings associated
with tetanus. Evidence of complications such as aspiration
pneumonia, pulmonary thromboembolism, or DIC may be seen
on necropsy in patients that die of severe cases.

Treatment and Prognosis
Specific Treatment
Tetanus antitoxin is widely available and should be administered
as a single dose IV (equine antitoxin) or IM (human antitoxin)
after an initial intradermal test dose to evaluate for an allergic
reaction (Table 72.1). Dogs that react to the test dose can be
premedicated with diphenhydramine and a low dose of
dexamethasone. Adverse reactions to antitoxin include vomiting,
retching, or tachypnea and may occur even in premedicated dogs.
16 Reduction in the rate of antitoxin administration or
discontinuation of treatment leads to resolution of clinical signs.
Administration of antitoxin does not reverse existing signs
because it does not enter nerve terminals, but it may neutralize
free toxin. A small amount of antitoxin can be administered

vetexamprep.ir

locally if a wound is identiﬁed. The eﬃcacy of tetanus antitoxin is
controversial, and the optimal dose is not known. In one study,
earlier IV administration of equine tetanus antitoxin did not
inﬂuence disease progression or mortality as opposed to
administration later in the course of disease. 16 Antitoxin
administration may prevent localized tetanus from generalizing.
For animals with tetanus, treatment with antimicrobials that
have activity against C. tetani is recommended. Appropriate
antimicrobials for treatment of tetanus include IV metronidazole
or penicillin G. Metronidazole is preferred because of its
improved penetration into purulent material and the fact that
penicillin can antagonize GABA. Studies in human patients have
also shown improved outcome with metronidazole as opposed to
procaine penicillin. 43 Once antitoxin has been administered and
spasms are controlled (see Supportive Care), wounds should be
managed appropriately. Earlier, appropriate antimicrobial
treatment and wound debridement were not shown to inﬂuence
progression or mortality in one small veterinary study in dogs. 16
However, early, deﬁnitive management with antitoxin, wound
management, and appropriate antimicrobial therapy is a
cornerstone of treatment in humans with tetanus, 44 and common
sense suggests that veterinary patients would beneﬁt from that
same level of care.

Supportive Care
Supportive care is an essential part of management for patients
with tetanus. The extent of care required depends on the severity
of illness. IV ﬂuids, soft bedding, frequent turning to prevent
decubital ulcers, application of ocular lubricant to prevent corneal
ulceration, bladder expression or urethral catheterization (ideally
intermi ent), enemas to relieve constipation, and nutritional
support in the form of hand feeding, feeding tubes, or parenteral
nutrition may be required. Force feeding is not recommended
because it is unlikely to satisfy caloric needs and can contribute to
the development of aspiration pneumonia.
To help minimize spasms, dogs or cats with generalized tetanus
should be placed in a quiet, dimly lit environment away from
excessive visual or auditory stimuli. Co on balls can be used as
earplugs. Sedatives and/or muscle relaxants such as

vetexamprep.ir

acepromazine, benzodiazepines, dantrolene, or baclofen may be
useful. Severely aﬀected animals may require a constant-rate
infusion of drugs such as pentobarbital, phenobarbital, or
propofol. Barbiturates are no longer recommended for treatment
of tetanus in humans, in whom benzodiazepines are the mainstay
for sedation and relaxation. 45 , 46 If human disease is severe,
drugs that cause neuromuscular blockade such as vecuronium are
used, but this necessitates mechanical ventilation. Methocarbamol
often appears ineﬀective and requires frequent administration, 16 ,
19 and thus its use is not recommended because it may delay
administration
of
more
eﬀective
medications.
Also,
benzodiazepines are preferred to methocarbamol because they are
GABA agonists and provide some sedation. Successful control of
muscle spasms relieves pain and hyperthermia. If used, opioids
should be administered with caution because they may contribute
to constipation or GI adverse eﬀects. Administration of
magnesium sulfate infusions has also been associated with
improvement in clinical signs; a dose of 70 mg/kg over 30 minutes
followed by an initial CRI of 100 mg/kg/day has been
recommended. Oral magnesium aspartate (12 mg/kg q12h) orally
can be continued for 14 days once this is feasible. 47
Fans and room temperature ﬂuids may be beneﬁcial for dogs
with tetanus-induced heat injury. Administration of atropine may
be required for animals with bradyarrhythmias (in dogs, HR < 60
beats/minute; in cats, HR < 120 beats/minute). Rarely,
bradyarrhythmias have required temporary pacemaker
placement. 16 Occasionally (< 10% of dogs with generalized
tetanus in a referral population), mechanical ventilation is
required to support respiration. 16 Temporary tracheostomy may
be required to bypass the larynx in cases of severe upper airway
obstruction. 18

Prognosis
Provided complications do not occur, prognosis is generally good
for animals with generalized tetanus. The overall 28-day survival
rate for dogs with generalized tetanus in one study was around
80%, 16 whereas in another study of 20 dogs it was only 50%. 19 A
classiﬁcation system has been developed to assess the severity of
tetanus in dogs for the purpose of prognostication (Table 72.2). 16
The survival rate for dogs that progressed to tetanus severity class
I or II was 100%, but it dropped to 60% for dogs that progressed to
tetanus severity class III or IV. 16 However, at the time of initial
evaluation, only 11% of 37 dogs were in class III or IV, and dogs
progressed to higher classes unpredictably, with 47% of the dogs
categorized in class III or IV when the highest recorded class was
assigned. Dogs with severe tetanus are more likely to develop
complications such as aspiration pneumonia or multiple organ
dysfunction than dogs with mild tetanus. In a few dogs that
recover (< 10% of dogs that develop generalized tetanus),
intermi ent localized muscle spasm continues to occur for many
months, which may be noticed by the owner during activities
such as sleeping or eating. 16
The prognosis for animals with localized tetanus is excellent
with supportive care of wound management and antimicrobial
treatment.

Immunity and Vaccination

vetexamprep.ir

Given the relative rarity of tetanus in dogs and cats, vaccination is
not recommended in these species. Recurrent tetanus has been
documented in people, so recovery from natural disease does not
necessarily result in protection from future episodes. 44 Thus,
preventative measures should be discussed with owners of pets
that recover from tetanus.

Prevention
Control of: (1) roaming, (2) exposure to plant awns, and (3)
aggressive interactions with other animals may reduce the chance
that wounds develop. If wounds are noticed, they should be
cleaned promptly with soap and water. Surgical instruments
should always be sterilized properly before use so that tetanus
spores are inactivated, and needles should never be reused.
Tetanus spores can be inactivated with iodine, glutaraldehyde,
hydrogen peroxide, or autoclaving at 121°C and 15 psi for 15
minutes.

Public Health Aspects
Animals with tetanus cannot transmit it directly to people who
handle them. The main risk that dogs with tetanus pose to
humans is through bite wounds, which can occur when owners
a empt to administer oral medications to animals with increased
jaw tone or spasm.
Tetanus in humans is rare in developed countries because most
children are vaccinated against the disease. When it occurs, it is
most often in people older than 65 years because of waning
immunity, and in injection drug users. 48 Worldwide, the vast
majority of cases occur in neonates from developing nations
because of lack of immunization.

Botulism
Epidemiology
Botulism is rare in dogs and even rarer in cats. Clinical disease in
dogs and cats follows ingestion of carrion that contains preformed
neurotoxin. Botulism outbreaks in dogs have been reported in
hunting foxhounds that have eaten domestic mammal or wild

vetexamprep.ir

animal carcasses. 4 , 49 Maggots can vector C. botulinum and BoNT
between bird carcasses, 50 and some cases of canine botulism have
followed ingestion of bird carrion. 5 , 8 , 9 , 51 At least one case was
associated with a botulism outbreak in waterfowl. 10 Most dogs
reported have been medium- to large-breed, intact male or intact
female dogs that vary in age; this ﬁnding is likely because the vast
majority of botulism cases in dogs have been reported in
foxhound packs. The only report of botulism in cats was an
outbreak of disease that occurred after several cats were fed
pelican carrion. 3 The relative resistance of dogs and cats to
botulism has been hypothesized to reﬂect an adaptive response to
a carnivorous lifestyle.

Modiﬁed from Burki JM, Sturges BK, Jandrey KE, et al. Risk

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Clostridium botulinum spores germinate in anaerobic conditions
and produce toxin. They grow best in temperatures that range

vetexamprep.ir

from 30°C to 37°C, so carrion in warm conditions is ideal for
BoNT production. The toxin is ingested, survives the acid stomach
conditions, and is absorbed into the bloodstream from the small
intestine. It then travels to peripheral cholinergic synapses, which
include the neuromuscular junction and autonomic synapses, and
inhibits release of acetylcholine (ACh) (Fig. 72.5). This leads to
ascending, symmetrical ﬂaccid paralysis, development of
megaesophagus, and signs of autonomic dysfunction. Clinical
signs usually occur within 12 to 72 hours after ingestion of
botulinum toxin and may be complicated by signs from dietary
indiscretion, although GI signs may also reﬂect the presence of
autonomic derangement. Disease progresses rapidly over 1 or 2
days, and then begins to resolve with supportive care. Rapid
development of signs after carrion ingestion is generally
associated with a more severe course of disease. Death can result
from respiratory muscle paralysis or aspiration of GI contents.
Abnormalities in aﬀected cats were ascending ﬂaccid paralysis,
lethargy, hypothermia, tachypnea, dehydration, and urinary
incontinence. 3

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 72.5

Mechanism of action of botulinum

toxin

Physical Examination Findings
Botulism causes an acutely progressive, ascending, bilaterally
symmetrical ﬂaccid paralysis. Physical examination ﬁndings
depend on the severity of intoxication. Fever is absent unless
aspiration pneumonia has developed. Mildly aﬀected animals
show only ataxia or pelvic limb paresis, whereas those with severe
intoxication are quadriplegic with absent voluntary motor activity
and are unable to rise from lateral recumbency. The ability to wag
the tail is often retained in dogs. 4 , 10 , 51 Segmental reﬂexes are
generally decreased or absent, and pain perception is preserved.

vetexamprep.ir

Patients usually experience constipation, and an “overﬂow”
bladder due to lower motor neuron dysfunction may be present.
Cranial nerve examination can reveal decreased function,
especially facial nerve function and a decreased gag reﬂex,
sometimes accompanied by ptyalism. 4 , 5 , 51 , 52 Dysphonia is
common. Decreased blinking can result in corneal ulceration, 5 , 6
and concomitant keratoconjunctivitis sicca has been reported. 9
Mydriasis with sluggish pupillary light reﬂexes has been
described. 4 , 52
TABLE 72.3

Occasionally tachycardia and tachypnea are present. Tachypnea
may result from diaphragmatic muscle weakness or secondary
aspiration pneumonia. Increased breath sounds may also be
present on thoracic auscultation of dogs with secondary
aspiration pneumonia. Physical examination ﬁndings in one
aﬀected cat consisted of hypothermia, lethargy, dehydration,
quadriplegia, and decreased segmental reﬂexes. 3 In general, the
sooner the onset of clinical signs after ingestion of toxin, the more
severe and long-lasting the course of disease. Most cases worsen
over the ﬁrst 1–2 days of clinical signs and are markedly
improved in less than a week.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of botulism is most often based on a history of recent
exposure to carrion, clinical signs, and exclusion of the few other
rule-outs; sometimes electrodiagnostic testing is performed. The
primary diﬀerential diagnoses for botulism are acute idiopathic
polyradiculoneuritis (coonhound paralysis), tick paralysis, acute
fulminant myasthenia gravis, coral snake envenomation,

vetexamprep.ir

ionophore toxicosis, and paralytic rabies. The intermediate
syndrome
of
organophosphate
intoxication
and
organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy are also possible,
though these syndromes are exceptionally rare in veterinary
medicine. A full history should be obtained for vaccination status
and possible exposure to organophosphate pesticides or
ionophore antimicrobial agents, and a close examination should
be performed for engorged ticks. An ACh receptor antibody assay
can be performed to rule out fulminant myasthenia gravis.
Serologic assays have been used to detect an antibody response to
BoNT. Finally, speciﬁc assays that detect BoNT in serum, GI
contents, or food can be performed (Table 72.3).

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Biochemical Tests, and
Urinalysis
Routine laboratory test results in animals with botulism are often
normal. Dehydration may result in hemoconcentration or prerenal
azotemia. Animals with aspiration pneumonia may have
leukogram changes.

Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
CSF analysis in dogs and cats with botulism is typically normal.

Diagnostic Imaging
Thoracic radiographs in dogs with botulism may be
unremarkable, or megaesophagus may be present (see Fig. 72.4B).
6 , 9 , 52 Aspiration pneumonia may occur. 4 , 9 , 52 Carrion bones
are occasionally present in the GI tract. Abdominal
ultrasonographic examination may be normal, or mild abdominal
lymphadenopathy may be identiﬁed.

Electrodiagnostic Tests
EMG and nerve conduction studies can be useful to support a
diagnosis of botulism (Table 72.4). Sedation or anesthesia for
electrophysiologic testing is generally not advisable in dogs with
megaesophagus and aspiration pneumonia, although this testing

vetexamprep.ir

has been performed without anesthesia in some cases. 4 EMG
evaluates the electrical activity in muscle. Using EMG, the
primary ﬁnding in dogs with botulism is prolonged or increased
insertional activity. 4 , 52 Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp
waves have also been noted. 4 , 9
Nerve conduction studies evaluate the quality and speed of
nerve responses following stimulation. Nerve conduction ﬁndings
in dogs with botulism include normal F waves (late waves that
decrease in magnitude or disappear in acute polyradiculoneuritis,
and thus distinguish the two diseases) and decreased magnitude
of the compound muscle action potential. 4 , 9 , 52 Repetitive nerve
stimulation at low frequencies can result in decremental
responses, but repetitive nerve stimulation at high frequencies in
dogs with botulism has no eﬀect on the muscle response. 52 Motor
nerve conduction velocity is normal 52 or decreased. 4

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Detection of C. botulinum, C. butyricum, or C. baratii bacteria in
source material, 3 , 6 or in the stomach contents, 3 vomitus, or feces
5 , 51 of aﬀected animals helps support the diagnosis of botulism,
but is neither sensitive nor speciﬁc for clinical disease.
Serologic Diagnosis
ELISA assays that detect the antibody response to botulinum
neurotoxin are available and were used to conﬁrm a diagnosis of
botulism in one dog. 5 A convalescent specimen collected 3 weeks
after the onset of illness was positive, but specimens collected at
the time the dog was ﬁrst evaluated and 10 days into the course of
disease were negative. Thus, the diagnosis is generally
retrospective with this method because most dogs have recovered
by the time seroconversion occurs.
Toxin Detection
Botulinum toxin can be detected in feces, 4 , 7 , 9 , 51 vomitus, 8 GI
contents collected at necropsy, source material (carrion), 3 , 9 or
serum. 4 , 8–10 , 12 , 51 Specimens should be held at 4°C, marked
with a warning label, and shipped immediately to the laboratory.

vetexamprep.ir

The most sensitive assay is a mouse inoculation assay, in which
untreated mice and mice treated with serotype-speciﬁc antitoxin
are inoculated with the specimen to determine if the antitoxin is
protective. 53 However, several days are required to run this assay
and it involves the sacriﬁce of laboratory animals. Toxin typespeciﬁc ELISA assays are available for rapid detection of BoNT C,
but standard ELISA assays lack sensitivity when compared with
mouse inoculation. Research eﬀorts have been focused on the
development of a variety of novel, rapid, highly sensitive, and
inexpensive diagnostic assays that detect minute quantities of
botulinum toxins. 53

CMAP, compound muscle action potential; MNCV, motor nerve conduction
velocity.

Pathologic Findings
There are no speciﬁc gross or histopathologic ﬁndings associated
with botulism.

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

Specific Treatment
There is no readily available speciﬁc treatment for botulism in
dogs. In the United States, heptavalent equine antitoxin is
available from the CDC for treatment of human botulism.
However, its availability is tightly controlled, so it may be
impossible to obtain for treatment of dogs and cats. 54
Antimicrobials are not indicated for the treatment of botulism,
because the disease is due to the ingestion of preformed toxin.

Supportive Care
Supportive care is an essential part of management. The extent of
care required depends on the severity of illness. IV ﬂuids, soft
bedding, frequent turning to prevent decubital ulcers, application
of ocular lubricant to prevent corneal ulceration, bladder
expression, enemas to relieve constipation, and nutritional
support in the form of hand feeding, feeding tubes, or total
parenteral nutrition may be required. Force feeding is not
recommended because it is unlikely to satisfy caloric needs and
can contribute to the development of aspiration pneumonia.
Occasionally, intermi ent positive pressure ventilation may be
required to support ventilation. Antimicrobial drugs should only
be used if secondary infection develops (e.g., bacterial pneumonia
or UTI). Aminoglycosides should be avoided because they may
contribute to neuromuscular blockade.

Prognosis
Provided complications do not occur, prognosis is generally good
for animals with botulism. Most animals are markedly improved
within a week of onset of clinical signs.

Immunity and Vaccination
Botulism is so rare in dogs and cats that vaccination against it is
considered unwarranted. Vaccination has been successful in other
species, and BoNT vaccine development is an active area of
research due to concerns about the toxin being used in
bioterrorism. 55

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
Prevention of botulism involves limiting access to carrion and
feeding heat-processed commercial diets that are unspoiled.
Although BoNT can be denatured through boiling, spores can
survive this treatment. Thus, cooked food should not be allowed
to stand for long periods before it is fed to pets. The spores of C.
botulinum are inactivated by pressure-cooking foods.

Public Health Aspects
Animals with botulism cannot transmit the condition directly to
people. Nevertheless, feces, tissues, or body ﬂuids from animals
with botulism should be handled with care and marked with
warning labels before they are submi ed to the laboratory
because the toxin may be present in these items and only minute
quantities are required to cause severe disease.
Three forms of botulism occur in people: infant botulism,
wound botulism, and food botulism. Infant botulism occurs as a
result of local production of botulinum toxin within the intestinal
tract by C. botulinum in the absence of the competing intestinal
microﬂora that are normally found in adults. Wound botulism
occurs almost exclusively as a result of injection of contaminated
heroin by IV drug users. Botulinum toxin preparations are used to
treat conditions such as strabismus, esophageal achalasia, cervical
dystonia, axillary hyperhydrosis (excessive sweating), or
blepharospasm. There are rare reports of iatrogenic botulism after
such use. 56 , 57 Life-threatening iatrogenic botulism has occurred
after use of botulinum preparations that were unlicensed for
cosmetic treatment of wrinkles. 58 Signiﬁcant concerns have been
raised about the possible use of botulinum toxin as an agent of
bioterrorism. This has stimulated considerable research on the
disease, which is otherwise very rare.

Case Example
Signalment

“Jenny,” a 6-year-old female spayed Labrador retriever from
Winters in northern California.

vetexamprep.ir

History

Jenny was brought to the University of California, Davis
veterinary emergency service early in the morning for a 2-hour
history of inability to stand. Her owners awoke to ﬁnd her in
another room, unable to get up for her morning walk. She
appeared anxious and was breathing with increased eﬀort, but
was still wagging her tail. She also did not want to eat breakfast.
There had been no known history of travel, toxins, trauma, or
tick exposure. Over the past 2 months, she had been treated
with prednisone (1 mg/kg, PO, daily for 5 days, followed by
0.74 mg/kg, PO, daily thereafter) for allergic dermatitis. Three
weeks before the onset of illness, she was treated with a short
course of cephalexin after an aural hematoma was repaired.
Jenny had been regularly vaccinated with rabies, distemper,
hepatitis, and parvovirus vaccines.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 27.2 kg.
General: Bright, alert, responsive, and hydrated. Laterally
recumbent and anxious. T = 101.0°F, HR = 140
beats/minute, panting.
Integument, eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Sutures were
present on the pinna of the right ear from the recent aural
hematoma repair. Moderate dental calculus and gingivitis
were present. There were no other abnormalities noted.
Musculoskeletal: BCS 5/9. The dog was unable to use the
pelvic limbs to bear weight.
Cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, genitourinary, and lymph
nodes: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were
present.

Neurologic Examination
Mentation: Appropriate, anxious.
Gait/Posture: The dog was non-ambulatory, but voluntary
movement was present in all four limbs. She was unable
to stand and support weight, but could crawl and shuﬄe.
She a empted to bear weight on her thoracic limbs and
could maintain sternal recumbency. When supported to

vetexamprep.ir

stand, the pelvic limbs collapsed and the thoracic limbs
were minimally able to bear weight.
Cranial nerves: Slightly reduced palpebral reﬂexes and
gag reﬂex. Absent corneal reﬂexes. No other deﬁcits were
noted.
Postural reactions: These were diﬃcult to assess because
of the dog’s inability to stand, but appeared decreased.
Segmental reﬂexes: Reduced muscle tone was present in
the thoracic limbs. Triceps, patella, and gastrocnemius
reﬂexes were decreased. Reduced thoracic limb
withdrawal reﬂexes were noted, but pelvic limb
withdrawal reﬂexes were intact. Panniculus and perineal
reﬂexes were also intact. Pain perception remained intact.
Spinal palpation: No apparent pain was present on
palpation or cervical manipulation.
Neuroanatomic localization: Neuromuscular disease.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 41.0% (40%–55%), MCV 69 fL (65–75 fL),
MCHC 36.6 g/dL (33–36 g/dL), WBC 5,800 cells/µL (6,000–
13,000 cells/µL), neutrophils 3,671 cells/µL (3,000–10,500
cells/µL), lymphocytes 1,769 cells/µL (1,000–4,000 cells/
µL), monocytes 197 cells/µL (150–1,200 cells/µL),
eosinophils 145 cells/µL (0–1,500 cells/µL), platelets
clumped but adequate (150,000–400,000 platelets/µL).
Serum biochemistry proﬁle: Sodium 146 mmol/L (145–154
mmol/L), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.6–5.3 mmol/L),
chloride 107 mmol/L (108–118 mmol/L), bicarbonate 21
mmol/L (16–26 mmol/L), phosphorus 2.3 mg/dL (3.0–6.2
mg/dL), calcium 11.4 mg/dL (9.7–11.5 mg/dL), BUN 15
mg/dL (5–21 mg/dL), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.3–1.2
mg/dL), glucose 105 mg/dL (64–123 mg/dL), total protein
7.1 g/dL (5.4–7.6 g/dL), albumin 4.2 g/dL (3.0–4.4 g/dL),
globulin 2.9 g/dL (1.8–3.9 g/dL), ALT 64 U/L (19–67 U/L),
AST 25 U/L (19–42 U/L), ALP 129 U/L (21–170 U/L),
creatine kinase 57 U/L (51–399 U/L), GGT 4 U/L (0–6 U/L),
cholesterol 204 mg/dL (135–361 mg/dL), total bilirubin 0.2
mg/dL (0–0.2 mg/dL).

vetexamprep.ir

Urinalysis: SpG 1.025; pH 7.0, trace protein (SSA), 1+
bilirubin, no hemoprotein, glucose, ketones, WBC/HPF,
RBC/HPF, bacteria or crystals in the sediment. Many lipid
droplets were present.

Imaging Findings

Thoracic radiographs: The cardiopulmonary structures were
within normal limits. There were mineralized opacities within
the stomach. There was a small amount of gas in the
midthoracic esophagus.
Abdominal ultrasound examination: Mild mesenteric
lymphadenomegaly was identiﬁed. No other abnormalities
were present.

Neuromuscular Testing

Edrophonium response test for myasthenia gravis: Negative.

Treatment

Jenny was admi ed to the intensive care unit and treated with
supportive care that included IV ﬂuids (lactated Ringer’s
solution with 20 mEq/L KCl at 75 mL/hour), soft bedding,
intermi ent manual bladder expression, physical therapy
(massage and passive ROM exercises), and frequent turning.
Treatment with prednisone was discontinued. Respiratory
function was monitored continuously by observation, serial
examination, and serial venous pCO2 measurements. After
repeated inspections for ticks, topical ﬁpronil was applied in
case the signs resulted from tick paralysis. Serum was
submi ed for an ACh receptor antibody titer, and feces were
submi ed for a botulinum toxin assay. Over the subsequent 12
to 18 hours, Jenny became anxious after she was fed canned
food and began to retch and hypersalivate. Thoracic
radiographs were repeated and showed megaesophagus (see
Fig. 72.4B). Severe tachycardia also developed (HR = 210
beats/minute). An ECG showed ventricular tachycardia
followed by supraventricular tachycardia. Systolic blood
pressure was 145 mmHg. Acepromazine was administered (0.01
mg/kg, IV, once), after which her HR decreased to 90
beats/minute, with a normal sinus rhythm. A second neurologic
examination showed progression of disease with reduced
cervical tone and an inability to hold up the head, tetraplegia

vetexamprep.ir

with absence of all segmental reﬂexes, and a reduced tail wag.
The owners were warned that mechanical ventilation may be
needed should the disease progress. Over the course of the next
day, dysphonia and a mild cough developed, and Jenny
regurgitated several times. Gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube
feeding or parenteral nutrition were oﬀered to the owner, but
were declined. Four days after admission, improvement in the
triceps reﬂex was noted, and on day 5, some voluntary
movement was noted in the pelvic and thoracic limbs. At that
time Jenny was successfully fed meatballs of canned dog food
by hand. She was kept in sternal recumbency for 30 minutes
after eating to minimize aspiration. On day 7, the ACh receptor
antibody and botulinum toxin assay results became available.
Serum acetylcholine receptor antibody titer: 0.05 nmol/L
(reference interval, < 0.6 nmol/L)
Botulinum toxin C mouse bioassay (fecal specimen): Positive
for type C botulinum toxin. An extract from the fecal specimen
was lethal in the bioassay. The eﬀects were eliminated by
heating the extract at 80°C for 10 minutes, which indicated that
the toxic eﬀects were due to a heat-labile toxin. Mice were also
protected from the eﬀects by anti–type C botulinum antisera
but not by anti–type A botulinum antisera.

Diagnosis
Botulism.

Outcome

On day 8 after hospitalization, thoracic radiographs showed
resolution of megaesophagus and no evidence of pneumonia.
By day 10, Jenny began to shuﬄe along the ﬂoor. All segmental
reﬂexes had returned but remained reduced. The dog was
discharged from the hospital with instructions for continued
care in the home environment. By day 15, Jenny’s owners
reported that her normal bark had returned, and she could
walk 20 steps and defecate and urinate unassisted. A month
after discharge she was re-examined and no abnormalities were
detected.

Comments

The main diﬀerential diagnoses considered for this dog were
myasthenia gravis and botulism. Initially, polyradiculoneuritis
was also considered, but the subsequent development of

vetexamprep.ir

megaesophagus was not consistent with this disorder.
Ultimately, a diagnosis of botulism was conﬁrmed through
assay of the stool for botulinum toxin. A history of carrion
ingestion was not known, but the dog lived in a semirural area,
and the presence of mineralized stomach contents suggested
that it had occurred. Prednisone administration may have
contributed to polyphagia and ingestion of carrion by this dog.

73: Yersinia pestis (Plague) and
Other Yersinioses
Bruno B. Chomel, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Descriptions of plague date back to around
1300 BC. The causative agent was isolated in 1894, in Hong
Kong by Alexandre Yersin. 1 , 2
• Cause: Yersinia pestis, a gram-negative coccobacillus (family
Enterobacterales).
• Affected Hosts: Yersinia pestis causes disease in rodents,
rabbits, wild carnivores, domestic dogs and cats, and humans.
Wild felids (such as mountain lions or bobcats), goats, deer,
antelope, camelids, and nonhuman primates can also develop
illness.
• Geographic Distribution: USA: Southwestern United States;
foci also exist in South East Asia, Africa (including the island
of Madagascar), and South America (Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, and
Ecuador).
• Major Mode of Transmission: Flea-borne, via an enormous
variety of rodent flea species; ingestion of infected rodents or
rabbits by cats and dogs. Human contamination reported by
sleeping with flea-infested pets.
• Major Clinical Signs: Fever, lethargy, inappetence,
lymphadenopathy, subcutaneous abscesses, hemoptysis
(dogs).
• Differential Diagnoses: Tularemia, cat bite abscesses,
Streptococcus spp. infections, feline infectious peritonitis,
leptospirosis (dogs), aspiration or foreign body pneumonia
(dogs).

vetexamprep.ir

• Human Health Significance: A small percentage (10%) of
human plague cases result from exposure to infected cats,
through bites, scratches, or respiratory droplet inhalation from
cats with pneumonic plague. Dogs and cats can also expose
humans through the carriage of infected fleas into households
(especially when sleeping with owners).

Etiology and Epidemiology
The genus Yersinia includes 11 diﬀerent species, three of which are
pathogenic in humans, cats, and dogs: Yersinia pestis, the agent of
plague, and the two enteropathogenic species Yersinia
pseudotuberculosis and Yersinia enterocolitica. Only Y. pestis is
transmi ed by arthropod vectors. Plague is caused by Y. pestis, a
coccobacillus of the family Enterobacterales. It is a nonmotile,
non–spore-forming, facultative anaerobic, gram-negative, bipolarstaining bacterium. The bacterium is non-saprophytic and
sensitive to desiccation and temperatures ≥ 40°C. However, it can
survive for several weeks to months in organic material such as
infected carcasses, and survival in contaminated soil has been
conﬁrmed in natural conditions for at least 24 days and in
experimental conditions for up to 40 weeks. 2 , 3 Cold
temperatures or freezing may prolong the viability of this
organism for years. The organism grows slowly in culture even at
its optimum temperature (28°C on blood agar or MacConkey
agar), so cultures should be held for at least 48 hours before being
discarded. Colonies are much smaller than those of other
Enterobacterales and may be overlooked. As recently as 1500 to
20,000 years ago, Y. pestis evolved from Y. pseudotuberculosis, a
relatively benign enteric bacterium that is transmi ed through
contact with contaminated food and water. 3 As part of its
transition from an enteric to vector-borne pathogen, Y. pestis has
acquired two unique plasmids (pPla and pMT1), possesses genes
required for persistence outside the vertebrate or vector, and
gained apparently new functions for several chromosomal genes.
Yersinia pestis produces a lipopolysaccharide endotoxin and a
capsular envelope containing the antiphagocytic principal fraction
I antigen. Three geographic variants of Y. pestis (orientalis, antiqua,

vetexamprep.ir

and mediaevalis) have been distinguished biochemically but have
identical virulence.
Yersinia pestis is maintained in wild burrowing rodents in rural
regions of Asia (including the Middle East), Africa, and the
Americas (Fig. 73.1). There is no plague in the Australian
continent and New Zealand, Oceania, Japan, Taiwan, the
Philippines, and Indonesia. The last case of plague in Europe was
reported after World War II. The organism is transmi ed between
rodents by rodent ﬂeas; humans, dogs, and cats are usually
accidental and “dead-end” hosts (although direct transmission
can occur through aerosols in humans and cats with pneumonic
disease). Fleas become infected when they feed on heavily
bacteremic rodents. The organism replicates in the ﬂea
gastrointestinal tract and creates in some ﬂea species, such as
Xenopsylla cheopis, the Oriental rat ﬂea, a blockage of the
proventriculus, located prior to the ﬂea stomach, which causes the
“starved” ﬂea to repeatedly and aggressively feed and regurgitate
bacteria into the bite site of a new host. 4 , 5 Infection is maintained
by an obligatory ﬂea-rodent-ﬂea cycle involving bacteremic
rodent hosts and their resident ﬂeas (Fig. 73.2). More than 80 ﬂea
species have been found to be naturally infected with Y. pestis, and
at least 28 ﬂea species occurring in North America have been
experimentally conﬁrmed as vectors. 6 A large number of ﬂea
species can transmit Y. pestis, but some ﬂea species, such as the
Oriental rat ﬂea (X. cheopis) worldwide and the ground squirrel
ﬂea (Oropsylla montana) in the western United States are
particularly eﬃcient vectors. Although nowhere near as eﬃcient
as these two ﬂeas as a vector, the cat ﬂea (Ctenocephalides felis), for
which the proventriculus blockage is usually absent, can infest
rodent reservoirs and also has the potential to transmit Y. pestis. 7
However, the rapid transit of Y. pestis in the cat ﬂea digestive tract
makes the cat ﬂea a poor plague vector. Yersinia pestis a ains very
high concentrations in rodent blood (108 organisms/mL) before
the death of the rodent occurs, which allows ﬂeas to acquire
suﬃcient numbers of bacteria for eﬃcient transmission to other
rodents. 8 Fleas can remain infected for more than a year, which
permits transmission long after the death of an infected rodent.
Eﬃcient transmission between rodents is enhanced by the fact
that rodent ﬂeas, which are temperature sensitive, will search for
a new warm-blooded host when their rodent host dies.
