TABLE 82.1

Cryptococcus neoformans Species Complex
Organisms that belong to the C. neoformans SC have a worldwide
distribution. They primarily infect human patients who are
immunocompromised, especially AIDS patients. The realized
environmental niche for C. neoformans SC organisms is weathered
bird (especially pigeon) guano which provides an alkaline,
hyperosmolar, nitrogen-rich environment that allows proliﬁc
growth. 39 They can also be found in decaying plant ma er in
hollows of certain trees. 40 The organism can remain viable for at
least 2 years in environments such as pigeon lofts. The majority of
human cryptococcal infections result from infection with C.
neoformans sensu stricto (ss) (VNI). 41 C. neoformans ss is the most
common Cryptococcus species isolated from dogs and cats in
southeastern Australia and accounts for more than 70% of
infections. 31 , 32 , 34 Across the United States, most dogs with
cryptococcosis are infected with C. neoformans SC organisms, but
infection of cats with this species is rare. 11 , 42

Cryptococcus gattii Species Complex
Organisms that belong to the C. ga ii SC are endemic in Australia,
New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Southeast Asia, parts of Latin
America, California, Mexico, Hawaii, Central and South Africa,
and, to a lesser extent, certain parts of Europe (Austria, Germany,
France, Italy, Greece, and Spain). 43 , 44 Since 1999, an epidemic of
infections with C. ga ii SC has occurred in humans and domestic
and wild animals in British Columbia in Canada, especially
Vancouver Island, and the Paciﬁc Northwest of the United States,

vetexamprep.ir

and infections have been occurring in humans at a rate higher
than that in other endemic regions. 45–49 The main species
identiﬁed in this epidemic has been C. deuteroga ii (molecular
types VGIIa and, to a much lesser extent, VGIIb and, in Oregon,
also VGIIc). Cryptococcus deuteroga ii (VGII) can be found on
living tree bark (Garry oak, maple, cedar, and pine) and in air,
and has also been found in freshwater and seawater. Proximity to
areas with soil disturbance was a risk factor for dogs and cats. 48
In California, almost all cats appear to be infected with C.
bacillisporus (VGIII), with occasional C. deuteroga ii (VGII)
infections. 11 , 42 The ecologic niche of C. bacillisporus (VGIII) in the
United States remains somewhat unclear, 49 but it has recently
been isolated from the bark of several tree species, including the
Canary Island pine, American Sweetgum, Pohutukawa tree,
Western Sycamore, and Blue Gum in southern California, as well
as from soil in public parks and areas in the Los Angeles and San
Diego regions. 50 However, as found for other endemic mycoses,
approximately 25% of aﬀected cats are housed exclusively
indoors. 11
In eastern Australia, 20% to 30% of human, feline, and canine
cryptococcosis is caused by C. ga ii SC organisms, 32 , 38 whereas
in Western Australia, approximately 50% of cats and dogs with
cryptococcosis are infected with C. ga ii SC organisms. 8 , 49 Most
C. ga ii isolates from eastern Australia belong to C. ga ii ss (VGI),
whilst C. deuteroga ii (VGII) is mostly seen in southwestern and
northern Australia. 8 , 51 Cryptococcus ga ii ss (VGI) in Australia is
very strongly associated with dead plant material in Eucalyptus
tree hollows. 5 , 52 Cats in rural environments are at risk of
infection. Recently, C. deuteroga ii (VGII) was identiﬁed in two
cats with nasal signs 53 and dogs with disseminated disease 54 , 55
from southeastern Brazil, and C. bacillisporus (VGIII) was
identiﬁed in a cat with a nasal cutaneous lesion from Chile. 56
In contrast to C. neoformans ss, C. deuteroga ii (VGII) isolates
from the Paciﬁc northwest and British Columbia can infect
apparently immunocompetent humans. 57
Cryptococcus
bacillisporus (VGIII) infections have been reported in
immunosuppressed humans in southern California. 58 When
disease occurs in immunocompetent hosts, it is often
characterized by the presence of pulmonary mass lesions

vetexamprep.ir

(cryptococcomas) and sometimes intracranial cryptococcomas. 59 ,
60 As a result, pulmonary cryptococcomas are more commonly
described in human patients infected with C. bacillisporus (VGIII)
compared with those infected with C. neoformans ss. 60

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Based on the small size of basidiospores, the lung is thought to be
the primary site of infection in humans. In cats, dogs, and koalas,
the nasal cavity may be the primary site of infection (see Fig. 82.1).
Cryptococcus neoformans ss has been shown to be a transient
colonizer of the nasal mucus of cats, dogs, and koalas in Australia,
5 , 61 whereas C. ga ii ss can be isolated in suﬃcient numbers and
with suﬃcient frequency to potentially even be considered part of
normal sinonasal ﬂora of koalas in certain environments. 62
Signiﬁcant pulmonary parenchymal involvement in these species
is rare, although lesions can be detected on pulmonary CT scans
and at necropsy. Importantly, the progression of disease from
colonization to subclinical disease and clinical disease is best
recognized in the koala. 5 , 62 , 63 Colonization of the nasal cavity
may be followed by development of cryptococcal rhinitis in some
(but not all) dogs and cats. However, some nasal cavity
involvement may result from hematogenous dissemination,
because injection of Cryptococcus spp. into the carotid artery of
cats can lead to development of lesions on the bridge of the nose.
Some localized cutaneous lesions may result from direct
cutaneous inoculation (e.g., after a cat scratch), but skin lesions are
usually interpreted as the result of dissemination or extension
from the nasal cavity.
The pathogenesis of cryptococcosis depends on the size of the
inoculum, virulence of the cryptococcal strain, and host
immunity. Cryptococcus has been aptly described as “a sugarcoated killer with designer genes.” 64 Cryptococcus has several
important virulence factors, including its polysaccharide capsule,
laccase (which makes melanin), mannitol, and other enzymes
such as phospholipase, urease, and superoxide dismutase. 17 , 59 ,
65 Capsular polysaccharide is continuously shed into the host’s
extracellular ﬂuid, which includes blood, urine, and CSF. The

vetexamprep.ir

capsule inhibits phagocytosis through its negative charge and via
blockage of the Fc portion of bound antibodies from interacting
with host phagocyte receptors. The capsule also depletes
complement and interferes with migration of leukocytes from the
bloodstream into infected tissues by causing them to shed selectin.
65 , 66 It also directly inhibits CMI by causing a shift from Th1 to a
Th2 type immune response. 66 The ability of C. neoformans SC and
C. ga ii SC organisms to grow at mammalian body temperature is
also an important virulence factor and is lacking in other species
of Cryptococcus. Both C. neoformans SC and C. ga ii SC organisms
can undergo phenotypic switching by altering the cell membrane
sterol composition and GXM structure allowing the organisms to
evade the host immune response. 67
The incubation period can range from 2 to 13 months. 68 , 69
Exposure and self-limiting infection may occur in some
individuals, with reactivation of viable cryptococci in residual
granulomatous
foci
months
or
years
later
with
59
immunosuppressive drug therapy or illness.
Because of this
delay, a travel history to areas where Cryptococcus is highly
endemic (such as British Columbia or the west coast of the United
States) may be present in animals and humans residing in
nonendemic regions. After infection is established within the lung
or nasal cavity, the organism can spread hematogenously via
macrophages to other sites, particularly the lymph nodes, eye,
skin, and CNS (see Fig. 82.1). Cryptococcus spp. can cross the
capillary endothelium and enter the CNS by traveling within
infected macrophages (“Trojan horse” mechanism). Free
organisms may also be able to penetrate the blood-brain barrier
by penetrating between damaged endothelial cells, or by
transcytosis, whereby free organisms cross through capillary
endothelial cells into the brain parenchyma, causing meningitis or
meningoencephalitis. 30 , 70 In humans, cerebral cryptococcosis is
often associated with increased intracranial pressure, and this
probably also occurs in cats and dogs. Spread of infection to the
eye, either along the optic nerves from the brain or as a result of
hematogenous spread, may result in concurrent cryptococcal optic
neuritis and chorioretinitis. In animals with nasal cavity
involvement, extension of infection into the brain may also follow
osteomyelitis of the cribriform plate or of the ventral wall of the

vetexamprep.ir

frontal sinus. Middle ear involvement can also occur. 71 Infection
also often spreads from the nasal cavity to the mandibular lymph
nodes.
Multifocal cutaneous involvement in cats and dogs reﬂects
hematogenous dissemination from the primary site of infection
(usually respiratory tract), as do lesions in bone (e.g., digits) or
periarticular soft tissues. Primary cutaneous lesions are rare,
although occur more frequently in species like the koala, due to
direct inoculation from heavily contaminated environments. Dogs
infected with C. neoformans ss often develop widely disseminated
disease, with involvement of sites such as the GI system, pancreas,
mesenteric lymph nodes, kidneys, myocardium, and thyroid
gland (Fig. 82.3). 11 , 33 , 72 , 73 In contrast, dogs infected with C.
deuteroga ii (VGII) in the United States tend to have isolated
caudal nasal cavity cryptococcomas, which can extend through
the cribriform plate into the brain (Fig. 82.4). Primary GI tract
cryptococcosis is rare but does seem to occur and may be
associated with C. deuteroga ii (VGII). 74 , 75

Clinical Features in Cats
Cryptococcosis is often a chronic infection in cats, and aﬀected
cats are usually otherwise well but occasionally have mild
lethargy and inappetence. Fever is rare, and when it occurs, it
tends to be of low grade. Upper respiratory tract signs due to
nasal cavity involvement are common including sneezing and
nasal discharge which can be mucopurulent, serous, or
hemorrhagic in nature. A ﬁrm to ﬂuctuant swelling over the
bridge of the nose may be present with or without mandibular
lymphadenopathy. Single or multifocal ulcerated or nonulcerated
cutaneous masses may also be present (Fig. 82.5). 76

vetexamprep.ir

Lower respiratory tract signs such as tachypnea are uncommon
but can occur as a result of pleural eﬀusion or severe mediastinal
lymphadenomegaly. Neurologic signs vary depending on the
location of lesions in and around the CNS (see Physical
Examination Findings), and, rarely, cats with CNS involvement
lack obvious neurologic signs. Optic neuritis and chorioretinitis
develop in as many as one third of aﬀected cats and almost
always indicate CNS involvement.
Other signs include peripheral lymphadenomegaly (which may
be unassociated with skin lesions and is often asymmetric),
lameness due to osteomyelitis or cryptococcal arthritis, and
swollen digits. Rarely, involvement of the abdominal lymph
nodes, kidneys, lower urinary tract, spleen, liver, thyroid, and
salivary glands occurs.
Clinical Features in Dogs
In contrast to cats, dogs frequently develop severe disseminated
disease. In one study, 80% of dogs had involvement of multiple
anatomic sites, and 50% of dogs had involvement of sites other
than the nasal cavity, skin, lungs, lymph nodes, kidney, eye, and
CNS. 11 Weight loss, lethargy, and inappetence are common
nonspeciﬁc ﬁndings. Rhinosinusitis from cryptococcosis may be
subclinical in dogs, so its incidence may be underestimated. 11 , 34
However, sneezing and mucopurulent nasal discharge can also
occur. Neurologic signs were present in two thirds of aﬀected
dogs from California. 11 Dogs can also primarily show signs of GI
or pancreatic involvement, such as vomiting, diarrhea, and
abdominal pain. 54 , 74 , 75

Cutaneous involvement is uncommon in dogs but, as in cats,
may be a marker for disseminated disease. Although rarely
detected antemortem, more than half of dogs have lower

are infrequently present in dogs include peripheral
lymphadenomegaly or lameness (due to osteomyelitis or arthritis)

Physical Examination Findings
Cats
Upper respiratory tract signs are common physical examination
ﬁndings in cats with cryptococcosis. These include sneezing;
snuﬄing; and mucopurulent, serous, or hemorrhagic nasal
discharge that is unilateral or bilateral. In some cats, a ﬂeshy mass
protrudes from the nostril. Other cats have one or more ﬁrm to
ﬂuctuant, ulcerated or nonulcerated, subcutaneous swellings over
the bridge of the nose. These swellings may communicate with the
frontal sinus or nasal cavity, and palpation of the lesions may
reveal crepitus due to subcutaneous emphysema. Cats with
nasopharyngeal cryptococcosis develop stertor, stridor, and,
occasionally, otitis media. Mandibular lymphadenopathy is often
present. Ulcerated or proliferative lesions of the buccal mucosa
can also be found. Multifocal skin lesions consist of nodules or
masses that are ﬂuctuant to ﬁrm, up to several centimeters in
diameter, and may ulcerate (see Fig. 82.5).

Neurologic examination abnormalities in cats with CNS
involvement include obtundation; atypical behavior; slow
menace, palpebral, or pupillary light responses; mydriasis or
anisocoria (Fig. 82.6A); twitching or tremors; and seizures,
circling, head pressing, ataxia, paresis, abnormal placing
reactions, head tilt, nystagmus, and spinal pain. 10 Fundoscopic
examination may reveal granulomatous chorioretinitis, exudative
retinal detachment, papilledema, evidence of optic neuritis,
and/or retinal hemorrhage (Fig. 82.6B). Severe ocular lesions or
optic neuritis may result in blindness with dilated and
unresponsive pupils.

Dogs
Many dogs with cryptococcosis are lethargic or obtunded because
of disseminated disease and/or CNS involvement. When fever
occurs, it is typically low grade. Other CNS signs in dogs include
absent or slow menace, gag, or pupillary light responses,
nystagmus, mydriasis, head tilt, strabismus, anisocoria, facial
paralysis, paraparesis, abnormal placing reactions, ataxia, circling,
seizures, twitching or tremors, reluctance to open the mouth,
absent or decreased segmental reﬂexes, and, commonly, cervical
hyperesthesia. 10 , 33 Some dogs show signs that resemble those of
cervical disc herniation. The most common ocular abnormalities
are chorioretinitis, papilledema, evidence of optic neuritis, and
retinal detachment. Decreased nasal airﬂow may be present in
dogs with nasal cavity cryptococcomas. Nodules, masses, or
ulcers may involve any portion of the integument, and the nose,
tongue, buccal mucosa, hard palate, lips, or nail beds.

a Clinical abnormalities vary depending on the Cryptococcus

species/molecular type, host species (dog versus cat) and level of
immunocompromise. For example, widely disseminated disease that
involves multiple parenchymal organs is most often seen in young
adult, often purebred dogs with Cryptococcus neoformans sensu stricto
(VNI) infection, resembling that in human AIDS patients. See text for
more details.

Diagnosis
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of cryptococcosis is usually straightforward
and based on evaluation of representative tissue specimens with
cytology, culture, and occasionally histopathology, with or
without serologic detection of cryptococcal antigen in body ﬂuids
(Table 82.2). Suitable specimens include nasal swabs, nasal
washings, needle aspirates from mass lesions or enlarged lymph
nodes, bronchoalveolar lavage specimens, pleural ﬂuid, CSF, and
urine.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Profile, and
Urinalysis
Changes in the CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis in animals
with cryptococcosis are generally mild and nonspeciﬁc. Mild to
moderate nonregenerative anemia; leukocytosis, often with
monocytosis; and eosinophilia are the most common ﬁndings.
Dogs with disseminated disease may have a neutrophilia with a
left shift. The serum biochemical proﬁle reﬂects speciﬁc organ
involvement in animals with disseminated disease. Occasionally,
cryptococcal yeasts are found on examination of the urine
sediment.

Cerebrospinal Fluid Examination

vetexamprep.ir

The CSF in cats and dogs with neurologic signs due to
cryptococcosis may have an increased protein concentration
(usually between 10 and 140 mg/dL in cats, but may be several
hundred or rarely more than 1,000 mg/dL in dogs). 10 Leukocyte
counts can range from 2 to more than 1000 cells/µL in both dogs
and cats. A mixed cellular pleocytosis is generally present, with
neutrophils or large mononuclear cells generally outnumbering
other cell types. Some dogs have a marked eosinophilic
pleocytosis. Cryptococcal yeasts are visible in most but not all
animals with cryptococcal meningitis (see Fig. 82.2). 10 Marked
deterioration in neurologic status occasionally occurs in animals
with CNS cryptococcosis immediately after CSF collection. Many
animals have intracranial mass lesions or increased CSF pressure,
which can increase the risk of cerebellar herniation following a
cisternal tap. Wherever possible, a empts to make a diagnosis
with serum antigen testing or collection of specimens from other
anatomic sites should be considered as an alternative to diagnosis
by CSF analysis.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Thoracic radiographs in dogs and cats are often normal. In some
animals, interstitial to alveolar inﬁltrates or small nodular lesions
are present. Occasionally, large pulmonary nodules, hilar
lymphadenopathy, a mediastinal granuloma, or pleural eﬀusion
are found. 58
Computed Tomography
In cats with nasal cryptococcosis, CT of the nasal cavity can reveal
soft tissue and ﬂuid opaciﬁcation of the nasal cavity or frontal
sinus, peripherally contrast-enhancing mass lesions of the nasal
planum, and lysis of the nasal bones or of the cribriform plate. 11
CT was used to document a contrast-enhancing right cranial lung
lobe mass that invaded the distal trachea and right mainstem
bronchus in a cat from Arizona. 78 In dogs, CT ﬁndings in the
nasal cavity include peripherally contrast-enhancing mass lesions
within the frontal sinuses, caudal nasal cavity, nasopharynx, or
the retrobulbar space and associated osteomyelitis (see Fig.

vetexamprep.ir

82.4A). CNS abnormalities such as ventricular dilation and intraaxial contrast-enhancing mass lesions have been described in dogs
using CT. 10 However, MRI is more sensitive for detection of CNS
lesions in human patients, 59 and the same is probably true for
dogs and cats.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI abnormalities in cats with CNS cryptococcosis consist of
single or multifocal contrast-enhancing mass lesions that tend to
be hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1weighted images, as well as mild to moderate, diﬀuse or focal
meningeal enhancement. 10 Some cats have lesions that appear
ﬂuid-ﬁlled on T2-weighted images but have a greater T1-weighted
intensity than expected for acellular ﬂuid (“high T2, low T1
lesions”; Fig. 82.7). 10 MRI in dogs may show contrast-enhancing
mass lesions that are hyperintense on T2-weighted images and of
variable intensity on T1-weighted images, as well as meningeal
enhancement (see Fig. 82.4B). Ventriculomegaly and/or cribriform
plate osteomyelitis may also be evident.
Sonographic Findings
Over 80% of cats with cryptococcosis have normal abdominal
ultrasound examinations. Cats with kidney involvement can have
iso- to hypoechoic intraparenchymal mass lesions on ultrasound,
with or without associated renal failure. These sometimes involve
the renal pelvis. However, cats with renal involvement can also
have normal abdominal ultrasound examinations. 11
Ultrasonographic ﬁndings in dogs include intra-abdominal
lymphadenomegaly, multifocal gastric and small intestinal
thickening, changes suggestive of pancreatitis, renal mass lesions,
and/or ascites (see Fig. 82.3). 11 , 73

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination
Cytologic examination can be performed on aspirates, body
ﬂuids, or impression smears of biopsy specimens. Romanowskytype stains, new methylene blue, and Gram stain are all
satisfactory for making a cytologic diagnosis. India ink can be

vetexamprep.ir

used to examine CSF for cryptococcal yeasts, which appear
unstained and silhoue ed against a black background. India ink
staining of CSF has been used in the diagnosis of human
cryptococcal infections (Fig. 82.8). 59 However, lymphocytes and
fat droplets can sometimes be confused with the organism.
Although cytologic examination of nasal or cutaneous exudates,
aspirates, or body ﬂuids for organisms is a rapid and sensitive test
for cryptococcosis, negative test results do not eliminate the
possibility of cryptococcosis. Generally, organisms are found only
by cytologic examination of CSF in 60% to 80% of dogs and cats. 11
If a suﬃcient index of suspicion exists, additional diagnostic tests
such as histopathology, antigen testing, and/or fungal culture are
indicated.
Fungal Culture
Cryptococcus spp. are readily cultured from aspirates, exudate,
CSF, urine, and tissue specimens. A empts to culture the
organism are recommended whenever possible before treatment
is initiated, because isolation conﬁrms the diagnosis, can be used
to diﬀerentiate C. ga ii SC from C. neoformans SC organisms, and
permits antifungal susceptibility testing for cases that
subsequently fail to respond adequately to antifungal drug
treatment. Some veterinary diagnostic laboratories still report all
Cryptococcus isolates as C. neoformans in the absence of tests to
discriminate between C. neoformans SC and C. ga ii SC organisms.
If the report lists C. neoformans as the isolate, the laboratory must
therefore be consulted to determine whether C. neoformans SC was
diﬀerentiated from C. ga ii SC. However, whether the clinician
needs to know whether the isolate belongs to the C. neoformans SC
or the C. ga ii SC is debatable because at this time, species
identiﬁcation
does
not
clearly
inﬂuence
treatment
recommendations or prognosis in dogs and cats. If Cryptococcus is
isolated from a contaminated site such as the nasal cavity, a
diagnosis of cryptococcosis should be supported with cytologic or
histopathologic evidence of active infection. This is because
subclinical colonization occurs in some animals.

Pathogenic Cryptococcus species grow on almost all laboratory
media, but fungal isolation media (such as Sabouraud’s dextrose
agar) and incubation temperatures of 25°C or 30°C in addition to
incubation at 37°C are preferred when fungi are being considered
in the diﬀerential diagnosis. Antibiotics are added to the medium
for isolation of Cryptococcus spp. from contaminated sites, such as
the nasal cavity. Colonies usually are visible in 2 to 3 days, but
sometimes incubation for up to 10 days is required. Unlike other
dimorphic fungi, Cryptococcus grows as a yeast, rather than a
mold, on routine fungal media and so is less likely to represent a
laboratory hazard than organisms that grow as molds. The
organisms form white, creamy colonies. Often colonies of the C.
ga ii SC are more mucoid than those of the C. neoformans SC. The
organism is identiﬁed based on its microscopic morphology and

vetexamprep.ir

either response to biochemical tests in commercial yeast
identiﬁcation kits or MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (see Chapter
4). Canavanine-glycine-bromothymol blue (CGB) agar is used to
diﬀerentiate between C. neoformans SC and C. ga ii SC isolates. 79
Unlike C. neoformans SC organisms, C. ga ii SC organisms grow
on CGB agar and turn the media a brilliant deep blue (Fig. 82.9).
Fungal culture of the CSF is frequently positive in patients with
CNS cryptococcosis and should be performed even if the
organism cannot be demonstrated cytologically or serologically.
Culture of urine specimens collected using cystocentesis is also
indicated when cryptococcosis is suspected, even when obvious
renal involvement is not present and cytologic abnormalities are
not present. Identiﬁcation of molecular types for epidemiologic
purposes requires specialized techniques such as multilocus
sequence typing or PCR ﬁngerprinting. However, MALDI-TOF
mass spectrometry can also rapidly diﬀerentiate between
Cryptococcus species, and may be used in veterinary clinical
microbiology laboratories for this purpose in the future. 80
Most cryptococcal isolates from dogs or cats are susceptible to
amphotericin B (AMB), 5-ﬂucytosine, and azoles. Rarely,
resistance to 5-ﬂucytosine and azole antifungal drugs (especially
ﬂuconazole) is detected. In general, MICs for ﬂuconazole are
higher than those for other azole drugs, and this does not imply
resistance in vivo. In the human literature, it has been suggested
that when the MIC rises during treatment, or if the initial MIC is
at least 16 µg/mL for ﬂuconazole, or at least 128 µg/mL for
ﬂucytosine, failure of antifungal drug treatment may result from
drug resistance. 59 There is evidence that organisms that belong to
the C. ga ii SC may be more resistant to ﬂuconazole than those
that belong to the C. neoformans SC. 81

Serologic Testing
Latex agglutination assays (referred to as the latex cryptococcal
antigen test [LCAT]) for detection of cryptococcal polysaccharide
capsular antigen are widely used for diagnosis of cryptococcosis
in veterinary patients and are sensitive and speciﬁc. 11 , 82 , 83
(Note: the latex agglutination assay oﬀered by Meridian
Biosciences is known as the Cryptococcal Latex Agglutination
System [CALAS]). Serologic assays detect the antigen of all
species in the C. neoformans SC and C. ga ii SC and can be used on
serum or CSF. These can provide a rapid diagnosis when
organisms cannot be visualized or cultured. When positive, serum

vetexamprep.ir

cryptococcal antigen assays can be advantageous in animals with
neurologic signs when CSF collection is unacceptably risky or if a
diagnosis of cryptococcosis is unlikely but requires additional
evidence for exclusion.
In human patients, commercial kits typically have at least 90%
sensitivity and 97% to 100% speciﬁcity. 59 Results have been
similar for small animal patients, 11 , 82 , 83 although false-negative
results may be more common in dogs than in cats. 11 Falsepositive test results are reduced when test specimens are
pretreated in the laboratory with pronase (a proteinase). 59 In
human patients, titers below 1:8 can represent false-positive
results, although false-positive titers of up to 1:200 have rarely
been detected in cats. 11 These cats had other causative etiologies
identiﬁed that explained their clinical signs. In some cats, these
low positive titers may represent subclinical colonization.
A empts to obtain cytologic or histopathologic conﬁrmation of
infection in animals with titers of 1:200 or less are recommended.
Antigen titers are frequently extremely high (>1:65,536) in cats
and dogs with cryptococcosis, but even a titer of 1:2 can indicate
cryptococcal infection. 82 Titer results from diﬀerent kits vary
considerably; therefore, the methodology should not be altered
when monitoring the response to treatment. A good prognosis is
indicated by a decrease in antigen titer, whereas a persistent titer
after treatment suggests continued infection. Reductions in the
titer typically lag behind clinical improvement. No correlation has
been found between pretreatment antigen titer and outcome.
Other detection methodologies exist including ELISA assays
and immunochromatography. A POC dipstick cryptococcal
antigen lateral ﬂow assay (CrAg, IMMY Diagnostics, Norman,
OK, USA) is one of the most reliable screening tests in human
medicine and has the beneﬁt of providing rapid test results. 84 It
has been validated in cats and dogs from Australia with a
sensitivity of 92% and 100% and speciﬁcity of 81% and 84%,
respectively. 85 In the United States, the assay had a sensitivity of
92% and speciﬁcity of 93.2% compared with the LCAT when
applied to cats and dogs with and without cryptococcosis.
Another POC assay (CryptoPS, Biosynex, Strasbourg, France)
correctly classiﬁed 8/10 tested LCAT-positive specimens and 56/59
LCAT-negative specimens (sensitivity 80%, speciﬁcity 94.9%). This

vetexamprep.ir

la er assay is semiquantitative, with high titer and low titer
bands, and oﬀers greater ease of use in practice than the IMMY
assay. However, suboptimal sensitivity of this assay when
compared with the IMMY assay has also been documented in
humans. 86 In animals recovering from cryptococcosis with
treatment, sometimes the POC assays were positive when LCAT
was negative, so these assays may be more sensitive for
monitoring treatment. 87 Use of a combination of POC assays and
LCAT may ultimately prove to oﬀer the highest sensitivity for
treatment monitoring, but whether this leads to reduced rates of
relapse requires further study.
Because the sensitivity of cryptococcal antigen testing is not
100%, cryptococcosis should not be ruled out on the basis of a
negative antigen titer alone. This is especially important in dogs,
because false negatives are more common in dogs than in cats. 11
False negatives are most common in animals with localized
ocular, CNS, or solitary cutaneous lesions. For dogs and cats
suspected to have cryptococcal meningoencephalomyelitis that
have negative serum antigen titers, CSF should be submi ed for
cytologic examination, antigen titers, and fungal culture.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Real-time PCR assays for Cryptococcus spp. are oﬀered on a
commercial basis by some veterinary diagnostic laboratories.
These assays can conﬁrm the presence of Cryptococcus DNA in
tissues or body ﬂuids when other means fail. However, because a
diagnosis of cryptococcosis is usually apparent based on the
methods described earlier, PCR is currently not regarded as a
routinely useful clinical tool. Because Cryptococcus DNA has been
detected using PCR assays in small intestinal contents from
healthy dogs and dogs with chronic enteropathies, 88 positive
results on intestinal biopsies may not reﬂect cryptococcosis.
Similarly, because subclinical nasal cavity colonization can occur,
positive results on nasal biopsies may not represent invasive
disease. Because false positives also have the potential to occur as
a result of contamination in the PCR laboratory, a PCR diagnosis
of cryptococcosis should always be supported by cytologic or
histopathologic evidence of infection and/or culture of
Cryptococcus spp. from a normally sterile site.

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic Findings
Gross lesions associated with cryptococcosis vary from gelatinous
masses that consist almost exclusively of organisms to wellordered granulomas or pyogranulomas that typically occur in
patients with improved CMI responses. The gelatinous
appearance is a reﬂection of the large amount of capsular
polysaccharide present in lesions. In sections stained with H&E,
Cryptococcus yeasts are faint, eosinophilic, round to oval bodies
that are surrounded by a clear halo (the unstained capsule). In
fact, the histopathologic lesion is often dominated by the negative
staining capsule, sometimes occupying most of the lesion. The
organism’s cell wall is more easily visualized with PAS,
methenamine silver, or Fontana-Masson stain, although the
capsule still does not stain well with these methods. With Mayer’s
mucicarmine stain, the cryptococcal capsule takes on a rose red
color, and the organism appears pink against a blue background.
Other fungi with similar morphologic features do not stain with
Mayer’s mucicarmine. Some Cryptococcus strains have poorly
developed capsules. Infections with capsular-deﬁcient organisms
were described in four cats from the United States (Texas and
upstate New York) with pyogranulomatous and eosinophilic
dermatitis; in some of these cases, it was possible to identify
infection with C. neoformans ss. 76 If necessary, IHC or the use of
molecular methods (PCR) can be used to diﬀerentiate Cryptococcus
from other fungi and molecular methods can provide information
on the identity of the species complex present. 89
Cats
In cats that die or are euthanized as a result of cryptococcosis,
histopathology of lesions within the nasal cavity may reveal
granulomatous rhinitis. CNS cryptococcosis consists of either
meningitis 58 or meningoencephalomyelitis, with single or
multiple cerebral granulomas (Fig. 82.10). Extension of infection
from the meninges along perforating arteries into the VirchowRobin spaces can result in cystic collections of yeast organisms
sometimes referred to as “soap-bubble lesions” and known as
10

include
pyogranulomatous to granulomatous chorioretinitis, optic

separation. Other aﬀected organs include skin and subcutaneous
tissues, kidneys, and lymph nodes. Renal granulomas have been
found in some cats with disseminated disease. Granulomas can
also occasionally be found in the spleen, adrenal glands, thyroid
glands, and liver.
Dogs
Dogs that die or are euthanized because of cryptococcosis often
have CNS infection, ocular involvement, or widely disseminated

Treatment
Treatment recommendations for dogs and cats with
cryptococcosis have been based on evidence-based studies
performed in human patients and clinical experiences; evidencebased studies are lacking for veterinary patients. The most
common problems encountered are the high cost of therapy,
requirement for multiple hospital visits, and the need for regular
medication of pets for a protracted period. Resistance to
antifungal medications is not common; however, development of
ﬂuconazole and ﬂucytosine resistance has been reported. 90–92
Immunocompromised animals (which may include purebred
dogs with no obvious underlying immunodeﬁciency) are
especially likely to have persistent or progressive infection in the
face of treatment. In many aﬀected animals, treatment must be
continued for years or the life of the animal. Surgical debulking

vetexamprep.ir

could be considered before treatment for large cryptococcomas to
improve drug penetration. However, even large cryptococcomas
can resolve with medical treatment alone, and surgery should
only be performed if lesions can be easily and safely resected. The
reader is referred to Chapter 11 for detailed information on
antifungal drugs.

Cats
Cats with localized cutaneous disease can sometimes be treated
successfully with azole monotherapy. The initial drug of choice is
ﬂuconazole (10 mg/kg, PO, q12h), because of its good penetration
of the brain, eye, and urinary tract; low cost; and minimal adverse
eﬀects.
Treatment should be continued until there is complete lesion
resolution and the cryptococcal antigen titer becomes negative. A
fourfold to ﬁvefold reduction in the antigen titer suggests an
adequate response. In cats with C. ga ii ss or C. neoformans ss
infections, this typically takes 2 to 12 months (median, 4 months),
32 although longer periods of therapy may be required for some
cats. For recovered animals that achieve an antigen titer of 0, the
titer can be monitored every 3 to 6 months so that any recurrence
is diagnosed early. However, in the authors’ experience, many
cats with C. deuteroga ii (VGII) and C. bacillisporus (VGIII)
infections in North America fail to respond completely to
ﬂuconazole treatment, antigen titers persist at high levels, and
relapse may ultimately occur after an initial treatment response.
In some of these cats, treatment with itraconazole (5–10 mg/kg,
PO, q24h [capsules] or 3–5 mg/kg, PO, q24h [solution]) can lead to
clinical remission. Itraconazole does not have good penetration
into the CNS; however, it has been used successfully to treat
cryptococcal meningitis. 35 , 83 , 93 Ketoconazole has also been used
with success when treating C. deuteroga ii infections from the
Vancouver Island region. 2 Serum liver enzyme activities should
be monitored monthly during treatment with azole antifungal
drugs to monitor for hepatotoxicity (see Chapter 11).
AMB is the most eﬀective anticryptococcal agent. Penetration of
the CNS and vitreous is poor, but clinical responses still occur in
cats and dogs with CNS and ocular cryptococcosis, presumably
because the blood-brain barrier is compromised. A combination of

vetexamprep.ir

AMB and 5-ﬂucytosine (250 mg, PO, q8h) is considered the
optimal therapy for cats (and humans, but not dogs) with CNS
cryptococcosis, or for those that fail to respond to azole drugs.
Fluconazole can be substituted for 5-ﬂucytosine if 5-ﬂucytosine is
unaﬀordable. However, 5-ﬂucytosine shows synergy when
combined with AMB and eﬀectively penetrates the blood-brain
barrier. Because resistance can develop rapidly when 5-ﬂucytosine
is used alone, it is used chieﬂy to improve the eﬃcacy of other
antifungal drugs. 92 Lipid-complexed AMB preparations are not
necessarily more eﬀective but are less nephrotoxic, which may
translate into greater eﬃcacy because higher doses can be used,
although at a substantially increased cost. In human patients,
higher doses of AMB more eﬀectively sterilize the CSF. The reader
is referred to Chapter 11 for dosing protocols for various
formulations of AMB. Treatment with 5-ﬂucytosine (or
ﬂuconazole) and AMB is continued for 2 to 4 weeks (ideally 4
weeks) or until azotemia develops, after which treatment is
continued with azole monotherapy. Additional courses of AMB
may be required to maintain clinical remission in some cats.
Although controlled trials have not been performed, some cats
with CNS cryptococcosis have shown apparent response to
addition of terbinaﬁne to the treatment regimen when other drugs
failed to resolve clinical signs. 94

Dogs
If aﬀordable to the owner, dogs with disseminated disease or CNS
involvement should be treated initially with deoxycholate or
lipid-complexed AMB and ﬂuconazole. Dogs treated with
ﬂucytosine frequently develop toxic epidermal necrolysis,
typically 10 to 14 days after starting therapy, which precludes
treatment with ﬂucytosine in this species. 95 Some dogs with CNS
involvement respond to azole monotherapy, although residual
neurologic signs may persist. 10 Other potential outcomes include
incomplete recovery, with persistent active infection despite
therapy, or relapse after prolonged clinical remission. In one dog,
surgical debridement of an extradural spinal cord granuloma
combined with ﬂuconazole treatment controlled spinal cord
infection. 96 Again, azoles are fungistatic and rely on a CMI
response and phagocytosis to remove cryptococcal yeasts from the

vetexamprep.ir

host, which may be lacking in some dogs with cryptococcosis.
Treatment of a dog with intestinal cryptococcosis with terbinaﬁne
was associated with long-term disease resolution when treatment
with azoles, surgical debulking, and AMB failed. 73

Other Antifungal Treatments
Other antifungal drugs that are eﬀective for treatment of
cryptococcosis include voriconazole and posaconazole. Both
drugs penetrate the CNS and are therefore potentially
advantageous for treatment of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis,
but urinary concentrations are low. However, virtually all cats
and some dogs do not tolerate voriconazole treatment because of
GI, neurologic, and cardiac adverse eﬀects. 97 , 98 In humans,
posaconazole 99 is well tolerated, and it has been used to treat
other fungal infections without complication in cats (see Chapter
11), so it could be an option for cats with refractory disease. 99 In
the future, novel drugs such as the azole isavuconazole may oﬀer
promise for treatment of cryptococcal infections in dogs and cats,
100 but pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies will be required
before agents used for humans can be considered safe and
eﬃcacious.

Supportive Care
Because many cats and dogs with CNS involvement deteriorate
clinically during initial treatment with antifungal drugs as a result
of the inﬂammatory response to dying yeasts, anti-inﬂammatory
doses of short-acting glucocorticoids may be necessary to support
animals with CNS cryptococcosis for the ﬁrst few days to weeks
of treatment and may increase survival rate at 10 days after
initiation of treatment. 10 Deterioration of neurologic status in the
ﬁrst few days of treatment is not a negative prognostic indicator if
the animal can be supported through this phase. Supportive care
with IV ﬂuid therapy, tube feeding, and antiseizure medications
may be necessary. Rarely, dogs or cats require supplemental
oxygen because of respiratory involvement.

Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

In general, cats show signiﬁcant clinical improvement within 1 to
2 weeks of starting therapy. In studies from Australia, around 75%
of cats were treated successfully. 8 , 32 As many as 60% of cats may
be cured after an initial course of therapy, although some cats that
show an initial favorable response to therapy can relapse,
sometimes as long as 10 years after therapy is discontinued. 32 In
one study, the median survival time of cats with CNS
cryptococcosis was only 13 days (range, 0–4,050 days), but a
median survival time was never reached if cats survived at least 3
days after diagnosis, so supportive care during this phase may be
critical. 10
The prognosis is more guarded for dogs. Six of 11 dogs with
cryptococcosis in Australia were treated successfully. 32 In a study
from the western United States 9 and another from southwestern
Australia, 5 the success rate was lower, around 30%. The median
survival time for dogs with CNS cryptococcosis was 7 days
(range, 0–3,680 days). 10
In human patients with cryptococcosis, negative prognostic
indicators include underlying immunosuppressive disease or
drugs, abnormal mental state, high organism burden at
presentation (as deﬁned by large numbers of yeasts in the CSF
and/or high antigen titers), and a poor anti-inﬂammatory
response in the CSF (<20 cells/µL). 101 The presence of CNS
disease appears to negatively aﬀect outcome in both cats and
dogs. 102 , 103 In dogs and cats with CNS involvement, the
presence of altered mental status at ﬁrst evaluation was associated
with increased mortality (P = .03). 10

Immunity And Vaccination
Cryptococcosis can occur in apparently immunocompetent or in
immunodeﬁcient individuals, although those with deﬁciencies of
CMI are most commonly infected. Production of Th1-type
cytokines such as IL-2, TNF-α, and IFN-γ and a granulomatous
inﬂammatory response are important for elimination of infection,
and decline in the CD4+ T-cell count to less than 50 to 100 cells/µL
correlates well with the risk of infection in HIV-infected humans.
59 No vaccines are available.

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
Prevention of cryptococcosis may be possible through avoidance
of exposure to ecologic niches of the organism, such as pigeon
feces. Nevertheless, cryptococcosis occurs in animals housed
exclusively indoors, and widespread exposure and recovery likely
occurs in endemic areas.

Public Health Aspects
Cryptococcosis is an important opportunistic fungal infection of
humans with AIDS, in particular those who are not treated with
highly active antiretroviral therapy. Human infection is acquired
from the environment and not by direct contact with infected
animals, although intense exposure to avian excrement has been
associated with some cryptococcosis cases in HIV-infected
humans. 104 Malignancy, chemotherapy, immunosuppressive
drug therapy, diabetes mellitus, splenectomy, cirrhosis, or
sarcoidosis can also predispose to the disease. Severe meningitis
and disseminated infections can develop in immunodeﬁcient
patients. Identiﬁcation of Cryptococcus spp. infection or
colonization of cats has been proposed as a sentinel for human
infection in Italy and Brazil. 53 , 105
The organism does not aerosolize from sites of tissue infection,
so the disease cannot spread among humans or animals. The
major public health signiﬁcance of infected pets is that cats may
act as a sentinel for infection of human beings, because of their
susceptibility to infection. In the diagnostic laboratory, culture of
Cryptococcus is not a signiﬁcant health hazard, because only the
yeast form is grown routinely, and this form does not aerosolize
from media. During handling of infected tissues or cultures,
precautions should be taken to prevent inadvertent cutaneous
inoculation of the organism. Veterinarians should consider patient
sedation for procedures that involve FNA in order to avoid
inadvertent needle-stick injuries, which have caused localized
cutaneous infection in the human health care se ing. 106 Because
sporotrichosis is a major diﬀerential diagnosis for cats with
cutaneous lesions, gloves should always be worn and hand
hygiene performed when handling cats with suspicious lesions
(see Chapter 84).

Case Example
Signalment

“Simon,” an 8-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat
from northern California.

History

Simon was evaluated by the University of California, Davis,
VMTH, for a 5-week history of progressive weakness,
inappetence, and weight loss. Initially the owners noted that he
was reluctant to jump and had a low tail carriage; intermi ent
episodes of head shaking and sneezing were also noted. He also
had episodes of clenching the furniture with his claws. Three
weeks before he was brought to the VMTH, Simon was seen at
a local veterinary clinic where a physical examination was
unremarkable. Broad-spectrum antimicrobial drugs were
prescribed (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and enroﬂoxacin for 7
days), and he was treated with subcutaneous ﬂuids (lactated
Ringer’s solution, 150 mL, once). Over the following 5 days his
clinical signs lessened, but then anorexia developed. Physical
examination 2 days after the onset of anorexia revealed a rectal
temperature of 102.5°F (39.2°C) and weight loss (from 3.7 kg at
the previous visit to 3.2 kg). A CBC and biochemistry panel
showed mild lymphopenia (1,157 cells/µL [reference range,
1500–7000 cells/µL]). Treatment with metronidazole (39 mg/kg,
PO, q24h) and prednisone (3 mg/kg, PO, q24h) was instituted.
Three days before he was brought to the VMTH, he began
panting and vocalizing. The metronidazole was discontinued
and the prednisone dose was reduced to 1.5 mg/kg, PO, q24h.
The following day, the owners noted that Simon’s eyelids were
twitching, and he urinated and defecated on himself in the li er
box. Clindamycin (6 mg/kg, PO, q12h) was prescribed for
suspected toxoplasmosis, and Simon was referred for further
evaluation.
Simon had no other previous medical or surgical history
apart from being neutered as a ki en. He had access to the
outdoors and there were no other cats in the household. There
had been no changes in his thirst or urination, no vomiting or
diarrhea, and he was last vaccinated at 5 years of age. He had

vetexamprep.ir

y
g
killed a large rat approximately 5 weeks earlier and had not
been himself since.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 2.9 kg.
General: Obtunded but responsive, estimated as 5%
dehydrated. T = 100.2°F (37.9°C), HR = 200 beats/minute,
RR = 60 breaths/minute, CRT < 2 seconds.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Bilateral mydriasis and
absent pupillary light reﬂexes were noted. There was no
evidence of nasal discharge and nasal airﬂow was
normal. Mucous membranes were pink and slightly
tacky. Fundic examination was within normal limits.
Musculoskeletal: BCS 4/9, ambulatory. The cat had a slow
gait with a short stride.
Respiratory: Tachypnea was present with a normal
respiratory eﬀort. Normal breath sounds were present on
auscultation.
Cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary, and lymph nodes: No
clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected. The
urinary bladder was small.
Neurologic examination: The cat was mildly obtunded,
walked with a crouched stance, and behaved as if
nonvisual. Bilateral mydriasis and absent menace and
pupillary light reﬂexes were conﬁrmed. Intermi ent
horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the left was
present. Cranial nerve examination was otherwise
normal. Placing and hopping reactions were delayed in
the left pelvic limb. There was a decreased left patellar
reﬂex, but other segmental reﬂexes were intact. There was
no apparent pain on spinal palpation, but the cat
appeared painful when the tail was raised.
Neuroanatomic location: multifocal CNS disease.

CBC: HCT 27.2% (30%–50%), MCV 48.3 fL (42–53 fL),
MCHC 29.8 g/dL (30–33.5 g/dL), reticulocytes 8,400 cells/
µL (7,000–60,000 cells/µL), WBC 12,360 cells/µL (4,500–

cells/µL), lymphocytes 828 cells/µL (1,000–7,000 cells/µL),

cells/µL (150–1,100 cells/µL), basophils 0 cells/µL (0–50
cells/µL), platelets 357,000/µL (180,000–500,000 platelets/
µL).
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 150 mmol/L (151–158
mmol/L), potassium 4.3 mmol/L (3.6–4.9 mmol/L),

7.5 g/dL (6.6–8.4 g/dL), albumin 3.8 g/dL (2.2–4.6 g/dL),
globulin 3.7 g/dL (2.8–5.4 g/dL), ALT 37 U/L (27–101 U/L),
AST 28 U/L (17–58 U/L), ALP 8 U/L (14–71 U/L), GGT < 3
U/L (0–4 U/L), cholesterol 177 mg/dL (89–258 mg/dL),

RBC/HPF, few amorphous crystals, few lipid droplets.
ELISA for FeLV antigen and FIV antibody: Negative.
Latex agglutination for Cryptococcus antigen (LCAT):
Positive at 1:32,768.

Imaging Findings
Plain thoracic and abdominal radiographs: The only
abnormality present was mild lateral spondylosis of the
caudal lumbar spine.
Abdominal ultrasonography: The liver was mildly
enlarged and contained multiple small hyperechoic foci.
In the kidneys, mild cortical hyperechogenicity and
decreased corticomedullary distinction were present.
Magnetic resonance imaging (brain): Precontrast images
showed a well-deﬁned, round T2-hyperintense, T1hypointense lesion in the gray ma er of the right cerebral
cortex at the junction of the parietal and occipital lobes
(see Fig. 82.7). Postcontrast images showed moderate

vetexamprep.ir

contrast enhancement of this lesion. There was mild
contrast enhancement of the meninges ventral to the right
preoptic area. There was moderate, focal contrast
enhancement of the gray ma er at the lateral aspect of the
right pyriform lobe. There was contrast enhancement of
the medial aspect of both pyriform lobes adjacent to the
hypophysis. Impressions: multifocal contrast-enhancing
lesions with T2 hyperintensity and a cystic lesion in the
right cerebral cortex.

Cytologic Findings
CSF analysis (cisternal): Protein concentration 29 mg/dL
(reference range, <25 mg/dL). The specimen had a
moderate increase in cellularity with a low number of
erythrocytes. Numerous thick-capsuled yeast organisms
with frequent narrow budding forms were noted,
consistent with Cryptococcus spp. Nucleated cells
consisted of nondegenerate neutrophils admixed with
low numbers of variably vacuolated macrophages and
small lymphocytes. The diﬀerential cell count was 83%
neutrophils, 7% small mononuclear cells, and 10% large
mononuclear cells.

Microbiologic Testing
Fungal culture (CSF): C. ga ii SC. Multilocus sequence
typing revealed that the organism belonged to C.
deuteroga ii molecular type VGIIa.

Diagnosis

C. deuteroga ii meningoencephalitis.

Treatment

Simon was treated with deoxycholate AMB (0.25 mg/kg in 30
mL 5% dextrose IV over 30 minutes on Monday, Wednesday,
and Friday for ﬁve treatments). Before and after this treatment,
0.9% NaCl was administered at twice maintenance rate and
kidney analytes were monitored. Flucytosine (62.5 mg, PO, q8h)

vetexamprep.ir

and prednisone (2.5 mg, PO, q24h) were also administered. An
esophagostomy tube was placed for enteral nutrition because of
persistent inappetence. By day 7, Simon appeared more alert,
pupillary light reﬂexes and menace responses were present but
weak, and nystagmus had resolved. He was discharged from
the hospital on day 12, with instructions to continue treatment
with ﬂuconazole (50 mg, PO, q12h) and prednisone (2.5 mg,
PO, q48h), in addition to esophagostomy tube feeding. On day
24, he was reevaluated for lethargy of several days’ duration.
Physical examination showed resolution of cranial nerve
abnormalities, but delayed hopping reactions in all limbs were
present. He was treated with six additional AMB treatments
over 2 weeks. He began eating, and the esophageal feeding tube
was removed on day 40. Three months after diagnosis, his
neurologic signs had almost completely resolved with the
exception of occasional tremors, persistent mild placing
reaction deﬁcits, and lumbosacral pain. A cryptococcal antigen
titer was positive at 1:65,536. The ﬂuconazole was replaced with
itraconazole solution (3 mg/kg, PO, q12h). After an additional
month, the antigen titer was 1:1024, a serum chemistry proﬁle
was unremarkable, and the owners felt that Simon was a
normal cat. The prednisone treatment was discontinued
thereafter. A year later, the antigen titer was 1:20. At a recheck
examination 2 years later, the cat was neurologically normal.
The owner declined further antigen testing and chose to
continue treatment with itraconazole.

Comments

This cat had CNS cryptococcosis caused by C. deuteroga ii
(molecular type VGIIa), a hypervirulent molecular type that
emerged in British Columbia and the Paciﬁc Northwest. The
treatment plan was limited by client’s ﬁnancial concerns, which
meant that the initial course of AMB and ﬂucytosine treatment
was short, and a second course of AMB was required.
Subsequently, treatment with ﬂuconazole was associated with
limited improvement, but a change to itraconazole was
followed by dramatic clinical improvement and reduction in
antigen titers.

83: Coccidioidomycosis and
Paracoccidioidomycosis
Polina Vishkautsan, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Coccidioides spp. was first described in 1892
(by the medical student Alejandro Posadas), in a person from
Buenos Aires, Argentina, where it was initially mistaken for a
protozoan (Coccidia). 1
• Cause: Coccidioidomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis
and Coccidioides posadasii (ascomycetes, no known
teleomorph).
• Affected Hosts: Primarily humans and dogs, but also a variety
of other animals that include cats, domestic farm animal
species, and a variety of wildlife hosts.
• Geographic Distribution: Southwestern United States,
northern Mexico, and parts of Central and South America
(northeastern Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Bolivia).
Recently cases have also appeared in eastern Washington in
the United States.
• Mode of Transmission: Inhalation of arthroconidia from the
environment; rarely cutaneous inoculation.
• Major Clinical Signs: Cough, fever, inappetence, weight loss,
tachypnea, increased respiratory effort, lameness,
subcutaneous masses or draining skin lesions,
lymphadenopathy, neurologic signs, ascites due to right-sided
heart failure (pericarditis), ocular lesions (uveitis,
chorioretinitis, endophthalmitis).
• Differential Diagnoses: Neoplasia, other deep mycoses,
mycobacteriosis, actinomycosis or nocardiosis, toxoplasmosis
or neosporosis, systemic immune-mediated disease.

vetexamprep.ir

• Human Health Significance: Direct transmission from animals
to humans does not usually occur, although sharps injuries or
bite wounds from affected animals may be a source of human
infection. Dogs are a sentinel for human exposure.

Coccidioidomycosis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Coccidioides spp. are dimorphic, soil-borne fungi that exist in the
environment as a mycelium and in tissues (at 37°C) as peculiar
structures known as spherules (Fig. 83.1). The mycelium consists of
chains of haploid, multinucleated, barrel-shaped arthroconidia (or
arthrospores) that alternate with smaller, thin-walled, nonviable
cells. The arthroconidia remain viable in the soil for long periods.
They ultimately fragment from each other and are subsequently
aerosolized and inhaled by animal hosts (Fig. 83.2). The inoculum
needed for infection can be small, even a few arthroconidia. 2 This
can be followed by the development of coccidioidomycosis, a
localized pulmonary disease or a serious multisystemic disease if
dissemination occurs in the face of an inadequate immune
response.
In the environment, Coccidioides spp. are distributed in the
lower Sonoran life zone, regions characterized by semi-arid to
arid soils, low elevations above sea level, and hot summers. The
organism has been aptly referred to as “the dust devil.” 3
Worldwide, Coccidioides spp. are found in the southwestern Unites
States, Mexico, and parts of Central and South America,
speciﬁcally northeastern Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras,
Venezuela, northeastern Brazil, the Chaco region in Argentina and
Paraguay, and Bolivia (Fig. 83.3). In the southwestern United
States, highly endemic regions are the south-central valley of
California, especially Bakersﬁeld (“valley fever”) and Arizona,
especially Tucson and Phoenix. 4 Other aﬀected states in the
United States are Utah, Nevada, New Mexico, and southwestern
Texas. Since 2010, cases in non-traveled dogs and humans have
been reported from Washington state. 5 , 6 Infections also occur in
non-endemic regions in dogs and humans that have a travel
history to endemic regions. Over the last two decades, the

vetexamprep.ir

incidence of coccidioidomycosis in humans and likely also dogs
has been on the rise (Fig. 83.4); 7 , 8 it has been speculated that this
may be the result of population growth in endemic areas, climate
change, a larger population of immunocompromised humans,
and increased recognition and reporting. 9 , 10
Two species of Coccidioides have been identiﬁed— Coccidioides
posadasii and Coccidioides immitis. These appear to cause similar
clinical manifestations and have similar antifungal drug
susceptibilities, but further studies are required. 11 The geographic
range of C. immitis is largely limited to endemic regions in
California and eastern Washington state, whereas C. posadasii is
found elsewhere. 7 , 12 However, there may be some overlap in the
distribution of these organisms. 13
Infection of animals and humans with Coccidioides spp. often
follows a cycle of moist conditions (required for growth of the
organism in the soil), a dry period, then soil disruption, such as
that may occur with heavy rainfall, earthquakes, dust storms,
prolonged droughts, or construction. 14–16 An association between
the presence of Coccidioides in the soil and small desert mammal
activity has been observed; these rodents may contribute to
distribution of the fungus in the soil, 7 and it has been suggested
that they may act as reservoirs of the fungus.
Dogs of any breed, age, or sex may be aﬀected, although largebreed, young adult dogs predominate in some case series. 17 , 18 In
dogs seen at the University of California-Davis VMTH, boxers,
poodles, pointers, Labrador and golden retrievers, German
shepherd dogs, Australian shepherds, Dalmatians, Sco ish
terriers, dachshunds, and beagles are over-represented when
compared with the hospital patient population. 19 When
compared with a control population of dogs with diseases other
than coccidioidomycosis, risk factors for coccidioidomycosis
among dogs seen at the University of California-Davis VMTH
were younger age (young adult rather than older adult), digging
behavior, and travel to Arizona or the California central valley. 20
In this study, predisposed breeds were viszlas, Dalmatians,
weimaraners, greyhounds, English pointers, bull terriers, Bri any
spaniels, and boxers. Risk factors for infection in dogs from
Arizona included being housed outdoors during the day rather
than indoors, roaming area more than 1 acre, and walking in the

vetexamprep.ir

desert. 21 Latent infections may also occur in dogs and these can
reactivate after treatment with immunosuppressive drugs, such as
glucocorticoids and chemotherapeutic agents, including after
previous recovery from coccidioidomycosis.
Although not as prevalent as in dogs, coccidioidomycosis also
occurs in cats. 22 , 23 In two separate case series of cats from
Arizona, cats ranged in age from 1 to 15 years (median, 5 years in
one study and 6.8 years in another) and there was no obvious sex
or breed predisposition. 22 , 23 Many cats were indoor only. 22
Only a small number of aﬀected cats in the combined studies were
co-infected with FIV or FeLV. Interestingly, a search of the UC
Davis VMTH and pathology database from 1990 to 2015 revealed
only one case of feline coccidioidomycosis, and that cat lived in
Arizona, which might suggest cats are less susceptible to C.
immitis infection than to C. posadasii infection.

Clinical Features

vetexamprep.ir

Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The clinical signs of coccidioidomycosis depend on factors such as
the infectious dose and the immune status of the host.
Arthroconidia are inhaled and are phagocytosed by alveolar
macrophages. They then enlarge into a spherule, which measures
8 to 100 µm in diameter. Hundreds of endospores then develop
within the spherule, which are released when the mature spherule
ruptures. These a ract neutrophils, which leads to a
pyogranulomatous inﬂammatory response. Each released
endospore that escapes immune destruction then enlarges into a
new spherule, and the cycle continues. Endospores can also revert
to mycelial growth when removed from the site of infection. In
hosts that are unable to mount an eﬀective immune response,
endospores disseminate by lymphatics to tracheobronchial lymph
nodes and hematogenously to a variety of body sites. Inoculation
coccidioidomycosis can rarely occur, and generally results in
lesions that are localized to the site of the wound. In one report, it
followed removal of a foxtail from a wound. 24 Cutaneous
coccidioidomycosis appears to be predominantly a sequela of
disseminated infection, whereas primary cutaneous infection is a
rare event. 25
Most infections in endemic areas are subclinical. 26
Development of clinical signs often follows a subacute to chronic
course, with variable and often mild systemic signs such as
intermi ent fever, lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss. 17 , 27
Many dogs otherwise appear healthy, with occasional periods of
inappetence. 17 Clinical signs may be present for days to years
before veterinary a ention is sought. 18 Signs of respiratory tract
involvement include a harsh cough, increased respiratory eﬀort,
tachypnea, and/or exercise intolerance. 18 , 27 Cough may be
chronic and is sometimes associated with gagging or retching;
occasionally it results from bronchial compression by enlarged
tracheobronchial lymph nodes. Rarely, diﬀuse pneumonia follows
a fulminant course, with signs that resemble acute bacterial
pneumonia or septic shock, as reported in immunocompromised
human patients. 4

vetexamprep.ir

Life cycle of Coccidioides spp.
Hyphae fragment into arthroconidia, which are
inhaled and form spherules in tissues. The
spherules rupture and release endospores,
which form new spherules. In some dogs, the
organism disseminates from the lungs to a
variety of other tissues, but especially local
lymph nodes, bone, skin, the pericardium, the
eye, and the CNS.
FIG. 83.2

A smaller percentage of infected dogs develop disseminated
infections. Sites of dissemination often include osteoarticular sites,
the CNS, skin, peripheral lymph nodes, eye, reproductive organs
(testes, prostate, and the uterus), and the pericardium. 18 , 19
Rarely, other sites such as the liver, spleen, GI tract, peritoneal
cavity, and urinary system are aﬀected. 17 Sometimes
dissemination to only one anatomic site is evident; in other dogs
multiple sites are involved. A history of respiratory signs may be
absent. 17 Bone involvement may manifest as lameness and/or one
or more ﬁrm swellings associated with the appendicular or axial
skeleton. Dogs with skin involvement may have ulcerated skin
lesions that drain serosanguinous ﬂuid, or subcutaneous masses
(Fig. 83.5). 17 , 25 Lesions are commonly located on the trunk for
both dogs and cats, and in over 50% of cases lesions aﬀect non-

vetexamprep.ir

appendicular skeletal regions. In most cases, skin lesions should
be considered separate sites of dissemination and not necessarily
an extension of coccidioidal osteomyelitis. 25 Neurologic signs
result from meningoencephalitis or mass lesions and include
obtundation, blindness, nystagmus, absent menace reﬂexes,
diminished gag responses, ataxia, abnormal placing reactions,
pacing, circling, cervical pain, tetraparesis and seizures. 18 , 28–30
Ocular
manifestations
of
coccidioidomycosis
include
chorioretinitis, uveitis, optic neuritis, and endophthalmitis. 18 , 31 ,
32 Involvement of abdominal organs such as the liver and GI tract
can lead to inappetence, vomiting, and/or diarrhea. 17 Pericarditis
may lead to signs of right-sided cardiac failure, with ascites and
pleural eﬀusion. 17

Clinical signs in aﬀected cats from Arizona have most often
been respiratory signs (cough, tachypnea, dyspnea) and skin
lesions, which may be nodular lesions, non-healing ulcers, or
plaque-like crusting lesions. 22 , 25 In addition to those, nonspeciﬁc
signs of weight loss, inappetence, and lethargy can be commonly
seen. Fever and lameness due to bone involvement can also occur;

vetexamprep.ir

lameness, paresis, or paraparesis was described in 22% of 51 cats
in one case series. 22
Physical Examination Findings
Fever is present in up to two-thirds of aﬀected dogs with
coccidioidomycosis (range, 103 to 106°F) on physical examination.
Other common ﬁndings in dogs are lethargy, weakness, thin body
condition or profound muscle atrophy, tachypnea, increased
respiratory eﬀort, inducible or spontaneous cough, and/or
increased lung sounds. 18 Lameness and ﬁrm, often painful bony
swellings with associated muscle atrophy may be present in dogs
with osteomyelitis. 33 Less often, focal or (very rarely) generalized
peripheral lymphadenomegaly, subcutaneous masses or draining
skin lesions, or swollen joints are present. Dogs with pericardial
coccidioidomycosis may have abdominal distention with a
palpable ﬂuid wave, tachycardia, tachypnea, jugular pulses,
muﬄed breath and heart sounds due to pleural eﬀusion, mucosal
pallor, prolonged capillary reﬁll time, and weak pulses. 34
Neurologic signs, when present, include seizures, obtundation,
apparent blindness, ataxia, nystagmus, spinal pain, circling, and
tetraparesis. The most common ocular abnormality is uveitis, but
keratitis, conjunctivitis, granulomatous chorioretinitis, optic
neuritis, retinal detachment, and endophthalmitis with secondary
glaucoma have also been described. 18 , 31 , 32
In cats with coccidioidomycosis, fever was reported in 31% of
48 cats in one study 23 and 8% of 51 cats in another. 22 Skin lesions
were present in more than 40% of cats, and included draining skin
lesions, subcutaneous granulomas, plaque-like crusting lesions,
and abscesses. 23 Tachypnea or increased respiratory eﬀort was
present in 25% of aﬀected cats in one study and in 39% in another;
and lameness has been noted in approximately 20% of cats.
Ocular abnormalities that include conjunctival masses, periorbital
swellings, chorioretinitis, retinal detachment, endophthalmitis,
and/or anterior uveitis have been described. 35 , 36 A small
percentage of cats have neurological signs such as hyperesthesia,
posterior paresis, seizures, and ataxia. Dissemination to
abdominal organs such as the spleen can occur. 37

Diagnosis
Coccidioidomycosis is usually suspected based on a history of
travel to or residence in an endemic region, and consistent clinical
signs and radiographic ﬁndings. Coccidioidomycosis should be
retained in the diﬀerential diagnoses for dogs and cats that have
formerly lived in or traveled through endemic areas, for the rest of

vetexamprep.ir

y
g
their lives and regardless of whether they have previously shown
any sign of infection. Because the disease’s geographic
distribution is changing as a result of climate change, population
shifts, and construction activity, early diagnosis requires a high
index of suspicion in the regions where new reports of disease in
people and animals become available. The diagnosis can be
conﬁrmed with cytologic examination of aspirates or body ﬂuids,
serologic assays that detect antibodies to Coccidioides spp.,
histopathology, and/or fungal culture (Table 83.1).
TABLE 83.1

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
CBC ﬁndings in dogs with coccidioidomycosis are nonspeciﬁc
and resemble those of other deep mycoses. Most aﬀected dogs
have mild, normocytic, normochromic, non-regenerative anemia

vetexamprep.ir

and mild leukocytosis. Leukocytosis results from a neutrophilia,
occasionally with a left shift and evidence of neutrophil toxicity. 18
, 34 A monocytosis and lymphopenia may also be present, but in
contrast to human infections, eosinophilia is not typically present.
Neutrophilia and monocytosis have also been described in
aﬀected cats. 22
Serum Biochemical Tests
Almost all dogs with coccidioidomycosis have hypoalbuminemia,
and approximately half of aﬀected dogs and cats have
hyperglobulinemia (up to 7.8 mg/dL in one study). 18 , 22 , 23
Hypoalbuminemia is usually mild to moderate, but rarely may be
more severe (< 1.5 g/dL). Uncommonly, mild hypercalcemia is
present. Increased activity of serum ALP may be present in some
dogs, possibly as a result of bone involvement.
Urinalysis
The urinalysis in dogs with coccidioidomycosis is often normal,
but signiﬁcant proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratios as
high as 9.5, reference range < 1) has been reported in some dogs. 18
In a series of chronic canine coccidioidomycosis cases, glomerular
lesions and proteinuria were documented. 38 Dogs with
coccidioidomycosis should be carefully screened for proteinuria
to initiate timely treatment. In addition, testing dogs with proteinlosing nephropathies that have resided in Coccidioides-endemic
areas for anti-Coccidioides antibodies has the potential to identify
an underlying cause.
CSF Analysis
CSF analysis in dogs with CNS coccidioidomycosis usually
reveals an increase in protein concentration (generally < 300
mg/dL, reference range < 25 mg/dL), and a mild to moderate
increase in the nucleated cell count (usually < 50 cells/µL,
reference range < 2 cells/µL). 18 The diﬀerential cell count may
show mixed, predominantly lymphocytic, mixed mononuclear, or
neutrophilic pleocytosis. Organisms are generally not observed.

osteosarcomas (Fig. 83.7). 17 , 22 , 23 , 33

Abdominal
ultrasound
examination
of

with

Mild

Coccidioides peritonitis may have echogenic, elongated plaques on
serosal surfaces and peritoneal eﬀusion. Ascites, hepatomegaly,
and distended hepatic veins may be evident in dogs with
pericarditis and right-sided heart failure. 34
Echocardiography in dogs with Coccidioides spp. pericarditis can
reveal thickening and mass lesions of the pericardium, adherence
of the pericardium to the epicardium, pericardial and pleural
eﬀusion, and evidence of cardiac tamponade (see Fig. 122.3). 34
Detection of pleural eﬀusion using thoracic ultrasound was
described in 2 of 51 cats with coccidioidomycosis from Arizona. 22

Advanced Imaging
Advanced imaging ﬁndings in dogs with coccidioidomycosis have
not been extensively reported in the literature. Focal, contrastenhancing intra-parenchymal mass lesions in the brain or
osteomyelitis of the skull may be identiﬁed on CT of the head. 39
Thoracic CT ﬁndings include contrast-enhancing miliary nodular
pulmonary lesions; single or multifocal larger nodules or masses;
tracheobronchial, sternal, or mediastinal lymphadenopathy; focal
regions of alveolar or peribronchial inﬁltrates; lobar consolidation;
pleural or mediastinal thickening; and rarely pleural eﬀusion (Fig.
83.8).
MRI of the brain in dogs with CNS coccidioidomycosis may
show focal or multifocal lesions within the brain (Fig. 83.9). 40 , 41
While human patients typically develop meningitis, mass lesions
may be more frequently identiﬁed in dogs. When granulomas are
present, they can share multiple MRI features with CNS neoplasia
or other infectious or inﬂammatory processes. Mass lesions may
have indistinct borders on post-contrast T1-weighted images. The
degree of intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images varies greatly.
30 Other ﬁndings include ventricular dilation and/or meningeal
enhancement. Bilaterally symmetric T2 hyperintense lesions
within the frontal lobes, caudate nuclei, and rostral internal
capsule, with variable evidence of faint, wispy, contrast
enhancement were described in a subpopulation of dogs with
CNS coccidioidomycosis from Arizona; schnauzers were
overrepresented. 41 Use of other diagnostic tests such as serology
or demonstration of the organism are needed for deﬁnitive
diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis.

Cytologic Examination
Cytologic examination of aspirates of aﬀected tissues, pleural
eﬀusion, or respiratory lavage specimens typically reveals
granulomatous or pyogranulomatous inﬂammation, sometimes
with rare multinucleated giant cells, sca ered eosinophils, and/or
a reactive lymphocyte population. However, occasionally a
suppurative inﬂammatory response predominates. Fungal
elements are often not found in ﬂuid specimens. Fluid specimens

vetexamprep.ir

should be centrifuged and multiple aspirates of masses or lymph
nodes should be collected to increase chance of detection. The
clinician should alert the laboratory if there is clinical suspicion of
coccidioidomycosis since often there are only very few organisms
on the slide; because of their large size, they have the potential to
be overlooked. Spherules may be visualized as round, deeply
basophilic, double-walled, slightly crinkled structures that range
in diameter from 8 to 70 µm. Spherules are generally low in
number, often associated with cellular aggregates, but often they
are not evident or easily identiﬁed. Usually their internal structure
is not easily discernable, but occasionally endospores are seen in
association with ruptured spherules (Fig. 83.10). The endospores
are 2 to 5 µm in diameter, are surrounded by a thin, non-staining
halo, and have small, round to oval, densely aggregated, eccentric
nuclei. Endospores may be found extracellularly or within
phagocytes. In one report, endospores were visualized in a ﬁneneedle aspirate from a bone lesion in the absence of spherules. 24
Because cytology is relatively insensitive for diagnosis of
coccidioidomycosis when compared with other deep mycoses,
serologic testing for coccidioidomycosis should always be
considered when cytology of tissue aspirates, body ﬂuids, or lung
washes
reveals
pyogranulomatous,
suppurative,
or
granulomatous inﬂammation but organisms are not seen, and
exposure to Coccidioides is possible based on the history.

Serologic Diagnosis
Serologic assays that detect antibodies to Coccidioides spp. are
important diagnostic tests for coccidioidomycosis because
organism detection assays have low sensitivity. Most diagnostic
laboratories screen serum specimens with qualitative gel
immunodiﬀusion (ID) assays for IgG or IgM antibodies (see
Chapter 2). Detection of IgM (tube precipitin) or IgG (complement
ﬁxating) antibodies is reported, depending on the antigen
preparation used in the assay. In dogs, IgM is detectable within 2
to 5 weeks of infection, and IgG appears after 8 to 12 weeks. 19
Quantiﬁcation of an IgG antibody response can then be performed
with quantitative ID, whereby serial dilutions of patient serum are
subjected to gel ID. 26 In human patients, the complement ﬁxation
test is often used for quantiﬁcation of IgG antibody, but frequent
false-positive results have been described with this method in
dogs as a result of anticomplementary properties of canine serum.
42 The complement ﬁxation test is positive in most cats with
coccidioidomycosis, with titers that range from 1:2 to 1:128. 23

vetexamprep.ir

False-negative serologic test results are extremely rare in dogs
with coccidioidomycosis tested at the author’s institution, 18 , 34
but they have been described in dogs from Arizona 42–44 and
rarely in cats. 22 False-negative results can occur in early infection
and therefore sometimes a follow-up serologic test should be
performed a few weeks later if clinical suspicion for
coccidioidomycosis still remains. False-negative serologic test
results can occur in immunocompromised patients. In people,
false-negative results have been reported in forms of disease with
a more benign clinical course, such as patients with isolated
pulmonary nodules.
Positive antibody titers usually range from 1:2 to 1:256; the
median titer was 1:32 in one study. 18 There appears to be no clear
correlation between the magnitude of the IgG titer and the
severity of illness in dogs. Dogs with active infection can have
titers as low as 1:2, and healthy dogs in hyperendemic areas in
Arizona can have titers as high as 1:16. 26 As a result, positive
titers of 1:16 or lower should always be interpreted in light of
clinicopathologic abnormalities and, in hyperendemic areas, other
diagnostic tests (such as cytology or histopathology) should also
be used to conﬁrm the diagnosis if possible. Rapid antibodydetection assays have been developed, including enzyme
immunoassays (EIAs) and an immunochromatographic lateral
ﬂow assay (LFA). A commercially available EIA (MiraVista
Laboratories, Indianapolis, IN, USA) was evaluated in dogs
compared to AGID and determined to have a sensitivity of 89.2%
and speciﬁcity of 97.2%. 46 Although this assay is rapid compared
to conventional gel ID, it requires shipment of specimens to a
commercial laboratory, specialized training, and equipment to
perform with delays in the time to diagnosis. A POC LFA for
detection of antibodies to Coccidioides (Sõna LFA, IMMY
Diagnostics, OK, USA), which received FDA approval for
diagnosis of human coccidioidomycosis, has recently been
assessed for the diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis in dogs. In a
study from Arizona, an overall agreement of 87.5% was noted
between the LFA and conventional gel ID. 47 Another study from
the UC Davis VMTH revealed a sensitivity of 89% and a
speciﬁcity of 100% when compared with conventional gel ID. 48
False negatives were observed in dogs with low gel ID titers, and

vetexamprep.ir

so conﬁrmatory testing is needed if the clinical suspicion for
coccidioidomycosis remains. Otherwise, this assay represents an
excellent rapid alternative to conventional gel ID.
A serologic assay that detects Coccidioides antigen in urine is
available for diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis in human patients,
such as in immunocompromised patients that lack the ability to
produce signiﬁcant quantities of antibody. However, preliminary
data suggest that this assay has unacceptable sensitivity (≤ 20%)
for diagnosis of canine coccidioidomycosis when serum, urine, or
both specimens are tested, and false-positive reactions occur in a
small proportion of dogs with blastomycosis or histoplasmosis. 49
