Fungal Culture
Coccidioides spp. can sometimes be isolated from clinical
specimens on routine fungal media in the laboratory, but a
negative culture result does not rule out coccidioidomycosis.
Growth of a gray-white, downy mold that is tan to brown when
visualized through the bo om of the plate usually appears after
incubation for several days. The organism can be identiﬁed based

vetexamprep.ir

on its light microscopic appearance, with or without molecular
methods. Culture of Coccidioides spp. is a serious laboratory health
hazard, and should be done by suitably equipped laboratories.
The clinician should warn the laboratory of the possibility of
dimorphic fungal infection if suspected.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Real-time PCR assays have been used for rapid detection of
Coccidioides spp. in respiratory specimens or CSF from aﬀected
humans, although sensitivity has been limited. 4 , 50 PCR assays
have also been used in epidemiological studies to identify major
growth sites for Coccidioides spp. in soil. 51 PCR assays have not
yet been widely applied to the diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis in
dogs and cats.
Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in dogs with coccidioidomycosis
include mo ling and consolidation of the pulmonary
parenchyma; single or multiple, pale masses, nodular lesions, or
emphysematous bullae within the lungs (Fig. 83.11); enlarged and
ﬁrm tracheobronchial, mediastinal or sternal lymph nodes;
plaque-like lesions on the pleura; and pleural and pericardial
eﬀusion. The interior of masses or nodules may be ﬁrm, caseous,
or liqueﬁed. The pericardium and epicardium may be thickened
with mass lesions and adhesions between the pericardium and
epicardium. 34 Ascites may also be present in dogs with
pericarditis. Dogs with disseminated disease may have diﬀuse
muscle atrophy, one or more enlarged peripheral lymph nodes,
irregular bony swellings with associated draining skin lesions,
and/or evidence of arthritis and synovitis. Meningoencephalitis
may be evident as mass lesions within the brain parenchyma,
ventricular dilation secondary to obstruction of CSF ﬂow by
inﬂammatory lesions, regional discoloration within the brain,
and/or discoloration and thickening of the meninges. Rarely
prostatic enlargement, hepatic congestion and friability,
multifocal nodular lesions within the myocardium or other
parenchymal organs, and ocular lesions are present.

Histopathology of aﬀected tissues reveals large numbers of

found at all. Use of special stains such as PAS and Gomori’s
methenamine silver can enhance organism identiﬁcation within

Treatment
Treatment of coccidioidomycosis typically requires a combination
of antifungal drug therapy and supportive care; in some cases,
surgery is required. Usually a minimum of 6 months of treatment
is required.
Antimicrobial Treatment
Animals with coccidioidomycosis can respond well to azole
monotherapy with ﬂuconazole or itraconazole. Ketoconazole has
been used successfully to treat dogs and cats in the past but is no
longer recommended owing to its lower activity and increased
rate of adverse eﬀects. Fluconazole is the least expensive azole
and may be a be er choice than itraconazole for dogs with CNS
involvement, because of its superior penetration of the CNS. The
dose of ﬂuconazole is 5 to 10 mg/kg PO q12h; for dogs with
disseminated or refractory pulmonary disease, doses of 10 mg/kg
PO q12h may be required. Occasionally, such high doses can lead
to inappetence or diarrhea, especially in the ﬁrst 1 to 2 weeks of
treatment. Itraconazole (5 mg/kg PO q24h) is preferred for

vetexamprep.ir

animals with bone involvement, based on clinical studies in
people, 53 and may be eﬀective in dogs that fail to respond to
treatment with ﬂuconazole. In human patients, itraconazole
demonstrated a greater response rate in a blinded comparison
with ﬂuconazole. 53 Compounded formulations of itraconazole
should be avoided. Small dogs are best treated with itraconazole
suspension (10 mg/mL), which has higher bioavailability than the
capsules (see Chapter 11). If capsules are used, they should be
administered with food. If clinical signs do not improve with
azole treatment, therapeutic drug monitoring could be considered
to ensure serum drug concentrations are adequate. Periodic
monitoring of liver enzymes is recommended for animals treated
with azole antifungals.
Treatment with deoxycholate or lipid-complexed amphotericin
B is recommended either alone or in combination with an azole
for dogs with refractory disease or severe disease (see Chapter 11
for dosing protocols). However, studies that compare
amphotericin B to azole therapy in dogs have not been performed.
Combination therapy with an azole and terbinaﬁne are
anecdotally reported as beneﬁcial in some dogs that become
refractory to single azole treatment. 25 Controlled studies are
lacking. Voriconazole and posaconazole have excellent in vivo
activity against Coccidioides spp. Both have been used to treat
refractory coccidioidomycosis in human patients. 4 These have
been used to treat aﬀected dogs 54 , 55 but use has been limited by
expense. Voriconazole could be considered for treatment of
refractory meningoencephalitis if client ﬁnances permit its use,
because it has excellent penetration of the CNS.

Nikkomycin Z is a narrow-spectrum anti-fungal drug with
potent in vitro activity against Coccidioides spp. It inhibits the
synthesis of chitin, a fungal cell wall component which mammals
lack. This drug is currently under development as an orphan drug
for the treatment of coccidioidomycosis in people, but its
prospects for commercial development are unclear. 56 It has
shown eﬃcacy in naturally aﬀected dogs and experimentally
infected mice. 57 , 58
Surgical Management
Ultimately, some dogs with severe and persistent osteomyelitis
require amputation to control the infection, and enucleation may
be required for dogs with endophthalmitis. In some situations,
spinal surgery is required in cases of discospondylitis or intraspinal granulomas that cause spinal cord compression. 59 , 60
Successful treatment of Coccidioides pericarditis has been reported
after subtotal pericardiectomy and epicardial excision, which

vetexamprep.ir

should be performed in conjunction with antifungal drug therapy.
The perioperative mortality rate in one study was reported as
24%, and the 2-year survival rate after discharge was 82%. 34
Supportive Care
Other treatments that may be required for dogs with severe
pulmonary coccidioidomycosis are similar to those described for
blastomycosis, and include oxygen supplementation, nebulization
and coupage, drainage of thoracic eﬀusions, nutritional support,
anti-inﬂammatory drugs, and intravenous ﬂuid therapy.
Concurrent treatment with glucocorticoids and anti-seizure
medications may be necessary to reduce the severity of neurologic
signs in dogs with CNS coccidioidomycosis. Topical prednisolone
acetate solution and anti-glaucoma agents may be required for
dogs with ocular lesions.

Prognosis
The prognosis for resolution for coccidioidomycosis depends on
the severity of infection and the extent of dissemination. The
duration of treatment ranges from 6 months to many years, and in
some cases (such as with bone or CNS involvement), life-long
treatment is needed. IgG antibody titers decrease with successful
treatment, which in general should be continued until lesions
resolve and the titer is 1:2 or lower. Residual radiographic
opacities may be present in some dogs as a result of scar tissue
formation. Dogs with localized pulmonary infection have the best
prognosis; the prognosis is less predictable for dogs with CNS
involvement. Long-term clinical remissions have been described
in dogs treated with ﬂuconazole for CNS coccidioidomycosis in
two recent reports from Arizona. 40 , 41 A 2021 report of 45 clientowned dogs with suspected intracranial coccidioidomycosis
described a mean duration of follow-up of 22.4 ± 20.5 months. 40
Some dogs with Coccidioides osteomyelitis may require life-long
azole therapy. 33

Immunity and Vaccination
Immunity to Coccidioides spp. depends primarily on cell-mediated
immunity, speciﬁcally T lymphocytes. No vaccine is currently

vetexamprep.ir

available commercially for prevention of the disease, but the
potential for eﬀective immunization exists because recovered
individuals rarely become reinfected. A variety of vaccine
strategies have been examined for prevention of human
coccidioidomycosis. 3 One candidate is a deletion mutant strain of
C. posadasii that lacks a homolog of the gene CPS1, a virulence
factor found in a maize pathogen. Vaccination of mice with this
deletion mutant strain has protected mice from lethal infection
with C. posadasii and C. immitis, and a vaccine based on this strain
is currently under development for prevention of Valley fever in
dogs. 3 An initial challenge study in a limited number of research
beagles showed protection from disease following a prime
followed by booster vaccination; subcutaneous swelling at the site
of vaccination was the main adverse eﬀect. 61 A single vaccination
did not result in protection. Should this vaccine be successful, it
may be a model for human vaccination.

Prevention
Prevention of coccidioidomycosis requires avoidance of
hyperendemic areas (especially parts of Arizona and south-central
California), which may not be possible. In endemic areas, dogs
should be kept away from sites of soil disturbance (such as
construction sites), and housed indoors during dust storms;
digging should be discouraged. Housing dogs indoors during the
day in endemic regions may reduce the chance of infection.
Nevertheless, it should be remembered that clinical infections
only develop in a minority of exposed dogs.

Public Health Aspects
Coccidioidomycosis is a serious infection in human patients and
has similar clinical manifestations to those described in dogs. As
noted earlier in this chapter, coccidioidomycosis is considered an
emerging infectious disease, and its incidence in people has
increased in Arizona and California in the last decade, possibly as
a result of population growth, immigration of immunologically
naïve people, and construction. In an endemic area, construction
and agricultural workers, archeologists, and excavators are at high
risk for coccidioidomycosis. 2 , 4 African American and Filipino

vetexamprep.ir

patients, as well as patients with AIDS and other causes of
immunosuppression and women in the third trimester of
pregnancy and immediately post-partum are at highest risk for
disseminated disease, which occurs in approximately 1% to 3% of
infected humans. 2
Because of their susceptibility to infection, dogs have been used
as a sentinel for human exposure to environmental sources of
Coccidioides spp. in seroprevalence studies. 20 , 62 Direct
transmission between infected veterinary patients and humans
has not been reported. However, fatal disease occurred in a
veterinary resident after necropsy of a horse with disseminated
disease. 63 Inoculation coccidioidomycosis was reported in a
veterinary technician from Arizona after a bite from a cat that was
later diagnosed with disseminated disease. 37
Inoculation coccidioidomycosis also has the potential to occur if
sharps injuries occur during aspiration of aﬀected tissues, surgical
procedures, or necropsy examinations. Proper sedation or
anesthesia should always be used if coccidioidomycosis is
suspected in dogs or cats seen at veterinary clinics and the
potential for a sharps injury exists. If accidental inoculation
occurs, immediate a ention should be sought from a physician.
Prolonged ﬂuconazole prophylaxis is generally recommended
with monitoring of Coccidioides serology and liver function tests.
Bandaging of skin lesions should be avoided because of a concern
for conversion of the organism to a mycelial form in drying
organic ma er exposed to air, although no documented instances
of transmission through exposure to bandages exist. Necropsies
should be performed without delay with suitable protective
clothing, and the carcasses of animals that die from
coccidioidomycosis should immediately be incinerated. For the
same reason, burial is not recommended because of the potential
for contamination of the environment. Fluconazole prophylaxis is
also indicated after accidental laboratory exposure to inocula. 64

Paracoccidioidomycosis
Paracoccidioidomycosis is a severe systemic mycosis, almost
exclusively of people, endemic in Latin America (Brazil,
Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela). The etiologic
agents are organisms that belong to the Paracoccidioides species

vetexamprep.ir

complex, such as Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and Paracoccidioides
lu ii. 65 , 66 The eco-epidemiological niche of those fungi is not
well characterized. 67 The main clinical characteristics in people
are development of granulomatous lesions in the lungs, lymph
nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. 68 Infections result from inhalation
of conidia. Paracoccidioides spp. have been rarely recovered from
animals. To date, the fungus has been isolated from a variety of
avian and mammalian species, including three dogs and a cat. 49 ,
52 , 69 Serologic studies have shown that other wild animals had
contact with the fungus but did not develop signs of the disease.
Serologic studies in Brazil showed seroprevalence of 31.6% in cats
67 and 14.8% to 80.5% in dogs. 70 Seropositivity was higher in dogs
and cats living in rural areas. 70 There are only three case reports
of clinical disease in dogs. The dogs all had peripheral
lymphadenomegaly, and variable evidence of other organ
involvement (pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, epididymitis, or
pyogranulomatous dermatitis), 65 , 69 , 71 resembling clinical signs
described in humans. The organism was found in peripheral
lymph nodes using cytologic examination or histopathology and
the organism was deﬁnitively identiﬁed using culture (which can
take 20 to 30 days for growth to occur) and/or molecular methods.
65 , 69 , 71 In cytologic preparations, the organism is 10 to 20 µm in
diameter, oval to elongated in shape, and has a thick cell wall;
simultaneous side-by-side budding of two or more daughter cells
from the parent cell has led to the description of a “Mickey
Mouse” and “pilot-wheel” appearance in the literature (Fig.
83.13A and B). 69 There is a granulomatous inﬂammatory
response, and multinucleated giant cells may be present. 69 On
histopathology, the organism may be diﬃcult to distinguish from
other fungal pathogens when the characteristic budding pa ern is
not identiﬁed (Fig. 83.13C). Itraconazole is the drug of choice and
was associated with good clinical responses in dogs. 65 , 69 , 71
Paracoccidioidomycosis was diagnosed in a cat that presented
with general systemic and neurologic signs. The cat was treated
successfully with ﬂuconazole and amphotericin B. 72
Paracoccidioidomycosis should be considered as a diﬀerential
diagnosis for dogs and cats that reside within endemic regions,
and it should be considered when yeast-like structures that
resemble organisms such as Sporothrix, Cryptococcus, or

vetexamprep.ir

Blastomyces are seen in tissues on histopathology. Increased
awareness of this disease in endemic regions may lead to
recognition of more cases.

Case Example
Signalment

“Jenny,” a 2-year-old female spayed Labrador retriever from
Oxnard in southwestern California.

History

Jenny was evaluated for a 2-month history of cough,
inappetence, and lethargy. For the ﬁrst 3 days of illness, the
owner noted only an intermi ent harsh, non-productive cough.
On day 4 of illness, the dog became lethargic and inappetent, so
she was taken to a local veterinary clinic. Thoracic radiographs
revealed alveolar inﬁltrates in the left cranial lung lobe. A
diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia was suspected, so Jenny was
treated with enroﬂoxacin (6 mg/kg PO q24h), clavulanic acidamoxicillin (12.5 mg/kg PO q12h), and metronidazole (8 mg/kg
PO q12h) for 2 weeks. After the ﬁrst week of treatment, there
was no improvement, so a long-acting cephalosporin was
administered (cefovecin, 8 mg/kg, SC, once). Two days later,
treatment with prednisone (0.3 mg/kg PO q12h) was initiated
which was followed by only mild improvement in the clinical
signs. Jenny’s owner then sought a second opinion on day 20
after onset of clinical signs, and Coccidioides serology was
performed. The titer was positive for IgG at 1:64. The
prednisone was discontinued and treatment was initiated with
ﬂuconazole (6.7 mg/kg PO q12h). However, after 1 month of
treatment, there had been no clinical improvement and thoracic
radiographs were unchanged. The ﬂuconazole was substituted
with a compounded itraconazole formulation (5 mg/kg PO
q12h). However, after an additional 2 weeks of treatment there
had been no further improvement in the cough, so the owner
sought a third opinion at the University of California, Davis.
According to the owner, Jenny had a poor appetite for dog
food but was eating home-cooked chicken, rice, and vegetables.
Her activity level had been low. The cough occurred many
times throughout the day and was unrelated to exercise and
eating. Occasionally she had paroxysms of cough with a
terminal retch. Other medical history included canine
parvovirus infection when she was 8 weeks old and “kennel
cough” when she was 9 months old, which resolved after 10
days. The owners lived in a semi-rural area just north of Los

vetexamprep.ir

Angeles. The only travel had been to Atascadero further north
on the California coast. She was the only animal in the
household. There had been ongoing construction around the
house to replace a septic system with a sewer, which began
approximately 4 to 6 weeks before the onset of clinical signs.

Physical Examination

General: Quiet but alert and responsive, hydrated. T =
102.6°F (39.2°C), P = 100 beats/min, R = 24 breaths/min,
CRT = 1 s.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No ocular abnormalities
noted. A dilated fundoscopic examination was
unremarkable.
Musculoskeletal: BCS 4/9. The dog was ambulatory with
no lameness or muscle atrophy.
Cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary, and lymph nodes: No
clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected.
Imaging Findings Thoracic radiographs were compared to
the two-view thoracic study performed 2 weeks
previously, which were available for review. The initial
radiographs showed a dense alveolar pa ern throughout
the left cranial lung lobe and increased opacity in the
region of the hilar lymph nodes with splaying of the
mainstem bronchi (see Fig. 83.6C). These abnormalities
improved slightly in the 10-day recheck interim, but
alveolar inﬁltrates were still present throughout the left
cranial lung lobe. There was a persistent, mild, diﬀuse
pulmonary interstitial pa ern in the remaining
pulmonary parenchyma, which was most severe in the
caudodorsal lung ﬁelds. This was considered excessive
for the age of the patient. The cardiovascular structures
were within normal limits.

Microbiologic Testing
Coccidioides serology: Positive by qualitative gel
immunodiﬀusion for complement ﬁxing antibody (IgG),
negative for IgM. Quantitative immunodiﬀusion revealed
an IgG titer of 1:128.

vetexamprep.ir

Serum itraconazole concentration: < 0.31 µg/mL
(undetectable).
Diagnosis Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis.
Treatment The itraconazole capsules prescribed at the
previous veterinary clinic were examined and found to
contain a white powder rather than granules. Treatment
was changed to brand name itraconazole (Sporonox),
because compounded formulations can be unstable.
Instructions were given to administer the itraconazole (5
mg/kg PO q24h) with food to improve absorption.
Aspirin was also prescribed (12 mg/kg PO q12h). One
month later, Jenny’s cough and activity level had
improved considerably. A CBC was within normal limits
and a biochemistry panel showed hypoalbuminemia (3.3
g/dL, reference range 3.4–4.3 g/dL) and
hyperglobulinemia (3.4 g/dL, reference range 1.7–3.1
g/dL). Liver enzyme activities were within reference
ranges. Thoracic radiographs showed resolution of hilar
lymphadenopathy with persistence of the alveolar
inﬁltrates in the left cranial lung lobe. The IgG antibody
titer to Coccidioides was 1:64. Three months later the cough
had resolved completely, and after 6 months of treatment,
there was complete resolution of thoracic radiographic
abnormalities and the titer was 1:32. At this point, the
owner switched to a generic formulation of itraconazole
due to ﬁnancial concerns. After an additional 3 and 6
months of treatment, the IgG titer was 1:16 and 1:8,
respectively, with no further clinical signs. Treatment was
continued for an additional 3 months (i.e., total of 15
months of treatment), and the dog remains alive at the
time of writing.

Comments

This is an interesting case of pulmonary coccidioidomycosis
that occurred outside the hyperendemic central valley region in
California. Exposure may have resulted from soil disturbance
as a result of sewer work. Because of the low suspicion for the
disease, the disease was mistaken for bacterial pneumonia. The
owner had limited ﬁnancial resources, so an extensive
respiratory workup (including respiratory lavage with cytology

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
p(
g
p
y
g
y
gy
and culture) was declined. When Coccidioides serology was
positive, ﬂuconazole was prescribed, but there was no
improvement. The decision to treat with a compounded
formulation of itraconazole was made because of client ﬁnancial
limitations, but serum drug levels with this treatment were
undetectable. Fortunately, disease ultimately resolved with a
change to a noncompounded formulation, and there was
progressive decline in serial IgG titers (which were always
performed by the same laboratory). Whether treatment beyond
complete resolution of the radiographic abnormalities was
necessary is debatable.

84: Sporotrichosis
Luisa H.M. Miranda, Isabella D.F. Gremião, Sandro A. Pereira, Rodrigo
C. Menezes, Tânia M.P. Schubach, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Sporothrix spp. (ascomycetes).
• First Described: Sporothrix schenckii was first described in
1896, in Maryland, United States, by Benjamin Schenk. 1
• Affected Hosts: Infection has been reported principally in
humans and cats, as well as in dogs and a variety of other
mammalian and avian species.
• Geographic Distribution: Tropical, subtropical, and temperate
zones worldwide.
• Route of Transmission: Cutaneous inoculation of conidia or
yeasts, or less frequently, inhalation of conidia.
• Major Clinical Signs: Cutaneous nodules or ulcerated skin
lesions, lymphangitis, lymphadenomegaly.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other systemic mycoses (especially
cryptococcosis in cats), mycobacterial infections, nocardiosis
or actinomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniosis, SCC, feline
eosinophilic granuloma complex, feline herpesviral dermatitis,
abscess, foreign body granulomas.
• Human Health Significance: Many human infections are
acquired from the environment, but direct transmission can
follow contact between infected cats and humans, and
especially cat bites or scratches.

Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

The fungal genus Sporothrix includes a group of thermodimorphic
pathogens that cause human and animal infections. 1 These
organisms are widespread in nature and have been isolated as a
saprobe from senescent or dead vegetation, such as thorns, hay,
straw, sphagnum moss, wood, and soil rich in decaying organic
ma er. Sporothrix sp. is most prevalent in warm, tropical, and
subtropical climate regions. It grows in the environment or in
culture at 25°C as a mycelium and converts to a small budding
yeasts in mammalian host tissues or in culture at 37°C. Infectivity
may result from selection of strains adapted to grow at
temperatures higher than 35°C. 2 Although all Sporothrix isolates
have in the past been grouped into the single species Sporothrix
schenckii, multiple genotypes exist that vary in virulence and
geographic distribution. 3–6 The classic agent S. schenckii now
comprises several molecular siblings nested in a clinical clade
with Sporothrix globosa, Sporothrix luriei, and Sporothrix brasiliensis,
7 with the la er being the most virulent. 8 The phylogenetically
distant environmental species Sporothrix mexicana, Sporothrix
pallida, Sporothrix chilensis, and Sporothrix humicola are rare agents
of sporotrichosis in mammals being nested in the environmental
clade. 8–13 However, the epidemiology of the various species of
Sporothrix is incompletely understood. Sporothrix brasiliensis is so
far restricted to Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. 14 , 15 , 16 Two
diﬀerent clusters of S. schenckii sensu stricto are prevalent in the
Americas and Asia, and in the Americas and Africa, respectively.
Sporothrix globosa is predominant in Asia and Europe, but rare in
the Americas and Africa. 9 Sporothrix schenckii, S. brasiliensis, S.
humicola, 17 and S. albicans have been isolated from cats, and S.
brasiliensis, S. schenckii, and S. luriei have been isolated from dogs.
18

Human sporotrichosis is distributed worldwide and is rare in
Europe, with endemic areas in Brazil, Peru, Mexico, South Africa,
China, and India. In Latin America, it is the most common
subcutaneous mycosis in humans. 19 Feline sporotrichosis has
been documented in the United States, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina,
Spain, Germany, India, Malaysia, Japan, Australia, Paraguay,
Thailand, and United Kingdom. 15 , 17 , 20–22 Reported cases of
canine sporotrichosis are from the United States, Brazil, Canada,
France, and Italy. 23–27 The classic infection results from direct

vetexamprep.ir

inoculation of the fungus into skin via contact with contaminated
plants or soil, or less frequently, by inhalation of conidia. Zoonotic
transmission occurs through bites or scratches of animals. Infected
cats are the main species implicated in the zoonotic transmission
of Sporothrix. Additionally, there have been reports of this mycosis
following bites or scratches by other animals, 28 such as
armadillos, birds, and rodents, although without a signiﬁcant
zoonotic potential. 29 The oral cavity and claws of most animals
are suggested to become contaminated from contact with the
environment, which would allow the transmission of the fungus
percutaneously through scratches or bites. However, the isolation
of the agent from the oral cavity and claws has only been reported
from cats. 30 Epidemics involving great numbers of people or
wide geographic regions are rare and usually related to a common
source of infection in the environment such as wood timbers and
sphagnum moss. 2 , 31 , 32 Sporothrix schenckii has primarily been
associated with sporadic transmission from the environment to
humans, cats, and dogs in developed countries (Fig. 84.1). There
were no reports of sporotrichosis epizootics before a cattransmi ed epidemic was reported in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. 14 , 33
Between 1998 and 2015, approximately 5,000 human cases were
recorded at Evandro Chagas National Institute of Infectious
Diseases, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 34 and
most of them were related to zoonotic transmission by infected
cats (Fig. 84.2A and B). 4 Most of the isolates from aﬀected
humans in Brazil were S. brasiliensis, but S. schenckii sensu stricto
and S. globosa were also isolated. 7 It seems that S. brasiliensis is
more likely associated with outbreaks of zoonotic sporotrichosis
related to transmission by cats (see Fig. 84.1). Since 1998, 244 dogs
were diagnosed through 2014 35 and 5,113 cats were diagnosed
through 2018 at the same institution, 14 so far representing the
largest outbreaks of this mycosis. 33 In Malaysia, cats seem to also
take part in the transmission of S. schenckii sensu stricto to humans,
as around 50% of the human cases from a case series reported a
previous episode of scratches or bites from cats. Sporotrichosis
due to S. schenckii sensu stricto was reported as the third principal
cause of death in cats submi ed to necropsy examination at a
veterinary teaching hospital in Malaysia. 36–45

vetexamprep.ir

Transmission of Sporothrix schenckii
and Sporothrix brasiliensis. A, Sporothrix
schenckii (Ss) is primarily transmitted through
contact with environmental sources. The
domestic cat may be infected and also be a
source of infection to humans, dogs and other
cats, primarily through scratches and bites. B,
Sporothrix brasiliensis (Sb) is primarily a
zoonotic pathogen that is transmitted from cats
to humans. It is suggested to have shifted from
an environment-adapted species to a felineadapted species. In this scenario, the hostshifting steps are as-yet unsolved, but Rattus
norvegicus has been hypothesized as a
potential passage host (possibly through
hunting behavior of cats). C, In the Sb zoonotic
cycle, cats are the main source of infection for
humans, dogs, and other cats, with resulting
outbreaks most likely occurring in urban and
periurban areas and affecting a larger number
of individuals, in comparison with environmentacquired sporotrichosis. Likewise, Sb-infected
cats may contaminate the environment not
only through scratching but also through feces
and following decomposition of their carcasses
in the environment.

vetexamprep.ir

Cats are the only species conﬁrmed as a source of infection of
Sporothrix sp., as demonstrated by isolation of fungus from skin
lesions, which are rich in fungi, nasal and oral cavities, and claws
of cats with sporotrichosis. The fungus isolation from the oral
cavity of apparently healthy cats from Rio de Janeiro that were in
contact with aﬀected animals range from 1.5% to 3.6%. 46 , 47 In
addition, in an endemic region in Peru, Sporothrix was isolated
from the nasal cavity and/or nails of two cats (2.4%) without
clinical signs of sporotrichosis. 48 The low prevalence of the
isolation of Sporothrix spp. from apparently healthy cats suggests
they contribute li le to the transmission and maintenance of the
disease. The mobility of cats in dwellings and surroundings, their
habit of scratching vegetation, and their ﬁghting behavior,
especially in non-neutered male cats, may improve dispersal of
the fungus in the environment. 49 , 50 Cats can be infected either
through the classic route (environmental sources) or through
scratches and bites during physical interaction with an infected
cat. Direct contact with the exudate from infected cats’ lesions is
also a potential route of transmission, presumably facilitated by a
previous breach in the skin integrity. Cat-to-cat transmission is the
main route described in S. brasiliensis transmission. 13 , 14 , 22 , 47
Canine sporotrichosis can be acquired during hunting activities
with possible introduction of the organism through thorn injuries
or wood splinters. However, in Brazil, the most frequent forms of
transmission to dogs were through scratches, bites or contact with
exudates from cutaneous lesions of cats. 23 No clear breed or sex
predisposition has been identiﬁed, and dogs in the Rio de Janeiro
epizootic ranged in age from 6 months to 12 years (median, 4
years). Mixed sporotrichosis and cryptococcosis was reported in a
dog from Ontario, Canada. 51

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The transmission of Sporothrix classically results from cutaneous
inoculation of organisms present in the environment, but can also
result from inhalation of conidia. The cutaneous inoculation of the
pathogen through scratches and bites by infected cats is also

vetexamprep.ir

described and represents the major route of transmission of S.
brasiliensis. Direct contact with cats that have sporotrichosis (even
without a history of a previous break in the skin) can result in
transmission. 46 Following inoculation, the fungus can remain in
the dermis and subcutaneous tissue at the inoculation site, spread
up regional lymphatics and produce lymphangitis and
lymphadenitis, or disseminate systemically through blood vessels.
The incubation time usually ranges from 3 to 30 days (within 14
days in average) in human and animal sporotrichosis, but can be
months. 29 The initial skin lesions are ﬁrm subcutaneous nodules
that slowly soften, generally draining purulent or hemorrhagic
content, and progress to form exudative ulcers with slightly
elevated well-deﬁned rims. 23 , 46

vetexamprep.ir

The optimal interaction of Sporothrix PAMPs and innate
immunity receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), has shown
to be determinant for phagocytosis and cytokine production. 52 , 53
After phagocytosis, the fungus can evade oxidative damage, such
as through production of melanin and mutations in stressactivated protein kinases. 54 , 55 The successful dissemination into
host tissues is strongly related to the pathogen’s ability of binding
to proteins in the extracellular matrix. In this context, cell wall
adhesins on the Sporothrix surface can bind to ﬁbronectin. 56 , 57
Organisms that are thermotolerant (able to survive at
temperatures closer to body temperature, or 37°C) may be more
likely to cause invasive disease. 52 , 53 , 58
The clinical form of the disease is determined principally by the
immunologic status of the host, the load and depth of the
inoculum, and the virulence of the infecting Sporothrix species. 59
Sporothrix brasiliensis, the principal species involved in zoonotic
transmission and the causative pathogen of feline sporotrichosis
in Brazil, is remarkably virulent, 60 and has been associated with
disseminated and atypical presentations of sporotrichosis in
humans. 61 , 62
The classiﬁcation of clinical forms used for humans includes
several
forms:
lymphocutaneous,
ﬁxed
cutaneous,
mucocutaneous, extracutaneous, and disseminated. More than
50% of human patients develop the lymphocutaneous form and
the infection spreads proximally along lymphatics, with formation
of multiple secondary nodules that may ulcerate (Fig. 84.3).
Among the extracutaneous forms in humans, osteoarticular and
pulmonary involvement are the most common. 54 , 63 Co-infection
with HIV and Sporothrix may be associated with disseminated
cutaneous lesions, systemic sporotrichosis, and hospitalization. 64
Dogs and cats frequently display more than one of these clinical
forms simultaneously. The most common lesions in dogs and cats
are cutaneous nodules and ulcers, sometimes with mucosal
involvement. Although the cutaneous-lymphatic form is the most
frequently seen in humans, this is not the case for cats, and

vetexamprep.ir

possibly not for dogs. 23 , 46 In a retrospective study involving 347
cats with sporotrichosis, the cutaneous-lymphatic form was
observed in only 19.3% of cats. 46
Cats are highly susceptible to Sporothrix infection. The spectrum
of clinical signs ranges from a single or multiple skin lesions to
fatal systemic forms due to hematogenous dissemination.
Multiple skin lesions in cats can occur because of multiple
inoculation sites, self-trauma, grooming, 46 or they can be a
manifestation of a systemic infection. Generalized disease is
frequently reported in cats with sporotrichosis, with involvement
of multiple organ systems. 65 , 66 The detection of the fungus by
histopathologic examination and/or by culture is described in the
lungs, heart, spleen, kidneys, lymph nodes, adrenal glands, and
liver of naturally infected cats. 66–68 Hematogenous spread may be
an early event and it was demonstrated by isolation of Sporothrix
from the peripheral blood of cats with widespread cutaneous
lesions as well as cats in good general condition with localized
lesions, even when no clinical signs suggestive of a septic
syndrome were observed. 30 , 69 Fatal disseminated cases are not
described in Asia, which is suggested to be due to the lower
thermotolerance of S. schenckii sensu stricto in comparison with S.
brasiliensis. 45 Co-infection with FIV does not appear to be a risk
factor for dissemination. 69
The occurrence of respiratory signs may also precede the
beginning of the cutaneous involvement and may be observed in
cats without skin lesions. 44 The high frequency of these signs, and
nasal mucosa and pulmonary lesions in cats with sporotrichosis,
as well as the isolation of Sporothrix from bronchoalveolar lavage
washings and from the lungs of necropsied cats, suggest that the
inhalation route of entry may have epidemiologic importance in
cats. 66 , 70

Physical Examination Findings
The most common clinical signs in dogs and cats are cutaneous
lesions. Extracutaneous signs are frequent, and primarily consist
of lymphadenomegaly and respiratory signs, such as sneezing,
nasal discharge, and dyspnea. Secondary bacterial infection may
occur. Other clinical signs that may be observed are anorexia,

vetexamprep.ir

hyporexia, vomiting, weight loss, and dehydration. 23 , 46
Hematologic and biochemical alterations observed in dogs and
cats are nonspeciﬁc. 23 , 46
Dogs
In dogs, as in humans, sporotrichosis is essentially a benign
disease, although disseminated forms may rarely develop. 71–73
The most common lesions in dogs are skin nodules and ulcers,
with frequent nasal mucosal involvement. Intranasal masses that
protrude from the nostrils can be observed. 23 , 74 The skin lesions
may be solitary or multiple and more frequently located on the
head, especially on the nose (Fig. 84.4), followed by the limbs and
thorax. Skin lesions on the nasal planum were observed in 56.8%
of 44 dogs in one study, and 20.5% of dogs had nasal mucosal
involvement, with isolated mucosal lesions in 3 (6.8%) dogs. The
high frequency of lesions on the muzzle of dogs may be explained
by injuries caused by cats that inhabit the same household
environments. 23 Rarely, lesions course along lymphatics, 23 , 65 , 70
, 74
when they are usually associated with regional
lymphadenomegaly. 23 Osteoarticular sporotrichosis occurs rarely
in dogs and may manifest clinically as lameness and synovial
eﬀusion. 74 , 75 Disseminated cutaneous sporotrichosis in
association with immunosuppressive therapy has been described
in a dog. 76

Cats
The most frequent clinical forms of feline sporotrichosis are
multiple skin lesions, usually in three or more anatomical sites,
with involvement of nasal mucosa. Generally, cats with
sporotrichosis exhibit good general health, 46 but lethargy,
anorexia, and fever may occur in systemic infection. 78
Skin lesions are characterized especially by nodules and ulcers.
Plaques and tumor-like lesions are also observed. 29 The main
aﬀected site for skin lesions is the head (Fig. 84.5), especially the
nasal region and the pinna. Other common sites are the distal
limbs, digits, and tail, but lesions can also be found elsewhere on
the body. Lesions of the conjunctiva (Fig. 84.6), and oral and
genital mucosa can also be present in some aﬀected cats. In
addition to skin and mucosal lesions, lymphangitis,
lymphadenomegaly, and extensive zones of necrosis that expose
muscle and bone can be observed. 46
Extracutaneous signs, particularly respiratory signs (sneezing,
dyspnea, and nasal discharge) and nasal mucosa involvement, are
frequent. Respiratory signs are observed in 42% of cats, mainly
sneezing (39%). 79 Nasal mucosa lesions and respiratory signs can
be associated with treatment failure and death. 79 , 80 The isolation
of Sporothrix from nasal swab specimens and the occurrence of
sneezing may precede appearance of skin lesions in some cases. 44
Sporotrichosis diﬀerential diagnosis in cats includes neoplasia
(mainly SCC), feline eosinophilic granuloma complex, bacterial
pyoderma,
mycobacteriosis,
nocardiosis,
actinomycosis,
cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, phaeohyphomycosis, American
tegumentary leishmaniosis, feline herpesviral dermatitis, and
severe allergic diseases (e.g., mosquito bites, ﬂea allergy
dermatosis), among others. The coexistence of sporotrichosis and
other skin diseases, like neoplasia, eosinophilic dermatosis,
bacterial pyoderma, dermatophytosis, and demodicosis should be
considered. 44 , 81

Diagnosis
A high degree of suspicion is required for the disease in nonendemic regions. Although clinical signs, patient history, and
epidemiologic data can suggest sporotrichosis, deﬁnitive
diagnosis depends on isolation of Sporothrix spp. in culture media.
Cytology and histopathology are very useful routine tools for the
preliminary diagnosis. IHC, serology and PCR are other options
for the diagnosis of sporotrichosis.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
In many dogs and cats with sporotrichosis, the CBC is
unremarkable. The most common abnormalities are mild anemia
and leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia, sometimes with a mild left
shift. 46 , 71 Monocytosis, eosinophilia, lymphocytosis, or
lymphopenia may also be present. Approximately 50% of the

vetexamprep.ir

dogs from the Rio de Janeiro epizootic were anemic, and around
20% had eosinophilia or neutrophilia. 23
Serum Chemistry Profile
The most frequent serum biochemistry ﬁndings in cats and dogs
with
sporotrichosis
are
hyperglobulinemia
and
hypoalbuminemia. Increased liver enzyme activities can occur in
aﬀected cats and dogs. 23 , 46
Urinalysis
Urinalysis in animals with sporotrichosis usually reveals no
clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
A pulmonary interstitial inﬁltrate was described in one aﬀected
cat. 66 Thoracic radiographs on one dog and ﬁve cats seen at the
author’s teaching hospital revealed no radiographic abnormalities.
Radiographs of bones that underlie skin lesions typically reveal
only soft tissue swelling; rarely is underlying osteomyelitis
detected.
Advanced imaging
CT of the nasal cavity in cats with lesions on the bridge of the
nose may reveal masses within the nasal cavity that invade
through nasal bones to involve the subcutaneous tissues (Fig.
84.7A and B). Severely thickened turbinate mucosa, an intranasal
soft tissue density mass, and focal osteolysis were reported on
nasal CT in a dog with signs of nasal cavity disease due to
sporotrichosis. 82

Microbiologic Tests
Specimens to be collected may include swab specimens of the
nasal cavities, exudative lesions, and purulent or seropurulent
content aspirated from nonulcerated nodular lesions, as well as
incisional skin biopsy specimens. 46 , 83 In cats, swab specimens of
exudative lesions are the recommended specimen for diagnosis of
Sporothrix infection. 46

vetexamprep.ir

p
Skin biopsies should be obtained from borders of active lesions
with a 3- to 4-mm surgical punch. Two tissue specimens can be
collected, one ﬁxed in 10% buﬀered formalin for histopathology
and immunohistochemical tests, and the second kept in a sterile
glass ﬂask with sterile saline and transported on ice to a
diagnostic laboratory for fungal culture, preferentially within 8–10
hours. 59 In dogs, the best results for fungal isolation are from
surgical skin biopsy specimens as they are more sensitive than
swab specimens of exudative lesions. 23 , 46
Suitable specimens for cytopathologic examination include
impression smears of ulcerated skin, exudates or biopsy
specimens (before placing in formalin), smears of swab specimens,
skin scrapings, or ﬁne-needle aspirates of abscesses and nodules.

To diagnose dissemination, whole blood can be directly seeded
in blood culture ﬂasks. 69 BAL is useful for diagnosis of
pulmonary involvement. 70 At necropsy, tissue specimens can be
collected for mycology, cytology, histopathology, and
immunohistochemical testing.
Cytopathologic Examination
The sensitivity of the cytopathologic examination of skin lesions
of cats with sporotrichosis ranges from 79% to 87%. 85 , 87 , 88 This
method is rapid, practical, and low cost, and a positive result can
allow initiation of antifungal treatment while awaiting the results
of culture. 87 , 89 However, despite cytopathology being highly
sensitive for diagnosis of feline sporotrichosis, its sensitivity drops
drastically after onset of antifungal treatment. 89 In dogs, a
sensitivity of 32% was observed. 83 , 87
Cytologic preparations stained with Wright or Romanowskytype or Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) stains permit good
visualization of the yeast cells. 83 , 86 With Wright or
Romanowsky-type staining, Sporothrix spp. appear as cigarshaped to oval or round budding yeasts that are 3–5 µm by 5–9
µm in maximum length, with blue cytoplasm and a single round
nucleus surrounded by a nonstaining cell wall (Fig. 84.8). 84 , 87
These organisms are seen mainly within the cytoplasm of
macrophages, and neutrophils and also extracellularly. 76 , 84 , 85
Sporothrix spp. may be confused with Histoplasma, Cryptococcus,
Candida, and Leishmania spp., and potentially other protozoan
parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum. 29
Fungal Culture

vetexamprep.ir

Fungal culture is the reference standard for the diagnosis of
sporotrichosis in animals and humans due to its high sensitivity
and speciﬁcity. The sensitivity of isolation from skin biopsies
exceeds 95% in both dogs and cats. 23 , 46 , 65 In addition, fungal
culture allows further identiﬁcation of Sporothrix at species level
by PCR. 7 , 8 However, it is time consuming, taking 10 to 15 days
to obtain results. Other disadvantages of culture are that falsenegative results can occur due to low fungal burden, prior
treatment with topical or systemic antifungal agents, inadequate
specimen size, deterioration of specimens during transport, and
contamination with bacteria.

with a single nucleus, and are surrounded by a

FIG. 84.8

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical material should be inoculated onto Sabouraud’s
dextrose agar with chloramphenicol and Sabouraud’s dextrose
agar with chloramphenicol plus cycloheximide and incubated at
25°C to 30°C. Mycelial growth of Sporothrix spp. can be observed
in 3 to 5 days, although sometimes several weeks of incubation
may be required. 58 Typical colonies are initially cream colored,
smooth, and moist, gradually becoming dark brown or black, as a
result of production of pigmented conidia, (Fig. 84.9A). However,
much variation among isolates and even among subcultures of the
same isolate can be observed. Various culture media can also
inﬂuence the color and texture of colonies. Identiﬁcation depends
on the morphologic characteristics of the mycelial form and its
conversion to the yeast form on blood agar or brain-heart infusion
(BHI) agar plus yeast extract agar when incubated at 37°C. The
microscopic characteristics of the mycelial form are slender,
hyaline, septate, and branched hyphae measuring 1.5 to 2 µm in
width. The conidia arise directly from the hyphae or from the
apex of thin conidiophores, with conidia in a ﬂowerlike
arrangement. The intensity of colony color is directly proportional
to the number of dark brown thick-walled conidia. The yeast
phase is pleomorphic, showing oval or cigar-shaped cells and
exhibiting single or multiple buds with elongated morphology.
The organism can then be identiﬁed based on light microscopic
appearance of the mold and yeast forms (see Fig. 84.9B and C).
Sporothrix species identiﬁcation requires subsequent molecular
analysis by specialized laboratories. 90 MALDI-TOF has also been
successfully applied for the diﬀerentiation of Sporothrix species. 91
Antifungal susceptibility testing can be performed, but
established breakpoints are not available.
Serologic Diagnosis
ELISAs that detect antibody to Sporothrix cell wall antigens have
been developed for diagnosis of human and feline sporotrichosis.
92–94 The best results for an ELISA’s sensitivity and speciﬁcity for
the diagnosis of feline sporotrichosis were 96% and 98%,
respectively, using S. schenckii crude exoantigen, and 90% and
98%, respectively, using a cell wall antigen (SsCBF). 83
ELISA and immunoblo ing suggest 3-carboxymuconate cyclase
(a 60-kDa protein in S. brasiliensis and a 70-kDa protein in S.

vetexamprep.ir

schenckii) as the immunodominant antigen in feline sporotrichosis
and a potential marker for serologic diagnosis. Although these
methods do not distinguish between S. brasiliensis and S. schenckii
infections, there is no reactivity when sera from healthy cats or
from cats with other infections were used, so speciﬁcity appears to
be promising. 94

Recently, the ELISA test using SsCBF was adapted and
validated for detecting IgG from sera of cats with sporotrichosis
and is currently commercially available in private laboratories in
Brazil. 22 , 95
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid-Based Testing
Conventional identiﬁcation methods are time consuming and
prone to misidentiﬁcation since there is an overlap of phenotypic
characteristics among the species of Sporothrix. Therefore, rapid
and accurate identiﬁcation of Sporothrix relies on the use of
molecular methods. PCR is an important tool used to identify
Sporothrix species from animals and humans, especially when

vetexamprep.ir

isolates are not identiﬁed by morphologic and physiologic
phenotyping. PCR sequencing targeting the calmodulin gene is
most used, but PCR sequencing targeting ITS1/2, large-subunit
(LSU) ribosomal DNA, β-tubulin, chitin synthase, 9 , 96 , 97 and
translation elongation factor 96 , 98 can also distinguish among
species of Sporothrix. Recently, more rapid molecular assays that
do not need sequencing for identiﬁcation were developed. These
include PCR ﬁngerprinting based on random ampliﬁcation of
polymorphic DNA (RAPD) using the universal primer T3B, 99
ampliﬁed fragment length polymorphisms, 98 PCR-restriction
fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs), 100 species-speciﬁc PCR,
101 and rolling-circle ampliﬁcation (RCA). 102–104 A PCR assay
targeting the chitin synthase 1 gene was used with success for
speciﬁc and rapid detection of Sporothrix DNA and identiﬁcation
at genus level in a biopsy specimen from a cat with sporotrichosis.
105 A species-speciﬁc PCR targeting calmodulin gene sequences
has also been described, including its direct application in clinical
specimens from cats with sporotrichosis. 101 , 106 In addition, RCA
has been used to successfully detect and identify Sporothrix from
both clinical and environmental specimens. 102

Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
In addition to cutaneous and mucosal lesions, the main gross
lesions in cats are small whitish nodular lesions measuring
approximately 1 mm in diameter on the pleural surface and
parenchyma of the lungs, and enlargement of lymph nodes. 65
Histopathologic Findings
Histopathology of cutaneous lesions of feline and canine
sporotrichosis is characterized by ulcerative and variable but
usually intense pyogranulomatous inﬂammatory reaction in the
dermis, which can reach the panniculus and subjacent skeletal
muscles. 107 , 108 The inﬂammatory inﬁltrate usually reveals a
predominance of neutrophils and macrophages, variable number
of plasma cells and lymphocytes. Eosinophils and mast cells can
be occasionally seen. 74 , 108 , 109 Multinucleated giant cells are
infrequent in dogs and cats compared with their occurrence in

vetexamprep.ir

humans. 108–110 The presence of Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon
(“asteroid bodies”) around yeasts is commonly described in
human infections, 111 but this is not typically observed in dogs or
cats. 107 , 111
There is a predominance of poorly formed granulomas (poorly
delineated) in cutaneous lesions from cats, dogs, and humans
with sporotrichosis. 23 , 107 , 108 , 110 Organized granulomas are less
common (approximately 11%) in skin lesions of cats (Fig. 84.10)
compared with dogs (38%–45%) and humans (38%). 23 , 107 , 108 ,
110 Cats tend to have poorly formed granulomas composed of
macrophages ﬁlled with yeast-like forms and a mild neutrophilic
and lymphoplasmacytic surrounding reaction (Fig. 84.11). 108

Systemic involvement is common in cats and a
pyogranulomatous inﬂammatory reaction and yeasts can be
observed in the lungs, spleen, lymph nodes, liver, kidneys,
adrenal glands, eyes, 66–68 skeletal muscles, and tongue. Cats with
intranasal sporotrichosis often have severe pyogranulomatous
rhinitis with osteomyelitis, osteolysis, and necrosis of hyaline
cartilage (Fig. 84.12). 44
Histopathologic ﬁndings are nonspeciﬁc and similar to those of
other pathogenic fungi and protozoans. 109 Therefore,
histochemical stains such as GMS and PAS are needed to
highlight Sporothrix spp. in tissues. 46 , 67 Sporothrix spp. yeasts are
oval or cigar-shaped, range in size from 4 µm to 6 µm, generally
exhibit a single bud with a narrow base, and are dark staining
using GMS (Fig. 84.13A) and pink using PAS. Pseudohyphae,
hyphae, and yeast-like forms with multiple budding are
occasionally seen. 39 , 44 , 68 Yeast-like forms of Sporothrix spp.
should be diﬀerentiated from those of Histoplasma spp., which are

vetexamprep.ir

smaller (2 µm to 4 µm), do not present cigar-shaped forms, and
are usually grouped in clusters inside macrophages. 112
The yeast-like forms of Sporothrix can be seen inside
neutrophils, macrophages, giant cells and osteoclasts, or
extracellularly in purulent exudate and inﬂamed areas. 44 In cats
with sporotrichosis, the number of Sporothrix organisms is usually
high and can be detected in 94% of histopathologic examinations
of skin biopsies stained by GMS. 46 , 67 , 68 , 108 Higher fungal loads
in skin lesions detected by histopathology (GMS) were linked to
young age and treatment failure with itraconazole (ITZ), as well
as to poorly formed granulomas with fewer inﬂammatory cells
and a longer time for wound healing. 80
In dogs, as in humans, the yeast-like forms are usually rare, and
the fungus is visualized in tissue specimens stained by PAS and
GMS in approximately 17% and 44% of cases, respectively. 23 , 110 ,
113 Use of GMS increases sensitivity when compared with PAS for
diagnosis of canine sporotrichosis. Around 58% of cases show a
maximum of ﬁve fungal elements in multiple histologic sections
of skin biopsies. 108 , 113
In order to increase the sensitivity of histologic diagnosis in
formalin-ﬁxed paraﬃn-embedded (FFPE) tissues from dogs, IHC
is recommended. An IHC protocol using a rabbit anti-Sporothrix
hyperimmune serum and an avidin-biotin detection system was
described for the diagnosis of Sporothrix in FFPE skin samples of
dogs (Fig. 84.13B) and cats. 113 The sensitivity of this assay was
65% in dogs and 88.6% in cats. 88 , 113 However, anti-Sporothrix
antibodies are not commercially available. 114

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of dogs and cats with sporotrichosis still represents a
challenge for veterinarians. 115 The cost and availability of
antifungal drugs vary and this often dictates the choices made. 74
Antifungal drugs for sporotrichosis include ketoconazole
(KTZ), ITZ, potassium iodide (KI), sodium iodide (NaI),
terbinaﬁne, ﬂuconazole (FLZ), or AMB. Treatment of animal
sporotrichosis should be continued for at least a month after
complete resolution of clinical signs. Other therapeutic options are
local thermotherapy, cryosurgery, and surgical resection of
cutaneous lesions. 116–118 Clinical and biochemical monitoring is
strongly recommended, 78 regardless of the prescribed treatment
regimen. ITZ is considered the drug of choice in human, feline,
and canine sporotrichosis treatment. 2 , 79 , 84 , 118 The

vetexamprep.ir

recommended dosage of ITZ capsules for the treatment of feline
or canine sporotrichosis is given with food to facilitate absorption
(Table 84.1). 46 , 84 ITZ solution permits more accurate dose
measurement and improved absorption and bioavailability at the
recommended dose so that dosages per unit body weight are
lower 46 (see Table 84.1); however, this formulation is not available
in some countries. Compounded formulations are not
recommended in substitution to the reference drug as they might
not be bioequivalent, while generic formulations can be a suitable
alternative (see Chapter 11). 22
Concurrent bacterial infections should be simultaneously
treated with an appropriate antibiotic/antibacterial agent. 119 Use
of glucocorticoids or any immunosuppressive drug is
contraindicated in dogs and cats during and after the treatment of
the disease, because the disease can worsen or recur. 78 , 120 There
are risks of fetal malformations associated with the use of KTZ
and KI. Administration of any azole, terbinaﬁne, 121 and KI 122
should be avoided during pregnancy.
Treatment response is assessed through clinical evaluation, and
cure is deﬁned as complete remission of cutaneous and
extracutaneous signs. The cooperation and persistence of the
owners is instrumental in a empting a successful response to
therapy. When sporotrichosis is not treated for an adequate time,
it often recurs, usually with respiratory signs.

Importantly, in regions where zoonotic transmission of
Sporothrix spp. occurs, the treatment of infected cats is one of the
main control measures of this mycosis.

Cats
Sporotrichosis is more diﬃcult to treat in cats than in dogs,
generally requiring a prolonged period of therapy. Four to six
months of treatment are usually necessary for a successful
outcome, but in some cats, treatment may last more than a year. 86
Additionally, even when there is remission of clinical signs,
fungal clearance cannot be conﬁrmed and recrudescence may
occur. 46
In a retrospective study, the eﬀectiveness and safety of ITZ and
KTZ were assessed for the treatment of 773 Sporothrix-infected
cats 79 : 598 cats received oral KTZ tablets and 175 cats received
oral ITZ capsules at dosages listed in Table 84.1. Clinical cure was
achieved in 238 (30.8%) cats, 171 (29%) with KTZ and 67 (38%)
with ITZ. The median treatment time using either KTZ or ITZ was
similar (26 to 28 weeks). Adverse eﬀects were reported in 39.6% of
the cats, with a higher occurrence in cats treated with KTZ.
Hyporexia was the most frequent adverse eﬀect, followed by
vomiting and/or diarrhea. The high prevalence of adverse eﬀects
was a ributed to the use of higher dosages than those usually
employed for the treatment of feline sporotrichosis. 46 , 78 , 84
Higher doses were used because of the diﬃculty in achieving
clinical cure with those recommended by the literature. 79
Nevertheless, the doses were similar to those used by other
authors for the treatment of cats with systemic mycoses such as
coccidioidomycosis and cryptococcosis. 123 , 124 When adverse GI
eﬀects related to KTZ and ITZ were observed, the total daily dose
was split in two equal parts and given every 12 hours instead of
every 24 hours. 78 , 84 Because of its eﬀectiveness and safety in cats,
ITZ has replaced KTZ in the treatment of feline sporotrichosis.
NaI or KI were otherwise considered the drugs of choice in
human and canine sporotrichosis, but serious adverse eﬀects have
limited their use, especially in cats. Oral administration of
supersaturated potassium iodide (SSKI) was used to treat
sporotrichosis in cats, dogs (see Table 84.1 for doses), or humans
in the past, before the widespread availability of ITZ. In the

vetexamprep.ir

treatment of feline sporotrichosis, controversial results have been
related with the use of SSKI or supersaturated sodium iodide
(SSNaI). Some authors reported clinical cure and others the
worsening of clinical condition and death. 125–127 Cats are very
sensitive to iodides, and adverse eﬀects can occur such as
anorexia, depression, vomiting, hypothermia, hyperthermia,
cardiovascular failure, cardiomyopathy, hyperexcitability,
muscular spasms, ptyalism, and diarrhea. 128
The use of KI capsules in lower doses than those previously
employed (see Table 84.1) has re-emerged as an eﬀective
alternative for the treatment of feline sporotrichosis. 129 , 130
Because of its extremely bi er taste, a capsule formulation of KI
has been used to treat aﬀected cats, with a cure rate of 48% after 4
to 5 months (median time to achieve clinical cure was around 19
weeks). 130 Inappetence occurred in 52% of cats, and a smaller
percentage of cats developed weight loss, diarrhea, or vomiting.
Increased liver enzyme activities can also occur. The dose range
used was 2.5 to 20 mg/kg, PO, q24h (median, 15 mg/kg). The dose
was increased in 2.5 mg/kg increments every 5 days from the
initial dose. Alterations in thyroid function can be an adverse
eﬀect of KI treatment in humans. 131
Higher cure rates in feline sporotrichosis have resulted from use
of a combination of KI capsules and ITZ. 129 The combination
allowed the reduction of KI dose (see Table 84.1) compared with
KI monotherapy, and led to a cure rate of 96.2% in a prospective
cohort study (Fig. 84.14A and B). Dose increments of 2.5 mg/kg at
every 30-day period were employed in those cats with worsening
or persistence of clinical signs. Adverse eﬀects were observed in
50% of the cats from this study and were managed with
temporary treatment interruption and/or the introduction of
hepatoprotective therapy with oral silymarin (30 mg/kg, PO,
q24h). Clinical adverse eﬀects, such as hyporexia, vomiting, and
weight loss, were reported in 20% of the cats, while a mild
elevation in transaminase activities was detected in almost 17% of
cats. The occurrence of clinical adverse eﬀect was similar to that
described for ITZ monotherapy and lower than that with the use
of KI alone. This is likely to be explained by lower doses of KI
when combined with ITZ, in comparison with KI monotherapy.

Cats with ITZ-refractory sporotrichosis can be treated with the
combination of ITZ and KI, notably when respiratory signs and
nasal mucosa lesions are present. 132 The primary indication for
AMB is the treatment of sporotrichosis refractory to ITZ. 116
Systemic administration of AMB by the IV route in cats is limited
because of its adverse eﬀects, mainly nephrotoxicity and
thrombophlebitis. 36 , 67 , 127 Intralesional AMB administration in
combination with ITZ was used successfully to treat ﬁxed or
multifocal cutaneous lesions in cats that were refractory to ITZ
alone. 116 , 133 The solution was prepared by addition of 5 mL of
2% lidocaine and 5 mL of distilled water to a 50-mg vial of AMB
(ﬁnal concentration, 5 mg/mL). A total of 0.5 to 1.5 mL (median 0.7
mL) was administered intralesionally once a week to once every
other week, and 73% of the cats were cured. The number of
treatment sessions ranged from 1 to 5 (median, 2 treatment
sessions per cat). Sterile abscess formation at the site of
administration occurred in 15% of cats. 133
Although terbinaﬁne has been eﬀective for treatment of
cutaneous forms of human sporotrichosis, 134 and in vitro
susceptibility studies have shown promising results, 135 its
employment for the treatment of feline sporotrichosis is poorly
described 46 and its eﬀectiveness and safety in cats are not known.
FLZ is recommended for lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis in
humans when the patient cannot tolerate other agents. In one cat
with disseminated sporotrichosis, cutaneous lesions and
respiratory signs resolved during treatment with FLZ, although
an additional course of treatment was needed following relapse. 74
The eﬀectiveness and safety of FLZ in the treatment of feline
sporotrichosis needs to be further clariﬁed.
Surgical resection of a lesion combined with antifungal therapy
can be an alternative after failure of antifungal treatment in

vetexamprep.ir

humans and cats, as long as the anatomic location of the lesions
enables surgical intervention. 38 , 136–138
Localized hyperthermia has been used as a safe and
inexpensive
method
to
treat
ﬁxed
cutaneous
and
lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis in human patients and was used
as the sole treatment in a cat with localized cutaneous disease. 139
In that case, a thermal bag that reached a temperature of 40°C to
42°C was applied twice daily for 15 minutes. When used alone,
this method is not likely to be eﬀective in animals with
disseminated disease.
Lastly, cryosurgery was apparently eﬀective in the treatment of
11 cats with sporotrichosis that were concurrently treated with
ITZ, 140 initiated prior to the cryosurgical procedure. The
treatment length until clinical cure ranged from 14 to 64 weeks
(median 32 weeks), after starting ITZ therapy. Although the
treatment duration until cure was longer than that reported with
other schemes, this protocol can be an option for cats that do not
tolerate higher doses of ITZ and in which systemic disease signs
are not observed.
Despite the occurrence of treatment failure in cats, clinical cure
may be achieved. The likelihood of cure is unrelated to the
severity of the initial clinical ﬁndings. However, involvement of
the nasal mucosa, respiratory signs, and high fungal loads
detected by cytologic examination or histopathology in skin
lesions are predictors of treatment failure with ITZ. 80 , 89 Coinfection with FIV does not seem to alter the likelihood of
treatment success. 47 Clinical cure following treatment has been
observed in the majority of the cats co-infected with FIV or FeLV.
Moreover, the diﬀerence between the median treatment time to
clinical cure in FIV-positive and FIV-negative cats was not
statistically signiﬁcant. 79
Relapse can occur between 3 and 18 months after
discontinuation of antifungal drug therapy. Spontaneous
regression of a persistent cutaneous lesion was also described in a
cat. 47 In animals with advanced disease, euthanasia may be
indicated. This should also be regarded as a management
alternative when long-standing clinical stagnation or progressive
worsening of clinical condition is observed even under adequate
therapeutic protocols. The expensive antifungal therapy and the

vetexamprep.ir

concerns for zoonotic transmission are additional factors in which
euthanasia is to be considered.

Dogs
Generally, canine sporotrichosis has a good prognosis and is
easily treated. Spontaneous regression of cutaneous lesions has
been described in a few cases 31 and dogs have remained lesionfree for 1 to 4 years on follow-up examinations. 23
ITZ capsules can be used to treat canine sporotrichosis (Fig.
84.15A and B) at recommended dosages (see Table 84.1) for 2 to 5
months. 23 Adverse eﬀects include anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea,
elevated hepatic enzyme activities, and cutaneous vasculitis (see
also Chapter 11). 141–143
Although KTZ is not the ﬁrst choice for treatment of canine
sporotrichosis, clinical cure was obtained with the recommended
dosage in Table 84.1 for 2 to 5 months. 23 Potential hepatotoxicity
should be monitored during therapy. 119 , 144
The treatment of canine sporotrichosis with oral administration
of a SSKI is also described (see Table 84.1), but dogs should be
monitored for any signs of iodism (mucopurulent oculonasal
discharges, salivation, and weakness). If toxicity occurs, the
medication should be discontinued for a week. If the adverse
eﬀects are mild, they may not recur, and therapy should then be
reinstituted. If the adverse eﬀects recur or the initial reactions

vetexamprep.ir

were severe, another drug should be considered. 78 Although the
eﬀectiveness of KI capsules (see Table 84.1) for treating canine
sporotrichosis is poorly known, a successful outcome was
described in one dog with no reported adverse eﬀects. 145
Recently, terbinaﬁne was described for the treatment of
sporotrichosis in two dogs, being successful even in the presence
of respiratory signs and nasal mucosa lesions. It may be a suitable
alternative in animals that do not tolerate ITZ therapy. 146

Immunity and Vaccination
Most of the knowledge on the immune response to Sporothrix
infection is derived from studies from human sporotrichosis and
animal models.
The immune response to Sporothrix infection involves both
innate and adaptive mechanisms. Elements from the Sporothrix
cell wall function as PAMPs for recognition by pa ern-recognition
receptors (PRRs), such as TLRs and C-type lectin receptors
(CLRs), 147 expressed by innate immune cells. 148 These contribute
to the enhancement of a further adaptive response. 149 , 150 The
generation of oxidative species during phagocytosis in the
experimental model is also involved in fungicidal activities. 151
Whether Sporothrix infection leads to a severe or a mild disease
clearly is aﬀected by the host’s immune response in murine and
human studies. Th1-dependent immunity, through CD4+ cells and
activated macrophages, persists as a required mechanism in the
defense to Sporothrix, 152 while the response to more virulent
strains of the fungus seem to be Th2-shifted. 153 Recently, Th17
also emerged as an important branch of immune response for
fungal clearance in sporotrichosis. 154
Cellular immunity is also recognized as important in the
response to feline infections. 155 Cats with localized sporotrichosis
that are in good general condition typically display wellorganized granulomatous lesions with a lower fungal burden and
a higher percentage of CD4+ cells in their peripheral blood when
compared with cats with disseminated sporotrichosis that exhibit
a poor general condition. The la er group of cats have poorly
organized granulomas and a high fungal burden, in association
with a higher percentage of CD8low cells. Although the CD8low

vetexamprep.ir

cells subset is connected to retroviral infections, such as HIV and
FIV 156 , 157 in humans and cats, respectively, this subset was
unrelated to FIV co-infection in the case of cats with
sporotrichosis.
Some authors believe that the severity of feline sporotrichosis
may be related to immunosuppression caused by co-infection
with FIV or FeLV. In a recent study, a poor general condition in
cats with sporotrichosis was correlated to FIV co-infection.
Likewise, the evaluation of cytokine levels in cats with
sporotrichosis revealed IL-10 expression to be signiﬁcantly higher
in FIV co-infected cats and in FeLV progressive infection than in
retrovirus-negative cats. 158 Considering IL-10 is a key cytokine in
the inhibition of Th1 immunity, its increase is believed to impair
the host’s optimal antifungal response. Still, severe sporotrichosis
is increasingly reported in cats independently of retrovirus coinfection or other apparent immunosuppression, which supports
the assumption that this disease develops in a diﬀerent manner in
cats. 46
Despite the importance of cellular immunity in resolution of
fungal infections, a humoral immune response contributes to the
overall response in sporotrichosis and fuels further studies for the
development of a vaccine. 159 Cell wall components have been
studied as a promising source of vaccine candidate antigens.
Passive immunization with antibodies to 3-carboxymuconate
cyclase antibodies, a 70-kDa cell wall glycoprotein (gp70) that is
important for fungal adherence to the extracellular matrix, 160
resulted in a protective eﬀect in mice, 161 even when T-cell–
deﬁcient animals were used. Moreover, yeast opsonization with
serum against cell wall proteins of S. schenckii markedly increases
phagocytosis and strongly inhibits the adhesion of the fungus to
ﬁbroblasts. In a similar way, the opsonization of the fungus by
antibodies anti-3-carboxymuconate cyclase enhanced phagocytic
ability of macrophages and elicits the release of proinﬂammatory
cytokines. 162 Carboxymuconate cyclase has been suggested as an
antigen candidate for the further development of an eﬀective
vaccine for animal and human use. 94
Another potential vaccine candidate from Sporothrix cell wall is
the protein enolase. In conjunction with the adjuvant
MontanideTM Pet Gel A (PGA), this protein has been shown to

vetexamprep.ir

induce a strong Th1 reaction in addition to high antibody levels
and decreased fungal load in the liver and spleen. 163 The use of a
recombinant
enolase-based
PGA-adjuvanted
vaccine
demonstrated a protective eﬀect in mice after challenge with
virulent Sporothrix species. 164
Despite the progress made in the past few years on the
discovery of potential vaccine candidates, an eﬀective vaccine for
preventing sporotrichosis is still not commercially available.

prevention
People handling cats with potential sporotrichosis should follow
the biosafety measures listed in Box 84.1. 165 In addition, isolation
of sick cats from other animals reared in the same environment is
indicated. Care must be taken to avoid cuts or penetrating injuries
when working with infected cats, and protective outerwear
should be worn. Proper physical restraint or sedation of
noncooperative animals must be done to allow complete
examination of lesions and the collection of specimens for
diagnosis.
Decontamination and cleaning of cages or transport containers
can be achieved with sodium hypochlorite (1%), for at least 10
minutes. If possible, sun drying is also beneﬁcial. After contact
with infected animals, surfaces should be cleaned and disinfected
with sodium hypochlorite solution (1%), for at least 10 minutes,
followed by alcohol 70%, using disposable paper towels. 166
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide and polihexametilene biguanide
(PHMB) are suitable alternatives to sodium hypochlorite.
An eﬀective and viable therapeutic regimen applied to cats as
well as public awareness programs on sporotrichosis prophylaxis
are required in endemic areas, encouraging the following:
responsible ownership, castration, cremation of dead cats,
conﬁnement of cats inside the home, limitation of the number of
cats per household, regular cleaning of dwellings, and proper
health care for cats. General public health measures such as basic
sanitation, regular garbage collection, and cleaning of uninhabited
lots are also required. 166

Public Health Aspects

vetexamprep.ir

Sporotrichosis is classically associated with contact with
contaminated plants or soil. Individuals with occupational risks
are gardeners, ﬂorists, forestry workers, agricultural workers,
farmers, hunters, ﬁshers, and carpenters. Outbreaks have been
reported after common exposure of multiple individuals to a
source of contaminated plant material. Laboratory-acquired
infections have also been described. 167 , 168
Since the 1990s, zoonotic sporotrichosis, related to the direct
transmission from infected cats, has emerged as an important
alternative route for the infection. The ﬁrst reported zoonotic
epidemic of this mycosis was identiﬁed in 1998 in the city and
surroundings of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and currently this region is
considered hyperendemic for zoonotic sporotrichosis. Cases have
occurred in an urban area mainly among people of
underprivileged socioeconomic level. Taking care of diseased cats
is the main factor associated with zoonotic transmission due to
contact with infectious lesions and due to the higher risk of
suﬀering scratches and bites when handling these cats. 6 Nearly
85% of aﬀected humans reported contact with sick cats, and more
than half of these individuals reported a history of a scratch or a
bite. Housewives (30%), students (18%), and veterinarians (5%)
were the primary at-risk populations. 5 Immunocompromised
humans, such as HIV-infected patients, are a high-risk population
and are susceptible to extracutaneous sporotrichosis with
involvement of multiple organs. 64 , 169 Atypical clinical
presentations as well as disseminated sporotrichosis in humans
have been associated with S. brasiliensis infection, with no
apparent connection to the host’s immune status. 170

Veterinary Clinics

• Personal protection equipment: disposable gloves, longsleeved impermeable gowns, closed-toe footwear. In
regions where epidemics occur, consider head covers, shoe

• Hair should be tied back.
• After handling animals or contaminated equipment,
remove gloves and wash hands with antiseptic

• In case of injury through protective clothing by piercing,
cu ing, biting, or scratching, the wound must be
immediately washed with soap and running water and
professional medical advice obtained.
• Use experienced physical or preferably chemical restraint
for examination of the animal or collection of specimens for
laboratory evaluation.
• Dispose of animal waste in infectious waste labeled bags.
• After euthanasia, animals should be placed in infectious
waste labeled bags and, after any necropsy examination,
the ﬁnal destination must be incineration.
• Needles and syringes and other disposable equipment used
to collect specimens should be disposed of in labeled
biohazard containers.
• Sharp items require approved rigid containers and soft
items can be disposed of in infectious waste labeled bags.
• Soiled gauze squares should be treated as biohazardous
and disposed of properly.
• Disposable gowns, gloves, and shoe and head covers
should be treated as biohazardous and disposed of

solution, accelerated hydrogen peroxide, or
polihexametilene biguanide (PHMB) for 10 minutes. For
impervious horizontal surfaces such as tables, alcohol (70%
ethanol) can be applied for additional 10 minutes following
a rinse of the hypochlorite solution. For smaller items, sun
