Owner
• Use disposable gloves when handling cats.

vetexamprep.ir

• Wash hands and arms after handling cats.
• Clothes should be washed in detergent and hot water and
sun dried.
• Crate and dishes should be reserved exclusively for the
infected pet and disinfected on a regular basis.
• Transport infected animals in plastic carriers instead of
wood or cardboard to facilitate cleaning.

The detection of Sporothrix strains on claws and in the oral
cavities of cats that are genetically identical to those causing
human disease provides evidence that zoonotic transmission can
occur through scratches or bites. 171 Isolation of organisms from
nasal secretions and cutaneous lesions implies the possibility of
transmission through secretions and exudates. In contrast, no
human cases were associated with a series of 23 veterinary cases
from northern California. 74 This remarkable diﬀerence in the
Brazilian zoonotic epidemic is probably due to the prevalence of
the highly virulent S. brasiliensis in association with a successful
route of transmission driven by cats. 172
In contrast to feline sporotrichosis, canine sporotrichosis is of
minimal zoonotic importance. Dogs are probably not directly
involved in the transmission of sporotrichosis in view of the
scarcity of yeasts in the lesions and the absence of Sporothrix in the
oral cavity. In addition, there is no conﬁrmation of human cases
associated with transmission by dogs in the Brazilian epidemic. 49
Interhuman transmission is rare. 173 , 174

Case Example
Signalment

“Milho,” a 2-year-old mongrel intact male cat from Rio de
Janeiro, Brazil.

History

Milho was examined at a reference center for diagnosis and
treatment of sporotrichosis in Rio de Janeiro because of

vetexamprep.ir

suspected sporotrichosis. The owner had observed skin lesions
on the cat for a month before referral.

Physical Examination

The cat weighed 4.1 kg and was in a good overall condition.
Clinical examination revealed multiple ulcerated skin lesions
distributed over the face (Fig. 84.16A), nasal region, cervical
region, hind limbs and fore limbs, as well as generalized
lymphadenomegaly.

Laboratory Findings

Exudates from the ulcerated lesions (pelvic limbs, thoracic
limbs, and cervical region) were collected under anesthesia
before and during follow-up by sterile swab and seeded on to
Sabouraud’s dextrose agar, followed by incubation at 25°C.
Suspected isolates were subcultivated on potato dextrose agar
medium at 25°C for macroscopic and microscopic morphologic
studies, and dimorphism (demonstration of both yeast and
mold forms) was demonstrated by conversion to the yeast form
on BHI agar medium at 37°C. For cytologic examination,
impression smears of the same skin lesions were made.
Yeast-like cells were observed on cytologic examination, and
Sporothrix spp. was isolated and identiﬁed from skin lesions
using fungal culture. Alterations identiﬁed on routine
hematology and serum biochemical panels were anemia,
leukocytosis, and hypoalbuminemia. The cat was positive for
FIV antibody and negative for FeLV antigen (SNAP Combo
FeLV/FIV, IDEXX Laboratories, ME, USA).

Treatment

Oral ITZ capsules, at a dose of 100 mg, PO, q24 h (24.4 mg/kg),
was prescribed. After 3 months of ITZ therapy, besides
worsening of the initial skin lesions (Fig. 84.16B), new skin
lesions and nasal mucosal involvement developed, together
with respiratory signs (sneezing and nasal discharge).
Sporothrix continued to be isolated from exudates during the
3 months of ITZ monotherapy, and impression smears were still
positive after 2 months, though with a progressive decrease in
the number of yeasts present.
Due to poor clinical response, KI capsules at the dose of 15
mg, PO, q24h (3.65 mg/kg) were administered, while continuing

vetexamprep.ir

ITZ (100 mg, PO, q24h). Both drugs were administered with
food by the owner.
Two weeks after the ITZ+KI association had been initiated,
the cat developed hyporexia. KI treatment was temporarily
suspended for 3 days and oral silymarin 30 mg/kg, q24h, was
administered. Within this period, the cat began eating normally,
and KI was reintroduced at half the dose on alternate days for
15 days. After that, the full KI dose (15 mg, q24h) was again
prescribed.
At the ﬁrst follow-up visit, around 30 days after the
introduction of KI, the cat had stopped sneezing and nasal
discharge was not observed. Cutaneous lesions were healing,
but lymphadenomegaly persisted.
At the following appointment, the owner reported hyporexia
and weight loss was documented. A palpable soft mass on the
left thoracic region (8 cm diameter) was detected on physical
examination, and needle aspiration cytology conﬁrmed abscess
formation with polymorphonuclear leukocytes, necrotic cells,
and numerous coccoid bacteria. After the drainage of the
abscess, oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid treatment was initiated
(25 mg/kg, PO, q12h for 14 days).
Because of the inappetence, treatment with both antifungal
drugs was temporarily suspended (15 days for ITZ and 20 days
for KI). The drugs were reintroduced as follows: ITZ 100 mg PO
q24h, and KI 7.5 mg PO q48h (1.8 mg/kg) for a week, then 15
mg PO q48h for a week, then 15 mg PO q24h. After 3 months of
combination therapy, the cat was considered cured with
complete healing of skin and mucosal lesions (Fig. 84.16C).
After clinical cure, treatment was continued for an additional
period of 4 weeks.

Comments

This cat demonstrated progression of clinical signs with the
emergence of nasal mucosa involvement, even while receiving
ITZ. Sporothrix brasiliensis is the most prevalent etiologic agent
in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and is described as the most virulent
among the Sporothrix species. A recent study demonstrated that
none of the tested strains of S. brasiliensis recovered from cats
were ITZ resistant. 175 Although antifungal susceptibility tests
were not performed in this case, it should be considered that
the causative strain may have exhibited some resistance to ITZ,

vetexamprep.ir

y

or alternatively, there may have been problems related to
absorption of ITZ. Therapeutic drug monitoring could have
also been considered, although 100 mg PO q24h is a high dose
of ITZ that can be associated with signiﬁcant adverse eﬀects in
cats. Still, the high susceptibility of cats to Sporothrix species is
not yet understood, but it is believed to be multifactorial.
The decrease in fungal burden during treatment suggests that
in spite of the clinical failure, the potential of this cat as a source
of infection was probably reduced. The use of KI capsules as a
combined therapy led to a favorable outcome. Hyporexia and
weight loss were managed as adverse eﬀects of the therapy.
However, the coincidental development of an abscess
(presumably a cat-bite abscess) may have been the cause of
hyporexia when they both occured at the same time.

85: Candidiasis and
Rhodotorulosis
Jane E. Sykes, and Krystle L. Reagan

KEY POINTS
•
First Described: The identification of Candida as a fungal
pathogen was recognized in Stockholm around 1840 (Fredrik
Berg), 1 but candidiasis was described as far back as around
400 BC by Hippocrates.
• Cause: Candida spp. (division Ascomycota, class
Saccharomycetes).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, cats, humans, and a variety of other
animal species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Usually invasion of commensal yeasts
secondary to immune suppression.
• Major Clinical Signs: Local dermatitis; otitis externa; keratitis;
LUTS; abdominal pain, icterus, and/or ascites due to
peritonitis; or severe systemic infections with fever,
inappetence, ocular inflammation, lameness due to
osteomyelitis, respiratory distress, icterus, vomiting.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other systemic fungal or bacterial
infections.
• Human Health Significance: Human infections by Candida
species result from invasion by normal flora, but human-tohuman transmission of Candida strains can also occur. The
potential for exchange of Candida species between animals
and humans is not known.

vetexamprep.ir

Candidiasis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Candida species are yeasts that are typically benign counterparts of
the normal GI, urogenital, and cutaneous ﬂora but can invade
tissues and cause disease as a result of disruption of normal host
defenses. Candida species can also be isolated from soil, inanimate
objects, and hospital environments. The yeasts are small (3 to 6
µm) and ovoid (blastospores) and reproduce by budding.
Budding results in the formation of new yeast cells,
pseudohyphae (chains of elongated yeast cells), and true septate
hyphae. Disease syndromes caused by Candida species that occur
in dogs and cats are listed in Box 85.1. More than 200 species of
Candida exist, but only a few species have been identiﬁed as
pathogens in dogs and cats (Table 85.1). 2–12 The most commonly
isolated species is Candida albicans, and only C. albicans appears to
cause disseminated disease in dogs and cats. However, an
epidemiologic shift with increasing numbers of non-C. albicans–
related infections in animals has been reported. 6 , 10 , 12 , 13 This
change has also been documented in humans and is of signiﬁcant
concern as non-C. albicans species exhibit higher rates of
ﬂuconazole resistance. 14 , 15
Local or disseminated infections where Candida is present with
a mixture of bacterial species can occur. Local infections (such as
UTIs) with two diﬀerent Candida species have also been reported.
10 , 16

When compared with human patients, candidiasis is
uncommonly described in dogs and cats. Predisposing factors in
dogs or cats with local or disseminated candidiasis have included
diabetes mellitus, 5 , 10 , 17 treatment with immunosuppressive
drugs or broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs, 10 , 12 , 18 a history of
GI surgery, 8 , 11 lower urinary tract disease other than infection
(e.g., urinary catheter placement, permanent stomata, atonic
bladder), 12 parvoviral infections, 19–21 and/or underlying
malignancy. 10 , 20 Often more than one of these factors is in the
history. Disseminated candidiasis has most often been described
in dogs, but also occurs in cats. 11 , 22 Although most animals have
underlying immunocompromising conditions, disseminated
candidiasis has been described in apparently immunocompetent

vetexamprep.ir

animals, 23 , 24 which may reﬂect an unidentiﬁed underlying
genetic immunodeﬁciency. Cats with FeLV or FIV infection do not
have higher rates for Candida colonization, 25 and those with
candidiasis usually test negative for FeLV and FIV. 16
Analysis of the authors’ hospital population suggests that cats
are at least as likely as dogs to develop Candida UTIs. 16 In other
studies, Candida species were isolated from the urine of 0.2% of
more than 8,000 dogs with UTIs 26 , 27 and 0.2% of more than 2,000
dogs with persistent or recurrent UTIs. 27 Administration of
antibacterial drugs is strongly associated with candiduria in dogs
and cats. 12 Lower urinary tract disease other than infection, such
as
cystostomy
tube
placement,
intermi ent
urinary
catheterization, and perineal urethrostomy, has been reported in
the history of some cats and dogs with Candida UTIs 6 , 10 , 12 and
is signiﬁcantly associated with candiduria in cats. 12 Local
mucocutaneous infections can occur at the site of long-term
placement of feeding tubes. 3

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
A combination of disruption of normal host barriers and
expression of virulence factors are likely necessary to allow
Candida spp. to invade the host. Administration of antibacterials
can lead to alterations in the normal bacterial ﬂora, allowing
Candida to proliferate. 28 , 29 Compromise to defenses of the lower
urinary tract with urinary catheter placement or alterations to
urine ﬂow (e.g., perineal urethrostomies) are risk factors for the
development of Candida UTIs. 6 , 12
Candida can adhere to a variety of tissue components, such as
epithelial and endothelial cells, as well as other bacteria and
inanimate objects, such as catheters and stents, via integrin-like
and carbohydrate adhesion molecules. 30 , 31 Candida yeasts
produce many proteins that are associated with infection
including hydrolases and heat shock proteins. 23 The yeasts
readily form bioﬁlms consisting of extracellular polymeric
polysaccharides and budding, pseudohyphal, and hyphal forms.
32 Bioﬁlm growth is enhanced by availability of carbon sources
such as glucose (glucosuric patients) and on some substrates such

vetexamprep.ir

as latex urinary catheter. 32 Formation of a bioﬁlm confers
resistance to antifungal drugs by allowing organisms at the center
of the bioﬁlm to slow growth rates, thus making cell cycle–
dependent antifungal agents less eﬀective. It also provides a
physical barrier against antifungal penetration with the
extracellular matrix and promotes the upregulation of drug eﬄux
pumps. 32

Within tissues, neutrophils are a key defense against Candida. 33
Candida blastospores are phagocytized and destroyed by
neutrophils. Mononuclear cells play a less important role.
Reactive oxygen species, hydrolytic enzymes, and antimicrobial
peptides contribute to the intracellular destruction of blastospores
by neutrophils. Thus, any condition that impairs neutrophil
numbers or function, such as neutropenia or diabetes mellitus,
predisposes dogs and cats to candidiasis. A large number of other
cytokines, complement, dendritic cells, and lymphocytes are also
involved in the immune response to Candida. 33 The formation of
hyphae by Candida promotes tissue invasion, which may be
followed by life-threatening fungemia and dissemination to
multiple organs. 34 This ability of Candida to change its
morphology (“morphologic dimorphism”) is thought to be an
important virulence factor.
Lower urinary tract candidiasis may be subclinical or associated
with dysuria, stranguria, and/or hematuria. Systemic signs of
pyrexia, lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss have also been
described in aﬀected dogs and cats, 6 but these signs may result
from the presence of other predisposing diseases. Ascending
infections may lead to development of Candida pyelonephritis.
Cutaneous candidiasis may manifest as erythema, scaling,
alopecia, erosions, and crusting, often where disruption of
cutaneous or mucocutaneous regions has occurred (such as a
previous surgical site or a feeding tube or cystotomy stoma).
Persistent disease in the face of systemic or topical treatment with
broad-spectrum antibiotics should raise suspicion for candidiasis.
Dogs with Candida otitis externa often have a history of chronic
bacterial otitis externa that has been treated aggressively with
systemic or topical antibacterials.
Overgrowth of Candida in the GI tract may occur in animals that
are immunosuppressed or treated with glucocorticoids and/or
broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs. In some cases, invasion of the

vetexamprep.ir

mucosa into the lamina propria or deeper tissues occurs (e.g.,
intestinal candidiasis). A Candida GI granuloma was diagnosed in
a cat after passage of an intestinal foreign body without previous
antibacterial drug administration or known cause of
immunosuppression. 35 Intestinal candidiasis is occasionally
identiﬁed at necropsy in puppies that die after treatment for
parvoviral enteritis and may be a reason for persistent vomiting,
diarrhea, and death despite aggressive ﬂuid and antibacterial
drug therapy. 21 Candida spp. may also contribute to ulcerative
glossitis in puppies with parvovirus infection (Fig. 85.1).
Candida albicans cholecystitis was reported in a 3-year-old cat
from upstate New York. 36 Although no clear underlying cause
could be identiﬁed, the cat had obstructive cholecystitis with what
appeared to be an organizing mucocele, and a nematode of
unknown identity was discovered in the cat’s esophageal feeding
tube during hospitalization. Another cat with diabetes mellitus
was described with pancreatitis associated with a Candida glabrata
infection. 37
Candida peritonitis can occur after intestinal and/or biliary
surgery or intestinal perforation secondary to NSAID
administration. 8 , 11 , 38 Recent treatment with broad-spectrum
antibacterial drugs is reported in most dogs that develop Candida
peritonitis. 38 Mixed infections with Candida and intestinal ﬂora
may develop. Aﬀected dogs are febrile, have abdominal pain, and
may have other GI signs such as vomiting and diarrhea.
Disseminated candidiasis results from hematogenous spread of
Candida from intestinal, urinary, or possibly corneal or cutaneous
sites. 17 , 39 , 40 A diagnosis of disseminated candidiasis should be
considered whenever Candida infections are identiﬁed in the eye,
skin, or urinary tract of an animal that has (or subsequently
develops) severe systemic illness. Clinical signs of disseminated
candidiasis in dogs include fever, inappetence, anorexia, weight
loss, and a variety of other clinical signs that reﬂect underlying
immunosuppressive disease processes and speciﬁc organs
involved. The la er can include the pancreas, liver, mesentery,
spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, lymph nodes, and, less often, the
bone, intestinal tract, eyes, meninges, thyroid, and/or prostate
gland. 5 , 17 , 20 , 23 , 39–44 Ocular signs in animals with disseminated
disease include keratitis and corneal ulceration, uveitis,

vetexamprep.ir

chorioretinitis, and endophthalmitis. 16 , 17 , 41 , 43 Candida keratitis
may also occur as a localized process, sometimes secondary to
aggressive treatment of corneal ulceration secondary to other
disease processes with topical broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs.
Thromboembolic disease may complicate disseminated infections.
Pulmonary thromboembolism may result in respiratory distress
and death. 5 , 16

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Laboratory abnormalities in dogs and cats with candidiasis result
from the underlying disease process (such as diabetes mellitus or
systemic neoplastic disease) as well as the location and severity of
the fungal infection. Laboratory abnormalities in dogs or cats with
Candida UTIs may be absent, or there may be evidence of renal
failure with azotemia and isosthenuria. Grossly, urine may
contain ﬂocculent white debris. Urinalysis may reveal proteinuria,
pyuria, and, in some cases, hematuria and/or Candida fungal
elements (see Case Example). Dogs and cats with disseminated
candidiasis or Candida peritonitis frequently have had
nonregenerative anemia and mild to marked neutrophilia with
bandemia and toxic neutrophil changes (in contrast to other deep
mycoses, where hematologic abnormalities are often mild or
absent). Lymphopenia may be present as a result of underlying
immunosuppressive illness or drug therapy. Some dogs are
thrombocytopenic and have coagulation abnormalities consistent
with DIC. 5 Findings on the serum biochemistry panel in dogs
with disseminated candidiasis are variable and nonspeciﬁc but
may include metabolic acidosis, moderate to severe
hypoalbuminemia, and increased liver enzyme activities. The cat
with Candida cholecystitis had marked hyperbilirubinemia (up to
33.8 mg/dL) and increased serum liver enzyme activities
associated with a concurrent hepatitis. 36

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain thoracic radiographs in dogs with disseminated candidiasis
may be unremarkable or show increased pulmonary interstitial
opacity, thoracic lymphadenomegaly, and/or pleural or
pericardial eﬀusion. 11 , 18 , 23 Abdominal ultrasound examination
in dogs with Candida peritonitis or disseminated disease may
reveal echogenic ascites ﬂuid, mesenteric hyperechogenicity,
changes
consistent
with
pancreatitis,
abdominal
lymphadenomegaly, or increased echogenicity of the renal

fungal balls may be detected as mobile, echogenic, spherical
structures without distal acoustic shadowing within the lumen of

vetexamprep.ir

Microbiologic Tests
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of candidiasis requires visualization of the
organism within lesions by cytologic or histopathologic
examination and conﬁrmation of its identity using culture.
Cytologic Examination
Candida blastospores (5–7 µm), pseudohyphae, and true hyphae
(3–5 µm-wide septate hyphae) can be visualized in swab
specimens from the ear canal (ear cytology); tape preparations
from the skin; urine sediment or other body ﬂuids (Fig. 85.2); or
ultrasound-guided aspirates of abdominal lesions.
Fungal Culture
Candida grows on routine bacteriologic media as well as fungal
media such as Sabouraud dextrose agar. Creamy white colonies
appear within 2 to 3 days, and so isolation of the yeast may be
reported when it is present in specimens submi ed for aerobic
bacterial culture, which are typically incubated only for this
period of time. If Candida is suspected based on the history, fungal
culture (rather than bacterial culture alone) should be requested
because Candida grows best on fungal isolation media. Because
Candida can be isolated from the skin and mucous membranes of
healthy dogs and cats, infection must be conﬁrmed with cytology
or histopathology when Candida is isolated from these sites.
Identiﬁcation of Candida isolates is based on morphology and
biochemical reactions. Preliminary diﬀerentiation of C. albicans
from other Candida species can be made based on the ability of C.
albicans to produce germ tubes when exposed to serum. MALDITOF MS (see Chapter 3) accurately and rapidly identiﬁes Candida
species 46 and may replace these methods in the future. Isolation
of Candida allows not only deﬁnitive identiﬁcation but also
antifungal susceptibility testing (see Fig. 4.16). This is important
for Candida because some isolates (especially Candida glabrata and
Candida krusei) can exhibit antifungal drug resistance.
Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings at necropsy in animals with
disseminated candidiasis include peritoneal or pleural eﬀusion,
enlarged and edematous lymph nodes, congestion and necrotic

vetexamprep.ir

whitish foci within aﬀected organs, evidence of tissue thrombosis,
and formation of a gray-white or yellow-green ﬁbrinonecrotic
layer on aﬀected mucosal surfaces. 5 , 11 , 21 , 23 , 40 , 44 Concurrent
underlying disease processes are also often identiﬁed.

inﬂammatory response that is composed primarily of neutrophils,
macrophages, and lymphocytes. Multinucleated giant cells may
also be present. 23 , 40 , 44 Pseudohyphae and hyphae predominate
in invasive infections (see Fig. 4.1). Evidence of blood vessel
invasion, thrombosing vasculitis, and infarction may be seen, with
multifocal mycotic granulomas in aﬀected organs. 40 The
organism is most readily visualized with special stains such as
PAS and Gomori’s methenamine silver. IHC has also been used to
identify Candida within lesions. 23 , 40 When mixed infections with
Candida and other bacteria are present, tissue Gram stains may
reveal bacterial rods and/or cocci in addition to gram-positive
fungal elements.

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of candidiasis should involve management of
underlying immunosuppressive disorders, if possible, and speciﬁc
antifungal drug treatment. Systemic antibacterial drugs should be
discontinued if not clearly indicated, or the spectrum of activity
should be narrowed as much as possible.
Cutaneous and corneal infections are usually treated with a
combination of topical antiseptics or antifungal medications and
systemic antifungal drugs until lesions resolve. 7
Dogs and cats with candiduria should receive antifungal
therapy as many of the underlying risk factors such as permanent
urinary tract stomata or neoplasia cannot be easily corrected and
ascending pyelonephritis has been reported. 5 , 10 , 17 Initial
therapy should be with antifungal drugs that achieve high
concentrations in the urine, such as ﬂuconazole, for 4 to 6 weeks.
Fungal urine culture should be used to conﬁrm resolution of
infection. Systemic antifungals alone may be adequate to resolve
Candida UTIs in some animals, although resolution has been
reported in some animals in the absence of antifungal drug
therapy. 10
Persistent infection may result from drug resistance, adverse
eﬀects of treatment that necessitate treatment discontinuation, or
inadequate drug penetration into fungal masses that line the
bladder wall (see Case Example). Intravesicular treatment with
1% clotrimazole may be eﬀective in these cases. 47 , 48 Under
anesthesia, the bladder is catheterized with a Foley catheter,
emptied, and then lavaged with sterile saline. The bladder is then
ﬁlled with 1% clotrimazole solution (e.g., 30 to 50 mL for a cat).
The animal is rotated to promote contact of the solution with the
uroepithelium, and after the solution has been in the bladder for
an hour, the catheter is removed and the animal is allowed to
recover. Treatment is continued weekly until Candida can no
longer be isolated from the urine. Typically one to four treatments
are required. 16 , 48 Ultrasound-guided administration of
clotrimazole via cystocentesis to a dog with Candida cystitis was
described in one report. 47
Successful treatment of systemic candidiasis in dogs or cats is
rarely described. One dog with Candida peritonitis was treated
successfully by surgical exploration and lavage of the abdomen,

vetexamprep.ir

placement of an abdominal drain, and IV ﬂuconazole. 8 In
addition, aggressive supportive measures were required that
included IV ﬂuid therapy, fresh frozen plasma, antiemetics,
gastroprotectants, total parenteral nutrition, and antibacterial
drugs for a suspected catheter-related infection. Antifungal drugs
other than ﬂuconazole used to treat invasive candidiasis in human
patients include amphotericin B (AMB) or an echinocandin such
as caspofungin, 49 both of which must be administered
parenterally.

Prevention
Prevention of candidiasis involves avoidance of excessive
immunosuppression, as well as discriminate use of antibacterial
drugs, which should be tailored to the results of culture and
susceptibility whenever possible. 12 Whether Candida species
carried on the hands of humans can colonize dogs and cats is not
known, but routine hand washing and the wearing of gloves
when immunosuppressed animals are handled or intravascular
devices are placed should minimize the chance of healthcareassociated infections. Although prophylactic antifungal drug
treatment has been used to prevent invasive candidiasis in human
high-risk groups, the low incidence of candidiasis in
immunosuppressed dogs and cats does not warrant the use of
prophylactic antifungal drugs in this group.

Public Health Aspects
Candida species (especially C. albicans) are common causes of
mucosal disease in humans. Since 2000, Candida has also emerged
as an extremely important cause of invasive infections owing to
the more widespread use of invasive medical devices and
immunosuppressive drugs. In hospitalized human patients,
Candida is reportedly the fourth most common organism isolated
from the bloodstream. 50 Although many human infections result
from invasion of tissues by commensal yeasts in the face of
immune suppression, horizontal transmission of Candida and
hospital-acquired infections have been described. 51 One Candida
species of particular concern is Candida auris, a highly drugresistant species of Candida that was ﬁrst reported as a nosocomial

vetexamprep.ir

pathogen in Japan in 2009 and has subsequently spread
worldwide. Whether Candida isolates from dogs or cats colonize
humans is not known. Zoonotic transmission of Candida
parapsilosis from dogs was suggested by the authors of a case
report that described two human cases of C. parapsilosis
perioriﬁcial dermatitis (one periocular and another perioral). 52
This was on the basis of a history in both cases of volunteering in
dog shelters, and historic evidence that dogs can be colonized by
C. parapsilosis. However, the prevalence of C. parapsilosis
colonization in dogs from the shelters was not investigated, and
no molecular studies were performed to show that isolates
colonizing the dogs were the same as those causing the two
human infections.

Rhodotorulosis
Rhodotorula spp. are saprophytic yeasts within the division
Basidiomycota (family Sporidiobolaceae). Previously thought to
be nonpathogenic, they are now considered emerging
opportunistic pathogens of humans and other animals. 53
Rhodotorula spp. are widespread in the environment and can be
found in air, soil, lakes, ocean water, dairy products, and fruit
juice. They are also commensal inhabitants of the skin, GI, and
upper respiratory tracts of mammals, and are common
contaminants of hospital surfaces, including endoscopes and
dialysis equipment. 53 They may be isolated in low numbers from
clinical specimens that may have become contaminated with
environmental bacteria or fungi.
Opportunistic infections with Rhodotorula spp. in humans are
very rare. When they occur, they most often are characterized by
fungemia in patients with central venous catheters, including
premature neonates, patients with hematologic malignancies, and
patients receiving central parenteral nutrition. 53 However, they
have also been identiﬁed as a cause of meningeal, skin, ocular,
peritoneal, and prosthetic infections in humans with other
immunocompromising conditions, including treatment with
broad-spectrum antibacterials. The most common species isolated
from humans is Rhodotorula mucilaginosa (approximately 70% of
isolates), followed by Rhodotorula glutinis (approximately 7%). 54 ,
55 In dogs, there have been fewer than ﬁve reports of Rhodotorula

vetexamprep.ir

spp. infection in the literature. Associated conditions were
granulomatous epididymitis, funguria, and pneumonia. 6 , 56 , 57
Care should be taken not to overinterpret light growth of
Rhodotorula from potentially contaminated sites as clinically
signiﬁcant infection, especially in the absence of intralesional
yeasts and when accompanied by mixed growth of bacterial
organisms or other fungal contaminants.
AMB is the most common antifungal agent used for treatment
of humans with Rhodotorula spp. infections, with a mortality rate
of approximately 10%. 53 Although successful therapy with
ﬂuconazole has also been reported, Rhodotorula spp. are resistant
to triazoles and echinocandins in vitro. 58 As with candidiasis,
treatment of rhodotorulosis should likely include identiﬁcation,
and correction, if possible, of any predisposing local or systemic
causes of altered immunity.

Case Example
Signalment

“Lizzie,” an 18-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat
from the San Francisco Bay area (Fig. 85.3A).

History

Lizzie was evaluated by the University of California, Davis,
VMTH, for a 12-hour history of dysuria and hematuria. The
owner described multiple episodes of urination and defecation
outside the li er box with stranguria, hematuria, and tenesmus.
Lizzie was also observed repeatedly grooming her perineum.
The cat had been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 10 years
previously, and more recently with feline bronchial disease, a
thoracolumbar (T3 to L3) myelopathy, generalized
osteoarthritis, chronic constipation, bilateral cataracts, CKD,
and recurrent bacteriuria (Streptococcus bovis group, Escherichia
coli, Enterococcus faecalis, then Aerococcus viridans). She also had
a cardiac murmur secondary to dynamic right ventricular
outﬂow tract obstruction. Historic bacteriuria had been treated
with a variety of antimicrobial drugs selected based on the
results of aerobic bacterial urine culture and susceptibility
(most recently doxycycline, but also amoxicillin-clavulanic acid

vetexamprep.ir

or marboﬂoxacin in the past). Her current medications
consisted of prozinc insulin (3.5 U, SC, q12h), lactulose (2 mL,
PO, q12h), a soluble ﬁber supplement (1 teaspoon with food
twice daily), inhaled ﬂuticasone (110-µg puﬀ, q12h),
theophylline (12 mg/kg, PO, q24h), and doxycycline (5 mg/kg,
PO, q12h). Her most recent blood work (collected 1 month
previously) showed a creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL (reference range,
1.1–2.2 mg/dL) and a BUN of 34 (reference range, 18–33 mg/dL),
which were similar to values obtained over the course of the
previous 5 years. She was an indoor-only cat and was fed a
commercial cat food with occasional turkey meat from the
delicatessen. Her appetite was good, there had been no weight
loss noted, her water consumption was unchanged, and there
had been no vomiting or diarrhea. She had not been vaccinated
for the past 4 years but was on regular ﬂea preventative
medication (nitenpyram as well as ﬁpronil).

Physical Examination

Body weight: 4.1 kg.
General: Quiet, alert, and responsive, T = 100.5°F (38.1°C),
HR = 170 beats/minute, RR = 28 breaths/minute, CRT <1
second, pale pink mucous membranes.
Integument: A dull, slightly unkempt haircoat with mild
scale was noted.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Immature cataracts were
present bilaterally, and all teeth were absent on
examination of the oral cavity. No other clinically
signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected.
Musculoskeletal: BCS was 4/9, and there was mild
generalized muscle atrophy. The cat was reluctant to
ambulate, and appeared painful on manipulation of the
elbows, stiﬂes, and coxofemoral joints bilaterally.
Crepitus was detected on manipulation of the tarsus.
Cardiovascular and respiratory systems: A grade II/VI left
parasternal heart murmur was auscultated. Pulses were
strong and synchronous. No other abnormalities were
detected.
Abdominal palpation: The abdomen was soft and
nonpainful. Both kidneys were small (approximately 2 cm
in diameter) and irregular. The urinary bladder was

vetexamprep.ir

y
approximately 5 cm in diameter and soft. Severe
erythema was noted around the vulva.
Lymph nodes: All were < 1 cm in diameter.

Laboratory Findings
Urinalysis: SpG 1.030; pH 6.0, 75 mg/dL protein, 1,000
mg/dL glucose, no ketones or bilirubin, 250 erythrocytes/
µL hemoprotein, >100 WBC/HPF, >100 RBC/HPF, few
transitional and squamous epithelial cells, many budding
yeast organisms.

Microbiologic Testing
Aerobic bacterial urine culture: 105 C. albicans/mL were
cultured.
Yeast antifungal drug susceptibility panel: Susceptible to
5-ﬂucytosine (0.5 µg/mL), caspofungin (0.25 µg/mL),
ﬂuconazole (0.25 µg/mL), itraconazole (0.06 µg/mL),
voriconazole (0.015 µg/mL). MICs for AMB and
posaconazole were 0.5 µg/mL and 0.03 µg/mL,
respectively (no interpretative criteria available).

Diagnosis

Susceptible C. albicans UTI.

Treatment

Lizzie was treated with ﬂuconazole (50 mg, PO, q12h). At a
recheck examination 10 days later, the owner reported ongoing
pollakiuria and incontinence. A fungal urine culture again
revealed 105 C. albicans/mL with a similar susceptibility proﬁle.
Addition of ﬂucytosine was recommended (250 mg, PO, q8h)
but was considered unaﬀordable to the owners. Treatment was
continued for another month with li le clinical improvement
and persistence of infection. A blood glucose curve revealed 2hourly blood glucose concentrations that were “high”, 470, 368,
300, 383, and 423 mg/dL, respectively, so the insulin dose was
increased to 4 U, q12h. Two weeks later, the owner described
some improvement in the urinary incontinence and reduction

vetexamprep.ir

in stranguria, but again 105 C. albicans/mL was cultured from
the urine, and persistent urine scalding was noted around the
perineum and on the pelvic limbs on physical examination.
Body weight was 3.8 kg, and a blood glucose curve revealed 2hourly blood glucose concentrations that were 457, 301, 209,
227, 300, and 296 mg/dL, respectively.
Topical treatment with clotrimazole was elected. Before the
procedure was performed, a preanesthetic evaluation was done.
A CBC showed a normocytic, normochromic, nonregenerative
anemia (HCT 28.3%; reference range [RR]: 30%–50%), mature
neutrophilia (15,206 cells/µL; RR; 2,000–9,000 cells/µL),
lymphopenia (919 cells/µL; RR: 1,000–7,000 cells/µL), and
monocytopenia (33 cells/µL; RR: 50–600 cells/µL). A serum
biochemistry proﬁle was unremarkable with the exceptions of a
BUN concentration of 49 mg/dL (RR: 18–33 mg/dL) and a
glucose concentration of 314 mg/dL (RR: 63–118 mg/dL).
Urinalysis showed a speciﬁc gravity of 1.022; pH 6.0, 25 mg/dL
protein, 1,000 mg/dL glucose, 0–2 WBC/HPF, 0–2 RBC/HPF,
and moderate numbers of budding yeast organisms and fungal
structures. Thoracic radiographs revealed mild cardiomegaly
and a diﬀuse, static bronchial pa ern consistent with the
previous diagnosis of feline bronchial disease. Abdominal
ultrasound ﬁndings included an enlarged and hyperechoic
liver, mild diﬀuse thickening of the GI mucosa and submucosa,
decreased renal corticomedullary distinction bilaterally with
thickening of the renal cortices, a markedly thickened and
irregular urinary bladder wall that contained hypoechoic, illdeﬁned nodules, and thick sediment within the urinary bladder
lumen. Cystoscopy revealed a large amount of white, ﬂuﬀy
debris adherent to an edematous bladder wall as well as in the
lumen (Fig. 85.3B). A 10F Foley catheter was placed over a
0.025-inch guidewire. The bladder was ﬂushed and the majority
of the debris removed. A total of 47 mL of 1% clotrimazole
solution was infused into the bladder, and the solution was
allowed to remain in place for 1 hour. The solution was
removed, and Lizzie was allowed to recover from anesthesia.
Treatment with ﬂuconazole was continued, although the dose
was lowered (25 mg, PO, q12h). At a recheck 2 weeks later, the
owners reported that Lizzie was more active and was no longer
pollakiuric, although she still urinated outside the li er box and

vetexamprep.ir

intermi ent vomiting had been noted. A CBC, biochemistry
panel, and urinalysis revealed nonregenerative anemia (HCT
21.2%); lymphopenia (349 cells/µL); monocytopenia (70 cells/
µL); increased activities of serum ALT (1028 U/L; RR: 27–101
U/L), AST (226 U/L; RR: 17–58 U/L), and ALP (223 U/L; RR: 14–
17 U/L); hypercholesterolemia (324 U/L; RR: 89–258 U/L); and
hyperbilirubinemia (0.7 mg/dL; RR: 0–0.2 mg/dL). Aerobic
bacterial urine culture revealed more than 105 CFU/mL of
hemolytic E. coli, and fungal culture of the urine was negative.
The ﬂuconazole was discontinued, after which the vomiting
ceased and liver enzyme activities returned to reference ranges.
Multiple bacterial UTIs were diagnosed over the following 6
months, but Candida was never again isolated from the urine.

Comments

In this cat, the C. albicans UTI may have occurred secondary to a
combination of factors that likely included poorly controlled
diabetes mellitus, CKD, neurologic disease, and repeated
treatment with broad-spectrum antimicrobial drugs. Systemic
antifungal drug treatment and improved control of diabetes
mellitus were initially used as treatment strategies but failed,
probably because of the large mats of fungus that were
adherent to the bladder wall. Fortunately, a single topical
clotrimazole treatment resulted in resolution of the yeast
infection. The hepatopathy that developed was thought to be
secondary to ﬂuconazole toxicity since it resolved when the
drug was discontinued.

86: Aspergillosis and
Penicilliosis
Vanessa R. Barrs, and Jonathan D. Dear

KEY POINTS
• Cause: Aspergillus spp. and Penicillium spp., which are
ascomycetes in the family Aspergillaceae, order Eurotiales. 1
• First Described: Invasive aspergillosis was first described in
1815 in a jackdaw bird (Meyer). 2 Aspergillosis was first
described in dogs in 1897 and in cats in 1982. 3
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, cats, humans, and a variety of other
animal species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Inhalation of fungal spores
(conidia) from the environment.
• Major Clinical Signs: Sinonasal aspergillosis and penicilliosis:
nasal discharge, sneezing, epistaxis, depigmentation of the
nares in dogs. Sino-orbital aspergillosis (cats): exophthalmos,
third eyelid prolapse, and oral mass lesions or ulcers in the
pterygopalatine fossa. Disseminated aspergillosis:
inappetence, weight loss, spinal pain, lameness, pelvic limb
paresis or paralysis, cough, vomiting, and tachypnea.
• Differential Diagnoses: Sinonasal aspergillosis: neoplasia,
inflammatory rhinitis, oronasal fistulas, cryptococcosis, nasal
mites (dogs), foreign bodies, and polyps (cats). Disseminated
aspergillosis and penicilliosis: bacterial discospondylitis,
bacterial pyelonephritis, and other systemic mold infections,
especially paecilomycosis.
• Human Health Significance: Human Aspergillus infections are
acquired from the environment. Aspergillus fumigatus is the

vetexamprep.ir

most prevalent airborne fungal pathogen in developed
countries. The global burden of aspergillosis is high;
approximately 3 million people have chronic pulmonary
aspergillosis and almost 5 million have allergic
bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Ten million
immunocompromised patients per year are at risk of
developing invasive aspergillosis, resulting in 200,000 new
cases per annum, with a mortality rate of > 50%. Direct
transmission from affected dogs and cats to humans does not
occur.

Aspergillosis and penicilliosis are diseases caused by pathogenic
fungi that belong to genus Aspergillus and Penicillium,
respectively. These fungi are ubiquitous, saprophytic, hyaline
molds that sporulate abundantly; their spores (conidia) can be
found in soil, water, air, and decaying vegetation. Conidia become
airborne after environmental disturbance and strong air currents.
Their small size keeps them airborne both indoors and outdoors. 4
It is estimated that an individual person inhales several hundred
Aspergillus conidia each day. 5 Aspergillus species, and very rarely
Penicillium species, cause a variety of noninvasive and invasive
forms of disease in dogs and cats that include keratomycosis,
fungal
otitis
externa,
fungal
rhinosinusitis
(FRS),
bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and disseminated invasive
aspergillosis (DIA). Aspergillus species known to cause disease in
dogs and cats are listed in Table 86.1. 6–23 The genus Aspergillus
contains several hundred individual species and can be divided
into six subgenera (Aspergillus, Polypaecilum, Cremei, Fumigati,
Nidulantes, and Circumdati) comprising 27 sections and 75 series. 24
The subgenera most frequently implicated in canine and feline
aspergillosis are Fumigati, Circumdati, and Nidulantes.
Teleomorphs (sexual forms) have been identiﬁed for some
Aspergillus and Penicillium species; the asexual state (anamorph)
comprises hyphae with mitotic spores (conidia), while the
teleomorph consists of fruiting bodies that contain meiotic spores
(ascospores) (Fig. 86.1). Teleomorphs are likely to be present in the
growth phase of these organisms, when growth has been longterm and the nutrients of the substrate favor sexual

vetexamprep.ir

diﬀerentiation. Under the previous dual nomenclature system, the
teleomorph of a fungus was assigned to a separate genus, which
had taxonomic precedence over the anamorph name. Most species
in section Nidulantes (one of nine sections in subgenus Nidulantes)
have a sexual state and were named Emericella. Similarly,
Neosartorya in section Fumigati (subgenus Fumigati) and Eurotium
in section Aspergilli were teleomorph genus names of Aspergillus
species with sexual states. In 2011, dual nomenclature was
abandoned in favor of a “one-fungus, one-name” taxonomic rule
in the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and
plants, under which teleomorph genus names have been
transferred into Aspergillus; for example, Neosartorya udagawae is
now Aspergillus udagawae. 25 This information is relevant for
veterinarians and microbiologists since clinically relevant reports
may have been published using either the anamorph or
teleomorph name of the fungus.
Because accurate identiﬁcation of Aspergillus and Penicillium
species requires advanced molecular techniques, organisms can be
misidentiﬁed based on their morphology in culture alone.
Because the etiology, epidemiology, clinical signs, diagnosis,
and treatment of upper respiratory tract (URT) aspergillosis, DIA,
and keratomycosis/otomycosis diﬀer, they are considered
separately in this chapter. The discussion is focused on
aspergillosis because of the rarity of penicilliosis; however, clinical
disease, diagnosis, and treatment are the same for penicilliosis.

Upper Respiratory Tract Aspergillosis
Etiology and Epidemiology
In dogs, sinonasal aspergillosis (SNA) is a subacute to chronic,
noninvasive disease of the nasal cavity and sinuses. It is most
often caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. Rarely, infection by other
species, such as Aspergillus niger complex organisms (e.g.,
Aspergillus tubingensis) or Aspergillus ﬂavus and the closely related
fungus Penicillium, occurs (see Table 86.1). SNA occurs worldwide,
with cases most commonly reported from the United States and
Australia. Any breed of dog can be aﬀected, but disease is most
common in large, nonbrachycephalic breeds, especially
golden/Labrador retrievers, German/Belgian shepherd dogs,

vetexamprep.ir

ro weilers, malamutes, and rough/Border collies. 26–40 Smaller
breeds most frequently aﬀected include bull terriers, Staﬀordshire
terriers, and miniature schnauzers. Dogs of any age can be
aﬀected (median age around 6 years). 26 , 32 , 35 , 41–45 Males appear
to be at greater risk of infection than females; of 459 reported
cases, 62% were male. 27–42 , 44–46 Systemic immunodeﬁciency or
concurrent systemic disease is rare in dogs with SNA. Local
sinonasal cavity disease including foreign bodies, neoplasia, and
trauma is occasionally identiﬁed.

vetexamprep.ir

a Some isolates have not been identified beyond the series level level

Two forms of FRS occur in cats—SNA and sino-orbital
aspergillosis (SOA). Similar to dogs, SNA is generally a
noninvasive mycosis, with plaques or mats of hyphae that adhere
to, but do not penetrate, the mucosal epithelium. By contrast, SOA
is a deeply invasive mycosis that extends beyond the nasal cavity
and paranasal sinuses to involve adjacent tissues including the
orbit. The ﬁrst case of feline FRS described was in a cat with SOA
in 1982, more than a century after SNA was ﬁrst described in

vetexamprep.ir

dogs. 3 Since then over 70 cases of FRS have been reported in cats,
mostly in the last decade. 3 , 6–9 , 11–13 , 47–62 Whether this increased
reporting frequency is due to increased disease awareness or
increased disease prevalence is not yet clear. Similar to canine
SNA, the majority of cases in cats are from Australia or the United
States, but cases from Japan, the United Kingdom, and mainland
Europe reﬂect the global environmental presence of saprophytic
Aspergillus species that cause these infections.

SNA in cats is most frequently caused by A. fumigatus. Other
species within subgenus Fumigati such as Aspergillus lentulus and
Aspergillus thermomutatus can also cause feline SNA (see Table
86.1). These closely related species are also called “cryptic” species
because of their close morphologic resemblance to A. fumigatus.
Accurate identiﬁcation of cryptic species requires molecular
techniques, and is important since antifungal resistance is
common among these species. Species from other subgenera
including A. niger and A. ﬂavus can also cause feline SNA.

vetexamprep.ir

In early descriptions of SOA, causative organisms were not
identiﬁed beyond the genus Aspergillus. 3 , 49 In several
subsequent cases, A. fumigatus was identiﬁed, but identiﬁcation
was not deﬁnitive since it was morphological. 54 Where molecular
methods have been used for deﬁnitive fungal identiﬁcation (>25
cases), a novel species of Aspergillus discovered in aﬀected cats,
Aspergillus felis, was the most common cause of SOA, followed by
A. udagawae. These species, in subgenus Fumigati, are cryptic
species related to A. fumigatus, and even more closely related to
Aspergillus viridinutans. There are currently 10 species in the A.
viridinutans species complex, and of these, 3 have been detected in
cats with SOA: A. felis, A. udagawae, and Aspergillus wyomingensis.
63

Brachycephalic breeds of Persian and related lineage
(Himalayans, exotic/British/Sco ish shorthair cats, ragdolls) are
predisposed to SNA and to SOA, but both conditions occur in any
breed. Disease can occur in cats of any age (median, 5 years) and
there is no sex predisposition. Most cats with URT aspergillosis
test negative for FeLV or FIV infection. SNA and SOA occasionally
occur in association with facial trauma, nasal neoplasia, and
inhaled plant material, as has been reported in canine SNA. 64 , 65

Pathogenesis
Sinonasal Aspergillosis
The pathogenesis of canine SNA is not fully understood despite
investigations of innate and adaptive immune responses. 68–73
There are three lines of defense against fungal respiratory
infection: (1) the respiratory mucosal epithelium traps and
removes inhaled conidia via the mucociliary escalator and acts as
an anatomic barrier to invasion; (2) fungal elements are
phagocytosed by host cells (monocytes, macrophages,
neutrophils, and respiratory epithelial cells) resulting in direct
pathogen killing; and (3) dendritic cells respond to phagocytosis

vetexamprep.ir

by promoting diﬀerentiation of naïve T cells into eﬀector T-helper
(Th) cell subtypes.
After inhalation, Aspergillus conidia that are not trapped and
removed by mucociliary defenses germinate, if temperature and
humidity are favorable, to form plaques of fungal hyphae that are
adherent to the sinonasal mucosa. Aspergillus conidia are coated
with hydrophobin proteins that facilitate mucosal adherence and
protect conidia from recognition of PAMPs by innate and
adaptive immune cells. 74 SNA is usually noninvasive; therefore,
fungal hyphae do not penetrate the mucosal epithelium.
Dendritic cells express pa ern recognition receptors (PRRs)
including C-type lectin receptors, TLRs, NOD-like receptors
(NLRs), and galectin family proteins that recognize speciﬁc fungal
epitopes and induce speciﬁc Th responses, which are an essential
determinant of host susceptibility or resistance to invasive
aspergillosis. 75 In the immune response of humans to A.
fumigatus, Th1 cytokine responses are generally protective, while
Th2 cytokine responses increase susceptibility to invasive disease.
Th17 responses are regulatory, promoting Th1 responses and
suppressing Th2 responses. Th17 responses are implicated in the
immunopathogenesis of chronic fungal infections by failure to
restrain inﬂammation after IL-17A-dependent neutrophil
recruitment. 75 T-regulatory (Treg) cells restrain exuberant
immune reactivity and limit tissue damage in many chronic
infections, but can handicap the eﬀect of protective immunity. In
addition to infected cells, or cells exposed to fungal PAMPs, Treg
cells are a principal source of IL-10.
Cytokine proﬁling of dogs with SNA demonstrated
upregulation of mRNA for cytokines associated with a Th1
response compared with normal controls or dogs with
lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis. 68 , 69 , 72 In addition, there was
upregulation of IL-10, which may limit the extent of local tissue
destruction, 76 but paradoxically could also impede clearance of
infection. Compared with normal dogs, dogs with SNA were
found to have signiﬁcantly higher expression of all 10 TLRs except
for TLR5, and of NLR2, but not NLR1 in the nasal mucosa. 73 A
subsequent mutational analysis of TLRs 2, 4 and 9 was performed,
70 since single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNPs) in these speciﬁc
TLRs have been associated with higher risk of fungal disease in

vetexamprep.ir

humans. 77 However, no SNPs associated with canine SNA were
detected.
The functional phenotype of peripheral blood mononuclear
cells (PBMCs) from normal dogs and dogs with SNA after
challenge with heat-inactivated A. fumigatus conidia has also been
determined. 71 There was signiﬁcantly greater expression of IL17A mRNA in PBMCs from aﬀected dogs compared with
controls, suggesting a role for a Th17-driven uncontrolled
inﬂammatory response that could counteract the host’s eﬀorts to
clear fungal infection through Th1-directed immunity.
Although SNA in dogs is noninvasive, it results in nasal
turbinate and paranasal bony lysis, which can be severe. This is
a ributed to the inﬂammatory response of the host. 78 In addition,
A. fumigatus synthesizes proteases, phospholipases, and toxic
secondary metabolites, which may contribute to tissue
destruction. 79 Other fungal metabolites unique to section Fumigati
have one or more virulence properties including cytotoxicity (e.g.,
fumiquinazolines, trypacidin), ability to induce ciliastasis (e.g.,
verruculogen, helvolic acid) or apoptosis; and inhibition of
immune responses, neutrophil responses, phagocytosis, and/or
angiogenesis (e.g., gliotoxin, fumagillin, pyripyropenes). 79
Sino-Orbital Aspergillosis
In SOA there is direct extension of a sinonasal infection to involve
paranasal structures, usually via lysis of the thin orbital bone. 8
Cats with SOA have granulomatous invasive mycotic
rhinosinusitis with submucosal hyphal invasion. 3 , 6 , 55 Once
infection reaches the orbit, multilobulated fungal granulomas
form in which hyphae are conﬁned centrally.
As orbital granulomas expand, they cause dorsolateral
displacement of the globe and bulge ventrally into the caudal oral
cavity. In advanced disease, local extension to involve the CNS
can occur, resulting in granulomatous mycotic meningitis.
Hematogenous dissemination to involve other organs was
reported in one case.80 A role for species-speciﬁc fungal virulence
factors in the development of disease is suspected since diﬀerent
fungal species cause SNA and SOA. The A. felis type strain,
isolated from a cat with SOA, had signiﬁcantly higher virulence in
Galleria melonella larvae than A. fumigatus. 81 Whether unique

vetexamprep.ir

fungal metabolites are involved in pathogenicity is not known, for
example, viriditoxin is produced by all members of the A.
viridinutans complex but not by A. fumigatus. 79

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of SNA in dogs include sneezing, reverse sneezing,
chronic serous to mucopurulent nasal discharge, depigmentation,
crusting or ulceration of the nasal planum, muzzle pain and, less
commonly, epistaxis (Fig. 86.2). Clinical signs are subtle early in
disease. Nasal discharge is initially unilateral but can become
bilateral as the disease progresses. Signs in advanced disease may
include lethargy, inappetence, and weight loss. Nasal pain can
manifest as pawing at the face, hiding, or withdrawal when
approached. Destruction or obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct
can lead to epiphora. Osteolysis of the cribriform plate is often
subclinical, but occasionally leads to meningitis with neurologic
signs such as obtundation or seizures. Clinical signs of SNA in
cats are similar although nasal depigmentation and signs of nasal
pain have not been reported.
Cats with SOA are usually examined because of signs
associated with a retrobulbar fungal granuloma including
unilateral exophthalmos, a prolapsed, inﬂamed third eyelid, and
blepharospasm or conjunctival discharge (Fig. 86.3). Exposure
keratitis is common and uveitis is sometimes present. Nasal signs
may be subtle or absent; however, the history usually reveals
sneezing or nasal discharge in the 6 months before examination.
In advanced disease, vision loss can occur due to severe ulcerative
keratitis or inﬁltration of the optic nerve and/or optic chiasm. 6 , 49
, 50 , 55 Exophthalmos may become bilateral and neurologic signs
may develop including seizures, nystagmus, circling, facial
muscle fasciculation, and hyperesthesia. 6 , 58 , 59 Inappetence and
dysphagia can also occur. 59
Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in dogs with SNA include
unilateral or bilateral serous or mucopurulent nasal discharge,
epistaxis, pain on palpation of the face, mild mandibular

vetexamprep.ir

lymphadenomegaly, depigmentation, crusting or ulceration of the
nares, and occasionally epiphora (see Fig. 86.2). Nasal airﬂow is
usually normal or increased because of turbinate lysis. Sometimes
palpation of the nasal bones or hard palate can reveal defects in
the underlying bone. Dogs with cribriform plate involvement and
meningitis may be obtunded or dehydrated. Dogs with severe
epistaxis can have melena on rectal examination secondary to
swallowed blood. Most aﬀected dogs are afebrile.
Physical examination ﬁndings in cats with SNA consist of
serous or mucopurulent nasal discharge, sneezing, stertor,
epistaxis, and, in some cases, mandibular lymphadenomegaly,
fever, or a discharging sinus over the nasal bridge or frontal sinus.
6 Cats with SOA most commonly have unilateral exophthalmos
with dorsolateral deviation of the globe and prolapse of the third
eyelid, which may also be inﬂamed. Corneal ulcers are usually
central and are readily visualized with ﬂuorescein stain (see Fig.
86.3). Other ocular signs variably present include miosis, an
absent pupillary light response, an absent menace response, and
signs of anterior or posterior uveitis. Resistance to retropulsion of
the globe and normal intraocular pressure readings on tonometry
enables diﬀerentiation of exophthalmos from buphthalmos.

Oral cavity involvement is ﬁrst visible as a submucosal swelling
in the pterygopalatine fossa adjacent to the last molar tooth,
which may become ulcerated (Fig. 86.4). Ulceration of the hard
palate occurs occasionally. Fungal invasion of maxillary
subcutaneous tissues causes facial swelling, which may be subtle
or severe and can ulcerate. 61 Fever and mandibular
lymphadenomegaly are variably present. In most cases, there is
no pain on opening of the mouth.

Diagnosis
Early diagnosis of URT aspergillosis relies on a high degree of
suspicion for the disease and availability of client ﬁnancial
resources because of a lack of uniformly available sensitive,
noninvasive diagnostic tests for the disease. Serologic tests are
performed early in investigation. Deﬁnitive diagnosis requires a
combination of imaging, visualization of fungal plaques by
rhinoscopy/sinuscopy (SNA), and identiﬁcation of fungal
elements on cytology or histopathology. Imaging should be
performed before rhinoscopy to avoid the inﬂuence of iatrogenic
hemorrhage on the results. Duplicate tissue or fungal plaques can
be stored frozen, as well as submi ed fresh for culture and in

vetexamprep.ir

formalin for histopathology. If fungal cultures are negative, frozen
tissues can be retrieved for molecular testing.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Dogs with SNA often have no abnormalities on CBC, serum
chemistry
proﬁle,
or
urinalysis.
Occasionally,
mild
nonregenerative anemia; mild neutrophilia, rarely with a left shift;
mild eosinophilia; and/or mild hypoalbuminemia are present. 10
Cats with SOA may have a mild mature neutrophilia and
sometimes mild to severe hyperglobulinemia. 6 , 49
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Plain skull radiographs in dogs or cats with SNA may show
unilateral or bilateral loss of turbinate detail, destruction of the
nasal septum, and/or increased soft tissue opacity within the nasal
cavity. The open-mouth view provides optimum evaluation of the
turbinates (Fig. 86.5A). A “skyline” view of the nasal sinuses may
show opaciﬁcation of one or both sinuses and frontal bone
hyperostosis (Fig. 86.5B). 33
Advanced Imaging
Whenever possible, CT or MRI are preferred imaging modalities
for the nasal cavity because of their increased sensitivity over
plain radiography for evaluation of the nasal cavity, sinuses, and
cribriform plate. 33 Bony changes are best appreciated on CT.
Sinonasal cavity involvement can be unilateral or bilateral in dogs,
and is usually bilateral and asymmetric in cats. 32 , 33 In some
animals, lesions are limited to the frontal sinus. 8 , 45 Findings on
CT or MRI in canine and feline SNA include moderate to severe
“cavitated” nasal turbinate lysis and defects in the nasal septum;
increased soft tissue opacity within the nasal cavity and/or sinuses
due to mucosal inﬂammation, ﬂuid accumulation, or fungal
plaques; hyperostosis of the frontal bones; and mandibular or
retropharyngeal lymph node enlargement. 8 , 32 , 33 , 45 Nasal
mucosal thickening is detected as a rim of soft tissue along the
nasal bones, maxillary recess, and frontal bone. Osteolysis of the
cribriform plate, orbital bone, frontal bones, and, rarely, the

vetexamprep.ir

maxillary or palatine bones may be present (Fig. 86.5C).
Meningeal enhancement is sometimes evident on contrast
administration in dogs with cribriform plate destruction. 41
Fungal plaques and mucosal secretions fail to enhance with
contrast and cannot be readily distinguished from each other.
Deposits of calcium-containing fungal metabolites that aggregate
to cause sinoliths are common in human maxillary sinus
mycetomas, but have only been reported in one cat with SNA
(rhinoliths), 50 one cat with SOA (sinolith), 8 and not in dogs.

Rhinoscopy and Sinuscopy
Visualization of fungal plaques by rhinoscopy and sinuscopy
conﬁrms the presence of mycotic rhinitis, and is a noninvasive,
reliable method for obtaining fungal plaques and mucosal
biopsies for cytology, histopathology, and fungal culture. Plaques
are white, gray, yellow, black, greenish, or a mixture of these
colors and are adhered to the nasal mucosa or mucosa of the
frontal sinus in cases of SNA. (Fig. 86.7). Cytologic examination is
important to establish a diagnosis of SNA since there are other
causes of mycotic rhinitis, and because mucopurulent exudates
can occasionally be mistaken for fungal plaques.

In dogs, nasopharyngoscopy is performed with a ﬂexible
endoscope, after which a rigid telescope or ﬂexible endoscope is
used to examine the rostral portions of the nasal cavity. In some

vetexamprep.ir

cases, extensive turbinate destruction allows a ﬂexible endoscope
to be passed directly into the frontal sinuses through the
nasofrontal opening. If this is not possible, but CT or MRI ﬁndings
suggest the possibility of frontal sinus lesions, trephination or
surgical exploration of the frontal sinuses is necessary to visualize
(and treat) this region. After trephination, a rigid endoscope can
be used to examine the frontal sinus through the trephination site.
Nasopharyngoscopy using a ﬂexible endoscope is useful in cats
to identify choanal and nasopharyngeal fungal plaques or
granulomas. In cats with SOA, although mycotic rhinitis is
usually present, fungal plaques are not seen on rhinoscopy
because of deep tissue invasion by fungal hyphae. The nasal
cavity is examined using a rigid rhinoscope. Indications for sinus
trephination are the same as for dogs.
Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination
Cytologic examination of blind or rhinoscopy-directed mucosal
swabs, brush specimens of the nasal cavity, or nasal biopsies from
dogs or cats with SNA can reveal ﬁlamentous fungal hyphae and
sometimes also conidia (Table 86.2). Hyphae stain well with
Wright stain. They are septate and branch at 45-degree angles (see
Fig. 4.3). Large numbers of degenerate neutrophils, ciliated
epithelial cells, and/or bacteria are also usually present. In one
study, the sensitivity of cytologic examination was 93% for
endoscopic-guided cytology brush specimens, and 100% for
squash preparations of biopsies of suspected mucosal fungal
plaques, but it was only 20% or less for nasal discharge or smears
made from blind swab specimens. 40

Fungal hyphae may be identiﬁed in cats with SOA on cytologic
examination of ﬁne-needle aspirates or squash preparations of
nasopharyngeal or retrobulbar masses biopsied via the oral cavity
or with ultrasound or CT guidance. However, because fungal
hyphae are conﬁned to central areas of granulomatous lesions,
they may be missed.
Serologic Diagnosis
The sensitivity of serologic tests to detect the fungal cell wall
antigen galactomannan (GM) or Aspergillus-speciﬁc antibodies in
aspergillosis is heavily inﬂuenced by host immunocompetence
(see Table 86.2). Antigen tests are aﬀected by host ability to clear
fungal antigen from the circulation, and antibody tests rely on an
adequate humoral immune response. A commercial ELISA to
detect GM in the serum (Platelia Aspergillus EIA, Bio-Rad) has a
sensitivity of up to 90% in systemically immunocompromised
patients, including neutropenic human patients with pulmonary
aspergillosis and dogs with DIA. 82 , 83 However, in nonneutropenic patients with pulmonary aspergillosis, the assay

vetexamprep.ir

sensitivity is < 30%. 82 , 84 , 85 Similarly, in dogs and cats with SNA,
GM also performs poorly (23%–24% sensitivity). 43 In
immunocompetent patients, GM is cleared by neutrophils, which
possess mannose-binding receptors, or is complexed by antibody.
86 , 87 Also, lack of tissue invasion in noninvasive mycoses such as
SNA may contribute to the lack of detectable circulating GM.
Assays to detect serum Aspergillus-speciﬁc antibodies include
immunodiﬀusion (ID) assays that detect precipitins, such as AGID
or counter immunoelectrophoresis (CIE) (see Fig. 2.7A), and
ELISA assays. In general, ID assays have lower sensitivity and
higher speciﬁcity than ELISAs for diagnosis of canine and feline
URT aspergillosis. However, clinical performance data for some
assays used in commercial veterinary diagnostic laboratories may
not be available. The sensitivity of one ID assay (Meridian
Bioscience, USA) for diagnosis was 57% to 77% for canine SNA 41–
43 and 43% for feline URT aspergillosis. 9 The speciﬁcity for both
assays was 98%–100%.The sensitivity and speciﬁcity of another ID
assay (Immuno-Mycologics, OK, USA) for canine SNA was 31%
and 97%, respectively. 88 The sensitivity and speciﬁcity of an
ELISA assay that detects antibodies against a commercial
Aspergillus antigen extract derived from A. fumigatus, A. niger, and
A. ﬂavus was 88% and 97%, respectively, for canine SNA and 95%
and 93%, respectively, for feline URT aspergillosis. 9 , 43 Thus,
negative results with these antibody assays do not rule out SNA,
but positive results strongly suggest the disease is present.

Fungal Culture
Aspergillus fumigatus can be readily grown on routine laboratory
media. Colonies of mold generally appear within 96 hours, but
occasionally longer incubation times are required. 44 In the
absence of supportive rhinoscopic, cytologic, or histopathologic
ﬁndings, positive cultures from the nasal cavity require cautious
interpretation because Aspergillus may be found within the URT of
healthy animals. Nevertheless, in two separate studies, no dogs
with nonfungal nasal disorders had positive culture results for
Aspergillus. 42 , 44 In one of these studies (which included 21 dogs
with SNA and 37 dogs with nonfungal nasal disease), the
sensitivity of fungal culture of endoscopic nasal tissue biopsies
(including nasal mucosa and fungal plaques if visualized) for
diagnosis of canine SNA was 81%. 42 In the other study, the
sensitivity of fungal culture of nasal mucosal biopsies at 37°C was
75%, 88% for fungal plaques and < 19% for blindly collected nasal
swab specimens (see Table 86.2). 44
The fungal pathogens that cause feline URT aspergillosis can
usually be isolated from tissue biopsies or fungal plaques on
commercial culture media such as Sabouraud’s dextrose agar or
malt extract agar. Of 23 cases of feline SNA and SOA, 22 were

vetexamprep.ir

culture-positive in one study. 6 One useful distinguishing feature
of the cryptic species in Aspergillus subgenus Fumigati that cause
URT aspergillosis in cats (e.g., A. felis) is their inability to grow at
50°C, in contrast to A. fumigatus, which does exhibit growth at
50°C. Fungal cultures from cats with URT aspergillosis can be
subcultured and incubated at 50°C to determine whether a cryptic
species is present. Fungal isolates that fail to grow at 50°C should
be submi ed for molecular testing for species identiﬁcation.
Cryptic species are also slower to sporulate than A. fumigatus and
have white or cream-colored fungal colonies before sporulation in
contrast to the rapidly sporulating grey-green colonies of A.
fumigatus (Fig. 86.8).
Identiﬁcation of Aspergillus species using macroscopic and
microscopic morphologic features is inaccurate and many cryptic
species within a complex cannot be reliably diﬀerentiated from
each other. Morphologic features in combination with
demonstration of fungal growth at 50°C is usually adequate to
diﬀerentiate A. fumigatus from cryptic species. 21 Accurate
identiﬁcation of other species in Aspergillus subgenus Fumigati
requires PCR and sequencing. Using DNA extracted directly from
fungal cultures, longer gene targets can be ampliﬁed than from
formalin-ﬁxed paraﬃn-embedded tissues, and ampliﬁcation of
the ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 region of rDNA (751 bp) using primers ITS1
and ITS4 is standard. For some species, ampliﬁcation of a
secondary identiﬁcation target such as calmodulin, β-tubulin, or
the RNA polymerase II second largest subunit (RPB2) is required
for deﬁnitive identiﬁcation. 89
MALDI-TOF MS is an alternative method for identiﬁcation of
Aspergillus species but has been limited by inadequate species and
strain spectra representation in commercial libraries (see Chapter
3). For example, of 55 clinical Aspergillus isolates from Australia,
69% were correctly identiﬁed using the commercial database
alone, but 93% were correctly identiﬁed when it was combined
with an in-house database constructed from strains of Aspergillus
circulating in Australia. 90
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
In veterinary medicine, the use of panfungal PCR assays for the
diagnosis of mycotic disease is increasing. PCR can lack
sensitivity for detection of fungi when compared with bacteria

vetexamprep.ir

y
g
p
due to problems associated with fungal cell wall lysis in order to
release DNA during the ﬁrst step of DNA extraction. PCR assays
targeting the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) gene cluster have the
broadest application because this gene is multicopy (>50,000
copies per haploid fungal genome). It also contains regions that
are highly conserved between fungal genera and that ﬂank highly
variable regions. Thus, universal primers can be designed based
on the conserved regions, and the resulting sequences enable
identiﬁcation to at least genus or species complex level. The rDNA
gene cluster comprises the small subunit rDNA (18S) gene, the
5.8S gene, and the large subunit (28S) gene. These regions are
separated by the intergenic transcribed spacer (ITS) regions, ITS1
and ITS2, which are the most hypervariable regions. PCR assays
that target the 361 bp ITS1 region (primers ITS1 and ITS2) or the
231 bp ITS2 region (primers ITS3 and ITS4) have been used to
identify fungal pathogens in fresh, frozen, or formalin-ﬁxed
canine and feline tissues. 91 , 92 In two studies, the sensitivity of
these PCR assays to correctly identify a fungal pathogen to genus
or species level was approximately 65%. 91 , 92 Real-time PCR
methods are increasingly used together with fungal antigen
detection tests for the diagnosis of pulmonary aspergillosis in
immunocompromised humans using blood (plasma or serum) or
bronchoalveolar lavage ﬂuid. 93 The use of real-time PCR assays to
detect Aspergillus DNA in nasal biopsy specimens was evaluated
for diagnosis of SNA in dogs, but assays evaluated had either
unacceptably high rates of false-positive test results (PenAsp
assay) or a low sensitivity (Aspergillus genus-speciﬁc PCR). 88 For
both assays, dogs with SNA had higher DNA copy numbers than
control dogs or dogs with lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis or
neoplasia, but there was considerable overlap in copy numbers
between dogs with SNA and those without SNA.

Pathologic Findings
The sensitivity of histologic examination of nasal mucosal biopsies
for diagnosis of SNA was approximately 80% in two studies in
which fungal plaques and adjacent mucosa were biopsied under
endoscopic guidance (see Table 86.2). 41 , 42 Biopsy of the nasal
mucosal tissue without the overlying fungal plaque can cause a
false-negative result. Special fungal stains (e.g., PAS or GMS)
increase the sensitivity of detection of fungal hyphae in histologic
sections.
Histopathology of nasal biopsies from dogs and cats with SNA
usually reveals mats of branching, septate fungal hyphae a ached
to nasal or sinus mucosa or within luminal exudates, in a
background
of
lymphoplasmacytic
and
neutrophilic
inﬂammation. Occasionally, the neutrophilic component
predominates. Variable numbers of macrophages and eosinophils
may also be present, as well as necrotic debris. Other ﬁndings
include osteolysis, turbinate remodeling, and intralesional
bacteria. Occasionally, intralesional plant material is detected.

vetexamprep.ir

Conidiophores and conidia can be found because the fungus is
exposed to air within the nasal cavity (Fig. 86.9).
In cats with SOA, retrobulbar fungal granulomas contain
central areas of coagulative necrosis in which fungal hyphae are
conﬁned and surrounded by peripheral zones of inﬂammatory
cells including neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, peripheral
ﬁbroblasts, lymphocytes, and plasma cells (Fig. 86.10A and B).
Inﬂammatory lesions can also eﬀace adjacent skeletal muscle and
bone. The globe is resistant to fungal invasion, but may be
aﬀected by keratitis and anterior uveitis. 6 , 49 , 55 , 58 There may be
invasion of adjacent structures including the nictitating
membrane, eyelid, optic nerve, and optic chiasm. 6 , 49 , 54 , 55 , 59
Mycotic invasion of the sinus or nasal mucosa may also be evident
(Fig. 86.10C).

Treatment and Prognosis
Successful treatment of SNA is challenging. Because of the large
size of the nasal cavity and sinuses, clinical signs are often not
apparent until disease is advanced. Delays in diagnosis can occur
because of the costly and invasive nature of diagnosis and
treatment and the need for specialized imaging techniques and
endoscopic expertise. Owners of adult dogs that develop
persistent nasal discharge (e.g., present for at least 1 week) should
be encouraged to pursue advanced imaging and rhinoscopy as
soon as possible so that the disease can be recognized and treated
early, especially in regions such as California and Australia where
there is a high disease incidence. Treatment with antibacterial
drugs alone is discouraged because primary bacterial infection of
the nasal cavity in adult dogs (in the absence of an underlying
causes such as neoplasia or fungal infection) is extremely rare.
In general, treatment of canine and feline SNA requires
thorough mechanical debridement of plaques with endoscopic
biopsy forceps and copious irrigation until no visible fungus
remains, which may necessitate extended anesthesia. In some
cases, treatment is performed immediately after imaging and
rhinoscopy, which further prolongs the period of anesthesia. If
plaques within the frontal sinuses cannot be accessed by
antegrade rhinoscopy through the nasofrontal opening, frontal
sinus trephination and cure age or open surgical debridement of

vetexamprep.ir

the frontal sinus may be required. Debridement of fungal plaques
is followed by repeated lavage with 0.9% saline and suction,
followed by topical antifungal drug therapy with clotrimazole or
enilconazole. Additional systemic antifungal drug treatment
could also be considered, but whether this improves the outcome
over topical therapy alone is unknown.

Canine Sinonasal Aspergillosis
A variety of noninvasive and invasive protocols for topical
antifungal drug treatment of canine SNA after debridement of
fungal plaques in the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses have been
described, with varied rates of success. Currently, there is a lack of
masked, randomized prospective clinical trials with consistent
and long-term follow-up evaluation that indicate clear beneﬁt of
one treatment over another. Complete debridement of fungal
plaques is associated with an improved ﬁrst treatment success
rate compared to partial debridement in dogs treated with topical
antifungal azole infusions.94 The protocol described here is used
at the University of California Davis, Veterinary Medical Teaching
Hospital (UCD VMTH). A similar protocol has been used
successfully to treat SNA in cats. 57
After thorough debridement of fungal plaques, a 24F Foley
catheter is retroﬂexed over the soft palate and the balloon inﬂated
until it can be palpated above the soft palate (Fig. 86.11).
Placement of the catheter can be facilitated by insertion of a stiﬀ
guidewire into the catheter. Alternatively, a ﬂexible catheter can
be advanced from the rostrum through the nasal passage and into
the oropharynx. The Foley catheter can then be sutured to this
second catheter and be drawn into the nasopharynx by
withdrawing the second catheter from the nasal folds. The tip of
the catheter can then be bent into a U shape and hooked over the
soft palate, after which the balloon is inﬂated. The nasopharynx is
packed with moistened laparotomy pads, a gauze pad is placed
over the incisive papilla, and the proximal end of the Foley
catheter is clamped across the guidewire to prevent leakage of
antifungal drug from the nasal cavity. The dog is then placed in
dorsal recumbency with the skull positioned vertically (at 90
degrees to the tabletop), the eyes are lubricated and a protective
wrap is placed around the muzzle to prevent spillage of
medication into the eye. Clotrimazole (1%) or enilconazole (1% or
2%) solution is then administered into each nasal passage until
full and a meniscus is visible. For large-breed dogs, 20 to 30 mL of
solution is administered per side initially, and medication is
dripped in to maintain ﬁlling of the nasal passage for 15
minutes.94 The catheters and sponges are then removed with the
dog’s head tilted downward at an angle of 30 degrees, and the
material is allowed to drain from the nasal cavity for 10 minutes.

vetexamprep.ir

Debridement and a second treatment are then routinely
performed 1 month later. Sometimes, a third treatment 1 month
after that may be necessary. Clotrimazole can be irritating to
tissues, and solutions with a propylene glycol vehicle can cause
nasopharyngeal irritation and edema. 95 , 96 In general, however,
clotrimazole solutions with a polyethylene glycol vehicle cause
minimal adverse eﬀects. Enilconazole solutions may be less
irritating, but there is no evidence that they are more eﬀective
than clotrimazole. They also tend to be less viscous, and may be
more likely to be aspirated as a result.

One retrospective study compared two minimally invasive
topical enilconazole infusion protocols after endoscopic plaque
