Clinical Manifestations

Hepatitis, myositis

Sarcocystis canis has been associated with hepatic, pulmonary,
cutaneous, and/or CNS infections in puppies less than 10 months of
age. 8–10 Reported cases have been from Maryland, Kansas, and
Colorado (United States), and one dog from Costa Rica. Sarcocystis
canis has also been reported as a cause of hepatitis in a California sea
lion and a Steller sea lion from Alaska, a striped dolphin from Spain,
a Hawaiian monk seal, polar bears, a chinchilla, a horse, and a black
bear. 32 Genetic characterization of the organism has been based on
DNA extracted from the liver of wildlife species with hepatitis. 32 The
deﬁnitive host of S. canis is unknown.
Sarcocystis caninum has been identiﬁed as a cause of systemic illness
and myositis/necrotizing myopathy in domestic dogs from Canada,
Finland, and the United States. 7 , 11 , 33 , 34 Sarcocystis caninum
sarcocysts also were identiﬁed in the muscle tissue from 2 of 37 dogs
on sale for dog meat consumption at a market in southwestern China.
35 The life cycle of this organism is also unknown.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs

vetexamprep.ir

After ingestion of infected muscles of intermediate host containing
the sarcocyst stage, bradyzoites enclosed in the sarcocyst are released
in the gut lumen and penetrate enterocytes, and transform into male
and female gamonts. After fertilization, oocysts are formed in the
lamina propria of small intestine. Oocysts sporulate in situ and
sporulated oocysts contain two sporocysts, each with four
sporozoites. Sporulated oocysts, but more often, sporocysts are
excreted in feces. Because oocysts are trapped in the lamina propria,
they are released at irregular intervals even several months after
initial infection. The intermediate host becomes infected by ingesting
food or water contaminated with sporocysts. The replicative cycle in
intermediate hosts varies depending on the Sarcocystis species
involved. In general, sporozoites released from sporocysts penetrate
the intestine and form schizonts, often in endothelial cells. After one
or more replicative cycles, the organisms encyst in the muscle as
sarcocysts, where they wait to be ingested by a carnivore.
Sarcocystis canis
Sarcocystis canis can cause hepatitis, meningoencephalitis, and
pneumonia in dogs, with most reports involving puppies. 8–10 Clinical
signs have been complicated by comorbidities such as CDV and
Blastomyces spp. infection, but include fever, lethargy, vomiting,
diarrhea, cough, abdominal eﬀusion, dehydration, obtundation,
ataxia, abnormal placing reactions, circling, nystagmus, and seizures.
8–10 The life cycle of S. canis is unknown. Organisms that are
morphologically similar to S. canis have also been found in noncanid
carnivores and marine mammals, 36–38 although application of
molecular methods is needed to conﬁrm these are truly S. canis. In
these intermediate hosts, only schizonts are present, and they are
primarily conﬁned to the liver. Recently, molecular methods were
used to identify infection with an S. canis-like organism as well as
Sarcocystis arctosi in a grizzly bear with fatal hepatic sarcocystosis. 39
Sarcocystis neurona
Most dogs and cats with S. neurona infections have had neurologic
signs secondary to meningoencephalomyelitis. 25–27 , 40 One dog with
pelvic limb paresis was treated with glucocorticoids, and after
temporary remission of signs, the dog developed progressive
tetraparesis with recumbency and hyperesthesia. 27 On retrospective
examination, dogs with neurologic sarcocystosis originally a ributed
to S. canis were found to be infected with S. neurona, and organisms

vetexamprep.ir

were found in extraneural tissues of some dogs. 40 One dog had
chorioretinitis in addition to meningoencephalitis. 26 Sarcocystis
neurona infection was also described in a dog with myositis and
muscle atrophy. 41 Sarcocysts were found in many skeletal muscles.
PCR testing conﬁrmed S. neurona in the muscle tissue, although the
dog had received immunosuppressive therapy for its clinical illness,
and whether the cysts were a cause of the disease or eﬀect of therapy
was uncertain.
Sarcocystis neurona–associated meningoencephalomyelitis was
described in a 13-week-old Burmese ki en from California with
progressive lethargy, vocalization, and hemiparesis. 28 Another 12week-old ki en from Illinois developed progressive neurologic signs
with ataxia 3 days after castration. 23 A third report described a 5month-old domestic shorthair from Indiana with fever, dull
mentation, spinal pain, muscle fasciculations, ataxia, postural reaction
deﬁcits, hyperesthesia, and anisocoria. 24 An S. neurona-like organism
was detected in the brain tissue using molecular analysis.
Sarcocystis caninum
Dogs infected with S. caninum have had a biphasic illness
characterized by variable fever, lethargy, anorexia, ptyalism, diarrhea,
dehydration, icterus, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, and
increased serum liver enzyme activities, followed by development of
generalized muscle stiﬀness, muscle atrophy and weakness, muscle
pain, delayed placing reactions, decreased segmental reﬂexes, and
increased CK activity. 11 The la er phase resembles a systemic
immune-mediated neuromuscular disease. The dog from Finland that
was co-infected with S. caninum and S. svanai had signs of
nonambulatory tetraparesis, and decreased to absent placing
reactions, but no evidence of muscle pain. 7

Diagnosis
A diagnosis of sarcocystosis should be considered in young (<1 year)
or immunosuppressed dogs and cats with systemic signs of illness,
especially involving the liver, CNS, or muscle. Diagnosis most often
relies on detection of protozoal organisms in tissues using light
microscopy and/or PCR assays. Diagnosis of intestinal infections is
dependent on microscopic examination following centrifugal zinc
sulfate fecal ﬂotation.

vetexamprep.ir

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Biochemistry Panel, and
Urinalysis
There are no speciﬁc hematologic or biochemical abnormalities that
suggest sarcocystosis. When laboratory ﬁndings have been reported,
the CBC has been normal or there has been evidence of mild
nonregenerative anemia, neutrophilia with a left shift and toxic
change, monocytosis or monocytopenia, lymphopenia, or mild to
moderate eosinophilia (up to 6,300 cells/µL). 7 , 8 , 11 , 25 , 33 , 34 Some
aﬀected dogs and cats have had thrombocytopenia. On the serum
chemistry panel, abnormalities have included hypoalbuminemia,
moderate to severe elevations in the activity of serum ALT (655–3,436
U/L), mild to moderate elevations in the activity of serum ALP (312–
2,203 U/L), mild to moderate hyperbilirubinemia, and/or increased
CK activity (623–13,206 U/L). 8 , 11 , 33 , 34 One dog with S. caninum/S.
svanai myopathy had only increased activity of serum AST (459 U/L)
and CK (5,018 U/L). 7 The urinalysis may be normal or show
bilirubinuria.
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
Findings on CSF analysis in dogs and cats with sarcocystosis have
been reported rarely. One dog with neuromuscular disease due to S.
caninum had a mild increase in CSF protein concentration (62 mg/dL).
11 A dog with encephalomyelitis secondary to infection with T. gondii
and S. neurona had lymphocytic pleocytosis (70 cells/µL) and a
moderate increase in CSF protein concentration (260 mg/dL). 25 A dog
seen at the author’s institution with Sarcocystis meningoencephalitis
was initially diagnosed with eosinophilic meningoencephalitis
because the CSF had a total nucleated cell count of 117 cells/uL with
23% eosinophils, 34% small mononuclear cells, 40% large
mononuclear cells, and 3% neutrophils, with 54 mg/dL protein. 42 In
contrast, a cat with S. neurona encephalomyelitis had neutrophilic
pleocytosis with both intracellular and extracellular merozoites. 24
Intracellular merozoites were also described in the CSF of a dog
infected with S. neurona. 26

Diagnostic Imaging
Reports of diagnostic imaging ﬁndings in dogs and cats with clinical
sarcocystosis have been limited. Findings on thoracic radiography in
two dogs were normal. 8 , 11 Hepatomegaly has been described on

vetexamprep.ir

abdominal radiography and ultrasound examination in dogs with
hepatitis. 8 , 34 Abdominal lymphadenomegaly and mild peritoneal
eﬀusion also have been described on abdominal ultrasound
examination. 8 , 34 MRI of the thoracolumbar spine of a dog that was
co-infected with S. neurona and T. gondii revealed focal spinal cord
enlargement at T4 to T6 and L2 to L4, with asymmetric
intramedullary parenchymal T2 hyperintensity with associated
contrast enhancement in these regions. 25 A dog with suspected S.
canis meningoencephalitis at the author’s institution had multifocal
T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense, contrast-enhancing regions throughout
the cerebrum, thalamus, midbrain, and brainstem with meningeal
enhancement (Fig. 95.2). Evidence of mandibular lymph node
reactivity was also present.

Electrodiagnostic Testing
Electrodiagnostic ﬁndings were described in one dog from the United
States with S. caninum myositis 11 and the dog from Finland with S.
caninum/S. svanai myopathy. 7 Electromyography (EMG) in the ﬁrst
case showed spontaneous activity with increased insertional activity
and ﬁbrillation potentials in a generalized distribution. There was
marked decrease in motor nerve conduction velocity, and compound
motor unit amplitudes were decreased with dispersion. In the dog
from Finland, EMG evaluation revealed no changes in insertional
activity and no spontaneous activity. Motor nerve conduction
velocity was normal and compound motor unit amplitudes showed
temporal dispersion with no decrement following repetitive nerve
stimulation. 7

Microbiologic Tests (Table 95.2)
Cytologic Examination
Cytological diagnosis of Sarcocystis infections has been reported in a
cat and a dog with S. neurona encephalomyelitis. Sarcocystis
merozoites were observed intracellularly and extracellularly in the
CSF, and measure 2–4 µm × 4–6 µm (Fig. 95.3). 24 , 26
Fecal Flotation
Fecal ﬂotation with sugar or zinc sulfate solutions can be used to
detect the sporocysts of Sarcocystis in feces. However, clinically
aﬀected dogs do not typically excrete oocysts. Sarcocystis is excreted
in feces fully sporulated, often as free sporocysts when examined

vetexamprep.ir

(Fig. 95.4). It is not possible to diﬀerentiate the species based on
sporocyst size or appearance using light microscopy. Free sporocysts
are small and not very dense, so they lie at a diﬀerent plane of focus
than other parasites.
Serology
Serologic assays for diagnosis of Sarcocystis infections in dogs and
cats are not available commercially. Diagnosis of S. neurona infection
in horses has involved immunoblot testing for speciﬁc antibodies to
S. neurona in CSF, but this is not commercially available for dogs and
cats due to the need for feline- and canine-speciﬁc antibody
conjugates. Infected dogs and cats most often have negative antibody
titers to Toxoplasma and Neospora. Nevertheless, positive antibody
titers have been described, 11 , 33 possibly as a result of previous
exposure to these pathogens.

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Real-time PCR assays are commercially available for detection of S.
neurona in horses and could be used on the CSF or aspirates of
aﬀected tissues from dogs and cats suspected to have S. neurona
infections, although the clinical sensitivity of these assays in dogs and
cats is unknown. Broad-spectrum Sarcocystis PCR assays that amplify
18S and ITS-1 gene sequences have been used on a research basis for
diagnosis. 11 , 24 , 27 , 34 , 40 , 41 Sequence analysis of PCR products has
limited ability to distinguish among Sarcocystis species, and typically
species identiﬁcation is based on sequence analysis of the ITS-1 gene
combined with phenotypic characteristics of the organisms using
light and transmission electron microscopy (e.g., sarcocyst

vetexamprep.ir

ultrastructure, lack of rhoptries in S. canis). As is the case for Neospora
and Toxoplasma, PCR results must always be interpreted in light of
clinicopathologic ﬁndings, because Sarcocystis DNA can be detected
in tissues from healthy dogs and cats.

Pathologic Findings
Gross lesions at necropsy may be absent, or ﬁndings such as
hepatomegaly, muscle atrophy, or spinal cord swelling and
discoloration may be present. 8 Histopathologic abnormalities in dogs
and cats with clinical Sarcocystis infections of the CNS have typically
included granulomatous or pyogranulomatous necrotizing
meningoencephalomyelitis with intralesional merozoites and
schizonts of varying stages of development (see Fig. 95.3). 26–28 , 40
Schizonts and merozoites have been reported within neurons and
other neuropil cells. The schizonts range in size from 3 to 25 µm × 5–
20 µm and contain up to 40 merozoites. The merozoites measure 1–2
× 2–5 µm and form rose es that may surround a residual body.
Perivascular cuﬃng with mixed mononuclear inﬂammatory cells
(lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes) and gliosis is commonly
reported in the gray and white ma er. Lesions have been in the
cerebral cortex, caudate nucleus, cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal
cord. 23 , 27 , 28 One dog with S. neurona infection had chorioretinitis in
addition to meningoencephalitis, with retinal necrosis and
detachment, and merozoites and schizonts in all layers of the retina.
26 There was also signiﬁcant involvement of skeletal muscle of the
tongue. Dogs with Sarcocystis hepatitis have had often widespread
hepatic necrosis and hepatic vasculitis with inﬁltrates of eosinophils,
neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. 8 , 10 , 40 In one dog, many
hepatocytes were reported to contain merozoites, sometimes forming
rose es. 8 Pulmonary Sarcocystis infections in dogs have been
characterized by necrotizing bronchiolitis and schizonts within
endothelial cells, epithelial cells, or macrophages, with concurrent
evidence of co-infections with organisms such as CDV. 9 The presence
of multinucleated giant cells has been reported in a variety of tissues
from multiple dogs and cats with Sarcocystis infections. 25 , 26 , 33 , 40
Dogs with S. caninum myositis have necrotizing myositis with mixed
mononuclear cell to pyogranulomatous inﬂammation and
intracellular sarcocysts, which measure up to 1200 µm long and 25 to
75 µm wide (Fig. 95.5). 7 , 11 The sarcocysts have a thin wall and
contain metrocytes peripherally and diﬀerentiating bradyzoites
centrally. The single dog with myositis thought to be secondary to S.

vetexamprep.ir

intralesional cysts that were smaller (40–100 µm × 15–40 µm) than
those described for S. caninum. The cysts contained many circularly
arranged metrocytes. 41

neurona antisera. 8

Treatment and Prognosis
Intestinal Infections
Sarcocystis species do not cause clinically relevant intestinal tract
lesions in dogs and cats, so treatment of intestinal infections is not
necessary.

Extraintestinal Infections
There are few reports of antiprotozoal treatment of dogs and cats
with clinical Sarcocystis infections because most aﬀected dogs and cats
have been diagnosed with sarcocystosis at necropsy. Clinical signs
worsened after glucocorticoid therapy in some animals, suggesting
that immunosuppression may allow for proliferation of the parasite.
Eﬀective treatment of horses has involved the use of ponazuril. Other
anticoccidial drugs such as clindamycin, tetracyclines, or antifolate
inhibitors might also be considered, especially if parenteral therapy is
considered (Table 95.3). A cat with encephalomyelitis thought to be
caused by S. neurona was treated with ponazuril followed by a
combination of clindamycin, pyrimethamine, and trimethoprim
sulfonamide, and recovered with the only residual neurologic
abnormality being delayed placing reaction in the right thoracic limb.
24 Treatment of a dog infected with S. caninum with decoquinate led
to resolution of signs of myositis, 11 and two others appeared to
respond clinically to treatment with clindamycin. 33 , 34
TABLE 95.3

Immunity and Vaccination
Immunity to Sarcocystis is cell-mediated. No vaccines exist for
prevention of disease in dogs and cats.

Prevention
Sarcocystis infections can be prevented by cooking all meat fed to
animals, prevention of hunting behavior, keeping cats indoors, or

vetexamprep.ir

feeding only commercially processed diets. Prevention of roaming
and coprophagy may reduce the chance that dogs act as intermediate
hosts.

Public Health Aspects
Humans can be deﬁnitive and intermediate hosts for certain species
of Sarcocystis. However, Sarcocystis species of dogs and cats do not
infect humans. The primary public health signiﬁcance of sarcocystosis
is that it can resemble rabies, and a number of dogs and cats with
Sarcocystis infections were euthanized because of a suspicion for
rabies virus infection. The potential for zoonotic transmission in
China through consumption of infected dog meat was raised in one
study where sarcocysts of S. caninum were found in 2 of 37 dogs on
sale for dog meat consumption at a market in southwestern China. 35

96: Leishmaniosis
Gad Baneth, Christine Petersen, Laia Solano-Gallego, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
•
First Described: The cause of visceral leishmaniasis was first
described in India in 1903 (separately by William Leishman
and Charles Donovan). 1
• Causes: Canine and feline leishmaniosis is caused by
Leishmania infantum (synonymous with Leishmania chagasi)
(class Kinetoplasta, family Trypanosomatidae). Other species
such as Leishmania braziliensis cause localized cutaneous
lesions in South America (American tegumentary
leishmaniosis).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs and less commonly cats; also humans,
rodents, wild canids, horses, and marsupial species.
• Geographic Distribution: Primarily southern Europe and the
Middle East, Asia, northern Africa, Central and South
America; also some parts of the United States. Travel-related
disease may occur in nonendemic regions worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Phlebotomus and Lutzomyia spp. sand
flies. Transmission through blood transfusion as well as
vertical transmission can occur.
• Major Clinical Signs: Weight loss, inappetence, scaling and/or
ulcerative non-pruritic cutaneous lesions, onychogryphosis,
keratoconjunctivitis, uveitis, lymphadenomegaly,
hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, lameness, signs of renal failure.
• Differential Diagnoses: Differential diagnoses in dogs with
systemic disease include canine monocytic ehrlichiosis,
babesiosis, histoplasmosis, brucellosis, hemic neoplasia,
other metastatic neoplasms, and primary autoimmune

vetexamprep.ir

diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus. Differential
diagnoses for cutaneous lesions in dogs include demodectic
mange, pyoderma, Malassezia dermatitis, cutaneous
vasculitis, and pemphigus foliaceus. Differential diagnoses for
cutaneous lesions in cats include cutaneous neoplasia,
cutaneous vasculitis, herpesviral dermatitis, and
dermatophytosis. The primary differential for American
tegumentary leishmaniosis is sporotrichosis.
• Human Health Significance: Human infections are primarily
transmitted by sand flies, and are caused by a large number
of different Leishmania species. Dogs are considered the
major reservoir for L. infantum infections. Precautions should
be taken when handling potentially infected tissue and blood
specimens.

Introduction
The leishmaniases are a group of infectious diseases that aﬀect
humans and domestic and wild animals worldwide and are
caused by members of the genus Leishmania. Leishmaniosis is the
preferred term for the disease in animals. 2 The infection is
transmi ed by sand ﬂies of the genus Phlebotomus in the Old
World (Europe, Asia, and Africa), and Lu omyia in the New
World (South, Central, and North America). Reservoir hosts vary
within diﬀerent geographic areas and can include domestic or
wild animals. Leishmaniosis caused by Leishmania infantum
(synonymous with Leishmania chagasi) 3 is a frequent cause of
clinical illness in dogs in some regions but is less common in cats.
4 Dogs are the major reservoir for canine and human L. infantum
infection in an area that stretches from Portugal to China and
across South, Central, and parts of North America (Fig. 96.1). As
reservoir hosts, dogs can infect feeding sand ﬂies and remain
subclinical carriers for extended periods. Canine leishmaniosis is
sometimes found in nonendemic countries because of
international tourists and immigrants who bring infected pets or
because of dog importation. Leishmaniosis due to L. infantum has
been reported among soldiers returning from Afghanistan. 5 , 6
Similarly, pet dogs belonging to military personnel and other

vetexamprep.ir

individuals from Leishmania-endemic regions are transported back
to the United States. Subclinical dogs can remain healthy for
months to years after being introduced or reintroduced to the
United States.
This chapter presents a global overview of leishmaniosis,
followed by two recognized geographic forms of emerging
disease in animals in the New World. The last section is devoted
to leishmaniosis in cats.

Overview of Leishmaniosis Worldwide
Leishmaniosis is caused by diphasic protozoans of the genus
Leishmania
in
the
class
Kinetoplasta
and
family
Trypanosomatidae. The genus Leishmania is divided into the
subgenera Leishmania and Viannia based on diﬀerences in the
location of parasite development within the sand ﬂy. Organisms
of the Viannia subgenus (e.g., Leishmania braziliensis) replicate in
the sand ﬂy hindgut (see Canine American Tegumentary
Leishmaniosis, later), in contrast to the midgut replication
characteristic of other Leishmania species. Several diﬀerent species
are recognized within the Leishmania and Viannia subgenera, and
classiﬁcation is primarily based on DNA sequence comparisons,
electrophoresis migration pa erns of isoenzymes (zymodemes),
and reactivity to monoclonal antibodies and to membrane-shed
antigens.
Phlebotomine sand ﬂies of the genus Phlebotomus in the Old
World (Europe, Asia, and Africa) and Lu omyia in the New World
(the Americas) are the natural vectors of leishmaniosis. Sand ﬂies
are small insects with a body length that seldom exceed 3 mm. 7
The biting activity of sand ﬂies is crepuscular (at twilight) and
nocturnal. In the Mediterranean and Asia, sand ﬂies are primarily
active in the warm months, from spring to late fall. In Latin
America, some sand ﬂy species are active throughout the year.
Sand ﬂies do not move long distances, and studies have shown
that they are seldom dispersed more than 1 km away from their
breeding sites. Many species of sand ﬂy exist, but only some of
them act as Leishmania vectors. Diﬀerent vector species may be
found in distinct geographic regions and ecologic niches. Some
sand ﬂy species exclusively transmit only one Leishmania species,
whereas others are vectors for multiple species. The capacity of

vetexamprep.ir

diﬀerent sand ﬂy species to act as vectors appears to be related to
the ability of promastigotes to speciﬁcally bind to ligands in the
sand ﬂy gut. When they do not bind to the sand ﬂy gut, the
parasites that initially replicated in the gut lumen are excreted
with the sand ﬂy feces and presumably do not reach the critical
mass needed to infect a host during a second blood meal. 8

The global distribution of visceral
leishmaniosis in humans and dogs.
FIG. 96.1

In vertebrate hosts, Leishmania is found in macrophages in its
nonﬂagellate form, the amastigote (Fig. 96.2). Amastigotes are
ovoid or round, 2.5 to 5 µm long and 1.5 to 2 µm wide. In addition
to a basophilic-staining nucleus, a rod-shaped, darker-staining
kinetoplast is visible with Wright or Giemsa stain (Fig. 96.3).
Amastigotes multiply by binary ﬁssion, and then subsequently
rupture out of the macrophage to infect new cells. Sand ﬂies can
ingest amastigotes when they become engorged with blood from
an infected host. In the sand ﬂy gut, amastigotes are released from
host cells; transform into the extracellular, ﬂagellated procyclic
promastigote (Fig. 96.4); and replicate. In an appropriate vector,
there is suﬃcient replication and regulated molecular changes in
the parasite’s cell surface and the parasite detaches from the
midgut epithelium. This results in anterior migration of infectious
metacyclic promastigotes into the foregut and mouthparts of the
vector. Promastigotes are injected with saliva into the skin of a

vetexamprep.ir

vertebrate host when the female sand ﬂy feeds again. After
inoculation into the host, the promastigotes lose their ﬂagella and
transform back into amastigotes (see Fig. 96.2).
About 30 diﬀerent Leishmania species are found in various parts
of the Old World and New World. Of these, about 20 cause a wide
spectrum of clinical illnesses in humans. 9 Most Leishmania spp.
that infect humans are zoonotic, and only a few are strictly
anthroponotic (i.e., transmi ed directly from human to human via
sand ﬂies). Human leishmaniasis is endemic in 88 countries—66
countries in the Old World and 22 in the New World—and aﬀects
the world’s poorest populations living mainly in rural and
suburban areas. 10 Approximately 12 million humans are infected
with leishmaniasis, and some 350 million humans are at risk of
acquiring the disease, with a yearly incidence of 1 to 1.5 million
new cases of cutaneous disease and 500,000 new cases of the
potentially fatal visceral form. 11 , 12 Disease caused by the various
Leishmania spp. in humans is divided into three forms according
to clinical features: cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), mucocutaneous
leishmaniasis, and visceral leishmaniasis (VL). Some species cause
more than one form. Anthroponotic VL caused by Leishmania
donovani is responsible for a large part of the fatalities due to the
visceral disease in humans and is present in East Africa,
Bangladesh, India, and Nepal. 10 Humans are the reservoir hosts
for L. donovani, and animals do not appear to play a signiﬁcant
role in the anthroponotic epidemiology of infection, 13 although
dog ownership has been associated with human leishmaniasis in
Ethiopia. 14 The main reservoir hosts for Leishmania spp. causing
CL and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis in humans are rodents and
other wild animal species. 15

vetexamprep.ir

The life cycle of Leishmania
infantum. Dogs, cats, and humans become
infected when they are bitten by a sand fly.
Promastigotes are inoculated into the dermis
and penetrate macrophages. Within the
macrophage, they transform into amastigotes
and replicate within a phagolysosome. The
macrophage ruptures and new macrophages
are infected. If the host fails to control the
infection in the skin, amastigotes disseminate
via regional lymphatics and the blood to infect
the entire reticuloendothelial system.
Amastigotes that are ingested by a female
sand fly during feeding convert back into
promastigotes, and replication of

Canine Leishmaniosis
Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

Domestic dogs are the main reservoirs for human leishmaniasis
caused by L. infantum in the Mediterranean basin, Middle East,
and South America. The low genetic variability of L. infantum, as
compared with other species of Leishmania, is consistent with its
more contemporary importation to the New World; it is thought
to have been introduced by infected dogs from Europe that
arrived with early se lers to the Americas. 16 Other species of
Leishmania that infect dogs in diﬀerent geographic regions include
L. donovani, Leishmania tropica, Leishmania major, L. braziliensis,
Leishmania mexicana, Leishmania peruviana, Leishmania panamensis,
17 and Leishmania amazonensis. 18
Seroprevalence studies from Spain, France, Italy, and Portugal
estimate that 2.5 million dogs in these countries are infected with
L. infantum, and infection is spreading north in Europe, reaching
the foothills of the Alps, 19 Pyrenees, 20 and northwestern Spain. 21
The number of infected dogs in South America is in the millions,
with high infection rates in some areas of Brazil and Venezuela. 22
In regions with a high infection rate among dogs, the incidence of
clinical VL in the general human population has generally been
low. In contrast, the rates of human exposure to Leishmania (as
determined by the prevalence of speciﬁc antibodies or positive
leishmanin skin test results) can be high. 22–25 This suggests that
either subclinical infection or protective immunity exists in
humans. Clinically healthy human blood donors from southern
France 26 and the Balearic Islands 27 , 28 also have a high rate of
infection. 29

vetexamprep.ir

Leishmania promastigotes grown in
culture. Note round nuclei and rod-shaped
kinetoplast (May-Grunwald-Giemsa stain,
×1000).
FIG. 96.4

Canine leishmaniosis caused by L. infantum is an important
cause of zoonotic disease in many endemic countries and areas,
including Spain, Portugal, southern France, Italy, Malta, Greece,
Turkey, Israel, Egypt, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco, Iraq, Iran, the
former Asian republics of the Soviet Union, Pakistan, China,
Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Venezuela. 30–34
Leishmaniosis may also be transmi ed in southern Germany. 35
Sporadic cases of canine leishmaniosis occur as a result of
importation or transport of infected dogs to countries where sand
ﬂy transmission of Leishmania does not occur, such as the
Netherlands, the United Kingdom, 36 and Sweden. 37 Because
many dogs in endemic areas harbor subclinical infections,
infection rates are often estimated not only by the presence of
clinical signs compatible with the disease but also by serologic test
results, demonstration of speciﬁc CMI responses against
Leishmania, and the presence of parasite DNA in tissues as
determined using PCR assays. Canine infection rates approach
70% to 90%, as shown by PCR and serology in highly endemic
foci, such as the Balearic Islands of Spain, 38 the Marseille area in
France, 39 throughout Greece, 40 and the Naples area in Italy. 41

vetexamprep.ir

This is a much higher prevalence of infection than that associated
with disease or determined by serology alone. It is thought that
most or all dogs in these areas are infected at some point during
their lives. 38 , 41 A low proportion of dogs succumb to the
infection and develop disease, whereas the majority of dogs are
resistant and harbor the pathogen subclinically. 17 , 42 In other
areas, infection is not as highly prevalent, possibly because of less
favorable environmental conditions for transmission and vectors.
22 , 43 The age distribution of clinical disease has two peaks, one in
young dogs (2 to 4 years old) and another in older dogs (more
than 7 years old) 44 Several dog breeds, including boxers, cocker
spaniels, Ro weilers and German shepherds, are apparently more
susceptible to disease. 44–46 Other breeds that arose and evolved in
endemic areas, such as the Ibizan hound from the Balearic Islands,
only develop mild forms of disease such as papular dermatitis
and possess protective cellular immunity. 47 , 48
In Europe and South America, sensitive xenodiagnostic studies,
involving feeding of vector sand ﬂies on dogs, have demonstrated
that dogs with or without clinical illness and with serum antibody
titers to Leishmania are a source of infection for a high proportion
of feeding sand ﬂies. 49 The percentage of infected sand ﬂies
increased with the presence and severity of clinical signs, high
anti-Leishmania antibody levels, and decrease in CD4+ T-cell
counts. 50–53 These ﬁndings corroborate that clinical disease and
high anti-Leishmania antibody levels are positively correlated with
high parasite burdens. 54 , 55 Risk of sand ﬂy-borne transmission is
reduced as parasite loads decline after treatment. 56–58
Although L. infantum is transmi ed most frequently through
the bites of sand ﬂies, other modes of transmission are possible. In
utero transmission has been documented in clinical reports 59 and
under experimental 60 and natural conditions as well as in
humans. 61 , 62 Venereal transmission of leishmaniosis from
infected males to healthy bitches can occur. 63 Transmission by
hematophagous arthropods other than sand ﬂies has been
investigated but not proven to have epidemiologic signiﬁcance.
Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks acquire Leishmania organisms in
their gut after feeding on infected dogs 64 ; however, the tick’s
competence as a vector has not been conﬁrmed. 65 Fleas have been

vetexamprep.ir

proposed as alternative vectors of Leishmania transmission, but
proof of transmission is still lacking. 66 , 67 Transmission by blood
transfusion has been reported 68 , 69 and is of special concern in
areas where blood donors are subclinical carriers of infection. 70 ,
71 Direct dog-to-dog transmission has been suspected in areas
where sand ﬂy vectors are apparently absent. 72 Modalities of
transmission other than by sand ﬂies require further investigation
to deﬁne their relative importance in the natural history and
epidemiology of leishmaniosis. 42
Infection of dogs occurs mostly in periurban or rural areas;
however, canine and human infections have been reported in
urban areas and pose a threat to the well-being of dogs, cats, and
humans. 73 , 74 The potential importance of reservoir hosts other
than domestic dogs in the epidemiology of L. infantum infection is
less well known. 49 Leishmania infantum infection has been
reported in many domestic animals from the Old and New
Worlds. 49 A high prevalence of infection based on positive serum
antibody titers and PCR results has been reported in domestic cats
in some areas of Europe 75 and Brazil. 76 Clinical disease occurs in
cats. 77–80 Infections have also been reported infrequently in horses
in Europe, 81 , 82 and South America 83 and cellular immunity tests
in horses have shown that exposure is more frequent than clinical
disease. 84 , 85 Serologic responses of pigs to L. infantum have been
described in Brazil. 86 Infection has been reported in a wide range
of wild carnivores and rodents in the Old World, including a seal.
49 , 87 In the New World, infection has been detected in crab-eating
foxes (Cerdocyon thous) and in a range of other carnivores and
rodents, including bats. 49 A high prevalence of infection exists in
populations of foxes in Europe and South America. 49 , 87 Clinical
disease has been reported in wild canids. 88 , 89 The majority of
reports in other domestic or wild mammals describe subclinical
infections.
Transmission of Leishmania to feeding sand ﬂies has been
conﬁrmed from humans, black rats, domestic cats, hares, 90 crabeating foxes, and opossums. These hosts, therefore, have the
potential to act as primary or secondary reservoirs. 49 , 87
However, infected crab-eating foxes in Brazil exhibited low rates
of transmission to the sand ﬂy Lu omyia longipalpis. Similar

vetexamprep.ir

results were found in humans, who were not considered to be
important as reservoirs of leishmaniosis in Brazil. 49 , 91
Although leishmaniosis is infrequently reported in humans and
domestic animals in North America, the disease has become
established in dogs, predominantly hunting hounds. No
autochthonous (local, non-travel-related) human cases have been
reported in association with these dogs. The ﬁrst report of
autochthonous leishmaniosis in dogs in the United States was in a
hunting hound in 1980. 92 An outbreak in 1999 among foxhounds
in a New York kennel revealed a puzzling epizootiologic situation
suggesting endemic transmission. 93 , 94 Organisms isolated from
infected dogs were typed biochemically as L. infantum zymodeme
MON-1, the most common zymodeme found in the
Mediterranean region, suggesting an origin from Europe and not
South America. Subsequent to the New York kennel investigation,
the CDC screened sera from 13,000 foxhounds from across North
America. Positive animals were found in 28 states and 2 Canadian
provinces. 72 Positive serum antibody reactivity to L. infantum was
identiﬁed in foxhounds from 69 kennels. Organisms isolated from
45 hounds across multiple states and provinces were again
identiﬁed as L. infantum MON-1 (Fig. 96.5). 72 Leishmaniosis
became enzootic in North American hunting hounds via vertical
transmission. 95 , 96 North American dogs with leishmaniosis have
the same clinical abnormalities as dogs from endemic areas. 97
Leishmaniosis can also be diagnosed in North America in any dog
breed originating from endemic areas following importation and
breeding of one or more infected dogs. Breeds include Corsicas,
Neapolitan Mastiﬀs, Spinones, Cane Corso, and potentially other
breeds. 98

Transplacental transmission can aﬀect almost all pups born to a
subclinically infected dam, and can lead to a full spectrum of
clinical outcomes over multiple years. 99 Vertical transmission of
Leishmania spp. occurs globally in both endemic and nonendemic
countries, and in humans as well as dogs, hamsters, and other
rodents. 62 Blood-to-blood contact due to ﬁghting, 100 or other
direct contact could also potentially lead to transmission, but
factors for direct transmission in the environment are poorly
understood. Because the most common Mediterranean L. infantum
strain (MON-1) has been identiﬁed in North America, the
possibility of a suitable North American vector has been a concern
for the persistence and potential spread of infection. The most
prevalent sand ﬂy in United States, found in 21 states as of 2012, is
Lu omyia shannoni. 101 Lu omyia shannoni develops heavy
parasite burdens when experimentally fed on dogs infected with

vetexamprep.ir

L. infantum 102 ; however, the vector competence of Lu. shannoni
for the natural transmission of the parasite to dogs has not been
established. Lu omyia longipalpis is found as far north as Mexico,
and Lu. longipalpis was able to transmit L. infantum from infected
North American foxhounds to hamsters. 103 Because the presence
and the role of sand ﬂies as the primary vector of leishmaniosis
have not been determined in North America, biologic
transmission by other insects has also been investigated and
rejected. 104 Evidence for transvaginal transfer of infection during
parturition or spread through milk is lacking. 105 Some
researchers have suggested the possibility of venereal
transmission 59 , 76 , 106 ; however, further investigation is needed.
Leishmaniosis has been reported in Canada 72 ; however, the
Canadian food inspection agency lists it as one of the “nonreportable list B” diseases.
Other Leishmania Species
Leishmania tropica occurs in the Old World and is a rare cause of
infection in dogs. Leishmania tropica is an important agent of CL in
humans in some parts of the Middle East and Africa. It also
caused VL in American soldiers returning from the Persian Gulf
after the 1991 Operation Desert Storm 107 and has been described
in patients from India. 108 It has been sporadically found in dogs
with cutaneous lesions from Tunisia, Morocco, and Israel, 109 , 110
and was described in a dog from Morocco with visceral
involvement and no dermal abnormalities, 111 as well as a dog
from Iran. 112 Leishmania major infection has been associated with
cutaneous disease in dogs in the Middle East. 113 , 114

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Infection of the vertebrate host starts when Leishmania
promastigotes are injected along with sand ﬂy saliva into the
vertebrate host’s dermis. These promastigotes are phagocytized
by localized immune phagocytes including dermal macrophages
and Langerhans cells. Surviving intracellular parasites shift to the
aﬂagellar amastigote phase and multiply within parasitophorous
vacuoles that have the characteristics of phagolysosomes. Upon

vetexamprep.ir

phagocyte rupture, freed amastigotes penetrate additional host
cells and disseminate primarily via lymphatic circulation from the
local bite site to the draining lymph node and further to
hemolymphatic organs including the spleen, bone marrow, liver,
and remote dermal areas. This establishes systemic infection.
Not every dog naturally or experimentally infected with
Leishmania develops disease. 115 The ability to mount a productive,
robust, pro-inﬂammatory immune response at the time of
infection and thereafter appears to be the most important factor in
determining whether dogs develop generalized infection or
remain healthy and whether infection will progress from a
subclinical to a clinical state. 105 Infection initially is subclinical
but can progress into clinical disease unless parasite replication is
controlled. Dogs that are able to control infection, restricting
parasite burden and remaining subclinical for long periods or life,
are considered clinically resistant. Infected animals predisposed to
disease either genetically, or due to secondary factors including
comorbid infection(s), poor nutrition or other immunosuppressive
disease or treatments, are considered susceptible. These same
factors, if they occur later in life, can also lead to loss of immune
control and progression of disease. 17 This occurs in human
patients with HIV and Leishmania co-infection, as well as cats
infected with FeLV or FIV. 4 , 116
The innate, or pa ern-based early immune response is the ﬁrst
line of defense encountered by Leishmania parasites when entering
a host. One of many mechanisms by which Leishmania parasites
evade innate immune defenses involves the ability of
promastigotes to survive within macrophage phagolysosomes by
producing surface glycolipids such as lipophosphoglycans that
may inhibit phagosome maturation. 117
A protective immune response to all Leishmania species, as an
intracellular pathogen, is dependent upon a Th1 response
including IL-12 production by dendritic cells and macrophages,
eﬃcient antigen presentation, and subsequent IFN-γ production
from T cells. 118 , 119 Innate immune system–based clearance of
Leishmania requires intracellular killing via production of oxygen
radicals within the phagolysosomes of infected cells. Critical
innate responses are mediated through detection of parasite
surface molecules, or PAMPs, detected by pa ern recognition

vetexamprep.ir

receptors, including TLRs, NOD-like receptors, and others. TLRs
appear to play an important role. 120 Generally speaking, TLR2
upregulation appears to be associated with disease, while TLR4
downregulation appears to be associated with disease progression
in dogs. 121 , 122 There is limited information regarding the role of
other TLRs such as TLR3 and TLR9, which recognize nucleic acids
in canine leishmaniosis. 120 , 123 Surface PAMPs are key
components in many current Leishmania vaccines as antigens,
adjuvants, or both. This response is enhanced by IFN-γ
stimulation of phagocytes by NK cells early after Leishmania
infection and by IFN-γ from CD4+ T cells at later stages of
infection, 124 also indicated by IL-17 expression by infected dogs.
123 Therefore, the initial understanding of a dichotomous immune
response (Th1/Th2) has been expanded to include additional types
of T-cell immunity including Th17, T-regulatory responses, and
others. 125 Although protective immunity for leishmaniosis is still
described as Th1, this response is likely to also contain elements of
a Th17 response and be dampened by a regulatory response,
leading to a mixed overall cytokine proﬁle. Shorter-term robust
Th1 responses are believed to control Leishmania infection, but
alone in chronic se ings or when combined with
hyperinﬂammatory Th17 responses, inﬂammation is harmful and
is likely to drive T cells to shift to IL-10–based regulatory immune
responses. 125 , 126 Regulatory immunity leads to T-cell exhaustion,
predominance of regulatory B-cell responses, hyperproduction of
immunoglobulins, expansion of parasite burden, and clinical
disease. 125 , 127 A strong DTH response with the leishmanin
intradermal skin test indicative of a CMI response to Leishmania
infection is found in resistant dogs that have been exposed to the
parasite, and is absent in severely ill dogs. 47 While elements of
cytokine production that provide protective immunity against
Leishmania spp. are thought to be understood (high IFN-γ, low IL10, and low IL-4), 126 development of protective immunity
through vaccination has been more challenging. 119 Vaccination as
immunotherapy for canine leishmaniosis has had conﬂicting
results. 125 , 128 These studies demonstrated successful stimulation
of a balanced Th1 response from canine cells following exposure
to a TLR agonist, but inclusion of a TLR4 agonist within a subunit
vaccine formulation was not successful in halting disease

vetexamprep.ir

progression. 129 , 130 Perhaps more importantly, healthy yet
infected dogs progressing to clinical leishmaniosis already have Tcell exhaustion, 127 which can interfere with the response to
vaccines or immunotherapeutics. 125 When exposed to vaccine
antigens and mitogen, CD4+ T cells from dogs with clinical
leishmaniosis had signiﬁcantly reduced proliferation and IFN-γ
production when compared with those from healthy dogs. At its
heart, leishmaniosis is an opportunistic infection which manifests
clinically when there is immune compromise. Therefore,
consideration of an animal’s immune status before starting any
immunomodulatory therapy, including vaccination, is important.
Susceptibility and resistance to canine leishmaniosis appear to
have a genetic basis. Studies on polymorphisms of the Slc11c1
(Solute carrier family 11 member a1) canine gene (formerly
NRAMP1), which encodes an iron transporter protein involved in
the control of intraphagosomal replication of parasites and
macrophage activation, implied that susceptible dogs have
polymorphism and mutations in this gene. 131–133 Similar
mutations have also been described in humans. 134 A DLA class II
DLA-DRB1 genotype, which is a dog MHC II allele, was linked to
the risk of susceptibility to leishmaniosis in an endemic area in
Brazil. 135 A similar HLA DQ/DR allele was identiﬁed to lead to
human susceptibility to leishmaniasis in a multicentric study of
patients in both India and Brazil. 136 Genome-wide analysis has
demonstrated that multiple loci are responsible for the
progression of Leishmania infection to clinical disease. Genetic
biomarkers of susceptibility to infection and disease in canines is
extensively reviewed elsewhere. 137
Canine leishmaniosis is a chronic disease, and clinical signs may
develop 3 months to 7 years or more after infection. T-cell regions
in the lymphoid organs become depleted, and antibodyproducing B-cell regions proliferate. The proliferation of B cells,
plasma cells, histiocytes, and macrophages results in generalized
lymphadenomegaly, splenomegaly, and hyperglobulinemia. As
with other chronic persistent intracellular infections, the
immunoglobulin response is usually excessive, not necessarily
targeted at parasite antigens, not protective, and often
detrimental. Autoantibodies in dogs with clinical leishmaniosis 138
, 139 are thought to be associated with the development of

vetexamprep.ir

pathologic phenomena such as ITP. 140 , 141 Serum anti-histone
antibodies have been associated with glomerulonephritis, and
antigen-antibody depositions were frequent in dogs with
leishmaniosis. 142 , 143 Impaired T-cell regulation with exuberant
regulatory B-cell activity leads to large amounts of circulating
immune complexes (CICs). 144 Deposition of CICs in the walls of
blood vessels may cause vasculitis, polyarthritis, uveitis, and
glomerulonephritis, the la er being the main cause of death.
Immune complexes that activate the complement cascade also
induce vasculitis and renal damage. 142 This important pathologic
mechanism is responsible for tissue necrosis and accounts for
dermal, visceral, and ocular lesions. Systemic vasculitis may lead
to visceral and cutaneous necrosis and rarely nervous system
involvement. 145–147 CICs may also include cryoglobulins. These
may precipitate in the blood vessels of the extremities when
exposed to cold and cause ischemic necrosis.
Canine leishmaniosis is most often associated with various skin
lesions, which can be generalized rather than local because L.
infantum disseminates systemically. 148 In addition, microscopic
lesions and intralesional amastigotes are detected in normalappearing skin from sick dogs as well as in clinically apparent
dermal lesions. 149 Extracellular matrix assessment in the skin of
sick dogs demonstrated a decrease in collagen type I and an
increase in collagen type III ﬁbers proportional to the severity of
the skin lesion and tissue destruction. 150 Dermatologic
abnormalities may occur in the apparent absence of other signs,
but any animal with dermal manifestations is likely to have
visceral involvement, because dissemination occurs before
generalized skin lesions develop. Cutaneous lesions are present in
56% to 90% of dogs with clinical leishmaniosis. 151–153 Several
dermatologic entities have been described, which are rarely
associated with pruritus: 152 , 154 , 155 (1) desquamative dermatitis
with alopecia, which can be generalized or localized to the face,
ears, and limbs (Fig. 96.6A); (2) ulcerative dermatitis over bony
prominences, and in mucocutaneous junctions, paws, and the ear
pinnae (Fig. 96.6B); (3) focal or multifocal nodular dermatitis; (4)
mucocutaneous proliferative dermatitis (Fig. 96.7); (5) papular
dermatitis (Fig. 96.8); (6) abnormally long or bri le nails

vetexamprep.ir

(onychogryphosis); (7) pustular dermatitis; (8) nasal and digital
hyperkeratosis; and (9) multifocal alopecia.
Dogs with leishmaniosis may show hemorrhagic diatheses,
manifested primarily as epistaxis, and less commonly as
hematuria and hemorrhagic diarrhea. Epistaxis appears to be the
result of multiple abnormalities of primary and secondary
hemostasis, such as thrombocytopathy, hyperglobulinemiainduced serum hyperviscosity, and lymphoplasmacytic or
granulomatous rhinitis with or without nasal mucosal ulceration.
156–158 Anemia usually develops as a sequela to inﬂammatory
disease or CKD, but may be aggravated by blood loss.
Lymphadenomegaly of multiple superﬁcial lymph nodes
frequently develops 159 with lymph nodes enlarging to two to six
times their normal size, occasionally mimicking lymphoma.
Splenomegaly is also common.
Approximately 16% to 80.5% of dogs have ocular lesions,
including conjunctivitis, blepharitis, keratoconjunctivitis, and
anterior or posterior uveitis, glaucoma, panuveitis, and
panophthalmitis (Fig. 96.9). 151 , 153 , 160–162 In keratoconjunctivitis
sicca, inﬂammatory inﬁltrates located around the lacrimal ducts
cause secretory retention and a decrease in tear production. 163
Less frequently, nictitating membrane or iris granulomas may be
identiﬁed. In the majority of cases, ocular signs are bilateral, while
unilateral ocular lesions are associated with an early diagnosis of
the disease.
Weight loss and muscle atrophy are the most common signs of
visceral involvement (Fig. 96.10). Some dogs lose weight despite a
ravenous appetite. Muscle weakness is associated with
mononuclear myositis, neutrophilic vasculitis, and IgG immune
complexes in muscle tissues in conjunction with serum antimyoﬁber antibodies. 164 , 165 Progressive CKD may be
accompanied by anorexia, obtundation, polyuria, polydipsia, and
vomiting. Transient diarrhea may occur. Kidney disease may be
the only abnormality apparent; dogs with CKD in endemic areas
should be tested for Leishmania infection.
In cases of overt disease, decreased physical activity is obvious
and related to somnolence, decreased endurance, and locomotion
disturbances. Locomotion disturbances may be caused by
neuralgia, erosive and nonerosive polyarthritis, polymyositis,
footpad clefts, interdigital ulcers, osteoarticular and osteolytic

vetexamprep.ir

Physical Examination Findings
Canine leishmaniosis may be subclinical, a self-limiting disease, or
the classical non–self-limiting and severe illness. 17 Canine
leishmaniosis due to L. infantum is often classiﬁed as visceral
disease in compliance with the classiﬁcation of the disease caused
by this pathogen in humans; however, dogs usually have both
visceral and cutaneous involvement. Canine leishmaniosis is
essentially a chronic systemic disease that may involve any organ,
tissue, and biological ﬂuid and is manifested by a plethora of
clinical signs and physical examination ﬁndings. 17 The main
historic and physical examination ﬁndings in typical cases are
skin lesions, local or generalized lymphadenomegaly, thin body
condition,
exercise
intolerance,
inappetence,
lethargy,
splenomegaly, polyuria and polydipsia, ocular lesions, epistaxis,
onychogryphosis, lameness, vomiting, and diarrhea (Table 96.1).
17 , 42 , 151 , 152 Rectal temperature may ﬂuctuate but is usually
normal. In some cases, ocular abnormalities are the only signs. 161
For this reason, it is important to perform a thorough
ophthalmologic examination in dogs with suspected
leishmaniosis. Epistaxis and cough are other clinical signs that

vetexamprep.ir

may be present in isolation or with other clinical signs (Fig. 96.11).

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of canine leishmaniosis is complex due to its
variable clinical manifestations and laboratory ﬁndings.
Vaccination eﬀorts to prevent leishmaniosis have increased the
complexity of diagnosis, as serologic tests may not distinguish
between naturally infected and vaccinated dogs. Pre-vaccination
screening tests are not suﬃciently sensitive to detect subclinically
infected dogs, resulting in the potential for vaccination of infected
animals, which then remain infectious to sand ﬂies. 184 Diagnosis
is usually performed to conﬁrm disease in a dog with signs
compatible with leishmaniosis as well as to monitor response to
treatment. However, detection of infection may also be pursued
for clinically healthy dogs in endemic regions such as blood

vetexamprep.ir

donors, breeding dogs, candidates for vaccination, dogs suspected
to have progression of disease, dogs travelling from endemic to
nonendemic countries, and to evaluate immune responses to
vaccination. 17 , 184 , 185 The diagnostic procedures used, and the
approach to interpretation of test results, will vary accordingly. 17
Accurate diagnosis requires an integrated approach consisting
of clinicopathologic tests and speciﬁc diagnostic assays. 17 Speciﬁc
assays include microscopic demonstration of parasites in cytologic
preparations or histopathologic specimens, serology, culture, or
nucleic acid detection.

Complete Blood Count
Mild to moderate nonregenerative anemia and lymphopenia are
frequently found on the CBC. Mild leukocytosis, leukopenia, and
pancytopenia are inconsistent ﬁndings. 158 , 186 Serum
hyperviscosity, thrombocytopathy, 158 secondary ITP, 141 impaired
secondary hemostasis, and ﬁbrinolysis 156 may also be detected.
Parasites are rarely detected in peripheral blood smears.

vetexamprep.ir

The most consistent serum biochemistry ﬁndings are serum
hyperproteinemia
with
hyperglobulinemia
and
hypoalbuminemia, which results in a decreased albumin/globulin
ratio. Serum globulin concentration ranges from mild to severe
(up to 8 g/dL). Leishmaniosis should be suspected in dogs from
endemic regions that have polyclonal beta and gamma
hyperglobulinemia with no apparent cause. Dogs with
leishmaniosis may have increases in the concentration of serum
acute-phase proteins such as CRP and ferritin and decreases in
negative acute phase proteins such as albumin and paraxoxanase
1 (PON1). 187 , 188 Mild increases of liver enzyme activities are
frequent; however, grossly elevated liver enzyme activities, severe
azotemia, or both are found in only a minority of dogs. 186
However, glomerulonephritis eventually develops with
progressive pathologic renal dysfunction. Azotemia has been
reported in 16% to 38% of dogs. Renal biomarkers, such as the
serum symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), may also be useful to
assess the extent of renal damage. 189 , 190 Test results for
antinuclear antibodies can be positive, especially if co-infections
are present. 139

Urinalysis
Dogs with leishmaniosis may have proteinuria or isosthenuria
secondary to glomerular and tubulointerstitial renal function

vetexamprep.ir

impairment, respectively. Cylindruria may be detected in some
dogs. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio and enzymuria have
been proposed as tests to assess the extent of renal damage. 191–193
Examination of Other Body Fluids
Lymphocytic and neutrophilic inﬂammation is observed with
Leishmania amastigotes in the synovial ﬂuid in dogs with both
erosive and nonerosive polyarthritis. 166 Dogs with neurologic
signs have most commonly a lymphocytic pleocytosis. 194 A
reduction in semen quality of dogs with leishmaniosis has been
reported with poor progressive motility and large score of total
sperm defects and detached normal heads. Semen quality is
partially reverted after long-term treatment. 195
Bone Marrow Examination
Bone marrow cytologic alterations described in canine
leishmaniosis include erythrophagocytosis, erythroid hypoplasia
and dysplasia, eosinophilic hypoplasia, granulocytic hyperplasia,
and increased numbers of lymphocytes and plasma cells. 196 , 197
Amastigotes may also be visible.
Diagnostic Imaging
Abdominal radiography or ultrasonography in dogs with
leishmaniosis may reveal abdominal lymphadenomegaly,
splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. Radiographic lesions of long
bones in dogs with bone involvement consist of soft periosteal
proliferation, increased or decreased intramedullary opacity,
and/or cortical and medullary destruction. 153 , 166 Lesions tend to
be bilateral and symmetric. Joint radiographs in dogs with signs
of arthritis may reveal erosive changes, or arthritis may be
nonerosive.
Microbiologic Tests (Table 96.3)
Organism Identification by Microscopy and Culture
Diagnosis can be based on cytologic or histologic identiﬁcation of
amastigotes, either in macrophages or free in routinely stained
smears. Organisms are often found in lymph nodes, splenic
aspirates, skin touch impressions, bone marrow, or other tissues

vetexamprep.ir

and body ﬂuids. 193 The speciﬁcity of these methods is virtually
100%, but depending on the time spent searching for parasites, the
maximum sensitivity is around 80% in dogs with clinical signs of
the disease and lower in subclinically infected seropositive dogs.
Cytologic studies may reveal few or no demonstrable parasites in
dogs with overt clinical signs of disease.
Serologic Diagnosis
Various serologic methods have been used to detect serum antiLeishmania antibodies. These include IFA testing, ELISA,
immunochromatography with rapid POC devices, direct
agglutination assays, and Western blo ing. In general, most of
these methods have good sensitivities and speciﬁcities for the
diagnosis of clinical leishmaniosis. However, sensitivity and
speciﬁcity greatly depend on the antigens employed. Wholeparasite extracts are sensitive for the detection of subclinical or
clinical infections but provide a somewhat lower speciﬁcity. 198
On the other hand, assays that include recombinant protein
antigens are very speciﬁc but may lack sensitivity for the detection
of clinically healthy infected dogs, depending on the antigen
employed. 199 The recombinant proteins reported to be highly
sensitive for detection of infection in dogs are K39, K26, KMP11,
SMT, 200 , 201 cysteine proteinase, 202 A2, 203 and the chimeric
protein Q. 204 Another study demonstrated the high sensitivity
and speciﬁcity of a ribosomal protein extract. 205
Negative test results may reﬂect delayed seroconversion in
some animals, which may take several months to occur. However,
many dogs with clinical signs seroconvert after a long incubation
period. Importantly, in endemic areas, positive serologic test
results do not imply that disease is due to Leishmania spp.
infection, because subclinical infections are widespread. Thus, for
diagnosis of disease (leishmaniosis), results must be interpreted in
conjunction with clinical ﬁndings and the results of cytologic and
histopathologic evaluation of aﬀected tissues. A diagnostic
algorithm summarizing the use of antibody titers for
leishmaniosis is shown in Fig. 96.12. High antibody levels are
associated with high tissue parasite loads and disease. 54 , 55 AntiLeishmania antibodies are rarely undetectable in infected dogs
with clinical signs of leishmaniosis. Therefore, a high positive

vetexamprep.ir

antibody titer strongly supports the diagnosis and is conclusive of
leishmaniosis in dogs with compatible clinical signs or
clinicopathologic abnormalities. 17 In cases with low antibody
titers and compatible clinical signs, the use of additional detection
methods is recommended to exclude or conﬁrm the disease
because a low positive titer result may be detected in dogs that are
subclinical carriers (see Fig. 96.12). 17

FIG. 96.12

Serologic tests also may detect antibodies that form secondary
to vaccination. This may not allow “diﬀerentiation between
infected and vaccinated animals” (DIVA). Serologic crossreactivity with other pathogens is possible with some tests,
especially those based on whole-parasite antigen. Cross-reactions

vetexamprep.ir

are less likely to occur when using recombinant peptides or
extracts 199 , 202 or ribosomal protein extracts. 205 Cross-reactivity
has been reported with other species of Leishmania 198 , 199 and
Trypanosoma. 206 Cross-reactivity is less likely to occur to Babesia
canis and E. canis antigens. 207
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Dased Testing
PCR demonstration of Leishmania DNA in tissues of infected
animals is sensitive. It is routinely used for diagnostic purposes,
research studies, and screening for canine blood donors. 208 , 209
The small subunit rRNA gene, the internal transcribed spacer of
the ribosomal operon, and high-copy sequences of kinetoplast
DNA (kDNA) have been used as targets. The kDNA assays are
considered the most sensitive due to the high copy number of this
target 210 and, therefore, are the most commonly employed
diagnostic assays. In contrast, rRNA assays are frequently used
for speciation but are less sensitive. PCR can be performed on
DNA extracted from tissues, blood, body ﬂuids, or even
histopathologic specimens. 211 , 212 PCR on bone marrow, lymph
node, spleen, or skin is most sensitive and speciﬁc for the
diagnosis of leishmaniosis. 213 , 214 PCR on whole blood, buﬀy
coat, and urine is less sensitive than the aforementioned tissues.
214 , 215 Conjunctival swab specimens can be collected
noninvasively and PCR on these specimens is accurate for
diagnosis of seropositive dogs with clinical leishmaniosis. 216–218
The clinical performance of molecular assays on other
noninvasively collected specimens such as oral swabs, 219 hair, 220 ,
221 and cerumen 222 is under investigation. PCR on cytologic
stained samples from the bone marrow 223 and cutaneous lesions
224 is sensitive and speciﬁc for the diagnosis of Leishmania
infection in dogs. Isothermal assays that have the potential to be
used as sensitive and speciﬁc POC tests have also been developed
and require further clinical validation. 225
Culture
The diagnosis may also be established by the culture of parasites
from tissues in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle medium or Schneider’s

vetexamprep.ir

Drosophila medium, but this can take weeks and is typically only
performed in the research se ing.
Pathologic Findings
Severely aﬀected animals are usually cachectic and suﬀer from
muscle atrophy. The skin and hemolymphatic organs are
primarily aﬀected. Generalized lymphadenomegaly and
splenomegaly are usually present. Hepatomegaly may be present,
but it is less common. Small, light-colored focal nodular
granulomas may develop in various organs, including the skin
and the kidneys. Mucosal ulcerations in the nasal cavity, stomach,
intestine, and colon are occasionally observed. Petechiae and
ecchymoses on mucosal and serosal membranes are present in
some cases. Osteolytic or proliferative periosteal lesions may be
found in various parts of the skeleton. 166
Most aﬀected tissues exhibit an inﬂammatory reaction
associated with macrophages in the presence or apparent absence
of amastigotes. Amastigote numbers may vary from very few
organisms within macrophages to large numbers in rarer events.
Lymphoplasmacytic inﬂammation is also common. Classical
histopathologic lesions have been described mainly in organs with
abundant mononuclear-phagocytic system cells such as the
spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow, liver, GI tract, 226 and skin.
Similar inﬂammatory pa erns may be observed in other tissues
such as the eyes 160 and nasal cavity. 158 Reactive lymphoid
hyperplasia is found in lymphoid organs including the lymph
nodes and spleen in association with monocytic hyperplasia in the
spleen and bone marrow 227–229 and variable numbers of
amastigotes.
The most common cutaneous ﬁndings are periadnexal nodular
to diﬀuse pyogranulomatous or granulomatous dermatitis,
together with orthokeratotic to parakeratotic hyperkeratosis,
acanthosis, crusting, and ulceration. Other histopathologic
pa erns, such as subcorneal pustular dermatitis, lichenoid
dermatitis, vasculitis, and panniculitis, have also been described.
17 , 149 , 154 , 167

Renal lesions include glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial
nephritis, and rarely amyloidosis. 230 , 231 , 232
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is more frequently

vetexamprep.ir

associated with CKD. Mesangioproliferative lesions and minimalchange glomerulonephritis have been detected in kidney tissue
from infected dogs without clinicopathologic evidence of renal
disease. 233
In the liver, mild changes have been observed with the presence
of individual or clustered macrophages, mostly within the
sinusoids. 234 Moderate changes, the most common ﬁnding, are
characterized by mononuclear inﬁltration in the portal space and
hepatic parenchyma. 234 , 235 Hepatic granulomas and
collagenogenesis (intralobular ﬁbrosis) have been reported. 235 , 236
More severe hepatic pathology is characterized by marked
lymphoplasmacytic portal hepatitis with occasional inﬁltration to
the parenchyma and portal ﬁbrosis. 234
Histopathologic changes in the eyes are observed, in order of
frequency, in the conjunctiva and limbus, ciliary body, iris, cornea,
sclera and iridocorneal angle, choroid, and optic nerve sheath,
with diﬀerent inﬂammatory pa erns and variable numbers of
amastigotes. 160
Pathologic changes in muscle are characterized by sca ered to
diﬀuse mononuclear myositis, myonecrosis, and endomysial
ﬁbrosis. 164 In the CNS, inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration including
lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells, and some neutrophils
was reported in the choroid plexi, subventricular zone, and
leptomeninges as well as around parenchymal blood vessels in
dogs with high anti-Leishmania antibody titers and clinical
leishmaniosis with or without neurologic signs. 237 Cerebral blood
vessel walls presented positive labeling against anti-Leishmania
antibody in a histopathologic study, suggesting the deposition of
circulating parasite antigens in the CNS. 237

No gross lesions are normally detected in the external or

only change in bitches was a mild to moderate vulvar dermatitis
with no changes in other genital organs. 238

facilitated by immunohistochemical methods such as

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

Canine leishmaniosis is more resistant to therapy than human
leishmaniosis, and only rarely are all Leishmania organisms
eliminated with available drugs. 241 , 242 Relapses necessitating
retreatment are the rule rather than the exception, although dogs
frequently become cured of the clinical disease. For a summary of
the main drug dosages and adverse eﬀects, see Table 96.4. 243
Follow-up and monitoring of clinical and laboratory parameters
of treated dogs and healthy infected dogs are essential for
adequate management. 17 , 184 A summary of the approach to
monitoring sick and clinically healthy dogs is shown in Table 96.5.
For decades, pentavalent antimonials have been the primary
drug for treatment of canine and human leishmaniosis. These
selectively inhibit the protozoal enzymes required for glycolytic
and fa y acid oxidation. Meglumine antimoniate (see Chapter 12)
is the main antimonial used for treatment of dogs. It is
administered at 75 to 100 mg/kg/day SC for 4 to 8 weeks and may
cause cutaneous cellulitis or abscesses at the injection site and be
potentially nephrotoxic. 56 , 57 , 243–246 The selection for L. infantum
strains that are resistant to pentavalent antimonials has been
reported in France, Spain, and Italy and is a veterinary and public
health concern. 247–249

meglumine antimoniate in combination with allopurinol. This is followed by
allopurinol for at least 6–12 months and is currently considered the most
effective treatment of L. infantum infections.
b Can be combined with allopurinol as an alternative to the meglumine

antimoniate. In such cases, treatment with allopurinol is continued for at least
6–12 months after miltefosine discontinuation.

Allopurinol is an indispensable part of the treatment of canine
leishmaniosis, frequently used in combination with other drugs. It
is a hypoxanthine compound that is metabolized by Leishmania
spp. to produce an analogue of inosine. The analogue is
incorporated into leishmanial RNA, causing faulty protein
translation and inhibition of parasite multiplication. It is
administered orally, has few adverse eﬀects, and is readily
available, even in the United States and countries where
meglumine antimoniate is not marketed. 250 , 251 A dose of 10
mg/kg, q12h, PO often results in remarkable clinical improvement
within 4 weeks and reduction of parasites to undetectable
numbers. However, relapses may occur once therapy has been
discontinued or while still on treatment due to selection for
allopurinol resistance. 252 Even after conscientious administration
of the drug for 6 months, complete recovery is rare, 253 and
deterioration of kidney function may continue during allopurinol
therapy despite resolution of dermal lesions and general
improvement in the clinical condition. Use of allopurinol causes
hyperxanthinuria, which may occasionally produce urolithiasis.
Combined treatment with meglumine antimoniate and
allopurinol is considered as the most eﬀective therapy and
constitutes the most frequently used protocol against the disease.
17 , 185 The combination is administered for 4 to 8 weeks, followed

vetexamprep.ir

by continuation with allopurinol alone usually for at least 12
months. 254
Miltefosine (see Chapter 12) is an alkylphospholipid with a
direct toxic eﬀect on Leishmania parasites that is eﬀective for the
treatment of human VL and has been introduced for use in
veterinary medicine. 255 , 256 It is administered to dogs at 2
mg/kg/day PO for 4 weeks and is an alternative to meglumine
antimoniate when combined with long-term allopurinol therapy.
243 , 257 , 258 In North America, miltefosine can be purchased from
Profounda Pharmaceuticals (Orlando, FL, USA).
Additional drugs that are not recommended as ﬁrst-line
therapy for canine leishmaniosis because of the adverse eﬀects
associated with treatment include pentamidine, amphotericin B
(AMB), and aminosidine. 259 , 260 Other drugs that have been
evaluated for antileishmanial eﬃcacy in dogs include
ketoconazole, metronidazole and spiramycin, and marboﬂoxacin.
185 In a trial comparing the eﬃcacy of conventional treatment with
meglumine antimoniate and allopurinol against use of
metronidazole and spiramycin, treated dogs showed some clinical
improvement without a parasitologic cure, similar to control dogs.
261

Additional treatment with immune system modulators for the
prevention of disease progression is reviewed elsewhere 262 and
includes dietary supplementation of nucleotides and active
hexose as an adjunctive therapy. 263 , 264
If dogs are seriously ill, and especially if they are in severe renal
failure, it may be necessary to restore ﬂuid and acid-base balances
before antileishmanial drugs are administered. The prognosis of
leishmaniosis depends on the severity of injury to the dog’s
systems at the time of diagnosis and the dog’s individual response
and rate of deterioration. In dogs that have not reached a
progressive state of renal failure, treatment frequently
signiﬁcantly improves dermal and visceral signs of the disease.
Immune responses were monitored in dogs before and after
treatment and have indicated that in some cases, parasite-speciﬁc
CMI that is absent before therapy is regained after drug
administration but may deteriorate again during a clinical relapse.

Staging
A clinical staging system for canine leishmaniosis divides the
disease into four clinical stages from mild to very severe disease
based on clinical signs, clinical laboratory abnormalities, and level

vetexamprep.ir

of serum anti-Leishmania antibodies. 184 This system is helpful for
decisions on the therapy most suitable for each patient and for
consideration of a prognosis (Table 96.6). The clinical stage may
change if the clinical health of the dog deteriorates or improves.

Prevention
Eﬀorts to control leishmaniosis in the canine populations in some
endemic countries are controversial and generally have not been
considered to be successful. 50 , 266–269 Culling sick and
seropositive dogs is obviously unacceptable to the owners, but it
is also ineﬀective in controlling spread of the disease because
subclinically infected dogs, and possibly wild canids are
additional sources of parasite transmission. Furthermore,
available methods for testing do not identify all infected dogs, and
a population of young susceptible puppies can replace the culled
animals. 43 , 268 Spraying for sand ﬂy vectors and eradicating their
presumptive breeding places has limited eﬀectiveness in
preventing spread of the disease. No prophylactic drug has yet
been shown to be eﬀective against infection, and medical
treatment of infected dogs with antileishmanial drugs is
ineﬀective in eliminating the parasite.
Sand ﬂy bites can be reduced by keeping dogs indoors during
the sand ﬂy season from dusk to dawn, avoiding microhabitats
favorable to sand ﬂies in the location where the dog spends time,
and using environmental insecticides and topical insecticides. 270
Topical insecticides for protecting dogs against sand ﬂy bites
include solutions, spot-on tubes, sprays, and collars. A spot-on
containing imidacloprid and permethrin is recommended for
dogs every 3 to 4 weeks for repelling sand ﬂies. 271–273
Deltamethrin-impregnated collars (see Chapter 13) can protect
dogs for about 8 months from more than 90% of bites from
Phlebotomus perniciosus, the primary vector of L. infantum in
France, Italy, and Spain; and Lu. longipalpis, a major South
American vector. 274–276 A controlled study on the eﬀect of using
collars on dogs in a focus of VL in Iran indicated that the
seroconversion rate after 1 year in dogs and children was
signiﬁcantly lower in intervention villages than in control villages.
277 Topical insecticide protection is valuable for dogs in endemic
regions during transmission seasons and for dogs traveling to

vetexamprep.ir

these areas. Use of collars or spot-on formulations on clientowned infected dogs treated medically and living in infected
areas is warranted.
Commercial vaccines to protect dogs against canine
leishmaniosis are available and widely used in Brazil and Europe.
Vaccination decreases the occurrence of clinical disease, however,
may not be as successful in preventing infection. 184 , 243 , 278
Domperidone is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist reported to act
by the stimulation of prolactin secretion which acts as a proinﬂammatory cytokine. It is also used as a prophylactic treatment
in dogs in some European countries. 279 An integrated control
approach that combines vaccination with the application of
topical insecticides could reduce the burden of infection in dog
populations in endemic countries. 243 There is no licensed vaccine
against leishmaniosis for veterinary use in the United States.
Euthanasia has been promoted to prevent leishmaniosis from
becoming established in North America in se ings where large
numbers of dogs are infected in kennel situations.

Public Health Considerations
VL is a serious human disease that may be fatal if untreated.
Malnutrition predisposes to progression of infection. 10 , 280 , 281
Traditionally, VL primarily aﬀected young children and infants,
but now it is also often a complication in adults infected with HIV
or those receiving cytostatic or immunosuppressive drugs. 116 , 282
Transmission of L. infantum from dogs to humans via sand ﬂies
is the primary route of infection. Several studies have investigated
the association between canine and human leishmaniosis in the
same region. 185 Increased prevalence of infection in the dog
population is associated with increased incidence of human
leishmaniosis. 283 Poor socioeconomic conditions are risk factors
for the association between canine and human infections, 282 and
dog density and infected dog ownership are risk factors for
infantile human leishmaniosis. 32 , 284 , 285 The link between dog
and human infections probably diﬀers from one region and
lifestyle to another and could depend on multiple factors
including human nutrition, time spent outdoors, the density of
dogs, and the behavior of sand ﬂy vectors. In southern Europe,

vetexamprep.ir

where human disease is often sporadic and the ratio between
clinically aﬀected humans and infected dogs is low, ownership of
dogs is usually not perceived as being associated with an
increased risk to humans. Despite this, studies from Europe have
established linkage between human and canine infection at the
population level. 284 Eﬀective control of canine leishmaniosis
could lead to a decrease in human leishmaniosis in endemic
regions. Control measures of canine leishmaniosis include
vaccines, topical insecticides, and environmental control of sand
ﬂies. 286
Transmission by direct contact between dogs and humans is
speculated to be rare, if it occurs at all. Transmission of L. infantum
through blood products has been reported in dogs that received
blood transfusions from infected canine donors and in humans. 69
Studies in Spain have documented transmission among IV drug
users as a result of shared needle use. 287 Therefore, direct contact
with contaminated hypodermic needles or with open wounds or
exudates from dogs with leishmaniosis should be avoided.
Direct blood-to-blood transmission would likely pose a far
smaller risk to humans than transmission by insects such as sand
ﬂies. However, as sand ﬂies are able to transmit L. infantum from
infected to susceptible dogs in North America, zoonotic vector
transmission might be possible. 103 , 288
Infected pets may remain disease carriers despite treatment. In
areas where sand ﬂy vectors are found, this poses a concern to
owners, veterinarians, and local public health and environmental
agencies. Before deciding on the fate of an infected pet, owners
should be consulted and educated about the disease, its zoonotic
nature, the prognosis for their dog, what should be expected from
therapy, and safety precautions that should be taken. A clear,
oﬃcial policy based on relevant research and a calculated
estimation of the risk to the community is desirable.

Canine American Tegumentary Leishmaniosis
American cutaneous (tegumentary) leishmaniosis (ATL) is caused
by multiple Leishmania species that belong to the subgenus
Viannia. These include L. braziliensis, L. mexicana and L. peruviana.
The condition aﬀects dogs and humans in Latin America;
infection in dogs has been reported from Brazil, Argentina,

vetexamprep.ir

Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, and Panama.
Leishmania braziliensis is the most widespread Leishmania species
causing ATL in South America. 289–291 Outbreaks of ATL have
been associated with jungle deforestation. 292

Anemia,
