107: Mosquitoes and Other
Blood-Feeding Flies
Meriam N. Saleh

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Aristotle gave true flies their name “Diptera”
(two-winged) in the fourth century BC. In Aristotle’s History of
Animals (335 BC), he accurately observed “the diptera have
the sting in the front” and “no insect with only two wings has a
sting in the rear.” The earliest Diptera appeared in the Triassic
period ca. 240 million years ago. 1
• Causes: A variety of blood-feeding flies feed on dogs and cats
in North America, including members of the families Culicidae
(e.g., mosquitoes), Simuliidae (e.g., black flies), Psychodidae
(e.g., sand flies), and Muscidae (e.g., stable flies).
• Affected Hosts: Blood-feeding flies feed on a wide variety of
reptiles, birds, and mammals, including dogs and cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Mosquitoes, black flies, and muscid
flies are found on every continent except Antarctica. Sand
flies can be found throughout tropical and subtropical Europe,
Asia, Africa, and in parts of the Americas.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Fly bites occur upon contact
with environments where blood-feeding flies are present. The
specific environment of risk varies with each particular fly
species.
• Major Clinical Signs: Blood-feeding flies cause skin lesions
leading to irritation, erythema, pruritus, inflammation,
hypersensitivity reactions, and anemia. In addition, bloodfeeding flies transmit numerous pathogens as biologic (e.g.,
Dirofilaria immitis) or mechanical (e.g., anthrax) vectors.

vetexamprep.ir

• Differential Diagnoses: Skin lesions from other ectoparasites
including ticks, mites, fleas, and lice; other cutaneous
hypersensitivities (e.g., atopic dermatitis); eosinophilic plaque;
autoimmune disorders; photoinduced dermatitis (e.g., solar
dermatitis, photosensitive dermatitis).
• Human Health Significance: Many species of blood-feeding
flies readily feed on humans.

Etiology And Epidemiology
True ﬂies (Diptera) are among the most varied order of insects.
Approximately 158,000 species have been described with great
diversity in their biology and life histories. 2 Historically the order
was divided into three major suborders: Nematocera containing
mosquitoes, black ﬂies, sand ﬂies, and gnats; Brachycera
containing horse ﬂies and deer ﬂies; and Cyclorrhapha containing
the house ﬂies, ﬂesh ﬂies, tsetse ﬂies, and keds. However, major
taxonomic revision has led to most current studies classifying the
true ﬂies into ﬁve infraorders: Culicomorpha (mosquitoes and
black ﬂies), Psychodomorpha (sand ﬂies), Brachycera (horse ﬂies,
deer ﬂies, and house ﬂies), Bibionomorpha (gnats), and
Tipulomorpha (crane ﬂies). 2 , 3 This chapter focuses on families
that contain blood-feeding Diptera known to feed on dogs and
cats: Culicidae and Simuliidae of the infraorder Culicomorpha,
Psychodidae of Psychodomorpha, and Muscidae of Brachycera.
Like other insects, the body of adult Diptera are divided into
three parts: the head, thorax, and abdomen. The head contains the
eyes, antennae, and specialized mouthparts that vary greatly
among species. Variation in antennae structure and number, along
with mouthpart morphology, play an important role in taxonomy
and species distinction. Blood-feeding Diptera have specialized
mouthparts made for piercing or biting the skin to imbibe blood
meals. 4 , 5 Hematophagous ﬂies ﬁrst appeared in the Jurassic
period, 6 , 7 and only a minority of known Diptera (approximately
11,000 species) have evolved to feed on blood. 8 Most Diptera have
two wings (one pair) as adults, although there are some species of
wingless adults. True ﬂies have modiﬁed structures called
halteres rather than hind wings; these club-shaped organs are

vetexamprep.ir

used for balance and are present even in the wingless Diptera. 8
Wing venation is also important for identiﬁcation and
classiﬁcation of diﬀerent species. The abdomen consists of 11 or
fewer segments, with the posterior segments modiﬁed for
copulation or ovipositing.
All Diptera have a complex life cycle and undergo complete
metamorphosis with egg, larval, pupal, and adult stages. The
larval stages are commonly referred to as maggots, while the
pupal stage usually involves development within a cocoon. 8 In
most blood-feeding species, only the female imbibes blood from
the host. However, there are some examples where both sexes
take blood meals (e.g., stable ﬂies). Feeding behavior is a major
component of a blood-feeding ﬂy’s ability to serve as a vector for a
pathogen, and diﬀerences in host preference or feeding pa erns
directly inﬂuence vector potential. Table 107.1 provides examples
of diﬀerent pathogens that can be transmi ed to dogs or cats by
members of each family.

Culicidae (Mosquitoes)
Adult mosquitoes are delicate ﬂies (Fig. 107.1) with long
segmented antennae and an extended proboscis containing a
bundle of stylets used in feeding. Mosquitoes persist and thrive in
a variety of environments. They feed on dogs, cats, people, and
many other animals worldwide; mosquitoes also transmit a wide
variety of human and veterinary disease agents. Important genera
that readily feed on and transmit pathogens to dogs and cats
include Aedes, Anopheles, Culex, and Psorophora. 9 , 10
The mosquito life cycle is depicted in Fig. 107.2. Mosquitoes
oviposit in aquatic environments or in dry areas that ﬂood
seasonally, with some species being able to utilize moist soil. 11 A
small body of water (e.g., a backyard puddle) can provide a
suitable habitat for a large number of eggs. In some species, eggs
remain dormant in dry conditions for months, hatching only after
an area is inundated by ﬂoods or heavy rain. Several abiotic
factors, particularly temperature and moisture, play a role in
determining when eggs will hatch or when pupae become adults.
11 , 12 After hatching, mosquito larvae molt four times within an
approximately 2-week period before pupating. The pupae may

vetexamprep.ir

persist from 2 days to a week depending on the species (Fig.
107.2).

Female mosquito (Aedes
aegypti).Note the delicate appearance and
long proboscis.

FIG. 107.1

TABLE 107.1

Only the female mosquito takes a blood meal, which is required
for oviposition, while the males feed on plant nectar. 13 In some
species the female undergoes autogeny (production of eggs
without a blood meal), but most only do so for an initial clutch. 11
The female mosquito takes blood meals every few days and rests
and develops eggs between feedings. 14 , 15 After oviposition the

vetexamprep.ir

female seeks a new host. Repeated feeding on new hosts
contributes greatly to pathogen transmission.
Mosquitoes utilize complex behaviors that support the location
of a host and subsequently a blood meal. Chemical cues such as
the detection of carbon dioxide, lactic acid, and acetone from the
skin, sweat, and breath may be used. 16 , 17 Mosquito mouthparts
have evolved to eﬃciently pierce skin and obtain a blood meal. 13
Mosquito saliva contains anticoagulants that are injected into the
wound during feeding; 13 if not interrupted, feeding is usually
concluded within 3 to 4 minutes. 18 Abdominal stretch receptors
alert the nervous system when adequate blood has been
consumed and feeding stops. 15

Simuliidae (Black flies)
Black ﬂies are among the smallest of the blood-feeding Diptera,
measuring 1 to 6 mm in length. Black ﬂies have stout bodies with
short segmented antennae and they vary in color from black or
gray to a yellow-brown. Sometimes referred to as the humpback
ﬂy because of the shape visible in proﬁle behind their head (Fig.
107.3), black ﬂies are a major pest of poultry and livestock, and
livestock deaths from hypersensitivity reactions, anemia, or toxin
from ﬂy saliva have been reported. 14 Black ﬂies also readily feed
on dogs and cats and can cause pruritic bloody lesions. 14 In areas
where black ﬂies are common, reports often describe dogs
plagued by swarms during the summer months. 19 , 20 Black ﬂies
are also considered a putative vector of Onchocerca lupi in dogs
and cats in the United States. 21 , 22
Like mosquitoes, black ﬂies also use water to complete their life
cycle (Fig. 107.4). Female black ﬂies deposit eggs in clear, running
water in natural areas. 23 Larval and pupal stages are adapted to
an aquatic environment, and only the females imbibe a blood
meal while the males feed on plant nectar, similar to mosquitoes.
23 Black ﬂies are notorious for their aggressive feeding and
markedly large swarms involving huge numbers of ﬂies;
asphyxiation of livestock has reportedly occurred following
inhalation due to the extreme abundance of black ﬂies at certain
times of the year. 24 , 25 Females oviposit on the water’s surface or
on partially submerged objects. 14 Species diﬀer in seasonality and

vetexamprep.ir

annual fecundity. In areas of North America with mild climates,
some species are multivoltine (produce multiple broods annually)
and can complete seven or more generations per year. 23 The eggs
of multivoltine species hatch in a few days, but eggs of univoltine
species (one brood of eggs per year) will not hatch until the
following year. In some species of black ﬂies, females can
reproduce without taking a blood meal; for these species the
mouthparts lack teeth and cannot cut the host’s skin. 23
Black ﬂies feed during the day, and their activity is highly
seasonal in temperate areas, with more feeding occurring during
the spring and summer. 8 Several host a ractants have been
identiﬁed, including carbon dioxide, host shape, size, and color. 16
The black ﬂy has short mouthparts consisting of serrated stylets
that cut into host skin. 8 Stylets enter the host’s skin and anchor
the mouthparts; blood then begins to pool at the feeding site and
is imbibed from the pool. 23 The saliva contains anticoagulants
and local anesthetic to enhance vasodilation. 26 Black ﬂies are
persistent feeders and often do not leave a host until completing
their blood meal, which can require as long as 3 to 6 minutes; this
behavior renders them poor mechanical vectors as they do not
take multiple interrupted feedings. 23

vetexamprep.ir

Mosquito life cycle.Female
mosquitoes oviposit in aquatic environments or
in dry areas that flood seasonally. Eggs are
deposited either in clusters called a raft or
singly depending on species. Larvae hatch and
molt four times before pupating. The pupae are
a nonfeeding stage and can persist from 2
days to a week depending on the species.
Once development is complete, adults emerge
and rest on the water surface to dry and then
fly off to find a blood meal.

Psychodidae (Sand flies)
Sand ﬂies of veterinary importance are in the subfamily
Phlebotomine. These small fuzzy-appearing ﬂies have long legs
and antennae (Fig. 107.5) and are readily distinguished from other
Diptera by wings held above the body forming a vertical “V”
shape. 27 The adults are weak ﬂiers and are mainly active at night.
Sand ﬂies can typically be found near breeding and resting sites
such as tree hollows, plant leaves, cracks and crevices between
rocks or other masonry, and other dark humid sites that oﬀer
shelter. 28 The sand ﬂy life cycle is depicted in Figure 107.6.
Breeding and ovipositing occur in humid and terrestrial areas. 28
Sand ﬂies are vectors of the protozoan parasite Leishmania spp.
(see Chapter 96).
Only female sand ﬂies feed on blood. As is the case with
Culicidae and Simuliidae, some sand ﬂy species are autogenous,
but females of these species need to imbibe blood meals for
successful oviposition. Blood feeding generally occurs on exposed
skin such as ears, nose, lips, and feet. 28 The sand ﬂy has tiny
mouthparts (less than 0.6 mm) and mandibles with teeth that cut

vetexamprep.ir

like scissors, creating a small pool of blood from which to imbibe
(similar to black ﬂies). 27 Less is known about the host-seeking
behavior and cues of sand ﬂies compared to mosquitoes. 29

Muscidae (Stable Flies)
Most Muscidae adults do not imbibe blood, but one subfamily,
the Stomoxyinae, contains several blood-feeding species. 30 The
stable ﬂy, Stomoxys calcitrans, is a ﬁlth ﬂy and a blood feeder of
medical and veterinary importance. Stable ﬂies closely resemble
the common house ﬂy (Musca domestica), but the mouthparts
diﬀer (Fig. 107.7A). Stable ﬂy mouthparts bear a nonretractable,
long, sharp proboscis for piercing the host skin and imbibing
blood (Fig. 107.7B). Unlike many other blood-feeding ﬂies, both
males and females imbibe blood. As a ﬁlth ﬂy, stable ﬂy eggs are
laid in decaying organic material such as damp hay, lawn
clippings, or animal manure. The complete life cycle is illustrated
in Figure 107.8. The adults mate in the air and do not spend
signiﬁcant time on the host.
Stable ﬂies are usually active and a acking hosts on warm days
and often stop seeking hosts and blood meals during cold
weather. 14 Livestock are the primary hosts, but stable ﬂies will
often feed on people and dogs, so much so that in some areas they
are commonly referred to as the dog ﬂy or kennel ﬂy, as dogs are
often repeatedly bi en. 30 Stable ﬂies are a common cause of
allergic ﬂy bite dermatitis in dogs, particularly in dogs housed in
outdoor kennels where they cannot readily escape the ﬂies. 31
Mechanical transmission of Trypanasoma evansi and Coxiella spp.
by Stomoxys spp. has been documented. 32

vetexamprep.ir

Black fly life cycle.Female black
flies oviposit after taking a blood meal,
depositing their eggs in clear running water.
The larval stages are adapted to an aquatic
lifestyle and anchor themselves to rocks,
vegetation, or other debris and feed on organic
matter in the current. After passing through
several instars (4–9 depending on the
species), the larvae spin cocoons and pupate
underwater. Pupae are attached to the
substrate via a silken thread. Adults emerge
from the pupae underwater and are carried to
the surface in a bubble of air. The mature adult
then searches for a blood meal.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Blood feeding by ﬂies causes a wide range of eﬀects, from no
reaction by the host, to general annoyance, the appearance of
pruritic bloody spots at the feeding site, and the potential for

vetexamprep.ir

pathogen transmission. Fly feeding injuries often result in
mechanical damage to the host skin and immediately underlying
tissues. A wound can form at the feeding site causing further
irritation, erythema, dermatitis, papular eruptions, and, in some
cases, hypersensitivity reactions. 33 Stable ﬂies can cause necrotic
dermatitis on the ear tips of dogs as well as exudative dermatitis.
34 Hypersensitivity reactions to mosquito feeding are particularly
common in some cats resulting in eosinophilic dermatitis that can
lead to nodules, scaling, and alopecia. 33 , 35
Excessive blood feeding by ﬂies can result in signiﬁcant blood
loss and subsequent anemia. Mosquitoes can ingest up to three
times their body weight when taking a blood meal, 36 and heavy
swarms have caused the death of ca le and horses, 37 , 38 therefore
exsanguination of smaller mammals is also possible, although
rare. The saliva of a biting ﬂy contains anticoagulants, toxins, and
other secretions that aid in blood ﬂow at the wound site and allow
the ﬂy to continue to successfully feed. 30 For example, sand ﬂies
inject a particularly powerful vasodilation peptide into the
feeding site which results in a pool of blood for feeding. 39
Salivary components also stimulate an immune response that
often results in local inﬂammation. In some instances, individual
dogs or cats may become hypersensitive, developing more severe
reactions as they encounter more ﬂies.

vetexamprep.ir

Sand fly life cycle.Female sand flies
oviposit after a blood meal and deposit eggs in
cracks and crevices between rocks or other
masonry, tree hollows, or other dark humid
areas that offer shelter. Sand flies progress
from egg, to larva going through four instars
before pupating and the emergence of adults.
Unlike mosquitoes and black flies, the
immature sand fly stages are not aquatic.

Physical Examination Findings
Blood feeding by ﬂies is often painful, although reactions vary
greatly among individual animals. Inﬂammatory reactions and
pruritus at the bite site are common. Local inﬂammation triggered
by blood-feeding ﬂies may result in the formation of wheals and
papules with a central puncture wound that may or may not be
bleeding. 40 Cats with mosquito bite hypersensitivity develop
lesions primarily on the haired skin of the nose, pinnae, and
margins of the paws (Fig. 107.9). 33 , 35 , 40 These lesions initially
appear as erythematous papules that, over time, become crusts,
erosions, areas of alopecia, or ulcers and may be either hyper- or
hypopigmented.

vetexamprep.ir

Stable fly life cycle.Stable flies
deposit eggs in moist, decaying organic matter
such as feces. The adult female deposits
multiple clutches of eggs, with each clutch
requiring a separate blood meal. Eggs hatch
into the first instar larvae, which feed and
mature through three instars. The third instar
larvae pupate in the organic material and adult
stable flies can fly within an hour of emerging.

Diagnosis
Deﬁnitive diagnosis can be achieved by identifying ﬂies directly;
however, observing ﬂies feeding on pets is unlikely. Because ﬂies
are usually not present on examination, a detailed history—
including a ention to the season and awareness of arthropods
commonly active in a given habitat and geographic region—is
necessary to help identify the cause of the skin lesions. The
identiﬁcation of a speciﬁc vector-borne disease or pathogen
transmi ed by the biting ﬂy also would indicate a previous ﬂy

vetexamprep.ir

bite. Diﬀerential diagnoses for blood-feeding ﬂies include other
arthropod bite wounds such as those induced by ticks, mites,
ﬂeas, lice, and bed bugs as well as a number of diﬀerent skin
conditions. Reactions to food and environmental antigens, head
and neck excoriations, photoinduced dermatitis, and autoimmune
conditions can result in similar lesions.
Biting ﬂies that readily feed on dogs or cats can be
diﬀerentiated from other ectoparasites morphologically. Diptera
bodies are diﬀerentiated into head, thorax, and abdomen. The
head contains the eyes, antennae, and specialized mouthparts
adapted for blood feeding that can vary greatly among species;
the thorax bears six legs and a pair of wings; and the abdomen
contains the reproductive organs. 4 , 5
Morphologic keys are available to identify all stages of biting
ﬂies. 41-43 If the adult ﬂy is available and the specimen is not
damaged, an identiﬁcation can be made by a trained
parasitologist or medical entomologist using morphologic keys. 14

, 30 , 44

Laboratory Abnormalities
Most bloodwork ﬁndings on animals with ﬂy bites are
unremarkable. When massive blood loss from feeding has
occurred, anemia can be present.

Pathologic Findings
Histopathologic Findings
Early ﬂy bite lesions may include a central area of epidermal
necrosis surrounded by edema and dermal hemorrhage; in some
cases, a hemorrhagic crust covers the necrotic area. Mixed
mononuclear, neutrophilic, and eosinophilic inﬂammatory
inﬁltrates may be present, along with intraepidermal eosinophils,
sometimes contained within eosinophilic pustules. 44 The
histologic ﬁndings of feline mosquito bite hypersensitivity include
extensive superﬁcial and deep perivascular and interstitial
eosinophilic and mixed dermatitis. Focal areas of degranulated
eosinophils with eosinophilic folliculitis and furunculosis may
also be present. 44

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Prognosis
Animals with hypersensitivity or other dermatologic reactions to
blood-feeding ﬂies should be treated as their clinical signs dictate.
Feline mosquito bite hypersensitivity can be addressed by
keeping the cat housed indoors and administering
immunomodulatory drugs such as glucocorticoids and
antihistamines until lesions resolve. 45 In the case of feline
mosquito bite hypersensitivity, as long as mosquitoes are kept
from biting, the reaction can be contained and the prognosis for
recovery is good, but the reappearance of mosquitoes and
subsequent bites will lead to continued hypersensitivity reactions.
45 As for all blood-feeding ﬂies, preventing contact with ﬂies is
crucial for a good prognosis. Repellents containing permethrin
can be helpful in limiting bites from mosquitoes, sand ﬂies, and
Stomoxys on dogs but cannot be used safely on cats. 46 Some
studies have documented reduced transmission of heartworm to
dogs when a mosquito repellent is used; this approach should
always be combined with consistent use of heartworm preventive
(see Chapter 111). 47 Dogs and cats that are routinely pestered by
blood-feeding ﬂies, particularly by persistent and aggressive
feeders such as black ﬂies or Stomoxys spp., should be kept
indoors to limit contact with the oﬀending ﬂies.

Immunity and Vaccination
The immune response to a biting ﬂy is largely directed against
salivary proteins. The saliva of blood-feeding ﬂies contains
numerous enzymes to assist in blood meal acquisition and
minimize the host immune response, including kinases that
destroy bradykinin, which is responsible for mediating pain and
itch in the host, as well as other histamine-binding proteins. 48 Fly
feeding activity induces both a Th1 and Th2 response in the host.
The Th1 respsonse is stimulated by salivary components that do
not function as antigens because of their low molecular weight,
but instead bind to collagen and other skin proteins of the host,
acting as haptens. 48 Repeated exposure to these haptens can
induce delayed hypersensitvity reactions.
Mosquito saliva has been shown to elicit an immune response
that leads to Type 1 and Type 4 hypersensitivity reactions as well

vetexamprep.ir

as IgE-mediated reactions and antibody-independent T-cell
reactions. 49 Mast cells also play a key role in the hypersensitivity
reactions caused by exposure to mosquito saliva. The adaptive
immune response to biting ﬂy saliva can also impact pathogen
transmission. Immunity to sand ﬂy saliva can lead to strong
protection against Leishmania spp. infection by limiting parasite
proliferation. 50 Numerous salivary proteins from diﬀerent sand
ﬂy species have been evaluated as potential candidates for
vaccines against leishmaniosis. 51 A phase I clinical trial in
humans showed that a mosquito vaccine appeared to be safe and
incited an immune response when adjuvanted. 52 However, at the
time of writing no commercially available vaccine exists for
mosquitoes, sand ﬂies, or any other biting ﬂies for any species.

Prevention
Keeping pets indoors and limiting contact between the pets and
blood-feeding ﬂies are particularly helpful in preventing ﬂy bites.
However, some biting ﬂies, especially certain endophilic mosquito
species, will readily enter the home or other buildings. 15 Ensuring
that windows and doors are properly screened will help prevent
access by mosquitoes. In addition, removing any potential
breeding sites, such as standing water for mosquitoes or decaying
vegetation associated with compost piles for Stomoxys spp., can
limit populations of biting ﬂies in the environment. 53 , 54
In dogs, some topical pyrethroids have eﬃcacy as mosquito,
sand ﬂy, and stable ﬂy repellents and can reduce the feeding
activity of these biting ﬂies. 55-58 In areas where vector
transmission of pathogens is common, permethrin or
deltamethrin repellents are used to protect pets from ﬂy feeding
and can reduce transmission risks. 59 Pyrethroid repellents have
also been shown to prevent sand ﬂies from transmi ing
Leishmania spp. to dogs in endemic areas. 57 , 60 An eﬀective
prevention strategy combines the use of safe, eﬀective repellents
with lifestyle management (habitat avoidance) to limit the contact
with blood-feeding ﬂies, and barriers to prevent mosquitoes and
other blood-feeding ﬂies from gaining entry into the home.
Isoxazoline insecticides will kill mosquitoes and sand ﬂies after
feeding; although their use does not prevent feeding altogether,

vetexamprep.ir

killing the ﬂies does reduce the overall population and limit
transmission to the next host. 61 , 62

Public Health Aspects
Mosquitoes and other biting ﬂies also are of signiﬁcant human
health importance. People often develop localized reactions from
arthropod feeding as well as hypersensitivity resulting in
erythema, pruritus, and edema. 63 Biting ﬂies also transmit a
number of pathogens to people. Recommended protection
methods include habitat modiﬁcations to reduce ﬂy populations,
avoiding areas with actively feeding ﬂies, wearing protective
clothing, and using repellents containing permethrin or N, Ndiethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET). No DEET-containing products
are labeled for veterinary use and DEET should not be used in
pets as seizures may result, especially in cats. 14 In leishmaniosisendemic regions, dogs can serve as a reservoir host; sand ﬂy
control on dogs has been shown to limit transmission risk to
people (see Chapter 96).

Case Example
Signalment
“Tom,” a 3-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair
from Glen Ellen, California, USA.
History: Tom was evaluated in June for multiple skin
nodules and ulcerations on his nasal planum and pinnae
that ﬁrst appeared in April (2 months previously). He had
a similar problem last spring that began as a few small
nodules on his nose and ears. His owner reported that the
nodules increase in number and eventually ulcerate if
untreated. The lesions were nonpruritic. Last spring, he
was treated with a glucocorticoid injection, ivermectin
IM, and possibly antimicrobials. The lesions resolved
completely until this episode. Tom is an indoor/outdoor
cat that lives on a half-acre of land with a dog, goats, and
chickens. None of the other animals have skin conditions.

vetexamprep.ir

Current Medications: Topical monthly ﬂea prevention
(owner unaware of name).
Other Medical History: Previous medical problems
included transient pyrexia of unknown origin a year
previously, and a migrating plant awn in the inguinal fat
pad a month previously that was removed surgically. At
that time the skin lesions were present. He was treated
with cefovecin sodium SC, but there was no change in the
skin lesions after the injection.

Physical Examination
Body weight: 6.2 kg
General: Bright, alert, hydrated, responsive. Mucous
membranes pink, HR 190, RR 50, temperature 100°F
(37.8°C)

Suspected mosquito bite
hypersensitivity dermatitis lesions on (A)
the bridge of the nose and (B) the pinna
of a 3-year-old male neutered domestic
shorthair. Courtesy of University of CaliforniaFIG. 107.9

Davis Veterinary Dermatology Service.

Integument: There was focal alopecia, crusting, and
ulceration on the bridge of the nose and multiple crusted
nodules on both pinnae (see Fig. 107.9A and B). A
thickened area of skin was present in the inguinal fat pad
where surgery had been performed a month previously.
No ectoparasites were evident.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mild gingivitis was present.

vetexamprep.ir

No other clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings were found on
physical examination.

Cytology Findings
Cytology of a skin scraping revealed increased numbers
of neutrophils and cocci.

Serology
A feline heartworm antibody test was negative.
Diagnosis:Suspected mosquito bite hypersensitivity.

Treatment

Tom was treated with a tapering course of prednisolone (1
mg/kg q12h PO for 5 days, then q24h for 5 days, then 0.5 mg/kg
q24h for 5 days then q48h for 5 days). He was also treated with
clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (10 mg/kg q12h PO). Monthly
treatment with topical selamectin was commenced. The lesions
resolved completely.

Comments

A presumptive diagnosis of mosquito bite hypersensitivity was
made in this cat based on the seasonality of disease, the cat’s
lifestyle and geographic location, and the suggestive
appearance and distribution of lesions. The owner was oﬀered a
biopsy but declined. Other diagnostic tests that could be
considered in this case are retrovirus testing as well as a
heartworm antigen test (see Chapter 111).

108: Myiasis
Jane E. Sykes, Lindsay Merkel, and Susan E. Li le

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Myiasis in humans and animals has been
recognized for centuries. The most well-accepted description
of myiasis was reported in 1965 by Fritz Zumpt, a German
entomologist. 1 Infestations with Cuterebra spp. in cats in the
United States were first described in the late 1800s. 2
• Cause: A variety of fly species that obligately or facultatively
infest the skin of vertebrates. The most common species that
infest dogs and cats belong to the order Diptera; families
Oestridae (bot flies or warble flies), Calliphoridae (blow flies),
Sarcophagidae (flesh flies), and Muscidae (house flies).
Examples include Cuterebra spp., Hypoderma spp.,
Dermatobia hominis, and Oestrus spp. (Oestridae);
Cochliomyia hominivorax, Lucilia spp., and Chrysomya spp.
(Calliphoridae); Sarcophaga spp. and Wohlfahrtia spp.
(Sarcophagidae); and Musca domestica (Muscidae).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, cats, and a large number of other
vertebrate host species, especially livestock and wildlife
species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide, although the geographic
distribution of individual fly species varies.
• Route of Transmission: For Cuterebra spp., eggs or larvae
that are normally deposited around rodent or lagomorph
burrows contaminate the skin and migrate into tissues. For
most other fly species, eggs or larvae are deposited directly
on to the vertebrate host. This may be where wounds or skin
maceration are present, around body orifices (e.g., nasal
cavity, perianal region), or on intact skin of weak or debilitated
animals that are unable to groom.

vetexamprep.ir

• Major Clinical Signs: Cutaneous ulceration, which may have a
putrid odor; subcutaneous masses (“warbles”), which may be
pruritic or have evidence of larval movement; upper
respiratory signs (e.g., sneezing, nasal discharge, stertorous
respiration); neurologic signs (e.g., seizures, paralysis);
ophthalmologic signs (impaired vision, uveitis, corneal edema,
ocular discharge, distortion of the globe).
• Differential Diagnoses: Depend on parasite location and
include a variety of other infectious diseases and neoplasia of
the skin, ocular tissues, upper respiratory tract, and CNS; and
migrating foreign bodies (e.g., plant awns). Aberrant CNS
migration by Cuterebra spp. has been identified as a cause of
feline ischemic encephalopathy in some regions.
• Human Health Significance: Humans can be infested by some
of the same Diptera species that infest dogs and cats; myiasis
is more often seen in impoverished people living in unhygienic
conditions, travelers returning from tropical jungles, and
children. Infestations are not directly transmitted from dogs
and cats to humans. Blow fly larvae, especially Lucilia
sericata, are also used as a recognized treatment in humans
for debridement of necrotic wounds.

Introduction
Myiasis is deﬁned as the infestation of live human and vertebrate
animals with dipterous larvae, which, at least for a certain period,
feed on the host’s dead or living tissue, liquid body-substances, or
ingested food. Myiasis has been divided into obligatory myiasis,
where a living host is required for ﬂy development, and facultative
myiasis, where ﬂies that normally use carrion or decaying organic
ma er for development occasionally infest macerated tissue or
wounds of living hosts. Pseudomyiasis is when maggots are found
in the intestinal or urogenital tract as passersby; they have
accidentally been swallowed or migrated into these areas without
actually feeding on tissues.
Myiasis may also be deﬁned based on the anatomic region
infested: cutaneous, auricular, ophthalmic, neurologic, urogenital,
GI, and nasopharyngeal. Cutaneous myiasis includes furuncular

vetexamprep.ir

(subcutaneous) myiasis, traumatic (superﬁcial cutaneous) myiasis, and
creeping obligatory myiasis. Creeping obligatory myiasis is when
dipteran larvae create burrows in the skin and is usually caused
by Gasterophilus spp. To date, this has not been reported in dogs or
cats. Ophthalmic myiasis has been divided into three types
depending on the location of aﬀected ocular tissues:
ophthalmomyiasis externa (orbital or external ocular tissues),
ophthalmomyiasis interna posterior (posterior portion of the globe),
and ophthalmomyiasis interna anterior (anterior chamber).
A large number of ﬂy species have been implicated in myiasis,
which can be broadly grouped into the families Oestridae (bot
ﬂies or warble ﬂies), Calliphoridae (blow ﬂies), Sarcophagidae
(ﬂesh ﬂies), and Muscidae (house ﬂies). Often the exact species of
Diptera involved is not identiﬁed in clinical cases. However,
examples of species that have been identiﬁed in dogs and cats are
listed in Table 108.1.

Cuterebra Spp. Infestations
(Cuterebriasis/Cuterebrosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Cuterebra spp. (family Oestridae) are large, bee-like ﬂies (bot ﬂies)
that normally deposit their eggs in or around rodent (depending
on the Cuterebra species, various squirrels, chipmunks, woodrats,
house mice) (subgenus Cuterebra) and lagomorph burrows
(subgenus Trypoderma). They are the most common cause of
furuncular myiasis in North America. Approximately 34 diﬀerent
species have been identiﬁed in North America, with
approximately 12 species in the subgenus Cuterebra and 22 in the
subgenus Trypoderma. 3 Adult ﬂies, which live only a few weeks,
lay 5 to 15 eggs per site (one to several thousand per lifetime) on
vegetation during the summer months, and in response to heat
from vertebrate hosts and optimal environmental conditions, eggs
hatch and release ﬁrst-stage larvae, which are 2 to 4 mm long (Fig.
108.1A). The sticky larvae then adhere to the fur of their target
hosts and penetrate the host body by entering natural oriﬁces.
Often this is the upper respiratory tract, especially the
nasopharyngeal or tracheal mucosa. Larvae then migrate through
pleural and peritoneal tissues to a subcutaneous location. After

vetexamprep.ir

about a week, the larva molts to the second instar, penetrates the
epidermis, and creates a small air pore (“warble pore”) by which
it uses to breathe and excrete waste. The second-stage instar is
gray to white and about 5 to 10 mm long. After another week,
development to a third-stage larva occurs, then the larva enlarges
the pore, emerges, drops to the ground, burrows into detritus and
soil, and pupates. At the pre-pupal stage, third-stage larvae may
be 2 to 4 cm long, are dark, thick, have two black mouth hooks,
and are covered in cuticular spines (platelets) (Fig. 108.1B). The
spines of Cuterebra species that prefer rodents have been described
as ﬂa ened and plate-like, occasionally somewhat conical, usually
biﬁd to many pointed in the anterior and posterior bands of
spines on most segments. In contrast, species that prefer
lagomorphs have conical, single-pointed spines, especially in the
anterior and posterior bands on most segments. 4 Precise species
determination is not possible based on larval morphology and
requires molecular assays or pupation in the laboratory
environment; unfortunately, larvae recovered from aberrant hosts
often will fail to pupate to adults. The total time for larval
maturation, from infection to exit from the warble, ranges from 3
to 8 weeks. The time required for the adult ﬂy to emerge from the
pupal case may be a month to several years.

vetexamprep.ir

TABLE 108.1

E, environment; H, host.

vetexamprep.ir

Dogs, cats, humans, and a variety of other wildlife species such
as raccoons and skunks are accidental or atypical hosts,
developing more severe clinical disease than rabbits and rodents,
sometimes with aberrant larval migration to sites such as the CNS
and upper respiratory tract. It has been suggested that most
infestations in dogs and cats involve Cuterebra spp. with a
preference for lagomorph burrows. 5 Most aﬀected dogs and cats
documented in the literature have been from the midwestern and
northeastern states of the United States, where only six diﬀerent
species of Cuterebra exist (Table 108.2). However, many cases have
also been reported from eastern Canada, 6 , 7 along with isolated
cases from other states of the United States (e.g., Georgia,
Louisiana, Florida, Kansas, Texas), where other species of
Cuterebra are present, potentially with slightly diﬀerent host
species as well as target site predilections. For example, in a case
report of ophthalmomyiasis externa in an 8-week old Sco ish
terrier puppy, it was suggested that Cuterebra jellisoni might be
involved, a species in the region that typically targets the head of
rabbits, especially periocular tissues. 8 Although unpublished in
the peer-reviewed literature, cases are common in Colorado (Jane
Sykes, personal communication), 9 , 10 and occasional cases occur
in the western United States (author’s personal observations). 11 ,

Infestations are usually recognized in late summer to early fall;
90% of 42 cases (20 dogs and 22 cats) in one study that included
cases from Michigan (United States) and Ontario (Canada) were
seen in July and August, and the remainder in September. 6 A

vetexamprep.ir

similar temporal pa ern of infection has been noted in cats with
CNS cuterebriasis. 13 , 14 The mean body weight of aﬀected dogs
in the series from Michigan and Ontario was 4.1 kg, and 80% of
dogs were ≤ 4.5 kg; only one dog weighed > 9.1 kg. Eight of the
dogs were Yorkshire terriers, and this breed was signiﬁcantly
overrepresented. A Yorkshire terrier with cerebral cuterebriasis
conﬁrmed molecularly to be C. abdominalis was also described
from Texas. 15 However, anecdotally, small-breed white-coated
dogs such as West Highland white terriers are most often aﬀected
in Colorado. Mean age of the dogs was 55.7 months (range, 8–110
months) and that of the cats was 17.8 months (range, 1–97
months); median age of 11 cats with CNS cuterebriasis was 2
years. 14 No sex predisposition has been noted. Both indoor-only,
indoor/outdoor, and exclusively outdoor animals were aﬀected;
however, free roaming increases risk for infection. Although only
one larva is usually identiﬁed, occasionally multiple larvae are
removed; the presence of multiple larvae has most often been
reported in ki ens, 6 which also have the potential to be infected
by larvae transferred from the fur of a queen.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical Examination
Findings
Furuncular myiasis in dogs and cats may occur when Cuterebra
spp. larvae penetrate wounds or migrate following inhalation or
ingestion to a subcutaneous location, forming subcutaneous
masses (furuncles or “warbles”) with a 2 to 4 mm air pore with
well-deﬁned margins. The exact route of migration to
subcutaneous tissues in domestic animals is unknown, but
evidence of migration through muscle and the peritoneal cavity
has been identiﬁed in some animals, suggesting a similar pa ern
of migration to that in rabbits or rodents. 6 Secretion of
collagenase, proteases, and other digestive enzymes by the larva
facilitates migration. Migrating larvae may also carry bacteria into
tissues that leads to secondary bacterial infection. Furuncles are
usually located on the head, neck, or trunk. The pore may ooze
serosanguinous ﬂuid such that the hair covering the furuncle
becomes ma ed. Occasionally, the larva may also be observed to
intermi ently extrude from the pore.

vetexamprep.ir

Aberrant migration of larvae can involve the nasal cavity,
pharynx, trachea, eye, and CNS. Occasionally, animals exhibit
systemic signs in association with infection, such as inappetence
or lethargy. Fever may also be present, possibly resulting from
secondary bacterial infection or toxins excreted by the migrating
larva. DIC, sepsis, and anuric renal failure secondary to acute
tubular necrosis have been documented in dogs, but not cats. 6
Animals with infection of the upper respiratory tract or pharynx
typically show signs that include epistaxis, sneezing, stertor, nasal
discharge, gagging, cough, or inspiratory stridor and dyspnea
with tracheal involvement. 6 , 12 , 16 Occasionally a larva is sneezed
out of the nasal cavity, coughed or vomited out, or extrudes from
the nares. Other physical examination ﬁndings include decreased
nasal airﬂow, and swelling of the soft palate or pharynx. Ocular
cuterebriasis is associated with ocular discharge, corneal edema,
periocular swelling or masses, chemosis, blepharospasm, uveitis,
and sometimes blindness. 17 , 18 A larva may be observed in
periocular masses (ophthalmomyiasis externa) or within the
anterior or posterior chambers (ophthalmomyiasis interna). 17
Involvement of the anterior chamber appears to incite more
inﬂammation than involvement of the posterior chamber. CNS
migration (cerebrospinal cuterebriasis) is most often reported in
cats, but also has been described in a small number of dogs. 19–21
Based on the frequent ﬁnding of Cuterebra spp. in the olfactory
bulbs or peduncles and cribriform plate at necropsy, it is
suspected that larvae gain access to the brain from the nasal
cavity. 14 The neurologic signs that follow depend on the path of
larval migration. Acute onset of seizures (documented in
approximately 25% of cats), head tilt, nystagmus, circling, falling
to one side, central blindness, evidence of cranial nerve
dysfunction, head pressing, obtundation, ataxia, abnormal placing
reactions, pelvic limb weakness, behavioral changes,
thermoregulatory disturbances, vomiting, and vocalization have
been described. 11 , 13 , 14 , 21–23 Signs are often lateralizing (and in
one study, left lateralizing), 14 typically progress rapidly and end
in death due to ischemic necrosis and inﬂammation; rarely,
recovery with or without residual neurologic signs occurs. Rarely
larvae are found within the spinal canal. 24 Respiratory signs
(especially sneezing) often precede CNS signs, most often by 1 to

vetexamprep.ir

2 weeks, but occasionally 4 to 10 weeks. 4 CNS cuterebriasis has
been suggested as the cause of feline ischemic encephalopathy,
based on a similar geographic distribution and seasonality as well
as ﬁndings on CNS histopathology 11 ; it has also been suggested
as a possible cause of feline idiopathic vestibular disease. 14 , 23

Diagnosis
Cuterebra spp. larvae have a characteristic appearance as described
above, and because other causes of myiasis in North America are
rare, in most cases, a diagnosis of cuterebriasis is made
presumptively, without conﬁrmation of their identity by a
parasitologist. If a larva is not visualized in the eye or extruding
from the air pore in the skin or upper respiratory tract, diagnosis
can also be made following biopsy. Clipping the hair over
cutaneous furuncles may be required in order to visualize the
pore. Cerebrospinal cuterebriasis is usually diagnosed at
necropsy, although ﬁndings on MRI examination of the brain may
be supportive of the diagnosis. In endemic regions, a history of
respiratory signs (especially sneezing) before the onset of
neurologic signs should raise suspicion for cerebrospinal
cuterebriasis, especially in the summer or early fall.
Cryptococcosis is an important diﬀerential diagnosis in cats with
this history.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Profile, Urinalysis,
and Clotting Function
Findings on routine blood work and urinalysis in dogs and cats
with cuterebriasis are nonspeciﬁc and may be normal.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis, eosinophilia, thrombocytopenia,
increased
serum
liver
enzyme
activity,
azotemia,
hypoalbuminemia, and hyperglobulinemia have been described
in some animals. 6 , 14 In the study of dogs and cats from Michigan
and Ontario, proteinuria was documented in all 13 animals that
had urinalysis performed; urine protein-to-creatinine ratios
(UPCRs) that were performed in six dogs were consistent with the
magnitude expected with glomerular proteinuria (3.2 to 16). Some
animals have granular casts in the urine. 6 Clo ing function is

vetexamprep.ir

usually normal, but evidence of DIC may be present in
infestations that are complicated by SIRS or sepsis.
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
The CSF in dogs and cats with cerebrospinal cuterebriasis may
have evidence of hemorrhage and pleocytosis, in some cases with
a predominance of eosinophils. 14 , 19 , 23 Total protein
concentration may be moderately to markedly increased. 19 , 21
Given that some animals have had evidence of increased
intracranial pressure, collection of CSF may carry some risk for
brain herniation; however, this has not been reported in the
literature.
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain radiography of aﬀected tissues can reveal soft tissue
submucosal or subcutaneous masses, sometimes with evidence of
chitinous larval fragments, which appear as radiodensities. 6 Brain
MRI of dogs and cats with cerebrospinal cuterebriasis can reveal
single tubular lesions (tracts) that course through the brain
parenchyma; these have been described as hyperintense with a
hypointense rim on T2-weighted images, and hypointense on T1weighted images, relative to normal gray ma er. In one case
report, the hypointense rim enhanced strongly with gadolinium
on T1-weighted images, and T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences
revealed evidence of edema surrounding the tract (hyperintense
signal). 19 Brain lesions extended from the cribriform plate,
suggesting entry through the nasal cavity. One cat had evidence
of subtentorial and transforaminal brain herniation, with
intraparenchymal
T2-hyperintense,
T1-contrast-enhancing
meandering tracts that correlated with eosinophilic tract lesions
on histopathology. 23 Few descriptions exist of the larvae
themselves, but blooming artifacts have been described on T2∗
(T2-star) sequences in humans with CNS myiasis that have the
potential to be caused by larval materials rather than hemorrhage
(Fig. 108.2). 25
Rhinoscopy and tracheoscopy in animals with respiratory
involvement allow direct visualization of warbles or larvae and in
some cases, endoscopic removal of larvae (Fig. 108.3). Larvae may
be observed to intermi ently extrude from a warble. 12

vetexamprep.ir

Parasitologic Tests
Serologic Diagnosis and Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic
Acid–Based Testing
No serologic tests are commercially available for diagnosis of
cuterebriasis in dogs and cats. However, development of an
ELISA assay that detects IgG antibodies to Cuterebra spp. antigen
was reported which showed some promise for aiding diagnosis
when larvae could not be visualized, especially in the case of
cerebrospinal cuterebriasis. 24 Unfortunately, for unclear reasons,
some cats with large larvae remained seronegative, and no further
developments on this assay have been reported at the time of
writing. PCR-based assays have been used to diﬀerentiate ﬂy
species causing myiasis in livestock (including Cuterebra spp.) 26 ,
27 and humans, 3 but these have only recently been applied for
identiﬁcation of larvae recovered from companion animals. 15
However the dearth of accurately identiﬁed specimens for
reference purposes makes molecular conﬁrmation diﬃcult in
many cases. 3 , 24

Pathologic Findings
Gross pathology of the brain in dogs and cats with CNS
involvement can reveal focal or multifocal areas of yellow
discoloration (malacia) and hemorrhage, often within the
olfactory bulbs or peduncles, with a single intralesional larva (Fig.
108.4). 13 Histopathology may reveal a larva within the brain
parenchyma accompanied by neutrophilic and or eosinophilic
meningoencephalitis. However, larvae are not found in many
cases. 14
Parasitic migratory tracts have most often been identiﬁed in or
near the caudate nucleus and thalamus in cats, and have been

vetexamprep.ir

characterized by spongy degeneration, cerebral infarction, and
hemorrhage; cerebrocortical necrosis; astrogliosis; and focal
granulomatous encephalitis surrounding a larva. 13 , 19 , 21 Larvae
have also been found at necropsy in association with the optic
nerve, cribriform plate, or ventral cranial cavity. 13 It has been
suggested that a larval toxin may induce some of the pathology
found within the brain that resembles that described for feline
ischemic encephalopathy.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of furuncular cuterebriasis or infestations that involve
the respiratory tract or eye involves removal of the larva using
forceps as well as broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy for
secondary bacterial infection. It has been recommended not to
squeeze or disrupt the larva during removal as release of antigens
has the potential to trigger an anaphylactic reaction, and residual
fragments may lead to a foreign body reaction and abscessation.
However, this is anecdotal and in practice, gentle compression of
the base of a cutaneous furuncle to extrude the larva rarely has
adverse consequences. The area should be debrided as much as
possible, lavaged with copious amounts of saline, and allowed to
heal by granulation. In human medicine, asphyxiation of the
larvae by covering the air pore with petrolatum jelly or other fa y
substances has been advocated to trigger spontaneous extrusion
of the larva, rather than removing it surgically. Such treatments
have not been documented in the veterinary literature. A short
(72-hour) course of NSAIDs may help to reduce pruritus
following extraction of cutaneous larvae, and for cases that
involve the nasopharynx or trachea, a tapering course of
glucocorticoids should be administered if there is severe swelling
that obstructs respiration. Where multiple larvae are identiﬁed,
administration of ivermectin should be considered (e.g., 100 to 400
µg/kg, PO, once). Application of topical ﬂuralaner or oral
sarolaner was used to successfully treat furuncular myiasis caused
by Dermatobia hominis in cats and dogs, respectively. 28 , 29 Larvae
located within the respiratory tract may be removed using
endoscopic guidance. 16 , 30 Descriptions exist of surgical
approaches to remove larvae of various stages from the tracheal
submucosa 12 , 16 and in cases of ophthalmomyiasis interna by

vetexamprep.ir

keratotomy or vitrectomy techniques. 12 , 17 , 31 , 32 IV ﬂuid therapy
and other supportive care measures may be required for
debilitated animals. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
and low-dose aspirin have been used to treat animals with
secondary protein-losing nephropathy. 19
The optimal treatment for suspected cerebrospinal cuterebriasis
is not known. Ivermectin has been the most commonly reported
antiparasitic treatment, with doses that range from 20 to 400
µg/kg SC or PO; in some cases, more than one treatment was
given at intervals ranging from q24h, q48h, and 14 days. 14 , 19 , 23
Ivermectin normally does not penetrate the blood-brain barrier; its
use has been based on the assumption that barrier disruption
occurs secondary to larval migration and inﬂammation and
evidence of eﬃcacy for treatment of other cerebrospinal myiases.
19 Death of larvae may trigger a type I hypersensitivity reaction,
and so pretreatment with diphenhydramine (4 mg/kg IM) 1 to 2
hours before ivermectin (400 µg/kg, SC, q24h for 3 treatments)
and dexamethasone (0.1 mg/kg IV) has been used in some cases. 14
, 19 It may be necessary to continue treatment with tapering antiinﬂammatory doses of glucocorticoids to reduce brain edema and
inﬂammation. Mannitol may also be indicated if increased
intracranial pressure is suspected. Surgical removal of a migrating
larva by craniotomy was a empted in one dog, but the larva was
not identiﬁed, and instead biopsy was performed. 19 This dog
ultimately recovered following treatment with an escalating dose
of ivermectin (20 µg/kg on day 1, 25 µg/kg on day 2, and 30 µg/kg
on day 3) and methylprednisolone sodium succinate (30 mg/kg IV
q24h). Recovery without ivermectin treatment also has been
described. 21 Anticonvulsants such as phenobarbital have been
used to manage seizures acutely, and were required for long-term
management of residual cluster seizures in one otherwise
recovered dog. 19 An overall mortality rate of 17% was reported
among 42 dogs and cats with cuterebriasis from North America. 6
Only 1 of 22 cats died, and this was as a result of suspected septic
peritonitis secondary to larval migration through the peritoneal
cavity. In contrast, 6 of 20 dogs died; all weighed ≤ 4.5 kg and had
SIRS, DIC, or both.

Prevention

vetexamprep.ir

Keeping cats indoors, limiting roaming of pets, and maintaining
yards to reduce long grass and rodent/lagomorph habitats can
help reduce infection. It is possible that the use of heartworm
prophylaxis and ﬂea control, including systemic insecticides (e.g.,
isoxazolines), may also reduce the risk of infection, but this has
not been evaluated experimentally. 6

Public Health Aspects
Human cases of cuterebriasis have been reported in North
America, including cases of ophthalmomyiasis, respiratory
infections, and cuterebrid cutaneous furunculosis. 33 Most cases
occur in the northeastern United States, with humans
encountering eggs or larvae when they engage in outdoor
activities. The rabbit bot ﬂy species Cuterebra buccata has been
identiﬁed as the cause of a small number of human myiasis cases
in the United States; however, as with dogs and cats, the species is
rarely identiﬁed. 3 Furuncles are most commonly identiﬁed in
lesions of the scalp, face, and neck down to the upper torso.
Cutaneous and respiratory infestation with C. buccata was
described in a 74-year-old man from Connecticut who reported
doing yard work, including mowing his lawn, without a shirt. 3
Similar lesions occur with Dermatobia hominis infestations (New
World or human bot ﬂy), which occurs in the Caribbean, Central
America, and South America. Although theoretically animals
could bring ﬁrst-stage Cuterebra spp. larvae adherent to their coats
into close proximity with humans, human disease is extremely
rare and no human case has been linked to contact with
companion animals.

Wound Myiasis (Maggot Infestation)
Etiologic Agents and Epidemiology
In North America, most maggots found associated with skin
wounds are facultative parasites that feed on decaying, necrotic
tissue and include members of the Calliphoridae (blow ﬂies),
Sarcophagidae (ﬂesh ﬂies), and, rarely, Muscidae (house ﬂies). In
other regions of the world, a few species are obligatory parasites
that feed on healthy tissue. Examples of obligatory myiasis ﬂies
include the primary New World screwworm ﬂy, Cochliomyia

vetexamprep.ir

hominivorax; the Old World screwworm ﬂy, Chrysomya bezziana;
the tumbu ﬂy, Cordylobia anthropophaga; and the spo ed ﬂesh ﬂy,
Wohlfahrtia magniﬁca. The la er two species are non–bot ﬂy agents
of furuncular myiasis not present in the Americas. 34
Diptera associated with wound myiasis have a similar life cycle.
Females deposit eggs or larvae on the edge of a wound or, for
some species, on a moist mucous membrane. For obligatory
myiasis ﬂies, a wound as small as a tick bite may be adequate. In
some patients, no primary trauma is identiﬁed. 34 Larvae feed on
necrotic tissue and decaying organic material (e.g., feces,
vegetation) adherent to the skin or, in the case of primary
screwworm larvae and other obligatory myiasis ﬂies, healthy
tissue. After 3 to 10 days on the host, fully developed larvae drop
to the environment and pupate in the soil. Environmental
development, activity of adult ﬂies, and fecundity are species,
temperature, and humidity dependent. Some species thrive in
more tropical areas, whereas others are found seasonally in
temperate regions. At lower temperatures, ﬂies may remain in the
pupal stage for several months. 34
Adult New World screwworm ﬂies are two to three times larger
than house ﬂies, metallic blue to blue-black, and have three stripes
along the dorsal surface; the center stripe of Co. hominivorax is
shorter than the outer ones, and in Cochliomyia macellaria all stripes
appear to be of the same length. 35 Larvae of Co. hominivorax grow
as long as 17 mm and can be identiﬁed by the presence of
pigmented tracheal trunks. Tissue destruction by feeding Co.
hominivorax may a ract other blow ﬂies resulting in a mixed
population of maggots. The primary screwworm can only survive
in areas with mild (warm) temperatures and adequate humidity,
and, although historically found in the southern United States, has
been eradicated from North America and most of Central
America. 36 Populations remain in southern Panama, South
America, and in some Caribbean islands with occasional reintroductions into North America reported. 37 , 38 Adult female Co.
hominivorax only mate once; large-scale release of sterile male ﬂies
allowed initial eradication and continues to be employed when reintroductions occur. 36 , 38 The Old World screwworm ﬂy, Ch.
bezziana, is found in tropical areas in Southeast Asia, Africa, the
Middle East, and some Paciﬁc islands. Adults are metallic green

vetexamprep.ir

or blue. Larvae have pigmented tracheal trunks, but the pa ern
diﬀers from that of Co. hominivorax. 35 Other Chrysomya spp.
(Chrysomya ruﬁfacies, Chrysomya putoria) primarily develop in
carcasses but are also involved in some cases of facultative
myiasis. 34 Cordylobia anthropophaga is unusual in that larvae hatch
from eggs deposited in the environment and then directly
penetrate the skin to develop in furuncles prior to emerging to
pupate in the environment, similar to bot ﬂies. 34
Like Chrysomya spp., Lucilia spp., Calliphora spp., and Phormia
spp. are referred to as bo le ﬂies due to the dramatic metallic
green or blue color of the adults. Lucilia sericata, the common
green bo le ﬂy, is found worldwide and thrives in warm humid
areas although it can also survive in drier regions. Although
associated with sheep, L. sericata will also deposit eggs on necrotic
tissue on dogs and cats, resulting in ﬂy strike. 39 Other Lucilia spp.
(e.g., Lucilia [Phaenicia] eximia), Calliphora spp. (e.g., Calliphora
vicina), and Phormia spp. (e.g., Phormia regina) can also be
involved. 40–43
Adult ﬂesh ﬂies (Sarcophagidae: Sarcophaga spp., Wohlfahrtia
spp.) are large, greyish ﬂies approximately twice as large as house
ﬂies and can be recognized by the distinct checkerboard pa ern
(Sarcophaga spp.) or rows of oval black spots (Wohlfahrtia spp.) on
the abdomen. 34 Female Sarcophaga spp. deposit fully formed
larvae (or, for some species, hatching eggs) onto decaying ﬂesh;
development to mature larvae can proceed in as li le as 3 to 4
days. Several Sarcophaga spp. (Sarcophaga pernix [= haemorrhoidalis],
Sarcophaga argyrostoma, Sarcophaga tibialis) have been reported in
cases of facultative myiasis in dogs and cats. 43 Larvae of W.
magniﬁca are obligatory parasites that infest wounds or natural
body oriﬁces (nares, ears, eyes, genitals) of mammals and birds in
southern Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. As with Sarcophaga
spp., female Wohlfahrtia spp. deposit formed larvae. Canine
infestations are often associated with livestock, especially small
ruminants, but infestations in shelter dogs have also been
reported. 44–46 Wohlfahrtia spp. in North America (Wohlfahrtia vigil,
Wohlfahrtia opaca) normally infest wildlife (fox, rabbits) and have
been historically reported in dogs and cats but are presently
considered rare causes of furuncular myiasis in the region. 47 , 48

vetexamprep.ir

House ﬂies (Musca domestica) occasionally lay eggs in decaying
tissues but are not a common cause of wound myiasis.
Wound myiasis disproportionally aﬀects animals in poor
condition that are kept outside. 49 Feral cats, and dogs and cats
that experience trauma and are not presented for treatment, are at
increased risk; ages vary and intact males are overrepresented. 50–
53 Fight-related wounds are considered particularly high risk. 53
Other identiﬁed risk factors include paresis and obesity. 41 , 43 An
association with exposure to livestock is evident in many case
reports, and cases of myiasis are more likely in months with
warm, humid weather when ﬂy activity is highest. 45 , 49

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical Examination
Findings
Facultative myiasis ﬂies are a racted to dogs and cats by the
presence of adherent blood, feces, or decaying tissue. Obligatory
species seek out pets kept outdoors regardless of overall
condition, although debilitated animals may be more susceptible.
Female ﬂies deposit eggs or larvae directly onto animals, selecting
warm, moist regions such as wounds, which may be as minor as
arthropod feeding lesions, or mucous membranes. Predisposing,
traumatic conditions that a ract female ﬂies include wounds that
develop following a ﬁght, fall, or vehicular collision; untreated
surgical incisions; abrasions from a collar; dermatitis associated
with infection, which may be secondary to fecal and urine
contamination of skin or ma ed fur; ectoparasite infestation; or
decubitus ulcers secondary to prolonged immobility. 39
Dogs and cats infested with maggots are malodorous and often
debilitated. Stabilizing the patient may be necessary prior to
instituting therapy. The extent of the infestation may be obscured
by the hair-coat, particularly in long-haired or dense-coated
animals, or by other material adherent to the wound. Careful
inspection, including clipping the hair, is usually necessary to
adequately assess overall condition; sedation with analgesia may
be required to allow full examination of aﬀected areas. A
complete history that includes questions about recent injuries,
pre-existing conditions, housing conditions, and, for potentially

vetexamprep.ir

introduced species of myiasis ﬂies, travel, can be helpful in
formulating an eﬀective treatment plan.

Diagnosis
In animals with wound myiasis, maggots are usually grossly
apparent on ulcerated skin lesions. To conﬁrm the etiology, a
representative sample of larvae should be removed with forceps,
placed in 70% ethanol, and submi ed to a diagnostic laboratory.
54 Mixed infestations commonly occur, including with primary
screwworm ﬂy; submi ing several larvae (20–30) collected from
diﬀerent areas is recommended. Third-stage larvae are more
readily identiﬁed; when possible, larger larvae should be selected
for submission. In cases of furuncular myiasis, larvae are removed
from subcutaneous cysts for identiﬁcation as described for
cuterebriasis.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Profile, Urinalysis,
and Clotting Function
Findings on routine blood work and urinalysis in dogs and cats
with wound myiasis may be normal or, if abnormal, associated
with either the infestation or the underlying condition. Dogs
infested with W. magniﬁca had neutrophilic leukocytosis, but all
other parameters were normal. 45 Some case reports of wound
myiasis describe increased serum hepatic enzyme activities,
increased CK concentration, and hypergammaglobulinemia, as
well as mild anemia, decreased serum albumin concentration, and
decreased serum albumin-to-globulin ratio. 55–54 Evidence of
dehydration due to ﬂuid loss may be present in dogs and cats
with advanced wound myiasis lesions.
Parasitologic Tests
Larval identiﬁcation is made by examining the spiracles, cuticular
spines, and, for Co. hominivorax, tracheal trunks. 54 If primary
screwworm ﬂies are suspected, representative specimens should
be placed in 70% ethanol and submi ed to a diagnostic
parasitologist for conﬁrmation of identiﬁcation. In many areas of
the world, including North America, primary screwworm ﬂies

vetexamprep.ir

must be promptly reported to regulatory agencies. 38 , 58 The
identity of larvae in ethanol can also be evaluated using molecular
assays; formalin distorts some morphologic features and reduces
utility for subsequent molecular assays. Morphologic
identiﬁcation of larvae of some ﬂy species can be challenging, and
appropriate keys should be used by a trained, boarded
entomologist or veterinary parasitologist. Many larvae cannot be
identiﬁed to species based on morphology alone, and molecular
data are not available for all species. In these cases, partnering
with a specialist to collect live larvae and rear them to adults can
allow identiﬁcation.
Pathologic Findings
Wound myiasis is usually present in ulcerated, necrotic tissue.
Invasion of major organs or sepsis following secondary infections
may occur. 59 Because wound myiasis is grossly apparent,
histopathology is not usually pursued. Examination of otic
discharge and preputial lavage ﬂuid from dogs with W. magniﬁca
infestations revealed bacterial cocci, neutrophils, and epithelial
cells; Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci
were isolated. 45

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of wound myiasis involves a combination of
insecticidal and manual removal of ﬂy larvae followed by wound
management. The hair should be clipped to visualize the extent of
the infestation. Systemic insecticides useful for treatment of
wound myiasis include nitenpyram, spinosad, sarolaner,
afoxolaner, milbemycin oxime, and other macrocyclic lactones.
Nitenpyram administered twice, 6 hours apart, to dogs infested
with Co. hominivorax resulted in expulsion of 86% of larvae by 6
hours and 94% by 18 hours; all larvae were killed as well as
expelled. 60 , 61 Administration of spinosad to dogs infested with
Co. hominivorax resulted in expulsion of most (70%) larvae by 6
hours after treatment although not all larvae were killed;
sarolaner expelled fewer larvae than spinosad but all (100%)
larvae in sarolaner-treated dogs were dead 24 hours after
treatment. 62 , 63 A combination spinosad/milbemycin treatment
killed all larvae by 7 hours post-treatment. In groups receiving

vetexamprep.ir

afoxolaner or spinosad, all larvae were killed within 24 hours. 61
Other approved isoxazolines (ﬂuralaner, lotilaner) are also
considered eﬀective. 64 Historically, topical organophosphates or
pyrethroids were applied to wounds, but their use has largely
been supplanted by systemic insecticides. 65 Any remaining larvae
in the wound after insecticide treatment should be manually
removed. Larvae can be removed from aﬀected tissues with
forceps and the tissue lavaged and cleaned with chlorhexidine
and povidone-iodine. 54
Insecticide treatment and manual removal of larvae alone are
not adequate for resolving cases of wound myiasis; careful wound
management, treatment of underlying conditions, and change in
owner care practices are also necessary. Once larvae are removed,
necrotic tissue should be debrided and other issues caused by
larvae or responsible for initial wounds appropriately addressed
(e.g., skin resection, complete excision to allow primary closure,
enucleation, amputation). Pain management (e.g., meloxicam, 0.2
mg/kg q24h until resolved) and both systemic and topical
antibiotic therapy should be provided as indicated; continuing
antibiotics for at least 2 weeks past clinical resolution is
recommended. 54 , 62 , 63 Larvae involved in furuncular myiasis
(e.g., W. magniﬁca, Co. anthropophaga) can be removed with forceps
and the skin lesion managed as described for cuterebriasis. 34
Prognosis is dependent on the extent of the lesions at
presentation, the body systems aﬀected, any underlying
conditions, and the ability of the owner to provide appropriate
housing and follow-up care. Uncomplicated cases or those in
which co-morbidities can be readily addressed are likely to
recover, even when infestations are severe.

Prevention
Keeping dogs and cats indoors and protected from ﬂies,
particularly when debilitated or if skin wounds are present,
largely eliminates risk of myiasis. Outdoor pets should be
routinely bathed, groomed to remove mats, and kept in clean, dry
areas free of fecal debris or other decomposing material (e.g.,
garbage, compost) that will a ract ﬂies; screening kennels if
possible is strongly encouraged. 54 Postsurgical discharge
instructions should advise owners to house pets indoors and

vetexamprep.ir

protected from ﬂies until wounds are completely healed,
particularly during warmer months. Pets with skin lesions,
including pyotraumatic or atopic dermatitis, or those infested
with mites, lice, ticks, or ﬂeas, are at increased risk. Addressing
other health issues, such as incontinence or malodorous dermatitis
or otitis externa, that might lead some owners to house animals
outdoors or in structures unprotected from ﬂies (e.g., sheds,
barns) supports prevention. Risk is higher for older, debilitated
dogs that may develop decubital ulcers and for intact dogs and
cats allowed to roam and thus prone to trauma or ﬁght wounds.
Accordingly, neutering indirectly reduces risk. 53 Routine use of
macrocyclic lactones for heartworm prevention and insecticides
for ﬂea control, including systemic isoxazolines, would be
expected to limit wound myiasis, but this has not been evaluated
experimentally.

Public Health Aspects
In areas where the ﬂies are endemic, primary screwworm ﬂy
larvae (Co. hominivorax, Ch. bezziana) feed on human as well as
animal tissues (Fig. 108.5). Myiasis caused by both species can
result in extensive tissue destruction, including bone loss; in
severe cases and without treatment, fatalities occur. 66–68 A
systematic review of 291 cases revealed that human infestation
with Ch. bezziana usually occurs in concert with poor hygiene, low
socioeconomic status, advanced age, substance abuse, or the
presence of underlying diseases including infections, age-related
diseases, and noninfectious chronic diseases. 67 Similar factors
have been identiﬁed in analysis of human cases of Co. hominivorax,
with infestations more common in warmer months and associated
with poor hygiene, psychiatric disorders, substance abuse, and coinfestation with lice or scabies; older men are overrepresented. 68 ,
69 In Africa, humans acquire Co. anthropophaga larvae from the
environment, developing furuncular myiasis on the arms,
abdomen, and lower back; other species of Cordylobia described
from humans include the Lund’s ﬂy, Cordylobia rodhaini. 70
Facultative wound myiasis readily develops on humans and is
usually associated with lack of access to housing, neglect, and the
presence of co-morbidities, including substance abuse and
peripheral vascular disease. Cases of wound myiasis in the United
States are more common in older men (average age 60 years,
male-to-female ratio 5.5:1). 59 Lucilia sericata is the most common
species, but other blow ﬂies and ﬂesh ﬂies have been described in
people. A majority of patients are homeless and present with
larvae from late spring through early fall. 59 In Brisbane, Australia,
where Lucilia cuprina was the most commonly identiﬁed species,
cases similarly occurred during warm weather and
disproportionately aﬀected elderly, ill, and debilitated patients. 71
do not contribute to the risk of facultative wound myiasis in
humans. Dogs are considered a reservoir of Co. anthropophaga in
Africa, and translocation of infested pets is a potential source for
re-introduction and geographic spread of primary screwworm
ﬂies, but dogs and cats are not epidemiologically important in the
life cycle of any other obligatory or facultative myiasis ﬂies. 34 , 38

vetexamprep.ir

Accidental Myiasis (Pseudomyiasis)
Accidental myiasis refers to the presence of larvae (maggots) in
feces or vomit of animals following ingestion of ﬂy eggs or larvae
in food, carrion, or garbage. 54 Common species include any of the
blow ﬂy or bo le ﬂy larvae that invade carcasses (Lucilia spp.,
Calliphora spp., Phormia spp.) or muscid ﬂies whose larvae develop
in decomposing food materials (e.g., Musca spp., Muscina spp.).
Sarcophaga spp. have also been detected in feces following
ingestion in carrion. 34 The larvae are present due to dietary
indiscretion, not because of ongoing development in the GI tract.
Since the pet is not infected, treatment is not indicated. 54
Accidental myiasis would be expected to be more commonly seen
in free-roaming pets that are likely to encounter and ingest
decomposing carcasses or ro ing food with ﬂy larvae.
Conﬁrmation of pseudomyiasis can be achieved by conﬁning the
pet for 2–3 days and feeding only fresh, commercial food; larvae
will no longer be evident in the feces.
Pseudomyiasis can also occur when larvae are found in feces
submi ed for parasite examination because specimens are
collected from the environment rather than per rectum. Female
ﬂies oviposit on uncovered feces in the environment almost
immediately after it is deposited, and larvae rapidly develop but
are not of diagnostic signiﬁcance. 72 When conﬁrmation of the
absence of larvae is desired, a fresh fecal specimen can be
collected and examined.
In humans, accidental myiasis is commonly associated with
Piophila casei, the cheese skipper, following ingestion of cured or
smoked meats and cheese on which the ﬂies have fed. 34 , 73 The
condition has also been reported in children and adults that ingest
Drosophila spp. on produce, meat with Sarcophaga spp., and in a
child fed overripe bananas with Muscina stabulans. 34 , 74 , 75

CSF Analysis

Total protein, 41 mg/dL; RBC, 163 cells/µL; total nucleated
cells, 9 cells/µL. Total nucleated cells comprised 70%
neutrophils, 7% small mononuclear cells, 19% large
mononuclear cells, and 4% eosinophils. The neutrophils
were largely non-degenerate although occasional hypersegmented and rare degenerate forms were identiﬁed.
The large mononuclear cells were often vacuolated. No
infectious agents were noted.
Diagnosis: Minimal mixed (neutrophilic and eosinophilic)
pleocytosis.

Serologic Tests
FeLV/FIV serology (IDEXX SNAP, IDEXX Laboratories,
ME, USA): Negative for FeLV antigen and FIV antibody.
Toxoplasma gondii IgG/IgM: Negative.

Diagnosis

Presumptive cerebrospinal cuterebriasis.

Treatment

Ivermectin (300 µg/kg PO, two doses, 48 hours apart),
prednisolone (0.7 mg/kg PO q12h), clindamycin (20 mg/kg q12h
for 7 days.)

vetexamprep.ir

Comments

Although not conﬁrmed, a diagnosis of CNS cuterebriasis
seemed likely in this cat based on the geographic location, time
of year, left lateralizing CNS signs, MRI ﬁndings (including the
structure in the nasopharyngeal wall, which may have
represented a furuncle), and negative T. gondii titers. Upon
recovery from the MRI, two partial seizures were observed, 12
hours apart, that involved the face. Following treatment, Prim
made a full recovery although the seizures continued and were
managed with zonisamide (7 mg/kg, PO, q12h). Three years
later, at the time of writing, she is still alive and otherwise
apparently healthy.
