109: Ticks
Jennifer E. Thomas, and Mason V. Reichard

KEY POINTS
• First Described: The earliest written records of ticks date to
ancient Greek literature. Homer mentioned ticks in his poem
Odyssey (800 BC) as did Aristotle in the History of Animals
(335 BC). Rhipicephalus sanguineus adults and nymphs were
recovered from a mummified dog dating to Roman Egypt. 1
Occurrence of ticks in the fossil record indicate the parasites
originated during the Cretaceous period (65–146 mya). 2
• Causes: Ticks that infest dogs and cats belong to two
taxonomic families, the Ixodidae or hard ticks, and the
Argasidae or soft ticks. The most common ticks found on dogs
and cats in North America are hard ticks and include
Amblyomma americanum (lone star tick), Amblyomma
maculatum (Gulf Coast tick), Dermacentor andersoni (Rocky
Mountain wood tick), Dermacentor occidentalis (Pacific Coast
tick), Dermacentor variabilis (American dog tick),
Haemaphysalis longicornis (longhorn tick), Ixodes pacificus
(western black-legged tick), Ixodes scapularis (deer tick;
black-legged tick), and Rhipicephalus sanguineus (brown dog
tick; kennel tick). The soft tick most commonly encountered in
dogs and cats is Otobius megnini (spinose ear tick). However,
other soft ticks including Ornithodoros spp. can also infest
dogs and cats.
• Affected Hosts: All dogs and cats are susceptible to tick
infestation.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide with the highest
abundances in tropical and temperate climates.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Contact with environments
contaminated with ticks. Intrastadial transfer of ticks from one

vetexamprep.ir

infested animal to another.
• Major Clinical Signs: Painful bite, erythema, pruritus,
inflammation, swelling, ulceration, hypersensitivity reactions,
otitis externa, paralysis, and anemia. Ticks are vectors of
several pathogens capable of resulting in severe disease with
variable clinical signs in dogs and cats.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other ectoparasites including mites,
fleas, lice, and bed bugs. For tick paralysis, key differential
diagnoses include botulism, polyradiculoneuritis, acute
peripheral neuropathies, snakebite, and hypokalemia.
• Human Health Significance: Several species of ticks (e.g., A.
americanum and I. scapularis) readily bite and feed on
humans. Pets that are not maintained on tick control can
transport ticks indoors increasing the risk of exposure to
humans. Owners removing embedded ticks from infested pets
with improper technique or without protection risk infections
with tick-borne pathogens.

Etiology
Ticks (Acari: Ixodida) are obligate parasites that feed on the blood
of vertebrates. There are about 900 extant species of ticks known. 3
These species are divided into three families: Ixodidae (hard ticks;
ca. 700 species), Argasidae (soft ticks; ca. 200 species), and
Nu alliellidae (one species, Nu alliella namaqua). Nu alliella
namaqua occurs only in southern Africa and exhibits biology
related to both hard and soft ticks as well as traits speciﬁc to itself.
This tick primarily infests lizards 4 and has not been reported
from dogs or cats.
Numerous species of ticks feed on dogs and cats throughout the
world (Table 109.1). 5 The focus of this chapter will be ticks in
North America 6 but the chapter will also mention important ticks
from other parts of the world. The ticks most commonly
recovered from dogs and cats include Amblyomma americanum,
Amblyomma maculatum, Dermacentor andersoni, Dermacentor
occidentalis, Dermacentor variabilis, Haemaphysalis longicornis, Ixodes
paciﬁcus, Ixodes scapularis, Rhipicephalus sanguineus, and Otobius
megnini (Tables 109.1 and 109.2; Figs. 109.1 and 109.2). 5 , 7 , 8 Ticks

vetexamprep.ir

are highly specialized arachnids with three distinct regions to
their bodies 9 : the gnathostoma (or capitululm), idiosoma (body),
and segmented appendages (legs). The gnathostoma contains the
mouthparts (e.g., palps, chelicerae, hypostome, basis capituli). The
idiosoma is the largest part of a tick and contains the internal
organs. Legs connect to the anterior half of the idiosoma through
coxae. The tarsus of the ﬁrst pairs of legs contains Haller’s organ.
Haller’s organ is a sensory structure used to locate hosts by
detecting odors, temperature, humidity, and possibly other
external stimuli. 9 Ticks also contain chemoreceptors in their palps
that help them sense their environment. 9 , 10
Hard and soft ticks diﬀer in several key characteristics. The
most conspicuous diﬀerence is that hard ticks possess a scutum.
The scutum is a sclerotized plate that covers nearly the entire
dorsal surface of males and the anterior half of females and
immature stages (larvae and nymphs). Soft ticks lack a scutum
and have a cuticle covered in mammillae. When examining hard
ticks from the dorsal aspect, mouthparts project anteriorly. The
mouthparts do not project beyond the anterior margin of the body
in adult soft ticks and can be visualized only from the ventrum.

Epidemiology
There are four developmental stages in the life cycle of ticks: eggs,
larvae, nymphs, and adults. There is li le variation on this basic
developmental plan for hard ticks in that each motile, feeding
stage (i.e., larvae, nymphs, and adults) feeds once on a host. Soft
ticks are more variable having more than one nymphal stage and
feeding multiple times as adults; the number of nymphal stages is
not consistent across species.
Hard ticks are categorized as one-, two-, or three-host ticks.
Three-host ticks are the most common and comprise the majority
of ticks that infest dogs and cats. Three-host ticks are deﬁned by
each feeding stage taking a blood meal from a host, falling oﬀ that
host, molting to the next stage, and then ﬁnding another host. For
the common three-host ticks of dogs and cats, adult ticks feed and
mate on the third host after which replete (fully fed) females drop
oﬀ the host and lay eggs in the environment. Larvae hatch from
the eggs and the cycle is repeated. For two-host ticks, fed larvae
are retained on the ﬁrst host, molt to the nymphal stage, feed, and

vetexamprep.ir

then drop oﬀ and molt to adults. Adults ﬁnd the second host
where they feed and mate. Larvae, nymphs, and adults of onehost ticks all feed on the same individual host animal without
spending time in the environment (oﬀ the host), between stages.
TABLE 109.1

In general, soft ticks utilize a multitude of hosts in their life
cycle. In addition to having multiple nymphal stages, soft ticks
display biology that distinguish them from hard ticks. Soft ticks
visit their vertebrate hosts only to take a blood meal and they feed
quickly (15 to 30 minutes). In some instances, soft ticks may not

vetexamprep.ir

take a blood meal before molting to the next life stage. Soft tick
females lay several clutches of eggs from a single blood meal and
may take multiple blood meals at various stages. In comparison,
hard ticks a ach and feed on their hosts from days to just over a
week depending on species and life cycle stage, only take one
blood meal per motile stage, and females deposit one clutch of
eggs from their single blood meal.
Ticks persist in two environments: on hosts and oﬀ hosts. Ticks
infest a wide variety of vertebrates including amphibians, reptiles,
birds, and mammals. Host predilection is the host preferred by a
tick species. Host range is the variety of hosts that a tick species
can utilize for a blood meal. Diﬀerent stages of ticks and tick
species often have diﬀerent host predilections and ranges (see
Table 109.2). Relatively few tick species feed on dogs and cats 11-14
with the majority parasitizing wildlife species. 6 , 15
Understanding the preferred host and the host range of ticks is
critical to understanding population dynamics of ticks, tick-borne
diseases, and the risks to pets and humans.
Dogs are signiﬁcant hosts for ticks throughout the world. 16
Examination of dogs seen at veterinary hospitals in 339 US cities
across 40 states from 2002 to 2004 demonstrated that ticks were
observed during 42,090 of 8,088,288 dog visits. 17 That is, the
prevalence of dog visits in which ticks were found was 0.52%
(95% CI, 0.51–0.53%). The highest prevalence of dogs with ticks
were in Oklahoma (2.5%; 2.3–2.7%), Arkansas (2.4%; 2.1–2.7%),
Connecticut (1.4%; 1.2–1.6%), West Virginia (1.3%; 1.1–1.6%), and
Rhode Island (1.2%; 1.0–1.5%). States with the lowest prevalence
of ticks on dogs included Michigan (0.03%; 0.02–0.06%), Utah
(0.04%; 0.03–0.06%), Nevada (0.05%; 0.04–0.07%), Colorado (0.1%;
0.09–0.1%), and Washington (0.2%; 0.1–0.2%). The highest
prevalence of ticks on dogs were observed late spring into
summer during April, May, June, and July. The lowest prevalence
was during winter in November, December, January, and
February. Factors that increased the risk for infestation were age
of 6 months to 1 year (OR [95% CI] = 1.54 [1.47–1.62]), male sex
(OR [95% CI] = 1.08 [1.06–1.10]) and being sexually intact (OR
[95% CI] = 1.46 [1.43–1.49]). 17 These factors likely indicate time
before client compliance with ectoparasite preventive regimens
and a tendency of intact animals to roam, increasing contact with
environments harboring ticks. Similarly, dogs less than 1 year of

Less information is known about ticks on cats, and primary
literature reports of cats naturally infested with ticks are limited to
a handful. 6 , 19-26 The importance of ticks infesting cats is often
overlooked possibly due to the misperception that cats are not
suitable hosts and are fastidious groomers. A survey of
ectoparasites on feral cats in Florida 20 only recovered a few adults
of A. americanum, D. variabilis, I. scapularis, and Rh. sanguineus. A
comparable survey of free-roaming cats in Oklahoma 25 also
demonstrated adults of A. americanum, D. variabilis, I. scapularis,
and Rh. sanguineus on 18.7% (15.9–21.9%) of the cats examined.
However, larvae and nymphs comprised 54.7% of the ticks
(mostly A. americanum) recovered from infested cats. Ticks were
found infesting cats in all months surveyed. 25

Three-host hard ticks are intermi ent parasites and spend 95%
of their lifespan in the external environment. 27 In general, soft
ticks spend even more time in the external environment and only
visit hosts brieﬂy to feed. Otobius megnini is an exception. This is a

vetexamprep.ir

soft tick whose larvae and two nymphal stages are parasitic in the
ear canal of dogs, cats, and other animals. 28 Adult O. megnini are
free living and do not feed.
Hard ticks thrive in habitats rich with vertebrate hosts, like
mammals, lizards, and ground-dwelling birds. The preferred
habitats for most wildlife ticks are brushy, wooded, or weedy
areas, especially moist woodlands and vegetated areas at the edge
of forests, along animal and hiking trails and in overgrown weedy
or grassy ﬁelds. One hard tick, Rh. sanguineus, is more likely to be
found in or around homes or kennels with dogs. Soft ticks are
generally found in animal burrows, dens, caves, or dilapidated
human dwellings such as huts, cabins, or sheds. In addition, soft
ticks readily thrive in hot and dry conditions. Dogs and cats
become infested with ticks through contact with contaminated
environments. Pets may also become infested with ticks through
intrastadial (same life stage) transfer from one infested animal to a
naïve one (e.g., an adult tick transfers from one dog in the
household to another pet). 29
In the external environment, tick survival is dependent upon a
multitude of factors including climate, vegetation, host
availability, photoperiod, and human activities. 30 Ticks that are
oﬀ hosts are most susceptible to arid conditions and temperature
extremes. 27 Mortality of ticks in the external environment results
from freezing in winter, dehydration during arid summers,
overheating during summer, drowning in ﬂoodwater, and
exhaustion of energy resources because they fail to ﬁnd a host. 31
Nonetheless, ticks are well adapted to survive oﬀ hosts and live
longer than any other arthropod without food or water. 27 Ticks
can become active at temperatures not thought to be conducive to
tick activity and they can occur in locations considered atypical by
most pet owners presenting unforeseen risks to pets. For example,
the threshold temperature in which I. scapularis adults quest is 4°C
(32°F). 32 Rhipicephalus sanguineus is adapted to completing its life
cycle indoors but can also survive outdoors in mild climates if
hosts and environmental refuges are available. 33 With the ability
to survive and reproduce indoors, as well as the ability to transmit
Ricke sia ricke sii (causative agent of Rocky Mountain spo ed
fever), Rh. sanguineus presents a signiﬁcant public health concern.

Current thinking suggests that human development and
population growth, movement of wild and domestic animals, and
climate change will all have an impact on tick distribution and
abundances. 35 , 36 What that impact will be has yet to be
determined. Within recent history, we have seen an expansion of
the ranges of A. americanum, A. maculatum, D. variabilis, and I.
scapularis. Amblyomma americanum, historically found in the
southeastern and southcentral United States, has expanded
rapidly in the northeast and Midwest. 37 Amblyomma maculatum
was historically found within a couple hundred miles of the Gulf
of Mexico. Over the last two decades, the geographic range of A.
maculatum has expanded northward along the Atlantic coast to
Maryland as well as north into mid-western states including
Arkansas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and southwestern Tennessee.
Dermacentor variabilis, historically found in prairie states and
provinces east of the Rocky Mountains, has moved westward and
northward in Canada. 38 and is now commonly found infesting
dogs and cats in Rocky Mountain states. 44 Finally, Ixodes
scapularis (historically found in the southcentral, southeastern,

vetexamprep.ir

northeastern, and upper Midwest) has expanded into Canada. 40
The distribution of I. scapularis in the United States has also
shifted. Since 1998 the number of counties in the United States
reporting I. scapularis has increased by 44.7%. 31 Moreover, the
greatest increase in the number of counties reporting I. scapularis
occurred in the northeastern states and upper Midwest. It has
been suggested that the historic foci of I. scapularis populations in
New England states and upper Midwest are converging in the
Ohio River Valley. 31 Haemaphysalis longicornis was initially found
in the United States on sheep in New Jersey in late 2017 41 and has
since been found in at least 17 states throughout the eastern and
southcentral United States.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
Insertion of mouthparts and feeding activities may result in
mechanical injury, irritation, inﬂammation, hypersensitivity
reactions, transmission of pathogens, and toxicosis (see tick
paralysis). A tick bite lesion is created upon insertion of the tick’s
chelicerae and hypostome into the host’s skin. 42 Once a tick ﬁnds
a suitable location, insertion of the mouthparts occurs in four
phases: surface coursing, superﬁcial a achment, cheliceral
insertion, and hypostomal envelopment. 43 Ticks may remain
a ached at one location or they may remove their mouthparts and
rea ach at a diﬀerent site. Insertion of chelicerae and the
hypostome are not adequate holdfast organs to support the
extended duration needed for ixodid ticks to feed. Most ixodid
ticks secrete cement proteins 44 for extended a achment. Tick
cement is a latex-like substance secreted by the tick within 5 to 30
minutes of a achment. 42 The cement hardens quickly forming a
gasket between the tick’s mouthparts (Fig. 109.3) and the host’s
epidermis, securing the a achment. Soft ticks do not produce
cement 42 and feed rapidly by inserting their mouth parts deeply
into their hosts.

vetexamprep.ir

Partially engorged Amblyomma
americanum female with cement cone
surrounding hypostome.
FIG. 109.3

Insertion of a tick’s mouthparts damages capillaries and small
blood vessels creating pools of extravasated blood that is ingested.
While on hosts, ticks are in a gorging state 27 and must modulate
the host’s defenses in order to successfully feed. A variety of
bioactive proteins and lipids are produced to combat host
hemostasis, tissue repair at the feeding site, and development of
an anti-tick response. Over 3500 putative salivary proteins have
been identiﬁed from a variety of tick species. 45 These substances
include anticoagulants, antiplatelet aggregators, vasodilators,
anti-inﬂammatories, and immunomodulators that allow ticks to
feed successfully to repletion. 46 Ticks are important vectors of
pathogens and transmit a greater variety of disease agents (Table
109.2) than any other arthropod vector group. 16 Transfer of
pathogens from ticks to hosts most commonly occurs through the
passage of contaminated saliva during feeding. 47 However, tickborne pathogens may also be transferred to hosts through
regurgitation, coxal ﬂuid, tick feces, 48 and ingestion of infected
ticks as seen with Hepatozoon americanum and Hepatozoon canis (see
Chapter 99). 49

vetexamprep.ir

Galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose Hypersensitivity Reactions
In humans, an association has been made between bites of certain
tick species and subsequent development of delayed (3 to 8 hours)
anaphylactic reactions to red meat. In 2009, it was reported that
bites from A. americanum induced a delayed anaphylaxis to red
meat in humans due to IgE antibodies against galactose-alpha-1,3galactose (alpha-gal) in the US. 50 , 51 Alpha-gal is a carbohydrate
naturally produced in all mammals besides humans, great apes,
and new-world monkeys. It is a carbohydrate moiety of posttranslational modiﬁcation of proteins for proper protein folding
and stability as well as intracellular movement of proteins. The
mechanism by which this antibody response develops has yet to
be determined. Possibilities include, but are not limited to: the
presence of alpha-gal in ticks to which hosts are exposed; host
antibody development against a non-alpha-gal carbohydrate or
protein which is cross-reactive with alpha-gal; and host exposure
to alpha-gal ingested from a previous blood meal, including from
the blood meal of the previous motile life stage. This phenomenon
has also been demonstrated in Europe (Ixodes ricinus), Australia
(Ixodes holocyclus), Asia (tick species not identiﬁed), and Central
America (Amblyomma cajennense suspected). 52 Food allergy as a
result of anti-alpha-gal antibodies is not likely to develop in dogs
and cats as these species naturally produce alpha-gal. Production
of anti-alpha-gal antibodies would represent a catastrophic
autoimmune disorder, unlikely to be overlooked.
Tick Paralysis
Tick paralysis results from the inoculation of toxins present in tick
saliva into hosts. Dogs, cats, and numerous other animals are
susceptible to these toxins. 53–55 Tick paralysis in animals and
humans occurs worldwide. 56 Most tick bites do not result in
paralysis and the condition is rare in North America.
Approximately 70 species of hard and soft ticks have been
implicated in, or suspected to cause, paralysis in hosts. 57 Most
cases of tick paralysis in dogs, cats, and humans in North America
are due to infestation with D. andersoni or D. variabilis. 57
However, all of the ticks common on dogs and cats in North
America are capable of causing tick paralysis. 54–57 Other
medically important ticks that cause paralysis are I. holocyclus

vetexamprep.ir

(eastern paralysis tick) and Ixodes cornuatus (southern paralysis
tick) in Australia 58 , 59 and Ixodes rubicundus and Rhipicephalus
evertis in Africa. 60 A third Ixodes species in Australia, Ixodes hirsti,
has been reported as a cause of paralysis in cats. 59 The onset of
paralysis coincides with rapid engorgement of female ticks
regardless of the species. 57 Feeding of male ticks does not result
in paralysis likely as a result of lower levels of saliva injected
during feeding compared to females. 61 Large numbers of larvae
or nymphs are believed to cause toxicosis. For Dermacentor
species, rapid engorgement of females occurs after mating with a
male after about 5 days of a achment and feeding. In cases of tick
paralysis in humans, ticks are commonly found a ached to the
scalp, behind the ear, the neck, and the groin. 56 In veterinary
medicine, it is commonly believed that ticks a ached to the head,
base of the skull, or along the spine are most likely to result in
paralysis. The ability of D. andersoni adults to cause paralysis is a
heritable trait and virulent strains of ticks can be selected. 60
Paralysis due to I. holocyclus results from a temperaturedependent inhibition of acetylcholine release from the
neuromuscular junction. 62 Muscle paralysis can be
experimentally induced by inhibiting the dependence of
transmi er release on extracellular calcium. 58 Direct
cardiotoxicity and GI signs (vomiting and regurgitation), with
aspiration pneumonia, have also been identiﬁed in dogs. The
exact mechanism of paralysis caused by D. andersoni is not known
and is thought to be distinct from that of I. holocyclus. 57 Feeding
D. andersoni females are known to aﬀect neurons of the eﬀerent
pathway but not the aﬀerent; the neuromuscular junction of
peripheral nerves is targeted through inhibition of acetylcholine
release from the synapse, suggesting a presynaptic target. 63

Clinical Signs
Tick bites are painful and irritating. They incite local
inﬂammatory reactions and pruritus. The a achment of a few
ticks is well tolerated by most dog and cat hosts. However, severe
infestations can lead to anemia 64 and possibly death by
exsanguination. It is important to remember that tick burden is
relative to patient size and concurrent morbidities. A female tick

vetexamprep.ir

will ingest between 0.5 and 1.5 mL of blood from the host,
depending on tick species. 65 Hypersensitivity reactions to tick
a achment and feeding may result in focal areas of necrosis and
ulceration; erythematous macules or nodules that may or may not
be pruritic and ulcerated; and pruritic pododermatitis. 66 Ticks
that feed in or around the ears (e.g., O. megnini) may cause
secondary otitis externa 67 and pruritic or painful ear disease
(head tilt, altered pinnal carriage). Cases of tick paralysis present
as acute, symmetric, ascending paresis/paralysis. The longer the
inciting tick(s) remains a ached, the higher the likelihood that
ascending neuromuscular paralysis will lead to respiratory failure
and death. Unilateral facial paralysis and anisocoria have been
noted in dogs and cats presenting with tick paralysis due to I.
holocyclus. 53 Additional signs include cough; gagging;
hypersalivation; inappetence; urinary incontinence due to
sphincter incompetence; and dyspnea and increased breath
sounds due to pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure, or
aspiration pneumonia. 68 , 69 Hypothermia may occur in
moribund animals. Physical examination ﬁndings can be
confounded if a tick-borne disease is also present. Sudden death
may also occur.

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings of dogs and cats infested with ticks
are highly variable. Cases with only a few ticks a ached will be
subclinical. Infestation by only a few ticks or by immature ticks
can be easily missed during physical examination. 25 Ticks can be
found a ached anywhere on a dog or cat requiring close
inspection of the entire surface of a pet, as well as mucous
membranes. If tick infestation is severe enough to lead to anemia,
expected ﬁndings may include dull mentation, generalized
weakness, pale mucous membranes, tachycardia, tachypnea, and
poor peripheral pulses. 64
Cutaneous lesions include erythematous macules, papules, or
nodules around the site of tick a achment (Fig. 109.4). These
lesions may be up to 2 cm in diameter. Surface ulceration/erosion
and crusting will develop after tick detachment and may be
subtle. Self-induced trauma may make the lesions more dramatic.
After a tick detaches or is removed, acute feeding lesions of 1 to 2

vetexamprep.ir

mm deep and 1 to 3 mm wide remain (Fig. 109.5). Tick bite lesions
typically heal in about 3 weeks but may be complicated by
secondary infection. Granuloma formation at the bite site has been
described in humans and domestic animals, and may persist for
months to years. 70 , 71
Dogs and cats with tick paralysis have generalized lower motor
neuron signs (including ataxia, lateral recumbency, decreased
withdrawal reﬂexes) and may also have signs related to the
respiratory and GI tract described earlier. Respiratory signs may
predominate in cats. 68

Diagnosis
Diagnosis is achieved by identifying ticks recovered from infested
pets during physical examination. The burden of ticks on pets can
range from a few that are subclinical to severe infestation that
results in anemia requiring a blood transfusion. 64 Thorough
examination of infested animals is often necessary to locate
immature stages of ticks that are easily missed because of their
small size. 25 Utilization of a ﬂea comb can help recover ticks but
combing is not eﬃcient for recovering small, a ached,
unengorged (i.e., ﬂat) ticks aligned close to the surface of the pet’s
skin. By examining dogs during peak activity times of A.
americanum, D. variabilis, I. scapularis, and Rh. sanguineus activity,
predilection sites have been described for each species. 72 Adult A.
americanum were evenly distributed on dogs including the
perianal region and between the pelvic limbs. However, 43% of A.
americanum adults were recovered from the ears, head, and neck
of infested dogs. The majority (80%) of adult D. variabilis were also
recovered from the ears, head, and neck of infested dogs. Adult I.
scapularis were most commonly recovered from anterior body
regions of infested dogs. Adult Rh. sanguineus were retrieved from
all body regions of dogs with the head, neck, and back being most
commonly infested. 72 Larvae and nymphs of Rh. sanguineus were
evenly distributed on infested dogs with the fewest on the
dorsum. Predilection sites of ears, head, interdigital spaces, back,
inguinal region, and axilla were also reported for Rh. sanguineus.

Diﬀerential diagnoses for acariasis includes infestation with
other parasites such as mites, ﬂeas (especially Echidnophaga
gallinacea, the sticktight ﬂea), lice, and bed bugs. Ticks are
arachnids that can be easily diﬀerentiated from other
ectoparasites. 13 , 73 Arachnids do not have wings, have four pairs
of legs in the adult stage, and undivided bodies. Insects (e.g., ﬂeas
and lice) have bodies divided into three regions (head, thorax, and
abdomen), six pair of legs, and mouthparts outside the head
capsule. Mites (see Chapter 110) are also arachnids but can be
easily distinguished from ticks. Ticks are larger than mites, and

vetexamprep.ir

have a leathery cuticle and spiracles near the coxa of the fourth
pair of legs. 6
Ticks are identiﬁed based on the morphology of key anatomical
structures. Dichotomous keys are available for identiﬁcation of
adults, 74 , 75 nymphs, 75–78 and larvae. 75 , 78–81 However,
dichotomous keys are problematic in that they are often limited to
speciﬁc taxa, life stage, or geographic location. Identiﬁcation of
immature ticks to species can be challenging and is not practical
in a clinical se ing. Common adult hard ticks (see Fig. 109.1) and
O. megnini (see Fig. 109.2) can be readily identiﬁed in clinic with
the aid of a magnifying lens or dissecting microscope. Websites
are available 82 , 83 to assist in gross identiﬁcation of common
adult ticks found on pets and humans.
Amblyomma americanum is a medium-sized, reddish-brown
bodied, ornate tick with long mouthparts and festoons. 84 The
female A. americanum is distinguished by a white spot (hence the
name “lone star” tick) on the posterior margin of the scutum.
Male A. americanum are readily identiﬁed having white spots on
the festoons. Amblyomma maculatum is a medium- to large-sized,
reddish-brown bodied, ornate tick with long mouthparts and
festoons. 85 This tick is distinguished from other ticks based on its
large size and diﬀuse pa ern of white on the scutum of both
males and females.
Dermacentor andersoni, D. occidentalis, and D. variabilis are
morphologically similar. They are medium- to large-sized,
reddish-brown bodied, ornate ticks with short mouthparts, a
square basis capitulum, and festoons. A primary diﬀerence
among these ticks is the geographic locales where they are most
abundant. Dermacentor andersoni, the Rocky Mountain wood tick,
is found in the Rocky Mountains in western North America. 86
Dermacentor occidentalis, the Paciﬁc Coast tick has a range
restricted to far western North America. 87 Dermacentor variabilis,
the American dog tick, is widely distributed in North America
east of the Rocky Mountains and some areas along the Paciﬁc
Coast (see Fig. 46.1 for maps). The coloration and pa erns of adult
Dermacentor spp. look most similar to those of A. maculatum and
the ticks may be confused for each other in areas where their
distributions overlap. Nonetheless, Dermacentor spp. are readily
diﬀerentiated from A. maculatum due to their short mouthparts.

vetexamprep.ir

Haemaphysalis longicornis is an inornate, reddish-brown,
medium-sized tick with rectangular basis capitulum, short mouth
parts, and lateral projection of the second palpal segment. 88
Morphologically, H. longicornis is most similar to and easily
mistaken for Rh. sanguineus. However, upon close inspection
under magniﬁcation, one can easily identify the ﬂared second
palpal segment of H. longicornis as compared to the ﬂared basis
capitulum of Rh. sanguineus (see following text).
Ixodes paciﬁcus and I. scapularis are morphologically similar
ticks. Ixodes paciﬁcus, the western black-legged tick, is found along
the west coast of the United States. 31 Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged tick or deer tick, is widely distributed in eastern North
America with dense populations in the northeast and upper
Midwest (see Fig. 45.2). 31 As their common names suggest, the
legs of these adult ticks are black as is their scutum. They have
long mouthparts and an anal groove located anterior to the anus;
this is also true for other ticks that belong to the Ixodes persulcatus
complex.
Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick or kennel tick, is
found throughout the world. 33 Rhipicephalus sanguineus is a
brown tick that is inornate and has a ﬂared basis capitulum and
short mouthparts.
Otobius megnini, the spinose ear tick, is the soft tick that is most
commonly encountered in dogs and cats. 7 This tick has no
scutum and only larvae and nymphs of O. megnini are parasitic,
infesting the ears of their hosts. 28 Larvae of O. megnini resemble
tiny shriveled grapes 7 and nymphs are covered in spines,
conveying its common name. Otobius megnini is most commonly
found in arid areas of western North America. 7 , 89
Tick paralysis is diagnosed when acute onset of ascending
paralysis is accompanied by tick infestation. Inciting tick(s) may
be diﬃcult to locate on the aﬀected animals necessitating a
complete and thorough search of the pet. Ticks may be a ached in
areas not typically considered including deep within the ears, in
the mouth (both mucosa and transverse palatine ridges of the
hard palate), preputial sheath, vulvar folds, and perianal folds.
Clinical laboratory tests are not available outside of research labs
to aid the veterinary practitioner in diagnosing tick paralysis nor
infestation with ticks. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by resolution of

vetexamprep.ir

clinical signs following tick removal. Clinical scoring systems
have been developed to classify neurologic and respiratory signs
in canine 69 , 90 and feline 68 , 91 tick paralysis patients for
prognostication purposes and to monitor recovery.

Laboratory Abnormalities
Responses of cats and dogs to infestation with ticks are nonspeciﬁc and variable. Most cases of infestation in which only a few
ticks are a ached are unremarkable. Laboratory abnormalities
range from no abnormalities to eosinophilia, hypoproteinemia,
and non-regenerative or regenerative anemia. No signiﬁcant
diﬀerence in CBC ﬁndings were detected in dogs repeatedly
infested with >50 adult Rh. sanguineus versus non-infested dogs. 92
Two dogs severely infested with nymphal and adult Rh.
sanguineus (i.e., thousands of ticks) were described with severe
regenerative anemia, hypoproteinemia, and leukocytosis. 64

Pathologic Findings
Histologic lesions of tick bites include congestion, edema, and
sometimes focal hemorrhage (Fig. 109.6). Inﬂammation consists of
perivascular to diﬀuse accumulations of neutrophils, eosinophils,
and basophils. 93 After about 24 hours of infestation with A.
americanum, there is mild, focal epidermal necrosis with a minimal
increase in dermal cellular inﬁltrates. The tick bite lesion extends
through the epidermis into the dermis. By 48 hours post
infestation, the predominant pa erns include a moderate
perivascular neutrophilic dermatitis with extension into the
dermis and subcutis, and a moderate diﬀuse neutrophilic
panniculitis. Coagulated collagen degeneration is observed by 48
hours. By 96 hours post infestation, a focally severe neutrophilic
dermatitis and panniculitis is observed, with focal areas of
necrosis and ﬁbrin deposition extending through the subcutis into
the muscle band of the deep subcutis. The most intense cellular
inﬁltration into the dermis and epidermis is by 96 hours post
infestation. Mast cells and mononuclear leukocytes are also
present. 94

Treatment And Prognosis
All a ached ticks should be removed from infested pets as
quickly as possible to minimize pathogenesis and reduce the
likelihood of pathogen transmission. For pets with only a few

vetexamprep.ir

ticks a ached, manual removal of ticks with gloved hands is
indicated. Ticks are easily removed using ﬁne-tipped tweezers.
The tick should be grasped as close to the surface of the skin as
possible and pulled perpendicular to the skin with steady, even
pressure. Jerking or twisting should be avoided as this will
increase the likelihood of breaking oﬀ the tick’s mouthparts. If
mouthparts do break oﬀ, they should be removed from the skin
with ﬁne-tipped tweezers. Ticks should not be squeezed or
crushed as this may cause the tick to regurgitate gut contents or
stimulate salivary gland secretion. After ticks are removed, the
lesion should be cleaned to reduce risk of secondary bacterial
infection, using dilute chlorhexidine or iodine, rubbing alcohol, or
soap and water.
Other popularized remedies suggesting that a ached ticks be
removed by some method of burning (e.g., lit match or cigare e),
suﬀocation (e.g., painting with ﬁngernail polish, petrolatum jelly,
oils), or chemical irritation (e.g., alcohol, oils, perfume,
diatomaceous earth) do not work, are ill-advised, and could
increase the risk of pathogen transmission to hosts.
Live, motile ticks can be secured by placing them in a sealed
plastic bag or adhering between two layers of tape. Secured ticks
should be disposed of in the trash. Ticks are also killed by longterm submersion in alcohol or freezing at −20°C for a minimum of
24 hours. Ticks can be tested for speciﬁc pathogens at various
commercial laboratories. Testing ticks for the presence or absence
of pathogens should not be used as a proxy for the clinical
assessment of a patient. It is impossible to tell if a pathogen was
transmi ed from a tick to a host by testing the tick after it has
been removed from the host. Tick pathogen screens are, by nature,
not comprehensive for all pathogens the tick may carry.
Pets heavily infested with ticks can be treated with an approved
acaricide (Table 109.3 and Chapter 13). Depending on the level of
infestation and the amount of injury that results, severely infested
animals may require treatment for secondary skin infections,
topical or systemic glucocorticoid therapy, ﬂuid therapy, and/or
blood transfusion. 64 Historically, it was recommended to bath
severely infested pets with warm water and an acaricidecontaining shampoo, sometimes daily until all ticks were
removed. 64 However, the majority of acaricide-containing
shampoos and dips available in the US market contain pyrethrins,

vetexamprep.ir

pyrethroids, and their synergists. As of 2021, amitraz dip for dogs
is not currently being manufactured in the United States.
Clinicians should weigh the risks of dermal irritation of exposing
broken and damaged skin to these compounds, along with
potential risks of increased dermal absorption of these
compounds in highly infested animals. Similar clinical judgment
should be used when considering topical sprays. Common topical
acaricidal sprays in the US market may contain a variety of active
ingredients, including: pyrethrins, pyrethroids, ﬁpronil,
etofenprox, and tetrachlorvinphos (see Table 109.3). Acaricidal
powders are generally avoided in small animal medicine due to
risk of respiratory irritation, eye irritation, and exposure to
veterinary staﬀ and clients. A clinician may elect to use an
eﬀective systemic acaricide for the patient, and determine if the
addition of an EPA-approved topical product is necessary.
Routine treatment and control of ticks on dogs and cats is
accomplished through regular and continuous use of approved
acaricides (see Table 109.3). Year-round use of acaricides on dog
and cats is warranted because pets are host to several tick species
that have varying degrees of activity throughout the year, ticks
can be active in colder months of the year, common ticks that
infest dogs and cats are expanding in distribution, and because
Rh. sanguineus can infest homes and kennels and be active indoors
throughout the year. All animals in close association with an
infested animal should be treated and maintained on an approved
acaricide.
In the United States, ectoparasiticides are regulated by the
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) or the FDA. As a general
rule, if a product is applied topically to an animal to treat
ectoparasites, and the compound is not absorbed systemically, it
likely falls under the jurisdiction of the EPA. If a product is
administered orally, by injection, or if it is applied topically for
systemic absorption, it likely falls under the jurisdiction of the
FDA. This distinction is important for practitioners to recognize,
because there is no legal extra-label use of products regulated by
the EPA. Label directions must be followed regarding species
treated, product concentration, product dosage, individuals
allowed to administer application, and re-treatment interval.
Because products regulated by the FDA are approved animal

vetexamprep.ir

drugs, extra-label use may be allowed under the Animal
Medicinal Drug Use and Clariﬁcation Act (AMDUCA).
Acaricides currently approved for use in cats and dogs are
formulated for topical (“spot on” products, collars, sprays) or oral
administration (see Table 109.3). Care must be taken to use
acaricides only on or in the host species for which they are
approved. Dog products should not be administered to cats, and
vice versa. In areas where ticks are abundant and there is
increased risk of infestation to pets, practitioners can combine tick
treatment and control products, alternating and overlapping
application of products yet keeping within label directions.
Acaricide resistance has been documented in various locations
throughout the world, predominately in livestock. 95 The
continued use and in some cases misuse of acaricides would be
expected to select for ticks that are drug-resistant. Resistance of A.
americanum to benzene hexachloride (BHC)/cyclodienes; D.
variabilis to BHC/cyclodienes and DDT; and Rh. sanguineus to
amitraz, BHC/cyclodienes, and organophosphates has been
reported. 96 Rhipicephalus sanguineus removed from dogs in
Florida and Texas were resistant to permethrin and tolerant to
ﬁpronil. 97 Rhipicephalus sanguineus from dogs in Yucatan, Mexico
were resistant to amitraz and cypermethrin, 98 and ivermectin. 99

Immunity And Vaccination
Both innate and acquired immune defenses are involved in the
response of hosts to tick a achment and feeding. Tick feeding
induces a complex array of host immune responses involving
antigen-presenting cells, T cells, B cells, antibodies, cytokines,
complement, basophils, mast cells, eosinophils, and a number of
other bioactive molecules. 100 Hosts show varying degrees of
susceptibility to ticks. Some hosts can develop resistance to ticks
after repeated infestations. Dogs are less likely to acquire
resistance to the host-adapted Rh. sanguineus 101 but do develop a
cutaneous, 102 immediate 92 hypersensitivity reaction induced by
the tick’s a achment and feeding.
In naïve hosts, local reactions to tick bites are inﬂammatory
with a predominance of neutrophils; in contrast, in sensitized
hosts, rapid and more intense reactions occur locally and
cutaneous lesions present at a greater distance from the site of
a achment with basophils, eosinophils, and neutrophils present
in the epidermis and dermis. 93 Cutaneous basophil
hypersensitivity, a form of delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH),
plays an important role in immunity to ticks. 93 Acquired
resistance to ticks manifests in reduced engorgement weight,
increased duration of feeding, decreased numbers of eggs,
reduced viability of eggs, inhibition of moulting, and death of
engorged ticks. 100
Ticks counteract innate and acquired host defenses by
producing a complex array of pharmacologically active proteins
diﬀerentially expressed over the course of tick feeding. 100 Distinct
diﬀerences occur in the composition of secreted proteins for
diﬀerent tick species. 103 Molecules produced in the salivary
glands of ticks function for vasodilation, platelet aggregation
inhibition, anticoagulation, ﬁbrinolysis, complement inhibition,

vetexamprep.ir

immunosuppression, immunomodulation, chemokine binding,
delayed wound healing, and angiogenesis. 46
No commercial vaccine exists for use in dogs and cats to
prevent ticks from a aching and feeding. A tick vaccine was
developed and commercialized in the early 1990s for control of
Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus (a one-host tick) on ca le in
several Latin American countries and in Australia. 104 The vaccine
contained recombinant Rh. (Boophilus) microplus gut antigens and
showed eﬃcacy by reducing the number of engorged female ticks,
their weight, and reproductive capacity. 104 Despite demonstrated
eﬃcacy when combined with strategic acaricide application and
integrated tick management, the vaccine experienced a number of
diﬃculties in commercialization. 104 Tick vaccines still oﬀer
promise for reducing tick burdens on animals while concurrently
reducing dependence on acaricides. Current research eﬀorts in
tick vaccine development target the unique physiology of ticks
and their dependence on a parasitic lifestyle, modern molecular
biology techniques, and bioinformatics. 105

Prevention
Veterinarians and pet owners should not rely solely on the
application of approved acaricides to pets to prevent infestation.
No compound is 100% eﬀective all of the time. Combining a tick
treatment and control plan for pets with other control strategies to
formulate an integrated tick management (ITM) 106 program
provides the most comprehensive and successful approach to
prevent infestation with ticks. The goal of an ITM program is to
reduce the risk of tick infestation on pets. This is accomplished by:
1. Maintaining all pets in a household on approved acaricides
for the entire year. Thoroughly checking pets each day for
ticks and removing any ticks as quickly as possible.
2. Modifying the habitat where pets reside to become less
suitable to ticks while oﬀ hosts. This includes keeping the
yard mowed, removing leaf li er, and trimming bushes
and trees that are overgrown to let in more sunlight.
3. Excluding other animals from the backyard where pets
spend their time. This includes adding secure fencing and,
moving bird feeders, water baths, and woodpiles. Keep

vetexamprep.ir

pets in managed areas to reduce the risk that they come in
contact with ticks.
4. Applying approved environmental acaricides that target
oﬀ-host ticks to the perimeter of a yard where natural
wooded areas come in contact with the lawn. Optimal
results are obtained using a trained and licensed pesticide
applicator.
5. Using targeted acaricide treatment of wildlife species that
are key reservoirs of ticks and tick-borne pathogens.
Several devices exist that target white-tailed deer 102-104
and small rodents 110 (Tick Control Tubes, Thermacell,
MA, USA) to deliver acaricides safely to wildlife and
reduce the size of tick populations.
Arguably, the biggest obstacle that veterinarians face when
implementing an eﬀective tick prevention program is owner
compliance. Analysis of 559 dog owners at 24 veterinary hospitals
across the United States demonstrated that the average owner
believed their pet needed only 10.5 months of ﬂea and tick
prevention despite their veterinarian’s recommendation of 12
months. 111 Moreover, only 62% of the 559 dog owners
remembered their veterinarian’s recommendation of 12 months of
ﬂea and tick prevention. 111 Common causes of tick product
failure include product not applied at correct frequency, product
not applied to all pets in a household, product improperly applied
by owner, insuﬃcient dosing rate by owner, unrealistic
expectations of owner (no compound is 100% eﬀective all of the
time), and overwhelming numbers of ticks in the environment.

Public Health Aspects
As for pets, tick bites in humans are painful and annoying.
Humans throughout the world are exposed to ticks 112 and ticks
are often found on people in the United States 113 and Canada. 114 ,
115 Most cases of tick infestation on humans are due to ixodid
ticks; however, cases of argasid tick bites of humans are also
reported. 112 , 116 Based on specimens submi ed to the US
National Tick Collection, 44 species of ticks (33 ixodid and 11
argasid) were recovered from infested humans. The predominant

vetexamprep.ir

tick species on humans was variable and predictable based on
geographic location in the United States. 113 All motile stages of A.
americanum were common in the southern United States and
Atlantic coastal states. Adults of D. variabilis and all stages of I.
scapularis were common on people in the eastern and northern
United States. In Rocky Mountain and western states, D. andersoni
was most common whereas in far western states, adult I. paciﬁcus
were most commonly recovered from humans. 113 Tick paralysis
in humans occurs worldwide. 56 , 117 , 118 In North America, the
majority of human tick paralysis cases are in the Paciﬁc northwest
of the United States and adjacent areas of southwestern Canada.
119 However, occurrence is rare. 56 Children 2 to 5 years old are at
highest risk. 120
Humans exposed to natural areas with wildlife present are at
increased risk of exposure to ticks and tick-borne diseases. 116
Outdoor activities related to contact with wood (e.g., si ing on
logs, gathering wood, si ing against trees, walking, stirring and
si ing on leaf li er, just si ing on leaf li er) resulted in greater
acquisition of I. paciﬁcus nymphs. 121 Coming in contact with wild
and domestic animals infested with ticks increases the risk of tick
bites to humans. 116 Maintaining pets on year-round tick
prevention under the direction of a veterinarian will minimize the
potential for animals to bring ticks into the home. Perhaps the
biggest impact ticks have on humans globally is as pathogen
vectors. 116 , 122 Ticks are second only to mosquitoes in this
respect, 16 and they will continue to play a signiﬁcant role in
emerging zoonotic diseases. 123–125

“Amos,” a 2-year-old mastiﬀ mix male dog from north-central
Oklahoma.

History

The mastiﬀ mix was reported to be roaming for 5 to 7 days and
a municipality’s Department of Animal Welfare was notiﬁed for
pick-up. The dog was given the name “Amos” and examined by
a veterinarian. After 4 days for stray hold (according to city
animal welfare protocol), Amos was presented to a local animal
shelter for castration and vaccination. Amos was adopted after
10 days at the shelter. There was no history of known
medication.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 31 kg (68 lb).
General: Quiet, alert, responsive. Body condition score
2/9. Euhydrated. T = 101.6°C (38.7°F). P = 100 beats/min, R
= 24 breaths/min, mucous membranes pink, CRT <2 s.
Integument, eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Dermatological
abnormalities were limited to the sites of ectoparasite
a achment. An asymmetric pa ern of a ached ticks was
present over the patient’s dorsum and convex surfaces of
the pinnae (Fig. 109.7). Nodular swellings underlay each
a achment point. The ticks were at various stages of
rapid engorgement. Mild small, loose scale was present
throughout the coat. Neither alopecia nor hypotrichosis
were seen. No adult ﬂeas were observed with ﬂea comb
exam. The interdigital webbing was normal. Ocular
mucopurulent discharge was noted OU with mild
hyperemia of the conjunctiva. There was mild ectropion
OU. Corneas were clear. A Schirmer tear test was normal.
Otoscopic examination revealed moderate brown, waxy
exudate adherent to non-erythematous, non-edematous
canal walls AU. Tympanic membranes intact AU. Nasal
oriﬁces free of discharge. Oral exam had no abnormalities
noted.
Musculoskeletal: Ambulation was assessed by allowing
the patient to roam in a small enclosure as Amos was not
accustomed to walking on a leash. All joints palpated had
normal range of motion with no swelling noted. There

vetexamprep.ir

was no evidence of pain, and weight bearing was equal
on all four limbs. Pain score was assessed to be 1/5.
Cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and
genitourinary: No murmurs or arrhythmias were
ausculted. All lung ﬁelds were clear on auscultation. No
cough was elicited on tracheal palpation. Abdominal
palpation was unremarkable. A smooth enlarged spleen
was noted. Unilateral cryptorchidism was noted with the
right testicle retained in the abdomen. Rectal examination
was unremarkable.
Lymph nodes: Within normal limits.
Neurologic examination: Patient interacts appropriately
with surroundings. No neurologic abnormalities were
detected during an abbreviated neurologic examination.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 39% (36%–60%), MCV 68 fL (58–79 fL), MCHC
35 g/dL (30–38 g/dL), WBC 17,500 cells/µL (4000–15,500
cells/µL), neutrophils 9450 cells/µL (2060–10,600 cells/µL),

Parasitological Testing
Gross parasites identiﬁed as Amblyomma maculatum (Gulf
Coast ticks) and Dermacentor variabilis (American dog
ticks).
Fecal ﬂotation (sugar with centrifugation) demonstrated
moderate numbers of Ancylostoma caninum (hookworm)
eggs.
SNAP 4Dx Plus test (IDEXX Laboratories): Negative for
Borreliella burgdorferi antibodies; negative for antibodies to
Anaplasma spp.; negative for antibodies to Ehrlichia canis,
E. ewingii; negative for Diroﬁlaria immitis antigen.

Diagnosis

Infestation with ticks, infection with hookworms; malnutrition.

Treatment

Amos was treated with 8.80% imidacloprid + 44.00%
permethrin + 0.44% pyriproxyfen (Advantix II, Bayer) for ticks
and 272 µg ivermectin + 227 mg pyrantel pamoate (Heartgard
Plus, Boehringer Ingelheim) for hookworms. He was vaccinated
for canine distemper, canine adenovirus type 2, canine
parainﬂuenza, canine parvovirus type 2, Bordetella
bronchiseptica, and rabies. Amos received a balanced,
commercially available dry dog food to improve his nutritional
status and elevate his body condition score.

Comments

This was a typical case of a stray dog seen at an animal shelter
in the southcentral United States. Amos was malnourished and
moderately infested with ticks. Upon further examination, he
was also found to be infected with hookworms. The moderate
eosinophilia and mild monocytosis was consistent with
parasitic infestation and infection. The extent of eosinophilia
caused by the ticks versus hookworms was not known. The
likelihood that a parasite will generate an eosinophilia is
proportional to the degree of tissue contact. Prolonged injection
of tick saliva, migration of juvenile A. caninum, and feeding of
adult A. caninum in the small intestines would all produce an
eosinophilia. It is possible that infection with vector-borne
pathogens was too recent for an antibody response to have
developed. The presence of fully engorged female A. maculatum

vetexamprep.ir

and D. variabilis suggested that infestation had been present for
at least 7 to 10 days, which is the average amount of time
required for female ticks to a ach, breed, engorge fully, and
detach. Both A. maculatum and D. variabilis are capable of
transmi ing pathogens to dogs (see Table 109.1). Due to the
substantial and year-round activity of various tick species in the
central United States and the potential for tick-borne pathogen
transmission, the necessity of continuous administration of
acaricides and control of other parasites was discussed with
Amos’ new owners.

110: Mites

KEY POINTS
Cheyletiella spp. (‘Walking Dandruff’)
• First Described: Cheyletiella parasitovorax was first described
from the fur of rabbits by Megnin in 1878 as the genus
“Cheyletus.” In 1885, Canestrini erected the genus
Cheyletiella. Robert Smiley described Cheyletiella yasguri as
a primary infestation on dogs in 1965, and Cheyletiella blakei
as a new species from cats in 1970.
• Cause: Cheyletiella yasguri, Cheyletiella blakei (family
Cheyletidae, order Actinedida).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs (C. yasguri), cats (C. blakei).
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Direct contact with infested
animals or with mites in the environment.
• Major Clinical Signs: Mild to moderate dermatitis, excessive
scaling, and alopecia usually along the dorsal aspect of the
head, neck, and back. Pruritus may be the primary presenting
complaint or, in subclinical carriers of mites, absent.
• Differential Diagnoses: Flea allergy dermatitis, other mite
infestations (Demodex spp., Notoedres cati, Otodectes
cynotis, Sarcoptes scabiei), lice, mosquito allergy,
dermatophytosis, bacterial pyoderma, Malassezia dermatitis,
atopic dermatitis, cutaneous adverse food reactions,
autoimmune disease.
• Human Health Significance: Humans, especially those in
frequent contact with infested animals through shared
households or animal care teams, are very susceptible to
infestation with Cheyletiella spp. and may develop pruritus

vetexamprep.ir

and a papular, erythematous dermatitis, particularly on
regions of the body in direct contact while holding infested
animals, such as the forearms or abdomen.
Demodex spp. (Hair Follicle Mites, Red Mange,
Demodicosis, Demodectic Mange)
• First Described: Demodex canis was first described by Leydig
in 1859. Demodex cati was first described by Megnin in 1877
as Demodex folliculorum var. cati, and then later as D. cati by
Hirst in 1919. In 1997, Hillier and Desch described Demodex
injai, and in 1999, Demodex gatoi was described from a cat in
Louisiana, United States, by Desch and Stewart. Morphologic
variants (e.g., “Demodex cornei”) have occasionally been
described but later synonymized with existing species. Skin
lesions and otitis externa caused by unnamed Demodex spp.
have also been reported.
• Cause: Demodex canis, Demodex injai, Demodex cati,
Demodex gatoi, Demodex sp. (family Demodicidae, suborder
Prostigmata, order Trombidiformes).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs (D. canis, D. injai); cats (D. cati, D. gatoi,
Demodex sp.).
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide, with D. canis and D. cati
reported more commonly and in a wider distribution than the
other species.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Most Demodex species are
thought to be transferred from dam to offspring early in the
neonatal period upon close contact during nursing. Some
species (e.g., D. gatoi) are contagious and can be transmitted
via direct contact among co-housed young or adult animals.
• Major Clinical Signs: Localized demodicosis: focal regions of
mild to moderate alopecia and hyperkeratosis, often on the
face and usually not pruritic. Generalized demodicosis
(juvenile or adult onset): moderate to severe alopecia,
erythema, and alopecia with folliculitis and furunculosis;
pustules and crusts are often present and secondary
pyoderma, which may be pruritic, can lead to sepsis. Lesions
develop anywhere on the body, including periorbital, pedal, or
associated with otitis externa.

vetexamprep.ir

• Differential Diagnoses: Flea allergy dermatitis, other mite
infestations (N. cati, O. cynotis, S. scabiei), lice, mosquito
allergy, dermatophytosis, bacterial pyoderma (often present
with demodicosis), Malassezia dermatitis, atopic dermatitis,
cutaneous adverse food reactions, autoimmune disease.
• Human Health Significance: None known. Demodex spp. of
dogs and cats are not transmitted to humans.
Sarcoptes scabiei (Itch Mite, Scabies, Sarcoptic Mange)
• First Described: Sarcoptes scabiei was first described in 1689
by Bonomo and Cestoni, and is widely considered to be the
first known human disease with a confirmed microscopic
etiology (Arlian and Morgan, 2017). Mites infesting different
hosts are generally regarded as somewhat host-specific
varieties of the larger S. scabiei species group.
• Cause: Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis (family Sarcoptidae, order
Sarcoptiformes).
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, wild canids, especially coyotes, wolves,
and red fox (Vulpes vulpes); rarely cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Highly contagious through
direct contact with infested animals.
• Major Clinical Signs: Intense pruritus, hyperkeratosis,
alopecia, self-excoriations. If chronic, weight loss and
decreased body condition. Lesions are often most
pronounced on the margins of pinnae, lateral elbows, and
lateral tarsi. If immunocompromised, profound hyperkeratosis
may develop in a condition referred to as “crusted scabies.”
• Differential Diagnoses: Flea allergy dermatitis, other mite
infestations (Demodex spp., O. cynotis), lice, mosquito allergy,
dermatophytosis, bacterial pyoderma, Malassezia dermatitis,
atopic dermatitis, cutaneous adverse food reactions,
autoimmune disease.
• Human Health Significance: Humans, especially those in
frequent contact with infested animals through shared
households or animal care teams, are very susceptible to
infestation with S. scabiei var. canis from dogs and may
develop pruritus and a papular, erythematous dermatitis,
particularly on regions of the body in direct contact while

vetexamprep.ir

holding infested animals, such as the forearms or abdomen.
However, outbreaks of human scabies that occur in shared
housing (e.g., nursing homes, prisons, dormitories) are
caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis and are of human
origin.
Notoedres cati (Feline Head and Neck Mange)
• First Described: Notoedres cati was first described as a small
feline Sarcoptes sp. by Hering in 1838, and then as a distinct
genus and species by Railliet in 1893.
• Cause: Notoedres cati (family Sarcoptidae, order
Sarcoptiformes).
• Affected Hosts: Cats, wild felids.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Highly contagious through
direct contact with infested animals.
• Major Clinical Signs: Intense pruritus, alopecia, and
hyperkeratotic crusts, particularly on the pinnae, head, and
feet, often presenting with self-excoriation which can be
severe.
• Differential Diagnoses: Flea allergy dermatitis, other mite
infestations (Demodex spp., O. cynotis), lice, mosquito allergy,
dermatophytosis, bacterial pyoderma, Malassezia dermatitis,
atopic dermatitis, cutaneous adverse food reactions,
autoimmune disease.
• Human Health Significance: Humans, especially those in
frequent contact with infested cats through shared households
or animal care teams, are very susceptible to infestation with
N. cati and may develop pruritus and a papular, erythematous
dermatitis, particularly on regions of the body in direct contact
while holding infested animals, such as the forearms or
abdomen.
Otodectes cynotis (Ear Mites)
• First Described: Ear mites were originally described as
Sarcoptes cynotis by Hering in 1838 and reclassified as
Otodectes cynotis by Neveu-Lemaire in 1938.
• Cause: Otodectes cynotis (family Psoroptidae, order
Sarcoptiformes).

vetexamprep.ir

• Affected Hosts: Cats, dogs.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Direct contact with infested
animals; transfer particularly common during neonatal period.
• Major Clinical Signs: Otitis externa characterized by otic
pruritus, excessive dark cerumen, head shaking, and, in some
cases, bloody discharge; mites usually confined to ear canal.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other otic mite infestations (Demodex
spp.), mosquito allergy, dermatophytosis, otitis externa
caused by bacteria or Malassezia, atopic dermatitis,
cutaneous adverse food reactions, autoimmune disease.
• Human Health Significance: Although rare, there are a few
isolated anecdotal case reports of human infestation with O.
cynotis.

Introduction
The term “mites” refers to a large, diverse group of arthropods in
the class Arachnida, subclass Acari, and include free-living,
commensal, and parasitic species. Closely related to ticks,
parasitic mites can cause considerable disease in infested hosts.
Knowledge of their preferred hosts, location, collection strategies,
and identifying features can assist in diagnosis and selection of
eﬀective treatment and control strategies. Most parasitic mites are
diﬃcult to observe without a light microscope. As obligate
parasites, most common mites remain on the host for the entirety
of their life cycle and are transmi ed among animals by direct
contact; because of this, large populations can develop on
susceptible animals. Chiggers (trombiculid mites) are a notable
exception and are acquired as larvae from the environment.

Cheyletiella SPP.
Etiology and Epidemiology
Cheyletiella spp. are prostigmatid mites that infest the fur and skin
of cats, dogs, and rabbits worldwide. The genus is easily
recognizable by its distinct, large palpal claws (Fig. 110.1).

vetexamprep.ir

Identifying Cheyletiella to the species level can be challenging.
Individual species are not host-speciﬁc but have strong host
associations, with Cheyletiella yasguri most commonly associated
with dogs, Cheyletiella blakei with cats, and Cheyletiella parasitovorax
with rabbits. All three species have been reported in human
Cheyletiella infestations. 1–3
The mites are intimate ectoparasites, spending their entire life
cycle on the host. They have six developmental stages: egg,
prelarva, larva, a ﬁrst and second nymphal stage, and adult. 4 All
motile stages are parasitic. Adult females deposit single, elliptical
eggs that range in size 190–260 µm by 110–140 µm. 1 , 5 Eggs are
wrapped in ﬁnely woven threads a ached to the hair shaft
approximately 2–3 mm above the base. 5
The prelarva and larva develop within the egg. The prelarva is a
legless, inactive, nonfeeding stage. The larva hatches from the egg
and molts through the ﬁrst (protonymph) and second
(deutonymph) nymphal stages before developing in to adults.
Adult Cheyletiella spp. are yellowish and large, barely visible to
the unaided eye. Adult females measure approximately 500 × 315
µm and males measure approximately 350 × 225 µm. 1 , 5 All
parasitic stages have large palpal claws that lie lateral to the
mouthparts (gnathostoma) and feather-like appendages
(empodia) at the distal extremities of the legs (tarsi) (see Fig.
110.1). The life cycle varies in duration from 21 to 35 days. 3 , 6–10
Cheyletiella spp. mites live in the hair of the host and travel to
the epidermis to feed on the keratin layer. 4 The mites do not
burrow in the epidermis. 3 , 9 Instead, they pierce the epidermis
with their chelicerae to feed on tissue ﬂuids. 3 , 5 Regardless of
humidity or temperature, immature stages and males die within
48 hours of leaving the host, whereas females may be hardier and
can live oﬀ the host for 10 days if kept in cool conditions. 5
Transmission of mites is by direct and indirect contact; mites
may also be acquired from the environment. Humans are
transiently infested and human-mediated transfer among animals
is possible. Infestations are contagious among young animals and
can spread quickly in multiple-animal situations, such as kennels
and ca eries. The introduction of a new cat or dog, even if
apparently healthy, is a risk factor for infestation of other animals
in the household. 11 , 12 Transmission is likely on fomites, such as

vetexamprep.ir

brushes and collars. “Phoresy,” whereby Cheyletiella spp. mites
a ach themselves to other arthropods for the purpose of travel,
has been suggested, including C. blakei and C. parasitovorax with
ﬂeas, and C. yasguri with the dog louse ﬂy, Hippobosca longipennis.

13-16

Pathogenesis
The feeding of mites on the keratin layer of the epidermis results
in a subacute, nonsuppurative dermatitis with slight
hyperkeratosis and vacuolization of epidermal cells. Varying
degrees of superﬁcial perivascular dermatitis may be observed
with nonspeciﬁc inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrate. 5 , 12 , 17 Occasionally,
lymphoplasmacytic dermatitis develops. Eosinophils vary from
few to many. Mite segments may be present in hyperkeratotic
stratum corneum. 10 , 12

Adult Cheyletiella sp., causative
agent of “walking dandruff” on dogs, cats, and
rabbits, are usually found in superficial
hyperkeratotic flakes shed from infested
animals. The large palpal claws (arrows)
