vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Features
Clinical signs associated with Cheyletiella sp. infestation include
scaling, crusting, and dermatitis; infestations may not cause
clinical signs in some individuals. Skin scaling, characterized by
powdery, meal-like scurf or dandruﬀ, is usually observed on the
dorsum, particularly in the sacral region. 5 , 6 , 18 Scaling may not
be obvious in animals that aggressively groom; self-trauma
commonly occurs. In severe cases, scaling and mites may be
present over most of the body surface. Pruritus can vary from
absent to severe. 6 , 18 The intensity of clinical signs may not be
proportionate to the mite density and is thought to be related to a
hypersensitivity reaction. 9 , 12 Infestations on young dogs may be
more severe, with older dogs more likely to be subclinical carriers.
3,5

Diagnosis
Direct Microscopic Examination
Diagnosis of cheyletiellosis is performed by directly visualizing
the mites or by microscopic examination of material collected
from the infested animal. Evidence of mites moving among
debris, often with adherent scales, has given cheyletiellosis the
common name of “walking dandruﬀ.” Combing is a
recommended diagnostic technique but fails to conﬁrm mites in
15% of infested dogs and 58% of cats. 9 , 19–21 To examine by
combing, the haircoat on the back, especially over the sacral area,
is parted and a ﬂea comb or brush used to collect scurf; scales and
other material are placed on dark paper and examined for
movement among the debris. Material can also be transferred to a
microscope slide with a few drops of mineral oil, a coverslip
applied, and examined microscopically. 19 Other collection
methods include using clear tape to examine scurf, superﬁcial
skin scrapes, and hair plucks to evaluate for eggs; clipping the
hair in long-haired animals may facilitate examination. 22 A
modiﬁed vacuum technique with in-line ﬁlters has been described
and was demonstrated to be more eﬃcient than tape preparations,
skin scraping, or hair plucking but is not widely available. 9 Fecal
ﬂotation may also demonstrate mites and their eggs, particularly
in cats that frequently groom. 8

vetexamprep.ir

Regardless of the method employed, ﬁnding mites may be
diﬃcult. 8 , 12 , 21 The number of mites present may be highly
variable and low, particularly if the animal is over-grooming or if
the area being sampled is small. 8 , 9 , 12 , 21 Combing in
combination with other diagnostic tests may yield be er results. 9
, 23 In some cases in which mites are not demonstrated but there is
considerable suspicion, empiric treatment may be warranted; in
these circumstances, other animals in the household should also
be treated. 23
Comparatively speaking, Cheyletiella spp. are one of the larger
mites encountered. Adults are yellowish, have a waist-like
appearance (more pronounced in females), and very large palps
that end with prehensile claws, giving the appearance of an extra
pair of legs. An M-shaped peritreme can be observed in the
gnathostome, just posterior to the chelicerae. The legs terminate
with comb-like appendages (empodia). In addition to the number
and arrangement of setae, the shape of the sensory organs
(solenidia) on genu I of the legs has been used to identify
Cheyletiella to species—the organs on C. yasguri are heart-shaped,
those on C. blakei are conical, and C. parasitovorax has spherical
organs. 4 However, there is much variation in solenidia shape in
immature stages, and variation can even sometimes be observed
on an individual adult. 4
Serology
Serologic assays have not been developed to detect Cheyletiella
spp. antibodies. In one study, protein electrophoresis was used to
assess infested dogs, but gammopathy was not demonstrated. 12
Immunologic cross-reactions between Cheyletiella spp. and the
dust mites Dermatophagoides farinae and Dermatophagoides
pteronyssinus have been documented, a phenomenon also
observed with other parasitic mites. 12
Laboratory Abnormalities
CBCs and chemistry panels from infested animals are generally
unremarkable. In one study, mild peripheral eosinophilia was
observed in 2 of 23 infested dogs that resolved after treatment. 12
Gross Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Scaling, crusting, and dermatitis are commonly seen in animals
with cheyletiellosis, although subclinical infestations also occur.
Lesions are most evident on the back, particularly over the sacral
region. Desquamation results in bran-like exfoliative debris in
aﬀected areas. In an uncomplicated case, very li le dermatitis or
pruritus is observed and alopecia is mild or absent. However,
papular, crusting eruptions, scabies-like lesions, alopecia, and
severe pruritus can develop due to hypersensitivity reactions. 10 ,

12 , 24

Treatment and Prognosis
No products are FDA label-approved for use against Cheyletiella
mites, but several eﬃcacious oﬀ-label treatments have been
described. Treatments reported to be eﬀective include
transdermal selamectin applied for 3 consecutive months to cats,
or every 2 weeks to dogs for four treatments; 8 , 23 two treatments
of transdermal moxidectin (applied in combination with
imidacloprid) administered 4 weeks apart also cleared Cheyletiella
sp. infestations in a group of dogs. 25 Sarolaner was reported to be
eﬀective in treating cheyletiellosis in four dogs; other systemic
isoxazolines are also expected to be eﬀective. 26 Milbemycin oxime
was also eﬀective in treating dogs (2 mg/kg, PO, q7d for 3 to 9
weeks). 12 Although eﬀective when given PO or SC, high-dose,
oﬀ-label large animal preparations of ivermectin or other
macrocyclic lactones are not recommended due to safety concerns;
if used, treatment must be continued weekly for as long as 6 to 8
weeks. 19–21
Topical ﬁpronil has been used with success to treat canine
cheyletiellosis using a 0.25% spray, and a 10% (w/v) spot-on was
eﬀective for cats. 27 , 28 Other topical therapies include lime sulfur
dips and pyrethroid sprays and shampoos. 22 Amitraz topically at
250 ppm has been used to treat canine cheyletiellosis but is
contraindicated in cats and is not considered the treatment of
choice for dogs and canine amitraz products are not available in
many areas. 19 , 29 An alternative topical treatment for cats and
dogs is 3-weekly baths with 1.0% selenium sulﬁde shampoo. 22
Regardless of the treatment used, continuing to treat for a
suﬃcient period of time is of particular importance. The treatment

vetexamprep.ir

period may be adjusted to address the severity of infestation,
number of animals involved, the product being used, housing
conditions, and the possibility of environmental contamination. 20
Because the mites are not highly host-speciﬁc and some animals
remain subclinical, all animals in a household or facility should be
treated simultaneously. Reinfestation from oﬀ-host females and
eggs is considered possible; accordingly, the environment should
be cleaned and treated with products that have acaricidal activity.
Bedding and grooming tools should be discarded, washed using
hot temperatures, or treated with an acaricide. Diagnostic
procedures should be repeated to ensure treatment success, but
due to the diﬃculty of isolating mites and the hardiness of eggs to
treatment, therapy should continue for at least 2 to 4 weeks after
signs have resolved regardless of the results of examination for
mites. 19 Hypersensitivity reactions and accompanying pruritus
may be alleviated if miticidal treatment is accompanied by a short
course of anti-inﬂammatory glucocorticoid treatment if not
contraindicated. Treatment of cheyletiellosis usually has a good
prognosis when all animals can be treated and reinfestation
prevented.

Immunity
Studies investigating the immune response during cheyletiellosis
have not been reported. Observations that young animals appear
predisposed to infestation and that infestations can be selflimiting suggests that immunity develops. 1 , 3 Severe cases are in
all probability the result of hypersensitivity reactions. 12

Prevention
Prevention of cheyletiellosis entails that there is no direct or
indirect transmission of the mite. When new pets are introduced
to a household, they should be checked for mites and treated.
Previously used grooming tools and other fomites should be
avoided. Routine use of products eﬀective against Cheyletiella spp.
(e.g., transdermal macrocyclic lactones, oral or transdermal
isoxazolines) would also be expected to limit infestations.
Anecdotal observations have been made that in warmer areas

vetexamprep.ir

where year-round ﬂea control is practiced, the prevalence of
Cheyletiella spp. mites has substantially decreased. 30

Public Health Aspects
Pet owners, animal care teams, and others who are in frequent
contact with infested animals are susceptible to developing
dermatitis associated with Cheyletiella spp. Approximately 20%–
40% of owners of infested animals are aﬀected. 1–4 , 7–9 , 18 Small,
pruritic, erythematous papules are most frequently observed on
areas of the body that are in contact while holding infested
animals, such as the arms, abdomen, or legs. 2 , 3 , 7 The lesions
develop into vesicles or pustules, and eventually demonstrate
central necrosis. 3 Arthralgia and peripheral eosinophilia have
been reported in some aﬀected individuals. 31 In some cases, the
ﬁrst indication that a pet is infested may be the owners’ dermatitis
if the pet is apparently healthy. Mites are rarely recovered from
people and do not reproduce on humans; treatment of all animals
in the household prevents further lesions from developing. 8

Demodex SPP.
Etiology and Epidemiology
Demodex spp. are prostigmatid mites that live primarily in the
pilosebaceous unit or the stratum corneum of mammals; mites
occasionally venture to the surface and can be transferred between
hosts of the same species by direct contact. At present, two species
infest dogs and three are reported from cats although additional
variants have been described. 32 Demodex spp. mites have
elongated bodies (Fig. 110.2) that consist of a cranial gnathosoma
where the mouthparts are located, a podosoma bearing short,
stubby legs, and a caudal opisthosoma; an anus is absent. Demodex
canis and Demodex cati are considered normal commensal fauna
ubiquitous on dogs and cats, respectively, live in the hair follicles
and sebaceous glands, and are transmi ed early in life by direct
contact from dams to nursing neonates. 33 , 34 Dogs may also
harbor Demodex injai, which has a long, thin opisthosoma and is
associated with hyperplasia of sebaceous glands and excess
sebum production. 32 Cats can be infested with a shorter,

vetexamprep.ir

unnamed Demodex sp., or with Demodex gatoi, which is very short
and stubby; both primarily infest the stratum corneum. 30

Elongated adults (A) and spindleshaped egg (B) of Demodex canis are readily
found on skin scrapes from dogs with
generalized demodicosis. Courtesy of Megan
FIG. 110.2

Lineberry, National Center for Veterinary Parasitology.

Demodex spp. females deposit eggs in the infested hair follicles.
Larvae hatch from eggs, feed, and molt, developing through two
nymphal stages before becoming adults. Comprehensive life
history studies on Demodex spp. of pets are lacking, but the life
cycle is thought to be completed in 14 to 21 days. Females are
diploid and males haploid. Infestations with D. canis and D. cati
are considered universal and treatment of contact animals is not
required to eﬀectively address cases. In contrast, D. gatoi can be
transferred between individual cats, and thus this mite should be
considered contagious and managed accordingly. 30 , 32

Pathogenesis
Most Demodex spp. mites are commensal organisms, and
populations are kept in check by the host immune system;
contagious feline D. gatoi infestations that spread in multi-cat
facilities are the exception. 32 Immune restriction occasionally fails
in young, otherwise healthy dogs, and in adult,
immunocompromised dogs or cats, allowing mite populations to
increase dramatically and leading to clinical disease. In dogs,

vetexamprep.ir

localized demodicosis and juvenile-onset generalized demodicosis
are thought to develop following temporary alterations in CMI;
the tendency to develop the condition has a genetic basis. 32
Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, speciﬁc DLA
haplotypes have been associated with juvenile-onset generalized
demodicosis in some predisposed breeds. 35
Risk factors associated with juvenile-onset (<1.5 years old)
generalized demodicosis in dogs include coccidiosis, hookworm
infection, pyoderma, short haircoat, and pit bull-type breed. 36
Although any breed of dog may be aﬀected, including mixed
breeds, increased risk of disease has been reported for the
American Staﬀordshire terrier, Staﬀordshire bull terrier, Chinese
shar-pei, French bulldog, English bulldog, pit bull-type dog,
boxer, Argentinian mastiﬀ, and Sealyham terrier. 35–37
Immunocompromising
conditions
and
the
use
of
immunosuppressive therapies are thought to be responsible for
adult-onset (>4 years old) canine demodicosis, and for feline
demodicosis caused by D. cati. 32 , 33 Conditions associated with
adult-onset canine demodicosis include hyperadrenocorticism,
hypothyroidism, leishmaniosis, and other vector-borne infections
(babesiosis, ehrlichiosis). A history of neoplasia or atopic
dermatitis has also been associated with generalized demodicosis
but may be related to chemotherapy or glucocorticoid treatment.
32 Wire-haired fox terriers and other terrier breeds are more often
reported with disease due to D. injai infestation and associated
hyperplastic sebaceous glands; aﬀected dogs are older (average
age of 8 years) and often have a history of allergy, endocrine
disease, neoplasia, or immunosuppression. 38–40
Predisposing conditions for feline demodicosis caused by D. cati
include FIV or FeLV infection, hyperadrenocorticism, systemic
lupus erythematosus, diabetes mellitus, and xanthoma. 32 , 33
Localized D. cati–associated feline demodicosis has been
described with squamous cell carcinoma. 41 Clear breed
predispositions have not been identiﬁed for feline demodicosis
although some consider the condition more common in Siamese
and Burmese cats. 30 Infestations with D. gatoi can result in
pruritis although not all infested cats develop clinical signs. 42
Clusters of feline D. gatoi infestations have been reported in multicat households involving several breeds and all ages of cats. 42

Clinical Features
Dogs
Dogs with localized demodicosis due to D. canis typically exhibit
few (1 to 4), small (≤2.5 cm diameter), nonpruritic areas of
alopecia and scaling. When localized, the condition is of only
minor cosmetic concern. In contrast, dogs with generalized
demodicosis can have moderate to severe disseminated skin
lesions, deep pyoderma, and systemic illness. 10 , 32 Juvenile-onset
generalized demodicosis develops in dogs less than 1.5 years of
age and is considered due to an underlying genetic defect,
whereas adult-onset (>4 years of age) is thought to be associated
with immunocompromising disease state or administration of
immunosuppressive drugs. 43 Mite proliferation in the hair
follicles and sebaceous glands leads to large focal or multifocal
areas of alopecia, comedone formation, and erythema, with
lesions often coalescing over time. Severe pododemodicosis may
develop and, when present on at least two feet, is considered
indicative of generalized demodicosis even if feet are the only area
aﬀected. Follicular hyperpigmentation can be evident. In dogs
with mild to moderate demodicosis due to D. canis infection but
without secondary bacterial infection, pruritus is usually absent.
As disease progresses and secondary bacterial or fungal infections
establish, associated pruritus may become evident. Over time,
deep, pustular pyoderma can develop with draining tracts,
lymphadenomegaly, fever, and lethargy; in the absent of
treatment, fatality from sepsis can occur. 32 Dogs with
demodicosis due to D. injai also present with alopecia and an
erythematous dermatitis as well as characteristic excessive sebum
production dorsally and hyperplastic sebaceous glands. 39
Cats
Cats with demodicosis due to D. cati infection develop localized
or generalized areas of alopecia, scale, crusting, and erythema;
pruritus is variable and pyoderma is rare. 30 Lesions most
commonly appear ﬁrst on the face and can be associated with
otitis externa either as the primary focus of the infestation or as
part of a generalized demodicosis. 44 Mite proliferation can also be
localized to carcinoma in situ lesions. In cats with clinical signs
due to D. gatoi, pruritus is often the primary owner complaint and

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
p
y
p
other clinical signs (e.g., alopecia) associated with excessive
grooming secondary to intense pruritus are often found on the
abdomen and thorax. Hypersensitivity appears to develop in
some cats infested with D. gatoi, while others remain subclinically
infected. 32 , 33 , 42 , 44 Due to the contagious nature of D. gatoi
infestations, many animals in a ca ery or multi-cat household
may harbor mites or experience clinical disease. 42 , 45 , 46

Diagnosis
Direct Microscopic Examination
Demodex spp. mites are readily recovered from dogs with
localized or generalized demodectic mange. Although considered
normal fauna, when present together with characteristic
pathology and in high enough numbers to readily detect using
light microscopic examination of skin scrapings, treatment is
indicated. To collect material for microscopic examination, a
scalpel blade with a small amount of mineral oil is used to scrape
aﬀected areas of skin in the direction of hair growth; application
of lateral pressure to a skin fold while scraping increases the
recovery of mites. Scrapes should be collected from multiple
aﬀected areas, when present. Primary lesions with pustules or
alopecia are more likely to have mites than ulcerated areas.
Collected material is transferred to microscope slides, coverslips
applied, and examined for mites. When infestations are active,
eggs may be numerous and all stages of mites (larvae, nymphs,
adults) present; mites are often active in fresh mineral oil
preparations. 32
Other methods useful to examine for mites include clear tape
preparations from patients with seborrheic dermatitis; direct
examination of purulent material expressed from pustules or
draining tracts in dogs with deep pyoderma; and trichograms or
hair plucks, which may be preferred for collecting specimens from
areas of the face and feet that are diﬃcult to scrape. If using
trichograms, many (50–100) plucked hairs should be collected,
transferred to a microscope slide with mineral oil, and applied to
a coverslip to facilitate examination. When lymphadenomegaly is
present, mites may be identiﬁed in lymph node aspirates. Otic
swabs allow identiﬁcation of Demodex sp. mites associated with
otitis externa. Mites ingested by dogs that chew aﬀected skin can

vetexamprep.ir

also be found on fecal ﬂotation; however, this method alone is not
considered a sensitive means of diagnosis. 32 , 34 In general,
recovery of Demodex sp. mites is more challenging in cats, and
especially from cats infested with D. gatoi, which is superﬁcial and
may elicit hypersensitivity leading to excessive grooming. 44 Cats
that are active groomers reduce mite populations on the skin and
may only have mites detected in feces. 46
To allow mites to be easily visualized, the microscope lighting
should be adjusted to optimize contrast by closing the condenser.
Demodex spp. mites are readily identiﬁed by their characteristic
shape (Fig. 110.2A); measurements that allow identiﬁcation of
diﬀerent species are provided in Table 110.1. Eggs are spindleshaped (Fig. 110.2B) and often recovered on fecal ﬂotation or skin
scraping at initial diagnosis before treatment is instituted. 34 The
number and stage of mites present in skin scrapings can be used
to monitor progress during treatment. As lesions resolve, mite
populations will be reduced; only a small number of adults may
be found, eggs are rare if present at all, and many mites are dead.
10

Serology
Serologic assays to conﬁrm demodicosis are not available.
Common Demodex spp. mites (e.g., D. canis, D. cati) are considered
part of normal ﬂora and infestations universal.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Dogs with generalized demodicosis and deep pyoderma may
have anemia of inﬂammatory disease or an inﬂammatory
leukogram; an elevated concentration of C-reactive protein and
haptoglobin, reduced butyrylcholinesterase activity, and reduced
paraoxonase-1 activity that normalize with treatment. 47 Cats may
have normal hemograms or changes associated with comorbidities. 33

Treatment and Prognosis
Dogs
Localized demodicosis usually resolves without treatment within
2 months. 32 If topical treatment is desired, benzoyl peroxide

vetexamprep.ir

shampoo or gel or rotenone ointment can be used. 32 , 43
Progression to generalized demodicosis is considered rare and
prognosis is excellent. Prescribing transdermal moxidectin and
imidacloprid for heartworm, intestinal parasite, and ﬂea control,
or an isoxazoline for ﬂea and tick control, would be expected to
protect against progression although this approach has not been
evaluated experimentally. Dogs with only demodectic otitis
externa or pododermatits beneﬁt from acaricidal treatment even
though mites and lesions are localized. 32 , 43
Dogs with juvenile-onset generalized demodicosis can usually
be treated with acaricides and, if indicated, antibiotics for
secondary bacterial pyoderma. Underlying conditions are not
considered common; further diagnostic testing is not considered
necessary and the prognosis for recovery is good. 32 In contrast,
adult-onset generalized demodicosis is a more serious condition
and successful treatment requires long-term commitment;
although most dogs recover with treatment, lifelong therapy may
be required in some patients to restrict mite proliferation,
particularly if the underlying condition cannot be identiﬁed and
addressed. Without treatment, fatalities can result, and relapse
following treatment is common, particularly when therapy is
terminated early. 32
Successful treatment of adult-onset generalized demodicosis
involves a thorough diagnostic evaluation to identify and address
any underlying conditions, management of pyoderma when
present, and acaricidal treatment of mites. Although recurrence
with estrus is considered anecdotal, intact females should be
spayed once the skin has healed to allow surgery to both limit
recurrence and breeding of susceptible animals. Topical
antimicrobial shampoos (e.g., benzoyl peroxide, chlorhexidine)
are adequate to manage secondary bacterial infections in most
cases; occasionally the severity of pyoderma and risk of sepsis
necessitates use of systemic antibiotics. Symptomatic relief may
result from acaricidal therapy alone, but recurrence is likely if
underlying conditions are not identiﬁed and addressed.
Continued regular monitoring of the overall health of dogs with
adult-onset generalized demodicosis is recommended as
underlying conditions not evident at initial presentation may
become apparent over time. 10 , 32 , 43

vetexamprep.ir

Widely available miticidal treatments include systemic
isoxazolines and macrocyclic lactones; all are oﬀ-label in the
United States. Systemic isoxazolines (afoxolaner, ﬂuralaner,
lotilaner, sarolaner) approved in dogs for ﬂea and tick control are
eﬀective against generalized demodicosis when administered
according to label directions, every 4 to 12 weeks depending on
product used. 32 , 48–57 Most (afoxolaner, ﬂuralaner, lotilaner) are
available for use in dogs > 8 weeks of age and all should be used
with caution in dogs with a history of seizures. Transdermal
moxidectin/imidacloprid administered weekly is eﬀective against
demodicosis and labeled for this purpose in Europe; use of
weekly transdermal moxidectin/imidacloprid is recommended
only for mild to moderate cases. 32 , 58 , 59 Milbemycin oxime (1 to
2 mg/kg/day PO) is also safe and eﬀective although cost of daily
use may be prohibitive. 56 , 60 Reports evaluating eﬃcacy of
milbemycin oxime/afoxolaner combination products are not yet
available. 32 Response to treatment should be monitored with
monthly skin scrapes and miticidal therapy continued for at least
8 weeks past ﬁrst negative skin scrape. 32

Although management is involved and the treatment course
may be long and expensive, most dogs with generalized
demodicosis can recover and euthanasia is no longer a common
consideration. The prognosis for recovery from generalized
demodicosis is be er in young dogs (<1.5 years) than in older
dogs. Spontaneous resolution from generalized demodicosis has
been reported in younger dogs although the incidence is
unknown and likely varies with breed and underlying condition.
32 , 43 , 59 Spontaneous resolution is not thought to occur in older
dogs; without treatment, the condition can be fatal.
Cats
Demodicosis in cats may be treated with topical dips, systemic
macrocyclic lactones, or systemic isoxazolines. Weekly lime sulfur
dips (2%) have long been a mainstay of feline demodicosis
treatment; weekly amitraz rinses (0.0125%) have also been used. 32
However, feline patients often do not tolerate both approaches
well, and when several individual cats in a multi-cat household
are aﬀected, application of topical, body-wide rinses weekly can
be challenging. Weekly administration of transdermal
moxidectin/imidacloprid is also eﬀective and more easily
achieved. 32 , 60 Fluralaner and sarolaner are also eﬀective for
treatment of feline demodicosis 61 – 63 ; other isoxazolines
approved for cats (i.e., lotilaner) may also be eﬀective.
Combination macrocyclic lactone/isoxazoline products (e.g.,
moxidectin/ﬂuralaner, selamectin/sarolaner) are available for cats;
inclusion of both drug classes in treatment likely supports
eﬃcacy.

Immunity
An underlying immune deﬁcit is considered responsible for
development of localized and generalized demodicosis;

vetexamprep.ir

addressing stress caused by poor nutrition or presence of other
infections improves patient health and supports treatment of
demodicosis. A comparison of pit bull terrier-type dogs with
juvenile-onset generalized demodicosis with healthy age- and
breed-matched controls revealed signiﬁcantly higher serum
concentrations of IL-2, IL-18, and monocyte chemoa ractant
protein-1 in dogs with generalized demodicosis, a ﬁnding
interpreted to reﬂect an appropriate immune response. 64
The beneﬁcial eﬀects of immunostimulants in demodicosis
treatment are not clear, and most studies evaluating potential
adjunctive therapies are small. 32 Inactivated Parapoxvirus ovis
administered subcutaneously together with amitraz dips
decreased time to remission (85 days) when compared with
amitraz dips alone (104 days). 65 Insuﬃcient evidence is available
to support use of vitamin E, muramyl dipeptide, or herbal and
homeopathic products in treatment of demodicosis. 43

Prevention
Judicious breeding can limit the number of li ers that develop
demodicosis. 10 The American Academy of Veterinary
Dermatology and the consensus guidelines from the World
Association for Veterinary Dermatology have consistently
recommended neutering all dogs with generalized demodicosis
and state that both dogs with demodicosis and their parents
should not be used for breeding. 32 Although more research is
needed, administering ﬂuralaner 10 days before breeding reduced
the number of puppies that developed disease. 66 Monthly
administration of moxidectin/imidacloprid may prevent relapse in
dogs with generalized demodectic mange. 67 Administering
isoxazolines reduces but does not eliminate populations of
Demodex sp. mites from treated dogs. 68 Routine administration of
isoxazolines would also be expected to support remission for dogs
with generalized demodicosis. Quarantine and prophylactic
treatment of newly acquired cats should limit introduction of D.
gatoi into a facility.
Underlying conditions should be identiﬁed and addressed
whenever possible. Improving nutrition, identifying and
eliminating intestinal parasites, and reducing environmental

vetexamprep.ir

stress in stray or rescued dogs supports recovery. Co-morbidities
and other inciting causes are not always identiﬁed, but one review
of 41 cases of adult-onset demodicosis identiﬁed exogenous
glucocorticoid use in allergy patients (24%), hyperadrenocorticism
(19%), chemotherapy (15%), and hypothyroidism (12%) as
common potential underlying problems. 69 Relapse after
treatment occurs in 10% to 45% of canine patients due to stress
(including during estrus, pregnancy, or lactation), as well as when
systemic diseases are not well controlled. 10 , 43 Avoiding
immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids, oclacitinib
maleate, cyclosporine) in patients with a history of generalized
demodicosis is also recommended to reduce incidence of relapse.
43

Public Health Aspects
Canine and feline demodicosis are not zoonotic. Humans develop
disease due to overgrowth of Demodex spp. mites that only infest
humans (Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis) and that are
normal commensals of hair follicles and sebaceous glands.
Lesions most commonly appear on the face and include acne,
rosacea, pityriasis folliculorum, and blepharitis. A meta-analysis
found that prevalence and density of Demodex spp. mites were
signiﬁcantly higher in patients with rosacea than in controls. 70 , 71

Sarcoptes Scabiei Var. Canis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis is a burrowing mite in the order
Sarcoptiformes, family Sarcoptidae. Sarcoptid mites have a
distinctly rounded morphology with short legs that scarcely
project beyond the body margin. The anterior pretarsi of S. scabiei
consist of long, unsegmented pedicels, also referred to as stalks,
that terminate in caruncles (suckers); females have these
structures on the ﬁrst and second pairs of legs, and males have
them on the ﬁrst, second, and fourth pair of legs. 34 The dorsum
has numerous transverse ridges and triangular scales or spines
and the anus is located at the posterior edge of the body. The S.
scabiei species complex is found worldwide and has been reported

vetexamprep.ir

from more than 100 species of mammals. 72 , 73 However,
infestations are generally regarded as caused by host-adapted
strains or “varieties” of the same core species, with host varieties
spread more readily among species to which each has adapted.
Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis is the strain reported from domestic
dogs and wild canids. Although S. scabiei var. canis will transfer to
and cause dermatitis on other hosts, including humans, these
infestations are generally considered self-limiting. 22 , 72 Sarcoptic
mange is rare in cats but occasionally reported. 22 , 74 Mites from
cats suspected to be S. scabiei may be Notoedres cati (see below) and
should be submi ed to a parasitologist with appropriate
diagnostic expertise for accurate diagnosis.
Sarcoptic mange has been described from domestic dogs and
wild canids worldwide. Sex and breed predilections have not
been reported, but younger dogs are overrepresented in case
series. 75 , 76 Mites are found in 1% or fewer of dogs in surveys and
are not recovered from many infested, clinically aﬀected dogs
even when pruritus is severe. 77–79 Accordingly, the true
prevalence of S. scabiei var. canis is not known. In areas where
infestations are common in dogs, antibodies may be present in a
majority of animals tested. One survey in Nigeria found
antibodies to S. scabiei in 67% of dogs. 78 A survey that utilized a
remote camera in Texas, United States, found lesions consistent
with sarcoptic mange in 72% of coyotes. 73 Sarcoptic mange is
considered a major mortality factor for red fox in the southeastern
United States, and mites are more readily recovered from wild
canids or domestic dogs with crusted scabies. 10 , 80
After mating, fertilized female mites burrow into the stratum
corneum, creating horizontal tunnels. The mites feed on ﬂuids
leaking from damaged tissues. While in tunnels, females oviposit
2 to 3 eggs per day over a lifespan of 2 months. The eggs hatch in
3 to 5 days. The larvae then crawl out onto the skin surface and
make shallow superﬁcial burrows termed “molting pockets”
wherein they feed and molt. After 2 to 3 days, larvae molt to the
nymphal stage and after 3 to 4 days, nymphs undergo two
subsequent molts to the adult stage. Males make their way to the
skin surface where they seek immature females. Mating may take
place on the skin surface or in molting pockets depending on the
location of the immature female. Immature and adult mites are

vetexamprep.ir

transmi ed by direct contact to other hosts and S. scabiei is
considered highly contagious; all dogs with known contact with
an infested dog should be treated. Infestation following indirect
contact via fomites (e.g., clippers, bedding) has also been reported
although oﬀ-host survival is limited. The entire life cycle usually
takes 17 to 21 days to complete, but generation times as short as
10 days have been described. 22

Pathogenesis
The burrowing activity of the fertilized female and its destructive
feeding behavior, as well as the deposition of eggs, molted
cuticles, and mite feces within the upper layers of the epidermis,
lead to varying levels of dermatitis characterized by intense
pruritus, alopecia, and hyperkeratotic lesions. Pruritus is observed
early after infestation and may be evident as early as 1 week prior
to development of lesions. A hypersensitivity reaction to mite
antigens, including mite feces, contributes to the pruritus. Mites
also release immunomodulating substances that shift immune
responses, including upregulation of IL-20 which may promote
hyperkeratosis. 72 , 81 Initial lesions consist of erythematous
maculopapular eruptions with alopecia and often ﬁrst appear in
areas where hair is sparse. Predilection sites include the ears,
particularly the margins of the pinnae, periocular region, face,
lateral elbows, and lateral hocks. As infestation spreads, the
ventral thorax and ventral abdomen may be aﬀected and lesions
can eventually cover the majority of the body. Extensive alopecia
and generalized lymphadenomegaly may be evident. 3 , 76 When
untreated, fatalities can result.
Biopsy of aﬀected areas reveals acanthosis, spongiosis,
hyperkeratosis, and prominent rete ridge formation; intracorneal
pustules may be present. 82 Biopsy lesions contain mixed cellular
inﬁltrates comprising mononuclear cells, neutrophils, plasma
cells, and mast cells. 83 Direct evidence of infestation (e.g., mites,
eggs, mite feces) conﬁrms infestation but may not be consistently
evident.
In
chronic
infestations,
licheniﬁcation
and
hyperpigmentation may be apparent and associated with selfexcoriation. Secondary bacterial infections are common and may
be promoted by mite-mediated inhibition of host complement. 84 ,
85 In some individuals, crusted scabies develops with profound

vetexamprep.ir

hyperkeratosis and an enormous number of mites present. In
humans, patients with crusted scabies develop a more
pronounced IgE response than patients with routine scabies. 86

Clinical Features
Intense pruritus is the most common clinical sign reported in dogs
with sarcoptic mange. In some case series, pruritus is reported in
only 56% to 74% of cases although severe hypersensitivity
reactions responsible for pruritus may limit mite populations,
precluding conﬁrmation of infestation and inclusion in case series
reports. 76 , 87 Other common signs include alopecia (43%), crusts
(41%–78%), lesions on the pinnae (41%), and scaling (24%–44%). 76
, 87 In one study evaluating treatment of naturally infested dogs,
pruritus, alopecia, and crusts or scales were reported in virtually
all cases. 88 Lesions may occur anywhere but are most
pronounced on the margins of the pinnae, lateral elbows, and
lateral tarsi. 3 , 10 However, sarcoptic mange should be considered
in any dog with a history of pruritus. Young or
immunocompromised animals may develop “crusted scabies”
characterized by marked, profound hyperkeratosis associated
with extremely large numbers of mites; patients with crusted
scabies are usually not pruritic. This condition is common in red
fox in the southeastern United States and has been reported in
young, malnourished dogs, dogs co-infected with Leishmania sp.,
and, rarely, in cats. 80 , 89 , 90

Diagnosis
Direct Microscopic Examination
Although mites are not recovered from approximately 50% of
canine patients, sarcoptic mange can be conﬁrmed directly by
identifying S. scabiei mites using microscopic examination of
multiple skin scrapes from the margin of aﬀected areas. To
perform skin scrapes, a small amount of mineral oil is applied to a
scalpel blade used to gently abrade aﬀected areas; the scurf thus
collected is transferred to a microscope slide, a coverslip applied,
and the material examined for characteristic mites. Females are
300–400 µm long and males are ∼250 µm long. Pretarsi on the
ﬁrst two pairs of legs have long, unsegmented pedicels each

vetexamprep.ir

bearing a caruncle; males also have these structures on the fourth
pair of legs. Numerous transverse ridges and triangular scales are
present on the dorsum and the anus is located at the posterior
edge of the body (Fig. 110.3). Because skin scraping is relatively
insensitive for conﬁrming a diagnosis of sarcoptic mange,
multiple areas should be examined and failure to detect mites
should not be used to eliminate S. scabiei var. canis as a potential
etiology. 10 , 22

Serology
Although not widely available, ELISAs have been developed to
support the diagnosis of S. scabiei in dogs. In ﬁeld evaluations
using microscopic detection of mites as the comparator, ELISA
has had 84%–96% sensitivity and 90% speciﬁcity. 78 , 91 Antibodies
are not detected until 4 weeks after infestation. Speciﬁcity can be
compromised by cross-reactivity with antibodies to common dust
mites (Dermatophagoides spp.) and false positives have been
reported in dogs with documented atopy associated with dust

vetexamprep.ir

mites.
Values on serum chemistry proﬁles are usually
unchanged. 94
Laboratory Abnormalities
Blood values in dogs with sarcoptic mange are largely
unremarkable. Hemoglobin and hematocrit concentrations
decrease with infestation, and neutrophil counts increase, but in
the absence of sepsis secondary to pyoderma, all remain within
normal limits. Eosinophilia is reported in some individual dogs
but is not consistently evident. 94
Gross Pathologic Findings
Dogs with sarcoptic mange develop erythematous, follicular,
papular dermatitis that is initially focal but spreads to become
multifocal and then generalized. Alopecia, hyperkeratosis, and
self-excoriations are common, and abundant crusts are often
noted. In the absence of treatment, secondary pyoderma
commonly develops. Mites are not easily recovered particularly
early in the course of disease; a high index of suspicion and
response to treatment can support a clinical diagnosis. 10 , 22

Treatment and Prognosis
Transdermal moxidectin and selamectin are FDA label-approved
for treatment of sarcoptic mange in dogs. In some countries,
amitraz dips or oral milbemycin oxime may also be approved. 95
Isoxazolines (e.g., afoxolaner, ﬂuralaner, lotilaner, sarolaner) have
been shown to be eﬀective; multiple doses may be necessary
depending on the product used. 87 , 88 , 95–97 Fipronil is labelapproved to aid in the control of sarcoptic mange and may help
limit infestations but is not recommended as a stand-alone
treatment. Older therapies, including high-dose, oﬀ-label
macrocyclic lactones intended for use in large animals or phosmet
dips are no longer recommended due to safety concerns and the
wide availability of safer, label-approved choices. Most dogs with
sarcoptic mange respond well to treatment. Pruritus is relieved
within a few days of instituting eﬀective acaricidal therapy, and
lesions resolve so long as treatment course is completed and
immunocompromise, malnutrition, or other co-morbidities can be
addressed.

vetexamprep.ir

Immunity
Both ﬁeld and experimental data indicate that dogs develop
immunity to S. scabiei var. canis. The preponderance of young
dogs in case series of clinical sarcoptic mange has been interpreted
as older dogs becoming less susceptible to infestation, presumably
due to prior exposure. 76 In experimental infestation trials, seven
of eight dogs developed immunity to S. scabiei var. canis; although
reinfested, immune dogs self-cleared mites within 1 to 2 months
of reinfestation and some dogs eliminated reinfestation in 3 to 4
weeks. 83 Biopsy specimens from immune dogs documented that
monocytes and neutrophils predominated in challenge
infestations and appeared more rapidly in sensitized dogs than in
naïve dogs undergoing a primary infestation; immune dogs also
had a more rapid antibody response that decreased as mite
populations decreased. 83

Prevention
Vaccines for S. scabiei are not available. Prevention requires
avoiding direct contact with dogs or wild canids that are likely to
harbor mites, limiting roaming, and routine use of control
products eﬀective against S. scabiei. 10 Dogs diagnosed with
sarcoptic mange should be conﬁned and all shared animal
facilities (e.g., dog parks, groomers, boarding kennels, dog day
care) avoided until treatment is completed and lesions are fully
resolved. All dogs in the same household or that have had direct
contact with an infested dog should be presumed infested and
treated simultaneously, including dogs that are not showing
evidence of clinical disease; subclinical carriers of mites contribute
to perpetuating infestations. 98 Routine use of products eﬀective
against S. scabiei (e.g., transdermal macrocyclic lactones, oral or
transdermal isoxazolines) would also be expected to limit
infestations.

Public Health Aspects
Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis is a human parasite that aﬀects
approximately 200 to 300 million people worldwide each year and
infests as many as 10% of children in developing countries. 99

vetexamprep.ir

Scabies is recognized as a neglected tropical disease by the WHO,
and cases appear to be increasing in developed countries. 100 , 101
Patients with primary scabies due to S. scabiei var. hominis, the
variety responsible for direct human-to-human transmission,
develop an erythematous, papular rash characterized by intense
pruritus; serpiginous burrows where mites have tunneled are
often apparent. Lesions associated with S. scabiei var. hominis most
commonly appear in the interdigital region, wrists, elbows, knees,
abdomen, and groin, and mites are transmi ed between humans
by prolonged, intimate contact. Institutional outbreaks are
frequently reported in nursing homes, dormitories, and prisons;
transmission among family members is also common but S. scabiei
var. hominis is not known to infest pets. 98 , 101 People are most
often treated with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin. 99
While zoonotic, cases of S. scabiei var. canis infestation are only a
concern in individuals that have direct contact with infested dogs
or wild canids. The rash usually develops within 1 to 4 days after
contact with an infested dog. Mites are rarely present and history
is key to reaching a diagnosis. 102 Although intensely pruritic,
once acquired by a person, S. scabiei var. canis mites do not
transfer to other humans. Preventing dermatitis associated with
zoonotic infestations requires use of appropriate preventives in
dogs to avoid development of infestations, prompt diagnosis and
treatment of infested dogs, and careful handling of dogs with skin
conditions consistent with mange or known to harbor mites. 98
Dogs or red fox with crusted scabies harbor a huge number of
mites and thus present an elevated zoonotic risk. Zoonotic
infestations may be managed symptomatically with topical
hydrocortisone creams or, if severe, treated systemically. 3 , 98

Notoedres Cati
Etiology and Epidemiology
Notoedres cati is a burrowing sarcoptid mite (order Sarcoptiformes,
family Sarcoptidae) of domestic cats and wild felids. Infestations
with N. cati have been reported in at least 18 diﬀerent host species,
including rabbits, and, rarely, dogs. 103 , 104 The parasite is most
commonly described from domestic cats and bobcats (Lynx rufus).
Although the rounded appearance and pretarsi (long, unjointed

vetexamprep.ir

pedicels ending in caruncles) are morphologically similar to S.
scabiei, N. cati is smaller (150–225 µm) than S. scabiei, lacks dorsal
spines, and the anus is dorsal rather than terminal (Fig. 110.4). 34
Other species of Notoedres infest rodents, procyonids, and bats. 103
The life cycle of N. cati is similar to that of S. scabiei, with larvae,
nymphs, and adults burrowing in the host skin, and requires
approximately 2 weeks. Females deposit eggs in burrows in the
skin of the face, ears, and, occasionally, legs of the host. Mites are
transferred between cats by direct contact. Cats infested with N.
cati are reported worldwide albeit less commonly than dogs with
S. scabiei var. canis. In North America, reports are more common
in the southern United States and Mexico. 30 , 103
A survey of feline parasites in pet cats from several countries in
Europe identiﬁed N. cati in only 3 of 1,519 cats but infestations are
considered more common in some countries, including Greece
(where prevalence in stray cats in a survey was 2.4%) and Brazil.
105–107 Local epizootics have also been reported and long-haired
cats are predisposed. 105 , 108 Infestations with N. cati are highly
contagious and may be seen as entire li ers aﬀected, in multi-cat
facilities, and in free-ranging felid populations. 10 , 108–110

vetexamprep.ir

Pathogenesis
Similar to S. scabiei, N. cati activity elicits inﬂammation. Mites
burrowing in the stratum corneum lead to an erythematous,
papular dermatitis that progresses to thickened skin covered with
crusts. Alopecia and intense pruritus are common, and secondary
infections occur, particularly with self-excoriation. 10

Clinical Features
Notoedric mange is characterized by intense pruritus and
development of hyperkeratotic crusts and alopecia on the dorsal
pinnae. Hypersensitivity contributes to pruritus and leads to
intense grooming which can result in secondary excoriations. In
chronically infested cats with advanced disease, anorexia, weight
loss, and poor condition may be evident. 10

Diagnosis
Direct Microscopic Examination

vetexamprep.ir

Mites are present in high numbers and are readily recovered in
skin scrapings from aﬀected areas. Although rare, S. scabiei has
been reported in cats; feline sarcoptiform mites must be carefully
examined to distinguish N. cati from those of S. scabiei. Use of
clear tape to collect material for microscopic examination from
aﬀected areas may be less stressful for feline patients and appears
to be of equal diagnostic sensitivity for N. cati. 107 Like other mites
(e.g., Demodex sp., Lynxacarus sp.), N. cati is occasionally detected
on fecal ﬂotation of infested cats due to ingestion during
grooming. 111 Fecal PCR has been developed for survey of wild
felid populations but is not commercially available for testing
domestic cats. 112
Serology
Serologic assays to detect antibodies to N. cati have not been
described, and S. scabiei ELISA is not validated for use in cats with
notoedric mange.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Clinical pathology values have not been described in cats with N.
cati infestations. Bobcats with notoedric mange have had low
serum creatinine concentrations, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte
abnormalities
(hyperphosphatemia,
hypernatremia,
and
hyperchloremia), as well as decreased serum cholesterol, albumin,
globulin, and total protein concentrations, presumably due to
protein loss across the aﬀected skin. 113
Gross Pathologic Findings
Notoedric mange most commonly presents as facial dermatitis,
often initially involving the anterior edge and dorsal surface of the
pinnae. As the infestation progresses, the head, neck, and dorsal
thorax may become aﬀected, and the skin becomes profoundly
thickened, wrinkled, and licheniﬁed. Lesions may also appear on
the feet, tail, and perineum following contact with aﬀected areas
during grooming. In chronic infestations, most of the body surface
can be aﬀected, peripheral lymphadopathy develops, and fatality
may occur. 10

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

Although FDA label-approved options to treat N. cati are not
available, treatment is similar to that recommended for S. scabiei,
with transdermal eprinomectin, moxidectin, or selamectin
recommended; combination products in which both active
ingredients
have
eﬃcacy
against
mites
(e.g.,
eprinomectin/ﬁpronil,
selamectin/sarolaner,
moxidectin/ﬂuralaner) are likely of even greater eﬃcacy. 114–116
Isoxazolines approved for cats (i.e., ﬂuralaner, lotilaner, sarolaner)
would also be considered eﬀective. High-dose oﬀ-label ca le
preparations of macrocyclic lactones have been used historically
but are not recommended due to safety concerns; repeating the
treatment at 14-day or monthly intervals may be necessary to
remove mites that hatch from eggs which remain after treatment
and eliminate the infestation. If a dip is preferred, a 2% to 3%
warm lime sulfur solution can be applied topically and allowed to
dry on the skin every 7 days for at least 6 weeks and until lesions
resolve. 10 Because some cats may be subclinical carriers, all cats in
the household should be treated for N. cati infestation regardless
of clinical appearance. Cats with notoedric mange respond well to
treatment so long as all cats in the household can be treated, reexposure is prevented, and treatment can be repeated, if
necessary, until infestations completely resolve. 10

Immunity
The extent to which cats develop immunity to N. cati has not been
investigated. The occurrence of epizootics in wild felid
populations that stabilize over time suggests that, although
notoedric mange can be responsible for population declines,
immunity may develop similar to what has been described for S.
scabiei in some wild canid populations. 103

Prevention
Vaccines are not available for prevention of N. cati infections.
Prevention involves keeping cats indoors, avoiding contact with
other cats likely to be infested, and, for multi-cat households,
treating new arrivals during initial quarantine to prevent
introduction. Although not evaluated experimentally, routine use
of control products eﬀective against mites, including macrocyclic

vetexamprep.ir

lactones and isoxazolines, would also be expected to prevent
infestation. 30 , 117 Cats with notoedric mange should be isolated
until cleared of the infestation. All li ermates or adult cats in the
same household should be treated regardless of clinical
appearance as subclinical infestations may be present in some
cats, creating a reservoir for future infestations. 10

Public Health Aspects
People in direct contact with infested cats often develop selflimiting dermatitis characterized by intense pruritus and an
erythematous papular rash; lesions are common on areas in
contact with infested cats including the hands, wrists, forearms,
and abdomen. 108 , 118 As with pruritus due to zoonotic S. scabiei
varieties, N. cati mites create a transient infestation in humans and
are not transmi ed to other humans. 10

Otodectes Cynotis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Otodectes cynotis (order Sarcoptiformes, family Psoroptidae) is the
common ear mite of domestic cats, dogs, and ferrets; infestations
have been reported in many other mammals. 30 Although most
commonly reported from domestic and free-roaming cats, O.
cynotis is well recognized as a parasite of ferrets and dogs. Adults
of O. cynotis are approximately the same size (300–450 µm) as S.
scabiei; at 350–450 µm, females may be grossly visible to the
unaided eye. The pretarsi consist of a caruncle (sucker) a ached
to a very short pedicel (stalk) on the ﬁrst two pairs of legs of the
female and all four pairs of legs on the male; males also have
distinct copulatory structures on the ventral surface. 34 Otodectes
cynotis is the only member of the genus.
Completion of the life cycle of O. cynotis requires approximately
3 weeks, with larvae, nymphs, and adults developing in the ear
canal and feeding on superﬁcial epidermal debris; under warmer
conditions, the life cycle is completed more rapidly. 30 Females
adhere eggs to the epidermal surface of the ear canal; larvae hatch
from eggs in approximately 4 days and then develop through two
nymphal stages (protonymph, deutonymph) to the adults. Motile

vetexamprep.ir

stages largely remain in the ceruminous exudate and cellular
material that accumulates in infested ears, occasionally venturing
to the surface. Mites are transferred between animals by direct
contact, including from dams to nursing young, and oﬀ-host
survival is limited. However, experimentally mites can survive for
5 to 17 days oﬀ host depending on temperature and relative
humidity. 119 , 120 Cats and, less commonly, dogs, infested with O.
cynotis are reported worldwide; ear mites are also very common
in ferrets and both wild and farmed foxes.
The prevalence of O. cynotis infestation in cats ranges from 0.9%
of pet cats in the United Kingdom to 37% of free-roaming cats in
the United States (Florida) (Table 110.2). 120–122 Failure to
microscopically examine otic exudate from every cat
underestimates prevalence and may explain some of the variation
seen. 121 , 122 In a multi-institutional survey of 1,519 cats in seven
diﬀerent countries in Europe, O. cynotis was present in 17.4% of
pet cats and was more commonly recovered from cats than any
other ectoparasite, including ﬂeas (15.5%). 106 Although
infestations are frequently found in ki ens and in cats with
outdoor access, age-related diﬀerences in prevalence have not
been clearly established in all feline populations and ear mite
infestations also occur in adult cats. 22 , 123–125 Prevalence in dogs
has ranged from 2.8% (Albania) to 6% (Brazil); age, sex, and breed
have not been associated with risk of infestation in dogs. 126 , 127
Otodectes cynotis is also commonly identiﬁed in pet ferrets and
wild canids. 128–131 In wild canid populations, O. cynotis
infestations tend to be focused in certain geographic areas. For
example, 4% of Arctic foxes across Iceland were infested, but all
were from a single county where the prevalence of infestation was
38%. 132

Pathogenesis
Infestation with O. cynotis is an important inciting cause of otitis
externa in cats and, less commonly, dogs. Ear mites do not burrow
but instead feed on superﬁcial epithelial cells and associated
exudate; occasionally tissue ﬂuid is imbibed. 10 The inﬂammatory
response leads to erythema of the ear canal and development of
dark brown, granular, ceruminous exudate. As mite populations

vetexamprep.ir

expand, miliary dermatitis may develop on adjacent areas of the
head and, less commonly, on the feet or tail following transfer
during grooming. 3 Some estimate that as many as 85% of feline
otitis externa cases and 50% of canine otitis externa cases are
caused by ear mites. 133 In a survey of free-roaming cats in
northern Italy, 55% had evidence of otitis externa with O. cynotis
found in a majority (53.3%) of aﬀected cats. 134 When treatment is
delayed, secondary bacterial and fungal infections can develop. 135
In some infested pets, diﬀuse hypersensitivity resembling ﬂea
allergy dermatitis and associated with ectopic mites has been
described. 10 The chronic ceruminous gland hyperplasia resulting
from untreated O. cynotis infestations has been associated with
development of ceruminous gland tumors. 131

Clinical Features
Ear mite infestations lead to a wide variety of clinical
presentations. Some infested animals appear normal, whereas
others develop intense otic pruritus accompanied by head shaking
and frequent, persistent scratching of the ears. Acne-like lesions
on the face have been described. 123 Aﬀected ears may contain
copious amounts of dark, granular discharge described as
resembling coﬀee grounds. In severe cases, self-excoriation leads

vetexamprep.ir

to traumatic injury of the skin, bleeding, development of aural
hematomas, and secondary infections. Purulent otitis externa may
develop. Dermatitis may also be seen, particularly when mites are
present outside the ear canals; common sites for ectopic mites and
associated alopecia and pruritus include the neck, back, feet, and
tail. 10 , 30 However, some animals will have large numbers of
mites with minimal discharge or pruritus evident. In cats, there is
not a clear correlation between the number of mites and the
severity of lesions that develop, or the amount of otic discharge
and the relative degree of pruritus. Dogs are usually pruritic with
only minimal discharge evident. 10

Diagnosis
Direct Microscopic Examination
Ear mites can be visualized directly during otoscopic examination
or by microscopic examination of exudate collected on a swab;
mineral oil aids in collection of material for examination and
transfer to a microscope slide. Direct microscopic examination of
material collected from the ear canal is key to reaching an accurate
diagnosis. In one study, otoscopic examination alone failed to
identify O. cynotis in 39% of infested cats, including eight cats
with an ear canal that appeared normal and had only mild
ceruminous exudate. 121 Another study showed that otoscopic
examination identiﬁed only 67% of infestations and that
sensitivity was increased by use of cure age to collect the
cerumen. 136 Flushing the external ear canal with a small amount
of mineral oil further enhances recovery and increases prevalence
of infestation when used for surveys of clinically normal pet cats
but is likely impractical in a clinical se ing. 123 Immature and
adult O. cynotis are motile when collected and are readily
identiﬁed by their large size (200–450 µm), characteristic rounded
appearance, and presence in the ear canal (Fig. 110.5). The other
mite occasionally found associated with otitis externa is Demodex
spp., which has a distinct elongated morphology. Males and
deutonymphs (pre-females) of O. cynotis are often found in
copulation; eggs are commonly seen within females or in collected
exudate. 34 Ectopic O. cynotis may occasionally be recovered on
skin scrape of the neck or tail. 10

vetexamprep.ir

Serology
Serologic tests for ear mites are not available. Cross-reactions with
dust mites can occur on intradermal skin tests similar to that seen
with S. scabiei and Cheyletiella spp. 137
Laboratory Abnormalities
Blood values in cats and dogs with O. cynotis infestations are
largely unremarkable. Signiﬁcant changes on CBCs, including
eosinophilia, have not been demonstrated. 138
Gross Pathologic Findings
Classically, O. cynotis induces erythematous hyperplasia and
hyperkeratosis in the ear canal epithelium. Pronounced
hyperplasia of the sebaceous and ceruminous glands is commonly
seen together with dilated blood vessels and increased numbers of
macrophages and mast cells. 10 , 30 Copious dark, ceruminous otic
discharge often packs the ear canal and must be removed to allow
complete examination. However, many cats and dogs conﬁrmed
to be infested as documented by the presence of mites on ear
swabs do not develop signiﬁcant pathology and otoscopic
examination is unremarkable. 121

(A) Adult Otodectes cynotis. (B)
Magnified view showing suckers at the end of
short pedicels on the first and second pair of
legs. Courtesy of Megan Lineberry, National Center for
FIG. 110.5

Veterinary Parasitology.

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

Otodectes cynotis is readily treated with macrocyclic lactones,
including otic preparations of ivermectin or milbemycin oxime
developed for treating ear mites, or transdermal, systemic
formulations of eprinomectin, moxidectin, or selamectin with
broad-spectrum eﬃcacy against many internal and external
parasites. 22 , 139 , 140 Otic preparations may lead to more rapid
clearance of mites. 141 Systemic isoxazolines (afoxolaner,
ﬂuralaner, lotilaner, sarolaner) are also eﬀective against ear mites
and may be given alone or in combination with macrocyclic
lactones to further support eﬃcacy. 142–148 In one study, a single
administration of a label-approved formulation of ﬂuralaner plus
moxidectin eliminated ear mites from treated cats. 147 Historically,
ear mites have been treated with otic preparations of pyrethrin,
rotenone, ﬁpronil, or lindane, or by using high-dose large animal
preparations of macrocyclic lactones oﬀ-label; toxicities have been
reported and these strategies are no longer recommended. 149
Mineral oil alone is eﬀective although repeated treatments are
needed, an overly aggressive approach can exacerbate otitis, and
an oily residue is left on the cats. 30 , 150
Otic cytology should be evaluated prior to cleaning; when
present, secondary bacterial or fungal infections should also be
treated. If debris is present, ear canals can be gently cleaned with
ceruminolytics to provide symptomatic relief to the patient and to
remove mites, taking care not to irritate the epidermal lining. 150
When otic acaricides are to be used, cleaning should occur before
application. Eliminating ectopic mites with systemic macrocyclic
lactones or isoxazolines should resolve traumatic alopecia
associated with excessive grooming due to pruritus from a diﬀuse
hypersensitivity reaction. If pruritus is severe, symptomatic care
may be indicated while infestations resolve. All dogs and cats in
contact with the patient should also be treated with acaricides;
subclinical infestations are common, and these animals may serve
as reservoirs to perpetuate the cycle of infestation. When the
primary patient and any direct contacts (e.g., other cats or dogs in
the household) can be treated, and any secondary infections
addressed, animals routinely recover. 10

Immunity

vetexamprep.ir

The negative association between age and intensity of O. cynotis
infestation suggests immunity may develop, and this reaction
could limit mite populations in older animals. 123 , 151 However,
ear mites are still present in many adult cats and dogs, and
reinfestation following treatment has been described. 137

Prevention
Preventing O. cynotis infestation can be achieved by avoiding
contact with other cats and dogs likely to be infested, including
keeping cats indoors and preventing roaming in dogs. Young
animals are particularly susceptible to acquiring infestations from
dams in the neonatal period due to prolonged, intimate contact
while nursing; treating breeding females before or during
pregnancy, prior to parturition, would be expected to eliminate
mites and reduce risk of transmission to ki ens and puppies. In
addition, routine use of products known to have eﬃcacy against
O. cynotis, including macrocyclic lactones and isoxazolines used to
control heartworm, intestinal parasites, ﬂeas, and ticks, would
also limit infestations with ear mites. 142–148 A combination
ﬁpronil, S-methoprene, eprinomectin, and praziquantel product
has been shown to protect cats from O. cynotis infestation. 152

Public Health Aspects
Although a few isolated cases of human infestation or dermatitis
associated with O. cynotis in pets have been reported,
transmission from pets to people appears quite rare. 153 , 154 Ear
mites pose minimal, if any, zoonotic risk.

Pneumonyssoides Caninum (Nasal Mite)
Nasal mites (Pneumonyssoides caninum, also Pneumonyssus
caninum) are an uncommon ﬁnding in pet dogs in most of the
world. The large (1.0–1.5 mm) mites live in paranasal sinuses and
nasal cavity, and transmission occurs with direct or indirect
contact between dogs. Nasal mites appear more common in
Scandinavia, with prevalence estimated to be 7% in Norway and
23% in Sweden. 163 , 164 One survey in Uppsala, Sweden
documented P. caninum in 20% of dogs surveyed; infestations

vetexamprep.ir

were more common in older (>3 years) and large-breed dogs, and
dolichocephalic breeds may be more commonly infested. 165 Cases
have also been described in North America and the United
Kingdom, but the true prevalence is not known. 166–169
Clinical signs vary from nasal irritation, nasal discharge,
sneezing, nasal pruritus, and stertorous breathing, to epistaxis,
hyposmia, and head shaking. 169 Diagnosis can be made by
visualizing mites with rhinoscopy or by retrograde saline nasal
ﬂush. 163 Nasal biopsy may reveal an eosinophilic inﬂammatory
response, and transient peripheral eosinophilia has been
described. 169 , 170 Selamectin applied every 2 weeks for three
treatments is eﬀective and clinical signs resolve within a few days
of initial treatment. 169 , 171 Milbemycin oxime (1 mg/kg, PO, q10d
× 3 doses) is also eﬀective. 163 All dogs in the home should be
treated. Nasal mites are not known to be zoonotic.

Lynxacarus Radovskyi (Fur Mite, Hair Clasping
Mite)
The fur mite, Lynxacarus radovskyi, is laterally compressed and
primarily found infesting cats in tropical areas. Mites a ach eggs
to the hairs of cats. Larvae, nymphs, and adults clasp the hairs
with the anterior end oriented toward the hair shaft (Fig. 110.6).
The complete life cycle has not been described, but oﬀ-host
survival is considered limited. 30 Mite populations are higher on
the caudal area of the body, including the base of the tail, tail tip,
and perianal region. 172 , 173 Lynxacarus radovskyi may be found on
more than 70% of pet cats in Malaysia and free-roaming cats in
the Caribbean. 172 , 173 Many infested cats are subclinically
infested, with pruritus, presumably due to a hypersensitivity
reaction, only occasionally observed. 174
Infested cats develop a dry, dull hair coat, alopecia, and,
occasionally, pruritus; the stippled appearance to the fur is often
described as “peppered.” Excessive grooming leads to alopecia
that is most pronounced in the perianal region, caudolateral hind
legs, base of tail, and abdomen. 173 An association between fur
mite infestation and feline eosinophilic granuloma complex has
been suggested. 175 Diagnosis can be made by identifying mites
grasping hairs plucked from aﬀected areas. Clear tape applied to

vetexamprep.ir

the fur also recovers mites and identiﬁes more infested animals.
172 Eﬀective treatments include moxidectin/imidacloprid or
selamectin applied every 2 weeks, ﬂuralaner once, or sarolaner. 173
, 173 , 176 , 177 All cats in the home should be treated. Humans in
contact with infested cats may develop a papular rash that
resolves with treatment of the pet. 178

Trombiculid Mites (Chiggers, Red Bugs, Berry
Bugs, Harvest Mites, Scrub Itch or Grass Itch
Mites)
Etiology and Epidemiology
Chiggers (family Trombiculidae, order Trombidiformes) are
minute, larval mites that cause chigger dermatitis (trombiculosis).
They are found in many tropical and temperate terrestrial
habitats. Although usually parasites of wildlife, trombiculids
occasionally found on dogs and cats include Eutrombicula spp.
(North, Central, and South America), Neotrombicula spp. and
Ericotrombidium spp. (Europe), and Leptotrombidium spp. (Asia,
Australia). 179–186 Over 1,200 species of trombiculid mites have
been identiﬁed, but many only as larvae. More than 50 species
have been recorded infesting humans and approximately 20 are
recognized as capable of causing animal and human disease.
Speciﬁc identiﬁcation is often not pursued, and the full diversity
of species involved is likely under-recognized. 183 Eutrombicula
alfredugessi is the most common and widespread chigger in the
Western Hemisphere and is found from Canada to Argentina and
the Caribbean. 187 In the United States, E. alfreddugesi is more
common east of the Rocky Mountains, Eutrombicula splendens is
found in the eastern United States, and Eutrombicula lipovskyi is
encountered in the southern United States from Arkansas,
Oklahoma and Kansas to Alabama and Tennessee. 187 Walchia
americana, a mite in the family Walchiidae and in the same
superfamily as the trombiculids (Trombiculoidea), is found in the
southwest and eastern United States, and commonly infests
squirrels and other rodents although larvae can infest cats. 180
Neotrombicula autumnalis, the harvest mite, is the most common
chigger in Europe, found throughout the continent and the British

vetexamprep.ir

Isles. 187 Neotrombicula inopinata is found in England, Spain and
France, and portions of central and Eastern Europe, from
Germany and Poland to Ukraine and the Northern Caucasus
region of Russia. 188 A related trombidioid mite of foxes,
Straelensia cynotis (family Leeuwenhoekiidae), parasitizes dogs in
Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, and Israel. 189–193 Leptotrombidium
spp., the vectors for scrub typhus, are found in Southeast Asia, the
southwestern Paciﬁc Islands, and northern Australia. 194

Adult Lynxacarus radovsky in hairs
collected from an infested cat. Courtesy of
FIG. 110.6

National Center for Veterinary Parasitology.

The life history of trombiculid mites encompasses the egg,
prelarva, larva, prenymph, nymph, tritonymph, and adult stages.
The female adult oviposits on the ground and larvae hatch and
begin to search for new hosts in 12 days. The larvae, which are
obligate parasites, have li le host speciﬁcity and will feed on a
wide variety of terrestrial vertebrates, including domestic animals
and humans. Larvae feed for 1 to 5 days, but generally, most will
complete feeding by the second day. Engorged larvae then drop
to the ground where they molt into the prenymph stage.
Following another molt, nymphs prey on invertebrates and,
following two more molts, become adults. Nymphal and adult
stages are either predatory on invertebrates or scavengers; they
are usually found in soil. The adults are typically bright red or
yellow, and about 1 mm in length. Covered in plumose setae,

vetexamprep.ir

adults appear to be covered in velvet and are sometimes referred
to as red velvet or true velvet mites.
Pets become infested when they encounter larval stages in the
environment, often in brushy areas frequented by wildlife. In
temperate regions, larvae usually begin to appear in the midsummer and their populations peak in the late summer and early
fall, and in tropical and subtropical areas, larval populations may
be host-seeking throughout the year. 187 , 195 , 196 The harvest mite,
N. autumnalis, is active on warm, sunny days 187 and E. alfreddugesi
larvae are most active at dawn and late afternoon–early evening,
with low levels of activity during the midday and night. 197

Clinical Features
Larvae are round, 0.2 to 0.5 mm long, often orange or red in color,
and have six legs. The mouthparts (gnathostoma) include the
chelicerae, or cu ing plates, that are used for piercing and holding
onto the host. A ached larvae eject saliva into the epidermis
through a buccal aperture. The saliva digests host tissue and aids
in formation of a stylostome, or feeding tube, through which the
larva can imbibe ﬂuid. After feeding, or if dislodged by the host,
the larva falls to the ground and the stylostome is left behind,
resulting in persistent, intense pruritus; chiggers do not burrow.
187 Irritation reactions appear to become more severe with
repeated feeding episodes, likely due to a hypersensitivity
reaction. In cats, the ears are most frequently infested, but clusters
of orange-red trombiculid larvae may be visible on margins of
pinnae, periorbital region, ventrum, or interdigital skin; alopecia
is often evident, and associated lesions are dry and crusted.
Papules, measuring 0.1 to 0.3 cm, may be observed with mild
wheals, crusting, and yellow exudate. Involvement of the feet may
present with swollen paws and cracked claws. 180 Pruritus was the
most common clinical sign although a majority (57%) of infested
cats in one study did not have clinical signs. 198 Neurologic signs
have been reported in dogs heavily infested with Neotrombicula
spp. 199 , 200
In contrast, larvae of S. cynotis infest hair follicles of dogs and
cause a nonpruritic nodular dermatitis on the dorsal head and
trunk; when severe, nodules may be painful and dogs lethargic
and anorexic. Infestations with S. cynotis are associated with

vetexamprep.ir

contact with fox dens where the nymph and adult mites live and
have been reported in dogs and, occasionally, cats, in Spain,
Portugal, France, and Israel. 189–191 , 193 , 201 Histologically, the
cysts comprise large, dilated hair follicles containing a larva; the
follicular epithelium is hyperplastic and inﬁltrates of plasma cells
and mast cells are evident. 190 Inﬂammatory inﬁltrates are usually
mild and eosinophils are rarely observed.

Diagnosis
When there is an abundant and recent infestation, clumps of
reddish- to orange-colored larvae can be observed on the skin.
Diagnosis of chiggers can be made by close inspection of lesions,
gently scraping mites from aﬀected areas or collecting with clear
tape, or, in the case of S. cynotis, examining biopsy specimens of
the nodular dermatitis.

Treatment and Prevention
Treatments for trombiculid mites reported to be eﬀective in cats
include transdermal selamectin or ﬁpronil. 202–205 Dogs have been
treated successfully with topical ﬁpronil, permethrinpyriproxyfen, and permethrin-ﬁpronil combinations. 202 , 206 , 207
Straelensia cynotis infestations do not consistently respond to
systemic treatment with ivermectin. 190 , 191 Treatment failures
may relate to the mite’s endofollicular location. Topical or
systemic antibiotics may be indicated to treat secondary
infections, and glucocorticoids would provide relief. Anecdotally,
isoxazolines may also have good eﬃcacy, eliminating chiggers on
dogs within 6–8 hours. 200
Modifying chigger habitat so as to make it inhospitable for mite
survival can reduce the likelihood of exposure. Routinely mowing
grassy areas, clearing brush, and raking leaves can decrease
chigger exposure. Reinfestation in cats (and dogs and humans, as
well) is very likely after treatment if there are no changes in
lifestyle. 198 Avoidance of sites where chiggers are active,
especially during the times of the year when larvae are active, is
useful in minimizing chigger exposure. Limiting activity in those
areas to the midday hours during chigger season may also

vetexamprep.ir

minimize exposure as the larvae are less likely to be seeking hosts
during the warmest and driest part of the day.

Public Health ASPECTS
Although humans are considered accidental hosts, about 20 mite
species are considered medically relevant because their bites can
elicit dermatitis and hypersensitivity reactions, as well as being
vector pathogens. 194 In addition, scrub typhus (tsutsugamushi
disease), caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi, is
transmi ed by chiggers of Leptotrombidium spp. in far eastern
Russia, the Korean Peninsula, Japan, South east Asia, India, and
northern coastal Australia. 194 Larvae are eﬃcient vectors because
the bacterium is transovarially transmi ed.
In humans, chigger bites usually occur on the lower limbs.
Small (1–2 mm) papules appear approximately 3 to 24 hours postexposure, which can develop into pustules. Intense pruritus
begins to subside after 1 week and accompanying skin lesions
may last 3 weeks.
People are advised to prevent mite exposure by avoiding
known and suspected chigger areas, wearing protective clothing,
and using repellents. Although direct contact with host-seeking
larvae on vegetation is the likeliest route of transmission, there are
two suspected cases of animal-to-human transmission in the
literature. 208 , 209

Case Example
Signalment

“Ginger,” a 5-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat
from Muscogee, Oklahoma, United States.

History

Ginger was evaluated in July for alopecia and mild to moderate
pruritus on the head, pinnae, and shoulder. Her owner
reported excessive grooming over the past month when the
lesions ﬁrst appeared; this included pawing at the ears,
scratching, and occasionally chewing the aﬀected area on the
shoulder. Ginger was an indoor-only cat that had been housed
in a long-term, limited access private shelter. Ginger joined the

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
g j
shelter population in April (3 months ago) following the death
of a previous owner. The owner’s impression was that Ginger
was removing her own hair with the excessive grooming,
perhaps due to stress, but she had not observed any diﬃcult
interactions with other cats in the facility. The current owner
managed the shelter and had not noted pruritus or similar skin
lesions in any of the other 14 cats in residence.

Current Medications:

Topical monthly ﬂea control (imidacloprid).

Other Medical History:

No medical problems or skin lesions were noted at intake.
Ginger was negative for feline retroviruses and feline
heartworm antigen. Giardia sp. cysts were present on fecal
ﬂotation in April; 3 days of fenbendazole (50 mg/kg) was
administered to avoid introducing Giardia sp. into the shelter
population. For the past 3 weeks, the owner had fed Ginger a
commercial hydrolyzed protein dry kibble diet; pruritus and
skin lesions persisted.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 6.4 kg; BCS 6/9.
General: Bright, alert, hydrated, responsive. Mucous
membranes pink, HR = 170 beats/minute, RR = 50
breaths/minute, T = 100.8°F (38.2°C).
Integument: Alopecia, scaling, and broken hairs were
evident on the dorsal neck, right shoulder and right
lateral thorax (Fig. 110.7). Alopecia and scaling were
present on the dorsal surface of the head and the external
pinnae; excoriations were noted on the left pinna. Flea
frass, ﬂeas, or other grossly apparent ectoparasites were
not recovered by combing. Fluorescence was not noted
with ultraviolet illumination of aﬀected areas; culture of
plucked hairs in dermatophyte test medium did not
reveal color change or fungal growth.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mild amount of light tan
cerumen in both ears. No other clinically signiﬁcant
ﬁndings were found on physical examination.

vetexamprep.ir

Skin Cytology and Skin Biopsy Findings

Mites were not evident on multiple (n = 6) skin scrapings
collected from aﬀected areas. Cytologic examinations of skin
scrapings revealed no signiﬁcant ﬁndings. Skin biopsy revealed
mild hyperkeratosis and mild to moderate perivascular
dermatitis.

Alopecia, mild erythema, and mild
to moderate scaling on the dorsal neck,
shoulder, and lateral thorax of a cat with
demodicosis.
