Fecal Flotation Findings

Demodex gatoi mites, with characteristic stubby appearance and
each approximately 90–110 µm long, were recovered on
centrifugal fecal ﬂotation using 33% zinc sulfate (Fig. 110.8). 45

Diagnosis

Demodex gatoi infestation.

Treatment

Ginger was treated with transdermal moxidectin/imidacloprid
administered weekly for three consecutive treatments and
monthly thereafter. Clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (10 mg/kg,
q12h, PO) was also administered; antibiotics were discontinued
after 7 days. The pruritus and associated lesions began to

vetexamprep.ir

resolve in the ﬁrst week of treatment. Mites were detected on
fecal ﬂotation 7 days after treatment but not at 14 days or 21
days. At 1-month follow-up examination, the skin appeared
normal.

Comments

Mites are not consistently recovered in skin scrapings from cats
with demodicosis, including those with D. gatoi infestation.
Examination of material collected with tape strips may be more
successful for conﬁrmation of diagnosis. 42 However, because
the pruritus associated with demodicosis causes cats to groom
excessively, mites are ingested and frequently identiﬁed on
fecal ﬂotation. 46 Fecal examination should be requested for cats
seen for pruritus. Skin biopsy was not necessary in this case and
could have been avoided if fecal ﬂotation had been performed
initially. Although this cat was treated with transdermal
moxidectin, isoxazolines (lotilaner, ﬂuralaner, sarolaner) are
available for cats, and sometimes in combination with
macrocyclic lactones (selamectin, moxidectin) and would also
be expected to be eﬀective. Unlike most other Demodex spp., D.
gatoi causes contagious pruritus and when co-housed, multiple
cats are often infested. 42 Ginger should be isolated until
treatment has been completed and other in-contact cats closely
evaluated for skin lesions. Prophylactic treatment of all cats in
the facility with selamectin/sarolaner or moxidectin/ﬂuralaner
may be warranted.

111: Heartworm and Related
Nematodes
C. Thomas Nelson

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Heartworm was first described in dogs in Italy
in 1626 1 and in the United States in 1847. 2
• Cause: Dirofilaria immitis, belonging to the superfamily
Filarioidea and family Onchocercidae. A related nematode,
Dirofilaria repens, is found in southern and central Europe,
Africa, and Asia but is not currently endemic in North America.
• Affected Hosts: Although canids (domestic dogs, coyotes,
foxes, wolves, and other wild canids) are the definitive hosts
for heartworms, the parasite has been found in more than 30
species of animals, including domestic cats and wild felids,
bears, ferrets, seals, sea lions, and humans.
• Intermediate Hosts: There are multiple mosquito vectors in
every region of the United States. More than 70 species of
mosquitoes have been shown to be capable of transmitting
heartworms; 25 species have been proven to be significant
vectors.
• Geographic Distribution: Heartworm is endemic in North,
Central, and South America; the Caribbean Islands; the
coastal regions of Africa, southern Europe, and Asia; Japan;
Indonesia; and Australia.
• Route of Transmission: Female mosquitoes feeding on a
microfilaremic canine host ingest microfilariae. The ingested
microfilariae undergo a transformation and two molts over a 2to 4-week period to become infective third-stage larvae (L3).
The L3 are then deposited on a dog’s skin in a droplet of

vetexamprep.ir

hemolymph by a feeding female mosquito. The L3 enter
through the bite wound into the subcutaneous tissue.
• Major Clinical Signs: Signs of heartworm disease can range
from a cough and exercise intolerance to dyspnea, abnormal
heart and lung sounds, hepatomegaly, syncope, ascites, and
death.
• Differential Diagnoses: These include primary pulmonary
diseases (pneumonia, chronic bronchitis, allergic lung
disease), pulmonary thromboembolism, pulmonary
hypertension, and right-sided heart failure.
• Human Health Significance: Dirofilaria immitis is of public
health concern even though the number of reports of infection
in humans is relatively small. The most common clinical
syndrome reported in human infections is the formation of a
pulmonary nodule or nodules within the lung parenchyma.

Canine Heartworm Disease
Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Heartworm disease is caused by the parasitic ﬁlarial nematode
Diroﬁlaria immitis, belonging to the superfamily Filarioidea and
family Onchocercidae. Nine ﬁlarial nematode species infect dogs
worldwide, and three have been diagnosed in the United States:
D. immitis, Diroﬁlaria repens, and Acanthocheilonema reconditum
(formerly Dipetalonema reconditum). Only D. immitis and A.
reconditum are considered endemic, but conditions exist for D.
repens to become established. Heartworm was ﬁrst described in
dogs in Italy in 1626 1 and in the United States in 1847. 2 Although
canids (domestic dogs, coyotes, foxes, wolves, and other wild
canids) are the deﬁnitive hosts for heartworms, the parasite has
been found in more than 30 species of animals, including
domestic cats and wild felids, bears, ferrets, seals, sea lions, and
humans. There has even been one conﬁrmed case in a bird. 3
Information speciﬁc to the cat is presented in the second part of
this chapter.
Heartworms are endemic in North, Central, and South America;
the Caribbean Islands; the coastal regions of Africa, southern

vetexamprep.ir

Europe, and Asia; Japan; Indonesia; and Australia. 4 , 5 In the
United States, heartworm has progressed from being a parasitic
disease primarily in the southeast to being diagnosed in all 50
states (Fig. 111.1). Alaska is the only state in which transmission
has not been documented; however, there are mosquito vectors
and climatic conditions present in regions of central Alaska to
support the transmission of heartworms for brief periods. 6 The
yearly incidence of identiﬁed cases of canine heartworm infection
continues to rise despite the availability of many
chemoprophylactic drugs. The increased incidence has been
prominent in the western half of the United States over the past 30
years. Two factors are likely responsible: (1) heartworm-infected
dogs have been relocated to western regions as humans have
moved from endemic areas, thus establishing a reservoir of
infection, and (2) mosquito habitats have been created as a result
of irrigation of newly developed areas and the subsequent inﬂux
of suitable vector mosquitoes. A sylvatic cycle has developed in
the coyote population, as the rate of heartworm infection is over
90% in many western areas. 7 The prevalence of infection
elsewhere in the United States varies by region with over 90% of
unprotected dogs along the Gulf Coast, lower Atlantic Coast, and
Mississippi River valley being infected. 8 The severity of clinical
illness also varies by region. The worm biomass in an infected dog
is typically higher in dogs coming from the high-prevalence areas
just listed. However, there are isolated pockets of infection with
high prevalence and severity of infection throughout the United
States.
The natural cycle and transmission of heartworms requires a
reservoir of infection, a competent mosquito vector, and favorable
climatic conditions. Unprotected domestic and feral dogs as well
as wild canids serve as the reservoir hosts. Relocation of
heartworm-infected dogs and expansion of the territories of
microﬁlaremic wild canids into other areas continue to precipitate
the spread of heartworms.
There are multiple mosquito vectors in every region of the
United States. 9 More than 70 species of mosquitoes have been
shown to be capable of transmi ing heartworms; 25 species have
been proven to be signiﬁcant vectors. Importation of new
mosquito species into an area, environmental changes created by
humans, and natural climatic conditions can aﬀect heartworm

vetexamprep.ir

transmission. Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito), originally
introduced into southeast Texas in 1985, has increased the
exposure rate of dogs in many regions of the United States. 10 This
mosquito can now be found in 35 states primarily in the
Southeast, the Midwest, and the Atlantic seaboard as far north as
New Jersey, southern New York, and Pennsylvania. 11 This large
urban-dwelling mosquito can reproduce in small watercontaining vessels such as ﬂower pots. It voraciously feeds
throughout the day, not just at dusk and dawn. The female lives
for 3 months and is capable of overwintering. Aedes albopictus was
introduced into Italy in 1990 and has spread over much of
southern Europe, becoming a major vector of D. immitis and D.
repens. Aedes sierrensis (western tree-hole mosquito) has had its
geographic range extended in the western United States as a result
of the continuing development of previously semiarid areas by
the installation of irrigation systems and the planting of trees in
new urban home sites.
Laboratory studies have determined that a minimum
temperature of 57°F is necessary for the development of
heartworm larvae to the infective third-stage larva (L3). 12 This has
led to the common practice of seasonal, rather than year-round,
heartworm prevention in states north of the 37th parallel.
Unfortunately, the heat island eﬀect (Fig. 111.2) in urban areas can
create microenvironments that are capable of supporting
heartworm larva development even during winter months in
northern states. 13 Furthermore, Culex spp. mosquitoes are
competent vectors that are frequently found indoors. Therefore,
transmission can continue even during cooler months in large
indoor kennels. These factors along with the northward spread of
A. albopictus have prompted the American Heartworm Society
(AHS) to recommend year-round administration of heartworm
preventive to dogs and cats in the continental United States and
Hawaii. 14
A knowledge of the heartworm life cycle is important for
development and implementation of prevention and treatment
strategies (Fig. 111.3). The life cycle of D. immitis is 7 to 9 months
(210 to 270 days). Female mosquitoes feeding on a microﬁlaremic
canine host ingest microﬁlariae. The ingested microﬁlariae then
undergo a transformation into ﬁrst-stage larvae (L1) after entering

vetexamprep.ir

a mosquito. 15 The L1 will undergo two molts over the next 2 to 4
weeks, depending on the average ambient temperature, at which
time they become infective L3. The L3 are then deposited on the
dog’s skin in a droplet of hemolymph by a feeding female
mosquito (Fig. 111.3A). The L3 enter through the bite wound into
the subcutaneous tissue, where most L3 molt to fourth-stage
larvae (L4) within a couple of days. The L4 migrates in the
subcutaneous tissue and muscle toward the thorax, and from
approximately 50 to 70 days after initial infection L4 undergo a
ﬁnal molt to juvenile worms. These juvenile worms subsequently
penetrate the muscle tissue and eventually enter the circulation.
Historically, the juvenile worm has been referred to as a ﬁfthstage larva (L5). Because this stage does not undergo another molt,
it should not be considered a larval stage. It is an immature or
juvenile worm that matures into an adult over the next several
months. After entering a peripheral vein, the blood then carries
immature worms to and through the heart and into the
pulmonary arteries, arriving as early as 70 days PI. 16 By 120 days
PI, virtually all juvenile worms have entered the pulmonary
vasculature. Final maturation to adult worms and mating occurs
in the pulmonary vessels. Microﬁlariae are then produced,
typically around 180 to 210 days (but up to 270 days) PI,
completing the life cycle. Mature adult males range from 15 to 18
cm in length and females from 25 to 30 cm with a life expectancy
of 5 to 7 years. 17

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Heartworm infections primarily cause damage to the pulmonary
arteries and lungs. Juvenile worms entering the pulmonary
vasculature 3 months PI initiate an eosinophilia and eosinophilic
pneumonitis. 18 Mature worms cause endothelial damage to
pulmonary vessels, villous proliferation, and neutrophilic
inﬁltrates in the vessel walls (Fig. 111.3B). Heartworms harbor the
ricke sial endosymbiont Wolbachia pipientis that produces
Wolbachia surface proteins (WSPs). These WSPs activate IL-8
transcription and stimulate chemokinesis in canine neutrophils. 19
In dogs infected with D. immitis, neutrophils accumulate in the
pulmonary arterial walls and may help incite the pulmonary
vasculature changes that develop. WSPs can be detected using
IHC in glomerular capillaries from heartworm-infected dogs (Fig.
111.4) which suggests that glomerulonephropathy associated with
heartworm disease may be the direct result of D. immitis that
harbor Wolbachia. 20 The WSP also stimulates IL-10 and
prostaglandin E2 responses and IFN-γ production and IgG1

vetexamprep.ir

antibody responses in humans infected with Onchocerca volvulus,
another ﬁlarial nematode that harbors Wolbachia. 21
The severity of disease can be aﬀected by the number of worms
and the duration of the infection; but of equal importance, if not
greater, is the activity level of the dog. Dogs in which 50 worms
were surgically implanted and that were exercise-restricted took
longer to develop clinical disease, and developed less pulmonary
vascular resistance, than dogs infected with 14 heartworms that
were allowed moderate activity. 22 This is also evident in naturally
infected dogs in which there is no correlation between the number
of heartworms and pulmonary vascular resistance, indicating that
the individual host-parasite interaction plays an important role in
the severity of disease. 22 Results of a subsequent study included
similar ﬁndings in dogs being treated with melarsomine. 23
Whereas live heartworms can cause endarteritis and muscular
hypertrophy of arteriole walls, primarily of the caudal pulmonary
arteries, the pathologic changes seen in clinical disease are
primarily the result of the eﬀects of dying heartworms. As worms
die from either natural causes or as a result of administration of
adulticidal drugs, they decompose. Small worm fragments lodge
in the distal pulmonary arteriole and capillary beds in the caudal
lung lobes, blocking blood ﬂow. These worm fragments, along
with the inﬂammation that they elicit and platelet aggregation,
result in pulmonary thromboembolism. During periods of
increased activity or exercise, the increased blood ﬂow to these
blocked vessels can cause fragile capillaries to rupture with
resultant pulmonary hemorrhage and subsequent ﬁbrosis. 24 This
ﬁbrosis, along with the release of vasoactive substances by
heartworms, leads to increased pulmonary vascular resistance
and subsequent pulmonary hypertension. 25 The sequelae to these
pulmonary vascular events is cor pulmonale and potential rightsided heart failure.
Ectopic lesions, due to aberrant migration of worms into the
eye, CNS, abdominal cavity, and systemic circulation, can occur.
15 “Caval syndrome,” which occurs in a small percentage of cases,
results from heartworms located in the posterior vena cava and
right atrium causing interference with tricuspid valve function
(see Fig. 111.3C). Luminal obstruction, which can result in a
peracute hemolytic crisis from traumatic injury to erythrocytes,

vetexamprep.ir

contributes to the development of overt right-sided heart failure.
“Caval syndrome” is usually associated with excessively large
worm burdens in the right ventricle and atrium and may result
from a combination of cardiac insuﬃciency and increased
pulmonary vascular resistance, which allows the heartworms in
the pulmonary artery to move back into the right heart.
Glomerulonephropathy may also occur as a result of antigenantibody complexes leading to proteinuria, and anemia,
hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria are often present (Table
111.1).
Many dogs infected with heartworms have no clinical signs,
because dogs can tolerate live heartworms very well, especially if
they are not very active. Factors that can aﬀect the onset of clinical
signs are the number of worms present in relationship to the size
of the dog; the duration of infection; the individual host response
to the parasite; and, most importantly, the activity level of the
dog. Clinical signs usually develop gradually, with a mild cough
being the most common sign noticed. This will be followed by
exercise intolerance and an unthrifty appearance. Clinical signs
associated with more advanced disease can also develop acutely
as a result of the natural death and disintegration of a heartworm
that leads to sudden pulmonary thromboembolism. As the
disease progresses and pulmonary pathology worsens, signs
associated with right-sided heart involvement such as abnormal
heart sounds and ascites appear. 15 Dogs that have experienced
pulmonary thromboembolism from dead worms may be febrile
and have hemoptysis. Those with caval syndrome present with
acute, often profound, lethargy and weakness. Four classes of
heartworm disease have been described with associated clinical
signs (see Table 111.1). Classiﬁcation of disease based on clinical
severity has been used to determine treatment strategies and
prognosis. However, although class 3 patients are statistically at a
greater risk for severe complications and death after treatment,
class 1 and 2 patients can experience the same levels of
complications. 14 Dogs with caval syndrome (class 4) are severely
ill and require surgery to survive.

vetexamprep.ir

Life cycle of heartworm infection.
Microfilaria are ingested by the mosquito. After
undergoing transformation to first-stage larvae
(L1), they undergo two molts over a period that
can span 10 to 28 days, depending on ambient
temperature. During this transformation, they
first enter the malpighian tubules, then the
body cavity, finally migrating toward the head
and into the labium. (A) During feeding, the
third-stage larvae (L3) are deposited in a
droplet of hemolymph (white arrows) on the
animal’s skin surface and migrate into
subcutaneous tissue. In dogs, they molt into
fourth-stage larvae (L4) within 3 to 4 days postinfection (PI), and migrate in the subcutaneous
tissue and muscle moving toward the thorax.
L4 molt into juvenile worms (sexually immature
adult stage) within 50 to 70 days PI. Juvenile
worms enter the venous circulation within the
muscle tissue and between 70 and 120 days
PI have migrated to the heart and pulmonary
FIG. 111.3

vetexamprep.ir

vasculature. The juvenile worm grows to a
sexually mature adult during the range of 120
to 210 days PI, and female worms release
increasing levels of antigen. In dogs,
pulmonary vascular changes include blunting
of the arteries, intraluminal thrombi and
pulmonary hypertension (B). Adult worms
usually reside in the pulmonary arteries and in
severe infections, in the right side of the heart
including the cranial and caudal vena cava
(arrows indicate right pulmonary artery [RPA]).
(C) A heart from a dog with caval syndrome as
viewed from the right ventricle toward the
tricuspid valve (TV). A mass of heartworms
completely occludes the valve preventing it
from closing. Right atrial, ventricular, and
pulmonary artery enlargement are apparent. In
cats, 90% to 95% of infections do not go past
the juvenile stage, and 50% of cats have
negative antibody titer results by 8 months.
Dying immature worms produce heartwormassociated respiratory disease (HARD)
syndrome consisting of occlusive hypertrophy
of pulmonary arterioles, peribronchial
infiltrates, and alveolar inflammatory infiltrates
and consolidation. A, Courtesy Boehringer
Ingleheim; B, Photographic images courtesy of Stephen
Jones, DVM.

Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in dogs with heartworm disease
may be normal in mild or early infections. Dogs may exhibit a thin
body condition, tachypnea, dyspnea, a right-sided heart murmur
from tricuspid insuﬃciency, cardiac gallop, and jugular
distension with pulsation. Auscultation of lung ﬁelds could reveal
pulmonary crackles primarily in the caudal lung lobes. Dogs with
caval syndrome are severely lethargic, have pale mucous
membranes and delayed capillary reﬁll time, weak peripheral
pulses, and often have dark urine due to hemoglobinuria.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of heartworm disease is primarily done using
serum immunoassays, but other testing modalities are useful in
determining the severity of disease present.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Abnormal clinical laboratory results occur but are not uniquely
diagnostic for heartworm infection. Hemogram abnormalities
may
include
eosinophilia,
basophilia,
neutrophilia,
nonregenerative anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Elevated liver
enzyme activities, azotemia, and hyperbilirubinemia may be
noted in results of serum chemistries, and proteinuria may be
detected on urinalysis.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Radiography is an eﬀective way of evaluating the severity of
cardiopulmonary disease, and before the availability of serologic
testing, it was the method used to diagnose occult
(nonmicroﬁlaremic) heartworm disease. The heart silhoue e
appears as a reversed “D” and caudal lobar pulmonary arteries
are enlarged, tortuous, and often truncated. These vascular
changes are accompanied by varying degrees of pulmonary
parenchymal disease (Fig. 111.5). 26
Parasitologic Tests
The AHS recommends annual screening using both a
microﬁlariae and an antigen test for all dogs over 7 months of age;
and testing is indicated 6 months after starting prophylaxis in
dogs over 8 weeks of age; before starting prophylaxis in dogs over
7 months of age; and on days 0, 180, and 360 when there has been
noncompliance or a change in prophylactic treatment product.
Detection of Microfilaria
Microﬁlaria can be identiﬁed microscopically by direct
examination of a drop of anticoagulated blood, with concentration
techniques using a Millipore ﬁlter, or centrifugation using the
modiﬁed Kno ’s procedure (see Chapter 5). Microﬁlariae may not
be detected in as many as 20% of heartworm-infected dogs. These
“occult” infections may occur as a result of single-sex infections,
host immune responses suppressing reproduction, and if the dog
has been on a heartworm preventive. 15 For various reasons,
microﬁlariae may be present in dogs with negative blood antigen
result. It is possible for puppies to acquire microﬁlariae in utero
when the bitch has a high microﬁlaria count. Because microﬁlariae
can survive in the dog’s bloodstream for over 2 years, dogs treated
with an adulticide or dogs whose infection has cleared naturally

vetexamprep.ir

can have microﬁlariae and have negative antigen test results.
Heartworm microﬁlariae must be diﬀerentiated from those of A.
reconditum (Fig. 111.6 and Table 111.2).

Acanthocheilonema reconditum
(top) and Dirofilaria immitis (bottom). Courtesy
FIG. 111.6

Serologic Testing
Antigen detection, which, together with microﬁlaria testing is the
recommended method for diagnostic screening in dogs, is
accomplished by using one of several commercially available
antigen tests kits. These are available as POC tests or well-based
tests that are used by reference laboratories to process large
numbers of specimens. These tests detect a glycoprotein secreted
mainly by adult female heartworms and are the most sensitive
diagnostic method currently available.
Commercially available antigen test systems are based on
enzyme immunoassay methods that have been adapted to
laboratory or POC kits. The sensitivity (95% to 100%) and
speciﬁcity (100%) of these test systems are excellent in infections
when three or more female worms are present. Most POC test kit
systems have low sensitivity in dogs with fewer than three female

vetexamprep.ir

worms. In dogs with one female worm, the sensitivity ranged
from 65% to 85%, and with two female worms, it ranged from
85% to 95%. 27 However, when comparing the presence or absence
of female worms at necropsy, the sensitivity of one in-clinic
instrument-based agglutination immunoassay test system ranged
between 50% and 72% compared with 92% and 99.6% for a kitbased enzyme immunoassay. 28 False-positive results are rare,
and, therefore, it is be er to accept rather than reject a positive test
result. However, it is prudent to repeat a test when positive
results are found for dogs residing in hypoendemic areas, and in
animals that receive heartworm preventive. Conﬁrmation of the
positive test result can be obtained if circulating microﬁlaria are
identiﬁed, or if another positive result is generated using a
diﬀerent type of antigen test. An animal with clinical signs of
heartworm disease that has a negative test result should also be
retested. The amount of antigen present in the circulation can be
quantitated and does have a relationship to the number of female
worms, but this is not an accurate determination of the total worm
burden. Male and immature female worms could be present but
not producing detectable antigen. Likewise, shortly after the death
of a female worm, large amounts of antigen are released into the
circulation, giving the appearance of a heavy worm burden in
quantitative test results. 14
False-negative test results occur most commonly when
infections are light, female worms are still immature, only male
worms are present, and/or the test kit instructions have not been
followed. There are also documented cases of antigen blocking,
presumably from antigen-antibody complexes, interfering with
antigen testing, resulting in false-negative test results. Laboratory
studies have shown that heating the sample test-tube to 104°C for
10 minutes degrades the complexes, which releases antigen,
yielding more accurate results. 29 , 30 The routine heating of all
blood samples is not recommended at this time as this is contrary
to the label instructions for these tests and could interfere with the
results of combination tests that include an antibody test for
detection of other infectious agents. Due to this, and other
mentioned considerations, heartworm test results should only be
recorded as positive or no antigen detected (NAD) and should not
be wri en as “negative.” Antigen test results should be

vetexamprep.ir

interpreted carefully, taking other relevant clinical information
into consideration.

Antigen may be detected as early as 5 months PI and
consistently by 7 months PI. Antigenemia may be delayed until 9
months PI in some infected dogs that receive preventives.
Microﬁlaria can be detected microscopically 6 months PI, by
examining fresh blood, or with concentration techniques.
Screening dogs for the presence of microﬁlaria is complementary
to antigen testing, because it adds sensitivity without
compromising speciﬁcity, 31 conﬁrms the infection and alerts the
veterinarian of a potential adverse reaction that may occur after
administration of microﬁlaricidal doses of macrocyclic lactones.
Because of the prepatent period, dogs should not be tested with
either microﬁlariae or antigen tests until they are at least 7 months
old. 14
Molecular diagnostic methods are occasionally used in research
for diagnosis of heartworm infection. A multiplex PCR assay has
been developed that can detect and discriminate D. immitis from
D. repens. 32

Treatment
Successful management and treatment of heartworm disease
requires a thorough understanding of the life cycle of D. immitis,
the host-parasite relationship, and the susceptibility of the various
life stages to microﬁlaricidal and adulticidal drugs. The goals of

vetexamprep.ir

any heartworm treatment are to improve the clinical condition of
the animal and to eliminate all adult heartworms and
developmental stages with minimal post-treatment complications.
Before initiation of therapy, a thorough physical examination,
clinical laboratory testing, and thoracic radiographs should be
performed. Clinical or laboratory problems of concern should be
controlled or stabilized before the dog receives adulticidal
therapy. This may involve the administration of glucocorticoids to
reduce pulmonary inﬂammation as well as angiotensinconverting enzyme inhibitors to improve cardiac function. In
severe cases of right-sided heart failure, abdominal drainage may
be necessary to remove ascitic ﬂuid to initially reduce
diaphragmatic pressure followed by maintenance therapy with
furosemide and sildenaﬁl (see Table 111.3 for doses of drugs used
to treat canine heartworm disease).
Caval syndrome is an often fatal manifestation of heartworm
disease in dogs that have a high worm burden that obstructs
blood ﬂow. Severe pulmonary arteriolar hypertension and
decreased cardiac output occur. Heartworms can be surgically
extracted via a right jugular venotomy and introduction of
alligator forceps, a ﬂexible snare, or brush (Fig. 111.7). 33 The use
of a C-arm imaging device is useful but not imperative. This
procedure is done as an emergency measure that is reserved for
dogs with this syndrome. Medical management of heartworm
disease is used in all other patients as discussed in the following
sections.
Melarsomine
Melarsomine is an arsenic-based drug and is the only adulticidal
drug approved by the FDA for heartworm treatment in the United
States. It is administered by deep intramuscular injection into the
epaxial lumbar muscles. The two-dose protocol recommended on
the package insert for treating class 1 and 2 heartworm infections
(see Table 111.1) kills 90% of adult worms present. The “alternate”
or three-dose protocol recommended for treating class 3
heartworm infections kills 98% of the adult worms.
Approximately 50% of adult worms are killed by the ﬁrst dose,
and most of the remaining worms are killed by the second and
third injection administered 4 to 8 weeks later. The three-dose

vetexamprep.ir

protocol is recommended by the AHS as the adulticidal treatment
of choice because of its increased safety margin and eﬃcacy.
Macrocyclic Lactones
The heartworm preventive products belonging to the macrocyclic
lactones contain ivermectin, milbemycin, moxidectin, or
selamectin. In the past, long-term administration of heartworm
preventives has been advocated to prevent reinfection while
waiting for existing adult heartworms to die. This approach is not
recommended because it can take 2 to 3 years to completely clear
the infection, during which time pulmonary and cardiovascular
abnormalities can progress (Fig. 111.8). There is also the chance of
selection for resistant strains of D. immitis.

Heartworm cuticle after 3 years of
ivermectin preventive administration. Courtesy of

Stephen Jones, DVM.

Doxycycline
Because the metabolites (WSP) of Wolbachia contribute to the
disease process, doxycycline has been the subject of several
studies in heartworm treatment, and is now being used in the
treatment of several human ﬁlarial diseases. Results of two

vetexamprep.ir

studies were compared: heartworm test–positive dogs treated
with ivermectin and doxycycline before melarsomine injections
versus those with melarsomine alone had fewer gross pulmonary
pathologic changes associated with the death of the heartworms.
34 , 35 In one study, there was a 78% reduction in heartworm
numbers using ivermectin and doxycycline only after 36 weeks of
therapy. 34 Other studies have shown similar results. 36
Histopathologic changes in the lung tissue included an intense
inﬂammatory reaction and positive staining for WSP in the dogs
treated with melarsomine. The inﬂammation was signiﬁcantly
reduced and staining for WSP was virtually absent in dogs
receiving
doxycycline-ivermectin-melarsomine
combination
therapy (Fig. 111.9). 37 Doxycycline administered at 10 mg/kg
q12h for 4 weeks eliminates the presence of Wolbachia DNA. The
dose can be reduced to 5 mg/kg q12h if GI adverse eﬀects occur.
In one study, 40% of heartworm-infected dogs receiving
doxycycline developed elevated serum liver enzyme activities.
This does not appear to be clinically signiﬁcant in dogs with
normal liver function. The elevated activities are transient and
they typically return to pretreatment values without intervention.
38 Microﬁlariae from dogs treated with doxycycline developed
into L3 after ingestion by mosquitoes, but those L3 did not develop
into adult worms when inoculated into a new canid host. This
impaired maturation of L3 would result in decreased transmission
and reduces the potential for selection of resistant strains of D.
immitis. 39 , 40
Macrocyclic Lactones/Doxycycline Combinations
Select macrocyclic lactones (ivermectin and moxidectin) coupled
with doxycycline individually suppress embryogenesis and
weaken adult heartworms. Administration of doxycycline in
combination with ivermectin provided more rapid adulticidal
activity than ivermectin alone, and reduced Wolbachia burden to a
greater extent than doxycycline alone. 41 Topical moxidectin in
combination with doxycycline had 95.9% eﬃcacy in killing adult
worms after 10 months of treatment. 42 In cases where arsenic
therapy is not possible or is contraindicated, the use of a monthly
heartworm preventive containing ivermectin or topical
moxidectin along with doxycycline at 10 mg/kg q12h for a 4-week

vetexamprep.ir

period might be considered. This protocol is not recommended by
the AHS as a standard ﬁrst-line treatment but instead as a salvage
procedure. The safety and long-term eﬀects of these protocols
have not been evaluated. An antigen test should be performed
every 6 months and the dog not considered cleared until two
consecutive negative heartworm antigen tests have been obtained.
Heat treatment of samples from dogs being treated with only
preventive and doxycycline prior to antigen testing is necessary
because false-negative antigen tests are common in such patients.
43 If a dog treated this way is still antigen positive after 1 year,
doxycycline therapy should be repeated. Exercise should be
rigidly restricted for the duration of the treatment process.

Prednisone
Thromboembolism is an unavoidable sequela of any heartworm
treatment protocol. Emboli primarily consist of worm fragments
with associated perivascular inﬂammation; grossly visible clots
are not usually present. The treatment of choice to help reduce the
inﬂammatory response is prednisone. The dosage is 0.5 mg/kg
q12h for the ﬁrst week, 0.5 mg/kg q24h for the second week, and
0.5 mg/kg q48h for 1 to 2 weeks. Aspirin had been advocated in

vetexamprep.ir

years past, but has been shown to be contraindicated in
heartworm treatments because it leads to greater pulmonary
vascular extravasation of blood. Prednisone reduces parenchymal
and arterial wall damage resulting in less reparative ﬁbrosis.
Arterial elasticity is be er preserved, which leads to reduced
pulmonary vascular resistance, and subsequently fewer rightsided heart complications. 44 In dogs experimentally infected with
heartworms, eﬃcacy of therapy with melarsomine and
prednisone was the same as that in dogs treated only with
melarsomine, in either two- or three-dose protocols. 45
AHS-Recommended Treatment Protocol
The treatment protocol outlined in Table 111.4 is designed to
eliminate Wolbachia organisms and allows time for clearance of
Wolbachia-associated metabolites such as WSP. Pretreatment with
a macrocyclic lactone heartworm preventive and doxycycline
halts embryogenesis and makes the adult worms unthrifty and
smaller. This is followed by the three-dose melarsomine protocol,
which provides a 99% kill rate of adult worms. Results of a
retrospective study of naturally infected dogs treated with the
AHS protocol compared with an identical protocol with the
exception of doxycycline showed a decrease in overall posttreatment complications and mortality with the AHS protocol. 46
A second study that compared cardiopulmonary biomarkers
between a classic melarsomine two-injection protocol and the
AHS approach showed higher levels of D-dimer in the
melarsomine treatment group. 47

Prognosis
Most heartworm infections can be cleared successfully, but there
is usually residual damage to the pulmonary vasculature and
parenchyma. The extent of the damage depends on the number of
worms, activity level of the dog before and after treatment, and
the host-parasite relationship. Strict exercise restriction during
and after treatment along with utilizing the AHS treatment
protocol provides the best opportunity to minimize permanent
lung damage. 46

commercially marketed as vaccine eﬃcacy was less than the

Prevention
Diroﬁlaria immitis infection can be prevented with commercially
available macrocyclic lactone heartworm preventives (see Table
13.2), which should be recommended no later than 8 weeks of age.
These products vary in their claims of eﬃcacy against other
internal and external parasites and are oﬀered as orally
administered ﬂavored or chewable tablets (ivermectin,
milbemycin oxime, and moxidectin), as topically applied liquids
(moxidectin and selamectin), or as a slow-release formulation of
subcutaneously injected drug (moxidectin). The oral and topical

vetexamprep.ir

forms are administered once monthly, and the injectable product
licensed in the United States is available in a 6-month and 12month formulation. 14 The macrocyclic lactones are formulated to
kill the tissue stages (L3 and L4) of D. immitis. The ﬁnal molt from
L4 to juvenile worm can occur as early as 50 days PI, so it is
imperative that the product be given at a 30-day interval, because
late L4 stages have reduced susceptibility. 48 These preparations
also help to control other internal and external parasites. 49
There have been increased reports of lack of eﬃcacy (LOE)
according to the Center for Veterinary Medicine of the FDA. 50
Evidence of LOE is deﬁned by the FDA as having positive
heartworm test results in the face of consistent heartworm
preventive use. Unless the injectable form is given, it is very
diﬃcult to assess client compliance with regard to product
administration. Other reasons for LOE are possible. Underdosing
may occur in animals that have gained weight. Dosing intervals
may be prolonged beyond eﬃcacy, because doses may be
inadvertently skipped or animals may fail to retain a dose because
they spit out or vomit tablets shortly after administration. There is
also the possibility of biological variation in how an individual
animal metabolizes a drug or whether or not a strain of D. immitis
has developed drug resistance.
In experimental studies that have evaluated these products
against apparently resistant strains of D. immitis, dogs being given
preventives developed adult worms. 51 , 52 Therefore, the drugs
generally cannot be assumed to be 100% eﬀective and clients
should be so informed. Furthermore, genetic variations associated
with decreased susceptibility to macrocyclic lactones occur among
D. immitis isolates, indicating resistant strains exist. 53 , 54 Because
drug resistance is selected for and does not randomly develop, it
is imperative that any dog suspected of harboring a more tolerant
or resistant strain be treated immediately with an adulticidal
protocol that incorporates doxycycline and melarsomine.
Doxycycline will eliminate Wolbachia and reduce the potential for
transmission of the resistant strain. A three-injection melarsomine
treatment protocol will eliminate 98% of the total worm burden.
With this protocol, usually 100% of the male worms needed for
sexual reproduction will be eliminated, thus impairing
microﬁlaria production. This approach, along with the extensive

vetexamprep.ir

refugia of wild-type genes, may limit resistance from becoming
widespread.
Addition of topical products that repel and kill mosquitoes will
also enhance the eﬃcacy of the macrocyclic lactones. Use of a
topical
dinotefuran-permethrin-pyriproxyfen
product
in
conjunction with a macrocyclic lactone heartworm preventive was
able to prevent experimental heartworm infection by a known
resistant strain. 55 Reduction of exposure to mosquitoes through
standard environmental control of mosquitoes and their breeding
environments, and when possible, reducing outdoor exposure
during key mosquito feeding periods is also recommended.
Diethylcarbamazine citrate is an older medication that is no
longer marketed in the United States but is still available for
heartworm prevention in other parts of the world. Its eﬀect is at
the molt between L3 and L4 and, therefore, it must be given every
day to be eﬀective.

Public Health Aspects
Diroﬁlaria immitis is of public health concern, even though the
number of reports of infection in humans is relatively small.
However, there is no serologic test to detect infection, so invasive
procedures that involve biopsy of lesions is usually necessary. 56
The most common clinical syndrome reported in human
infections is the formation of a pulmonary nodule or nodules
within the lung parenchyma. 57 , 58 This lesion appears on
radiographs as circular density and has been described as a “coin
lesion.” These lesions resemble those of pulmonary
adenocarcinomas and often are not diagnosed until after a person
has undergone a thoracotomy for the removal of a lung lobe.
Histopathologic ﬁndings are granulomatous inﬂammation
surrounding the remnants of an immature heartworm.
Granulomatous lesions have also been recorded in the eye, skin,
testicle, and other tissues. 58 Infected dogs or blood with
microﬁlaria do not present a direct risk of infection to humans
because the parasite can only be transmi ed by mosquitoes.
Prevention is best accomplished through mosquito-abatement
programs and by using mosquito repellents, wearing protective
clothing, and remaining indoors during mosquito feeding

vetexamprep.ir

periods. See Chapter 13 for further information on insect control
measures.

Feline Heartworm Disease
Etiology And Epidemiology
Heartworm disease was ﬁrst discovered in cats in Brazil in 1921 59
and in the United States in 1922. 60 Its geographic distribution
mirrors that of canine heartworm infections, as long as there is a
competent mosquito vector present that will feed on both dogs
and cats. 61 The means of transmission and life cycle are identical
in the cat and dog until the juvenile heartworm (also referred to as
an immature adult or ﬁfth stage) reaches the pulmonary arteries
(see Fig. 111.3). Most juvenile worms in dogs mature to adults
over 3 to 4 months, after which they mate and produce
microﬁlariae. However, in the cat, most of the juvenile worms die
3 to 4 months PI, resulting in an abbreviated infection. 62 In a
small percentage of cats, a few worms mature to be adults and
live for 2 to 4 years. 63 Microﬁlaria will be produced and may be
found 8 months PI in 20% of mature worm infections. They will
be removed from the circulation by the cat’s immune response
within 2 months and not found again. 62

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
There are three stages of heartworm disease in cats. The ﬁrst stage
begins shortly after the arrival of the juvenile worms in the caudal
pulmonary arteries 75 days PI. There is an acute vascular and
parenchymal inﬂammatory response to the presence and
subsequent death of most of these immature worms
approximately 90 days PI. Light and electron microscopic lesions
can be detected in the lungs of experimentally infected cats as
early as 42 days PI. 64 Vascular disease can be found in the caudal
lung lobes by day 75 PI, followed by interstitial and alveolar
disease by day 90 PI. 65 , 66 The vascular lesions are described as
severe muscular hypertrophy of the medium- and small-sized
arteries. These same types of lesions are found in cats that have
positive results for anti-heartworm antibodies but have no adult

vetexamprep.ir

heartworms at necropsy. 66 Therefore, cats do not have to have
fully mature adult worms to have pulmonary disease.
A study of experimentally infected cats compared the
pulmonary pathologic changes between cats receiving heartworm
prevention, cats with abbreviated juvenile worm infections, and
cats with adult heartworms. Vascular lesions were found in both
cats that had mature heartworms and cats with abbreviated
infections (Fig. 111.10). The lesions in the bronchioles and alveoli
of the abbreviated juvenile worm were almost identical to those
found in cats with adult worm infections (Figs. 111.11 and 111.12).
68 Thus, pulmonary disease occurs in cats as a result of juvenile
worm infections even if they do not progress to the mature adult
worm stage. Because heartworm disease in the cat is primarily a
pulmonary disease, the term “heartworm-associated respiratory
disease” (HARD) has been adopted to describe heartworm
infections in cats. 68 , 69

eosin stain, ×20). Courtesy Drs. Ray Dillon and

Byron Blagburn, Auburn University, Auburn, AL.

Adult heartworms have the ability to suppress the activity of
the pulmonary intravascular macrophage, the main component of
the cat’s reticuloendothelial system. 70 , 71 Therefore, if the juvenile
worm matures to the adult worm, suppression of the host
immune response occurs and there may be some resolution of
clinical signs. However, when heartworms die, this
downregulation of the immune system ceases and the
degenerating parasite causes an intense inﬂammatory reaction
and thromboembolism, which can lead to a catastrophic acute
lung injury and sudden death. Sudden death has been reported to
occur in 10% to 20% of cats with mature adult heartworm
infections. 63 , 72 If the cat survives this insult, there is hyperplasia
of type II alveolar cells, which replace the normal type I cell, and
may cause permanent pulmonary dysfunction. 24 , 71 This can lead
to chronic respiratory disease, the third manifestation of
heartworm disease in cats.
Arterial intimal proliferation of the pulmonary arteries,
resembling the characteristic heartworm arteritis found in dogs,
can occur in cats. These lesions are localized and ordinarily fail to
cause suﬃcient obstruction to produce clinically signiﬁcant
pulmonary hypertension in cats. Consequently, right ventricular

vetexamprep.ir

hypertrophy and right heart failure are less common in cats than
in dogs. Ectopic migration of worms, however, appears more
common in cats.
Proteinuria occurs as a consistent complication in
experimentally infected cats. 73 Naturally infected cats also have a
greater prevalence of proteinuria (90% versus 35%) than do ageand gender-matched control cats. 73 The mechanism for the
proteinuria is presumed to be renal in origin; however, further
investigation is needed to determine its cause and signiﬁcance.
The most common clinical signs observed in cats are cough or
dyspnea (64%) and intermi ent vomiting unrelated to eating
(38%); 28% of infected cats are clinically healthy. 72 The large
proportion of subclinically aﬀected cats is probably a result of the
sedentary lifestyle of many cats, because exercise is a major factor
in precipitating cardiopulmonary manifestations of heartworm
disease
in
dogs.
Ascites,
hydrothorax,
chylothorax,
pneumothorax, ataxia, seizures, and syncope have been reported
in cats, but are uncommon. A peracute syndrome consisting of
some combination of signs including respiratory distress, ataxia,
collapse, seizures, hemoptysis, or sometimes sudden death may
arise without warning.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of heartworm disease in cats can be challenging
because there is no test that can reliably detect all stages of disease
(Table 111.5). Running multiple tests increases the chances of
making a diagnosis. It is diﬃcult to make a diagnosis using a
single method unless there is a positive antigen test result or a
worm is found on ultrasound. Additional testing must be
considered if results do not support clinical suspicion. In a study
of 22 heartworm-infected cats, where thoracic radiography,
echocardiography, and antigen and antibody testing were
performed, pulmonary enlargement was detected using
radiography in 64%; worms were visualized by echocardiography
in 64%; 55% had antigen-positive results; and 82% had antibodypositive results. 74 In a multicenter study of 215 cats when clinical
signs were correlated to serologic and radiographic ﬁndings, 44%
of cats with coughing or dyspnea and intermi ent vomiting

vetexamprep.ir

unrelated to eating had positive antibody test results. 75 This was
twice the positive antibody result rate for clinically healthy cats in
the same geographic area. Of cats with radiographic signs
consistent with heartworm disease, 58% had positive antibody
test results. 76
Diagnostic Imaging
Radiology
A bronchointerstitial lung pa ern (Fig. 111.13A) can also be found
in cats with heartworm disease but is not speciﬁc. The most
common radiographic abnormality is an enlargement of what
appears to be the right caudal lobar pulmonary artery, which is
best seen in a ventrodorsal view (Fig. 111.13B and C). This
apparent enlargement is a result of inﬂammatory inﬁltrates
surrounding the vessel and producing a radiographic shadow.
Cats with these lesions may be misdiagnosed as having allergic
bronchitis or asthma, and if treated with glucocorticoids, the
radiographic signs improve, further supporting the misdiagnosis.
Other less commonly seen ﬁndings are hyperinﬂation of the lungs
with ﬂa ening of the diaphragm, focal parenchymal
radiodensities, consolidated lung lobes, pleural eﬀusion, and
pneumothorax. The use of radiography does have limitations, as
found in one study where only 6 of 10 cats with heartworm
antigen-positive test results had radiographic signs consistent
with heartworm disease. 76

Echocardiography
Ultrasound examination can detect adult heartworm infections,
but the caudal pulmonary arteries must be examined up to the

vetexamprep.ir

bifurcation within the lung ﬁelds, because this is where most
adult heartworms are found. The cuticle of the adult heartworm is
strongly echogenic and produces short, segmented, parallel lines
(“heartworm signatures”) where the imaging plane crosses the
worm (Fig. 111.14). Heartworm signatures on echocardiography
have been described as “equal signs” (=). Because the imaging
beam may cross the worm multiple times, quantiﬁcation of the
number of worms is diﬃcult. Reports cite echocardiography as
detecting heartworms in 68% of naturally infected cats 77 and 88%
of experimentally infected cats. 78
Microfilarial Detection
Microﬁlaremia in the cat is rare for multiple reasons. More than
90% of infections in cats are abbreviated and do not reach the
adult stage. When adult worms are present, the infections are
frequently single sex, and if microﬁlariae are produced, their
presence is transient because the cat’s immune response will
eliminate them from circulation.
Serologic Testing
Antigen Detection
Both antigen and antibody testing are available for cats, but a
thorough understanding of their limitations is essential for
interpretation of results. Antigen tests are considered the gold
standard for diagnosis of heartworm disease in dogs. Because the
available antigen tests detect a glycoprotein primarily produced
by the uterus of the mature female worm, these tests will not
detect early or male-only worm infections as readily. The most
common form of heartworm disease in cats results from the death
of juvenile worms at 3 to 4 months PI and will not be detected by
an antigen test. If mature adult heartworms do develop, most cats
have only one or two adult worms. Single-sex infections are
common, and these are frequently male-only infections. Multiple
studies have reported the sensitivity of antigen test in mature
heartworm infections to be 50% to 86%. 79–81 Antigen-antibody
complexes, as described earlier in this chapter for dogs, also occur
in cats further decreasing sensitivity. 82 Blocked antigen is
particularly common early in feline infection, and multiple testing

vetexamprep.ir

modalities may be needed to reach a diagnosis. 83 Blocked antigen
was identiﬁed in 5.3% of shelter and free-roaming cats in the
southern United States and a majority (77%) were also antibody
positive. 84 As a result, a negative antigen test result cannot be
used to rule out heartworm infections in cats.
Antibody Detection
Tests that measure serum antibody detect infection with late L4,
juvenile and adult worm infections. They have been reported to
be 93% to 100% sensitive in experimental models 85 , 86 but are less
sensitive in naturally infected cats. A retrospective study
involving 50 cats with heartworms had a 14% false-negative
antibody test result rate. 72 Results of a necropsy study of shelter
cats in Texas revealed 50% false-negative antibody test results. 80
In a similar necropsy study of shelter cats in Florida, 11% to 68%
had false-negative test results using eight diﬀerent antibody test
methods. 81 In this study, 21 of 31 cats with heartworms had
negative test results on at least one of six antibody methods that
were evaluated. A number of the assays described in these
references are no longer available. Clearly however, a negative
antibody test result cannot be used to rule out heartworm
infection in cats, and more sensitive and speciﬁc assays are badly
needed for diagnosis of heartworm infection in cats.

Treatment And Prognosis
Table 111.6 summarizes the drug dosages used to treat cats with
heartworm disease. Cats with clinical or radiographic signs of
heartworm disease should be treated with daily antiinﬂammatory doses of glucocorticoids (prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg
PO). This dosage should be reduced on a weekly basis, over a 3- to
4-week period. If clinical signs recur or persist, then alternate-day
glucocorticoid therapy is given at the lowest dose eﬀective for
control of clinical signs. Radiographic evaluation and serologic
testing are repeated periodically to monitor the course of the
disease. Infected cats can be started on a once-monthly heartworm
preventive, because cats are rarely microﬁlaremic, and even when
microﬁlaria are present, their numbers are low, so reactions do
not occur.
Cats with acute respiratory distress should be given oxygen and
“shock doses” of glucocorticoids (dexamethasone sodium
phosphate, 1 to 2 mg/kg, IM or IV; or prednisolone sodium
succinate, 50 to 100 mg/cat, IV) and bronchodilators (such as
theophylline or terbutaline). Supportive therapy (IV ﬂuids and
external thermal regulation) is maintained until the cat’s clinical
condition is stabilized.

vetexamprep.ir

Results of retrospective studies are that between 10% to 20% of
cats with adult heartworm infections will die within 4 years. 63 If
cats are diagnosed with adult heartworms by antigen test or
echocardiography, their owners must be made aware of this risk
and instructed to seek prompt medical a ention at any sign of
respiratory distress, because timely treatment is critical. It may be
prudent to send home dexamethasone sodium phosphate (10 mg),
with instruction to administer it IM in case of a respiratory
emergency, to initiate treatment. This is not in lieu of, but before,
seeking emergency veterinary care.
There is no form of adulticidal therapy proven to improve the
survival rate of heartworm-infected cats. Theoretically, the use of
antileukotrienes might help because cytokines contribute to the
disease process. IL-8 is produced in response to Wolbachia, an
intracellular ricke sial endosymbiont found in all stages of
heartworms and IL-4 can be found in the secretions recovered by
bronchoalveolar lavage from heartworm-infected cats. There is
anecdotal evidence that antileukotrienes such as montelukast (2
mg, PO, q24h) may be beneﬁcial in thwarting a respiratory crisis
in heartworm-infected cats. 87
Doxycycline therapy is another theoretical treatment option.
Elimination of Wolbachia reduces the pathologic changes
associated with worm death in dogs. 34 , 35 Doxycycline is now
being used to treat some ﬁlarial nematode infections in humans. 88
, 89 Although this form of therapy in cats is unproven, considering
the 20% chance of a heartworm-related death in cats with adult
worms, its use could be considered in cases where the owner
wants to pursue all options. The recommended protocol would be
to administer doxycycline 5 mg/kg q12h for 1 month with oncemonthly administration of a macrocyclic lactone heartworm
preventive. If doxycycline hyclate is used, a suspension is
preferred to prevent esophagitis and potential esophageal
strictures. If tablets are used, follow with a minimum of 6 mL of
water.
Although not shown to improve outcomes or survival,
heartworms can be surgically extracted via a right jugular
venotomy and introduction of a ﬂexible snare or brush that is
guided into the pulmonary artery using a C-arm imaging device.
During removal, care must be taken to keep the worms intact,

vetexamprep.ir

because partial or complete traumatic transection of a worm may
result in acute circulatory collapse and death. 90

Prevention
All cats in endemic areas, whether residing indoors or outdoors,
should receive heartworm preventives. Indoor cats are at similar
risk of exposure as outdoor cats. There are many commercially
available products on the market labeled for cats that are safe and
virtually 100% eﬀective (see Chapter 13). Ivermectin is available as
a chewable treat, milbemycin as a ﬂavored tablet, and selamectin,
eprinomectin, and moxidectin as topical applications. All
products have activity against D. immitis as well as a variety of
other internal and external parasites. 69 Of 400 animal sheltering
agencies in the southeastern United States, only 23% performed
heartworm testing and 31% provided preventive medication for
cats for cats. 91 Expense and the perception that the risk of feline
infection in the region was low were reasons for these low
prevalences. Further ﬁnancial support and education are required
concerning this disease in cats.

Public Health Aspects

Case Example
Signalment

“Possum,” a 2-year-old female spayed blue heeler from
Roanoke, AL.

History

Possum’s owner reported that Possum had shown signs of
lethargy, cough, and inappetence for several days. When
abdominal distention was noted and she vomited a few times,
Possum was taken to her regular veterinarian where a rectal
temperature of 105°F and harsh lung sounds were documented.
A presumptive diagnosis of pneumonia was made, as well as
possible intestinal obstruction, as the dog had a history of
chewing and swallowing foreign objects. Possum was

vetexamprep.ir

discharged with a course of antibiotics and instructions to
return the following day for abdominal radiographs if vomiting
continued. That evening the abdominal distention became more
pronounced and labored respirations developed, so Possum
was taken to a 24-hour facility where she was admi ed to the
critical care unit. Possum was up to date on core vaccines and
was given monthly ivermectin-based heartworm preventive.
Upon further questioning, the owner admi ed to missing an
occasional dose and that the preventive had not been started
until the dog was 6 months old.

Current Medications

Ivermectin 136 µg/pyrantel 114 mg PO q30d for monthly
heartworm prevention and intestinal parasite control.

Physical Examination
Body weight: 15 kg.
General: Quiet, alert and responsive. Ambulatory on all
four limbs. Temperature = 102.1°F (38.9°C), HR = 132
beats/minute, respiratory rate = 148 breaths/minute,
mucous membranes pale pink, CRT = 2 seconds.
Integument: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No signiﬁcant abnormalities.
Musculoskeletal: BCS of 5/9; no clinically signiﬁcant
abnormalities.
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic murmur loudest at
sternum.
Respiratory: Breath sounds harsh with labored breathing.
GI and genitourinary: Abdomen distended and ﬁrm but
not painful. Urinary tract appears normal.
Lymph nodes: Within normal limits.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 42.8% (37%–55%), MCV 74.3 fL (60–77 fL),
MCHC 33.6 g/dL (30–37.5 g/dL), WBC 23,680 cells/µL
(5,500–16,900 cells/µL), neutrophils 20,550 cells/µL (2,000–

cells/µL), monocytes 1,900 cells/µL (300–2,000 cells/µL),
platelets 264,000 platelets/µL (175,000-500,000 platelets/
µL).
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 147 mmol/L (144–160
mmol/L), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.8 mmol/L),
chloride 111 mmol/L (109–122 mmol/L), BUN 22 mg/dL

Imaging Findings
Thoracic radiographs: Enlarged reversed D cardiac

Evidence of pulmonary embolism of the left caudal lobar
artery was identiﬁed (Fig. 111.15).
Abdominal radiographs: No evidence of GI foreign body
obstruction. Loss of abdominal detail suggesting ascites
(Fig. 111.16).
Abdominal ultrasound: Hepatic congestion, distended

Abdominocentesis was performed and yielded
serosanguineous ﬂuid.
Fluid analysis: Color – serosanguineous; total solids 2.8
g/dL, few mesothelial cells and RBCs noted on
microscopic review, no bacteria. Consistent with a
modiﬁed transudate.
Fecal examination: No parasite ova seen.
Heartworm test: Antigen strong positive, no microﬁlariae
on Kno ’s test.

Diagnosis

Class 3 heartworm disease.

Treatment

vetexamprep.ir

Possum was placed on ﬂow-by oxygen and 450 mL of
serosanguineous ﬂuid was removed from the abdominal cavity
to relieve severe abdominal distension, which was considered
to be impacting respiration. The dog was also started on
prednisone 10 mg q24h for 2 weeks then reduced to 10 mg
q48h, doxycycline 150 mg q12h for 30 days, enalapril 5 mg
q12h, and furosemide 12.5 mg. Possum responded favorably to
therapy and was weaned oﬀ oxygen within 24 hours and
released from the hospital the following day with instructions
for strict exercise restriction for the duration of treatment.

Possum returned for a recheck examination 2 weeks later.
Her appetite had returned, her lung sounds were greatly
improved and the heart murmur was no longer noted.
Radiographs showed signiﬁcant improvement, and the dog was
scheduled to start melarsomine therapy in 6 weeks.
Possum continued to do well clinically although signiﬁcant
abnormalities persisted on thoracic radiography (Fig. 111.17A).
The ﬁrst melarsomine injection was given on day 62. The dose
of prednisone was increased to 10 mg q24h for 2 weeks, then

vetexamprep.ir

the dosage interval was reduced to q48h. The furosemide
dosage interval was decreased to q48h. The owners were
reminded of the importance of exercise restriction. The second
and third melarsomine injections were given on days 97 and 98.
Again, the prednisone dosage interval was increased to q24h for
2 weeks then reduced to q48h. Possum returned on day 128 for
a recheck. No abnormalities were detected on physical
examination, and the furosemide, enalapril, and prednisone
doses were reduced by 50%. On day 160, thoracic radiographs
revealed reduction in the size of the right heart and pulmonary
arteries (Fig. 111.17B). The owner perceived that Possum had a
normal appetite and activity level. The enalapril, furosemide,
and prednisone were discontinued and Possum was allowed to
resume normal activity. Follow-up radiographs taken 7 years
later revealed persistent cardiac, vascular and pulmonary
parenchymal changes that resulted from worm death (Fig.
111.17C).

Comments

This dog was not treated with preventives until 6 months of
age. When preventive treatment was initiated, she was not
tested 6 months later and was likely infected during the ﬁrst
few months of life. By starting a dog in a highly endemic region
on preventives after 6 months of age (i.e., after infection), a
“slow kill” form of heartworm treatment was essentially
implemented, which is not recommended. Death of worms lead
to pulmonary thromboembolism and right-sided heart failure
at an early age, and was likely exacerbated by the fact that she
was a very active dog. Puppies should be started on heartworm
preventives no later than 8 weeks of age, and if started after 8
weeks of age, they should be tested 6 months later.
Possum was treated with the protocol described in this
chapter. Although the heartworm infection was cleared and the
dog survived, the radiographs taken 7 years later revealed how
permanent damage to cardiopulmonary structures can occur.

112: Ascarids
Michael J. Yabsley, and Sarah G.H. Sapp

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati have been
recognized since the late 1700s. Toxascaris leonina was first
described in 1902. Baylisascaris procyonis was first described
in raccoons (Procyon lotor) in Poland in 1951, and first
reported in dogs in 1988 (Michigan, United States).
• Cause: Ascarids (order Ascaridida) are large robust
nematodes that primarily infect the small intestine of their
definitive hosts. The anterior end of this group of nematodes
has three prominent lips and males lack copulatory bursa.
Representatives of this group include important pathogens of
several domestic animals, wildlife species, and humans. This
chapter will focus on the four primary ascarid species that
infect dogs and cats: Toxocara canis and Toxascaris leonina
in dogs, Toxocara cati and T. leonina in cats, and
Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon roundworm), which rarely
occurs in dogs.
• Affected Hosts: Domestic dogs and wild canids can become
infected with T. canis and T. leonina, whereas domestic cats
and wild felids are the hosts of T. cati and T. leonina. Although
the raccoon is the primary host of B. procyonis, domestic dogs
can develop patent infections.
• Paratenic Hosts: An intermediate host is not required for
ascarids, but many species utilize paratenic hosts. Rodents
are the primary paratenic host species, although birds can
also become infected with Toxocara spp. and B. procyonis.
• Geographic Distribution: Toxocara canis, T. cati, and T.
leonina have cosmopolitan distributions. Baylisascaris
procyonis is native to many regions of the United States and

vetexamprep.ir

Canada but has been introduced to parts of Asia and Europe
through translocation of raccoons.
• Route of Transmission: Toxocara canis can be transmitted to
canids by ingestion of embryonated eggs or paratenic hosts or
by transplacental or transmammary routes. Toxocara cati can
be transmitted to felids by ingestion of embryonated eggs or
paratenic hosts and through the transmammary route.
Toxascaris leonina is transmitted to canids or felids by
ingestion of embryonated eggs or paratenic hosts.
Baylisascaris procyonis is transmitted to canids by ingestion
of embryonated eggs or paratenic hosts.
• Major Clinical Signs: Young dogs and cats are more likely to
develop signs which may include unthriftiness, lethargy,
abdominal tenderness, rough haircoat, poor body condition
and potbellied appearance, cough, and mucoid diarrhea. Adult
animals are less likely to develop signs, as are those animals
with low parasite burdens.
• Differential Diagnoses: Parasitic ova of other GI helminths
must be differentiated from ascarid eggs. In dogs and cats,
other large parasitic helminths or pseudoparasites (e.g.,
Physaloptera spp., free-living planarian Bipalium, horsehair
worms/nematomorpha) may be passed in feces or vomitus
and must be differentiated from ascarids.
• Human Health Significance: Toxocara spp. and B. procyonis
are zoonotic. Infections are acquired by ingestion of
embryonated eggs in the environment.

Toxocara Canis
Etiologic Agent
The common dog roundworm Toxocara canis is one of three
ascarids that occur in the small intestine of domestic dogs. The
other two ascarids are Toxascaris leonina and Baylisascaris procyonis
(raccoon roundworm); the la er rarely occurs in dogs. Toxocara
canis is transmi ed to dogs by ingestion of embryonated eggs or
paratenic hosts, or by transplacental or transmammary routes (see
Transmission, later in this section). Infection is of zoonotic

vetexamprep.ir

importance because of the potential for T. canis to cause ocular
larva migrans (OLM) and visceral larva migrans (VLM) in
humans.
Toxocara canis can most readily be distinguished from T. leonina
by the presence of cervical alae in T. leonina which are absent or
inconspicuous in T. canis (Table 112.1; Fig. 112.1). In addition, the
eggs of these two species are easily distinguished based on
morphology but not size (see Table 112.1; Fig. 112.2). Eggs of T.
canis are pi ed, whereas T. leonina are smooth with an undulating,
prominent vitelline membrane on the inner boundary of the shell
(which is not apparent in T. canis). Therefore, if there is any doubt
to identity of adult worms, female worms can be teased open and
egg morphology examined. Eggs of T. canis are most similar to
those of B. procyonis; eggs of the la er tend to be smaller in
diameter with a zygote that usually does not ﬁll the shell, and
possess a darker coat that is less distinctly pi ed (see Fig. 112.2). 1
Another species, Toxocara tanuki, has been described from the
raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) in South Korea and Japan,
but it has not been reported in domestic dogs. 2 Morphologically,
T. tanuki is similar to T. canis (similar width of cervical alae and
egg size) but the two can be distinguished based on spicule length
(T. tanuki spicules are longer than those of T. canis and T. cati) and
by sequence analysis of several gene targets.

Epidemiology
Toxocara canis is ubiquitous in canine populations worldwide and
the prevalence varies among regions. 3–14 In the United States,
prevalence varies considerably among studies in diﬀerent regions
or among diﬀerent populations of dogs (e.g., owned dogs with
low risk of infection versus stray/shelter dogs). However, even in
areas where infection is believed to be infrequent, prevalence can
change. For example, using a long-term dataset (capcvet.org), the
prevalence of T. canis in dogs in Colorado was shown to have
increased nearly 36% between 2013 and 2017. 15 Although lower
in prevalence, T. leonina is considered widespread in canid
populations.

Age resistance to T. canis is well documented but not absolute.
Puppies spontaneously lose many adult worms after 6–8 weeks
and patent infections are less likely to develop in dogs older than
6 months following ingestion of eggs. 16 In subsequent exposures,
larvae are more likely to undergo somatic migration than to

vetexamprep.ir

successfully complete the tracheal migration necessary for
development. However, patent infections are still capable of
developing in adult dogs and are detected occasionally; these
dogs, even with low worm burdens, are suﬃcient to provide
substantial environmental contamination; transmission. 17 , 18
Male dogs are somewhat more frequently infected than female
dogs, although it is not clear if this is due to biological or
epidemiologic factors, 19–21 and the opposite has also been noted.
22 Among owned dogs, prevalence is generally greater in dogs
used for hunting or pastoral purposes than in companion dogs. 20

, 23–25

vetexamprep.ir

Eggs of four ascarid species found
in domestic dogs and cats: (A) Toxocara canis,
(B) Toxocara cati, (C) Toxascaris leonina, and

FIG. 112.2

Similar to most ascarids, large numbers of eggs are passed by
infected dogs. Each female worm can release thousands of eggs,
so a single puppy could excrete 10,000 to more than 100,000 eggs
per gram of feces (EPG). 26–28 Eggs passed by dogs are
unembryonated and require at least 2–4 weeks under ideal
conditions to become infectious. Larval development ceases below
10°C and most larvae die if frozen (–15°C). 29 Once embryonated,
eggs retain infectivity for a considerable period of time, up to 14
months in experimental se ings, and are generally resistant to
freezing. 30 , 31
Seasonality has been noted for identiﬁcation of T. canis in dogs
in the United States. 32–34 Evaluation of more than 39 million fecal

vetexamprep.ir

ﬂoat test results at national service laboratories from 2012 to 2018
compiled by the CAPC (capcvet.org) revealed monthly prevalence
of detection was consistent among years but highest (2.4%–2.7%)
in the winter (December–January) and lowest (1.2%–1.5%) in the
summer (May–June). 35 Similar seasonality was noted for
whipworms, but the opposite seasonality was noted for
hookworms, indicating that year-round control of intestinal
parasites is important. On Prince Edward Island, Canada, the
highest prevalence of T. canis infections in dogs occurred in the
autumn (September–December) and winter (December–March). 22
Numerous studies have shown that T. canis eggs may adhere to
the haircoat of dogs and possibly present a risk, if a small one, for
transmission to humans or other animals with direct contact to pet
dogs. 36–39 In one study, 100% of stray puppies and over half of
stray adult dogs had Toxocara spp. eggs adhering to perianal hair.
Puppies also had a signiﬁcantly higher mean concentration of
eggs on hair (1,499 EPG) versus adult dogs (mean 42 EPG). 40
Among owned dogs, 8.8% were positive for Toxocara spp. eggs on
hair on the head, neck, back, and/or perianal areas.
Concentrations were very low compared to stray dogs (mean 4.4
EPG). 41 Despite the frequency of contamination, the risk of
transmission is negligible unless these adherent eggs are
embryonated. Eggs are capable of developing on hair in a
laboratory environment, although dogs would likely groom away
this fecal contamination before embryonation could occur. 42
While most studies have recovered predominately nonviable or
unembryonated eggs, some dogs acquire embryonated eggs on
fur from contaminated environments. 36 Appropriate hand
hygiene after contact with dog fur should be observed to reduce
risk of zoonotic transmission, particularly for dog groomers and
individuals caring for stray dogs, especially young puppies.

of Toxocara canis.
