There is growing interest in the canine and public health risks
associated with contamination of the environment with T. canis
eggs. Numerous studies have shown that soil and/or dog feces in
dog parks, city parks, children’s playgrounds, etc. can contain
Toxocara spp. eggs. 43–46 In a 2020 study from the United States, 9%
of 3,006 fecal specimens from dogs that were using oﬀ-leash parks
were positive for at least one intestinal nematode, 17 of which
were ascarids. 47 Overall, intestinal parasites were detected in over
20% of dogs and at 85% of dog parks across the study areas.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
Toxocara canis is transmi ed to canid hosts by numerous routes
including the ingestion of embryonated eggs from the
environment or ingestion of paratenic hosts (Fig. 112.3). However,
transplacental, and to a lesser extent transmammary, routes of

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
transmission are very common, which is why nearly all puppies
are born infected or become infected early in life. The migration of
larvae in the canine host is complex and inﬂuenced by age, route
of infection, and host immunity.
Transmission by Egg Ingestion
When eggs with infectious third-stage larvae (L3) are ingested by
young dogs, the eggs hatch in the duodenum and the L3 penetrate
the small intestinal wall to enter circulation. Within approximately
24 hours, circulating larvae are transported to the liver via the
portal vein where they exit via the vena cava and are carried to
the lungs. Larvae exit the circulation through the alveoli, then are
coughed up and swallowed, reentering the GI tract in what is
referred to as hepatotracheal migration. Once in the stomach, the L3
molt to L4; another molt to the L5 (subadult) stage occurs in the
small intestine. It takes approximately 1 to 2 weeks for this
migration to be completed. Completion of maturation and
patency typically occurs after 4 to 6 weeks, tending towards
longer periods in older experimentally inoculated animals. 17 , 19
Some larvae do not complete the hepatotracheal migration;
instead they reenter circulation after exiting the lungs. These
larvae then undergo somatic migration and cause VLM. When
larvae become trapped in capillaries during migration, they
become encapsulated in granulomas produced by host immune
mechanisms and arrest at the L3 stage.
An interesting observation regarding infection via ingestion of
eggs is the eﬀect of dose on infection success. Ascarid-naïve
puppies inoculated with 10 to 1,000 eggs developed intestinal
infections, but no infections were detected in those inoculated
with 10,000 eggs, suggesting this resistance is not a result of preexisting immunity. 48 Similar results have been observed with 3week-old puppies inoculated with 3,000 eggs. 49
Transmission by Paratenic Host Ingestion
When a susceptible paratenic host, such as a rodent or bird,
ingests infectious eggs, the larvae hatch in the GI tract and enter
the circulation. Larvae in paratenic hosts do not undergo
hepatotracheal migration, but instead undergo somatic migration
and accumulate in the liver, lung, kidney, skeletal muscle, and

vetexamprep.ir

nervous tissues. 50 Invasion of the CNS by larvae is referred to as
neural larva migrans (NLM), and these migrating larvae may
produce neurologic disease which can be fatal. Larvae can also
invade the eye (OLM) and cause vision damage or blindness.
Larvae can remain viable in tissues of paratenic hosts for months
to years. 50–54 Experimentally, cockroaches and earthworms can
ingest eggs and serve as paratenic hosts. 53–56 Reviews of the
ecology and impacts of Toxocara spp. infections in paratenic hosts
have been published. 50 , 54
These larvae, regardless of location in the paratenic host, are
infectious to the canine deﬁnitive host or other paratenic hosts. 57
When a dog ingests larvae in paratenic host tissues, tracheal
migration may not always occur, presumably because larvae have
developed suﬃciently during migration within the paratenic host.
58 In experimental inoculations of dogs with T. canis larvae within
mouse tissues, infection develops, in some instances, without
breaching the GI tract as few to no larvae are recovered from sites
other than the GI wall/lumen. 49 , 58 When development proceeds
without tracheal migration, prepatent periods (PPPs) tend to be
short (as early as 33 days in one experimental infection study). 57
Transplacental and Transmammary Transmission
The majority of, if not all, infections of very young puppies with T.
canis are acquired through the transplacental (intrauterine,
prenatal) route. Infection of the dam either during gestation or
prior to conception can result in vertical transmission. Hypobiotic
larvae in tissues of the dam can become reactivated during
gestation, but it is unknown how long these larvae can persist.
The mechanism by which hypobiotic larvae become activated is
also not understood, although it is likely mediated by complex
hormonal changes (e.g., estradiol, progestin, prolactin) and
immunosuppression that occur during pregnancy. 59 The timing
of infection of a dam during gestation can impact transplacental
transmission, with more frequent transmission occurring when
dams become infected later in gestation. 60 For example,
inoculation at 35 days post-conception did not result in
transmission, whereas ﬁve of six pups from a dam inoculated at
56 days post-conception had larvae within their tissues. 60 In
another study, larvae were ﬁrst noted in a single fetus in a dam

vetexamprep.ir

infected 43 days post-conception, and the infection of dams after
47 days post-conception resulted in the presence of larvae within
fetuses. 61
In puppies born to experimentally inoculated pregnant dams,
L3 were present in the heart and lungs of the puppies at
parturition. Larvae had migrated to the GI tract within 3 days and
molted to the L4 stage with in ∼1 week. In these puppies, mature
T. canis were detected as early as 3 weeks post-parturition. 49 , 61
Larvae that fail to establish infection in the intestine in young
puppies may be passed in the feces. Dams may become reinfected
postpartum by swallowing these expelled larvae during grooming
of pups. 62 Also, adult worms are frequently expelled in large
numbers by older puppies, especially around 9 to 10 weeks or age.
Lactogenic (transmammary) transmission can also occur, but
this is considered a minor route of infection in dogs compared
with the transplacental route. 63 As with larvae acquired through
ingestion of paratenic hosts, the ingested L3 do not undergo
hepatotracheal migration.
Transplacental transmission has also been demonstrated in
paratenic hosts. Experimental infections in mice revealed the
presence of larvae in the placenta and fetal tissues after
inoculation at mid-gestation. This process is generally thought to
be prolactin-mediated. 59 , 64
Clinical Signs and Physical Examination Abnormalities
Clinical signs of T. canis infestation are most severe and most
likely to occur in young puppies. Most adult dogs with intestinal
T. canis infections are subclinically infected. Heavy burdens can
cause unthriftiness, abdominal tenderness, poor body condition,
lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, and cough. Puppies will often
present with a “potbellied” appearance. Extremely high worm
burdens can cause intestinal obstructions or intussusception.
Larval migration though the lungs creates hemorrhage, but
respiratory distress is not usually evident unless infections are
particularly intense. In rare cases, very young puppies may die
acutely due to the migration of large numbers of prenatally
acquired larvae out of the lungs after birth. In some cases, puppies
vomit developing mature worms when worm burdens are high.

vetexamprep.ir

Rarely, migrating larvae may become encapsulated in
granulomas and, if numbers of larvae are high, cause morbidity or
mortality. 65 , 66 A few unusual cases of retinitis a ributed to
ocular toxocariasis in puppies have been reported. In one case,
four puppies developed retinopathy leading to blindness, and T.
canis larvae were recovered from the eye of the one puppy that
was necropsied. These puppies had been fed raw pork liver,
which may have contained a large number of encysted larvae. 67
Toxocara canis is capable of causing VLM in cats following
experimental inoculation. Cats inoculated with T. canis eggs
developed granulomatous lesions in the liver, lungs, and kidneys
accompanied with peripheral eosinophilia, but clinical signs were
mild to absent. 68 However, a naturally infected cat that was
evaluated for pyrexia and eosinophilic pulmonary endarteritis
had disseminated lesions containing T. canis larvae, suggesting
that migrating T. canis larvae are capable of causing disease in cats
in the ﬁeld. 69

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities and Diagnostic Imaging
Laboratory abnormalities in dogs with T. canis infections are
nonspeciﬁc; peripheral eosinophilia may be present, and
increased serum liver enzyme activities have been documented as
a result of hepatic migration. 58 Radiographs may reveal diﬀuse
mixed pulmonary opacities as a result of larval migration.
Ascarids may be visible as linear foreign objects within the GI
tract following barium administration; they may also be seen on
ultrasound examination as two non-shadowing parallel
hyperechoic lines (“train tracks”) on longitudinal section and
ring-shaped hyperechoic structures on transverse section (Fig.
112.4). In one study from Sardinia, Italy, ascarids were visible in
the intestinal tract of newborn puppies using ultrasonography on
days 10, 15, 20, and 25 after birth, even before eggs were visible on
zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation. 70
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination

vetexamprep.ir

All dogs should be tested for ascarid infections by fecal ﬂotation
with centrifugation (see Chapter 5), although all puppies should
be assumed infected and thus dewormed. Recently, a commercial
test that detects antigens shed by developing and adult ascarids
has become available. 71 Puppies should be tested more frequently
than adult dogs; testing at least four times a year for puppies and
at least 1 to 2 times a year for adults is recommended.

Ascarid eggs ﬂoat in most salt- and sugar-based ﬂotation
solutions (e.g., ZnSO4 SpG 1.18; sugar SpG 1.25). Although
ascarids produce large numbers of eggs, increased sensitivity is
gained from using centrifugation of fecal ﬂoats. This is especially
important because not all parasites in dogs may produce large
numbers of ova. Toxocara spp. eggs must be diﬀerentiated from
those of T. leonina and B. procyonis (see Table 112.1; Fig. 112.2; see

vetexamprep.ir

also section on Etiology, earlier). Coprophagy is an important
consideration when examining fecal ﬂoats, especially if the dog
has access to cat feces, as eggs of T. canis and T. cati are
morphologically similar. If a dog tests positive for Toxocara spp.
eggs but the history suggests a patent infection is unlikely (e.g.,
owner compliance regarding monthly preventive use is not in
question or dog has had recent treatment), additional fecal
specimens should be evaluated after the dog has been leashconﬁned to prevent coprophagy.
An ELISA that detects antigens produced by immature and
adult ascarids is available (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook,
ME, USA). 72 Because this test can detect antigens released by
immature worms, detection of infection can occur before patency.
Experimentally, the ELISA detected T. canis coproantigen 31 to 38
days PI. 71 Single-sex infections can also be detected. However, the
assay does not diﬀerentiate between the ascarid species, so
microscopic examination of feces is still recommended (e.g.,
patent infections with either T. canis or B. procyonis can result in a
positive ELISA result). 73 As noted earlier, coprophagy may
confuse interpretation of coproantigen test results; if a dog is
coproantigen negative but fecal ﬂoat positive, one should consider
coprophagy. Several studies have noted that a high number of
canine fecal specimens with Toxocara spp. eggs actually harbor T.
cati eggs. 74 , 75 Additionally, older dogs are more likely to have
discordant results (antigen negative, fecal egg positive). 72
Retesting of specimens after prevention of coprophagy should be
recommended.

Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in puppies that die as a result of large
numbers of migrating ascarids include pulmonary congestion and
hemorrhages, as well as hepatic congestion (which may be
secondary to shock). On histopathology, eosinophilic enteritis,
hepatitis, and interstitial pneumonia may be identiﬁed with
intralesional ascarid larvae (Fig. 112.5).

Treatment And Prevention
Treatment for T. canis is necessary for several reasons: (1)
treatment of clinically ill dogs, (2) to prevent contamination of the
environment with environmentally resistant eggs, (3) to prevent
transmission from the dam to puppies, and (4) to reduce the risk
of human disease. All dogs should be on a monthly product with
eﬃcacy against T. canis to limit reinfections. Also, limiting the
ability of dogs to ingest possible paratenic hosts will minimize
infection risk. Another ﬁnal consideration for prevention of
infection in dogs is to avoid raw diets; raw animal tissues (e.g.,
liver) can be a source of infection if tissues include Toxocara spp.
larvae, as has been noted in humans.
Currently, numerous anthelmintics are approved for the
treatment of T. canis including fenbendazole, milbemycin oxime,
moxidectin, and pyrantel pamoate. In addition, pyrantel in
combination with ivermectin, pyrantel in combination with
ivermectin and praziquantel, and febantel in combination with
pyrantel and praziquantel are approved for treatment of T. canis
infections (see h ps://capcvet.org/parasite-product-applications/).
All are eﬀective when administered at the label-approved dose;
repeated treatment may be necessary to eliminate all stages.
To prevent excretion of eggs into the environment, all pups
should be routinely treated at 2, 4, 6, and 8 weeks of age and then
placed on a monthly preventive with activity against T. canis.
Nursing dams should be treated for ascarids on the same schedule
as the puppies. If possible, pregnant dams should be treated
during pregnancy to prevent vertical transmission to the pups.
Daily fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO, q24h), selamectin (6–12 mg/kg

vetexamprep.ir

applied topically), and monthly topical moxidectin/imidacloprid
have been shown to prevent infection from dam to pups when
administered late in pregnancy. 76–78

Public Health Aspects
VLM in humans can likely occur with both T. canis and T. cati
infections, although most cases are thought to be associated with
T. canis infection. Most cases are reported in children due to
geophagia/pica. Signs and symptoms are generally nonspeciﬁc
and variable depending on which tissues larvae migrate through,
which can complicate diagnosis. Common manifestations of acute
infection include fever, cough, abdominal pain, eosinophilia, and
sometimes respiratory signs; diagnosis is conﬁrmed with case
history and serologic testing (typically, a T. canis excretorysecretory ELISA to detect speciﬁc IgG). 79 Toxocara canis larvae
rarely invade the brain, but there are a few documented cases of
cerebral toxocariasis. 80 Children should be encouraged to practice
hand hygiene and be prevented from engaging in geophagia to
prevent exposure to T. canis eggs.
OLM causes diﬀuse unilateral subacute retinitis (DUSN)
involving unilateral vision loss and strabismus, again more in
children than adults (Fig. 112.6). Symptoms can wax and wane, or
it may be an incidental ﬁnding on routine ocular examination.
Granuloma formation may be misdiagnosed as retinoblastoma
and result in unnecessary enucleation, so awareness of ocular
toxocariasis is critical for physicians. 81 Unlike VLM, OLM is
thought to be associated with exposure to a low number of eggs,
which would not generate a suﬃcient immune response to
prevent larvae from invading the eye. 82 Furthermore, this low
degree of immunologic activation complicates diagnosis as
antibody levels may be minimal to undetectable. 83
Antibodies to Toxocara spp. have been detected in people
throughout the world, but seroprevalence varies regionally and
with socioeconomic development. 84 In the United States, three
large nationally representative surveys revealed that 5.1% to
13.9% of individuals were seropositive, with the greatest
prevalence among lower socioeconomic strata. 85–88 The presence
of antibodies in otherwise asymptomatic individuals is sometimes
referred to as covert toxocariasis. Multiple epidemiologic studies

vetexamprep.ir

p
p
g
have found statistical associations between covert toxocariasis and
other health conditions such as urticaria, allergies, diminished
lung capacity, occult seizures, and cognitive delay in children,
although the role of Toxocara as the causative agent is not always
clear. 89

Toxocara Cati
Etiologic Agent
The cat roundworm, T. cati, is the most common ascarid detected
in domestic cats. Unlike T. leonina, the other ascarid likely to be
found in domestic cats, adult T. cati have very prominent, broad,
“arrow-shaped” cervical alae which are less prominent and more
spear-shaped in T. leonina (see Table 112.1; Fig. 112.1). In addition,
the eggs of these two species are easily distinguished based on
morphology, but not size (see Table 112.1; Fig. 112.2). Eggs of T.
cati are pi ed, whereas T. leonina are smooth, and T. leonina eggs
contain prominent vitelline membranes which are absent in T. cati.
Therefore, if there is any doubt to identity of adult worms, female
worms can be teased open and egg morphology examined. In a
geographically limited area of Asia, a third ascarid (Toxocara
malayasiensis) has been reported from domestic cats.
Morphologically, T. malayasiensis lacks the prominent broad
cervical alae of T. cati (thus is morphologically most similar to T.
canis).

Epidemiology
Toxocara cati is widespread in felid populations worldwide,
although the prevalence varies among regions. 5–9 , 11–13 , 90 Its
prevalence tends to be highest in shelter/unowned cats or cats
without veterinary care; prevalence in these groups is often > 20%.
This high prevalence in free-roaming cats likely explains the
frequently detected contamination of outdoor spaces (e.g., parks,
children’s playgrounds). 46 , 91 , 92 In many of these environmental
studies, more T. cati eggs were detected than T. canis eggs. Similar
to T. canis in dogs, T. cati prevalence varies seasonally in cats
(highest prevalence in winter) and in the environment. 34 , 91
The PPP can be as early as 21 days if infections develop from
ingestion of paratenic hosts but can take approximately 38 to 55
days if infections follow egg ingestion. As for T. canis, large
numbers of eggs can be passed in the feces of infected cats,
although egg numbers are more variable and generally range
from 200 to 23,000 EPG. Eggs require about 3 weeks in an
oxygenated environment to become infective. No development
occurs below 10°C. 29
Dogs may develop VLM following ingestion of T. cati eggs, with
larvae recovered from the skeletal muscle and lung tissue, but

vetexamprep.ir

patent intestinal infections have never been successfully
established in dogs. 93
Toxocara cati has been reported in cats worldwide. It has also
been reported in wild felids. 94 Prevalence varies greatly based on
location and host factors. 5–9 , 11–13 , 90 Young cats (<1 year) are
more commonly infected than older cats. 14 , 16 , 95 , 96 Stray cats
have a much greater prevalence of T. cati infection versus owned
cats, and among owned cats, those with outdoor access are at
increased risk of infection. 97–100 Cats receiving more than three
anthelmintic treatments per year had a signiﬁcantly reduced
prevalence compared with those receiving fewer, although
prevalence was still 10.4% in this group. 97
Toxocara cati is frequently detected in soil specimens,
particularly in urban areas. For example, in Poland, T. cati was
more prevalent in soil in urban regions than T. canis, presumably
due to the presence of feral cats. 101 However, the majority of
surveys do not distinguish between the Toxocara species, so data
on individual Toxocara species and environmental contamination
is limited. 102

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical Examination
Findings
Similar to T. canis infection in dogs, transmission of T. cati to cats
can occur after ingestion of either infectious eggs or paratenic host
tissues containing larvae (Fig. 112.7). Transmammary
transmission from dam to oﬀspring occurs but is less important
than the other two routes. Currently there is no evidence to
suggest that prenatal or transplacental transmission occurs in cats
even though it is a major transmission route for T. canis in dogs. 93
, 103 , 104

Transmission by Egg Ingestion
As with T. canis infections, ingestion of T. cati eggs is followed by
hepatotracheal migration. During the ﬁrst 5 to 10 days after
infection, the larvae migrate through the liver and lungs; some of
the larvae migrate up the trachea, where they are swallowed.
Other larvae migrate to muscle tissues. Those that return to the

vetexamprep.ir

stomach enter the stomach wall and begin to grow from about
0.3–0.4 mm in length to approximately 1.0 mm, at which point
they molt to the L4 stage and enter the intestinal lumen. 93 L4
stages proceed to develop to adults after passage into the lumen.

Life cycle and transmission routes
of Toxocara cati.
FIG. 112.7

Transmission by Paratenic Host Ingestion
Predation of paratenic hosts such as rodents, birds, and some
invertebrates (earthworms, beetles) is likely the most important
transmission route for T. cati infections. When vertebrate hosts
ingest eggs, the larvae migrate through the liver, lungs, skeletal
muscle, and other tissues where they can remain infectious for
several months. 54 , 105 In general, fewer T. cati larvae migrate to
the CNS or eyes compared with T. canis; however, should they
migrate into these tissues, they can cause clinical disease. 106–108 In
a mouse model, T. cati appeared to have a preference for the

vetexamprep.ir

cerebellum, whereas T. canis localized primarily in the cerebrum.
109 These diﬀerences may explain observed behavioral diﬀerences
in neurologic manifestations between T. canis– and T. cati–induced
neurotoxocariasis. 110 Although most work on paratenic hosts
revolves around understanding transmission to cats, disease due
to larval migrans can be important for vulnerable or endangered
species (e.g., North Island brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli)). 111
Reviews of the ecology and impacts of T. cati infections on
paratenic hosts have been published. 50 , 54 Within paratenic hosts,
larval width diﬀerentiates T. cati (maximum 18 µm) from T. canis
(generally ≥ 18 µm). Several PCR assays have also been developed
for detection and distinction of ascarid larvae in tissues and other
specimens. 112 , 113 When larvae in paratenic host tissues are
ingested by cats, they generally do not undergo hepatotracheal
migration, although a few larvae may be recovered from the lungs
or liver.
Transmammary Transmission
Transmammary transmission is most likely to occur following
acute infection during pregnancy or soon after birth, after which
the larvae migrate to mammary glands and infect nursing ki ens.
However, transmammary transmission also has been documented
from chronically infected queens. Larvae are abundant in
mammary glands and appear in milk throughout lactation. 95
Larvae acquired by ki ens via this route do not undergo
hepatotracheal migration.
Larva migrans can follow egg ingestion in cats. When large
numbers of eggs are ingested, early migration of larvae in lungs
can produce focal hemorrhages, pulmonary arterial lesions, and
inﬂammation, resulting in dyspnea and cough. Complete vessel
occlusion can occur as a result of arterial wall hyperplasia. 114 , 115
In cats that were experimentally infected with 6,000 eggs,
treatment
with
a
commercial
preventive
(topical
moxidectin/imidacloprid) prior to inoculation did not prevent
larval migration through the lungs, although it did ameliorate
pathologic changes to some degree and prevented maturation in
the intestine. 116 Therefore T. cati larva migrans should be
considered as a diﬀerential diagnosis in cases of acute and chronic
lung disease in cats even if a preventive is being utilized.

Intestinal infections with mature T. cati are nearly always

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities and Diagnostic Imaging
Cats infected with T. cati may have peripheral eosinophilia.
Radiographic and CT ﬁndings due to pulmonary migration in
experimentally inoculated cats have been described and include a
patchy to diﬀuse bronchointerstitial pa ern and enlarged
pulmonary arteries, which appeared similar to changes associated
with Diroﬁlaria immitis and Aelurostrongylus abstrusus infection
(Fig. 112.8). 116
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
As for dogs, cats should be tested for ascarid infections by fecal
ﬂotation with centrifugation. Ki ens should be tested at least four
times during their ﬁrst year and then one to two times annually as
adults. Cats can be infected with T. cati and/or T. leonina but, as
described earlier, their eggs are readily diﬀerentiated (see Table
112.1; Fig. 112.2). A commercial ELISA that detects antigens
produced by immature and adult ascarids has become available
and can be used to detect T. cati antigens in fecal specimens. 71
Migration of T. cati adults into the stomach can cause vomiting,
so adult worms are commonly detected in the vomitus of cats
(Fig. 112.9). These worms must be diﬀerentiated from Physaloptera
spp. nematodes which are also commonly present in vomitus of
cats. Ascarids are larger and have three prominent lips, whereas
Physaloptera are smaller and have a triangle-shaped anterior end
that often has a swelling of the cuticle (see Chapter 116).
Nonparasitic free-living planarians (Bipalium) can also be found in
the vomitus of cats and are identiﬁed by their large triangleshaped anterior end.

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic Findings
Ki ens that were experimentally inoculated with larvated T. cati
eggs had multifocal depressed lesions on the surface of their lungs
at necropsy. Histopathologic ﬁndings included pulmonary artery
intimal and smooth muscle hyperplasia that was associated with
bronchial inﬂammation as well as inﬂammatory inﬁltrates within
the alveolar interstitium (Fig. 112.10).

Treatment
There are numerous commercially available products for the
treatment of ascarids in cats and many of these products, when
used regularly, limit reinfection (e.g., fenbendazole, milbemycin
oxime, eprinomectin, moxidectin, selamectin, emodepside,
pyrantel pamoate, and combinations thereof; see Chapter 13). An
interactive quick product reference guide that lists all of the
currently approved drugs for treatment of T. cati and other
parasites
can
be
found
on
the
CAPC
website
(h ps://capcvet.org/parasite-product-applications/). Treatment of
larva migrans in the cat may also be needed, especially since
disease can be associated with migration through the lung and
other tissues. Topical emodepside/praziquantel (Profender;
Elanco) is approved for the treatment of larvae, and eﬃcacy was
98.5% when used to treat ki ens 5 days after inoculation with T.
cati. However, oral milbemycin oxime/praziquantel was not
eﬃcacious. 117
Vertical transmission may be prevented by treatment of
pregnant queens before parturition. Application of topical
emodepside/praziquantel 5–6 days before parturition in
experimentally inoculated queens resulted in negative fecal egg
counts in both the queen and li er, where untreated queens and
their ki ens were coproscopically positive. 118 When queens were
inoculated with eggs daily from 50 to 60 days after conception,

vetexamprep.ir

then treated with the same topical medication, treatment was
98.7% eﬃcacious in preventing vertical transmission to ki ens. 119

Public Health ASPECTS
Most reports of human toxocariasis (VLM or OLM) are presumed
to be due to T. canis, but a few reports of conﬁrmed T. cati larva
migrans have been detected by biopsy. 120 , 121 Additional cases of
T. cati larva migrans likely exist given the global distribution of
the parasite, but current serologic diagnostic techniques cannot
distinguish between the two species. 83 , 122 A high antibody titer
to T. cati antigen but a low titer to T. canis antigen may be
suggestive of T. cati infection.
Rarely, adult T. cati are recovered from vomit or feces of
humans, typically children. Given the lack of seroconversion and
consistent clinical signs, and the low likelihood that T. cati could
mature in the human intestine, these cases may have been the
result of children consuming adult T. cati possibly passed by pet
cats. 123 , 124

Toxascaris Leonina
Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Toxascaris leonina can be found in both wild and domestic canids
and felids, although in most locations, the prevalence in domestic
animals is lower compared with Toxocara spp. 3 , 96 As noted
earlier, the anterior end of the worm and egg morphology can be
used to diﬀerentiate T. leonina from Toxocara spp. (see Table 112.1;
Figs. 112.1 and 112.2).
Worldwide, T. leonina is a common parasite of many wild felids
and canids. Wild felid hosts include nearly all extant species
across subfamilies Pantherinae (e.g., lions, tigers, ocelots) and
Felinae (e.g., bobcats, wildcats, pumas, leopards). Within Canidae,
infection has been reported in foxes, wolves, jackals, and coyotes,
among others. Molecular studies have suggested that T. leonina is
a species complex consisting of three phylogenetically distinct
clades; a canid clade (domestic dogs, wolf), a felid clade (cheetah,
lynx, tigers), and parasites from foxes. However, additional work
is needed to determine if the canid and felid parasites are genetic

vetexamprep.ir

variants or separate species. 125 , 126 Interestingly, T. leonina was
recently molecularly conﬁrmed in an ∼17,000-year-old coprolite
from a cougar (Puma concolor) from Argentina. 127
Younger dogs are more likely to be infected; however,
prevalence does not drop oﬀ as sharply with age as it does for
Toxocara spp. 128 , 129 Patent infections have been detected in
weaning-age puppies, presumably from contamination of the
whelping environment by the dam. 130 The rapid development of
T. leonina eggs relative to Toxocara spp. necessitates rigorous
sanitation of facilities to prevent reinfections after treatment.
Because of the wide host range and persistence of eggs, T. leonina
infection is common among captive wildlife species that do not
receive regular preventives. 131
Unlike Toxocara spp., T. leonina does not undergo liver-lungtracheal migration in the host and completes development solely
within the GI tract. After ingestion of larvated eggs or tissues from
infected paratenic hosts, larvae penetrate into the intestinal
mucosa and emerge into the lumen after 3 to 4 weeks of
development as either L4 stage or small adults. The PPPs range
from 45 to 80 days (average, ∼50 days). 132 , 133 Eggs of T. leonina
reach infectivity more rapidly than those of Toxocara spp. or
Baylisascaris spp., capable of becoming embryonated as soon as 4
days to 1 week under ideal conditions. Also, T. leonina eggs can
develop at low temperatures (6°C–8°C). 134 Vertical transmission
of T. leonina does not occur due to lack of somatic migration. 132
Although T. leonina infects both dogs and cats, some studies
suggest there may be some host-adapted strains. Cats inoculated
with eggs of T. leonina derived from a dog did not develop patent
infections; either no larvae were recovered or arrested L3 were
found months after inoculation. However, cats were successfully
infected when fed mice infected with canine-strain larvae. 132 , 133
Some dogs inoculated with “feline-strain” eggs became infected,
whereas others did not develop patent infections. 133 In addition,
morphologic variation (esophageal length diﬀerences) has been
noted among canine- and feline-derived isolates. 133 , 135
Occasionally, larvae persist in the intestinal wall or lumen as L4
stage in developmental arrest. In a cat experimentally co-infected
with T. leonina and T. cati, the PPP of T. leonina was prolonged to

vetexamprep.ir

22 weeks, and at necropsy 1 year after inoculation, many
immature L4 and few adult T. leonina were found, suggesting that
competition may occur. 133
In paratenic hosts, T. leonina undergoes somatic migration; the
majority of larvae become encapsulated in the mesentery and
intestinal wall. A smaller proportion are recovered from other
organs (liver, lung, skeletal muscle). 133 , 136 Migration to the brain
has not been observed. 136 Some evidence suggests that hostadapted strains (i.e., canine and feline isolates) may have
diﬀerential growth characteristics in the paratenic host. 133
Overall, T. leonina infection is associated with few or no clinical
signs. Very heavy infections may cause unthriftiness and GI
distress.

Diagnosis, Treatment And Prevention
See sections earlier on Toxocara spp. infections.

Public Health Aspects
There are no conﬁrmed cases of T. leonina larva migrans in
humans. One unusual report of infection with adult worms exists
in which nematodes were purportedly extracted from a
subcutaneous abscess 137 ; however, this could represent a
misidentiﬁcation with other large nematodes that would be more
likely to cause such signs (e.g., Eustrongylides, Diroﬁlaria,
Onchocerca). Toxascaris leonina can cause VLM in paratenic hosts,
so it is possible that some human VLM cases that are assumed to
be Toxocara spp. infections may be due to T. leonina infection.
However, there appears to be li le or no serologic cross-reaction
between these genera based on the excretory-secretory antigen
fractions commonly used for diagnosis of Toxocara spp. VLM in
humans. 138 , 139

Baylisascaris Procyonis
Etiologic Agent And Epidemiology
Baylisascaris procyonis, a common zoonotic ascarid of raccoons
(Procyon lotor), is widespread in North America. Domestic dogs
can serve as alternative deﬁnitive hosts and excrete eggs into the

vetexamprep.ir

gg
environment or can act as paratenic hosts and develop clinical
disease due to larva migration. 73 , 140 Morphologically, adults
resemble T. canis and diﬀer from T. leonina by the presence of
inconspicuous cervical alae (see Table 112.1; Fig. 112.1). The males
of B. procyonis can be diﬀerentiated from those of T. canis by the
presence of a roughened anal patch. Eggs of B. procyonis can be
diﬀerentiated from those of T. leonina by their smooth egg shells
and polar ﬁlaments (see Fig. 112.2). As noted previously, T. canis
and B. procyonis eggs can be diﬃcult to distinguish, but the la er
tend to be darker amber and are more ellipsoid.
TABLE 112.2

CNS, central nervous system; CSF, cer ebrospinal fluid; ELISA, enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay; NS, not specified.
a Had access to a cage that had previously housed a raccoon suggesting

ingestion of larvated eggs as the likely route of exposure; however, only one of
three puppies in the litter became ill.
b Larvae in tissues of infected laboratory mice.

Although there are numerous other Baylisascaris spp. in North
America (e.g., B. columnaris in skunks, B. transfuga in bears), none
have been reported from domestic dogs. However, diagnosis of
infection in dogs is generally by fecal examination and the eggs of

vetexamprep.ir

most Baylisascaris spp. cannot be reliably distinguished based on
morphology. 141
Sporadic patent infections have been reported in the United
States and Canada and a 2017 report of reference laboratory data
described Baylisascaris spp. eggs in 504/9,486,672 (0.005%) fecal
specimens. 140 , 142 Prevalence was also low in a study on Prince
Edward Island, Canada (7/242 dogs; 0.36%). 143 However,
prevalence in stray dogs or dogs not receiving regular veterinary
care is likely higher. Also, unreported infections may be detected
during POC fecal examinations or as a result of misidentiﬁcation
of eggs as Toxocara spp. eggs. In the United States, prevalence in
dogs was lower in the southern and central regions, which
corresponds with the known prevalence and distribution of the
parasite in raccoons. 142 Most of these positive dogs were large
breeds in the sporting and working groups (AKC breed
classiﬁcations). These dogs may be more likely to be kept
outdoors unsupervised where they have access to raccoon feces
and/or infected paratenic hosts, such as rodents. Like the eggs of
other ascarids, B. procyonis eggs are extremely hardy and are
resistant to low and freezing temperatures, desiccation, and
disinfectants. 144 , 145 Only temperatures > 60°C will destroy eggs
145 although bleach removes their mammilated outer layer,
making them easier to remove from surfaces.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs, and Physical Examination
Findings
The life cycle of B. procyonis is similar to that of other ascarids.
Like raccoons, dogs can develop patent infections (i.e., act as
deﬁnitive hosts) but unlike raccoons, some infected dogs,
particularly puppies, can develop VLM. Deﬁnitive hosts are
infected when they ingest embryonated eggs or tissues of infected
paratenic hosts. Depending on the route of infection, the PPP for
dogs can range from 42 to 48 days after ingestion of paratenic
hosts to ∼60 days after infection with eggs, although data are
limited. 146 , 147 Some PPPs may be longer. 73 It is unknown if B.
procyonis larvae undergo hepatotracheal migration in the
deﬁnitive host after egg ingestion as reported for Toxocara

vetexamprep.ir

infections, although this has been reported for Baylisascaris laevis
in rodents. 148 Eggs excreted in feces require 2 to 3 weeks under
ideal conditions to embryonate.
When eggs are ingested by paratenic hosts (including dogs),
they hatch and larvae exit the GI tract and migrate through
tissues. After an initial liver-lung migration, larvae migrate
throughout the somatic tissues of the host, including the CNS and
eyes, causing NLM and OLM, respectively. As with Toxocara spp.,
VLM can also produce disease if signiﬁcant numbers of larvae are
present. The paratenic host range is remarkably broad and
encompasses over 150 species of mammals and birds. 140
Some evidence exists for vertical transmission of Baylisascaris
spp. in deﬁnitive and paratenic hosts. Baylisascaris procyonis eggs
have been detected in the feces of puppies as young as 2 months
of age 140 , 142 and Baylisascaris sp. larvae were detected in a
neonatal lamb with neurologic disease suggesting infection via
the transplacental or transmammary route. 149 Additionally, B.
transfuga (a parasite of bears) was found in the cerebrum of two
newborn sibling moose calves with neurologic disease who were
born to a dam shot for aggressive behavior. 150
Migration of larvae in susceptible paratenic hosts can lead to
VLM, NLM, and/or OLM; these can be severe or fatal. When
larvae hatch from eggs, they are ∼300 µm in length but within
10–15 days grow to ∼1,500–1,800 µm. Histologically, these larvae
are ∼60–80 µm in diameter and have distinct lateral alae visible
in cross-section. In contrast, larvae of Toxocara spp. and T. leonina
are signiﬁcantly shorter and have smaller diameters (see Table
112.1). The larger size of Baylisascaris spp. larvae compared with
Toxocara spp. larvae and the growth of larvae during migration
leads to more signiﬁcant inﬂammation and tissue damage.
In raccoons, intestinal infections with B. procyonis are nearly
always subclinical and the same is likely true for dogs when they
act as deﬁnitive hosts. Very high worm burdens could
theoretically cause signs that are similar to heavy T. canis
infections. However, because dogs are not the normal deﬁnitive
host for B. procyonis, such high worm burdens may not develop.
In the few case reports that exist, burdens ranged from only 2 to
13 worms. 1 , 151 Also, not all dogs experimentally exposed to B.

vetexamprep.ir

procyonis develop infections, which is further indication that they
are not an ideal host for the parasite (Table 112.2). 73 , 146 , 147
Cerebral baylisascariasis in paratenic hosts can result in
behavioral changes, agitation, ataxia, lethargy, and confusion that
deteriorates into paralysis, seizures, coma, and death. Eosinophilic
meningitis or encephalomyelitis with moderate to high peripheral
eosinophilia are common outcomes of CNS infection. Although
ocular manifestations are poorly studied in animals, Baylisascarisassociated OLM in humans is often associated with DUSN which
can lead to diminished vision or blindness. 140 Although most
natural paratenic hosts are rodents or birds, there have been cases
in numerous species of lagomorphs, and carnivores, as well as
domestic animals (e.g., sheep, chickens) and captive exotics (e.g.,
primates, prosimians, marsupials, ﬂying fox, parrots). 140
Several cases of larva migrans in puppies have been reported
(see Table 112.2). Puppies generally showed neurologic signs, and
larvae morphologically consistent with B. procyonis were found in
association with inﬂammatory lesions. However, not all puppies
develop disease; there have been several instances of puppies (<2
months) passing eggs in feces which were presumed to be early
patent infections. 140 , 142 NLM has also been experimentally
induced in adult dogs inoculated with high doses of B. procyonis
eggs (see Table 112.2). Two dogs given > 100,000 embryonated
eggs developed clinical signs by 2–3 days PI, including lethargy,
pale mucosa, anorexia, ataxia, and reduced activity (which was
likely due to VLM). By 10 days PI, their condition deteriorated
and severe neurologic signs (inability to stand or right self,
extensor rigidity, repetitive limb movements) developed and both
dogs died by 14 days PI. Both dogs had large, ulcerated,
hemorrhagic foci in the pyloric stomach presumably due to larvae
migration out of the GI tract. 152 Two additional dogs were given
10,000 eggs and although one remained clinically normal, the
other developed ataxia and incoordination by 19 days PI.
However, this dog never developed signs as severe as the other
two dogs given a higher dose. Some behavioral changes and
agitation were noted in a dog inoculated with 50,000 eggs, but no
neurologic disease developed. No major histologic lesions were
noted in the dogs receiving 10,000 to 50,000 eggs. 152 In another

vetexamprep.ir

study, a single dog given 5,000 eggs orally did not develop any
clinical disease and no larvae were recovered from tissues. 153

Diagnosis
Centrifugal fecal ﬂotation to recover eggs is the primary method
for diagnosis of patent Baylisascaris spp. infections in dogs. Given
their morphologic similarities, care should be taken to distinguish
Baylisascaris spp. eggs from those of T. canis (see Fig. 112.2).
Coprophagy has the potential to contribute to diagnostic
confusion in domestic dogs. For example, oocysts of Eimieria spp.,
common raccoon parasites, were detected in 15% of canine fecal
specimens positive for Baylisascaris spp. eggs. 142 The ﬁnding of
embryonated Baylisascaris spp. eggs or Eimeria spp. oocysts
indicates that coprophagy has occurred.
PCR-based protocols can be used to conﬁrm the presence of
Baylisascaris spp. eggs in fecal specimens. 154 Also, a commercial
coproantigen ELISA (IDEXX Laboratories Inc., Westbrook, ME),
developed for the detection of more common roundworm genera
(Toxocara, Toxascaris), can also detect antigen shed from B.
procyonis in the intestine. 73
A diagnosis of B. procyonis larva migrans cannot be conﬁrmed
antemortem as serologic tests are not available for dogs. A history
of exposure to raccoon feces can suggest a risk. Larvae recovered
from tissues by artiﬁcial digestion or in histologic sections can be
identiﬁed morphologically and/or with molecular tools. It is
possible that B. procyonis NLM in dogs is under-recognized given
these diagnostic challenges and the variable nature of disease
progression and clinical signs.

Treatment And Prevention
There are no anthelmintics approved for the treatment of B.
procyonis in dogs. However, anthelmintics labeled for treatment of
T. canis appear eﬀective for the elimination of intestinal B.
procyonis infections. Single doses of pyrantel (20 mg/kg) and
moxidectin (1 mg/kg) were eﬃcacious in experimentally infected
raccoons. 155 Three daily doses of fenbendazole (50 mg/kg) and
ﬂubendazole (22 mg/kg) were also eﬀective. 155 High-burden
infections may require re-treatment to eliminate all worms. For

vetexamprep.ir

example, in a study of B. procyonis–infected dogs, a single oral
dose of milbemycin oxime was eﬀective for dogs infected with 25
worms; but in two dogs with more than 25 nematodes, infection
was not eliminated using this protocol. 142
Treatment of Baylisascaris spp. larva migrans in dogs has not
been investigated. In some recent human cases, early intervention
with anthelmintics (typically albendazole, use of which should be
avoided in dogs and cats) and glucocorticoids to control
inﬂammation resulted in favorable clinical outcomes with full or
nearly full recoveries. 156 , 157
Use of monthly products labeled for prevention of other
ascarids should control B. procyonis infection. Prevention of
coprophagy is important for two reasons: it prevents exposure
and the subsequent development of a patent infection and/or
larva migrans and also prevents passive excretion of B. procyonis
eggs by dogs into a domestic environment.
Preventing contact with captive raccoons and any
structures/substrates that may be contaminated is also important.
Raccoons should not be kept as pets, and any raccoons in captivity
should be routinely examined for B. procyonis infection and
treated if necessary.

Public Health Aspects
Over 50 human cerebral and ocular baylisascariasis cases have
been reported. Case fatality rates for NLM are ∼40%; however,
treatment is more successful now given improved diagnostic tests
as well as increased awareness. 140 , 157 However, NLM survivors
are still frequently left with permanent sequelae, and OLM can
cause permanent vision defects. 140 While human infections are
rare, the potentially severe consequences warrant awareness and
prevention eﬀorts. Some infections may occur covertly as with
toxocariasis; however, the implications of seropositivity in
asymptomatic individuals are not well understood. 158
Although prevalence is very low in dogs, infected dogs may
represent a greater risk for human and other companion animal
exposure due to their indiscriminate defecation habits (versus
raccoons that utilize deﬁned latrine sites). No human cases have
been linked to contact with infected dogs, but veterinarians
should provide information to clients about the risks of B.

vetexamprep.ir

procyonis infection and prevention strategies, especially in areas
where raccoons are ubiquitous and the parasite occurs at a high
prevalence.

Other Ascarids
Toxocara MalayASIensis Infection
A relatively recently described species, Toxocara malayasiensis, has
been detected in domestic cats in Southeast Asia. Toxocara
malayasiensis shares many morphologic characteristics with T.
canis but can be diﬀerentiated based on appearance of cervical
alae in transverse section (curved versus straight in T. canis),
shorter spicule length, and lip morphology. 159 Molecular analysis
also supports the validity of this species. 160
Li le is known about the distribution and epidemiology of T.
malayasiensis in cats. Worms collected from domestic cats in China
and Malaysia were conﬁrmed to be T. malayasiensis using nucleic
acid–based methods. 161 In stray cats from Malaysia, the
prevalence of T. malayasiensis infection was higher than that of T.
cati infection. 162 This emphasizes the need for further
investigation into potential cryptic Toxocara species globally.

Lagochilascaris SPP. Infection
The genus Lagochilascaris includes zoonotic ascarids of domestic
and wild felids from Mexico south to Argentina. This genus is
distinguished from other Ascarididae based on unique lip and
anterior end morphology; involutions in each lip create a “harelipped” appearance (for which the genus is named), and the lips
are of equal width to or wider than the cuticular collar. The two
primary species that infect domestic cats are Lagochilascaris minor
and Lagochilascaris major. The females of both species are 18 to 22
mm long, while males are 17 to 20 mm. 163 The lips of L. major
protrude over the collar more compared with L. minor. Eggs of
both species are similarly sized, ∼60 µm wide and generally
spherical, with a prominently pi ed surface, but the species diﬀer
in the number of pits on the surface of the eggs (L. minor 15 to 25;
L. major 33 to 45).

vetexamprep.ir

The life cycle of L. minor has been elucidated in experimental
infections. 164 The adult nematodes form tumor-like masses and
ﬁstulous lesions in the larynx, pharynx, tongue, and palate, and
occasionally in the esophagus and stomach of cats, although this
is not always observed (especially in wild felids, presumably the
“natural” host). Clinical signs became apparent within 10 days of
inoculation, including dyspnea, poor body condition, decreased
vocalization, decreased activity, and frequent sneezing. 164 One
study observed mild to moderate neurologic impairment in some
experimentally infected cats, such as imbalance, mild ataxia, and
torticollis, although other cats appeared normal in behavior. 165
Infections became patent ∼2 weeks PI and eggs were excreted
in feces. 164 Some lesions contained adults at variable stages,
larvae, and embryonated eggs, suggesting that autoinfection may
occur. 164 , 165 Lagochilascaris spp. are believed to be obligatory
heteroxenous (requiring at least two host species to complete their
life cycle) as no cats inoculated with eggs of L. minor became
infected, but all mice inoculated with eggs developed VLM. 164 It
is possible that young cats could become infected through egg
ingestion, but this has not been evaluated. Natural infections of L.
minor in domestic cats are variable in presentation, ranging from
benign subcutaneous nodules around the head and neck to large,
ﬁstulated abscesses in the upper respiratory tract. 166–169 Both
young (<1 year) and adult cats are susceptible.
The life cycle of L. major has not been demonstrated
experimentally, but is presumably similar; reports of natural
infections in cats exist and resemble those of L. minor. The adults
of L. major may cause ﬁstulated, purulent pharyngeal abscesses
that result in cough, dyspnea, and diﬃculty swallowing. 163
Abscesses may contain 50 or more adult worms.
In humans, larvae migrate to subcutaneous sites of the head,
neck, throat and particularly the submandibular area, where large
nodules may develop. If these form in proximity to the eyes,
severe, persistent ocular disease may result. 170 At least one
human case has been associated with fatal NLM. 171 More than 60
cases have been reported in Mexico, Trinidad, Suriname,
Venezuela, Colombia, Bolivia, Brazil, and Argentina. 172 The
transmission route to humans is unknown, although in some
communities it may be due to the practice of eating wild

vetexamprep.ir

intermediate hosts such as capybara, agouti, and opossums. 165 ,
173 One suspected L. major larva migrans case has been reported
from a dog and involved a purulent abscess. 174
Treatment in humans and felids typically involves surgical
excision of the nodules, followed by lavage of the area and
anthelmintic therapy to remove any remaining larvae. Levamisole
and ivermectin appear to be the drugs of choice;
diethylcarbamazine and benzimidazoles appear to lack eﬃcacy in
some human cases and experimental infections. 175–177 Prolonged
or multiple rounds of anthelmintic therapy may be required to
prevent recrudescence via autoinfection. 170 Antibiotic treatment
may be necessary if secondary bacterial infection of subcutaneous
abscesses has occurred.

Case Example
Signalment

“Chloe,” a 4-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat
from Edmond, Oklahoma, United States.

History

Chloe was evaluated in April for a recent episode of acute
vomiting. Her owners reported ﬁnding motile nematodes in the
vomitus; one was brought for examination (see Fig. 112.9).
Chloe was an indoor/outdoor cat that lived in a wooded
subdivision. She was current on vaccinations and wore a
ﬂumethrin/imidacloprid collar for ﬂea and tick control. Her
owners denied that she hunted often but reported occasionally
ﬁnding dead, eviscerated mice and birds around their home.
Current medications: No treatments other than the
ﬂumethrin/imidacloprid collar. Owners reported
applying a new collar each March.
Other medical history: Previous medical problems
included ﬂea infestation and ear mites as a ki en, both of
which resolved with treatment. Owners declined earlier
recommendations for comprehensive monthly internal
parasite control (selamectin), opting instead to only
protect Chloe from ﬂeas and ticks.

vetexamprep.ir

Physical Examination
Body weight: 3.7 kg; BCS: 4/9.
General: Bright, alert, hydrated, responsive. Mucous
membranes pink, HR = 180 beats/minute, RR = 40
beats/minute, T = 101.2°F (38.4°C).
GI and genitourinary: Normal palpation. No abdominal
mass, pain, or other abnormalities detected.
Integument: Normal haircoat. No ectoparasites were
evident.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat; musculoskeletal; respiratory;
cardiovascular; lymph nodes: No clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings
were noted.
Fecal ﬂotation, fecal antigen test, and parasite identiﬁcation
results: Numerous eggs of T. cati were present on examination
of zinc sulfate centrifugal fecal ﬂotation, and fecal specimen
was positive for antigen of Toxocara spp. (FecalDx®, IDEXX
Laboratories, Inc.). The adult nematode (see Fig. 112.9) was
morphologically identiﬁed as a female T. cati ascarid.

Serology

A feline heartworm antibody test and antigen test were
negative.

Diagnosis

Toxocara cati infection.

Treatment

Chloe was treated with a single transdermal dose of
emodepside/praziquantel.
Topical
moxidectin/ﬂuralaner
administered every 8 weeks was commenced and the owners
were advised to discontinue the ﬂumethrin/imidacloprid collar.
No further incidents of vomiting were reported.

Comments

A deﬁnitive diagnosis of T. cati infection was made based on
identiﬁcation of adult worms in vomitus, eggs on fecal ﬂotation,
and antigen detected in feces. Although normally present in the
small intestine, ascarids often migrate in a retrograde manner to
the stomach, irritate the gastric mucosa, and are expelled
through vomiting. The distinct arrowhead-shaped anterior end

vetexamprep.ir

allows adults of T. cati to be distinguished from those of
Physaloptera spp., another nematode found in cat vomit us that
requires a diﬀerent treatment (see Chapter 116). Treatment with
emodepside/praziquantel was recommended to address
potential co-infection with Taenia sp. tapeworms which are
diﬃcult to detect on fecal examination and commonly found
together with ascarid infections in cats with access to prey
species. 178 Treating only with moxidectin/ﬂuralaner every 2
months would eliminate the T. cati infection and address the
need for ongoing ﬂea and tick control but would not provide
eﬃcacy against tapeworms.

113: Hookworms
Dwight D. Bowman, Araceli Lucio-Forster, and Alice C.Y. Lee

KEY POINTS
• First Described: The canine hookworm, now known as
Ancylostoma caninum, was first described by Ercolani in a
veterinary textbook in Italy in 1859, and in 1911, the species
was moved to the genus Ancylostoma. 1 Ancylostoma
tubaeforme was first described by Zeder in 1800 as a
hookworm of the cat; it was later considered the same as the
dog hookworm until 1962 when Burrows showed it was a
distinct species. 2 Ancylostoma braziliense was described as
a new species by de Faria in 1910 from specimens collected
from dogs and cats in Brazil. It was then synonymized with
Ancylostoma ceylanicum until 1951 when Biocca showed they
were distinct species. 3 Ancylostoma ceylanicum was first
described by Looss in 1911 1 based on specimens from a
civet and then in three people in India. 4 Uncinaria
stenocephala was initially named Dochmoides stenocephala
in France in 1884 by Railliet and then later transferred to the
genus Uncinaria.
• Cause: Five members of the hookworm family
Ancylostomatidae: Ancylostoma caninum (canine
ancylostomiasis), Ancylostoma tubaeforme (feline
ancylostomiasis), Ancylostoma braziliense (the creeping
eruption hookworm of people), Uncinaria stenocephala
(canine uncinariasis), and in tropical areas of Australasia,
Ancylostoma ceylanicum (causing ancylostomiasis in dogs,
cats, and humans).
• Affected Hosts: Ancylostoma caninum is a parasite of dogs
and other canids; A. tubaeforme is a parasite of the domestic

vetexamprep.ir

cat and other felids; A. braziliense is a parasite of canids and
felids; adults of A. ceylanicum can be found in canids, felids,
and people; and U. stenocephala is found in dogs, foxes, and
other canids. There are no intermediate hosts; however, all
these hookworms can utilize some invertebrates and
mammals as paratenic hosts.
• Geographic Distribution: Ancylostoma caninum and A.
tubaeforme have a cosmopolitan distribution. Ancylostoma
braziliense tends to be restricted to the southeastern United
States and the coastal areas of the Atlantic, through the
Caribbean, the eastern coastal areas of Mexico, Central and
South America, southeast Asia, and the northern coast of
Australia. Ancylostoma ceylanicum occurs in India, Taiwan,
central Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo, and likely New
Guinea; it is also in Surinam in South America. Uncinaria
stenocephala is found in the northern United States and
Canada, as well as the EU, Africa, and it has been reported
from Australia.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Hookworms infect their final
hosts through either oral or percutaneous routes.
Ancylostoma caninum is the only species capable of infecting
offspring through transmammary transmission. Relative to
transmission into their carnivorous final hosts, all four species
of Ancylostoma persist in the tissues of murine paratenic
hosts for extended periods, with the exception being A.
ceylanicum where a very small percentage of larvae (<1%)
survive in mice one month PI. It has been reported that the
larvae of U. stenocephala can also persist in the tissues of
mice after either oral or percutaneous infection; however,
others consider U. stenocephala to have strictly a direct life
cycle.
• Major Clinical Signs: When present in sufficient numbers,
hookworms can cause anemia, leading to pale mucous
membranes, tachycardia, and lethargy. Inappetence,
emaciation or failure to gain weight, and poor haircoat are
often evident. During acute infections, feces can contain blood
and mucus. Dark, tarry feces may be produced when there is
significant blood loss into the intestinal lumen.

vetexamprep.ir

• Differential Diagnoses: Other parasitisms (e.g., fleas, ticks,
coccidia, Babesia spp.), bacterial or viral enteritis (e.g.,
parvovirus, feline panleukopenia virus, Salmonella,
enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli), IMHA, hemotropic
Mycoplasma infections, FeLV or FIV infections, portosystemic
shunt, hereditary hemophilia, toxicity (e.g., rodenticide,
NSAID, garlic, onion), and neoplasia.
• Human Health Significance: Ancylostoma braziliense and, to a
lesser extent, A. caninum cause cutaneous larva migrans in
humans (“creeping eruption”). Ancylostoma caninum can
mature to the adult stage in the human intestine on rare
occasions, eliciting an eosinophilic enteritis.

Etiology and Epidemiology
Hookworm infections in cats and dogs are caused by species of
nematodes in the genera Ancylostoma and Uncinaria. The species of
Ancylostoma infecting companion animals in the Americas include:
Ancylostoma caninum in dogs, Ancylostoma tubaeforme in cats, and
Ancylostoma braziliense in both hosts. Uncinaria stenocephala infects
dogs and other canids, and although the nematode has been
previously reported in cats, infections in feline hosts are rare. In
companion animals, these parasites are important because of the
anemia they induce as they feed from the mucosa of the small
intestine. The major diﬀerences in the pathology induced in their
hosts are related to: (1) the modes of infection utilized by each
species, and (2) the amount of blood loss induced by individual
worms within the intestinal tract, which varies with the species of
hookworm involved. Aside from the exotic Ancylostoma ceylanicum
that routinely develops to the adult stage in humans, the zoonotic
importance of canine and feline hookworms stems from the
ability of the larvae to penetrate skin and produce cutaneous
lesions in humans.
The general life cycle of hookworms requires that the feces from
an infected host be deposited at a site where it will be mixed with
porous soil that remains moist; in this manner, the eggs will be
protected from being overly heated, frozen, or dried. Then, in
about a week, larvae develop within the egg, hatch as ﬁrst-stage

vetexamprep.ir

larvae, feed and grow, molt twice, and become non-feeding
infective third-stage larvae. The larvae of A. caninum develop
optimally at 25°C to 30°C, taking only 3 days to become infective
at 30°C compared to 22 days if maintained at 15°C. 5 Ancylostoma
tubaeforme and U. stenocephala develop optimally at 20°C. 5 , 6 Fecal
cultures harboring both A. caninum and U. stenocephala eggs, if
held at 15°C, will produce only U. stenocephala larvae 8 days after
the cultures are initiated; the eggs and larvae of U. stenocephala are
tolerant to cold and can survive temperatures near freezing, for
days to weeks, while the same conditions will kill A. caninum eggs
and larvae in a few days. 5 There have been no similar studies on
the development of A. braziliense, but its presence only in warmer
climes would suggest that it develops most successfully at
warmer temperatures and may not develop in soils of colder
climates.
Infective-stage hookworm larvae that develop in the soil can
enter their ﬁnal canine or feline hosts in three diﬀerent ways. One
means of infection is to penetrate the skin, be carried to the lungs
via the circulatory system, and then enter the intestine after
migrating up the trachea and being swallowed. Second, they can
be ingested as free larvae from the soil or on contaminated plants
or fomites. Third, they can be ingested as infective-stage larvae in
the tissues of prey paratenic hosts. All four species of Ancylostoma
persist in tissues of rodent paratenic hosts for extended periods,
with the exception of A. ceylanicum where a small percentage of
larvae (< 1%) survive in mice a month PI. 7–9 Additional work with
A. caninum has shown that it will persist in the tissues of
cockroaches, rodents, cats, sheep, and goats. 10 Chickens appear
refractory to A. caninum larval infection with < 1% of the inoculum
being recovered from muscle after 2 months, 11 and no larvae
were recovered from chickens 20 days after infection with A.
tubaeforme. 7 Uncinaria stenocephala can also persist in the tissues of
mice after oral or percutaneous infection 12 ; however, others
consider U. stenocephala to have strictly a direct life cycle. 13
Ancylostoma caninum of dogs is the only species discussed herein
that infects neonates through transmammary transmission (Fig.
113.1). 14 In this case, larvae that have been sequestered in the
tissues of the dam will enter the mammary gland and make their
way into the milk after the female begins lactation. Thus, very

vetexamprep.ir

young pups can be infected with a large number of A. caninum
relative to their body size, which can lead to severe and even fatal
anemia. The pre-patent and patent periods for A. caninum, A.
tubaeforme, A. braziliense, and U. stenocephala, respectively, are: 15–
26, 18–28, 14–16, and 15–17 days before eggs are produced; and
about 6, 18–24, 4–8, and 6–12 months of egg excretion. 15–18
Ancylostoma caninum and A. tubaeforme have a cosmopolitan
geographic distribution. Uncinaria stenocephala, the most cold
tolerant of the species, 19 is found in the northern United States
and Canada, as well as in the EU, Africa, and has been reported
from Australia. 20 The CAPC prevalence maps for the United
States show the results for over 10 million dog fecal examinations;
in 2021, about 2.9% contained hookworm eggs. The CAPC maps
for cats, representing almost 1.8 million fecal specimens, show
that 0.8% contained hookworm eggs. Much higher infection rates
were reported in animals not receiving routine veterinary care or
endoparasitic treatments, and those having access to prey and
contaminated environments. 21–23 The areas with the highest
prevalence rates were in the southeastern and southcentral states,
and the areas with the lowest rates of infection were the
southwestern states. Ancylostoma braziliense, based on reported
cases of “creeping eruption” in humans and surveys of dogs and
cats in the United States, is located mainly in the southeastern and
southcentral states bordering the shores of the Atlantic and the
Gulf of Mexico. 24–26 Globally, cutaneous larva migrans (CLM)
occurs in warmer climates, is endemic in many countries in the
developing world, and has increasingly been a problem in
southern Europe. The disease has been a problem among travelers
returning to North America from the Caribbean 27 ; a study that
included over 17,000 travelers consulting specialized travel or
tropical medicine clinics on six continents after holidays identiﬁed
the disease in 2%–3% of patients. 28 Sites of exposure, in
decreasing order of frequency, were the Caribbean, Southeast
Asia, Central America and South America, and the northern coast
of Australia. 15 , 29 (see Public Health Signiﬁcance). Ancylostoma
ceylanicum occurs in India, Taiwan, central Thailand, Malaysia,
Indonesia, Borneo, and likely New Guinea; it is also in Surinam in
South America. 15 , 29

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
The disease produced by adult hookworms is anemia. In 1992, Dr.
Jay Georgi, who for years studied blood loss from hookworm
infection and haemonchosis, described the blood lost due to A.
caninum as follows: “The amount of blood removed is directly
proportional to the weight of adult hookworms in the small
intestine and amounts to a daily loss of about 30 µL of
erythrocytes per mg of worm. An adult female A. caninum weighs
2.0 to 2.6 mg and a male, about 0.8 mg. Therefore, a population of
only 50 females and 25 males would exact a toll of about 4 mL of
erythrocytes each day, a substantial drain on the hemopoietic
resources of any puppy. The imposition of such a burden during
the nursing period could prove fatal. To make ma ers worse,
peak blood loss is experienced even before eggs appear in the
feces. This not only renders diagnosis diﬃcult but constitutes a
sudden hemorrhagic shock that very young puppies are illequipped to compensate. The other species of Ancylostoma remove
less blood than A. caninum, and U. stenocephala least of all.” 30–32
It has also been estimated that amount of blood lost in dogs per
worm is 10–200 µL for A. caninum, 14 µL for A. ceylanicum, 1 µL
for A. braziliense, and 0.3 µL for U. stenocephala. 31 Thus, A. caninum
causes far greater blood loss than the other species. In the case of
puppies, not only do they have a markedly lower total blood
volume than adults but also they do not receive large amounts of
iron in the milk from the dam, limiting their ability to regenerate
red blood cells. By the end of the third week postpartum, a
heavily infected pup can lose 25% of its circulating erythrocyte
volume; this can be fatal. 33
The same number of worms will cause as much blood loss in an
adult dog as they do in puppies, however, a well-nourished adult
dog can compensate for the blood loss. “Compensated” and
“decompensated” hookworm disease has been described. 30 In
compensated disease, well-maintained dogs will have no signs
other than fecal egg excretion or reductions in erythrocyte
parameters. In decompensated hookworm disease, animals that
are malnourished or emaciated may require supportive protein

vetexamprep.ir

and iron supplements along with treatment for intestinal
hookworms.
Hookworms secrete a family of anticoagulative proteins into the
host blood that prevents ﬁbrin clot formation and also enhances
the dissolution of formed clots. They act by several mechanisms,
including inhibition of platelet aggregation and clo ing factor
activity (Xa, VIIa/tissue factor complex), as well as degradation of
ﬁbrinogen into nonfunctional components. 34 , 35 Consequently,
hemorrhage can continue from hookworm-abandoned feeding
sites within the intestine until hemostasis is re-established (Fig.
113.2). This intestinal hemorrhage, in combination with that lost
through direct feeding by the worms, contributes to anemia and
hypoproteinemia in heavily infected animals.
Dogs and cats infected with hookworm species other than A.
caninum can have large numbers of worms without signiﬁcant
clinical signs, because these other species are not passed directly
from the mother to oﬀspring, they cause less blood loss per worm,
and they are less pathogenic. However, all hookworm infections
cause blood loss, and signs are commensurate with the number of
worms present. Thus, a high egg count in adult animals indicates
a larger number of adult female worms, and greater blood loss
than an animal with low egg counts, in most cases. Though
anemia is uncommon with U. stenocephala and A. braziliense
infections, hypoproteinemia may still develop as a result of
villous atrophy with associated malabsorption and protein loss. 36
Additionally, intestinal mucosal thickening can be observed when
U. stenocephala worm numbers reach 1,000 or more. 36

vetexamprep.ir

Life cycle of Ancylostoma caninum,
the most common hookworm in dogs in the
United States. The nematode can infect dogs
in the same manner as the other hookworms
of cats and dogs (i.e., ingestion of free larvae
from the environment, ingestion of larvae in
prey tissues, and through skin penetration), but
it is the only hookworm species in these hosts
that is capable of transmammary transmission
through the reactivation of hypobiotic larvae
from the tissues of the dam.

Clinical Signs and Physical Examination Findings
Peracute clinical disease is seen in neonatal pups infected by A.
caninum through transmammary transmission. Pups often appear
healthy in the ﬁrst week of life, then rapidly deteriorate and die at
2–3 weeks of age. Acute disease aﬀects older pups and ki ens,
and even adult animals exposed to overwhelming numbers of
infectious larvae. Clinical signs include diarrhea with melena
and/or mucus, mucosal pallor, lethargy, inappetence, emaciation
or failure to gain weight, and poor haircoat. Tachycardia,
tachypnea, and weak pulses may be present on physical
examination in severely anemic and hypoproteinemic animals. In
peracute—and sometimes acute—hookworm disease, clinical
signs may occur before eggs appear in the feces, so an accurate
diagnosis relies on a good history and physical examination
ﬁndings. Animals with chronic, compensated hookworm
infections are subclinically infected, though decreases in
hematologic parameters such as erythrocyte count and
hemoglobin concentration may be evident.

vetexamprep.ir

Uncinaria stenocephala infection is most commonly associated
with dermatitis, though Ancylostoma spp. are also capable. These
cutaneous manifestations typically occur in kenneled greyhounds.
37 There is typically dermatitis with keratitis of the paw pads, but
associated lesions can also often be observed on the ventral thorax
and abdomen as well as the limbs. Thickened intestinal loops may
also be palpable on physical examination in heavy infections of U.
stenocephala.

Diagnosis
Fecal Analysis
Fecal Flotation
Patent hookworm infections may be diagnosed by recovery of
eggs from fresh or refrigerated fecal specimens examined by
routine fecal centrifugal ﬂotation; stationary (noncentrifuged)
ﬂotations will recover a markedly lower percentage of hookworm
eggs from any given fecal specimens. Hookworm eggs are thinshelled, smooth and oval, containing an embryo in a morula
(generally 4–8 cells) stage. Careful measurement of length and
width, and consideration of the host species, can aid identiﬁcation
of the species of hookworm involved. The eggs of A. caninum and
A. tubaeforme are similarly sized, but can be distinguished based
upon the host speciﬁcity of the parasite. Dogs and cats can both be
infected with A. braziliense, but the smaller egg of this species
allows it to be distinguished from the dog- and cat-speciﬁc
hookworms. Uncinaria stenocephala eggs are larger than any of the
Ancylostoma spp. (Fig. 113.3). The egg measurements (length by
width) of the four hookworm species in micrometers are: 48–57 ×
34–39 µm for A. braziliense, 58–66 × 38–42 µm for A. tubaeforme, 58–
76 × 36–41 µm for A. caninum, and 71–92 × 35–58 µm for U.
stenocephala. 38 , 39 Mixed infections are possible. In the case of U.
stenocephala, the major confounder in fecal examinations is the
presence of strongyle or trichostrongyle eggs in the feces of a dog
that has ingested either prey or the feces of ruminants, equids, or
other animals.
