Fecal Antigen Detection
Coproantigen detection of hookworms via a fecal ELISA is
commercially available (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook, ME,
USA). This test can detect a protein excreted by Ancylostoma spp.
and U. stenocephala worms in the intestine of cats and dogs, but
cannot diﬀerentiate species. This test detects both patent and
nonpatent infections, i.e., young and adult nematodes of either sex
in the intestine. 40 It is recommended that coproantigen testing be
paired with fecal centrifugal ﬂotation tests to optimize detection
of concurrent infections and to provide information on egg
excretion (and hence environmental contamination).
Adult Nematode Morphology
Adult worms recovered from the feces or during necropsy may be
identiﬁed to species level by examination of the buccal capsule
and the teeth present on its anterior margin. Ancylostoma species

vetexamprep.ir

can be diﬀerentiated by the number of teeth present: one large
tooth on either side of the midline in A. braziliense, and three
lateral teeth on either side for A. caninum and A. tubaeforme.
Uncinaria stenocephala, on the other hand, is armed with a cu ing
plate on each side rather than teeth (Fig. 113.4). Although adult A.
caninum resemble A. tubaeforme, they can be diﬀerentiated based
on the length of the spicules of the males. However, cats and dogs
are refractory to infections with A. caninum and A. tubaeforme,
respectively, so such eﬀorts for diﬀerentiation are seldom
warranted.
Molecular Identification
Molecular identiﬁcation of hookworm eggs, larvae, or adults to
the species level is possible by performing PCR ampliﬁcationsequencing. In early 2022, a real-time PCR assay was released in
North America that detects the DNA of Ancylostoma spp. and U.
stenocephala as part of a panel designed to detect the DNA of 20
diﬀerent parasites (KeyScreen GI Parasite PCR, Antech, CA, USA).
The assay also detects a genetic marker for benzimidazole
(fenbendazole) resistance in A. caninum (see Treatment, below).
Additional peer-reviewed studies are required to assess the
performance of this panel.

Laboratory Abnormalities
In animals with hookworm infections, the CBC may reveal acute
normocytic, normochromic anemia progressing to microcytic,
hypochromic anemia. Eosinophilia may also be observed.
Hypoalbuminemia is present in severe cases, and increased BUN
concentration may be evident as a result of intestinal bleeding.

Diagnostic Imaging
Although not practical or economical as a primary means of
diagnosing hookworm infection, intestinal hookworms in both
dogs and cats can be detected using conventional ﬂexible
endoscopy (see Fig. 113.2). 41 Capsule endoscopy is another
option in dogs. 42

Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Grossly, translucent, white, or red-colored nematodes up to 2 cm
long are found a ached to the intestinal mucosa in hookworm
infections. Pinpoint red lesions are visible in the mucosa at sites
where hookworms previously fed. The contents of the intestinal
lumen are dark red in color due to waste produced by the
hookworms and ongoing hemorrhage. In severely anemic
animals, extreme pallor of the intestines, liver, and other internal
organs is observed. Serous eﬀusion may be found in the
abdominal and thoracic cavities as a consequence of
hypoproteinemia. Intestinal thickening may be apparent in
animals heavily infected with U. stenocephala.

Treatment and Prognosis
Products approved for A. caninum treatment in dogs include
fenbendazole, milbemycin, moxidectin, pyrantel, and a
pyrantel/febantel/praziquantel combination. All of these, aside
from milbemycin, are also labeled for treatment of U. stenocephala
infections. The ivermectin-based heartworm preventives that
contain a pyrantel component also are labeled for the treatment of
A. braziliense infections. Approved products for the treatment of A.
tubaeforme infection in cats include emodepside, ivermectin,
milbemycin, moxidectin, pyrantel, and selamectin; in cats, the
ivermectin dose used for heartworm prophylaxis is also approved
for treatment of A. braziliense infections.
The prognosis for recovery from acute and chronic hookworm
disease is good to excellent after eﬀective anthelmintic treatment.
Unfortunately, in recent years, veterinarians have observed an
increase in the number of cases where A. caninum infections have
not been successfully cleared by treatment with multiple doses or
even multiple classes of anthelmintics approved for this purpose.
Initially the “larval leak” phenomenon was suspected to be largely
responsible (see Prevention, below), but subsequently, emergence
of anthelmintic resistance has been documented in A. caninum in
the United States. Resistance of A. caninum to pyrantel was ﬁrst
reported in pet dogs in Australia in 2007. 43 In the United States,
resistance was ﬁrst suspected in pet greyhounds that failed to stop
excreting hookworm eggs despite aggressive treatment with a
combination of topical moxidectin, oral pyrantel, and oral
febantel. However, uncertainty about client compliance limited

vetexamprep.ir

full interpretation. 44 Subsequent work with hookworm isolates
from pet greyhounds and pet dogs of other breeds conﬁrmed
infection with multidrug resistant A. caninum through poor
reduction in fecal egg counts and elevated resistance ratios. 45 , 46
The problem appears to have initially developed in greyhound
kennels, and although resistance is also described from other
breeds, greyhounds are overrepresented in reports of A. caninum
resistance. 47 Initial data indicate that canine hookworms resistant
to pyrantel, benzimidazoles, and macrocyclic lactones can be
cleared with emodepside treatment. 48 An oral product containing
emodepside is available for dogs in Europe (but not in the United
States) and is eﬀective for treating A. caninum infections. 49 A
topical feline emodepside product is available in the United States
and appears eﬀective against multidrug resistant hookworm
infections when administered to dogs orally. However, due to
toxicity concerns, the topical feline formulation should only be
administered orally to dogs by a veterinarian and care must be
taken to avoid severe reactions in heartworm-infected dogs. 50 The
geographic distribution of multidrug resistant hookworm
populations in the United States has not been fully deﬁned but
appears widespread. It is strongly recommended that
veterinarians follow up with suspected resistant cases posttreatment to conﬁrm that egg excretion has ceased. If egg
clearance cannot be accomplished, owners must be careful to
promptly dispose of feces to prevent larval development that may
lead to reinfection of the dog or infection risk for humans.
Emodepside treatment under the close supervision of a
veterinarian may also be considered. 50

The prognosis for recovery from peracute hookworm disease
due to A. caninum is guarded to poor, even when eﬀective
treatment is instituted. Whole blood transfusion and other colloid
therapy are often necessary for supportive care and to allow time
for worms to be killed by anthelmintics. Supplemental oxygen
may be required. Additional ongoing support in the form of iron
supplementation and a high-protein diet is warranted.

Immunity and Vaccination
Greyhounds appear to develop immunity to infections with U.
stenocephala. 51 A vaccine for hookworms was previously available

vetexamprep.ir

that utilized irradiated larvae, similar to the commercial vaccine
for the bovine lungworm, Dictyocaulus viviparus. 52 Thus, dogs do
develop immunity to hookworm infections, but it does not appear
to be sterile immunity. Also, work has shown that when dogs
receive less than adequate nutrition, their immunity wanes and
they can be reinfected with hookworms. 53

Prevention
With current heartworm prevention products that are eﬀective
against hookworm infections, along with the other excellent
anthelmintics labeled for treatment of hookworms, there is every
reason to believe that hookworm infections can be controlled
through routine prevention. Dogs and cats receiving broadspectrum heartworm prevention should in most instances remain
relatively hookworm-free (caveat: dormant larvae present in the
tissues are not removed until they reactivate, migrate to the
intestines, and are killed when the next dose of anthelmintic is
administered). If they are not receiving such prevention, cats and
dogs should have two to four fecal examinations each year to
insure that any worms detected at that time are removed through
proper treatment. Some intact females, especially rescue dogs,
may have large numbers of sequestered larvae in their tissues that
can reactivate and infect nursing pups, and there is currently no
approved means of preventing transmammary infection in these
dogs. Thus, veterinarians need to remain aware that post-natal
hookworm infections are likely to occur and can prove fatal to
pups. For all puppies, the recommendation is to deworm with
pyrantel every 2 weeks beginning at 2 weeks of age until they can
be transitioned to a monthly heartworm preventive product with
activity against hookworms. For a dam with a history of A.
caninum-related peracute disease in a previous li er, decreased
transmission to subsequent li ers can be achieved by the oﬀ-label
use of one of the following: daily fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO,
given from the 40th day of gestation to the 14th day postpartum;
this regimen can be costly), ivermectin (0.5 mg/kg, SC, given 4–9
days before parturition and then again 10 days later), transdermal
moxidectin (4–4.6 mg/kg given on the 56th day of gestation), or
injectable moxidectin (1 mg/kg, SC, on the 55th day of gestation).
54

vetexamprep.ir

Some dogs persistently excrete eggs in spite of treatment. Even
when treatment successfully removes the population of worms in
the intestine, sequestered larvae in the dog’s tissues—the same
ones that awaken to infect pups—constantly reactivate to
repopulate the intestine and mature to egg-producing adults. 55–57
This “larval leak” phenomenon was a common occurrence before
monthly control products became available. Some dogs on
monthly preventives, especially those coming from heavily
contaminated environments, continue to shed eggs despite many
months of repeated hookworm treatments. In these dogs, the goal
should be to use the monthly preventives to remove any worms
reactivated since the last dose in order to maintain low
populations of feeding worms in the intestine, and preclude
disease in the animal as well as egg excretion into the
environment.

Public Health Aspects
The hookworms of dogs and cats in the United States can all
penetrate the skin of mammals. At the same time, the vast
majority of reports of creeping eruption from hookworms occur in
areas where the species A. braziliense is found. Ancylostoma
braziliense is also the species for which larvae have been recovered
from human skin and identiﬁed using molecular methods. 58
Migrating larvae cause pruritic, serpiginous tracks in the skin that
can persist for weeks if not treated (Fig. 113.5).

vetexamprep.ir

Serpiginous tracts secondary to
cutaneous larva migrans. Reprinted from Kinkaid L,
FIG. 113.5

Klowak M, Klowak S, et al. Management of imported
cutaneous larva migrans: A case series and mini-review.
Travel Med Infect Dis. 2015;13:382–387.

An often overlooked aspect of canine and feline hookworm
infections is that these parasites utilize mammalian paratenic
hosts as part of their life cycles. All four of these hookworms
persist for long periods in the tissues of rodents, and a hookworm
larva was identiﬁed in a muscle biopsy from a person 3 months
after diagnosis of CLM. 59 Ancylostoma caninum larvae can persist
in the muscles of sheep after percutaneous infection. 10 Thus, it
seems likely that in patients with CLM, larvae will migrate into
the musculature where they will begin a long-term residence.
Among the hookworm species found in the United States, only
A. caninum is known to develop to the adult stage in humans. The
worms have been found in the intestine and cause eosinophilic
enteritis with abdominal pain as the main symptom. 21

Case Example

vetexamprep.ir

Signalment

“Tonka,” a 13-week-old intact male basset hound from Ithaca,
NY, USA.

History

Tonka’s owner reported a 24-hour history of lethargy and
inappetence, with one episode of a small amount of bile being
vomited. Tonka had had diarrhea with intermi ently black and
tarry feces since he was acquired from a local breeder 1 week
ago. He had been eating, drinking, and urinating normally up
until the previous day. According to the owner, Tonka had
been vaccinated by the breeder at 8 and 12 weeks of age with a
“9-way” vaccine, and had also been dewormed. He was not on
any current medications.

Physical Examination Findings

Body weight: 7.6 kg.
General: Quiet, alert, and responsive. Temperature =
100.5°F (38.1°C), HR = 188 beats/minute, RR = 24
breaths/minute, pale mucous membranes, CRT < 2
seconds.
Integument: Normal haircoat. No petechiation and no
evidence of ectoparasites.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mild waxy debris within both
ear canals. No other abnormalities noted.
Cardiovascular: Sinus tachycardia. Femoral pulses strong
and synchronous. No murmurs were detected on
auscultation. Mucous membranes were pale and tacky.
GI and genitourinary: The abdomen was large and
distended, with ﬂuid-ﬁlled intestinal loops. No pain was
elicited upon palpation. No other abnormalities noted.
Musculoskeletal, respiratory, lymph nodes: No clinically
signiﬁcant abnormalities noted.

Laboratory Findings
Rapid assessment tests: PCV 17%, TP 5.1 g/dL, BUN 15–26
mg/dL.
Coagulation panels: PT and aPTT within normal limits.

vetexamprep.ir

Parvovirus fecal antigen ELISA test: Negative.
Blood smear: Normal RBC morphology with no
spherocytes observed. WBCs (lymphocytes, neutrophils,
eosinophils) were subjectively increased. Approximately
15 platelets/HPF were observed.

Fecal Examination Results
Fecal ﬂotation: Ancylostoma caninum eggs, >100 per 10×
ﬁeld.

Diagnosis

Anemia due to ancylostomiasis.

Treatment

Tonka was given an IV bolus of 20 mL/kg of Plasmalyte for
cardiovascular support, followed by 175 mL of packed RBCs.
Anthelmintic treatment was initiated with fenbendazole (50
mg/kg, PO, q24h for 3 days). Famotidine (0.5 mg/kg, q12h) and
sucralfate (0.5 g slurry, q8h) for 5 days were also prescribed for
gastroprotection.

Comments

This puppy was evaluated by a veterinary emergency service. It
was unclear from the history provided by the owners what
drug and protocol the breeder used for deworming. Based on
the severity of the clinical signs, the large numbers of eggs in
the feces, and the large numbers of A. caninum worms passed in
the feces a day after the initiation of anthelmintic treatment
(Fig. 113.6), it seemed likely that whatever parasite protocol the
breeder utilized was insuﬃcient for hookworm control.
Adherence to the recommendation for deworming every 2
weeks starting at 2 weeks of age until puppies can be placed on
a broad-spectrum heartworm preventive should prevent this
condition.

David A. Elsemore, and Jennifer K. Ke is

KEY POINTS
• First Described: Trichuris vulpis was first described in 1789 by
von Frölich, who isolated it from a dog in Europe. Trichuris
serrata and Trichuris campanula, described in 1879 and 1888,
respectively, were first isolated from cats in Brazil by von
Linstow. 1 , 2 It has been proposed that these are the same
species and should be renamed Trichuris felis. 3
• Cause: Trichuris vulpis, which occurs in dogs, and Trichuris
felis (Trichuris serrata and Trichuris campanula), which occurs
in cats, are commonly referred to as whipworms (family
Trichuridae).
• Affected Hosts: Trichuris vulpis infects dogs and wild canids.
Trichuris felis infects domestic cats and wild felids.
• Geographic Distribution: The distribution of T. vulpis is
worldwide, although prevalence is reportedly lower in
extremely cold and extremely hot arid climatic zones. 1
Trichuris felis is considered a more exotic infection except in
tropical and sub-tropical zones with infection being common in
South America and the Caribbean. Less frequent reports of
infection have come from the USA, Australia, and Europe.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs and cats become infected with
whipworms by ingestion of eggs with infective first-stage
larvae.
• Major Clinical Signs: In general, T. vulpis infections are of low
pathogenicity. However, infections can be associated with
intermittent diarrhea and, with heavy infections, chronic and/or
severe diarrhea, dehydration, lethargy, anorexia, and anemia.
Little is known regarding feline disease. Theoretically, cats

vetexamprep.ir

could have similar clinical signs as dogs, although there are
no published case studies suggesting infection results in
clinical signs.
• Differential Diagnoses: The clinical signs are representative of
many large bowel disorders (gastroenteritis, dietary
indiscretion, gastrointestinal foreign body, inflammatory bowel
disease, and other nematode infections). In some cases,
infection can be associated with pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism.
Presence of Trichuris eggs does not necessarily indicate that
whipworms are the cause of the clinical signs, given the
general low pathogenicity of infection.
• Human Health Significance: Trichuris vulpis has been
proposed as a zoonotic pathogen. While there have been a
few reported human infections, genetic sequencing to confirm
the Trichuris sp. has been limited. There are no reports of T.
felis infecting humans.

Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Dogs
Trichuris spp. belong to the superfamily Trichinelloidea and the
family Trichuridae. While the name of this genus can be
translated as “hair-tail,” it is actually the anterior portion (forming
up to ¾ of the body) that is ﬁlamentous and the posterior portion
that is thick, resulting in the typical whip-like appearance. 4
Trichuris vulpis adults range from 4.5 to 7.5 cm in length (Fig.
114.1). 5 They have a stichosome esophagus and a bacillary band
in the esophageal region. The male adults have a single spicule
and a coiled posterior while the females have a straight uterus and
straight posterior. 6 The eggs range from 70 to 90 µm long by 30 to
50 µm wide, are lemon shaped with symmetrical bipolar plugs,
and contain a single cell in fresh feces (Fig. 114.2). 5 , 7 , 8
Several experimental infections have been conducted to
determine the life cycle of T. vulpis (Fig. 114.3). 7 , 9–11 Infection
occurs via ingestion of an egg with an infective ﬁrst-stage larva.
On arrival in the small intestine, the plugs are digested and the
larvae are released primarily in the duodenum and upper portion

vetexamprep.ir

of the jejunum with some delayed until the upper portion of the
ileum. 9 , 11 The larvae enter the mucosa via the crypts of
Lieberkühn where they remain tightly coiled for 6 to 15 days. 9 , 11
Some minor destruction of the host tissue cells surrounding the
larvae can occur. By 15 days PI, the larvae enter the lumen and
travel to the cecum or colon where they enter the mucosa, molt
three times, and then mature to adults. As the larvae molt from an
immature stage (which are not whip-shaped and more uniform in
diameter) to an adult, the anterior end remains in the epithelium
and the posterior end begins to protrude into the lumen. The ﬁnal
adult worm lives with the anterior esophagus in a “tunnel” in the
mucosa, formed by the destruction of the lateral membranes while
the apical and basal surfaces remain intact. 12 The embedded
portion of the adult worm is normally limited to the superﬁcial
tunica propria although some individual nematodes penetrate
more deeply into lymph follicles resulting in focal coagulative
necrosis surrounding the region. 7 , 9–11
In low-burden infections, T. vulpis can be found crowded
together in the cecum. However, in heavier infections, the worms
also can be found in the colon and, rarely, near the rectum. The
prepatent period is long (70 to 112 days) with the single-cell eggs
excreted in the feces. 7 , 9–11 , 13 Adult worms can live for several
months to over a year with female worms having the capability of
excreting 1000 to 5000 eggs per day, with potentially fewer eggs
per female with high burden infections. 7 , 9 , 13 , 14 While the
impact of crowding has not been well studied in dogs, Trichuris
spp. in other hosts have been shown to decrease in size and
fecundity with higher burden infections. 15–18 Also, egg excretion
can vary signiﬁcantly on a daily basis. The eggs require <2 weeks
to 1.5 months to develop to the infective stage, depending on the
soil temperature and moisture level (e.g., 1.5 months at 20°C, 1
month at 25 to 30°C). 7 , 19 , 20 Infective eggs contain a ﬁrst-stage
larvae and have a slightly rounder appearance. At cool
temperatures (e.g., 4°C), development can be delayed but resumes
when temperatures increase, while long periods of freezing
temperatures and direct sunlight can destroy eggs. Though
generally considered relatively hardy, Trichuris eggs do not
survive desiccation and heat as well as ascarid eggs do. 7 , 10 , 11 ,

19–21

vetexamprep.ir

Given the susceptibility of eggs to freezing temperatures and
arid conditions, it is not surprising that prevalence of infections in
dogs is lower in hot arid regions and regions with long cold
winters. While challenging to compare prevalence studies due to
diﬀerences in the diagnostic methods used and source of dogs, it
appears that prevalence in well-cared-for pet dogs is decreased in
many regions, likely a ributable to regular anthelmintic
treatment. Data from CAPC indicate that prevalence in pet dogs is
<1% in the United States (vs. 8 to 81% in the US in the 1930s to
1950s) and <0.5% in Canada. 7 , 21 Other United States–based
studies have found prevalence to range from <1% to 10%. 22 , 23 In
Australia, a study from 1975 showed a prevalence of 60.6% in
shelter dogs, whereas a study from 2004–2005 found only 3.1% to
be infected, with <1% of owned dogs infected. 24 In Europe, more
contemporary studies have also indicated that prevalence is
generally low among owned dogs (0.1 to <4%) although it is
higher in regions of Greece, Hungary, and Italy (9.6 to 23.3%). 4 , 25
, 26 Higher prevalences (14 to >50%) have been documented in
dogs from rural areas, kennels, shelters, and stray dogs as well as
other regions of the world, which is likely reﬂective of parasite
control and dog ownership practices. 27–32

In addition to occurring worldwide in domestic dogs, T. vulpis
has been documented in red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), coyotes (Canis
latrans), and wolves (Canis lupus) in the United States, Europe,
Asia, and Africa with prevalences ranging from 0.5 to 33%, and an
indication that in the Netherlands, it might be increasing in
prevalence. 33–39 These canids could serve as a source of
environmental contamination and hence domestic dog infection.

Cats
Much less is known about the whipworm species that infect cats
and their epidemiology when compared with dog whipworm
species. While two separate species, Trichuris serrata and Trichuris
campanula, were described, it has been proposed that they are one
species and should be renamed Trichuris felis. 3 In the original
descriptions, the presence of a vulva appendage in T. serrata and

vetexamprep.ir

diﬀerences in the size of the adults, spicule, and eggs were used as
diﬀering characteristics. 1 , 2 Trichuris serrata adult females range
from 14.7 to 49.5 mm in length; males from 12.8 to 40 mm; and
their eggs are 54 to 60 µm long by 35 to 40 µm wide. Trichuris
campanula adult females range from 22.5 to 31.5 mm in length;
males from 21.5 to 36 mm; and their eggs are 63 to 72 µm long by
34 to 39 µm wide. 40–43 Given that adult worm size can vary based
on infection intensity and variation in egg size has been
demonstrated with other Trichuris spp., size is an unreliable
characteristic for species diﬀerentiation. 15 , 16 Twenty-two females
(with the vulva appendage and classiﬁed as T. serrata) and 12
males harvested from 12 cats and eggs from the feces of nine of
these cats were measured and shown to overlap with the
measurements for T. serrata and T. campanula, supporting the
theory that there is just one species. 43 While the 18S rRNA gene of
these “T. serrata” were sequenced, at the time of writing,
sequences are not available from Trichuris spp. from cats that lack
the vulva appendage. 44 Therefore it remains to be determined if
cats host two Trichuris species or one. Given the lack of
information on the separate species, these are, herein, referred to
as T. felis (Figs. 114.4–114.6).
Based on one experimental study, the prepatent period of T. felis
is believed to range from 62 to 91 days. 42 The life cycle is the same
as that of T. vulpis. However, since it has not been as extensively
studied as T. vulpis, less is known about the timeframe for each
stage of development. Less also is known about the factors that
inﬂuence egg development, although they are likely similar to T.
vulpis and other Trichuris species.
Trichuris felis are generally present in low prevalence in much of
the world with most reported infections occurring in the
Caribbean and South America. 3 In a study from Argentina, 16%
of cats were infected. 45 On St. Ki s, 71% of feral cats and 22% of
owned cats were positive. 46 , 47 In a 1975 study from Australia,
1.5% of cats were infected, although infections have not been
reported in more recent studies. 24 , 48 In the United States there
have been infrequent reports of infection in cats from the
Midwest, Southeast, and Northeast. A study from 2003 reported a
prevalence of 0.03% in owned cats. 3 , 42 , 49 A 2015 study of a
shelter in Miami, Florida, however, found 25 (38%) of 65 cats to be

vetexamprep.ir

infected, suggesting that prevalence can be higher among certain
regional populations. 50 In Europe, most prevalence studies have
not detected Trichuris sp. in cats. 51 , 52 However, two studies from
Italy (one with owned and the other stray cats) and a study from
Serbia (owned cats) found 0.9 to 2.9% to be infected; these
infections were referred to as T. vulpis. 26 , 53 Based on a small
study in Nigeria where 5.8% of cats were positive, feline Trichuris
sp. infection also occurs in Africa. 54

Trichuris felis infections have been reported in two oncillas
(Leopardus tigrinus, 1851 in Brazil and 1963 in Venezuela) and from
ocelots (Leopardus pardalis, 1937 in Trinidad; Oncifelis geoﬀroyi,
2005 in Argentina). 3 , 40 , 55

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
During the prepatent stage of infection, the embedding of larvae
in the mucosa of the small intestine can cause mechanical damage
resulting in localized inﬂammation, mucosal hyperemia, and
hemorrhage. 7 , 9–11 , 56 Immature and adult worms in the cecum
(and colon in heavy infections) also cause mechanical damage to
the mucosa due to the penetration and movement of the
embedded anterior end and mouth stylet. Hemorrhage and
inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration of the mucosa and submucosa are
localized around worms. 7 , 9–11 , 56 Trichuris spp. release cytolytic
and hemolytic enzymes, believed to enable them to consume
tissue ﬂuids that contribute to the localized reactions. 9 , 11 , 56
Trichuris also consume blood (at a low level compared to
hookworms) and mucosal epithelium. 57
In many cases, T. vulpis infection is of low pathogenicity and
there are no or limited clinical signs. The most common clinical
sign is intermi ent diarrhea with variable hematochezia and

vetexamprep.ir

mucus secondary to the mechanical damage being caused by the
worms. These signs can begin during the prepatent period. In
heavy infections, diarrhea can be severe and chronic leading to
dehydration. 5 , 8 Weight loss, anorexia, and lethargy also can
occur in severe infections, especially those associated with
pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism (pseudo-Addison’s disease) (Box
114.1). 58–64 Anemia is listed in many references as a clinical sign;
however, few experimental infections have been able to induce
anemia, and in other hosts (e.g., children with Trichuris trichiura
infestation) there has not been a strong association of infection
with anemia. 65 Studies with Trichuris muris and Trichuris suis
have demonstrated a parasite-microbiota interaction which could
increase the pathology and clinical signs; however, the changes in
microbiota have not been consistent. 66–68 While not studied with
T. vulpis, this variable interaction with the microbiota has the
potential
to
explain
the
occurrence
of
pseudohypoadrenocorticism.

No clinical signs have been associated with T. felis infections in
cats. This apparent lack of clinical disease has been a ributed to
most infections being low intensity (1 to 10 adult worms). 3
However, cats can harbor >100 adult worms, so more studies are
required to ascertain whether infections in cats can be associated
with signs of disease. 43 , 45

Physical Examination Findings
Most dogs have no abnormal ﬁndings on physical examination
except in high-intensity infections. 5 , 8 Infections with a large

vetexamprep.ir

number of whipworms may result in chronic or severe diarrhea,
with dehydration, lethargy, weight loss, pale mucus membranes,
and even hypothermia noted on physical examination.
Dehydration may be severe and can lead to acute collapse,
bradycardia, and weak pulses. 58–64 Rectal examination may
indicate the presence of diarrheic feces with blood ﬂecks and
mucus. Rectal prolapse has not been associated with T. vulpis
infection in dogs as it has in humans and pigs.
No abnormal physical examination ﬁndings have been reported
in cats with T. felis infections.

Diagnosis
The most common method used to identify T. vulpis and T. felis
infection is fecal examination for the identiﬁcation of eggs. A
commercial fecal antigen test (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc.,
Westbrook, ME USA) became available in 2015 but is not in a POC
format. Adult T. vulpis worms can be seen at necropsy, and the
stichosome esophagus and bacillary bands can be used for
identiﬁcation in histology. Because of the long prepatent period,
clinical signs can appear before eggs can be detected in the feces.
Intermi ent shedding can also lead to failure to detect infection
on a single fecal ﬂotation. In these situations, failure to treat dogs
with chronic diarrhea can result in the somewhat unfortunate
occasional diagnosis with colonoscopy, a signiﬁcantly more costly
procedure than assessment of response to treatment (Fig. 114.7).

Laboratory Abnormalities
In cases of pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism, hyponatremia,
metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalemia are present. An
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test can be used
to rule out true hypoadrenocorticism. Basal and poststimulation
cortisol levels will be normal and aldosterone normal or high
(Table 114.1). 58–64

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification

vetexamprep.ir

Trichuris vulpis and T. felis eggs can be identiﬁed by fecal
examination with the preferred method being centrifugation with
Sheather’s sugar ﬂotation solution. While other solutions can be
used, the solution should have a speciﬁc gravity of at least 1.2,
given that T. vulpis eggs have a speciﬁc gravity of 1.15. 66 Eggs can
be intermi ently shed and therefore multiple fecal examinations
over a one-week period might be required. Centrifugation with
Sheather’s sugar ﬂotation solution can be used to detect many
other GI parasites, and co-infections with other parasites and
whipworms are common. The presence of intestinal parasite coinfection can make it more complicated to determine the cause of
the clinical signs.
While the eggs of Trichuris spp. are distinct (oval, yellowishbrown, and thick-shelled, with two polar plugs), they can be
confused with Eucoleus aerophilus (syn. Capillaria aerophila),
Eucoleus boehmi, and Aoncotheca putorii (Table 114.2). Also, if fecal
material is contaminated with urine, Trichuris eggs must be
distinguished from Pearsonema plica (Capillaria plica). 69–71
Misdiagnosis is more likely to occur with T. felis infections, due to
the similarity in size with Eucoleus spp. eggs. Because of this, some
cases of T. felis diagnosed in the United States may have
represented Eucoleus infections and vice versa. 3 , 71 However, in
regions where T. felis is uncommon, it is reasonable to
presumptively identify eggs with bipolar plugs as Eucoleus eggs,
provided there is no travel history. Bipolar plugged eggs also may
be found in cat feces following consumption of rodents or other
wildlife harboring infection with Trichuris spp. or Capillaria spp. 69
Conﬁning the pet to prevent additional predation or coprophagy
and repeating fecal ﬂotation 2 to 3 days later should facilitate
diﬀerentiation of these pseudoinfections.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Speciﬁc PCR assays have been used to detect nucleic acid of
Trichuris spp. in feces. However, this approach is not used for
clinical specimens, is not eﬀective for eggs (unless eggs are ﬁrst
crushed to release nucleic acid), and sequencing is required to
diﬀerentiate the species. 72–74
Fecal Antigen Testing

vetexamprep.ir

A fecal antigen test (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Westbrook, ME,
USA) became available in 2015 and was oﬀered at some
commercial veterinary diagnostic laboratories. This test has been
validated for detection of T. vulpis and T. felis antigen and can
detect infections not identiﬁable on fecal examination including
single-sex infections (male or female) and prepatent infections.
Antigen tests also have been demonstrated to diﬀerentiate
between true infection and eggs in feces from coprophagy. 50 , 75 ,

76

Pathologic Findings
Adult Trichuris spp. can be seen grossly at necropsy with either
only the posterior end visible in the lumen or whole worms with
the classic whip shape in the lumen of the cecum and colon. In
heavy infections, if the adult whipworms have released from the
mucosa, they will be tangled together forming a “Medusa’s head”
(Fig. 114.8). Occasionally, the worms contain a reddish or pinkish
ﬂuid due to blood consumption. In histopathologic sections, the
stichosome esophagus and the bacillary band(s) are key
characteristics for diﬀerentiation from other nematodes.
Histologic changes that can be observed include pyknotic nuclei
in cells of the lamina propria, coagulative necrosis, hyperemia,
and lymphocytic invasion. Immediately after infection, hyperemia
in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa and desquamation of the
epithelium can be seen. Larvae in the lamina muscularis of the
duodenum and jejunum are surrounded with clusters of

vetexamprep.ir

eosinophils. Larvae and adults in the cecum and colon are
associated with diﬀuse lymphohistiocytic inﬁltration of the
submucosa and mucosa. Mucoid dystrophy and vascular
hyperemia also are present. 56 , 77

Treatment and Prognosis
Several anthelmintics are approved for the treatment of T. vulpis
(Table 114.3). Repeat treatments (e.g., 3 monthly treatments) are
usually recommended since few anthelmintics have eﬃcacy
against the immature stages and reinfection from a contaminated
environment is common. Trichuris spp. can be dose-limiting
parasites for some anthelmintics and the best treatment and
control are achieved with consistent use of monthly broadspectrum anthelmintics. When infection is associated with
pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism, complete recovery is possible with
prompt treatment for the infection and supportive therapy for the
dehydration. As with all cases of severe dehydration and
electrolyte imbalance, slow correction of the serum sodium
concentration is required to prevent CNS disorders and death.
Hypokalemia can develop in these pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism–
associated cases if mineralocorticoids for hypoadrenocorticism are
administered; however, the hypokalemia will resolve when
steroid administration is stopped. 60
No anthelmintics are registered for the treatment of T. felis and
few studies have been conducted to assess eﬃcacy of the available
anthelmintics. Compounds eﬀective against T. vulpis are
considered likely eﬀective against T. felis. In one case report,
fenbendazole (Panacur 10% oral suspension, Merck Animal
Health) at 50 mg/kg administered for 5 days was eﬀective at
treating a cat infected with T. felis. 78 In a small study, emodepside
(Profender Topical Solution, Elanco) at 3 to 15 mg/kg also was
eﬀective. 79

Immunity and Vaccination
Dogs and cats do not develop strong immunity and are
susceptible to reinfection. Self-curing and some resistance to
reinfection has been noted in a few dogs that were experimentally
infected. However, dogs and cats of all ages, regardless of

vetexamprep.ir

previous exposure, have been identiﬁed with Trichuris spp.
infestations. Therefore, any immunity that develops appears to be
of a limited nature. Vaccination is not available.

Prevention
Given the hardiness of whipworm eggs, the key to prevention is
removal of feces from the environment. This recommendation
applies to gardens, yards, public parks, and other locations where
dogs and cats roam. Once soil contamination has occurred,
removing eggs is not feasible. In kennels and shelters, thorough
cleaning is important. Regular fecal examinations using
centrifugation and antigen testing, especially in adult dogs and
cats (in areas where feline infections are prevalent), with prompt
treatment of all positive animals, can assist in decreasing
environmental contamination. Given the long prepatent period
and the lower eﬃcacy of treatments against immature stages,
multiple treatments may be required. Alternatively, use of
treatments with eﬃcacy against immature stages of whipworms
or the use of monthly broad-spectrum anthelmintics with eﬃcacy
against whipworms can be used to control and prevent infections.

For T. felis, given the lack of information regarding the optimal
conditions for egg development, it is unclear if the prevalence of
this parasite could increase outside the Caribbean and South
America. It is possible that the distribution of this parasite could
extend with global climate change and translocation of cats. Given
increased travel of pet cats with owners, measures should be
implemented to prevent transport of T. felis to nonendemic
locations. Treatment should be administered before departure
from endemic areas with follow-up fecal examinations and
treatment as needed upon arrival in nonendemic areas.

Public Health Aspects

vetexamprep.ir

There have been no reports of T. felis infecting humans. Zoonotic
transmission of T. vulpis has been proposed with reports of T.
vulpis completing its development in humans. Reported incidence
has ranged from <0.2% to >7% with infections primarily in
children. 80 , 81 These infections have been asymptomatic or
caused clinical signs ranging from abdominal upset, diarrhea,
nausea, vomiting, and eosinophilia. Humans have their own
species of Trichuris, T. trichiura, which can be misidentiﬁed as T.
vulpis; disease caused by T. trichiura primarily occurs in children
living in poverty in the tropics and subtropics. Adult worms
(excreted post treatment) can be distinguished based on spicule
length and cloaca of the males and the vagina and uterus of the
females, with T. trichiura convoluted and T. vulpis straight. 16
Traditionally, however, egg size has been used to distinguish T.
vulpis from T. trichiura infections in humans. Trichuris trichiura
eggs (50–56 µm by 21–26 µm) are normally half the size of T.
vulpis (72–90 µm by 32–40 µm); however, a small percentage of T.
trichiura eggs overlap in size with T. vulpis. Therefore, when egg
size is used to determine the species infecting people,
misidentiﬁcation can occur. 16 , 78 , 80 Trichuris vulpis has rarely
been reported to cause visceral larva migrans in people 82 ;
however, none of these reports have been conﬁrmed and the
evidence more strongly suggests that these were not T. vulpis
infections, particularly since there is no evidence of larval
migration with T. vulpis.

Case Example
Signalment

“Rusty,” an 8-year-old female spayed boxer mix from
Tennessee, USA.

History

The owner reported that Rusty had a history of weight loss,
lethargy, and anorexia. The last recorded body weight (4 years
previously) was 34 kg. Vaccinations were not current and the
dog was not on any medications, including heartworm
preventive.

Physical Examination

vetexamprep.ir

Ambulatory on all four limbs. Body weight: 23.4 kg.
Temperature = 99.5°F (37.5°C).
Faint/muﬄed heart sounds, strong pulses, and slightly
increased respiratory noise. No signiﬁcant abnormalities were
noted in examination of the eyes, ears, nose, and throat.
Mucous membranes pink and tacky; decreased skin turgor.
Lymph nodes were normal. Abdominal palpation was
unremarkable. No evidence of ectoparasites. After
hospitalization, Rusty had an episode of voluminous diarrhea,
which was liquid in consistency and without obvious blood or
mucus.

Laboratory Findings

CBC: WBC 35,820 cells/µL (6000–17,000 cells/µL),
neutrophils 32,550 cells/µL (3000–12,000 cells/µL), HCT
60% (37–55%); all other parameters were within the
normal range.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: BUN 118 mg/dL (7–25 mg/dL),
creatinine 2.5 mg/dL (0.3–1.4 mg/dL), phosphorus 11.3
mg/dL (2.9–6.6 mg/dL), glucose 267 mg/dL (60–110
mg/dL), potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.7–5.8 mmol/L), sodium
109 mmol/L (138–160 mmol/L); all other parameters were
within the normal range.
ACTH stimulation test (cosyntropin, 125 mg, IV) with
samples taken at times 0 (<1.0 µg/dL; normal range 1.0–
5.0 µg/dL) and 1 hour (6.1 µg/dL; normal range 8–17
µg/dL).

Imaging Findings

Thoracic radiographs revealed decreased cardiac size, clear
lung ﬁelds, and no pleural eﬀusion or masses.

Microbiologic Testing

Fecal ﬂotation revealed large numbers of hookworm and
whipworm eggs.

Diagnosis

Pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism secondary to whipworm and
hookworm infestation. The initial diﬀerential diagnoses were

vetexamprep.ir

hypoadrenocorticism
(Addison’s
disease),
infestation, neoplasia, and renal failure.

whipworm

Treatment

After initial examination, Rusty was hospitalized for IV ﬂuid
administration; dexamethasone sodium phosphate was also
administered (4 mg, once, IV). On the following day, when the
fecal and ACTH stimulation results became available, IV ﬂuids
were continued and the following medications were started:
sucralfate 1 g PO q12h and fenbendazole PO q24h for 3 days.

Comments

Rusty’s condition rapidly improved and he began eating and
drinking by the evening after the ﬁrst dose of fenbendazole.
Stools were ﬁrm within 2 days of instituting treatment and
electrolyte and renal values were normal when retested 3 days
after treatment commenced. The fenbendazole treatment was
repeated 3 weeks and 3 months later.
Case example provided courtesy of Dr. Gary Del Gaudio.

115: Tapeworms
Christopher B. Adolph, and Andrew S. Peregrine

KEY POINTS
Dipylidium caninum
• First Described: Dipylidium caninum has been known to infect
pets since ancient times. Linnaeus named this parasite Taenia
cania in 1758; Leuckart created the genus Dipylidium in 1863.
• Cause: Dipylidium caninum (order Cyclophyllidea).
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Affected Hosts: Dogs and cats, as well as other canids and
felids, serve as definitive hosts for adult D. caninum.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Infected definitive hosts
intermittently shed segments that contain egg packets which
break down in the environment. When a suitable arthropod
intermediate host (e.g., Ctenocephalides felis felis [flea],
Trichodectes canis [biting louse]) ingests the eggs, a
metacestode stage (a cysticercoid) develops within the
arthropod. Final hosts become infected and develop patent
intestinal infections upon ingestion of an infected intermediate
host.
• Major Clinical Signs: Heavy infections in dogs and cats may
cause constipation and diarrhea. However, the most common
clinical situation arises when an owner discovers segments in
the hair coat, bedding, or recently passed feces, of a healthy
animal.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other GI parasites, dietary indiscretion,
pancreatitis, intestinal bacterial overgrowth, IBD, GI neoplasia,
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, GI
foreign body, and intestinal perforation. When segments are

vetexamprep.ir

present, these need to be differentiated from other tapeworms
that shed segments.
• Human Health Significance: Dipylidium caninum occasionally
infects people that accidentally ingest infected fleas.
Taenia spp.
• First Described: Taenia was first described by Linnaeus in
1758.
• Cause: Multiple cyclophyllidean species that belong to the
family Taeniidae. The family contains two generally accepted
genera: Taenia and Echinococcus.
• Geographic Distribution: Essentially worldwide. However, the
importance of different Taenia species varies depending on
the geographic region.
• Affected Hosts: Taenia pisiformis, Taenia crassiceps, Taenia
hydatigena, Taenia ovis, Taenia serialis, and Taenia multiceps
all infect dogs as the definitive host. The predominant Taenia
species infecting cats globally is Taenia taeniaeformis.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Infected dogs and cats
intermittently pass egg-laden segments into the environment.
Eggs are then consumed by a suitable mammalian
intermediate host (e.g., rabbit, sheep, mice, rats) resulting in
the formation of the metacestode, larval, tapeworm in that
host’s tissues; the type of metacestode varies with the Taenia
spp. involved. Dogs and cats develop patent intestinal
infections after consuming an infected intermediate host.
• Major Clinical Signs: Intestinal infections with Taenia spp. in
dogs and cats have long been thought to be well tolerated
with no associated clinical signs. When clinical signs occur,
they are relatively non-specific and may include vomiting and
diarrhea. Rarely, cats require an enterotomy to relieve a
cestode impaction.
• Differential Diagnoses: Differentials include other GI parasites,
dietary indiscretion, pancreatitis, intestinal bacterial
overgrowth, IBD, GI neoplasia, exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, GI foreign body, and
intestinal perforation. When segments are present, these
need to be differentiated microscopically from segments of
other tapeworms.

vetexamprep.ir

• Human Health Significance: In general, zoonotic Taenia spp.
are limited to species that utilize cattle and pigs as
intermediate hosts (e.g., T. saginata, T. solium); dogs and cats
are not involved in the life cycles. However, adult T.
taeniaeformis have been recovered from the intestinal tract of
humans. Humans may also occasionally be infected with the
metacestode stage of T. multiceps or T. serialis, which utilize
dogs as a definitive host. When eggs are accidentally
ingested by humans, they hatch in the GI tract; oncospheres
are released and circulate in the bloodstream until they lodge
in organs where coenuri develop. For T. multiceps, coenuri
may be found in the brain and eyes, while those of T. serialis
are found in subcutaneous tissue.
Echinococcus spp.
• First Described: Echinococcus granulosus s.l. was first
described by Batsch in 1786, and Echinococcus multilocularis
was first described by Leuckart in 1863.
• Causes: Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato (s.l.) and
Echinococcus multilocularis (family Taeniidae).
• Geographic Distribution: Echinococcus granulosus s.l.
comprises multiple genotypes/species that differ in their
geographic distribution due to differences in host specificity.
The genotype most important for human disease is E.
granulosus sensu stricto (s.s.), which is primarily associated
with sheep and found worldwide. Echinococcus multilocularis
occurs throughout much of the northern hemisphere (Europe,
Asia, and North America).
• Affected Hosts: Adult stages of both cestodes are a few
millimeters in length and occur in the small intestine of
carnivores. Definitive hosts for E. granulosus s.l. are primarily
dogs and, to a lesser extent, wild canids, which excrete
infective eggs into the environment in feces. Echinococcus
multilocularis occurs primarily in a wildlife cycle with wild
canids (arctic/red fox, coyote, raccoon dog, wolf) as definitive
hosts. Dogs, and to a lesser extent cats, may also be
definitive hosts. Dogs occasionally may also be accidental
hosts that develop metacestodes.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Ingestion of E. granulosus s.l.
eggs by intermediate hosts (e.g., sheep, cattle, goats, pigs,

vetexamprep.ir

horses) and accidental hosts (e.g., people) results in the
development of a hydatid cyst within the liver, lungs, or other
internal organs. The resultant disease is termed cystic
echinococcosis (CE). After ingestion of E. multilocularis eggs
by rodents, the typical intermediate host, the metacestode
stage develops most commonly within the liver, behaves like
an invasive tumor, and produces alveolar echinococcosis
(AE). Ingestion of eggs by accidental hosts (e.g., people,
dogs) also results in AE. Thus, dogs can be both definitive
and accidental hosts for E. multilocularis. Dogs, cats, and wild
canids develop intestinal infections following ingestion of
metacestode-infected rodents.
• Major Clinical Signs: Intestinal infections are rarely clinical. AE
in dogs is typically associated with hepatic injury; clinical signs
include abdominal pain and/or distension, lethargy, anorexia,
and vomiting.
• Differential Diagnoses: Both cats and dogs excrete eggs
morphologically identical to those of Taenia spp. and require
DNA analysis to determine the genus/species. Differential
diagnoses for hepatic AE in dogs include tumors, abscesses,
and cysts (sterile, congenital).
• Human Health Significance: Most species of E. granulosus s.l.
can infect people. However, globally, most human cases of
CE are due to E. granulosus s.s. (sheep strain). This strain
occurs in both domestic and wildlife cycles. However, the
domestic cycle is of particular zoonotic significance as human
infections are typically associated with ingestion of eggs in the
feces of dogs. The resultant hydatid cysts are usually large,
fluid-filled structures that behave like a space-occupying
lesion. While often clinically silent, they may cause CE, a
potentially severe disease of the liver, lungs, bone, brain, or
other organs. While E. multilocularis occurs in wild and
domestic life cycles, most human infections are associated
with ingestion of eggs in the feces of dogs. In humans, AE is
typically associated with development of the metacestode
stage in the liver and has a high case fatality rate when left
untreated; the metacestode behaves like an invasive tumor
and often metastasizes to other organs. The clinical
incubation period is 5 to 15 years. Both AE and, to a lesser

vetexamprep.ir

extent, CE, have high pathogenic potential and are
considered two of the most important helminthic zoonoses. In
a veterinary environment, infection risk in people when
handling dogs and cats can essentially be eliminated by strict
attention to hand hygiene.
Mesocestoides spp.
• First Described: Valliant described Mesocestoides ambiguous
in 1863.
• Causes: Cestodes that belong to the Mesocestoides genus.
Questions remain as to how to define the species because the
life cycle has not been fully defined for any species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, cats, and raccoons are definitive hosts
for Mesocestoides spp.; there are a variety of intermediate
hosts (e.g., mammals, amphibians, birds, reptiles). Peritoneal
larval cestodiasis occasionally occurs in dogs or cats following
ingestion of an infected intermediate host.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Definitive hosts become
infected by ingesting intermediate hosts that contain the
second metacestode stage, a tetrathyridium, located in the
peritoneal cavity. The first intermediate stage is thought to be
a cysticercoid that develops from an oncosphere in a
coprophagic insect, but this has yet to be proven. Tetrathyridia
develop into adult tapeworms in the intestinal tract of the
definitive host. Subsequently, sections of the strobila, or body,
are excreted in feces, rather than individual segments like D.
caninum or Taenia spp. Segments contain eggs that vary in
maturity. Peritoneal larval cestodiasis occurs when dogs and
cats ingest an infected intermediate host and larval parasites
migrate through the intestinal wall and multiply as the
tetrathyridial stage within the peritoneal cavity by asexually
dividing or budding.
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs and cats infected with
Mesocestoides spp. typically have subclinical intestinal
infections. Dogs with peritoneal larval cestodiasis may show
abdominal distention with or without systemic signs of
anorexia, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, ascites,
and tachypnea. Clinical signs in one cat from Sicily, Italy

vetexamprep.ir

included anorexia, moderate abdominal swelling, cough, and
dyspnea.
• Differential Diagnoses: Mesocestoides spp. segments are
significantly smaller than those of more common cestodes
(i.e., D. caninum and Taenia spp.) and may be confused with
those of Echinococcus spp. Differentials for peritoneal larval
cestodiasis include other causes of ascites, such as rightsided heart failure, neoplasia, pancreatitis, GI foreign body,
and intestinal perforation.
• Human Health Significance: Rarely, humans can become
infected with adult Mesocestoides spp. by ingestion of
undercooked organs (e.g., raw snake liver, chicken viscera)
containing tetrathyridia leading to abdominal pain and
passage of segments in the stool. Infected dogs and cats are
not a direct zoonotic risk to people.
Diphyllobothrium spp.
• First Described: Linnaeus, 1758.
• Causes: Cestodes of the Diphyllobothrium genus (family
Diphyllobothriidae). Globally, Diphyllobothrium latum
(Dibothriocephalus latus) is the most important species.
• Geographic Distribution: Diphyllobothrium latum has a
circumboreal distribution involving Alaska, the Great Lakes
region of the USA/Canada, northern Europe, Russia, and
parts of Asia and South America.
• Affected Hosts: Adult tapeworms occur in the small intestine of
dogs, cats, people, pigs, foxes, mink, and other fish-eating
animals.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Ingestion of the plerocercoid
stage in raw or undercooked freshwater fish.
• Major Clinical Signs: Infections in both dogs and cats are
typically subclinical.
• Differential Diagnoses: Segments of D. latum within feces are
typically larger in size than those of Spirometra spp., Taenia
spp., and D. caninum. Unlike Taenia spp. and D. caninum,
segments of D. latum and Spirometra spp. have a medial
uterine pore.
• Human Health Significance: Humans acquire D. latum
infection by ingestion of raw or undercooked fish; infections

vetexamprep.ir

are most commonly asymptomatic. Dogs and cats infected
with D. latum are not a direct risk to human health.
Spirometra spp.
• First Described: Rudolphi first described Spirometra
erinaceieuropaei (syn. Diphyllobothrium erinaceieuropaei) in
1819. In 1882, Mason described Spirometra mansoni. In
1935, Mueller described Spirometra mansonoides.
• Causes: Spirometra spp. (family Diphyllobothriidae); a
cestode closely related to Diphyllobothrium spp.
• Geographic Distribution: Spirometra erinaceieuropaei occurs
in Asia, Australia, and Europe. Spirometra mansonoides
occurs in North and South America. Spirometra mansoni is
predominantly found in Asia.
• Affected Hosts: Adult Spirometra spp. occur in the small
intestine of dogs, cats, wild felids, wild canids, raccoons, and
other carnivores. Proliferative sparganosis (proliferation of
plerocercoids) occasionally occurs in the abdominal or
thoracic cavity, or connective tissue, of dogs and cats.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Infected definitive hosts shed
eggs in feces that hatch in water to release a coracidium.
When ingested by freshwater copepods (e.g., Cyclops spp.),
the coracidium develops into a procercoid. Following ingestion
of infected copepods by a second intermediate host (e.g.,
amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals), the procercoid
develops into a plerocercoid (or spargana). Definitive hosts
become infected following ingestion of muscle or connective
tissue of second intermediate hosts or paratenic hosts
containing a plerocercoid. The plerocercoid then attaches to
the intestinal wall and develops into an adult tapeworm.
Proliferative sparganosis occurs following ingestion of water
containing copepods infected with procercoids, or
plerocercoids in second intermediate hosts or paratenic hosts.
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs and cats infected with adult
Spirometra spp. often have subclinical infections. However,
enteritis, diarrhea, weight loss, and vomiting have been
associated with infection, particularly in cats. Occasionally, the
only evidence of infection is the presentation of chains of
segments by owners to a veterinarian. Clinical signs

vetexamprep.ir

associated with proliferative sparganosis depend on the
location of the plerocercoids.
• Differential Diagnoses (Intestinal Infections): Other GI
parasites, dietary indiscretion, pancreatitis, intestinal bacterial
overgrowth, IBD, GI neoplasia, exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, and GI foreign body.
• Human Health Significance: Spirometra spp. cause
sparganosis in people. This occurs when the plerocercoid
stage (spargana) is transferred to humans following ingestion
of raw or undercooked meat (e.g., frog) or when copepods
infected with the procercoid larval stage are consumed by
drinking untreated water. This condition is rare, and usually
presents as a subcutaneous nodule containing a plerocercoid.
However, in some cases, proliferative sparganosis involving
the CNS or other organs has been reported.

Introduction
Cestodes are ﬂatworms that are divided into two orders of
veterinary signiﬁcance, Cyclophyllidea and Diphyllobothriidea
(formerly Pseudophyllidea). 1 The Cyclophyllidea comprise
Dipylidium caninum, Echinococcus spp., Mesocestoides spp., and
Taenia spp. The Diphyllobothriidea, or primitive tapeworms,
contain Diphyllobothrium spp. and Spirometra spp.. Deﬁnitions that
are related to cestode infections are shown in Box 115.1.

Dipylidium caninum
Etiology and Epidemiology
Dipylidium caninum is the only Dipylidium species of veterinary
importance and commonly infects dogs, cats, and other canids
and felids. Molecular characterization of D. caninum isolates
obtained from infected ﬂeas and proglo ids of both dogs and cats
has demonstrated the existence of two distinct genotypes,
suggesting the possibility of two separate species within D.
caninum. Extensive evaluation of infected ﬂeas from the United
States and Europe as well as adult tapeworms from South Africa,
France, and China has demonstrated that the two genotypes (dog

vetexamprep.ir

and cat) generally appear to be species speciﬁc around the world.
2 The success of this tapeworm can partially be a ributed to the
global distribution of ﬂea intermediate hosts. However, multiple
additional factors are involved including societal a itudes toward
dogs and cats as pets, ability and willingness to institute proper
ﬂea control, and the low sensitivity of current detection methods.
Thus, D. caninum has been documented in North America, 3 South
America (e.g., Brazil), 4 Europe, 5 the Middle East (e.g., Iran), 6
Russia, 7 Asia (e.g., China), 8 and Africa (e.g., Nigeria). 9
Dogs and cats become infected when they ingest arthropod
intermediate hosts that include ﬂeas (Ctenocephalides felis,
Ctenocephalides canis, and Pulex irritans) and chewing lice
(Trichodectes canis) (Fig. 115.1). 3 Dogs and cats pass gravid
segments intermi ently in feces. Pre-adult stages of the
intermediate host (e.g., ﬂea larvae) ingest eggs of the cestode once
the segment breaks down in the environment. As the intermediate
host develops to adulthood, the oncosphere (tapeworm embryo)
develops to the metacestode stage, a cysticercoid, within the
intermediate host. Dogs and cats become infected when infected
arthropods are ingested. The cysticercoid then develops to an
adult tapeworm within the lumen of the small intestine and
a aches to the small intestine wall via muscular suckers on the
scolex and small hooks on the rostellum. The body of the
tapeworm (strobila) elongates and the most mature (gravid)
segments on the distal end detach and are passed in feces. Gravid
segments may be shed by dogs and cats as soon as 2 to 3 weeks
after being infected with cysticercoids. 10 , 11
Proglo ids do not have an opening for eggs to escape and each
segment is packed with eggs. The oncospheres are contained
within a packet and each packet may contain 25 to 30 oncospheres
(Fig. 115.2A). 3 Evidence of the longevity of D. caninum is unclear;
estimates vary widely, from as short as 3 months to 3 years. 12

Life cycle of Dipylidium caninum.

Previous surveys in New Jersey and Wisconsin, USA, reported
D. caninum prevalences of 10.4% and 13.0% in cats, respectively.
The same two surveys also reported prevalences for dogs of 0.4%

vetexamprep.ir

and 4.0%, respectively. 13 , 14 In the New Jersey survey, 318 feral
cats were examined by both fecal ﬂotation and necropsy; 33 were
infected with D. caninum at necropsy (10.4%); none tested positive
by zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation. In a more recent survey in
Oklahoma, USA, 40 of 116 (34.5%) cats were positive for D.
caninum at necropsy; however, 0 of 40 of these infections were
detected utilizing two diﬀerent ﬂotation methods (passive and
centrifugal). 15 These data indicate that prevalence determinations
based solely on fecal examination underestimate the true
prevalence of infection. This ﬁnding is consistent with the
biological characteristic of proglo ids passing singly in feces
without release of eggs in the intestinal tract. 16

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Adult D. caninum cause li le pathology and are well tolerated by
the host. Dogs and cats with tapeworm proglo ids visible on the
perineal area, or detected in freshly passed feces, have been
observed to drag their anus on the ground. However, such
behavior can also happen in the absence of infection. 11
Occasionally, cats infected with D. caninum have developed
convulsions and seizures. 10 More commonly, young animals with
clinical signs exhibit an unthrifty, potbellied appearance. 17

vetexamprep.ir

In a 2015 survey in Oklahoma, cats infected with D. caninum
had gross intestinal lesions, including distension of the small
intestine, mural thickening, hemorrhage, and ulceration in

vetexamprep.ir

association with the presence of tapeworms. Because of this, it
appears that the current understanding of pathology associated
with intestinal tapeworm infections requires more study. 15
Most clients have strong emotional reactions to detecting a
proglo id in their pet’s feces or on the pet’s perianal region and
will often contact their veterinarian for assistance. Diﬀerentiating
proglo ids of D. caninum from other cestodes will allow the
clinician to appropriately treat the current infection, because
certain tapeworms require higher dosages of anticestodal
medications and for longer periods of time, and to address the
risk of reinfection.

Diagnosis
Adult D. caninum tapeworms may be detected at necropsy and are
usually 15 to 30 cm in length (Fig. 115.2C). 10 The scolex has a
retractable rostellum with 30 to 150 small thorn-like hooks
arranged in circles and four muscular suckers (Fig. 115.2B).
Gravid segments are 10 to 12 mm in length, narrowed at both
ends, and contain two genital pores. The common name,
“cucumber seed” tapeworm, is based on the appearance of the
gravid segment (Fig. 115.2D and E). 3 Diagnosis of D. caninum
antemortem typically relies on detection of the characteristic
proglo id on the host or in the feces, as well as detection of the
characteristic egg packet on fecal ﬂotation. However, egg packets
can be diﬃcult to ﬂoat and astute veterinary team members are
more likely to detect proglo ids on gross examination than egg
packets on ﬂotation. 15 Occasionally, the egg packet may be
disrupted during specimen preparation and individual eggs
observed in feces. Generally, high speciﬁc gravity solutions (e.g.,
Sheather’s sucrose solution, SpG 1.27) have a higher probability of
ﬂoating heavier helminth eggs than lower speciﬁc gravity
solutions. 18
Tapeworm proglo ids should be deﬁnitively identiﬁed prior to
initiating anticestodal therapy. Environmental structures may be
confused for proglo ids, and determining the genus of the
tapeworm and addressing risk factors is important to prevent
reinfection. Rehydrating suspected proglo ids in water or saline
for 10 to 30 minutes prior to microscopic examination often aids
identiﬁcation of the bilateral genital pores characteristic of D.

vetexamprep.ir

caninum (see Fig. 115.2D and E). Eggs can be observed by adding a
drop of saline and crushing the proglo id between two glass
slides. Occasionally, proglo ids are sterile and one may only
observe calcareous corpuscles (ovoid mineral concentrations that
contain calcium carbonite) that vary in size from 2 to 30 µm. 19
However, these are typical of all cestodes. Regardless of the
detection method (ﬂotation or proglo id preparation), egg
packets are 120 to 200 µm long and contain 25 to 30 individual
ova. Each egg measures 35 to 60 µm and contains a hexacanth
embryo (see Fig. 115.2A). 20 Copro-antigen and PCR detection
methods are not yet commercially available for detection of D.
caninum infections but would be expected to dramatically
improve diagnosis. These strategies have been used on a research
basis to detect D. caninum in ﬂeas and to diﬀerentiate D. caninum
from other cestode species. 21 , 22

Treatment and Prognosis
Eﬀective treatment of D. caninum infections requires both
treatment for tapeworms and for the ﬂea intermediate host. To
avoid reinfection, every dog and cat on the premise must be
treated for ﬂeas. Treatment with appropriate anticestodal
medication at both the time of the initial diagnosis and at
conclusion of environmental ﬂea elimination (2 to 4 months is a
reasonable expectation with proper ﬂea control of all pets) will
eliminate all current and newly acquired tapeworms.
Praziquantel is available as both oral and injectable
formulations for both dogs and cats. Dogs and cats are dosed at 5
mg/kg PO or 5.7 mg/kg when administered either SC or IM (Table
115.1). These dosages eliminate 100% of the adult and immature
stages. 23 Praziquantel (12 mg/kg) is also available as a topical
formulation in combination with emodepside or eprinomectin,
and as a standalone formulation (8 mg/kg) for cats. Epsiprantel is
an oral medication with eﬃcacy against adult stages of D. caninum
and is dosed at 5.5 mg/kg in dogs and 2.75 mg/kg in cats. 11
Nitroscanate is approved for use in dogs in some countries. A
dosage of 25 mg/kg eliminated natural infections with D. caninum.
24 However, nitroscanate is approved in Canada for treatment of
D. caninum infections in dogs at a dosage of 50 mg/kg.
Nitazoxanide has been given to dogs and cats infected with D.

vetexamprep.ir

caninum and was 100% eﬀective at a single dosage of 100 mg/kg. 25
Over the last few years, there have been reports of D. caninum
infections in dogs in the USA that could not be eliminated despite
eﬀective ﬂea control and therapeutic dosages of either
praziquantel or epsiprantel. Cases were resolved following
treatment with either nitroscanate or a compounded
pyrantel/praziquantel/oxantel formulation. 26
TABLE 115.1

B, both dog and cat; C, cat; D, dog; TD, transdermal.

Prevention
With proper ﬂea control and use of an eﬀective anticestodal
medication, D. caninum infections should be eliminated and the
risk of reinfection minimized.

Public Health Aspects
Dipylidium caninum can infect people. Young children are at
greatest risk due to their propensity to sample their environment
orally leading to ingestion of ﬂea intermediate hosts. 27 Human
infections have been reported worldwide. A recent publication
described 349 human cases of dipylidiasis, distributed among 24
countries; more than 100 cases were reported in Italy, followed by
the USA (86 cases), Japan (81 cases), China (30 cases), Chile (18
cases), Poland (6 cases), India (5 cases), and Mexico, Brazil,
Canada, Sri Lanka, and Uruguay (each had 2). Individual cases
were reported in other countries. More than two-thirds of the
cases were in small children. 28 Most humans with dipylidiasis are
asymptomatic; however, anal pruritus, diarrhea, or mild
abdominal pain may occur. Flea control in pets should eliminate

vetexamprep.ir

environmental infestations and minimize the risk of human
infection.

Taenia spp. Infections
Etiology and Epidemiology
The Taenia genus belongs to the cyclophyllidean group of
tapeworms and has multiple species that utilize dogs, and one
that utilizes cats, as deﬁnitive hosts. Like D. caninum, deﬁnitive
hosts are infected by ingestion of the metacestode (immature or
larval) stage within the tissues of an intermediate host (Fig. 115.3).
Taenia species typically form one of three diﬀerent kinds of
metacestode: a cysticercus, strobilocercus, or coenurus (Table
115.2). A cysticercus is composed of a single bladder within which
is a single immature parasite with a protoscolex. A strobilocercus
also consists of a single bladder that contains a single immature
parasite; however, unlike a cysticercus, the strobilocercus contains
a protoscolex with a long segmented body. Thus, elongation and
segmentation has begun in the intermediate host. A coenurus is
composed of a single bladder, within which are many
protoscolices; each protoscolex has the potential to develop into a
mature tapeworm. Dogs are infected with Taenia pisiformis when
the cysticercus is consumed in the viscera of rabbits or rodents
(see Table 115.2). For Taenia crassiceps, dogs are infected when the
cysticercus is consumed in the viscera of rodents. Dogs are
infected with Taenia hydatigena when the cysticercus is consumed
in the viscera of ruminants, horses, and pigs. Taenia ovis infects
dogs when the cysticercus is ingested in the muscle of sheep or
goats (see Table 115.2). The metacestode stage of Taenia multiceps is
a coenurus and infects dogs following consumption of the brain
or spine of sheep or ca le. The metacestode of Taenia serialis is also
a coenurus and infects dogs following consumption of connective
tissue of rabbits or rodents. Cats are infected with T. taeniaeformis
by ingesting rodents containing a strobilocercus, typically within
the liver (see Table 115.2). 3

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 115.3

Life cycle of Taenia pisiformis.

Once the metacestode stage is consumed by a dog or cat, it
develops into an adult tapeworm in the lumen of the small
intestine. Gravid tapeworm segments containing eggs detach and
are excreted in feces. Taenia pisiformis reaches patency in
approximately 56 days, T. crassiceps in 27 to 31 days, T. hydatigena
in 51 days, T. ovis in 42 to 63 days, T. multiceps in 30 days, T. serialis
in 1 to 2 months, and T. taeniaeformis in 40 days. 11 , 29 If a suitable
intermediate host ingests the eggs, which are immediately
infective in fresh feces, the oncosphere hatches, penetrates the
intestinal wall, and migrates to the preferred organ. Here the
embryo grows, cavitates, and forms the metacestode stage that is
infective to the deﬁnitive host. 11
Necropsy surveys indicate that Taenia spp. infections are
common in dogs and cats; prevalences in North America have
been reported between 25.0% and 29.7% for dogs (T. pisiformis),

vetexamprep.ir

and between 25.9 and 33.0% in cats (T. taeniaeformis). 13–15 In Iran,
90 dogs were necropsied; T. hydatigena was recovered in 43%, T.
multiceps in 11%, and T. ovis in 3%. 6 In Albania, 111 dogs were
necropsied; T. hydatigena was recovered in 2.7%. 30
When fecal ﬂotation is utilized as the sole detection method, the
observed prevalence of infection is typically much lower than that
observed by necropsy. 13 , 15 , 31 However, the sensitivity of fecal
ﬂotation depends on the ﬂotation method used. For example, in a
2015 study from Oklahoma, 30/116 (25.9%) cats were detected as
infected with T. taeniaeformis by necropsy. Fecal ﬂotation was
performed on all the cats utilizing two ﬂotation methods: passive
ﬂotation with NaNO3 and centrifugal ﬂotation with Sheather’s
sucrose solution. Centrifugal ﬂotation detected 8/30 infected cats
(26.7%); passive ﬂotation detected only 3/30 infected cats (10.0%).
15 In fecal ﬂotations, Taenia species eggs are morphologically
indistinguishable from one another and from Echinococcus spp.; a
diagnosis to species level requires identiﬁcation of adults
procured at necropsy or the use of molecular techniques. For
example, a recent study in Turkey demonstrated that 27 of 100
dogs were positive for taeniid eggs by centrifugal ﬂotation and
sedimentation. Echinococcus granulosus-speciﬁc PCR products
were obtained in 14/27 (51.9%) taeniid specimens. Since additional
PCR analysis was not conducted, the remaining 13/27 positive
taeniid specimens can be presumed to be other Echinococcus or
Taenia spp. 32

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs

vetexamprep.ir

The current dogma is that Taenia spp. infections in dogs and cats
are generally not associated with clinical signs. As for dipylidiasis,
some infected animals will exhibit scooting behavior associated
with anal pruritus, but other conditions such as impacted anal
glands will lead to the same behavior. Several case reports
describe cats with Taenia sp. impactions. 33 , 34
Dogs and cats are rarely infected with the metacestode stages of
Taenia spp. However, disseminated abdominal, thoracic, or
subcutaneous cysticercosis due to T. crassiceps has been reported
in dogs; 35–37 a compromised immune system may have played a
role in the pathogenesis. Occasional cases of feline cerebral
coenurosis due to T. serialis have been described in Australia and
North America. In all cases the diagnosis was made at necropsy
following morphological identiﬁcation of cerebral coenuri (i.e.,
ﬂuid-ﬁlled cysts containing characteristic protosolices). Taenia
serialis normally utilizes a dog as the deﬁnitive host and a
lagomorph or rodent as the intermediate host. The rare cat that
develops cerebral coenurosis presumably is infected by ingesting
eggs passed by an infected dog; the larvae then aberrantly migrate
to the cat’s cerebrum. 38 Neurocysticercosis due to T. crassiceps has
been rarely described in cats. 39

Diagnosis
When fully intact Taenia spp. are grossly identiﬁed, characteristic
features include a scolex with four suckers and a non-retractable
rostellum armed with two rows of hooks (Fig. 115.4A). Depending
on the maturity of the specimen, the length of the tapeworm can
range from tens to hundreds of centimeters. The segments are
rectangular with alternating unilateral genital pores (Fig. 115.4B
and C). Typical taeniid eggs are usually observed in gravid
segments (Fig. 115.4D). Morphologic identiﬁcation is based on the
number and size of rostellar hooks and the morphology of mature
segments. 40 It is recommended that fresh (in saline) specimens be
submi ed to a reference laboratory for speciation eﬀorts; ﬁxation
in formalin may preclude proper identiﬁcation.
Diagnosis of Taenia spp. infection in dogs and cats is most
commonly based on detection of segments on the haircoat or skin
of the host or in freshly passed feces, as well as detection of eggs
by fecal ﬂotation. As for D. caninum, both methods are very

vetexamprep.ir

insensitive; 15 , 31 segments are excreted intermi ently and eggs
are only present in feces if the segment is damaged in the GI tract
or during preparation of the fecal specimen for examination.
However, segments should be examined when present as
identiﬁcation informs advice on prevention of reinfection. A
single lateral genital pore may be observed (see Fig. 115.4B) which
diﬀerentiates Taenia spp. from D. caninum. Furthermore, segments
can be diﬀerentiated from those of Echinococcus spp. as Taenia spp.
segments are more rectangular and much larger (Fig. 115.5). As
with other tapeworms, the presence of calcareous corpuscles
allows one to distinguish between a cestode segment and a
pseudoparasite (e.g., small foreign body). 41 Molecular techniques
allow identiﬁcation of adult parasites or segments to the species
level. 42
Eggs may be identiﬁed in segments or free in feces. They have a
thick shell wall with radial striations, are brown, and 25 to 40 µm
in
diameter.

Two methods for characterization of taeniid eggs in fecal

antigen can be detected in feces weeks before patency, the levels

for several months in formalin-ﬁxed feces, and copro-antigen

Treatment and Prognosis
Praziquantel or epsiprantel are eﬀective for treatment of Taenia
spp. infections using the same dosages as used for D. caninum
(Table 115.3). 23 In the USA, fenbendazole is approved at 50 mg/kg
q24h for 3 consecutive days for T. pisiformis in dogs; in the UK, the

vetexamprep.ir

same drug dosage is approved for use in dogs and cats for Taenia
spp.. Nitroscanate is approved in some countries for use in dogs; a
dosage of 50 mg/kg was 98% eﬀective against T. hydatigena, T. ovis,
and T. pisiformis. 24 Nitazoxanide has been used to treat dogs and
cats infected with T. pisiformis and T. taeniaeformis, respectively.
The drug was 100% eﬀective against both cestodes at a single dose
of 100 mg/kg. 25

Prevention
Prevention of Taenia spp. infections is essentially limited to
minimizing the risk of ingestion of infected intermediate hosts,
which requires conﬁnement. Ideally, the Taenia species infecting a
dog or cat should be identiﬁed as this will allow one to determine
the most likely source of infection. Pets can then be administered
an eﬀective anticestodal medication periodically based on risk
factors for exposure. Depending on the Taenia spp. involved,
Taenia spp. that infect dogs and cats have PPPs of 27 to 63 days
(see Table 115.2). If limiting predation of intermediate hosts is not
possible, anticestodal medication could be considered every 6 to
12 weeks; preventive treatment at intervals slightly greater than
the PPP typically provides adequate control because not all
intermediate hosts are infected with the metacestode.

Public Health Aspects
Occasionally, the metacestode stages of T. crassiceps, T. multiceps,
T. serialis, and T. taeniaeformis have been described in people.
However, overall, the risk of zoonotic infection by these Taenia
spp. is very low and often associated with immunosuppression; 45
infections are likely acquired via ingestion of eggs in the feces of
dogs or cats. Dogs and cats are not involved in the life cycle of T.
saginata (beef tapeworm) and T. solium (pork tapeworm).
