Echinococcus spp. Infections (Echinococcosis)
Etiology and Epidemiology
All species in the genus Echinococcus have a predator-prey,
indirect life cycle that commonly involves wildlife. However,
some occur in signiﬁcant domestic life cycles. The adult
tapeworms of all species are only a few millimeters in length and
reside within the small intestine of carnivores, especially canids.
Intermediate hosts range from livestock to rodents. Most species
are infective for people. However, globally, the two most
important species are E. granulosus sensu lato (s.l.) and
Echinococcus multilocularis.
Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato Infections
Echinococcus granulosus s.l. occurs in animals and people and is
found worldwide, except for Greenland and Iceland which are
considered free of the parasite. 46 This etiologic agent is composed
of multiple genotypes/species that diﬀer in host speciﬁcity,
morphology, geographical distribution, and human pathogenicity
(Table 115.4). 47–49 Dogs are the deﬁnitive host for most
genotypes/species. However, wild canids can also be deﬁnitive

vetexamprep.ir

hosts for some. Following ingestion of eggs, the intermediate
stage, a hydatid cyst, develops within internal organs of
intermediate hosts (primarily ruminants, horses, pigs) and
accidental hosts (people and other mammals). The resultant
disease is termed cystic echinococcosis (CE). Furthermore, while
most species/strains of E. granulosus s.l. have been associated with
CE in people, the majority of human cases are due to E. granulosus
sensu stricto (s.s.) (sheep strain) (dangerous dog tapeworm, dwarf
dog tapeworm). 48 , 50 This genotype is therefore the primary
focus of the rest of this section.
Dogs are the primary deﬁnitive host for E. granulosus s.s.
However, wild canids such as foxes, coyotes, and dingoes may
also serve as deﬁnitive hosts. Domestic herbivores and omnivores
(e.g., sheep, ca le, buﬀalo, goat, camel, pig) are the predominant
intermediate hosts. Furthermore, while sheep are the primary
intermediate host in many regions, reindeer constitute the
primary intermediate host in parts of northern Europe and
northern Russia; camels are the main reservoir in parts of the
Middle East. 51
Adult tapeworms develop within the small intestine of
deﬁnitive hosts and live for approximately 6 months. Once
segments are fully mature, they usually disintegrate within the
intestine to release eggs that are shed in feces and are immediately
infective. Both intermediate hosts and accidental hosts, including
people, are infected by ingestion of eggs. Subsequently,
oncospheres hatch from eggs within the small intestine, penetrate
blood vessels, and travel primarily to the liver where they develop
into hydatid cysts, the metacestode stage. Hydatid cysts are
composed of an outer acellular laminated layer and an inner
germinal layer. Weeks to months following infection, the germinal
layer may generate brood capsules, 0.25 to 1.5 mm in diameter,
that each contain up to approximately 40 protoscolices. Brood
capsule walls may subsequently rupture. Thus, hydatid cysts
occur either as a single, ﬂuid-ﬁlled, cyst or one large cyst
containing multiple smaller cysts; hydatid ﬂuid is composed of
protoscolices, calcareous corpuscles, and potentially brood
capsules that collectively are referred to as “hydatid sand”. Cysts
may take 6 to 12 months to mature and, depending on the host
species, age of the animal, and organ involved, may vary in
diameter from 1 mm to 20 cm. In intermediate hosts and people,

vetexamprep.ir

the liver and lungs are the primary organs involved. Less
commonly, cysts develop in body cavities, the CNS, eye, kidney,
muscle, or spleen. Cysts may remain viable for lengthy periods
(Fig. 115.6). The life cycle is completed when fertile hydatid cysts
are eaten by dogs and wild canids. In dogs, the PPP is 34 to 58
days. 52 , 53
Although E. granulosus s.s. occurs in wildlife species, it is the
domestic life cycle that is of particular zoonotic concern. Thus, CE
in people is especially common in parts of Africa, Asia, Australia,
Europe, the Middle East, and South America where the following
condition(s) occur that facilitate establishment of the domestic
cycle: (1) large sheep and dog populations, (2) dogs that have
access to dead livestock or oﬀal, (3) cestocide treatment of dogs is
lacking, (4) communities have a low socioeconomic status.
Prevalences of hydatid cyst detection in sheep in excess of 40%
have been demonstrated in parts of China, Ethiopia, Iran, Italy,
and Kyrgystan. 51 While few studies have evaluated the
prevalence of E. granuosus s.l. in dogs in many of these regions, in
some areas of Italy the prevalence of hydatid cysts in sheep has
been 23.5% to 27.9%; in the same areas, 24.6% of dogs were coproantigen-positive for E. granulosus s.l.; signiﬁcant levels of CE have
been identiﬁed in people in the same region. 54

feces, or on the skin and coat, of dogs. Unfortunately, li le

In moist environments, eggs can remain viable for weeks to
months. However, the duration of viability is greatly reduced in
low humidity. At temperatures of 75 to 100°C, eggs are destroyed
within minutes; at −80°C this takes approximately 48 hours.
Commonly used chemical disinfectants do not destroy eggs. 53
While cats are not deﬁnitive hosts for E. granulosus s.l., a few
cases of CE have been reported in cats. CE due to E. granulosus s.s.
(genotype 1) has been described in cats from Russia and Uruguay;
57 , 58 and CE due to E. granulosus s.l. was reported in a cat in
Turkey. 59 One of the cats was co-infected with FIV; 58 the other
two cats were not tested for retrovirus infection.
Echinococcus multilocularis (Dwarf Fox Tapeworm)
Echinococcus multilocularis is a zoonotic tapeworm that occurs
throughout the northern hemisphere, primarily in a wildlifeassociated life cycle. Across its distribution, only minor genetic
variation has been observed. 60 In North America, E. multilocularis
has historically been considered to occur in two distinct
geographic regions: the Northern Tundra Zone that extends from
the west coast of Alaska to parts of the Canadian arctic, 61 and the
North Central Region that includes the southern parts of three
Canadian provinces (Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba) and 13
midwestern US states (North Dakota, South Dakota, Iowa,
Minnesota, Montana, Wyoming, Nebraska, Illinois, Wisconsin,
Indiana, Ohio, Missouri, Michigan). 61–63 However, the
geographical range has been expanding into parts of British
Columbia and Ontario, Canada. 64 , 65 In Europe, the parasite has
historically occurred in Austria, France, Germany, and
Swi erland. However, over the last two decades the distribution
of the parasite has extended into western, northern, and eastern
parts of Europe, involving a total of 21 countries; those with the
highest prevalence of infection in deﬁnitive hosts (>10%) include
the Czech Republic, Estonia, France, Germany, Latvia,
Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, and Swi erland.

vetexamprep.ir

European countries currently free of E. multilocularis in wild
canids are Finland, Ireland, the United Kingdom, and mainland
Norway. 66 , 67 The parasite also occurs throughout much of the
Middle East (e.g., Turkey, Iran) and Asia (e.g., Russia, China,
Japan). 68 , 69
Adult E. multilocularis reside within the distal small intestine of
deﬁnitive hosts, which are primarily wild canids. In Europe, the
red fox is the primary deﬁnitive host. In North America, coyotes,
wolves, and arctic foxes also harbor adult parasites and may play
a signiﬁcant role in the epidemiology. Domestic dogs may also be
deﬁnitive hosts. Dogs also can play an important role in the
epidemiology in parts of Alaska and Asia (e.g., China). 53 , 70
Domestic cats and wild felids occasionally develop intestinal
infections but are of minor importance in the epidemiology due to
the short duration, and low levels, of fecal egg excretion. 71
Like E. granulosus s.l. eggs, eggs of E. multilocularis are
morphologically indistinguishable from eggs of Taenia spp. and
are immediately infective for intermediate and accidental hosts.
Intermediate hosts for E. multilocularis are primarily wild rodents.
72 Accidental hosts include humans, non-human primates, pigs,
horses, and dogs. Both intermediate and accidental hosts become
infected by ingestion of eggs (Fig. 115.7). Subsequently, an
oncosphere hatches from the egg, typically travels to the liver via
the hepatic portal circulation, and develops into the metacestode.
This stage comprises numerous small vesicles that vary in size
from <1 mm to 3 cm in diameter; the wall is composed of an outer
laminated layer and an inner germinal epithelium from which
multiple protoscolices may develop. In intermediate hosts that are
highly susceptible to infection, protoscolices develop in 2 to 4
months. In less susceptible hosts, the rate of development is
slower or the number of protoscolices that develop is reduced or
absent. Unlike hydatid cysts caused by E. granulosus s.l., the
metacestode of E. multilocularis undergoes exogenous budding.
During this process, the metacestode buds smaller portions of its
cystic-like structure that invade neighboring tissue and may
spread to distant organs, mimicking an invasive tumor. 46 By the
time clinical signs develop, there is usually substantive
involvement of the liver. The resultant disease, alveolar
echinococcosis (AE), is usually associated with extensive hepatic

vetexamprep.ir

damage and occasionally spreads to other locations (e.g., lungs,
brain, bone). The life cycle is completed when an infected
intermediate host is ingested by a deﬁnitive host; development of
adult tapeworms takes approximately 4 to 5 weeks. 71 Thereafter,
egg excretion usually lasts a few weeks. However, some parasites
persist for up to 12 months. In experimental work, the duration
and level of egg excretion in cats has been substantively less than
in dogs. 73 , 74

Across Europe, pooled prevalence estimates of infection in red
foxes range from <1% to >50%. 67 Furthermore, within endemic
areas the focal prevalence of infection in red foxes shows regional
variability. 75 , 76 High prevalences have been observed in fox
populations that have established in multiple European cities over

vetexamprep.ir

the last two decades. For example, in Geneva, Stu gart, and
Zurich in Swi erland, the prevalence of infection in red foxes
ranges from 17% to 44%. 77 This, in turn, has been associated with
the establishment of urban parasite life cycles. For example, fecal
analysis of 660 randomly selected, privately owned dogs in a
densely populated part of eastern Swi erland demonstrated an E.
multilocularis prevalence of 0.3%; in the same area, 0.4% of 263 cats
were infected. 78 Among dogs in endemic European countries, a
pooled estimate for the prevalence of intestinal infections was
0.3%. 67 However, among dogs that roam freely and have access to
rodents, a prevalence as high as 8.1% has been described. 79
Infected dogs, particularly in urban environments, constitute a
signiﬁcant risk for human infection. For example, in central
Europe, 4% to 19% of environmental contamination with E.
multilocularis eggs is associated with domestic dogs. The
contribution of cats is considered insigniﬁcant (<0.3%). 80 Within
North America, there are very few reports of intestinal infections
in dogs or cats in either the USA or Canada. Historically,
prevalences of infection up to 12% have been observed in some
dog populations on St. Lawrence Island, Alaska. 81 However,
outside Alaska, intestinal infections in dogs appear to have been
evaluated only three times; using molecular methods, E.
multilocularis was identiﬁed in feces of 1/218 (0.5%) dogs in
Alberta 63 and 0/477 (0%) dogs in Ontario 82 ; an intestinal
infection has recently been described in a dog in Missouri. 83
Similarly, only ﬁve cats have been reported with intestinal
infections (three in Saskatchewan; 84 two in North Dakota). 85
Under central European summer conditions, with adequate
moisture, eggs of E. multilocularis survive in the environment for 2
to 3 months. Under cooler conditions and at −20°C, eggs may
remain viable for months. However, as with E. granulosus s.l., eggs
are susceptible to desiccation. Temperatures in excess of 70°C
inactivate eggs. At −80°C, infectivity is lost after 48 hours. 53
Alveolar Echinococcosis in Dogs
Since the late 1980s, cases of AE, primarily involving the liver,
have been described in domestic dogs in Swi erland, Germany,
France, and Belgium. 72 , 86 These cases are thought to occur either
as a result of ingestion of large numbers of infective eggs (e.g., in

vetexamprep.ir

the feces of foxes) or by autoinfection in association with the
presence of adult E. multilocularis in the small intestine. 87 , 88 Of
the cases seen in Swi erland, the median age at diagnosis is 3.1
years (range = 1.1–10.7 years), with no signiﬁcant breed
predilection. 88
Prior to 2009, AE had not been diagnosed in a dog in North
America. However, in 2009, hepatic AE was diagnosed in a 3-yearold dog that had lived permanently in British Columbia, 64 a
Canadian province previously considered free of E. multilocularis.
Subsequently, examination of wild canids in the area where the
dog resided indicated that 11/33 (33%) were infected with E.
multilocularis. 89 Between 2009 and 2020, at least 25 dogs have been
described with AE in Canada: in British Columbia, Alberta,
Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and southern Ontario. 19 , 65 , 69 , 90 , 91
Furthermore, the Ontario dogs were generally from an area where
the prevalence of E. multilocularis in wild canids is >30%. 92 In
2020, AE was described in an 8-year-old Labrador retriever that
was acquired as a puppy from Mississippi and brought to
Virginia, 93 which is the ﬁrst case reported in the United States.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Echinococcus granulosus s.l. Infection
Dogs (definitive host)
Parasites are typically found in the proximal small intestine,
deeply embedded within crypts and a ached to the mucosa via
the scolex. This usually results in minimal damage, even when
substantive parasite burdens are present (similar to Fig. 115.8);
minor damage to the epithelium and mild cellular inﬁltration of
the mucosa may be observed. Thus, intestinal infections are
typically subclinical, even when large numbers of parasites are
present. When parasite burdens are heavy, segments of
Echinococcus spp. are occasionally found on the perianal region or
in feces; they are white and 0.5 to 3.0 mm long.
Cats (accidental hosts)

vetexamprep.ir

In all three cats described in the literature, large numbers (>150) of
ﬂuid-ﬁlled, transparent-white, hydatid cysts, 0.1 to 5.0 cm in
diameter, were found free in the abdomen and a ached to serosal
surfaces. In one cat, multiple cysts were also present within
hepatic parenchyma. 57–59 However, despite substantive cyst
burdens, minimal pathology was described. Signs were primarily
associated with a progressive space-occupying lesion within the
abdomen; all cats had a history of progressive abdominal
enlargement. Additional clinical signs included anorexia, dull
mentation, polydipsia, dyspnea, and constipation. 57–59 One of the
three cats was co-infected with FIV; 58 immunosuppression has
been associated with an increased risk of AE in people. 94

Echinococcus multilocularis Infection
Dogs and cats (definitive hosts)
Adult parasites are found a ached to the small intestinal mucosa
via the scolex, typically deep within intestinal crypts (see Fig.
115.8). Intestinal burdens in dogs are much greater than in cats. 71
However, even when large numbers of parasites are present,
lesions are minimal and infections are rarely clinical.
Dogs (accidental hosts)

vetexamprep.ir

Cases of AE in dogs are typically associated with lesions in the
liver; usually, there is signiﬁcant involvement by the time a
diagnosis is made, with lesions up to 10 to 15 cm in diameter.
Furthermore, because of the ability of the metacestode to
metastasize, secondary lesions may be found elsewhere in the
body, both within and outside the abdomen. 95 Dogs with AE
usually have signs of abdominal distention, lethargy, anorexia,
and vomiting. 87 , 88 Other, less common, signs include abdominal
pain, diarrhea, weight loss, polypnea, fever, and polyphagia.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Profile, and
Urinalysis
In dogs and cats with Echinococcus spp. intestinal infections, the
CBC, serum biochemical tests, and urinalysis are typically
unremarkable. In a European study on 11 dogs with AE, the most
common serum chemistry abnormalities were hypoalbuminemia
(10/11), hyperproteinemia (9/11), increased serum amylase (7/11),
and hyperglobulinemia (3/11). Increased liver enzyme activities
were only observed in 2/11 dogs. The most signiﬁcant CBC
abnormality was a decreased PCV (3/11). 96
Diagnostic Imaging
Sonographic Findings
In dogs with AE, abdominal ultrasound typically reveals the
presence of one or more large, heterogeneous, poorly limited,
cavitated hepatic masses, with or without wall mineralization.
Usually, there is a thick hyperechoic outer surface, an irregular
inner surface, and a centrally located cavity ﬁlled with echogenic
ﬂuid. 88 , 96 Non-cavitated ultrasound pa erns are thought to
represent early inﬁltration prior to central liquefaction or cavity
formation. A lack of vascularity of masses is evident. 96 Extension
to neighboring organs is observed in approximately one-third of
cases. Free abdominal ﬂuid is present in a similar proportion and
is generally a ributed to rupture of cystic structures. 88

vetexamprep.ir

Advanced Imaging
CT of dogs with AE usually reveals cystic to cavitated, or
granular, masses within liver lobes; cavitated masses have a
hypoa enuating center and a distinct hypera enuating wall (Fig.
115.9). 96 , 97 Mineralization may be observed in walls of cavitated
masses. The absence of enhancement within masses has been
observed and is a characteristic CT feature of AE in people. 98
Progressive mineralization over time is considered a sign of
chronic disease and of dystrophic tissue metaplasia because of
medical therapy. 99 A lack of vascularity of masses is evident. 96
Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
In many dogs, ultrasound-guided ﬁne-needle aspirates of
intralesional or peritoneal ﬂuid generates specimens with
cytologic morphology consistent with AE, namely, calcareous
corpuscles and folded membranous structures (Fig. 115.10). 19
While the former may be associated with any cestode, the folded
membranes have only been described in AE cases.
Isolation and Identification
In heavy parasite burdens, a presumptive diagnosis of intestinal
infection may be made if segments are found in feces or on the
perianal region. However, Echinococcus spp. segments are much
smaller than those of Taenia spp. and Dipylidium caninum (see Fig.
115.5) and usually disintegrate before being passed in feces. Eggs
of Echinococcus spp. may be found in feces using ﬂotation
methods. However, this is insensitive and the eggs are
indistinguishable from Taenia spp. eggs (see Taenia earlier in this
chapter). 20 , 53 Eggs of both species are immediately infective for
people and appropriate biosecurity practices must be followed
when handling intestinal contents and feces.
At necropsy, adult parasites are most likely to be found by: (1)
stereoscopic examination of the small intestine, (2) intestinal
scraping, and (3) examination of small intestine wash ﬂuid using
the sedimentation and counting technique (SCT). 100 The la er
method has the highest sensitivity. Echinococcus granulosus s.l. are
generally located within the proximal small intestine. Adult

vetexamprep.ir

parasites are 1 to 7 mm in length with a scolex containing two
rows of hooks and four suckers. Typically, three (two to six)
segments are present. The genital pore is located approximately
equidistant from either end of the segment. Echinococcus
multilocularis are generally located within the distal small
intestine. 101 Adult parasites are 2 to 4 mm in length with a scolex
containing two rows of hooks and four suckers. Typically, ﬁve
(two to six) segments are present. The genital pore is located
within the anterior half of the segment.
The sensitivity of necropsy examination for diagnosis of
intestinal echinococcosis is high (>97%). However, when low
parasite burdens are present (<6 parasites), false-negative results
may occur, particularly if SCT is not performed. 102 Conﬁrmation
of the parasite species recovered can be carried out by DNA
analysis. 103

Serologic Diagnosis (Fecal Antigen Detection)
Multiple copro-antigen-detection ELISAs have been developed for
examining fecal specimens from dogs for Echinococcus spp. but are
generally genus speciﬁc. Sensitivities of these tests range from
60% to 92%; speciﬁcities range from 70% to 96%. Copro-antigen
ELISA sensitivity is inﬂuenced by parasite burden. 53 , 102 Crossreactions are generally associated with infection with T. hydatigena
but likely also occur with other Taenia spp.. Thus, when used on
dogs or cats, copro-antigen ELISA-positive results should ideally
be conﬁrmed with nucleic acid–based testing. 53

vetexamprep.ir

Serology
Most dogs with AE develop antibodies to an E. multilocularisspeciﬁc antigen. 88 , 104 At the time of writing, this diagnostic tool
is only available at the Universities of Bern and Zurich,
Swi erland. Due to abortive infections, some dogs will
seroconvert but not develop AE. 105 , 106
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Multiple PCR-based assays have been described for detection of E.
granulosus s.l. 102 and E. multilocularis, some of which require
isolation of eggs. While most assays have high speciﬁcity,
sensitivity has been variable; some methods have low sensitivity,
presumably due to PCR inhibitors in feces or intermi ent
shedding of eggs. One E. multilocularis PCR assay had an overall
sensitivity of 88%; in animals with more than 100 parasites,
sensitivity was 95.7%; speciﬁcity was at least 99.9%. This assay
was selected for use in national surveillance programs of wild
canids in Europe and has been used to detect infection in fecal
specimens from dogs and cats. 107
Multiple Echinococcus species-speciﬁc assays also have been
developed for use on tissue specimens. For example, DNA
sequence data for PCR-generated fragments of the mitochondrial
12S rRNA gene 108 and restriction fragment length polymorphism
analysis of the 12S rRNA gene and NADH dehydrogenase 1 gene 109
can be used to conﬁrm the presence of E. multilocularis. Similar
methods are available for detection and identiﬁcation of E.
granulosus s.l. 48 , 102

Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
In dogs with hepatic AE, multiple nodular ﬁrm pale-tan masses
are typically present that can be readily mistaken for neoplasia, or
sometimes abscesses, without histologic examination (Fig.
115.11A). Furthermore, while the liver is the most common organ
aﬀected, extension(s) into neighboring organs such as the
omentum, peritoneum, and diaphragm may occur. 88 Exogenous
budding of the metacestode has also been associated with lesions
in the lungs, spleen, vertebral bodies, brain, and prostate of dogs.
87 , 97

Histopathologic Findings
Histological examination of tissue biopsies is extremely helpful
for diagnosis of AE as morphology is characteristic for E.
multilocularis; 64 , 72 hepatic architecture is replaced by multi-

vetexamprep.ir

loculated coalescing cystic structures surrounded by ﬁbrosis. 88
Lining individual cysts is an eosinophilic hyaline membrane
(“laminated layer”) that stains with PAS (Fig. 115.11B and C). The
inner lining of the hyaline membrane is typically composed of a
germinal epithelial layer and a basophilic matrix that contains
occasional calcareous corpuscles. Intraluminal protoscolices are
sometimes observed. A prominent chronic eosinophilic and
granulomatous inﬂammation is also usually present. The
combination of histopathology and a positive E. multilocularis
species-speciﬁc PCR assay is the gold standard for diagnosis of
AE. 88 , 109

Treatment and Prognosis
E. granulosus s.l. and E. multilocularis Intestinal Infections
Praziquantel is most commonly used and typically recommended
as a single treatment as it kills both adult and immature parasites
in the intestine (see Table 115.5). 110 However, two treatments 24
hours apart are recommended for E. multilocularis infections to
ensure adequate dosing. Epsiprantel may also be used but eﬃcacy
is typically less than that of praziquantel. 111 Neither praziquantel
nor epsiprantel are ovicidal, and infective eggs may be shed in
feces for up to 3 days following treatment. As a result, when
treating infected dogs and cats, animals should be maintained in
an environment that is easy to clean, feces should be safely
disposed of for 3 days following treatment, animals should be
washed entirely after treatment using a shampoo to remove eggs
from the coat, and people should ideally wear mouth protection
(e.g., surgical mask or cloth face covering), gloves, and protective
clothing. 3

Alveolar Echinococcosis

vetexamprep.ir

The metacestode of E. multilocularis in the abdomen of dogs does
not constitute a direct risk to human health. However, some dogs
with hepatic AE may also have patent intestinal infections 112 and
therefore may constitute a zoonotic risk. Thus, as soon as a
presumptive diagnosis of hepatic AE is made, dogs should be
treated with praziquantel to eliminate intestinal infection; 110
treatment should be repeated 24 hours later. Praziquantel has
li le eﬃcacy against the metacestode.
Once a deﬁnitive diagnosis of AE is made, treatment should be
initiated with albendazole at 10 mg/kg PO q24h for life. 96 In some
dogs, albendazole can cause bone marrow toxicity leading to
aplastic anemia. 113 Therefore dogs receiving albendazole should
be monitored weekly for 1 month, then every 3 to 4 months
thereafter, with a CBC. This treatment regimen is recommended
whether or not surgical excision is pursued. As in people, surgery
is only recommended if complete removal of the metacestode can
be achieved. 88 Dogs with any type of intervention (albendazole,
surgery, or both) live signiﬁcantly longer than those that have no
intervention. 88 At present, there is no evidence that debulking
surgery (cytoreduction) followed by treatment with albendazole
results in a superior outcome compared to treatment with
albendazole alone. 88
Historically, it has been assumed that medical management of
dogs with AE is associated with short-term survival. However,
four of six dogs managed with only daily albendazole were in
remission 0.5, 0.5, 2.6, and 9.5 years after the initial diagnosis. 88

Immunity and Vaccination
A recombinant vaccine (EG95) for E. granulosus s.l. has been
developed for use in sheep and ca le intermediate hosts which
results in a substantive reduction (>95%) in hydatid cyst burdens.
As such, this vaccine is approved for use in a number of countries
(e.g., Argentina, China) 53 , 114 , 115 and constitutes a useful tool in
E. granulosus s.l. control programs. A similar vaccine is currently
being developed for AE in people. 68 Although vaccines are not
available for dogs, they have been considered desirable, and
vaccine trials in dogs have yielded promising results. 115

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
E. granulosus s.l. Infections
In some countries with high prevalence of infection in dogs and
high incidence of CE in people, control programs have been
implemented (e.g., Argentina, Chile, Cyprus, New Zealand,
Uruguay) that include: (1) strict regulation of animal slaughter
and disposal of oﬀal, (2) control of dog populations, (3) treatment
of all dogs every 6 weeks with a cestocide, and (4) education of the
public about transmission of E. granulosus s.l. and the importance
of cooking raw oﬀal or freezing it at −18°C for a minimum of 3
days prior to feeding it to dogs. 3 , 116 , 117 Such programs are
costly and take >10 years before the prevalence of infection in
dogs and intermediate hosts declines to low levels. Incorporation
of (EG95) vaccination of both intermediate and deﬁnitive hosts
into these control programs will likely have a more rapid and
sustainable impact on the prevalence of infection in diﬀerent
hosts. 53 , 115
E. multilocularis Infections
In areas endemic for E. multilocularis, administration of
praziquantel at 5.0 mg/kg PO every 4 weeks is recommended for
dogs with access to rodents. 88 In such areas, a risk assessment
should be carried out on a regular basis to determine if such
preventive treatment is necessary. Since AE in dogs may be
associated with autoinfection, such a protocol may also reduce the
risk of AE in dogs.
In order to reduce the risk of importation of E. multilocularis into
countries free of this parasite, some countries require dogs from
endemic areas to be treated with a cestocide at the time of entry,
for example, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, mainland Norway, Malta,
and the United Kingdom. 118 , 119

Public Health Aspects
People only become infected with E. granulosus s.l. and E.
multilocularis by ingestion of eggs. Thus, in a veterinary
environment, this will typically only occur by contamination of
hands. Since the eggs of both parasites are immediately infective
in fresh feces of dogs or cats, strict a ention to hand hygiene

vetexamprep.ir

whenever handling feces, materials contaminated by feces, or a
potentially infected animal will eﬀectively eliminate the risk of
infection. When performing a necropsy on a dog potentially
infected with Echinococcus spp., masks, gloves, and protective
clothing should be used if the intestine is opened.
Cystic Echinococcosis
While many genotypes/species of E. granulosus s.l. infect people,
>88% of human infections that have been typed are E. granulosus
s.s. genotype G1, 48 indicating that sheep are the intermediate
hosts. Many infections in people remain clinically inapparent for
lengthy periods, even when large hydatid cyst(s) are present. 120
Disease ranges from mild to fatal and is associated with the spaceoccupying nature of cysts that usually occur in the liver and lungs
and, less commonly, in the bone, CNS, or spleen. Liver
involvement is typically associated with abdominal pain. With
lung involvement, patients may present with chest pain, cough,
dyspnea, and hemoptysis. 121 Diagnosis is based on detection of
cysts by imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) combined with
Echinococcus spp. serology. 120 Surgical excision is the preferred
management as this is the only approach likely to result in cure.
122 When surgery is not an option, prolonged treatment with
albendazole or mebendazole is carried out which, while usually
not curative, reduces the cyst size and the associated clinical signs.
122

Alveolar Echinococcosis
Only approximately 1% to 10% of people that are exposed to eggs
of E. multilocularis and seroconvert develop disease. 68 , 98 When
infections are not eliminated, the clinical incubation period is 5 to
15 years. People usually present with symptoms associated with
hepatic neoplasia, such as epigastric pain, fatigue, jaundice, and
weight loss. 122 , 123 Disease has been reported in all ages, but is
most commonly diagnosed in people aged 50 to 55 years. 124 , 125
AE is usually diagnosed by imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI)
followed by Echinococcus spp. serology. However, imaging is
usually suggestive of a neoplasm; suspicion of AE typically only
occurs after histological examination of a biopsy. 120

vetexamprep.ir

AE in people often presents in an advanced stage 124 and
mortality rates are typically much greater than CE. When left
untreated, AE has a chronic course that lasts weeks to years.
Surgical excision of the entire lesion, followed by treatment with a
benzimidazole (albendazole or mebendazole), is the only
intervention that can result in cure, but is an option for only
approximately one-third of cases. For individuals with nonresectable lesions, long-term treatment with a benzimidazole is
recommended. 68 Since this treatment is parasitostatic rather than
parasitocidal, regular imaging (e.g., PET scan) is required to
determine the duration of therapy; in some individuals, life-long
treatment may be required. 123 Data from Europe indicate that the
10-year survival rate in untreated individuals is 6% to 25%.
However, this increases to 80% to 89% in people on long-term
benzimidazole treatment. 126
In a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of the
literature, risk factors associated with AE in people included dogrelated factors (e.g., playing with dogs, dog ownership), gender
(being female), vocational factors (e.g., being a farmer, handling
foxes), sociocultural factors (e.g., low income), and human habits
(e.g., chewing grass). However, these potential risk factors likely
vary in importance in diﬀerent endemic areas of the world. 127 For
example, strong associations between AE in people and dogs have
been observed in parts of Alaska and China. 81 , 128 If exposure of
people to E. multilocularis eggs is a concern, serological testing for
up to 12 months following exposure is recommended. 129–131
In North America, despite the large geographic distribution of
E. multilocularis in wildlife, only a small number of cases of
autochthonous alveolar echinococcosis in people had been
described before 2013—one from Manitoba in 1937, 132 and one
from Minnesota in 1977. 133 This low number of cases led some to
conclude that the genetic variants of E. multilocularis occurring in
North America are of lower infectivity or pathogenicity for people
than those in Europe. 134 However, since 2013, reports of disease
in humans associated with a European-type strain began to
emerge, including seventeen cases from Alberta, one from
Saskatechewan, and one from Vermont, USA. 135 , 136 The case
from Vermont was a 36-year-old woman who owned a dog and
had grown up fox-hunting in Maryland; she had traveled

vetexamprep.ir

extensively throughout the USA, Costa Rica, Rome/Naples, and
Montreal, but not to regions in Europe or Canada where the
majority of European haplotype strain cases have been described.

Mesocestoides spp. Infection
Etiology and Epidemiology
There is still much to learn about Mesocestoides spp., including the
number of species and the identity of the ﬁrst intermediate hosts.
137 , 138 At present, there are no accepted speciﬁc criteria that can
be used to deﬁne a species, so numerous species appear in the
literature. In 1932, Witenberg recognized one species,
Mesocestoides lineatus in dogs, foxes, jackals, and cats, and
synonymized or discounted 24 described species. 17 , 139 In 1980,
Loos-Frank created the name Mesocestoides leptothylacus for the
species commonly found in foxes in Europe. 140 In 1991, Etges
proposed the name Mesocestoides vogae to replace the species
Mesocestoides corti ﬁrst described by Hoeppi in 1925, utilizing
specimens collected from a mouse in Colorado, USA. 141 The most
common European species are M. vogae, M. leptothylacus, and M.
lineatus. However, some authors believe the name of the la er is
taxonomically incorrect; the ﬁrst descriptions were based on
specimens that were not available for future authors to compare
and none of the descriptions matched the original description.
Therefore it has been proposed that all descriptions under the
name M. lineatus be revised. 140
Mesocestoides spp. occasionally infect dogs and cats, and
essentially have a worldwide distribution. In Europe, the adult
stage of Mesocestoides spp. occurs mainly in foxes, with a
prevalence in some areas of up to 70%. 142 The prevalence in dogs
and cats is considerably less. For example, the prevalence of
Mesocestoides spp. in feral cats in Denmark at necropsy was 3.0%.
143 The prevalence of Mesocestoides spp. in owned cats in central
Italy was 1.2% by fecal ﬂotation. 144 In Iran, M. lineatus was
reported in 19% of stray dogs at necropsy. 145 In Russia, M.
lineatus was found in 1.7% to 23.5% of dogs at necropsy. 146
Mesocestoides spp. have also been reported in North and South
America. 147 , 148 In North American dogs and cats, both fecal
examination and necropsy studies have revealed a low prevalence

vetexamprep.ir

(0%–1%); infections are more commonly detected in the
southeastern and western United States. 14 , 15 , 148 , 149
Adult Mesocestoides spp. develop in the intestine of dogs and
cats following ingestion of the infective metacestode stage
(tetrathyridium) within the abdominal cavity of various
intermediate hosts, which include over 200 species of reptiles,
amphibians, mammals, and birds (Fig. 115.12). 150 However,
strangely, despite this breadth of information, the ﬁrst stage and
ﬁrst intermediate host for Mesocestoides spp. remain a mystery. It
is currently believed that a cysticercoid stage occurs in an
arthropod such as an ant, and that this precedes the tetrathyridial
stage. However, experimental infections have yet to conﬁrm this.
137 , 151 One study examined thousands of soil-inhabiting
invertebrates from areas heavily contaminated with Mesocestoides
spp. gravid segments shed by experimentally infected foxes, but
cysticercoids were not found. 137

ingestion of a ﬁrst-stage larva in the still-unidentiﬁed ﬁrst
intermediate host or a tetrathyridium in a second intermediate
host. 152 In M. vogae (syn. M. corti), both the tetrathyridium and
adult tapeworm can undergo asexual reproduction. 153 Thus, this
species can repopulate the intestinal tract without further
exposure if not eliminated by anthelmintic treatment. 154 Chronic
glucocorticoid treatment may be a risk factor for peritoneal
disease in dogs; Welsh Corgis appeared to be over-represented in
a study of 60 dogs from the United States, comprising 10% of the
aﬀected dogs. 155

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Intestinal infection appears to be subclinical in dogs and cats.
Most reported cases of peritoneal infections have been dogs from
North America. Of 60 dogs in the United States with peritoneal
infections, most (50) were from California, with three cases from
Oregon, and single cases from Washington, Arizona, Florida, and
Oklahoma. 155 Single cases have also been reported in dogs from
New Mexico and Washington state, and British Columbia,
Canada. 138 , 156 , 157 Additional aﬀected dogs have been reported
in other countries (e.g., Germany, Japan). 142 , 158 Disease is
associated with asexual division or budding of the parasite and
development of large numbers in the peritoneal cavity; viable
tetrathyridial or non-viable acephalic metacestodes may be
produced. Infected dogs and cats may appear clinically normal,
especially if infected with relatively few metacestodes; subclinical
infections may be an incidental ﬁnding during abdominal
surgery. Clinically aﬀected dogs may have abdominal distension
secondary to ascites, anorexia, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea,
and tachypnea. 155 Some aﬀected cats have abdominal pain and
vomiting. 152 , 159 , 160

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
In dogs with peritoneal larval cestodiasis, leukocytosis,
eosinophilia, and thrombocytopenia have been demonstrated on

vetexamprep.ir

CBC. Serum chemistry analysis may show azotemia,
hyperphosphatemia, hyponatremia, panhypoproteinemia, and
hyperbilirubinemia. 142 , 158
Diagnostic Imaging
Abdominal radiographs typically show a general loss of detail
secondary to ascites. Abdominal ultrasound may reveal round,
thin-walled, anechoic cysts. Some may contain a 1-mm to 5-mm
rounded structure compatible with a tetrathyridium. 142 , 158 , 159
Large quantities of hyperechoic free peritoneal ﬂuid is often
present that is highly suggestive of the disease (Fig. 115.13).
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
Diagnosis of intestinal infections is by detection of segments in
feces (Fig. 115.14A and B) or, rarely, detection of eggs via fecal
ﬂotation (Fig. 115.14C). Gravid segments are 3 to 4 mm in size and
club shaped; they are similar in size to segments of Echinococcus
spp. but smaller than those of Taenia spp. and D. caninum (see Fig.
115.5). For deﬁnitive identiﬁcation, segments should be ﬂa ened
between two glass slides after adding water or saline to the
segment; the genital pore is positioned mid-ventrally.
Furthermore, Mesocestoides spp. possess a thick-walled
parauterine organ in mature segments where eggs accumulate;
this is rarely found in other cyclophyllideans. 11 , 161 Segments can
also be disrupted to release eggs (if present). As for other
cestodes, calcareous corpuscles also may be seen. 41
Although fecal ﬂotation is insensitive (as for other cestode
infections), Mesocestoides eggs are unique; they are 30 to 40 µm in
diameter and possess a thin, clear, smooth shell wall. Hooks of the
hexacanth embryo can help distinguish the egg from a
pseudoparasite. 3
Cytologic Diagnosis
Peritoneal larval cestodiasis is diagnosed by detection of either
tetrathyridia or calcareous corpuscles in abdominal ﬂuid;
abdominal ﬂuid is collected via centesis or during an exploratory
laparotomy. 153 Grossly, free fragments of white, ﬂocculated

vetexamprep.ir

material that vary in size from less than 1 mm to 5 mm may be
seen in abdominal ﬂuid that appears clear to serosanguinous (Fig.
115.15). Microscopically, tetrathyridia of Mesocestoides spp. have
four suckers, calcareous corpuscles, and the absence of hooks or a
rostellum (Fig. 115.16). 142 , 158 , 159

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Molecular methods can be used to deﬁnitively identify acephalic
metacestodes. 138 PCR-DNA analysis targeting the mitochondrial
(mt) 12S rRNA gene and mt cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 gene
has been used to identify M. vogae (syn. M. corti), 158 as well as the
mt 12S rRNA gene of M. lineatus. 142

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

A single dose of praziquantel (5 mg/kg PO or 5.7 mg/kg SC or IM)
can eliminate intestinal Mesocestoides spp. infections in dogs and
cats (Table 115.6). 11 , 162 However, dogs with peritoneal infections
require long-term use of high dosages of fenbendazole (100 mg/kg
q12h for 28 days) along with peritoneal lavage following
laparotomy to remove tetrathyridia (see Table 115.6). 138 One case
report concluded that praziquantel was more eﬀective than
fenbendazole at treating canine peritoneal cestodiasis; however,
this was only in one dog that had previously been treated with
fenbendazole. In this case, praziquantel was dosed at 5.0 mg/kg
and repeated 15 days later. 163 Long-term follow-up is indicated as
some dogs will experience recurrence of clinical disease even after
28 days of high dosages of fenbendazole. 155 Dogs that fail
fenbendazole treatment or have adverse eﬀects of high-dose
fenbendazole (typically gastrointestinal or neurologic signs in the
editor’s experience) after peritoneal lavage may respond to 8
mg/kg praziquantel q24h for 2 weeks (Sykes JE, personal
observations).
In the 60 dogs from California, Oregon, Washington, Arizona,
Florida, and Oklahoma, dogs received one, two, or three of the
following treatment options: surgery/lavage, fenbendazole at any
dosage, or fenbendazole at 100 mg/kg for >28 days (termed high
dose). Overall, survival was 72.3% at 6 months and 60.5% at 1
year. Both clinical severity at the time of diagnosis and treatment
regimen signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced the treatment outcome; dogs
treated with high-dose fenbendazole, or both peritoneal
lavage/surgery and any dosage of fenbendazole, had less than
one-ﬁfth the risk of dying compared to dogs that were not treated
in this manner. 155 If there is a history of chronic treatment with
glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive medications, these
should be tapered and discontinued if possible.

Prevention
The only preventive measure available is minimizing the risk of
consumption of intermediate hosts by dogs and cats. Since the
tetrathyridium stage (the stage infective to dogs and cats) has
been reported in over 200 species of reptiles, amphibians,
mammals, and birds, the best recommendation is to limit
unsupervised roaming outdoors. 150

Public Health Aspects
Humans have very rarely been reported to develop intestinal
adult Mesocestoides spp. infections, but infected dogs and cats are
not a direct risk to humans. The ﬁrst report of a human infection

vetexamprep.ir

was in Texas, USA (1942), where a girl was diagnosed with an M.
lineatus infection. 164 Other cases include a 19-month-old boy from
Louisiana diagnosed with an M. variabilis infection; the proposed
origin of infection was food-borne. 165 Six other human cases of M.
lineatus or Mesocestoides spp. have been reported in the USA in
Texas, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio, Mississippi, and California. 166
In Japan, a 35-year-old man was diagnosed with M. lineatus
infection and thought most likely to have acquired the infection
by eating raw snake liver. 167 These infections all appeared to be
well tolerated and were diagnosed by ﬁnding segments in the
feces. Treatment with praziquantel is typically eﬀective. In
addition, niclosamide and paromomycin sulfate have been used.
166 , 167

Diphyllobothrium spp. Infection
Etiology and Epidemiology
The Diphyllobothrium genus contains approximately 50 species of
which 14 have been reported in humans. 168 All occur as adult
parasites within the intestinal tract of ﬁsh-eating mammals and
birds. Globally, Diphyllobothrium latum (Dibothriocephalus latus) 169
is the most important species. Regionally important species
include Diphyllobothrium dendriticum (Russia, Argentina, Chile)
and Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense (Paciﬁc Coast of Asia and North
America). 168 , 170
Diphyllobothrium latum (the ﬁsh tapeworm, broad tapeworm)
infects both dogs and cats; other deﬁnitive hosts include humans,
bears, foxes, pigs, mink, and seals. The parasite occurs in North
America (Alaska and the Great Lakes region of Canada and the
USA), northern Europe (Estonia, Finland, Hungary, Lithuania,
Poland, Sweden and sub-Alpine lakes in France, Italy,
Swi erland), and Russia. However, cases have also been reported
in South America (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Peru) and occasionally
in parts of Asia (Japan, Korea, Philippines, Taiwan). 171–173

Diphyllobothrium latum has a three-host life cycle (Fig. 115.17).
Adult parasites occur within the small intestine of dogs, cats,
people, and other deﬁnitive hosts. Each parasite releases up to
1,000,000 eggs per day in to the intestinal contents via a single
uterine pore that is present in each segment. 174 Eggs are then
shed into the environment in feces. In fresh water, a ciliated
coracidium hatches from the egg 174 and is ingested by the ﬁrst
intermediate host, aquatic copepods (Cyclops and Diaptomus
species). 175 The coracidium matures into a procercoid within the
body cavity of the copepod. When ingested by the second
intermediate host, fresh water ﬁsh, the procercoid invades the
peritoneal cavity, internal organs, or muscles and matures to a 1to 3-cm long pleroceroid that resembles a small tapeworm.
Plerocercoids can survive for extended periods in these locations.
176 If a ﬁsh infected with a plerocercoid is ingested by another ﬁsh,
the plerocercoid can transfer to the new ﬁsh, that is, ﬁsh may be
paratenic hosts. Dogs, cats, and other deﬁnitive hosts develop
intestinal infections after consuming ﬁsh infected with a
plerocercoid. In dogs and cats, the prepatent period is 5 to 6
weeks. 11

Prevalence of infection in these species is highly variable.
However, in Lake Geneva, France/Swi erland, the prevalence of
plerocercoids in perch in 2003–2005 was 4% to 10%. 178 By
contrast, in Lake Como, Italy, the prevalence of infection from
2013 to 2014 in perch and pike was 25.4% and 84.2%, respectively.
179

Li le information is available on the prevalence of D. latum in
dogs and cats. In North America, most infections are diagnosed in
dogs. 3 In Europe, D. latum infections are generally rare. Thus, in
dog populations examined in both Finland and Swi erland, D.
latum infections were detected in 0.4% of dogs. 180 , 181 By contrast,
in parts of Russia, up to 90% of cats have been shown to be
infected. 182 , 183
One of the most important components of the epidemiology of
D. latum is contamination of freshwater environments by
untreated human sewage, although dogs can also be an important
source of environmental contamination. 184 , 185

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs

vetexamprep.ir

Intestinal infections in both dogs and cats are usually subclinical.
While anemia has been associated with D. latum intestinal
infections in people, this phenomenon has not been described in
naturally infected dogs or cats. Experimental D. latum infections
in dogs have been associated with decreased red cell numbers and
decreased total hemoglobin levels. 186 The possibility of infection
is generally only considered after owners report the presence of
chains of segments (typically empty of eggs) in feces. 3

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Laboratory abnormalities are generally unremarkable in dogs and
cats with D. latum infections.
Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Adult D. latum are found in the small intestine and measure 1 to
12 m in length. As with other pseudophyllidean tapeworms, the
scolex lacks hooks and suckers. Instead, it contains two shallow
longitudinal grooves (bothria). The strobila contains up to 3000
segments. Anterior segments are broader than long (width = 12–20
mm); posterior segments are approximately square shaped (Fig.
115.18). Segments have a number of characteristic features that
include a medioventral uterine pore and a centrally located,
rose e-shaped uterus. Unlike the more common tapeworms of
dogs and cats (i.e., Taenia spp. and D. caninum), segments of D.
latum continuously release eggs until the uterine contents are
exhausted. Thus, terminal segments are typically not gravid, that
is, do not contain eggs. Furthermore, they usually detach in
chains, not individually.
Eggs of D. latum are oval, light brown, have an operculum at
one pole, and measure 58 to 76 µm × 40 to 51 µm. They resemble
eggs produced by Spirometra spp. and digenetic trematodes.
However, a pore is often visible in the shell wall at the pole
opposite the operculum in association with a small amount of
material that protrudes from it (Fig. 115.18C). Eggs may be
recovered by fecal ﬂotation but are most readily detected using
sedimentation. 20 , 176 Precise identiﬁcation of diﬀerent

vetexamprep.ir

Diphyllobothrium species is most reliably achieved by PCR
sequencing. 187

Treatment and Prognosis
Praziquantel has been reported to be eﬃcacious for treatment of
D. latum infections in dogs and cats, but increased dosages are
required beyond label recommendations (Table 115.7). Some
authors have reported eﬃcacy in dogs at 7.5 mg/kg, PO, either
singly or for 2 consecutive days. 11 , 188 However, both the authors
of this chapter and others have observed infections in dogs that
have not been eliminated by these dosage regimens. A single dose
of 35 mg/kg eliminated D. latum from infected cats 189 and has
eliminated infections in dogs (Andrew Peregrine, unpublished
observations).

Prevention
Diphyllobothrium latum infections in dogs and cats are acquired by
ingestion of raw or undercooked ﬁsh. However, freezing ﬁsh for
over 48 hours at −18°C, or cooking ﬁsh (core temperature ≥ 50°C)
for ≥ 5 minutes, will eliminate infection risk. 178 Preventing
animals from roaming freely or scavenging dead ﬁsh will also
prevent infection. 190

Public Health Aspects
Diphyllobothrium latum infection is an important ﬁsh-borne
zoonosis, 172 but dogs and cats infected with D. latum are not a
direct risk to humans. Worldwide, approximately 20 million
people are infected with Diphyllobothrium spp., of which D. latum
and D. nihonkaiense are the most common. 172 , 178 As with dogs
and cats, human infections are acquired by ingestion of raw or
undercooked ﬁsh that contains plerocercoids. Smoking or
marinating ﬁsh typically does not kill the plerocercoid. 191

vetexamprep.ir

Increased consumption of carpaccio, ceviche, sushi, sashimi, and
other dishes made from raw ﬁsh has been associated with
increased risk of D. latum infection in people. 172 , 184 Intestinal
infections in people are typically clinically silent. However, some
individuals experience poorly deﬁned symptoms that may
include mild abdominal discomfort, nausea, diarrhea,
constipation, and weakness. Occasionally, heavy, prolonged D.
latum infections may result in a megaloblastic anemia due to
absorption of vitamin B12 by tapeworms. 192 Infections are readily
eliminated by treatment with praziquantel or niclosamide. 178

Spirometra spp. Infection
Etiology and Epidemiology
Spirometra spp. are diphyllobothridean tapeworms and infect wild
and domestic carnivores, including cats and occasionally dogs.
The most important species appear to be Spirometra
erinaceieuropaei/Spirometra erinacei (Asia, Australia, Europe),
Spirometra mansonoides (North and South America), and Spirometra
mansoni (Asia). Adult parasites are found in the small intestine of
cats, dogs, and wild carnivores. 193 In the USA, infection is most
common in cats in the Gulf Coast and southeastern states, with
additional reports from Hawaii, New Jersey, New York, and
Pennsylvania. 194 In stray cat populations from Syracuse, New
York and New Jersey, the prevalence was 3% and 1%,
respectively. 13 , 195 Spirometra sp. was detected in 7.9% of shelter
cats in Florida. 196 Typically, higher prevalences have been
detected in the Gulf Coast states of southeastern United States
(e.g., Florida) where aquatic ecosystems support the life cycle of
Spirometra spp. In a necropsy study in Brazil, 4.1% of cats were
infected with S. mansonoides. 4 In northern Portugal, 0.3% of dogs
living on farms were positive for Spirometra sp. using fecal
ﬂotation and sedimentation. 197 In Iran, Spirometra spp. were
found in 7.4% of dogs and 33.3% of cats at necropsy. 198 In Japan,
1.7% of owned cats were infected with S. erinacei as determined
using fecal sedimentation. 199 In China, 40.5% of cats and 27.5% of
dogs from 23 villages had eggs of S. mansoni detected in feces
using the Kato-Ka technique. 200 In Malaysia, 9.2% of stray cats

vetexamprep.ir

and 3.5% of stray dogs were positive for Spirometra sp. by fecal
sedimentation. 201 In Thailand, 4.0% of cats and 0.6% of dogs from
an animal refuge were infected with S. mansoni by fecal
sedimentation. 202

FIG. 115.19

Life cycle of Spirometra sp.

Like Diphyllobothrium spp., Spirometra spp. diﬀer from the more
common cyclophyllidean tapeworms in several aspects of their
life cycle (Fig. 115.19). Firstly, they shed individual eggs into the
intestinal tract through a mid-ventral uterine pore of individual
segments, rather than detach an egg-laden segment from the
strobila. Secondly, the egg is operculated, hatches once it reaches
water, and releases a ciliated coracidium that is free-swimming.
The coracidium is then ingested by the ﬁrst intermediate host, a

vetexamprep.ir

copepod (e.g., Cyclops spp.) and matures into a procercoid.
Thereafter, infected copepods are consumed accidentally by the
second intermediate host (i.e., amphibians, reptiles, birds,
rodents) while drinking water. In the second intermediate host,
the procercoid develops into a plerocercoid, also referred to as a
spargana, in the muscle or connective tissue. The plerocercoid
stage is highly paratenic, meaning it can remain in this stage
through a series of paratenic hosts. For example, if a tadpole is
infected with plerocercoids and is consumed by a water snake, the
plerocercoids will migrate through the snake’s tissues but remain
as plerocercoids in this new paratenic host. The parasite will
survive this way until an infected paratenic host is ultimately
consumed by a carnivore deﬁnitive host (e.g., cat or dog). This
increases the odds that Spirometra spp. cestodes ﬁnd their way
into a deﬁnitive host. When an infected second intermediate host,
or paratenic host, is consumed by a deﬁnitive host, the
plerocercoid a aches to the small intestine wall and develops into
an adult tapeworm. The prepatent period is 10 to 60 days in dogs
and cats. Furthermore, infection can persist up to 3.5 years in cats.
194 , 195 , 203 The duration of infection in dogs is unclear.
When plerocercoids are ingested by accidental hosts (e.g.,
rodents, pigs, humans), they may penetrate the intestinal wall and
invade serous cavities, connective tissue, or internal organs
(proliferative sparganosis). Such infections occasionally also occur
in dogs, cats, and other deﬁnitive hosts. 195 , 204–206

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Infection with adult Spirometra spp. appears to be well tolerated
by cats and dogs; however, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss
have been reported. 13 , 195 The mechanism underlying disease has
not been fully elucidated. Selective uptake of vitamin B12 by the
adult and plerocercoid stage has been demonstrated, 207 but the
signiﬁcance of this phenomenon in cats and dogs is unknown.
Clinical signs usually resolve quickly following treatment.
In sparganosis, spargana proliferate in abdominal and thoracic
cavities, aﬀecting the stomach, lungs, liver, and spleen, as well as
in subcutaneous tissues. This is associated with chronic

vetexamprep.ir

inﬂammation and ﬁbrosis. Proliferative sparganosis is rare, but
has been reported in dogs from Australia, 205 and cats and dogs
from the USA. 204 , 206 Probable exposure routes include ingestion
of copepods infected with procercoids in contaminated drinking
water, and ingestion of plerocercoids in second intermediate or
paratenic hosts. 3 Clinical signs vary depending on the tissue
involved and disease can range from mild to severe. In
Gainesville, Florida, USA, a 6-year-old cat was evaluated for
abdominal pain; physical examination revealed a palpable
abdominal mass. Proliferative sparganosis was diagnosed at
necropsy; the liver and spleen and wall of the cat’s stomach
contained numerous spargana. 204 Two cats from southern
Georgia were described that had subcutaneous cystlike masses. 208
In Tampa, Florida, a 21-month-old border collie was evaluated for
progressive right thoracic limb lameness and subcutaneous
edema. The subcutaneous tissue and intermuscular fascia
contained multiple cavities ﬁlled with spargana. Septic pleuritis
and peritonitis were detected later in the course of the disease. At
necropsy, multiple spargana were found in the pleural and
peritoneal cavities. 206 In Australia, ﬁve dogs have been reported
with sparganosis; spargana were detected free in the abdominal
cavity, in association with chronic ﬁbrinous peritonitis or
inﬂammation of the serosal surface of the GI tract or liver. Signs in
three dogs included a palpable abdominal mass (n = 1) and
abdominal distension (n = 2); in the remaining two dogs,
sparganosis was an incidental ﬁnding at surgery (n = 2). 205
Another dog from southeastern Australia was evaluated for
pneumothorax secondary to pulmonary involvement; exploratory
thoracotomy revealed numerous white nodules throughout the
pleura and pulmonary parenchyma (Fig. 115.20). 209

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities and Diagnostic Imaging
In animals with proliferative sparganosis, laboratory
abnormalities and diagnostic imaging ﬁndings depend on the
location of aﬀected tissues. For example, pneumothorax was
evident in one dog on plain thoracic radiographs, together with

vetexamprep.ir

irregular soft-tissue opacities in the region of the distal eighth and
ninth ribs (Fig. 115.20A).
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
Short (usually < 5 cm) chains of mature segments may be
recovered from feces or vomit. Occasionally, longer chains are
recovered (Fig. 115.21A and B). These segments can be identiﬁed
as diphyllobothridean tapeworms by the presence of a medial
uterine pore and operculated eggs within segments. 3 , 194
Eggs can be recovered by ﬂotation. However, lower SpG
ﬂotation solutions may be inadequate to ﬂoat the heavy eggs; the
diagnostic sensitivity of ﬂotation methods using ZnSO4 (speciﬁc
gravity 1.18) or NaNO3 (speciﬁc gravity 1.18) is signiﬁcantly less
than sucrose (speciﬁc gravity 1.27) for recovery of Spirometra spp.
eggs. 194 , 210 Fecal sedimentation can also be used to recover
Spirometra spp. eggs. 20 Spirometra spp. eggs are yellow-brown
and 60 to 75 µm × 35 to 37 µm, have an operculum at one end, and
are narrowed at both ends (Fig. 115.21C). They may be mistaken
for the similar, but more rounded, eggs of Diphyllobothrium spp. 3 ,
20 Geographic location can suggest the species involved. In the
Americas, while D. latum is most common in the Great Lakes
region of North America, S. mansonoides is most common in the
southeastern USA and parts of South America. 17 , 194 Eggs of
Spirometra spp. can also be mistaken for trematode eggs. Both
Spirometra spp. and Paragonimus spp. produce eggs that are
unembryonated when shed, but Spirometra spp. eggs are smaller
than those of Paragonimus kellico i (lung ﬂuke; North America;
eggs 75–118 µm × 42–67 µm) and other Paragonimus species
around the world (e.g., Paragonimus westermani, the Japanese lung
ﬂuke, and Paragonimus heterotremus in Asia). The liver ﬂuke of cats
(Platynosomum concinnum), found in the southeastern USA and the
Caribbean, produces smaller operculated eggs that contain a
miracidium (see Chapter 118). 11 , 20 , 194
Recovery of plerocercoids from tissue is necessary for diagnosis
of sparganosis. Additionally, molecular identiﬁcation can be
performed by isolating DNA from segments of the tapeworm.
PCR assays have been utilized to identify S. erinacei 209 , 211 and S.

vetexamprep.ir

mansonoides. 212 In dogs, inﬂammatory tissue cysts may be ﬁlled
with both intact and degenerate white spargana surrounded by
red, cloudy, thick ﬂuid. 206 Microscopic ﬁndings include large
numbers of spargana surrounded by large numbers of
pyogranulomatous inﬂammatory cells in variably sized cystic
spaces and reactive ﬁbrocollagenous stroma. Larval parenchyma
is strongly PAS positive. 208 The absence of scolices and suckers
helps diﬀerentiate plerocercoid larvae from those of
cyclophyllidean tapeworms (Mesocestoides, Echinococcus spp.).

Treatment and Prognosis
There is no approved treatment for infection with Spirometra spp.
in dogs or cats. Treating animals infected with adult parasites
requires higher dosages of praziquantel than is required for Taenia
spp. or D. caninum; a protocol of 25 mg/kg of praziquantel (PO or
SC) for 2 consecutive days is eﬀective (Table 115.8). 194 Treatment
of proliferative sparganosis in dogs utilizing combination therapy
with praziquantel (50 mg/kg SC once a week for 3 weeks) and
fenbendazole (100 mg/kg PO q12h for 28 days), along with
abdominal lavage to remove as many plerocercoids as possible,
may be a empted, but prognosis is guarded. 206 There is also a
report of a dog surviving proliferative sparganosis utilizing a
protocol of alternating 3-week courses of mebendazole (20 mg/kg
PO q24h for 21 days) and praziquantel (5 mg/kg PO q24h for 21
days) for 3 months. 205 The eﬀect of substituting other
benzimidazoles for mebendazole is unknown. 3

Prevention
While reinfection in endemic areas is likely, the only preventive
measure is to limit access to intermediate host species. 194
Therefore limiting a dog’s or cat’s access to amphibians, birds,
reptiles, and small mammals that are potential intermediate hosts
should aid in preventing Spirometra spp. infections.

Public Health Aspects
Sparganosis of humans is caused by the plerocercoid stage of
various tapeworms within the Spirometra genus. Humans can be
infected by several routes including drinking water containing
copepods infected with procercoids, ingesting the ﬂesh of second
intermediate hosts infected with plerocercoids (e.g., snakes, frogs),
and via direct migration into a wound or across a mucous
membrane from infected ﬂesh (e.g., applying the incised body of a
freshly caught frog to an open wound or injured eye as a
traditional poultice). 11 , 203 , 213 Human sparganosis is a foodborne disease, therefore the risk of a human developing
sparganosis directly from an infected dog or cat is minimal.
Epidemiological data suggest that the most common cause of
human sparganosis is consumption of raw freshwater frogs or
snakes. 203 Human sparganosis most often presents as
subcutaneous nodules containing a plerocercoid; scrotal and
breast nodules are also described, and surgical removal is
indicated. 214 , 215 Occasionally, the plerocercoid develops in the
lungs, peritoneal cavity, eyes, or CNS. Cerebral sparganosis is of
particular concern as it may be associated with neurological signs
and even death. 194 Such infections have primarily been described
in eastern and southeastern Asia.

Case Example
Signalment

“Zoe,” a 5-year-old female, spayed, shar-pei/beagle mix that
lived in southern Ontario, Canada.

History

Zoe was evaluated at a Veterinary Emergency and Referral
Hospital in southern Ontario with a history of urinary
incontinence for the previous 18 months. She was able to
urinate and postured normally during micturition. There was
no history of polyuria, polydipsia, or stranguria. Bloodwork
and urinalysis performed 12 months earlier by the referring
veterinarian were unremarkable, but at this visit a CBC
revealed non-regenerative anemia (HCT 34% [RR, 38–57%],
MCHC 32.1 [RR: 32.6-39.2 g/L]). On urinalysis, SpG was 1.026;
some calcium oxalate crystals were noted. The urine
protein:creatinine ratio was unremarkable and aerobic bacterial
urine culture was negative. An abdominal ultrasound
examination revealed no abnormalities of the urinary tract.
However, a poorly deﬁned, 5 × 3 cm mass was detected within
the left liver lobe adjacent to the diaphragm. Due to the location
of the lesion, ﬁne-needle aspirates were not possible. Thoracic

vetexamprep.ir

radiographs were unremarkable. An abdominal CT scan
revealed a 4.5-cm diameter, rounded mass lesion in the left
cranioventral and lateral aspect of the hepatic parenchyma in
close proximity to the diaphragm. The mass was suspected to
involve the left medial and left lateral lobes (see Fig. 115.9).
After contrast administration, small septations were evident in
the lesion creating a subtle honeycomb appearance. The
periportal, gastric, splenic, and pancreaticoduodenal lymph
nodes were mildly enlarged. No other abnormalities were
detected.
Zoe was started on phenylpropanolamine for suspected
sphincter mechanism incontinence. However, the incontinence
appeared to worsen. The phenylpropanolamine dose was
increased, but without improvement. Zoe had a history of
aggression and was known to bite dogs and people. As a result,
limited physical examinations had been performed; sedation
was required for any procedure. Two months after being seen at
the referral hospital, Zoe was evaluated at Ontario Veterinary
College. At that time the owner reported she had been eating
and drinking normally; no vomiting or diarrhea had been
noted. She was still incontinent despite daily treatment with
phenylpropanolamine.

Physical Examination Findings

The dog was bright, alert, and responsive. Body weight was
19.8 kg. After sedation (15 µg/kg dexmedetomidine IM and 0.4
mg/kg butorphanol IM), pulse was 48/minute, respiration rate
was 28/minute, temperature was 99.3°F (37.4°C). No heart
murmurs, arrhythmias, or abnormal breath sounds were
auscultated. No masses or organomegaly were detected on
abdominal palpation. No abnormalities of the genitourinary
tract were detected. All other parameters were unremarkable.

Laboratory Findings

A PCV and total protein by refractometry were unremarkable.

Imaging Findings

Abdominal ultrasound examination revealed an 8 × 8 × 6 cm
mass in the left liver, close to the diaphragm, with echogenic
material in the center.
The initial diﬀerential diagnosis for the hepatic mass was
hepatic neoplasia (hepatocellular carcinoma, adenoma,

vetexamprep.ir

hemangiosarcoma, lymphoma, other) or a benign liver mass
(nodular regeneration, granuloma, hematoma). In order to
obtain a biopsy specimen, exploratory laparotomy was
performed. A 7 × 6 × 4 cm mass was identiﬁed within the left
medial liver lobe that was white/brown and slightly nodular
(see Fig. 115.11A). The aﬀected lobe was removed using a
thoracoabdominal stapler; two circumferential ligatures were
placed on remaining hilar vessels. The remainder of the liver
and other abdominal organs were grossly unremarkable.

Pathologic Findings

On cut section, the resected mass was soft, white, and irregular,
and contained multiple small (1 to 5 mm) cavities. On
histopathology, eﬀacing and replacing 80% to 90% of the
hepatic parenchyma was a well-demarcated, partially
encapsulated, expansile nodule composed of coalescing cystic
spaces. These spaces were surrounded by abundant, variably
mature, ﬁbrovascular tissue and mixed inﬂammatory cells.
Cystic spaces were lined by a variably folded eosinophilic,
homogeneous, laminated (hyaline) membrane and an inner,
variably intact, germinal epithelial layer. Cysts contained
eosinophilic necrotic debris and mixed inﬂammatory cells. Rare
small calcareous corpuscles were observed. However, no
protoscolices were seen in the sections (see Fig. 115.11B). The
same tissue sections stained positive with PAS stain.

Microbiologic Testing

Fresh frozen liver tissue was submi ed for PCR testing. A
PCR product was generated using primers speciﬁc for E.
multilocularis. 109 The sequence generated was 100%
identical (344/344 bp) to reference sequence of E.
multilocularis.
DiagnosisHepatic alveolar echinococcosis (AE).
TreatmentZoe was treated with praziquantel (5 mg/kg
PO), to eliminate a potential intestinal infection. When the
results of nucleic acid testing became available, treatment
with albendazole (10 mg/kg PO q24h) for life was
commenced.

Comments

vetexamprep.ir

Because this mass was located at the liver hilus, it was possible
that a small amount of aﬀected liver tissue remained after
surgery. Treatment with albendazole was therefore particularly
important. Since albendazole can occasionally cause bone
marrow suppression in dogs, a CBC was recommended every
week for the ﬁrst month, monthly for the ﬁrst 3 months, then
every 3 months thereafter. A repeat abdominal ultrasound/CT
scan was recommended every 6 to 12 months to monitor for
recurrent disease. The diagnosis of AE in this case was an
incidental ﬁnding and not likely associated with the urinary
incontinence, which remained unresolved.
