116: Miscellaneous Nematode
Infections
Jennifer K. Ke is, Susan E. Li le, and Judit M. Wulcan

KEY POINTS
Physaloptera spp. Infection
• First Described: Physaloptera praeputialis was first isolated
from a domestic cat and described in 1889 (von Linstow).
Physaloptera rara was first isolated from a domestic dog in
North America and described in 1918 (Hall and Wigdor).
• Cause: Physaloptera praeputialis and Physaloptera rara.
• Affected Hosts: Domestic and wild dogs and cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide (P. praeputialis), North
America (P. rara).
• Route of Transmission: Ingestion of intermediate insect or
paratenic hosts.
• Major Clinical Signs: May cause chronic intermittent vomiting.
Infections often are subclinical.
• Differential Diagnosis: Any GI or systemic cause of chronic
vomiting (e.g., idiopathic gastritis, gastric foreign body, gastric
neoplasia, food intolerance/allergy, chronic pancreatitis). Eggs
must be differentiated from those of Spirocerca lupi. Vomited
nematodes must be differentiated from Toxocara canis,
Toxocara cati, and Toxascaris leonina.
• Human Health Significance: Physaloptera spp. of dogs and
cats are not considered a zoonosis.
Spirocerca lupi Infection
• First Described: Karl Asmund Rudolphi (Swedish
parasitologist and “father” of helminthology), 1809.

vetexamprep.ir

• Cause: Spirocerca lupi (esophageal worm), superfamily
Spiruroidea, order Spirurida.
• Affected Hosts: Domestic dogs, wild canids, and other
carnivores; rarely cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide but primarily in tropical
and subtropical regions with the highest prevalence in the
southern United States, Brazil, the Caribbean, South Africa,
and the Middle East.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs become infected after ingestion
of the intermediate host (coprophagous beetles in the family
Scarabaeidae, order Coleoptera) or paratenic hosts (e.g.,
birds, frogs, lizards and other reptiles, rodents) containing a
third-stage larva.
• Major Clinical Signs: Vomiting or regurgitation, odynophagia,
ptyalism, respiratory difficulty, cough, weight loss, and fever.
• Differential Diagnoses: Differentials for regurgitation include
esophageal foreign bodies, esophageal strictures, esophageal
neoplasia or granulomas of other origin, and megaesophagus.
Differentials for vomiting include any GI or systemic cause of
chronic vomiting (e.g., idiopathic gastritis, gastric foreign body,
gastric neoplasia, food intolerance/allergy, chronic
pancreatitis). Eggs must be differentiated from Physaloptera
spp.
• Human Health Significance: Spirocerca lupi infection is not
considered a zoonosis.
Strongyloides spp. Infection
• First Described: Larval stages of Strongyloides stercoralis
were first isolated from human feces in 1876; the first
identification of natural infection in a dog was in 1914. In cats,
Strongyloides planiceps was isolated by Leiper from a rusty
tiger cat (Felis planiceps) in 1927. Strongyloides felis was first
isolated from cats in India in 1925. While Strongyloides
tumefaciens was first noted in cats in the USA in 1929, it was
not described or named until 1941.
• Cause: Strongyloides are commonly referred to as
threadworms and belong to the family Strongyloididae in the
order Rhabditida.

vetexamprep.ir

• Affected Hosts: Strongyloides stercoralis occurs in dogs, cats,
non-human primates, and people. Strongyloides felis and S.
tumefaciens have been described in domestic and wild cats;
S. planiceps in domestic and wild cats, dogs, and wild
carnivores.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Route of Transmission: Oral, percutaneous, and, less
frequently, transmammary infections occur in dogs. Oral and
percutaneous transmission occur in cats.
• Major Clinical Signs: Subclinical infections are common.
Cough and other signs of bronchial involvement can occur in
the early stage of infection in dogs. Severe enteritis with
profuse diarrhea can occur in the later stage of infection. Skin
papules are sometimes seen when larvae enter the dog
percutaneously. In cats, clinical signs are rare, but diarrhea
has been reported in some infections.
• Differential Diagnoses: The clinical signs are nonspecific and
must be differentiated from other causes of diarrhea, for
example, dietary, infectious, inflammatory, toxic, or
extraintestinal causes of diarrhea. In puppies, S. stercoralis
must be differentiated from other parasites that have larval
lung migration stages (e.g., Toxocara canis, Ancylostoma
caninum), cause diarrhea, and are able to enter the animal
percutaneously (e.g., Ancylostoma caninum, Uncinaria
stenocephala). In cats and dogs, recovered larvae must be
distinguished from lungworm; hookworm larvae.
• Human Health Significance: Strongyloides stercoralis can be
transmitted from dogs to people and from people to dogs.
Zoonotic transmission of cat Strongyloides has not been
studied; there have been no reports of Strongyloides being
transmitted from cats to people.
Mammomonogamus spp. Infection
• First Described: Mammomonogamus ierei (synonym
Syngamus ierei) was first described by Buckley in 1934, who
isolated it from a domestic cat in Trinidad.
Mammomonogamus auris (synonym Syngamus auris) was
first described by Faust and Tank in 1934, who isolated it from
the middle ear of several cats in China.

vetexamprep.ir

• Cause: Mammomonogamus ierei and Mammomonogamus
auris, which occur in cats, are commonly referred to as
gapeworms. These nematodes belong to the family
Syngamidae.
• Affected Hosts: Mammomonogamus ierei and M. auris infect
domestic cats.
• Geographic Distribution: The distribution of
Mammomonogamus is disparate, with M. ierei reported in the
Caribbean and M. auris found in Asia.
• Route of Transmission: Unknown. Given the life cycle of other
parasites in this family, it is likely that paratenic hosts are
involved.
• Major Clinical Signs: Subclinical infections are common.
However, infections can be associated with inflammation of
the nasopharynx resulting in a mucoid nasal discharge,
coughing, sneezing episodes, and weight loss with M. ierei.
Head shaking has been seen in a cat with M. auris infection.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other infections that cause nasal
discharge and sneezing (e.g., viral infections, Eucoleus
aerophilus, Cuterebra spp.). In the case of M. auris,
Otodectes cynotis also can result in head shaking. The dark
cerumen associated with O. cynotis infection does not occur
with M. auris infection. Eggs of M. ierei and M. auris can be
seen in a fecal flotation.
• Human Health Significance: There are no reports of M. ierei
and M. auris infecting humans and neither are believed to be
zoonotic.
Dioctophyme renale Infection
• First Described: Dioctophyme renale was first described by
the German zoologist Johann Goeze in 1782; earlier reports
of giant kidney worms date back to the late 1500s.
• Cause: Dioctophyme renale, the giant kidney worm, is the
largest parasitic nematode of domestic animals (family
Dioctophymidae in the order Ascaridida).
• Affected Hosts: Most cases of D. renale in domestic animals
are reported in dogs, with infections occasionally seen in cats
and other host species, including humans. Fish-eating

vetexamprep.ir

vertebrates, especially mink and other mustelids, are the
natural definitive host.
• Geographic Distribution: Dioctophyme renale has a sporadic,
worldwide distribution although reports of infection are rare in
Africa and Asia. The parasite is widespread in the Americas
and has been reported from dogs and other hosts from
Canada to Brazil.
• Route of Transmission: Eggs are shed in the urine of infected
definitive hosts. First-stage larvae develop inside the eggs
and hatch following ingestion by aquatic oligochaete annelid
intermediate hosts found in the detritus of ponds and streams.
Third-stage larvae develop within the tissues of the annelids
and may be passed to paratenic hosts, such as fish and frogs,
when they ingest the intermediate hosts. Dogs and other final
hosts are infected upon ingestion of annelids, or, more
commonly, by ingesting third-stage larvae in fish paratenic
hosts.
• Major Clinical Signs: Most infections are subclinical. Some
dogs have hematuria, renal pain, renal enlargement,
abdominal pain, and abdominal effusion. Development of
worms in subcutaneous fat has also been reported.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other causes of cystitis; renal
neoplasia; or a retroperitoneal, abdominal, or subcutaneous
mass. Abdominal D. renale infection in cats can resemble FIP.
Eggs of D. renale are not always present in urine sediment
and thus diagnosis may sometimes be made by ultrasound or
exploratory laparotomy.
• Human Health Significance: Although rare, zoonotic infections
with D. renale have been reported and are associated with
ingestion of larvae in undercooked fish or frogs.
Dracunculus insignis Infection
• First Described: Dracunculus spp. have been described since
antiquity. Dracunculus medinensis was described by Linnaeus
in 1758, and Dracunculus insignis by Leidy in 1858.
• Cause: Dracunculus insignis, a subcutaneous worm of
raccoons and other carnivores that also infects dogs, is a
spirurid nematode closely related to the human Guinea worm,
Dracunculus medinensis.

vetexamprep.ir

• Affected Hosts: Most cases of D. insignis infection in domestic
animals are reported in dogs, although ferrets are also
susceptible; a limited number of cases have been described in
cats. Wild carnivores, especially raccoons, are most
commonly infected and considered the natural definitive host
of this parasite in North America. Although primarily a human
parasite, D. medinensis also readily infects dogs in endemic
areas.
• Geographic Distribution: Dracunculus insignis has only been
reported from Canada and the United States. Due to
concerted eradication efforts, D. medinensis is currently
limited to three countries in Africa. Other Dracunculus spp.
have been reported from mammals, snakes, and turtles in the
Western Hemisphere and from snakes in Europe, Africa, Asia,
and Australia.
• Route of Transmission: Gravid female Dracunculus spp.
migrate to the extremities of the definitive host and form
subcutaneous cysts. The presence of the nematode induces
the formation of blisters; when immersed in water, the uterus
of the nematode ruptures, releasing hundreds of thousands of
larvae into the water. The motile larvae are ingested by
copepod intermediate hosts. After third-stage larvae develop,
copepods are ingested by definitive hosts drinking water; the
nematodes then migrate to subcutaneous locations, mature,
mate, and eventually form new cysts to continue the life cycle.
Alternatively, infected copepods may be ingested by aquatic
vertebrates which can then serve as paratenic hosts.
• Major Clinical Signs: Dogs with D. insignis present with
fluctuant subcutaneous swellings, usually on a distal extremity
or, less commonly, the thorax. Lesions are often pruritic and
painful. The skin may appear ulcerated or bear a patent
opening; when the affected limb is immersed in water, an
adult nematode may emerge.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other, more common causes of
subcutaneous masses include lipoma, reactive lymph nodes,
neoplasia, or other dermal parasites (e.g., Cuterebra,
Dirofilaria repens). However, the distinct location on a distal
extremity and, when present, the appearance of a patent ulcer
through which a nematode emerges, considerably narrows

vetexamprep.ir

potential diagnoses. Specimen collection using fine-needle
aspiration often leads to recovery of D. insignis larvae. Long
female nematodes may be encountered during surgical
exploration of the cystic lesion.
• Human Health Significance: Human infection is most
commonly by D. medinensis. Recent reports of D. medinensis
in domestic dogs have created challenges in the final stages
of eradication efforts for the human Guinea worm.
Ocular Nematodes
• First Described: Onchocerca lupi was first described in a feral
wolf in Russia. Thelazia callipaeda was first described by
Ralliet and Henry in 1910 and Thelazia californiensis by Price
in 1930.
• Cause: Onchocerca lupi and Thelazia spp. Aberrant migration
has also resulted in other species of nematodes reported from
the eye, including Dirofilaria spp., Dracunculus spp., and
Toxocara spp.
• Affected Hosts: Onchocerca lupi is primarily a parasite of
domestic dogs although feline onchocerciasis has been
reported. Thelazia callipaeda and T. californiensis are
described from dogs and cats with occasional reports from
wildlife definitive hosts. Other Thelazia spp. infect the eyes of
large animals.
• Geographic Distribution: Ocular nematodes occur sporadically
around the world, with O. lupi reported from northern Asia,
southern and central Europe, and the southwestern United
States; T. callipaeda from Asia and, more recently, Europe;
and T. californiensis from western North America.
• Route of Transmission: The life cycle of O. lupi is not fully
understood, but other Onchocerca spp. are transmitted
between definitive hosts by arthropod intermediate hosts,
including black flies (Simulium spp.) and biting midges
(Culicoides spp.). Thelazia spp. are transmitted by muscid
flies feeding around the eyes.
• Major Clinical Signs: Ocular lesions due to O. lupi and
Thelazia spp. may be mild to severe although many animals
appear largely subclinical. In the acute phase of O. lupi
infection, general ocular discomfort is seen with excessive
lacrimation and photophobia. In chronic infections, nodules

vetexamprep.ir

develop on the sclera, conjunctiva, and eyelids. Infection with
Thelazia spp. may be associated with chronic conjunctivitis
but nodules are not present.
• Differential Diagnoses: Many infectious, inflammatory, and
traumatic conditions can cause ocular irritation and
conjunctivitis. However, once nematodes are visualized coiled
in inflammatory tissue on the conjunctiva (O. lupi) or free
under the eyelids or nictitating membrane (Thelazia spp.), the
diagnostic list of differentials is short. Other nematodes that
occasionally migrate aberrantly to the eyes include
Angiostrongylus vasorum, Dirofilaria spp., Dracunculs
insignis, Toxocara spp., and Trichinella spiralis (eyelid).
• Human Health Significance: Human infection with both O. lupi
and Thelazia spp. occasionally occurs resulting in ocular
irritation, excessive lacrimation, and the presence of
intraocular nematodes.

Introduction
This chapter reviews clinically relevant aspects of several
nematode parasites of dogs and cats that are occasionally
encountered in veterinary practice. Some aﬀect the GI system,
including Physaloptera, a stomach worm associated with chronic
vomiting, and Strongyloides stercoralis. Strongyloides stercoralis is a
nematode that alternates between a free-living and parasitic
lifestyle and that, when parasitizing the small intestine, can
induce severe diarrhea, particularly in puppies. Other nematodes
in this chapter may cause esophageal (Spirocerca lupi), otic or
nasopharyngeal (Mammomonogamus spp.), dermal (Dracunculus
insignis), renal (Dioctophyme renale), or ocular (Onchocerca lupi,
Thelazia spp.) pathology.

Physaloptera spp. Infection
Etiology and Epidemiology
Physaloptera is a genus of spirurid nematodes belonging to the
family Physalopteridae in the order Spirurida. Numerous species
have been reported in a variety of vertebrate hosts worldwide, but

vetexamprep.ir

only two species, Physaloptera praeputialis and Physaloptera rara, are
regularly reported in dogs and cats. Physaloptera praeputialis, ﬁrst
described in 1889 (von Linstow), occurs worldwide and is
considered primarily a parasite of cats, although it infects a
variety of other mammals including domestic dogs, foxes, and
wild felids. 1–5 Physaloptera rara, ﬁrst described in 1918 (Hall and
Wigdor), occurs in North America and is considered primarily a
parasite of coyotes but also is found in domestic dogs and cats,
raccoons, and other wild animals. 1 , 2 , 6–8
Adult nematodes are between 2 and 6 cm long, white or pink,
and have a cephalic collar and triangular, toothed pseudolabia.
The males are slightly shorter than the females and have
pedunculated caudal papillae and alae, joined anterior to the anus
(Fig. 116.1). 3 , 6 , 9 Physaloptera praeputialis can be diﬀerentiated
from P. rara by a cuticular sheath that covers the posterior end. 2
The eggs of the two species are indistinguishable and are small (49
to 59 µm x 30 to 34 µm), oval, thick-shelled, and contain fully
formed larvae in fresh feces (Fig. 116.2). 2 , 10 , 11
The life cycle of Physaloptera spp. includes intermediate insect
hosts from the orders Coleoptera, Orthoptera, and Bla odea
(beetles, crickets, and roaches) and paratenic hosts (snakes,
lizards, frogs, hedgehogs). The complete diversity of insect and
paratenic hosts is unknown. Cats and dogs become infected via
the consumption of intermediate or paratenic hosts or feces from
these hosts containing third-stage larvae (L3). Adult Physaloptera
spp. and larvae reside mainly in the stomach with some also
found in the cranial duodenum, usually with their anterior end
a ached to the mucosa. 9 , 12 Larvae are not known to migrate. The
prepatent period ranges from as few as 35 days to 156 days, with
most infections requiring at least 60 days to reach patency. This
wide variation in the prepatent period is potentially due to the
source of infection (intermediate or paratenic host). 2 , 3 , 6 , 12 In
cats and dogs, most infections consist of only a few adult worms
(1 to 8), although much higher numbers have been found in feral
cats (25 to 30). 13 , 14

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 116.2

Physaloptera spp. occur worldwide with most reports of
infections in cats and dogs from North and South America,
Australia, and Asia. There have only been a few reports of
Physaloptera spp. in Europe and Africa in domestic dogs and cats.
2 , 15 In domestic dogs and cats, prevalence is typically below 5%
with most studies in dogs showing a prevalence of <2% and cats
with the higher prevalence. 10 , 15–24 This contrasts with some
older studies from the 1940s to the mid-1980s where prevalence in
cats was found to be from 20% to 40% and diﬀers from wildlife
species where it can be over 50%. 6 , 25 , 5 , 26 , 27
Given the issues with diagnosis using many common fecal
ﬂotation solutions with lower speciﬁc gravity (e.g., <1.3), the
prevalence of Physaloptera spp. in domestic dogs and cats could be
underestimated. At the same time, prevalence could be decreasing
with more widespread use of regular monthly heartworm

vetexamprep.ir

preventives. Conversely, the high prevalence in wildlife species
could potentially pose a concern where these animals frequent
urban areas, which could increase exposure of domestic dogs and
cats.

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Physaloptera spp. a ach to the gastric or duodenal mucosa and
feed on blood and tissue. Adult and immature Physaloptera can
induce a catarrhal gastritis which may manifest as chronic,
intermi ent vomiting. Diarrhea, anorexia, and weight loss also
can occur, although many infections are subclinical. 13 , 18 , 28
Diﬀerentials for Physaloptera spp. are broad and can include any
GI or systemic cause of chronic vomiting (e.g., idiopathic gastritis,
gastric foreign body, gastric neoplasia, food intolerance/allergy,
chronic pancreatitis). 29

Diagnosis
Physaloptera eggs are particularly heavy compared to other
common nematode eggs and occur intermi ently in feces; overall
egg numbers can be low when infections are of low intensity. 30 In
addition, clinical signs can be induced by larval stages before eggs
are present in the feces. Therefore fecal diagnosis is insensitive.
When eggs are present, ﬂotation methods with solutions of
speciﬁc gravity >1.3 can be used; however, many standard
ﬂotation solutions are <1.3 SpG. 31 , 32 Direct smear can overcome
the heavy egg issue but also lacks sensitivity due to the limited
quantity of feces examined. 18 , 31–33 When eggs are seen, they
must be diﬀerentiated from those of Spirocerca lupi.
Frequently, a diagnosis is made when dogs or cats vomit
nematodes or following gastroscopy. 13 , 28 When nematodes are
vomited, they must be diﬀerentiated from Toxocara canis, Toxocara
cati, and Toxascaris leonina. Although adult worms are readily
visible using gastroscopy, immature stages, which also induce
clinical signs, might be more challenging to see. Peripheral
eosinophilia has been reported in a minority of cases. 13 , 28

vetexamprep.ir

On gross necropsy examination the gastric wall may be normal
or thickened, with mucosal petechiae or ecchymoses.
Histologically, a diﬀuse lymphoplasmacytic gastritis is most
commonly reported, sometimes with concurrent mucosal
congestion, catarrhal gastritis, and histiocytic or eosinophilic
inﬁltrates. 13 , 14

Treatment and Prognosis
No anthelmintics are registered for the treatment of Physaloptera
spp. infections in cats and dogs. Pyrantel pamoate (20 mg/kg PO
repeated at 2 week intervals for a total of 2 to 3 administrations) is
recommended, and with this treatment, prognosis is good. 33
Treatment with lower and single doses of pyrantel pamoate has
shown limited eﬃcacy; pyrantel pamoate (5 to 20 mg/kg PO) did
not clear infections in cats. 34 , 35 In a single case report of infection
in a dog, 5 mg/kg administered twice at a 2-week interval was
eﬀective; however, in a study of 10 dogs in which adult worms
were removed via endoscopy prior to treatment, 15 mg/kg
administered twice at 2- to 3-week intervals did not result in
resolution of clinical signs in two dogs. 13 , 18 Other anthelmintics
that have been used include ivermectin (200 µg/kg SC) in two
dogs and two cats, fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO q24h for three
days) in a single dog after manual removal of worms by
endoscopy, and levamisole (8 mg/kg SC) in two cats. 13 , 28 The
dose of ivermectin used was signiﬁcantly higher than that in
heartworm preventives and should not be used in sensitive
breeds.
Endoscopic removal of adult nematodes can be eﬀective.
However, not all adult nematodes may be seen and larval stages
can remain, requiring a follow-up anthelmintic treatment. 13 , 33

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
There are no published data suggesting that dogs and cats
develop immunity to reinfection and there are no vaccines to
prevent infection. The primary means of prevention is to limit
access to intermediate and paratenic hosts. No studies on the
eﬃcacy of monthly heartworm preventives (e.g., macrocyclic
lactones) in preventing the establishment of Physaloptera spp. have

vetexamprep.ir

been performed; however, data with ivermectin suggest that
monthly heartworm preventives could limit infections. 28 , 33

Public Health Aspects
Physaloptera spp. of dogs and cats are not considered zoonotic.

Spirocerca lupi Infection (Spirocercosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Spirocerca lupi, ﬁrst described by Rudolphi in 1809, belongs to the
superfamily Spiruroidea in the order Spirurida. 36 Spirocerca lupi
infects domestic and wild canids with some other mammals such
as raccoons occasionally serving as a ﬁnal host. 37–40 Adult S. lupi
reside in nodules in the esophagus, are pink to red in color, and
range in size from 3 to 7 cm, with the males being smaller than the
females. 41–43 The eggs released by the female worms enter the
lumen of the esophagus and are passed in the feces. Eggs
recovered from fresh feces contain a ﬁrst-stage larva (L1) and are
thick-shelled, elongated with parallel sides, and range in size from
20 to 37 µm x 11 to 18 µm (Fig. 116.3). 41 , 43 , 44 Coprophagous
beetles from the family Scarabaeidae, order Coleoptera consume
the eggs whereby the larva is released, develops to the third stage,
and encysts. Dogs become infected when they ingest beetles with
third-stage larvae (L3) or by consuming paratenic hosts such as
birds, frogs, lizards and other reptiles, and rodents (Fig. 116.4). 41 ,
45–47 Once consumed, the L are released in the stomach of the dog
3
and proceed to penetrate the stomach mucosa and migrate toward
the thoracic aorta via the gastric and celiac arteries. This migration
typically requires 3 weeks. Once in the wall of the thoracic artery,
the nematode develops to an immature adult stage in
approximately 3 months, after which it migrates to the esophagus
where further development to the adult stage occurs. During
development from a larva to a mature adult, a tissue reaction
develops in the esophageal wall, resulting in the esophageal
nodule in which the adult nematode lives (Fig. 116.5). These
nodules initially consist of granulation-like tissue, which later
gradually is replaced by proliferating ﬁbroblasts. They are often

vetexamprep.ir

incorrectly referred to as granulomas. 41 , 43 , 45 The prepatent
period is 3 to 6 months. 41 , 43

Life cycle of Spirocerca lupi.

Most reports of S. lupi infection in dogs are from the southern
United States (Alabama, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Texas), South
and Central America (Brazil, Mexico), the Caribbean, the Middle
East, and South Africa with infrequent reports in Europe. 41 , 42 , 45
, 48–51 In general, occurrence in domestic dogs is <1% although in
some areas, particularly in stray dogs, it can be as high as 40%. 22 ,
25 , 52–54 The density of intermediate and paratenic hosts inﬂuences
diﬀerences in occurrence in rural and urban areas and prevalence
can be underestimated if less-sensitive diagnostic methods are
used and overestimated if based solely on stray dogs. 45 , 49 Older
dogs, working and sporting dogs, and large-breed dogs are at risk
of infection. 49 , 55

vetexamprep.ir

Spirocerca lupi adult and
esophageal nodule; adults range from 3 to 7
cm long. Courtesy of Ross University School of
FIG. 116.5

Veterinary Medicine.

Incidence has decreased in some locations and in Italy it is
referred to as an “old-fashioned” parasite due to its lack of
occurrence. 40 Reasons cited for decreasing prevalence are use of
insecticides killing the intermediate host, changes in dog diets,
and use of monthly heartworm preventives. 41 , 45 In endemic
areas where macrocyclic lactones are used as a preventive, there is
some concern that anthelmintic resistance development could
occur. While no resistance has been documented, it does require
investigation. 49
In locations where S. lupi currently is rare in domestic dogs,
there are concerns that migration of wild animal hosts,
urbanization of foxes and raccoons, and the movement of
domestic dogs could pose a risk of reintroduction or increased
occurrence. 40 , 56 , 57 In the USA, S. lupi has been identiﬁed in
foxes and coyotes in Florida, Texas, and New Mexico, all areas
where S. lupi is reported in domestic dogs. 27 , 39

Clinical Features

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Larval migration, esophageal nodules, and secondary infections
can cause clinical signs in S. lupi infections. While the clinical
signs can be severe, many infections are subclinical, with
extensive pathology occurring prior to diagnosis.
The esophageal nodules may be single or few, <1 to several cm
in diameter, and are typically located just a few centimeters
cranial to the caudal esophageal sphincter. 45 , 49 , 58–61 The
nodules may undergo malignant transformation and
approximately 20% of aﬀected dogs are diagnosed with either
esophageal ﬁbrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or undiﬀerentiated
sarcoma. 45 , 49 , 59 These tumors may metastasize to lungs and
other organs. 62 , 63 Small benign esophageal nodules can be
subclinical, whereas larger nodules can disrupt normal
swallowing, causing clinical signs such as regurgitation/vomiting,
odynophagia, and weight loss. 45 , 49 , 59–61 Respiratory signs such
as cough or dyspnea are not uncommon and may be secondary to
physical compression by esophageal nodules or complications
associated with migration or malignant transformation. 49 , 59 , 60 ,
64 Fever may be present on physical examination.
A frequent but typically subclinical concurrent ﬁnding is a
caudal thoracic spondylitis, which is seen in approximately 30% of
cases. The pathogenesis of this periosteal bone reaction is not
known, but is so rarely seen without S. lupi lesions that the
combination of a caudal esophageal mass and caudal thoracic
spondylitis by some is considered pathognomonic. 59–61
Concurrent hypertrophic osteopathy, which may present as
lameness and/or swollen, hard extremities, is sometimes seen,
including salivary gland enlargement and hypersalivation. 59 Both
conditions have been reported to resolve with resolution of the
esophageal lesion. The pathogenesis of both of these conditions is
unknown. 65–67
Clinical disease caused by aberrant or standard migration can
occur with or without concurrent esophageal lesions. Migrating
larvae can cause permanent intimal scars and aneurysms in the
thoracic aorta. In some cases, the weakened aorta may rupture,
causing sudden death. 41 , 52 , 68 , 69 In other cases, migration from
the aorta to the esophagus causes mediastinitis, pleuritis, or

vetexamprep.ir

pyothorax. 59 , 64 There also have been reports of thromboembolic
disease, likely caused by turbulent blood ﬂow through aortic
aneurysms, presenting as peracute paresis/paralysis of pelvic
limbs; and painful, cold, dysfunctional lower extremities with
absent or weak femoral pulses. 70 , 71 Aberrant migration of larvae
is not uncommon and nodules containing worms have been found
in many thoracic and abdominal organs. 60 There are several
reports of aberrant migration through the spinal cord presenting
as acute-onset paresis or paralysis of one or both pelvic limbs.
Apart from neurological deﬁcits associated with spinal lesions,
physical examination ﬁndings in these cases included pain along
the spine. 72–75

Diagnosis
A diagnosis of canine spirocercosis heavily relies on diagnostic
imaging and esophageal endoscopy. Clinical pathological ﬁndings
are variable and unspeciﬁc. Findings compatible with
inﬂammation such as inﬂammatory leukograms (typically
characterized by neutrophilia and/or monocytosis), evidence of an
acute phase reaction (e.g., increased serum CRP concentration),
and non-regenerative anemia are sometimes, but not always, seen.
45 , 76

Fecal analyses are of limited sensitivity for several reasons:
pathology from larval migration and nodule formation can occur
before egg excretion; high egg production occurs for only a short
time at the beginning of patency; and few or no eggs are shed in
single-sex infections, nodules that lack opercula, and late in
infection if neoplastic conversion has occurred. 41 , 43–45 , 77
Regardless of the fecal analysis method used, none consistently
achieves >70% sensitivity. 44 , 48 , 60 , 77 Examination of repeated
fecal specimens improves detection, but by only 8 to 28%. 60
Unlike with Physaloptera spp., use of higher speciﬁc gravity
ﬂotation solutions does not improve sensitivity and can damage
the eggs. 44 Nucleic acid–based detection methods have limited
application in fecal diagnosis but could enable diagnosis using
tissue specimens and have the potential to increase detection
during early infection. 77

vetexamprep.ir

Where infections are endemic, a tentative diagnosis can be
made on identiﬁcation of a soft-tissue mass in the caudal
esophagus. The esophageal masses in clinically aﬀected patients
can be large enough to be seen on thoracic radiographs. 45
Radiographs also can be used to detect concurrent thoracic
spondylitis, hypertrophic osteopathy, and other disease
complications. Sensitivity of radiographs for nodule detection
may be improved with administration of liquid barium sulfate in
subclinically infected dogs where screening is considered
desirable in order to prevent malignant transformation in
hyperendemic regions. 48
Esophageal endoscopy is useful for conﬁrmation or detection of
smaller lesions but requires general anesthesia and can only detect
nodules and adult nematodes that are protruding into the lumen
of the esophagus. 48 , 78 Computed tomography, in addition to
detecting small esophageal nodules, can be used to detect
extraesophageal nodules, aortic lesions, and potential metastasis
in cases of neoplastic transformation. 45
Endoscopic-guided biopsy has high speciﬁcity but low
sensitivity for diagnosis of malignant transformation; instead,
diagnosis is often made after surgical excision or on necropsy. In
sections of nodules collected at necropsy, nematodes, eggs, or
migratory tracts can be seen in most nonneoplastic nodules, but in
only a minority of neoplastic nodules. 59
The diagnosis of intraspinal S. lupi infection is extraordinarily
challenging as esophageal nodules and patent infections are not
always present. Nonspeciﬁc changes can be seen on CT or MRI.
CSF analysis regularly shows marked pleocytosis with variable
proportions of neutrophils and eosinophils; however, deﬁnitive
diagnosis usually is made by direct visualization of nematodes
during surgery or at necropsy. 72 There is one case report,
however, where nematode eggs were visualized directly in CSF. 79

Treatment and Prognosis
There are no registered anthelmintics for the treatment of S. lupi.
In dogs without neoplastic nodules, treatment with doramectin,
milbemycin oxime, and moxidectin halts egg excretion, resolves
clinical signs (if present) within weeks, and results in
disappearance of esophageal nodules in 95 to > 500 days (Table

vetexamprep.ir

116.1). These macrocyclic lactones must be used with caution in
certain dog breeds. There have been mixed reports of ivermectin
eﬃcacy (0.4 mg/kg, SC, six doses at 2-week intervals; 0.6 mg/kg,
SC, two doses at 2-week intervals). 49 , 80 Levamisole does not
appear to be eﬀective. 40 Prognosis, with treatment, is typically
good for cases without malignant transformation. 45 , 59 , 81 This
requires early detection, even in subclinically infected dogs, which
can be challenging due to the limitations of routine fecal
diagnostic methods.
Surgical treatment is required for dogs with neoplastic
transformation. Partial esophagectomies may be successful, but
median survival time after surgery is usually short (3 to 9
months), with metastatic disease reported as the most common
cause of death. 63 , 82 , 83 More recently, transendoscopic
esophageal mass ablation has been described as a method for
removing nodules. 82 , 84 , 85 Removal of nodules is often combined
with chemotherapy (doxorubicin or carboplatin as monotherapies
or combined), but neither the use nor the type of drug has been
demonstrated to increase survival time. 82 Esophageal resections
have been a empted but are typically not successful, as patients
often die within the immediate postoperative period. 63

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
There is no indication that dogs develop immunity to reinfection
and there is no vaccine available. Prevention should focus on
limiting a dog’s access to the intermediate and paratenic hosts.
Removal of vomit and feces from the environment can decrease
dung beetle access to the eggs.
Moxidectin 2.5%/imidacloprid 10% (Advocate for dogs in
Europe and Advantage Multi in the USA; previously Bayer, now
Elanco) applied monthly is approved in Europe as a preventive
for S. lupi infection. Natural exposure studies have shown a
preventive fraction of 94.7%. 86 Other macrocyclic lactones are
active against immature stages, reducing establishment of S. lupi
adults and the size of nodules. Milbemycin oxime (minimum 0.5
mg/kg, monthly for up to six treatments) decreased aortic lesions,
establishment in the thoracic aorta, and establishment of adults;
eﬃcacy for prevention of adult infections ranged from 92.3% to
100% in experimental and natural infections. 87-89 Doramectin and
ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg every 3 months) have been used as

vetexamprep.ir

preventives in endemic areas, although the eﬃcacy of these
regimens have not been evaluated. 49

Public Health Aspects
Spirocerca lupi has not been identiﬁed as a zoonosis.

Strongyloides spp. (Strongyloidiasis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Strongyloides stercoralis (family Strongyloididae, order Rhabditida)
has a unique life cycle; adult females reside in the host and
reproduce via parthenogenesis (asexual reproduction), and freeliving adult females and males reproduce sexually. In dogs,
females reside in the small intestine and can be identiﬁed by their
ﬁlariform esophagus, which is approximately one third of the
length of their body. Larvated eggs and, more commonly, ﬁrststage rhabditiform larvae (L1) with straight tails can be recovered
in host feces. These larvae can develop to L3 (homogonic cycle),
or, depending on environmental conditions, free-living adult
rhabditiform female and male nematodes (heterogonic cycle) that
produce oﬀspring that develop into infective L3. The
environmental cycle can take as few as 2 days (homogonic cycle)
and as long as 7 days (heterogonic cycle). 90-95 Infective L3
primarily enter the host percutaneously. Oral infection can occur,
although this more typically results in penetration of the oral
mucosa by L3. 96 , 97 The migration route varies with strain and
species; pulmonary migration is common but not required. 98
Some larvae can arrest but the majority reach the small intestine
within 4 to 6 days. The female then develops in the mucosal
epithelium and lays eggs in small intestinal crypts. The prepatent
period ranges from 5 to 21 days. Strongyloides stercoralis females
range from slightly < 2 mm to 3.5 mm; mean egg dimensions are
42 to 58 µm x 30 to 34 µm; and L1 recovered in feces are
approximately 180 to 380 µm long with most 250 to 300 µm long.
90 , 91 , 93 , 97

Although less common, transmammary infection is possible if
the infection in the mother occurs in late gestation or early
lactation. 99 , 100 Autoinfection is rare but can occur with the L1

vetexamprep.ir

hatching from the egg and molting into an L3 while in the host. 101
, 102 Hyperinfection, used to refer to high levels of autoinfection
and migrating larvae, also can occur. In humans, “disseminated
infection” refers to the migration of larvae beyond the GI tract,
peritoneum, and lungs. This term is not directly applicable to
dogs since the normal migratory route can be extrapulmonary.
The life cycle of Strongyloides in cats has not been as extensively
studied but likely is similar to that in dogs with a few important
exceptions. Female Strongyloides spp. worms in cats also can
inhabit the colon and neither transmammary, autoinfection nor
hyperinfection have been conﬁrmed. 93-95 Also, with Strongyloides
planiceps, embryonated eggs almost as large as Ancylostoma eggs
are found in the feces instead of L1. 93
While S. stercoralis is the species found in dogs, the species
infecting cats is much less clear. Strongyloides planiceps, ﬁrst
isolated in 1927 and described in 1943, has only been reported in
cats and some wildlife species in Malaya and Japan. 93 , 103
Strongyloides felis, described in 1925, has been reported in India
and Australia. 91 , 95 Strongyloides tumefaciens, the last to be
described (1941) and the only species in which the parasitic female
resides in the large intestine, has been reported in North and
South America. 94 , 104-106 Reports of S. stercoralis in cats have been
infrequent although it has been proposed that S. felis and S.
tumefaciens are strains or subspecies of S. stercoralis; this has been
supported by work with dog and human strains. 91 , 107-111
Nematodes in tissue that were thought to be S. tumefaciens based
on lesion location and pathology were recently subjected to PCRsequencing and determined to be S. stercoralis, supporting the
theory of strains or subspecies. 112 However, given the diﬀerence
in morphology that exists, S. planiceps is likely a distinct species.
Hence, in the rest of this chapter, infections in cats are referred to
as Strongyloides spp. unless the information is speciﬁc to S.
planiceps.
In both cats and dogs, Strongyloides spp. occur worldwide,
although prevalence is typically low; most studies report a
prevalence of <5% in dogs (range, 0 to 50%). 113-124 The higher
prevalence is reported more in tropical and subtropical regions. In
cats, prevalence is typically 0 to 4% but up to 46% has been seen in
some populations. 24 , 95 , 125-128 Strongyloides infections in dogs

vetexamprep.ir

and cats are likely underreported, given that release of eggs and
L1 can be intermi ent and routine fecal diagnostic methods lack
sensitivity for Strongyloides spp. detection.

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Most Strongyloides spp. infections in dogs and cats are subclinical.
Dogs with heavy infections can have chronic intermi ent diarrhea
and weight loss or stunted growth. Feces is typically of watery,
mucoid consistency and can contain blood. Severe infections may
be fatal. 114 , 115 , 121 , 123 In some cases, GI signs are preceded by
respiratory signs and hemorrhagic pododermatitis. These signs
may be caused by pulmonary migration and percutaneous
infection, respectively. 129 , 130 As in humans, Strongyloides
infection of dogs with immunosuppressive conditions (e.g.,
glucocorticoid therapy) can result in accelerated autoinfection or
hyperinfection that is associated with exacerbated GI and
pulmonary signs. 101 , 102 , 130 , 131 Less is known about clinical
signs of infection in cats. However, infections have been
associated with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and death. 94 , 104 ,

105

Diagnosis
Strongyloides infection is challenging to diagnose using
conventional fecal analysis techniques due to a low parasite load
and irregular larval output. Use of serial specimen collection and
the Baermann test can increase sensitivity. 132 When L1 are
recovered (Fig. 116.6), Strongyloides spp. larvae can be
diﬀerentiated from Ancylostoma spp. larvae by their shorter buccal
capsule and a prominent genital primordium. If ﬁlariform L3 are
seen, these can be distinguished by their truncated notched tail
and long esophagus. If eggs are seen, they are larvated in fresh
feces and are smaller than Ancylostoma spp. eggs.
There are no commercially available serological or PCR assays
for detection of Strongyloides spp. in dogs or cats. PCR methods
have had variable sensitivity when used to detect Strongyloides

vetexamprep.ir

spp. in humans. IFA tests and ELISA have good sensitivity but are
of limited availability. 119

CBC and serum chemistry results in clinically aﬀected animals
are nonspeciﬁc and may include stress leukograms, mild anemia,
hypoproteinemia, and increased serum CRP. 121 While
eosinophilia is typically associated with many parasitic infections,
it is not consistently seen with Strongyloides spp. infections. 121 , 133
On necropsy, parasitic females are typically located in the
duodenal mucosa. The nematodes are small and may easily be
overlooked on gross examination, but can be found on
microscopic examination of duodenal scrapings or on
histopathological sections. Pathological ﬁndings in clinically
aﬀected dogs range from none to mild to marked
lymphoplasmacytic enteritis and may, in addition to the
duodenum, aﬀect the proximal jejunum, or occasionally the whole
intestinal tract. 114 , 121 , 129 Strongyloides spp. also can be found in
the anterior portion of the small intestine in cats. 95 However, in
cats, parasitic female adult nematodes also can be found within
nodules in the colonic submucosa (Figs. 116.7 and 116.8). 94 , 105 ,

112

Treatment and Prognosis
No anthelmintics are registered for the treatment of Strongyloides
in dogs and cats, and eﬀective doses are higher than those

vetexamprep.ir

required for most other GI nematode infections. In dogs,
ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg PO), fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO for 3 to 5
days), and albendazole (100 mg/kg PO twice daily for 3 days)
have been used. 134-136 In the treatment of hyperinfections,
ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg PO) administered every 4 days with a total
of three or four administrations and fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO)
for 7 to 14 days have been used. 136 Due to toxicity concerns,
extra-label use of high-dose ivermectin or albendazole is not
recommended in dogs or cats. Less is known about eﬀective
treatments in cats although ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg PO) and
thiabendazole (25 mg/kg PO q12h for 2 days) have been
suggested. Fenbendazole (20 mg/kg PO for 3 days), pyrantel
emboate (12.5 mg/kg PO), and pyrantel pamoate (25 mg/kg PO)
were not eﬀective in cats. 137
With treatment, dogs fully recover from non-hyperinfections.
The prognosis for dogs with hyperinfections is poor. In cats, very
li le work on treatment has been performed and prognosis is
diﬃcult to assess. Most cats are subclinically infected.

Immunity and Prevention
Dogs develop limited immunity to reinfection with S. stercoralis.
Infections can be chronic with female worms living for months or
longer. Immunosuppression can result in recrudescence of larval
shedding, higher autoinfection, and extensive dissemination of
the larvae, which can be fatal. 101 , 130 , 133 , 138 Development of
immunity has not been studied in cats. Prevention is primarily
through hygiene, especially in kennel situations.

Public Health Aspects
Strongyloides stercoralis is zoonotic. DNA and RNA sequencing
have shown that people and dogs share some strains of S.
stercoralis, while others are host speciﬁc, therefore people

vetexamprep.ir

potentially serve as a source of infection for dogs and vice versa.
107-111

Even if zoonotic infections are strain-speciﬁc, S. stercoralis must
be considered a serious zoonosis. Between 30 and 100 million
people are estimated to be infected with S. stercoralis worldwide.
In the USA, community-based studies suggest a prevalence of
2.7% 139 ; IgG seroprevalences of 12 to 77% have been reported in
certain immigrant groups in North America from southeast Asia,
Somalia, and Sudan. Hyperinfection, while rare, can be fatal and
people with asymptomatic infections can develop hyperinfection
when glucocorticoids are administered.
There have been no reports of cat Strongyloides spp. infecting
people, and the role of cat infections in providing a reservoir for
human or dog infections is unknown.

Mammomonogamus spp. Infections
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Mammomonogamus spp. (family Syngamidae) typically reside in
the upper respiratory tract. While ﬁve species have been described
in either domestic or wild cats, three of the species,
Mammomonogamus
dispar,
Mammomonogamus
felis,
and
Mammomonogamus mcgaughei, have only been seen once or twice
and are likely conspeciﬁc with other Mammomonogamus spp. 140
The remaining two species, Mammomonogamus ierei and
Mammomonogamus auris, infect domestic cats and have been
associated with upper respiratory signs and head shaking,
respectively. 141 , 142 Both M. ierei and M. auris were ﬁrst described
in 1934; M. ierei was isolated from a domestic cat in Trinidad 143
and M. auris from the middle ear of several cats in China. 144
There have been reports of Mammomonogamus spp. infections in
wild felids, but the species involved are unclear.
Mammomonogamus laryngeus, a species found in ruminants, is
morphologically similar to M. ierei and the two species have
overlapping distribution. While it has been suggested that they
might be synonyms, genetic sequence information does not
support this theory. 140

vetexamprep.ir

Mammomonogamus ierei adult
female and male; females range from 13.8 to
23.8 mm long and the males range from 3 to
6.9 mm long. Courtesy of J. Ketzis.
FIG. 116.9

Mammomonogamus spp. are thick-bodied nematodes with large
buccal capsules. They are characterized by the “Y” shape formed
by male and female adult worms a ached in permanent
copulation (Fig. 116.9). The males are less than half the length of
the females. Adult M. ierei reside in the nares and nasopharynx
and are red to reddish-brown, and M. auris adults reside in the
middle ear and are orange to red. 140 , 143 , 144 Both are considered
haematophagous. Location in the host is the main diﬀerentiating
feature for the two species. Sizes of the male and female worms
are similar: M. ierei females are 13.8 to 23.8 mm long and the males
are 3 to 6.9 mm long; M. auris females are 13.7 to 30 mm long and
males are 3.3 to 8.1 mm long. 140 , 143-145

vetexamprep.ir

Mammomonogamus ierei egg in a
Sheather’s sugar flotation; eggs are 78 to 100
μm long x 46 to 58 μm wide. Courtesy of J.
FIG. 116.10

Ketzis.

The eggs of both species can be found in feces or sputum with
the eggs of M. ierei also found in nasal discharge. The eggs are
oval with a clear, slightly thick shell and are 78 to 100 µm long x
46 to 58 µm wide (Fig. 116.10). 143-145 In fresh fecal material, the
eggs are in the four- to eight-celled morula stage. 143 , 144
The complete life cycle of the various Mammomonogamus species
has yet to be determined. Neither oral infection nor percutaneous
infection has been successful in limited studies, as is the case for
other Mammomonogamus species. 143 , 146 It has been hypothesized
that paratenic hosts are involved. The migratory path of the larvae
to their respective predilection sites is not known. For M. ierei,
eggs are likely coughed up and swallowed while those of M. auris
are believed to pass down the Eustachian tubes into the pharynx
where they are swallowed. 143 , 144 Larvae develop to the third
stage in the egg before hatching and there are no data on
diﬀerentiating the eggs or L3 of the two species. The prepatent

vetexamprep.ir

period is unknown but is potentially as short as a few days and as
long as 2 weeks or more. 147-150
All conﬁrmed reports of M. ierei infection have come from the
Caribbean islands. Mammomonogamus auris occurs in Asia with
reports from China, Japan, Sri Lanka, and islands in the northwest
Paciﬁc Ocean. 140 , 142 , 144 , 145 , 151 There have been sporadic
reports from other locations with the species not identiﬁed. 140 , 152
There are few recent studies on prevalence of infection in cats in
endemic areas. A 2015 study from St. Ki s of 41 owned cats
(indoor/outdoor and indoor only) found 2% to be infected and a
2010 study from the same location with 100 feral cats found 45%
to be infected. 153 , 154 In less recent studies in the Caribbean,
prevalence ranged from 32.5% to 47%. 142 , 141 In the case of M.
auris, a 1934 study in China found 11 (23%) of 48 cats to be
infected, and 5.6% (7 of 124 cats) were found to be infected in a
1982 study from Japan. 144 , 145 Li le is known about infection
intensity; one to four pairs of worms are most often seen although
27 pairs of M. ierei were described in one cat and six pairs of M.
auris in another cat. 141 , 143 , 144

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Most cats are subclinically infected. Clinical signs have included
mucoid nasal discharge, cough, sneezing episodes, upper
respiratory tract congestion, open mouth breathing, and weight
loss with M. ierei. 141 , 153 , 155 Head shaking has been seen in a cat
with M. auris infection. 142 Inﬂammation and hemorrhage of the
nasopharyngeal mucosa have been observed in infections with
both species. 141 , 143 , 144 In cats with M. auris infection, the
tympanic membrane appears unaﬀected. 144

Diagnosis
Mammomonogamus spp. infections can be conﬁrmed via fecal or
sputum ﬂotation. While simple ﬂotation, direct smear, and
sedimentation have been used, ﬂotation with centrifugation and
Sheather’s sugar ﬂotation solution (1.27 to 1.3 SpG) appears to be

vetexamprep.ir

the most sensitive method. 140 , 154 On otoscopic examination, M.
auris adults can be visible and on occasion M. ierei can be expelled
during a sneeze. Both species can be recovered at necropsy, with
M. ierei ﬁrmly a ached to the mucosa. 141 , 143

Treatment and Prognosis
In a single case report, fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO q24h for 5
days) was eﬀective for the treatment of an M. ierei infection. 155
Selamectin and a combination of thiabendazole, dexamethasone,
and neomycin were used to treat an M. auris infection. 142
Thiabendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin have been used
with apparent success to treat Mammomonogamus spp. in other
hosts, which suggests that both benzimidazoles and macrocyclic
lactones could be eﬀective. 147 Physical removal of nematodes
from the ear also is possible and on occasion, cats eliminate the
nematodes with forceful sneezing. With treatment or physical
removal of the worms, cats fully recover. 141 , 142 , 152 , 155

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
Cats are not known to develop immunity to Mammomonogamus
spp. infection and there is no vaccine. Given that the route of
infection is unknown, control/prevention measures are unclear.
However, since infection is likely through paratenic hosts,
preventing cats from hunting should decrease infection in
endemic areas.

Public Health Aspects
Neither M. ierei nor M. auris has been identiﬁed as zoonotic.
Reports of Mammomonogamus spp. infecting people are extremely
rare (approximately 100 cases in the literature), almost always
associated with residence in or travel to the Caribbean or Brazil,
and largely a ributed to M. laryngeus. In humans, infections
involve the trachea and are followed by violent coughing until the
worms are expelled. 148 Molecular studies of Mammomonogamus
spp. found in people are required to conﬁrm that the species
involved is the same as that infecting ruminants.

Dioctophyme Renale Infection
(Dioctophymatosis, Dioctophymiasis)
Etiology and Epidemiology
Dioctophyme renale (also referred to as Dioctophyma renale,
especially in the human literature), the giant kidney worm, is the
largest nematode of domestic animals. The parasite has a
sporadic, worldwide distribution although reports of infection are
rare in Africa and Asia. It is widespread in the Americas and has
been reported from dogs and other hosts from Canada to Brazil.
Adults are usually dark red and thick, often measuring 1 cm or
more in diameter; immature worms may be creamy white and
smaller. Females are larger than males, and may measure as long
as 50 to 100 cm. Dioctophyme renale is found in a variety of ﬁsheating mammals; mink and other mustelids are considered
deﬁnitive hosts. Adult nematodes do not become as large when in
mink. In domestic animals, infection with D. renale is most
commonly reported in dogs and, occasionally, cats, but has also
been described in pigs, ca le, and horses. 156 , 157 Whether the
name of the genus was Dioctophyme or Dipctophyma was
contentious for over 2 centuries, but was resolved as
“Dioctophyme” in 1989 (International Commission on Zoological
Nomenclature).
Eggs are passed in the urine of an infected host and are longlived in the environment. First-stage larvae develop within eggs, a
process dependent on temperature; larvae may develop in as early
as 30 days at 25 to 30°C or as late as 7 months at lower
temperatures. 158 Aquatic oligochaete annelids commonly referred
to as mud worms (e.g., Lumbriculus variegatus) serve as
intermediate hosts. The annelids ingest the eggs; the larvae then
hatch, penetrate the tissues, and develop through successive molts
to third-stage larvae. These larvae are immediately infective to
mink and dog deﬁnitive hosts if annelids are ingested. However,
more commonly, a ﬁsh or frog bridges the ecologic gap by
ingesting the annelid and serving as a paratenic host. 158
Mink, dogs, and, rarely, cats become infected when they ingest
infective larvae in the tissues of paratenic hosts, most commonly
freshwater ﬁsh. Larvae emerge from paratenic host tissues,
penetrate the wall of the duodenum, and migrate directly to the

vetexamprep.ir

kidney. Based on anatomical proximity to the duodenum, the
right kidney is most frequently infected. Adult worms develop
over several months, with infections becoming patent in 4 to 6
months or as long as 2 years. 158 Adult worms also can remain in
the abdominal cavity.
Infection of dogs with D. renale is largely sporadic and few
epidemiologic studies have been undertaken. Dogs with D. renale
infection in Manitoba were co-infected with Metorchis conjunctus
and clinically normal when examined, but at necropsy had
extensive destruction of the right kidney and, occasionally,
hypertrophied left kidneys. 159 In Brazil, dogs with D. renale
infection were more likely to be female, fed ﬁsh or ﬁsh oﬀal by
their owners, known to eat frogs, and reported to drink water
from a river known to harbor infected annelids. 159 Some authors
do not consider dogs to be deﬁnitive hosts because few worms are
usually present in infected dogs and infections are often not
patent. However, eggs recovered from dogs have been shown to
be fertile and develop larvae, and thus dogs are thought to
contribute to transmission of the parasite in some environments.
160

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
A majority of renal infections are unilateral, involving only the
right kidney, and subclinical; when both kidneys are involved,
disease is more severe. When clinical signs are present, hematuria,
polyuria, and pyuria are most commonly reported. Renal pain or
generalized abdominal pain may be present. Some dogs are
reluctant to move and anorexia, ascites, weight loss, and
polydipsia may be present. When renal damage is severe, dogs
can develop uremia, with associated lethargy, anorexia, and
seizures. Adhesions and peritonitis may develop when D. renale is
present in the abdominal cavity. 156 , 161
Adult worms in the renal pelvis cause compression atrophy
resulting in hemorrhagic, suppurative pyelitis. Over time, the
renal tubules atrophy and ﬁbrose, the pelvis dilates, and the entire
parenchyma is lost resulting in a renal capsule that contains only
large, coiled D. renale and hemorrhagic exudate. Adult worms in

vetexamprep.ir

the abdominal cavity can result in adhesions and a
serosanguinous exudate. Entrapment of a liver lobe with
subsequent rupture and hemoperitoneum has been reported. A
minority of dogs have both renal and abdominal D. renale
nematodes. 157

Egg of Dioctophyme renale in
urine sediment; eggs are 60 to 80 μm x 40 to
47 μm, oval, and have a dramatically
corrugated surface. Courtesy of National Center for
FIG. 116.11

Veterinary Parasitology, Oklahoma State University.

Diagnosis
Classical diagnosis of D. renale infection relies on detection of the
characteristic eggs in urine sediment. Eggs are not detected in all
infected patients; many dogs with a single nematode in the renal
pelvis, and all dogs with nematodes only in the abdominal cavity,
will not be excreting eggs in urine. When present, the eggs of D.
renale have a distinct appearance; they are oval, 60 to 80 µm x 40
to 47 µm, often yellowish to brown in color, and have bipolar

vetexamprep.ir

plugs and a dramatically pi ed, rough outer coat (Fig. 116.11). A
serum ELISA has been developed for research use but is not
available commercially. 160
Infection with D. renale may also be suspected radiographically
when a distended right kidney is evident, but ultrasonography is
preferred for conﬁrmation. The large adults of D. renale will
appear as ring-like structures with hyperechoic walls and a
hypoechoic core that, when viewed laterally, are arrayed as bands
in the renal pelvis of the right kidney. 162 Because confusion with
normal structures can occur, ultrasound should be interpreted
with care when a empting to identify D. renale in the abdominal
cavity. When nematodes are present in the renal pelvis,
compressive atrophy of the parenchyma is often evident; in
advanced cases, nothing remains of the aﬀected kidney except a
capsule containing the adult worms and hemorrhagic exudate.
Entire adult nematodes are also occasionally found free or
encysted in the abdominal cavity during routine surgical
procedures such as ovariohysterectomy. They can also be found
encapsulated during exploration of cystic lesions in tissues such
as mammary glands, subcutaneous fat in the inguinal region, or
mesenteric lymph nodes. 156 , 163 Adult worms have also been
found in the urinary bladder, uterus, ovary, and urethra. The
nematodes are usually dark red and very large; females are 30 to
100 cm x 1 cm and males are 15 to 45 cm x 0.5 cm. Histologic
examination of aﬀected tissues with encapsulated nematodes may
reveal cross-sections of the distinct eggs, which appear as
birefringent double-walled circular structures with regular radial
striations. 164

Treatment and Prognosis
Nephrectomy is recommended for animals with only one aﬀected
kidney as complete atrophy of the renal parenchyma is usually
present; most dogs recover well. 165 Less commonly, in patients
with both kidneys aﬀected, nephrotomy may be a empted to
remove the parasites and allow recovery of renal function but the
prognosis is more guarded; careful evaluation of remaining renal
structure and function should guide surgical decisions.
Exploratory laparotomy to remove any nematodes free in the
abdominal cavity is also recommended. Ectopic worms in

vetexamprep.ir

subcutaneous fat or mammary tissue can also be removed
surgically; when lesions are not complicated, the prognosis for
recovery is excellent.

Immunity and Prevention
Prevention strategies focus on not feeding raw ﬁsh or ﬁsh oﬀal to
dogs or cats and keeping pets conﬁned to prevent ingestion of
frogs or other potential paratenic hosts. Infection may also occur
by direct ingestion of the aquatic oligochaete annelid intermediate
hosts in water, but this route is considered less common.
Immunity to infection has not been described.

Public Health Aspects
Human infection with D. renale is extremely rare (approximately
40 cases in the literature) but has been reported following
ingestion of undercooked ﬁsh or frogs, as well as contaminated
unﬁltered and unboiled water. 164 , 166 , 167 Most cases have been
from China. 168 Occasionally, nematodes develop in the kidneys
or retroperitoneal space but in most cases developing larvae
become encapsulated in subcutaneous nodules.

Dracunculus Insignis Infection (Dracunculosis)
Etiology and Epidemiology
Dracunculus insignis is a spirurid nematode closely related to the
human Guinea worm, Dracunculus medinensis. 169 Dracunculus
insignis causes subcutaneous infections in raccoons and other
carnivores, including domestic dogs. Dracunculus spp. have been
described since antiquity. Dracunculus medinensis was described
by the Swedish botanist Linnaeus in 1758, and D. insignis by Leidy
(Pennsylvania, USA) in 1858. 158 Traditional treatments in people
involved slowly winding the female nematodes around a stick
over a period of several days.
Adult female Dracunculus spp. are long and thin and usually
found coiled in subcutaneous cysts. Most reports of D. insignis
include female nematodes 20 to 30 cm in length although longer
specimens have been described; males die in subcutaneous tissues
before the mature cysts form and are rarely encountered in

vetexamprep.ir

clinical cases. Dracunculus insignis infections only occur in North
America (especially in the southeast); wild carnivores, especially
raccoons, are most commonly infected and considered the natural
deﬁnitive host. Most cases of D. insignis infection in domestic
animals are reported in dogs, although ferrets are also susceptible;
a limited number of cases have been described in cats. 170-174
Because males are necessary to conﬁrm species identiﬁcation,
although assumed D. insignis, most of these are now considered to
be reports of Dracunculus sp. infection. Although primarily a
human parasite, D. medinensis also infects dogs in Africa. 174 , 175
Larvae are deposited directly into water from ulcerative
cutaneous lesions on the limbs of the deﬁnitive hosts and ingested
by cyclopoid copepod intermediate hosts, which are small
crustaceans found widely in freshwater and saltwater habitats.
First-stage larvae molt to third-stage in 3 to 4 weeks at
temperatures of 24°C; at lower temperatures, development in the
copepod is delayed or does not occur. 176 , 177 Infected copepods
may be ingested directly by deﬁnitive hosts when they drink
water, or by paratenic hosts, notably frogs, with deﬁnitive hosts
ultimately infected through predation. Male and female
Dracunculus spp. become sexually mature in approximately 2 to 3
months and mate in the subcutaneous tissues of the thorax or
inguinal region; in experimental studies, fertilized females are
identiﬁed as early as 4 months PI. Males die in the subcutaneous
tissue after mating, while females migrate to the extremities, form
cysts, become gravid, and release larvae into water. After larvae
are expelled the females senesce and calcify. 158
The identiﬁcation of D. insignis infections in wildlife species
follows a seasonal pa ern. Historically, the highest prevalence of
mature females in subcutaneous cysts was reported in the spring
and early summer; these infections result from ingestion of
copepods or paratenic hosts the previous year as mature females
take as long as 10 to 12 months to develop in the deﬁnitive host.
178 A 2018 review of infections in North American dogs and cats
showed that dogs could be diagnosed with dracunculosis in every
month of the year, but 72% of infected dogs were seen in
December to May, with the highest number of cases in March. 174
Although less common, D. insignis infections in cats were also
seen between November and April. Cases were widespread

vetexamprep.ir

throughout eastern North America. The average age at initial
examination was 5.3 years, although patients ranged from 7
months to 15 years of age; no sex predilection was observed. 174

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Most dogs infected with D. insignis are evaluated for non-painful
skin nodules or subcutaneous swellings that are usually located
on the extremities. Other common locations include the thoracic
and abdominal wall, although nodules have been reported from a
variety of locations including the head. 174 The skin overlying the
nodule may be ulcerated or bear a patent opening; when the
aﬀected limb is immersed in water, an adult nematode may
emerge. 179 Localized hair loss is often seen. Occasionally lesions
are pruritic.
Nodule formation and ulceration are thought to be due to the
inﬂammatory response to the adult female nematode. Ulcer
formation is necessary to allow release of the larvae from the
uterus into water to continue the life cycle. Most infected dogs
have a single nodule containing only one adult female nematode,
but multiple nodules and multiple nematodes have been reported.
In one particularly severe case, more than 100 nematodes were
removed from a dog over the course of a year. 180

Diagnosis
When characteristic nematodes are encountered in subcutaneous
cysts on a leg, diagnosis is straightforward. Fine-needle aspirate of
the subcutaneous cyst usually yields serosanguineous ﬂuid
containing numerous Dracunculus spp. larvae with a distinctly
long, thin tail and measuring 600 to 800 µm (Fig. 116.12). Females
can be removed by careful dissection (see Treatment); intact
nematodes should be submi ed to a diagnostic veterinary
parasitologist for conﬁrmation of their identity. This is
particularly important when adults suspected to be Dracunculus
spp. are recovered from unusual locations such as the eye or
scrotum. Specimens can be submi ed immediately in saline;
alternatively, placing nematodes in 70% ethanol preserves key

vetexamprep.ir

morphologic features while also allowing subsequent evaluation
of key nucleic acid sequences. Formalin is not recommended.
Deﬁnitive morphologic conﬁrmation of the species requires
recovery of males which are usually not available. 175

Larvae of Dracunculus insignis.
Often present on fine-needle aspirate from a
cyst containing adult female worms; the larvae
are approximately 600 to 800 μm long and
have a long, thin tapering tail. Courtesy of National

FIG. 116.12

Center for Veterinary Parasitology, Oklahoma State
University.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of D. insignis in dogs with uncomplicated skin lesions
usually involves careful surgical exploration of subcutaneous
cysts and removal of any nematodes present followed by routine
wound management. Care should be taken not to cut or break the
nematodes during removal. Anthelmintic protocols to prevent or
treat infection have not been reported. Some dogs that develop

vetexamprep.ir

lesions are reported by their owners to be current on heartworm
preventives, and experimental treatment trials in ferrets using
ivermectin, albendazole, or diethylcarbamazine were not
rewarding. 174 , 181 Despite the lack of data, follow-up treatment
with macrocyclic lactones, including ivermectin at 0.2 mg/kg
administered parenterally and repeated in 2 weeks, or
transdermal 2.5% moxidectin/10% imidacloprid at the labelapproved dose, is often recommended to a empt to eliminate
developing, immature larvae that have not yet formed
subcutaneous cysts. Prognosis is good in uncomplicated cases that
involve a single nematode in the skin. When nematodes have
migrated aberrantly, such as to the eye, scrotum, or other
locations, or when numerous cysts are present, surgical removal is
still recommended but prognosis may be more guarded.

Immunity and Prevention
Limiting D. insignis infection in dogs requires complete avoidance
of ingestion of copepod intermediate hosts in natural bodies of
water or predation on potential paratenic hosts. Dogs should be
prevented from roaming, particularly in areas where raccoons or
other deﬁnitive hosts known to be infected with D. insignis are
also present.

Public Health Aspects
Human infections with D. insignis have not been reported despite
the fact that non-human primates are susceptible to experimental
infection. 182 Dracunculus medinensis, also known as the Guinea
worm or Medina worm, is currently limited in distribution to
three countries in Africa; historically this parasite was much more
widespread in Africa, southwestern Asia, and to a lesser extent,
northeastern South America and the West Indies. Infection follows
ingestion of water contaminated with infected copepods, with
transmission occurring when people stand in water when ﬁlling
water containers. Extensive eradication eﬀorts have dramatically
reduced both the number and geographic distribution of D.
medinensis cases in people in Africa. 183 Canine infections with D.
medinensis, while low in number and restricted geographically,
continue to be monitored.

vetexamprep.ir

Ocular Nematode Infections
Etiology and Epidemiology
Ocular nematodes reported from small animals include
Onchocerca lupi in dogs, and Thelazia spp. in dogs and, less
commonly, cats. Aberrant migration has also resulted in other
species of nematodes reported from the eye, including Diroﬁlaria
spp., Dracunculus spp., and Toxocara spp. Onchocerca lupi was ﬁrst
described in a feral wolf in Russia, 184 and causes onchocerciasis
in dogs in northern Asia, southern and central Europe, and the
southwestern United States. Thelazia callipaeda was ﬁrst described
by Ralliet and Henry (France) in 1910; infections occur in Asia,
and more recently in Europe. Thelazia californiensis was ﬁrst
described by Price in 1930 and causes infections in dogs in
western North America.
Onchocerca lupi infections are most commonly reported in
domestic dogs although occasionally the parasite has been
described in captive wild canids, domestic cats, and people. 185 ,
186 Prevalence of infection is highest in adult dogs over 3 years of
age, likely due to the very long development time of the
nematodes, and particularly common in dogs kept outside. 187
German shepherds are overrepresented in case series. 188 , 189 In a
survey in Greece and Portugal, 8.4% of adult dogs were infected.
190 Many infected dogs are subclinically infected. Knowledge of
the epidemiology of O. lupi infections is hindered by lack of a full
understanding of the vectors and intermediate hosts. In
California, Simulium tribulatum was identiﬁed as a putative vector
when PCR surveys revealed 2.8% harbored DNA of O. lupi. 191
Adults of O. lupi are found in conjunctival nodules and produce
microﬁlaria which are distributed in the skin. Blood-feeding ﬂy
vectors ingest these microﬁlaria which then develop to third-stage
larvae and are transmi ed to the next host by subsequent feeding.
158

Thelazia callipaeda and T. californiensis are described from dogs
and cats with occasional reports from wildlife deﬁnitive hosts.
Other Thelazia spp. infect the eyes of large animals. 158 Adults of
Thelazia spp. are found in the conjunctiva, under the nictitating
membrane, or in the lacrimal glands of deﬁnitive hosts. Larvae are
shed in lachrymal secretions and are ingested by muscid ﬂies

vetexamprep.ir

feeding around the eyes. In Europe, T. callipaeda vectors are
Phortica and Amiota spp., and drosophilid fruit ﬂies. Prevalence in
dogs can reach up to 40 to 60% in highly endemic areas. 192 , 193 In
North America, T. californiensis is thought to be transmi ed by
latrine ﬂies (Fannia spp.) although fruit ﬂies may also be involved.
Third-stage larvae develop in the ﬂies in approximately 2 weeks,
migrate to the mouthparts, and are deposited directly into the
eyes of the next host when the ﬂy again feeds. 158

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs, Pathogenesis, and Physical Examination
Findings
Onchocerca lupi infections result in the development of episcleral
and subconjunctival nodules. In acute infections, dogs have
conjunctivitis with episcleral and conjunctival hyperemia and
periorbital swelling (Fig. 116.13A). As infections become chronic,
mature nematodes are found within granulomatous nodules in
the sclera, conjunctiva, orbital fascia, or eyelid. Exophthalmos and
protrusion of the nictitating membrane may be present, along
with edema, ocular discharge, lacrimation, and photophobia.
Nematodes or nematode fragments are present in excised
nodules. Occasionally, mild dermatitis develops in response to
microﬁlaria in the skin. 187 , 194
The presence of larval and adult Thelazia sp. results in
lacrimation, ocular discharge, epiphora, conjunctivitis, keratitis,
and, when trauma is severe or prolonged, corneal ulcers.
Conjunctivitis appears more severe when gravid females are
present. Thelazia sp. adults have a serrated cuticle that causes
damage to the corneal epithelium; the resultant ocular discharge
is both characteristic of the disease seen and important to
continuing the life cycle by a racting secretophagous ﬂy
intermediate hosts. Nematodes are readily observed and collected
during ocular examination (Fig. 116.14). 192 , 195

Diagnosis
Ocular onchocerciasis can be conﬁrmed when nematodes are
found within excised orbital nodules (Fig. 116.13B). Examination
of saline digest of skin snips reveals microﬁlaria; preferred

vetexamprep.ir

locations where O. lupi microﬁlaria concentrate include the head,
ears, and intrascapular region. 190 Microﬁlaria are not present in
blood and heartworm antigen tests do not appear to cross-react
with antigen of O. lupi.
Thelazia spp. infections are diagnosed directly by observation of
nematodes in the conjunctival sac (Fig. 116.14). Often several
nematodes are present, necessitating thorough examination to
allow complete removal. Once removed, nematodes can be
submi ed to a specialist for conﬁrmation of identity by
morphology, including the presence of distinct transverse
striations on the cuticle. 192 Specimens should be submi ed in 70%
ethanol or 0.9% saline to preserve nucleic acid for ampliﬁcation.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of ocular O. lupi in dogs involves surgical removal of
the nodules and the nematodes followed by anthelmintics to
eliminate any remaining nematodes, reducing the recurrence of
nodules after surgery (Fig. 116.13C). 187 Melarsomine (two
injections 24 hours apart) and macrocyclic lactones are
recommended. 188 However, some dogs infected with O. lupi were
reportedly current on heartworm prevention and thus it is not
clear if all macrocyclic lactone–based heartworm preventives
protect dogs from infection. With appropriate surgery and
postsurgical care, most dogs recover from ocular onchocerciasis.
187 , 188 One dog that appeared refractory to treatment appeared to
beneﬁt from addition of doxycycline for nematode-associated
Wolbachia spp. infection (5–10 mg/kg PO q12h) as well as topical
demecarium bromide (1 drop q12h in aﬀected eye), which induces
miosis and may have some activity against Onchocerca spp. (Fig.
116.13).
Macrocyclic lactones (extra-label) are eﬀective for treatment of
Thelazia spp., including application of label-approved doses of
transdermal moxidectin/imidacloprid or oral milbemycin oxime.
196 , 197 Worms can also be manually extracted using forceps after
application of topical proparacaine (Fig. 116.14). Prognosis for
recovery is excellent, and treatment with sustained-release
injectable moxidectin also provides protection. 198

vetexamprep.ir

Immunity and Prevention
Preventing infection with O. lupi and Thelazia spp. requires
protecting dogs and cats from the ﬂy intermediate hosts. Keeping
animals inside behind screens should reduce the risk of infection.
Pyrethroid repellents in the form of topical, liquid permethrin
spot-on products or deltamethrin collars are available for dogs
and would also be expected to provide some protection from
infection. A study in France showed that transdermal 2.5%
moxidectin/10% imidacloprid protected dogs from Thelazia
callipaeda infection; 199 a similar strategy may also be eﬀective for
treating O. lupi infections early, before development of clinical
signs.
