Public Health Aspects
Human infection with both O. lupi and Thelazia spp. occasionally
occurs, resulting in ocular irritation, excessive lacrimation, and the
presence of intraocular nematodes. 200-202 Patients with O. lupi
infections in most areas of the world develop conjunctival
hyperemia and subconjunctival nodules containing nematodes;
diagnosis is usually made upon histopathologic examination of
excised tissues. In the United States, human patients are more
commonly reported to have subdermal, spinal, and orbital
nodules. In addition to removal of aﬀected tissues and nematodes,
treatment involves a combination of anthelmintics and antibiotics
together with glucocorticoids to reduce inﬂammation. 203 , 204
Patients with Thelazia spp. infections generally report ocular
discomfort and a foreign body sensation; nematodes are identiﬁed
directly upon ophthalmologic examination and removed with
forceps. 191 Prevention of zoonotic infection with O. lupi and
Thelazia spp. requires avoiding contact with the respective ﬂy
vectors.

Case Example
Signalment

“Pirro,” an adult male neutered mixed breed dog from St. Ki s,
West Indies.

History

Pirro was seen for lethargy, anorexia, and regurgitation
(approximately once daily), which were of a few days’
duration.
Pirro was adopted from an animal neglect situation 10
months before initial examination. At that time he was treated
with Drontal Plus (praziquantel/pyrantel pamoate/febantel),
and shortly thereafter he was vaccinated and started on
monthly
heartworm
preventives
(ivermectin/pyrantel
pamoate). Shortly after adoption, a ﬁrm, indolent, 2 × 2 cm
prominence was noted over the left third metatarsal.

Physical Examination

vetexamprep.ir

The dog was in adequate body condition (BCS 3/5). Apart from
mild pyrexia, and an approximately 4 × 4 cm ﬁrm, indolent
swelling over the left dorsal metatarsals, physical examination
ﬁndings were within normal limits.

Laboratory Findings

There was moderate hypoalbuminemia (1.3 g/dL, reference
interval 2.5–4.4 g/dL) and mild hyperglobulinemia (6.3 g/dL,
reference interval 2.3–5.2 g/dL). All other CBC and serum
biochemical parameters were within normal limits.
Fecal ﬂotation and sedimentation: No parasite oocysts, ova,
or larvae were seen.

Imaging Findings

Thoracic radiographs: A soft-tissue opacity, compatible with an
esophageal mass was seen in the caudal thorax.
Left distal pelvic limb radiographs: Palisades of periosteal
new bones were seen on the dorsal surface of the left metatarsal
bones, consistent with hypertrophic osteopathy.
Esophagoscopy: A large (9 × 6 × 6 cm) intraluminal mass with
superﬁcial hemorrhage was partly obliterating the caudal
esophageal lumen.

Pathologic Findings

Endoscopic biopsies: Histopathology revealed necrotic debris
admixed with pieces of plant material.
Surgical biopsy (via gastrotomy): Osteosarcoma.

Diagnosis

Distal esophageal osteosarcoma.

Treatment

The dog was initially treated with ivermectin for presumed S.
lupi infection. A lack of clinical response and the biopsy
diagnosis of osteosarcoma led to a decision of humane
euthanasia.

Necropsy Findings

The antemortem diagnoses of caudal esophageal osteosarcoma
and hypertrophic osteopathy was conﬁrmed at necropsy. No
adult or larval stages of S. lupi were found.

Comments

In this case, an underlying previous spirocercosis was
presumed based on the ﬁnding of an esophageal osteosarcoma

vetexamprep.ir

in an endemic region.
Case example provided courtesy of Ross University School of
Veterinary Medicine.

117: Nematode Infections of the
Respiratory Tract
Gary A. Conboy, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
Aelurostrongylus abstrusus Infection
(Aelurostrongylosis)
• First Described: First recovered from a cat in 1890, the cat
lungworm was described and named as Strongylus abstrusus
by Railliet in France in 1898 and renamed Aelurostrongylus
abstrusus by Cameron in 1927.
• Causes: Aelurostrongylus abstrusus (cat lungworm).
Nematode in the superfamily Metastrongyloidea, family
Angiostrongylidae.
• Affected Hosts: Adult worms occur in the terminal bronchioles
and alveolar ducts in the lungs of cats and some wild felids.
• Intermediate Hosts: Terrestrial gastropods (slugs and land
snails) serve as intermediate hosts. Various amphibians,
birds, reptiles, and rodents can serve as paratenic hosts.
• Geographic Distribution: Endemic throughout the world and
reported from all continents except Antarctica.
• Route of Transmission: Cats may acquire infection by the
ingestion of infective third-stage larvae in the tissues of the
terrestrial gastropod intermediate hosts (slugs, land snails);
however, transmission probably more commonly occurs by
the ingestion of infected paratenic hosts (amphibians, birds,
reptiles, rodents). Infection may also occur through ingestion
of infective third-stage larvae released into the environment by
infected gastropods.

vetexamprep.ir

• Major Clinical Signs: Cough, nasal discharge, tachypnea, and
dyspnea. Weight loss and emaciation may occur in some
cases. Infections can be fatal.
• Differential Diagnoses: Allergic respiratory disease, bacterial
or viral pneumonia or infection with lungfluke (Paragonimus
kellicotti), other metastrongyloids (Oslerus rostratus,
Troglostrongylus spp.), or the capillarid nematode Eucoleus
aerophilus.
• Human Health Significance: There are no reports of zoonotic
infection; A. abstrusus is not considered a human health
concern.
Crenosoma vulpis Infection (Crenosomosis)
• First Described: Recovered by Dujardin from a specimen
bottle in a natural history museum in Paris in 1844, the fox
lungworm was described and named as Liorhynchus vulpis
and renamed Crenosoma vulpis by Railliet in 1915.
• Cause: Crenosoma vulpis (fox lungworm); nematode in the
superfamily Metastrongyloidea, family Crenosomatidae.
• Affected Hosts: Adult worms occur in the bronchi, bronchioles,
and trachea of dogs, wild canids, bears, badgers, and
martens.
• Intermediate Hosts: Terrestrial gastropods (slugs and land
snails).
• Geographic Distribution: Endemic in the northeastern quarter
of North America as well parts of Europe and Asia.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs acquire infection by ingestion of
infective third-stage larvae in the tissues of the terrestrial
gastropod intermediate hosts (slugs, land snails). Infection
may also occur through ingestion of infective third-stage
larvae released into the environment by infected gastropods.
• Major Clinical Signs: Chronic productive cough, gagging.
• Differential Diagnoses: Airway collapse, chronic bronchitis,
airway neoplasia, eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy, or other
infectious respiratory diseases that can cause cough.
Parasitic infections on the differential diagnosis list when
examining fecal specimens include lung fluke (Paragonimus
kellicotti), other metastrongyloids (Angiostrongylus vasorum,
Filaroides hirthi, Filaroides milksi, Oslerus osleri), the

vetexamprep.ir

capillarid nematode Eucoleus aerophilus, or intestinal
threadworm (Strongyloides stercoralis).
• Human Health Significance: There are no reports of zoonotic
infection; presently C. vulpis is not considered a human health
concern.
Filaroides spp. Infection (Filaroidiosis)
• First Described: Filaroides milksi was first recovered and
described from a dog in New York by Whitlock in 1956.
Filaroides hirthi was first detected by Hirth and Hottendorf in
research beagles in New York in 1973 and described and
named by Georgi and Anderson in 1975.
• Causes: Filaroides hirthi and Filaroides milksi are nematodes
in the superfamily Metastrongyloidea, family Filaroididae.
These species are similar in morphology so there is some
debate as to whether they may be the same species.
• Affected Hosts: Filaroides hirthi infection has only been
reported in dogs. Subclinical infections have been reported in
laboratory colony research beagles. Prevalence within
research colonies may be high. Infrequent cases with severe
clinical disease have been reported in client-owned dogs.
These are usually associated with concurrent
immunosuppression or some underlying disease process.
Filaroides milksi has been reported from dogs and skunks.
• Intermediate Hosts: None—both species have a direct life
cycle; L1 are the infective stage.
• Geographic Distribution: Filaroides hirthi has been reported
from the USA, Canada, Europe, Australia, Israel, and Japan.
Filaroides milksi has been reported from the USA.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs acquire F. hirthi infection by
ingestion of L1 larvae in sputum, feces, or vomitus. The life
cycle of F. milksi is unknown.
• Major Clinical Signs: Adult worms of both species occur in
bronchioles and embedded in the lung parenchyma. Most F.
hirthi infections are likely subclinical. With immunosuppression
or the presence of another underlying disease or stress
condition, a potentially fatal hyperinfection with signs of
dyspnea, cough, cyanosis, and obtundation may occur.

vetexamprep.ir

• Differential Diagnoses: Other severe pulmonary conditions
including CDV infection, bacterial bronchopneumonia (e.g.,
bordetellosis, Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus),
toxoplasmosis, fungal pneumonia, heartworm disease, leftsided congestive heart failure, pulmonary thromboembolism,
idiopathic eosinophilic pulmonary diseases, and infection with
other metastrongyloid, capillarid, or trematode lungworms.
• Human Health Significance: There are no reports of zoonotic
infection; neither Filaroides species is considered a human
health concern.
Oslerus osleri Infection (Oslerosis)
• First Described: First recovered from dogs in Montreal,
Canada by Sir William Osler in 1877, Oslerus osleri was
described and named by Cobbold in 1879.
• Cause: Oslerus osleri is a nematode in the superfamily
Metastrongyloidea, family Filaroididae.
• Affected Hosts: Wild and domestic canids.
• Intermediate Hosts: None—the life cycle is direct; L1 are the
infective stage.
• Geographic Distribution: Reported from all continents except
Antarctica.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs acquire infection by the
ingestion of infective L1 in sputum or vomitus.
• Major Clinical Signs: Adult worms occur in nodules clustered
at the bifurcation of the trachea. Signs include a nonproductive hacking cough which may be paroxysmal,
wheezing and in severe cases dyspnea, cyanosis,
bronchospasm, and emaciation may occur. Infection can be
fatal.
• Differential Diagnoses and Human Health Significance: See
Filaroides spp. infection.
Angiostrongylus vasorum Infection (Angiostrongylosis)
• First Described: Angiostrongylus vasorum was first described
in 1853 in a dog from southern France.
• Causes: Angiostrongylus vasorum (French heartworm), is a
nematode in the superfamily Metastrongyloidea, family
Angiostrongylidae.

vetexamprep.ir

• Affected Hosts: Domestic and wild canids, especially domestic
dogs and red foxes.
• Intermediate Hosts: Terrestrial gastropods (slugs and land
snails) are the primary intermediate hosts. Frogs can also
serve as intermediate hosts. Both frogs and chickens can be
paratenic hosts.
• Geographic Distribution: Infection is endemic throughout most
of Europe, parts of Africa, and South America, and in North
America it is restricted to the Canadian provinces of
Newfoundland-Labrador and most recently in Nova Scotia.
• Route of Transmission: Dogs acquire infection by the
ingestion of infective L3 in the tissues of terrestrial gastropod
intermediate hosts (slugs, land snails), or infected paratenic
hosts (such as frogs or chickens). Infection may also occur
through ingestion of infective L3 released into the environment
by infected gastropods. The importance of paratenic hosts or
environmental contamination in transmission is unclear.
• Major Clinical Signs: Cough, gagging, dyspnea, tachypnea,
exercise intolerance, evidence of bleeding disorders,
neurological signs, uveitis, anorexia. Infections can be fatal.
• Differential Diagnoses: These include heartworm disease,
other infectious causes of tracheitis and bronchopneumonia
including other lungworms (metastrongyloids, Eucoleus
aerophilus, Paragonimus kellicotti), systemic neoplasia,
anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity, pulmonary
thromboembolism, pulmonic stenosis, cardiomyopathy, and a
variety of infectious and inflammatory disorders of the CNS
and eye (rabies, CDV infection, toxoplasmosis, neosporosis,
cryptococcosis, other CNS-migrating parasitic diseases such
as Baylisascaris procyonis migration and cerebrospinal
myiasis).
• Human Health Significance: Angiostrongylus vasorum does
not infect humans.
Eucoleus aerophilus and Eucoleus boehmi Infection
(Eucoleosis/Capillariosis)
• First Described: First recovered from a wolf in 1839 by Creplin
(Eucoleus aerophilus) and from the frontal sinuses of a wolf
(Eucoleus boehmi) in 1953 by Supperer.

vetexamprep.ir

• Cause: Eucoleus aerophilus (previously Capillaria aerophila)
and Eucoleus boehmi (previously Capillaria boehmi) are
nematodes in the superfamily Trichinelloidea, family
Trichuridae, subfamily Capillariinae that parasitize the trachea,
bronchi, and bronchioles (E. aerophilus) and nasal cavity and
frontal sinuses (E. boehmi).
• Affected Hosts: Eucoleus aerophilus: Dogs, cats, wild
carnivores (e.g., mustelids, foxes), occasionally people.
Eucoleus boehmi: Dogs and various wild canids.
• Intermediate Hosts: The life cycle is unclear. Direct (i.e.,
without an intermediate host) or indirect involving earthworms
have been proposed for both Eucoleus species.
• Geographic Distribution: Endemic throughout the world.
• Route of Transmission: Whether definitive hosts acquire
infection by the ingestion of larvated eggs (fecal-oral) or
earthworm intermediate hosts is unknown.
• Major Clinical Signs: Most infections are subclinical. Nonproductive cough, nasal discharge, sneezing, tachypnea, and
dyspnea may occur with heavy infections. Secondary bacterial
bronchopneumonia may occur and may exacerbate clinical
signs.
• Differential Diagnoses: These include allergic respiratory
disease, bacterial, fungal, or viral pneumonia or infection with
lungfluke (Paragonimus kellicotti), or other metastrongyloids
(Angiostrongylus vasorum, Crenosoma vulpis, Filaroides
hirthi, Oslerus osleri in dogs; Aelurostrongylus abstrusus,
Oslerus rostratus, Troglostrongylus spp. in cats). In dogs, the
bipolar-plugged eggs may also be mistaken for those of
Trichuris vulpis.
• Human Health Significance: Very rare (< 20) cases of human
infection by E. aerophilus exist in the literature.

Overview of Metastrongyloid Infections of the
Respiratory Tract
Metastrongyloids (“lungworms”) are a varied group of nematode
parasites of mammals. As the common name suggests, most

vetexamprep.ir

species occur in the lungs; however, a few species occur in the
pulmonary artery, veins, or frontal sinuses of the host. The life
cycles for the majority of metastrongyloids are indirect, most often
involving terrestrial gastropods as intermediate hosts; however,
direct life cycles occur in a few species. 1 Although the signiﬁcance
remains unclear, recent studies have indicated that spontaneous
shedding of infective third-stage larvae (L3) into the environment
by infected gastropods is widespread within the metastrongyloids
and that these L3 survive outside the host for several weeks to up
to 4 months. 2 Therefore animals have the potential to acquire
infections through ingestion or licking of grass and other plant
sources. In North America, Aelurostongylus abstrusus occurs in the
lungs of cats and Angiostrongylus vasorum in the pulmonary
arteries and Crenosoma vulpis, Filaroides hirthi, Filaroides milksi, and
Oslerus osleri in the lungs of dogs. 3 First-stage larvae (L1) are
passed in the feces of infected dogs or cats for each of these
species. Typical of the metastrongyloids, fecal larval excretion
pa erns may be sporadic. 4 Due to sporadic larval excretion and
diﬃculty in recovery and identiﬁcation of nematode larvae,
diagnosis of metastrongyloid infection in dogs and cats tends to
be challenging. An additional and perhaps the most signiﬁcant
impediment to diagnosis is a failure to consider metastrongyloid
infection as a diﬀerential diagnosis in dogs and cats with signs of
respiratory disease.

Aelurostrongylus abstrusus Infection
(Aelurostrongylosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Aelurostrongylus abstrusus adult worms are 4 to 10 mm in length. 5
The bursa in males is greatly reduced, and the vulva in females is
near the anus just anterior to the tail. 6 Mature females produce
undiﬀerentiated eggs which develop in the lung tissue and hatch
L1.
Aelurostrongylus abstrusus infects cats and wild felids (Amur cat,
cheetah, Eurasian lynx, leopard, lion, ocelot, tiger) and has a
worldwide distribution. 7–9 In North America, infection has been
reported in the eastern USA (Alabama, Connecticut, Florida,

vetexamprep.ir

Georgia, Maryland, Massachuse s, New Jersey, New York, North
Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia) and
in the western coastal states (California, Oregon, Washington) as
well as in Hawaii and Puerto Rico. 10–14 In Canada, infection has
been reported in Ontario and diagnosis based on fecal
examination has occurred in British Columbia, NewfoundlandLabrador, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia (author’s
unpublished observations). 15 In other global regions, infection
has been reported in Africa (Kenya, South Africa), Asia, Australia,
Europe (Albania, Bulgaria, Denmark, England, France, Germany,
Greece, Hungary, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania,
Scotland, Serbia, Spain, Swi erland, Turkey), the Middle East
(Iran, Israel), and South America (Argentina, Brazil). 16–30 Infection
in cats has been reported with increasing frequency in Europe in
the last decade. 31 There have also been reports of A. abstrusus
infection in dogs based solely on detection of L1 on fecal
examination. 10 These may be spurious diagnoses due to
coprophagy. A empts to experimentally infect dogs with A.
abstrusus have been unsuccessful indicating dogs are probably not
a susceptible host. 5
The prevalence of infection varies within endemic regions. Fecal
ﬂotation surveys, which likely underestimate prevalence,
indicated A. abstrusus infection rates in North America in cats as
low as 0.1 to 1.1% in Pennsylvania, Connecticut, and New Jersey
to 6.2% in upstate New York. 10–12 , 32 Although it may reﬂect a
regional diﬀerence, a much higher prevalence (18.5%) was found
in a fecal survey of cats in Alabama which utilized the more
sensitive Baermann technique. 33 Various surveys have found
prevalence values that range from 0.5 to 50% in Europe and 14 to
39.2% in Australia. 31 Infection appears to be more common in
younger cats (3 months to 3 years), cats with access to outdoors,
and in those living in rural environments. 17 , 27 , 34–38

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis
The life cycle of A. abstrusus is indirect involving terrestrial
gastropods as intermediate hosts (Fig. 117.1). L1 are passed in the
feces of infected felids; slugs and land snails become infected

vetexamprep.ir

while feeding on cat excrement. L3 develop in tissues of the
gastropod in about 3 to 4 weeks. 1 Cats acquire infection by
ingestion of L3 contained in the gastropod or in a wide range of
paratenic hosts (amphibians, reptiles, birds, small rodents). 1
Recent studies have indicated that infected gastropods
spontaneously excrete L3 into the environment; this may be an
additional exposure route for cats or paratenic host species by
direct ingestion of L3 through ingestion of plant material. 2 The
PPP is about 5 to 6 weeks; infected cats may excrete L1 in feces for
about 2 to 7 months (peak excretion 10 to 17 weeks PI). 14 , 39 , 40 A
prolonged period of larval excretion (1 to 2 years) occurs in some
cats. 39 , 40 L1 may survive for 5 months in moist soil. 14 In cats that
have been re-exposed, there is a delayed onset of patency, a
reduced excretion level, and a more erratic larval excretion pa ern
than that typical of a ﬁrst exposure. 39 , 40 Cats may excrete large
numbers of L1 in the feces with counts as high as 144,800 larvae
per gram of feces. 36
Heavy infections can result in severe, potentially fatal,
interstitial bronchopneumonia. Severe clinical disease occurred 6
weeks PI in experimentally infected ki ens fed 800 L3. 41 Chronic
catarrhal eosinophilic bronchiolitis occurs in response to the
presence of adult worms, eggs, and larvae. A necropsy survey of
anesthetic-associated deaths in cats in New York found 9% were
infected with A. abstrusus. 42 The infections were subclinical at the
time of anesthesia and it was speculated that death may have
occurred due to hypoxia and systemic hypotension secondary to
lungworm infection resulting in cardiovascular collapse and
arrest. Pneumothorax and pyothorax secondary to A. abstrusus
infection has been reported in a ki en. Migrating L3 may have
become contaminated with Salmonella typhimurium in the lumen of
the intestine and carried it to the lungs. 43 Although rare, there
have been several reports of invasion of the large intestine by L1 of
A. abstrusus; in one of these cases, hyperinfection was considered
the cause of death. 44 , 45

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 117.1

Life cycle of Aelurostrongylus

abstrusus.
Clinical Signs and Physical Examination Abnormalities
Most infections are subclinical and self-limiting. 14 , 21 , 39 Heavily
infected cats show signs of cough, wheezing, dyspnea, and may
suﬀer from anorexia and emaciation. Most cats are afebrile.
Usually, cough can be elicited on tracheal palpation. Increased
vesicular lung sounds may be noted on auscultation. Enlarged
mandibular lymph nodes, nasal discharge, and increased
respiratory rate (> 50/min) may be noted. 46

Diagnosis
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of A. abstrusus infection is achieved by the
detection of L1 in the feces or mucus of infected cats. The L1 can be
speciﬁcally identiﬁed based on size and morphology. Larvae can
be detected in feces by both direct smear and ﬂotation; however,
the method of choice is the Baermann technique (see Chapter 5).
In general, larval excretion in the feces of animals infected with
metastrongyloids tends to be sporadic. 4 In A. abstrusus infections,
the fecal larval excretion pa ern becomes sporadic typically after
10 to 17 weeks of infection. 14 As a consequence, false-negative
fecal examination results can occur. Examination of multiple fecal
specimens increases detection sensitivity; most recommendations
suggest the evaluation of three fecal specimens before discounting
the possibility of metastrongyloid infection. 4
Laboratory Abnormalities

vetexamprep.ir

In many cases, no abnormalities are detected. The CBC may show
a peripheral eosinophilia. 47
Diagnostic Imaging
Radiographic changes usually involve a mixed pa ern
(bronchointerstitital
and
alveolar),
or
may
show
bronchointerstitial, bronchial, or diﬀuse unstructured interstitial
pa erns (Fig. 117.2). 31 , 38 , 48 , 49 CT ﬁndings have also been
described and include mixed pulmonary pa erns with a “ground
glass” appearance, interstitial-alveolar pa erns, pulmonary
nodules, tracheobronchial or mediastinal lymphadenomegaly,
and subpleural thickening. 49–51 No evidence of pulmonary
hypertension was identiﬁed using imaging and echocardiography
in one study of 14 infected cats from Italy. 49 Bronchoscopic
ﬁndings in aﬀected cats include airway hyperemia and stenosis,
increased bronchial mucus, airway collapse, and bronchiectasis
(Fig. 117.3). In a small study that compared ﬁndings in 24 cats
with aelurostrongylosis to 12 cats with feline idiopathic bronchial
disease, bronchiectasis was only found in cats with
aelurostrongylosis; airway hyperemia, epithelial irregularities,
and bronchial stenosis were more often found in cats with
bronchial disease. 52
Microbiologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
Although insensitive, examination of a direct fecal smear for L1 is
the simplest, least expensive, and quickest diagnostic test. A small
speck of feces is mixed in a single drop of saline or water on a
slide, cover-slipped, and examined microscopically for L1. In one
study, direct smears identiﬁed larvae in 3 of 12 A. abstrususinfected cats. 21 This test will only detect cats that excrete high
numbers of larvae in the feces.

vetexamprep.ir

Lateral thoracic radiograph showing
a severe, diffuse, bronchointerstitial pattern
with peribronchial cuffing in a 6-month-old
intact female Himalayan cat with
Aelurostrongylus abstrusus infection. Courtesy of
FIG. 117.2

University of California-Davis Diagnostic Imaging
Service.

Centrifugal fecal ﬂotation using zinc sulfate (ZnSO4), sodium
chloride, or sugar has been used to detect L1. Flotation is less
sensitive than the Baermann method and larval morphology may
be damaged by the high speciﬁc gravity ﬂotation media; this can
complicate identiﬁcation. Detection sensitivity of centrifugal
ﬂotation using ZnSO4 was reported to be superior to that of sugar
but both were inferior to the Baermann technique. 53
The Baermann technique is the most sensitive method for
detection of most species of nematode larvae. 4 Larval detection
by this method requires that the L1 are vigorous and motile. Only
fresh fecal specimens should be evaluated. In cats this usually
means restricting the use of a clean li erbox to one cat and
collecting the next available specimen. Feces that cannot be
submi ed within several hours of collection should be

vetexamprep.ir

refrigerated. False-positive results can occur if specimens are
incubated at room temperature for about a day before collection
due to the presence of newly hatched Ancylostoma tubaeforme eggs.
Additionally, specimens collected from grass or soil can be
invaded by free-living nematodes if left for prolonged periods on
the ground before collection. 4 Aelurostrongylus abstrusus L1 are
360–400 µm in length. There is a cephalic bu on (symmetrical
indentations along the rostral edge of the head) present at the
anterior end and the tail ends in a distinctive S-shaped kink with a
dorsal spine (Fig. 117.4). Immobilization of the L1 by the addition
of a drop of dilute iodine (1:10) facilitates a detailed examination
of the morphology. 4
Cytologic Diagnosis
Analysis of respiratory lavage specimens in cats may reveal
increased cell counts with mixed neutrophilic and eosinophilic
inﬂammation, as found in cats with idiopathic bronchial disease.
However, bronchoalveolar lavage specimens were normal in 21%
of 24 cats in one study, and only 33% of specimens had evidence
of eosinophilic inﬂammation. 52 Larvae may also be recovered
from transtracheal wash or bronchoalveolar lavage specimens. In
one study, larvae were found in bronchoalveolar lavage
specimens from 5 (21%) of 24 cats with aelurostrongylosis (Fig.
117.5).

Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
A PCR assay for A. abstrusus infection used on Baermann
sediment, feces, and pharyngeal swabs has been developed and
shows promise; it had a reported speciﬁcity of 100% and
sensitivity of 96.6%. 53–55
Pathologic Findings
Yellow, ﬁrm protruding nodules (1–10 mm in diameter) may be
apparent throughout the lungs on necropsy examination of cats

vetexamprep.ir

with aelurostrongylosis. Histologically, a granulomatous
(eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes, and multinucleated giant
cells) response occurs around adult worms, eggs, and larvae (Fig.
117.6). The uterus of adult female worms contain only
undiﬀerentiated eggs and undiﬀerentiated eggs may be visible in
the lung parenchyma. In most metastrongyloid species infecting
companion animals, adult females produce fully formed L1; only
in the Angiostrongylidae (including A. abstrusus and
Angiostrongylus chabaudi in wild felids) are undiﬀerentiated eggs
produced. 1 Although domestic cats are susceptible to infection
with Angiostrongylus spp., infections are very rare and the few
infections reported have been non-patent. 56 Therefore the
detection of undiﬀerentiated metastrongyloid eggs in the lung
parenchyma of cats in histologic sections is nearly pathognomonic
for A. abstrusus infection. There is hypertrophy and hyperplasia of
smooth muscle in the walls of bronchioles and alveolar ducts. 21 ,
31 Identiﬁcation of A. abstrusus nematodes may be an incidental
ﬁnding on necropsy of cats with other disorders.

Treatment and Prognosis
Emodepside, eprinomectin, fenbendazole, moxidectin, and
selamectin have been used to treat cats with aelurostrongylosis.
Based on fecal larval counts, emodepside (3 mg/kg, in
combination with praziquantel) had an eﬃcacy of 99% when used
in a single topical application and 100% with two bi-weekly
applications. 57 , 58 In an eﬃcacy study based on total worm
counts at necropsy, a single application of 3 mg/kg emodepside
had an eﬃcacy of 73%; with two doses 14 days apart, the eﬃcacy
rose to 99%. 59
Based on fecal larval counts, an eﬃcacy of 90% was reported for
a single topical application of eprinomectin (with ﬁpronil and
praziquantel) at 0.5 mg/kg in naturally infected cats. 60 Eﬃcacies
of 91.6 to 98.9% with a single application and 99.9% after two
treatments of eprinomectin (0.5 mg/kg) was reported in cats
infected with A. abstrusus. 61
Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 days) greatly reduced
but did not eliminate larval excretion in A. abstrusus-infected cats.
57 , 62 Extension of treatment duration appears to increase

vetexamprep.ir

eﬀectiveness. Dosages of 20 mg/kg for 5 days, 25 mg/kg for 5
days, and 50 mg/kg for 15 days have all been reported as eﬀective
treatments. 63–65 The eﬃcacy of a single topical application of
moxidectin (in combination with imidacloprid) at 1 mg/kg was
100% based on fecal larval counts. 66 Eﬃcacy of topical moxidectin
based on necropsy worm counts was reduced to 88% for a single
application; administering two to three monthly applications
resulted in an eﬃcacy of 99 to 100% when used as either a
treatment or preventive. 67 A single topical application of
selamectin (6 mg/kg) resulted in cessation of fecal larval excretion
in one of three naturally infected cats. 63 Administration of two
selamectin treatments 23 days apart resulted in clinical
improvement and negative post-treatment fecal examinations in 9
of 10 naturally infected cats. 68
With timely diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is good. Case
reports of fatal infections often involve prolonged periods of time
from the onset of clinical disease to diagnosis. To what degree a
delay in diagnosis contributes to a fatal outcome is unknown.
Some airway changes, such as bronchiectasis, may be irreversible
and predispose cats to chronic bronchial disease.

Immunity and Vaccination
Infection in most cats is mild and self-limiting. Re-exposed cats
have a delayed onset of patency and tend to shed lower numbers
of larvae than that occurring with naïve exposures. 39 , 40 Cats
likely develop some degree of immunity through previous
exposure. No vaccines are currently available.

Prevention
Curtailing access of cats to the outdoors limits exposure to
terrestrial gastropods and paratenic hosts. Topical eprinomectin
and moxidectin have potential for use as monthly preventive
treatments. 61 , 67 Most of the anthelmintics with activity against
A. abstrusus are approved for monthly use to prevent infection
with a range of diﬀerent parasites. To what degree cats receiving
monthly treatments with these anthelmintics are protected from
developing clinical aelurostrongylosis is unknown.

vetexamprep.ir

Public Health Aspects
There are no reports of zoonotic infection with A. abstrusus, and
currently A. abstrusus is not considered to have any public health
signiﬁcance.

Metastrongyloids Of Wild Felids
Reports from Europe have indicated a growing recognition that
domestic cats acquire infection with metastrongyloids
(Angiostrongylus chabaudi, Oslerus rostratus, Troglostrongylus
brevior, Troglostrongylus subcrenatus) that naturally occur in wild
felids. 56 , 69 Previously, domestic cats infected with these wild
felid lungworms were likely misdiagnosed as having A. abstrusus
infections. In North America, O. rostratus and Troglostrongylus
wilsoni have been reported from lynx and bobcats in the USA
(Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, North Carolina, Texas, Virginia,
West Virginia) and Canada (Alberta, Nova Scotia, Ontario). 70–75
To date, there have been no reports of domestic cat infection with
either of these wild felid metastrongyloids in North America.

Crenosoma vulpis Infection (Crenosomosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Adult Crenosoma vulpis nematodes are 4 to 15 mm in length and
are characterized by a distinctive anterior-end morphology; there
are 18 to 26 ringlike folds in the cuticle. 3 Males possess a
copulatory bursa, and female worms produce thin-shelled
larvated eggs which hatch shortly after being laid.
The deﬁnitive hosts of C. vulpis are primarily wild and domestic
canids. The natural deﬁnitive host is the red fox (Vulpes vulpes).
Infection has also been reported in such wildlife as the arctic fox
(Alopex lagopus), gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), coyote (Canis
latrans), raccoon-dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides), and wolf (Canis
lupus) and non-canid hosts such as the badger (Meles meles), black
bear (Ursus americanus), and martens (Martes spp.). 1 Wildlife,
particularly red fox, serve as reservoir hosts of infection for dogs.
In North America, C. vulpis is mainly restricted to the northeast.
Endemic infection in dogs or wild canids has been reported in
Canada (New Brunswick, Newfoundland-Labrador, Nova Scotia,

vetexamprep.ir

Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec) and the USA (Illinois,
Massachuse s, New York). 76–82 The sole report of infection
outside this region was in an arctic fox on St. Lawrence Island,
Alaska. 83 Endemic infections have been reported throughout
most of Europe. 30 Infection in a dog based on fecal examination
was reported in South Korea. 84 Prevalence of infection in the red
fox in North America ranges from 21 to 87% and is particularly
high in the Atlantic Canadian provinces. 78 , 79 , 82
Dogs acquire C. vulpis infection by ingestion of infective L3 in
the tissues of the terrestrial gastropod intermediate hosts. 1
Multiple slug and land snail species appear to be suitable
intermediate hosts; however, gastropod species involved in
natural infections are unknown. 3 Infected gastropods release L3
in mucus trails and feces; shed L3 may survive for periods of
weeks to months free in the environment. Therefore the potential
exists that dogs may also acquire infection when they ingest L3
during consumption of grass and other vegetation. 2 The
prevalence of infection in dogs is unknown for most regions. A
necropsy survey of humane society dogs on Prince Edward
Island, Canada, found 3.2% were infected with C. vulpis. 76
Crenosomosis is a frequent cause of chronic canine respiratory
disease in Atlantic Canada with C. vulpis infection detected in 21%
of the dogs with chronic cough. 85 There are no age, breed, or sex
predispositions. Ages of infected dogs have ranged from 3 months
to 16 years. In North America, the majority of the diagnoses occur
from November to May. 85

Clinical Features
Upon ingestion, L3 penetrate the duodenal wall, enter the liver,
and travel to the heart and lungs via the hepatic portal circulation.
The L3 break through the pulmonary capillaries into the alveolar
airspace and migrate to the bronchioles and bronchi to mature to
the adult stage. In cases of heavy infection, adult worms may also
be found in the trachea. The PPP is 18 to 21 days and the adult
worm lifespan is about 10 months. 1 The magnitude of the
exposure dose necessary to cause clinical disease and the
prodromal period are unknown. The consequences of repeated

vetexamprep.ir

exposure are also unknown. Infection results in eosinophilic
bronchitis; signs consist solely of chronic, usually productive
cough which may be accompanied by gagging. 86 , 87 The gagging
may be so pronounced that the owner may perceive that the dog
has esophageal obstruction. Aﬀected dogs are otherwise usually
bright, alert, and responsive with normal temperature and
appetite. Mild hyperpnea may be detected. In most cases, a cough
response is easily elicited through tracheal palpation. 86 , 87

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Bloodwork results in dogs with crenosomosis are generally
unremarkable. Eosinophilia, basophilia, and mild monocytosis
may be detected on CBC. 87
Diagnostic Imaging
Thoracic radiographs in aﬀected dogs may reveal an interstitial to
bronchointerstitial pa ern; focal alveolar pa erns have also been
described. 86 , 87 Findings on thoracic CT include diﬀuse bronchial
wall
thickening,
parenchymal
consolidation,
multifocal
peribronchial “ground glass” a enuation, parenchymal bands,
and cylindrical bronchiectasis. 88 Airway mucus and hyperemia,
irregular bronchial wall thickening, nodules, and adult worms
may be visualized on bronchoscopy (Fig. 117.7). 89–91 Occasionally,
adult worms may be identiﬁed using bronchoscopy when
Baermann fecal examination is negative. 89
Microbiologic Tests
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of crenosomosis is best achieved by detection
and identiﬁcation of L1 in feces or sputum of infected dogs. Fecal
ﬂotation lacks detection sensitivity for C. vulpis L1. In specimens
where L1 are present, the morphology may be too severely
aﬀected by osmotic damage to allow larval identiﬁcation.
Centrifugal fecal ﬂotation using zinc sulfate as the ﬂotation media
has been reported to detect C. vulpis larvae in about 10% of
infected dogs. 85 The fecal examination method of choice is the
Baermann technique (see Chapter 5). 3 As for aelurostrongylosis,
the intermi ent shedding pa ern typical of metastrongyloids
limits sensitivity. In order to minimize the chance of a falsenegative result, submission of feces from 3 consecutive days is
recommended. 3 , 4
Recovered larvae should be killed by addition of a drop of
dilute (1:10) iodine prior to examination on microscopy. Larvae
are identiﬁed based on size (264 to 340 µm in length) and
morphology (cephalic bu on, long esophagus, tail ends in a
simple point lacking kinks and spines but showing a slight
deﬂection) (Fig. 117.8). 4 A false-positive diagnosis of

vetexamprep.ir

crenosomosis can occur as a result of larvae excreted passively as
a result of coprophagia or predation. Additionally, fecal
specimens collected from grass or soil hours to days after deposit
may be invaded by free-living nematodes, which may be confused
with C. vulpis. Finally, if fresh feces are not examined, hookworm
eggs in fecal specimens may hatch and release larvae, which can
also be confused with metastrongyloids. 4

vulpis recovered on Baermann examination of

Cytologic Diagnosis
Analysis of respiratory lavage specimens in dogs with
crenosomosis may reveal increased cell counts with mixed
neutrophilic and eosinophilic inﬂammation. In one study of 10
aﬀected dogs, bronchial lavage specimens revealed a
predominance of eosinophils in seven dogs, eosinophils and
neutrophils in two dogs, and neutrophils in one dog; larvae were
identiﬁed in specimens from ﬁve dogs. 87
Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Since there have been no reports of fatal infection, details on gross
and histologic lesions in dogs are limited. Slightly depressed red
to purple discolored areas of consolidation in the mid to ventral
portions of the lung lobes have been reported. On histopathology,
multifocal histiocytic, eosinophilic bronchopneumonia may be
present with complete blockage by inﬂammatory cells,
nematodes, and debris occurring in bronchioles and in some
cases, bronchi (Fig. 117.9). 92

Treatment and Prognosis
Fenbendazole, milbemycin oxime, and moxidectin have been used
to treat dogs infected with C. vulpis. Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO,
q24h for 3 to 10 days) has been used widely with resolution of
clinical signs and cessation of larval excretion. 86 , 93 Milbemycin
oxime (0.5 mg/kg, PO, single dose) had an eﬃcacy of 99% in the
treatment of experimentally infected dogs. 85 , 92 A single topical
application of moxidectin (2.5 mg/kg) was similarly eﬀective. 94
The prognosis is excellent. In most dogs, full recovery occurs
within 7 to 10 days of anthelmintic treatment. In some dogs,
cough worsens in the ﬁrst 48 hours after treatment. This is
invariably followed by marked improvement and a full recovery.

Immunity and Vaccination
As for cats with A. abstrusus infections, the onset of fecal larval
shedding is delayed and the number of larvae shed is greatly
reduced in dogs that have been re-infected with C. vulpis (author’s
unpublished observations). This likely reﬂects the induction of
some degree of immunity from exposure. No vaccines are
available.

Prevention
Dogs placed on monthly milbemycin oxime or topical moxidectin
for heartworm prevention or other reasons are unlikely to develop
clinical disease due to C. vulpis infection.

Public Health Aspects
Crenosoma vulpis is not considered to have any public health
signiﬁcance.

Filaroides spp. Infection (Filaroidosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

Filaroides milksi was ﬁrst found in 1956 as an incidental ﬁnding at
necropsy in the bronchioles and coiled in nests in the lung
parenchyma of a 10-year-old Boston terrier. 95 Adult worms were
3.4 to 10.9 mm in length. Filaroides hirthi was ﬁrst reported, also as
an incidental ﬁnding at necropsy, in the bronchioles and lung
parenchyma of beagles from a purpose-bred research colony in
1975. 96 , 97 Adult worms were 2.3 to 13 mm in length. The
morphology of both species is similar, with the vulva in the
female located near the anus just anterior to the termination of the
tail and the male tail lacking a well-developed bursa. 6 The two
species are diﬀerentiated based on subtle diﬀerences in worm size
and male spicule morphology and length. 98 Whether the two are
diﬀerent species or the same has been the subject of some debate.
98–100 There are few reports of F. milksi infection in dogs. Diagnosis
based solely on histopathology has been reported in dogs in
Australia, Canada, and the USA. 101–103 However, diﬀerentiation
between F. hirthi and F. milksi is not possible based on
histopathology and therefore these may have been F. hirthi. 100
Since the original description of F. milksi infection in 1956, there is
only one other report of its diagnosis in a dog based on recovery
and identiﬁcation of adult male worms from a dog in Michigan.
104 There have been several reports of F. milksi infection in skunks.

99 , 105

Filaroides hirthi infection has been reported in laboratory
research dogs from Australia, Germany, Great Britain, Israel,
Japan, and the USA, with a prevalence of infection in colonies as
high as 78%. 96 , 106–111 However, most likely as a result of
heightened awareness and control eﬀorts, there have been no
reports of infection in laboratory research beagle colonies since
1996. Diagnosis has been relatively rare in non-research colony
dogs. Infected client-owned dogs have been reported from the
USA (Alabama, Georgia, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas,
Washington), Europe (France, England, Ireland, Spain), and
Australia. 112–122 Most case reports involve young (< 3 years of age)
toy breed dogs (Chihuahua, toy poodle, West Highland white
terrier, Yorkshire terrier).
The life cycle of F. milksi is unknown. Transmission of F. hirthi
occurs by ingestion of infective L1 usually through coprophagy of
fresh fecal material or in sputum, saliva, or vomitus. In research

vetexamprep.ir

beagle colonies, this is thought to occur from mother to pup by 4
to 5 weeks of age through exposure to feces from infected dams.
123 The PPP is 35 days. 124 Infections appear to be long lived and
may persist due to re-exposure to infective L1 through
autoinfection. 125

Clinical Features
Adult worms of both species occur in bronchioles and embedded
in the lung parenchyma. Most infections of F. hirthi in dogs are
probably subclinical. Clinical signs are usually associated with
immunosuppression or comorbid diseases. Glucocorticoid
therapy, concurrent demodectic mange, CDV infection, severe
trauma, and neoplasia have all been associated with clinical
disease. 108 , 109 , 112-114 , 116 , 117 Presumably, through autoinfection
such dogs develop massive hyperinfections with life-threatening
granulomatous pneumonia; larvae have also been found in
mesenteric lymph nodes, the intestinal wall, and the liver. Most
often, aﬀected dogs develop a non-productive cough that
progresses to dyspnea, tachypnea, cyanosis, and sometimes death.
Dogs may become emaciated.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Eosinophilia may be detected on bloodwork. Other bloodwork
abnormalities may be detected depending on the presence of coexisting diseases.
Diagnostic Imaging
Radiographic changes are non-speciﬁc. Radiographs may show an
interstitial pa ern with linear and nodular inﬁltrates involving all
lung lobes. 113 , 117 , 119 , 126 Bronchoscopy can be done to rule out
the possibility of Oslerus osleri infection. The absence of nodules at
the bifurcation of the trachea in a dog in which L1 are detected
suggests Filaroides spp. infection.
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination

vetexamprep.ir

Complicating the diagnosis of Filaroides spp. infection is the lack
of a reliable fecal examination method. For reasons poorly
understood, the L1 of Filaroides spp. excreted in feces of infected
dogs lack vigor to the point of being moribund and are therefore
not reliably recovered by the Baermann method. 124 Zinc sulfate
centrifugal ﬂotation has greater detection sensitivity than the
Baermann method but is still insensitive. Osmotic damage due to
the high speciﬁc gravity ﬂotation media may obscure the larval
morphology preventing accurate identiﬁcation. Larvae can be
detected using fecal sedimentation, but this is time-consuming
and laborious to perform.
Larval detection is best achieved through examination of
sputum, saliva, or respiratory lavage specimens. This is the
method of choice; larvated eggs and L1 may be detected. The eggs
are thin walled and measure about 38 × 80 µm; L1 are 240 to 290
µm in length and have a bluntly rounded head (i.e., lack a
cephalic bu on) and the tail has a kink (Fig. 117.10). 124 The L1 of
Filaroides spp. and Oslerus osleri are diﬃcult to diﬀerentiate due to
similarities in size and morphology.

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic Findings
Grossly, the lungs of dogs infected with Filaroides spp. are ﬁrm
and red. A large number of thin (35 to 102 µm wide) adult worms
may be observed extruding from the cut surface of the lung tissue.
Histopathology reveals granulomatous verminous pneumonia
with adult worms in bronchioles and nested in the lung
parenchyma. In some cases, only eggs and larvae are observed.
Hepatic granulomas surrounding worms have also been also
observed. 108 , 109 , 112 , 113 , 115-117 , 124 In massive infections, larvae
may be found in mesenteric lymph nodes, liver, the intestinal
wall, and the lungs. 108

Treatment and Prognosis
There is no anthelmintic approved for use in the treatment of
Filaroides spp. infection in dogs. Albendazole, fenbendazole, and

vetexamprep.ir

ivermectin have been used to treat dogs infected with F. hirthi. 3
Albendazole and high-dose ivermectin are not approved for use
in dogs and, due to safety concerns, are not recommended.
Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO q24h) for 14 to 21 days has been used
to successfully treat several dogs with clinical disease signs due to
F. hirthi infection. 114 , 117 , 121 One dog was successfully treated
with fenbendazole at 100 mg/kg PO q24h for 7 days. 122
Depending on the nature of the predisposing disease condition,
prognosis may be guarded to poor. Infections in
immunocompromised dogs may be overwhelming and fatal
despite treatment.

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
Routine use of anthelmintics should prevent Filaroides spp.
infections in research dogs.

Public Health Aspects
Neither Filaroides spp. is considered to have any public health
signiﬁcance.

Oslerus osleri Infection (Oslerosis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Oslerus osleri infects the trachea and bronchi of dogs and various
wild canids (coyotes, dingos, wolves). 1 Adult worms are 6.5 to
13.5 mm long; males lack a well-developed bursa and the vulva
and anus in females occurs at the termination of the tail. 6 , 127
Adult worms reside within wart-like nodules that are a ached to
the surface of the lumen in the trachea and bronchi clustered at
the bifurcation. 127 , 128 Nodules range in size from 1 to 14 mm and
can become conﬂuent if present in large numbers. 129–135 Nodules
from naturally infected coyotes contained 1 to > 100 worms per
nodule. 136
Oslerus osleri has a worldwide distribution. In North America,
infection has been reported in wild and domestic canids in the
USA (Alabama, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut,
Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Hawaii, Kansas, Massachuse s, Michigan,
Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North

vetexamprep.ir

Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South
Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wyoming), Canada (Alberta,
British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan,
Nova Scotia), and Mexico. 13 , 137–148 Other endemic regions of the
world include Australia, parts of Europe, Japan, New Zealand,
and South Africa. 127–129 , 131 , 133–135 , 149–153 Infection can be
common in wild canids, particularly in coyotes and Australian
dingos, with a prevalence as high as 52%. 148 However, wild
canids do not appear to serve as an infection reservoir for dogs;
dogs exposed to infective larvae recovered from coyotes failed to
become infected. 146 Infection in dogs appears to be relatively
infrequent. 13 However, O. osleri infection was found to be the
cause of 18% of the cases of chronic respiratory disease in dogs in
a retrospective survey from the 1980s in England. 149
The O. oslerus life cycle is direct with the L1 as the infective
stage. Female worms partially protrude through pores in the
nodule to deposit thin-shelled larvated eggs (90 × 60 µm) into the
lumen of the trachea and bronchi. The eggs hatch releasing the L1
while in the process of being coughed up to either pass to the
outside in the saliva or be swallowed and pass in the feces. 1 As
for F. hirthi, larvae recovered from the feces tend to be sluggish
and are often found to be dead and degenerating. Transmission in
wild canids is thought to occur at the time of weaning from dam
to puppy by regurgitative feeding. 150 Transmission in domestic
dogs is likely also from dam to puppy but occurs more through
exposure to L1 in saliva when the dam cleans puppies by licking.
148 Infection may also follow ingestion of larvae in contaminating
fecal ma er but this is likely of lesser importance. 128 , 150 The PPP
is about 70 to 126 days. 150 , 154 Consistent with exposure at an
early age, infections are more common in younger dogs (6 months
to 2 years of age). 148 , 149 , 155

Clinical Features
After ingestion, L1 penetrate through the wall of the duodenum
and travel to the heart via the lymphatics or hepatic portal
circulation; they then travel to the lungs via the pulmonary artery.
Immature worms arrive in the trachea about 34 days after

vetexamprep.ir

exposure and by 70 days PI, nodules that contain adult worms
become apparent. 150 In heavily infected dogs, nodules may be so
large and numerous that they may obstruct 50% to almost the
entire lumen of the trachea and bronchi. 130–132 , 149 , 152 Infection
results in a chronic, non-productive cough which may become
worse with exercise and is readily elicited on tracheal palpation.
In some cases, wheezing, dyspnea, and cyanosis occur. 148
Severely aﬀected dogs will show weight loss, emaciation, collapse,
and even death. 156 Pneumothorax secondary to bronchial rupture
was reported in one dog. 130 Subclinical infections occur in some
dogs.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Bloodwork ﬁndings are mild and non-speciﬁc; a peripheral
eosinophilia may be detected.
Diagnostic Imaging
Tracheal nodules or narrowing of the tracheal lumen secondary to
a mural soft-tissue mass are occasionally visible using thoracic
radiography. 131 , 132 , 134 , 135 , 149 , 155 , 157 , 158 Deﬁnitive diagnosis
of O. osleri infection occurs by detection of the nodules by
bronchoscopy (Fig. 117.11) along with the identiﬁcation of
nematode larvae with consistent morphology from respiratory
specimens or feces. The absence of nodules at the bifurcation of
the trachea in a dog excreting such larvae indicates Filaroides spp.
infection.
Microbiologic Tests
The same fecal examination challenges that exist for Filaroides spp.
exist for O. osleri. The diagnostic test of choice is examination of
respiratory lavage specimens for larvated eggs and L1. The eggs
are thin walled and measure about 60 × 90 µm; L1 have a bluntly
rounded head (i.e., lack a cephalic bu on) and a kinked tail. 150
Larvae recovered from mucus are 232 to 266 µm in length; those
recovered from feces measure 326 to 378 µm (Fig. 117.12A). 128 , 151
The L1 of F. hirthi, F. milksi, and O. osleri are similar in size and
morphology. 4

Pathologic Findings
Grossly, nodules are readily seen a ached to the epithelial surface
of the lumen in the trachea and bronchi clustered at the
bifurcation. Individual nodules may be as large as 12 mm in
diameter and contain adult worms coiled inside. Portions of
female worms may be seen extruding out from the surface of the
nodule. The presence of coiled adult worms in the nodule with
the females containing a uterus with developing larvated eggs can
be conﬁrmed on histopathology, either following endoscopic
biopsy of tracheal nodules or at necropsy (Fig. 117.12B). 128

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Prognosis
There are no anthelmintics approved for use in the treatment of
dogs infected with O. osleri. Variable results using a number of
older anthelmintics (diethylcarbamazine, thiacetarsemide,
thiabendazole, levamisole, oxfendazole) have been cited in the
literature. 133 , 155 , 157 , 159–162 Currently, fenbendazole and highdose ivermectin are treatment options. Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg
PO q24h) for 7 to 14 days was reported to be eﬀective in 19 of 20
dogs with clinical O. osleri infections. 149 The one remaining dog
required a second 14-day course of treatment and although it
showed marked clinical improvement, it still had evidence of a
few tracheal nodules and a small number of larvae present on
post-treatment examination. Fenbendazole at the same dose for
approximately 1 month was reportedly eﬀective in another dog
with severe tracheal involvement. 158 Ivermectin (0.4 mg/kg, SC,
repeated every 3 weeks for 4 treatments) was reported to be
eﬀective in the treatment of four dogs resulting in a clinical cure
and resolution of tracheobronchial nodules. 163 This dose of
ivermectin is not safe to administer to collies, collie-type breeds,
and other dogs with a mutation in the multidrug resistance gene
(mdr1). Marked clinical improvement was reported in a dog given
a single oral dose of ivermectin (0.4 mg/kg); however, nodules
persisted after treatment. 133 In general, prognosis for recovery
following appropriate treatment is good to excellent.

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
Routine use of anthelmintics should prevent Oslerus spp.
infections.

Public Health Aspects
There are no reports of zoonotic infection with O. osleri and it is
not considered to have any public health signiﬁcance.

Angiostronglyus vasorum Infections
(Angiostrongylosis)
Etiology and Epidemiology
Angiostrongylus vasorum (French heartworm) is a nematode in the
superfamily Metastrongyloidea, family Angiostrongylidae.
Angiostrongylus vasorum was ﬁrst described in 1853 in a dog from
southern France. 164 The life cycle is indirect with a wide variety of
gastropods (slugs and land snails) as well as the frog as
intermediate hosts, and both frogs and chickens reported as
paratenic hosts (Figure 117.13). Although the precise role it may
play in natural infection is unknown, the possibility of exposure
through direct ingestion of L3 has been suggested. Recent studies
have shown a portion of the infective L3 contained in the tissues of
infected gastropods are shed into the environment where they can
survive outside of a host for several weeks to several months. 2
This suggests that dogs might become infected through licking or

vetexamprep.ir

eating grass and other plant materials. 2 Somewhat limited in
geographic distribution, A. vasorum has shown a remarkable
capability for expansion over the past 40 years with endemic foci
currently occurring in southwestern France, the United Kingdom
(espeically southwestern England and Wales), Ireland, Denmark;
sporadic cases from other parts of Scandinavia (Finland, Sweden),
the Netherlands, Austria, Swi erland, Italy, Hungary, Spain,
Greece, Turkey, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Uganda, and
Canada. Angiostrongylus vasorum is a signiﬁcant pathogen of dogs,
causing life-threatening cardiopulmonary and neurological
disease. Various species of foxes, particularly the red fox, are
considered to be the natural deﬁnitive host, but infections can also
occur in other wild canids including the wolf (Canis lupus), coyote
(Canis latrans), and jackal (Canis aureus). Disease is occasionally
recognized in nonendemic regions following importation of
infected dogs, including a dog imported into the United States
(Michigan) from Ireland, 165 a dog imported into Canada (Alberta)
from Cornwall, England, and another imported into Australia
(Perth, Western Australia) from southern England. 166 , 167
Autochthonous cases in domestic dogs have not been reported
from the United States, but infection based on histopathology was
recognized in 2014 in a red fox from West Virginia; 168 and a focus
of infection has been identiﬁed in domestic dogs, red foxes, and
subsequently coyotes in Newfoundland, Canada. 169 Recently,
infection in coyotes has been reported from the Canadian
province of Nova Scotia, indicating the parasite has spread from
the island of Newfoundland to the mainland. The ongoing
expansion of the geographic range of this parasite has raised
concern about its impact following introduction into nonendemic
regions as a result of climate change and the movement of foxes
and gastropods (international movement of gastropods as a result
of horticulture industry activities is signiﬁcant). 170 Computer
modelling has predicted that there is a high likelihood that the
parasite will become established in much of North America,
becoming endemic throughout the eastern half of the continent
and in the states and provinces on the west coast. 171

vetexamprep.ir

FIG. 117.13

Life cycle of Angiostrongylus

vasorum.
In endemic regions, the overall prevalence of infection in
domestic dogs has ranged from 0.3 to 9.8%, and depends on
factors such as the coprological method used to detect L1 and the
dog population studied (e.g., stray vs. owned dogs). In contrast,
the prevalence of infection in foxes has ranged from 5 to 56%. 172
Increased awareness of the parasite and improved diagnostic
testing has likely contributed to disease emergence as well. 173
Although infections with A. vasorum have been reported from
South America (primarily Brazil, but also Argentina and
Colombia), 174 molecular studies suggest that isolates from Europe
and South America may be genetically distinct. 175
There is no clear breed predisposition for angiostrongylosis. In
the United Kingdom, purebred dogs, especially Cavalier King
Charles spaniels, Staﬀordshire bull terriers, and beagles have been
overrepresented. 172 , 176 Studies from other countries have shown
no breed predisposition; in Newfoundland, Canada, hunting dogs
were at greatest risk. 171 , 172 The median age of dogs in one case
series was 10 months, 176 and in another survey of 160 dogs, over
50% of aﬀected dogs were ≤ 1 year of age. 177 However, dogs from
3 months to 14 years of age have been aﬀected. No breed

vetexamprep.ir

predilection has been identiﬁed. In Canada, the majority of the
cases are diagnosed from October to March with a similar winterspring pa ern (December to May) reported in Denmark. 176

Clinical Features
Adult nematodes live within the pulmonary arteries and right
ventricle where they deposit undiﬀerentiated eggs. The eggs
lodge in capillaries in the lungs where they become larvated and
hatch. The L1 break through the pulmonary capillaries into the
airways, are coughed up, swallowed, and passed in the feces. L1
are ingested by the snail, slug, or frog intermediate host and
mature into L3 over about 10 to 16 days when conditions are
optimal. 172 Domestic dogs acquire infection by ingesting
intermediate or paratenic hosts; although the epidemiological
signiﬁcance remains unknown, infection may also be acquired by
consumption of vegetation contaminated with L3 released from
gastropods in feces and mucus. 2 , 178 Frogs and chickens can act
as paratenic hosts after ingestion of slugs or snails. 179 The L3 are
then released into the intestinal tract and migrate to the
mesenteric lymph nodes, where they develop into L4. L4 migrate
via the portal vasculature and liver to the lung by 9 to 10 days PI.
The PPP is 38 to 57 days, but can range from 28 to 108 days (see
Figure 117.13). 172
Clinical signs of infection in domestic dogs can range from
subclinical to life-threatening, with varying organ involvement;
the disease has been referred to as “the great pretender” 180
because of the varying manifestations of illness. Respiratory signs
are the most common manifestations of infection. The
granulomatous response to the developing eggs and movement of
L1 through the capillary wall into the alveolar airspace results in
ﬁbrosis which eventually can aﬀect large areas of the lungs. 181
This in turn is responsible for signs of productive or nonproductive cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, syncope, exercise
intolerance, and sometimes ascites. Increased lung sounds and a
right-sided heart murmur secondary to tricuspid regurgitation
may be detected on thoracic auscultation. Dogs may develop a
coagulopathy that results in hemorrhage. Hemorrhage may lead

vetexamprep.ir

to anemia with evidence of mucosal pallor on physical
examination. Signs of hemorrhage include scleral ecchymoses,
hyphema, retinal hemorrhage, epistaxis, hemoptysis, melena,
gingival bleeding, excessive post-surgical bleeding, subcutaneous
hematomas, or thoracic or abdominal cavity hemorrhage. The
pathogenesis of the coagulopathy is poorly understood, but
chronic DIC has been suggested to play a role. 182–184 Neurologic
signs in dogs with A. vasorum infection are usually secondary to
CNS hemorrhage, and include seizures, ataxia, nystagmus,
blindness, tremors, paralysis, and coma. Rarely CNS signs have
been reported to occur as a result of aberrant migration of L1. 167 ,
185 The acute onset of neurological signs may be the only evidence
of infection. 186 Other reported signs include vomiting, diarrhea,
abdominal pain, lumbar pain, inappetence, and weight loss.
Sudden death may occur secondary to abdominal, cerebral, or
thoracic hemorrhage or the rupture of a major blood vessel due to
worm migrations. 184 , 187 Aberrant migration of L1 has also been
identiﬁed to the skin, myocardium, kidney, spleen, adrenal gland,
thyroid gland, diaphragm, and pancreas. 172 , 177
Rarely, visualization of aberrant migrating larvae in the anterior
chamber has been reported on ocular examination, sometimes
with accompanying signs of blepharospasm, epiphora, uveitis,
episcleral congestion, hyphema, and corneal edema. 188

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Profile, and
Urinalysis
Findings on bloodwork are non-speciﬁc and include nonregenerative or regenerative anemia, leukocytosis due to a
neutrophilia, bandemia, lymphopenia, mild to moderate
eosinophilia (up to 2800 cells/µL in one study) and/or mild
basophilia, and mild to moderate thrombocytopenia. Findings on
serum
chemistry
proﬁle
are
variable
and
include
hyperglobulinemia, hypercalcemia, azotemia, and increased
activity of serum ALP. Hypercalcemia has been reported

vetexamprep.ir

secondary to granulomatous inﬂammation. 185 , 189 Urinalysis is
often unremarkable, but proteinuria has been reported. 190
Clotting Function
In dogs with evidence of a coagulopathy secondary to A. vasorum
infection, coagulation test results are variable. In one study of 30
aﬀected dogs, 18 dogs had signs of bleeding on physical
examination. 183 Of these 18 dogs, 17 had thromboelastography
results consistent with hypocoagulation. A total of 22 of 25 dogs
had increased D-dimer concentrations, and ﬁbrinogen
concentrations were signiﬁcantly lower in dogs with evidence of
hemorrhage compared with those that did not. Although
coagulation times (PT and APTT) were abnormal in some dogs,
these were not associated with clinically evident hemorrhage.
Cytologic Analysis of Body Fluids
Analysis of the CSF in dogs with neurological signs may show no
abnormalities or a mixed pleocytosis, variable degrees of
hemorrhage, and increased protein concentration. Eosinophilic
pleocytosis and L1 were reported in the CSF of a dog with CNS
signs secondary to aberrant larval migration. 185
Bronchoalveolar lavage specimens have increased cellularity
with a predominance of neutrophils; eosinophils may also be
present. In one study, L1 were found in 7 of 10 specimens. 176
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Findings on thoracic radiography include interstitial, bronchial,
and/or alveolar lung pa erns with a patchy, peripheral
distribution; mild pleural eﬀusion; pneumothorax; subcutaneous
emphysema; and a widened cranial mediastinum. Right
ventricular enlargement may be evident as well as truncated
pulmonary arteries, but these ﬁndings are more common with
diroﬁlariasis (see Chapter 111). 190
Advanced Imaging
MRI of the brain and spinal cord of dogs with A. vasorum infection
and neurological signs may reveal evidence of intramedullary and

vetexamprep.ir

intraparenchymal hemorrhage, including ill-deﬁned T1isointense, T2-hyperintense lesions and areas of signal void that
are consistent with infarction on T2-weighted image gradient echo
sequences. 186 , 191 In cases where CNS signs have been secondary
to aberrant larval migration, evidence of focal meningitis has been
described, with meningeal thickening and hyperintensity in T2weighted images. 185
Sonographic Findings
Echocardiography can reveal evidence of pulmonary
hypertension with concentric and eccentric right ventricular
hypertrophy, right atrial dilation, tricuspid valve regurgitation,
pulmonic valve insuﬃciency, and a bulging interatrial septum. In
one dog, a ruptured chordae tendineae was evident as a systolic
ﬂail of the anterior leaﬂet of the tricuspid valve, which
represented the ﬁrst report of tricuspid valve chordae tendineae
rupture in any dog. 192 Abdominal ultrasonography may reveal
ascites and distended hepatic veins in dogs with right-sided
congestive heart failure.
Parasitological Tests
Adult worms may be identiﬁed at necropsy. They are
approximately one-tenth the size of adult D. immitis; males are 14
to 18 mm long, with visible bursa, bursal rays, and spicules and
females are 18 to 25 mm long and have the “barber’s pole”
appearance that has been described for Haemonchus spp. (Fig.
117.14). 172 L1, the form shed in the feces, can be detected using
the Baermann technique on feces and respiratory lavage
specimens and are occasionally detected in the CSF or eye. They
are 340 to 399 µm long, have an anterior cephalic bu on, and their
tail ends with a marked kink with a dorsal spine (Fig. 117.15). In
contrast, Crenosoma vulpis larvae have a straight tail and Oslerus
spp. and Filaroides spp. larvae have a kinked tail but lack the
dorsal spine. Because the larvae are highly motile, accurate
identiﬁcation requires the immobilization of the L1 in order to
examine them in detail. This can be achieved by the application of
a drop of diluted Lugol’s iodine (1:10) to the edge of the coverslip.
Zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation may also reveal larvae, but is only 60%
sensitive compared with the Baermann technique. Because the

vetexamprep.ir

Baermann technique is time-consuming, a direct smear, which
may detect L1 in about half of the infections, can be used in order
to rapidly assess for larvae initially. If the direct smear is negative,
a Baermann examination should be done. Regardless of the
method used, false-negative results can occur as a result of
intermi ent excretion of larvae in the feces. Examination of
multiple (at least three) fecal specimens collected over a 7- to 10day period or daily for 3 consecutive days can increase sensitivity.
With the availability of tests for circulating antigen and PCR
assays, which can be used in combination with fecal examination,
the requirement for serial fecal examinations may be reduced.

Serologic Diagnosis
Sensitive and speciﬁc ELISA assays have been developed for
detection of circulating antigens and antibodies to A. vasorum and
can detect infection before 7 weeks PI, the period of patency.
These assays have been made available by some university
diagnostic laboratories. A rapid (15-minute) POC antigendetection assay is also available in Europe (Angio Detect, IDEXX
Laboratories). When applied to 214 dogs with suspected or
conﬁrmed disease, the sensitivity of this assay compared with the
Baermann assay was 97.1% and speciﬁcity was 98.9%; there was
no evidence of cross-reactivity with other common nematode
parasites, including Diroﬁlaria immitis. 193 However, in one study
of experimentally inoculated dogs, the Baermann assay became
positive at 8 weeks, laboratory ELISA antigen assay at 11 weeks,
and the POC assay at 14 weeks after inoculation, so the sensitivity
of the POC assay may be low early in the course of infection. 194
Antibody testing has the potential to be positive with subclinical
infection or in recovered dogs, so may lack predictive value.

The POC assay has been used to look for evidence of other
angiostrongylid infections in domestic cats in Europe that were
either positive or negative (50 cats each) for metastrongyloid
nematodes on Baermann examination, none of which were
positive. Cross-reactivity occurs with antigens of Gurltia

vetexamprep.ir

paralysans, a related metastrongyloid nematode found in domestic
and wild felids in South America. 195 Gurltia paralysans has a
tropism for veins of the subarachnoid space, and causes chronic
eosinophilic meningomyelitis and progressive paraparesis in cats
(gurltiosis).
The POC assay has also been used to monitor resolution of
infection with treatment, 196 but can also remain positive up to 7
weeks after treatment, possibly due to slow elimination of
antigens from dying worms. 194
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Nucleic acid–based assays have been developed to detect A.
vasorum DNA. These have been used to identify the parasite in
gastropod intermediate hosts, as well as to detect infection in
respiratory lavage specimens. In one study, use of a real-time PCR
assay for A. vasorum on bronchoalveolar lavage specimens was
more sensitive than Baermann analysis or detection of circulating
antigen using the IDEXX POC assay. 197
Pathologic Findings
Gross ﬁndings at necropsy include mo led and congested lungs,
multifocal pleural ﬁbrosis, evidence of systemic petechial or
ecchymotic hemorrhages, and adult worms in the pulmonary
arteries (Fig. 117.16A and B). Histopathology of the lungs in dogs
infected with A. vasorum reveals multifocal granulomas in the
periphery of the lungs that is accompanied by hemorrhage,
arterial thrombosis, periarteritis, and with chronicity, ﬁbrosis (Fig.
117.16C and D). Detection of undiﬀerentiated metastrongyloid
eggs together with L1 in histologic sections of the lungs is
considered pathognomonic for A. vasorum infection in the dog.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of A. vasorum infections has most often involved the
use of fenbendazole (20–50 mg/kg PO for 5 to 21 days or 20–25
mg/kg PO for 20 days), topical moxidectin/imidocloprid
(minimum 2.5 mg/kg moxidectin and up to 6.25 mg/kg; minimum
10 mg/kg imidacloprid and up to 25 mg/kg; one or two monthly
treatments), or milbemycin oxime (0.5 mg/kg PO once weekly for
4 weeks). 190 Use of the la er two protocols represents licensed
use in Europe. In addition, supportive care measures are often
needed depending on clinical signs present, such as intravenous
ﬂuids, blood products, supplemental oxygen, anticonvulsants,
treatment for congestive heart failure (diuretics, angiotensinconverting enzyme inhibitors), and sildenaﬁl.

Immunity and Prevention
On recovery from infection, dogs are not immune and can
experience repeated infections. Repeated infection also has been
documented experimentally. 190 No vaccine is available.
Prevention relies on minimizing access to slugs and snails as well
as regular treatment with prophylactic anthelmintics. Licensed
prophylactic
treatments
in
Europe
are
topical
moxidectin/ivermectin or oral milbemycin oxime in combination
products. A single dose of a moxidectin (24 µg/kg) in combination
with sarolaner (1.2 mg/kg) and pyrantel (5 mg/kg) (Simparica
Trio, Zoetis) had a 95% eﬃcacy in prevention of development of

vetexamprep.ir

immature adults in dogs experimentally infected with A. vasorum;
doses of 3 mg/kg and 12 mg/kg had eﬃcacies of 7.2% and 54.5%,
respectively. 198 Milbemycin oxime (0.75 to 1.0 mg/kg, PO) in
combination with spinosad had an eﬃcacy of 98.8% when
administered 30 days after exposure to A. vasorum. 199

Public Health Aspects
Angiostrongylus vasorum does not infect humans.

Non-Metastrongyloid Nematode Infections Of
The Respiratory Tract
Eucoleus Aerophilus And Eucoleus Boehmi
Infection (Eucoleosis/Capillariasis)
Eucoleus aerophilus and Eucoleus boehmi (previously Capillaria spp.;
the species name Capillaria aerophila was revised to Eucoleus
aerophilus) are trichuroid nematodes with a worldwide
distribution that infect the lower and upper respiratory tract,
respectively. Infection with E. aerophilus occurs in dogs, cats, and
various wild animals; E. boehmi infection only occurs in dogs and
wild canids. Adult worms are embedded in the mucosal
epithelium—E. aerophilus in the trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles;
and E. boehmi in the turbinates of the nasal cavity. The life cycle of
both nematode species is incompletely described although
earthworms have been proposed as a possible intermediate host
for E. boehmi. 200 Adults mate and produce bipolar-plugged eggs
that are coughed up, swallowed, and passed unembryonated in
the feces. Most infections appear to be subclinical, but animals
infected with E. aerophilus may show episodes of non-productive
cough, gagging, retching, tachypnea, and dyspnea. Secondary
bacterial infections may lead to bronchopneumonia and a
productive cough, and death can result from heavy infections. 201
Dogs infected with E. boehmi may show signs of sneezing, reverse
sneezing, and/or nasal discharge. In addition, aberrant migration
of E. boehmi to the CNS was reported in a dog from Texas that was
evaluated for seizures and a possible meningioma based on
ﬁndings on MRI. 202

vetexamprep.ir

Thoracic radiographs in dogs and cats infected with E.
aerophilus may show tracheal narrowing and mixed pulmonary
pa erns if secondary bacterial infection occurs. The nematodes
can be visualized and retrieved for identiﬁcation of adults and
eggs using tracheobronchoscopy (E. aerophilus) or rhinoscopy (E.
boehmi). Identiﬁcation of eggs on centrifugal fecal ﬂotation can
also be used for diagnosis. 3 , 203 The eggs have bipolar plugs,
similar to those of whipworms. Because the eggs of these
nematodes may be misidentiﬁed as Trichuris spp., the true
prevalence of Eucoleus spp. infections in dogs may be
underestimated. Capillarid eggs can be diﬀerentiated from those
of Trichuris spp. based on their morphologic appearance (Table
117.1). The eggs of T. vulpis are larger (72–90 × 32–40 µm) with a
smooth shell wall surface, the plugs are symmetrical on the
longitudinal midline (in most eggs), and the plugs have a series of
“threaded” lines making them appear as if they were “screwed”
into the shell wall (Fig. 117.17A). In contrast, capillarid (Eucoleus
spp.) eggs are smaller, the plugs are asymmetrical on the
longitudinal midline (in most eggs), the plugs lack “threaded”
lines, and there is a surface shell wall pa ern unique to each
species (Fig. 117.17B). Eggs of E. aerophilus are 58–79 × 29–40 µm
in size and the shell wall surface has a net-like pa ern of
interconnected ridges (Fig. 117.18A and B). Eggs of E. boehmi are
54–60 × 30–35 µm in size and the shell wall surface is covered with
small pits (Fig. 117.18C and D). 3 , 4 In addition, a PCR assay that
detects the mitochondrial cox1 gene of nematodes in the subfamily
Capillariinae has been used to identify Eucoleus spp. in stool
specimens and diﬀerentiate them from T. vulpis. 203

There are currently no anthelmintics approved for use in the
treatment of dogs and cats infected with E. aerophilus or dogs
infected with E. boehmi. Eprinomectin, fenbendazole, and
moxidectin have been used to successfully treat cats infected with
E. aerophilus. A single topical application of eprinomectin (0.5
mg/kg) in combination with ﬁpronil, (S)-methoprene, and
praziquantel had an eﬃcacy of 82.4% in cats naturally infected
with E. aerophilus. In a case report involving a single animal,
fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 14 days) was reported as an
eﬀective treatment in a cat; clinical signs resolved after treatment;
however, a second 14-day course was required due to a return of
egg excretion. 204 Eﬃcacies (based on fecal egg counts) of 99.8 to
100% were reported with topical moxidectin (1.0 mg/kg)

vetexamprep.ir

combined with imidicloprid in cats infected with E. aerophilus. 205 ,
206 Fenbendazole and milbemycin oxime have been used to
successfully treat dogs infected with E. aerophilus. Treatment with
fenbendazole (50 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 14 days) resulted in a
clinical cure and the cessation of fecal egg shedding in a dog with
Addison’s disease also infected with E. aerophilus. 207 Negative
fecal examination results occurred after the ﬁrst treatment of eight
dogs infected with E. aerophilus in a 6-month ﬁeld study on
monthly use of milbemycin oxime (0.5–1.0 mg/kg) combined with
afoxolaner. 208 Fenbendazole, ivermectin, and moxidectin have
been used successfully to treat dogs infected with E. boehmi.
Fenbendazole at several dosages (50 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 14 days
or 110 mg/kg q12h for 14 days), ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg, PO, once),
and milbemycin oxime (2 mg/kg, PO, once) have been reported to
be eﬀective in the treatment of dogs infected with E. boehmi. 202 ,
209–211 In several ﬁeld studies using topical moxidectin (2.5–6.25
mg/kg) in combination with imidacloprid to treat dogs naturally
infected with E. boehmi, reported eﬃcacies based on fecal egg
counts were 99 to 99.7% with a single application and 100% after
two applications. 203 A short course of glucocorticoids may be
indicated for animals with severe respiratory diﬃculty to reduce
tracheitis or bronchitis (e.g., prednisolone sodium succinate,
dexamethasone sodium phosphate). There have been several
reports of treatment failures with multiple anthelmintics
(fenbendazole, milbemycin oxime, and moxidectin) in dogs
infected with E. aerophilus and E. boehmi. 212 , 213 Whether failure to
respond adequately to treatment reﬂects reinfection from the
environment or is due to some other factor remains unknown. In
some cases, further treatments are required, as well as eﬀorts to
clean the environment and limit coprophagy by dogs. Posttreatment fecal surveillance to monitor anthelmintic eﬀectiveness
is extremely important in the management of cases of capillarid
infections in both dogs and cats. Rare (< 20) cases of human
infection by E. aerophilus have been reported in the literature. 214
