Case Example
Signalment

“Sass,” a 1-year-old intact female toy poodle from West
Sacramento in northern California.

History

Sass was evaluated at the University of California-Davis VMTH
for a 6-month history of chronic intermi ent cough and gagging
that began 1 month after she was acquired. Episodes of clinical
signs were sometimes associated with inappetence and lethargy
and persisted for several weeks at a time; at least 8 episodes
were reported. The cough was not associated with eating,
drinking, or exercise. Diagnostics performed at several other
veterinary clinics over the course of illness included thoracic
and abdominal radiographs, CBC, chemistry proﬁle, pancreatic
lipase immunoreactivity, and a direct fecal smear and ﬂotation,
all of which had been negative. Sass had also been treated with
clavulanic acid-amoxicillin and doxycycline with mild clinical
improvement.

Current Medications
None

Other Medical History

There was no other known medical history. Sass was an
indoor/outdoor dog and was current on routine vaccinations.
The owner reported feeding a homemade chicken- and ricebased diet with some potato and dry dog food added.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 2.5 kg
Sass was quiet, alert, and responsive; had pale pink mucous
membranes, HR 140 beats/min, RR 30 breaths/min, T = 102°F,
and BCS 5/9. A cough was easily elicited on tracheal palpation.
No other clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were identiﬁed on
physical examination.
Centrifugal zinc sulfate fecal ﬂotation and Baermann
examination: Negative for parasites.

Imaging Findings

Tracheal ﬂuoroscopy: There was no evidence of tracheal
collapse when a cough was elicited. However, dynamic

vetexamprep.ir

narrowing of the mainstem bronchi was noted that was
suggestive of bronchiectasis.
Bronchoscopy: Four soft-tissue nodules were identiﬁed at
the level of the carina (see Fig. 117.11). The remainder of
the respiratory tract was within normal limits.

Cytology Findings

Bronchoalveolar lavage: Total nucleated cell count 1940 cells/µL
with 9% neutrophils, 4% lymphocytes, 16% macrophages, 65%
eosinophils, and 6% mast cells. The cytofuge specimen was
highly cellular with moderate accumulations of mucinous
material in a clear background. Large numbers of eosinophils
were admixed with macrophages, some of which contained
foamy cytoplasmic vacuoles.
Impression smear of nodule biopsy: There were numerous
parasite larvae either free or within eggs in a moderately
cellular background.

Histopathology of Nodule Biopsy (see Fig.
117.12B)

Sections are composed of nodules of extensively inﬂamed
ﬁbrous connective tissue that contains numerous tangential and
cross sections of nematode parasites. The nodules are variably
covered by a pseudostratiﬁed columnar ciliated-to-low
cuboidal epithelium. The nematodes have a pseudocoelomic
body cavity and an intestine. Consistent with metastrongyloids,
the cuticle is smooth, the intestine is composed of a few
multinucleate cells with short microvilli, and the uterus of
female worms contain developing L1. There are a few free
larvae within the inﬂammatory nodules. Many of the
nematodes are surrounded by a dense ﬁbrous capsule.
Inﬂammatory cells include numerous lymphocytes, plasma
cells, and histiocytes that extensively expand the submucosal
ﬁbrovascular connective tissue separating collagen bundles.

Diagnosis

Oslerus osleri infection.

Treatment

Fenbendazole, 50 mg/kg PO q12h for 14 days and butorphanol
(0.05 mg/kg PO up to q8h) for cough. Larvae were not detected

vetexamprep.ir

on zinc sulfate centrifugal ﬂotation and simple sedimentation
fecal examinations performed 2 weeks later and the dog had
improved clinically. The owner was informed that a second
bronchoscopy to re-evaluate the nodules was advisable and
additional treatment may be required. However, 2 days later
she was brought to the emergency room when her owners
found her vomiting and obtunded in their back yard. She was
found to be in hypovolemic shock and was diagnosed with
hemoabdomen. The owners elected euthanasia based on the
guarded prognosis and ﬁnancial concerns.

Comments

This dog was diagnosed with O. osleri infection based on the
presence of nodules that contained parasitic larvae that had
morphology supportive of that diagnosis. Larvae were not
detected in the feces both before and after treatment by any of
the methods employed (Baermann, ﬂotation, sedimentation).
Baermann examination has poor detection sensitivity due to the
moribund state of O. osleri L1 excreted in the feces; the primary
use of the Baermann test in this case was to screen for possible
infection with A. vasorum or C. vulpis. Although zinc sulfate
centrifugal ﬂotation has greater detection sensitivity than the
Baermann examination, it also has a low sensitivity. The most
reliable fecal examination method for detecting O. osleri L1 is
fecal sedimentation. Due to the considerable time and eﬀort
necessary to perform the fecal sedimentation test, it is useful to
a empt to detect the larvae ﬁrst by zinc sulfate centrifugal
ﬂotation. Larvae were also not detected by fecal sedimentation
and this was likely due to the erratic shedding pa ern typical of
metastrongyloids. Had the O. osleri infection diagnosis not been
made by the detection of nodules and larvae on bronchoscopy,
further fecal specimens would have been requested before
ruling out lungworm infection. The cause of the hemoabdomen
was unknown, but the dog was reported to roam freely
outdoors and had access to rodenticide, so anticoagulant
rodenticide toxicity was considered most likely in light of the
signalment and history.

118: Trematodes
Karen F. Snowden, and Jennifer K. Ke is

KEY POINTS
Heterobilharzia americana Infection
(Heterobilharziasis/Canine Schistosomiasis)
• First Described: Heterobilharzia americana was first described
as an adult worm recovered from a bobcat (Lynx rufus) in
1929, and more fully described in specimens from a raccoon
(Procyon lotor) in 1943. The parasite was first reported in
dogs in Louisiana in 1961.
• Cause: Heterobilharzia americana (Platyhelminthes,
Trematoda, Digenea, Strigeidida, Schistosomatidoidea,
Schistosomatidae).
• Affected Hosts: A variety of wildlife hosts, most commonly the
raccoon (P. lotor). Dogs are the most frequently identified
domestic animal hosts, but the parasite has also been shown
to cause disease in horses and llama.
• Intermediate hosts: Freshwater snails in the lymnaeid family,
with Galba (previously Fossaria or Lymnaea), Galba humilis,
and Pseudosuccinia columella confirmed as intermediate
hosts by experimental infection.
• Geographic Distribution: Primarily the southeastern United
States, but the range appears to be expanding.
• Route of Transmission: Penetration of intact skin by the larval
cercarial stage that is released from snails in fresh water.
• Major Clinical Signs: Many infections are subclinical, but the
most frequent signs are chronic or recurrent diarrhea, weight
loss, and sometimes hematochezia in response to adult
parasites in the mesenteric veins and migrating eggs in the
intestinal mucosa. Hepatic fibrosis and pancreatitis can occur

vetexamprep.ir

due to inflammatory changes associated with hematogenously
disseminated eggs in various tissues.
• Differential Diagnoses: Depending on signs, these are a wide
variety of neoplastic, toxic, or infectious/inflammatory causes.
In a case series review, possible differentials included
cholecalciferol toxicity, ethylene glycol toxicity, lymphoma, and
pancreatitis. A variety of infectious pathogens can cause
enteritis and hemorrhagic diarrhea. The differential diagnosis
for hypercalcemia (sometimes present) includes malignancyassociated disease, endocrinopathies, renal failure, or a
variety of infectious or inflammatory diseases.
• Human Health Significance: No human infections with H.
americana have been reported. However, it is possible that
the free-swimming cercarial stage may be able to penetrate
human skin causing “cercarial dermatitis” as reported from the
closely related avian schistosomes found in waterfowl.
Paragonimus kellicotti Infection (Paragonomiasis)
• First Described: Paragonimus kellicotti was described as a
new species by Ward in 1908 after a careful review of eggs
and other parasitologic specimens from humans from different
geographic localities.
• Cause: Over a dozen respiratory trematode species have
been described in dogs and cats on a global basis. In the
United States, Paragonimus kellicotti (Platyhelminthes,
Trematoda, Paragonomidae) is the helminth parasite that
localizes in cystic spaces in the lung parenchyma of dogs and
cats.
• Affected Hosts: Paragonimus spp. infect domestic dogs and
cats, and less frequently are reported in a variety of wildlife
hosts and humans.
• Intermediate hosts: The first intermediate hosts for
Paragonimus spp. are aquatic snails, and the second
intermediate hosts are typically crabs or crayfish, depending
on the parasite species. For P. kellicotti, reported snail
intermediate hosts include Pomatiopsis lapidaria, Pomatiopsis
cincinnatiensis or Oncomelania nosophora, and the crayfish
hosts, Cambarus spp. or Orconectes spp.

vetexamprep.ir

• Geographic Distribution: Various species of Paragonimus are
globally distributed in temperate climates, with P. kellicotti
being the important species in North America.
• Route of Transmission: Mammalian hosts become infected by
ingesting the metacercaria larval stage found in the tissues of
the second intermediate host (crab or crayfish). Ingestion of
infected paratenic hosts may also occur.
• Major Clinical Signs: Paragonimus infections may be
subclinical or may be associated with signs of respiratory
disease, most often intermittent or chronic cough.
• Differential Diagnoses: Paragonimus kellicotti is found in cystic
spaces in the pulmonary parenchyma, so major differential
diagnostic considerations include pulmonary abscesses,
metastatic neoplasia, cavitated neoplasms, and mycotic
pneumonia.
• Human Health Significance: Paragonimus kellicotti is a
zoonotic parasite that causes respiratory disease in humans.
Humans become infected through the ingestion of raw or
undercooked crab or crayfish intermediate hosts, so contact
with dogs or cats does not pose a direct risk to humans.
Platynosomum illiciens Infection (Platynosomiasis)
• First Described: Platynosomum illiciens (synonyms
Platynosomum concinnum and Platynosomum fastosum) was
isolated from civet cat by Braun in 1901 (named Dicrocelium
concinnum) and Felis minuta by Kossack in 1910. Other
potential synonyms are Dicrocelium lanceolatum var
symmetricum and Concinnum concinnum.
• Cause: Platynosomum illiciens (previously Platynosomum
fastosum), a liver fluke of cats, which belongs to the class
Trematoda and family Dicrocoeliidae.
• Affected Hosts: Domestic cats and a variety of wild cats.
Platynosomum spp. also have been found in other hosts (e.g.,
opossums, ferrets, mice, non-human primates, and birds); it is
unclear if these are true or incidental hosts, or if it is P. illiciens
or another species in these hosts.
• Intermediate and paratenic hosts: The first intermediate host
of P. illiciens is a land snail (e.g., Subulina octona). Isopods
(Oniscidea spp. and Nagurus spp.) are considered the

vetexamprep.ir

primary second intermediate host. Paratenic hosts include
reptiles and amphibians (e.g., Anolis spp., Hemidactylus spp.,
Tropidurus spp., Bufo spp.) with mice potentially serving as
paratenic hosts and final hosts.
• Geographic Distribution: Tropical and subtropical regions of
the world, including those in Central and South America, the
Caribbean, Asia, and Africa. In North America, P. illiciens
occurs in Florida; there are no reports of infection in cats from
Europe.
• Route of Transmission: Ingestion of excysted metacercariae in
paratenic hosts or encysted metacercariae in a second
intermediate host.
• Major Clinical Signs: Most infections are subclinical. Clinical
signs are consistent with liver disease and include anorexia,
weight loss, jaundice, vomiting and diarrhea.
• Differential Diagnoses: Differentials include polycystic liver
disease, biliary carcinoma, and other nonparasitic causes of
liver disease. When geographic distribution overlaps or cats
have traveled between endemic areas, differentials include
other fluke species that infect the liver and bile ducts (e.g.,
Opisthorchis felineus).
• Human Health Significance: Platynosomum illiciens is not
considered to be zoonotic.
Alaria spp. Infections
• First Described: The mesocercaria larval stage of Alaria
marcianae was first described by La Rue (1917) in a garter
snake and named Cercaria marcianae. 1 Walton (1949)
proposed the scientific name A. marcianae based on studies
in frogs. 2 The first description of Alaria alata was attributed to
Goeze (1782). Adult Alaria parasites were first described in
naturally infected cats (A. marcianae) and dogs (Alaria canis)
in 1965. 3 Additional species have been described in dogs,
cats, and a number of wildlife hosts, and several parasite
species have been synonymized. Due to challenges in
parasite identification, several clinical reports use only the
genus name (Alaria sp.)
• Cause: Members of the genus Alaria are Diplostomatid
trematode parasites that localize in the small intestine of the

vetexamprep.ir

definitive mammalian host. Multiple species have been
described in the cat and dog, especially Alaria marcianae
(cats) and Alaria alata (dogs).
• Affected Hosts: Domestic dogs, domestic cats, a variety of
wild canids and felids, and other small mammals serve as
definitive hosts.
• First intermediate host: In the United States, planorbid snails
including Heliosoma trivola and Heliosoma campanulatum;
other snail species are first intermediate hosts on other
continents.
• Second intermediate host: In the United States, frogs in the
Ranidae family, including Rana catesbeiana, Rana clamitans,
Rana utricularia, Myla cinerea, and Gastrophryne
carolinensis. Other amphibian intermediate hosts have been
identified for various Alaria spp.
• Paratenic host: A number of nonessential hosts such as
rodents, frogs, garter snakes, feral swine, and domestic
chickens have been described and may be important in
maintaining the parasite until the life cycle is completed in the
carnivore definitive host.
• Geographic Distribution: Temperate climates across North
America from Canada to Louisiana, Mexico, and South
America; Europe; Middle East; and Africa.
• Route of Transmission: Ingestion of an intermediate or
paratenic host that contain mesocercaria.
• Major Clinical Signs: Adult Alaria spp. attach to the small
intestinal mucosa but do not cause signs in dogs and cats. In
other hosts, adult flukes may cause enteritis, and migrating
larval stages may cause damage, inflammation, and
hemorrhage in the lungs or other viscera.
• Differential Diagnoses: Infections are subclinical, so this is not
applicable.
• Human Health Significance: Alaria spp. are generally
considered zoonotic parasites. The migrating larval
mesocercariae may cause serious clinical disease, and
human fatalities have been reported. Humans become
infected by ingesting raw or poorly cooked frogs or paratenic

vetexamprep.ir

hosts, but human association with infected dogs or cats does
not pose a direct transmission risk.

Heterobilharzia Americana Infection
(Heterobilharziasis/Canine Schistosomiasis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Heterobilharzia americana (Platyhelminthes, Trematoda, Digenea,
Strigeidida, Schistosomatidoidea, Schistosomatidae) is a
trematode parasite of wildlife and domestic mammals in North
America, and it is the only species in this genus. 4–9 It was
originally described by Price (1929) who reported an adult worm
in a bobcat (Lynx rufus) in Florida, and was later redescribed from
specimens recovered from a raccoon (Procyon lotor) in Texas. 4 , 5
The parasite was ﬁrst described in dogs in Louisiana in 1961. 6
Heterobilharzia americana belongs to the Schistomatidae family that
includes several species such as Schistosoma mansoni, Schistosoma
haematobium, and Schistosoma japonicum that are of global
importance as “neglected tropical disease” pathogens in humans.
10 Adult worms of the majority of these species infect the blood
vessels of the host intestine, with a few species infecting the
vasculature of other organs. This group of parasites are informally
called “schistosomes” and the clinical infection is often referred to
as “schistosomiasis.”
The life cycle of the parasite is maintained in wildlife and has
been reported most frequently in raccoons, 11 , 12 as well a variety
of other mammals including nutria (Myocastor coypus), swamp
rabbit (Sylvilagus aquaticus), 6 opossum (Didelphis virginianis), 13
beaver (Castor canadensis), 14 and white-tailed deer (Odocoileus
virginianus). 15 Heterobilharzia americana has also been identiﬁed in
various wild carnivores such as coyote (Canis latrans), 16 mink
(Mustela vison), 11 and black bear (Ursus americanus). 12 On
occasion, H. americana also infects horses (Equus ferus caballus) and
zebras (Equus burchelli boehmi). 17 , 18
Cases in dogs have been reported across the southern United
States, including Louisiana, Florida, North Carolina, Kansas,
Arkansas, Georgia, and Texas. 7 , 19–21 The identiﬁcation of cases in

vetexamprep.ir

the last decade from California, Oklahoma, Kansas, Utah, and
Illinois indicates a wider geographic distribution of the parasite
than is generally recognized (Sykes, unpublished observations). 21
, 23 , 24

The life cycle of H. americana requires fresh water for
transmission among hosts (Fig. 118.1). Long slender adult male
and female worms (6 to 12 mm in length) are typically paired in
copula, and reside in the mesenteric veins. Eggs that contain
already developed miracidia are excreted from adult females in
mesenteric veins. The eggs then migrate through the small
intestinal tissue to the gut lumen and are passed in feces. When
eggs are deposited in water, the larval miracidium hatches and
infects the ﬁrst intermediate host, small conical aquatic lymnaeid
snails (Galba (previously Fossaria or Lymnaea) cubensis,
Pseudosuccinia columella, Galba humulis). 25–28 Following asexual
multiplication through two sporocyst larval stages, motile
cercarial larvae are released from the snails into the water and
actively penetrate the intact skin of mammalian hosts. The
prepatent period (PPP) is estimated at 2 to 4 months based on egg
excretion at 61 to 70 days and 65 to 121 days in a small number of
experimentally infected dogs in two studies. 27 , 29 The longevity
of adult Heterobilharzia in the mammalian deﬁnitive host has not
been well studied, but closely related schistosome adult parasites
live an average of 3 to 10 years and have been documented for as
long as 40 years in humans. 10

Only limited information is available on risk factors for canine
schistosomiasis. In one report of 214 cases from Texas, the age
range was 3 months to 17 years (median 5.5 years) with an even
gender distribution. 7 All American Kennel Club breed groups
were represented, with herding and sporting breeds and mixed
breed dogs in the highest numbers. Aﬀected dogs typically have
an outdoor lifestyle with exposure to fresh water sources, which is
consistent with the route of parasite transmission. No signiﬁcant

vetexamprep.ir

seasonality has been noted, but for 12 cases more than one dog in
a household was infected, suggesting that multiple dogs were
exposed to a common infected water source.

Clinical Features
The clinical signs associated with heterobilharziasis range widely
from no clinical signs to signs with a fatal outcome, and various
stages of the parasite life cycle result in a spectrum of clinical
problems. The presence of paired adult parasites in the mesenteric
veins and migration of eggs through the intestinal wall from the
serosa to the intestinal lumen typically results in signs associated
with inﬂammatory intestinal lesions including intermi ent
diarrhea with or without blood and mucus, anorexia/hyporexia,
weight loss of variable duration, and hematochezia. 7 , 8 , 21 , 30–32
Additionally, eggs may be carried by portal circulation to the liver
causing chronic granulomatous inﬂammation and hepatic ﬁbrosis.
7 Less frequently, eggs disseminate hematogenously to other
organs including pancreas, spleen, lungs, lymph nodes, and
kidneys and cause granulomatous inﬂammation resulting in
organ-speciﬁc
problems
such
as
pancreatitis
and
7
,
32–34
glomerulonephritis.
The intensity and duration of infection
impact the spectrum and severity of clinical problems.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of H. americana infections can be challenging because
the parasite infection is under-recognized and the clinical signs
are nonspeciﬁc and varied. Often infection is diagnosed at
necropsy, and sometimes it is considered an incidental ﬁnding
rather than the primary cause of clinical disease or fatality. In one
retrospective case series of 22 dogs, the diagnosis was obtained by
necropsy, histopathology, or fecal examination; in approximately
one third of cases, H. americana infection was an incidental
ﬁnding. 32 In another review of 238 cases, the diagnosis was
conﬁrmed by histopathology, egg identiﬁcation on fecal
examinations, or fecal PCR assays; a number of cases were
positive using multiple methods. 7 In that study, infection was
considered an incidental ﬁnding in 42% of dogs. In another
retrospective evaluation of 60 cases from 2010 to 2019, diagnosis

vetexamprep.ir

was made most commonly by fecal PCR alone (82%) followed by
identiﬁcation of eggs in feces or lesions on histopathology, and
infection considered incidental in 12%. 22
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
Consistent hematologic changes in white or red blood cell counts
are not seen in association with infection with this parasite
although a mild anemia has been noted in a few case reports,
probably secondary to chronic inﬂammation. 20 , 31 , 32 Anemia
was reported in 18% and eosinophil count > 500/µL in 42% of
dogs conﬁrmed to be infected. 22
Serum Chemistry Profile and Urinalysis
The most frequently reported clinical chemistry abnormalities are
hyperglobulinemia
and
a
variable,
but
inconsistent,
hypercalcemia. 7 , 21 , 30–32 , 34 In one case series, more than 40% of
dogs infected with H. americana were hypergammglobulinemic,
while hypercalcemia caused by H. americana was identiﬁed in a
minority (7%) of infected dogs and 17% were hypocalcemic. 22
Parathyroid hormone or parathyroid hormone-related protein
concentrations have been within normal limits or increased. 21 , 30 ,
31 , 34 In some patients with H. americana infection, renal function
is compromised based on increased BUN and/or creatinine
concentrations, or signiﬁcant proteinuria that suggests the
presence of glomerulitis. 7 , 21 , 33 Other clinical chemistry changes
occasionally reported include increased serum liver enzyme
activities (ALT and/or ALP) or hypoalbuminemia. 7 , 12 , 20 , 22 , 32–

35

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Imaging techniques may be suggestive of granulomatous
inﬂammatory tissue changes associated with chronic H. americana
infection. Abdominal radiography can be helpful in documenting
focal mineralized lesions associated with the chronic granulomas

vetexamprep.ir

that may be distributed in the small intestine or other tissues. 21 ,
35 , 36 Hepatomegaly may also be noted. 31
Sonographic Findings
In a few canine case reports, abdominal ultrasonography showed
thickened walls of small intestinal loops or enlarged mesenteric
lymph nodes and splenomegaly. 20 , 21 , 34 In one case series, 8 of
13 infected dogs had hepatic abnormalities on abdominal
ultrasonography. 32 One of the often-noted lesions in chronic
infections are hyperechoic foci in small intestine and sometimes
kidney or liver indicating egg-associated mineralized granulomas.
21 , 31 , 36 , 37

Parasitologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
Detection of eggs using fecal sedimentation test is a simple but
insensitive diagnostic method that can be conducted in a primary
care se ing. 38 Since adult female H. americana intermi ently
produce thin-shelled eggs (clear to golden, round to oval, 74–113 ×
60–80 µm) that are passed in feces, the likelihood of egg detection
is increased if the test is conducted on three or more fecal
specimens collected on diﬀerent days (Fig. 118.2A). Unlike most
trematode eggs, there is no obvious operculum as a distinctive
morphologic feature, but a freshly voided egg contains a
developed miracidium which serves as a distinguishing
characteristic. Since these larval miracidia readily hatch from eggs
in fresh water, it is important to use saline (0.9% to 1.2% NaCl)
rather than water in the fecal sedimentation test. In multiple case
reports, trematode eggs were recovered by sedimentation,
conﬁrming active infections, and often negative tests were
considered as an indicator of successful treatment. 21 , 31
Although eggs can be identiﬁed on a direct fecal smear or saline
wet mount, those methods have very low sensitivity and are not
recommended for diagnosis. 33 In several case reports, no eggs
were recovered by fecal ﬂotation, the most widely used routine
parasitologic fecal screening test. 20 , 21 , 30 These negative results
are not surprising since most trematode eggs are relatively dense
and are not typically recovered by ﬂotation methods.

vetexamprep.ir

Cytologic Diagnosis
Heterobilharzia americana infection can be diagnosed by light
microscopic examination of biopsied tissues retrieved by upper GI
endoscopy, exploratory laparotomy, or FNA. 19–21 , 23 , 31–33
Diagnosis is usually inferred based on the presence of eggs or egg
fragments, or characteristic multifocal granulomatous lesions in
the intestine, liver, or sometimes other tissues. In 24 dogs where
diagnosis of H. americana infection was achieved by biopsy, 7
associated disease was present in 16 dogs, whereas the parasite
was considered an incidental ﬁnding in 8 dogs. Interestingly,
heterobilharziasis was not considered as a diﬀerential diagnosis in
14 of those cases, and biopsies were conducted based on
suspected neoplasia or other hepatic disease. The sensitivity of
biopsies for diagnosis depends on the intensity and distribution of
granulomas and eggs in various tissues and the size of the
specimen collected.

Serologic Diagnosis
Numerous immunologic methods for diagnosis of human
schistosomiasis are described in the scientiﬁc literature. Both
antigen and parasite-speciﬁc antibody detection tests are
commercially available for use in individual cases or in serologic
surveys in humans. 10 Since several antigens have been shown to
be highly conserved among various schistosome species, it is
likely that some of these tests could be adapted for veterinary use.
However, a lack of demand for these tests on a large scale makes
it unlikely that tests validated for use in dogs will be available in
the near future. In an interesting case report, an antigen capture
ELISA detecting schistosome circulating anodic antigen and
designed for human use was positive in a conﬁrmed canine case.
20 Repeated ELISA testing showed a decrease in serum antigen
level following anthelmintic treatment.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
While molecular diagnostic methods are increasingly used for
detection of schistosome parasites in human infections, there is
limited information on the molecular detection of H. americana in
animals. At the time of writing, there is one commercially
available fecal H. americana qPCR test for dogs (Texas A&M
University, Gastrointestinal Laboratory, College Station, TX).
Although commonly used for diagnosis at some academic centers,

vetexamprep.ir

a full description of the methodology, gene target, sensitivity and
speciﬁcity are not available. 21
In another case report, the identity of histologically apparent
parasites was conﬁrmed at necropsy as H. americana. End-point
(conventional) PCR ampliﬁcation and sequencing of a 487 base
pair sequence of the parasite small subunit rRNA gene was
successfully completed using formalin-ﬁxed, paraﬃn-embedded
tissue from liver and small intestine. 35
Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
Commonly reported gross lesions in dogs infected with H.
americana include segmental areas of thickened small intestinal
walls and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. 34 , 35 Other ﬁndings
sometimes include pale, ﬁrm (ﬁbrotic) liver, or pale kidneys with
or without pale, ﬁrm foci of mineralized granulomas. 34 In some
case reports, macroscopic lesions included ﬁrm white areas of
dystrophic mineralization in the heart, thoracic aorta, kidney, or
intercostal muscle. 30 , 35
Histopathologic Findings
The most notable histopathologic ﬁnding in dogs with
heterobilharziasis is granulomatous inﬂammation associated with
eggs that are disseminated in a variety of tissues. In 39 dogs that
were necropsied, the most commonly aﬀected tissues were small
intestine, liver, and pancreas, with occasional egg-associated
lesions in the large intestine and rectum, kidney, and lung. 7 Thinwalled, clear to golden-colored eggs or egg shell fragments are
sometimes visualized microscopically in association with
granulomas in various tissues (Fig. 118.3). In the small intestine,
eggs are sometimes arranged in linear rows as they migrate
through the intestinal wall to enter the lumen. 5 , 35 Sections of
adult parasites may be identiﬁed in veins of the small intestine,
colon, rectum, liver, lung, or pancreas. In addition to granulomas,
local to focally extensive lymphoplasmacytic and sometimes
eosinophilic inﬂammation can be present. Other reported
histopathologic changes include ﬁbrosis, hemosiderin pigment in
macrophages, focal mineralization associated with granulomas,

vetexamprep.ir

and bile duct hyperplasia. In hypercalcemic dogs, dystrophic
mineralization has been noted in the gastric mucosa, cardiac
tissues, and skeletal muscle. 30 , 34 , 35

Treatment and Prognosis
No anthelmintics are label-approved for the treatment of H.
americana infection and current extra-label recommendations are
mostly anecdotal. No data from clinical trials comparing diﬀerent
treatment protocols have been published. Praziquantel and
fenbendazole have been used individually, sequentially, or in
combination in various clinical reports (Table 118.1). In several
cases, praziquantel at varying doses was generally eﬀective. The
canine dose of praziquantel labeled for the control of cestodes (5
mg/kg, PO) is inadequate for treating many trematode infections.
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice for human schistosome
infections (40 to 60 mg/kg, PO, depending on the parasite species).
10 The most signiﬁcant adverse eﬀect of high-dose praziquantel is
GI irritation and vomiting, which can be mitigated by dividing the
daily dose into several treatments and administering the drug
with food.

Immunity and Vaccination
No vaccines are available for canine schistosomiasis, and studies
regarding protective immunity have not been reported.
Reinfection has been noted in multiple clinical cases, so it is
unlikely that dogs develop protective immunity.

Prevention
Based on the mode of transmission, the most obvious way to
prevent infection is to limit dog access to surface water locations
(wading or swimming in water). The lymnaeid snail intermediate
hosts are typically found in shallow, stagnant fresh water such as
persistent puddles and pond edges (not fast-running streams).
They are small, conical snails which may not be obvious based on
casual observation of the aquatic environment. 25 , 26 Since
raccoons are common hosts, the presence of wildlife around a
water source would increase the likelihood of contamination of
the area with egg-containing feces, leading to establishment of the
life cycle. Historically, the use of molluscicides for snail control
was recommended in developing countries as part of human
schistosome control programs, but no such eﬀorts have been
reported in the United States for this parasite. 41

vetexamprep.ir

Public Health Aspects
There are no reports of human infection with adult H. americana,
and the parasite is not considered a zoonotic risk. However, it is
theoretically possible that if larval cercariae have access to
humans who are wading/swimming in fresh water, the parasite
should be able to penetrate intact skin. The transient pruritic rash
called “cercarial dermatitis” is typically a ributed to skin
penetration by the cercariae of avian schistosome parasites that
are associated with ducks and other waterfowl that use the
aquatic environment. 42 It is unknown whether H. americana
cercariae may play a minor role in causing transient cercarial
dermatitis in humans or other mammalian hosts.

Paragonimus Kellicotti Infection
(Paragonomiasis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
On a global basis, a number of trematodes in the genus
Paragonimus and the closely related genera Euparagonimus and
Pagumogonimus infect the respiratory tract of dogs or cats (Table
118.2). 43–45 Various species have been reported in dogs and cats
across the Americas, Africa, and Asia. All have indirect life cycles
involving an aquatic snail ﬁrst intermediate host and a second
intermediate host, usually a crab or crayﬁsh, ingested by the
mammalian deﬁnitive host (Table 118.3). 46 , 47 Ingestion of
infected paratenic hosts may also lead to infection. 48 This chapter
will focus on Paragonimus kellico i, which is geographically
located in much of the eastern half of North America from Canada
to Louisiana, and the Mississippi River basin. 49 , 50
The monoecious (hermaphrodite) adult trematode occurs in the
lung parenchyma of a number of mammalian hosts including
dogs, cats, a variety of wildlife species (skunk, red fox, coyote,
raccoon, bobcat, mink), and rarely humans. 49–51 Adults are
approximately 10 × 5 mm in size, ovoid, with typical oral and
ventral suckers, and are found in pairs within encapsulated cysts
in the lung parenchyma with connections to bronchiole airways.
Operculated eggs are shed from adult ﬂukes, coughed up in
bronchial secretions, swallowed, and passed in feces. The life cycle

vetexamprep.ir

requires fresh water for several stages. When eggs are deposited
in water, the larval miracidium stage develops and hatches from
the egg and infects the ﬁrst intermediate host, aquatic snails
(Pomatiopsis lapidaria, Pomatiopsis cincinnatiensis, Oncomelania
nosophora). 45 , 46 Following asexual replication as sporocyst and
redia stages, cercarial larvae are released into water, penetrate the
second intermediate crayﬁsh host (Cambarus spp., Orconectes spp.),
and develop to metacercaria. 49 The mammalian deﬁnitive host
becomes infected through ingestion of an infected crayﬁsh or
paratenic host such as an infected rodent, so infection is possible
in a dog or cat without direct access to crayﬁsh and fresh water. 48
Metacercariae excyst in the duodenum, penetrate the intestinal
wall into the peritoneal cavity, then migrate through the
abdominal wall and diaphragm to the lungs, where they become
encapsulated and mature into adults. Infections have been
reported to last as long as 4 years in a dog, following a PPP of 5 to
7 weeks. 49 Human infections with the parasite have been
reported to persist for several decades. 50

Most descriptions of P. kellico i infections in dogs and cats are
included in the literature as case reports, and li le information on
risk factors is available. In a Louisiana survey of domestic cats
with respiratory tract disease, 3 of 65 cats with clinical signs were
infected with P. kellico i, whereas 0 of 65 control cats were
infected. 52 In a 5-year survey of parasitic infections in dogs and
cats from New Jersey that was published in 1965, eggs of P.
kellico i were identiﬁed in three cats and one dog. 45 In a survey of
123 stray adult dogs from Michigan from 1964, P. kellico i was
identiﬁed in a single animal. 44

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical Features
In dogs or cats, P. kellico i infections are often subclinical. Longlived adult ﬂukes localize in cystic spaces in lung parenchyma
and intermi ently shed eggs into the bronchial tree. Clinical
disease in naturally infected dogs is characterized by a chronic or
intermi ent cough, which may be productive with frothy white
sputum. 53 , 54 A mild, intermi ent cough was the most frequently
reported clinical sign in experimentally infected dogs. 55 Similarly,
infected cats may have a mild cough. 56 In a study of 10 infected
client-owned cats, the predominant reason for evaluation was
cough. 57 In another feline case series, four of ﬁve infected cats
were seen with a history of cough lasting from 3 days to 1 year. 58
Over time, exercise or exertion may exacerbate the cough in some
animals. Infrequently, parasitic cysts may rupture causing acute
pneumothorax, sometimes with sudden death. 55 , 59–61

Most animals are afebrile with an adequate appetite and normal

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of pulmonary paragonimiasis is usually based on
recognition of suggestive lesions on thoracic radiographs.

vetexamprep.ir

Conﬁrmation of the infection is usually based on detection of
Paragonimus eggs in fecal specimens or respiratory secretions.
Laboratory Abnormalities
CBC and serum chemistry test results are often within normal
limits in naturally and experimentally infected cats and dogs. 62–64
In a case series of 10 infected cats, leukocyte counts ranged from
normal to slightly high, sometimes with a neutrophilia or an
eosinophilia. 57 Serum chemistry results for total protein
concentration, BUN, and serum ALT activity in those cats were
within normal limits. In a single canine case report, total serum
protein was elevated with a hyperglobulinemia and
hypoalbuminemia. 53 Secondary pneumonia in association with
Paragonimus infection may be associated with elevated WBC
counts and neutrophilia. 59
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Cystic structures containing adult parasites are radiographically
detectable on thoracic radiographs in both dogs and cats. 53 , 59 , 62
, 65 Lesions are described as interstitial nodular opacities or as
thin-walled cavitated pulmonary cystic structures, usually
ranging from 2 to 5 cm in diameter. Air-ﬁlled cysts containing
adult parasites may be multilocular. The caudal lung lobes are
most frequently aﬀected. 59 Other abnormalities include
secondary pneumonia, peribronchial inﬁltrates, or rarely
pneumothorax due to rupture of a cyst. Diﬀerential diagnoses
include pulmonary abscesses, metastatic neoplasia, cavitated
neoplasms, and mycotic pneumonia. 58 Findings on thoracic CT
have been described in human patients and include peripheral
lung nodules that are 1 to 3.5 cm in size with peripheral ground
glass opacity. Sometimes linear tracks may be seen connecting
nodules to the pleural surface. 66 One dog seen at the editor’s
institution had a solitary soft tissue spherical mass in the right
dorsal aspect of the accessory lung lobe. The mass was adjacent to
the pleura, associated with the bronchus and had a medial
mineralized portion (Fig. 118.4A and B).

Parasitologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal Examination
Deﬁnitive diagnosis of P. kellico i infection is made by detection of
the oval, yellow-brown operculated egg (74–118 × 42–67 µm) in
feces or respiratory secretions (Fig. 118.2B). 35 Eggs have a
distinctive lip or ridge along the edge of the operculum,
sometimes described as “ﬂask-shaped,” that is a key diagnostic
feature. When evaluating fecal specimens, the eggs are dense and
are diﬃcult to detect in fecal ﬂotation tests, so a fecal
sedimentation test is the parasitologic method of choice. Eggs are
excreted intermi ently; a single fecal sedimentation test has a low
sensitivity and multiple tests on multiple fecal specimens may
increase the likelihood of egg detection.
Cytologic Diagnosis
Although adult ﬂukes in lung parenchymal cysts are not
visualized on bronchoscopy, characteristic “ﬂask-shaped” eggs
may be detected by cytologic evaluation of bronchial lavage
secretions. 53
Serologic Diagnosis and Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
No immunodiagnostic tests have been reported as diagnostic tools
for detection of P. kellico i infection in dogs or cats. The use of
several experimental immunodiagnostic assays for Paragonimus
westermani, Paragonimus siamensis, or Paragonimus heterotremus has
been described in scientiﬁc literature to detect antibody
production in experimentally infected cats. 67 , 68 Similarly, PCRbased assays have been used experimentally to detect P.
heterotremus DNA in feces of experimentally infected cats, but the
use of molecular tests that detect P. kellico i DNA has not been
reported for diagnostic purposes in dogs or cats. 69 , 70
Pathologic Findings
At necropsy, subpleural cystic lesions up to several centimeters in
size may be visualized as raised dark reddish-brown nodules on
the lung surface, or may be located deeper in the lung
parenchyma. On cut section, the nodules have a thin, dense
ﬁbrotic capsule and usually contain one or two adult ﬂukes along

vetexamprep.ir

with a small amount of brownish ﬂuid (Fig. 118.5). 59 Bronchial
lymph nodes may or may not be enlarged. Pulmonary areas
adjacent to the parasitic nodules are usually grossly and
histologically normal. Histologically, parasitic cystic structures are
composed of ﬁbrous capsular tissue with a variable collection of
mixed inﬂammatory inﬁltrate cells including macrophages,
plasma cells, and eosinophils surrounding the cyst wall (Fig.
118.6). 65 , 71 Sometimes eggs may also be visualized in the lung
parenchyma or small bronchioles surrounded with a localized
granulomatous inﬂammatory inﬁltrate.

Treatment and Prognosis
No anthelminthics are label-approved for the treatment of
Paragonimus spp. infection in dogs or cats. However, praziquantel,
fenbendazole, and albendazole have been reported to be eﬀective
in a variety of studies (Table 118.4). Multiday treatment of dogs or
cats with praziquantel administered at higher than the labeled
dose has been generally reported as successful. 54 , 64 , 72 , 73 The
most signiﬁcant adverse eﬀect of high-dose praziquantel is GI
irritation and vomiting, which may be mitigated by dividing the
the daily dose into several treatments and administering the drug
with food. The recommended treatment for human
paragonimiasis is also praziquantel (25 mg/kg, q8h, for 3 days). 50

Successful, multiday, high-dose fenbendazole treatment has
also been reported in naturally infected cats and experimentally
infected dogs. 63 , 74 Similarly, albendazole administered in
varying doses for a prolonged period has been reported as
eﬀective in a small number of experimentally infected cats and in
one naturally infected dog (see Table 118.4). 75 , 76 Albendazole is
not label-approved for use in dogs or cats and can induce aplastic
anemia, so alternative therapies are suggested.

Immunity and Vaccination
No vaccines are available for paragonomiasis, and studies
regarding protective immunity have not been reported.

Prevention

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention of paragonomiasis is focused on limiting dog and cat
access to crayﬁsh and their aquatic habitat, as well as paratenic
hosts such as rodents. Since a variety of wild mammals can serve
as reservoir hosts, proximity to wildlife associated with ponds or
streams increases the likelihood that the parasite life cycle will
become established in a local environment.

Public Health Aspects
Pulmonary paragonimiasis is considered a foodborne infection
that aﬀects as many as 23 million people, primarily in Asia and
Africa. 51 Most of these infections are a ributed to P. westermani or
other closely related species. 51 , 77 A limited number of
autochthonous cases of North American paragonimiasis have
been described in humans caused by P. kellico i infection and
associated with ingestion of raw or undercooked crayﬁsh. 51 , 78
Clinical disease in humans ranges from asymptomatic to serious
respiratory disease, with similar clinical expression as the disease

vetexamprep.ir

in dogs and cats. Eosinophilic meningitis has also been reported.
79

Frequency of transmission in humans depends on dietary habits
since mammalian deﬁnitive hosts, including humans, become
infected by ingesting metacercaria in crab or crayﬁsh intermediate
hosts. Therefore, although P. kellico i is considered a parasite with
zoonotic potential, direct or indirect contact with infected pets or
mammalian wildlife poses no direct risk to humans.

Platynosomum Illiciens (Previously Fastosum)
Infection (Platynosomiasis)
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology
Platynosomum illiciens (previously fastosum) belongs to the family
Dicrocoeliidae and is synonymous with Platynosomum concinnum
and Platynosomum fastosum. While most literature has used
“fastosum” for infections in mammals and “illiciens” for infections
in birds, molecular studies indicate these are the same with the
trematode having a low host speciﬁcity. The name P. illiciens has
been recommended rather than P. fastosum and so will be used
from this point onwards. 80–85 Adult P. illiciens is found in the
intrahepatic biliary ducts of the ﬁnal host, domestic cats and a
variety of wild cats, 86–88 and other hosts including non-human
primates, opossums, birds of prey and parrots, 84 with no
predilection for a speciﬁc hepatic lobe or lobule, and the
gallbladder. 89 In heavy infections, adult trematodes also can be
found within the pancreatic ducts, small intestine, and lungs. 87 ,
88 , 90 Mature P. illiciens are 2.1 to 8 mm long and 0.5 to 2.5 mm
wide (Fig. 118.7). 81 , 91 , 92 The location of the testes, ventral
sucker, ovaries, and vitelline glands can be used to distinguish P.
illiciens from other ﬂukes in the biliary system in areas where
more than one species is endemic (Fig. 118.7 and Table 118.5). 81

vetexamprep.ir

The eggs, which are smaller than those produced by many
other ﬂuke species, are light brown, more oval than round,
approximately 30 × 50 µm, and have an operculum that can be
obscure (Fig. 118.8). 81 , 88 Damaged and immature eggs also occur
in feces. Damaged eggs are shrunken and clear to pink; and
immature eggs are clear, more ovoid, and smaller (16–20 × 27–30
µm). 88 , 92
The life cycle of P. illiciens is indirect and utilizes two
intermediate hosts and several paratenic hosts (Fig. 118.9). 81 , 93–95
Cats become infected when they ingest excysted metacercariae in
a paratenic host or encysted metacercariae in the second
intermediate host. Metacercariae are released in the intestine and
the immature ﬂukes travel to the common bile duct and within 3

vetexamprep.ir

days develop a digestive tract. In the following weeks, the ﬂuke
increases in size and the reproductive tract develops. Full
maturity is reached in 8 to 12 weeks. Mature adult P. illiciens
release 10 to 100 eggs per day which are stored within the gallbladder, released with bile into the GI tract, and excreted in feces.
81 The life span of P. illiciens can be > 1.5 years. 89
Eggs are ingested by land snails (primarily Subulina octona but
also Eulota similaris), the ﬁrst intermediate host, resulting in the
release of miracidia which move to the snails’ connective tissues
surrounding the respiratory tract. In the respiratory cavity,
sporocysts develop resulting in cercariae. The cercariae release a
glandulous ﬂuid that helps the sporocysts exit the snail and reenter the environment via the respiratory tract or the tunica
propria, killing the snail in the process. Moisture and decreased
light signal the exit of the sporocysts. A snail on average releases
7.6 sporocysts (approximately 134 cercariae) with the process
from miracidium to sporocyst release requiring approximately 60
days. 81 , 89 , 91 , 96
Isopods are considered the most likely second intermediate
hosts. 81 , 89 , 91 , 96 These are tiny terrestrial crustaceans
(woodlice), speciﬁcally Oniscidea sp. (“roly-polys”) and Nagurus
sp. (e.g., the “greenhouse woodlouse”). These consume cercariae
in the environment, which then mature to metacercariae and
encyst. Cats can become infected if they consume isopods,
although most infections are believed to originate from the
consumption of a paratenic host. In paratenic hosts the
metacercariae excyst and reside in the hepatic and biliary systems.
For many years, lizards, particularly Anolis spp. lizards (anoles),
were considered an obligate paratenic host, resulting in the
common name of “lizard poisoning” for platynosomiasis.
Subsequent work has shown that several other lizard species (e.g.
Tropidurus spp., Hemidactylus spp., Lygosoma metallicum), toads
(Bufo spp.), frogs (Eleutherodactylus spp.), and, potentially, mice
also can serve as paratenic hosts. 81 , 89 , 91 , 96–98 There are few
studies on the prevalence and impact of metacercariae in
paratenic hosts. A study from Puerto Rico found > 30% of Anolis
spp. lizards examined to be infected (mean number of 16
metacercariae) with heavy infections (e.g., >300 metacercariae)
associated with hyperplasia of the bile duct and atrophy of the
gallbladder. 81

vetexamprep.ir

g

Platynosomum illiciens can be found in cats in the Caribbean and
other tropical and subtropical regions of the world, including
Central and South America, southern areas of North America,
Asia, and Africa. 88 , 90 , 93–95 , 99–102 In Australia, P. illiciens was
found in cats in quarantine and treatment was pursued to prevent
importation of the parasite. 103 In North America, P. illiciens
occurs in Florida and Texas in the United States. It also has been
found in cats outside of these regions such as in Ohio, Illinois, and
Oklahoma within the United States; and Siberia, Russia. In some
of these cases, the cats have originated from endemic areas. 104 , 105
However, travel was not demonstrated in all cases indicating that
P. illiciens might have the potential to be present in or spread to
nonendemic areas. This is supported by the presence of the
trematode in non-feline hosts in areas where P. illiciens is not
considered endemic in felids.

Within endemic areas, there are few recent studies on
prevalence of infection in cats. Studies from St. Ki s in the
Caribbean suggest that 22% of owned cats (indoor/outdoor and
indoor only) and 81% of free-roaming cats are infected, with other
Caribbean islands reporting a prevalence of <15% to >80%. 88 , 100 ,
102 The prevalence in Brazil has been reported as <3% to >42%; in
Yucatan, Mexico as 45%; and in diﬀerent Asian countries, <1% to
73%. 1 , 88 , 106 , 107 Because paratenic hosts can gain access to
homes, both indoor and outdoor cats are at risk for infection. 102 ,

108

Infection burden ranges from 1 to >4,000 ﬂukes with average
burden of 202 in St. Ki s and 110 in Yucatan; approximately one
fourth of cats have high-burden infections (>125 ﬂukes). 92 , 95
Older cats are more likely to be infected than younger cats, and
some studies have suggested that female cats are more likely to be
infected than male cats, a diﬀerence a ributed to hunting
behavior to feed oﬀspring. 95 , 109
While domestic and wild cats have been considered to be the
deﬁnitive ﬁnal host, other animals can be infected. Mice (Mus
musculus) and birds (Australian parakeets, Melopsi acus undulatus)
have been successfully experimentally infected with P. illiciens
metacercariae, although the infection establishment level was
lower than in cats. 89 , 91 , 96 Platynosomum adults also have been
found in opossums (Didelphis virginiana), ferrets (Grisson vi atus),
skunks (Spilogale putorius), North American hawks (Buteo
platypterus), and nonhuman primates (marmosets, [Callithrix
jachhus], orangutans [Pongo pygmaeus], monkeys [Macaca spp.]). 93 ,
97 , 110–115 Molecular studies now suggest that all of these hosts
contain the same species of Platynosoumum, indicating that the
distribution is much larger then previously deﬁned.

Clinical Features

vetexamprep.ir

Most cats are subclinically infected and signs, when they do occur,
are nonspeciﬁc. The presence of the ﬂukes in the biliary system is
associated
with
hepatic
cirrhosis,
cholangitis,
and
cholangiohepatitis. The occurrence of clinical signs are related to
the parasitic load within the biliary system, level of continuous
exposure to infection, chronicity of infection, and the cats’
individual reaction to the parasite. 109 Increasing liver and biliary
tract pathology result in general malaise, poor body condition,
anorexia, weight loss, alopecia, vomiting, diarrhea, emaciation,
dehydration, anemia, enlarged abdomen, hepatic encephalopathy,
and progressive icterus. 89 , 109 , 116–119 On physical examination,
hepatomegaly can be palpable.
While few studies have been conducted on the pathogenesis of
P. illiciens infection, much can be extrapolated from the more
studied liver ﬂukes such as Clonorchis spp., Opisthorchis spp.,
Dicrocoelium spp., and Fasciola hepatica. Immature and adult ﬂukes
cause mechanical destruction of liver tissue via migration,
a achment, and feeding. Localized toxic reactions and localized
inﬂammatory reactions occur with ﬂuke excretion/secretion
products leading to eosinophilia. Fluke maturation and growth
leads to bile duct dilation and adenomatous hyperplasia with duct
dilation contributing to parenchymal cell damage and altered
duct walls resulting in blood leakage. Younger ﬂukes are believed
to reside in the intrahepatic biliary ducts with more mature and
larger ﬂukes migrating to the extrahepatic biliary ducts. 91 As the
ﬂukes mature and their growth rate decreases, ﬁbrotic connective
tissues around the bile duct decrease bile and ﬂuke
excretion/secretion product ﬂow into the parenchymal tissue
limiting parenchymal tissue pathology.
Partial mechanical obstruction of the common bile duct or
irritation of the common bile duct resulting in dyskinesia causes
bile retention. Bile stagnation is believed to result in an
environment conducive to secondary bacterial infections;
however, li le is known about secondary bacterial infection with
P. illiciens infection. 88 , 97 , 109 , 110 , 120 With Clonorchis spp.
infections, development of biliary calculi also has been a ributed
to bile stagnation and these are considered a factor in the
occurrence of cholangiocarcinoma. While choleliths have not been
identiﬁed in P. illiciens infections, cholangiocarcinomas have been
noted, albeit rarely.

vetexamprep.ir

In experimental infections that involve a single exposure,
clinical signs have not been seen during the early stages of
infection. Approximately 2 months PI, lethargy, inappetence,
slight weight loss, and abdominal distension have been
documented with exposure to large numbers of trematodes,
although most clinical signs resolved by 4 months PI with the cats
remaining subclinical for up to an additional year. Less is known
about progression of clinical signs during natural, continuous
exposure. Natural infections of cats with > 125 ﬂukes have been
classiﬁed as high-intensity infections, with infection associated
with pathology and clinical signs. Conversely, cats with > 1,000
ﬂukes have been subclinical. It is possible that diﬀerences in
pathology and clinical signs might diﬀer between cats infected by
consumption of a few paratenic hosts with a high number of
metacercariae compared with those that develop more chronic
infections as they consume many paratenic hosts that each harbor
only a few metacercariae.

Diagnosis
Fecal analysis is the recommended method for diagnosis of
platynosomiasis. 88 , 121 However, the number of eggs recovered
might not reﬂect the intensity of infection and negative fecal
specimens can occur in heavy infections where there is partial or
complete occlusion of bile ducts. 87 , 102 , 121 Bile collected using
percutaneous ultrasound-guided cholecystocentesis can be used
as an alternative to fecal specimen for retrieval of eggs and might
be a more sensitive method. 122 Laboratory ﬁndings, abdominal

vetexamprep.ir

ultrasound examination, and liver biopsy also can be useful for
assessing the extent of liver damage but do not reveal ﬁndings
speciﬁc for P. illiciens infection. 114 , 118 At necropsy, adult P.
illiciens can be recovered from the liver and/or gallbladder and
eggs can be found in bile.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Routine bloodwork can assist in determining the cause of liver
disease and assessment of the extent of liver damage. The
leukogram may be normal; however, an inﬂammatory leukogram
with eosinophilia is a common ﬁnding, and occasionally a
neutrophilia. 88 , 119 Anemia can be present in some infected cats.
119 Increased activities of serum AST and ALT can occur 4 to 5
months after infection and are indicative of cholestasis and
hepatocyte damage. 88 , 108 , 110 , 118 , 119 Serum ALP activity may
be normal, which is not unusual for cats even with severe or
obstructive cholestastic disease. 123 Serum total bilirubin and bile
acid concentrations may be increased in proportion to the severity
of the infection. Serum pancreatic enzyme activities can also
increase with P. illiciens invasion.
Diagnostic Imaging
The results of abdominal ultrasound examination are nonspeciﬁc
in cats infected with P. illiciens, with some studies ﬁnding no
signiﬁcant abnormalities of the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver of
infected cats. 87 , 123 , 124 However, in endemic areas and when P.
illiciens infection is suspected, changes in these structures would
support examining multiple fecal specimens or bile for eggs.
Changes that have been noted include distention of the
gallbladder with a hyperechoic wall, distended and tortuous bile
ducts and common bile duct, and hepatomegaly. 114 , 123–126 In one
case study, cystic structures consistent with intrahepatic biliary
duct dilatation were observed. 108 While P. illiciens can invade the
pancreas, ultrasonographic changes to the pancreas have not been
described. 126 Some relationship between intensity of infection
and pathologic changes detected with ultrasound has been noted,
but changes are likely also to be related to the chronicity of the
infection. 109 , 123–125

vetexamprep.ir

Parasitologic Tests
Diagnosis Using Fecal or Bile Examination
Two fecal diagnostic methods for egg recovery have been
proposed as the “gold-standard” for diagnosis of platynosomiasis:
traditional formalin-ether sedimentation and the more sensitive
double centrifugation (500 g for 5 minutes) with Sheather’s sugar
ﬂotation solution (SpG ≥ 1.27). 94 , 100 , 121 , 127 , 128 Safety issues
with the use of formalin-ether solutions make this method less
desirable, and centrifugation and ﬂotation also permit
identiﬁcation of a greater variety of other parasites. 129 Falsenegative results can occur due to intermi ent egg excretion in
feces, biliary obstruction, and low numbers of eggs in general. 89 ,
118 , 130 Multiple fecal analyses, as well as complementary
diagnostics should be performed before eliminating P. illiciens
infection as a cause of liver disease in cats.

Light microscopic examination of bile can be a more sensitive
diagnostic method than fecal analysis. Use of 10 to 20 µL in a
direct smear preparation is considered suﬃcient to identify eggs
(Fig. 118.8B). 102 , 122 , 130 In severe platynosomiasis, few to no eggs
may be found in feces due to biliary obstruction, but are present
in bile. 118 Bile collection, via percutaneous ultrasound-guided
cholecystocentesis, can be safely performed in P. illiciens–positive
cats even in cases when severe pathology of the gallbladder is
present. 122
Pathologic Findings
At necropsy, P. illiciens adults can be collected from the liver and
gallbladder. To recover the parasites, the liver can be cut into
pieces (approximately 1 to 2 cm) and massaged and washed over
a sieve. The gallbladder also can be opened and washed over a
sieve to retrieve adult ﬂukes. Bile can be collected and a direct
smear viewed using a 10× objective (100× magniﬁcation) for
identiﬁcation of eggs, which can be more sensitive than adult
trematode collection. 123
Gross pathologic ﬁndings include icterus, hepatomegaly, an
accentuated hepatic parenchymal lobular or reticular pa ern,
intraparenchymal parasitic cysts, biliary obstruction, a distended
gallbladder, ascites (usually a transudate), and abdominal
lymphadenomegaly (Fig. 118.10). 88–90 , 95 , 104 , 105 , 108 , 116 , 119 ,
130–132 Cholangiocarcinomas and polycystic livers have been
described in a few cats. 108 , 131 , 133
Histologic ﬁndings include: atrophy and fa y inﬁltration of
hepatocytes, hepatic and biliary duct ﬁbrosis, hyperplasia of
epithelium lining biliary tubules, and inﬁltration by eosinophils,
lymphocytes, plasma calls, and neutrophils. 89 , 109 , 116–119 , 130–134
Ultimately, this is associated with increasingly severe cholangitis
and nonsuppurative cholangiohepatitis. If cholangiocarcinomas
develop, metastasis to other organs may follow. 130 , 133

Treatment and Prognosis
The treatment of choice for platynosomiasis is praziquantel (20–40
mg/kg, PO, q24h for 3–10 days). This use and dose is extra-label
but within tested safety limits for healthy cats. Adverse events

vetexamprep.ir

may include GI irritation causing vomiting, diarrhea, and
salivation. Praziquantel disrupts the tegument of ﬂukes causing
permeability alterations in the membrane, disintegration of the
tegument, and spastic paralysis. 135–137 The antigen presentation of
the trematode to the host changes, permi ing it to be recognized
by the host immune system; hence the host’s immune system can
work synergistically with the treatment to eliminate the infection.
136 , 137 Disintegration of the tegument and spastic paralysis
results in increased release of eggs with corresponding higher
fecal egg counts after treatment. In most P. illiciens infections, if
there are no signs of liver failure, prognosis is good with
praziquantel treatment. Prognosis is poor in cats with diﬀuse liver
pathology and with clinical signs of liver failure, with euthanasia
being the outcome in many case studies. 99 , 108 , 118 , 119 Immature
ﬂukes may be more resistant to treatment, so treatment may need
to be repeated 2 to 12 weeks later. 88 , 137–139 Drugs found
insuﬃcient to treat P. illiciens infections include fenbendazole,
mebendazole, levamisole, thiabendazole, diamphenethide,
rafoxanide, and pyrantel pamoate. 89 , 103 , 134
The eﬃcacy of the praziquantel dose and dosing regimen is
based on case series rather than on controlled studies. In one
study, ﬁve cats infected with adult mature ﬂukes were treated
with a single dose of praziquantel at 20 mg/kg, after which they
appeared to be cured. 103 The use of 10 mg/kg for 3 consecutive
days resulted in reversal of clinical signs in mildly to moderately
ill cats. 90 In a ﬁeld study with seven cats, 20 mg/kg, q24h, for 3
days and repeated 3 months later resulted in cure, although the
assessment of cure was based on single fecal egg counts following
formalin-ether sedimentation. 140
Oral administration of 20 mg/kg praziquantel can be
challenging for the pet owner. Also, in high-burden infections,
mass trematode death has the potential to cause acute bile duct
blockage, which may worsen outcome. Alternative regimens of 20
mg/kg, IM, q24h, for 3 days or lower doses of praziquantel have
been investigated with limited success. 92 In a study of six
naturally infected cats with immature and adult ﬂukes,
praziquantel at 20 mg/kg, IM, for 3 days cured three cats based on
ﬂuke counts performed at necropsy 10 days after treatment. Two
of the remaining cats had low-burden infections (1–2 ﬂukes) and

vetexamprep.ir

one cat had 40 ﬂukes. 92 Adverse events from injection
administration may include pain and/or swelling at the site of
injection, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle tremors, weakness or
lassitude, and anorexia. In addition, in a small study where one
cat received 27 mg/kg, gross muscle pathology was noted at the
injection site (paralumbar muscle) at necropsy. Histopathology
revealed focal rhabdomyositis with evidence of myoﬁber
regeneration. 92
A dose of 5 mg/kg (the labeled dose of praziquantel, although
the use is extra-label) administered twice at a 2- to 4-week interval
has been proposed. In a case study, fecal egg excretion ceased
after the initial dose but recommenced weeks later. After a second
5-mg dose, fecal egg count remained negative over an 8-month
monitoring period. 141 In a study of six cats with natural infections
(unknown ﬂuke maturity), none of the cats were cured, based on
ﬂuke counts at necropsy, after being administered 5 mg/kg, twice,
2 weeks apart. However, egg counts and ﬂuke burden decreased.
100 An advantage of this dose is that fewer tablets are
administered and products in which praziquantel is combined
with nematicides could be used, increasing the options available
in a clinical se ing. While this lower dose can be more convenient
to administer, without further proof of eﬃcacy it should be used
with caution.
Regardless of the dose and regimen used, eﬃcacy of treatment
should be assessed, since chronic infections contribute to ongoing
hepatobiliary damage. Fecal egg counts to assess eﬃcacy should
not be performed until 14 days after treatment. As a result of slow
release from the bile or a few surviving adult ﬂukes, eggs can
continue to be excreted at low levels intermi ently for up to 9
weeks post treatment. 103
Other treatments administered to P. illiciens–infected cats with
complicated infections include ﬂuid therapy, nutritional support,
antimicrobial drugs for secondary bacterial cholangiohepatitis,
cholecystotomy, cholecystectomy, complete or partial liver
lobectomy, or choledochoenterostomy. Prognosis is poor in these
situations. 142

Immunity

vetexamprep.ir

Cats do not develop immunity to P. illiciens infection. Chronic
infections and reinfection are common.

Prevention
Given the variety of intermediate and paratenic hosts, prevention
of infection in endemic areas is challenging. Even indoor cats are
at risk with paratenic hosts such as anoles able to enter homes. In
endemic areas, regular examination of feces of indoor and
outdoor cats is needed to identify infections and treat them before
extensive biliary tract pathology develops. Administration of
monthly praziquantel might be beneﬁcial for cats at a high risk of
infection, although the eﬃcacy of the low dose of praziquantel is
uncertain and the potential exists for selection for anthelminticresistant parasites. The selection for resistant ﬂukes has been
suspected in the case of other ﬂuke species in other hosts,
although most cases of reduced treatment eﬃcacy have been
a ributed to overwhelming infections or incorrect dose. 135 , 137
Reports of P. illiciens infection in cats outside endemic areas are
a concern. While most of these cats have a history of travel from
an endemic area, it is unknown if P. illiciens can adapt to other
intermediate hosts and establish in new locations. Therefore,
measures should be implemented to prevent transport of P.
illiciens to currently nonendemic locations. Treatment should be
administered before departure from endemic areas with followup fecal examinations and treatment as needed after arrival in
nonendemic areas. Given the long PPP, need for repeated
treatments to eliminate infection, the lack of sensitivity of the
diagnostic methods, and the long lifespan of adult ﬂukes,
prevention of transporting infections to nonendemic areas
represents a challenge.

Public Health Aspects
Platynosomum illiciens is not considered a public health issue.
There have been no reports of human infections.

Alaria SPP. Infections
Etiologic Agent and Epidemiology

vetexamprep.ir

Members of the genus Alaria are Diplostomatid trematode
parasites that localize in the small intestine of a variety of
domestic and wild carnivores. Species described in domestic dogs
and cats include A. alata (Goeze, 1782), A. marcianae (La Rue, 1917
and Walton, 1949); A. canis (La Rue & Fallis, 1936); Alaria
arisaemoides (Augustine & Uribe, 1927); Alaria americana (Hall &
Wigdor, 1918); Alaria nasuae (La Rue & Townsend, 1932); and
Alaria minnesotae (Chandler, 1954) (Table 118.6). 1 , 143–147 Several
Alaria species such as A. canis, A. minnesotae, and A. americana
have been considered synonymous with A. marcianae by some
authors, 148–152 while separate species identities are supported by
other reports. 153 In relatively recent scientiﬁc literature, A.
marcianae is most frequently identiﬁed in the intestinal tract of
domestic cats, whereas A. alata is reported primarily in dogs. Due
to challenges in morphologic identiﬁcation of the various species
in some clinical reports, the parasite is identiﬁed only to the genus
level as Alaria sp. 154–158
The life cycle of Alaria spp. is complex with multiple life stages
in at least three hosts. In addition to dogs and cats, adult parasites
are found in the small intestine of a variety of wild carnivores
including wolves (Canis lupus), red fox (Vulpes vulpes), grey fox
(Urocyon cinereoargenteus), mountain lion (Felis (Puma) concolor),
striped skunk (Mephistis mephistis), and coyote (C. latrans). 147 , 148 ,
152 , 159 , 160 The relative importance of these wildlife reservoirs
with regard to dog or cat infections is unclear.
Alaria adults usually range in length from 1.5 to 4 mm and have
an unusual two-compartment body structure. The ﬂa ened
forebody contains oral and ventral suckers and a bulbous
trybocytic organ, and a aches to the intestinal mucosa. The
cylindrical hind body contains the reproductive organs and
extends into the lumen of the small intestine. 143 , 148 , 161 Large,
oval eggs with indistinct opercula (98–134 × 62–68 µm) are shed in
the feces of the deﬁnitive host (Fig. 118.2C). 35 When the egg
contacts fresh water, the larval miracidium develops and hatches
in about 2 weeks. The motile miracidia infect planorbid snails of
the genus Helisoma and undergo asexual replication as sporocysts.
Motile cercaria are released into the water and penetrate the skin
of larval amphibians (tadpoles) and transform into mesocercaria.
Several frog species serve as second intermediate hosts by

vetexamprep.ir

maintaining the larval stage in tissues as an adult. 148 , 159 , 162
Alternatively, the infected tadpole may be ingested by frogs,
snakes, rodents, chickens, or other paratenic hosts. 148 The dog or
cat deﬁnitive host becomes infected by ingesting an infected frog
or paratenic host.
TABLE 118.6

C, cat; D, dog; DH, definitive host; F, frog (second intermediate host); IH,
intermediate host; NR, not reported; S, snail (first intermediate host).
a Reference list associated with this table available on request to the chapter

authors. For more description of reports of Alaria spp., please see Möhl K,
Grosse K, Hamedy A, et al. Biology of Alaria spp. and human exposition risk to
Alaria mesocercariae: a review. Parasitol Res. 2009;105:1–15.
b Geographic source of infection not clearly identified in case report.

Once ingested by a dog or cat, mesocercariae migrate through
the diaphragm, transform into metacercariae in the respiratory
tract, pass up the bronchial tree, and are swallowed to develop to
adults in the small intestine. 148 , 161 , 162 In a single cat that was
experimentally infected with A. marcianae, egg excretion was ﬁrst
noted 19 days after feeding mesocercariae. 148 The longevity of
adult parasites in the cat or dog intestine is unclear.
In an unusual alternative transmission pathway for a typical
trematode, based on experimental infections, A. marcianae can be
transmi ed through a transmammary route. 163 Mesocercariae
were recovered from mammary tissues of lactating queens. In one
report, inoculation of a single queen resulted in infection of 21 of

vetexamprep.ir

her ki ens over the course of 5 li ers, and after 3 years, viable
larvae were still present in the mammary tissue. 163 They were
also found in ki ens born from uninfected queens transferred to
infected queens for nursing.
Alaria spp. have been reported in dogs or cats in temperate
regions of several continents including the Americas, Europe, the
Middle East, and a single report in Africa (see Table 118.6). In
some epidemiologic surveys, the species of Alaria was not
reported. It is unclear how these parasites were identiﬁed to the
species level since the egg morphology for various Alaria spp. is
not microscopically distinguishable. A report from Oklahoma,
United States, that evaluated several thousand canine and feline
fecal specimens identiﬁed Alaria spp. eggs in 9.0% of free-roaming
cats and 1.8% of rescue and shelter dogs 164 ; infections were less
commonly detected in client-owned cats (1.4%) and dogs (0.2%).

Clinical Features
Adult parasites a ach to the small intestinal mucosa. However, no
signs of enteritis or other tissue damage have speciﬁcally been
reported in dogs and cats. 165 In a single case report, adults of A.
arisaemoides were surgically removed from the small intestine of a
4-month-old Labrador retriever puppy with a history of vomiting,
anorexia, and chronic signs of malnutrition. 166 It has been
suggested that the migration of mesocercariae could cause tissue
damage or hemorrhage, particularly in the lungs, but clinical
signs consistent with these migrations have been reported in
infected cats. 161 However, two diﬀerent disease pa erns have
been suggested in other hosts: adult ﬂukes causing intestinal
inﬂammation and larval migrations causing “metacercarial
alariosis” in lungs and other viscera. 159

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of Alaria infection in dogs or cats is primarily based
on ﬁnding large, oval unembryonated eggs (62–68 × 98–134 µm) in
feces of the infected host (see Fig. 118.2C). 146 Adult trematodes
a ached to small intestinal mucosa may be identiﬁed on necropsy
and are sometimes considered incidental ﬁndings.

vetexamprep.ir

Parasitologic Tests
Since trematode eggs are usually dense and are not routinely
recovered by fecal ﬂotation techniques, fecal sedimentation is the
diagnostic method of choice. Egg excretion can be intermi ent;
sensitivity is improved by testing multiple fecal specimens from
diﬀerent days. No immunodiagnostic or molecular assays have
been reported as diagnostic tools for detection of Alaria spp.
infections in dogs or cats. In one survey of adult parasites
recovered from foxes in Ireland, parasite identity was conﬁrmed
as A. alata by sequencing of a DNA fragment ampliﬁed using a
broad-spectrum 18S rRNA PCR assay. 160
Pathologic Findings
In several parasitologic surveys, necropsy examination was
performed to determine parasite infection status. 154 , 167 , 168
However, no gross or histopathologic evaluations of host tissues
were pursued. Similarly, for several Alaria species, the life cycles
have been completed experimentally to characterize the various
larval and adult parasite stages. 143 , 148 , 169 No evaluations of host
tissues were conducted in those studies.

Treatment and Prognosis
No anthelminthics are label-approved for the treatment of Alaria
spp. in dogs or cats, and no treatment trials have been reported.
Praziquantel is anecdotally recommended at the label-approved
dose since the drug has eﬃcacy against some trematodes as well
as cestodes. 161 , 165

Immunity, Vaccination, and Prevention
No vaccines are available for Alaria spp. infection, and studies
regarding protective immunity have not been reported.
Dogs or cats become infected with Alaria spp. by ingesting frogs
or paratenic hosts infected with mesocercariae, and conﬁnement
of pets indoors or in well-managed outdoor areas should decrease
the risk of scavenging infected intermediate hosts. Since a variety
of wild carnivores may also serve as deﬁnitive hosts, the presence
of wildlife may allow the parasite life cycle to become established
in the local environment, increasing the possibility of infection in

vetexamprep.ir

pets. Access to aquatic habitats with frogs may increase exposure
risk.

Public Health Aspects
A few human infections with Alaria sp. have been documented
and at least two human fatalities caused by infection with A.
americana have been reported. 159 , 170 , 171 Humans become
infected by ingesting poorly cooked frogs; contact with infected
dogs or cats or their feces poses no direct risk to humans.

Case Example
Signalment

“Trooper,” a 5-year-old male neutered Labrador retriever from
Austin, Texas.

History

According to his owner, Trooper had a 4-month history of
progressive weight loss, inappetence, and lethargy. He was
drinking normally. The owner reported multiple intermi ent
episodes of diarrhea and soft stools, sometimes with blood. The
other dog in the household, “Sergeant,” a 4-year-old neutered
male pointer mix, was reported to be clinically normal. The
dogs lived in an urban neighborhood but were periodically
taken to a nearby farm property to run, play, and swim in the
farm pond.

Current Medications:

Monthly heartworm preventive and
medications were administered regularly.

Other Medical History:

ﬂea/tick

control

Trooper was neutered at a young age and was generally healthy
with annual wellness visits to the local veterinary clinic.
Previous pelvic radiographs indicated mild hip dysplasia. Both
dogs were up to date on vaccinations including distemper,
hepatitis, parvovirus, Bordetella, and rabies.

Physical Examination

vetexamprep.ir

General: Active, alert, and responsive. Temperature =
101.1°F (38.4°C), HR = 72 beats/minute, panting, mucous
membranes pink, CRT = 1 second. There were no
clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings on examination of the
integument, eyes, ears, nose, cardiovascular system,
respiratory system, and peripheral lymph nodes.
Musculoskeletal: BCS of 4/9 was noted with symmetrical
muscle overdevelopment in shoulders, and some minor
symmetrical muscle loss in hips, a ributed to hip
dysplasia.
GI: Abdominal palpation revealed a somewhat tense
abdomen with possible enlargement of mesenteric lymph
nodes. No abnormalities were detected on rectal
examination, and no feces were present in the rectum.

Laboratory Findings

CBC: HCT 36% (35%–52%), WBC 14,800 cells/µL (4,000–15,500
cells/µL), platelets adequate.

Cytology Findings

Impression smear of intestinal biopsies: Heterobilharzia americana
eggs and egg fragments were present in small numbers in the
intestinal tissue (see Fig. 118.3C). Mononuclear and neutrophilic
inﬂammation and granulomatous inﬂammatory tissue reaction
was noted in association with the presence of parasite eggs.

Fecal Examination

Centrifugal fecal ﬂotation (NaNO3 solution, SpG 1.25):
negative for parasite eggs, cysts, oocysts.
Fecal sedimentation: Heterobilharzia americana eggs < 1 per
10× ﬁeld (see Fig. 118.2A).
DiagnosisCanine heterobilharziasis (canine
schistosomiasis).

Additional Case Information

Because of the diagnosis of heterobilharziasis in Trooper, a fecal
sedimentation test was also conducted for the clinically normal
cohort dog, “Sergeant.” Eggs were also detected in the feces of

vetexamprep.ir

that dog; therefore, both dogs received praziquantel and
fenbendazole combination treatment.

Treatment

Praziquantel, 25 mg/kg twice daily with food for 2 days;
fenbendazole, 50 mg/kg/day for 10 days with food.

Comments

Trooper was diagnosed with canine heterobilharziasis (canine
schistosomiasis) based on identiﬁcation of characteristic eggs in
an impression smear of an endoscopic biopsy. Subsequently,
the parasite infection was conﬁrmed through the identiﬁcation
of parasite eggs on a fecal sedimentation test. Another clinically
normal dog that shared the same environment, “Sergeant,” was
also positive for eggs on a fecal sedimentation test. Both dogs
received praziquantel/fenbendazole treatment, and fecal
sedimentation tests were negative at 2 and 3 months posttreatment. The dogs likely became infected with H. americana by
penetration of cercariae in water while swimming in a farm
pond where infected wildlife (raccoon, coyote, etc.) could be
found in the local environment.
