Section 6

Infectious Diseases of Body
Systems and Clinical Problems
Jane E. Sykes

The ﬁnal section of this book discusses infectious diseases of
speciﬁc body systems such as the skin, musculoskeletal system,
respiratory and gastrointestinal systems, central nervous system,
eye, and genitourinary tract. It also includes chapters on systemic
problems such as bloodstream infections, infections of the
immunocompromised, and fever. These chapters are designed to
help readers develop a knowledge of the possible infectious
agents that could cause or contribute to disorders of diﬀerent
anatomic body systems, the optimum approach to diagnosis, and
what treatments should be implemented should an infectious
disease be strongly suspected or conﬁrmed as the cause. Most
discussion is limited to bacterial infections. For many bacterial
infections, the recommended duration of treatment has typically
been shortened, and recommended ﬁrst-line antibiotic choices for
most conditions have been tailored based on our knowledge of
susceptibility pa erns to improve antimicrobial stewardship.
Following on from this, in sites where commensal bacteria are
present, it has been increasingly recognized that sometimes
disease follows disruption of the microbiome, or dysbiosis. As a
result of the availability of high-throughput sequencing
technology (also known as next-generation sequencing), the last 5
years have seen a rapid expansion of our understanding of the
dog and cat microbiome in diﬀerent body systems and how
diﬀerent disorders and treatments modify viral, bacterial, and
fungal populations. These techniques are described in more detail
in Chapter 125 (Gastrointestinal and Intra-abdominal Infections),

vetexamprep.ir

but referred to in multiple chapters in this section. Analysis of
eﬀects of diﬀerent variables on thousands of bacterial and fungal
species requires reference to phyla and classes instead of
individual species, classiﬁcations which veterinary practitioners
are often less familiar with. It is likely that familiarity with
populations of microorganisms will increase with further
elucidation of the clinical relevance of microbiome analyses.
The ﬁnal chapter of this book discusses the approach to
diagnosis of fever of unknown origin. In this case, an infectious
disease might be suspected but no localizing signs are available to
narrow the list of diﬀerential diagnoses. Without localizing signs,
it can be helpful to refer to tables that provide a categorized list of
infectious diseases to consider for diagnostic eﬀorts; these are
included at the end of the chapter. In complex cases involving
fever of unknown origin, the astute clinician should be sure to
consider snuﬄeupagitis (see Chapter 77, Miscellaneous Bacterial
Infections). Perhaps SARS-CoV-2 should also be considered. Alas,
further research is needed (FRIN). 1

119: Pyoderma, Otitis Externa
and Otitis Media
Stephen D. White, and Lyne e K. Cole

KEY POINTS
Pyoderma
• Cause: Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, Staphylococcus
aureus, and Staphylococcus schleiferi. Occasionally
coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species.
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, less commonly cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: Epidermal collarettes, pruritus, erythema,
papules, pustules, alopecia. Deep pyoderma is characterized
by deep nodules and fistulous tracts. Local lymphadenopathy
may be present. Hyperpigmentation and lichenification occur
with chronicity.
• Differential Diagnoses: Superficial pyoderma: pemphigus
foliaceus, dermatophytosis, demodicosis, allergic dermatitis,
drug eruptions, erythema multiforme, Malassezia dermatitis.
Deep pyoderma: sterile pyogranulomatous dermatitis, sterile
nodular panniculitis, juvenile cellulitis, neoplasia, foreign body
reactions, deep cutaneous mycoses, pythiosis.
• Human Health Significance: Staphylococcus
pseudintermedius prefers not to colonize humans, but
zoonotic transmission has been reported. Staphylococcus
aureus infection in dogs likely represents reverse zoonotic
transmission from humans to dogs. Staphylococcus schleiferi
has also been reported to infect humans.
Otitis Externa and Otitis Media

vetexamprep.ir

• Cause: The most common bacterial organisms identified in
cases of infectious otitis externa and otitis media are
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius and Pseudomonas
aeruginosa. Less common bacterial cocci include
Staphylococcus schleiferi, Staphylococcus aureus,
enterococci, and β-hemolytic streptococci, while less common
bacterial rods include Proteus mirabilis, Escherichia coli,
Corynebacterium spp., and Klebsiella spp. The most common
fungal cause of infectious otitis externa and otitis media is
Malassezia pachydermatis; other uncommon to rare fungal
pathogens include Candida spp. and Aspergillus spp.
• Affected Hosts: Dogs, less commonly cats.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: The most common clinical signs of otitis
externa include otic pruritus (head shaking, scratching,
rubbing ears on the floor), otic erythema, otic exudate, otic
pain, and odor. With chronicity, proliferative changes and
ulceration occur. Vestibular signs, deafness, Horner’s
syndrome, nystagmus, and facial paralysis may be present
with middle and inner ear involvement.
• Differential Diagnoses: Otitis externa is not an isolated
disease of the ear canal, but rather a syndrome that reflects
underlying dermatologic disease. The etiologies of otitis
externa are classified into predisposing factors, primary
causes, and perpetuating factors. Differentials for otitis
media/otitis interna depend on the clinical signs. For animals
with peripheral vestibular signs and nystagmus, diseases to
consider include feline idiopathic vestibular disease, geriatric
canine vestibular disease, and hypothyroidism, while
differentials for Horner’s syndrome include FeLV infection,
retrobulbar injury, and idiopathic causes.
• Human Health Significance: Zoonotic transmission of S.
pseudintermedius from the skin and ears of dogs to humans is
very uncommon but has been reported. Owners should be
advised to wash their hands frequently or wear gloves while
handing their pet with known or suspected drug-resistant
infectious otitis externa or otitis media.

vetexamprep.ir

Bacterial Pyoderma
Etiology and Epidemiology
Pyoderma is deﬁned as a pyogenic infection of the skin, although
pus may not always be grossly evident. The bacteria most
commonly associated with pyoderma in dogs are Staphylococcus
pseudintermedius (previously identiﬁed as Staphylococcus
intermedius), 1 , 2 Staphylococcus aureus, and Staphylococcus schleiferi
(both S. schleiferi subsp. coagulans, which is coagulase positive, and
S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi, which is coagulase negative) roughly
in that order of frequency. 3 , 4 The role of other coagulasenegative staphylococcal (CoNS) species is probably more
important than previously thought. 5 Gram-negative bacteria such
as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus spp., and Escherichia coli may be
involved in dogs with deep pyoderma. 6 These organisms are
thought to invade secondary to alteration of local environmental
conditions by S. pseudintermedius.
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is a normal resident of mucosal
sites such as the anus and nares and is thought to colonize the
skin transiently following grooming and excessive licking in dogs
with pruritus, 3 , 7 although more recent microbiome studies have
shown that it can colonize the skin of healthy dogs. 2 , 8 Resident
ﬂora of healthy canine skin in these studies have primarily been
staphylococci (especially S. pseudintermedius), Streptococcus spp.,
anaerobes, and Malassezia spp. The exact number of species that
make up the canine cutaneous biome is continually expanding as
various higher throughput methods are brought to bear on this
research. 8 , 9 Similar research is ongoing in cats. 10 , 11 In one
study that used next-generation sequencing, Staphylococcus
epidermidis was the most abundant Staphylococcus spp. isolate
found on the skin of healthy cats; Staphylococcus felis and
Staphylococcus capitis were the most abundant isolates from the
skin of allergic cats. 11
In cats, pyoderma is less common, and is more likely to be
caused by either S. aureus or S. pseudintermedius. 12 Feline acne is
often a form of deep pyoderma, complicated by keratinization
abnormalities.
Pyoderma is usually secondary to some disruption in the
animal’s cutaneous barrier and/or immune system. The usual

vetexamprep.ir

primary diseases are allergic (ﬂea allergy, atopic dermatitis,
cutaneous adverse food reaction [CAFR]), endocrine
(hypothyroidism, hyperadrenocorticism, diabetes mellitus [less
commonly]), or demodicosis, but other diseases that cause severe
pruritus or suppress the immune system have occasionally been
implicated.
Over the past decade, clonal spread of methicillin-resistant S.
pseudintermedius (MRSP) has occurred across Europe and North
America. 13 Methicillin resistance has also been described among
S. aureus (MRSA) and S. schleiferi (MRSS) isolates from dogs and
cats with pyoderma. 4 , 14 These methicillin-resistant staphylococci
(MRS) encode an altered penicillin binding protein (PBP) that
confers resistance to all β-lactam antimicrobials, and many also
demonstrate resistance to other antimicrobials becoming MDR
isolates (see Chapter 51). 14

Clinical Features
Classification of Pyoderma
Three broad classiﬁcations of pyoderma exist, based on the depth
of skin and presumed follicle involvement: surface pyoderma,
superﬁcial pyoderma, and deep pyoderma.
Surface Pyoderma
Surface pyoderma occurs when bacteria proliferate on the surface
of the skin and incite an inﬂammatory response, without invading
the skin. Surface pyodermas include intertrigo (“fold”
pyodermas), pyotraumatic dermatitis (“hot spots”), and
mucocutaneous pyoderma, which most commonly aﬀects German
shepherd dogs. 15 Intertrigo may be found on the lip, face, vulva,
and tail. Pyotraumatic dermatitis occurs secondary to self-trauma,
such as that secondary to ﬂea allergy dermatitis, and is commonly
found in the lumbosacral area. Clinical signs include erythema,
variable pruritus, alopecia, moist exudation, and a foul odor.
Chronic lesions may be characterized by licheniﬁcation and
hyperpigmentation. Mucocutaneous pyoderma is characterized
by erosions and ulcerations with or without crusting, which
involve the lips, nasal planum, nares, perioral skin, and
sometimes the anus, vulva, prepuce, and eyelids. This may have
an immunologic as well as a bacterial etiology, and is

vetexamprep.ir

histologically identical to discoid lupus erythematosus; thus
diﬀerentiation between these diseases should be made clinically
and based upon response to antibiotics. 12 , 16
Microbial overgrowth syndrome has also been categorized as a
surface pyoderma when it involves bacteria. 17 Microbial
overgrowth syndrome usually involves the ventral aspect of the
body and is characterized by erythema, pruritus, a foul odor,
erythema, alopecia, hyperpigmentation, licheniﬁcation, and
excoriations, but no evidence of papules, pustules, epidermal
collare es, or crusts. 17
Superficial Pyoderma
In superﬁcial pyoderma, bacteria infect the superﬁcial epidermal
layers that lie immediately under the stratum corneum and/or the
portion of the hair follicle above the sebaceous duct (the
infundibulum). This is the most common type of pyoderma. It
includes superﬁcial bacterial folliculitis, superﬁcial spreading
pyoderma, and impetigo or juvenile pustular dermatitis (“puppy
pyoderma”). Early lesions of superﬁcial pyoderma are
erythematous follicular papules (papules from which a hair shaft
protrudes). As pus accumulates within the epidermis and hair
follicles, these lesions become pustules. Papules and pustules are
primary skin lesions. Epidermal collare es are circles of
epidermal scale with a free edge facing toward the center of the
circle (Fig. 119.1), and may be remnants of ruptured pustules. In
thick-coated dogs, the scale may become trapped throughout the
haircoat as the epidermal collare es exfoliate. Microscopically,
epidermal collare es consist of interfollicular, epidermal
spongiotic pustules. 18 This may mean that epidermal collare es
do not always denote a folliculitis, although they almost always
denote a pyoderma. 19 Hair fragments are shed from damaged
follicles, which results in alopecia. Crusted papules, epidermal
collare es, and alopecia are secondary lesions.

Impetigo generally occurs in dogs less than a year of age. In
impetigo, pustules are conﬁned to the epidermis, without
follicular involvement, and are most commonly found in the
poorly haired (glabrous) areas on the ventral abdomen and

vetexamprep.ir

inguinal region and around the chin. The pustules often evolve
into honey-colored crusts.
Deep Pyoderma
Deep pyoderma is deﬁned by infection deep within the hair
follicle, with or without follicular rupture (furunculosis) (Fig.
119.2). Nodules with or without ﬁstulous tracts may be present.
German shepherd dogs seem prone to a more severe and
extensive form of deep pyoderma 20 —the frequency of this form
seems to have diminished concurrently with the advent of more
eﬀective medications for ﬂea control. Other examples of deep
pyoderma include pedal folliculitis and furunculosis, pressurepoint pyoderma, pyotraumatic folliculitis and furunculosis, and
muzzle folliculitis and furunculosis (“canine acne”). A similar
process is seen in cats (“feline acne”). 21 , 22
Physical Examination Findings
Because the lesions of bacterial pyoderma are directly visible, in
many cases, diagnosis can be made based on a thorough physical
examination. Use of a hand lens may be helpful. In some cases,
clipping of small areas of the haircoat may be required. This can
help to identify epidermal collare es in dogs with dry scale.
Careful a ention should be paid to the presence of follicular
papules, pustules, crusted papules, epidermal collare es,
alopecia, nodules, ﬁstulous tracts, and the presence or absence of
pruritus. The distribution of lesions should be noted because it
can be a clue to underlying disease, such as demodicosis or ﬂea
allergy. In dogs with deep pyoderma, the skin may feel warm to
the touch and peripheral lymphadenomegaly may be detected.

Diagnosis
The diagnostic approach to pyoderma should involve
conﬁrmation of the presence of pyoderma and a thorough search
for possible underlying causes. The diﬀerential diagnosis includes
many diseases that predispose to and/or mimic pyoderma, such
as demodicosis, dermatophytosis, and pemphigus foliaceus (see
Key Points). When crusts are present, corniﬁcation disorders
should be considered, although crusting may also result from self-

vetexamprep.ir

trauma. The presence or absence of Malassezia spp. must also be
determined (Chapter 79).
In addition to a thorough physical examination, diagnostic
procedures that may be necessary include skin scrapings,
cytologic examination, aerobic bacterial culture and susceptibility
testing, and skin biopsy. Dermatophyte culture is indicated when
dermatophytosis is suspected or needs to be ruled out (see
Chapter 78). Identiﬁcation and subsequent treatment of
underlying allergic skin disease may require additional testing
such as intradermal skin testing, serologic tests for environmental
allergy, and/or a limited allergen diet trial.
Skin Scrapings
Skin scrapings should be performed in any dog suspected to have
pyoderma to assess for underlying demodicosis. Pustules or
papules that are associated with hair follicles should be targeted,
because Demodex mites have a predilection for this site.
Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination
Cytology can be performed on tape preparations of the skin or
smears made after swabbing pustules or draining tracts. Cytologic
examination is essential in order to identify concurrent infection
with Malassezia spp. Slides should be air-dried and stained with a
modiﬁed Wright stain such as Diﬀ-Quik. The presence of cocci
suggests a staphylococcal infection (Fig. 119.3). Infection is
supported by the presence of degenerate neutrophils and
intracellular cocci. Inﬂammatory cells may be absent in dogs with
underlying immunosuppressive disorders or those receiving
glucocorticoid treatment. It is the opinion of the authors that the
failure to see cocci on cytologic examination does NOT rule out a
staphylococcal pyoderma, especially if clinical signs such as
epidermal collare es are present.
Culture and Susceptibility Testing
Due to the rapidly increasing prevalence of MRS worldwide,
aerobic bacterial culture and susceptibility testing is playing a
more important role in diagnosis of canine pyoderma. While
probably not necessary for dogs with a ﬁrst-time diagnosis of

vetexamprep.ir

pyoderma, culture and susceptibility testing is never
contraindicated and should always be oﬀered in dogs with
recurrent or refractory pyoderma, a history of recent treatment
with systemic antimicrobial drugs, or who have had surgery or a
hospital stay within the previous 6 to 12 months. 14 Refractory
pyoderma is deﬁned as pyoderma that fails to respond to
treatment within a 3- to 4-week treatment period. Culture also can
deﬁnitively identify the staphylococcal species involved, which
may have public health implications (see Public Health Aspects,
later). The results of culture and susceptibility testing must
always be interpreted in light of the clinical signs present and any
history of antimicrobial drug treatment.

with inducible clindamycin resistance.
• Choice of a tetracycline is complicated by the fact that

The best lesions for culture in dogs with superﬁcial pyoderma
are pustules. A thorough search for pustules is recommended.
Pustules can be ruptured using a sterile needle, and a swab used
to obtain purulent material. If pustules cannot be detected, culture
can be performed on swab specimens collected from the skin that
lies beneath crusts or from under the edge of epidermal
collare es. 19 No surface antisepsis should be performed. Any hair
should be clipped from the lesion using sterile scissors, and crusts
should be lifted with sterile forceps. Alternatively, a sterile
culture e can be rolled two to three times over the collare e.
Papules can be biopsied using local anesthesia and submi ed for
culture. In this case, surface antisepsis with a single 70% alcohol
wipe may be performed before collection of the biopsy. Culture of
biopsy specimens from nodules and furuncles is best for dogs
with deep pyoderma. After collection of the biopsy, the epidermis
can be removed using a sterile blade and the deeper tissues
submi ed for macerated tissue culture.

vetexamprep.ir

Minimum reporting by microbiology laboratories should
include complete speciation of staphylococci—regardless of tube
coagulase status—and complete antibiotic susceptibility results.
The pathogenic potential of any CoNS isolate obtained from a
skin lesion should be interpreted in light of the clinical ﬁndings
and with respect to any other pathogenic species of bacteria that
may be co-isolated with it. 23 Other suggestions about
interpretation of susceptibility panels are outlined in Box 119.1.
Pathologic Findings
Findings on histopathology in dogs with uncomplicated
pyoderma include a neutrophilic inﬁltrate and abundant bacterial
organisms. Folliculitis, furunculosis, or the features noted in
epidermal collare es 18 (described above) are all potential
ﬁndings. Histopathologic evaluation of skin biopsy specimens
allows classiﬁcation of the extent and type of pyoderma and
identiﬁcation of other conditions such as allergic dermatitis,
demodicosis, dermatophytosis, pemphigus foliaceus, neoplasia,
deep mycoses, and vasculitides. Biopsy should be considered in
recurrent or refractory cases, in dogs with deep pyoderma, or
when the underlying cause is not apparent. Biopsies can be
performed under local anesthesia using a 6-mm punch biopsy.
When possible, the biopsy specimen can be halved with half
submi ed for culture and half for histopathology. The biopsy site
should be sutured after the specimen has been collected.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Molecular strain typing methods are research tools used to
investigate the epidemiology and ecology of MRS. However, at
this time, strain typing often has no impact on patient- or cliniclevel management, even in the context of most outbreaks. 23

Treatment and Prognosis
Factors to consider when treating dogs for pyoderma include the
underlying disease, the severity and extent of lesions, and the
local geographic prevalence of staphylococcal resistance.
Veterinarians’ reliance on systemic antimicrobial drug treatment
has been challenged by the increasing prevalence of MDR
staphylococci. Topical treatments that help to restore skin

vetexamprep.ir

structure and function, as well as topical antimicrobial therapy,
should be considered as alternatives. In dogs with mild disease,
treatment aimed at the underlying disorder may be suﬃcient to
resolve infection (see Prevention). Guidelines for the treatment of
superﬁcial bacterial pyoderma have been developed by ISCAID. 24
Topical Treatments
Topical therapy should be used as the sole on-animal antibacterial
treatment for surface and superﬁcial infections whenever the pet
and owner can be expected to be compliant.
Antibacterial shampoos may be eﬀective alone in some dogs
with surface or mild superﬁcial pyoderma and should be used as
adjunctive therapy in dogs with deep pyoderma. They aid in
debridement, reduce surface bacterial numbers, and decrease pain
and pruritus. Options include shampoos that contain ethyl lactate,
chlorhexidine, miconazole (in combination with chlorhexidine),
benzoyl peroxide, or sodium hypochlorite. Initially, they should
be used at least twice weekly with a 10-minute contact time. A
combination of chlorhexidine and miconazole may be particularly
eﬀective. 25 Benzoyl peroxide shampoos can be drying and so are
best reserved for dogs with greasy dermatitides. Daily
shampooing may be required for dogs with deep pyoderma. If
available, treatment with daily whirlpool baths containing
chlorhexidine may also be helpful for these dogs. Important
points about shampooing are noted in Box 119.2.
Topical antimicrobial drugs and antiseptics in ointment or
cream form result in high concentrations of drug at the skin
surface that can overwhelm bacterial drug resistance mechanisms,
and can be useful when pyoderma is limited to small areas of
skin. Aside from having the potential to be messy, these drugs
have minimal adverse eﬀects and result in minimal exposure of
bystander organisms (such as intestinal ﬂora) to antimicrobial
drugs. Examples of topical drugs with excellent activity against
staphylococci include neomycin, gentamicin, polymyxin B,
bacitracin, hydroxyl acids (such as acetic acid), novobiocin, and
silver sulfadiazine. Mupirocin and fusidic acid are additional
topical antimicrobial drug preparations that may also be useful
for treatment of pyoderma that is restricted to small areas. While
resistance to mupirocin and fusidic acid has been documented in
MRSA isolates from humans, 26 , 27 in vitro evidence of resistance

vetexamprep.ir

of S. pseudintermedius to these two medications is rare. 27 , 28
However, there is a report of subclinical nasal carriage of a
mupirocin-resistant MRSA isolate in a pet dog, so some caution is
warranted. 29

decreased lathering tendency of medical shampoos.

Systemic Antimicrobial Drug Therapy
When pyoderma is widespread, deep, or topical treatment is
ineﬀective or impractical, treatment with systemic antimicrobial
drugs may be required. If an antibiotic is selected for empiric
treatment, it should be based on the local prevalence of resistance,

vetexamprep.ir

and narrow-spectrum drugs that target staphylococci are
preferable. Clindamycin, ﬁrst-generation cephalosporins (such as
cephalexin), lincomycin, and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid are
reasonable ﬁrst choices (Table 119.1). Other acceptable alternatives
when the local regional susceptibility of S. pseudintermedius is
known include doxycycline, trimethoprim- or ormetoprimpotentiated sulfonamides.
The use of third-generation cephalosporins for empiric therapy
is controversial because their use in particular has been associated
with selection for MRS in humans and they have the potential to
select for resistant populations of gram-negative bacteria in the GI
tract. 30 Whether this holds true for dogs and cats is unknown at
present. What is known is that the percentage of MRS and MDR
isolates among all species of Staphylococcus is increasing. 14 , 23 , 31
However, there is li le evidence for a diﬀerence in outcome
between MRS and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus infections
in animals, and the prognosis for MRS skin infections in pets is
good, depending on the underlying cause and co-morbidities. 23
It is currently recommended that treatment be for a minimum
of 4 weeks for superﬁcial pyoderma and 8 weeks for deep
pyoderma. Dogs should be re-evaluated at the end of the
suggested periods while still receiving antibiotic therapy.
Continued clinical signs such as pruritus in the face of resolution
of the pyoderma (reduction or absence of epidermal collare es or
follicular papules) should prompt investigation of underlying
diseases. For superﬁcial pyodermas, treatment should be
continued for at least 7 days beyond clinical resolution of lesions,
because inﬂammation subsides before infection is completely
resolved. For deep or recurrent superﬁcial pyoderma, treatment
should be continued for 14 days beyond clinical resolution. It is
possible that in the future, shorter durations of treatment may be
recommended to reduce antimicrobial selection pressure,
especially when combinations of topical and systemic treatment
are used together with control of the underlying cause.

Although intermi ent administration of antimicrobials on a

with recurrent pyodermas, there is concern for induction of

initiated in the early 1980s, when the current high incidence of

vetexamprep.ir

resistance was not present, and it may not be relevant or advisable
at this time. If necessary, referral to a veterinary dermatologist is
recommended.

Prevention
Prevention of recurring pyoderma relies on addressing the
underlying cause or causes whenever possible. This may involve
investigating the possibility of food allergy, ﬂea allergy, atopic
dermatitis, Demodex spp. infestation, hypothyroidism, or
hyperadrenocorticism. This could include skin scraping, initiating
or increasing ﬂea control, frequent bathing to restore skin
condition, dietary management for dogs with food allergies,
management of atopic dogs, and/or breeding practices that aim to
select against atopic dogs and dogs with abundant skin folds.
Speciﬁc prevention of MRS infections relies on hand washing,
disinfection practices, as well as judicious use of antimicrobial
drugs, as outlined earlier. Previous treatment with antibiotics,
previous hospitalization, and cohabitant dogs have been
identiﬁed as risk factors for the development of infection with
MRS. 14 , 32 , 33 There is currently not enough evidence to
recommend routine decolonization of MRS carrier animals. 23
When treatment of the underlying cause or use of topical
therapy is unsuccessful in preventing recurrence of pyoderma,
subcutaneous administration of autogenous bacterins or
commercial bacterial antigens (such as Staphage Lysate, Delmont
Laboratories, USA) may be beneﬁcial in some dogs. 34 , 35 These
are generally given once or twice weekly.

Public Health Aspects
In vitro studies have shown that the majority of S. pseudintermedius
adhere be er to canine than human corneocytes. 36 However,
human infection has been reported occasionally, including among
veterinarians. 37 , 38 In these cases, pet dog contact was reported
and suggested to be the source of infection. In one case, an isolate
from the dog matched that isolated from the human as
determined using pulsed-ﬁeld gel electrophoresis.
In contrast, contact with human hospitals and children may be
risk factors for acquisition of MRSA infections by dogs, as S.

vetexamprep.ir

aureus infections in dogs appear to be a reverse zoonosis. MRSA
isolated from animals has been shown to be human clonal in
nature. 39 Colonization is generally transient in dogs and cats, so
speciﬁc treatment to decolonize dogs and cats is neither necessary
nor eﬀective. 40 See the suggested reading list for a complete
discussion of screening for MRSA in both dogs and humans. 23
Although it may be carried elsewhere on the body, S. schleiferi
subsp. coagulans has been isolated primarily from dogs with otitis
externa and has been reported as a cause of endocarditis in an
immunocompromised person, while S. schleiferi subsp. schleiferi
was reported as causing a prostatic abscess and bacteremia in a
man. 41 , 42
Frequent and proper hand washing using soap and water and
disinfectant foams or gels is the number one practice that limits
spread of these infections in human hospitals. Hands should be
washed before and after handling each patient. Clean clothing
should be worn and doctors’ coats changed regularly. A ention
should be paid to regular disinfection of other fomites such as
stethoscopes, cell phones, rectal thermometers, computer
keyboards and mice, calculators, and bandage scissors.
Disinfectant wipes that contain alcohol or accelerated hydrogen
peroxide can be used to clean these surfaces.

Otitis Externa and Otitis Media
Etiology and Epidemiology
Otitis Externa
Otitis externa is deﬁned as inﬂammation of the external ear canal;
in some cases, the inﬂammation may extend onto the surface of
the pinna. Etiologies of otitis externa have been divided into
predisposing factors, primary causes, and perpetuating factors
(Box 119.3). Successful treatment of otitis externa depends on
identiﬁcation, along with controlling or eliminating these factors
and causes. Simply treating the complicating infection without
addressing the primary cause, or eliminating the primary cause
without control of the secondary infection, likely will result in
treatment failure.

In a retrospective study evaluating 100 dogs with acute (37%)
and chronic-recurrent (63%) otitis externa, the most common
primary causes were allergic dermatitis (n = 43 dogs; e.g., CAFR,
canine atopic dermatitis), parasites (13 dogs), and grass awns (12
dogs). 43 Most bacterial and yeast infections are perpetuating

vetexamprep.ir

factors and therefore are secondary to the primary, underlying
disease. In cats, the most common primary causes of recurrent
otitis externa are Otodectes cynotis and nasopharyngeal polyps.
Unlike dogs, underlying allergic diseases such as CAFRs and
feline atopic skin syndrome are much less commonly associated
with secondary infectious otitis externa. A rare painful idiopathic
proliferative and necrotizing feline otitis externa (PNOE) has been
reported, which may or may not involve the concave pinnae. 44 , 45
In health, the external ear canal is colonized by numerous
bacterial as well as yeast species. Species that can be cultured from
the external ears of dogs without ear disease include CoNS,
Bacillus spp., coagulase-positive staphylococci (e.g., S.
pseudintermedius), E. coli, Corynebacterium spp., streptococci,
Micrococcus spp., and Malassezia spp. However, it is uncommon to
culture bacteria from healthy ears (with the exception of Bacillus
spp., CoNS, and low numbers of coagulase-positive
staphylococci). Pseudomonas spp. and Proteus spp. are rarely
cultured from clinically healthy ears. Instead, these
microorganisms proliferate when there is inﬂammation in the ear
canal as a result of primary conditions. Although less common, S.
schleiferi subsp. schleiferi also has been isolated from the external
ear canal of dogs. More recent studies that have used nextgeneration sequencing to analyze the microbiota of healthy ears
have shown a diverse microbial community with the most
abundant species being Cutibacterium acnes (previously
Propionibacterium acnes), S. pseudintermedius, and Streptococcus spp.
8

Bacterial organisms cultured from the external ear canal in dogs
with chronic otitis externa include S. pseudintermedius, P.
aeruginosa, Proteus spp., β-streptococci, Corynebacterium spp.,
Enterococcus spp., and E. coli, with the most commonly identiﬁed
cocci and rods being S. pseudintermedius and P. aeruginosa,
respectively. Using next-generation sequencing, the most
abundant species were Malassezia spp., S. pseudintermedius, S.
schleiferi, and a variety of anaerobes. 8 Knowledge of the most
likely organism based on cytologic examination allows one to
commence early and targeted antimicrobial therapy.
Staphylococcus schleiferi subsp. schleiferi has been isolated from
the ears of dogs with recurrent otitis, and S. schleiferi subsp.
coagulans can be found in dogs with both ﬁrst-time and recurrent

vetexamprep.ir

otitis externa. Infectious otitis externa is much less common in cats
than in dogs. Organisms identiﬁed in the ear canals of cats
associated with otitis externa include CoNS, S. aureus, S.
pseudintermedius, and Pasteurella spp.
Otomycoses have been reported in dogs and cats, with the most
common organism being Malassezia pachydermatis; Candida spp. is
an uncommon fungal pathogen. Aspergillus spp. is a rare cause of
otitis externa and otitis media in both dogs and cats. 46
The ear mite O. cynotis may be responsible for most feline cases
of otitis externa; dogs have a much lower prevalence of this
infestation. Most animals develop a hypersensitivity reaction to
the mite that results in an inﬂammatory reaction; however, some
animals are subclinical carriers. In others, the inﬂammation may
lead to a secondary bacterial or yeast-associated otitis externa that
can eventually result in the death of the mites.
In a study of 3,707 small animal consultations from 20 general
practices, the reported prevalence of otitis externa was 4.5% for
dogs (of 2,322 dogs) and 1.2% for cats (of 1,043 cats). 47 Breeds that
are overrepresented among dogs with otitis externa include the
cocker spaniel, Jura des Alpes, and Bri any spaniel. 43 However,
any breed as well as mixed-breed dogs may develop otitis externa.
Among cats, the incidence of otitis externa has been reported to be
highest in Himalayan and Persian cats. 48
Otitis Media
Otitis media is deﬁned as inﬂammation of the middle ear. Causes
of otitis media may be divided into those that are infectious and
those that are noninfectious. Infectious otitis media (bacterial,
fungal) is an important perpetuating cause of recurrent otitis
externa. Animals may traumatize their external ears because of
discomfort caused by irritation in the middle ear. Infectious otitis
media occurs as a direct extension from an existing otitis externa
through a ruptured tympanic membrane. Less common routes of
infection include extension through the auditory tube or the
hematogenous route. The reported prevalence of infectious otitis
media in dogs with acute otitis externa is 16%, whereas in dogs
with chronic, recurrent otitis externa the reported prevalence is
50% to 82.5%. 49 , 50 Although a ruptured tympanic membrane is
indicative of otitis media, the presence of an intact tympanic

vetexamprep.ir

membrane does not rule out otitis media because the defect in the
membrane may have healed.
The middle ear of dogs, like the external ear canal, has a
resident microﬂora consisting of low numbers of yeasts and
bacteria including E. coli, Staphylococcus spp., Branhamella spp.,
Streptococcus spp., Enterococcus spp., Bacillus spp., Bordetella
bronchiseptica, and Clostridium perfringens. The most common
organisms isolated from dogs with infectious otitis media include
yeasts, S. pseudintermedius, P. aeruginosa, Proteus spp., β-hemolytic
streptococci, Corynebacterium spp., and Enterococcus spp. The
resident microﬂora of the feline middle ear has not been
described. In cats with infectious otitis media secondary to
nasopharyngeal polyps, the most common bacterial organism
identiﬁed was S. pseudintermedius. Other bacterial organisms in
the middle ears of cats with infectious otitis media include P.
aeruginosa, B. bronchiseptica, Bacteroides spp., Fusobacterium spp.,
and Mycoplasma spp.
There are also noninfectious causes of otitis media (congenital
palatine defects, trigeminal nerve disorders, primary secretory
otitis media [PSOM], otic masses, cholesteatomas, cholesterol
granulomas, sinonasal disease, parasitic nematodes, trauma, grass
awns). Congenital palatine defects (i.e., secondary cleft palate, soft
palate hypoplasia) have been associated with radiographic signs
of middle ear disease in both dogs and cats. 51–53 Neurologic signs
indicative of otitis media were identiﬁed in cats but not in dogs.
Trigeminal nerve disorders due to neoplasia, neuritis, or
neuropathy in dogs have been associated with a middle ear
eﬀusion. Interruption of trigeminal nerve innervation of the tensor
veli palatine muscle (which opens the pharyngeal opening of the
auditory tube) alters the function of the auditory tube, which
could result in the middle ear eﬀusion. PSOM has been described
in the Cavalier King Charles spaniel. These dogs do not have a
history of concurrent otitis externa. Clinical signs include
moderate to severe pain in the head or cervical region; neck/ear
scratching; neurologic signs, such as facial paralysis, nystagmus,
or head tilt; and hearing loss. 54 , 55 An increased soft palate
thickness and decreased nasopharyngeal dimension are
associated with bilateral middle ear eﬀusion in this breed. These
changes may then result in auditory tube dysfunction with
resultant bullae eﬀusion. 56–58 The majority of middle ear and

vetexamprep.ir

external ear cultures from these dogs are negative, so the role of
bacteria in this disorder remains unclear. 59
Masses can occur in the external ear canal as well as in the
middle ear and can be neoplastic (benign or malignant) or
nonneoplastic. Ceruminal gland neoplasia is the most common
neoplastic mass of the external ear canal. In cats, these tumors are
usually malignant, whereas in dogs, they are usually benign.
Tumors that occur in both the ear canal and tympanic bulla are
usually malignant, but biopsy is needed for conﬁrmation.
Nasopharyngeal (inﬂammatory) polyps are nonneoplastic masses.
Although inﬂammatory polyps can contribute to chronic
recurrent otitis externa, they originate in the auditory tube and
can expand into the tympanic bulla or pharynx or both. Whereas
inﬂammatory polyps are common in cats, especially ki ens, they
are relatively uncommon in dogs. 60 Feline ceruminal
cystomatosis is an uncommon, nonneoplastic otic condition
consisting of striking multiple blue-gray to purple papules and
nodules often mistaken for melanotic or vascular tumors. 61 It is
important to biopsy all masses for histopathologic identiﬁcation.
Cholesteatomas are abnormal growths of the epithelium within
the middle ear consisting of keratinizing stratiﬁed squamous
epithelium, inﬂammatory cells, and ceruminous debris. These
may occur congenitally or secondary to chronic otitis media.
Cholesterol granulomas are granulomatous lesions containing
cholesterol crystals that may also occur in the middle ear. These
two entities can present similarly, but cholesteatomas typically
cause more bony destruction of the tympanic bulla and more
severe clinical signs and have only been reported in dogs, while
cholesterol granulomas have been reported in both dogs and cats.
Furthermore, in dogs, cholesteatomas and cholesterol granulomas
may co-exist. 61–63
Cats with sinonasal disease (e.g., rhinitis, neoplasia) are at
increased risk of having concurrent bulla eﬀusion and may not
exhibit any clinical signs of middle ear disease. 64
Mammomonogamus auris, a strongylid nematode that resides in the
middle ear, has been identiﬁed as the cause of head shaking in
domestic cats in Asia and the Caribbean (see Chapter 116). 65 , 66
Otoliths (stone-like mineral concretions of necrotic material
within the bulla) of the middle ear have been reported in three

vetexamprep.ir

dogs. The clinical signiﬁcance of otoliths is unknown, as only one
of the dogs reported with these had clinical signs of vestibular
disease. 67 In a retrospective study, stalked bony globular
structures that have been named hyperostotic tympanic bone spicules
were identiﬁed in the middle ear; these should be considered on a
diﬀerential diagnosis list for otolith-like structures identiﬁed on a
CT scan but can only be diﬀerentiated from otoliths histologically.
68

Clinical Features
The most common clinical signs of otitis externa include otic
pruritus (head shaking, scratching, rubbing ears on the ﬂoor), otic
erythema, otic exudate, otic pain, and odor. Additional clinical
signs (e.g., pedal pruritus, indicating primary underlying allergic

vetexamprep.ir

disease) may be present and identiﬁcation of these signs can help
with determination of the primary cause of the otitis externa.
Usually, the only clinical signs of otitis media are those also
seen with otitis externa listed above. Speciﬁc clinical signs
indicative of otitis media are facial nerve paralysis and Horner’s
syndrome. Injury to the facial nerve, as it courses near the middle
ear, produces clinical signs such as drooping of or inability to
move the ear or lip, drooling of saliva, or decreased or absent
palpebral reﬂex. In one study, 21.5% of 79 dogs and 18.8% of 16
cats had facial neuropathy (facial paresis, paralysis, hemifacial
spasm, or contracture) secondary to otitis media/interna. Cocker
spaniels with facial neuropathy were more likely to have otitis
media/interna as the underlying cause compared to other breeds
with facial neuropathy. 69 Horner’s syndrome is due to injury to
the sympathetic nerve ﬁbers, which course near the middle ear,
and is characterized by ptosis, miosis, enophthalmos, and
protrusion of the nictitating membrane. In one study of Horner’s
syndrome, the underlying cause was otitis media/interna in 27%
of cats and 2.7% of dogs. 70 Keratoconjunctivitis sicca may occur if
the parasympathetic nerves that innervate the tear gland are
injured. The parasympathetic nerve ﬁbers course with the facial
nerve, so keratitis may be aggravated by concurrent facial
paralysis.
Otitis media may lead to otitis interna, which is associated with
damage to the vestibular and cochlear branches of cranial nerve
eight (CN VIII). Clinical signs of otitis interna include horizontal
nystagmus, asymmetrical ataxia, head tilt, circling, falling, or
rolling toward the aﬀected side.
Physical Examination Findings
Obtaining a complete and thorough history from the owner is
critical before a physical examination is performed. Providing the
client with a dermatologic history form to complete before the
appointment can facilitate this (Box 119.4).
A complete dermatologic examination as well as an otic
examination should be performed. In some cases, a neurologic
examination may be needed if concurrent otitis media or otitis
interna is suspected. However, the most common clinical sign of
otitis media is recurrent otitis externa. A head tilt, circling, and
nystagmus may indicate otitis interna. Central extension of otitis

vetexamprep.ir

media/interna into the adjacent subarachnoid space
brainstem can be a life-threatening complication. 71 , 72

The pinnae should be examined for alopecia and excoriations.

occluding the canal. In chronic or recurrent otitis externa, an
increase in the otic discharge is evident, along with varying
degrees of hyperplasia and canal stenosis (Fig. 119.5). Palpation of

The otic examination is performed with either a handheld or

the vertical and horizontal ear canal for evidence of hyperplasia,
stenosis, and ulceration. It is also used to evaluate the amount,
consistency, and color of the otic exudate. If possible, the
tympanic membrane is examined. In some instances, there is so
much disease in the ear canal that otic examination is not possible.
In those cases, the otic examination is delayed until after initial
treatments have been implemented.

Diagnosis
The diagnostic approach to otitis includes identiﬁcation and
management of the primary cause as well as identiﬁcation and
treatment of the infectious (e.g., bacteria, Malassezia) agent(s). In
addition, predisposing factors need to be controlled or eliminated.
Perpetuating factors such as otitis media and progressive
pathologic changes must be diagnosed and treated. If all aspects
of otitis are not identiﬁed, treated, and managed, the otitis will
become recurrent and chronic. Additional diagnostics to identify
predisposing factors may include, but are not limited to, a food
trial, serum allergy testing, biopsy, skin scraping, or clinical
laboratory evaluation (CBC, biochemical proﬁle, thyroid testing).
Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination
After the otoscopic examination, otic exudate should be collected
for cytologic evaluation using a co on swab. Specimens should be
collected from each external ear canal because the organisms may
diﬀer between ears and a separate, clean otoscopic cone should be
used for each ear to prevent cross-contamination. It is also
important to soak otoscopic cones for 20 minutes before their use,
in either 2% chlorhexidine gluconate or a dual quaternary
ammonium compound (Cetylcide-II). 74 If otoscopic cones are to
be stored in a solution, the optimum solution is glutaraldehyde
(Cetylcide-G) (glutaraldehyde). 75
The material obtained is rolled onto a microscope slide, which is
heat ﬁxed, then stained with a Romanowsky-type stain (Wright
stain, Giemsa stain, Diﬀ-Quik) or Gram stain. After staining, the
slides should be rinsed and allowed to dry. If there is a possibility
of the patient having aural mites, a second specimen should be
obtained from each ear. The co on tip should be rolled into a
drop of mineral oil on a slide, a cover-slip placed on top of the
slide, and examined for Otodectes or Demodex mites.
Once the slide for cytologic evaluation is dry, it should be
viewed microscopically. The slide is ﬁrst scanned with the low
power lens (10× objective; 100× magniﬁcation) to ﬁnd keratinized
squamous epithelial cells or inﬂammatory cells, which are
typically associated with infectious agents. Once these are located,

vetexamprep.ir

they should be examined under oil immersion (100× objective;
1000× magniﬁcation). Smears should be evaluated for the number
and morphology of bacteria, the number of yeast, the number and
type of leukocytes, the presence of excessive cerumen, the
presence of excessive keratinized squamous epithelial cells, and
the presence of neoplastic cells. Ten ﬁelds under oil immersion
should be evaluated, allowing estimation of the number of
organisms and leukocytes in those 10 ﬁelds. For consistency, a
grading system of the numbers of organisms and leukocytes
counted should be developed. In one report, 2 or fewer yeast
organisms per high-dry ﬁeld (HDF, 40× objective, 400×
magniﬁcation) in dogs and cats were within reference limits,
whereas 5 or more yeast per HDF in dogs and 12 or more yeast in
cats were abnormal. 76 Any rod bacteria detected cytologically
should be considered abnormal. For coccoid bacteria, 5 or fewer
per HDF in dogs and 4 or fewer per HDF in cats were within
reference limits, whereas 25 or more per HDF in dogs and 15 or
more per HDF in cats were considered of pathogenic signiﬁcance.
The intermediate values were considered suspect, and the
decision to treat should be based on clinical signs as well as the
results of cytology. Cytologic examination should be performed at
the initial visit as well as at each recheck to monitor the response
to therapy. Evaluation for mites should be conducted with the low
power lens (10× objective; 100× magniﬁcation) with the condenser
in the lowest position. Leukocytes should not be present on
cytologic examination of otic specimens from healthy patients and
only on occasion are identiﬁed from animals with ceruminous
otitis; however, leukocytes may be abundant in purulent otic
debris.
Culture and Susceptibility Testing
Bacterial culture and susceptibility testing are not needed at every
visit. The purpose of performing bacterial culture and
susceptibility testing is to identify the organism(s) present in the
ear and to be used to guide the use of systemic (oral) antimicrobial
therapy. Topical otic antimicrobial treatments may a ain 100 to
1,000 times higher drug concentrations in the ear than can be
a ained in the plasma. This exposes the bacteria to very high
concentrations of the antimicrobial agent, far exceeding the levels
that may be a ained with an orally administered antimicrobial

vetexamprep.ir

agent. Therefore, susceptibility testing is not clinically useful for
determining the appropriate topical otic antimicrobial agent.
Some examples of indications to perform a bacterial culture are
when rod-shaped bacteria are detected cytologically (to verify the
organism is P. aeruginosa), when the patient is not responding to
appropriate oral empiric therapy, or when otitis media is
suspected (to identify an oral antibiotic for treatment).
Diagnostic Imaging
General anesthesia is required to perform diagnostic imaging
procedures and is recommended to properly ﬂush and clean the
ears for examination of the deep canal if discomfort of the patient
or occlusion of the canal have prevented adequate visualization.
Anesthesia, rather than sedation, is also imperative for
myringotomy because endotracheal intubation prevents any of
the otic ﬂush solutions that enter the auditory tube from reaching
the nasopharynx and larynx. A general recommended order of
procedure follows.

Once the patient is under anesthesia, radiographic imaging
should be done ﬁrst, because cleaning or ﬂushing ﬂuid in the ears
can obscure structures that require visualization. Radiographic
imaging (bulla radiographs, CT, MRI) is indicated when there is
chronic otitis externa, or if neurologic signs (facial paralysis,
Horner’s syndrome, vestibular disturbances, deafness) are
present, to determine the extent of involvement of the middle and

vetexamprep.ir

inner ear. Radiographic changes indicative of middle ear disease
include increased soft tissue opacity in the tympanic bulla,
sclerosis and thickening of the tympanic bulla wall, sclerosis and
bony proliferation of the petrous temporal bone, bone lysis of the
bulla and petrous temporal bone, and increased soft tissue opacity
within the tympanic bulla. However, normal radiographic
imaging results do not rule out otitis media. With signiﬁcant
radiographic changes, such as sclerosis or lysis, surgical
intervention (total ear canal ablation with bulla osteotomy or
ventral bulla osteotomy) may be required for resolution. The most
commonly used radiographic projections for examining the bullae
include the dorsoventral, right and left lateral obliques, and
rostroventral-caudodorsal open-mouth views. The rostroventralcaudodorsal open-mouth view is the most useful projection but
the most diﬃcult to obtain. It is valuable for comparing the
thickness and opacity of the osseous bullae for asymmetry, which
reﬂects chronic osteomyelitis. In cats, the rostro 10 degrees ventrocaudodorsal oblique view is easier to perform and as accurate as
the rostroventral-caudodorsal open-mouth view. 77
CT examination allows cross-sectional imaging of the external,
middle, and internal parts of the ear and is used to be er deﬁne
bony structures. The overall accuracy and speciﬁcity of CT and
conventional radiography for the diagnosis of otitis media are
similar; however, CT is a more sensitive indicator of otitis media.
78 , 79 Both CT and conventional radiography are more accurate
for predicting severity of otitis media, rather than its presence, 78
and the absence of radiographic evidence of otitis media does not
rule it out. Evidence of otitis media on CT images include change
in the bulla contour, presence of bony proliferation, or osteolysis
of the bulla, with or without increased ﬂuid or tissue within the
bulla (Fig. 119.9). MRI and CT are complimentary modalities: MRI
is superior to CT for detecting soft tissue changes, in the inner ear
and brain, while CT is superior to MRI for detecting bony
changes, such as in the bullae (Fig. 119.10A and B).

Ultrasound imaging of the canine tympanic bulla has been

their ear canals as well as the bulla via a myringotomy 83 ; cadaver

the accuracy of ultrasonographic results is operator dependent. 85

Positive-contrast ear canalography can be used to help evaluate
the patency of the tympanic membrane. A 1:1 concentration of
either iohexol or urograﬁn and sterile saline is infused into the ear
canals of an anesthetized dog, and pre- and postcontrast bullae
radiographs are performed. The presence of the contrast medium
in the bulla conﬁrms a ruptured tympanic membrane; however,
lack of contrast medium in the tympanic bulla does not rule it out.
This procedure should always be the last imaging procedure,
because it will obscure details of all the other methods.
Specimen Collection During Deep Ear Flushing and Cleaning
Knowledge of the anatomy of the middle ear is important to
understand the relationship of the inner ear structures to the
middle ear, in order to avoid damaging them during ﬂushing or
myringotomy. Possible complications of these procedures are
Horner’s syndrome, facial nerve paralysis, vestibular
disturbances, and deafness. Owners should understand these
complications and sign a consent form before the procedure.
The middle ear consists of an air-ﬁlled tympanic cavity, three
auditory ossicles and their associated muscles and ligaments, and
the tympanic membrane (Fig. 119.11). The round (cochlear)
window is covered by a thin membrane that oscillates to dissipate
the vibratory energy of the perilymph in the scala tympani
(tympanic duct). The oval (vestibular) window lies above the
round window adjacent to the pars ﬂaccida. It is covered by a thin

vetexamprep.ir

diaphragm to which the footplate of the stapes is a ached.
Movement of the stapes against the vestibular window is
transmi ed to the perilymph. When ﬂushing the middle ear, one
must be very careful to avoid damaging these windows, which in
turn can damage the inner ear. The auditory tube equalizes
pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane. The tympanic
cavity consists of a small epitympanic recess, a large ventral
cavity, and the tympanic cavity proper. In dogs, there is an
elliptical opening in the dorsal wall of the ventral cavity (the bulla
septum), which communicates with the tympanic cavity proper.
Therefore, in dogs, both compartments of the bulla can be ﬂushed.
The middle ear cavity of cats is divided by a septum into two
separate cavities. In the small dorsolateral compartment lie the
auditory ossicles, the ostium of the auditory tube, and the
tympanic membrane. The larger ventromedial compartment is the
air-ﬁlled tympanic bulla. In order to remove exudate or a mass
from the ventromedial compartment, the bony septum needs to be
perforated and thus can only be accessed surgically. Rough
handling of the septum may result in damage to the
postganglionic sympathetic nerves, resulting in Horner’s
syndrome.

vetexamprep.ir

Structures of the external, middle,
and inner ear of the dog. Courtesy of The Ohio

State University, Columbus, OH.

Deep ear ﬂushing is best done under general anesthesia to
completely clean and evaluate the ear and tympanic membrane.
Indications for deep ﬂushing are chronic, recurrent otitis externa;
persistence of exudate in the external canals despite at-home
cleaning; lack of response to medical management; and the
presence of concurrent neurologic deﬁcits that suggest middle or
inner ear disease. First, the external ear canal is soaked for 10
minutes with a non-ototoxic ceruminolytic ear cleaner. Cerumene
(Vetoquinol, Buena, NJ) is recommended, because unlike most
ceruminolytic agents, it is non-ototoxic. The ear is then ﬂushed
with warm sterile isotonic saline and a bulb syringe used to
remove large debris and exudate. This is followed by ﬂushing
with saline using a 12-mL syringe a ached to an 8F
polypropylene catheter passed through an otoscopic cone.
Additional ear cleaning is performed using a video otoscope with
an external ﬂushing unit, if available.
The tympanic membrane can then be visualized. If the
tympanic membrane is not intact, then the patient most likely has
otitis media, and additional specimens should be obtained from
the middle ear cavity. If a handheld otoscope is being used, this
can be done by inserting a small sterile otoscopic cone into the
horizontal ear canal and passing a sterile swab into the middle ear

vetexamprep.ir

p
g
cavity. The ﬁrst swab is used for bacterial culture and
susceptibility testing. A second swab is used to collect a specimen
for cytologic analysis. If a video otoscope is used, an open-end
3.5F diameter “Tomcat” catheter or 5F catheter a ached to a 12mL syringe is placed through the otoscope port. Sterile saline (1
mL) is ﬂushed into the middle ear cavity and aspirated back for
cytologic evaluation, and this process is repeated to obtain a
specimen for culture. After this, the middle ear can be cleaned by
ﬂushing repeatedly with a 12-mL syringe containing 1 mL of
warm sterile isotonic saline through the catheter placed in the
middle ear. This procedure is repeated until the aspirated saline is
clear.
Once the ear canal has been cleaned, any masses noted in the
vertical ear canal, horizontal ear canal, or middle ear should be
biopsied using biopsy forceps and submi ed for histopathology.
The biopsy should be the last procedure performed, because
blood from the biopsy site may obscure visualization of more
proximal structures in the ear. Foreign bodies can also be
visualized and removed using forceps.
Myringotomy for Specimen Collection
If the tympanic membrane is intact but the pars tensa appears
abnormal, or if otitis media was diagnosed on imaging, a
myringotomy is needed to obtain diagnostic specimens and to
ﬂush the middle ear cavity. An intact tympanic membrane does
not rule out otitis media. Using a handheld otoscope, the cone is
inserted into the horizontal ear canal and the tympanic membrane
visualized. Using a small sterile swab passed through the
otoscope, a perforation is made into the caudoventral quadrant of
the tympanic membrane (the pars tensa). The swab is then
removed and retained for culture. A second swab is inserted into
the original incision for cytologic analysis. If a video otoscope is
used, one of the catheters described above for ﬂushing is placed
through the otoscope port, and used to perforate the caudoventral
quadrant of the pars tensa (Fig. 119.12). Sterile saline (1 mL) is
ﬂushed into the middle ear cavity and aspirated back using a 12mL syringe. The ﬁrst specimen is used for culture and the second
for cytologic evaluation. Thereafter, the middle ear is ﬂushed as
described above. Provided the ear is kept free of infection after

vetexamprep.ir

myringotomy, the tympanic membrane should heal in 21 to 35
days.

Flushing the middle ear with saline does not eliminate all
bacteria from the tympanic cavity in dogs with otitis media. 86
However, when middle ear ﬂushing was combined with at-home
treatment, the otitis media resolved in 36 of 44 dogs, with a mean
time to resolution of 117 days (range 30 to 360 days). At-home

vetexamprep.ir

treatment included otic cleaners and antimicrobial agents (40 dogs
treated with both topical and systemic antimicrobial agents and 4
treated with topical agents only). 87

Treatment
The most common treatment for infectious otitis externa are
cleaning and drying agents and combination antimicrobial/antiinﬂammatory topical therapies. In severe cases, the epithelium in
addition to the lumen of the vertical ear canal is infected, 50 and
oral antimicrobial agents are indicated as well. The probability of
successful management of the ear disease without topical therapy
is low. Furthermore, when inﬂammation and associated ear pain
is severe, a short course of systemic glucocorticoids is indicated in
addition to topical therapies. For parasitic otitis externa, such as
ear mites, topical or systemic therapies are used.
The goals of medical management of otitis media are to reduce
inﬂammation and resolve infection. As for otitis externa, topical
therapy is recommended and may include ear cleaning and
drying agents, glucocorticoids, antibacterials, and antifungals.
Systemic antibacterials and antifungals are indicated in patients
with otitis media. The selection of systemic antibacterial agents
should be made based on culture and susceptibility results from
the middle ear. However, therapy may be initiated based on
cytologic results while awaiting the culture results.
Cleansing Agents (Table 119.2)
Topical cleaning agents are divided into ceruminolytic agents and
cleansing and drying agents. Ceruminolytic agents remove
ceruminous and purulent exudate from the external ear canal
during ear ﬂushing. They may also be sent home with the owner
if the tympanic membrane is intact. These agents work by
surfactant, detergent, or eﬀervescent activity. They are
contraindicated with a ruptured tympanic membrane, because
many are ototoxic, with the exception of the squalene-containing
ceruminolytic Cerumene (Vetoquinol, Buena, NJ). Water-miscible
preparations containing dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate or
propylene glycol are well tolerated. Oils, such as squalene or
mineral oil, are eﬀective but messy. Products containing urea

vetexamprep.ir

peroxide are very potent and recommended for in-hospital use
only.
Once the ear has been ﬂushed with the ceruminolytic, at-home
cleaning is done with a topical cleaning and drying agent in order
to minimize exudate accumulation. Most products contain acids,
some in combination with isopropyl alcohol, to dry the ear canal
and discourage overgrowth of bacterial and yeast organisms.
These products may also be used after swimming or bathing to
prevent “swimmer’s ear.” Cleansing and drying agents are also
used before topical antimicrobial agents for treatment of
infectious otitis externa.
In vitro antimicrobial eﬃcacy has been demonstrated for
EpiOtic Advanced (Virbac Corporation, Fort Worth, TX),
MalAcetic Otic (Dechra Veterinary Products, Overland Park, KS),
and TrizCHLOR Flush (Tromethamine [Tris], EDTA,
chlorhexidine 0.15%, Dechra Veterinary Products). Antimicrobial
activity has been demonstrated for EpiOtic Advanced in dogs
with bacterial- and yeast-related otitis externa, whereas MalAcetic
Otic has beneﬁt for dogs with yeast-related otitis externa. In some
cases, use of these products for cleaning and drying alone may be
suﬃcient to treat infection.
Application of Ear Cleaners
In some cases of otitis, the exudate in the ear canal can be kept to a
minimum with routine at-home cleaning. The frequency of ear
cleaner application depends on the chronicity of the otitis externa,
the severity of the infection, and the amount of exudate in the ear
canal. The goal is to begin treatment with the most frequent
application (e.g., daily) and over time, decrease to a maintenance
frequency (e.g., weekly). It is important to explain proper cleaning
technique to the owner, and in some cases demonstrate the
technique. The owner should ﬁll the ear with the cleaner, gently
massage the ear, let the animal shake its head, then gently wipe
the opening of the vertical ear canal with a co on ball or gauze
sponge. The use of co on-tipped applicators to clean the ear
should be discouraged, because it can cause trauma to an already
inﬂamed ear, induce ulcerations in the ear canal, or push exudate
further down the ear canal. In some cases when at-home cleaning
is ineﬀective or there is too much exudate in the ear canal, in-

vetexamprep.ir

hospital deep ear ﬂushing is the best option for cleaning the ear
(see Deep Ear Flushing and Cleaning earlier).
Topical Glucocorticoid Therapy
Glucocorticoids are antipruritic, anti-inﬂammatory, and
antiproliferative. During acute otitis, the ear canal becomes
edematous and erythematous. As the inﬂammation progresses,
the dermis becomes inﬁltrated with inﬂammatory cells. Apocrine
glands dilate and become hyperplastic, which leads to excessive
cerumen production. Glucocorticoids decrease both inﬂammation
and sebaceous and apocrine secretions. Therefore, they decrease
the pain, pruritus, stenosis, and edema associated with otitis.
They are usually used in combination with other agents, but may
be beneﬁcial when used alone in treatment of allergic animals
with otitis and in some animals with ceruminous otitis. To
prevent iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism, the lowest potency
glucocorticoid at the lowest frequency needed to control otitis,
should be used. Cort/Astrin Solution (Vedco, St. Joseph, MO)
contains a low-potency topical glucocorticoid (1% hydrocortisone)
in addition to a drying solution (Burrow’s solution) in a watermiscible propylene glycol base. A more potent product is Synotic
Otic Solution (Zoetis, Inc., Parsippany, NJ, USA), which contains
0.01% ﬂuocinolone acetonide and 60% dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO). DMSO is anti-inﬂammatory and facilitates the
absorption of ﬂuocinolone into the epidermis and dermis. This
product is very eﬀective in the management of proliferative otitis.

Topical Antimicrobial Therapy
Topical antimicrobial therapy is indicated in all cases of otitis
externa (Table 119.3). Commercially available topical preparations
usually contain various combinations of glucocorticoids,
antibacterials, and/or antifungals in a vehicle base. Selection of the

vetexamprep.ir

active ingredient of the topical product should be based on
cytology results. The patient’s progress while on these
medications should be monitored cytologically at each reevaluation and the topical therapy adjusted accordingly. Most
topical otic treatments are administered twice daily, and the
volume administered should reﬂect the size of the animal’s ear
canal, ranging from a few drops in very small dogs and cats to up
to 1 mL in large-breed dogs. Topical antiseptics such as acetic acid
and chlorhexidine have also been used to treat otitis externa.
However, these products are usually used in addition to topical
antimicrobials.
Most cases of acute bacterial otitis externa, whether due to
gram-positive or gram-negative organisms (even P. aeruginosa),
respond to aminoglycosides (e.g., neomycin, gentamicin).
Antifungal agents are used in cases of acute or chronic otitis
externa caused by Malassezia spp. or Candida spp. Ingredients that
are active against yeast include nystatin, miconazole,
ketoconazole, posaconazole, terbinaﬁne, and clotrimazole.
Furthermore, animals with acute otitis externa usually have
clinical improvement after a short course of topical antimicrobial
agents, such as a “triple” combination product (antibacterial,
antifungal, glucocorticoid), either in an ointment vehicle (e.g.,
Otomax, Merck Animal Health, Madison, NJ) or solution vehicle
(e.g., Tresaderm, Boehringer Ingelheim, Duluth, GA). Newer
FDA-approved topical antimicrobials (e.g., Claro Otic Solution,
Elanco Animal Health and Osurnia Otic gel, Dechra) which are
administered in the clinic may be preferred, as the client does not
have to treat the ears at home and these products are eﬃcacious
for 30 to 45 days, respectively. Unlike lanolin otic packs, these
products coat the ear canal, and do not “pack” the ear and cause
temporary conductive hearing loss.
Chronic or recurrent otitis externa does not respond as well to
products that contain an ointment or suspension vehicle, possibly
because it is diﬃcult for an ointment or suspension to penetrate
the stenotic and hyperplastic ear canals. Products containing a
solution, emulsion, gel, or lotion vehicle are preferred.
Chronic infections due to P. aeruginosa are one of the most
challenging otic diseases to treat because of P. aeruginosa’s high
level of resistance to antimicrobial agents. Antibacterial
treatments for acute otitis externa are usually not eﬀective, and

vetexamprep.ir

the next line of topical antimicrobial agents is needed, which
includes enroﬂoxacin, orbiﬂoxacin, silver sulfadiazine, and
polymyxin B. Presoaking the ear canals for 15 minutes with a
tromethamine EDTA (Tris-EDTA) product before application of
the topical otic agent is recommended. Cell surfaces of gramnegative bacteria are damaged by exposure to EDTA, whereas
tromethamine (Tris) enhances the antibacterial eﬀect of EDTA.
None of the commercially available otic topical treatments or
any extra-label otic preparations are labeled for use with a
perforated tympanic membrane. However, some of these products
have been used to treat otic infections in dogs with otitis media.
Ototoxicity and Topical Otic Treatments
It is the author’s (LKC) opinion that the use of ointment- or
suspension-based otic topical agents or otic packs in ears with a
perforated tympanic membrane should be avoided. Owners
should always be warned of the possibility of neurologic signs
following administration of topical medications when the
tympanic membrane is damaged.
Numerous compounds and classes of compounds of drugs can
be ototoxic, including antibiotics (e.g., aminoglycosides), loop
diuretics, antiseptics (e.g., chlorhexidine), antineoplastic agents,
and miscellaneous agents (e.g., ceruminolytic agents). Toxicity
may result from parenteral or topical applications. In veterinary
medicine, topical otic use of aminoglycosides, chlorhexidine, and
ceruminolytic agents is common. Few studies have been
published evaluating ototoxicity of topically administered agents.
Topical aminoglycosides and topical chlorhexidine are ototoxic in
humans as well as in cats. However, treatment of healthy
greyhounds with experimentally ruptured tympanic membranes
with topical gentamicin sulfate 88 or topical 0.2% chlorhexidine 89
for 21 days failed to induce clinical vestibular or brainstem
auditory evoked potential changes. Another study evaluated the
ototoxicity of four ceruminolytic agents instilled into the middle
ears of 24 dogs: these each contained dioctyl sodium
sulfosuccinate; carbamide peroxide; triethanolamine; and
squalene, respectively. Only the product that contained 25%
squalene (Cerumene) did not cause morphologic and/or histologic
changes in the majority of bulla at necropsy on day 29. 90 Results
of a study determined that a Tris-EDTA and polyhexamethylene

vetexamprep.ir

biguanide solution was not ototoxic when applied daily to dogs’
ears for 21 and 14 days, with an intact and experimentally
ruptured tympanic membrane, respectively. 91
Systemic Glucocorticoid Therapy
When severe chronic changes to the ear canal exist, treatment with
systemic glucocorticoids for an initial period of 2 to 3 weeks, with
re-evaluation at the end of the treatment period, is recommended.
Dose and frequency should be adjusted depending on the severity
of the otitis. For mild otitis externa in dogs, prednisone or
prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg, PO, q24h for 7 days) can be used. Dose
frequency is then decreased to every other day. For more chronic
changes, 1 mg/kg, q24h is used; for severe disease, 2 mg/kg, q24h,
for 3 days is used, and then the dose is decreased to 1 mg/kg,
q24h. Although rarely needed, prednisolone or dexamethasone
can be used in cats.
Systemic Antimicrobial Therapy (see Table 119.1)
In most cases of otitis externa, topical antimicrobial treatment is
suﬃcient. However, in severe cases, deep infection of ear tissue is
present, and both topical and systemic therapy is necessary.
Although every a empt should be made to treat topically, some
owners are not able to administer topical medications properly, in
which case systemic antimicrobial therapy may be required. Oral
antibacterial selection is the same for otitis media as for otitis
externa and should be based on culture and susceptibility results
(see Table 119.1).
While awaiting culture results, empiric treatment for otitis may
be initiated based on the cytologic results. Good empiric oral
antimicrobial choices if cocci are seen include amoxicillinclavulanic acid or cephalexin. Poor choices would be penicillin,
ampicillin, and amoxicillin.
If rods are detected cytologically, P. aeruginosa should be
suspected. Fluoroquinolones are appropriate choices, with
reported susceptibilities of P. aeruginosa isolates from ears of 75%,
66.7%, and 46.9% for ciproﬂoxacin, marboﬂoxacin, and
enroﬂoxacin, respectively. 92 , 93 However, variable absorption has
been reported for ciproﬂoxacin in dogs, so the use of this oral
antibiotic in some patients could result in treatment failure. 94

vetexamprep.ir

If the bacterial culture and susceptibility data indicate
intermediate susceptibility or resistance to the chosen
antimicrobial agent, the oral drug should be discontinued.
Another drug to which the bacteria are susceptible should be
started, if one exists. As noted above, MICs are irrelevant for
topical drugs because of the high concentrations reached. In the
case of MDR P. aeruginosa or other bacteria, the only option is
topical therapy alone to treat the infection.
In most cases of M. pachydermatis otitis externa, systemic
therapy is not indicated. However, for severe yeast otitis externa,
an oral antifungal agent (usually an azole or terbinaﬁne) may be
administered in addition to a topical antifungal medication (see
Chapters 11 and 79).
Surgical Therapy
Animals that fail to respond to medical management of otitis
media are candidates for surgical intervention. In dogs with endstage otitis externa, the surgery of choice is total ear canal ablation
with lateral bulla osteotomy (TECABO) and bulla cure age. This
procedure removes the infected ear canal tissues as well as a
portion of the ventrolateral wall of the osseous bulla to aid in
complete removal of debris and epithelium within the tympanic
cavity. Bacterial cultures should be obtained from the tissue
(mucosa) and exudate from the tympanic bulla during this
procedure. This procedure has a potential for numerous
postoperative complications; however, they are usually shortlived and resolve with medical treatment. Recurrent infectious
otitis media occurs in approximately 10% of dogs after TECABO.
Because these recurrences rarely respond to systemic antibacterial
treatment alone, a second surgical procedure (ventral bulla
osteotomy and cure age) may be required to resolve the otitis
media. 95
Inﬂammatory polyps in the cat are usually treated surgically via
a ventral bulla osteotomy. However, if the inﬂammatory polyp is
in the nasopharyngeal region only, traction, plus postoperative
prednisolone at anti-inﬂammatory dosages, is an eﬀective
alternative to surgery. 92 Inﬂammatory polyps in the dog are
uncommon and have been successfully treated by either a ventral
bulla osteotomy or TECABO. 60

vetexamprep.ir

Prognosis
The prognosis for infectious otitis externa is good for cases that
are acute, those without progressive pathologic changes to the ear
canal (stenosis, hyperplasia), those without concurrent otitis
media, and those for which the underlying primary disease has
been diagnosed and controlled. Chronic otitis media may occur if
infection does not completely resolve. Rarely, an aural
cholesteatoma (epithelial-lined cavity) will develop in the middle
ear secondary to chronic otitis media. Should these complications
develop, and if the ear becomes calciﬁed, the prognosis for
medical management is poor, and surgical intervention is
required for resolution. Intracranial sepsis is a rare complication
of bacterial otitis media/interna, but may have grave
consequences if it is not diagnosed and treated promptly. 96

Case Example
Signalment

“Colonel”, a 3-year-old golden retriever living in the Central
Valley of California.

History

The dog was evaluated for a history of pruritus for
approximately 2 months. Pruritus was ﬁrst noted on the ventral
abdomen, but had since spread to the axilla and on the ventral
neck. The dog was on ﬂea control (afoxolaner monthly), as was
the cat in the household (selamectin monthly). A plant awn had
been removed from between the 3rd and 4th digits of the left
pelvic limb paw 1 month previously, for which the dog
received ampicillin PO for 10 days.

Physical Examination

Multiple epidermal collare es and erythema were found on the
entire ventrum and ventral neck. There was interdigital
erythema, especially on the thoracic limbs.

Cytology Findings

Deep skin scraping: No evidence of Demodex spp.

vetexamprep.ir

Multiple superﬁcial scrapings: No evidence of Sarcoptes
scabei (in addition, treatment with afoxolaner made mite
infestation unlikely).
Acetate tape preparations (inguinal, axillary and ventral
neck areas): many neutrophils with numerous
intracellular and extracellular cocci.

Microbiologic Findings

Aerobic bacterial culture (epidermal collare e; done because of
the recent exposure to antimicrobial drugs): Staphylococcus
pseudintermedius, resistant to ampicillin but otherwise broadly
susceptible, including to cephalexin.

Diagnosis

Superﬁcial pyoderma.

Treatment

Cephalexin (30 mg/kg, PO, q12h) for 30 days.

Outcome

At a follow-up examination 2 weeks after starting cephalexin,
pruritus had reduced by approximately 30%, along with
reduction in erythema and the number of epidermal collare es.
Cytologic examination of tape preparations showed fewer
neutrophils and cocci than at the initial visit. Follow-up at 30
days after starting treatment continued to show lessened
erythema, epidermal collare es, neutrophils, and cocci, but the
pruritus persisted. Because of concern for an underlying
allergy, a hypoallergenic diet trial using a prescription diet
composed of proteins to which the dog had not been previously
exposed was used. The owners were instructed to stop all other
foods, and switched to a topical anti-ﬂea product (afoxalaner is
ﬂavored with soy protein). Because there was still both
cytologic and clinical evidence of the pyoderma, cephalexin was
continued for another 30 days. After the second month of the
cephalexin, the erythema, epidermal collare es, and pyoderma
had resolved, and cytologic examination of tape preparations
revealed no abnormal ﬁndings. Cephalexin was discontinued.
After another month of feeding the new diet, the dog remained
apparently healthy. The original diet was reinstated, and after 5
days the pruritus returned.

vetexamprep.ir

Comments

This dog had a dietary allergy, which led to pruritus.
Mechanical trauma from pruritus led to disruption of the
cutaneous barrier, with secondary S. pseudintermedius
pyoderma. This resolved with the cephalexin, and was
apparently making a 30% contribution to the pruritus. After the
owners re-commenced the prescription diet, they then tried
adding various proteins for a week at a time. With this
approach, a beef allergy was identiﬁed. The owner was
instructed to avoid beef protein-based diets in the future. The
afoxolaner was recommenced.
