120: Abscesses and Cellulitis
Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Abscesses and cellulitis occur in any tissue and are one of the
most frequent conditions of cats.
• Anaerobes and Pasteurella multocida are most often isolated
from abscesses when culture is performed.
• Many abscesses will heal following incision and drainage.
Lavage with copious volumes of saline and surgical
placement of a Penrose drain may also be indicated. For large
abscesses or where there is evidence of cellulitis and
systemic signs, treatment with antimicrobials for 5 to 10 days
is recommended. A drug with activity against anaerobes and
Pasteurella spp. is recommended, such as amoxicillin.
• In endemic regions, plague and tularemia should be
considered as differential diagnoses for abscesses in dogs
and cats with systemic illness, lymphadenomegaly, fever, and
subcutaneous lesions because of their zoonotic significance.
When lesions are in the inguinal region of cats, mycobacterial
infections should be considered because routine surgical
approaches to treatment have the potential to exacerbate
disease.
• Testing for FeLV and FIV should be considered for cats with
bite and fight wounds, with a follow-up test no earlier than 60
days later.

Etiology and Pathogenesis

vetexamprep.ir

Abscesses, which are characterized by an accumulation of pus,
can occur in any tissue. Subcutaneous abscesses are the most
common bacterial infections of feline skin and probably the most
common site of abscess formation in dogs and cats (Fig. 120.1).
The following discussion focuses on feline cutaneous abscesses,
although the principles of diagnosis and treatment are similar in
any location. In general, abscesses are more commonly diagnosed
in cats than in dogs, likely because of frequent ﬁghting behavior
and needle-like teeth and claws that facilitate inoculation of
bacteria under the skin through a small wound. Feline skin is also
elastic and readily seals over small contaminated puncture
wounds, with accumulation of subcutaneous exudate. The size
and extent of abscessation also depends on the overlying skin
tension, amount of dead space, and gravitation of exudate below
the point of penetration. Pus-ﬁlled cavities that form above a
puncture site drain easily. Cavities that gravitate below the
puncture site may repeatedly drain through the puncture site
without complete resolution.
Because subcutaneous abscesses in cats usually result from bites
and scratches, the most common organisms found within them
are resident oral microﬂora (Table 120.1). Anaerobes are isolated
from more than two-thirds of abscesses, and the most common
facultative aerobe isolated is Pasteurella multocida. Chapter 75
includes a more detailed discussion of bacteria isolated from catbite wounds. Cats that sustain bite injuries are more likely to
become infected with FIV and to a lesser extent FeLV. 1

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs and Physical Examination
Findings
Cat-bite/ﬁght abscesses are usually located around the limbs,
head, dorsum, and base of the tail. Some cats have discernable
cutaneous masses with few other signs of illness, whereas more
extensive infection is associated with fever (103.6° F to 105.2°
[39.7° C to 40.6°C]), anorexia, lethargy, and regional
lymphadenomegaly. Pain is usually present at the site of infection,
and obvious swelling or warmth may or may not be present.
Mature abscesses that are at the point of rupture are usually

vetexamprep.ir

tender with a soft, ﬂuctuant central area. Erythema or
discoloration is occasionally apparent. Drainage of purulent
material occurs spontaneously or after surgical lancing. Foulsmelling, red-brown discharges occur, especially with tissue
necrosis and anaerobic bacterial infection (Fig. 120.2). Systemic
signs often resolve once the abscess ruptures, and the only
evidence of infection may be ma ed hair at the site of drainage.
Careful examination in the area of swelling usually reveals a small
puncture wound covered by a crust. Recurrent abscesses at the
same site suggest underlying osteomyelitis or neoplasia, poor
surgical drainage, immunodeﬁciency (e.g., FeLV or FIV infection),
antimicrobial resistance, or the presence of a foreign body.
Abscesses associated with foreign bodies, underlying
osteomyelitis, or certain fastidious organisms such as Nocardia or
Mycobacterium, or fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii also tend to
recur, persist, or spread in tissues. Abscesses in dogs and cats are
often associated with noticeable regional lymphadenomegaly.
Sometimes the overlying skin may become necrotic.
Additional clinical manifestations reﬂect possible involvement
of other organs or tissues. Lameness or paralysis may be apparent
with myositis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, or discospondylitis.
Stiﬀness, lethargy, nuchal rigidity, or seizures can be seen with
meningitis. Osteomyelitis may be manifested by chronic or
recurrent draining ﬁstulas that only temporarily respond to
antibacterial drugs. Respiratory distress, dyspnea, and stridor are
noted with pyothorax or abscesses that occur in the cervical
region. Vestibular signs can be noted if otitis media or interna
develops. Signs of bacteremia and systemic infection include
malaise and fever or reﬂect those of another organ system of
hematogenous localization.
Retrobulbar abscesses or cellulitis are associated with proptosis,
decreased globe mobility, oculonasal discharge, chemosis,
conjunctival congestion, protrusion of the third eyelid, pain while
opening the mouth, periocular swelling or discomfort, lethargy,
weight loss, and fever. Corneal ulcers may develop from exposure
keratitis or self-trauma associated with retrobulbar pain. In some
cases, swelling and discoloration may be seen caudal to the
maxillary molar teeth on opening the mouth.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of abscesses and cellulitis is usually based on the
history and physical examination ﬁndings. The possibility of an

vetexamprep.ir

abscess should also be considered in cats that develop acute or
subacute fever of unknown origin before extensive and invasive
diagnostic tests are performed. It should be considered in cats that
are acutely anorexic and/or lame, even in the absence of a
subcutaneous swelling, given that formation of visible abscesses
may be delayed or hidden. In endemic regions, plague and
tularemia should be on the diﬀerential diagnosis list in febrile cats
with subcutaneous swellings, lymphadenopathy, and fever.
Although much rarer than cat-bite abscesses, they have the
potential to cause life-threatening infections in exposed humans.
Atypical bacteria such as Nocardia spp., Mycobacterium spp., and
fungal pathogens, especially Sporothrix spp. and Cryptococcus spp.,
should be considered should there be a lack of response to
standard treatment. Mycobacterial infections should be high on
the diﬀerential diagnosis list for subcutaneous lesions that occur
in the inguinal region of cats. It is critical that these be considered
early because a empts to drain these abscesses surgically as if
they were routine bacterial infections have the potential to spread
infection further in tissues and worsen disease.
Culture of typical abscess wounds is not generally indicated
because surgical debridement with or without empiric
antimicrobial therapy is often eﬀective, anaerobes are diﬃcult to
culture, and aerobic and anaerobic culture adds signiﬁcant
expense for owners. In addition, unless there is evidence of
systemic illness, laboratory ﬁndings on bloodwork usually do not
reveal abnormalities that would change treatment. Testing for
retroviruses is recommended for cats with an unknown retrovirus
status. Because it can take several weeks for cats to become FeLV
antigen–positive or FIV antibody–positive after exposure,
retesting is recommended 2 months after a cat is seen for a cat
ﬁght wound. 1

Ultrasonography can be used to view the extent of a swelling,
locate accumulations of ﬂuid or pus in soft-tissue planes, and
evaluate for foreign bodies, which are more common in dogs than
in cats. Grass awns characteristically appear as double or triple
spindle-shaped echogenic objects within soft tissues. 2 , 3

vetexamprep.ir

Minimally invasive ultrasound-guided retrieval of foreign
material has also been helpful in avoiding standard surgical
methods. 2 , 4 Instillation of radiographic contrast medium may be
helpful in determining the extent or depth of a draining ﬁstulous
tract if a foreign body is likely, although improvements in
ultrasound image quality have reduced the requirement for such
procedures. Use of ultrasound guidance to inject methylene blue
dye around a plant awn can facilitate identiﬁcation and removal
of awns during surgery.
Chronic or recurrent draining abscesses should be evaluated by
radiography for underlying osteomyelitis, by cytology and culture
for possible fungal or atypical bacterial infection, or by surgical
exploration for the presence of a foreign body or ﬂy larva.

Treatment
Abscesses vary in severity and in the extent of therapeutic
intervention required. Small, localized abscesses that drain
spontaneously by the time animals are examined require that the
hair around the wound be clipped, and the margins of the wound
be cleaned. Should abscesses not be open, incision and drainage
(IAD) may be needed under sedation or general anesthesia. The
abscess cavity should then be lavaged with copious amounts of
normal saline (500 mL–1 L) or a dilute antiseptic such as 0.05%
chlorhexidine or 0.1% povidone iodine. Consideration should be
given to the use of normal saline. There is no evidence that
antiseptics improve outcome; they have the potential to damage
tissue, and severe nosocomial infections have been reported in
association with use of antiseptic solutions that become
contaminated with antiseptic-resistant bacteria such as
Pseudomonas spp.. In one report, ﬁve cats developed Burkholderia
cepacia complex (formerly Pseudomonas cepacia) skin infections and
the organism was isolated from a 2% chlorhexidine scrub solution
in the clinic; two cats developed sepsis and died. 5 More extensive
infections that cause signs of systemic illness may require
parenteral antibacterial administration, surgical drainage, or
supportive care with hospitalization and intravenous ﬂuid
administration. Considerable variability in the approach to
treatment of cutaneous abscesses has been observed in human
medicine. 6

vetexamprep.ir

Antibacterial Therapy
Antibacterial therapy has a decided but not absolute role in the
management of abscesses in cats. Although mortality and
complications resulting from abscesses have been reduced with
the use of antibacterials, these agents should not be given
indiscriminately or in the absence of other adjunctive measures.
Antibacterials alone are ineﬀective in penetrating walled-oﬀ
abscesses that require drainage. Indiscriminate antimicrobial use
may also select for drug-resistant bacteria or cause drug reactions.
7

Although antimicrobials are often routinely used in veterinary
practice for cat-bite abscesses, drainage and lavage may be
suﬃcient to resolve the abscesses in many cases. In human
medicine, antimicrobials are only considered necessary when
there are systemic signs of infection, comorbidities such as
immunosuppressive illnesses and diabetes mellitus, or if there is
extensive (> 5 cm in humans) surrounding cellulitis. 8 No
diﬀerence in outcome was identiﬁed when humans with
uncomplicated subcutaneous abscesses were treated with
drainage with or without antimicrobials. 9 If antimicrobials are
used, they should be given for a short duration (e.g., 5 to 7 days).
Penicillin derivatives such as amoxicillin are antibacterials of
choice for treating abscesses because they are active against
Pasteurella spp. and anaerobes; addition of clavulanic acid is
generally not necessary, adds expense, and is more likely to cause
GI adverse eﬀects (Table 120.2). Other antimicrobials likely to be
eﬀective are clindamycin and metronidazole, but these are less
well tolerated by cats. Although eﬀective against pathogens found
in cat-bite abscesses, 10-12 widespread use of third-generation
cephalosporins (e.g., cefovecin, cefpodoxime) and pradoﬂoxacin
has raised concerns about selection for resistant bacterial
populations. 13 Cefovecin is widely used because it requires only a
single injection, and one study from Australia showed that the
most common reason for administration of cefovecin in cats was
cat ﬁght injuries and abscesses. 13 In another study of 4.4 million
veterinary visit records from Australia, cefovecin and clavulanic
acid-amoxicillin were the most common antimicrobials prescribed
for dogs and cats. 14 Although convenient, because of concerns
about resistance, cefovecin and pradoﬂoxacin should only be used

vetexamprep.ir

for treatment of cat-bite abscesses when there is a need for
antibiotics and oral amoxicillin is not tolerated. In general,
systemic antibacterial therapy may be beneﬁcial in minimizing
abscess formation when given immediately after bite wound
contamination in order to prevent abscess formation or with
diﬀuse cellulitis (see also Chapter 75). Antimicrobial treatment of
abscesses in cats should also be considered when there are
systemic signs of illness and lesions are large. Without surgical
drainage, medical therapy could be continued for 7 to 10 days.

Surgery
Diﬀuse cellulitis or early abscesses may need to be monitored for
accumulation of pus before surgical drainage is performed.
Applying warm compresses daily may hasten this process.
Surgical therapy usually involves creating drainage openings at
the most ventral portion of an abscess cavity. Controversy exists
as to the degree and type of surgical closure indicated. The
abscess cavity can be debrided and a small portion of overlying
skin removed to prevent premature closure. Placement of a
Penrose drain that exits at the lowest point of incision with partial
closure can also be used to maintain a drainage opening. The
drain should only have a ventral exit through a new stab incision;
the proximal aspect of the drain should be placed in the dorsal
aspect of the wound and can be secured to the skin in this location
with a ma ress suture. The drain should be removed within 3 to 5
days when drainage becomes serosanguineous or decreases in
volume.
TABLE 120.2

Surgical drainage must be established whenever abscess
formation occurs within closed cavities. Retrobulbar abscesses can
be drained by passing a probe from immediately behind the last

vetexamprep.ir

upper molar upward into the retrobulbar space. Infraorbital
abscesses are usually associated with infection of the upper
carnassial tooth, which must be extracted. Abscesses of the middle
ear also require surgical drainage with debridement of bone
because of the loculation of pus within cavities surrounded by
bone. Abscesses associated with underlying osteomyelitis must be
treated by surgical debridement of infected bone. Foreign bodies
or material must be removed from abscess cavities before they
heal.
Castration and indoor housing are recommended as a
preventive measure to abscess formation because they reduce the
ﬁghting and roaming behavior of male cats.

121: Osteomyelitis,
Discospondylitis, and
Infectious Arthritis
Jane E. Sykes, and Amy S. Kapatkin

KEY POINTS
• Causes: The most common causes of osteomyelitis and
infectious monoarthritis in dogs are Staphylococcus spp., but
streptococci, other gram-negative bacteria, anaerobes, and
fungi may be involved. Bartonella, Nocardia, and
Mycobacterium can also cause osteomyelitis. Brucella can
cause osteomyelitis and discospondylitis. Polyarthritis may be
caused by a wide range of gram-positive and gram-negative
bacteria; vector-borne bacterial pathogens (Rickettsia
rickettsii, Ehrlichia canis, Anaplasma phagocytophilum,
Ehrlichia ewingii, Borrelia burgdorferi); protozoa (Leishmania);
and fungi.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide, although the prevalence
of brucellosis and vector-borne and fungal causes varies
geographically.
• Major Clinical Signs: Pain, lameness, fever, inappetence,
lethargy, draining skin lesions, and soft tissue swelling may
occur with osteomyelitis. Spinal pain, fever, lethargy,
inappetence, and pelvic limb paresis or paralysis can occur
with discospondylitis. A stiff gait, reluctance to move,
lameness, fever, inappetence, lethargy, and swollen joints
may occur with polyarthritis.
• Differential Diagnoses: Differential diagnoses for suspected
osteomyelitis, monoarthritis, and discospondylitis include bone
neoplasia, sterile foreign body reactions, and degenerative

vetexamprep.ir

osteoarthritis. Primary immune-mediated polyarthritis is the
major differential diagnosis for suspected infectious
polyarthritis.
• Human Health Significance: When draining wounds are
present, resistant bacteria such as methicillin-resistant
Staphylococcus spp. associated with osteomyelitis and
arthritis in dogs and cats may have the potential to colonize
human patients. Discospondylitis and polyarthritis caused by
Brucella spp. can be transmitted to humans through contact
with infected urine. Because vector-borne pathogens and
fungi of importance to human health can cause polyarthritis,
hospital staff should take special care to avoid sharps injuries
when working with animals with polyarthritis.

Infectious osteomyelitis is deﬁned as infection of the cortical bone,
periosteum, and myeloid cavity, and the associated inﬂammatory
response. The axial and/or appendicular skeleton may be
involved. Discospondylitis refers to inﬂammation of the
intervertebral discs and adjacent cartilaginous endplates, and
almost always results from infection by bacteria or fungi. Infectious
arthritis refers to inﬂammation of the synovium, synovial ﬂuid,
and associated cartilage secondary to infectious causes.
Osteomyelitis, discospondylitis, and arthritis can result from:
(1) hematogenous spread of bacteria or fungi to these sites, or (2)
from direct introduction of bacteria as a result of penetrating
wounds or surgery. When fungi are involved, molds such as
Aspergillus spp. or Paecilomyces spp. are more likely than yeasts to
cause osteomyelitis and discospondylitis (especially in genetically
predisposed breeds such as German shepherds, see Chapter 86);
Candida has rarely been associated with discospondylitis in dogs. 1
In contrast, osteomyelitis can be caused by opportunistic molds or
dimorphic fungi, especially Coccidioides spp. or Blastomyces spp.
Fungal arthritis is uncommon but has been associated with
infection by Coccidioides spp., Blastomyces spp., and Cryptococcus
spp.

Osteomyelitis

vetexamprep.ir

Etiologic Agents and Epidemiology
Bacterial osteomyelitis most often results from direct introduction
of bacteria into wounds adjacent to bone. Bacteria can be
introduced into the bone as a result of penetrating foreign bodies,
surgical wounds (especially orthopedic surgeries with implant
placement), traumatic wounds, bite wounds, or extension of soft
tissue infections. In one study from Brazil, 78% of cases followed a
motor vehicle accident, 17% dog bite wounds, and 5% were
secondary to pododermatitis. 2 Human research shows a low
incidence of osteomyelitis for elective procedures, but high (33%)
reinfection rates after a Staphylococcus infection occurs. There are
three ways that staphylococci from an implant bioﬁlm invade
bone tissue and evade inactivation: (1) formation of abscesses in
the soft tissues and bone marrow; (2) glycocalyx formation on the
implant; and (3) colonization of the osteocyte lacuna-canalicular
network of cortical bone. 3 Veterinary orthopedic infection rates
are poorly reported. Infection rates reported depend on the
orthopedic procedure. 4 Tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO)
surgery for cranial cruciate rupture, one of the most common
orthopedic surgical procedures performed, has a postoperative
implant removal rate of 2.7% to 8.5% because of conﬁrmed
implant-associated infection. 5–11 For unknown reasons, the
surgical site infection (SSI) rate after TPLO appears to be higher
than that after routine “clean” orthopedic surgeries that involve
osteotomy (as opposed to fracture repair). In a report that was
published before the TPLO procedure was described, the overall
infection rate after any orthopedic surgery procedure was 3 (<1%)
of 502 surgeries. 12 In contrast, radiographically detectable
osteomyelitis was reported in 14 (7.3%) of 193 dogs that
underwent TPLO surgery and was the single most common
complication of the procedure. 6 A 1% rate of osteomyelitis was
reported in a prospective study of 100 dogs undergoing stiﬂe
surgery, whereas the incision infection rate was 8%. 13 One recent
review reported TPLO infection rates that ranged from 0.8% to
14.3%. 14 Total joint replacement infection rate was reported to be
up to 11%. 4 , 15 , 16 Infection rate after fracture repair varies. It was
9 (8%) of 110 surgeries in one study. 17 In this study, 20% of the
fractures were open. Open fractures were 4 times more likely to be

vetexamprep.ir

contaminated with bacteria at the time of surgery than the closed
fractures, and contaminated wounds were 5 times more likely to
develop complications (seroma, drainage, and dehiscence) than
those without contamination. Distal radius/ulna and tibial
fractures were 10.5 times and 7.5 times more likely to be
contaminated than femoral fractures, respectively. Animals with a
normal postoperative temperature and a clean surgical wound
did not develop postoperative complications.
Although gram-positive aerobes such as staphylococci and, to a
lesser extent, streptococci predominate as a cause of osteomyelitis
in dogs and cats, the organisms present and the bone(s) aﬀected
generally reﬂect the underlying type of injury that led to infection.
For example, osteomyelitis that follows SSI is often caused by
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, a common commensal of canine
skin (Table 121.1). Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative
bacterial infections can also cause orthopedic SSIs. 8 In contrast,
anaerobes (e.g., Bacteroides, Cutibacterium acnes, Peptostreptococcus,
Clostridium, Fusobacterium, Actinomyces) and aerobic gram-positive
bacteria (staphylococci, enterococci, streptococci) or gramnegative bacteria (Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella
pneumoniae, Proteus, Pasteurella) predominate in osteomyelitis that
results from bite wound infections, tooth root abscesses, or
penetrating foreign bodies. 18 , 19 Such mixed bacterial infections
are also common in dogs with digital osteomyelitis. Anaerobes
were isolated from 64% of osteomyelitis cases in dogs in one
study. 19
Osteomyelitis secondary to bacteremia, also known as
hematogenous osteomyelitis, is very rare and usually aﬀects young to
middle-aged animals. 4 , 20 The metaphyseal regions are often
involved, sometimes with extension to the epiphyses and joints
(Fig. 121.1). The pathogenesis remains obscure. It has been
suggested that discontinuous endothelium in the primary
spongiosa may predispose to extravasation of erythrocytes and
bacteria in this region. 21 In humans, acute hematogenous
osteomyelitis results from bacterial seeding secondary to transient
bacteremia, which may result from conditions such as otitis
media. Trauma to the bone and upregulation of bacterial
virulence factors may also be important for allowing
establishment of infection. 22 Sternal, pelvic, and vertebral

vetexamprep.ir

osteomyelitis can also result from hematogenous spread of
bacteria. 20 Osteomyelitis occasionally also results from
hematogenous spread of fastidious bacteria such as Brucella,
Bartonella, Mycobacterium, Nocardia, and Nocardiopsis spp.

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
The development of bacterial osteomyelitis requires the presence
not only of bacteria but also of compromised bone. Bone necrosis
can result from trauma (i.e., fracture), surgery, or underlying bone
neoplasia. Bacteria adhere to ﬁbronectin, a connective tissue
glycoprotein, through the use of a variety of adhesins. The
presence of foreign material promotes persistence of infection in
the form of bioﬁlm (Fig. 121.2). Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, S.
aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and E. coli are particularly apt to
form bioﬁlms. Adherent bacteria produce a matrix of condensed
exopolysaccharides known as a glycocalyx. 23 The bioﬁlm is
composed of a cluster of microorganisms and glycocalyx on an
inanimate surface. Embedded in the bioﬁlm mixture of
glycocalyx, host-derived serum proteins, and cellular debris,
bacteria often form into microcolonies. Within bioﬁlm, bacteria
evade opsonization and phagocytosis and are protected from the
eﬀects of antimicrobial drugs. Staphylococci can reside within
osteoblasts, and when cell death occurs, they are released and can
re-establish a productive infection. 23 Bacteria within bioﬁlms
intercommunicate via cytokines (quorum sensing), and this
appears to assist them in their ability to evade host defense
mechanisms. Bone sequestra can also become colonized by
bacteria, which evade host defenses in the absence of adequate
blood supply. Loose implants and fracture instability contribute to
bone resorption, compromised blood supply, and persistent
infection. 21 Some implant types are more apt to be colonized by
bacteria. Stainless-steel plates have been associated with a higher
risk of SSIs than titanium plates. 24 In one study, Slocum TPLO
plates were more likely to be removed than other types of TPLO
plates because of local bacterial infection and clinical signs of
inﬂammation. 11 In another retrospective study of 104 TPLO
procedures, the rate of SSI was higher among dogs treated with

vetexamprep.ir

Synthes implants than among those with Slocum implants, but
there was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the rate of infection among
the New Generation, Synthes, and Slocum implants. 25

Inﬂammatory cells recruited to the site of infection release
enzymes that cause additional bone necrosis, with destruction of
cancellous and cortical bone and abscessation of associated soft
tissue. The end result is focal swelling, pain, draining skin lesions,
and lameness. Small draining skin lesions often represent the “tip
of the iceberg”, with extensive bone involvement hidden beneath
the skin (see Fig. 121.2). The presence of anaerobes can be
associated with a foul odor or gas production. Fever, inappetence,

vetexamprep.ir

lethargy, and leukocytosis are occasionally present in animals
with acute osteomyelitis but are often absent in chronic
osteomyelitis. In a 2018 study of dogs that required removal of
tibial tuberosity advancement (TTA) cages to resolve SSIs, the
mean time to appearance of signs related to SSI was 403 days after
surgery (median: 287 days, range: 10 to 1,547 days). 26
Occasionally, infection reactivates in dogs years after surgery and
implant placement. In human patients, latent periods between
infection and development of osteomyelitis can last many
decades. 27
Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in dogs and cats with osteomyelitis
include lameness, localized pain, soft tissue swelling, muscle
atrophy, and the presence of draining tracts. Fever and lethargy
can also be identiﬁed in some animals.

Diagnosis
In most cases, osteomyelitis is diagnosed on the basis of history,
physical examination, and diagnostic imaging ﬁndings. Aerobic
and anaerobic bacterial culture of aﬀected bone or any implants
present is required for deﬁnitive diagnosis.
Laboratory Abnormalities
The CBC of animals with osteomyelitis may be unremarkable or
reveal mild anemia, neutrophilia with bandemia, and
monocytosis. The serum biochemistry panel and urinalysis are
usually unremarkable, unless bacteremia or other systemic
disease is also present.

vetexamprep.ir

Pathogenesis of osteomyelitis.
Necrotic bone is colonized by bacteria, which
adhere to fibronectin and in the presence of
foreign material (in this case, an implant) can
form biofilm. Biofilm consists of bacterial
aggregates embedded in a matrix of
exopolysaccharide (bacterial slime). The
biofilm protects the bacteria from antibodies,
phagocytosis, and antimicrobial drugs.
FIG. 121.2

Diagnostic Imaging
Radiographic changes in dogs and cats with osteomyelitis vary
considerably in extent and character. In some dogs and cats, only
soft tissue swelling may be evident. Plain radiography is
insensitive and can be poorly speciﬁc for diagnosis of
osteomyelitis, and interpretation can vary from one boardcertiﬁed radiologist to another. In one study, plain radiographic
ﬁndings were interpreted as osteomyelitis by two radiologists in
only ﬁve of eight dogs with experimentally induced osteomyelitis.
28 One radiologist diagnosed osteomyelitis in only three of the
eight dogs, but that radiologist was less likely than the other
radiologists to diagnose osteomyelitis when infection was absent.

vetexamprep.ir

When radiographic bony changes are evident, they consist of
periosteal proliferation, which may be smooth or speculated; focal
osteopenia with cortical resorption or thinning; loss of trabecular
markings; lucency around implants such as cages, plates, or
screws; and sequestration (Fig. 121.3). Pathologic fractures may be
evident in dogs with fungal osteomyelitis. Scintigraphy with
technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate, gallium-67 citrate,
and indium-111-labeled leukocytes has been used in human
medicine but is considered expensive and can lack speciﬁcity. 29
Bone scintigraphy has also been used for diagnosis of
hematogenous arthritis in dogs with multiple site involvement. 20
Ultrasound
imaging,
contrast
CT,
MRI,
and
18Fﬂurodeoxyglucose PET are sensitive diagnostic tools and may be
useful for identiﬁcation of sequestra, foreign material, and abscess
formation. IV administration of ultraparamagnetic iron oxide
nanoparticles during MRI, which are taken up by macrophages,
has shown promise for detection of vertebral osteomyelitis and
diﬀerentiation of osteomyelitis from aseptic inﬂammation. 4 , 30 , 31
Serum immunoassays that detect antibody responses to
staphylococcal proteins, such as iron acquisition proteins and
secreted toxins, have also shown utility for diagnosis and
prognostication in human patients with osteomyelitis, although
they can lack speciﬁcity due to previous exposure or
asymptomatic colonization. 3

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture and susceptibility should
be performed on aspirates of pus, bone biopsies, or removed
implants from dogs and cats with osteomyelitis. Aspirates should
be collected in a sterile manner from the focus of infection to
avoid contamination with surface bacteria (e.g., via aspiration of
lesions through healthy skin after skin antisepsis, or through
collection of biopsies or implants during surgical exploration).
Negative culture results may reﬂect an insuﬃcient specimen size,
or the presence of fastidious bacteria such as anaerobes, Bartonella,
Brucella, Nocardia, or Mycobacterium spp. Sonication of implants
removed from humans that had implant-associated osteomyelitis
increased the sensitivity of culture from 67% to 90%. 32 Blood
cultures should be performed if hematogenous osteomyelitis is
suspected based on the history and clinical ﬁndings (young
animal, multiple sites aﬀected, sternal or vertebral involvement,
other systemic illness, or immunosuppression).

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic Findings
Pathologic ﬁndings in osteomyelitis depend on the causative
agent and chronicity of infection. Inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrates may
range
from
suppurative
(acute
osteomyelitis)
to
pyogranulomatous or lymphoplasmacytic. The neutrophilic
inﬁltrate in dogs with acute osteomyelitis may be accompanied by
the presence of ﬁbrin, free red blood cells, and necrotic debris.
There may be evidence of bone resorption with multinucleated
osteoclasts and new bone and ﬁbrous tissue formation. In some
cases, intralesional bacteria or fragments of foreign material (such
as plant material) are observed (Fig. 121.4).

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment recommendations for focal osteomyelitis secondary to
trauma, surgery, or foreign body penetration depends on the
severity and chronicity of disease, the location of osteomyelitis,
the presence or absence of foreign material or implant, and the
extent of blood supply to the bone. In animals with fractures,
early detection and treatment of osteomyelitis is critical to prevent
extensive bone necrosis and nonunion. Antimicrobial drug
treatment alone is usually not suﬃcient to resolve chronic
bacterial osteomyelitis, because sequestra and bioﬁlm are
avascular and are not eﬀectively penetrated by antimicrobial
drugs. In general, treatment requires debridement, removal of
sequestra and foreign material, dead space removal, copious
lavage with sterile saline, rigid fracture stabilization, systemic
and/or local administration of appropriate antimicrobial drugs,
and grafting of bone deﬁcits. Because implants may ultimately
need to be removed to resolve infection, fractures may need
stabilization through alternative means, such as external skeletal
ﬁxation or one- or two-stage implant replacement revision
surgeries. Removal of the infected implant and replacing it at the
time of debridement helps to prevent colonization of the lacunar
canaliculi by staphylococci. 33 Maintenance of bone stabilization is
considered paramount in human medicine, because unstable
fractures or surgical sites are considerably more prone to infection
than those that are stable. 29 It is considered be er to leave an
implant in place and maintain stabilization than to remove an
implant early. In a study of 121 people with infection after

vetexamprep.ir

fracture ﬁxation, approximately 70% of the time, stable implants
could be salvaged following extensive irrigation, debridement,
and appropriate systemic antibiotics. 34 Systemic antimicrobial
drug therapy (and often regional antibiotic therapy in the form of
antimicrobial drug–impregnated beads or gel) is required while
the bone heals. In some cases, foci of osteomyelitis may be
removed en bloc without the need for further graft placement or
stabilization (e.g., digital osteomyelitis). Resected bone should be
submi ed for histopathology (to conﬁrm the presence of
osteomyelitis and identify other processes such as fungal infection
or neoplasia) as well as aerobic and anaerobic culture and
susceptibility testing. Wounds are left open after debridement if
continued debridement is needed via wet-to-dry bandaging. In
severely infected cases, vacuum-assisted wound closure
techniques are recommended. If all nonviable tissue has been
removed, closed irrigation systems or vascularized tissue ﬂaps
may be used to manage dead space. A sterile dressing should be
used to cover the wounds, with daily bandage changes until
exudation resolves. If needed, autogenous cancellous bone graft
placement is delayed until infection has been controlled and
granulation tissue has begun to ﬁll the wound (usually 1 to 2
weeks after initiation of antimicrobial drug treatment). 35 When
graft placement or fracture stabilization is not possible because of
ﬁnancial concerns or uncontrollable infection, amputation may be
necessary.
The choice of antimicrobial drugs should be based on the
results of aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture and
susceptibility. If the animal is stable, treatment should be
withheld until results are available, and medications to manage
pain should be administered. If earlier antimicrobial treatment is
deemed necessary pending the results of culture and
susceptibility, the drug chosen should be based on the history
(e.g., postsurgical infection versus bite wound infection) and local
prevalence data for the practice (Table 121.2). The presence of
anaerobes should be assumed if anaerobic culture is not
performed, or anaerobes are not isolated, especially if the
underlying insult was a bite wound or a traumatic injury.
Clindamycin is a reasonable initial choice for infections that could
include susceptible staphylococci and/or anaerobic bacteria and
was eﬀective in experimental models of S. aureus osteomyelitis in

vetexamprep.ir

dogs, 36 but a signiﬁcant proportion of MRS exhibit clindamycin
resistance or inducible clindamycin resistance (see Chapter 51). In
a study of dogs with osteomyelitis from Brazil, nearly 60% of
isolates exhibited clindamycin resistance. 2 In that study, a greater
proportion of isolates (79%) were susceptible to amoxicillinclavulanic acid. If gram-negative bacteria or MRS are suspected,
the addition of an aminoglycoside may be necessary if treatment
must be instituted before the results of culture and susceptibility
become available. However, aminoglycosides penetrate poorly
into purulent material, so adequate debridement is essential.
Combinations of antibiotics are sometimes required in animals
with polymicrobial infections. Systemic antibiotic treatment
should be continued for at least 4 to 6 weeks. Longer periods of
treatment may be required in some dogs and cats, especially if an
implant is present. The duration of therapy should be considered
on a case-by-case basis, depending on the underlying problem
(fracture, corrective osteotomy, bite wound), the likely organisms
present, and depth of infection. Antimicrobial drugs should be
given parenterally in the hospital for at least the ﬁrst 3 to 5 days,
and for longer if possible. There is evidence that use of
ﬂuoroquinolones may delay bone healing, and so in human
medicine it is recommended that the use of ﬂuoroquinolones be
avoided if possible. 29 The use of linezolid has been reported for
treatment of MDR orthopedic MRSP SSIs in 4 dogs. 37 Adverse
eﬀects of vomiting, lethargy, and anorexia (2 dogs) and
regenerative anemia (1 dog) were reported. Infections recurred in
2 dogs after discontinuation of treatment.

In addition to systemic treatment, antibiotic-impregnated beads
or gel can be used to treat chronic osteomyelitis and septic
arthritis in dogs. 38 , 39 Beads are prepared in the operating room
by mixing an antimicrobial drug with commercially available
calcium sulfate bead sets and se ing through the use of a rubber
mold. The beads are placed at the site of infection, where they
deliver high concentrations of drug to the site (e.g., initially 500fold that of normal serum concentrations with systemic
treatment), sometimes for several weeks, without systemic
adverse eﬀects. 40 The antimicrobial drugs used are generally heat
stable, hydrophilic, and have activity against MRS, such as
aminoglycosides (gentamicin or tobramycin) or vancomycin.
Gentamicin-impregnated beads were shown to reduce bioﬁlm
formation by methicillin-resistant S. pseudintermedius. 41 Other
products include antibiotic-impregnated collagen, bone graft
substitutes such as calcium phosphate (Fig. 121.5), and a variety of
synthetic polymers such as polylactic acid, polylactide-coglycolides, and cross-linked polydimethylsiloxane. 40 Tobramycinimpregnated calcium phosphate beads have been used
successfully to treat osteomyelitis in dogs. 39 Polymers have been
engineered to control the duration and concentration of antibiotic
treatment at the site. Hydrogel is another medium to deliver
antibiotics. The gel is aliquoted and then sterilized before use. It
has to be refrigerated and mixed with the antimicrobial of choice
in a hood to avoid contamination. The gel can be injected through
a rubber catheter or placed in the site before wound closure. It has
the advantage of being less expensive than beads but has a shorter
duration of antimicrobial elution. The gel may be preferred when
the infection is near a joint or a surgical approach is not being
used. 38 Recently, IV administration of activated mesenchymal
stem cells in conjunction with antibiotic therapy has also shown

vetexamprep.ir

eﬃcacy for treatment of chronic osteomyelitis. 42 Optimization of
local antibiotic delivery systems in order to promote continuous
delivery of appropriate concentrations of antibiotics, while
avoiding colonization of the materials used, is currently the
subject of extensive research.

Prevention
Although not a substitute for sterile surgical technique and strict
hospital infection control measures (see Chapter 15), perioperative
antimicrobial drug treatment is an accepted aid for prevention of
soft tissue surgical infections and osteomyelitis, especially when
orthopedic implants are anticipated. Recommendations published

vetexamprep.ir

for human medicine state that adequate prophylaxis requires: (1)
antimicrobial agents with activity against organisms likely to be
encountered in the surgical ﬁeld; (2) timely preoperative
antimicrobial drug administration (within 60 minutes of incision);
(3) bactericidal concentrations of drug in the serum and tissues
during the time that the wound is open; and (4) a duration of 24
hours after surgery. 43 Additional intraoperative doses should be
given if the procedure lasts longer than two half-lives of the drug
being administered (usually at least 2 hours). However, one study
showed that administration of antibiotics longer than 60 minutes
before incision was associated with a higher SSI rate than when
antibiotics were administered within 60 minutes of incision, but
the risk of SSI did not increase if antibiotic administration
occurred after incision. 44 In practices where the prevalence of
postoperative infections with MRS is low, preoperative treatment
with cefazolin may be eﬀective. Where the regional prevalence of
skin colonization with MRS is high (e.g., >10%), preoperative
treatment with cefazolin and an aminoglycoside such as amikacin
could be used. Nevertheless, use of perioperative vancomycin in
humans undergoing orthopedic procedures to prevent SSI was
associated with an increased risk of SSI (OR 1.75), whereas
administration of cefazolin decreased the risk of SSI (OR 0.49). 44
Whether administration of antimicrobials for multiple days
postoperatively decreases the risk of infections after orthopedic
procedures in dogs has been controversial, with some studies
showing no signiﬁcant beneﬁt, and others showing reduction in
the prevalence of SSIs. In a prospective study of 400 dogs that
underwent implant surgery, dogs were randomized to receive
either 5 days of postoperative antibiotics, or only perioperative
antibiotics. The rate of SSI was similar between the two groups. 45
In another prospective study of 100 dogs undergoing clean
orthopedic procedures that required stainless-steel plates,
postoperative administration of antimicrobials (cephalexin or
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid) for 7 days was associated with a lower
risk of SSI (4.3%) than for dogs that did not receive postoperative
antimicrobials. 46 Prophylactic treatment should never be
continued for longer than 24 hours after surgery because it can
select for drug-resistant bacterial infections. In human patients,
antibiotic-impregnated implants have been used to prevent

vetexamprep.ir

a achment of bacteria to their surface. 3 , 40 , 47 Silver-impregnated
coatings show promise for prevention of colonization by S.
pseudintermedius. 48 Minimization of surgery time, careful surgical
technique, and use of plate types that are associated with a lower
risk of postoperative infection (i.e., non–Slocum-type TPLO
plates) may also prevent postsurgical osteomyelitis. 11 Metals used
in implants should be of the same type (e.g., plate and screws) to
minimize the chance of galvanic corrosion. Galvanic corrosion
occurs when metals of diﬀerent electrochemical properties are
placed in close proximity in an electrolytic environment. This can
predispose to implant loosening, local infection, or sarcoma
formation. 49 Currently, it is considered acceptable to leave
implants in place after healing unless the animal has persistent
pain associated with the implant, or radiographic evidence of
osteomyelitis or osteopenia is present. This is because the process
of implant removal itself can be costly and may be followed by
osteomyelitis or fracture. However, owners of pets with implants
should be advised that although rare, possible long-term
complications of implant placement include reactivation of
infection in the future or development of malignancy at the
implant site.

Public Health Aspects
Dogs and cats with bacterial osteomyelitis can shed antibioticresistant gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria that have the
potential to colonize humans and later be a source of human
infection. Infections acquired after orthopedic surgeries, especially
TPLOs, and joint replacements are problematic. Most dogs are
infected with S. pseudintermedius, but a smaller percentage of dogs
are infected with S. aureus, which is more likely to colonize
humans (see Table 121.1). However, in some cases, the human in
the household may have been the source of S. aureus infection.
Some hospitals experience a high prevalence (>10%) of
postoperative wound infections with MRS. In a case-control study
that included dogs with methicillin-resistant S. aureus infection
(cases) and dogs with methicillin-susceptible S. aureus infection
(controls), surgical implant placement was associated with a 33fold increased risk of methicillin-resistant S. aureus infection (P =
.001). 50 Infected osteomyelitis wounds should be covered with a

vetexamprep.ir

suitable dressing at all times, and owners should be advised to
wear gloves when handling their pets (especially if the wound is
infected) and to wash their hands properly afterwards. In the
hospital, animals with draining orthopedic surgical wound
infections due to methicillin-resistant or MDR bacteria should be
handled by a limited number of individuals who wear gloves, a
gown, and dedicated equipment, and signage should be posted.
Hand washing should be performed after protective wear is
removed, and all equipment used should be disinfected properly
(see Chapter 15).

Discospondylitis
Etiologic Agents, Pathogenesis, and
Epidemiology
Discospondylitis most often follows hematogenous spread of
bacteria or fungi to the cartilaginous vertebral endplates, with
extension to the intervertebral discs. Bacteria or fungi are thought
to lodge in the endplates because blood ﬂow slows in this region.

vetexamprep.ir

In most cases, the source of infection cannot be identiﬁed, but
infection can originate from the urogenital tract, abscesses, skin
wounds, respiratory tract infections, or the oral cavity.
Occasionally, discospondylitis follows extension of infection from
an adjacent site, such as following vertebral column SSIs,
complications of epidural anesthesia, bite wounds, or migrating
grass awns.
Risk factors for discospondylitis in dogs include male sex, older
age, and breed. 1 Predisposed breeds are often large-breed dogs,
such as great Danes, boxers, ro weilers, English bulldogs,
German shepherd dogs, and Doberman pinschers. German
shepherds and Rhodesian ridgebacks are predisposed to systemic
mold infections that can target the intervertebral discs. 51
Although discospondylitis is frequently diagnosed in Labrador
and golden retrievers, these dogs are popular breeds and were not
found to be at risk. 1 Discospondylitis is extremely rare in cats and
usually follows trauma such as cat bites, with associated
meningomyelitis. 52–56 Concurrent disorders identiﬁed in dogs
include genitourinary tract infections (prostatitis, orchitis,
metritis, and/or UTI), pyoderma and otitis, immunosuppressive
drug treatment, heartworm disease, recent vertebral column
surgery, respiratory tract infection, bite wounds and other
traumatic injuries, migrating foreign bodies, recent nonvertebral
surgery, septic arthritis, severe intestinal parasitism, and infective
endocarditis.
The incidence of discospondylitis in dogs and prevalence of
diﬀerent causative infectious agents vary geographically. In one
study in the United States, the incidence of discospondylitis was
higher in the southern states than in the northern states. 1 In 123
dogs with discospondylitis from the southern United States, the
most common pathogen isolated was Staphylococcus (41% of 63
isolates), followed by Streptococcus (12%), and E. coli (11%). 1 Other
bacteria included Klebsiella, Brucella canis, Pseudomonas, Proteus,
and Actinomyces spp. (<10% each). When the results of Brucella
serology and culture were combined, 13 of the dogs were
diagnosed with brucellosis. Only two dogs were infected with
fungal organisms, one with Candida tropicalis and the other with
an unidentiﬁed fungal agent. Mixed infections were detected in 11
(9%) dogs. In 23 dogs with discospondylitis from the Paciﬁc

vetexamprep.ir

northwest of the United States, 10 of 18 isolates were
staphylococci, 3 were streptococci, and 3 were E. coli; Brucella
infection was not reported and a ﬁlamentous fungal species
(Phialemonium or Paecilomyces) was isolated from two dogs. 57 In
contrast, ﬁlamentous fungal species were isolated from nearly one
third of dogs diagnosed with discospondylitis at the University of
California, Davis (Table 121.3). The most common bacterial isolate
was methicillin-susceptible S. pseudintermedius; MRS were not
detected. In more than half of dogs with discospondylitis, the
causative agent is not identiﬁed. Lumbar discospondylitis caused
by Actinomyces spp. and anaerobic bacteria may occur as a result
of migration of inhaled grass awns, which lodge in the
retroperitoneal space. Sexually intact male dogs and dogs from
the southeastern states are at increased risk for B. canis
discospondylitis, 58 but it can occur in any region and in dogs of
any sex. In a German study, 4 dogs with B. canis discospondylitis
were described; the dogs were young (7–30 months of age) and
had been imported into Germany from eastern Europe (Moldavia,
Macedonia, Romania). 59 Other reported agents include
Enterobacter, Nocardia, Salmonella, and Erysipelothrix. 60–64

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of discospondylitis include fever, lethargy,
inappetence, weight loss, spinal pain, a hunched stance, lameness,
reluctance to move, and/or reluctance to jump or climb stairs. The
duration of signs is extremely variable, but are usually present for
less than 1 month. 58 Spinal cord compression as a result of
vertebral subluxation, abscess formation, disc protrusion or
extrusion, and soft tissue proliferation can lead to neurologic
deﬁcits such as delayed or absent placing reactions, paresis with
ataxia or paralysis, and loss of deep pain sensation. Neurologic
deﬁcits were detected in 59 (48%) of 123 dogs in one study. 1 In
another study, paresis or paralysis was detected in 20 (87%) of 23
dogs and 8 of these dogs were nonambulatory. 58 The neurologic
signs reﬂect the severity and location of discospondylitis lesions;
in the la er study, the severity of neurologic signs was correlated
with the number of compressive lesions and the percentage of

vetexamprep.ir

spinal cord or cauda equina compression. 58 The majority (50% to
60%) of dogs have lesions in the thoracolumbar spine (especially
the lumbosacral junction); cervical lesions are present in fewer
than 20% of dogs. 1 , 58 , 65 , 66 Around 30% to 40% of dogs have
multiple lesions. Thus, tetraparesis (which reﬂects the presence of
compressive cervical lesions) is less common (<5% of dogs) than
pelvic limb paresis or paralysis (33% of dogs). The location of
discospondylitis lesions (e.g., L7 to S1 versus C5 to C6) does not
seem to aﬀect the likelihood of cord compression. 66

Physical Examination Findings
Dogs with discospondylitis may have fever (although it is often
absent), lethargy, weakness, and pain on palpation or
manipulation of the spine. Spinal pain is not consistently present.
In some dogs, pain is diﬃcult to localize or manifests as apparent
abdominal pain when the abdomen is palpated, especially if
upward pressure is placed on the spine. Dogs with neurologic
deﬁcits can be tetraparetic or have pelvic limb paresis or paralysis.
Loss of deep pain sensation can occur in dogs with severe
compression lesions. Neurologic examination may reveal delayed
or absent placing reactions and exaggerated or reduced segmental
reﬂexes. Evaluation for abnormalities that reﬂect the presence of
concurrent disorders (such as cardiac murmurs in dogs with
endocarditis or swollen joints in dogs with polyarthritis) should

vetexamprep.ir

be carefully performed. Occasionally, discospondylitis is an
incidental ﬁnding on plain radiography (performed to evaluate
concurrent disease such as fever of unknown origin), and clinical
signs that suggest discospondylitis are absent.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of discospondylitis is based on physical examination
ﬁndings; imaging (plain radiography, CT/MRI); culture of blood,
CSF, or aspirates of disc material; and serologic testing for Brucella
spp. (antibody tests) or fungi (antigen tests). The reader is referred
to Chapter 71 (Brucellosis) and Chapter 86 (Aspergillosis and
Penicilliosis) for information on serologic testing for these
diseases. Serologic testing for Aspergillus galactomannan antigen
is inexpensive, and positive results (galactomannan indices > 1.5)
correlate strongly with an underlying mold infection. 67 Rarely,
mixed infections with bacteria and fungi occur, and bacterial
contaminants can complicate interpretation of blood and disc
aspirates. Thus, all dogs with discospondylitis should ideally be
tested for Aspergillus antigen before antibiotic treatment is
initiated. It is especially important to test predisposed breeds such
as German shepherds and Rhodesian ridgebacks. Aﬀected dogs
should be evaluated for evidence of disease at other anatomic
sites. If possible, this should consist of thoracic radiographs and
abdominal
ultrasound,
echocardiography
(for
infective
endocarditis), and aerobic bacterial culture of the urine.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Often the CBC and biochemistry panel are surprisingly
unremarkable in dogs with discospondylitis. There may be mild
to moderate neutrophilia with bandemia and/or lymphopenia on
the CBC. Mild hypoalbuminemia and mild to moderate
hyperglobulinemia are the most common abnormalities on the
biochemistry panel. Dogs with fungal discospondylitis may be
azotemic because of concurrent fungal pyelonephritis. 51
Urinalysis may show pyuria, bacteriuria, funguria, proteinuria,
and/or cylindruria in dogs with concurrent UTIs. Analysis of the
CSF often reveals mild to markedly increased CSF protein
concentration and rarely increased total nucleated cell count. 57

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Radiographic changes in dogs (and cats) with discospondylitis
include narrowing or widening of the intervertebral space,
irregularity or lysis of the vertebral body endplates, endplate
lucency, sclerosis at the margins of bone loss, proliferative or
osteolytic lesions within adjacent vertebral bones and bridging
spondylosis, and, in some cases, vertebral subluxation or fracture
(Fig. 121.6). 63 It has been suggested that there may be diﬀerences
in the radiographic appearance of lesions in young dogs when
compared with adult dogs, but more studies would help to verify
this. Because multiple disc spaces are frequently aﬀected,
radiographs of the entire spine should be performed to properly
assess the extent and severity of disease. Radiographic changes
may lag behind clinical signs for as long as 6 weeks in dogs with
discospondylitis, so radiographs should be repeated every 1 to 2
weeks if discospondylitis is suspected and plain radiographs are
initially normal. Alternatively, advanced imaging with CT or MRI
may reveal lesions not seen on plain radiographs. Plain
radiography does not allow visualization of the degree of spinal
cord compression, so advanced imaging is required to further
evaluate dogs with neurologic signs. Ultrasonography may be
useful for detection of retroperitoneal grass awns in dogs with
localized lumbar discospondylitis on plain radiography, and can
also show changes associated with discospondylitis, such as loss
of reverberation artefact. Bone phase nuclear scintigraphy may
also be helpful for diagnosis.
Contrast Radiography
Myelography can identify the site(s), type (vertebral subluxation
or soft tissue proliferation), and extent of spinal cord compression
in dogs with discospondylitis and allow planning for
decompressive surgery (Fig. 121.7). 66 However, MRI is less
invasive, more sensitive, and is now the preferred method for
diagnosis of cord compression due to discospondylitis.
Advanced Imaging
CT and MRI may have increased sensitivity for diagnosis of
discospondylitis when compared with plain radiography. MRI is

vetexamprep.ir

p

p

g p y
the gold standard for diagnosis of discospondylitis in human
patients and is the method of choice for diagnosis and
characterization of discospondylitis in dogs. 57 , 63 , 65 , 68 Aﬀected
vertebral bodies are classically hypointense on T1-weighted
images (which illustrate bone lesions) and may be hypointense
(most commonly), isointense, or hyperintense on T2-weighted
images when compared with normal surrounding structures. 57 ,
65 T2-weighted images highlight tissues with high water content,
including the nucleus pulposus, CSF, epidural fat, and
inﬂammatory lesions. Hyperintensity of the vertebral bodies in
dogs is even more commonly observed in short tau inversion
recovery (STIR) images, which suppress the signal from fat. Two
adjacent vertebrae are consistently involved. Intervertebral discs
are hyperintense on T2-weighted and STIR images when
discospondylitis is present. Marked uniform or heterogenous
contrast enhancement is usually apparent in vertebral endplates,
within the disc, and in surrounding soft tissue (Fig. 121.8).
Paravertebral soft tissues may also be hyperintense on T2weighted and especially STIR images. 57 Hyperintensity of
adjacent spinal cord on T2-weighted images has also been
described. 63 With more chronic infection, there is loss of
deﬁnition and cortical continuity and destruction of cortical
margins in T1-weighted images. Distortion and narrowing of the
disc space is also apparent, and subluxation and disc protrusion
with associated spinal cord compression can be easily identiﬁed.
The severity of spinal cord compression on MRI correlates with
severity of neurologic signs, whereas this does not appear to be
true for myelography.

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
The optimal specimens for identiﬁcation of the causative agent of
discospondylitis are blood or ﬂuoroscopically guided disc
aspirates (or biopsies performed during decompressive surgery),
because organisms isolated from these specimens are most likely
to reﬂect those involved in disc destruction. Blood cultures are
indicated in all dogs with discospondylitis (see Chapter 3 for
blood culture technique and interpretation). Because anaerobes
are uncommonly isolated from dogs with discospondylitis and
they have predictable susceptibilities, the decision to perform
anaerobic blood culture should be considered in light of any
underlying disease processes and client ﬁnancial constraints.
Negative blood cultures occur in more than half of dogs with
discospondylitis and may reﬂect low-level bacteremia or

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
y
fungemia, the presence of fastidious or unculturable organisms
such as Brucella or anaerobes, or recent antimicrobial drug
treatment. Urine cultures may reveal the causative organism
when blood cultures are negative, but not uncommonly bacterial
species present in the urine diﬀer from the organism present in
aﬀected discs. However, isolation of a mold species from the urine
suggests a disseminated mycosis. Serologic testing for Aspergillus
antigen and Brucella antibody should be performed in dogs with
culture-negative discospondylitis. Aspergillus serology should also
be considered for dogs that have blood culture-positive
discospondylitis, especially in predisposed breeds (such as
German shepherds, Rhodesian ridgebacks, vizslas) because mixed
infections with fungi and bacteria can rarely occur. Dogs with
Paecilomyces discospondylitis can have positive Aspergillus serum
and urine antigen tests due to serologic cross-reactions between
these fungi. 67
When blood cultures are negative, disc aspirates can be
obtained under anesthesia with ﬂuoroscopic (or other advanced
imaging such as CT) guidance after preparation of the skin in a
sterile manner. 69 Aspiration is performed with a 22-G, 1.5- to 2.5inch spinal needle into a syringe that contains a small amount of
sterile saline. In one study, 0.3 to 0.5 mL of sterile saline was
injected and immediately reaspirated, 69 but dry aspiration can
also be performed into the needle. The saline in the syringe can
then be used to ﬂush the contents of the needle into a plain sterile
tube, which is submi ed for bacterial and fungal culture. Only 3
of 11 aspirates or biopsies were positive in one study. 1 However,
in another study, positive bacterial cultures were obtained in 9 of
12 disc aspirates. 69 Other specimens that may yield growth
include CSF, aspirates of cellulitis or abscesses adjacent to sites of
discospondylitis, or synovial ﬂuid. When disease is present at
other sites, every eﬀort should be made to perform culture for
aerobic and anaerobic bacteria and fungi from these sites in order
to identify an infectious etiology.

Pathologic Findings
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in dogs with discospondylitis include
the presence of pus and necrotic debris in the intervertebral disc
spaces, irregularity and collapse of the disc spaces, and
discoloration and friability of the vertebral endplates (Fig. 121.9).
Protrusion of disc material and compression of the spinal cord
may be apparent. There may also be evidence of bony callus
material (ankylosing spondylosis). The nature of the inﬂammatory
inﬁltrates on histopathology varies with the chronicity of the
lesions and the underlying cause. For example, fungal
discospondylitis may be associated with granulomatous or
pyogranulomatous inﬂammation and intralesional fungal hyphae,
whereas chronic bacterial discospondylitis lesions typically
display neutrophilic and lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates, with
perilesional ﬁbrosis and granulation tissue. Osteonecrosis may be
present, as well as necrosis of the compressed spinal tissue.

vetexamprep.ir

that had multifocal discospondylitis caused by
Aspergillus spp. The L6-L7 disc space (arrow)
is collapsed with degenerate disc material,

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of discospondylitis involves prolonged antimicrobial
drug treatment and strict restriction of movement for several
weeks to prevent herniation of disc material or subluxation, with a
gradual increase in movement once lesions have healed. It is
important to stress to owners of dogs with discospondylitis that it
is a serious, life-threatening condition. Analgesics such as fentanyl
patches can also be administered provided they do not encourage
excessive movement. NSAIDs may also be beneﬁcial. Gabapentin

vetexamprep.ir

y
p
may alleviate neurogenic pain and can be used with opioids and
nonsteroidal drugs. 70
The antibiotic chosen to treat discospondylitis should ideally be
based on the results of culture and susceptibility. Treatment
recommendations for dogs with Brucella discospondylitis are
described in Chapter 71. Dogs with fungal discospondylitis
should be treated with antifungal drugs that have activity against
molds, such as voriconazole (if ﬁnances allow) or itraconazole (not
ﬂuconazole, which is not active against molds) with or without
amphotericin B; prognosis is guarded, and lifelong treatment may
be required (see Chapter 86). Dogs with culture-negative
discospondylitis that have negative serum or urine Aspergillus
galactomannan antigen tests should be treated with high doses of
a drug with activity against susceptible staphylococci and E. coli,
such as amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or cephalexin (see Table 121.2).
Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid also has activity against penicillinaseproducing anaerobes. However, occasionally gram-negative
organisms such as K. pneumoniae or P. aeruginosa, and MRSP cause
discospondylitis, and these may not respond to treatment with βlactam drugs. Addition of a ﬂuoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside
should be considered if there is no improvement after 1 week of
treatment with a β-lactam drug. Linezolid was used successfully
in one case report to treat a dog with MDR MRSP
discospondylitis. 71 Use of critical antimicrobials such as linezolid
should be based on culture and susceptibility testing. For dogs
that are systemically unwell or that have neurologic
abnormalities, antimicrobials should be administered parenterally
in the hospital for as long as possible (ideally at least 10 days)
before changing to oral administration. Antimicrobial drugs
should be administered for at least 6 to 8 weeks; in some cases,
treatment may need to be extended for many months. In one
study, the mean ± standard deviation for duration of antimicrobial
treatment in dogs that were cured of discospondylitis was 54 ± 45
weeks; for dogs with staphylococcal infections, it was 74 ± 62
weeks. 1 Dogs with fungal discospondylitis may require lifelong
treatment with antifungal drugs (see Chapter 86). Dogs should be
reevaluated clinically and radiographically every 3 to 4 weeks.
Improvement is characterized by resolution of bone lysis, sclerosis
of bone, and vertebral fusion, although radiographic
improvement can lag behind clinical improvement by 1 to 2

vetexamprep.ir

months, and there may be progression of osteolysis in addition to
sclerosis and increased osseous proliferation within the ﬁrst
month. 63 It has been recommended that antimicrobial drug
treatment be continued until lysis resolves completely, but
whether this is truly needed is controversial. MRI may be the most
sensitive imaging technique to conﬁrm resolution of active
infection, but requires general anesthesia. Imaging should also be
performed 1 to 2 months after antimicrobial drugs are
discontinued. If clinical deterioration occurs during treatment,
additional imaging (ideally with MRI) should be oﬀered to
evaluate for development of new lesions, abscessation,
subluxation, fracture, or disc protrusion.
Dogs with severe neurologic deﬁcits (such as paralysis) may
require decompressive surgery, debridement of abscesses or
vertebral osteomyelitis, and stabilization of the vertebral column.
Discospondylitis of L7-S1 may be a particular therapeutic
challenge. Although antimicrobial therapy will produce an
apparent initial cure, relapse will occur in about 25% of cases,
possibly due to residual instability of the intervertebral
articulation that predisposes the disc to reinfection or prevents
total resolution of the original infection by interfering with
neovascularization. Surgical distraction and arthrodesis of the
articular facets between L7 and S1 is recommended by some
clinicians in conjunction with antibacterial therapy.
Return of neurologic function can sometimes occur with
antimicrobial drug treatment alone, provided deep pain is
present. Decompressive surgery should be performed within 24
hours if deep pain is absent. Referral to a specialist surgeon is
recommended in this situation. In one study, 9 of 27 dogs with
discospondylitis received some form of decompressive surgery. 66
Physical therapy may also be beneﬁcial in these animals.

Public Health Aspects
The most important public health consideration in dogs with
discospondylitis is the possibility of Brucella infection. Human
disease has occurred as a result of contact with dogs with B. canis
discospondylitis and is typically an inﬂuenza-like illness. The
possibility of B. canis infection should be considered in all dogs
with discospondylitis, and precautions such as routine hand

vetexamprep.ir

washing, minimization of exposure to urine, and the wearing of
gloves should be taken until appropriate diagnostic testing has
ruled out Brucella as a cause.

Arthritis
Etiologic Agents, Pathogenesis, and
Epidemiology
Infectious arthritis may be classiﬁed as monoarthritis or
polyarthritis. Bacterial monoarthritis can follow orthopedic
surgeries that involve the joint (such as TPLOs, arthroscopies, or
joint arthrodesis), spread from soft tissue or bone infection at
adjacent sites, or result from trauma or bite wound infections.
Less commonly, monoarthritis follows systemic spread of bacteria
to a single joint. Bacterial causes of monoarthritis are similar to
those involved in osteomyelitis; the most common causes are
Staphylococcus spp., especially S. pseudintermedius but also S. aureus
and CoNS. Other reported causes are Streptococcus canis and
Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus, E. coli, and P. aeruginosa. 72 ,

73

Systemic spread of bacteria to the joints more often results in
polyarthritis. Infection with a variety of bacteria, protozoa, fungi,
and, rarely, viruses (West Nile virus in dogs, calicivirus in cats)
have been associated with polyarthritis in dogs and cats. In areas
where tick-borne infections are endemic, the most common
bacterial causes are Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia ewingii,
Ehrlichia canis, Borrelia burgdorferi, and Ricke sia ricke sii, but non–
vector-borne bacteria such as S. canis, S. aureus, Erysipelothrix,
Salmonella, Brucella, and mycoplasmas can also be involved.
Although its importance as a cause of polyarthritis remains
unclear, Bartonella should also be considered. Endocarditis is
frequently (if not almost always) present in dogs with
polyarthritis caused by facultative aerobic gram-positive and
gram-negative bacteria, and among dogs with endocarditis, S.
canis infections are most likely to be associated with polyarthritis.
Worldwide, the most important cause of protozoal polyarthritis in
dogs is Leishmania. Fungal polyarthritis is uncommon but can
result from infection by dimorphic fungi and, very rarely, molds
such as Aspergillus. Infectious polyarthritis is an important

vetexamprep.ir

diﬀerential diagnosis for primary (idiopathic) immune-mediated
polyarthritis (IMPA) in dogs. Although infectious polyarthritis is
less common than primary IMPA, failure to identify an
underlying infection can have disastrous consequences when
treatment with immunosuppressive drugs is initiated. In some
cases, polyarthritis is a secondary immune-mediated reaction to
systemic infections that are not localized in the joint (in human
medicine, a condition known as “reactive arthritis”).
After bacterial localization in the joint, an acute inﬂammatory
response occurs within the joint. There is a marked synovial
eﬀusion, causing increased intra-articular pressure, ischemia, and
release or activation of cartilage matrix-damaging enzymes.
Cartilage damage occurs quickly and, if severe, is irreversible.
Glycosaminoglycan depletion occurs within the ﬁrst 5 days
followed by cartilage softening and ﬁssuring. This leads to
mechanical weakening of the subchondral bone, as well as the
cascade of changes within the synovial ﬂuid and articular
cartilage. After recovery from infection, persistent inactivated
antigens or bacterial fragments may perpetuate the inﬂammatory
process.

Clinical Features
Clinical signs of monoarthritis may be acute or chronic in onset
and include variable fever, lethargy, inappetence, lameness that
involves a single limb, and a swollen joint that may be
erythematous, warm to the touch, and occasionally drain purulent
or blood-tinged ﬂuid (Fig. 121.10). The draining lymph node may
be enlarged and ﬁrm. Occasionally, edema of the distal limb may
be apparent. The most common joints aﬀected in one study were
the stiﬂe and elbow joints, followed by the tarsi and coxofemoral
joints, and signs developed within 2 to over 8 weeks after articular
or periarticular surgery. 72 In polyarthritis, multiple peripheral
joints are aﬀected, and dogs (and less commonly cats) show signs
of recumbency, reluctance to move, generalized peripheral
lymphadenopathy, a stiﬀ gait, and/or shifting leg lameness;
drainage of ﬂuid is not usually apparent. Dogs with bacterial
polyarthritis can also show signs of severe sepsis.

Diagnosis

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnosis of infectious arthritis is based on the history, clinical
signs, and cytology and culture of joint ﬂuid; serologic assays for
B. canis and fungal pathogens; and/or molecular diagnostic and/or
serologic testing for vector-borne pathogens in endemic regions.
Blood cultures may also allow identiﬁcation of the underlying
etiology in dogs with bacterial polyarthritis. As for
discospondylitis, dogs with bacterial polyarthritis should ideally
be evaluated for evidence of disease at other sites with thoracic
radiographs, spinal radiographs (for concurrent discospondylitis)
and abdominal ultrasound, echocardiography (for endocarditis),
and aerobic bacterial culture of the urine. However, it should be
kept in mind that bacterial isolates made from urine may
represent unrelated subclinical bacteriuria.

vetexamprep.ir
