Laboratory Abnormalities
Routine laboratory testing in animals with bacterial arthritis
typically shows leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia, which can be
accompanied by bandemia. The CBC may also be normal.
Thrombocytopenia may be present in dogs with bacteremia or
vector-borne bacterial infections and should prompt diagnostic
evaluation for vector-borne infections with PCR assays and
serology, or at least assessment of response to treatment with
doxycycline in the absence of client funds to pursue a diagnosis.
Urinalysis may be normal or show pyuria, bacteriuria,
proteinuria, and/or cylindruria in dogs with concurrent aerobic
bacterial UTIs.
Synovial ﬂuid from aﬀected joints is often yellow or bloodtinged, cloudy, increased in volume, and thin or watery in
consistency (normal synovial ﬂuid is clear and tenacious).
Cytologic examination of synovial ﬂuid reveals increased
numbers of leukocytes (>5000 cells/µL), with a predominance of
nondegenerate and/or degenerate neutrophils. Importantly, in the
majority of dogs with septic arthritis, degenerate neutrophils are
not visualized, 72 , 73 so the presence of only nondegenerate
neutrophils does not rule out an underlying bacterial infection.
Rarely, bacteria or fungal organisms are visualized extracellularly
or within leukocytes. Morulae are occasionally seen within
neutrophils in synovial ﬂuid of dogs infected with A.
phagocytophilum or E. ewingii (see Fig. 45.1C).
Diagnostic Imaging
When changes are apparent, radiographs of the joints in dogs and
cats with infectious arthritis most often reveal soft tissue swelling
and joint eﬀusion. In severe and chronic bacterial monoarthritis,
associated osteomyelitis may be present, with subchondral bone
lysis, articular erosion, and periarticular new bone formation.

vetexamprep.ir

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Conﬁrmation of bacterial arthritis requires culture of synovial
ﬂuid or of the synovium itself. Synovial ﬂuid from dogs with
neutrophilic polyarthritis should be submi ed for aerobic
bacterial culture and susceptibility, and anaerobic, fungal, or
Mycoplasma culture should at least be considered if the history is
suggestive. Inoculation of blood culture bo les with synovial
ﬂuids followed by subculture may increase sensitivity. Situations
in which anaerobic culture may be indicated include a history of
foreign body (such as plant awn) exposure or bite wounds.
Although rare, the possibility of Mycoplasma arthritis should be
considered in cats and dogs with a history of immune
compromise, surgery, or bite wounds, and when treatment with
β-lactam drugs fails (see Chapter 57). Dogs with fungal
polyarthritis may have lesions elsewhere (e.g., chorioretinitis,
pulmonary disease) that support a diagnosis of disseminated
fungal disease. However, anaerobic and Mycoplasma culture may
be insensitive (especially when there are delays in specimen
transport to the laboratory); Mycoplasma and fungal cultures
require prolonged incubation; and anaerobes, fungi, and
mycoplasmas tend to have predictable susceptibilities. Broadspectrum 16S rRNA PCR has also been used to detect and speciate
bacteria in synovial ﬂuid from dogs, but in one study, it was not
more sensitive than culture and yielded more false-positive
results. 74 Aerobic blood cultures may assist in identiﬁcation of
bacteria involved in polyarthritis.
If arthroscopy or arthrotomy is performed as part of evaluation
and treatment of bacterial monoarthritis, a biopsy of the
synovium could also be submi ed for culture and susceptibility
and may yield growth when synovial ﬂuid culture is negative. 73
In most cases, synovial ﬂuid culture alone is suﬃcient for
diagnosis of bacterial arthritis.

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of infectious arthritis depends on whether one joint is
involved or whether polyarthritis is present, as well as on the
identity of the causative agent. Infectious monoarthritis may

vetexamprep.ir

require surgical exploration, lavage and drainage, and treatment
with appropriate antimicrobial drugs based on the results of
culture and susceptibility. Monoarthritis is considered a surgical
emergency, and lavage should be performed immediately after
diagnosis, either via an ingress-egress approach, an arthroscope,
or with open surgery. For ingress-egress lavage, large-bore (14- to
16-G) needles are inserted percutaneously into two to three ﬂuid
pockets around the joint while the animal is heavily sedated or
anesthetized. Several liters of sterile saline is then administered
through one portal under pressure and allowed to drain from the
other portal(s). The sites of ingress and egress are switched until
the ﬂuid becomes clear. Arthroscopy can also be used.
Arthrotomy may be necessary if there are large accumulations of
ﬁbrin or inspissated purulent debris that cannot be eﬀectively
ﬂushed from the joint. If implants are present, they should be
removed when healing has occurred or if stabilization has failed.
If the implant is stable but the bone has not healed, lavage is
performed and the implant is often left in place because bone can
heal if rigidly stable despite infection. Implant exchange is the
“gold standard” in human medicine to decrease the bacterial load
from the bioﬁlm. 3 Cost may be prohibitive in animals and
subjectively, many of the cases in animals will heal with rigid
stability and can be removed later. Usually, the implant must
ultimately be removed and should be done as soon as possible
after healing. Antimicrobial drugs should initially be given
parenterally if possible. Treatment should continue until implants
can be removed if left in place. Once implants are removed,
treatment may need to be continued for another 2 to 4 weeks,
depending on the severity of infection. If local antibiotic therapy is
used in associated osteomyelitis lesions (i.e., impregnated beads),
systemic antimicrobial drug treatment should also be used.
Activated mesenchymal stem cells IV can be considered as an
adjunct therapy with antibiotics. 42 The prognosis depends on the
degree of cartilage and bone destruction, the degree to which
progressive osteoarthritis occurs, and the joint aﬀected.
Unfortunately, evidence-based clinical studies that document
long-term prognosis or prognostic indicators for infectious
monoarthritis are not available. In one retrospective study, dogs
that fully recovered tended to have a shorter duration of lameness
before treatment (median, 11 days compared with 26 days) and

vetexamprep.ir

lower synovial ﬂuid cell counts (median, 54 × 109 cells/mL
compared with 100 × 109 cells/mL) than dogs that never fully
recovered, and had signiﬁcantly lower body weights (median, 29
kg compared with 44 kg). 72
Polyarthritis caused by vector-borne bacteria usually responds
to treatment with doxycycline within 24 to 48 hours.
Antimicrobials for treatment of polyarthritis caused by other
bacteria should be selected based on the results of cytologic
examination of synovial ﬂuid (cocci versus rods) and culture and
susceptibility of blood or synovial ﬂuid. Because streptococci,
staphylococci, and Erysipelothrix are usually involved, a β-lactam
drug such as amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (or amoxicillin if
streptococci are more likely) could be used. Because bacterial
polyarthritis is frequently associated with endocarditis or
discospondylitis, the duration of treatment should be based on
resolution of these lesions. The reader is referred to Chapters 122
and 123 for additional information on treatment of bacteremia and
sepsis.

Public Health Aspects
Polyarthritis can be caused by organisms of public health
signiﬁcance, such as Salmonella, Brucella, S. aureus, pathogenic
fungi, Leishmania, and vector-borne bacterial pathogens of
importance to human health. This should be kept in mind when
handling dogs with polyarthritis. Care should be taken to avoid
needle-stick injuries during venipuncture, arthrocentesis, and
aspiration of other tissues such as lymph nodes. Deep sedation or
anesthesia is recommended for arthrocentesis.

Case Example
Signalment

“Tilly,” a 10-year-old female spayed greyhound/pit bull terrier
mix from Davis, CA (Fig. 121.11).

History

Tilly was brought to the University of California, Davis, VMTH
Orthopedic Surgery service, for evaluation of a draining tract
on her left medial proximal tibia that developed after a TTA

vetexamprep.ir

p
p
surgery for left cranial cruciate ligament tear. The ligament tear
had been diagnosed at the VMTH 15 months previously after
an acute onset of lameness, and the surgery was performed 2
months after diagnosis at another veterinary hospital after there
had been no improvement with conservative management
(activity restriction and antiinﬂammatory drugs). Immediately
after the surgery, the dog was placed on a 10-day course of
doxycycline. The tract was ﬁrst observed 2 weeks after the
doxycycline course had ﬁnished, and the owner (a veterinary
student) noted that the tract subsequently healed over, then
drained again. When the wound initially appeared, treatment
with doxycycline was reinstituted for a month, with no
improvement. A radiograph of the limb was performed at the
end of the course of treatment at the VMTH. Soft tissue swelling
was identiﬁed at the medial aspect of the stiﬂe, but there was no
radiographic evidence of implant infection or motion. Regional
osteopenia of the left tibial tuberosity and proximal tibia was
present, and there was progressive left stiﬂe osteoarthrosis.
Culture of the wound yielded very small numbers of S. canis
and a CoNS. The wound subsequently closed over again and
antibiotic treatment was not initiated, but 11 months later the
tract reappeared. Since the surgery, the incision had appeared
healthy. Tilly had been bearing progressively more weight on
the limb, although some lameness persisted. Other treatments
had included activity restriction and carprofen (2 mg/kg, PO,
q12h) for pain relief. Tilly had no other signiﬁcant medical
history apart from multiple lipomas that had been evaluated
with FNA cytology, which had not changed in size.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 37.2 kg.
General: Bright, alert, responsive. T = 101.0°F (38.3°C), HR
= 80 beats/minute, panting.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No abnormalities were
identiﬁed apart from moderate periodontal disease.
Musculoskeletal: Left pelvic limb lameness was present,
but there was intermi ent right pelvic limb lameness and
muscle atrophy of both pelvic limbs. There was pain on
extension of both coxofemoral joints. Examination of the
left pelvic limb revealed a 1-cm, open round wound on

vetexamprep.ir

p
p
the medial aspect of the proximal left tibia, which oozed
serosanguineous ﬂuid. A positive cranial drawer sign and
tibial thrust were present.

Tilly, 10-year old female
spayed greyhound–pit bull terrier mix
that developed osteomyelitis at the site
of a left tibial tuberosity advancement
surgery.
FIG. 121.11

All other systems: No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities
were detected.

Imaging Findings

Plain radiographs (pelvis): Bilaterally there was poor coverage
of the femoral heads by the acetabulae. The femoral heads and
necks were thickened and irregularly margined. There was
periarticular osteophytosis of the acetabulae. Atrophy of the
pelvic musculature was appreciated bilaterally although
somewhat worse on the left than the right. Findings were

vetexamprep.ir

consistent with bilateral hip dysplasia with severe degenerative
change.
Plain radiographs (left stiﬂe): The implants associated with
the TTA procedure were in place and intact (see Fig. 121.5A and
B). The osteotomy site had ﬁlled in with bone to some extent,
although the site was still visible nearly its entire length, and
bridging bone was absent at the proximal aspect of the
osteotomy and around the basket implant. There was thinning
of the cortical bone adjacent to the TTA plate that was
associated with the tibial tuberosity and proximal tibial

the distal-most screw, which suggested implant-associated

osteotomy; severe canine hip dysplasia.

Treatment

Surgical exploration of the left stiﬂe joint was performed. The
draining tract was followed to the plate and screws. The TTA
plate and screws were removed. The cage was removed by
drilling around it, which left a 2-cm round defect in the tibia.
During the procedure, it was discovered that a titanium plate
had been used together with 316L steel screws, which led to
concerns that osteomyelitis may have developed secondary to a
galvanic reaction. The area was extensively ﬂushed, and the
defect was ﬁlled with calcium sulfate beads. Beads were also
placed in the area previously occupied by the plate (see Fig.
121.5C). The fascia, subcutaneous tissue, and skin were closed,
and a modiﬁed Robert-Jones bandage was placed. Aerobic and
anaerobic bacterial cultures of the implant yielded small
numbers of methicillin-susceptible S. pseudintermedius. The
organism was resistant to ampicillin, penicillin, ticarcillin, and
doxycycline. Tilly was therefore treated with amoxicillinclavulanic acid (10 mg/kg, PO, q12h). At the time of suture

vetexamprep.ir

removal 2 weeks later, Tilly was weight bearing on the left
pelvic limb, and the draining tract had resolved. A small
draining tract reappeared 2 weeks later, and a swab from the
tract again grew S. pseudintermedius with the same antibiogram,
but only from the enrichment broth. Treatment was continued
for an additional month, all lesions resolved, and lameness was
reduced. Several years later, the dog was doing well and there
had been no recurrence of draining tracts (see Fig. 121.5D).

Comments

Diagnosis and treatment of osteomyelitis in this case was
delayed because of the lag in radiographic changes and the
appearance and disappearance of the draining tract. This
illustrates the diﬃculties associated with diagnosis of
osteomyelitis. Although unconﬁrmed, use of two diﬀerent
metals may have contributed to development of osteomyelitis
in this dog, which required costly and diﬃcult surgical
intervention with implant removal. The defects were closed
with biodegradable beads and infection resolved after 2 months
of systemic antimicrobial drug treatment, based on the results
of culture and susceptibility.

122: Cardiovascular Infections (Bacteremia,
Endocarditis, Myocarditis, Infectious
Pericarditis)
Steven E. Epstein, Joshua A. Stern, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Causes: Most common bacterial causes are staphylococci, streptococci, and
Escherichia coli. Gram-negative bacterial etiologies predominate in cats. Culturenegative infections of the bloodstream may be caused by Bartonella spp. or other
fastidious bacteria. Anaerobes, fungi, and mycobacteria are less commonly involved.
Rickettsia rickettsii can cause vasculitis and myocarditis.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: Highly variable. Fever, inappetence, lethargy, and tachycardia
are common with sepsis. GI signs such as vomiting and diarrhea may also be
present. Additional findings in infective endocarditis patients include cardiac
murmurs, lameness, and neurologic signs due to thromboembolic disease. Spinal
pain, paresis or paralysis may occur when discospondylitis complicates bacteremia
or fungemia.
• Differential Diagnoses: Noninfectious conditions that can mimic sepsis include
pancreatitis, trauma, hypoadrenocorticism, heat stroke, anaphylaxis, pulmonary
thromboembolism, hemorrhage, cardiac tamponade, and some toxicities. Dogs with
primary immune-mediated disorders may also show clinical signs that resemble
those of chronic bacteremia and infective endocarditis. The major differential for
infectious pericarditis is idiopathic or benign pericardial effusion and neoplastic
disorders such as mesothelioma.
• Human Health Significance: Dogs and cats with cardiovascular infections may be
infected with pathogens that have the potential to cause disease in humans, such as
Salmonella spp., Bartonella spp., Brucella spp., and R. rickettsii.

EtiologIC Agents, Epidemiology and Clinical Features
A variety of pathogens can cause infections of the cardiovascular system, including
viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and parasites. This chapter focuses on bacterial
infections of the cardiovascular system; information on other types of pathogens can be
found in their respective chapters in this book. Bacterial infections of the cardiovascular
system include bacteremia, infective endocarditis (IE), myocarditis, and infectious
pericarditis. These infections are frequently associated with sepsis, or the host systemic
inﬂammatory response to infection. Various terminologies are used to deﬁne the clinical
manifestations associated with sepsis (see Chapter 123).

Bacteremia

vetexamprep.ir

Bacteremia has been deﬁned as uncomplicated and complicated bacteremia (Table 122.1).
Transient, low-level (≤10 CFU/mL) subclinical bacteremia follows a variety of procedures
such as dental prophylaxis, endoscopy, GI surgery, and catheter placement. This is
typically cleared rapidly (within 15 to 30 minutes) by a functional mononuclear
phagocyte system. However, persistent release of large numbers of bacteria into the
bloodstream can overwhelm the host immune response and culminates in clinically
signiﬁcant bacteremia. Overwhelming bacteremia can occur with disorders such as
pyelonephritis, pyothorax, severe pyoderma, bacterial peritonitis, pyometra, pneumonia,
pancreatitis, a variety of GI disorders, bite wounds, orthopedic infections, or catheterrelated infections. Underlying immune system dysfunction (such as occurs with diabetes
mellitus, malignancy, and neutropenia) also predisposes to clinically signiﬁcant
bacteremia because unhindered multiplication of bacteria occurs in the bloodstream.
The most common organisms isolated from the bloodstream of sick, bacteremic dogs
are Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp. (especially Streptococcus canis), and Escherichia
coli (Table 122.2). 1 Less than 10% of bacteremic dogs in the authors’ hospital are infected
with anaerobes, but in a study of critically ill dogs and cats from Colorado, anaerobes
were isolated from 31% of 39 dogs and 40% of 10 cats. 2 With the exception of
bartonellosis, bacteremia is less commonly recognized in cats than in dogs, and usually
results from infection with gram-negative bacterial pathogens. 1 Polymicrobial infections
of the blood are common and typically occur in 10% to 20% of dogs and cats with
positive blood culture results. Mixed infections with two or more diﬀerent strains of a
single bacterial species can also occur. Polymicrobial infections often occur when
anaerobes are involved or secondary to compromise of the GI tract.
In addition to sepsis and septic shock (see Chapter 123), bacteremia may be followed
by the development of IE, discospondylitis, and metastatic abscess formation in a variety
of tissues. Chronic bacteremia may be associated with secondary immune-mediated
disorders, especially immune-mediated polyarthritis and glomerulonephritis, and rarely
IMHA. This can result in erroneous diagnosis of a primary immune-mediated disorder
and inappropriate treatment with immunosuppressive drugs, sometimes with fatal
outcome.

Infective Endocarditis
The reported incidence of canine IE has ranged from < 0.1% of cases evaluated by
veterinary teaching hospitals to approximately 1% of cases evaluated by veterinary
cardiologists. 3–6 IE is uncommonly diagnosed in cats; in one study, cats with IE
represented < 0.01% of cats evaluated by a university teaching hospital. 7 Most cats were
diagnosed with congestive heart failure (CHF) at the time of IE diagnosis and prognosis
was poor. Dogs with IE are typically middle aged to older, large-breed dogs such as
German shepherd dogs, golden and Labrador retrievers, Weimaraners, mastiﬀs, and
ro weilers. For unclear reasons, male dogs are aﬀected approximately twice as often as
females. Factors that predispose to IE are similar to those that predispose to continuous
bacteremia. However, virulence factors possessed by bacteria subsequently impact
whether IE develops, which explains why some bacterial species (especially grampositive bacteria) are more likely to produce IE than others (gram-negative bacteria).
Although congenital heart defects, especially subaortic stenosis (SAS), may predispose
young dogs to development of IE, the vast majority of dogs with SAS never develop IE,
and over 80% of dogs with IE have no identiﬁable underlying cardiac abnormality. 5 , 8 It
remains unclear if the associated risk of IE in patients with SAS is related to the
pathophysiology of this condition or simply an association secondary to the increased
incidence of IE in large-breed dogs and a similarly increased incidence of this common,
inherited heart disease in this population of large, sporting-breed dogs. Furthermore, IE
is rarely diagnosed in small-breed dogs, which are predisposed to myxomatous mitral

vetexamprep.ir

valve degeneration. The observed link between periodontal disease and IE in human
subjects is less clear in dogs and cats. One study found no association between
periodontal disease and IE in dogs., 8 A 2016 investigation identiﬁed the same
enterococcal pathogen from the mouth and IE lesions in 7 out of 32 dogs with IE and
periodontal disease. 9 However, in 2021 this publication was retracted because of
concerns about the validity of the results. 10

The most commonly reported etiologic agents in canine IE are streptococci,
staphylococci, and to a lesser extent, gram-negative rods, enterococci, and Bartonella spp.
(Table 122.3). 4 , 8 , 11–13 Organisms that are less commonly incriminated include fungi,
gram-positive rods, mycobacteria, and anaerobes. In dogs, the mitral and/or the aortic
valves are most commonly aﬀected (Fig. 122.1). The larger, septal leaﬂet of the mitral
valve may be more commonly aﬀected than the mural leaﬂet. 5 The tricuspid valve and
ventricular wall are rarely involved. This distribution correlates with the degree of
pressure that rests on the closed valve. Classically, vegetative lesions develop along the
line of valve closure. In a case series of cats with IE, the aortic valve was aﬀected 62% of
the time while the mitral valve was aﬀected in 38% of cats. 7
The development of IE begins with colonization of a heart valve by bacteria, and
deposition of ﬁbrin, platelets, leukocytes, and erythrocytes. Colonization may be
facilitated by changes in the valve surface as a result of turbulent blood ﬂow, which in
turn leads to the deposition of platelets, ﬁbrin, and ﬁbronectin; the end result is a sterile
vegetation, or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis. Bacteria then adhere to this matrix,
induce inﬂammatory cytokine and tissue factor release, and become covered with
additional layers of platelets and ﬁbrin, which promote bacterial growth to extremely
high densities in an environment that is protected from the immune system. Properties
of bacteria known to promote valve colonization include adhesins such as ﬁmA in
streptococci, and clumping factor and ﬁbronectin-binding proteins in staphylococci, 14 ,
15 as well as factors that cause platelet aggregation. Portions of the vegetation that results
can then dislodge and embolize in a variety of diﬀerent tissues, especially the kidneys,
spleen, brain, joints, and muscles, with a huge spectrum of associated clinical
manifestations. Thromboembolic complications are more likely to occur in dogs with
mitral valve involvement than those with aortic valve IE. 5 Regardless of the valve

vetexamprep.ir

aﬀected, valvular dysfunction can lead to impaired cardiac output and CHF. CHF
secondary to moderate to severe valvular insuﬃciency is a common sequela to IE in cats.
7

As in humans, IE in dogs may be best classiﬁed on the basis of the etiologic agent
involved, because the etiologic agent often determines the clinical course of disease,
disease manifestations, prognosis, and the most appropriate antimicrobial drugs for
treatment. For example, Bartonella IE is more likely to involve the aortic valve than the
mitral valve; often occurs in the absence of fever; has a high prevalence of CHF when
compared with IE caused by other bacterial pathogens; and is negatively correlated with
survival (see Fig. 70.7). In contrast, S. canis IE usually involves the mitral valve and is
often associated with neutrophilic polyarthritis. Dogs with gram-negative IE appear less
likely to develop CHF than those with IE caused by other pathogens. 11
The clinical signs and physical examination abnormalities that occur with IE are
extremely variable and depend not only on the causative organism but also on the valve
aﬀected, the presence or absence of thromboembolic complications, and the sites and
extent of thromboembolism. Common historic ﬁndings include lethargy; inappetence;
locomotory problems such as lameness, shifting lameness, joint pain, reluctance to
move, and inability to walk; as well as vomiting, respiratory diﬃculty, weight loss,
and/or cough. Locomotory abnormalities can result from peripheral arterial
thromboembolism,
embolic
or
immune-mediated
polyarthritis,
neurologic
abnormalities, and rarely, hypertrophic osteopathy. The most common initial physical
examination ﬁndings in dogs with IE are fever, tachycardia, and a cardiac murmur
(Table 122.4). 5 In one study of dogs with IE, fever was documented in the history or
serial physical examinations of only 41 (60%) of 68 dogs with IE, and a cardiac murmur
in 53 (76%) of 70 dogs with IE, so an absence of fever or a cardiac murmur does not
make IE an unlikely diagnosis. 5 Although diastolic murmurs may be suggestive of IE,
more than 90% of dogs with murmurs due to IE have systolic murmurs.

Infectious Myocarditis
Infectious myocarditis in dogs and cats usually results from hematogenous spread of
microorganisms to the myocardium or extension of IE lesions to the myocardium.
Viruses, bacteria, protozoa, or fungi may be involved. Certain organisms appear to have
a particular tropism for the myocardium (Table 122.5). Infectious myocarditis is rare in
cats.
Myocarditis may be subclinical or result in a variety of arrhythmias, CHF, or sudden
death. Simultaneous infection of a variety of other organs is frequent for the majority of
pathogens that cause myocarditis, so clinical signs of systemic infection (fever, lethargy)
and other organ dysfunction are often present. In one case series of dogs with
myocarditis, fever was present in 21% of dogs and a heart murmur in 19%. 16 Deﬁnitive
diagnosis is often only made at necropsy.

Infectious Pericarditis
Infectious pericarditis may result from direct inoculation of organisms into the
pericardium (such as occurs with penetrating wounds), 17 , 18 extension of infection from
adjacent organs such as the pleural space or lungs, or hematogenous dissemination of
viral, bacterial, protozoal, or fungal pathogens to the pericardium. Bite wounds or grass
awn migration often result in mixed aerobic-anaerobic infections that involve organisms
such as Actinomyces spp. (see Chapter 59). Infectious pericarditis as a result of
hematogenous spread of pathogens is rare. Idiopathic pericardial eﬀusion and heart
base neoplasia are the most common causes of inﬂammatory or hemorrhagic pericardial
eﬀusion in dogs; neoplasia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were the most common
causes of pericardial eﬀusion in cats in one study. 19 Pathogens with particular tropism
for the pericardial sac include FIP virus and Coccidioides spp. Pericardial eﬀusion was
also reported in association with Leishmania infection. 20 Pericarditis results in diastolic
cardiac dysfunction with subsequent development of right-sided heart failure, which is
manifested as weak pulses, tachycardia, jugular venous pulsation or distension, ascites,
and pleural eﬀusion. Muﬄed heart sounds may be detected on cardiac auscultation as a
result of pericardial and/or pleural eﬀusion.

Infective endocarditis. Vegetations are attached to the
mitral and aortic valves and may be mobile or sessile.

Diagnosis
Antemortem diagnosis of bacteremia is based on culture of bacteria from the
bloodstream. Reasons to consider blood culture are shown in Box 122.1. The diagnosis of
IE is based on a set of criteria modiﬁed from the Duke criteria used for diagnosis of IE in
human patients, which consider the results of blood culture and echocardiography as
major criteria, and other clinical manifestations of IE as minor criteria (Table 122.6).
Diagnosis of infective pericarditis relies on echocardiography and the results of cytologic
examination and culture of pericardial ﬂuid, or alternatively, histopathologic
examination and culture of pericardial biopsies obtained during thoracotomy or
thoracoscopy. In dogs and cats, infectious myocarditis is usually a necropsy diagnosis
because myocardial biopsy is rarely performed. However, bacterial myocarditis may be
suspected based on echocardiographic abnormalities, the presence of arrhythmias,
increased serum cardiac troponin I, concentration and positive blood cultures or
serologic testing.

Serum Biochemical Tests
The serum chemistry proﬁle may show evidence of sepsis, or bacterial embolization and
infarction. Abnormalities include azotemia, increased activities of liver enzymes, mild to
moderate hyperbilirubinemia (usually < 5 mg/dL), and electrolyte and acid-base
abnormalities (such as a high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to azotemia or lactic

vetexamprep.ir

acidosis). Hyperglycemia may be present early in sepsis in cats while hypoglycemia may
develop in either cats or dogs. Hypoglycemia may also be present as a result of
decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis or upregulation of non–insulin-dependent glucose
transporters. Hypoalbuminemia occurs in most dogs with IE, ranges from mild to
severe, and may result from decreased hepatic production, increased vascular
permeability, or as part of the inﬂammatory response (albumin is a negative acute-phase
reactant protein). Dogs with thromboembolism to muscle tissue may have markedly
increased activity of serum CK.
TABLE 122.6

Definite endocarditis: 2 major criteria, or histopathologic confirmation of endocarditis.
Possible endocarditis: Positive echocardiographic findings and 1 minor criteria, or 1 major and 3 minor
criteria, or 5 minor criteria. In recent human guidelines, 1 major and 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria, are
considered sufficient evidence for diagnosis of definitive endocarditis. 24

Urinalysis
Urinalysis ﬁndings in dogs and cats with bacteremia or IE may include proteinuria,
pyuria, cylindruria, microscopic hematuria, and bacteriuria. Severe proteinuria (urine
protein-to-creatinine ratio > 5) may occur as a result of glomerular damage in dogs with
IE which may contribute to a hypercoagulable state.
Coagulation Profile
Dogs and cats with DIC may have prolonged aPTT and PT, increased concentrations of
ﬁbrin degradation products or D-dimers, and/or decreased concentrations of plasma
ﬁbrinogen and antithrombin. If viscoelastic testing is used, either hyper- or
hypocoagulability may be documented in dogs. 21 In dogs with IE, PT is often shortened,
and ﬁbrinogen concentration is often increased. 5

Cardiac Biomarkers
A large body of evidence has accumulated to support that cardiac biomarkers, such as
the N-terminal fragment of the prohormone B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)
and cardiac troponin I, represent biochemical tests with acceptable sensitivity and
speciﬁcity for the diagnosis of myocardial injury, stress, or stretch. 22 , 23 Serum cardiac
troponin I is a useful, quantitative assessment of myocardial injury. Although not
speciﬁc for endocarditis or myocarditis, one study showed that serum cardiac troponin I
concentrations were signiﬁcantly higher in dogs with IE (n = 29) than dogs with stage-B
myxomatous mitral valve disease (n = 27) and dogs with immune-mediated disease (n =
16).25 A cut-oﬀ value of 0.625 ng/mL had 100% speciﬁcity and 52% sensitivity for
diagnosis of IE in that study. Severe myocardial injury such as myocardial infarction and
myocarditis is commonly associated with signiﬁcantly increased concentrations of
serum cardiac biomarker molecules. However, a small percentage of dogs with
myocarditis may have normal serum cardiac troponin I concentrations. 16 Ultimately,

vetexamprep.ir

increased concentrations of cardiac biomarkers supports a diagnosis of cardiovascular
infection but is not required for diagnosis.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Thoracic radiographs in dogs with IE often show no detectable abnormalities. When
present, abnormal ﬁndings include pulmonary inﬁltrates as a result of pneumonia,
ARDS or CHF; generalized cardiomegaly; left atrial enlargement; pulmonary venous
distension; mild pleural eﬀusion; and occasionally, even microcardia or vascular
a enuation (see Fig. 70.10). Infectious pericarditis may be associated with radiographic
evidence of pleural eﬀusion or cardiomegaly. Changes to the intervertebral disc spaces
that suggest discospondylitis may also be detected in dogs with bacteremia or
endocarditis (see Chapter 121).
Echocardiography
Echocardiography is indicated when IE, myocarditis, or pericarditis is suspected based
on the history and physical examination ﬁndings (such as fever, arrhythmia, a new
murmur, or signs of left- or right-sided CHF). It is also indicated for all dogs and cats
with bacteremia, even in the absence of a cardiac murmur or arrhythmia; for dogs with
neutrophilic polyarthritis; and for dogs and cats with evidence of systemic
thromboembolic disease. Echocardiographic ﬁndings in IE can include valvular
hyperechogenicity, thickening and irregularity, and valvular vegetations, which may be
nodular, discrete, or have a shaggy or moth-eaten appearance (Fig. 122.2 and see Fig.
70.13). Large vegetations may oscillate or vibrate, and follow-up echocardiography
sometimes reveals disappearance of a vegetative lesion in association with
thromboembolism. Mild or severe valvular regurgitation or insuﬃciency may be present
in association with lesions. Other echocardiographic ﬁndings include left ventricular
eccentric hypertrophy, chamber dilation, mural hyperechogenicity, ruptured chordae
tendineae, acquired defects in the valves or myocardium, and mild pericardial eﬀusion.
Echocardiography is a sensitive tool for diagnosis of IE (87.5% in one study of dogs with
IE when necropsy was used as the gold standard), 5 but negative results do not
completely rule out the possibility of IE. Echocardiography is also useful for monitoring
treatment of IE (see Treatment).
Echocardiographic ﬁndings in infectious pericarditis include pericardial eﬀusion,
adhesions of the pericardium to the epicardium, and sometimes focal or diﬀuse
pericardial thickening and hyperechogenicity (Fig. 122.3). Restrictive disease is
characterized by impairment of diastole, with decreased left ventricular internal
dimensions during diastole, and variation of blood ﬂow velocity across the mitral valve
with the respiratory cycle (increased with expiration and decreased with inspiration). In
addition, deviation of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle can occur during
inspiration and right ventricle during expiration. Echocardiographic ﬁndings in
myocarditis may include a heterogeneous appearance to the ventricular myocardium,
systolic dysfunction, and volume overload. 16 Regional septal or free-wall motion
abnormalities may be seen in areas of more severe ischemia or infarction.

Abdominal Sonographic Findings
Sonographic abnormalities may be present in a variety of organs in dogs with IE, and
may reﬂect underlying disease processes (such as neoplasia or bacterial peritonitis) or
septic thromboembolism. Infarction and hemorrhage secondary to thromboembolic
disease may result in focal cavitary or hypoechoic lesions in the spleen (Fig. 122.4) or
focal hyperechoic or hypoechoic lesions in the kidney. Thrombi may be found in the iliac
arteries or aorta.

Microbiologic Tests
Culture
Routine blood cultures assist in identiﬁcation of infecting pathogens and permit
susceptibility testing. Ideally, at least three blood cultures should be obtained from
separate sites within a 24-hour period. A suggested protocol for blood cultures is
outlined in Chapter 3 (Box 3.2). Although the use of separate venipuncture sites has been
suggested, this is not considered essential for diagnosis of human IE; however, the use of
indwelling catheters should be avoided. 24 If a catheter-related bloodstream infection is
suspected, collection of paired specimens has been recommended in humans, with one
specimen collected from the catheter prior to removal and the other collected from a
peripheral site. 26 The skin should be prepared in the same manner used for surgery, and
utmost care should be taken to avoid contamination with commensal bacteria. Because
IE is generally associated with continuous bacteremia, positive results in a single bo le
should be interpreted with caution. Positive results for Bacillus spp. or coagulasenegative staphylococci in a single bo le generally reﬂect contamination.
The decision to perform anaerobic blood culture should be considered in light of the
animal’s underlying disease process and client ﬁnancial constraints. For example,
anaerobic culture may not be cost eﬀective in dogs with IE, given the rare involvement
of anaerobes in this condition. Anaerobes are more likely to be present in dogs with
histories that suggest involvement of plant awn foreign bodies, bite wounds, GI, or
biliary tract compromise.
False-negative blood cultures may occur as a result of low-level bacteremia or
fungemia, the presence of fastidious or unculturable organisms such as Bartonella,
insuﬃcient specimen size, or recent antimicrobial treatment. Nevertheless, blood culture
is still indicated in animals with a history of antimicrobial treatment, especially if
antimicrobials have only been administered for 2 to 3 days. If an animal with IE is in
stable condition, discontinuation of existing antibiotic treatment for several days (ideally
7 to 10 days) could be considered before blood cultures are obtained. Speciﬁc culture
and serology for Bartonella is also indicated in dogs and cats with IE or suspected

vetexamprep.ir

myocarditis (see Chapter 70). This should be considered even if routine blood cultures
are positive, because polymicrobial infections that include Bartonella spp. and other
bacteria can occur. 11 Special media used to isolate Bartonella spp. (Bartonella alphaProteobacteria growth medium [BAPGM]) may also yield other fastidious bacteria such
as Sphingomonas spp., the clinical signiﬁcance of which requires further study. 27
Serologic testing for Brucella antibody and Aspergillus antigen could also be considered
for dogs with culture-negative IE (see Chapters 71 and 86, respectively).
A empts should also be made to isolate causative organism(s) from other sites that
are suspected to be a source of infection based on the history and clinical ﬁndings.
Appropriate specimens could include transtracheal or bronchoalveolar lavage
specimens, urine, ascites ﬂuid, wounds, or pleural eﬀusion. UTIs may reﬂect ascending
pyelonephritis or spread of bacteria from the blood into the urine. However, bacteria
cultured from the urine may not always reﬂect those present in the bloodstream, 11 so
blood cultures should always be performed even when urine cultures are positive.
Isolation of the same organism from the blood as well as an additional site facilitates
interpretation of the signiﬁcance of a single positive blood culture and aids decisions
regarding appropriate antimicrobial drug treatment.
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
PCR assays have been used to rapidly detect bacterial DNA within whole blood and
especially valvular tissue (obtained at necropsy) of animals with IE, and are especially
useful for detection of fastidious bacteria such as Bartonella spp. within the heart valves
(see Chapter 70). These assays use broad-range primers that target bacterial 16S
ribosomal subunit DNA, and the identity of the organism is determined by sequence
analysis of resulting PCR products.
In one prospective study that examined the performance of a conventional broadrange bacterial PCR assay on whole blood for diagnosis of the etiology of IE in 18 dogs,
there was no diﬀerence in the overall sensitivity of the PCR assay and culture, but the
combined use of the PCR assay and blood culture was more sensitive than the use of
either assay alone. 28 This was because the PCR assay detected several fastidious
organisms, which included Bartonella vinsonii, Brucella, and Granulicatella adiacens, but
appeared less sensitive than culture for detection of less fastidious organisms such as
streptococci. Studies that include larger numbers of dogs and cats, and that examine the
performance of other PCR assays such as real-time PCR assays are required before
broad-range bacterial PCR can be recommended for routine diagnosis of bacteremia and
IE in dogs and cats, but they show promise when used in conjunction with blood
cultures. Of major concern is the possibility of false positives with highly sensitive PCR
assays due to detection of contaminating bacteria. Even in human medicine, evidence is
considered insuﬃcient to recommend the routine use of whole blood or serum real-time
PCR assays for the diagnosis of culture-negative IE. 24

Pathologic Findings
There are no speciﬁc pathologic ﬁndings in sepsis or bacteremia, but underlying causes
such as pneumonia, pyometra, or peritonitis may be apparent. Microabscesses may be
present in multiple tissues of animals with bacteremia. Isolation of the same bacterial
species from multiple diﬀerent tissues is supportive of a diagnosis of bacteremia.
Pathologic ﬁndings in IE include valvular vegetations; avulsion or perforation of
valvular structures; and gross and histopathologic evidence of infarction, widespread
thrombosis, and CHF (Fig. 122.5). The inﬂammatory process may be chronic, with
lymphoplasmacytic and histiocytic cell inﬁltrates and ﬁbrosis; or acute, suppurative, and
ﬁbrinous, with or without microscopically visible intralesional bacteria (see Fig. 50.7).
Bartonella IE is characterized by chronic inﬂammation and may be associated with

vetexamprep.ir

valvular mineralization (see Fig. 70.14), whereas IE due to other microorganisms may be
acute or chronic, and is rarely associated with valvular mineralization. 11 Use of tissue
Gram stains and silver stains can reveal the presence of organisms within valvular
vegetations. Necrotizing vasculitis may also be present in organs such as the lungs,
myocardium, kidney, spleen, liver, and/or brain. Erythrophagocytosis has been
described in reticuloendothelial tissues of dogs with IE due to gram-positive cocci.
Membranoproliferative, membranous, or necrosuppurative glomerulonephritis may also
be identiﬁed. 5
Gross examination of the heart of animals with myocarditis may reveal focal or
multifocal areas of myocardial pallor and/or friability. Histopathologic characterization
of myocarditis in dogs showed that the most frequent type of inﬂammation present in
the myocardium was lymphoplasmacytic, although granulocytic and eosinophilic
inﬂammation may also be present. 29 The pericardium of dogs and cats with pericarditis
may be thickened and discolored, and pericardial eﬀusion may be present.
Histopathology reveals acute or chronic inﬂammatory inﬁltrates, depending on the
underlying cause, sometimes with intralesional bacteria or fungi.

Treatment and Prognosis
The mainstay of treatment of bacteremia, IE, sepsis, and bacterial myocarditis or
pericarditis is early antimicrobial drug treatment. The initial choice of antimicrobial
drugs should be based on knowledge of the prevalent bacterial species and their
antimicrobial drug susceptibilities for each hospital and/or geographic region, as well as
the likely source of infection (which provides information about the likely bacterial
species involved) (Tables 122.7 and 122.8). The presence or absence of IE and/or sepsis
also aﬀects treatment recommendations. The treatment of sepsis and septic shock is
covered in detail in Chapter 123.
In addition to antimicrobial drug therapy, the underlying cause of infection or chronic
bacteremia should be identiﬁed and removed if possible. All catheters or devices should
be removed and replaced at new sites if they are still needed. An a empt should be
made to locate foreign bodies such as grass awns with imaging techniques and
surgically remove them. Surgery may be required to resolve GI compromise, such as
occurs with foreign bodies, intestinal neoplasia, or torsion. Underlying
immunosuppressive disease such as neoplasia or diabetes mellitus should be identiﬁed
and treated if possible.

Infective Endocarditis
Guidelines for the treatment of IE in humans have been published and updated. 24 , 30
However, many factors considered for treatment of human patients do not apply to dogs
and cats, and include the availability of valve replacement; penicillin allergy in some
patients; the higher incidence of infections with MRS and VRE; evidence that supports
use of speciﬁc antimicrobial drugs or drug combinations; and the possibility of long
hospitalization times for parenteral antimicrobial drug therapy. In many human IE
patients, valve replacement is also essential for resolution. Indications for cardiac
surgery in humans include severe acute regurgitation or valve obstruction with
refractory pulmonary edema; uncontrolled infection with enlarging vegetations;
persistent fever and positive blood culture for at least 10 days after appropriate
antimicrobial drug treatment is commenced, infection caused by fungi or MDR bacteria,
and large vegetations (> 10 mm) in association with embolic episodes or other
complications, and isolated large vegetations (> 15 mm). 24
For dogs and cats, valve replacement is not a readily available option, so treatment
must rely on antimicrobial drugs and resolution of any predisposing factors. Where the
local prevalence of MDR gram-negative bacteria and MRS is low, a combination of
ampicillin and an aminoglycoside is a good choice for empiric treatment of IE pending
the results of culture and susceptibility. Where MDR gram-negative bacteria and MRS
are locally prevalent, empiric recommendations made for human patients could be
considered for dogs and cats pending the results of culture and susceptibility, provided

vetexamprep.ir

there is a chance of treatment success in the absence of valve replacement. When severe
sepsis is absent and IE follows an indolent course, it is recommended in human patients
that antimicrobial treatment be withheld pending the results of culture and
susceptibility, or a combination of penicillin with or without low-dose gentamicin (1
mg/kg, IV, q12h) be administered until results are available. Aminoglycosides are used
at this low dose, twice daily for their synergistic activity with penicillin against
enterococci and viridans streptococci, which are uncommon causes of IE in dogs.
Empiric treatment protocols that have activity against drug-resistant bacteria are used in
human patients pending results of culture and susceptibility when severe sepsis is
present, such as vancomycin and low-dose gentamicin (no risk factors present for gramnegative bacterial infection), or vancomycin and meropenem (risk factors present for
MDR Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas infection). However, the use of vancomycin and
meropenem in dogs and cats has been controversial and may not be permi ed or
feasible in some geographic locations.
Recommendations for treatment of IE in dogs once the microbial etiology is known
are shown in Table 122.9. Intravenous antimicrobial drugs should be continued in
hospital for as long as possible (ideally at least 7 to 10 days). A switch to oral
medications is not recommended for human IE patients because of poor activity when
compared with IV medications. 24 However, oral antibiotic treatment has been used with
success to treat some dogs with IE and may be the only viable option. At-home
treatment with IV drugs through peripheral indwelling catheters may be possible for
some dogs, but dog, owner, and drug factors should be considered very carefully and
proper client education is critical. If oral antimicrobial drugs are used, bactericidal drugs
with good oral bioavailability are preferable.
The role of antiplatelet therapy is controversial in human and veterinary patients with
IE. The importance of thromboembolic disease in canine and feline IE is well
documented; however, prospective studies identifying any risks or beneﬁts of
concomitant antiplatelet therapy are lacking. In the authors’ hospital, the use of
antiplatelet therapy such as clopidogrel is largely driven by clinician preference.
Antiplatelet therapy is administered to animals considered at risk of or with clinical
evidence of thromboembolic events such as those with spontaneous contrast on
echocardiography, or ultrasonographic evidence of organ infarction. Given the high
frequency of CHF and apparent thromboembolic events associated with IE in cats,
antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel may be warranted in this population. 7 The use of
antiplatelet therapy should be carefully weighed against the risk of hemorrhage
particularly in patients with concurrent thrombocytopenia or potential hypocoagulable
states.
Medical treatment should be continued for at least 4 to 6 weeks, and until the
underlying disease process has resolved, and valvular lesions have also resolved based
on echocardiographic examinations. In the authors’ experience, this treatment often
extends well beyond 6 weeks before resolution of lesions is observed. Echocardiography
should be repeated after 4 weeks, or earlier if there is evidence of complications (CHF,
embolic disease) or inadequate treatment response. Successful resolution of IE is
associated with reduction in size and consolidation of valvular vegetations. With
unsuccessful treatment, lesions remain unchanged, and/or new lesions may appear on
other valves. 5

TABLE 122.9

Infective Pericarditis
In addition to speciﬁc antimicrobial drug treatment, surgery may be required in dogs
with infective pericarditis in order to debride the pericardium and minimize cardiac
diastolic function. This carries a signiﬁcant risk of mortality, and if feasible, referral to an
experienced cardiac surgeon is recommended.

Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs and cats that develop IE, myocarditis, or pericarditis is guarded
and depends on underlying disease processes, the severity of organ damage, and the
etiologic agent or agents. In a study of dogs with IE, mortality rate due to IE was at least
40/71 (56%), and median survival time was only 54 days. 5 Factors strongly associated
with negative outcome in dogs with IE were thrombocytopenia, increased serum
creatinine concentration, renal complications, thromboembolic complications, and IE
associated with Bartonella infection.

Prevention
Methods to prevent bloodstream infections and sepsis include limitation of the use of
invasive devices and catheters unless absolutely necessary and a ention to routine
hygiene in the hospital to minimize nosocomial infections. Other measures include
management of immunosuppressive disorders such as diabetes mellitus, minimizing use
of immunosuppressive drugs such as glucocorticoids, and prompt a ention to wounds
or other underlying infections that have the potential to spread to the bloodstream.
The role of prophylactic antimicrobial drugs to prevent bacteremia and sepsis has
been controversial. Beneﬁcial outcomes have been reported when antimicrobials are
used to prevent infection after chemotherapy. In one study, the use of a 14-day course of
a trimethoprim-sulfonamide reduced morbidity and mortality in dogs with
osteosarcoma or lymphoma during the ﬁrst 14 days after treatment with doxorubicin. 31
In human patients a 7-day course of a ﬂuoroquinolone during the expected neutropenic
period after chemotherapy for solid tumors and lymphomas was shown to reduce the
incidence of fever, probable infection, and hospitalization. 32 Prophylactic treatment with
antimicrobial drugs could also be considered for animals with severe neutropenia (<500
cells/µL), although more studies are required that examine the prevalence of bacteremia
in neutropenic animals and the beneﬁts of prophylactic antimicrobial drug treatment.
Finally, prophylactic antimicrobial drug treatment has been suggested for dogs and cats

vetexamprep.ir

with congenital heart defects that undergo dental procedures, but evidence to support
the need for this practice is lacking.

Public Health Aspects
Dogs with bloodstream infections may harbor bacteria such as MRSA that have the
potential to colonize humans, and so routine precautions should be taken when these
dogs are handled, with special a ention to hand hygiene and fomite disinfection. Dogs
and cats with signs of cardiovascular infection may also be infected with important
human pathogens such as Salmonella spp., Bartonella spp., Brucella spp., and Ricke sia
ricke sii, so caution should be taken when handling blood from animals with
cardiovascular infections and needle-stick injuries should be avoided.

Case Example
Signalment

“Rugby,” a 12-year-old male neutered Labrador retriever from Napa, CA.

History

Rugby was seen at the University of California-Davis, VMTH emergency service for
treatment of possible sepsis. One week before he was evaluated, he had been
swimming in the lake in the owner’s backyard and when exiting was shivering and
reluctant to move. Since then, he has had a waxing and waning appetite. Over the last
day, he had been unwilling to walk. He was taken to the local veterinary clinic that
evening where his temperature was 104.6°F (40.3°C), he was laterally recumbent,
moderately obtunded, had thoracolumbar pain, and had decreased patellar reﬂexes
bilaterally. Blood work showed moderate leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia,
hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and a mildly elevated activity of serum ALP.
Oscillometric blood pressure was normal, and hydromorphone was administered.
Abdominal radiographs showed bridging spondylosis and multiple narrowed
intervertebral disc spaces. Rugby was up to date on vaccinations, including for rabies.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 44 kg.
General: Obtunded, laterally recumbent, T = 104.4°F (40.2°C), HR = 120
beats/minute, RR = 20 breaths/minute, mucous membranes dark pink, CRT = 1 s.
Integument: Multiple generalized small freely moveable subcutaneous masses.
Musculoskeletal: Nonambulatory and unable to stand. BCS was 8/9.
Cardiovascular: A grade 3/6 systolic murmur with a musical quality was
auscultated. Strong, symmetric femoral pulses were palpated bilaterally with
frequent pulse deﬁcits noted.
Respiratory: Increased bronchovesicular sounds were present in all ﬁelds.
Abdominal palpation: Moderate abdominal distention was noted. Palpation was
diﬃcult because of recumbency and the large size of the patient.
Neurologic evaluation: Mentation was severely obtunded with intact cranial
nerves. Postural placing reactions were delayed to absent in all limbs, worse in
the pelvic limbs. Segmental reﬂexes were intact bilaterally. Apparent pain on
palpation of caudal thoracic vertebra. Neuroanatomic localization: Intracranial
+/– T3-L3 myelopathy.
All other systems: No abnormalities detected.

Diagnosis

Streptococcus dysgalactiae IE with arterial thromboembolus formation.

Treatment and Outcome

Lactated Ringer’s solution with 2.5% supplemental dextrose was started at a
maintenance ﬂuid rate to maintain normoglycemia and ampicillin/sulbactam constant
rate infusion (CRI) was started (6 mg/kg/hour), enroﬂoxacin (15 mg/kg, IV, q24h), and
hydromorphone (0.05 mg/kg, IV, q4h). Continuous ECG and arterial blood pressure
monitoring, and urine output via urinary catheter were started. Mean arterial pressure
was > 80 mmHg overnight and supplemental oxygen was provided via nasal cannulas
to keep PaO2 > 80 mmHg. Over the next 3 days, the patient’s mentation steadily
improved and he was able to stand for short periods with support. However, he
remained anorexic. On day 4, the arterial blood pressure tracing suddenly
disappeared from continuous blood pressure monitoring; on abdominal ultrasound
examination, a thrombus was detected in the caudal abdominal aorta that extended
into the right external iliac artery. Multiple cortical renal infarcts were also present. A
nasogastric tube was placed and a commercial liquid diet was fed starting at 25% RER
to increase until full RER was reached 3 days later. Enoxaparin (0.8 mg/kg, SC, q6h)
and clopidogrel (75 mg by nasogastric tube q24h) were started on day 4. On day 8, a
recheck CBC showed a mild neutrophilia (23,800 cells/µL) and normalization of
platelet count (304,000 platelets/µL). Biochemical analysis showed persistent
hyperbilirubinemia (1.1 mg/dL) and hypoalbuminemia (1.6 g/dL). The ampicillinsulbactam CRI was switched to intermi ent dosing (50 mg/kg, IV, q8h). The dog was
still not able to stand independently, but could with support. Over the following 6
days, his ambulatory status improved until he could walk with harness support. His
appetite returned so he was consuming 1.25 RER voluntarily. On day 14, a focused
recheck abdominal ultrasound showed diminishing clot size in the aorta and external
iliac artery. He was discharged on day 15 with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (17 mg/kg,
PO, q12h) and enroﬂoxacin (11 mg/kg, PO, q12h) along with his anticoagulant
medications until scheduled recheck in 2 weeks.

Comments

This dog had mitral valve IE with associated sepsis. Echocardiography was performed
as the patient had a fever and a new-onset murmur. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were
initiated based on the level of illness of the patient and multiple potential sources of
infection (endocarditis and aspiration pneumonia). An antibiotic CRI of a beta-lactam
was initiated in an a empt to provide 100% of time > MIC. It is likely that the arterial
thrombus represented a thromboembolus based on the presence of a large oscillating
valvular vegetation; portions of such lesions may break oﬀ and embolize in the
periphery. The source of bacteremia and endocarditis was not apparent.

123: Sepsis
Deborah Silverstein, and Cynthia M. O o

KEY POINTS
• Sepsis is the systemic inflammatory response to an infectious
agent. The presence of organ function is now included in the
human definitions.
• The pathophysiology of sepsis is complex and includes both a
proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory response that, when
exuberant, can lead to organ dysfunction and death of the host.
• Potential septic foci should be determined as soon as possible,
and cultures of infected fluid or tissue obtained to help guide longterm therapy.
• Pending culture results, treatment should be aimed at the most
likely etiologic agent(s) and tissue infected.
• Intensive monitoring and aggressive supportive care are of utmost
importance to increase the chance for survival. The presence of
multiple organ dysfunction syndrome increases the mortality rate.
• The prognosis for patients with sepsis relies on the severity and
pathogenicity of the underlying infection, as well as the ability to
provide appropriate and early treatment.

Definitions and Epidemiology
Bacteremia is deﬁned as live microorganisms in circulation. Endotoxemia
refers to circulation of the LPS component of the gram-negative
bacterial cell wall and may or may not be associated with the presence
of live bacteria. Sepsis represents the clinical signs associated with a
systemic inﬂammatory response to an infectious agent. 1 More
recently, sepsis was redeﬁned as a life-threatening organ dysfunction
caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. 2 Bacteremia in
dogs and cats is expected to occur in a variety of infections (e.g.,
peritonitis, mastitis, prostatitis, pneumonia, pulmonary abscess,

vetexamprep.ir

pyothorax, pyometra, pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal abscess, biliary
tract infections), as well as during dentistry, but is not always
associated with a systemic inﬂammatory response. 3
Subclinical bacteremia probably also occurs during rectal palpation,
intestinal endoscopy and surgery, and when indwelling venous or
arterial catheters have been placed. Normally, circulating bacteria are
cleared by the mononuclear-phagocyte system; therefore, blood
cultures are not always reliable in documenting bacteremia. Bacterial
molecules, along with molecules from other infectious agents (e.g.,
fungi, virus), are referred to as “pathogen-associated molecular
pa erns” or PAMPs. 4 Macrophages and other cells of the innate
immune system recognize these PAMPs through toll-like receptors
(TLRs) and initiate a complex local inﬂammatory response and
upregulate systemic host defenses, thus preparing the animal to
combat potential spread of infection. 5
Typical clinical signs associated with bacteremia include altered
body temperature, tachycardia, tachypnea, and neutrophilia or
neutropenia; these signs represent the systemic inﬂammatory response
syndrome (SIRS) which, when initiated by an infectious agent and
accompanied by organ dysfunction, is referred to as sepsis. Not all
patients with bacteremia demonstrate clinical signs of sepsis. 3
Dysregulated inﬂammation and SIRS is characterized by a complex
cytokine-mediated response and can also be initiated by endogenous
danger signals (danger-associated molecular pathogens or DAMPs)
from damaged cells as a result of trauma, pancreatitis, hypoxia, and
other insults. 4 The host beneﬁts if the inﬂammatory response remains
localized and balanced by anti-inﬂammatory pathways; however,
systemic inﬂammation or failure to resolve the inﬂammatory response
can lead to high mortality.
The terminologies SIRS and sepsis were clariﬁed in the 1990s in
human medicine 1 ; relevant terms and the various categories of
severity are deﬁned in Table 123.1. SIRS criteria, however, are very
insensitive and nonspeciﬁc features of sepsis that were designed to
identify patients eligible for clinical trials of antisepsis therapies
(Tables 123.2 and 123.3). Subsequently, a human consensus conference
6 identiﬁed a more elaborate classiﬁcation system (PIRO) that focuses
on host factors (predisposition), infectious agent factors (infection), the
host-organism interaction (response), and the consequences of
systemic inﬂammation (organ failure) (Table 123.4). In 2016, updated
deﬁnitions were introduced in an a empt to more accurately identify
patients at high risk for morbidity and mortality from sepsis. These
new deﬁnitions, Sepsis-3, are based on the presence of an abnormal

vetexamprep.ir

mentation using the Glasgow coma scale, RR > 20 breaths/minute,
and/or a Doppler blood pressure < 100 mmHg. 2 , 5 The terms SIRS and
severe sepsis were eliminated. Sepsis or severe inﬂammatory diseases
often lead to an inappropriate, dysregulated generalized systemic
response that leads to a progression of severe sepsis, septic shock, and
ultimately multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) (see Table
123.1). 7 This chapter will continue to refer to the terms SIRS and
severe sepsis because they have been core to so many studies in the
recent past that have contributed to our understanding of sepsis, and
the PIRO system cannot be applied to animals. Much of our
knowledge of sepsis has been derived from experimental animal
models and human (and a few veterinary) clinical studies. Animal
models of sepsis can be divided by the type of insult, the route of
administration of the infectious agent or substance, and the endpoints
of the study. 8 One of the most commonly used agents to study the
physiologic response to systemic bacteria has relied on the use of
endotoxin. Endotoxin (lipopolysacharride [LPS]) consists of a lipid A
moiety (the toxic component) and polysaccharides (O antigens) (see
Fig. 53.2). LPS is released from the outer membrane of gram-negative
bacteria when they lyse and is normally conﬁned within the gut and
portal circulation. The source of endotoxin is usually a member of the
Enterbacterales family (Escherichia spp., Klebsiella spp., Enterobacter
spp., Proteus spp.), as well as Pseudomonas spp. Studies of endotoxemia
are highly reproducible, but administration of endotoxin to animal
models does not account for all of the factors involved in clinical
conditions in which endotoxin is a component of the disease. The
innate immune system has evolved to recognize and respond to LPS in
tissues and ﬂuids early in gram-negative infections. 9 A major function
of the innate immune system is to recognize threats to host survival.
These threats can be exogenous or pathogen-associated (PAMPs), or
endogenous danger signals released from damaged or dying cells
(DAMPs). 4 The pathway for recognition of endotoxin has been well
deﬁned and is the prototypical example of activation of the innate
immune response. The innate immune system is also capable of
recognizing gram-positive bacterial products, ﬂagellin, bacterial or
viral DNA, and fungal products via the TLR (Table 123.5). 10 , 11

The prevalence of naturally occurring sepsis in dogs and cats is
unknown, even though the dog has been used for many years as a
model of sepsis and endotoxemia for humans. 12 Risk factors for
endotoxemia, with or without concurrent bacteremia, in dogs include
canine parvovirus (CPV) enteritis, gastric dilation and volvulus,
pyometra, mastitis, other gram-negative infections, and heat stroke.
Endotoxemia can develop when hepatic clearance of LPS is reduced, as
in hepatic insuﬃciency and portosystemic shunts. Obstructive biliary
disease may be a risk factor because bile salts bind endotoxin in the
gut. Endotoxin may also play an important role in the pathogenesis of
severe acute pancreatitis in dogs. 13 In the dog, sepsis is most
commonly associated with disruption of the normal mucosal barrier
and movement of bacteria into the circulation or tissues. The most
commonly reported causes of sepsis in dogs include peritonitis (from
GI or urogenital origins) and pneumonia. 14–16 Dogs receiving
chemotherapy are susceptible to developing sepsis. 17 Smaller dogs
with lymphoma, after receiving doxorubicin, or vincristine are at
highest risk.
Sepsis is recognized less commonly in cats. Even severely aﬀected
cats do not commonly display the classic hyperdynamic signs of sepsis
(tachycardia, red mucous membranes, fever, bounding/hyperkinetic
pulses), making diagnosis a challenge. 18 , 19 In an experimental study
of low-dose endotoxin infusion, cats developed hypotension but not
tachycardia. 20 Risk factors for severe sepsis in cats include pyothorax,
septic peritonitis, bacteremia secondary to GI disease, pneumonia,
endocarditis, pyelonephritis, osteomyelitis, pyometra, and bite
wounds. 21 In cats with pyothorax, identiﬁed risk factors include
indoor-outdoor environment and multicat households. 22 In cats with
peritonitis, neoplasia 23 or trauma 24 are the most commonly
recognized causes. Endotoxemia is likely a component of some of these
infections. Sepsis is also recognized as a cause of neonatal death in
puppies and ki ens.

In a human study performed in a tertiary care hospital, 68% of

with hypotension or hypoperfusion, and only 4% developed septic
shock. Not all patients, even those who developed septic shock, had
bacteremia. Pneumonia and UTIs were the most common sources of

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Molecular Pathogenesis
The clinical signs of sepsis described earlier in this chapter occur as a
result of expression of proinﬂammatory cytokines and activation of the
coagulation cascade. 5 Endotoxin is released into the intestinal lumen

vetexamprep.ir

or tissues when gram-negative bacteria lyse, as occurs with rapid
bacterial replication or with bactericidal action of some antibacterials.
Within the intestinal lumen, most endotoxin is bound by bile salts and
contained by the mucosal barrier; the small amounts normally
absorbed into the portal circulation are cleared by hepatic
macrophages. Endotoxin absorbed through the lymphatic system is
cleared in regional lymph nodes. Thus, endotoxin levels in the
systemic circulation are usually extremely low to immeasurable.
Clinical signs of endotoxemia occur only when binding and clearance
mechanisms are overwhelmed. Bacteria can also translocate into the
bloodstream as a result of disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier.
Bacteria and other pathogens can also gain access to the circulatory
system from other mucosal surfaces, surgical or traumatic wounds, or
invasive monitoring devices. The innate immune system is equipped
with pa ern recognition receptors that allow a response without prior
exposure to the pathogen. These receptors are part of the TLR
pathway. 5 , 10 , 11
The ﬁrst step in recognition of gram-negative bacteria is the binding
of LPS to the acute-phase protein known as LPS-binding protein (the
canine molecule has been described and cloned). 26 This protein
complexes with LPS and shu les it to the macrophage, where the
complex
binds
to
the
surface
receptor,
CD14,
a
glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored membrane protein that lacks a
transmembrane domain. CD14 can be shed from cells, and soluble
(free) CD14-endotoxin complexes can bind to endothelial cells and
induce a cytokine response. Recognition of the TLR4 receptor provided
the missing link between LPS binding to CD14 and the initiation of the
signaling cascade. 27

In response to the activation of the TLR4 receptor, transcription
factor NF-κB (originally identiﬁed in B cells) is activated and leads to
the expression of many cytokines. 28 This activation requires the
recruitment and activation of a series of adapter proteins and signaling
molecules. Myeloid diﬀerentiation primary response protein 88
(MyD88) is an adapter protein found on all of the TLR. TLR4 activation
and MyD88 recruitment leads to the activation of the IL-1 receptorassociated kinase (IRAK) family members, and TNF receptorassociated factor-6 subsequent signaling pathways. Phosphorylated
IRAK1 associates with TRAF6 and forms a complex with another
signaling molecule, transforming growth factor β activated kinase
(TAK1). NF-κB resides in the cytoplasm as a complex with inhibitory
proteins of the inhibitors of NF-κB (I-κB) family. Eventually, TAK1
activation leads to phosphorylation of the I-κB kinase complex (IKK),
releasing the transcription factor, NF-κB. 9 This also leads to activation
of the NF-κB pathway. 9 , 10 Activation of NF-κB via phosphorylation
of the inhibitory proteins (referred to as the canonical pathway of
activation) can be triggered by cellular interactions with bacteria and
bacterial products, viruses, parasites, and cytokines, involving
activation of the TRL receptors 2, 3, 5, 6, and 9, or cytokine receptors. 28
The phosphorylation step involves three IKKs and results in

the inhibitory I-κB, NF-κB is free to translocate to the nucleus and
regulate expression of numerous genes involved in the inﬂammatory
response. NF-κB can also be activated independent of the IKK complex
by hypoxia, free radicals, and ultraviolet radiation. 28 Activation of NFκB may be a biomarker of inﬂammation and serve as a therapeutic
target for diseases of excessive inﬂammation. The wide range of genes
regulated by NF-κB, however, may result in untoward systemic eﬀects
if the transcription factor is completely inhibited. Similar to endotoxin,
products of gram-positive bacteria, fungi, and bacterial or viral DNA
are capable of binding TLR receptors and activating the innate immune
response. In SIRS, the innate immune system is activated by DAMPs
such as the DNA-binding protein, high mobility group box 1
(HMGB1). 29 This highly conserved ubiquitous nuclear protein is
released from cells dying from necrosis and, after acetylation or ADP
ribosylation, can be actively secreted by macrophages, monocytes, and
dendritic cells. HMGB1 activates TLRs 2, 4, and 9 and the receptor for
advanced glycation end products. In addition, HMGB1 can enhance
the response to other danger signals. Circulating HMGB1 levels persist
longer than most other cytokines in acute inﬂammatory states, and
HMGB1 may represent a therapeutic target to limit inﬂammation.
HMGB1 induces the release of numerous cytokines from inﬂammatory
cells, including TNF-α, IL-1 α and β, IL-1 receptor antagonist, IL-6, IL8, and macrophage inﬂammatory protein-1 α and β.
The macrophage is the main cell of the innate immune system that
initiates the response to PAMPs and DAMPs (Fig. 123.1). The early
macrophage response to endotoxin is characterized by release of
multifunctional proinﬂammatory cytokines, especially IL-1β and TNFα. In dogs, TNF-α levels increase within 15 minutes of exposure to
LPS, peak at 2 hours, and return to baseline levels in 4 hours. TNF-α
mediates many immune and inﬂammatory functions, as well as further
stimulating macrophages to secrete IL-1, IL-6, macrophage colonystimulating factor, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating
factor. IL-1 is released in similar burst fashion; it is a major costimulator of Th2 cells, stimulates the acute-phase response, induces
fever, and has a multitude of other proinﬂammatory eﬀects. Other
cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-8, and IFN-α, are additional early mediators
in sepsis. 30 Proinﬂammatory cytokines are released early and
transiently in response to endotoxin, before the animal shows clinical
signs. Novel therapeutics directed toward these mediators have not
demonstrated signiﬁcant beneﬁt in most human clinical trials. 31
However, late mediators, such as HMGB1, may be more appropriate
therapeutic targets. 21 The cytokine cascades increase the levels or

vetexamprep.ir

activity (or both) of inﬂammatory phospholipid-derived mediators
(prostacyclin, thromboxane, and platelet-activating factor), 32
coagulation factors, complement, reactive oxygen species, and nitric
oxide (NO; which is an important molecule associated with
hypotension), 33–36 endothelin-1 (a vasoconstrictor), 37 β-endorphin,
histamine, serotonin, vasopressin, angiotensin II, and catecholamines.
The biologic eﬀects of these mediators include neutrophil activation,
aggregation, and chemotaxis; platelet activation and aggregation; a
procoagulable state; increased activity of plasma proteases; and
vasodilation and potentially systemic hypotension, generalized
endothelial inﬂammation, increased vascular permeability, and GI
ulceration. 38 , 39 Lysosomal enzymes such as elastase and
chymotrypsin deplete ﬁbronectin and activate blood clo ing,
triggering DIC.

There are multiple eﬀects of sepsis on the coagulation cascade (Fig.
123.2). 40 Sepsis promotes coagulation, inhibits anticoagulation, and
impairs ﬁbrinolysis. Early in sepsis, patients exhibit a procoagulant
state which is followed by DIC. 41 , 42 Inﬂammation leads to the

vetexamprep.ir

exposure and induction of tissue factor, a potent procoagulant that
complexes with factor VII(a) to activate factor IX and factor X and
eventually lead to ﬁbrin formation. Platelets are also activated by
endotoxin, proinﬂammatory cytokines, and thrombin. Endothelial cell
damage associated with sepsis results in the release of von
Willebrand’s factor and further platelet aggregation. Activation of
platelets leads to release of proinﬂammatory mediators and
consumption of platelets. Clinically, septic patients frequently have
low platelet counts. The three main anticoagulant protein systems,
antithrombin (AT), tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI), and protein
C (PC), are all deranged during sepsis. Endothelial cells are actively
involved in the production/activation of TFPI and PC. TFPI is secreted
by and then bound to endothelial cells and inhibits the activation of
factor X by tissue factor–factor VII(a) complexes. Sepsis impairs the
binding of TFPI to endothelial cells and appears to decrease its
eﬀectiveness. The other anticoagulant protein that relies on normal
endothelial function is PC. Healthy endothelial cells express the
surface protein thrombomodulin, which binds circulating thrombin
(see Figs. 123.2 and 123.3). When thrombin is bound to
thrombomodulin, it is not available for cleavage by ﬁbrinogen, and the
complex acts to cleave PC into active PC (aPC). Endothelial cells
exposed to cytokines have a reduction in thrombomodulin expression;
thus, less PC can be activated. In addition, aPC is consumed in the
inactivation of factor Va and factor VIIIa. Septic patients and dogs have
reduced PC, which may be related to survival. 43 The only clinical trial
in sepsis that has shown any outcome beneﬁt was a trial of aPC in
patients with severe sepsis. 44 Unfortunately, the beneﬁts of aPC do not
seem to be generalizable to wider populations, 45 and has subsequently
been withdrawn from the sepsis market. In addition, the expense and
species speciﬁcity of the recombinant aPC have precluded clinical trials
in dogs. A major advance that resulted from investigations of aPC was
recognition of the interaction between coagulation and inﬂammation.
aPC
inhibits
neutrophil-endothelial
interactions,
limits
proinﬂammatory cytokine production, blocks chemotaxis of
neutrophils, and protects endothelial barrier function. 45
