In addition to increased activation of procoagulants and decreased
anticoagulants, ﬁbrinolysis is also impaired during sepsis. Initially,
plasmin (the main ﬁbrinolytic protein) activation is accelerated by
increased release of plasminogen activators (tissue plasminogen
activator and urokinase-type plasminogen activator) from the
endothelial cells. This eﬀect is short-lived as cytokines induce the
production and release of plasminogen activator inhibitor. 40
Thrombin-activatable ﬁbrinolysis inhibitor antigen was increased in
dogs with sepsis and not in other evaluated diseases. 47 Fibrin
deposition results from impairment of all components of the
coagulation cascade and can contribute to tissue hypoxia and
development of multiple organ dysfunction.

vetexamprep.ir

The innate immune system includes the complement system. 48
Complement functions in neutrophil chemotaxis, drawing neutrophils
to the sites of infection and inﬂammation, enhancing clearance of
bacteria through opsonization, and causing lysis of cells (both bacterial
and host). Complement is also involved in the integration between the
innate and adaptive immune system and facilitates removal of
apoptotic cells and immune complexes. Complement can be activated
by one of three pathways, all of which converge with the activation of
C3. Cleavage of C3 leads to production of the anaphylatoxin C3a and
the eventual cleavage and activation of C5. C5 cleavage produces the
chemotactic protein and anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, a major
component of the membrane a ack complex responsible for lysing
cells. The classic pathway is activated by immune complexes on cells,
apoptotic cells, and some bacteria and viruses. The mannose-binding
lectin pathway provides an antibody-independent mechanism to
activate the complement cascade by binding bacterial mannose
residues. Independent of antibody binding, endotoxin and other
surface molecules on bacteria activate the alternate pathway. 48 , 49 In
sepsis, high levels of C3a and C5a are associated with a worse
prognosis. In addition to its role as a chemotactic protein, C5a activates
endothelial cells, causes vasodilation, and increases vascular
permeability. Like many inﬂammatory mediators, the eﬀects of C5a
appear to be complex. C5 can be proinﬂammatory or protective or
even lead to immune paralysis. The response, at least in part, appears
to depend on the amount of C5a, the receptor it binds, and the
presence of proinﬂammatory or anti-inﬂammatory cytokines. 50
Strategies to limit C5 activation continue to be investigated.
If the systemic inﬂammatory state progresses, structural and
metabolic changes develop in vascular endothelial cells. Endothelial
adhesion molecules are upregulated, and neutrophils and platelets are
sequestered in various organs. The endothelium also becomes more
permeable, and plasma proteins move from the intravascular space to
the interstitium, resulting in edema. In addition to the vasodilation
mentioned earlier, the vascular endothelium may become
unresponsive to commonly used vasopressor therapy, a condition
termed catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock.
Despite normalization of macrohemodynamic indices (blood
pressure, perfusion, and global tissue oxygenation), multiorgan
dysfunction and failure may still develop in septic patients. Advances
in the ability to study the microcirculation have found alterations in
blood ﬂow through the arterioles, capillaries, and venules. These
changes have signiﬁcant prognostic implications in people with severe

vetexamprep.ir

sepsis. 51 Even though the percentage of perfused small vessels and
vascular density are similar at the onset of shock in both survivors and
nonsurvivors, small vessel perfusion improves with time only in
survivors. 52 , 53 However, both survivors and nonsurvivors have
similar measures of global perfusion and cardiovascular parameters
after initial stabilization, demonstrating that microcirculation, not
macrocirculation, is important for determining prognosis and survival.
This may provide a valuable monitoring tool in veterinary patients to
help guide diagnostic and therapeutic decisions and monitoring. 9
Concurrent with inﬂammatory mediator upregulation, antiinﬂammatory mediators are secreted to balance and limit the
inﬂammatory response. An insuﬃcient or inappropriate antiinﬂammatory response can allow sepsis to progress. 38
The prevailing theory has been that sepsis is a result of a cytokine
storm, leading to uncontrolled systemic inﬂammation. Newer studies
indicate that, for at least some patients, the hyperinﬂammatory state is
followed by severe acute immunosuppression, caused by the apoptosis
of B cells, CD4+ T cells, and follicular dendritic cells. The mechanism of
immunosuppression is not known; however, release of endogenous
glucocorticoids may be an important contributor. 54 Thyroid hormone
production and secretion have been impaired in endotoxin-treated
dogs. 55
In summary, PAMPs act as a signal to the immune system that
pathogens have invaded the host, whereas DAMPs are signals of
damage to host cells (see Fig. 123.1). A localized response along with a
primed or controlled systemic response is beneﬁcial in containing and
resolving the infection, whereas an uncontrolled host response leads to
systemic inﬂammation, immunosuppression, severe sepsis, septic
shock, and ultimately organ failure.
Organ Dysfunction in Sepsis
Abnormalities of the coagulation and ﬁbrinolytic pathways play a
major role in the development of organ dysfunction in septic patients.
Mechanisms for derangements of the coagulation system include: (1)
activation of the coagulation cascade; (2) defective physiologic
anticoagulant pathways; and (3) impaired ﬁbrinolysis. Clinically,
activation of procoagulant pathways can lead to an early
hypercoagulable or prothrombotic state that is diﬃcult to diagnose but
can contribute to organ dysfunction through inﬂammatory mediators
and development of microthrombi. As sepsis progresses, coagulation
disorders reﬂect a consumptive coagulopathy, impairment of

vetexamprep.ir

anticoagulant mechanisms, and inhibition of ﬁbrinolysis that is
recognized clinically as DIC. 44 , 56–59
Cardiovascular system
Disruption of normal cardiovascular function is common in patients
with sepsis. Circulating cytokines have been implicated in leading to
these derangements via three primary mechanisms: increased vascular
endothelial permeability, which allows leakage of intravascular ﬂuid
into the extravascular space, leading to hypovolemia and tissue edema;
impaired cardiac contractility and subsequent decrease in cardiac
output; and heterogenous loss of vasomotor tone, causing
maldistribution of blood ﬂow. Although a single “myocardial
depressant factor” was previously implicated as the cause of impaired
cardiac performance in septic animals and humans, several circulating
cytokines have been found to play a role (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-2, and
IL-6). 60 , 61 Additional factors might include alterations in intracellular
calcium traﬃcking with a reduction in systolic intracellular calcium
concentration and decreased myocyte contraction; downregulation of
beta receptors in the heart; and myocardial “hibernation” to preserve
cardiac myocytes via decrease in oxygen consumption, energy
requirements, and ATP demands. 50 , 62
Respiratory system
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a severe form of acute
lung injury (ALI), is the manifestation of lung injury that may occur in
human and veterinary patients with sepsis and SIRS. 63–66 ARDS and
ALI are labels that describe the syndrome of SIRS- or sepsis-associated
lung injury, rather than disease entities themselves. Impaired gas
exchange in patients with ALI and ARDS is multifactorial and involves
endothelial and epithelial injury; neutrophil-dependent lung injury;
proinﬂammatory cytokines; abnormalities of the coagulation system;
and abnormalities in the production, composition, and function of
surfactant. Ultimately there is an accumulation of protein-rich ﬂuid in
the alveoli and inﬁltration of the alveolar interstitial space with
inﬂammatory cells, ﬂuid, and debris. This is typically recognized as
alveolar inﬁltrates on thoracic radiographs. The lungs are the shock
organ in cats and are especially vulnerable to injury during sepsis in
this species; tachypnea was a common ﬁnding in cats with severe
sepsis and, although only 11 of 29 cats in one study had an underlying
respiratory cause of sepsis (pneumonia or pyothorax), 17 of 29 had
clinical or radiographic signs of respiratory disease. 18 Septic cats are
commonly ﬂuid intolerant and quite susceptible to ﬂuid overload.

vetexamprep.ir

Veterinary deﬁnitions for the development of ARDS and ALI have
been published (Box 123.1). 67
Urinary system
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common sequela to sepsis in humans. A
retrospective study proposed a scoring system for AKI in dogs (Box
123.2). Although there are no veterinary clinical studies that have
investigated the incidence of AKI in patients with sepsis, retrospective
sepsis studies and clinical impression suggest that sepsis-induced AKI
is infrequent in dogs and cats, except in dogs with severe babesiosis. 18
, 23 , 68 , 69 Dogs with bacterial endocarditis may be another exception.
70 Sepsis-associated AKI has been historically a ributed to acute
tubular necrosis secondary to renal ischemia (e.g., due to aﬀerent
arteriolar vasoconstriction and/or poor cardiac output). 37 , 70–72
However, sepsis-associated AKI may be more complicated than a
simple reduction in renal blood ﬂow. 29 , 71–73 Tissue injury may be due
to ischemia-reperfusion injury and/or activation of macrophages and
neutrophils; alterations in NO metabolism; cytopathic hypoxia; and
renal apoptosis. Reactive oxygen species may contribute to
vasoconstriction directly or through depletion of endogenous
vasodilators such as prostacyclin and NO. Apoptotic pathways may be
activated in reaction to potentially lethal insults (e.g., TNF, ischemia,
bacterial toxins). 71 , 72 Based on the human literature and retrospective
veterinary studies, there has been debate as to the role of hydroxyethyl
starch in contributing to AKI in veterinary patients. 74 , 75

Neurologic dysfunction
Sepsis-associated neurologic dysfunction is poorly characterized or
understood. CNS signs such as decreased alertness, stupor, coma, or
seizures are common in people with septic shock. Anatomic,
histopathologic, and reversible neurologic changes may be responsible
for these derangements, including a direct eﬀect from toxins of
infectious organisms, a reduction in cerebral blood ﬂow, capillary
leakage, and dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier. 76 , 77 The
incidence and pathogenesis of neurologic dysfunction in dogs and cats
with sepsis remains to be determined.

vetexamprep.ir

Gastrointestinal and hepatic systems
GI dysfunction in septic patients often manifests as ileus, poor
tolerance to enteral feedings, vomiting, diarrhea, GI ulceration,
melena, and hematochezia. Subsequent disturbances often include
malnutrition, ﬂuid and electrolyte losses, and small intestinal bacterial
overgrowth. An increase in GI mucosal permeability frequently occurs
and may predispose the patient to bacterial translocation into the
lymphatics and/or the bloodstream. Human patients in the ICU were
found to have altered microbiota that were associated with
inﬂammation, contained a loss of diversity, and were more pathogenic
than healthy individuals. 78 Because of the prominent role of the liver
in host defense, the derangements in liver function can contribute to
both the initiation and progression of sepsis. The reticuloendothelial
system of the liver acts as a ﬁrst line of defense in clearing bacteria and
their products; therefore, liver dysfunction leads to a spillover of these
products into the systemic circulation. Possible mechanisms of
increased GI epithelial permeability and hepatic dysfunction include
dysregulation of blood ﬂow, alterations in energy metabolism and
mitochondrial function, oxidant stress, or direct eﬀects of cytokines
promoting apoptosis. 79–82 The liver is commonly referred to as the
“shock organ” in dogs, and hepatic dysfunction can result in
hypoalbuminemia, coagulopathies, hypoglycemia, icterus, mental
depression, and encephalopathy. Decreased albumin levels may also
result from loss into the extravascular space, a shift toward production
of acute-phase proteins, and, secondary to LPS-induced
downregulation of NF-κB.
Microcirculatory system
In addition to alterations in smooth muscle tone and microcirculatory
perfusion, vascular endothelial cells are also commonly involved in the
septic process. 83–85 This negatively inﬂuences their normal roles in
antithrombosis, proﬁbrinolysis, and inhibition of platelet and
leukocyte aggregation, often resulting in DIC and further negative
eﬀects on microcirculatory perfusion. In addition, sepsis-induced
alterations in vascular endothelial function and perfused capillary
density may result in capillary leak syndromes and heterogenous
blood ﬂow within organs. Tissue ischemia may result from decreases
in both diﬀusive (i.e., tissue edema) and convective (i.e., decreased
perfused capillary density) oxygen delivery, possibly due to changes in
the endothelial glycocalyx. 86–90 In this sense, endothelial dysfunction
can be implicated as the “motor of MODS.” Technology such as
sidestream dark ﬁeld imaging has been studied in dogs and cats and

vetexamprep.ir

enables
visualization
and
assessment
of
microcirculatory
derangements during sepsis and in response to therapy. 51–53 , 91 , 92
The use of endothelial biomarkers such as endocan, syndecan-1,
angiopoietin-2, and soluble vascular endothelial cadherin (sVEcadherin) to predict the severity of sepsis and outcome is currently
under investigation in human medicine. 93 , 94 Proteomic panels have
also been used to identify diﬀerential inﬂammatory biomarker
expression that could help to predict outcome in patients with sepsis.
95

Diagnosis
The clinical features of sepsis result from the systemic inﬂammatory
response to microbial products. The diagnosis of sepsis is often
presumptive in clinical practice, based on the accumulation of
clinicopathologic and biochemical data. Although a “sepsis test” does
not exist, it is possible to use the patient’s clinical picture combined
with a high level of suspicion to quite accurately diagnose a septic
patient. However, it has been reported that 82% and 60% of bacteremic
dogs and cats, respectively, were found to suﬀer from clinical sepsis in
one retrospective study. 3 It is important to maintain a high index of
suspicion for sepsis since recent studies found that 6.2% of cats and
4.2% of dogs admi ed to a hospital were septic and 1.5% of cats and
1.6% of dogs developed sepsis while hospitalized. 96 , 97
The diagnosis of sepsis must always begin with suspicion based on
the patient’s clinical signs and history. Additional diagnostics that may
be indicated include imaging of the thorax and abdomen, spinal
radiographs, echocardiography, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, tracheal
or bronchoalveolar lavage, arthrocentesis, and CSF collection. The use
of serum biomarkers is an area of intense investigation and may prove
quite useful in diﬀerentiating septic and nonseptic SIRS in dogs and
cats. 98 , 99

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
The most common hematologic abnormalities in people with sepsis
include anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and activation of the
hemostatic system. 100 Similar changes have been reported in dogs and
cats. 15 , 18 , 23 , 101 , 102 A leukocytosis with bandemia and cytologic
evidence of toxic neutrophils indicate ongoing and premature release
of leukocytes from the bone marrow and continued inﬂammation. 101

vetexamprep.ir

Increased vascular endothelial permeability due to vasculitis, platelet
sequestration in the lymphoreticular system, and DIC can all
contribute to thrombocytopenia. Blood loss (e.g., GI loss secondary to
poor perfusion and ulcerations), hemolysis, and/or decreased
erythrocyte production may all lead to anemia (more common in septic
cats than dogs). Potential causes of anemia in septic animals include
premature clearance by the reticuloendothelial system with a lowgrade hemolysis and increased susceptibility to oxidative damage
leading to a Heinz body anemia, especially in cats. 102–105
Serum Chemistry Profile
Biochemical proﬁle changes in animals with sepsis are typically
reﬂective of the underlying disease process (e.g., azotemia with
pyelonephritis), but may also be due to sepsis-induced changes (e.g.,
cholestasis). Patients with severe sepsis and septic shock often develop
derangements indicative of organ dysfunction or failure (e.g., hepatic
failure, DIC). Some of the more common, nonspeciﬁc abnormalities
include hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, and
hyperbilirubinemia. 15 , 18 , 56 , 106 , 107
Clotting Function
DIC is common in humans and animals with sepsis. 15 , 42 , 47 , 108 , 109
Hemostatic
derangements
are
typically
characterized
by
hypercoagulability initially, then hypocoagulability as the disease
progresses. It is often challenging to diagnose hypercoagulability
clinically; therefore, this stage is often overlooked. Some potential clues
might include a progressively decreasing platelet count and ﬁbrinogen
levels, low AT activity, elevated D-dimers and ﬁbrin/ﬁbrinogen
degradation products (FDPs), the presence of schistocytes on blood
smear evaluation, evidence of hypercoagulability using viscoelastic
indices, or clinical evidence of abnormal clo ing (e.g., catheters,
anticoagulated blood samples, vascular thromboses to major organs).
The later hypocoagulable state is more frequently recognized clinically
and typiﬁes the progression of a septic patient into DIC. 15 , 42 A
statistically signiﬁcant lower PC and AT activity and higher PT, PTT,
D-dimer, and FDPs compared with controls have been described. 15
Dogs with naturally occurring CPV enteritis had decreased AT activity
and increased maximum amplitude on the thromboelastogram,
consistent with hypercoagulability. 42 Hematologic and hemostatic
changes in septic animals are summarized in Table 123.6.
Biomarkers

vetexamprep.ir

Early detection of sepsis is desirable because mortality increases with
the development of organ dysfunction, hypotension, and
hyperlactatemia. Early clinical signs such as tachypnea, tachycardia,
fever, and leukocytosis are nonspeciﬁc, so research investigating the
use of biomarkers is ongoing. Ideal biomarkers of sepsis would be able
to not only detect the presence of infection but also temporally track
severity of infection and progression from sepsis to septic shock. Their
ability to allow monitoring response to treatment and provide
prognostic information is also desirable. Potential categories of early
diagnostic biomarkers might include markers of infection (e.g., LPS,
bacterial DNA), markers of cellular responsiveness (intercellular
cellular adhesion molecule 1, CD11/CD18), 110 and products of
inﬂammatory cells and humoral activation (ILs, AT, aPC). 15
Procalcitonin and neutrophil CD64 appear to be potentially useful
biomarkers for human sepsis, but their application to veterinary
patients is yet to be deﬁned. 111–114 Heparin-binding protein was more
predictive of septic shock in people compared with several other wellstudied biomarkers. 115 Additional biomarkers that have received
a ention in people include IL-6, aPC, IL-8, acute-phase proteins (CRP,
amyloid A, haptoglobin, ﬁbrinogen, α-1-acid glycoprotein, and
ceruloplasmin),
LPS,
LPS-binding
protein,
nitrate/nitrite
concentrations (byproducts of NO metabolism), soluble intercellular
cellular adhesion molecule 1, AT, TFPI, CD14, CD11b/CD18, T-cell
function assays, IL-12, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, and
IL-1 receptor antagonist. 116–119 Serum IL-6 has been studied in
experimental models of endotoxemia or inﬂammation in dogs; this
biomarker rises within hours, stays elevated for days when
inﬂammation persists, and may have a prognostic role in this species.
120–123 Initial serum CRP concentration in dogs with sepsis did not
correlate with survival. 124 , 125 However, decreasing concentrations
were observed with recovery from sepsis. Monocyte chemoa ractant
protein-1 is increased in critically ill dogs and highest levels have been
observed in those with sepsis. 126 This level of cytokine mediator in
dogs appeared to increase in proportion to the severity of sepsis,
similar to what has been observed in humans. aPC is decreased in
septic human patients and canine models of sepsis and represents a
therapeutic target that reduces mortality in limited populations with
severe sepsis. 127–129 Treatment of sepsis with aPC failed to improve
survival in a large randomized clinical trial, 130 the product, when it
was available was quite costly and species speciﬁc; therefore, clinical
use of this product was not investigated in veterinary medicine.
Plasma von Willebrand factor antigen concentration, a marker of

vetexamprep.ir

endothelial activation, was increased in dogs with sepsis compared
with that in clinically healthy control dogs. 131 However, there was no
signiﬁcant diﬀerence between levels in surviving and nonsurviving
dogs.

Microbiologic Tests
Bacterial Isolation and Identification
The identiﬁcation of a septic focus and the procurement of infected
tissue or ﬂuid for culture and sensitivity testing are of paramount
importance. Although this might be diﬃcult in certain patients (e.g.,
those that are unstable, coagulopathic), cytology or histopathology can
also be used to make a deﬁnitive diagnosis of infection. 16 , 18 , 23 , 132
Specimen collection is further described in Chapter 3. Faster
turnaround times for canine and feline blood cultures (<24 hours) may
soon be clinically available to help guide earlier therapy. 133
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing and
Metagenomic Approaches
Rapid NAAT tests are increasingly being used in human medicine for
rapid identiﬁcation of pathogens associated with sepsis. Such assays
may detect more pathogens than culture, have a shorter turnaround
time, and may still be positive in the face of empirical antimicrobial
therapy. 134–136 Commercially-available diagnostic tests that use
metagenomic approaches such as next-generation sequencing (NGS)
are also increasingly available and in clinical use in human patients; an
example is the Karius NGS test (Karius, CA, USA). At the time of
writing, these assays can be expensive and their performance and
value requires further study. 136

Pathologic Findings
Because sepsis is not a speciﬁc disease, but rather a clinical entity
describing the host response to systemic inﬂammation initiated by a
pathogen, there are no speciﬁc gross or histopathologic ﬁndings that
are diagnostic for sepsis. Histologic ﬁndings associated with SIRS
include widespread vascular endothelial injury, neutrophil
margination, edema, and microthrombosis. The focus of infection will
often represent the key pathologic abnormality (e.g., CPV enteritis,
pyometra, bacterial endocarditis).
Necropsy studies do not deﬁnitively reveal the cause of death in
many human patients with sepsis, and there is frequently discordance
between histologic ﬁndings and the degree of clinical and laboratory
indices of organ dysfunction. One possible reason for this might be the
occurrence of cell stunning, in which sepsis activates defense

vetexamprep.ir

g
p
mechanisms that cause cellular processes to be reduced to basic
housekeeping roles, but further investigation is required. Many
animals develop secondary organ dysfunction that may prove lifethreatening; derangements of the coagulation, cardiovascular,
respiratory, renal, GI, hepatic, and microcirculatory systems are most
common.

Treatment
The mainstay of therapy for septic patients remains source control to
remove the inciting cause and provide supportive care.

Circulatory Support
Septic patients commonly suﬀer from circulatory collapse despite
volume resuscitation; therefore, cardiovascular support is a primary
objective of treatment. To maintain adequate tissue perfusion and
prevent the development of MODS, aggressive ﬂuid therapy is
essential. Isotonic crystalloids, hypertonic crystalloid solutions,
synthetic colloids, and blood component therapy are typically
administered during ﬂuid resuscitation and maintenance of the septic
patient. 137 , 138 Many septic patients have increased vascular
endothelial permeability and hypoalbuminemia; thus, judicious use of
ﬂuid products is recommended. Synthetic colloids may prove helpful
in animals with severe decreases in colloid osmotic pressure, and
colloidal blood component therapy, including human/canine albumin
or plasma, may be beneﬁcial in animals that are severely
hypoalbuminemic or coagulopathic, respectively. Although not proven
in small animals, the use of hydroxyethyl starch in humans with sepsis
has been found to increase the risk for AKI. 139 Because large volumes
of fresh frozen plasma are required for albumin replacement (e.g., 22
mL/kg of plasma to raise the albumin concentration by 0.5 g/dL), 140
fresh frozen plasma is used primarily for animals that are
coagulopathic or to prevent a further decline in those with severe
hypoalbuminemia.
Human and canine serum albumin are in the early stages of clinical
use in veterinary medicine, and further research is ongoing. The 25%
human serum albumin solution is hyperoncotic (100 mmHg) and
should be used judiciously in patients with limited ﬂuid tolerance.
Anemia and thrombocytopenia may prompt the use of erythrocyte- or
platelet-containing products (e.g., packed RBCs, fresh whole blood,
lyophilized platelets). In contrast to the debated value of placement of
a central venous catheter in humans, in veterinary patients this tool

vetexamprep.ir

provides a way to monitor trends in central venous pressures during
aggressive ﬂuid therapy. 137 In a landmark study, the use of early goaldirected therapy, including central venous oxygen saturation, was
shown to improve outcome in humans with sepsis and septic shock 141
; however, subsequent large-scale clinical trials failed to conﬁrm a
survival beneﬁt of this approach. 142 , 143 Noninvasive cardiac output
monitoring may prove useful in management of septic patients by
providing trends in systemic vascular resistance, cardiac output, and
pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. 143 This information will assist
with treatment decisions regarding the use of ﬂuids, vasopressors,
and/or inotropes. Frequent monitoring of body weight and urine
output via placement of an indwelling urinary catheter is also helpful
in assessing total ﬂuid balance. Various ﬂuid types and doses can be
found in Table 123.7.

Cardiovascular Support
Persistent hypotension (mean arterial pressure less than 65 mmHg or
Doppler less than 90 mmHg) despite restoration of a normal
intravascular volume signals the need for vasopressor and/or inotropic
therapy to support oxygen delivery to the tissues and prevent organ
damage. 141 , 144 The choice of treatment drug depends on the clinical
picture combined with objective information regarding the septic
patient (Table 123.8). Vasopressors such as norepinephrine, dopamine,
phenylephrine, and vasopressin are typically used in patients with
peripheral vasodilation. The use of dopamine has been discouraged in
septic humans due to an increased risk for arrhythmias, but this has
not been proven in dogs or cats. 145 Phenylephrine is a pure α-agonist,
whereas norepinephrine and dopamine have a combination of both αand β-agonist activity. 146 Vasopressin, also known as antidiuretic
hormone, is a nonadrenergic vasopressor agent that aids in the
regulation of free water balance in healthy animals, but serves as an
important endogenous vasoconstrictor during states of hypotension.
147 Decreased vasopressin concentrations have been found in animals
and humans with catecholamine-refractory shock, and exogenous
vasopressin treatment works synergistically with adrenergic pressor
substances, primarily norepinephrine. Therapeutic restoration of blood
vasopressin levels in patients suﬀering from shock works primarily via
the vasopressin-1 receptor to cause vasoconstriction of most capillary
vessels, although the cerebral, renal, pulmonary, and mesenteric
vessels are spared with low-dose therapy. 148 , 149 A combination of
vasopressin and glucocorticoids may further increase survival. 150 Use

vetexamprep.ir

of vasopressin in dogs and cats is limited thus far, but preliminary
ﬁndings in dogs are promising. 151–153
Hypotensive animals that are most likely to beneﬁt from vasopressor
therapy include those with clinical evidence of peripheral vasodilation,
such as bright red mucous membranes, bounding pulses, and fast
CRTs. However, cats rarely exhibit these signs. Invasive or noninvasive
measurements of systemic vascular resistance can also guide the use of
vasopressor therapy but can be diﬃcult to measure in the clinical
se ing. Vasoconstricting drugs are often eﬀective at increasing arterial
blood pressure but may also result in excessive vasoconstriction to
some areas, particularly the splanchnic and/or renal circulation, which
may lead to GI and/or renal ischemia and dysfunction. Especially in
the septic canine patient, splanchnic vasoconstriction may exacerbate
the endotoxemia by compromising normal intestinal integrity and
enabling bacterial translocation into the bloodstream.
Positive inotropes such as dobutamine are generally used in septic
patients with evidence of impaired myocardial contractility (e.g.,
decreased fractional shortening on M-mode echocardiography,
decreased cardiac output on invasive or noninvasive measurements of
cardiac output). The β-agonist drug most commonly used for the
treatment of decreased systolic function is dobutamine, although
isoproterenol, epinephrine, and dopamine also have beta-adrenergic
activity. 148

Antimicrobial Use in Sepsis
The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines were updated in 2012,
2016, and 2021 and recommend the administration of broad-spectrum
antibacterial therapy within 1 hour of diagnosis of severe sepsis or
septic shock. 154 , 155 Timely localization of the septic focus and
procurement of infected tissue or ﬂuid for bacterial identiﬁcation and
determination of antibacterial susceptibility are of paramount
importance in the treatment of a septic patient. However, sample
collection may be impossible because of cardiopulmonary instability or
the presence of a coagulopathy in some patients. Pending culture and
susceptibility results, empiric antibacterial therapy should be selected
based on the following factors: antibacterial properties (bactericidal
versus static); the expected bacterial ﬂora in the aﬀected tissue; the
ability of the antibacterial to penetrate the infected tissue; recent
history of antibacterial use and considerations for resistance; and
source of infection (whether nosocomial or community-acquired).
Readers are referred to Chapters 8 and 10 for further details.
Appropriate empiric therapy is vital for success. Broad-spectrum
bactericidal antimicrobial agents are typically administered to septic
patients via the IV route. Adjustments are made pending availability of
antibacterial susceptibility testing results. Box 123.3 contains examples
of four-quadrant, empiric therapy (i.e., eﬀective against many grampositive and gram-negative aerobes and anaerobes). One study
highlighted the importance of appropriate antibacterial selection; in
ﬁve dogs in which inappropriate antibacterial drugs were empirically
administered, mortality was 80%. 16 Studies have failed to show an
association between appropriate antimicrobial use and mortality 156 ,
157 ; the complexity of management of septic patients warrants a
prospective study to deﬁne the impact of early appropriate
antimicrobial administration. Polymyxin B, an antibacterial which

vetexamprep.ir

binds to the lipid A subunit of endotoxin molecules, has been used in
the treatment of cats with experimental endotoxemia. 158 When
administered IV, at a rate of 1 mg/kg over 30 minutes, polymyxin B
reduced the plasma TNF activity and increased leukocyte counts with
no adverse eﬀect. Further studies in naturally aﬀected cats will be
helpful to determine its clinical eﬃcacy. Delaying administration of
antimicrobials or withholding their use in a septic patient increases the
ability of the organisms to reproduce, spread, and induce a greater
inﬂammatory response.

Gastrointestinal Protectants
The initial strategy to prevent GI complications in critically ill dogs
and cats is to ensure adequate GI perfusion and employ early enteral
nutrition. High-risk patients should receive pharmacologic
prophylaxis for stress-related GI hemorrhage. Based on the available
evidence in human medicine, it appears that proton pump inhibitors
(PPIs) are superior to histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs), which
are superior to sucralfate in the prevention of stress-related mucosal
disease in adult critical care patients. 159–161 Drugs available include
omeprazole (0.7–1.0 mg/kg, PO, q24h); pantoprazole (0.7–1.0 mg/kg,
IV, q12–24h); famotidine (0.5–1.0 mg/kg, IV, q12–24h); and sucralfate
(0.25–1 g/25 kg, PO, q6–8h). Lower doses of sucralfate (0.1–0.2 mg/kg)
have claimed equal eﬃcacy. 162

Additional Treatment Strategies for Sepsis
There have been a number of landmark studies in human medicine
regarding treatment strategies for sepsis over the past several years,
some of which have subsequently been called into question. Some

vetexamprep.ir

q
y
q
strategies, however, may also prove applicable to small animal
medicine, although further research is needed. These highly acclaimed
strategies include early goal-directed therapy to direct resuscitation
treatment of relative adrenal insuﬃciency, tight glycemic control,
neutralization of endotoxin, and physiologic anticoagulant therapy.
The beneﬁts of treatment of human patients with IV vitamin C and
thiamine in combination with hydrocortisone is also being studied. 163
This has occurred in response to evidence of low vitamin C and
thiamine concentrations in septic patients, and some initial evidence of
positive outcomes in initial human clinical trials.
Early goal-directed therapy was initially shown to decrease
mortality and severity of illness in humans with sepsis, although more
recent investigations have not conﬁrmed these earlier ﬁndings. 141 , 144 ,
164 Preliminary evidence suggests a beneﬁcial response in dogs treated
with goal-directed therapy. 165 This invasive approach uses multiple
criteria, including central venous oxygen saturation > 70%, central
venous pressure ≥ 8–12 mmHg, mean arterial pressure ≥ 65 mmHg,
urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/hour, oxygen saturation ≥ 93%, and
hematocrit ≥ 30%, as a rapid goal within the ﬁrst 6 hours of
hospitalization in humans. In an observational study, 166 38% of canine
shock patients had central venous oxygen saturation < 70% despite
normalization of blood pressure, HR, and physical parameters.
Although formal studies have not been performed in veterinary
patients, it seems reasonable to expect that a rapid correction of
hemodynamic and organ function indices would be beneﬁcial to the
animal. The use of central venous oxygen saturation monitoring in
animals is limited, primarily because of the expense of the equipment
required.
The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is crucial for host response
to infection. The early inﬂammatory response to sepsis stimulates
endogenous release of cortisol, which subsequently modulates the
synthesis and release of pro- and anti-inﬂammatory mediators to
restrict inﬂammation of infected tissues. The cause of critical illnessrelated corticosteroid insuﬃciency (CIRCI) 167 in septic patients
appears to be multifactorial, including factors such as vascular or
ischemic damage, inﬂammation, and apoptosis within the
hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; use of drugs that modify cortisol
metabolism; and/or tissue resistance to glucocorticoids. 168 , 169 CIRCI
may occur in up to 70% of people with sepsis and is correlated to
hypotension and death in these patients. Preliminary research in dogs,
cats, and foals suggests that a similar phenomenon also occurs with
critical illness in these species. 170–174 Sepsis-induced CIRCI in humans

vetexamprep.ir

is not easily diagnosed and a ma er of considerable controversy. 45
Some recommendations suggested that a diagnosis could be made by
identifying a basal cortisol less than 10 µg/dL or a change in cortisol
(delta cortisol) of less than 9 µg/dL after administration of ACTH.
Administration of ACTH to diagnose the syndrome is no longer
recommended, rather administration of hydrocortisone is
recommended in patients who have not responded to adequate ﬂuid
resuscitation and vasopressor therapy. 155 The use of physiologic doses
of hydrocortisone has been found to improve 28-day mortality rates
and decrease the duration of vasopressor therapy in septic humans
with a poor response to ACTH testing. 175 However, one systematic
review performed in 2013 found no clear beneﬁt of glucocorticoids on
mortality, although subgroup analysis of low-dose glucocorticoid use
is suggestive of a beneﬁcial drug eﬀect on short-term mortality,
particularly in more critically ill patients. 155 In contrast, a 2019 metaanalysis showed faster shock reversal, fewer vasopressor-dependent
days and decreased length of ICU stay, in addition to a reduced 28-day
mortality rate. In summary, although routine use of hydrocortisone in
adults with sepsis is still controversial, its use is recommended in adult
patients with septic shock who are poorly responsive to ﬂuid and
vasopressor therapy, as well as pediatric patients with suspected or
proven adrenal insuﬃciency. 153 , 176 , 177 The diagnosis and treatment
of CIRCI in veterinary medicine is also subject to controversy. 170 In
one study, critically ill dogs with a delta cortisol ≤ 83 nmol/L were
almost six times as likely to need vasopressor therapy. 174 Similar to
the Surviving Sepsis Guidelines for humans, 155 the use of
hydrocortisone should be limited to those veterinary patients in shock
who have not responded to adequate ﬂuid resuscitation and
vasopressor treatment, until further evidence provides more speciﬁc
recommendations.
Prevention of hyperglycemia in septic and critically ill patients has
been the focus of much research, and glycemic control was
recommended in the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Guidelines. 153 , 155 , 178–181
Although there are several etiologies for the elevated glucose in septic
animals, hepatic insulin resistance appears to play a major role. 181
Hyperglycemia may serve to potentiate the proinﬂammatory response
and cause endothelial and neutrophil dysfunction. 182 , 183 A decrease
in morbidity and mortality, as well as the incidence of sepsis, was
found when intensive insulin therapy was used to strictly regulate
glucose levels (e.g., >180 mg/dL) in critically ill humans. 155 , 184–187
Tight glycemic control (glucose < 110 mg/dL) is associated with an
increased prevalence of hypoglycemia. In a series of randomized

vetexamprep.ir

controlled studies, tight glycemic control was either associated with no
improvement or an increase in mortality and a high incidence of
hypoglycemia. 155 Current recommendations from the Surviving
Sepsis Guidelines are to maintain blood glucose ≤ 180 mg/dL. 155 There
are few studies concerning glucose monitoring in small animals, but
preliminary data show a similar trend. 188–191 Until there is more
evidence of a broad beneﬁt and institution of precise monitoring in
small animals, the risk of hypoglycemia likely outweighs the beneﬁt of
tight glucose control. Critically ill small animal patients may beneﬁt
from strategies to maintain their glucose between 80 and 180 mg/dL.
Directed therapy of sepsis has a empted to follow the advances in
our understanding of the cascade of inﬂammation. 192 The most
common and potent trigger of SIRS in sepsis is bacterial endotoxin.
Several strategies have been investigated to eliminate or neutralize
endotoxin. The list of promising agents included glucocorticoids, antiendotoxin antibodies, competitive inhibitors (e.g., lipid X), and natural
inhibitors (e.g., bactericidal permeability increasing protein). Despite
survival beneﬁts in experimental animals, none of these agents has
proven successful in human or veterinary (bactericidal permeability
increasing protein) trials. 193 , 194 One of the proposed reasons for the
failure of this strategy was that endotoxin is an early and transient
mediator that initiates the cascade of events in the host immune
response. Therefore, in the next wave of investigations, a ention was
directed toward the inﬂammatory cytokines and other later mediators.
Similar to the experience with endotoxin inhibition, inhibition of
cytokines and other individual inﬂammatory mediators has failed to
show beneﬁt and, in some cases, was detrimental. These circulating
mediators have been demonstrated in septic veterinary patients, but
there are no veterinary clinical trials investigating inhibition of these
compounds. Immune paralysis has been recognized in some patients
with sepsis. Immune stimulation using granulocyte colony-stimulating
factor in puppies with CPV was not beneﬁcial. 195 However,
investigations in experimental animals and clinical trials are ongoing.
Overall strategies targeting individual mediators of sepsis have failed.
The use of aPC therapy in humans with septic shock has received
much a ention over the past 10 years as it was the only directed
therapy that had shown any beneﬁt in human sepsis clinical trials. aPC
inhibits factor Va and factor VIIIa and has eﬀects on in vitro
coagulation, ﬁbrinolysis, and the immune system. Although initial
studies showed a decrease in mortality in patients with sepsis and
septic shock, subsequent trials failed to demonstrate a beneﬁt and the
drug was withdrawn from the market. 130 , 196 aCP was quite expensive

vetexamprep.ir

and associated with an increased risk of serious bleeding in humans;
the human formulation was known to have a short half-life and to be
antigenic in dogs and, therefore, was not well studied in small animals.

Novel Drugs With Potential for Benefit in Sepsis
Nitric Oxide
NO is an important molecule in vasoregulation and the immune
system. 197 In the endothelial cell, the enzyme responsible for NO
production (endothelial NO synthase) is constitutively expressed. In
the vascular system, NO is released at low levels and mediates
vascular smooth muscle relaxation and opposes the interactions
between endothelial cells and leukocytes. In the inﬂammatory
response, macrophages are responsible for generation of large
quantities (100-fold greater than the endothelial cells) of NO that are
important in bactericidal activity. Excessive production of NO leads to
tissue damage, particularly as a result of interactions with superoxide
and the formation of the highly reactive peroxynitrite. The eﬀects of
sepsis on NO synthesis are complex. Although NO is implicated as a
mediator of septic hypotension and cardiac depression (among other
things), global inhibition of NO has multiple adverse eﬀects and has
failed to demonstrate a beneﬁt in human clinical trials. 198
Statins
Statins have been used in the treatment and prevention of
atherosclerosis and lower serum lipids through the inhibition of 3hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase. These drugs also
aﬀect intracellular signaling, including NF-κB activation, in the
inﬂammatory response. The anti-inﬂammatory eﬀects of statins have
been documented on both innate and acquired immunity, the
coagulation system (promoting an anticoagulant state and enhancing
the synthesis of aCP), and the vascular endothelium (improving
endothelial function and normalizing NO production). Despite
evidence from experimental studies and a meta-analysis of the
observational studies, 199–201 two published randomized controlled
trials evaluating statins in patients with ARDS 202 , 203 failed to
demonstrate a beneﬁt of treatment.
Toll-Like Receptor Antagonists
The a empt to intervene in the response to endotoxin has not proven
beneﬁcial in the past through anti-endotoxin antibodies, soluble CD14
(which conversely increased the inﬂammatory response), or through

vetexamprep.ir

LPS-binding agents (BPI). Another target of the endotoxin pathway
has been the TLR4 receptor. In a phase II clinical trial, one TLR4
antagonist did not show any more adverse events than the placebo and
overall did not change mortality. In a phase III multinational study of
1,961 patients with severe sepsis, treatment with a TLR4 antagonist
failed to demonstrate an eﬀect on mortality. 204 Targeting TLR
pathways continues to be an area of investigation for treatment of
sepsis. 205 , 206
High Mortality Group Box 1
HMGB1 is a nuclear protein that has been shown to be a late
biomarker in sepsis. Serum levels of HMGB1 are measurable in mouse
models of sepsis/endotoxemia within 8 hours and remain elevated for
up to 32 hours. 29 , 207 In addition to its value as a biomarker, it appears
that HMGB1 mediates part of the inﬂammatory response, thus making
it a potential target for therapy. Antibodies to HMGB1 were protective
in a mouse model of sepsis, even when they were administered 24
hours after the onset of sepsis. 207 Several agents have been shown to
modify HMGB1 activity or release and these include anticoagulant
agents (i.e., AT, thrombomodulin), endogenous hormones (i.e., insulin,
vasoactive intestinal peptide, ghrelin), vagus nerve stimulation, green
tea, the Chinese herb danshen, and ethyl pyruvate. Despite promising
experimental studies, there are no clinical trials documenting the
beneﬁt of HMGB1 inhibition in patients with sepsis. 29 , 208 , 209
Nuclear Factor-κB Inhibitors
Although NF-κB is a major transcription factor involved in the
inﬂammatory response, it is also vital in several other pathways
including the anti-inﬂammatory response and antiapoptotic pathways.
Several compounds known to inﬂuence NF-κB signaling have failed
clinical trials, (e.g., glucocorticoids, NSAIDs, antioxidants). These
drugs have numerous other eﬀects, and potentially improved
speciﬁcity and selective timing of administration will still have a role
in the future of sepsis therapy. 209
Individualized Approach
One concept that arises from the PIRO scheme (see Table 123.4) is that
each patient may require tailored therapy based on predisposition,
age, sex, genetic background, and, in the case of veterinary patients,
species and breed. Furthermore, the type and location of infection
inﬂuence how a patient is treated. This approach is employed in
antibacterial selection, but as additional information accumulates, it

vetexamprep.ir

may also guide speciﬁc treatment that enhances or downregulates
speciﬁc signaling pathways. Deﬁning the host response as monitored
by biomarkers is becoming more commonplace and has great potential
to identify patients that could beneﬁt from either suppression or
enhancement of the host immune response depending on whether the
patient was in a state of hyperinﬂammation or immune paralysis. The
ﬁnal component of PIRO is organ failure. One of the few advances in
treating septic patients has come from implementing “protective
ventilation” strategies in which low (6 mL/kg) tidal volume mechanical
ventilation is used in patients with ARDS. Individualizing treatments
and multimodal approaches are likely to be important in sepsis, given
the heterogeneity in the patients and the inciting cause and the
dynamic nature of response to sepsis. 209

Prognosis
Most dogs suﬀering from sepsis have a guarded prognosis. The
published survival rate in dogs and cats with sepsis is 33% to 68%,
respectively, and survival in animals with septic shock is worse. 15 , 168 ,
210 , 211 Mortality rate increases as the number of dysfunctional organ
systems increases. 7 In septic peritonitis, this survival rate does not
seem to have improved over the past 20 years despite improvements in
critical care management. 14 To maximize success, appropriate
diagnostics as well as timely and aggressive therapeutic support are
necessary. Future studies in veterinary medicine will likely focus on
novel diagnostic modalities as well as superior treatment options.

Case Example
Signalment

“Opal,” a 9-year-old, female spayed Siamese cat from Philadelphia,
PA.

History

Opal’s owner reported a 1-week history of fever, lethargy, and
anorexia. There had been no vomiting, diarrhea, coughing, or
sneezing. Two months prior to evaluation, the owner noticed that
the cat was drinking and urinating more than usual for 1 week, but
this resolved without treatment. Opal was an indoor-only cat with
no travel history and was up to date on all vaccinations. Opal was
not on ﬂea, tick, or heartworm preventative. Opal received no

vetexamprep.ir

medications and had no prior medical history. She ate a commercial
cat food and there was no recent diet change.

Physical Examination

Body weight: 3.4 kg.
General: Quiet, alert, and responsive. Ambulatory on all four
limbs. Temperature = 104.1°F (40.1°C), HR = 140 beats/minute,
RR = 52 breaths/minute, mucous membranes pale and dry,
CRT = 1.5 second.
Integument: A full, mildly dry haircoat was present and there
was no evidence of ectoparasites.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: No signiﬁcant abnormalities were
noted. There was intermi ent ptyalism and a mild amount of
brown waxy debris in both ear canals.
Musculoskeletal: A BCS of 4/9 with symmetrical muscling was
noted.

Cardiovascular: Weak femoral pulses were noted. No
murmurs or arrhythmias were detected on thoracic

Respiratory: An increased RR was observed and there were
clear breath sounds in all lung ﬁelds on auscultation.
GI and genitourinary: The cranial abdomen was tense with
abdominal splinting upon abdominal palpation. No masses
were palpated, although the liver and kidneys were
subjectively enlarged. A rectal examination was not
performed.
Lymph nodes: All peripheral lymph nodes were < 0.5 cm.
Doppler BP: 60 mmHg (120–160 mmHg)

Laboratory Findings
CBC: HCT 31.0% (31.7%–48.0%), MCV 51.2 fL (36.7–53.7 fL),
MCHC 31.1 g/dL (30.1–35.6 g/dL), WBC 13.9 × 103 cells/µL

platelets/µL (175,000–500,000 platelets/µL). A clinical
pathologist reviewed the slide and noted moderate toxic
changes in many WBCs. Bacterial rods were noted
infrequently within neutrophils (Fig. 123.4) and rarely
extracellularly.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Sodium 149 mmol/L (146–157

magnesium 3.3 mg/dL (1.9–2.6 mg/dL).
Urinalysis: SpG 1.024; pH 7.0, 3+ protein (SSA), 2+ glucose, no
ketones, no bilirubin, 4+ hemoprotein, 31–40 WBC/HPF, 0–5
RBC/HPF, mild epithelial cells, moderate bacterial rods.
Urine culture: >100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli, susceptible to

Blood culture and susceptibility testing: Escherichia coli
resistant to ampicillin with or without clavulanate or

vetexamprep.ir

sulbactam.
SNAP FeLV/ FIV ELISA antigen/antibody (IDEXX
Laboratories): Negative.

Imaging Findings
Thoracic radiographs: The cardiovascular and pulmonary
structures appeared within normal limits.
Abdominal ultrasound: There was a small amount of sludge in
the gallbladder. The right kidney was enlarged (47.4 mm long)
with pyelectasia (3.9mm). Mild to moderate retroperitoneal
eﬀusion with perirenal steatitis and renal mineralization were
present. The right ureter was dilated throughout its length
(proximal: 3.5 mm in diameter; mid: 3.6 mm; distal: 4.2 mm)
with a thickened wall. Within the ureter at the ureterovesicular
junction there was a 2.0-mm calculus. The left kidney had
decreased corticomedullary deﬁnition with hyperechoic
speckling throughout the medullary cavity. Several calculi
were within the renal pelvis (largest 3.9 mm in length). The
left lobe of the pancreas was mildly heterogeneous with
hyperechoic foci throughout, and there was a mild rim of
hyperechoic surrounding fat. Very scant free peritoneal
eﬀusion was seen.

Treatment

Aggressive ﬂuid therapy was instituted due to the hypotension.
Despite 30 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid ﬂuids administered over 45
minutes, blood pressure only increased to 85 mmHg.
Norepinephrine was administered at 0.1–0.5 µg/kg/minute as an IV
infusion as needed to keep Doppler BP ≥ 100 mmHg. A vasopressin
infusion was also necessary to maintain normotension (0.5–0.8
mU/kg/hour). An isotonic ﬂuid infusion was administered at 4
mL/kg/hour. Clindamycin (10 mg/kg, IV, q12h) and ceftazidime (40
mg/kg, IV, q6h) were administered pending blood and urine culture
results. Clindamycin was discontinued after 72 hours when
susceptibility testing from the cultures was completed.
Opal developed clinically signiﬁcant anemia and became
coagulopathic based on a prolonged PT and APTT. Packed RBCs (15
mL/kg) and fresh frozen plasma were administered. Vitamin K1 was
also administered (1 mg/kg, SC, q24h). Treatment with
gastroprotectants, including pantoprazole (1 mg/kg, IV, q 24h) and
maropitant (1 mg/kg, IV, q24h), were also started. Analgesia with

vetexamprep.ir

methadone (0.1–0.2 mg/kg, IV, q4h) was initially used for pain
control. This was later switched to a fentanyl infusion for
management of continued discomfort (2–4 µg/kg/hour IV). A repeat
ultrasound 1 and 2 days following initial evaluation revealed that
the ureteral calculus had passed into the urinary bladder. Surgery
was therefore not necessary.

Comments

This cat had several abnormalities that are common in cats with
sepsis. Although this species does not get the classic hyperdynamic
physical examination changes, as typically seen in dogs, the
presence of an increased rectal temperature, bradycardia, and
tachypnea represents a SIRS. The additional ﬁndings of pale mucous
membranes, poor femoral pulse quality, hypotension, mildly
increased bilirubin, toxicity and a left shift on the CBC, and the
presence of bacteria in the intracellular and extracellular space upon
blood smear evaluation all raise the suspicion for sepsis. Multiple
organ dysfunction, as evidenced by vasoplegia and coagulopathy, is
common and frequently involves additional organs such as the
heart, lungs, GI tract, liver, and kidneys. The need for vasopressor
therapy following ﬂuid resuscitation indicates the cat was suﬀering
from septic shock. Aggressive, rapid, and empiric therapy pending
culture and susceptibility led to a successful outcome in this cat.

KEY POINTS
Bacterial Tracheobronchitis and Pneumonia
• Causes: Primary bacterial pathogens include Bordetella
bronchiseptica and Mycoplasma spp. A wide variety of
secondary bacterial pathogens can also be implicated
including anaerobes, Escherichia coli, Pasteurella spp.,
Staphylococcus spp., and Streptococcus spp.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Community acquired (contagious) or
secondary to aspiration or impaired local or systemic immune
defenses.
• Major Clinical Signs: Cough, nasal discharge, sneeze,
tachypnea, respiratory distress, cyanosis, and systemic signs
of illness (lethargy, anorexia, fever).
• Differential Diagnoses: Differentials for bacterial
tracheobronchitis include other nonbacterial infectious airway
disorders (primarily viral and parasitic), noninfectious
inflammatory airway disease, and structural airway disorders;
differentials for bacterial pneumonia include other infectious
pneumonia (viral [especially CDV infection], fungal, parasitic,
protozoal), noninfectious inflammatory pneumonia (sterile
aspiration pneumonia and foreign body pneumonia),
neoplasia, interstitial lung disease, cardiogenic or
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, pulmonary vascular
disease, and hemorrhage.

vetexamprep.ir

• Human Health Significance: Bordetella bronchiseptica can
cause disease in immunocompromised humans. While further
study is needed, MDR bacteria colonizing the canine and
feline respiratory tract may be able to colonize humans.
Bacterial Pyothorax
• Causes: Pyothorax is often polymicrobial. Anaerobic bacteria
and mixtures of anaerobic and facultative aerobic bacteria are
common in both dogs and cats. Although more often cultured
from the pleural fluid of cats, Pasteurella is also implicated in
both species.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Primary Mode of Transmission: Direct inoculation of the
pleural cavity (e.g., migrating foreign material, bite wounds,
trauma), extension of local infection (e.g., pneumonia, lung
abscess, thoracic wall infection), hematogenous spread.
• Major Clinical Signs: Restrictive respiratory pattern (rapid,
shallow respiration with increased inspiratory effort),
obtundation, exercise intolerance, cough, lethargy, anorexia,
weight loss, and fever. Cats may exhibit hypothermia,
bradycardia, and hypersalivation.
• Differential Diagnoses: Other nonbacterial infections that can
be associated with pleural effusion (e.g., Aspergillus spp.),
chylothorax, hemothorax, neoplasia, FIP (cats).
• Human Health Significance: Because commensal organisms
of the oral cavity and upper respiratory tract are most typically
associated with pyothorax in dogs and cats, pyothorax does
not have human health significance.

Bacterial Tracheobronchitis and Pneumonia
Etiology, Epidemiology, and Pathogenesis
There is a continuum between the conducting airways and
pulmonary parenchyma without a physical barrier separating the
respiratory tract from the external environment. In healthy dogs,
cultivable bacteria have been identiﬁed from the upper airways,
lower airways, and thoracotomy-derived pulmonary parenchyma,
with the assumption that bacteria identiﬁed in the lung were

vetexamprep.ir

p
g
transient populations derived from the pharynx due to aspiration.
1 In cats, an analogous study with culture of lung tissue has not
been performed, but healthy cats similarly have cultivable bacteria
from their upper and lower airways.
Common bacterial isolates have been obtained from nasal
swabs (Table 124.1) and airway lavage specimens (Table 124.2) of
clinically healthy dogs and cats. In one study, bacterial isolates
from the trachea in healthy dogs included Streptococcus spp.,
Staphylococcus spp., Pasteurella multocida, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and
Corynebacterium spp.; when considering simultaneous positive
cultures from the pharynx and trachea, in 80% of dogs, the same
organism found in the trachea was identiﬁed in the pharynx. 2
These results underscore the fact that presence of bacteria
cultured from the respiratory tract does not equate with infection;
healthy dogs and cats have an abundance of respiratory
commensal organisms. Respiratory disease may occur due to a
shift in abundance of one or more commensal species to create
inﬂammation and damage to tissue. Certain bacteria considered to
be contagious may also exist as part of the respiratory
microbiome, including Bordetella bronchiseptica, Mycoplasma spp.,
and some Streptococcus strains. Bacterial respiratory tract
infections may also originate from primary pathogens in the
environment and/or reservoir hosts such as Nocardia spp.,
Mycobacterium spp., or Yersinia spp.
Complimentary techniques to standard laboratory-based
cultures have provided a wealth of information on resident
complex microbial populations in the respiratory tract. Using
next-generation sequencing of microbial DNA, healthy dogs have
been shown to harbor a rich and diverse respiratory microbiota. 3–
5 While bacterial communities from the upper and lower airways
are topographically continuous, sharing many bacterial species,
there are distinct diﬀerences between sites suggesting each
possesses unique resident communities, and lower airway
populations are not solely a reﬂection of aspirated upper airway
bacteria. 3 Healthy cats evaluated over time demonstrated a rich
lower airway microbiome with dynamic respiratory bacterial
populations. 6 The microbiome of the feline nasal cavity has also
been examined, and was shown to display a high degree of
individual variability; the most prevalent species in healthy cats

vetexamprep.ir

and cats with URTD was Moraxella spp. 7 Use of DNA-based
sequencing to characterize resident bacterial populations may
provide insight to interpretation of microbial cultures as well as
aid in an understanding of the impact of the respiratory
microbiome on health and disease. Similar to GI dysbiosis in
which disruption of the normally dominating species and
imbalances of other minority species has been associated with a
variety of local and systemic illnesses, respiratory dysbiosis has
been identiﬁed in dogs and cats with inﬂammatory airway disease
8 , 9 and dogs treated with antimicrobial drugs. 5 Understanding
deviations from a healthy respiratory microbiome is relevant to
tracheobronchial and pulmonary bacterial infections and is a ﬁeld
that is still in its infancy.

Identiﬁcation of bacteria solely using routine cultures is not
synonymous with bacterial infection. A positive culture needs to
be interpreted in light of clinical signs, evidence of concurrent
suppurative inﬂammation ideally with intracellular bacteria, and
bacterial growth conditions (e.g., heavy growth, single species). In
general, the host eﬀectively prevents bacterial respiratory
infections by physical and chemical barriers and the innate and
adaptive immune system. Traditionally, bacterial infection of the

vetexamprep.ir

airways or pulmonary parenchyma has been thought to result
secondary to inhalation of primary respiratory pathogens
(aerosols or direct oronasal contact), macro- or microaspiration,
compromised respiratory defenses, direct extension (e.g.,
migrating foreign body, penetrating wound, bronchoesophageal
ﬁstula), or hematogenous spread. Additional research is needed to
determine the role of dysbiosis in bacterial tracheobronchitis and
pneumonia when co-morbid respiratory disorders alter the local
microenvironment.

Bacterial tracheobronchitis and pneumonia are two separate
disease syndromes that can share routes of exposure (and thus
types of infecting bacteria) as well as predisposing factors of

vetexamprep.ir

susceptibility. Both conditions can be acute or chronic and
primary or secondary.
Primary bacterial tracheobronchitis in immunocompetent dogs
(i.e., community-acquired CIRD complex; the reader is referred to
Chapter 28 for more details) is generally self-limiting with
supportive care. Primary bacterial tracheobronchitis in cats is rare,
with very common upper respiratory tract infections nearly
always causing nasal and ocular but not tracheobronchial
pathology. Unlike in dogs where B. bronchiseptica is often
considered a highly contagious primary pathogen, B.
bronchiseptica can be found in healthy cats and in cats without
cough (with or without upper respiratory tract infections) housed
in shelters with canine outbreaks. 10 , 11 Mycoplasma species are
considered normal commensals of the upper respiratory tract and
have the potential to be opportunistic invaders. A empts to
isolate Mycoplasma spp. from the lower airway of clinically
healthy cats have not been successful, 12 , 13 but they are typically
associated with concurrent airway disease suggesting that they
are most likely opportunistic invaders. Their role as a primary
pathogen causing bronchitis is still unclear (see Suggested
Reading list for more information). 14 (Editor’s note: In 2021, a
novel bacterial species belonging to the genus Filobacterium was
reported in association with chronic neutrophilic bronchitis in cats
from Europe and Australia. 15 The name Filobacterium felis was
proposed; a related organism, Filobacterium rodentium (previously
cilia-associated respiratory bacillus [CARB]) is considered a
primary pathogen of rodents. The existence of similar organisms
has been described in cats with and without respiratory disease
from the United States. 16 , 17
Secondary bacterial tracheobronchitis is usually associated with
inﬂammatory or structural airway disease of the dog and cat and
can be responsible for clinical disease exacerbation. Bacterial
tracheobronchitis has been reported secondary to airway collapse,
18 , 19 chronic bronchitis, eosinophilic bronchitis/eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy, bronchiectasis, or bronchomalacia in dogs.
In cats, reports of positive bacterial cultures have been linked to
airway disease including asthma, chronic bronchitis, and
bronchiectasis. Bacterial tracheobronchitis that is associated with
bacterial species that are not “community-acquired” should

vetexamprep.ir

prompt a search for an underlying disorder. It is reiterated that
identifying cultivable bacteria does not necessarily imply active
infection.
