Dogs
Tracheal Collapse (Fig. 124.1A)
While bacteria can be frequently cultured from specimens
collected from the trachea in dogs with tracheal collapse, the
absence of concurrent evidence of inﬂammation or intracellular
bacteria makes diagnosis of secondary bacterial infections

vetexamprep.ir

unlikely in most cases. 19 The prevalence of positive bacterial
cultures of dogs with tracheal collapse decreased in one study
after tracheal stent placement. 20
Chronic Bronchitis
Chronic bronchitis is classically associated with cough, mucus
hypersecretion, and neutrophilic airway inﬂammation. 21 Chronic
bronchitis is considered a sterile process that occurs secondary to
airway epithelial damage and impaired mucociliary function.
While dogs with chronic bronchitis have impaired mucosal
defense and can theoretically be predisposed to infection,
infection appears uncommon especially when quantitative, not
qualitative cultures are performed. 22 Qualitative cultures using
the threshold of > 1.7 × 103 CFU/mL of BAL ﬂuid are proposed to
represent clinically relevant bacterial growth. Unlike qualitative
cultures, quantitative cultures take into consideration the
possibility of contamination from upper airways and/or
microaspiration (subclinical aspiration of upper GI secretions)
without true infection.
Eosinophilic Bronchopneumopathy
Eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy has been associated with
positive BAL cultures (albeit qualitative) including growth of
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, and Aeromonas spp., among
others. 23 As eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy can be associated
with bronchiectasis, it is unclear if the aforementioned identiﬁed
bacteria were a sequela to eosinophilic inﬂammation and/or
bronchiectasis. Another study of 75 dogs with eosinophilic
inﬂammation
in
BAL
ﬂuid
(due
to
eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy, eosinophilic bronchitis, or eosinophilic
pneumonia) reported bacterial growth in BAL cultures rarely;
only three dogs had positive culture results (Pasteurella spp.,
Pasteurella canis, and mixed growth of Escherichia coli and
Streptococcus spp.). 24
Bronchiectasis (Fig. 124.1B)
Bronchiectasis may be a consequence of primary ciliary
dyskinesia, chronic bronchitis, infectious pneumonia, eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy, and tracheal collapse. 24–28 Bronchiectasis

vetexamprep.ir

can also predispose to recurrent bacterial infection because of
poor clearance of mucus and exudate in the distal airways and
impaired local immune responses. This in turn creates a vicious
cycle of inﬂammation, secondary infection, and further airway
damage. In one study of dogs with bronchiectasis, bacterial
growth from airway lavage specimens was frequent (17/18 dogs)
with a variety of bacterial species isolated as either alone (7 dogs)
or as part of polymicrobial infections (10 dogs). 26 In another
study, bacteria (predominantly Streptococcus spp., Pasteurella spp.,
enterics, and Stenotrophomonas maltophila) were isolated in 24/86
dogs (28%) with bronchiectasis. 27
Bronchomalacia (Fig. 124.1C)
In bronchomalacia, weakened bronchial walls, with associated
static or dynamic reduction of airway diameters results in clinical
signs of cough, wheeze, and respiratory distress. In one study,
intracellular bacteria were noted on cytologic examination of BAL
specimens in 25/45 dogs with bronchomalacia; cultures were not
performed. 29 Another study documented intra- and extracellular
bacteria in 39% of specimens, with cultures yielding one isolate in
62% and two isolates in 39% of specimens. 30 The most common
isolates were B. bronchiseptica, Alcaligenes spp., Pasteurella spp., and
Bacillus spp. Dogs that had bronchoscopic evaluation for other
causes of cough that had concurrent tracheal and bronchial
collapse were less likely to have bacterial infection than dogs
without evidence of airway collapse. 31
Bacterial Pneumonia
Bacterial pneumonia generally arises due to local or systemic
immune compromise and can be life-threatening. Primary
bacterial pneumonia caused by B. bronchiseptica, virulent strains of
Streptococcus spp., and possibly Mycoplasma (particularly
Mycoplasma cynos) tends to occur most frequently in dogs under a
year of age, and dogs with immune defects (overexuberant or
insuﬃcient immune responses), concurrent respiratory infections,
or those in stressful or overcrowded environments. 32–34 Dogs
with a variety of predisposing factors including dysphagia,
regurgitation, gastroesophageal reﬂux, vomiting, diminished
consciousness (secondary to drugs including anesthesia, or

vetexamprep.ir

neurologic disease), and impaired airway defenses (e.g.,
brachycephalic airway syndrome) can develop aspiration
pneumonia. 35–41 Aerodigestive disorders often go unrecognized
because aspiration pneumonia can develop in the absence of GI
signs. 42
Aspiration pneumonia is not synonymous with bacterial
infection, as a sterile chemical pneumonitis may occur. Commonly
identiﬁed bacteria from dogs with aspiration pneumonia include
E. coli, Mycoplasma spp., Pasteurella spp., Staphylococcus spp.,
Klebsiella spp., and Enterococcus spp. 38 Impaired airway defenses
can also cause pneumonia even in the absence of aspiration, and
these disorders can be congenital or acquired. 43 Direct extension
of bacterial infection to the parenchyma can occur from inhaled 35
or migrating foreign bodies. 39 , 44 , 45 The most common isolates
from dogs with foreign bodies include anaerobes, Pasteurella spp.,
Streptococcus spp., and Actinomyces spp. 46 Often foreign bodies
are inhaled into caudodorsal principle bronchi; in other words the
accessory, right, and left caudal bronchi.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia represents a type of
nosocomial infection that is hospital-acquired. 39 Patients
requiring mechanical ventilation have a diﬀerent spectrum of
bacterial isolates from airway cultures when compared with other
patients with respiratory disease; these isolates are more likely to
be resistant to the common antimicrobials used to treat patients
with pneumonia. 47
Cats
Chronic Bronchitis
In cats, secondary bacterial bronchitis is far less common than
noninfectious inﬂammatory airway disease. Importantly,
quantitative tracheobronchial lavage cultures in healthy cats were
positive in 8 of 24 cats in one study 12 and 10 of 13 (77%) in
another. 10 In the la er study, cultures yielded 100–100,000
CFU/mL, and organisms such as Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus
spp., B. bronchiseptica, and P. multocida were identiﬁed. In that
same study, 42% of cats with bronchopulmonary disease (i.e.,
asthma and chronic bronchitis) had positive cultures, mostly
yielding low numbers of bacteria. 10 Positive cultures for

vetexamprep.ir

Mycoplasma species were not identiﬁed in the ﬁrst study or
performed in the second, but are of interest as in human asthma,
mycoplasmas are postulated to contribute to induction of and
exacerbation of disease. In a more recent study, Mycoplasma spp.
were detected in BAL ﬂuid from 6 of 17 cats with asthma/chronic
bronchitis and 4 of 9 sick cats without respiratory disease, which
was not a signiﬁcant diﬀerence. 48 Overall, bacterial bronchitis
(without involvement of the pulmonary parenchyma) in cats is
rare, with 1/245 cats with necropsy-conﬁrmed lower respiratory
tract infection a ributed to bronchitis alone. 49
Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis in cats has been associated with inﬂammatory
airway disease, pneumonia, and neoplasia. 50–53 Radiographic
evidence of bronchiectasis was noted in 43% of cats with
aspiration pneumonia, inﬂammatory airway disease, and
bronchopneumonia in one study. 53 It has also been reported in
cats with bronchial dysgenesis, presumptive primary ciliary
dyskinesia, and broncholithiasis. 54–56 Bronchiectasis is rarely
described in cats when compared with dogs, with too few positive
cultures to reliably report common bacterial species that act as
secondary invaders. 50
Bacterial Pneumonia
Bacterial pneumonia is rare in the cat. Even when present, it may
be diﬃcult to identify as some cats may lack clinical signs,
inﬂammatory leukograms, or classic radiographic lesions. 57
Bacteria often gain access to the respiratory tract through a
hematogenous route, including from the GI tract, uterus,
umbilicus, gingiva, and bite wounds. 57 Other reported routes
include inhalation (aspiration or from inhaling airborne bacteria)
and local extension. 53 , 57 Although an uncommon condition in
the cat compared with the dog, approximately one third of cats
treated for laryngeal paralysis with bilateral arytenoid
lateralization developed aspiration pneumonia. 58 The most
common underlying conditions in cats with aspiration pneumonia
in another study from a tertiary referral institution were
megaesophagus, esophageal stricture, esophageal dysmotility,
and acute or chronic vomiting; 27% had a recent history of general

vetexamprep.ir

anesthesia. 53 Mycoplasmas, Pasteurella spp., Streptococcus spp.,
and anaerobes represented the most common bacterial isolates
from airway lavage specimens from cats with bronchopneumonia.
53 In contrast, mycoplasmas were not isolated from cats with
aspiration pneumonia; cultures from these cats yielded aerobic
gram-positive or gram-negative bacteria and/or anaerobes.

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs and Physical Examination Findings
Dogs with primary or secondary bacterial bronchitis may show no
signs, or have respiratory signs, generally cough. Contagious
causes of tracheobronchitis may be associated with involvement
of other parts of the respiratory tract, thus additional clinical signs
referable to those sites may be noted (e.g., sneezing or nasal
discharge, see Chapter 28). Dogs with secondary bacterial
bronchitis may have clinical signs associated with an underlying
disorder, for example, stridor or wheeze with airway collapse.
Secondary infection should be suspected in stable patients with
chronic tracheobronchial disorders that suddenly develop signs of
disease exacerbation.
If systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or inappetence are
present, this should prompt search for pneumonia or another comorbid respiratory condition as systemic signs are rarely seen in
dogs with bacterial bronchitis. There should be a high index of
suspicion for CDV infection in young dogs that develop these
signs. Canine bacterial pneumonia may be associated with local
signs such as nasal discharge, cough, tachypnea, adventitial lung
sounds, decreased lung sounds in regions of consolidation,
exercise intolerance, respiratory distress (mixed inspiratory and
expiratory distress), and cyanosis; additionally, systemic signs can
be seen such as fever, anorexia, lethargy, dehydration, weakness,
and weight loss. 38 , 39 , 59 Some animals with pneumonia show no
signs or only a few of these signs. Hemoptysis is rare but reported
in dogs. 60 Other clinical signs may reﬂect an underlying illness,
for example, vomiting or regurgitation in the case of aspiration
pneumonia. 38
As mentioned above, there is controversy about the role of B.
bronchiseptica and Mycoplasma spp. in feline tracheobronchitis as
these organisms can be isolated from many clinically healthy cats

vetexamprep.ir

that lack respiratory signs (see Chapters 55 and 57). 48 Cats with
secondary bronchial infection may be subclinically infected or
have clinical signs (usually cough; sometimes wheeze, tachypnea,
and respiratory distress) relative to their underlying inﬂammatory
airway disease or bronchiectasis. 10 , 48 , 50 Many owners do not
recognize cough in cats, confusing it with “hacking” up hairballs
or retching. Cats with aspiration pneumonia may show only
systemic signs of illness such as fever, lethargy, and/or
inappetence. In contrast to dogs, cats with pneumonia often lack
clinical respiratory signs, especially cough. In one retrospective
study, cough was signiﬁcantly more common in cats with
bacterial pneumonia (25/26 cats, 96%) or inﬂammatory airway
disease (30/44 cats, 68%) than in cats with aspiration pneumonia
(8/33 cats, 24%). In another study of cats with fatal infectious
pneumonia (of which 54% were bacterial), 36% lacked clinical
signs referable to the respiratory tract. 57 Of the cats displaying
respiratory signs, tachypnea or respiratory distress and nasal
discharge were most common; cough was present in only 8% of
cats. Systemic signs of illness (anorexia, lethargy, and fever) were
absent in 41% of these cats despite histopathologic evidence of
systemic infection in 74% of cats. A high index of suspicion for
pneumonia is required in cats, especially if evidence of infection
exists in other organs. In a review of 21 cases of lower respiratory
tract infection in cats that were not all fatal, signs were chronic
cough (11), acute cough (6), respiratory distress (2), anorexia (1),
and neurologic signs (1). 61

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of bacterial tracheobronchitis or pneumonia is
made based on a combination of historical information (e.g.,
exposure to contagious pathogens, underlying co-morbid
respiratory conditions or disorders predisposing to aspiration,
etc.), clinical signs, radiographic ﬁndings and ideally ﬁndings on
cytologic examination of respiratory specimens (suppurative
inﬂammation with extra- or intracellular bacteria), and a positive
culture. With the exception of the transtracheal wash and FNA,
collection of respiratory specimens is performed under general
anesthesia. A step-wise approach should be taken: functional
laryngeal examination using doxapram to stimulate deep

vetexamprep.ir

respiration, thorough oropharyngeal examination (including
sweeping the tonsillar crypts for foreign material), CT imaging (if
indicated), endoscopic examination of the trachea and bronchi (if
indicated), collection of respiratory specimens for cytology and
culture, and choanal examination (retroﬂexed view using an
endoscope). Before anesthesia, there are a wide variety of
minimally invasive respiratory diagnostics that can help deﬁne
underlying or concurrent conditions and gauge severity, extent,
and cause of infection (discussed below).
Laboratory Findings
Complete Blood Count, Serum Biochemical Profile, and
Urinalysis
Although not speciﬁc to the respiratory system, the minimum
database, including a CBC, serum biochemical proﬁle, and
urinalysis, can provide useful information regarding systemic
health. Especially in the case of bacterial pneumonia, a systemic
response to infection or organ dysfunction may be detected. Dogs
and cats with bacterial pneumonia can have normal or abnormal
leukograms. 38 , 39 , 57 , 59 Abnormalities include a neutrophilia
with a left shift or neutropenia. Peripheral eosinophilia may be
present in dogs with eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy 23 , 24 or
cats with asthma. 62 Because bacterial pneumonia can result from
hematogenous spread of bacterial infection originating elsewhere
in the body, sepsis and multiple organ dysfunction can contribute
to morbidity and mortality, making a serum biochemical proﬁle
and urinalysis useful to determine the extent of disease. They may
also reﬂect an underlying disorder associated with impaired
immune function (e.g., endocrinopathy). 43
Diagnostic Tests for Pathogens Other Than Bacteria
Other infectious agents aﬀecting the respiratory tract should be
considered in the diﬀerential diagnosis (viruses such as CDV,
atypical bacteria, protozoa such as Toxoplasma gondii, fungi, and
parasites), with diagnostic tests selected based on the history
(geographic location, season, length of illness, other systemic
signs), minimum database (e.g., presence of thrombocytopenia),
and physical examination ﬁndings. Tests may include fecal
analysis (fecal ﬂotation or Baermann analysis for parasites) or

vetexamprep.ir

y
y
p
blood or urine testing (e.g., serology for antibodies to Leptospira, T.
gondii; parasite or fungal antigen testing).
Assessment of Oxygenation and Ventilatory Status
Arterial blood gas analysis is useful to determine the severity of
respiratory compromise as it can provide information on gas
exchange and acid-base balance which can be disrupted with
bacterial respiratory disease (in particular pneumonia).
Hypoxemia (PaO2 ≤ 80 mmHg at sea level) can be detected in
roughly three quarters of dogs with aspiration pneumonia that
have arterial blood gases measured. 38 , 59 Hypocapnia or
hypercapnia has also been described. 59 The alveolar-arterial (A-a)
oxygen gradient can be increased; values > 15 mmHg indicate
lung dysfunction. 38 Serial use of arterial blood gas measurements
can help to determine what treatment to use (e.g., supplemental
oxygen, mechanical ventilation) as well as provide information on
response to treatment. Pulse oximetry is a simple, rapid, widely
available, and noninvasive indicator of oxygen status, but is
relatively insensitive and does not provide information on
ventilatory or acid-base status. In patients receiving mechanical
ventilation, capnography can provide information about
ventilatory status.
Diagnostic Imaging
Radiography, ﬂuoroscopy, ultrasonography, and CT have been
used to image the respiratory tract. Each have distinct advantages
and disadvantages.
Plain Radiography
Thoracic and possibly cervical radiography should be performed
ﬁrst, with a minimum of two views (lateral and ventrodorsal or
dorsoventral); however, both right and left lateral views are
recommended because diﬀerential aeration that results from
positional atelectasis can improve or impair visualization of
lesions. 39 Static airway collapse may be appreciated with
standard views (Fig. 124.2), however, inspiratory and expiratory
cervical and thoracic radiographs aid in diagnosis of dynamic
tracheal or mainstem bronchial collapse. Thoracic radiography
may demonstrate bronchial or bronchointerstitial pa erns with

vetexamprep.ir

chronic bronchitis, eosinophilic bronchitis (Fig. 124.3), or feline
asthma, with hyperinﬂation and/or lobar atelectasis in the la er
condition. 62 , 63 Radiographic ﬁndings in eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy in dogs include a bronchial or
bronchointerstitial pa ern or an alveolar pa ern; bronchiectasis
was seen in 26% of cases in one report 23 and 60% in another. 24

Radiographic features of bronchiectasis include thickened
airway walls with a lack of tapering as the airways track to the
periphery with either a cylindrical or saccular (cystic) shape (Fig.
124.4). 26 , 50 Dogs with bronchomalacia generally lack
radiographic evidence of bronchial collapse, but can have
bronchial or bronchointerstitial pa erns, poor visibility of their
lobar bronchi, or have normal radiographs. 29 , 30 In dogs and cats
with pneumonia, interstitial, alveolar, and mixed pa erns are
commonly seen with focal, multifocal, and diﬀuse distributions. 39
, 57 Aspiration pneumonia in dogs most commonly aﬀects the
right middle lung lobe, and plant awn pneumonia frequently
involves the accessory and caudal lobes; however, any lung lobe
can be aﬀected. 38 , 39 , 45 Right middle lung lobe consolidation in

vetexamprep.ir

cats can occur not only with aspiration pneumonia but also with
bronchopneumonia and inﬂammatory airway disease. 53
Videofluoroscopy
Videoﬂuoroscopy allows visualization of the intra- and extrathoracic trachea and mainstem bronchi during the breathing cycle
and with spontaneous and induced cough. It can be helpful for
diagnosis of airway collapse that is not appreciated on static plain
radiographs. Videoﬂuoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) can also
be used to determine if a swallowing disorder may be
contributing to aspiration pneumonia. 42 , 64 Although underrecognized, there are many respiratory disorders that result from
aspiration (aside from aspiration pneumonia) which aﬀect the
airways and parenchyma and can contribute to secondary
bacterial infections. 35
Ultrasonographic Examination
Thoracic ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the lungs and
pleural space in cases of lung lobe consolidation, masses,
pulmonary abscess, and foreign bodies. 44 , 45 , 65 A combination of
transthoracic,
transesophageal,
and
intraoperative
ultrasonography helped to identify 91% of dogs with migrating
grass awns in one study. 44 Lung ultrasonography was also useful
for identiﬁcation and monitoring of cardiogenic pulmonary
edema; this is evidenced by an increase in the number of artifacts
known as “B-lines” caused by increased pulmonary water. 67
Ultrasonography can also be used to guide collection of
specimens by FNA. The Vet BLUE (veterinary bedside lung
ultrasound exam) scan is emerging as a rapid POC examination
used to screen dogs and cats with respiratory compromise,
including those with lung consolidation. 67 , 68 A major limitation
of ultrasound is the requirement for lesions to extend to the
periphery as ultrasound cannot penetrate through aerated lung.
Computed Tomography
Cervical and thoracic CT can be performed to obtain further
information regarding structural abnormalities and provide more
accurate correlative information with histopathologic lesions.
Advantages over plain radiography include increased sensitivity

vetexamprep.ir

and ability to provide three-dimensional reconstructions to
eliminate superimposition of body parts. In particular, CT is more
sensitive for detection of bronchiectasis than plain radiography. 39
It can also be a useful tool for surgical planning. Paired
inspiratory and expiratory scans achieved with breath holds at
end inspiration and end expiration can highlight dynamic airway
collapse inclusive of tracheal collapse and bronchomalacia (Fig.
124.5A and B). Peribronchial cuﬃng or increases in the
peribronchovascular density may be seen with inﬂammatory
airway disorders. CT changes associated with eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy include increased bronchial wall
thickening, intraluminal bronchial plugging, opacity of the
parenchyma (e.g., nodules and masses), and bronchiectasis. 69
Pneumonia can present with increased opacity of the lung
including ground glass opacity and consolidation. In some cases,
foreign bodies may be seen, such as in airways. 39 , 45 CT ﬁndings
can also raise suspicion for some infectious diseases of the lung
other than “routine” bacterial infections, such as mycobacterial,
fungal, and parasitic diseases.
Tracheobronchoscopy
Endoscopic examination allows direct visualization of the trachea
and bronchi which is valuable for diagnosing structural
abnormalities such as tracheal collapse, bronchiectasis, and
bronchomalacia (see Fig. 124.1A–C). Nonspeciﬁc changes
associated with inﬂammatory airway disease such as thickened
mucosa, hyperemia, and mucus hypersecretion may also be seen.
Another use of endoscopy is to facilitate collection of specimens
using brush catheters, transbronchial needles, BAL, and biopsy
forceps for culture or microscopic examination from locally
aﬀected areas of the lung. Endoscopy can also be used to remove
foreign bodies (e.g., grass awn) (Fig. 124.6).

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
Specimens for cytologic evaluation can be collected using FNA,
transtracheal washing, endotracheal washing, BAL, bronchial
brushing, or by making impression smears from tissue collected
using biopsy forceps. Visible strands of exudate may then be
teased onto a microscope slide, smeared, and stained. Small
quantities of material can be centrifuged and smears made of the
sediment. New methylene blue wet mounts and Wright-Giemsa
or Gram stain of air-dried smears can be used for identiﬁcation of
cellular elements and bacteria. Bacterial infections are typically
associated with degenerate neutrophils and intracellular bacteria;
in addition, excess mucus, proteinaceous material, and activated
alveolar macrophages can be present. Bacteria are demonstrable
only in a fraction of washings from pneumonic animals, and their
absence in cytologic specimens, especially if the patient has been
placed on antibacterial therapy, does not rule out bacterial
pneumonia.

vetexamprep.ir

Transtracheal lavage. This is well tolerated by the majority of
large dogs and requires only minimal restraint of the
unanesthetized patient, although some dogs require mild
sedation. Endotracheal washing with anesthesia (see later
discussion) is usually used for small dogs and cats. Although
complications from transtracheal washing and aspiration are
uncommon, the procedure is not without risk. Transtracheal
washing should not be a empted in the fractious or
uncooperative patient without adequate chemical and manual
restraint. Contraindications include defects in hemostasis, severe
pyoderma of the ventral skin of the neck, and respiratory distress.
The most common complication associated with transtracheal
washing is subcutaneous emphysema. Other complications
include endotracheal hemorrhage, tracheal laceration, and
infection at the puncture site.
Endotracheal lavage. Endotracheal lavage is recommended for
small dogs and cats and requires short-acting general anesthesia.
The volume of sterile nonbacteriostatic saline recommended has
ranged in small animals from 3 to 10 mL per animal. Advantages
of endotracheal lavage over transtracheal lavage is avoidance of
tracheal injury, the need for minimal supplies, and its ease in cats
and small dogs. Disadvantages are the potential for
oropharyngeal contamination, a lack of airway visualization to
guide specimen collection, especially when focal disease is
present, and comparatively poor retrieval of ﬂuid when compared
with BAL.
Blind BAL technique. A blind BAL can be performed using shortacting general anesthesia without an endoscope. 70 This method is
similar to endotracheal lavage except the red rubber catheter used
is advanced through the endotracheal tube until gentle resistance
is felt; this should correspond to wedging in a small airway. The
catheter should be measured against the endotracheal tube before
the procedure to ensure it advances well past the point of the end
of the tube. The authors use 10 mL aliquots of saline in patients ≤
3 kg, and 20 mL aliquots of saline in patients > 3 kg. If negative
pressure is felt during aspiration, the catheter is slightly
withdrawn, and suction reapplied until air appears in the syringe.
The presence of foam in the lavage reﬂective of surfactant
indicates a deep wash. With bacterial infection, the BAL ﬂuid may
be visibly purulent.

vetexamprep.ir

Bronchoscope-guided BAL. Bronchoscope-guided BAL allows
collection of a specimen from an aﬀected airway or lung lobe. In
general, cytologic preparations collected using this method are
superior to those obtained by transtracheal or endotracheal lavage
because larger volumes of cells and proteinaceous materials are
obtained from the deeper portions of the lungs. Collection of
multiple specimens from diﬀerent parts of the lung is
recommended when disease is multifocal or diﬀuse, as ﬁndings
may vary from one lobe to another. 39 Suppurative inﬂammation
with or without intra- or extracellular bacteria supports a
diagnosis of bacterial infection. Quantiﬁcation of bacteria present
is needed to distinguish lower airway contamination or transient
colonization from actual infection. In addition to BAL, brush
catheters can be passed through the biopsy channel of the
endoscope to obtain specimens. Given the expense of a catheter
system that can be used only once, the authors feel there is no
advantage of using brush catheters compared with BAL for
identiﬁcation of bacterial infection.

Fine-needle aspiration. FNA can be performed without guidance
in or with the aid of ultrasound, ﬂuoroscopy, CT, or endoscopy to
procure material for culture and cytologic examination. 71–73
Transthoracic FNA may have a higher diagnostic yield than

vetexamprep.ir

lavage (especially tracheal washings and blind BAL) when focal
lesions are present. Transbronchial needle aspiration can be
performed using bronchoscopic guidance. Needles that are
designed to pass through the endoscope can be used to aspirate
enlarged hilar lymph nodes or discrete masses. Use of FNA
(typically with a 25 or 27 gauge, 1.5” needle and a 6-mL syringe) is
less risky than use of a Tru-Cut needle, which can cause severe
pulmonary hemorrhage or pneumothorax. The recommended size
of the needle is 25 or 27 gauge and 1.5 inches in length but may
vary depending on patient size.
Culture and Susceptibility Testing
Specimens obtained by FNA or transtracheal or BAL should be
cultured for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Mycoplasmas can
either be cultured using special media (requires laboratory
notiﬁcation) or Mycoplasma-speciﬁc PCR assays can be requested.
The la er is more sensitive because many Mycoplasma species are
very fastidious or uncultivable, although the clinical signiﬁcance
of positive Mycoplasma spp. PCR results is unclear. A Gram stain
can help make an early diagnosis of bacterial infection, and an
acid-fast stain may be of use in dogs with suspected
Mycobacterium spp. or Nocardia spp. infections. Bacterial
colonization versus infection must be diﬀerentiated by use of
cytology and quantitative bacterial cultures. 22 The threshold for
clinically relevant bacterial growth in BAL specimens from dogs is
proposed to be over 1.7 × 103 CFU/mL of BAL ﬂuid. 22 The
identiﬁcation of more than two intracellular bacteria after
microscopic examination of 50 oil immersion ﬁelds of a Gramstained slide also supports the presence of bacterial infection. 22
Dogs or cats with severe bacterial pneumonia may have
substantial respiratory compromise, and invasive airway
specimen collection can be risky and/or relatively contraindicated.
While yet to be deﬁnitively proven, in some cases, blood cultures
could represent an option to identify relevant bacteria and
provide information about antimicrobial susceptibility. Further
studies need to be performed to determine the utility of blood
cultures in dogs and cats with bacterial pneumonia.
Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Histopathologic specimens of the respiratory tract can be obtained
by endoscopic biopsy (generally either masses or superﬁcial
mucosal tissue), surgical biopsy (thoracoscopy or thoracotomy),
and, rarely, for consolidated and peripheral mass-like lesions,
ultrasound or CT-guided biopsy. Histopathologic evaluation of
masses within the upper and lower respiratory tracts can help
conﬁrm a deﬁnitive diagnosis of an underlying/predisposing
cause of infection and identify intralesional bacteria. Special stains
can also be applied to increase the sensitivity of organism
detection. This assessment must be coupled with culture to
deﬁnitively identify causative agents and determine their
antimicrobial susceptibility. Although invasive, biopsy can
provide complementary and additional information in
complicated cases of pulmonary parenchymal disease, 51 , 74 , 75
and lung lobectomy may provide cure in cases of isolated
bronchiectasis, foreign body pneumonia, and isolated lobar
pneumonia unresolved by antimicrobial therapy. It also allows
collection of larger specimens for culture and molecular detection
methods (with improved sensitivity than techniques such as FNA
or airway lavage).

Treatment
When designing a therapeutic plan for a patient with bacterial
bronchitis or pneumonia, an investigation for all co-morbid
conditions is important as secondary infections may not fully
resolve or will recur if the primary disease condition is not
simultaneously treated. In addition, because the presence of
bacteria does not necessarily equate with infection, positive
cultures must be interpreted in light of clinical signs and
clinicopathologic ﬁndings. Veterinarians play an important role in
promoting antimicrobial stewardship, so indiscriminate use of
antibiotics should be avoided. Antibiotics should not be a ﬁrst-line
drug for dogs with acute cough in the absence of systemic signs
where CIRD complex is suspected, as many are of viral etiology
and the vast majority resolve with supportive care. 76 They are
also not recommended for dogs with uncomplicated tracheal
collapse or cats with cough that is likely secondary to
inﬂammatory lower airway disease. To minimize selection for
antimicrobial resistance, whenever possible, culture and

vetexamprep.ir

susceptibility testing should be used to guide antimicrobial
therapy. Additionally, certain antibiotics do not pass the bloodbronchus barrier, and while they may be useful for pneumonia,
are not eﬀective for bacterial bronchitis. Antimicrobials such as
tetracyclines and ﬂuoroquinolones are examples of drugs that
cross the blood-bronchus barrier.
More aggressive antimicrobial therapy is indicated for bacterial
pneumonia when compared with upper airway infections.
Supportive therapies (discussed in more detail below) including
systemic and airway hydration, nebulization and coupage, and
supplemental oxygen are also important components of therapy,
especially in severe cases. Cough suppressants are absolutely
contraindicated in cases of pneumonia, as they prevent the
beneﬁcial reﬂex intended to clear secretions from the respiratory
tract. Furosemide should be given only if critical to manage
congestive heart failure as it will dry respiratory secretions and
impair activity of the mucociliary apparatus. If furosemide is
administered, increasing the frequency or duration of
nebulization may help counterbalance this. Antihistamines are
also known to dry secretions and should be avoided. There have
been no studies on the use of bronchodilators in bacterial
pneumonia in dogs or cats, but they may worsen
ventilation:perfusion mismatch by dilating airways leading to
consolidated regions of lung where gas exchange is ineﬀective. It
is the authors’ opinion that bronchodilators are most
appropriately used in cats with evidence of bronchospasm (e.g.,
asthma). Although not routinely recommended, a trial in cats
might be warranted for emergency treatment of bronchospasm
and acute respiratory distress with terbutaline (0.01–0.02 mg/kg
SC). Care must be taken with administration of theophylline if
chloramphenicol or ﬂuoroquinolones are being used concurrently
because these drugs increase the serum theophylline
concentration. Other suggested treatments without scientiﬁc
evidence of eﬃcacy in canine or feline bacterial pneumonia
include N-acetylcysteine, NSAIDs, and glucocorticoids.
Identification and Management of Underlying Causes
A comprehensive discussion of the treatment for underlying
disorders contributing to secondary bacterial infection of the
lower respiratory tract is beyond the scope of this chapter, but

vetexamprep.ir

brief mention of management/treatment strategies is warranted.
Tracheal collapse requires a combination of weight management,
avoidance of triggers of clinical signs (robust exercise, excitement,
etc.), use of a harness instead of a neck collar, cough suppressants,
and anxiolytics/sedatives. Canine chronic bronchitis, whether
eosinophilic or neutrophilic, and feline chronic bronchitis and
asthma, should be managed with avoidance of inhaled triggers
(antigens such as environmental smoke; particulates such as
cleaning aerosols/powders or dusty cat li er; or allergens), weight
management, and glucocorticoids (oral or inhaled, tapered to the
lowest eﬀective dose). The use of bronchodilators is best reserved
for asthmatic cats with episodic expiratory respiratory distress.
Recurrent infections are particularly problematic in patients with
bronchiectasis. If bronchiectasis is conﬁned to a single lobe,
surgical lobectomy may be curative. If bronchiectasis is
generalized, recurrent infections must be managed as they arise,
and low doses of glucocorticoids (0.25–0.5 mg/kg of prednisone or
prednisolone in dogs and cats, respectively) may help reduce
concurrent inﬂammation. Reduction of environmental inhaled
irritants and allergens and weight management are also helpful;
airway humidiﬁcation may help reduce tenacious secretions.
Bronchomalacia, like bronchiectasis, also requires management of
underlying or co-morbid respiratory conditions and may beneﬁt
from environmental modulation, weight management, and airway
humidiﬁcation. If sterile inﬂammation is documented during a
period where there is no concurrent infection, addition of lowdose glucocorticoid therapy may also be helpful. Bronchodilators
have not been proven to be useful for this condition as airway
smooth muscle constriction is not part of the underlying
pathology.
Implementing appropriate husbandry practices and when
available (based on patient risk), vaccination for causes of
contagious tracheobronchitis may help reduce incidence of these
diseases. As previously mentioned, identifying underlying causes
of bacterial pneumonia and addressing them directly is also
important in the overall management strategy and to help prevent
recurrence.
Antimicrobial Drug Treatment

vetexamprep.ir

No single antibacterial drug is routinely eﬀective against the wide
variety of organisms causing bacterial pneumonia. Selection of an
antibacterial drug based on identiﬁcation of the pathogen and its
antimicrobial susceptibility results in recovery of substantially
more patients than when therapy is empiric. 77 Recent
antimicrobial therapy that is empiric also negatively impacts
susceptibility to subsequently required antimicrobials. 78 Over
half (57.4%) of dogs with pneumonia previously treated
empirically with antibiotics and subsequently referred for airway
lavage were infected with bacteria that exhibited resistance to the
empirically used antibiotic. 78 Thus, if absolutely necessary to
select an antimicrobial without culture and susceptibility testing,
recently administered antimicrobials should be avoided.
Morphologic characteristics of bacteria on a Gram-stained slide
can aid in selection of an antibacterial drug while awaiting the
results of bacterial culture and susceptibility. 22 Doxycycline has
been recommended for treatment of suspected B. bronchiseptica or
Mycoplasma spp. pneumonia. 76 When streptococcal pneumonia is
suspected (e.g., shelter outbreak of pneumonia associated with
Gram-positive cocci), a penicillin is the drug of choice. 76
Additional detail on treatment of dogs with pneumonia due to
CIRD complex can be found in Chapter 28.
Because aspiration pneumonia is not always associated with
bacterial infection, routine antimicrobial use is controversial.
Antimicrobial treatment should ideally be delayed until
secondary bacterial infection can be documented or until the
animal fails to respond appropriately to other supportive therapy.
When infection plays a role in aspiration pneumonia, a
multiplicity of aerobic and anaerobic organisms can be involved,
38 and combination antimicrobial therapy may be required, ideally
guided by results of culture and susceptibility. Cough or
respiratory distress, fever, leukocytosis, and radiographic
evidence of severe interstitial or alveolar pa erns do not
deﬁnitively prove the pneumonia is due to bacterial infection. In
one study of canine aspiration pneumonia, roughly 25% of dogs
had negative cultures; however, only 47 of 125 dogs in this study
had airway lavage cultures and only 2 of 126 dogs had BAL
instead of an upper airway wash, so focal infections may have
been overlooked. 38 The consensus opinion of the Working Group

vetexamprep.ir

of ISCAID is that in the absence of evidence of systemic sepsis,
either no treatment or parenteral treatment with a beta-lactam
antimicrobial may be suﬃcient for cases of aspiration pneumonia.
76

Empiric antimicrobial therapy is particularly important to
initiate early (within 1 to 2 hours) in dogs or cats with evidence of
sepsis (see Chapter 123). A broad-spectrum parenteral
antimicrobial strategy should be considered to address the
possibility of gram-negative bacteria (e.g., a ﬂuoroquinolone) and
gram-positive and anaerobic bacteria (e.g., ampicillin or
clindamycin) which is later adjusted based on culture and
susceptibility results. 76 The reader is referred to ISCAID Working
Group Guidelines (see Suggested Reading list) for detailed
discussion of antimicrobial treatment options for canine and feline
respiratory tract infections, including doses and other
considerations. 76 Regardless of initial selection of antimicrobial,
results of culture and susceptibility testing should be used to
modify therapy, including de-escalation when possible.
In stable patients with documented evidence of bacterial
infection of the airways or pulmonary parenchyma, oral antibiotic
monotherapy that is prescribed on an outpatient basis should be
suﬃcient. If patients are hospitalized, parenteral antimicrobial
therapy is recommended regardless of disease severity; when
discharged from the hospital, they can be transitioned to oral
antimicrobials. 76
Routine
intratracheal
or
aerosol
administration
of
antimicrobials is not recommended in pneumonia. With severe
alveolar consolidation in pneumonia, airway penetration of
antimicrobials is inferior to systemic administration. Inhaled
aminoglycosides have been used to treat refractory B.
bronchiseptica pneumonia in dogs, but concerns have been raised
about the possibility of toxicity. Treatment of experimental dogs
with inhaled gentamicin at 7, 14, and 41 mg/kg was associated
with renal tubular necrosis at the highest dose, but with no
evidence of respiratory tract irritation (in contrast to ﬁndings in
rats in the same report). 79 Another study of dogs with naturally
occurring B. bronchiseptica pneumonia concluded that use of an
undiluted 5% solution of gentamicin in a nebulizer for 10 minutes
twice daily was safe and eﬀective. 80

vetexamprep.ir

Duration of antimicrobial therapy for bacterial pneumonia has
long been recommended for 3–6 or more weeks, and at least 1–2
weeks beyond clinical and radiographic resolution of signs of
disease. 39 This recommendation has not been based on evidence
and diﬀers from recommendations for humans with bacterial
pneumonia. In humans, meta-analyses show that in randomized
controlled clinical trials of bacterial pneumonia, use of longer
courses of antibiotics versus shorter courses do not lead to
signiﬁcant diﬀerences with respect to clinical success, bacterial
eradication, adverse eﬀects, or mortality. 81 Additionally,
radiographic improvement in humans lags far behind the clinical
response and oﬀers no beneﬁt in identifying treatment failure
over physician or patient assessment of symptoms, underscoring
the lack of utility of this diagnostic to guide therapy. 81–83 Until
controlled peer-reviewed studies can be performed, the ISCAID
Working Group consensus statement recommends reevaluation of
patients with pneumonia in 10 to 14 days after initiating
antimicrobial therapy. 76 One prospective study reported no
diﬀerence in outcome in dogs treated for 10 days with pneumonia
compared with those treated for 21 days. 84 While the best means
to monitor eﬃcacy of therapy is currently lacking, consensus
opinion is that a recheck should consist of physical examination,
CBC, and thoracic radiography, keeping in mind that
radiographic changes may lag behind clinical improvement.
Ancillary Supportive Therapy
Maintenance of normal systemic and airway hydration is an
important therapeutic objective in hospitalized patients with
bacterial pneumonia. Dehydration hinders mucociliary clearance
and mobilization of secretions because normal respiratory
secretions are more than 90% water. Judicious use of IV ﬂuids is
recommended. Airway hydration can be directly addressed using
aerosol therapy to mobilize secretions by adding water to the
mucociliary blanket. A nebulizer that produces particles between
0.5 and 3.0 µm ensures that water is deposited in the lower
airways. Water vaporizers or humidiﬁers are inadequate because
the water particulate size is larger and droplets are generally
deposited in the nasal cavity. For nebulization, the animal is
placed in an enclosed chamber, and a bland aerosol (normal

vetexamprep.ir

saline) is nebulized into the chamber. Physiotherapy should
always be performed immediately after aerosolization to enhance
secretion clearance. Methods include increased cough frequency
by chest wall coupage or tracheal manipulation, mild exercise,
and postural drainage. The animal should be nebulized two to six
times daily for 10 to 20 minutes per treatment. Careful a ention
must be paid to appropriate cleaning/sterilization of the nebulizer.
Animals with severe tachypnea, respiratory distress, or
moderate to marked hypoxemia (arterial oxygen tension below 80
mmHg or SpO2 < 94% on room air) require supplemental oxygen
therapy. Oxygen should be humidiﬁed to prevent drying of
respiratory membranes. Oxygen can be administered in a cage, by
intratracheal cannula or nasal catheter (unilateral or bilateral), or
in intubated patients with or without a mechanical ventilator.
Mechanical ventilation may be required when there is severe
hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen supplementation or evidence
of labored respiration with inappropriate oxygenation for the
degree of ventilation and with increasing PaCO2 (i.e., impending
respiratory muscle fatigue). High-ﬂow oxygen therapy using
high-ﬂow nasal prongs may be an alternative approach for dogs
failing traditional oxygen therapy when mechanical ventilation is
not a viable option. 85
If aspiration pneumonia is a complicating factor or has the
potential to be a complicating factor, maintaining sternal
recumbency with the cranial part of the body elevated, and
minimizing gastric volume by small frequent feedings or use of
antiemetics or prokinetics (e.g., maropitant, ondansetron,
cisapride) can be considered. A pilot study in four dogs with
acquired idiopathic megaesophagus indicated a potential beneﬁt
of
at-home
intermi ent
esophageal
suctioning
(via
esophagostomy tube or per os) for prevention of aspiration
pneumonia, and deserves further study as a long-term
management strategy. 86 A perioperative IV CRI of
metoclopramide did not aﬀect the incidence of aspiration
pneumonia in dogs undergoing arytenoid lateralization surgery.
87 If a patient with bacterial pneumonia is receiving
immunosuppressants or chemotherapeutics and it can be safely
done, temporary withdrawal of these drugs or a decrease in their
dose may aid in resolution of pneumonia.

vetexamprep.ir

Surgery
Surgical intervention may be required in patients in which
appropriate antimicrobial therapy has failed to fully resolve all
clinical and/or radiographic lesions. For example, surgery may be
indicated if, after discontinuing antimicrobial therapy, pneumonia
recurs in the same lobe, which may raise suspicion for a foreign
body or focal bronchiectasis. In some pulmonary abscesses, a
residual nidus of infection may persist even after long-term
antimicrobial therapy. Lobectomy may be curative. Additionally,
histopathologic examination of lung biopsies may reveal evidence
of co-morbid respiratory conditions requiring targeted therapy.

Prognosis
Bacterial tracheobronchitis and bacterial bronchitis are not
generally considered life-threatening, but bacterial infection can
be an important contributor to clinical signs and exacerbation of
co-morbid respiratory conditions. Prognosis depends on the
severity of disease, response to treatment, and reversibility of
pathology, if any.
Studies have shown survival to discharge rates of dogs with
“community-acquired” pneumonia to be 96% and with aspiration
pneumonia to be 77%–83%. 37 , 38 , 78 There was no association
between survival rates and more severe evidence of disease on
radiographs or duration of hospitalization in one study, 37 but
multiple lobe involvement had a worse outcome than single lobe
involvement in another study. 38 Prognosis for survival was not
correlated with the number or types of bacteria responsible for
aspiration pneumonia, the underlying cause for aspiration, or the
existence of multiple underlying reasons for aspiration. 37 , 38
When evaluating long-term follow-up in dogs having unilateral
arytenoid lateralization with postoperative aspiration pneumonia,
1-, 2-, 3-, and 4-year survival rates were 83%, 64%, 52%, and 26%,
respectively, underscoring the importance of the larynx in upper
airway protection. 36 Collectively, these ﬁndings demonstrate the
importance of identifying and aggressively managing any
underlying cause for aspiration to prevent subsequent recurrence
of pneumonia and other permanent damage to the airways and
pulmonary parenchyma (e.g., bronchiectasis).

vetexamprep.ir

Prevention
Contagious causes of bacterial tracheobronchitis and pneumonia
can be prevented using good husbandry practices and targeted
vaccination (see Chapters 17, 22, 26, and 28). For secondary
bacterial infections of the respiratory tract, appropriate early
identiﬁcation and management of underlying disorders is critical.
The risk of aspiration pneumonia can be minimized by fasting
prior to anesthesia, altering feeding practices in dysphagic dogs
(optimizing food/liquid consistency, low-fat diets and prokinetics
to facilitate gastric emptying, upright feedings, and in some cases
[e.g., megaesophagus] placement of gastric tubes with multiple
frequent feedings), and use of antiemetics for animals with severe
or protracted vomiting. Prophylactic antimicrobials are not
recommended for animals with recurrent aspiration. Overuse or
inappropriate use of antimicrobials is likely to predispose patients
to infections with MDR bacteria.

Public Health Aspects
Humans and their pets share the same environment, and close
contact can lead to exposure of susceptible humans with zoonotic
pathogens. A few bacterial pathogens causative of respiratory
tract infection in dogs and cats are considered to have the
potential to be zoonotic including B. bronchiseptica, Streptococcus
equi subsp. zooepidemicus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Yersinia
spp. 88 The likelihood of infection as well as the severity of disease
is higher in immunocompromised humans. Routes of
transmission of zoonotic bacteria are unclear but could include
inhalation of aerosols and ingestion; thus, immunocompromised
individuals should minimize contact with dogs that are sneezing
or coughing, and routine precautions including use of appropriate
personal protective equipment and thorough hand washing are
prudent for all in-contact humans. An additional concern given
widespread and often indiscriminate veterinary use of
antimicrobials is the MDR bacteria that may be isolated from the
respiratory tract as was demonstrated in one dog with
bronchopneumonia. 89

Pyothorax

vetexamprep.ir

Etiology, Epidemiology, and Pathogenesis
Purulent pleuritis, pyothorax, and thoracic empyema describe
septic processes of the pleural cavity that are associated with
exudate accumulation. The pleural cavity normally contains a
small amount of transudative ﬂuid. With bacterial infections, the
resultant host inﬂammatory immune response leads to alterations
in vascular permeability and lymphatic function leading to an
eﬀusion rich in cells and protein.
Pyothorax can result from either local or systemic disease. Local
disease follows extension of infection from the thoracic wall,
tracheobronchial tree, pulmonary parenchyma, or esophagus.
Examples include bacterial infection from penetrating bite
wounds, parapneumonic spread, migrating foreign bodies or
parasites, thoracic trauma (including iatrogenic inoculation), and
esophageal perforation, among others. Pyothorax that is part of a
systemic disease process implies hematogenous or lymphatic
spread of bacteria.
Deﬁnitive identiﬁcation of the source of bacterial pleuritis is
frequently not achieved. 90 Pleural infections are commonly
polymicrobial in nature. 45 , 91–98 There is a high prevalence of
obligate anaerobic bacteria as sole pathogens or in combination of
facultative aerobes and other anaerobes. 95–97 The most prevalent
organisms isolated from pleural exudate of the dog and cat are
summarized in Table 124.3.

Dogs

vetexamprep.ir

Pyothorax in dogs most commonly occurs in young adult medium
to large breeds, especially of working and sporting varieties. 92 , 93
, 95 These breeds are thought to be at risk because they are prone
to grass awn inhalation during vigorous exercise. When
Actinomyces spp. are isolated, there should be a high index of
suspicion for plant material (grass awns) as the underlying cause.
99 , 100 Barbed awns migrate down the bronchial tree, carrying
commensal microﬂora from the oropharyngeal cavity into the
lung parenchyma. The awns may exit the visceral pleura and
enter the pleural cavity where they can cause pyothorax. The
relative importance of grass awns as a cause of pyothorax in dogs
may be regionally variable, with only 3 of 50 dogs in a UK
retrospective study being associated with plant inhalation. 93
Pyothorax may also occur in dogs due to penetrating trauma to
the thoracic wall, bite wounds, or esophageal trauma. For
example, the esophageal parasite Spirocerca lupi has also been
responsible for pyothorax in dogs from damage to the esophagus
at the site of granulomas and leakage of esophageal material into
the thoracic cavity (see Chapter 117). 101 Pyothorax can also be a
complication of thoracic drainage techniques (e.g., thoracostomy
tube placement and maintenance) or thoracic surgery. 102 , 103
When pyothorax is a complication of indwelling thoracostomy
tubes, it is typically diagnosed within 4 days of tube placement.
102

Cats
Risk factors for pyothorax in cats include young age and being
part of a multiple-cat household, but not indoor or outdoor status
(i.e., free roaming does not appear to increase risk). 96 Possible
overrepresentation of male cats has been documented in some
studies, but this has not been a statistically signiﬁcant ﬁnding.
Feline pyothorax generally results from contamination of the
pleural cavity with oropharyngeal ﬂora. The most common
aerobic organism isolated in feline pyothorax is Pasteurella,
although anaerobes are frequently cultured as well. 91 , 94 , 96 , 97
Parapneumonic spread and bite wounds are the most common
routes of infection. 91 , 104 Previously, bite wounds were thought
to be the major route of infection, especially in young, freeroaming intact male cats. 105 However, with more cats being

vetexamprep.ir

neutered and kept indoors, pyothorax secondary to bite wounds
is seen less frequently.

Clinical Signs and Physical Examination
Findings
Clinical signs of pyothorax result from restrictive respiratory
disease, including increased respiratory rate, shallow respirations,
inspiratory respiratory distress, and orthopnea. Other signs
include obtundation, exercise intolerance, cough, lethargy,
anorexia, weight loss, and fever. Physical examination may reveal
muﬄed heart sounds and decreased breath sounds in the
dependent areas of the thorax. Chronic or severe infections may
result in a dehydrated, debilitated, collapsed, or hypothermic

vetexamprep.ir

y
p
yp
patient. Approximately one half of cats with pyothorax develop
sepsis. 96 In cats with pyothorax, hypersalivation and bradycardia
can occur and are associated with a worse clinical outcome. 96 , 106

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of pyothorax in dogs and cats is usually established
based on radiography and microbiologic and cytologic analyses of
pleural eﬀusion (summarized in Tables 124.3 and 124.4).
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Biochemical Tests, and
Urinalysis
Abnormalities on CBC are typically nonspeciﬁc including mild-tomoderate nonregenerative anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis of
varying severity with or without a left shift, and presence of toxic
neutrophils. 91 , 93 , 95 , 96 , 107 , 108 In some patients, the CBC may
be unremarkable. In cases of sepsis and concurrent DIC,
thrombocytopenia may also be present. Serum biochemistry
proﬁle abnormalities may include hyponatremia, hypochloremia,
hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, azotemia, hyperglycemia
or hypoglycemia, and hypocalcemia. 93–96 Hyperbilirubinemia
may also be present in cats. 94 , 96

Diagnostic Imaging
Thoracic Radiography
Pleural eﬀusion is noted on thoracic radiography, particularly if
this is performed prior to thoracocentesis. Bilateral eﬀusion is
most common, but unilateral eﬀusion may be seen. 91–93 , 95 , 96 , 109
Thoracic radiography should be repeated after drainage of pleural

vetexamprep.ir

eﬀusion to evaluate for underlying etiology such as lesions in the
pulmonary parenchyma, pleural space, and lymphadenomegaly.
Ultrasonographic Examination
Thoracic ultrasound (TFAST) can be used to visualize pleural
eﬀusion location and presence of ﬁbrinous adhesions. Pleural
eﬀusion associated with pyothorax is typically echogenic.
Ultrasonographic examination can also be used to further evaluate
consolidated lung parenchyma, possible abscesses, intrathoracic
masses, and thoracic lymph nodes. In some cases, foreign material
(e.g., plant awns) may be identiﬁed. 45 , 110 Ultrasound can be
useful to guide needles for specimen collection or thoracocentesis,
particularly when loculated ﬂuid is present.
Advanced Imaging
CT may provide more detail regarding pulmonary parenchymal
lesions and correlates well with ﬁndings at surgery (Fig. 124.7). 111
CT reliably provides information on the presence and volume of
pleural ﬂuid. 111 Pleural gas may be noted, either due to
procedures such as thoracocentesis or as a result of plant foreign
body migration. 111 Pleural thickening, mediastinal lesions, and
lymphadenomegaly can all be reliably detected. 111 Improved
identiﬁcation of pulmonary parenchymal lesions is also a beneﬁt
of CT over plain radiography, and lesions may be identiﬁed that
are not evident at surgery. 111 For this reason, CT results can be
useful to guide surgical intervention. Use of a combination of CT
and bronchoscopy may be most eﬀective for identiﬁcation of
migrating plant awns. 112

Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Diagnosis
Grossly, pleural exudate obtained using thoracocentesis from
dogs and cats with pyothorax is typically turbid and/or
hemorrhagic and may contain ﬂocculent debris. In anaerobic
infections, it may also be malodorous. Sulfur granules within the
eﬀusion may be visualized with Actinomyces spp. or Nocardia spp.
infections. Bacteria can often be identiﬁed microscopically, and

vetexamprep.ir

mixed populations of bacteria may be noted; however, failure to
identify bacteria does not rule out bacterial pyothorax. Infection
with nonstaining bacteria such as Mycoplasma spp. or a history of
antimicrobial therapy may mean bacteria are not visible.
Actinomyces or Nocardia infection should be suspected if
ﬁlamentous bacteria are seen microscopically (Fig. 124.8).

Culture and Susceptibility Testing
Specimens for aerobic and anaerobic culture should be collected
before antimicrobial administration whenever possible. Pleural
ﬂuid should be placed into appropriate tubes, including anaerobic
transport medium, with minimal exposure to air to optimize the
chance of positive cultures. Specimens intended for anaerobic
culture should not be refrigerated and should be processed with
minimal delay. 90 Consideration should also be given to speciﬁc
culture for Mycoplasma spp., and it is recommended that the
laboratory be informed if there is a clinical suspicion of
Actinomyces spp. or Nocardia spp. infection. Because anaerobic
cultures and Mycoplasma spp. cultures are often low yield when
transported to a commercial diagnostic laboratory from a practice
environment (as opposed to immediate submission to an on-site
laboratory as occurs in teaching hospital environments), aerobic
bacterial culture and empiric therapy for anaerobes (which are
almost always present) is a suitable alternative.

Treatment
Treatment of pyothorax should be prompt and aggressive. Initial
goals are to relieve respiratory distress by removal of eﬀusion
from the pleural space, to provide appropriate IV ﬂuid therapy
and supportive care, and to inactivate bacteria using systemic
antimicrobial drugs.
Drainage and Lavage
Drainage of pleural exudates is essential for management of
pyothorax. Delayed pleural drainage leads to incomplete
resolution of signs and predisposes to formation of loculated
abscesses and ﬁbrosis, which could necessitate later thoracotomy.
Placement of indwelling thoracostomy tubes has been

vetexamprep.ir

recommended as the initial treatment of choice in most cats, with
95% of cats having resolution when this is combined with
appropriate concurrent antibacterial drug therapy. 91 Dogs may
also beneﬁt from indwelling tube placement and aggressive
medical management. Indwelling tubes have the advantages of
closed chest drainage and facilitate pleural ﬂuid sampling to
monitor therapeutic response; the tubes also allow direct
instillation of isotonic lavage ﬂuid (with or without additives) into
the pleural space (see later). Disadvantages of indwelling tubes
include challenges associated with maintenance of drain
placement and patency and the risks of pneumothorax and
infection. 102 Large-bore thoracostomy tubes have been
traditionally utilized to minimize the chance of obstruction with
purulent ﬂuid. However, small-bore wire-guided thoracostomy
tubes have been shown to be suitable for the management of
pyothorax without any occurrences of tube obstruction. 113 When
these tubes were used, thoracic lavage was incorporated into the
management protocol, which may explain why obstruction did
not occur. Small-bore tubes oﬀer advantages such as patient
tolerance of placement and ease of placement.
After ﬂuid removal, radiographs should be taken to more
accurately evaluate the pulmonary parenchyma, pleural space,
and mediastinum for lesions that may alter treatment plans.
Additionally, post-drainage radiographs can be used to assess
whether drainage is complete, especially on the contralateral side.
If ﬂuid removal is incomplete, bilateral tube placement may be
required. Intermi ent suction every 2 to 4 hours or continuous
suction can be used. 114 Use of one-way continuous suction
requires close monitoring as the risk of potentially fatal
complications in cases of malfunction is increased. The median
duration of indwelling thoracostomy tubes for drainage has been
approximately 6 to 7 days (range, a few hours to 21 days). 91–93 , 96
A single-needle thoracocentesis has not been routinely
advocated for management of pyothorax although one study
reported complete long-term resolution of pyothorax in 15 of 16
dogs after complete drainage and 6 weeks of treatment with
ampicillin and metronidazole. 107 Single drainage protocols are
usually not curative if pulmonary lobar masses (associated with
abscesses or consolidation) are evident by radiography after initial

vetexamprep.ir

ﬂuid drainage. Repeated thoracocentesis is relatively simple and
inexpensive but is generally not recommended due to associated
morbidity.
Thoracic lavage may be performed through indwelling
thoracostomy tubes. There is controversy about the eﬃcacy of
lavage of the pleural cavity. Lavage may facilitate removal of
accumulated pus and bacteria and break down clots and ﬁbrin
bands; in addition, it may dilute bacteria and other inﬂammatory
mediators. However, prospective studies are lacking. Some
retrospective studies have suggested that lavage led to decreased
duration of thoracostomy tube drainage 93 and increased the
likelihood of survival. 92 However, one retrospective study in cats
concluded that thoracic lavage should not be routinely
recommended as the beneﬁts of lavage did not outweigh the risks.
96 Lavage has been implemented as part of a medical management
protocol in some studies with apparently good success 91–93 , 115 ;
however, it is unclear how much of the beneﬁcial outcome was
directly related to lavage and not to the other medical
management strategies or diﬀerences in patient populations.
Fluid volumes for lavage are generally 10 to 20 mL/kg of
warmed 0.9% saline infused slowly over 5 to 10 minutes two to
four times per day. 116 Respiratory pa ern and eﬀort are
monitored closely during infusion, and infusion is discontinued
and ﬂuid immediately aspirated if respiratory distress occurs. The
ﬂuid volume can then be reduced for subsequent lavage. The
patient can be rotated from side to side, or mild coupage can be
performed followed by immediate removal of any accessible ﬂuid.
Lavage can be continued until the removed ﬂuid is clear of pus.
Cytologic improvement is exhibited by decreasing cell count, with
loss of degenerative changes in neutrophils, and absence of
bacteria. Repeated culture is also recommended to conﬁrm
resolution of infection. Addition of antimicrobial agents to the
lavage ﬂuid is controversial and is currently not recommended
based on limited data. 76
Antimicrobial Therapy
Systemic antimicrobial therapy is indicated for pyothorax, but it is
usually insuﬃcient without lavage or drainage of the infected
pleural cavity. Initial empiric antibacterial selection should be

vetexamprep.ir

active against a mixture of facultative and obligate anaerobic
bacteria. 76 , 97 Penicillin or penicillin derivatives are often given
because they are active against obligate anaerobes, Pasteurella
spp., or Actinomyces spp. As an initial empirical choice, a
combination of a ﬂuoroquinolone (e.g., enroﬂoxacin or
marboﬂoxacin) with a penicillin or clindamycin is recommended.
76 Culture and susceptibility testing should be evaluated in light
of clinical condition for further adjustments to antibacterial
therapy. Regardless of the anaerobic or facultative anaerobic
bacteria that are cultured, the regimen should always contain
drugs eﬀective against anaerobes. Systemic antibacterial therapy
should ideally be continued for at least 4 to 6 weeks. 76
Surgery
Surgical intervention is more costly, particularly when medical
management has been a empted ﬁrst and failed. 117 Therefore, it
is important to try to identify candidates that require surgical
intervention as early in the disease course as possible. 117
Evidence of foreign material, pulmonary or mediastinal masses,
radiographic evidence of ﬂuid encapsulation, repeated blockage
of drainage tubes, recurrent pneumothorax, and lack of signiﬁcant
improvement in ﬂuid consistency during lavage are indications
for surgical exploration and/or lobectomy. 93 , 95 , 96 Because
Actinomyces spp. have been associated with a high likelihood of
plant material, 100 , 118 , 119 isolation of these bacteria is another
potential indication for surgical exploration. Although surgical
exploration is expensive, one report suggested that dogs having
surgical exploration and debridement followed by medical
management have a be er outcome after treatment than those
undergoing pleural evacuation and lavage alone. 95 Thoracoscopy
(or video-assisted thoracic surgery, VATS) is a less invasive
alternative to thoracotomy. 109 , 120 , 121 In one study, conversion to
open thoracotomy was only required for 2 of 14 dogs with
pyothorax that underwent thoracoscopy, and only 1 dog had
recurrence of pyothorax that required a second surgery 17 months
later (median follow-up time: 143 days, range: 14–2,402 days). 121
Monitoring

vetexamprep.ir

Radiographic monitoring is essential during treatment and
follow-up of pleural infections. Serial radiographic examinations
should be performed ﬁrst after initial thoracocentesis, when the
chest tube is removed, 10 to 14 days after starting antibacterial
therapy, and at completion of therapy. 76 Additionally,
radiographs can be acquired 1 to 2 weeks after discontinuing
antimicrobials to monitor for subclinical recurrence of disease. If
there is persistence of eﬀusion or recurrence, repeated
thoracocentesis, ﬂuid analysis, and culture and susceptibility
should be performed.

Prognosis
The highest period of mortality for dogs and cats with pyothorax
is within the initial 48 hours of drainage and stabilization. 93 After
that time, prognosis improves. Survival to discharge of 74% and
long-term survival of 63% were reported in one study, 92 whereas
other studies have reported higher percentages. 93 , 107 , 117
Recurrence rates have been reported to be < 20% with most
recurrences occurring within a few months of discharge 92 , 93 , 95 ,

96 , 107 , 109 , 115 , 117

Prevention
When possible, reducing exposure of dogs to areas where grass
awns are prominent may assist in pyothorax prevention.
Grooming dogs that are exposed to areas of abundant grass awns
thoroughly and frequently may reduce the risk of related
complications. 100 Housing cats indoors and in stable colonies may
reduce the risk of pyothorax.

Case Example
Signalment

“Sam,” a 5-year-old, female, intact, English pointer from the
southeastern United States.

History

vetexamprep.ir

Sam was evaluated for a 3-day history of behavioral change and
2-day history of anorexia. Labored breathing was noted the
morning of evaluation which prompted presentation on an
emergent basis. The patient was up-to-date on vaccinations and
routine parasite prevention. The dog lived in an outdoor kennel
se ing and was an active ﬁeld trial dog that traveled frequently
to events. There was no history of prior illness.

Physical Examination Findings

Body weight: 17.5 kg, BCS 3/9.
General: Obtunded but responsive, 5% dehydration, T =
102.4°F (39.1°C), HR = 140 beats/minute, RR = 50
breaths/minute, mucous membranes pink, CRT = 2
seconds.
Ears, eyes, nose, and throat: Mild mucoid ocular
discharge bilaterally.
Respiratory: Restrictive respiratory pa ern (shallow with
greater eﬀort on inspiration), decreased bronchovesicular
sounds ventrally over both the right and left thorax.
Lymph nodes: Mild bilateral lymphadenomegaly of the
superﬁcial cervical lymph nodes.
No clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were noted in other
systems following full physical examination.

Laboratory Findings
CBC: Hct 44.1% (38.7%–59.2%), MCV 69.6 fL (60.5–73.8
fL), MCHC 34.6 mg/dL (32–37.2 mg/dL), platelets 468,000/
µL (152,000–518,000 platelets/µL), WBC 28,820 cells/µL
(5,090–17,410 cells/µL), neutrophils 26,806 cells/µL (2,600–
10,400 cells/µL), band neutrophils 576 cells/µL (0–300
cells/µL), lymphocytes 865 cells/µL (390–6,730 cells/µL),
monocytes 576 cells/µL (160–1,160 cells/µL), eosinophils 0
cells/µL (10–2,050 cells/µL), cell morphology – slight toxic
granulocytes.
Serum chemistry proﬁle: Total protein 6.4 g/dL (5.5–7.7
g/dL), albumin 1.6 g/dL (3–4.3 g/dL), globulin 4.8 g/dL (2–
4.3 g/dL), ALP 177 U/L (14–152 U/L), ALT 22 U/L (13–151
U/L), AST 29 U/L (18–55 U/L), total bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL

vetexamprep.ir

(0–0.2 mg/dL), creatine kinase 145 U/L (53–337 U/L), BUN
9.0 mg/dL (9–34 mg/dL), creatinine 0.3 mg/dL (0.5–1.6
mg/dL), calcium 9.1 mg/dL (9.6–12 mg/dL), phosphorus
5.5 mg/dL (2.6–7.9 mg/dL), glucose 84 mg/dL (76–116
mg/dL), cholesterol 328 mg/dL (132–335 mg/dL),
bicarbonate 15.2 mmol/L (14–29 mmol/L), sodium 141
mmol/L (142–151 mmol/L), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.6–4.9
mmol/L), chloride 104 mmol/L (105–117 mmol/L).

Imaging Findings

At the time of initial examination, a brief thoracic ultrasound
was performed and conﬁrmed the presence of pleural eﬀusion.
Thoracic radiographs revealed a moderate amount of pleural
eﬀusion characterized by retraction of the lung lobes, partial
silhoue ing of the cardiac outline and numerous pleural ﬁssure
lines. An alveolar pa ern was also noted within the caudal
aspect of the left cranial lung lobe. Interpretation: Pleural
eﬀusion. Alveolar pa ern within the caudal aspect of the left
cranial lung lobe was most consistent with pneumonia. An
underlying presence of a foreign body could not be ruled out.

Cytologic Findings

A pleural eﬀusion specimen was obtained for analysis using
thoracocentesis.
Fluid analysis: Color: red; transparency: cloudy; nucleated
cells: 124,900/µL; RBC: 370,000/µL; protein: 4.0 g/dL;
speciﬁc gravity: 1.027.
Cytologic description: Predominance of neutrophils with
fewer macrophages and sca ered reactive mesothelial
cells. Neutrophils were degenerative, and low numbers
had phagocytized thin, ﬁlamentous rod bacteria and
fewer small cocci. Bacteria were also seen free in the
background.
Interpretation: Septic inﬂammation.

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic and anaerobic culture: Actinomyces spp. from broth
only and heavy growth of Bacteroides capillosus.

vetexamprep.ir

Diagnosis

Bacterial pyothorax.

Treatment

The patient was stabilized upon initial presentation with
thoracocentesis and IV ﬂuid therapy. Once results of the pleural
ﬂuid analysis were available, an exploratory thoracotomy was
performed via median sternotomy. Eﬀusion was suctioned
from the thoracic cavity and thorough lavage was performed.
The right caudal lung lobe was abnormal in appearance with an
apparent mass present, and a right caudal lung lobectomy was
performed. Foreign material was not visualized within the
thoracic cavity. A thoracostomy tube was placed on the right
side.
The patient recovered from surgery without complication. IV
ﬂuids were continued postoperatively, postoperative analgesic
therapy was instituted, and empiric antimicrobial therapy was
begun with ampicillin-sulbactam (30 mg/kg, IV, q8h) and
clindamycin (11 mg/kg, IV, q12h). Pleural eﬀusion was
manually suctioned q4h. The thoracostomy tube was removed
on day 5 post-hospitalization when very li le pleural ﬂuid
production was documented, and antibiotic therapy was
transitioned to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (20 mg/kg, PO, q12h)
and clindamycin (8 mg/kg, PO, q12h). Histopathology of
surgically resected lung tissue revealed focal suppurative
pneumonia, chronic pyogranulomatous pleuritis, and
mediastinitis. Sam was discharged on day 6 of hospitalization.
He continued to recover well after discharge. No evidence of
recurrence was documented as of follow-up 18 months after
discharge.

Comments

The growth of Actinomyces spp. and the mass lesion in one lung
lobe in this dog suggested the possibility of plant awn
migration as a cause of the pyothorax.
