125: Gastrointestinal and IntraAbdominal Infections
Jane E. Sykes, Ingrid Balsa, William
T.N. Culp, Boaz Arzi, Sina Marsilio, and Stanley L. Marks

KEY POINTS
• Causes: A wide variety of gram-negative and gram-positive
bacteria can infect the GI tract and peritoneal cavity, including
Escherichia coli, Enterococcus spp., other gram-negative
aerobes, Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus spp. and
anaerobes. Candida spp. may also be involved, particularly in
immunocompromised patients or patients receiving
antibacterial drug therapy. Viruses, atypical bacteria (e.g.,
Mycobacterium spp.), protozoa (e.g., Toxoplasma gondii,
Giardia duodenalis, Tritrichomonas blagburni), endemic fungi
(e.g., Histoplasma spp.), algae (Prototheca spp.), and
helminth parasites also cause GI disease.
• Mode of Transmission: Most GI infections result from
opportunistic invasion by commensal bacteria and fungi of the
GI and urogenital tracts. Other pathogens are transmitted by a
variety of different routes.
• Major Clinical Signs: Signs are extremely variable depending
on the site of infection, the underlying etiology, and the
immunocompetence of the host, but include dysphagia,
hypersalivation, inappetence, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and
abdominal pain.
• Human Health Significance: Enteric bacteria involved may be
multidrug-resistant organisms that have the potential to
colonize humans. In addition, certain assemblages of Giardia
duodenalis have the potential to be zoonotic.

vetexamprep.ir

The Gastrointestinal Microbiome and
Metabolome
Thousands of microbial species reside within the GI tract as
commensal organisms. The resident gut microbiome is composed
of viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotic organisms that perform a
number of vital functions, including resisting colonization with
pathogenic microbes by maintaining oxygen tension, competing
with nutrients, and producing antibacterial substances
(bacteriocins); assisting with nutrient breakdown and
synthesizing essential vitamins and short-chain fa y acids;
stimulating and maintaining mucosal immunity; metabolizing
bile acids and drugs; and inactivating potentially carcinogenic and
toxic ingested substances. 1 , 2 Antimicrobial administration can
induce gut dysbiosis, with broad-spectrum antibiotics causing
rapid and signiﬁcant drops in taxonomic richness, diversity, and
evenness. In addition, disruption of the gut microbiome as a result
of disease, immunosuppression, or antimicrobial therapy can
adversely aﬀect the health of the GI tract and has the potential to
allow organisms that are normally nonpathogenic to proliferate
opportunistically and cause disease.
For decades, our understanding of the identity and quantity of
the resident microﬂora was hampered because of a reliance on
traditional culture methods. This is because the use of culture
methods overestimates the species that are culturable and
underestimates those that are fastidious or unculturable. The
more recent advent of high-throughput molecular approaches has
revolutionized our understanding of the intestinal microbiome in
health and disease, especially when layered upon our existing
knowledge based on culture-dependent methods. Application of
next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods (also known as
massive parallel sequencing) allows rapid sequencing of 1 million
to 43 billion short reads (up to 1000 bp) with each run. Microbial
DNA is ampliﬁed using PCR and then sequenced; several
diﬀerent types of sequencing methods can be used but common
methods applied are 454 pyrosequencing, reversible dye
terminator (Illumina) sequencing, and real-time sequencing. 3 The
PCR assays used commonly target bacterial 16S rRNA genes. The
internal transcribed spacer (ITS) gene has also been used as a
target; across bacterial populations, the ITS gene is more variable

vetexamprep.ir

than the 16S rRNA gene, and so ITS gene PCR methods oﬀer
improved discrimination between bacterial species (taxonomic
resolution). In-depth whole metagenomic sequencing (WMS)
methods capture total microbial DNA (rather than just 16S rRNA
gene information) and are not subject to bias that results from
preferential ampliﬁcation of certain 16S rRNA gene sequences;
however, they are more expensive than ampliﬁcation-based
methods and so ampliﬁcation-based methods continue to be
utilized. 2 The use of mixed methodology across studies and often
small numbers of animals has led to considerable variation in
microbiome composition results, but as more studies accumulate,
our understanding of the canine and feline microbiome is
improving. Targeted techniques such as FISH (see Chapter 6) are
complementary to these studies and allow identiﬁcation of
bacteria or fungi within lesions in formalin-ﬁxed tissues (Fig.
125.1).
Because microbiome analysis provides information on the
identity of hundreds of bacterial species, including many
previously unidentiﬁed organisms, data are usually presented by
grouping bacteria into phyla, and within phyla, orders.
Descriptions of microbial populations generally only refer to
individual species when those species represent a signiﬁcant
proportion of organisms within an order. Table 125.1 provides
examples of common phyla found within the GI tract, and some
of the orders and species within those phyla. A phylum can
contain both aerobes and anaerobes, but they tend to be primarily
gram-negative or gram-positive species (e.g., organisms that
belong to the Firmicutes are generally gram positive).
Terms used to describe microbiome communities include
diversity, richness, abundance, and evenness. Richness is the total
number of bacterial species present in a microbiome; a rich
microbiome has many species present. Species diversity is a
measure of the number of species and the abundance of each
species. Alpha-diversity is the diversity within a particular region
or sample, and beta-diversity is the diversity between two regions
or samples (measured as the number of species that are unique to
each region being compared). Evenness describes the distribution
of abundance across a population; an even population is when all
species in the population have the same abundance. Indices have
been developed in order to quantify diversity (e.g., Shannon’s

vetexamprep.ir

index) and evenness (e.g., Pielou’s evenness index) using
mathematical equations. A canine dysbiosis index (DI) is a PCRbased algorithm that allows veterinarians to quantify gut
dysbiosis and can be used to monitor disease progression and
response to treatment. 4 A DI ≥ 2 indicates dysbiosis, a negative DI
suggests normobiosis, and values in between have been
considered equivocal. 5 Antimicrobial administration induces a
rapid and signiﬁcant drop in taxonomic richness, diversity, and
evenness. In light of this phenomenon, there has been renewed
vigor to study the eﬀects of probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal
microbiota transplantation (FMT) on reversing intestinal dysbiosis
and optimizing the intestinal microbiome.

Several studies also have described the metabolic products
generated by the canine and feline intestinal microbiota, including
volatile fa y acids; amino acids such as tryptophan; lactate;
ammonia; and other end products. 6 , 7 The chemical signature
that results is reﬂective of the bacterial populations present, and is
referred to as the GI metabolome.

Infections of the Oral Cavity

vetexamprep.ir

The Oral Microbiome
The resident microbial ﬂora of the canine and feline oral cavity is
composed of a wide variety of aerobic bacteria and facultative and
obligate anaerobic bacteria, mycoplasmas, and yeasts, but diﬀers
signiﬁcantly from that in humans. Examples of anaerobes found
in canine saliva using culture include Actinomyces, Streptococcus,
and Granulicatella (previously nutritionally variant streptococci),
and in dental plaque, Porphyromonas, Actinomyces, and Neisseria. 8
High-throughput sequencing methods have demonstrated the
diversity of species in the bacterial and fungal biomes in the oral
cavity of healthy dogs and cats and those with periodontal
disease, with considerable variations from one anatomic region to
another. 9 In one study, three diﬀerent niches were identiﬁed in
dogs—saliva, supragingival plaque, and the soft-tissue structures
of the tongue and buccal mucosa. 9 The most abundant organisms
were Filofactor villosus for supragingival plaque (5% of total DNA
composition), an unclassiﬁed Pasteurellaceae for buccal mucosa
(12%), Conchiformibius sp. for the dorsal tongue mucosa (17%), and
an unclassiﬁed Escherichia coli-Shigella sp. for saliva (20%).
Proteobacteria were the dominant group for all of the sites except
supragingival plaque, where Firmicutes were dominant.
Supragingival plaque also exhibited the greatest microbial
diversity. Capnocytophaga,
Porphyromonas,
Neisseria,
and
Fusobacterium spp. were all observed among core microbiota. In
healthy cats, the most prevalent species in swabs from the oral
cavity in one study was an unidentiﬁed Pasteurellaceae (19%),
followed by Moraxella spp. (11%). When the subgingival
microbiota was examined, Porphyromonas spp. was most
abundant, followed by Moraxella spp. and Fusobacterium. 10 In
another study of cats with and without periodontal disease, the
most abundant genera in healthy cats were Enhydrobacter,
Moraxella, and Capnocytophaga spp. 11 Organisms that are found to
a greater extent in cats with periodontal disease than healthy cats
are Filofactor spp. and the spirochete Treponema spp.
Antimicrobial agents used in treating oral infections such as
gingivitis and stomatitis should be chosen with the composition of
the resident microﬂora in mind. However, clearly not all
organisms that comprise the resident microﬂora are capable of
causing disease or replicating when inoculated into tissue;

vetexamprep.ir

bacterial virulence factors, the local tissue environment, and the
host response to infection ultimately inﬂuence what bacteria are
able to replicate and cause pathology. Some of the organisms are
found in bite wound infections (see Chapter 75).

Gingivitis and Periodontitis
Inﬂammation and recession of the gingival margins are common
ﬁndings in dogs and cats. Factors that predispose dogs and cats to
periodontal disease include tooth crowding and rotation,
persistent deciduous dentition, malocclusions, congenital
abnormalities, trauma, soft food diets, and genetic factors. 12
Lesions are initially caused by excessive accumulation of dental
plaque resulting from deposition of by-products from breakdown
of food and saliva by normal resident microﬂora. Plaque is an
organic matrix of salivary glycoproteins and polysaccharides that
adheres to the tooth surface and provides sites for oral bacteria to
proliferate. Resident bacteria produce a glycopolysaccharide
referred to as a glycocalyx, which facilitates the a achment of other
bacteria. This bioﬁlm is further consolidated into a ﬁlm, or plaque.
Plaque accumulation results in inﬂammation of the gingiva.
Plaque can become mineralized, resulting in calculus deposition
(Fig. 125.2). The deposition of calculus facilitates additional
plaque formation and periodontal inﬂammation.
In dogs, periodontitis is associated with proliferation of grampositive and gram-negative anaerobic organisms that belong to
the Firmicutes, Actinobacteria (such as Actinomyces spp.),
Bacteroidetes (especially Porphyromonas spp. and Fusobacterium
spp.), and Spirochaetes (e.g., Treponema spp.). 13 , 14 In humans,
periodontitis has been associated with an increased population of
Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Treponema
denticola (collectively referred to as “the red complex”). 15 Pups
have very few Porphyromonas species in their dental plaque;
however, bacterial numbers increase as puppies mature and
inevitably periodontal disease develops. Although spirochetes
such as Treponema spp. have been considered important
pathogens in canine periodontal disease, one study found no
diﬀerence in the prevalence of various Treponema species as
detected using nucleic acid–based methods in gingival plaque
from dogs with and without periodontal disease. 16

vetexamprep.ir

TABLE 125.1

Subgingival plaque incites an inﬂammatory response in the
gingival tissue that can lead to chronic periodontal disease with
eventual loss of teeth. Early bacterial damage occurs in the
subgingival epithelial tissues with penetration of the interdental
rete pegs. Many bacteria possess proteolytic enzymes that allow
them to colonize and invade periodontal tissues. Periodontal
pathogens destroy the integrity of the dentition and oral mucosae.
Endodontal disease and periodontitis can also develop
whenever tooth damage occurs, exposing the dental pulp. Acute
periapical periodontitis (i.e., periapical lesion) begins within 20
days of pulp exposure in dogs and progresses with time. 17
Fractures of teeth usually result in pulp infection before
revascularization of the canal by vital tissue can occur. In
advanced human root canal infections, anaerobes, corynebacteria,
and streptococci predominate. 18 Although not widely practiced in
veterinary medicine and human endodontics, debridement and

vetexamprep.ir

treatment of the canal with a triple antibacterial paste
(ciproﬂoxacin, minocycline, and metronidazole) in a resorbable
matrix base early after injury may eliminate endodontal infection
and promote revascularization of the pulp canal. 19
Radiographic examination of the teeth and associated bony
structures is required to determine the condition of the tooth roots
and secondary bone or tooth resorption before treatment.
Furthermore, endodontal involvement, neoplastic destruction of
bone, and nasal and sinus passages can be evaluated to determine
the extent of disease before treatment.
Treatment includes the extraction of severely aﬀected teeth,
debridement of necrotic or proliferative gingival margins, root
planing with cure es, and scaling calculi from the remaining
involved supragingival and subgingival dental surfaces by
manual or ultrasonic means. Complete removal of all
supragingival and subgingival calculus and plaque is essential in
control of periodontal disease. More aggressive surgical
debridement is needed for advanced periodontal disease.
Although bacterial pathogens are important in periodontitis,
antimicrobial therapy alone does not eliminate progression of
disease. Because proinﬂammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, Il-1β,
and matrix metalloproteinases have been important in the
progression of periodontal disease, a variety of anti-inﬂammatory
and immunomodulatory drugs and dietary supplements have
been examined as treatments. 20 , 21 Genetic predisposition to
periodontal disease in humans may reﬂect diﬀerences in cytokine
responses to invasion of tissues by oral cavity bacteria. 21 Oral
IFN-α administered to dogs and cats with naturally occurring
gingivitis reduced both periodontal bacterial counts and
associated gingival inﬂammation. 22 , 23 The use of antiinﬂammatory diets or supplements with omega-3 fa y acids may
reduce the local gingival inﬂammatory response and has shown
some beneﬁt in small human clinical trials. 24 However, a
prospective study in dogs showed no beneﬁt for reduction of
gingivitis, plaque, or calculus when a diet supplemented with
either corn oil or ﬁsh oil was fed. 25

Although administration of systemic antimicrobial drugs such
as tetracyclines, clindamycin, metronidazole, and tinidazole have
been shown to reduce gingivitis, plaque accumulation, halitosis,
and alveolar bone resorption in dogs and cats, 26-28 the use and
eﬃcacy of systemic antimicrobial therapy for this purpose has
been questioned as an alternative for indicated dental procedures
29 and may select for antimicrobial-resistant bacterial populations.
Currently it is recommended by AAHA that the use of systemic
antimicrobials in conjunction with dental procedures be
considered on a case-by-case basis. 30 In most cases, antimicrobials
are not required. Postoperative treatment with clindamycin or
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is indicated for at least 7 to 14 days if
there is radiographic evidence of osteomyelitis. 30 Treatment for
several days before surgery has been suggested for animals with
Stage IV disease to facilitate tissue handling, but this may not be
necessary and has the potential to select for resistant bacteria.
Perioceutics are pharmaceutical formulations that are placed
into periodontal pockets to allow for sustained antimicrobial
activity against periodontal pathogens. They are used as an
adjunct to scaling and cleaning the dental surfaces. The

vetexamprep.ir

perioceutics containing antimicrobials are delivered into the
periodontal pocket via a blunt cannula. Once there, the
biodegradable polymer gels coagulate, allowing for sustained
release of the drug for up to 13 weeks. Products that contain 2%
clindamycin gel or 8.5% doxycycline hyclate are available for
veterinary use. 12 Their use has been recommended by AAHA
when a > 5-mm cleaned pocket exists in dogs with Stage II or
Stage III periodontal disease. However, one study evaluated the
use of these gels in conjunction with closed root planing in dogs
with periodontal pockets that ranged from 3.5 to 5.5 mm deep. 12
Use of the gels did not lead to greater improvement in periodontal
disease indices over closed root planing alone.
Long-term intermi ent periodontal care for dogs is highly
recommended because it slows the progression of gingival
recession and depth of periodontal crevices that develop in dogs
not receiving dental hygiene. 31 Gingival enlargement and abscess
formation are sequelae of calculus formation. 32 The type of
microﬂora present, diet, and the animal’s chewing habits may
inﬂuence the formation of calculus. 33 , 34 Daily tooth brushing is
more eﬀective than diet for optimization of oral health in dogs; in
one study it was three times as eﬀective at controlling plaque
accumulation than a dental diet or daily dental chews. 35 Tooth
brushing has also been shown to be eﬀective in cats. 36 , 37 The use
of special diets supplemented with dental chews can reduce
calculus deposition further in dogs and cats. 37 Feeding of a
commercial dental food to dogs signiﬁcantly reduced plaque and
gingivitis by 39% and 36%, respectively, compared with daily
feeding of a control dry-food diet. 38 Cats fed large kibbles with
mechanical cleaning qualities had less gingivitis and calculus than
cats on small kibble diets with or without daily brushing. 39
Flushing dental surfaces once daily with 0.1% to 0.2%
chlorhexidine and/or alternate-day brushing may delay
accumulation of dental calculus. A commercial product
formulated especially for dental purposes (Nolvadent, Zoetis)
does not stain teeth blue like other chlorhexidine formulations.
Daily application of chlorhexidine gel was eﬀective in reducing
recurrence of dental plaque in dogs. 40 Numerous cleansers and
brushes have been developed for daily brushing of dogs’ teeth,
and they warrant consideration when a dog has a tendency to

vetexamprep.ir

form calculus. Oral probiotics have been examined for their ability
to prevent the growth of pathogenic bacteria or modulate mucosal
immunity in the oral cavity. Oral probiotic bacteria should adhere
to and colonize on dental tissue and should be part of the bioﬁlm.
They should not ferment sugars, which subsequently lowers the
pH and is detrimental to dental health. 41 A split-mouth, doubleblind randomized pilot study, involving eight beagle dogs with
moderate experimentally induced periodontitis, documented the
impact of multiple subgingival applications of pellets containing
Streptococcus sanguinis, Streptococcus salivarius, and Streptococcus
mitis. 42 The bone density within periodontal pockets treated with
the beneﬁcial bacteria improved signiﬁcantly after 12 weeks,
whereas there was a nonsigniﬁcant change in the control group
that received a single root planing at baseline. In addition, there
was a signiﬁcant increase in the alveolar bone level at the end of
the study based on repeat radiographs compared to the control
group. Unfortunately, a randomized controlled clinical trial in
humans with Stage III periodontitis showed no beneﬁt of a
Lactobacillus probiotic or azithromycin as an adjunct to scaling and
root planing. 43 Also, a study that examined the eﬀect of an oral
probiotic containing Enterococcus faecium (Fortiﬂora, Purina)
showed no change in the oral microbiota of dogs, which remained
stable over a 7-week time period regardless of diet or
administration of the probiotic. 44 More needs to be known about
what organisms are capable of restoring and maintaining health
when delivered in a probiotic format. The Veterinary Oral Health
Council website lists products that have been shown to be
eﬀective for retarding plaque and calculus deposition in dogs and
cats (vohc.org/all_accepted_products.html).
A P. denticanis-gulae-salivosa bacterin that was commercially
available as an aid in preventing periodontal disease is no longer
licensed due to concerns surrounding lack of eﬃcacy.
Systemic Effects of Oral or Periodontal Infections
Ophthalmic manifestations can occur from dental disease because
of the close proximity of the caudal maxillary teeth and the orbit.
Systemic complications of periodontal disease, including cerebral
and myocardial infarction, systemic hypertension, adverse
pregnancy outcomes and early mortality, have been described in

vetexamprep.ir

people. 45 , 46 Human patients with poorly controlled diabetes
mellitus are at an increased risk of developing periodontal disease
47 and resolution of periodontal inﬂammation can improve
metabolic control of blood glucose in diabetics. 48
Associations between periodontal inﬂammation and heart
(endocarditis, cardiomyopathy), liver, and kidney (CKD) disease
have been reported in dogs. 49-53 These have included studies that
have correlated lesions at necropsy with whole mouth periodontal
scoring. In other retrospective studies, no statistical association
was found between bacterial endocarditis in dogs and either
dental or oral surgical procedures or oral infection. 54 , 55
However, detailed prospective screening and grading of oral
cavity changes were not undertaken in these studies.
Bacteremia associated with dental manipulations may be
subclinical or has the potential to cause sepsis or subsequently
result in bacterial endocarditis or localized embolic tissue
infections (see Chapter 122). In cats with periodontitis undergoing
dental scaling and extraction, 36% had positive blood culture
results at the time of the dental procedures. 56 Bacteria most
commonly
isolated
were
Cutibacterium
(formerly
Propionibacterium) acnes, Pasteurella multocida, and Staphylococcus
epidermidis. None of the cats subsequently became ill. Similarly,
blood culture results have shown subclinical bacteremia in 30% of
dogs with periodontal disease undergoing periodontal treatment
and tooth extraction, although a group of control dogs that were
anesthetized but that did not undergo dental procedures had a
similar prevalence of bacteremia. 57 It is generally recommended
that dental procedures should not be performed at the same time
as other surgical procedures, because the release of bacteria from
the dental procedure may have the potential to establish
themselves in tissue injured or devitalized by routine surgical
procedures, sutures, or foreign implants. Current guidelines from
AAHA recommend that intraoperative antibiotic administration
be used for immunosuppressed animals or those with implants or
subaortic stenosis to reduce the likelihood of bacteremia. A
rational approach is to follow the recommendations for
prophylactic antimicrobial use for “dirty” surgical procedures or
when the implications of a surgical site infection may be
devastating (see Chapter 76). In summary, the goal is to maintain

vetexamprep.ir

therapeutic drug levels throughout the period of risk by
administering the ﬁrst dose IV 30 to 60 minutes before starting the
procedure, with intraoperative dosing every 2 half-lives of the
antimicrobial as long as the procedure is underway. Ampicillin is
a rational choice for dental procedures, and it has a half-life of 20
minutes in the dog and 72 minutes in the cat, meaning
intraoperative redosing is indicated every 40 and 145 minutes,
respectively. Prerinsing the oral cavity with chlorhexidine
solutions can also be performed just before the procedure. Drug
administration should be terminated no longer than 24 hours after
the dental procedure because no additional beneﬁts are gained
and additional antimicrobial exposure increases the risk of
selection for resistant bacteria. Interestingly, IV administration of
aqueous penicillin during ultrasonic scaling in dogs did not alter
the prevalence of bacteremia before or after dental manipulation.
58 More studies are required to examine the eﬀects of
intraoperative antimicrobial administration on bacteremia in dogs
undergoing dental procedures and whether prophylaxis impacts
outcomes.
Because of the large numbers of bacteria in the oral cavity and
especially the gingival crevices, public health considerations are
important when dental procedures are performed. Face masks,
ocular shields, and gloves should always be worn by humans who
clean animals’ teeth. In addition, bioﬁlms that form on the inside
surface of water lines of ultrasonic scalers may harbor Legionella
species, which might produce acute pneumonia in susceptible
individuals. 59

Glossitis and Stomatitis
Glossitis may be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protozoa.
Fungi such as Blastomyces spp. and protozoa such as Leishmania
spp. typically cause nodular tongue lesions. 60 Viral causes in dogs
include CDV, canine calicivirus, and CPV. In cats, FCV and FHV-1
can cause lingual ulceration as well as ulceration of the buccal
mucosa. Ricke sia ricke sii can cause lingual ulceration as a result
of endothelial cell damage. Primary physical injury can occur via
trauma, bite wounds, burns, caustic substances, and foreign
bodies, with secondary infection with bacteria or Candida spp.
Lesions in the mouth that disrupt the normal host barriers include

vetexamprep.ir

those caused by eosinophilic granuloma complex and neoplasms
such as squamous cell carcinoma and epitheliotropic T-cell
lymphoma. Systemic disorders that may lead to lingual ulceration
include uremia; autoimmune diseases such as pemphigus
vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, erythema multiforme, and systemic
lupus erythematosus; and embolic disease (including septic
thromboemboli). Organisms are not often found on histologic
examination; however, suppuration and overlying ulceration are
usually apparent. Foreign material such as hair, bone, or plant
ma er can be present in lingual wound infections.
The most prevalent disorders associated with gingivostomatitis
in dogs and cats are canine chronic ulcerative stomatitis (CUS;
also known as chronic ulcerative paradental stomatitis) and feline
gingivostomatitis. Canine CUS is a chronic painful ulcerative
condition of the mouth with an unclear pathogenesis. 61
Predisposed breeds include the Maltese terrier, Cavalier King
Charles spaniel, greyhound, and Labrador retriever. Male
neutered dogs are also overrepresented. Ulcers typically occur on
the buccal mucosa opposite the dental plaque, but can also occur
on the lateral margins of the tongue, the palatoglossal folds, and
the mucocutaneous border of the lips (Fig. 125.3). Histopathology
reveals a lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrate at the interface between the
mucosal epithelium and the subepithelial connective tissue that is
comprised of CD79+ B cells, plasma cells, CD3+ T cells, and
regulatory T cells. 61 , 62 There has also been evidence of IL-17
expression in the lesions, a cytokine that is often associated with
regulation of autoimmune diseases. Infectious agents have not
been identiﬁed in association with CUS. Extraction of teeth
opposite the ulcers may result in clinical improvement. 61

Feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS) is a common and
painful disease of the oral cavity characterized by inﬂammation of
the buccal and caudal oral mucosa, lateral to the palatoglossal
folds. Ulcerative/erosive and proliferative phenotypes have been
described (Fig. 125.4). 63 Often young adult cats are aﬀected, and
in some cats there may be minimal evidence of accompanying
periodontal disease. However, most cats with FCGS often have
signiﬁcant generalized periodontitis and are more likely to have
external inﬂammatory root resorptive lesions. 64 Aﬀected cats may
show evidence of dysphagia with reduced appetite, weight loss,
halitosis, ptyalism, pawing at the mouth, and reduced grooming.
Some of the signs may also result from esophagitis, which has
been detected using endoscopy in aﬀected cats. 65
Although a variety of infectious agents have been associated
with this disorder, direct causation has not been proven because
most of the pathogens postulated to play a role commonly infect
cats without causing clinical signs; these have included FeLV, FIV,
FCV, FHV-1, and Bartonella spp. 63 , 66-68 The strongest associations
have been made with FCV infections, although not all evidence
has supported a role for this virus (see Chapter 35). 63 Disease

vetexamprep.ir

pp
(

)
may occur in a number of cats within a household and tends to be
recurrent after the initial treatment or is unresponsive to
treatment. Cessation of FCV shedding was associated with
resolution of chronic gingivostomatitis in one cat. 67 Coinfections
with FIV or FeLV may result in more severe lesions. In one study,
cats with chronic gingivostomatitis were more likely to shed FCV
and FHV-1 together than either virus alone. 68 Biopsy of aﬀected
regions reveals lymphoplasmacytic inﬂammation. Large numbers
of B cells and both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells can be found within the
lesions, as well as regulatory T cells. 69 In another study,
compared with nondiseased cats, aﬀected cats showed a
signiﬁcant increase in expression of IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12
(p35 and p40), and IFN-γ. 70 The predominant bacterial species
present in the oral cavity of cats with FCGS in one study with
Pasteurella multocida subsp. multocida. 71 Hyperproteinemia due to
a polyclonal gammopathy is often present on the serum chemistry
panel, and may be moderate to severe, likely reﬂective of chronic
antigenic stimulation.
Treatment with antibiotics that have activity against anaerobes
(such as clindamycin) can result in some improvement; however,
the response is temporary. Other medical treatments that have
been used are topical lactoferrin and oral IFN-ω (see Chapter 9).
Treatment with prednisolone may also result in some clinical
improvement, but long-term treatment tends to have gradual
reduction in eﬃcacy and is not recommended because of adverse
eﬀects. 63 Although the number of cats was small, treatment with
cyclosporine also seemed to be eﬀective when compared to a
placebo-treated group, and 5 of 11 cats followed for 3 or more
months remained in remission. 72 If cyclosporine is used,
measurement of trough concentrations is recommended on a
regular basis to avoid excessive immunosuppression, and the
drug should be used at the lowest possible dose that controls
clinical signs. To date, the most eﬀective treatment has been
proper management of periodontal disease, and, for refractory
cases, partial- or full-mouth tooth extractions. Because the
outcome following extraction of all premolar and molar teeth does
not appear to diﬀer signiﬁcantly from that following full-mouth
extractions, premolar-molar extraction has been recommended
initially, moving to full-mouth extraction 1 to 4 months later if

vetexamprep.ir

there is insuﬃcient reduction in clinical signs. 63 , 73 In cases with
generalized periodontitis and stomatitis, full-mouth tooth
extraction is recommended. It is estimated that approximately
20% to 30% of cats will show minimal or no improvement.

Infections of the Esophagus and Stomach
Infections of the esophageal wall in dogs and cats usually follow
esophageal perforation or full-thickness ulceration secondary to
foreign bodies, esophageal neoplasia, or gastroesophageal reﬂux
during anesthesia. 74 Uncommon infectious causes of esophagitis
that have been documented in dogs include Candida spp.
esophagitis and Pythium insidiosum esophagitis. Candida spp. were
isolated from two immunocompromised chow-chow puppies that
were coinfected with CAdV-2 and CDV, 75 and Pythium-associated
esophagitis was conﬁrmed on necropsy in two dogs from rural
Tennessee, USA. 76 One of the authors (SLM) has also conﬁrmed
Pythium-associated esophagitis in three dysphagic large-breed
hunting dogs from northern California via esophageal biopsy and
immunohistochemistry, and positive serum anti-P. insidiosum
ELISA. Nevertheless, uncommon complications, esophageal
abscesses, mediastinal empyema, or pyothorax may result.
Migrating plant awns have been incriminated as an underlying
cause in some cases. 77 Clinical signs include inappetence,
ptyalism, fever, lethargy, weight loss, regurgitation, odynophagia,
tachypnea, cough, and abdominal pain. 77 , 78 One dog developed
respiratory distress secondary to tracheal collapse and bilateral
laryngeal paralysis that were associated with a paratracheal
abscess that had entrapped the recurrent laryngeal nerves. 79 Plain
radiography may show evidence of pleural eﬀusion or mass
lesions associated with the esophagus. CT imaging and
ultrasound may also be useful for visualizing esophageal abscess
lesions. 77 , 78 Esophagoscopy ﬁndings were normal in several
dogs and a cat with caudal mediastinal paraesophageal abscesses.
77 , 78 Treatment has generally involved open surgical drainage
(lateral thoracotomy or median sternotomy) or omentalization
through a diaphragmatic incision. Antimicrobials indicated for
pyothorax are likely to be appropriate for paraesophageal
abscesses.

Because of the acidic milieu of the stomach and the presence of
pepsin, the stomach has relatively low concentrations of resident
microﬂora relative to other portions of the GI tract, and bacterial
gastritis and gastric abscesses rarely occur. Physaloptera spp.
infection can cause gastritis, and should be considered in dogs
and cats with chronic vomiting, especially those with a history of
consuming insects or vertebrate prey (see Chapter 116). A higher
dose and longer duration of fenbendazole in combination with
pyrantel pamoate is recommended for treatment of suspected or
conﬁrmed infections. Reinfection is common in some dogs and
should not be viewed as treatment failure. Ollulanus tricuspis
nematodes are worms found in the gastric mucosa of the cat, and
rarely in dogs. 80 , 81 The parasite has a direct life cycle and does
not require an intermediate host. Clinical signs of chronic
vomiting, weight loss, and anorexia are most commonly reported.
Eﬀective therapies include tetramisole at 5 mg/kg (single dose)
and fenbendazole at 50 mg/kg (PO q24h for 5 days).
The reader is referred to Chapter 66 for information on gastric
helicobacteriosis.

Infections of the Intestinal Tract
The Intestinal Microbiome
Concentrations of bacteria in the proximal small bowel are
relatively low because of the inﬂuence of gastric acid and bile, but
they gradually increase toward the ileocecal region. Numbers of

vetexamprep.ir

microorganisms in the distal small bowel or the large bowel are
not aﬀected by feeding and remain relatively constant after meals.
Increased numbers of resident organisms may be found in the
stomach and upper small intestine, or pathogenic organisms may
proliferate when normal bowel defenses are impaired. Excessive
use of acid suppressants, intestinal obstruction, ileus, impaired
bile acid signaling, exocrine pancreatic insuﬃciency, or decreased
mucosal or IgA secretions can result in disruption of the normal
microbiome and bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine. 82 In
contrast to cats with GI illness, clinically healthy cats have much
higher concentrations of bacteria in the duodenum and jejunum.
83 , 84

Puppies and ki ens lacking normal microﬂora at birth derive
their microﬂora from exposure to their dam and li ermates or
from their environment by 2 to 3 weeks of life. 85 Studies
performed using 16S rRNA gene PCR methods have shown that
the composition of the intestinal microﬂora may change with age
in dogs and cats, with Enterobacterales and enterococci
decreasing in abundance with age in cats, and lactobacilli and
enterococci decreasing in abundance with age in dogs. 86 , 87
Another study that used 16S rRNA gene PCR showed that the
microbial diversity in dogs tended to decrease as dogs aged. 88
Changes in diet, nutritional status, and physiologic state of the
host may inﬂuence the proportions of residing bacteria. 2 , 89 Small
intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) in dogs is a condition
thought to result from dysbiosis, and is most commonly
associated with exocrine pancreatic insuﬃciency, ileus,
malabsorption of nutrients, and deﬁciency of sIgA. The diagnosis
of SIBO is a topic of debate, because it has traditionally been
deﬁned as proliferation of small intestinal bacteria to
concentrations > 105/mL, which have now been identiﬁed even in
healthy dogs. 90 The term “intestinal dysbiosis” is far more
common in dogs, and refers to an alteration of the intestinal
microbiota independent of bacterial numbers.
In general, the important phyla that make up the intestinal
microbiota in dogs and cats are Fusobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and
Firmicutes. Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria are the two other
major taxa present. Some of the more important genera are

vetexamprep.ir

Fusobacterium, Lactobacillus, Streptococcus (dogs) and Enterococcus
(cats), Clostridium, Prevotella, and Bacteroides.
Use of 16S rRNA gene pyrosequencing has shown that the
stomach of healthy dogs is primarily occupied by Proteobacteria
(99.6%), with a predominance of Helicobacter. The remaining
organisms belong to the Firmicutes, primarily Lactobacillus. 82 The
duodenum and upper jejunum primarily harbor aerobes and
facultative anaerobes. The main phyla of the duodenum in dogs
are
Firmicutes
(approximately
45%),
Proteobacteria
(approximately 20%), and Bacteroidetes (approximately 10%). 82 ,
91 Prevalent orders in duodenal ﬂuid have included Clostridiales
and Lactobacillales, with only low numbers of the anaerobes
Fusobacteriales and Bacteroidales. 92 In the jejunal mucosa, the
ratio of Firmicutes to Proteobacteria appears to change, with one
study showing 47% of the microbiome to be Proteobacteria
(primarily Gamma Proteobacteria) and 15% to be Firmicutes; the
remaining phyla were Spirochaetes (15%), Actinobacteria (11%),
Bacteroidetes (6%), and Fusobacteria (4%). 93 In jejunal ﬂuid,
Clostridiales and Lactobacillales remained prevalent, but
Enterobacterales and Fusobacteriales were identiﬁed in greater
concentrations than in duodenal juice. 93 In colonic contents,
Proteobacteria have diminished dramatically (comprising < 2% of
organisms; this includes E. coli) and the population is dominated
by Fusobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes, in even
distribution. 93 The same phyla are found in canine fecal
specimens, although the distribution has varied among studies; in
most studies, Firmicutes have comprised a signiﬁcant proportion
of organisms, especially clostridia. 94 The maximum numbers of
microorganisms and the greatest biodiversity are found in the
large intestine when compared with the small intestine. 92 A
single gram of feces contains 1011 to 1012 organisms and 15,000 to
36,000 diﬀerent species. 95 , 96 The concentration of many
anaerobes is reduced in the feces during diarrhea because these
organisms normally require intestinal stasis and low oxygen
tension for growth.
The composition and concentration of the intestinal microﬂora
is altered in dogs with GI disease. For example, in one study of
dogs with acute diarrhea, episodes of diarrhea were associated
with increased abundance of Clostridiales (especially Clostridium

vetexamprep.ir

perfringens) and enterococci. 97 In dogs with inﬂammatory bowel
disease (IBD), one study showed reduced species richness and a
higher proportion of Enterobacterales; 91 another found a greater
proportion of Proteobacteria and a lower abundance of Clostridia.
98 Dogs with chronic enteropathies (food-responsive, antibioticresponsive, or immunosuppressant-responsive) are also
signiﬁcantly more likely to have positive dysbiosis indices when
compared with healthy dogs. 5 Although treatment of dogs with
immunosuppressant-responsive enteropathies (IBD) results in
clinical improvement, microbial dysbiosis may persist. 99
The eﬀect of intestinal disease on the GI microbiome in cats has
also been examined, although relatively few studies exist. In
addition, studies that have examined the microbiome of healthy
cats have had somewhat conﬂicting results, with diﬀerent
percentages of the major phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroides,
Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria) varying between individuals
and being inﬂuenced by age and diet. 100 , 101 A study that used
Illumina sequencing showed that cats with chronic enteropathies
(IBD and alimentary small cell lymphoma) had reduced fecal
bacterial population diversity when compared with healthy cats,
with an increase in Enterobacterales and Streptococcaceae and a
decrease in abundance of organisms that belonged to the phyla
Firmicutes and Actinobacteria (Biﬁdobacterium) and Bacteroidetes.
102 There were no detectable diﬀerences between cats with IBD
and cats with small cell lymphoma.
The prevalence and diversity of fungal organisms in the GI tract
of dogs and cats has had limited study. The most abundant
phylum in both healthy dogs and dogs with acute diarrhea in one
study that used pyrosequencing was Ascomycota (approximately
98%), followed by Basidiomycota (1%). 103 In both groups, the
most abundant genus was Candida, the primary species being
Candida natalensis. In another study that used similar
methodology, Ascomycota was the most abundant phylum in
dogs and the only phylum identiﬁed in cats. 104 In that study, the
most abundant genus in dogs was Nacaseomyces and in cats were
Saccharomyces and Aspergillus.
The Effect of Diet on the Microbiome

vetexamprep.ir

Dietary composition can impact the diversity and abundance of
diﬀerent bacterial species in the microbiome. In one study,
feeding a raw food diet to dogs was associated with increased
abundance of Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria in the fecal
microbiota; in dogs fed a commercial diet, Firmicutes were more
abundant. 89 It is important to consider the diﬀerences in the
macronutrient composition of raw and commercial diets, because
the increased ﬁber and carbohydrate in a commercial extruded
diet can impact the microbiota signiﬁcantly. A prebiotic is deﬁned
as a “nondigestible food ingredient which beneﬁcially aﬀects the
host by selectively stimulating the growth of and/or activates the
metabolism of one or a limited number of health-promoting
bacteria in the intestinal tract.” 105 A variety of prebiotics have
been added to dog and cat diets in order to promote GI health.
The most common prebiotics studied are fructans, although other
prebiotics such as mannans, lactosucrose, and lactulose are also
being evaluated. Short-chain fructooligosaccharides (scFOSs) are
polymers of glucose that have been added to commercial diets as
a source of soluble ﬁber. They occur naturally in plants or
mammalian milk, or are synthesized from fermentation. Chicory
root is one example of a naturally occurring source of scFOS.
Other natural sources rich in soluble ﬁber are oat bran or wheat
pulp. scFOSs are not digested by the mammalian small intestine,
and they reach the colon intact. There they are fermented by
anaerobic bacteria such as Biﬁdobacterium spp. or lactobacilli into
short-chain fa y acids such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate.
These anaerobic organisms proliferate and inhibit growth of other
potentially pathogenic microbes such as Clostridium species and E.
coli. Fructan supplementation a enuated some of the pathologic
responses to experimental Salmonella challenge of weanling pups.
106 In general, studies evaluating the eﬀect of dietary
supplementation with scFOS have shown an increase in fecal
biﬁdobacteria and lower fecal clostridia numbers in dogs. 94
However, these studies relied upon traditional culture methods to
identify and quantify relative proportions of bacteria. When 16S
rRNA gene pyrosequencing was used to assess the eﬀect of a diet
that contained beet pulp on fecal microbiota in dogs, the
abundance of Clostridia increased within the Firmicutes and the
abundance of the phyla Actinobacteria and Fusobacteria
decreased. 107 The appearance of butyrate-producing bacterial

vetexamprep.ir

pp
y
p
g
species that may possess anti-inﬂammatory eﬀects was also noted.
Administration of a scFOS or pectin-based diet to cats was
associated with an increase in the abundance of Biﬁdobacterium
and Lactobacillus, respectively, when compared with a control diet.
108 In this study, genus-speciﬁc PCR assays were used to amplify
bacterial DNA.
Probiotics
Probiotics are viable microorganisms that, when administered
orally in adequate amounts, confer a health beneﬁt on the host.
Enterococci, lactobacilli, and biﬁdobacteria—normal colonic
inhabitants—have often been administered after antimicrobial
treatment, intestinal infections, weaning, stress, or dietary changes
in an a empt to reestablish the intestinal microbiota. Many of
these microorganisms become transient constituents of the enteric
microﬂora. In humans, these bacteria have been administered in
the form of yogurt, cheese, and milk products, and eﬀorts have
been made to include these in canine and feline diets. Theoretical
beneﬁts of probiotics include the production of antibacterial
substances (bacteriocins) and competitive inhibition of pathogen
and toxin adherence to the intestinal epithelium, reestablishment
of enteric microﬂora after antimicrobial treatment, enhancement
of host innate immunity, regulation of host immune responses,
and regulation of intestinal epithelial cell functions. Synbiotics are
combinations of prebiotics and probiotics.
A number of studies addressing the role of probiotics in the
management of canine and feline diarrhea have been published to
date, with most studies evaluating the eﬃcacy of this therapeutic
modality for the management of acute diarrhea, and results have
been mixed depending on the type of probiotic and the
underlying disorder being managed. The eﬀect of probiotics in
both healthy dogs and those with enteropathies have been
published, with mixed results. Two studies were randomized,
placebo-controlled clinical trials of dogs with food-responsive
enteropathy. 109 , 110 In one of those studies, all of the dogs
clinically improved when placed on an elimination diet. However,
they showed no speciﬁc changes in the inﬂammatory cytokine
pa erns or any speciﬁc beneﬁt of a probiotic. 109 In the second
study, 110 dogs with acute diarrhea, with or without vomiting,
were divided into placebo or probiotic groups. The probiotic

vetexamprep.ir

p
p
g
p
p
formulation consisted of a mixture of live strains of Lactobacillus,
Bacillus, and Pediococcus species. The mean time from treatment to
resolution of the diarrhea was 1 day shorter in the probiotic
group. Administration of Lactobacillus keﬁri to dogs, a species
found in keﬁr, had no impact on fecal IgA concentrations or the
composition of the microbiome. 111 Several publications have
described beneﬁcial eﬀects in prospective studies of a probiotic
that contains four strains of Lactobacillus, three strains of
Biﬁdobacterium, and Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus.
Treatment of dogs with IBD with this probiotic in one randomized
study appeared to have the same eﬀect as treatment with
metronidazole and prednisone, with improvement in clinical and
histopathological scores. 99 In another multicenter study, dogs
with IBD were randomized to receive treatment with diet and
prednisone alone; or diet, prednisone, and the eight-strain
probiotic. 112 There was rapid clinical remission in both groups
over 60 days despite no improvement in inﬂammation assessed
histopathologically; dogs treated with diet and prednisone alone
had an increase in Biﬁdobacterium spp. using FISH on endoscopic
biopsies, and those treated with the probiotic had an increase in
Lactobacillus spp. Treatment of healthy dogs with this 8-strain
probiotic preparation as a dietary supplement for 60 days resulted
in a decrease in the abundance of C. perfringens and an increase in
the abundance of Biﬁdobacterium and Lactobacillus spp. when
compared to a control group fed the diet alone. 113 Treatment of
healthy dogs and dogs with food-responsive diarrhea with a
synbiotic that contained Enterococcus faecium, FOS, and gum arabic
had no impact on fecal microbiota diversity or richness. 114
Additional studies are warranted in dogs to further assess the
immunomodulatory eﬀects of probiotics and to evaluate their
safety.
There are fewer publications pertaining to probiotic use in cats,
and one randomized, placebo-controlled study in 217 shelter cats
administered the probiotic, Enterococcus faecium SF68 or placebo,
showed that the percentage of cats with diarrhea ≥ 2 days was
signiﬁcantly lower (P = 0.03) in the probiotic group (7.4%) when
compared with the placebo group (20.7%). 115 One study showed
that a microencapsulated probiotic formulation that contained
three Lactobacillus species—Biﬁdobacterium biﬁdum, Enterococcus

vetexamprep.ir

faecium, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae—was able to modulate the
fecal microbiota of healthy cats by increasing lactic acid bacterial
counts. 116 A mixture of FOS and gum arabic was used for
encapsulation. Treatment of laboratory-reared cats with
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for 7 days with or without Enterococcus
faecium strain SF68 for 14 days was associated with decreased
microbiome diversity in both groups, with no detectable
diﬀerences between groups. 117 However, the probiotic-treated
cats had improved diarrhea scores when compared with the cats
treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid alone.
Fecal Microbiota Transplantation
FMT can be infused by various methods, including nasogastric
tube,
nasojejunal
tube,
upper
tract
endoscopy
(esophagogastroduodenoscopy), colonoscopy, or retention enema,
and has been used to treat dysbiosis associated with a wide array
of disorders in humans. The therapeutic modality has recently
received a ention for treatment of refractory chronic
enteropathies and acute diarrheas in dogs and cats. A fresh fecal
specimen is collected from a healthy donor dog or cat, mixed with
saline or another isotonic solution, ﬁltered to remove particulate
ma er, and administered by endoscopy into the colon or enema.
Repeated treatments may be given on a regular basis (such as
every 3 to 5 days or even on a weekly basis). An optimum method
of preparation, dose, or dosing frequency has not been
established. Apparent clinical responses to treatment have
occurred in animals that were refractory to traditional medical
therapies. 118 , 119 In one report, the fecal microbiome of a recipient
dog converted to that of the donor after multiple treatments, with
a dramatic decrease in the abundance of Proteobacteria and
increase in the abundance of Fusobacteria. 118 As in humans,
randomized prospective studies are required to evaluate the
eﬃcacy of FMT to treat enteropathies in dogs and cats. Although
complications associated with FMT are extremely infrequent in
people, the risk of infectious hazards needs to be taken seriously,
particularly in recipients who are severely immunocompromised.
A recent report of infection with extended-spectrum betalactamase (ESBL)-producing E. coli in two human patients
following FMT underscores the importance of comprehensive

vetexamprep.ir

screening of donors and of the material to be transplanted. 120
Both of the ill recipients had severe underlying diseases – cirrhosis
with hepatic encephalopathy in one and hematologic dysplasia
treated by means of hematopoietic-cell transplantation in the
other. Both patients also had concomitant and previous use of
antibiotics that were broadly active against gut luminal bacteria,
which may have diminished the microbiota that normally provide
resistance to introduced pathogens. Both recipients developed
severe infections following FMT and one of the patients died after
they received FMT capsules from the same donor. It is readily
apparent that FMT may carry risks that can only be identiﬁed
after the fact, and improved screening of FMT donors and of the
material to be transplanted should help reduce the risks of
infections by known pathogens. It is highly probable that as the
use of FMT is broadened in veterinary medicine and more
compromised patients are treated, complications may be more
frequently observed.
Bacterial Translocation
The GI tract is a known reservoir of microorganisms, which under
certain circumstances can spread via the portal circulation or
intestinal lymphatics to extraintestinal sites, including the
mesenteric lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and pancreas, and to other
organs by systemic circulation. In one study of 50 clinically
healthy entire females undergoing ovariohysterectomy, a variety
of aerobic and anaerobic bacterial species could be isolated using
culture from the mesenteric lymph nodes of 26 dogs; in most dogs
a single isolate was obtained. 121 Corresponding peripheral
venous and portal venous blood cultures yielded a gram-positive
coccus and a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species from the
peripheral blood of one of the dogs. It is highly plausible that the
prevalence of bacterial translocation in healthy dogs is even
higher than that documented in this study given the limitations
and insensitivity of routine bacterial culture compared to
molecular-based methods. In the human literature, bacterial
translocation has been divided into “healthy” translocation,
whereby bacteria and fragments of bacteria (DNA, LPS,
peptidoglycan, ﬂagellin) are continuously presented to the
reticuloendothelial system in the liver and serve to promote host
immunity. In contrast, “pathologic” bacterial translocation occurs

vetexamprep.ir

when signiﬁcant numbers of bacteria are able to cross a damaged
intestinal barrier in a sustained manner and cause or contribute to
disease (Fig. 125.5).
Pathologic bacterial translocation occurs with conditions of
reduced mucosal perfusion; these can result from systemic
hypotension, decreased peristalsis (such as with intestinal
obstruction or ileus), intestinal resection, abdominal trauma,
burns, abdominal radiation therapy, pancreatitis, and obstructive
biliary disease. Paradoxically, antimicrobial therapy has been
shown to promote bacterial translocation in mouse models. 122
Administration of glucocorticoids or NSAIDs can result in
reduction in GI mucus production, a normal protective defense of
the bowel against bacteria. In one study of 448 humans
undergoing laparotomy in the United Kingdom, bacterial
translocation was detected in 15% of patients, with the main
species isolated being E. coli. 123 Furthermore, 41% of patients that
had evidence of bacterial translocation developed septic
complications, compared with only 14% of those that did not have
evidence of bacterial translocation. Furthermore, gut microbes
were responsible for the majority of septic events. Bacteria may
translocate via transcellular or paracellular pathways; paracellular
translocation of bacteria and LPS is facilitated by disruption of
tight junctions. Currently the best approach to prevention of
bacterial translocation is early treatment of the underlying
condition, and the use of intraoperative antimicrobial drugs
during contaminated procedures (see Chapter 76). A number of
treatments, such as dietary modiﬁcation with antioxidants,
prebiotics, probiotics, and vitamin D have been suggested to
reduce the impact of chronic translocation of bacteria and LPS in
humans with chronic disease states by working to improve the
integrity of the mucosal barrier. 124

Pathophysiologic Mechanisms of Infectious
Diarrhea
Enteropathogenic organisms, unlike resident and nonpathogenic
transient microﬂora, have acquired means of overcoming the host
defense mechanisms and the inhibitory properties of the normal
microﬂora. Adherence factors (e.g., somatic pili) that permit
intestinal pathogens to establish infection also allow them to

vetexamprep.ir

a ach to, multiply on, and colonize the intestinal mucosa. Some
pathogenic bacteria that cause diarrhea remain on the mucosal
surface and produce potent enterotoxins that disrupt ﬂuid ﬂux
across the intestinal mucosa. Others are able to penetrate intact
epithelial cells, producing inﬂammatory damage in the
underlying mucosa. Enteric viruses damage the intestine by
replicating within and destroying selected populations of
epithelial cells. Often, multiple mechanisms are involved. Various
mechanisms by which microorganisms produce intestinal injury
are covered in relevant chapters on enteropathic viruses and
bacteria in this book.
