Diagnosis of Acute Infectious Gastroenteritis
Diagnosis of many enteropathogenic infections is notoriously
challenging because many organisms are present in both healthy
and sick dogs and cats. When outbreaks of diarrhea occur, testing
specimens from multiple aﬀected and unaﬀected animals is
recommended, because an organism is more likely to be the cause
of illness when found in more than one animal and when more
prevalent in diarrheic than nondiarrheic animals. Examination of
fecal smears from a wet-prep may be useful when positive for
Tritrichomonas blagburni or Giardia spp., but this is a highly
insensitive diagnostic approach. Many veterinary diagnostic
laboratories oﬀer “GI panels” which comprise a combination of
diagnostic tests for organisms that have the potential to cause
diarrhea. An understanding of the limitations of each of the assays
included in these panels is critical for proper interpretation. For
example, some panels include culture on selective media for
Salmonella and Campylobacter and ELISA assays that detect
clostridial toxins; some are panels that combine fecal ﬂotation for
parasites with special stains for Giardia (e.g., direct FA) or
Cryptosporidium (e.g., direct FA, acid fast stains); and others are
PCR-based assays that detect clostridial toxin genes or the DNA of
multiple diﬀerent enteric viral, bacterial, and protozoal
pathogens. It should be emphasized that the detection of bacterial
DNA does not equate with infection, and that the detection of
toxin genes does not equate with expression of that gene.
Collection of a suﬃcient quantity of fresh feces is important, with
the amount required depending on the assay being performed.
The laboratory (or laboratory’s website) should be consulted for
information on the correct specimen type, quantity, and handling
and transport conditions. Speciﬁc pathogen chapters in this book

vetexamprep.ir

also include information on specimen collection and handling to
optimize diagnostic yield.

Treatment of Acute Infectious Gastroenteritis
Fluid and electrolyte administration is probably one of the most
important therapeutic strategies for the management of the
diarrheic animal. Fluids should be given intravenously when
severe shock and hypotension, obtundation, or persistent
vomiting or ileus accompanies the diarrheic episode. Animals
with less severe manifestations of disease can receive
subcutaneous ﬂuids. When ﬁnances preclude hospitalization and
dehydration is mild, acute diarrhea without vomiting can
sometimes be treated successfully with speciﬁc oral ﬂuid
preparations. 125 Oral ﬂuid therapy is based on the observation
that glucose is actively absorbed by the normal small bowel and
sodium is carried with it in an approximately equimolar ratio.
Solutions containing glucose or sodium, either alone or in an
imbalanced ratio of a decreased concentration, are not eﬀective in
reversing ﬂuid and electrolyte ﬂux across the intestinal mucosa. In
one study, an oral rehydration solution designed for dogs
(Hydrolyte, Advanced Nutritional Support, Elka Park, NY) was
used to treat dogs with acute hemorrhagic diarrhea. 125 Dogs were
oﬀered the solution every 4 hours, the volume was calculated
based on estimated dehydration, maintenance requirements, and
estimated ongoing losses. Two-thirds of the dogs voluntarily
consumed the solution, and the cost of treatment was signiﬁcantly
lower for this group than dogs treated with IV ﬂuids.
Antimicrobials are rarely indicated for treatment of acute
gastroenteritis. They should only be used when episodes of
diarrhea or vomiting are accompanied by signs of systemic illness,
including fever, severe lethargy, and impending shock, and the
presence of leukopenia or leukocytosis with a marked left shift.
These ﬁndings suggest sepsis secondary to translocation of
microbes or their toxins. Use of antimicrobials to treat
uncomplicated diarrhea may be harmful, altering the intestinal
microbiome deleteriously, reducing competitive exclusion of
pathogenic species by nonpathogenic commensals, and selecting
for resistant bacterial populations. Treatment of healthy dogs with
metronidazole for 14 days was associated with a reduction in

vetexamprep.ir

richness of the fecal microbiome with increased abundance of
Proteobacteria and decreased abundance of Fusobacteria and
Bacteroidetes (assessed using 16S rRNA gene PCR-Illumina
sequencing). Furthermore, disturbances in the population
persisted for 4 weeks after the drug was discontinued. 6 When
indicated, antibacterial therapy should be combined with
supportive care measures such as dietary modiﬁcation, ﬂuid
therapy, and antiemetics. In addition to complicated diarrhea
with suspected bacterial translocation, antimicrobial treatment is
indicated for antibiotic-responsive chronic diarrhea and
granulomatous colitis. Antibiotic-responsive chronic diarrhea
(ARD) and acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS) are
described in the following section; information on granulomatous
colitis can be found in Chapter 63.

Acute Hemorrhagic Diarrhea Syndrome
AHDS (previously known as hemorrhagic gastroenteritis [HGE])
is a syndrome characterized by acute onset of profuse, mucoid,
bloody diarrhea, sometimes (80% of cases) with vomiting. The
name of the syndrome was changed because of the frequent lack
of gastric involvement. Acute hemorrhagic diarrheal syndrome
associated with Clostridium perfringens infection has primarily
been described in small-breed dogs between 2 and 4 years of age
(see Chapter 64). Aﬀected dogs are often lethargic, dehydrated,
and may show evidence of abdominal pain on palpation. The
syndrome is also marked by hematologic ﬁndings that include
relative polycythemia, with a normal or low plasma protein
concentration, and coagulation test results suggestive of DIC and
occasionally, acute oliguric renal failure.
The pathogenesis of AHDS is unknown, but many clinical and
laboratory ﬁndings are similar to those produced in dogs by
experimental administration of bacterial endotoxin or
enterotoxins with resultant DIC. Allergic, hereditary,
autoimmune, and infectious causes for AHDS have been
proposed. Currently it is believed that most cases may result from
clostridial overgrowth and production of the pore-forming toxin
NetF by C. perfringens. 126 , 127 The prevalence of positive PCR
results for the NetF and NetE genes in dogs with AHDS (48%) was
signiﬁcantly higher than in healthy control dogs (12%) and dogs

vetexamprep.ir

with parvovirus enteritis (0%). 128 Other pathogens may also play
a role. For example, in one report of a dog that was seen for
hemorrhagic diarrhea and found to have severe acute proteinlosing enteropathy, mucosally invasive enterococci were
identiﬁed in intestinal biopsies using FISH. 129
Diagnosis of the syndrome of AHDS is based on historical,
clinical, and laboratory ﬁndings, and exclusion of other causes.
The detection of Clostridium perfringens type A strains that encode
the pore-forming toxin NetF also suggests AHDS, but these
strains can be found in healthy dogs and negative results do not
exclude a diagnosis of AHDS.
Rehydration and diuresis with polyionic isotonic ﬂuids are the
most important components of treatment. Prognosis is good, with
most dogs recovering within 48 hours, although stool consistency
may take 7 to 10 days to normalize. Antimicrobial therapy is not
warranted for most of these dogs, unless there are signs of
systemic illness, including fever, impending shock, marked
neutropenia, or neutrophilia with a left shift, or unless the patient
is immunocompromised (chemotherapy for cancer, poorly
controlled diabetes). One study showed no diﬀerence in outcome
for dogs with AHDS lacking signs of sepsis when clavulanic acidamoxicillin was used as part of treatment when compared with no
antimicrobials. 130 The drugs of choice for the management of
Clostridium perfringens-associated diarrhea include amoxicillin or
metronidazole, and antimicrobials are typically administered for <
7 days.

Antibiotic-Responsive Chronic Diarrhea in
Dogs (Tylosin-Responsive Chronic Diarrhea)
Chronic or intermi ent diarrhea of small intestinal character that
responds to tylosin therapy has been described in dogs. 131 , 132
Aﬀected dogs are usually middle-aged, large-breed dogs. The
diarrhea is chronic or intermi ent in nature, and typically watery,
mucoid, or bloody in consistency. The frequency of defecation
varies markedly depending on whether the diarrhea is associated
with the small or large bowel. In addition, borborygmus and
ﬂatulence are common with a low prevalence of vomiting, weight
loss, or hyporexia. Diagnostic investigation is important to rule
out underlying causes for these signs and to help conﬁrm the

vetexamprep.ir

diagnosis of ARD (a diagnosis of exclusion). Treatment of dogs
with ARD utilizing anthelmintics, antiprotozoals, antiinﬂammatories, immunosuppressives, probiotics, prebiotics, other
antimicrobials, pancreatic enzymes, or dietary modiﬁcations is
typically unrewarding. The presence of known enteropathogenic
bacteria has not been detected. The presence of an as-yet
undiscovered tylosin-susceptible enteropathogen or an antiinﬂammatory eﬀect of tylosin have been speculated as possible
reasons for response to treatment. 132 Tylosin causes a marked
alteration in the bacterial ﬂora of dogs, with an increase in fecal
enterococci and lactobacilli, and a probiotic eﬀect has most
recently been suggested as its mechanism of action. 93 , 131 The
recommended dose for tylosin is 5 to 10 mg/kg PO q12 to 24h for
an initial period of 4 weeks. 133 If signs relapse at this stage, then a
longer course of therapy may be required. Many cases require
long-term or lifelong therapy to maintain remission of signs.
Alternative therapeutic strategies including administration of
probiotics or FMT are currently being investigated. For further
information on tylosin see Chapter 10.

Pancreatitis and Pancreatic Abscesses
Pancreatitis in dogs and cats is usually noninfectious in etiology,
and secondary bacterial infection of the pancreas is rare.
Nevertheless, infectious diseases should remain on the diﬀerential
diagnosis list as possible etiologies when a diagnosis of suspected
pancreatitis is made, especially when signs of other organ
involvement exist or when response to conventional treatment is
poor. In dogs, pancreatitis can be caused by Leptospira spp. and
fungi such as Cryptococcus neoformans, often as part of a more
widely disseminated infection. Toxoplasma gondii can also cause
pancreatitis. Enterococcus hirae enteropathy was associated with
ascending cholangitis and pancreatitis in a ki en. 134 Pancreatic
abscesses are usually sterile and treatment requires surgical
intervention and drainage. 135 , 136
Use of antibacterials in dogs and cats with pancreatitis is
controversial. In animals with noninfectious necrotizing
pancreatitis, local intestinal damage as a result of spillage of
pancreatic enzymes and decreased intestinal perfusion can cause
bacterial translocation from the intestine to the diseased

vetexamprep.ir

pancreatic tissue, with the potential for secondary bacterial
infection. Bacterial infection may also occur as a result of infection
that ascends the pancreatic ducts. In cats, experimental
inoculation of pancreatic ducts with E. coli resulted in infection
with concurrent pancreatitis, whereas bacteria were cleared in cats
with healthy pancreatic tissue. 137 When antimicrobial therapy
was started 12 hours after inoculation, infection developed in 73%
of animals receiving no antibacterials and in none of the cats
receiving antibacterials. In dogs with intestinal colonization by
genetically labeled E. coli, organisms had spread to the pancreas
and mesenteric lymph nodes after experimentally induced
pancreatitis. 138
If antibiotics are used, they should be capable of penetrating
damaged pancreatic tissue and have activity against enteric
bacteria. Parenteral administration is typically required because
aﬀected animals are usually vomiting or have evidence of nausea,
and decreased GI perfusion may impair bioavailability. Drugs
that reach adequate concentrations in inﬂamed pancreatic tissue
that could be considered are clindamycin, metronidazole, a
ﬂuoroquinolone, or third-generation cephalosporins.

Bacterial Peritonitis and Intra-Abdominal
Abscesses
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Bacterial peritonitis can be classiﬁed as primary, secondary, or
tertiary/recurrent secondary. Primary bacterial peritonitis, or
spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, is an uncommonly reported
scenario where there is no identiﬁable intraperitoneal source of
infection or history of a peritoneal penetration. 139 , 140 This type of
infection appears to be more common in cats than in dogs. In 56%
of reported canine cases of primary bacterial peritonitis and 100%
of feline cases, bacterial culture yielded only one isolate with the
majority of organisms in both species being gram positive. 139
Although the pathophysiology is not entirely elucidated, the most
common route of infection is believed to be hematogenous spread.
Infection may also follow dissemination by the lymphatic route,
or transmural migration from the GI or genitourinary (GU) tract.
Because primary bacterial peritonitis is uncommon in dogs and

vetexamprep.ir

cats, risk factors have not been identiﬁed. Primary bacterial
peritonitis occurs with greater frequency in humans with
impaired immune systems, alcoholic cirrhosis, nephrotic
syndrome, malignancy, and acute viral hepatitis. 141-143
Secondary bacterial peritonitis is the most common type of
bacterial peritonitis. In approximately 60% of dogs and cats, it
results from leakage of commensal bacteria from the GI tract due
to either postsurgical wound dehiscence or rupture or perforation
of the GI tract. 144 , 145 Rupture and perforation may occur as
sequelae to gastric dilatation-volvulus, perforating ulcers,
intestinal mass lesions, or a foreign body. Generalized secondary
bacterial peritonitis or localized secondary peritonitis potentially
with intra-abdominal abscess formation may also follow
pancreatitis, penetrating abdominal wounds, ischemic intestinal
injury (e.g., intussusception, foreign bodies, torsion) (Fig. 125.6),
rupture of viscera (gallbladder, pyometra, urinary tract), and
surgical contamination. Bile salts, along with gastric mucin,
hemoglobin, and barium have the potential to enhance the
severity of peritonitis. Idiopathic purulent mesenteric
lymphadenitis or lymph node abscessation may be infectious or
noninfectious with 50% of cases from one case series yielding
positive bacterial cultures. 146

vetexamprep.ir

Ischemic injury secondary to partial
mesenteric torsion in a cat. Though no
perforation was identified in the intestine, E.
coli, Enterococcus sp., and anaerobes were
cultured from a peritoneal swab.
FIG. 125.6

Tertiary peritonitis may be deﬁned as intra-abdominal infection
that persists or recurs 48 hours following successful and adequate
surgical source control. There is uncertainty in the human and
veterinary literature how best to diagnose and treat this disease
process; however, it is associated with nosocomial or resistant
infections in human medicine. True tertiary peritonitis is rarely
reported in the veterinary literature. However, some studies
describe patients that have failed treatment for secondary septic
peritonitis as having recurrent septic secondary peritonitis
following a perceived successful surgical source control. 147 , 148
This description could ﬁt the deﬁnition of tertiary peritonitis.
Dogs that were at risk for recurrent secondary peritonitis were
those that had lower serum albumin concentrations, higher PCVs,
and septic peritonitis of GI origin, especially when GI foreign
bodies were present. 148
Bacterial species involved in peritonitis often reﬂect the normal
ﬂora of the GI tract. Secondary bacterial peritonitis is commonly
polymicrobial. 149 , 150 Mixed aerobic-anaerobic infections, with up

vetexamprep.ir

to four diﬀerent bacterial species, occur in more than 50% of
aﬀected dogs and cats. 139 , 149 Escherichia coli is the most common
isolate from both dogs and cats, followed by Enterococcus and
Clostridium spp. 139 , 149 , 151 Other isolates include staphylococci,
streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Acinetobacter spp., a variety
of anaerobes, gram-negative Enterobacterales (Proteus , Citrobacter
, Serratia , Klebsiella , or Enterobacter spp.), Actinomyces spp., or, in
cats, Pasteurella multocida. 152 , 153 In one study, a greater
proportion of dogs with primary peritonitis had gram-positive
bacterial infections than dogs with secondary peritonitis. 139
Uncommonly, Candida albicans can be isolated, especially if there
is a history of antibiotic treatment. 154 , 155

Clinical Signs and Physical Examination
Findings
The most common clinical signs in dogs and cats with bacterial
peritonitis are lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, and diarrhea,
although clinical signs can be quite variable. Weakness and
collapse can also occur in animals with septic shock. Diarrhea and
vomiting may result from intestinal hypermotility or ileus or may
be secondary to underlying intestinal disease.
Physical examination ﬁndings may include dull mentation,
fever, dehydration, mucosal pallor, abdominal pain, thin body
condition, abdominal enlargement, and a palpable ﬂuid wave due
to ﬂuid accumulation. 139 , 149 , 156 Peritoneal ﬂuid generally
cannot be detected on physical examination until the volume
reaches greater than 10 mL/kg. 157 Tachypnea or tachycardia may
be present; however, some aﬀected animals, and especially cats,
show none of these signs. More than one-third of cats lack any
evidence of abdominal pain. 149 , 156 Signs of septic shock may be
present, including tachycardia, tachypnea, weak pulses, and
injected mucous membranes in dogs, or hypothermia and
bradycardia in cats (see Chapter 123).

Diagnosis
Preoperative diagnosis of bacterial peritonitis is based on
abdominal imaging ﬁndings, cytologic examination of peritoneal
ﬂuid, and aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture of the ﬂuid.

vetexamprep.ir

Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count, Serum Chemistry Panel, and
Urinalysis
Qualitative and quantitative abnormalities in leukocytes are
common with septic peritonitis; however, they are generally
nonspeciﬁc. Anemia of inﬂammatory disease is common.
Depending on severity of disease, an increase or decrease in
neutrophils may be present along with a regenerative or
degenerative left shift. 158 Thrombocytopenia may be present in
animals with septic shock and DIC. 159 Changes on the serum
chemistry panel include electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities
and/or hypoalbuminemia due to inﬂammation or third-space
losses. Mild to moderate increases in serum liver enzyme
activities may be detected. Hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia may
be detected and hyperbilirubinemia can be present. 139 , 149 In
patients with vomiting and diarrhea pre-renal azotemia may be
present. Azotemia may be post-renal in animals with a ruptured
urinary tract. Several abnormalities may be present on blood gas
analysis depending on severity of disease. Increased serum lactate
concentration has received the most a ention in the veterinary
literature.
Clotting Function
Although not indicated in all dogs with septic peritonitis, a subset
of dogs and cats that develop DIC as a sequela to bacterial
peritonitis may have PT or APTT prolongation, increased plasma
D-dimer or ﬁbrin degradation product concentrations, and/or
decreased plasma antithrombin concentration, therefore
coagulation panel evaluation may be considered in dogs with
bacterial peritonitis.
Diagnostic Imaging
Imaging of the abdomen should ideally take place prior to
abdominocentesis to avoid iatrogenic pneumoperitoneum and the
inadvertent misdiagnosis of ruptured abdominal viscera.
Plain Radiography

vetexamprep.ir

Abdominal radiographs in dogs and cats with diﬀuse septic
peritonitis may show loss of serosal detail potentially indicating
free peritoneal ﬂuid, presence of free gas, identiﬁcation of foreign
material, segmental dilation of bowel, or the presence of abnormal
organ enlargement. Oral administration of a contrast agent may
be used to be er identify GI foreign bodies, ileus, or evidence of
perforation. Barium should not be used as a GI contrast agent
when there is concern for perforation as it can contribute to
peritonitis.
Sonographic Findings
Findings on abdominal ultrasound examination include focal or
diﬀuse hyperechogenicity of the mesentery and the presence of
even small quantities of ascites. The echogenicity of the ascites
will diﬀer depending on its cellularity. Evidence of underlying
disease may be present, such as an intestinal mass or foreign
body. Though nonspeciﬁc, corrugation of the small intestine with
or without increase in intestinal wall thickness has been associated
with peritonitis. Focal bowel ischemia and associated localized
peritonitis can also be detected with ultrasound. The presence of
pneumoperitoneum; a dilated, air-ﬁlled stomach or bowel loops;
or severe abdominal pain may interfere with complete ultrasound
examination of some patients.
Advanced Imaging
Although not routinely used for the evaluation of septic
peritonitis in veterinary patients, abdominal CT scans are the
imaging modality of choice in humans with acute peritonitis. Its
lack of routine use in veterinary medicine may be due to
availability, cost, or the need for general anesthesia. In veterinary
patients, a CT scan is most useful in cases of penetrating
abdominal wounds secondary to trauma or focal abscessation.
Analysis of Peritoneal Fluid
Specimens for cytologic examination from animals with
peritonitis may be collected by blind or ultrasound-guided
abdominal paracentesis or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL).
With the increased availability and sensitivity of ultrasound to
detect and guide collection of small quantities of undiluted intraabdominal ﬂuid, DPL is now uncommonly performed. Ascites

vetexamprep.ir

ﬂuid should be collected in a sterile EDTA tube for cytologic
examination, and a sterile red top tube for aerobic and anaerobic
bacterial culture and susceptibility testing.
Ascites ﬂuid from dogs and cats with bacterial peritonitis is
typically a modiﬁed transudate or exudate, although ﬂuid from
dogs with primary peritonitis may be more likely to be a modiﬁed
transudate or transudate. 139 Fluid analysis from most animals
with peritonitis reveals a high protein concentration and an
increased erythrocyte and total nucleated cell count (usually >500
cells/µL and up to 160,000 cells/µL). There is typically a
predominance of neutrophils that may have a degenerate
appearance, and foreign material and/or intracellular and
extracellular bacteria may be seen. The presence of intracellular
bacteria is generally considered diagnostic for bacterial peritonitis.
The presence of bile pigments suggests the hepatobiliary system is
the origin of peritonitis.
Because absence of bacteria does not rule out bacterial
peritonitis, submission of ﬂuid for culture is essential to guide
appropriate antimicrobial therapy, especially with the rise in
prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. 149 , 160 Although it is
preferable to submit specimens after therapeutic lavage at
surgery, one study showed that culture results were the same
regardless of whether samples were collected before or after
therapeutic lavage. 161
In addition to cytologic examination and culture of ascites ﬂuid,
other tests may be performed on the ﬂuid to be er characterize
the type and source of the peritonitis. Comparing blood glucose
and lactate concentrations to that of the abdominal ﬂuid has
proven to be useful to diagnose dogs with septic peritonitis. A
blood-to-ﬂuid glucose diﬀerence greater than 20 mg/dL was 100%
sensitive and 100% speciﬁc for a diagnosis of bacterial peritonitis
in one study of dogs and cats. 152 A peritoneal ﬂuid lactate level
greater than 2.5 mmol/L had 100% sensitivity and 91% speciﬁcity
for diagnosis a septic eﬀusion in dogs; however, this was not
repeatable in cats. 162 Another report examined a variety of
biomarkers as predictors of septic peritonitis in dogs. 163 Glucose,
the chemokine CCL2, IL-6, IL-10, and lactate were found in
signiﬁcantly higher concentrations in peritoneal ﬂuid than in
serum, and serum lactate concentration was the most useful

vetexamprep.ir

predictor. Lactate and glucose concentrations should only be used
as a guide to help predict septic peritonitis in dogs that have not
recently undergone an exploratory celiotomy, which has the
potential to create similar perturbations based on studies in
healthy research animals. 164 No single cut-oﬀ oﬀers 100%
sensitivity and speciﬁcity for distinguishing septic from nonseptic
peritonitis. Measurement of ﬂuid concentrations of creatinine,
potassium, and total bilirubin and comparing these concentrations
to those in serum can be helpful for identifying uroperitoneum or
bile peritonitis (Table 125.2). 165
TABLE 125.2

Treatment
Antimicrobial Drugs
Intravenous antimicrobial drugs should be initiated as soon as a
patient has been diagnosed with septic peritonitis. While waiting
for culture and susceptibility test results, a knowledge of whether
cocci or rods are present may be considered to help tailor
antibiotic therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy can also be
selected based on the probable source of infection, if one is
suspected. However, because most infections are polymicrobial,
and unculturable anaerobes may be present, initial therapy should
be broad-spectrum, with activity against gram-positive and gramnegative bacteria, as well as anaerobes and aerobic bacteria.
Suggested empiric antibiotic options for septic patients are
outlined in Chapters 122 and 123. De-escalation of the type of
antimicrobial may be considered when bacterial culture and
susceptibility results are available.

vetexamprep.ir

Surgery
The standard treatment for secondary bacterial peritonitis is
emergent exploratory laparotomy with surgical source control
and proper antibiotic therapy; however, without proper surgical
debridement, lavage, and drainage, it is unlikely that
antimicrobial therapy alone will be successful. It is recommended
that the patient is hemodynamically stable prior to anesthesia and
surgical exploration. Surgical exploration for primary bacterial
peritonitis may not be indicated; however, diagnosis of these
conditions may require exploratory surgery.
Surgery should be performed via a standard ventral midline
celiotomy from xiphoid to pubis. The entire peritoneal cavity
should be explored in a systematic fashion. The source of the
bacteria should be removed, in most cases, or repaired. The use of
monoﬁlament suture is generally recommended whenever
possible. Placement of omentum adjacent to the surgical area
(intestinal resection and anastomosis) or abscess cavity should be
considered to enhance blood ﬂow and lymphatic drainage.
Copious peritoneal lavage with warm isotonic saline should be
continued until the ﬂuid returning via suction is clear (suggested
200 to 300 mL/kg). It is recommended, though not required, that a
closed suction drain, such as a Jackson-Pra drain, be placed. 166
Open peritoneal drainage is only recommended in cases of severe
visceral contamination or when a planned re-exploratory surgery
is required. 167 Likewise, there are reports of the use of vacuumassisted peritoneal drainage in the veterinary literature. At this
time, open drainage and vacuum-assisted drainage have not been
shown to result in superior outcomes to closed suction drains and
both carry signiﬁcant added expense and a second anesthetic
event to ultimately close the abdomen. 168 However, randomized,
prospective, clinical trials regarding the need for and the optimal
type of drain in patients with septic peritonitis are lacking in
veterinary medicine.

Supportive Care
Patients with bacterial peritonitis often require intensive
supportive care and monitoring regarding ﬂuid replacement,
cardiovascular
stability,
and
electrolyte
derangements.

vetexamprep.ir

Additionally, transfusion, nutritional support, and analgesics are
all important factors for consideration in patients with bacterial
peritonitis. Use of surgically placed gastrostomy tubes for enteral
nutrition is recommended and was associated with a low rate of
complications. 169 Though essential for successful outcome in
these patients, discussion of these topics is outside the scope of
this chapter and the authors refer readers to other texts.
Additionally, anesthetic protocols for patients with septic
peritonitis is outside the scope of this chapter; however, a recent
retrospective article on intraoperative lidocaine constant rate
infusions indicated signiﬁcantly greater short-term survival than
in dogs that did not receive lidocaine intraoperatively. 170

Prognosis
Survival rates of 32% to 87% have been reported in dogs with
secondary peritonitis. 139 , 151 , 159 , 166 , 168 , 170 Survival rates of
44% to 70% after surgery have been reported for cats. 139 , 149 , 156 ,
171 In the author’s experience hospitalization times vary greatly;
however, most range from 3 to 10 days. When death occurs, it
usually results from septic shock, DIC, lack of source control, or
multiple organ dysfunction; prolonged hospitalization is often
due to pancreatitis and/or ileus. Negative prognostic indicators
identiﬁed in dogs with bacterial peritonitis include a diagnosis of
primary as opposed to secondary peritonitis, 139 and preoperative
anemia, leukocytosis, or hypoproteinemia. 172 Hypoproteinemia
(<5 g/dL) and hypoalbuminemia (< 2.5 g/dL) has been correlated
with an increased risk of leakage after intestinal anastomosis and
resultant peritonitis; 173 however, these ﬁndings have not been
consistent among studies. 174 Lower serum albumin concentration
and increased PCV were risk factors for recurrent secondary
peritonitis in one study, as was a GI source of peritonitis,
especially foreign bodies. 148 Dogs with a foreign body were 7
times more likely to require a second surgery than those with GI
sepsis occurring for reasons other than a foreign body. 148
Postoperative administration of glucocorticoids has been
identiﬁed as a risk factor for death in dogs with septic peritonitis.
173 Low preoperative median serum ALT activity (56 U/L for
surviving cats compared with 179 U/L for nonsurvivors) was the

vetexamprep.ir

only positive prognostic indicator in one study of cats with
peritonitis. 149 Signiﬁcant diﬀerences between ALT and gammaglutamyl transferase values were noted between survivors and
nonsurvivors in dogs. 145 In another study, a high plasma lactate
concentration was a negative prognostic indicator in cats with
bacterial peritonitis. 156 In a retrospective study of 83 dogs with
septic peritonitis, admission plasma lactate concentrations were
also correlated with survival. 175 Admission plasma lactate
concentrations > 4 mmol/L yielded a sensitivity of 36% and a
speciﬁcity of 92% for nonsurvival. Because these prognostic
factors were determined using retrospective studies with diﬀerent
populations and treatments, it is diﬃcult to make ﬁrm
conclusions, especially in the face of conﬂicting results between
studies.

Management of Surgical Contamination
Surgical contamination and spillage of organ contents can often be
anticipated, and a knowledge of the normal enteric ﬂora can assist
in appropriate choice of prophylactic antibiotics (Table 125.3).
Spillage of intestinal contents in dogs and cats can be minimized
by appropriate isolation of bowel loops and stomach with
laparotomy pads and appropriate use of an assistant and suction.
Although previously advocated in experimental models of septic
peritonitis, intra-abdominal instillation of antimicrobials and
disinfectants (e.g., povidone-iodine) is not recommend and can
lead to chemical peritonitis. Sterile saline used alone (without
systemic antimicrobials) to lavage the abdominal cavity as
described above has been unsuccessful in consistently resulting in
negative bacterial cultures, despite its diluting eﬀect on the spilled
material. 153

Case Example
Signalment

“Colby,” a 2-year-old male golden retriever from Davis in
northern California.

History

Colby had a 3-week history of waxing and waning lethargy and
inappetence that had worsened the week before examination.
One week before examination at the University of California,
Davis VMTH, he was examined at an emergency clinic.
Abnormalities found on bloodwork were a leukocytosis (22,820
cells/µL) due to a mature neutrophilia (20,470 cells/µL); the
serum chemistry panel was unremarkable. Abdominal
radiographs showed decreased detail in the caudal abdomen
secondary to small volume of eﬀusion or peritonitis, and

vetexamprep.ir

gastroenteritis was suspected. Colby was discharged with
instructions to feed a bland, low-fat diet.

Physical Examination

General: Bright, alert, responsive, with adequate hydration; T:
101.5°F (38.6°C), HR: 80 beats/min with strong, symmetrical
pulses. Respiration was panting, pink mucous membranes, CRT
2s, weight 29 kg, BCS 5/9. The remainder of the physical
examination indicated no clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities.
There was mild dental calculus; the abdomen was soft and
nonpainful, with no palpable masses; a rectal examination
revealed some evidence of liquid stool.

Laboratory Findings

A CBC revealed a leukocytosis (21,750 cells/µL; RR, 6000–13,000
cells/µL) with 18,270/µL mature neutrophils (RR, 3000–10,500
cells/µL), and 870 bands/µL with slight toxicity. The serum
biochemistry panel revealed only mild hypochloremia 107
mmol/L (108–118 mmol/L), hypocalcemia 9.5 mg/dL (9.7–11.5
mg/dL),
hypoglycemia
63
mg/dL
(64–123
mg/dL),
hypoalbuminemia
2.9
g/dL
(3.0–4.4
g/dL),
and
hyperglobulinemia 4.0 g/dL (1.8–3.9 g/dL). A urinalysis was
unremarkable, Spec cPL® (IDEXX Laboratories) within
reference range, and serum resting cortisol concentration 1.3
µg/dL.

Imaging Findings

Abdominal ultrasound: In the mid descending colon there is
focal severe thickening of the colonic wall. An adjacent thickwalled, ﬂuid and gas-ﬁlled structure, extending toward
midline, is conﬂuent with the colonic wall and gas is seen
tracking through the colonic wall and into this adjacent
structure. The surrounding mesentery is hyperechoic and there
is a small volume of echogenic ﬂuid surrounding the colon,
adjacent small bowel, and mesentery. The remainder of the
colon as well as the small intestinal tract and stomach are
within normal limits. There are multiple severely enlarged,
rounded, hypoechoic to heterogenous lymph nodes between
the abnormal portion of the colon and the left kidney. A more
caudal colic lymph node is also enlarged and hypoechoic. The
spleen contains multiple small, hypoechoic nodules. The

vetexamprep.ir

prostate is hyperechoic and large, consistent with the intact
status of the patient.
Impressions: Focal colonic thickening and perforation with
adjacent abscess formation; diﬀerentials include perforating
foreign body, perforating neoplasia, or fungal infection. The
adjacent mesentery and ﬂuid may represent septic or sterile
peritonitis. Severely abnormal adjacent lymph nodes may be
reactive, but are concerning for metastatic or round cell
neoplasia. Splenic nodules have a typically benign appearance,
although metastatic or disseminated round cell neoplasia is not
excluded.

Cytology Findings

Cytologic examination of an ultrasound-guided ﬁne-needle
aspirate of an enlarged lymph node in the caudal abdomen: A
markedly expanded population of large lymphocytes is present.
These cells have a small amount of deeply basophilic
cytoplasm. Nuclear chromatin is ﬁnely stippled and prominent
nucleoli are observed, and there are many mitotic ﬁgures. The
lymphocytes are CD79a positive, CD3 negative using
immunostaining.

Diagnosis

B-cell lymphoma, high grade.

Treatment

Surgery was recommended to address the colonic perforation
and associated abscess. Preoperatively, Colby was treated with
intravenous ﬂuids and parenteral ampicillin-sulbactam,
enroﬂoxacin, maropitant, and methadone. Exploratory
laparotomy was performed and the colonic mass was resected.
The abdomen was lavaged and a closed suction drain was
placed.

Microbiologic Testing

Sample: purulent ﬂuid from colonic mass.
Direct smear: moderate numbers small gram-negative
rods, very small numbers thin ﬁlamentous gram-negative
rods, very small numbers large gram-positive rods.
Aerobic culture: very small numbers hemolytic E. coli
(susceptible to all antimicrobials tested) and fastidious
gram-negative rods. Anaerobic culture: large numbers

vetexamprep.ir

Bacteroides spp./Prevotella spp. (β-lactamase negative),
Peptostreptococcus anaerobius and Fusobacterium nucleatum
(β-lactamase negative).

Diagnosis

Localized secondary septic peritonitis secondary to ruptured
colonic large B-cell lymphoma.

Outcome

After the surgery, Colby was treated with L-asparaginase for
lymphoma. He recovered for 5 days in hospital and was
subsequently discharged. Ten days after the surgery, he
continued chemotherapy with the Medical Oncology Service.
Histopathology of the mass was consistent with completely
excised colonic B-cell lymphoma with serosal perforation and
mucosal ulceration.
Comments: In this case, spillage of colonic contents was
contained by the mesentery and omentum, leading to a
localized septic peritonitis. Colby recovered uneventfully from
surgery with appropriate antibiotic therapy and supportive
care, and experienced complete remission with chemotherapy
(CHOP—cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and
prednisone). Three years later (at the time of writing), he
remains in remission.

126: Hepatobiliary Infections
Jane E. Sykes, Sina Marsilio, and Stanley L. Marks

KEY POINTS
• The liver and biliary tree contain a complex immune defense
system that protects the body against bacteria that enter from
the portal system, through arterial channels, or that ascend
the biliary tree. Diseases that disrupt these processes can
predispose to infection.
• Bacteria that most commonly cause hepatobiliary infections
are Escherichia coli, Enterococcus spp., and anaerobes; less
often other gram-negative aerobes, Streptococcus and
Staphylococcus spp. are involved.
• Several viruses, atypical bacteria, protozoa, fungi, and
helminths also can cause hepatobiliary infections in dogs and
cats.
• Major clinical signs of bacterial cholangitis or
cholangiohepatitis are inappetence, lethargy, fever, vomiting,
diarrhea, abdominal pain, and icterus.
• Ultrasound is a relatively sensitive tool for imaging the
hepatobiliary system and can be used to guide collection of
specimens for cytologic examination and culture.
• Treatment includes antimicrobial drugs and supportive care for
hepatobiliary disease; cholecystectomy may be required when
biliary tract obstruction is severe, gall bladder mucocele is
present, there is rupture of the biliary tract, or cholelithiasis.

Hepatobiliary Infections

vetexamprep.ir

Hepatobiliary infections include a variety of viral, bacterial,
protozoal, or fungal infections that can spread hematogenously to
the liver as part of a systemic infection; ascending infections of the
biliary tree; and possibly bacterial translocation from the portal
circulation (Table 126.1). The focus of this chapter is bacterial
infections of the biliary tree; hepatic abscesses are considered in a
separate section that follows. The main mechanism thought to be
involved is ascending infections of the biliary tree, although
hematogenous spread and bacterial translocation from the portal
system are other proposed mechanisms. 1 , 2 Ascension of bacteria
occurs when normal hepatic defense mechanisms are
overwhelmed (Box 126.1). Those mechanisms include the
mechanical barrier presented by the sphincter of Oddi, the
ﬂushing action of bile, antibacterial eﬀects of bile salts, and local
immune defenses as described in the following text (IgA, mucus,
Kupﬀer cells). Inﬂammatory bowel disease, neoplasia,
inﬂammatory liver disease, biliary obstruction, and systemic
immunosuppression can all interfere with these mechanisms and
predispose to infection. An understanding of normal
hepatobiliary defense mechanisms can facilitate improved
understanding of the pathogenesis and treatment of hepatobiliary
infections.

Normal Hepatobiliary Defense Mechanisms
Kupffer Cells
Hepatic Kupﬀer cells comprise the largest compartment of tissue
macrophages in the body, representing 80 to 90% of the total ﬁxed
macrophages and approximately 35% of the nonparenchymal
liver cells. 3 , 4 Residing mainly within the lumen of hepatic
sinusoids and adherent to endothelial cells by long cytoplasmic
processes, Kupﬀer cells are most numerous in the periportal area
(zone 1, see later) where they oﬀer ﬁrst-line defense against
bacteria, endotoxin, and microbial debris delivered from the GI
tract. 3 A number of other immune cells also participate in the
hepatic innate immune response by patrolling sinusoids,
including natural killer cells and γδ-T cells. 3
Activation of Kupﬀer cells by endotoxin and other signaling
molecules is mechanistic to their protective and disease-producing

vetexamprep.ir

eﬀects. Kupﬀer cells possess both Fc and C3 receptors and
phagocytize a wide variety of opsonized and nonopsonized
particulates. 3 Kupﬀer cells express complement receptor of the Ig
superfamily (CRIg), which is a receptor for C3. This can directly
bind lipoteichoic acid, a pathogen-associated molecular pa ern
associated with gram-positive bacteria, without the need for
complement activation. 3
Normally, hepatic Kupﬀer cells eﬃciently clear endotoxin to
a enuate systemic exposure. Endotoxin extraction is enabled by
LPS-binding glycoproteins on hepatocytes that facilitate transfer
to high-aﬃnity LPS receptors on Kupﬀer cells. Contact with LPS
activates Kupﬀer cells directly via TLR signaling or indirectly by
triggering complement activation. On exposure to endotoxin,
activation of Kupﬀer cells initiates a multitude of signaling
pathways resulting in a spectrum of inﬂammatory responses. 4
However, there is a degree of “endotoxin tolerance” that results
from constant, low-level exposure of the liver to endotoxin. 5 , 6
Because enteric bile acids bind and inactivate endotoxin,
patients with extrahepatic bile duct occlusion or severe
intrahepatic cholestasis with impaired enterohepatic bile acid
circulation have higher risk for endotoxin translocation. 7 Dogs
with induced chronic liver disease associated with intrahepatic
portal hypertension and acquired portosystemic shunts develop
signiﬁcantly greater endotoxin concentrations in portal venous,
hepatic venous, and caudal vena cava blood, compared to healthy
control dogs. 8
On activation, Kupﬀer cells release superoxide radicals,
hydrogen peroxide, nitric oxide, hydrolytic enzymes, and
eicosanoids (prostaglandins and leukotrienes) that can assist in
antigen destruction. They also release a large number of
immunoregulatory and inﬂammatory cytokines, including Il-1, Il6, TNF-α, platelet-activating factor, transforming growth factor-β,
and IFN-γ. Kupﬀer cells associated with zone 1 are larger, more
phagocytic, and generate greater amounts of TNF-α, Il-1,
prostaglandin E, and lysosomal enzymes. Less-active Kupﬀer cells
are associated with zone 3; these exhibit greater cytotoxic activity
to some stimuli and are more easily activated. Nitric oxide
released by Kupﬀer cells mediates a wide variety of physiologic
events, including vasodilation, neutrophil chemotaxis, and

vetexamprep.ir

adhesion of neutrophils to vascular endothelium (response to
bacteria or endotoxin). 9 As potent inducers of inﬂammatory
cytokines, Kupﬀer cells are implicated in pathologic events
resulting in liver injury. 10 Later, during the course of an infection,
other cells including hepatocytes, T lymphocytes, and
immigrating phagocytes (monocytes and neutrophils) contribute
cytokines to the inﬂammatory process. Kupﬀer cells have been
shown to be critical in T cell priming in the liver. 3 In addition,
sophisticated imaging techniques have shown T cells to populate
the liver from secondary lymphoid organs, adhere to platelets,
crawl along sinusoids, and interact with liver sinusoidal
endothelial cells. When they encounter a pathogen, they secrete
IFN-γ to eradicate the infection. 3

Biliary Epithelial Cells (Cholangiocytes)
Cholangiocytes (biliary epithelial cells) in larger bile ducts express
the polymeric IgA receptor (secretory component) that localizes
secretory IgA (S-IgA) to the ductal system. Uptake from the
basolateral side of the cholangiocyte is followed by transport to
the luminal ductal surface, where the secretory component is

vetexamprep.ir

cleaved from but secreted with S-IgA into bile. Cholangiocytes
from larger intrahepatic bile ducts, septal bile ducts, interlobular
bile ducts, and bile ductules express TLRs that bind a variety of
ligands including bacterial molecules, double-stranded messenger
RNA (mRNA), LPS, and ﬂagellin. In the presence of inﬂammatory
cytokines, cholangiocytes also can activate the (proinﬂammatory)
NF-κB pathway. Cholangiocytes also produce the antimicrobial
peptides defensin and cathelicidin, part of the innate immune
system, that defend the biliary tree against gram-positive and
gram-negative bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and viruses.
Expression of cathelicidin in biliary epithelium is enhanced by
exposure to endogenous and therapeutic bile salts (e.g.,
ursodeoxycholic acid). In biliary inﬂammation, cholangiocytes
also recruit CD4+ T cells as well as immature dendritic cells to
provide defense against antigenic and microbial challenge.
Cholangiocytes also express a variety of leukocyte and vascular
adhesion molecules that can facilitate tissue-speciﬁc leukocyte
migration, slowing leukocyte circulation near damaged
epithelium and traﬃcking cells to the targeted site of injury.
Expression of antigen-presenting molecules on cholangiocytes
also may contribute to local immune defense.
Bile
Secretory IgA is the major immunoglobulin in bile; IgG and IgM
are present in much smaller quantities. Bile contains
approximately twice the concentration of S-IgA as found in the
upper intestinal ﬂuid. 11 Bile and IgA each inﬂuence the enteric
bacterial population (type, number of organisms, and enterocyte
adherence). Normal physiologic choleresis mechanically clears the
biliary pathways of microbial organisms and particulate debris.
This function is thwarted in cholestatic disorders. A normal
biliary-enterobacterial cycle permits rapid elimination of bacteria
that have entered the biliary system where locally produced IgA
prevents epithelial invasion. 12 , 13 Bile salts also have antibacterial
action. In health, tight junctions between hepatocytes (abu ing
canaliculi) resist bacterial entry into canalicular bile.
Experimental models have helped clarify the physiologic
signiﬁcance of enteric portal bacteremia. Infusion of 105 to 107
bacteria into the splenic vein of normal adult cats signiﬁcantly
retards bile ﬂow and causes bacterobilia within 30 minutes.

vetexamprep.ir

However, in the presence of extrahepatic bile duct obstruction,
only modest bacterial inocula (103) lead to bacterobilia within the
same time frame. As bacteria enter sinusoidal blood, some are
phagocytized (Kupﬀer cells and neutrophils) and killed while
others remain viable entering bile. 14 Experimental studies
conﬁrm that any cause of cholestasis can augment development of
bacterobilia,
including
the
cholestasis
resulting
from
endotoxemia. The presence of bacteria within choleliths also can
sustain bacterial infections in the biliary tree. 15 Enteric organisms
in bile may dehydroxylate and deconjugate bile acids, generating
membranocytolytic forms that are capable of provoking
cholestasis, oxidant cell injury, and cell apoptosis.

Transient or episodic portal bacteremia likely explains the
unexpected isolation of bacterial organisms from liver or bile in
animals with illnesses thought not to be primarily bacterial in
origin, especially if specimens are collected after surgical
manipulations of visceral structures. A discussion of bacterial

infections
can
lead
to
suppurative
cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis, cholecystitis, choledochitis, and
cholelithiasis. 16-23 Cholangitis is inﬂammation of intrahepatic bile

vetexamprep.ir

ducts, whereas cholangiohepatitis is inﬂammation of the bile ducts
that has spread to the adjacent liver parenchyma. The use of the
term “cholangitis” (rather than “cholangiohepatitis”) has been
recommended by the WSAVA Liver Diseases and Pathology
Standardization Research Group, because inﬂammatory
disruption of the limiting plate to involve hepatic parenchyma is
not a consistent feature and if present, is usually an extension of a
primary cholangitis. For these reasons, the term “cholangitis” will
be used from this point onwards.
In cats, cholangitis has been classiﬁed histologically as
neutrophilic cholangitis, lymphocytic cholangitis, or chronic cholangitis
associated with liver ﬂuke infestation. 24 Neutrophilic cholangitis may
be further subclassiﬁed as acute or chronic depending on the
presence of ﬁbrosis, ﬁbroplasia, or bile duct proliferation. 25
Neutrophilic cholangitis is thought to develop as a result of
ascending bacterial infection from the GI tract, which may occur
secondary to IBD and/or pancreatitis (Fig. 126.1); however, a
study evaluating the utility of FISH for the detection of bacteria in
feline inﬂammatory liver disease observed intrahepatic bacteria
located predominantly within portal vessels and venous
sinusoids, or the hepatic parenchyma near the capsule. This
spatial distribution of bacteria within the livers of cats with
inﬂammatory liver disease is inconsistent with an ascending
bacterial infection from the GI tract, and more consistent with the
translocation of enteric bacteria across the mucosal barrier into the
portal circulation. 1 In contrast, bacteria that are localized within
the bile ducts are more likely to have ascended secondary to
pancreatic and hepatobiliary reﬂux in the face of intestinal
inﬂammation, pancreatitis, and biliary disease (triaditis) as a
consequence of the common entry of the pancreatic and common
bile ducts into the intestine. Not all cats with cholangitis have
histologic evidence of associated pancreatitis or IBD; studies have
indicated that the prevalence of triaditis in cats with cholangitis is
32 to 50%. 26 Cats with acute cholangitis tend to be younger than
those with chronic cholangitis. 25 , 27 Retrovirus infection does not
appear to be a predisposing factor. The cause of lymphocytic
cholangitis is unclear, although it is thought to be an immunemediated condition. 28 Chronic cholangitis associated with liver
ﬂuke infestation is rare and is primarily reported from regions

vetexamprep.ir

with subtropical climates such as the southeastern United States
and Hawaii, but disease can occur in nonendemic areas in
traveled cats. Although several diﬀerent ﬂuke species may be
involved, the most prevalent appears to be Platynosomum illiciens
(see Chapter 118). 29

Choledochitis is inﬂammation of the common bile duct, whereas
cholecystitis is inﬂammation of the gall bladder, and may or may
not be associated with cholangitis or choledochitis. In some
instances, necrotizing and/or emphysematous cholecystitis can

vetexamprep.ir

occur, which may lead to perforation of the gall bladder wall and
septic bile peritonitis. Cholelithiasis is stone formation within the
biliary tree. In some instances, cholelithiasis or neoplasia of the
biliary tree may predispose to cholangitis and necrotizing
cholecystitis (Fig. 126.2). 20 , 21 Alternatively, it has been suggested
that bacterial cholecystitis may predispose to stone formation
through bacterial deconjugation of soluble bilirubin glucuronide
to insoluble unconjugated bilirubin and glucuronic acid. 19
Culture of bile is more sensitive than culture of liver
parenchyma in both dogs and cats with hepatobiliary disease. In
one large study, approximately 30% of biliary cultures were
positive in dogs and cats, whereas hepatic cultures were positive
in 14% of cats and 5% of dogs. 23 In cats, more than 80% of biliary
cultures yielded a single bacterial species, whereas multiple
bacterial species were isolated from approximately 50% of dogs.
Bacterial species isolated from cats include anaerobes, a variety of
Enterobacterales, Enterococcus, Streptococcus, or Staphylococcus
species. 1 , 16 , 23 , 25 Dogs are most commonly infected with E. coli,
Enterococcus spp., and/or anaerobes, primarily Bacteroides and
Clostridium species. 17-21 , 23 , 30-32 Staphylococcus spp., other gramnegative aerobes (Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, and
Pseudomonas aeruginosa), and Streptococcus spp. may also be
isolated from dogs, and Helicobacter spp. have also been
implicated as a cause of chronic hepatitis in dogs and possibly
cats (see Chapter 66). 24 , 33 Salmonella in cats and Campylobacter in
dogs may also cause cholecystitis. Although rare, emphysematous
cholecystitis in dogs and cats is usually caused by Clostridium spp.
or E. coli. 34

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs and Physical Examination Abnormalities
The most common clinical signs of hepatobiliary infection in both
dogs and cats are lethargy, inappetence, vomiting, weight loss,
and diarrhea, although subclinical infections can also occur. 16 , 17 ,
22 , 25 , 27 , 30 , 35 Signs may be chronic, acute, and rarely peracute. 17
, 36 Peracute disease can occur with necrotizing cholecystitis and
rupture of the gall bladder wall, and may be associated with
clinical signs of septic shock. Hypersalivation may be evident in

vetexamprep.ir

cats with neutrophilic cholangitis. 16 Physical examination may
reveal fever, lethargy, dehydration, icterus, and thin body
condition, with or without pain on palpation of the abdomen.
Hepatomegaly may also be identiﬁed. 25 Some animals may be
tachycardic or tachypneic.

Diagnosis
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count
The CBC may show leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia, increased
numbers of band neutrophils, and occasionally monocytosis. 16-18 ,
22 , 25 , 27 , 36 Cats with neutrophilic cholangitis have higher
segmented and band neutrophil counts compared to cats with
lymphocytic cholangitis. 24 Some cats with neutrophilic
cholangitis may be leukopenic with or without a left shift. 16 , 25
Lymphopenia and/or anemia may also be present.
Serum Biochemical Tests
Dogs with cholangitis or cholecystitis typically have increased
activities of ALT, ALP, and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT),
and hyperbilirubinemia. 30 , 31 At least 50% of cats with cholangitis
have mild to moderate increases in the activity of ALT and/or ALP
(usually < 1000 U/L). Increased activity of GGT is usually
documented; however, some cats with cholangitis may have
normal ALT, ALP, and GGT activity. 25 Hyperbilirubinemia is
present in approximately two-thirds of cats. Along with higher
neutrophil counts, cats with neutrophilic cholangitis have higher
activities of ALT and higher total bilirubin concentration than cats
with lymphocytic cholangitis. 24 Electrolyte abnormalities may be
present secondary to GI losses in animals with vomiting or
diarrhea. 16 , 27 Hypocholesterolemia, hyperglobulinemia, and
hypoalbuminemia
are
uncommonly
identiﬁed.
Hypercholesterolemia may be present in dogs with cholestasis or
bile duct obstruction, but is uncommonly present in cats. 18 , 20 , 22
Despite the diﬀerences observed in hematological and
biochemical parameters in cats with neutrophilic versus
lymphocytic forms of cholangitis, there is tremendous overlap in

vetexamprep.ir

laboratory ﬁndings between the two forms of cholangitis, and
caution should be heeded in relying upon the laboratory results to
diﬀerentiate these forms of cholangitis.

Coagulation Profile
Coagulation abnormalities such as prolongations of PT and PTT
may be present in dogs and cats with hepatobiliary infections,
either secondary to impaired absorption of vitamin K secondary
to biliary obstruction, or potentially as a result of liver
dysfunction. 17 , 27
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
The most common ﬁnding on abdominal radiography of dogs and
cats with cholecystitis and cholangitis is hepatomegaly, which
may be variable. 22 , 27 Uncommonly, single or multiple
radiopaque choleliths are visible, although choleliths may also be
radiolucent (see Fig. 126.2). 18-20 , 35 Linear mineralization of the
biliary tree has been described in some animals with
cholelithiasis, 35 whereas other animals may reveal no
abnormalities. Emphysematous cholecystitis is characterized by
the presence of gas in the liver in the region of the gall bladder.
Loss of abdominal detail may be present if gall bladder rupture
and septic bile peritonitis has occurred. 17
Sonographic Findings
Ultrasound examination provides important information and can
inﬂuence decision-making in animals with cholangitis. 31 Findings
on ultrasound in dogs and cats with cholangitis are similar and
include hepatomegaly, normal or abnormal hepatic echotexture
with a homogenous or heterogenous increase in echogenicity,
prominent portal vasculature, ascites, a thickened and
hyperechogenic gall bladder wall, and sediment within the gall
bladder. 16-18 , 22 , 24 , 25 , 31 , 38 , 39 The gall bladder wall may also

vetexamprep.ir

appear irregular and contain polypoid mass lesions. Abdominal
pain in the right cranial quadrant may be evident during the
procedure. Choleliths may occasionally be identiﬁed within the
biliary tract as hyperechoic masses or linear structures with
acoustic shadowing. 35 Distention of the biliary tract may be
evident, sometimes with tortuosity of the cystic and common bile
duct (Fig. 126.3). 16 , 17 , 38 Concurrent evidence of pancreatic
and/or intestinal wall disease may be present in cats. 25
Ultrasound cannot be used to diﬀerentiate neutrophilic from
lymphocytic cholangitis in cats. Intramural gas may be identiﬁed
in animals with emphysematous cholecystitis (Fig. 126.4). Rupture
of the gall bladder may also be detected using ultrasound, which
is an indication for emergency surgery. 31 However, one study of
219 dogs with gall bladder mucoceles suggested that the
sensitivity of abdominal ultrasound for detection of gall bladder
rupture was low, only 56% (95% CI, 40–71%), whereas the
speciﬁcity was 92% (95% CI, 85–96%). 40
Microbiologic Tests
Cytologic Examination
Cytologic examination of bile collected by percutaneous
ultrasound-guided
cholecystocentesis
(or
intraoperative
cholecystocentesis) may reveal increased numbers of degenerate
neutrophils, small and/or large mononuclear cells, and in some
cases, a mixed or monomorphic bacterial population. 16 , 30
Identiﬁcation of multilobular nuclear remnants, representing
degenerate neutrophils, may be the only evidence of an
inﬂammatory response owing to the detergent eﬀects of bile on
cell membranes. Thus, in biliary sepsis, bacterial organisms are
commonly observed in biliary debris, with or without a welldeﬁned exudative response. Examination of only the liquid
partition of bile may fail to disclose bacterial organisms readily
identiﬁed in the heavier biliary sediment. Thus, cholecystocentesis
performed with the objective of identifying bacterobilia should
include sampling of both nonparticulate and sediment portions.
Standard protocol consists of introducing a 22-G needle (a ached
to an extension set, three-way stopcock, and 10-mL syringe)
through the ventral or ventrolateral portion of the liver into the

vetexamprep.ir

gall bladder. Cats and dogs are either heavily sedated or placed
under general anesthesia for the procedure. Sampling should be
done to completely empty the gall bladder to minimize
postcentesis bile leakage and to optimize collection of dependent
sediment. It is possible that percutaneous drainage of infected bile
may also have a therapeutic beneﬁt, although this requires further
study.

Culture
Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture should be performed on
bile collected by ultrasound-guided or intraoperative
cholecystocentesis or liver biopsies. An approximately 22%
isolation frequency of fastidious anaerobes among isolated
bacteria from cats justiﬁes submission of specimens for anaerobic
culture. 41 Bile is more likely to yield positive results; however,
bacteria are best retrieved from bile in which the gall bladder has
been nearly completely emptied (3–5 mL in cats). The sensitivity
of culture was also improved by combining tissue, bile, and

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
g
41
,
30
crushed choleliths for inoculation.
Although it is generally
accepted that bile is sterile in healthy dogs and cats, 2 , 42 transient
cytologic and microbiologic evidence of bactibilia has been
identiﬁed in healthy dogs. 43 Liver tissue from healthy dogs and
cats can also harbor a variety of enteric bacterial species. 1 , 44
Thus, the results of bile culture should be interpreted in light of
clinical and cytologic ﬁndings. Antibiotic resistance among
bacteria isolated from the bile of dogs and cats with cholecystitis
and cholangitis has been described in several studies, and so
culture and susceptibility testing is suggested whenever possible.
23 , 31 When cholecystocentesis is undesirable because of concerns
for gall bladder rupture (see Cytological Examination), blood
cultures may be useful, although the utility of blood culture in
dogs and cats with cholecystitis has not been studied. In human
patients, bile cultures are positive in 50 to 95% of patients with
acute cholecystitis, and blood cultures are positive in 30 to 40% of
patients. 45
Pathologic Findings
Neutrophilic cholangitis in cats varies considerably on
histopathology in severity, chronicity, and the extent of associated
hepatic parenchymal involvement. 25 , 37 FISH has been used to
identify bacteria within the hepatobiliary system in cats; bacteria
were more likely to be identiﬁed in portal vessels, venous
sinusoids, and parenchyma (12 of 13 cats) than the bile duct (1 of
13 cats). 1 Concurrent hepatic lipidosis may also be present. In a
small percentage of aﬀected cats, complete or partial biliary
obstruction may be identiﬁed as a result of inﬂammation,
neoplasia, or cholelithiasis. Other ﬁndings in aﬀected cats include
acute or chronic pancreatitis (65% of cats in one study), and/or
inﬂammatory bowel disease or intestinal lymphoma (46% of cats).
25 , 26 Histopathology of the gall bladder wall in both dogs and
cats with cholecystitis may reveal mucosal and glandular
hyperplasia,
and
thickening
and
neutrophilic
or
lymphoplasmacytic inﬂammation of the gall bladder wall. 18 , 22 ,

25

Choleliths in cats are most often composed of calcium
carbonate, although they also may comprise a mixture of
cholesterol, calcium bilirubinate, and calcium carbonate. 18 , 20 In

vetexamprep.ir

dogs they are often composed of calcium bilirubinate, bilirubin, or
a mixture of bilirubin and cholesterol. Aged female small-breed
dogs (dachshunds, poodles, miniature schnauzers) were
predisposed to cholelithiasis in one study. 19

Treatment
Treatment of cholangitis and cholecystitis typically consists of
supportive care and antibiotic administration. Dogs and cats with
necrotizing
or
emphysematous
cholecystitis
require
cholecystectomy. Cholecystectomy could also be considered to
prevent recurrence of cholelithiasis in animals with chronic
cholecystitis. Cholecystectomy, biliary stenting procedures, and/or
biliary diversion surgery may be required for animals with
obstructive processes such as cholelithiasis, biliary neoplasia, or
obstructive cholangitis. 19 , 20 Because cholecystotomy or biliary
diversion surgery often results in dehiscence and septic bile
peritonitis if bacterial cholecystitis or choledochitis is present,
cholecystectomy has been recommended for dogs with
cholelithiasis as opposed to cholecystotomy. 19 When compared
with other surgical biliary procedures, cholecystectomy has been
associated with good clinical outcomes in dogs and cats, but any
condition that requires biliary surgery carries a guarded
prognosis.
Antimicrobial Drug Treatment and Supportive Care
Empirically administered antibiotics should target gram-negative
enteric bacterial species, Enterococcus spp., and anaerobes and be
concentrated in bile. Cytologic examination of bile was shown to
correlate well with culture results in one study and can be used to
guide initial therapy. 46 Suitable antibiotics include ampicillinsulbactam or clavulanic acid-amoxicillin, or a ﬂuoroquinolone
with metronidazole, although resistance to clavulanic acidamoxicillin or enroﬂoxacin has been documented among biliary
isolates from dogs and cats. 22 Based on the results of cultures
from 248 dogs and cats evaluated for hepatobiliary disease, it was
concluded that broad-spectrum empirical coverage could be
achieved with a combination of a ﬂuoroquinolone, penicillin, and
metronidazole (reduce dose by 50% in cats with hepatobiliary
disease), or a ﬂuoroquinolone combined with clavulanic acid-

vetexamprep.ir

amoxicillin or clindamycin. 23 Again, because resistance can occur,
culture and antimicrobial susceptibility results should then be
used to adjust treatment. In human patients, speciﬁc treatment of
Enterococcus spp. biliary infections may not be necessary when
other concurrent bacterial infections are being managed, as the
Enterococcus spp. infection tends to resolve when the other
infections are treated. 45 Supportive treatments that should be
considered include IV crystalloid ﬂuids with or without colloids,
glucose supplementation, antiemetics (e.g., maropitant,
ondansetron), nutritional support by parenteral or enteral means
(with a restricted fat diet), ursodiol, S-adenosylmethionine, and
parenteral vitamin K supplementation.

Prognosis
The prognosis for cats with neutrophilic cholangitis is fair to
good, with mean survival times greater than 1 year. 16 , 27 Poor
outcomes may be related to the presence of underlying disease
that contributes to mortality such as neoplasia. 20 , 27 Among 168
cats with suppurative cholangitis-cholangiohepatitis syndrome,
infection (as identiﬁed by IHC), and the presence of gram-positive
bacteria by culture in conjunction with positive IHC, were
associated with a signiﬁcantly shorter long-term survival time of
283 days following diagnosis. 41 The presence of septic bile
peritonitis was associated with mortality in one study of dogs that
underwent extrahepatic biliary surgery; over 50% of dogs with
septic bile peritonitis died. 21 In another study, 9 of 23 dogs with
necrotizing cholecystitis died. 17

Hepatic Abscesses
Hepatic abscesses are uncommon in dogs and very rare in cats. 47 ,
48 They may be associated with ascending bacterial infection of
the biliary tree, translocation of portal bacteria, or hematogenous
spread of bacteria to the liver, although the source of bacteremia
in some animals is unclear. Because bacteria can be found in the
liver of healthy dogs, abscessation may also develop when these
bacteria proliferate secondary to compromise of normal defenses
(such as hepatic necrosis). 44 Aﬀected animals are typically middle
aged to older, 47 , 48 and the mean age of aﬀected dogs or cats is 10

vetexamprep.ir

g
g
g
years. The abscesses may be acute or chronic, single or multiple,
and macroabscesses or microabscesses may form. Pancreatitis,
diabetes mellitus, other hepatobiliary diseases, neoplasia, colonic
surgery, cholelithiasis, or chronic phenobarbital or glucocorticoid
administration have been involved in the histories of aﬀected
dogs. 48–50 Migrating plant awn foreign bodies may also be an
underlying cause. 50 Concurrent conditions reported in cats have
included IBD, pancreatitis, hepatobiliary neoplasia, chronic
cholecystitis, colonic surgery, or congestive heart failure. 47 Many
aﬀected cats have concurrent bacteriuria.
The most common bacterial species isolated from hepatic
abscesses in both dogs and cats is E. coli. In dogs, other species
have included Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus, and
Clostridium species. In cats, Bacteroides, Enterococcus, and
Streptococcus spp. have been isolated, often in mixed infections
with E. coli. Blood cultures are also often positive. 47 , 48 Clinical
signs and laboratory abnormalities are similar to those for other
hepatobiliary infections, except that severe illness and signs of
septic shock are often present. Evidence of bleeding diatheses may
be present. Marked neutrophilia or neutropenia, bandemia, toxic
neutrophils, anemia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia may be
present on the CBC. Hypoalbuminemia and coagulation
abnormalities are common. 47 , 48 Abdominal radiographs may be
unremarkable or they may show hepatomegaly or a hepatic mass
eﬀect, poor abdominal serosal detail, and/or pneumoperitoneum
if abscess rupture has occurred (Fig. 126.5). Thoracic radiography
often reveals interstitial, bronchiolar, or alveolar lung inﬁltrates, 47
, 48 which may result from associated embolic or aspiration
pneumonia. Ultrasonographic examination of the abdomen
reveals one or more hypoechoic, anechoic, or heteroechoic hepatic
masses, with or without peritoneal eﬀusion. In some cases, gas
may be evident within the masses (see Fig. 126.5).
Antemortem diagnosis usually relies on cytologic examination
of ultrasound-guided ﬁne-needle aspirates of these masses, which
reveals large numbers of degenerate neutrophils. Abscesses may
also be discovered during exploratory laparotomy (e.g., in dogs
and cats with bacterial peritonitis). Culture and susceptibility of
aspirates of the liver abscesses, free peritoneal ﬂuid, and/or blood
should be performed. Eﬀective treatment of solitary abscesses

vetexamprep.ir

relies on appropriate antimicrobial drug treatment together with
complete or partial liver lobectomy, or abscess drainage and
omentalization. With the exception of microabscesses,
antimicrobial drug therapy alone is often ineﬀective. Aggressive
supportive care in an intensive care unit may be required. Initial
antimicrobial drug treatment should be broad spectrum, after
which it should be adjusted based on the results of culture and
susceptibility testing. Mortality rates of 79% and 50% have been
reported for cats and dogs, respectively. 47 The prognosis appears
to be especially poor when multiple hepatic abscesses are present.
47 , 48

Case Example

“George,” a 16-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair from
northern California.

History

George was evaluated for a 2-day history of vomiting and
progressive lethargy and inappetence. The owners reported
that the vomiting occurred six times at the onset of illness and
was associated with apparent abdominal pain, but had since
resolved. The day he became ill, he was seen at an emergency
clinic where a CBC showed only a mild left shift (479 band
neutrophils), a chemistry panel showed mild hypokalemia (3.1
mmol/L, reference range 3.6–4.9 mmol/L), and a total serum T4
concentration was markedly increased (10.2 µg/dL, reference
range,
1.1–3.3
µg/dL).
Recurrent
pancreatitis
and
hyperthyroidism were initially suspected and George was
treated with subcutaneous lactated Ringer’s solution (200 mL,
SC, q24h), mucosal buprenorphine (0.2 mg/kg, PO, q8h to
q12h), and ondansetron (0.2 mg/kg, PO, q12h). However,
because George became inappetent and lethargic, he was
returned for re-evaluation the following day.
Other past pertinent medical history: George had been
diagnosed with pancreatitis 8 months previously. He was also
diagnosed with a biliary cystadenoma via ultrasound at that
time. He had been hospitalized for 9 days and treated with
jejunostomy tube feeding. Since then, he had been well until
this recent onset of illness.

Body weight: 6.1 kg.

Integument: Full, clean haircoat.

with normal gait.
Cardiovascular: Gallop sound with no murmurs or
arrhythmias auscultated. Femoral pulses strong and
synchronous.

ﬁelds.
Genitourinary/GI: Soft, mildly painful abdomen. The
bladder was small.
Other systems, including peripheral lymph nodes: No

hypera enuating. There was diﬀuse thickening of the
muscularis layer of the small bowel. There was no

Thoracic radiographs: The cardiac silhoue e appeared
mildly enlarged. There was a mild bronchointerstitial

result from a systolic click. New ﬁndings on the CBC
were mild, nonregenerative normocytic, normochromic
anemia (HCT 29.9%, RR, 30–50%), with a WBC of 11,580
cells/µL (4,500–14,000 cells/µL), 4053 neutrophils/µL

(2,000–9,000 cells/µL), bandemia (3,242 cells/µL) without

Microbiologic Testing

Cytologic examination (bile): Smears had light blue
backgrounds and contained a moderate amount of
unidentiﬁed material. Nucleated cells were not found, but
there were many short, plump coccobacilli observed.
Most of the bacteria were in large clusters, but a few
groups were in chains. During detailed evaluation, no
inﬂammatory cells were recognized. Interpretation:
possible severe sepsis.
Peritoneal ﬂuid analysis: Grossly the ﬂuid was pink and
cloudy, and it had a yellow, clear supernatant. The total
protein concentration was 2.8 g/dL and there were

vetexamprep.ir

100,000 RBC/µL. There were 5,380 nucleated cells/µL,
with 70% nondegenerate neutrophils, 6% small and welldiﬀerentiated lymphocytes, 7% foamy macrophages, and

Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture (bile): Large numbers
of Enterococcus faecium. No anaerobes were cultured. The isolate
was susceptible to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (≤ 4 µg/mL),
ampicillin (≤ 0.25 µg/mL), penicillin (0.12 µg/mL),

µg/mL).
Aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture (ascites): Very small
numbers of Enterococcus faecium. The antibiogram was identical
to the isolate from the bile.

Diagnosis

Bacterial cholecystitis and peritonitis caused by E. faecium;
pancreatitis and secondary hepatic lipidosis. Hyperthyroidism.
A concurrent chronic enteropathy was also likely present in
light of the ultrasound changes (thickened muscularis layer)
with concurrent hypocobalaminemia and hypofolatemia.

Treatment

Medical treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam (30 mg/kg, IV,
q8h) and enroﬂoxacin (5 mg/kg, IV, q24h) was commenced on
day 3 of hospitalization, before the results of culture and
susceptibility were available. Treatment was also continued
with IV ﬂuids, buprenorphine, omeprazole, ondansetron, and
nutritional support via the esophagostomy feeding tube with a
slurry of a commercially available gastroenteric diet (Purina
ProPlan Veterinary Diets EN Gastroenteric Feline Formula,
q4h). Surgery was considered, but because George was
medically stable, a decision was made to continue medical
treatment with close observation and serial CBC and abdominal
ultrasound examinations. Within 12 hours of antibiotic
treatment, George was brighter. A repeat abdominal ultrasound
showed no changes with the exception of mildly enlarged and
hypoechoic mesenteric lymph nodes. The CBC showed
persistent nonregenerative anemia (HCT of 26.4%), 10,181

vetexamprep.ir

moderately toxic neutrophils/µL, 5,553 bands/µL, 185
metamyelocytes/µL, and a normal platelet count (305,000/µL).
On day 5 of hospitalization, abdominal ultrasonography
showed a decrease in the amount of ascites. The enroﬂoxacin
was discontinued when the results of culture and susceptibility
became available. On day 6, the CBC showed a stable HCT,
9,366 moderately toxic neutrophils/µL, 2,810 bands/µL, and no
metamyelocytes. A serum chemistry panel was unremarkable
and the total bilirubin had decreased to 0.1 mg/dL. On day 8,
George began eating a small amount of food on his own and the
CBC showed further improvement with 6,048 neutrophils/µL
with no evidence of toxicity, 336 bands/µL, and a mild
monocytosis (896 cells/ µL). He was discharged from hospital
the following day with instructions to continue tube feeding,
ondansetron (0.3 mg/kg, PO, q24h), omeprazole (1 mg/kg, PO,
q12h), and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (15 mg/kg, PO, q12h). At
a recheck 1 week later, the owner reported that George had
been doing well at home, although he had vomited three times
over the course of the week. Physical examination was
unremarkable, apart from the thyroid nodule and evidence of
mild weight loss (body weight, 5.6 kg compared with 5.9 kg at
discharge). A CBC showed a HCT of 30%, 10,592 neutrophils/
µL, and 132 bands/µL. A serum chemistry panel was within
normal limits and the total T4 concentration was 8.2 µg/dL.
Treatment with methimazole (1.25 mg q12h) was initiated for
the hyperthyroidism, but because of continued vomiting, this
was discontinued after three doses. George’s demeanor and
appetite continued to improve. A week later he was eating
canned and dry food on his own with no vomiting, a CBC
showed no abnormalities, and the antibiotics were
discontinued. The esophagostomy feeding tube was removed 3
weeks later, and methimazole was reinstituted, after which his
T4 normalized. George was still doing well at follow-up 6
months later.

Comments

In this cat, cholecystitis and bacterial peritonitis were diagnosed
based on cytologic and microbiologic analysis of bile and
peritoneal ﬂuid. However, there were no ultrasonographic
abnormalities within the biliary tract, and cytologic evidence of
infection in the peritoneal ﬂuid was absent. Pancreatitis or an

vetexamprep.ir

underlying chronic enteropathy may have predisposed the cat
to ascending infection of the biliary tract, or infection may have
occurred secondary to bacterial translocation. The lack of an
inﬂammatory reaction in the bile was unusual, but it may have
resulted from marked neutrophil disruption in a toxic
environment. Isolation of the same bacterial organism from
both the bile and the peritoneal ﬂuid and the rapid clinical
response to antibiotic treatment suggested that Enterococcus
played a role in disease in this cat, although the clinical signs
and hematologic abnormalities may also have resulted from
severe pancreatitis and suspected hepatic lipidosis. Surgery was
postponed because the peritonitis appeared to be very mild,
and there was a concern that it could exacerbate the
pancreatitis. Fortunately, the cat made a complete recovery.
