127: Infections of the
Genitourinary Tract
Jodi L. Westropp, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
• Causes: The most common cause of genitourinary tract
infections is Escherichia coli, but other gram-negative
bacteria, staphylococci, and streptococci may also be
involved. Anaerobic bacterial infections are rare causes of
genitourinary tract infections, but may be involved in
pyometra.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Major Clinical Signs: No signs, or dysuria, hematuria, or
pollakiuria may occur with lower UTI. Acute pyelonephritis,
prostatitis, and pyometra may be accompanied by fever or
abdominal pain. Lethargy, inappetence, vomiting, or diarrhea
may occur with sepsis. Pyometra may be accompanied by
abdominal distention and/or a vaginal discharge. Prostatitis
may be accompanied by dyschezia, dysuria, and a purulent or
hemorrhagic urethral discharge.
• Differential Diagnoses: Feline idiopathic/interstitial cystitis,
bladder neoplasia, or cystolithiasis (bacterial cystitis); toxicity,
leptospirosis, and fungal or protozoal pyelonephritis
(pyelonephritis); pregnancy, mucometra, or hydrometra
(pyometra); benign prostatic hyperplasia, paraprostatic cysts,
and prostatic neoplasia (prostatitis).
• Human Health Significance: MDR uropathogens might have
the potential to colonize human patients.

vetexamprep.ir

Introduction
Infections of the genitourinary tract include sporadic bacterial
cystitis, recurrent bacterial cystitis, pyelonephritis, renal abscesses,
prostatitis, epididymitis and orchitis, metritis, pyometra, and
potentially bacterial vaginitis. Lower UTI can also be caused by
Candida spp. (see Chapter 85), and some fungi, especially molds
such as Aspergillus spp., can infect the upper urinary tract leading
to fungal pyelonephritis (see Chapter 86). This chapter focuses on
bacterial infections of the urogenital tract; information on
infections by other types of pathogens such as protozoa and
nematodes can be found in other respective chapters in this book.
UTI and genital infections can occur separately or concomitantly.
Terminology regarding lower UTI has been addressed in the 2019
guidelines regarding diagnosis and management of bacterial UTI
in dogs and cats by the ISCAID. 1 Sporadic bacterial cystitis
(formerly known as uncomplicated UTI), in which a bacterial
infection in the bladder results in inﬂammation and associated
lower urinary tract signs (stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria, and
dysuria), is a common reason for veterinary visits and
antimicrobial administration. This often occurs in otherwise
healthy nonpregnant females and to a lesser extent, castrated
males and cats. While possible, comorbidities such as
endocrinopathies, intervertebral disc disease, and urinary stones
are rarely identiﬁed in this group. Generally, animals with
sporadic bacterial cystitis have had known or suspected UTI fewer
than three times in the last 12 months. Complicated bacterial
cystitis has also been described in dogs and cats; however, it is
often diﬃcult to determine if the bacterial cystitis is truly
uncomplicated; underlying predispositions may be present.
In human medicine, recurrent bacterial cystitis implies three or
more bacterial cystitis events within a 12-month period, or more
than two events in a 6-month period; the same deﬁnition has been
adopted in veterinary medicine. 1 In this case, predisposing
patient factors are often identiﬁed, such as immune suppression,
kidney disease, hypercortisolism, diabetes mellitus, urolithiasis,
neoplasia, micturition disorders, ectopic ureters, and other
anatomic abnormalities such as urethral strictures or cystic
diverticulum. 2 While clinical cystitis can occur secondary to these
conditions, these co-morbidities also have been associated with

vetexamprep.ir

subclinical bacteriuria (SBU). Recurrent bacterial cystitis may
reﬂect refractory (or persistent) infection, relapsing infection, or
reinfection (Table 127.1). Without the use of molecular techniques
(e.g., pulsed-ﬁeld gel electrophoresis), it may not be possible to
distinguish between relapsing infection and reinfection if the
same bacterial species is isolated repeatedly, because a diﬀerent
strain may be present. Enterococcus spp. and Pseudomonas spp.
may be more commonly found in dogs with persistent or
recurrent UTI than dogs with simple uncomplicated UTI. 3 Some
bacteria such as Escherichia coli can invade and form microcolonies
within the uroepithelial cells (Fig. 127.1), 4 which may contribute
to persistent infection in the face of antimicrobial treatment.
Bacteria may also be able to form bioﬁlms in association with the
bladder wall (“deep-seated” infections), or on urinary implants
such as stents and urinary catheters. Escherichia coli isolated from
the urinary tract of dogs have been reported to frequently form
bioﬁlms; 52.6% of isolates were capable of forming bioﬁlms in one
study. Because no clinical distinguishing feature was found,
bioﬁlm formation should be considered whenever E. coli bacterial
UTI is diagnosed. Bioﬁlm formation was actually associated with
greater susceptibility to antimicrobial drugs, suggesting that the
antimicrobial tolerance may not be related to the presence of a
resistance gene, but further studies are needed. 5 The use of
antimicrobial-coated urinary catheters may reduce bioﬁlm
formation. 6

Pathogenesis of urinary tract
infection by uropathogenic Escherichia coli
(UPEC). (A) UPEC colonizing the
gastrointestinal tract, perineum, or vagina
ascend into the urinary bladder to cause
cystitis, which may be accompanied by lower
urinary tract signs. They can also ascend into
the kidneys to cause pyelonephritis. (B) In the
urinary bladder, individual bacteria adhere to
and invade superficial urothelial cells in a
FimH-dependent manner. There they undergo
clonal expansion to form biofilm-like
intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs),
where they can evade normal host mechanical
and immunologic clearance mechanisms.
Bacteria then form filaments that flux out of the
cells into the bladder urine, where they then
bind to adjacent cells and begin a new
infection cycle. From Klein RD, Hultgren SJ. Urinary

Pyelonephritis can result when bacteria ascend into the renal
pelvis and parenchyma from the lower urinary tract (see Fig.

vetexamprep.ir

127.1); less commonly, hematogenous spread to the kidney occurs.
A single bacterial species (most often E. coli) is isolated from the
urine of approximately three quarters of dogs with pyelonephritis,
with two species isolated in 8% of dogs and three species from
only 2% of dogs. Pyelonephritis may be acute or chronic. Strains
of E. coli that cause pyelonephritis have greater ability to adhere to
cells than strains that cause cystitis. Adhesins located on the tip of
E. coli ﬁmbriae adhere to glycolipid residues on tubular, collecting
duct and bladder epithelial cells. In humans with pyelonephritis,
both P and type I ﬁmbriae appear to be important in colonization
of the renal pelvis (Fig. 127.2). 7 , 8 Other E. coli virulence factors
associated with pyelonephritis include hemolysin, cytotoxic
necrotizing factor, the iron scavenger aerobactin, and a serum
protease known as Sat. Fimbriae are also important in the
pathogenesis of Proteus spp. pyelonephritis. 9 The medulla is more
sensitive to colonization than the cortex, possibly owing to
impaired host defenses in a high-osmolality, low-pH and low–
blood ﬂow milieu. Organisms adhere to pelvic and distal and
proximal tubular epithelium, and have been observed
intracellularly. Considerable renal injury results from the
inﬂammatory response to infection. Aggregation of neutrophils
within capillaries and induction of vascular spasm by bacterial
toxins and/or cytokines can contribute to renal ischemia.
These infections should not be confused with SBU (also referred
to as asymptomatic bacteriuria or ASB in humans). This term is
used to describe the presence of bacteria in the urine, as
determined by a positive bacterial culture in the absence of lower
urinary tract signs (LUTS). The term “subclinical UTI” could be
applied to dogs and cats if cytologic evidence of infection (e.g.,
pyuria or hematuria) is present, 10 but in human patients, the term
SBU is used even in the presence of these abnormalities. SBU is
commonly identiﬁed in dogs and cats, especially those with
underlying endocrinopathies, kidney disease, micturition
disorders, as well as dogs treated with glucocorticoids or
cyclosporine. 11–15 In dogs evaluated in a primary care se ing,
bacteriuria was documented in 23 (12.7%) of 181 nonproteinuric
specimens and 23 (8%) of the 286 proteinuric specimens. Of these
46 positive specimens, 31 were from dogs with SBU. 16 In a
retrospective study that included 182 dogs with CKD, 33 (18.1%)
had a positive aerobic bacterial urine culture. The highest

vetexamprep.ir

p
g
prevalence of positive cultures was found for dogs with SBU
(45%), with E. coli as the most frequently observed isolate. 17 In
one study of dogs treated with glucocorticoids for dermatologic
disorders, 18% of 127 dogs had bacteriuria in the absence of
clinical signs, whereas none of 94 dogs that had not received
glucocorticoids had bacteriuria. 15 SBU has a prevalence of 10%–
13% in cats; females were 21 times more likely to have a positive
culture than male cats. 18 The extent to which antibiotic treatment
is important in dogs or cats with SBU is not clear (see Treatment).

Pathophysiology
Infections of the genitourinary tract usually follow impairment of
normal host defenses and invasion by bacteria that are part of the
normal ﬂora (see Fig. 127.1). Less commonly, infection results
from hematogenous spread to urogenital organs secondary to
bacteremia. Speciﬁc pathogens such as Leptospira spp., Borrelia
(Borreliella [incertae sedis]) burgdorferi, and Leishmania spp. that
injure the kidneys secondary to systemic infection are described in
Chapters 68, 69, and 96.
In healthy dogs and cats, bacteria are not found in upper
urinary tract or prostate gland. In anestrus and diestrus, the
uterus is also a sterile environment. The vagina, vestibule,
prepuce, and distal urethra have a resident microﬂora. Normal
ﬂora should also be considered when results of aerobic bacterial
cultures of urine, semen, or the preputial area are interpreted. In
humans, recurrent infections can be associated with alterations in
the normal vaginal microbiome, which is an important factor in
host defense against pathogenic organisms. The resident
microﬂora competes with pathogenic bacteria for nutrients and
can interfere with adherence of pathogenic bacteria to vaginal
epithelial receptors. Lactobacilli isolated from the vagina of dogs
showed antimicrobial activity against Proteus mirabilis,
Staphylococcus aureus, and E. coli. 19 The most common canine
vaginal isolates reported in the dog are E. coli and Staphylococcus
pseudintermedius. Vaginal lactic acid-producing bacteria were
reported less often, with Enterococcus canintestini being the most
common. 20
Other factors that prevent bacterial colonization of the bladder
include the glycosaminoglycan layer that covers bladder
transitional epithelium, frequent voiding, the normal urethral
microﬂora, antimicrobial properties of urine, an appropriate host
immune response, and a functional urethral sphincter.
Commensal bacteria that reside in the distal urethra, prepuce, and
vagina invade opportunistically when these mechanisms are
disturbed. The most common pathogen involved in all
genitourinary tract infections is E. coli, which has a particular
propensity to adhere to epithelial cells of the genitourinary tract.
Others include coagulase-positive and coagulase-negative
staphylococci; Enterococcus spp.; other aerobic gram-negative

vetexamprep.ir

bacilli such as Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, and Pseudomonas
aeruginosa; Corynebacterium spp.; streptococci; and mycoplasmas.
Anaerobic bacteria are also found in the genital tract of female
dogs, and may contribute to pyometra and metritis. In addition to
impaired host defenses, a variety of bacterial virulence factors
may impact the nature of the organisms that ultimately invade
tissues and cause disease. The importance of virulence factors in
uropathogenic E. coli infections is described in Chapter 53.

Upper and Lower Urinary Tract Infections
Etiology and Epidemiology
Sporadic bacterial cystitis is commonly diagnosed in dogs.
Although mixed bacterial infections can occur, the vast majority of
these infections involve a single bacterial species. 21 The most
common uropathogen isolated is E. coli, which accounts for
approximately 50% of all isolates, followed by Staphylococcus,
Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and Streptococcus spp.
Mycoplasmas have also been isolated from dogs with bacterial
cystitis, although their clinical signiﬁcance has been unclear
because they are usually isolated from dogs that have other
disorders of the lower urinary tract, such as underlying neoplasia
or cystolithiasis. Spayed females and older dogs are at increased
risk for infection; the mean age at diagnosis is 7 to 8 years. 3 , 21 As
a result of breakdown in host defense mechanisms, systemic
disorders such as acute or chronic kidney disease,
hyperadrenocorticism, diabetes mellitus, and systemic neoplasia
also predispose dogs to bacterial colonization of lower urinary
tract. However, in many of these cases, SBU may be present and
treatment with antimicrobials is not warranted (see later) (Table
127.2).

The prevalence of sporadic cystitis in cats ranges from just 1% to
3%. 22–24 However, other studies have reported a higher
prevalence of bacterial cystitis; 44/134 (33%) of cats with
obstructive and nonobstructive feline lower urinary tract disease
had bacteriuria from the Norwegian School of Veterinary Science.

While bacteriuria (clinical or subclinical) in cats is more often

Uncommon forms of bacterial cystitis in dogs and cats are
encrusting cystitis and emphysematous cystitis. Encrusting cystitis is
caused by the gram-positive bacterium Corynebacterium
urealyticum. Urease production by this organism leads to
precipitation of large amounts of struvite and calcium phosphate
within the bladder and along the bladder and urethral mucosa,
and in some cases within the ureters and renal pelvis. 28–31 Most
animals with C. urealyticum infections have severe LUTS and
underlying co-morbidities such as urinary retention, urolithiasis,
or ectopic ureters. Antimicrobial resistance is common and
treatment should be implemented based on susceptibility testing.
Use of an acidifying diet is warranted and endoscopic or surgical
urothelial debridement may be required.

vetexamprep.ir

Emphysematous cystitis is characterized by the production of
gas by bacteria within the bladder wall (Fig. 127.3). The most
common cause is E. coli, but Clostridium spp. may also be
involved. 32 , 33 The majority of dogs and cats that develop E. coli
emphysematous cystitis have co-morbidities. In one study,
diabetes mellitus was reported in 33% of 27 dogs, neurologic
disease in 26%, and adrenal disease in 19%. 32 In diabetics, gas
production may result from fermentation of glucose to gas
products by E. coli. In the absence of glucose, proteins such as
albumin may be fermented to gas. Emphysematous cystitis
caused by Clostridium perfringens occurs in the absence of diabetes
mellitus. 33 , 34

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of bacterial cystitis can include LUTS such as
dysuria, hematuria, stranguria, and pollakiuria. Some clinical
signs might be less apparent, such as subtle urinary incontinence
or licking of perivulvar or prepucial area. Owners might also
complain of foul-smelling urine. Cats may urinate outside the
li er box (periuria or inappropriate urination). In some dogs, such
as those with neurologic disorders like paraplegia, it can be
diﬃcult to ascertain if the animal is exhibiting signs of discomfort
from the infection. Short-term treatment (see later) can be
considered and the dog’s clinical response closely monitored.
Rarely, lethargy may accompany sporadic cystitis, but fever and
hyporexia are not present.
Acute or acute-on-chronic pyelonephritis may result in
decreased appetite, lethargy, variable fever, hematuria, and
clinical signs of uremia, such as vomiting and diarrhea. Polyuria
and polydipsia may also be present, or dogs with advanced
disease may be anuric. Dogs and cats with chronic pyelonephritis
may show no signs, or show only polyuria and polydipsia.
Physical Examination Findings
Physical examination ﬁndings in dogs or cats with bacterial
cystitis may be unremarkable, or there may be mild urine staining
of the perineum. Some dogs may present with urinary
incontinence and evidence of urine scalding or a strong ammonia-

vetexamprep.ir

like odor may be present. Underlying disorders that predispose to
bacterial cystitis may also be apparent (such as a recessed vulva
and associated vulvar fold dermatitis).
Occasionally, abdominal pain may be detected on palpation of
the abdomen of dogs or cats with bacterial cystitis, but more often
this is seen with acute pyelonephritis or when concurrent
prostatitis is present. The bladder is often small in dogs or cats
due to persistent inﬂammation and associated frequent voiding
(pollakiuria); a thickened bladder wall may also be palpated. If a
large, turgid bladder is present in dogs or cats with a UTI,
urethral obstruction due to neoplasia, calculi, encrusting cystitis,
or proliferative urethritis (PU) should be suspected. Fever is not
present in dogs and cats with infections localized to the lower
urinary tract, and is variable in dogs and cats with pyelonephritis.
Dogs and cats with severe pyelonephritis may show evidence of
lethargy, dehydration, and signs of severe sepsis or septic shock
(e.g., tachycardia or bradycardia, tachypnea, prolonged capillary
reﬁll time).

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of sporadic bacterial cystitis or pyelonephritis is based
on the clinical signs present, laboratory abnormalities, imaging
ﬁndings, and culture of urine. Most cases of acute pyelonephritis
arise from ascension of the fecal-derived organisms. Acute
pyelonephritis with E. coli (at least in children) is associated with
type 1 and type P pili, with the la er more frequently identiﬁed.
Renal scarring is noted in children due to activation of NF-κB,
which perpetuates the inﬂammatory response, fever, and
neutrophil recruitment (see Fig. 127.2). 35 The presence of fever or
leukocytosis in addition to a positive bacterial urine culture
should increase suspicion for concurrent bacterial pyelonephritis;
prostatitis or pyometra should also be considered (see relevant
sections later in this chapter). Ultrasound examination ﬁndings
also can support the diagnosis and assist in the identiﬁcation of
predisposing disorders such as neoplasia, anatomic abnormalities,
or the presence of calculi or foreign material. At a minimum,
collection of urine by cystocentesis followed by complete
urinalysis (with sediment examination) and quantitative aerobic
bacterial urine culture are recommended to conﬁrm the presence

vetexamprep.ir

of bacterial UTI for dogs or cats with signs of lower urinary tract
disease. 1 , 10 Additional diagnostics are indicated for animals that
have recurrent LUTS or those with systemic signs such as fever,
weight loss, or inappetence. The owners of animals that are
diagnosed with a suspected sporadic bacterial cystitis should
always be advised that other predisposing underlying disease
may be present.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Complete Blood Count and Serum Biochemical Tests
Animals with infections localized to the lower urinary tract
typically have no hematologic or serum biochemistry
abnormalities. The diagnosis of pyelonephritis can be diﬃcult.
Animals with pyelonephritis may have mild anemia, leukocytosis
due to a neutrophilia, increased band neutrophils, and
monocytosis. A degenerative left shift, toxic neutrophils, and
thrombocytopenia may also be present. The serum biochemistry
panel may show azotemia. Due to the potential for renal scarring
and other complications in children with acute pyelonephritis,
various novel biomarkers have been evaluated to identify early
kidney injury. These include CRP, IL-6, IL-8, plasma neutrophil
gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), 36 kidney injury molecule1 (uKIM -1) 37 and procalcitonin (PCT). 38 Several of these
biomarkers may be useful for predicting and possibly managing
acute pyelonephritis, but none are clinically available in
veterinary medicine at this time. The la er (PCT) is intriguing
because it is an early and reliable marker of serious bacterial
infections and sepsis. 39 SDMA can be a useful marker of
glomerular ﬁltration rate (GFR) in cats and dogs and is used for
screening for early detection of kidney injury. Like many of the
biomarkers, it is not speciﬁc for pyelonephritis, 40 but is clinically
available. Other markers such as cystatin C, NGAL, and
homocysteine have also been investigated in dogs. 41
Hypoalbuminemia and electrolyte abnormalities may be
present in dogs or cats with pyelonephritis. However,
pyelonephritis may be present in animals with normal CBC and
serum biochemical panels. While research is underway to identify
biomarkers speciﬁc for renal parenchymal infection, currently the

vetexamprep.ir

clinician must collate all physical examination, imaging, and
biochemical ﬁndings and decide if treatment for pyelonephritis is
warranted.
Urinalysis
The urinalysis is usually the initial screening test for dogs with
LUTS. Of 52 private practices in Denmark evaluating 151 dogs
with LUTS, the veterinarian performed a urine dipstick 99% of the
time and sediment examination in 80%. Only 56% of those
samples were submi ed for culture. 42 Findings on the urinalysis
in dogs and cats with UTI can include isosthenuria, pyuria,
hematuria, proteinuria, and bacteriuria. Animals with
pyelonephritis may have cylindruria, and small amounts of
glucose may be present in dogs with altered proximal tubular
function. However, the urinalysis may also be unremarkable, even
in dogs and cats with pyelonephritis. Infections with ureaseproducing bacteria such as staphylococci, Proteus spp., and C.
urealyticum may be associated with a high urine pH and the
presence of struvite crystals. The urine protein to creatinine ratio
(UPCR) in dogs with pyelonephritis may be increased as a result
of renal tubular or glomerular injury. However, an elevated UPCR
may be noted in dogs with sporadic cystitis as well as those with
SBU. 16 In patients with a high suspicion of pyelonephritis but
negative urine culture, blood cultures and/or nephropyelocentesis
should be considered.
Coagulation Profile
Evidence of coagulation abnormalities may be present in animals
with severe pyelonephritis that develop severe sepsis or septic
shock (see Chapter 123).
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Dogs or cats with sporadic bacterial cystitis alone generally have
no radiographic abnormalities. The bladder of animals with
pollakiuria may be small. Emphysematous cystitis is characterized
by the presence of radiolucencies within the bladder lumen
and/or in association with the bladder wall (see Fig. 127.3).
Radiopaque cystic or renal (“staghorn”) calculi may be visible in

vetexamprep.ir

dogs with struvite calculi secondary to infections with
Staphylococcus spp. or Proteus spp. (Fig. 127.4).
Renomegaly may be present with acute pyelonephritis, or the
kidneys may be small and irregular in dogs or cats with chronic
pyelonephritis.

Sonographic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Ultrasound examination of the urogenital tract is a noninvasive
method to obtain information about the extent and severity of
disease and underlying causes such as neoplasia, calculi, or
foreign bodies. It does not permit visualization of the entire
urethra, and urethral abnormalities (e.g., evidence of PU) may be
overlooked in some animals if only ultrasound is used for
imaging purposes. Ultrasound examination of the bladder may be
unremarkable or show a mild to moderately thickened bladder
wall in dogs or cats with bacterial cystitis. Increased echogenicity
of the urine may be present. Rarely the bladder wall is severely
thickened (Fig. 127.5). Animals with emphysematous cystitis may
have a hyperechoic bladder wall with acoustic shadow artifacts.
Shadow artifacts may also occur as a result of the presence of
cystic calculi.
Dogs or cats with pyelonephritis may have a normal abdominal
ultrasound examination, or blunting of the renal papilla,
pyelectasia, irregularity of the renal contour, and evidence of
hydronephrosis (Fig. 127.6). However, renal pelvic dilatation can
occur in animals with normal renal function, diuresis, and outﬂow
tract obstruction, and there is considerable overlap in the extent of
dilatation between groups. 43 Dogs and cats with severe
pyelonephritis may have hyperechoic material within the renal
pelvis, or the renal pelvis may be anechoic and contain
hyperechoic debris. 44 Sometimes the surrounding mesentery is
hyperechoic, and perinephric anechoic ﬂuid may be present due
to localized peritonitis. Other nonspeciﬁc ﬁndings in
pyelonephritis can include increased renal cortical echogenicity,
and decreased corticomedullary deﬁnition. The diagnosis of
pyelonephritis should not be made solely based on
ultrasonographic ﬁndings.

Contrast Radiography and Cystoscopy
Intravenous contrast urography was utilized to identify renal
pelvic enlargement and assist in the diagnosis of pyelonephritis,
but has largely been replaced by abdominal ultrasonography for
this purpose, which is less invasive and can be an excellent tool to
identify predisposing factors such as uroliths, diverticuli,
neoplasia, and polypoid cystitis. While cystoscopy can be
considered for select patients with recurrent UTI, it is not often
recommended for women when other imaging such as
ultrasonography is normal, 45 and cystoscopy performed solely
for recurrent UTI in women was reported to be low yield. 46 In 163
women with recurrent UTI, cystourethroscopy rarely (3.8%)
identiﬁed a unique lesion (i.e., pertinent uroendoscopic ﬁnding)
that was not previously identiﬁed by ultrasound (111 women) or
contrast CT (22 women). 47 In dogs with recurrent UTI, nonspeciﬁc cystourethroscopic and vaginoscopic ﬁndings such as
mucosal edema, lymphoid follicles and vestibulovaginal septal
remnants were noted in 45/53 (85%) dogs, but no comparisons
were made in this study between endoscopic and
ultrasonographic ﬁndings. 48 In addition, this study did not
determine if these ﬁndings were clinically relevant or related to
the LUTS for which the dog was being evaluated. Preliminary
data in dogs with recurrent UTI found that cystoscopy ﬁndings
were in agreement with the ultrasonographic ﬁndings in 26/30
(87%) dogs evaluated. 49 In dogs, cystoscopy can be considered if
bladder or urethral biopsy is indicated for histopathology. Culture
of the bladder or urethral tissue can be considered, as well as
techniques such as FISH when the possibility of a deep-seated
infection exists, as bladder wall infection may not be associated
with positive urine cultures in some dogs. 50 Furthermore, ﬁve
dogs with PU had negative urine and tissue cultures when FISH
was positive. There was no association detected between the type
of urethral inﬂammation and the results of urine and tissue
culture or FISH. 51 However, if obtaining biopsy specimens for

vetexamprep.ir

culture, it is ideal to collect these when the dog has a negative
urine culture and not receiving antimicrobial therapy, which can
be diﬃcult to achieve in some patients. Contrast
cystourethrography can also be useful for diagnosis of anatomic
abnormalities, particularly urethral lesions, when cystoscopy is
not available.

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Quantitative aerobic bacterial culture and susceptibility testing is
strongly recommended for dogs or cats with UTI before starting
antimicrobial drugs, because of the possibility of antimicrobial
drug resistance, which has been well recognized among E. coli

vetexamprep.ir

strains isolated from dogs and cats with genitourinary tract
infections. 52 , 53 It is especially warranted in dogs and cats with
recurrent UTI that have received previous antimicrobials for UTI
treatment. Isolates from dogs that had received amoxicillin,
doxycycline, or enroﬂoxacin 30 days before culture results were
obtained were signiﬁcantly more likely to be resistant than those
from dogs that did not receive those antimicrobials before urine
cultures were obtained. 2 Guidelines for diagnosis of bacterial UTI
in dogs and cats have been published. 1 , 10 Ideally, urine should
be collected by cystocentesis; if this is not possible or
contraindicated (e.g., coagulopathy or lower urinary tract
neoplasia), urethral catheterization can be considered. Although
any pathogens isolated from specimens collected by cystocentesis
are likely signiﬁcant, the presence of > 103 CFU/mL of bacteria is
unlikely to result from skin contamination alone. If specimens are
collected using catheterization, colony counts that exceed > 104
CFU/mL for male dogs and > 105 CFU/mL for female dogs are
considered clinically signiﬁcant. 1 , 10 Free-catch (midstream
voiding) specimen collection is not recommended for dogs or cats
because it is highly susceptible to contamination. Aerobic bacterial
urine culture from a specimen collected by cystocentesis conﬁrms
the presence of bacterial infection in animals with LUTS. Culture
can also help to diﬀerentiate reinfection from relapse should a UTI
return. 1 , 10 Culture of a single organism from a mucosal swab
collected from a site such as the urethra does not imply disease
causation because commensal bacteria may be isolated in pure
cultures from healthy dogs and cats. Specimens for culture and
susceptibility testing should be refrigerated immediately and
submi ed to the laboratory as soon as possible. The results of
culture for specimens that reach the laboratory > 24 hours after
collection should be interpreted with caution because falsenegative and false-positive test results can occur. For dogs and
cats with recurrent UTI that undergo surgery, culture of a bladder
wall biopsy or cystoliths can be considered, but a decision to treat
should be based on the presence of clinical signs.
Inexpensive urine “paddles” have been marketed for in-house
veterinary diagnosis of UTI, which consist of two diﬀerent types
of agar on either side of a plastic paddle (see also Chapter 3, Fig.
3.6). The media are inoculated with urine collected by

vetexamprep.ir

cystocentesis and the paddles are then incubated and examined
daily for growth; sensitivity and speciﬁcity of this POC test was
97.3% and 98.6%, respectively; however, the paddles do take
approximately 24 hours before results are available to interpret. 54
A rapid immunoassay (RapidBac Vet, Silver Lake Research,
Azusa, CA, USA) is also marketed as a POC test for detection of
bacteriuria in cats and dogs with a 90% sensitivity and 96.6%
speciﬁcity reported when applied to a small number of specimens.
Of 200 canine urine samples, 38 (19%) were considered associated
with a UTI based on the urine collection method and signiﬁicant
bacteriuria. For these samples, the sensitivity and speciﬁcity of the
rapid immunoassay was 97.8% and 98.8%, respectively. The
agreement with the reference laboratory was considered
substantial. 55 In another study of 22 urine specimens from dogs,
sensitivity and speciﬁcity were 73% and 91%, respectively; for
specimens with over 1000 CFU/mL of bacteria identiﬁed using
culture, sensitivity and speciﬁcity were 80% and 91%,
respectively. 56 Assay results are available in 20 minutes. These
POC tests can be useful screening tools for patients with LUTS
when client ﬁnances do not permit submission of specimens to a
microbiology laboratory for culture. If positive results are
obtained, ideally a urine specimen should then be submi ed to a
microbiology laboratory for culture and susceptibility testing in
order to select the most appropriate antimicrobial drug. If
performed in-house, bacterial culture should only be performed in
clinics with appropriate laboratory facilities, proper BSL
containment and waste management, and adequately trained
personnel. 10
If a urinary catheter is present, culture should be performed if
clinical signs of infection are present (e.g., hematuria, suspected
bacteremia). 10 The catheter should be removed and cystocentesis
performed after the bladder is allowed to ﬁll with urine.
Alternatively, the catheter could be removed, replaced with a new
catheter if necessary, and a urine specimen collected through the
new catheter after removal of several milliliters of urine to clear
the catheter. Urine culture should never be submi ed from
specimens collected from the urine bag because it is likely to yield
growth of organisms forming bioﬁlm on the bag or catheter; there
is no indication to culture the catheter tip.

vetexamprep.ir

Bacteria cultured from the urine are usually those involved in
pyelonephritis, when pyelonephritis is present. However, a
negative urine culture does not rule out pyelonephritis.
Pyonephrosis, a collection of sloughed urothelium and
inﬂammatory cells in the dilated renal collecting system, is a
complication that can be caused by partial or complete ureteral
obstruction with concurrent upper tract infection. The diagnosis
of pyelonephritis can be challenging clinically. Ultrasound-guided
nephropyelocentesis can be considered when renal pelvic dilation
is present to obtain urine for culture, but this is not usually
required for eﬀective treatment of pyelonephritis. Blood cultures
should also be considered in animals with acute pyelonephritis,
especially when signs of severe sepsis are present.
Laboratories that perform susceptibility testing for
uropathogens should adhere to local guidelines for test
performance and reporting (such as the Clinical and Laboratory
Standards Institute [CLSI] in North America and the European
Commi ee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing [EUCAST] in
Europe) (see Chapter 3). Breakpoints for systemic infections also
apply to UTI. However, provided renal function is normal, many
antimicrobials achieve much higher concentrations in urine than
they do in serum. Therefore, use of some antimicrobials may
eradicate the UTI despite predicted resistance. This is especially
true for treatment of staphylococcal UTI with penicillins and
cephalosporins. Urinary breakpoints are available for ampicillin
or amoxicillin in dogs (≤8 µg/mL), amoxicillin-clavulanate in dogs
and cats (<8/4 µg/mL), and nitrofurantoin. These should only be
used when infection is conﬁned to the lower urinary tract.
Pathologic Findings
Pathologic ﬁndings in dogs with bacterial cystitis and
pyelonephritis depend on the chronicity of the infection, the
underlying cause, and the uropathogens present. Acute infections
are associated with a dense neutrophilic inﬁltrate on
histopathology and intralesional bacteria may be identiﬁed.
Chronic infections may be associated with histiocytic or
lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates.

Treatment and Prognosis

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment of UTI consists of: (1) removal or management of the
underlying cause of infection and (2) antimicrobial treatment.
Treatment with antimicrobial drugs alone without a ention to an
underlying cause frequently leads to recurrent infection and
selection for resistant bacteria. Because of the increasing
prevalence of MDR E. coli and staphylococci in dogs and cats with
UTI, provided the patient is stable and sepsis is absent,
consideration should be given to delaying antimicrobial drug
treatment until the results of culture and susceptibility are
available. This is especially true for dogs and cats with recurrent
UTI that have a history of antimicrobial drug treatment. Empiric
treatment while awaiting the results of culture and susceptibility
could be considered to relieve discomfort if present in dogs that
have not received previous antimicrobial treatment. The use of
NSAIDs can be considered (with extreme caution in cats) to
relieve clinical signs while pending susceptibility testing. When
pyelonephritis or sepsis is present or suspected, treatment should
commence immediately with broad-spectrum antimicrobials that
have activity against MDR gram-negative bacteria (see Chapter
123).

options for severe sepsis.

Sporadic Bacterial Cystitis
Published guidelines provide detailed recommendations for
treatment of sporadic cystitis. 1 In most situations, rational choices
for initial treatment of sporadic cystitis include amoxicillin or
trimethoprim-sulfonamide (Table 127.3). Amoxicillin-clavulanic
acid could be considered if regional susceptibility trends suggest a
high (>10%) prevalence of β-lactamase production by
uropathogens isolated. 1 , 10 However, evidence of a need for

vetexamprep.ir

clavulanic acid is lacking and may not be necessary due to the
high urinary concentrations of amoxicillin that are achieved in
most animals. Trimethoprim-sulfonamides are an excellent
option, but do have a greater association with adverse events such
as hepatotoxicity, and immune-mediated diseases. Resolution of
clinical signs (i.e., clinical cure) is the goal of therapy, rather than
elimination of bacteriuria. Once culture and susceptibility results
are available, the initially chosen antimicrobial drug should either
be continued (if a clinical response has occurred) for a total of 3 to
5 days or switched to an alternative drug (if clinical cure has not
been achieved) with activity against the pathogen isolated and
that enters urine in high concentrations. A treatment duration of 3
to 5 days has been recommended by the ISCAID Antimicrobial
Working Group; however, 10 to 14 days of treatment is still
routinely prescribed. 1 , 10 While there are numerous studies
evaluating and supporting short-course therapy for UTI in
humans, studies in the veterinary ﬁeld are lacking. One study
showed that treatment of dogs that had sporadic cystitis with
high-dose enroﬂoxacin (20 mg/kg) for 3 days was not inferior to
treatment with clavulanic acid-amoxicillin for 14 days (see Table
127.3). 57 Another study of dogs with naturally occurring UTI that
evaluated short durations of treatment with trimethoprimsulfonamide compared with longer duration of treatment with
cephalosporins found that no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the
microbiologic or clinical cure rates were reported between the two
groups in short- or long-term (>30 days) evaluation, but long-term
treatment cure rates were low in both groups. 58
Recurrent Bacterial Cystitis
Investigation of an underlying cause is strongly recommended in
animals with recurrent UTI. For animals where reinfections are
conﬁrmed (i.e., recurrent infections with diﬀering bacterial strains
or species), a thorough evaluation for micturition disorders
(urinary incontinence or urine retention), perivulvar inﬂammation
and infection, or predisposing systemic abnormalities should be
performed.
Care should be taken not to overinterpret the ﬁnding of a
recessed vulva. While the incidence of bacteriuria improved in 19
of 22 dogs after vulvoplasty, 59% of those dogs had perivulvar
dermatitis which also improved. Moreover, 14 of 34 dogs had

vetexamprep.ir

signs such as urinary incontinence, and perivulvar dermatitis at
an older age suggesting multiple contributing factors for recurrent
infections. While 16 dogs with UTI and hooded vulva improved
clinically (i.e., decreased recurrence of UTI) after episioplasty, 3 of
16 had concurrent cystic calculi, and 12 of 16 dogs had concurrent
perivulvar dermatitis, which also resolved. 59
For animals with a relapsing infection (i.e., recurrent UTI with
the same pathogen strain), the pathogen susceptibility should be
reviewed, as well as the antimicrobial dose and duration. A
thorough investigation for a nidus of infection (e.g., urinary
calculi, polyp or deep-seated infection) should be considered.
Referral to an internal medicine specialist should be considered
for further diagnostic tests, including advanced imaging.
Antimicrobial drugs should be selected on the basis of culture and
susceptibility test results, and preference should be given to drugs
that are excreted in the urine in active form. If excreted in the
urine, drugs with intermediate susceptibility could be used to
treat UTI that is resistant to other appropriate drug choices;
however, a higher dose (for concentration-dependent
antimicrobials) or dosing frequency (for time-dependent
antimicrobials) should be considered. Nitrofurantoin should be
considered for UTI that is resistant to other oral antimicrobial
drugs that are excreted in the urine and only administered when
the infection is isolated to the lower urinary tract. Nitrofurantoin
should never be used to treat prostatitis or pyelonephritis due to
poor tissue penetration. When mixed infections are present,
antimicrobial drug treatment ideally should be directed at all
organisms present. In mixed infections that involve Enterococcus
spp., the Enterococcus spp. infection will typically resolve when
other organisms present are successfully treated. 10 There is no
evidence to suggest that longer antimicrobial treatment duration
(10 to 14 days) is needed for animals with recurrent UTI. The
primary objective for treatment is clinical cure (resolution of
clinical signs); microbiologic cure is not always achievable in some
patients with co-morbidities that cannot be corrected. Longer
courses (14 days) can be considered for some relapsing infections,
particularly for suspected deep-seated infections. Aerobic
bacterial urine culture could be considered 5 to 7 days after
initiating treatment, but if clinical cure is achieved, a change in
treatment may not be warranted even if a positive bacterial

vetexamprep.ir

culture is documented. If no clinical signs are present,
management should be as for SBU (see later).
As mentioned earlier, urolithiasis in the urinary tract can serve
as a nidus for infection and reason for relapsing infections,
particularly in dogs. Stone removal is advised if appropriate
(bladder, urethral stones) and consideration for a ureteral stent or
subcutaneous ureteral bypass in patients presenting with ureteral
obstruction. In dogs presenting with suspected struvite
urolithiasis, dissolution with a calculolytic diet and concurrent
antimicrobials (in dogs) should be prescribed. Traditionally,
antimicrobials are recommended for the entire dissolution
protocol in dogs. Shorter courses of antimicrobial therapy
combined with a calculolytic diet may be eﬃcacious; an induced
canine struvite model provided limited evidence for struvite
dissolution without antimicrobials 60 ; however, dissolution will
likely take longer utilizing this strategy. In one study, the target
urinary pH appeared appropriate for struvite dissolution (pH =
5.9–6.1) at day 45 in dogs with struvite urolithiasis following only
7 days of antimicrobial administration during the ﬁrst week
combined with a calculolytic diet. However, radiographic
evidence of struvite dissolution was not provided. 60 At this point,
no deﬁnitive guidelines exist for the timing and duration of
antimicrobial therapy in humans 61 or dogs with struvite uroliths.
Future studies should consider this to improve antimicrobial
stewardship. Recommendations for shorter course therapy have
been suggested for dogs. 1 Regardless of the strategy
implemented, patients should be re-evaluated on a regular basis
and treatment adjusted based on clinical ﬁndings using diagnostic
imaging and laboratory ﬁndings (serum chemistry, urinalysis,
urine culture).
There is no evidence that direct instillation of antimicrobials,
antiseptics, glycosaminoglycans, or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)
directly into the bladder via a urinary catheter is eﬀective for
treatment of recurrent UTI. These compounds are rapidly
eliminated from the bladder during micturition and may be
locally irritating, which may predispose further to infection with
drug-resistant bacteria. Approaches that have been used to
prevent recurrence are detailed in the Prevention section.
Subclinical Bacteriuria

vetexamprep.ir

In humans, there is abundant support that antimicrobial treatment
is not warranted for ASB. No evidence of an association between
SBU and risk of sepsis, pyelonephritis, or other complications
exists. Data in veterinary medicine are limited. Of 67 nonazotemic
cats that had urine cultures performed on ﬁve occasions over 3
years, the presence of SBU in cats did not adversely impact
survival even though antimicrobial treatment was withheld. 18 In
cats with CKD, no diﬀerence was noted in the frequency of CKD
progression between cats with UTI and those with SBU or no
positive urine culture. However, the impact of not treating SBU on
progression of CKD or survival could not be assessed because in
this group, all cats received antimicrobial treatment. When nine
healthy dogs with SBU were followed for 3 months, four had
persistent bacteriuria and four transient; none developed signs
during this period. 62 Of 47 chronically paralyzed dogs that lacked
pelvic limb pain perception, 35 had at least one positive urine
culture and 13 dogs had recurrent bacteriuria. 63 Bacteriuria was
not associated with survival, but the diﬀerences in antimicrobial
treatment between the two groups were not clear. However,
resistant bacterial isolates were cultured from 46% of dogs with
recurrent positive urine cultures.
Treatment for humans with concurrent diabetes mellitus and
ASB is not recommended; the authors do not advocate screening
or treatment of SBU in dogs with stable diabetes mellitus or those
with hypercortisolism. Identifying clinical signs of bacterial
cystitis in some patients can be diﬃcult (e.g., paralyzed dogs); if
the clinician or owner is concerned for poor quality of life, a short
course (3 to 5 days) of antimicrobials can be considered and the
clinical signs charted during the course of therapy.
While both UTI and SBU have been described in cats and dogs
that have implants such as subcutaneous ureteral bypass devices
or ureteral stents, 64 whether SBU should be treated with
antimicrobials requires additional study. These devices are prone
to colonization with bacterial bioﬁlms, and bacteriuria can be
diﬃcult to eradicate. Treatment should be implemented if
azotemia has progressed (and no other underlying cause for the
progression has been documented) and serum creatinine or
SDMA re-evaluated. If no improvement is noted, further
antimicrobial treatment may not be indicated.

vetexamprep.ir

Animals with SBU should be evaluated for potential underlying
causes of SBU that need to be addressed. If no underlying
conditions are evident, treatment for SBU is not warranted. The
authors advise treatment for SBU only for patients that are
undergoing a urologic intervention (e.g., cystotomy or laser
ablation for ectopic ureter) and at least once for dogs with SBU
associated with Staphylococcus cystitis due to its association with
struvite urolithiasis. Treatment is also indicated for SBU when
there is an associated new or progressive azotemia, and the
response to antimicrobial therapy monitored (clinical signs,
severity of azotemia). Finally, urine cultures and treatment are
indicated, despite a lack of LUTS, in animals where systemic
infection is suspected.
Pyelonephritis
Treatment of dogs with acute pyelonephritis should be initiated
immediately, without waiting for culture and susceptibility test
results. Cytologic examination of stained urine sediment may
assist in initial selection of an antimicrobial drug (i.e., based on the
presence of rods versus cocci). The use of a ﬂuoroquinolone that is
excreted in the urine in active form (i.e., not diﬂoxacin) has been
recommended for gram-negative bacterial pyelonephritis,
provided regional susceptibility data do not show widespread
resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones. 1 , 10 The dosage used may need to
be altered depending on the severity of renal impairment. If
combination treatment is initiated and antimicrobial susceptibility
test results show susceptibility to only one drug, the other drug
should be discontinued. In older veterinary literature, treatment
durations of 4 to 6 weeks have been recommended for
pyelonephritis, but a shorter duration is likely adequate, as is
recommended in human medicine. Treatment for 10–14 days is
recommended by the ISCAID Working Group. Oral antimicrobial
therapy is justiﬁed for animals that are otherwise systemically
healthy and have a normal ﬂuid intake without vomiting.
Intravenous antimicrobials should be administered to animals
that are febrile, dehydrated, hyporexic, and/or vomiting. Dogs
with acute pyelonephritis may require hospitalization and
supportive care with IV ﬂuids and other medications used to treat
acute kidney injury or sepsis. The patient should be re-evaluated
and serum creatinine, urinalysis, and an aerobic bacterial urine

vetexamprep.ir

culture are recommended 1 week after completion of the
antimicrobial treatment. The clinical and biochemical response
should be evaluated. If a microbiologic cure is not documented,
the clinician should be certain the patient was evaluated properly
for underlying disorders (e.g., uroliths) and decide if the isolate is
associated with ongoing pyelonephritis or SBU and treated
accordingly. Underlying co-morbidities should be addressed if
possible.

Prevention and Non-antimicrobial Therapies
Prevention of lower UTI involves identiﬁcation and reversal of
underlying causes of disease, such as vulvar fold dermatitis or
congenital abnormalities such as ectopic ureter. Urinary
catheterization should only be used when necessary, and
intermi ent catheterization is preferred to indwelling
catheterization. If indwelling catheterization is required, a closed
sterile collection system should always be used, and the catheter
should be removed as soon as it is no longer required, because the
risk of ascending infection increases with every day the catheter is
left in place. Treatment of catheterized animals with antimicrobial
drugs may increase the risk of bacterial infection, 65 so
catheterized animals should only be treated with antimicrobial
drugs when necessary, and they should not be used in an a empt
to prevent urinary catheter infection. Routine antimicrobial
treatment after catheter removal is not indicated unless clinical
signs of UTI develop, because colonization that follows
catheterization is cleared once the catheter is removed and host
defenses are restored.
Many treatments for prevention of UTI in dogs and cats with a
history of recurrent disease have been considered. Currently,
there is no evidence that urinary adjunct treatments such as
antiseptics (e.g., methenamine), or nutritional supplements such
as cranberry juice extract are eﬀective in dogs or cats. There are
numerous alternative/adjunct therapies that have been
investigated for the prevention and treatment of recurrent
bacterial cystitis in humans as well as animal models such as
NSAIDS, estrogen compounds, intravesical glycosaminoglycans,
cranberry extract, and live biotherapeutic products. 66 The eﬃcacy
of cranberry extract for treatment of recurrent UTI in women has

vetexamprep.ir

been mixed. At the time of writing, the most recent placebocontrolled studies have shown no signiﬁcant eﬀect; however,
patient selection appears critical. A reduction in UTI recurrence
has been reported in other studies, 67 although it has not appeared
to be as eﬀective in patients with other co-morbidities. While
cranberry has been shown to prevent adherence of E. coli strains
in in vitro canine studies, no signiﬁcant diﬀerence was noted in
dogs with intervertebral disc disease to reduce the risk of UTI or
SBU compared with placebo. 68
Live biotherapeutic products appear promising for treatment of
recurrent UTI and have the potential to reduce the need for
antimicrobial therapy. Intravesicular administration of E. coli ASB
strain 83972 in human beings with recurrent UTI reduced the
symptoms of UTI and protected some patients from recurrent UTI
after serial catheterizations. In a recent veterinary pilot study,
intravesicular administration of ASB E. coli strain 212 to dogs with
recurrent UTI resulted in complete or nearly complete clinical
cures in four of nine dogs, and three had microbiologic cures at 2
weeks; one of these dogs had SBU after treatment (in addition to
ASB E. coli 212) and did not require antimicrobial therapy. Longterm follow-up urine cultures were only available for two dogs.
ASB E. coli 212 (as determined by PFGE analysis) was isolated 60
days after bacterial instillation and these two dogs remained free
of LUTS for more than 6 months. Three of the four dogs had the
ASB strain isolated from their urine at day 14. Further studies are
underway to investigate treatment with this live biotherapeutic
compared to antimicrobial administration in a larger population.
69

Public Health Aspects
Dogs and cats with UTI have a potential to act as a source of MDR
bacteria for humans. Similarities between uropathogenic E. coli
isolates from dogs and those from humans have been identiﬁed, 70
, 71 but diﬀerences also exist. 72 Owners of pets with MDR UTI
should always wash their hands after handling their pets, wear
gloves when medications are administered, and pets should be
taken to urinate away from other people and animals.

vetexamprep.ir

Orchitis, Epididymitis, and Prostatitis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Orchitis and epididymitis may occur in association with UTI in
intact male dogs, but is rare. Infection with Brucella canis should
always be suspected in dogs with epididymitis (see Chapter 71).
Escherichia coli accounts for most cases of bacterial prostatitis in
dogs, but occasionally other gram-negative and gram-positive
organisms, including atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma spp.
and Brucella spp., are involved. Bacterial prostatitis is extremely
rare in cats. 73

Clinical Features
Pathophysiology and Clinical Signs
Bacterial prostatitis in dogs may be acute or chronic. It often
accompanies benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostatic neoplasia,
most likely as a result of ascending infection secondary to altered
urinary defense mechanisms. Prostatitis should be suspected in
any intact male dog that develops a UTI. Dogs with bacterial
prostatitis may show infertility, fever, lethargy, decreased
appetite, weight loss, LUTS, purulent or hemorrhagic urethral
discharge, abdominal pain, and sometimes a stiﬀ gait. Tenesmus,
vomiting, and diarrhea may also occur in some dogs. Acute
bacterial prostatitis can be accompanied by severe sepsis or septic
shock (see Chapter 123). Formation of prostatic abscesses may be
followed by abscess rupture and peritonitis. Dogs with chronic
prostatitis may be lethargic or have no clinical signs of illness.
Physical Examination Findings
Dogs with acute bacterial prostatitis may exhibit pain on
palpation of the prostate. The prostate may be normal in size and
shape, or enlarged or irregularly shaped. Fluctuant regions may
be palpated if abscesses are present. Palpation of genitourinary
structures should always be performed cautiously when acute
bacterial prostatitis is suspected so that rupture of prostatic
abscesses does not occur. Hemorrhagic or purulent discharge may
be seen around the urethral oriﬁce. Dogs with severe acute
prostatitis may be dehydrated, febrile, obtunded, and show other
signs of severe sepsis or septic shock (e.g., tachycardia or

vetexamprep.ir

bradycardia, tachypnea, prolonged CRT). Intact male dogs with
bacterial orchitis or epididymitis may have testicular enlargement,
hyperemia, and pain on palpation of the testicles. This may
sometimes be present in association with prostatitis.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of prostatitis is based on clinical signs, laboratory
abnormalities, imaging ﬁndings, and culture of urine or prostatic
secretions. Measurement of serum canine prostate speciﬁc
esterase (CPSE) has been proposed as a biomarker for prostatic
disease in dogs 74 ; such biomarkers may ultimately be useful to
help distinguish benign prostatic hyperplasia from bacterial
prostatitis.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Animals with acute prostatitis may have mild anemia,
leukocytosis due to a neutrophilia, increased band neutrophils,
and monocytosis. A degenerative left shift, toxic neutrophils, and
thrombocytopenia may also be present. Hypoalbuminemia and
electrolyte abnormalities may be present, or there may be
evidence of organ dysfunction in dogs with septic shock.
Hyperglobulinemia may be present in dogs with chronic
prostatitis. The urinalysis may reveal abnormalities consistent
with UTI.
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain and Contrast Radiography
Plain radiography is of limited value for diagnosis of bacterial
prostatitis. Dogs with benign prostatic hypertrophy (BPH) or
prostatic abscesses may have prostatomegaly, with ventral and
cranial displacement of the bladder (deﬁned as a prostate
diameter > 70% of the distance between the pubis and the sacral
promontory). 75 Prostatic mineralization can rarely accompany
chronic bacterial prostatitis in intact dogs, but when present in a
neutered dog, mineralization strongly supports the presence of
prostatic neoplasia. 76 Extravasation of contrast material into the
prostate during retrograde contrast cystourethrography supports
a diagnosis of prostatitis or prostatic neoplasia.

Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Many dogs with prostatitis shed bacteria into the urine; therefore,
bacteria cultured from the urine are usually those involved in
prostatitis (for collection methods, see Isolation and Identiﬁcation
section for UTI, earlier). Prostatic involvement should be
suspected in any intact male dog with bacterial UTI. However, a
negative urine culture does not rule out the possibility of
prostatitis, and occasionally the organisms isolated from the urine
may diﬀer from those isolated from the prostate.
Collection of prostatic ﬂuid via ejaculation, prostatic wash, or
aspiration of the prostate or prostatic cysts is also recommended
for diagnosis of bacterial prostatitis, particularly if the patient is
refractory to treatment, neoplasia is suspected, or the urine
culture is negative, and the prostate ﬁndings are suggestive for
infection on ultrasonography. Aspirates of the prostate for culture
and cytology (if clinically indicated) can be done in dogs with
acute and chronic prostatitis; however, dogs with acute prostatitis
may require sedation for patient comfort. The presence of large
numbers of bacteria (>105 CFU/mL) together with an
inﬂammatory response suggests infection. Cytologic examination
and culture of ultrasound-guided aspirates of prostatic abscesses
has been used to assist diagnosis, but there is a risk of localized
peritonitis when abscessed tissues are aspirated.
Pathologic Findings
Dogs with acute prostatitis may have inﬁltrates of neutrophils
with or without intralesional bacteria in the prostate on
histopathology. Chronic infections may be associated with
histiocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates. In some cases,
prostatic hyperplasia or abscess formation are identiﬁed.

Treatment

vetexamprep.ir

Data are limited regarding the treatment duration for acute
bacterial prostatitis, but 4 weeks of treatment with appropriate
antimicrobials is recommended. For dogs with sepsis, parenteral
antimicrobial administration initially may be required. If
inﬂammation is severe, any drug appropriate for treatment of UTI
may still penetrate the prostate in the acute phase.
Drug penetration is impaired in dogs with chronic prostatitis
because of the blood-prostatic ﬂuid barrier. Drugs that eﬀectively
cross the prostatic barrier of dogs include enroﬂoxacin, oﬂoxacin,
marboﬂoxacin, trimethoprim, and chloramphenicol. Drugs such
as the penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, and
tetracyclines are not able to cross an intact blood-prostate barrier
and should be avoided, particularly in cases of chronic prostatitis.
Ciproﬂoxacin should not be administered due to its variable GI
absorption. Fosfomycin can be considered if an MDR gramnegative organism is isolated. Organisms may persist within the
prostate of dogs with chronic prostatitis despite appropriate
antimicrobial
drug
treatment.
Because
trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole and chloramphenicol are more likely to be
associated with adverse eﬀects when administered for prolonged
periods, a ﬂuoroquinolone such as enroﬂoxacin is the drug of
choice for initial treatment of gram-negative bacterial prostatitis. If
the MIC of the organism is between 0.5 and 1.0 µg/mL, the highest
dose of enroﬂoxacin is recommended (20 mg/kg, q24h).
Clindamycin may be a reasonable choice for dogs with grampositive bacterial prostatitis. Treatment of dogs with chronic
prostatitis should continue for at least 6 weeks. Cure may not be
possible without castration.
Surgical castration is recommended for dogs with prostatitis
and can be considered as soon as the dog is stable to undergo
anesthesia and surgery. The eﬃcacy of drugs that cause prostatic
involution, such as ﬁnasteride, is not clear, but ﬁnasteride
enhanced the resolution of infection in a rat model of chronic
prostatitis when administered with a ﬂuoroquinolone. 78 Prostatic
abscesses and paraprostatic or large intraprostatic cysts must also
be addressed and treated using ultrasound-guided drainage or
surgically if necessary. Castration and antimicrobial drug
treatment alone does not eﬀectively resolve prostatic abscesses.
Follow-up should consist of a return visit for examination 7 to
10 days after initiating treatment, and aerobic bacterial urine

vetexamprep.ir

culture should be considered at this time if a positive urine culture
was initially present. A return visit and examination should also
be performed 1 week after discontinuation of treatment, at which
time physical examination, urinalysis, urine culture, and prostatic
ﬂuid cytology and culture should be performed. Where available,
prostatic ultrasound may also provide useful information at these
follow-up times, and if possible, should be performed 1 week after
discontinuation of antimicrobial drugs.

Prevention
Routine castration reduces the risk of prostatitis, although
prostatitis can still occur in neutered animals.

Vaginitis, Metritis, and Pyometra
Etiology and Epidemiology
Bacterial vaginitis in adult bitches is usually secondary to an
underlying disorder such as neoplasia, foreign bodies (e.g., grass
awn), or seen concurrently with UTI or anatomic abnormalities
such as strictures. Puppy vaginitis is thought to be a consequence
of immaturity, rather than bacterial infection.

vetexamprep.ir

Uterus of an 11-year-old female
Pomeranian with pyometra during
ovariohysterectemy. The left uterine horn was
severely dilated and fluid-filled. Courtesy of
FIG. 127.8

University of California, Davis, Veterinary Anatomic
Pathology Service.

Metritis results from ascending infection of the uterus. It
usually occurs shortly after parturition (e.g., within a week), or
after obstetrical procedures, and may be associated with clinical
signs of lethargy, fever, decreased appetite, and purulent vaginal
discharge.
Pyometra is an accumulation of pus within the uterus (Fig.
127.8). The pathogenesis of pyometra is incompletely understood.
However, in contrast to metritis, pyometra most often seems to
occur as a result of increased serum progesterone concentrations,
which cause cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH), impaired
immune function, and decreased uterine contractility. The end
result for at least some dogs and cats is opportunistic bacterial
invasion, most often by E. coli strains that have virulence factors
typical of uropathogenic isolates. 70 , 79 Bacterial bioﬁlm may
contribute to resistance to host immune defenses and

vetexamprep.ir

antimicrobial drugs. 80 Other organisms that cause pyometra are
similar to those that cause UTI, with the exception that anaerobes
are more often involved, usually in mixed infections with other
bacteria. CEH is not an absolute requirement for development of
pyometra, and some animals with CEH never develop pyometra.
Exogenous estrogen administration (used to treat mismating), as
well as exogenous progesterone administration, have also been
associated with pyometra. 81 Rarely, pyometra occurs in
conjunction with uterine neoplasia. 82 , 83 Emphysematous
pyometra has been reported in dogs but is uncommon; less than
10 cases have been reported in the literature. 84–87 Etiologic agents
in emphysematous pyometra have included C. perfringens,
Citrobacter diversus, and P. aeruginosa.
In dogs, pyometra usually occurs in diestrus, but it can occur in
anestrus. Aﬀected dogs are usually middle-aged to older, intact
female dogs (mean age around 7 to 9 years), but pyometra has
been reported in dogs as young as 8 months of age. Older dogs
are likely to develop pyometra as a result of chronic and repeated
exposure to progesterone with progressive cycles, whereas
younger dogs may develop pyometra as a result of treatment of
mismatings with estrogens. Pyometra is prevalent in regions
where routine ovariohysterectomy of dogs is not widely
performed; it has been estimated that 19% of all intact bitches
develop pyometra before 10 years of age. 88 In a study from
Scandinavia, breeds of dogs with increased risk included collies,
ro weilers, Bernese mountain dogs, Cavalier King Charles
spaniels, English cocker spaniels, and golden retrievers. 89 , 90
Bitches that have never been pregnant are at increased risk for
development of pyometra compared with those that have had
li ers, but false pregnancy does not inﬂuence the risk for
pyometra in dogs. In cats, CEH also seems to underlie pyometra.
Cats with pyometra are generally > 3 years of age (mean, 5 years),
but pyometra may occur in cats of any age.

Clinical Features
Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of pyometra in dogs usually occur 2 to 10 weeks
after estrus or breeding, but occasionally occur as long as 15

vetexamprep.ir

weeks after estrus (mean, 7 weeks). In both dogs and cats, clinical
signs may be acute or chronic, and include lethargy, polyuria and
polydipsia, vomiting, weight loss, decreased appetite, diarrhea,
fever, and abdominal pain. Cats may have an unkempt haircoat.
However, some dogs or cats show no signs of illness. Animals
with open-cervix pyometra, the most common form of pyometra
(>60% of dogs), usually have purulent vaginal discharge. The
discharge may have a fetid odor, be mucopurulent, purulent, or
contain blood. Dogs or cats with closed-cervix pyometra do not have
vaginal discharge, but abdominal distention may be present.
Animals with closed pyometra are more likely to have severe
signs of systemic illness than those with open pyometra. 91 In one
study, sepsis was more likely to occur in dogs with closed-cervix
pyometra (77% of 39 dogs) than in dogs with open-cervix
pyometra (51% of 71 dogs). 91 Concurrent glomerular and
tubulointerstitial disease may also contribute to signs of polyuria
and polydipsia. 92 In some dogs or cats, pyometra may be
accompanied by severe sepsis or septic shock (see Chapter 123).
Peritonitis may occur secondary to rupture of the uterus when
disease is severe. Dogs with leukopenia were 18-fold more likely
to have peritonitis as a complication of surgery than those that
were not leukopenic. 93
Stump pyometra is an uncommon form of pyometra. It
sometimes occurs after remnants of the ovaries are inadvertently
left in place after ovariohysterectomy, but this is not always
identiﬁed. Stump pyometra occurs most commonly in dogs, but
has been reported in the cat. 94 Clinical signs are similar to
animals with pyometra. In addition, stump pyometras can
contribute to recurrent lower UTI. When evaluated by ultrasound,
the uterine stump was enlarged in a small group of dogs treated
with estriol for urinary incontinence, without apparent adverse
systemic eﬀects. 95
Physical Examination Findings
Purulent vaginal discharge, sometimes with a putrid odor, may be
present in animals with bacterial vaginitis or open pyometra.
Fever may be present in some dogs and cats with pyometra, and
is more likely in closed-cervix pyometra. Abdominal pain may be
present on palpation of the abdomen, which should always be

vetexamprep.ir

performed cautiously when pyometra is suspected so that rupture
of the uterus does not occur. Dogs and cats with severe pyometra
may be lethargic, dehydrated, and show signs of severe sepsis or
septic shock.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of vaginitis, metritis, and pyometra is based on
signalment and history, clinical signs, laboratory abnormalities,
imaging ﬁndings, and, in some cases, culture of the urine or
uterine contents obtained during surgery.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Acute metritis or pyometra (especially closed-cervix pyometra)
may be associated with anemia, leukocytosis due to a
neutrophilia, increased band neutrophils, degenerate left shifts,
toxic neutrophils, and monocytosis, especially if the cervix is
closed. 91 Thrombocytopenia and signs of organ dysfunction (such
as azotemia, increased serum ALP activity, and coagulation
abnormalities) may be detected in dogs with severe sepsis or
septic shock. Azotemia may also reﬂect the presence of concurrent
pyelonephritis. Hypoalbuminemia and electrolyte abnormalities
such as low serum sodium-to-potassium ratios may be present. 96 ,
97 Dogs and cats with chronic pyometra may have few laboratory
abnormalities; some animals with chronic pyometra may be
hyperglobulinemic. On urinalysis, there may be abnormalities
consistent with UTI. UPCRs may be increased as a result of renal
tubular or glomerular injury. 92
Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Radiographic changes in dogs with pyometra consist of the
presence of a large, coiled or tubular mass in the caudal and midabdomen, which displaces the small intestine cranially and
dorsally. However, the uterus may not be visible in dogs with
open pyometra. Diﬀerentiation of pyometra from pregnancy may
require ultrasound examination. Localized or generalized loss of
abdominal detail may be present in dogs with peritonitis
secondary to uterine or prostatic rupture.

vetexamprep.ir

Sonographic Findings
Ultrasound is the imaging technique of choice for diagnosis of
pyometra and diﬀerentiation of pyometra from pregnancy.
However, it may not eﬀectively distinguish pyometra from
mucometra or hydrometra. Dogs with pyometra have an enlarged
uterus, which is immediately dorsal to the bladder. The uterus
may be thin-walled and distended with echogenic intraluminal
ﬂuid, or have a thickened wall with anechoic areas due to
glandular proliferation and enlargement (CEH). 98 Assessment of
uterine blood ﬂow may help to distinguish pyometra from CEH,
one study showing that dogs with pyometra had signiﬁcantly
higher uterine blood ﬂow than dogs with CEH or healthy dogs. 99
In one dog with emphysematous pyometra, the uterus had a
homogenously hypoechoic wall and was distended with gas, in
contrast to the layered wall of the adjacent colon. 87 Stump
pyometra may be recognized as a hypoechoic structure that is
located dorsal and caudal to the urinary bladder (Fig. 127.9). It is
important to record any concurrent estrogen exposure or
administration when interpreting the uterine stump size in dogs.
The maximum uterine height/aorta ratio was greater in dogs
receiving estriol for urinary incontinence when compared with
healthy dogs not receiving estrogen therapy. While this structure
appeared ultrasonographically abnormal in these dogs, no clinical
consequences were noted. 95
Microbiologic Tests
Isolation and Identification
Bacteria cultured from the urine are usually those involved in
pyometra, although a negative urine culture does not rule out the
possibility of pyometra, and occasionally the organisms isolated
from the urine diﬀer from those isolated from the uterus. Fine
needle aspiration of the uterus is contraindicated because of the
risk of uterine rupture. Usually, the bacteria involved are initially
identiﬁed through culture of urine. Cystocentesis should always
be performed with ultrasound guidance in animals suspected to
have pyometra to avoid inadvertent perforation of the uterus. For
animals with open pyometra, culture of a swab specimen that has
been collected from the cranial aspect of the vagina could be

vetexamprep.ir

considered, but the identity of the bacteria cultured may or may
not be the same as those present within the uterus; therefore, this
approach is not recommended. Tissues removed surgically can be
submi ed for culture and susceptibility testing, and this should be
done despite the administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial
drugs before surgery, because these drugs are unlikely to
penetrate pus within the uterus. If possible, both anaerobic and
aerobic bacterial cultures should be performed for dogs or cats
with pyometra. Blood cultures could be considered when signs of
severe sepsis are present.

Pathologic Findings

vetexamprep.ir

As for other urogenital infections, acute pyometra is associated
with a dense neutrophilic inﬁltrate on histopathology (Fig. 127.10)
and intralesional bacteria may be identiﬁed; chronic infections
may be associated with histiocytic or lymphoplasmacytic
inﬁltrates. CEH (expansion of the endometrium with hyperplastic,
dilated to cystic glands) and corpora lutea may also be identiﬁed.

Treatment and Prognosis
The overall prognosis for dogs with pyometra is good, with one
study reporting an overall mortality rate of 10%, when
euthanasias are included, to as low as 1% for surgically treated
cases. 93 Sick dogs or cats with metritis or pyometra should be
treated aggressively with IV ﬂuids and broad-spectrum parenteral
antimicrobial drugs that have activity against gram-negative
bacteria and anaerobes, such as a combination of clindamycin and
a ﬂuoroquinolone. Ovariohysterectomy is strongly recommended
for animals with pyometra, and may need to be performed on an
emergency basis to resolve sepsis or septic shock. Caution is
required to avoid rupture of a distended or friable uterus during
surgery, because this has been associated with increased mortality
(<10% to around 50%). Risk factors for peritonitis in one study
were leukopenia and abnormal rectal temperature. 93
Laparoscopic approaches have been described, 100 but these
should be reserved for uncomplicated cases. Reevaluation should
be performed 1 week after discharge from hospital, and should
include physical examination, a CBC, biochemistry panel, and
urinalysis. Usually, there is a rapid response to treatment and
hematologic and biochemical abnormalities resolve within this
time period. The white cell count may increase dramatically after
surgery before it returns to normal. Antimicrobial drug treatment
should be continued for 7 to 10 days after ovariohysterectomy.

FIG. 127.10

In conjunction with antimicrobial drug treatment, medical
treatment with natural or synthetic prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α),
which causes lysis of the corpora lutea, to expel uterine contents
may be possible for dogs with open pyometra that are young (<6
years of age), and otherwise in good health (Table 127.4). Medical

vetexamprep.ir

treatment for pyometra alone is not recommended for dogs that
are systemically unwell, and the possibility of pregnancy must
ﬁrst be ruled out with ultrasound. Medical treatment is also less
a ractive for dogs with closed pyometra because: (1) it risks
uterine rupture; (2) it is less eﬀective than in dogs with open
pyometra; and (3) dogs are often systemically unwell. However, it
has been used with success in some dogs. Medical treatment is
most likely to be successful in dogs that are in late diestrus (>5
weeks after the end of estrus). Improvement is generally not
evident for at least 48 hours, and adverse reactions such as
restlessness, hypersalivation, panting, vocalization, vomiting,
diarrhea, mydriasis, and fever are common with PGF2α, so
treatment should be given in the morning on an empty stomach,
hospitalization and observation is recommended for at least 4
hours after the injection (or throughout the treatment period in
dogs with closed pyometra), and the dose should be carefully
calculated and be appropriate for the product used. Signs of shock
may develop in some dogs treated with PGF2α. Walking dogs for
20 to 40 minutes after drug administration (while adverse eﬀects
occur) may lessen the adverse eﬀects and also promotes close
observation. 101 The severity of signs tends to decrease with each
injection administered. Serial abdominal ultrasound examinations
are recommended every 2 days during treatment for dogs with
closed pyometra to evaluate for peritonitis. PGF2α can also be
used to treat postpartum metritis.
