a Day 1 = day of diagnosis.

Aglepristone (RU534) is a progesterone receptor antagonist that
is available in Europe for treatment of pyometra. Aglepristone
appears to be a safe and eﬀective alternative to PGF2α in both
dogs and cats. 102 Addition of low-dose cloprostenol (a synthetic
PGF2α derivative) to aglepristone in one study increased the
success rate in dogs with open pyometra from 60% to 84%. 103
Aglepristone (10 mg/kg SC) has been administered at 0, 1, and 6
days after diagnosis. A modiﬁed protocol where aglepristone is
administered at 0, 2, 5, and 8 days after diagnosis, together with a
relatively short (6 days) duration of clavulanic acid-amoxicillin
therapy was eﬀective in all of 47 dogs, without the need for
ovariohysterectomy, compared with 89% of 26 dogs using the
traditional protocol. 104 No recurrence was noted in a 24-month
follow-up period, and approximately 80% of dogs subsequently
whelped.
All dogs treated medically should be re-evaluated 2 weeks after
treatment. If signs of pyometra persist, culture of a swab specimen
obtained from the cranial vaginal vault should be performed to
determine if resistance to antimicrobials is present, and treatment
should be repeated a second time or surgery performed. The
measurement of serum progesterone to monitor eﬀective
treatment is not necessary because it does not change treatment

vetexamprep.ir

recommendations. After successful treatment, the dog or cat
should be bred at each subsequent cycle until pregnancy occurs.
The chance that subsequent pregnancy will occur is over 80%, and
the vast majority of dogs that respond go on to have more than
one li er. Once the dog or cat is no longer required as a breeding
animal, it should be neutered.

Prevention
Routine ovariohysterectomy reduces the risk of pyometra,
although stump pyometra can still occur in neutered animals.
There is no known treatment for CEH. Use of estrogens to treat
mismatings is not recommended.

Case Example
Signalment
“Molly,” a 6-year-old female spayed shih
Sacramento, CA.

u mix from

History
Molly was brought to the University of California, Davis
VMTH for evaluation of recently diagnosed
nephrolithiasis and hematuria. Three weeks previously,
Molly’s groomer noted blood on the towel she had been
si ing on. The owners subsequently observed blood in
Molly’s urine and took her to their local veterinary clinic.
There had been no stranguria, polyuria, polydipsia, or
change in the frequency of urination. Blood work was
performed in the clinic; the hematocrit was 56.5% and
thrombocytopenia (86,000 platelets/µL) was present. A
urine dipstick analysis revealed 2+ protein, a pH of 8,
hematuria, and pyuria. The urine SpG was 1.014. A 3-cm
opacity in the right renal pelvis that was consistent with a
nephrolith was found on abdominal radiographs (see Fig.
127.4). The kidneys had a mildly irregular shape but were

vetexamprep.ir

normal in size. Treatment with amoxicillin was initiated
(23 mg/kg, PO, q12h for 10 days). After 12 days, the dog
was evaluated for dental prophylaxis. A CBC showed a
hematocrit of 50% and persistent thrombocytopenia
(51,000 platelets/µL). An abdominal ultrasound
(performed by a mobile board-certiﬁed veterinary
radiologist) showed a 2.9-cm right renal pelvic calculus
and a 7-mm left renal pelvic calculus. The kidneys were
normal in size but had a mildly irregular shape. There
was moderate thickening of the apical wall of the urinary
bladder, with small (4 mm) apical polyp formation.
Moderate ﬂocculent suspended debris was present within
the urine and multiple very small sand-like calculi were
present. All other organs evaluated were within normal
limits.
Other Medical HistoryThere had been no history of
vomiting, diarrhea, coughing, sneezing, or trauma. Molly
had traveled frequently to Oregon and Nevada. There
had been no change in her water consumption. She was
fed a stone dissolution diet (Royal Canin Urinary SO),
which had been prescribed 4 years ago when crystals
were seen in her urine on urinalysis, as part of a wellness
examination. She was also occasionally fed dog treats. She
had been vaccinated for CDV, CAdV, CPV, and rabies;
and Bordetella bronchiseptica, CCoV, leptospirosis, and
Lyme disease. She was treated with imidacloprid and
ivermectin for ﬂea and heartworm prophylaxis,
respectively, each month.

Physical Examination
Body weight: 10.8 kg.
General: Bright and alert, hydrated. T = 101.6°F (38.7°C),
HR = 128 beats/minute, RR = 32 breaths/minute, mucous
membranes pink and moist, CRT < 1 second.
Eyes, ears, nose, and throat: Mild epiphora bilaterally.
There was mild dental calculus and gingivitis. Otherwise
no clinically signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected.

vetexamprep.ir

Integument: Abdomen clipped from previous ultrasound
examination with healing clipper wounds. There was a 1cm ecchymosis on the ventral abdomen.
Musculoskeletal: BCS 7/9. Ambulatory with normal gait.
Cardiovascular: Sinus arrhythmia. No murmurs
auscultated. Femoral pulses strong and synchronous.
Genitourinary/GI: Soft, mildly painful abdomen. The
bladder was moderate sized. Rectal examination was
unremarkable. There was no vulvar discharge and no
evidence of perivulvar dermatitis. A slightly recessed
vulva was present.
Other systems, including peripheral lymph nodes: No
clinically signiﬁcant ﬁndings.

vetexamprep.ir

WBC/HPF, 30–50 RBC/HPF, no crystals or casts, many
rods, rafts of atypical transitional cells, many degenerated

Coagulation panel: PT 9.9 seconds (7.5–10.5 seconds), PTT
8.4 seconds (9.0–12.0 seconds), ﬁbrinogen 395 mg/dL (90–
255 mg/dL).

Microbiologic Testing
Direct smear of urine: Moderate numbers of gramnegative rods and gram-positive cocci were visualized.
Aerobic bacterial urine culture and susceptibility
(cystocentesis specimen): 105 CFU/mL Proteus mirabilis, P.
mirabilis (non-swarming strain), and Enterococcus faecalis.
Both Proteus spp. were resistant to ampicillin (≥256
µg/mL) but susceptible to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (4
µg/mL), cephalexin (8 µg/mL), chloramphenicol (≤16
µg/mL), enroﬂoxacin (≤1 µg/mL), tetracycline (64 µg/mL),
and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (≤4 µg/mL). The E.
faecalis was susceptible to ampicillin, clavulanic acidamoxicillin (≤2 µg/mL), chloramphenicol (≤16 µg/mL),
enroﬂoxacin (≤1 µg/mL), and tetracycline (16 µg/mL).

Diagnosis

Proteus mirabilis and E. faecalis cystitis and suspected
pyelonephritis with nephrolithiasis, with possible secondary
ITP.

Treatment

Molly was treated with enroﬂoxacin (7 mg/kg, PO, q24h). The
following day her platelet count had increased to 31,000
platelets/µL, and by day 3 of treatment it was 64,000 platelets/
µL. After 7 days of treatment, a CBC showed a neutrophil count
of 5,700/µL, no band neutrophils, and the platelet count was
79,000 platelets/µL. A urine culture obtained by cystocentesis at
this time showed 104 CFU/mL of E. coli and E. faecalis. The E. coli
was resistant to ampicillin, cephalexin, enroﬂoxacin,
tetracycline,
and
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole,
but
susceptible to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (64 µg/mL). The
susceptibility of the E. faecalis had not changed, with the

vetexamprep.ir

exception that the MIC for tetracycline was 32 µg/mL.
Treatment was changed to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin (23
mg/kg, PO, q12h). When re-evaluated 3 weeks later, she had no
clinical signs of illness. A CBC showed only mild
thrombocytopenia (146,000 platelets/µL, with an MPV of 12.6
fL). However, bacteria and large numbers of WBCs were still
present in the urine sediment, the urine pH was 8.0, and E. coli
with the same susceptibility pa ern was again isolated from the
urine. An extended panel showed susceptibility to amikacin (≤4
µg/mL) and imipenem-cilastatin (≤1 µg/mL), but resistance to
cefazolin, cefoxitin, cefpodoxime, cephalothin, gentamicin,
marboﬂoxacin, orbiﬂoxacin, and ticarcillin-clavulanic acid. The
dosage of clavulanic acid-amoxicillin was increased to 23
mg/kg, PO, q8h. The diet was changed to a stone dissolution
diet. After an additional month, urinalysis ﬁndings were
unchanged and the same E. coli was again isolated from the
urine. The platelet count was 244,000 platelets/µL and a
biochemistry panel was unremarkable. Abdominal radiographs
and ultrasound showed no evidence of nephrolithiasis, but
multiple small, rounded mineral opacities were present in the
region of the right ureter.
Antimicrobial drug treatment was ultimately changed to
amikacin (15 mg/kg, SC, q24h) 2 weeks later because an E. coli
was isolated that was resistant to clavulanic acid-amoxicillin.
Kidney values were monitored every 2 weeks during amikacin
treatment to evaluate for nephrotoxicity. The urine then became
sterile and ultrasound examination showed disappearance of all
urinary calculi over a 2-month period, after which antimicrobial
drug treatment was discontinued and the diet was changed to a
maintenance diet. Because of the recessed vulva and the dog’s
excess body condition, a weight loss program was discussed
with the owner. Molly was diagnosed with a subclinical
Enterobacter aerogenes UTI 2 months later, which was broadly
susceptible to antimicrobial drugs and treated with
enroﬂoxacin. The platelet count was within the reference range.
Further evaluation for underlying conditions predisposing to
recurrent UTI (contrast cystourethrography and cystoscopy),
followed by vulvoplasty if no other abnormalities were
detected, were oﬀered to the owners but further treatment and
evaluation was not pursued. The dog remained alive, untreated,

vetexamprep.ir

and without clinical signs 4 years later, at which time
hematology and biochemistry panel results were unremarkable,
but MDR E. coli was repeatedly isolated from the urine.

Comments

This is an interesting case of bacterial cystitis and
pyelonephritis associated with struvite nephrolithiasis, and
probable secondary ITP. The struvite urolithiasis was likely
secondary to the P. mirabilis infection. Months of antimicrobial
treatment were necessary because of bacterial sequestration
within urinary calculi. This may have explained continued
isolation of bacteria from the urine in the face of antimicrobial
drug treatment, although ultimately resolution of the E. coli
infection quickly followed the change in antimicrobial drug
choice. Meropenem would have been another appropriate
choice based on the susceptibility of the organism isolated, but
is often reserved for life-threatening infections in human
patients. Fortunately, dissolution of the nephroliths occurred
with antimicrobial and dietary therapy, and surgery to remove
infected uroliths was not required. Continued UTI was a likely
sequela in this dog in the absence of successful identiﬁcation
and treatment of an underlying cause. Although treatment of
the UTI was necessary during nephrolith dissolution, treatment
of the subclinical E. aerogenes infection may not have been
necessary.

128: Ocular Infections
Jean Stiles

KEY POINTS
• Infections of the eye can involve the ocular surface and
adnexal structures, intraocular structures, or both.
• Infections of the ocular surface and adnexal structures often
result from invasion by commensals when normal barriers are
disrupted, and include infectious blepharitis, conjunctivitis,
keratitis, dacryocystitis, and orbital infection.
• Intraocular infections may arise secondary to local injury or
occur as part of a systemic process. A large number of
viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and helminths can cause
intraocular disease. Sometimes ocular abnormalities are the
only outward clinical manifestation of systemic infectious
disease.
• Examination of specimens from ocular tissues or ocular fluids
can facilitate diagnosis of ocular infectious diseases, and may
assist in the diagnosis of systemic infections.
• Treatment of ocular disorders typically involves topical
administration of antimicrobials and anti-inflammatory drugs,
as well as specific therapy that is directed at underlying
causes. Systemic antimicrobial drugs or glucocorticoids are
occasionally required.

Infections of the Ocular Surface and Adnexa
Etiology, Epidemiology, and Pathogenesis
Most surface bacterial infections follow other debilitating
conditions that potentiate the pathogenicity of organisms that are

vetexamprep.ir

indigenous to the ocular surface. Despite the fact that all dogs
probably have indigenous bacteria in their conjunctival cul-de-sac,
bacterial isolation rates of between 46% and 91% have been
reported from apparently healthy dogs (Table 128.1). Variations in
the type and frequency of isolates may be a result of geography,
culture technique, breed, and season. Fungi are isolated from the
conjunctival sac of 10 to 22% of dogs. 1 , 2
Cats have a relatively lower prevalence of cultivable bacteria in
their conjunctival sacs. 3 Bacteria or mycoplasmas have been
isolated from 34% of conjunctival specimens and 25% of lid
margin specimens. In one study of 50 cats (100 eyes), no
organisms were isolated from 42% of the cats, bacteria were
isolated from the conjunctival sacs of 34% of cats (47% of eyes),
and fungi were isolated from 26% of the cats (14% of eyes) (Table
128.2). No anaerobes were isolated. 4
Abnormalities that contribute to local nidi of infection, such as
those of the nasolacrimal (NL) system and meibomian glands or
structures adjacent to the eye (ears, lip folds), should be sought
and corrected to overcome persistent or recurring infection.
Control of the resident ocular ﬂora of clinically healthy animals is
maintained by rinsing of the ocular surface with tears and
blinking, which directs tears into the NL system. Tears also
contain IgA and other antibacterial substances such as lactoferrin
and lysozyme. Competitive interactions among the indigenous
ﬂora keep the numbers of organisms lower, whereas disrupting
this balance may cause an overgrowth of one species. Conditions
that damage the ocular surface, such as keratoconjunctivitis sicca
(KCS), ultraviolet or other radiation, immune suppression, and
trauma can allow indigenous bacteria to adhere and proliferate to
produce disease. To become established, bacteria must adhere,
replicate, and then invade the tissue. Invasion subsequently
incites inﬂammation. Tissue damage results from a combination
of pathogen toxins and enzymes such as collagenase, elastase, and
cathepsins that are liberated by the neutrophilic response. 5
Bacteria that produce proteolytic enzymes such as Pseudomonas
aeruginosa typically cause rapidly progressive “melting” corneal
ulcers.

Clinical Features and Treatment

vetexamprep.ir

Blepharitis
Dogs
Blepharitis (inﬂammation of the eyelids) can develop secondary to
bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infection. Blepharitis can result from
other dermatologic diseases, and sometimes may occur in
conjunction with ocular diseases, such as conjunctivitis. Allergic
skin disease was the most common underlying cause in 102 dogs
from Germany with blepharitis (52% of dogs), followed by
infectious/parasitic disease (22%), autoimmune disease (18%), and
neoplasia (5%). 6 Brachycephalic breeds were at risk for
blepharitis when compared to the hospital population. Infectious
diseases were demodicosis, leishmaniosis, and dermatophytosis.
Parasitic infection of the eyelids was always accompanied by
periocular dermatitis. Secondary bacterial infection of the eyelids
may occur with any of these conditions, as well as with KCS.
Staphylococcus spp. can cause primary blepharitis and can also
generate a hypersensitivity reaction. Pruritis can lead to selftrauma, which exacerbates the blepharitis. In a 2020 study,
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius was isolated from 38 (40%) of 72
dogs and 24 cats with conjunctivitis/blepharitis, keratitis, or
uveitis, and 3 (8%) of the 38 isolates were methicillin-resistant; 2 of
the isolates were from dogs with conjunctivitis/blepharitis. 7
Clinical features of blepharitis include eyelid swelling,
erythema, skin ulceration, chalazia (granulomatous foci of
inﬂammation along meibomian glands), pruritis, and ocular
discharge (serous or purulent) (Fig. 128.1).
Treatment of bacterial blepharitis should include cleansing the
skin with a povidone-iodine solution (1:50 dilution) and
application of a broad-spectrum ophthalmic antibiotic ointment to
aﬀected skin and the eye q6-8h. If the skin is very inﬂamed, a
product that contains an antibiotic and dexamethasone is
indicated. Severe blepharitis may require systemic antibiotic
therapy such as a cephalosporin and possibly anti-inﬂammatory
doses of an oral glucocorticoid. Oral prednisone at antiinﬂammatory to immunosuppressive doses was not found to
inﬂuence tear production in healthy dogs and those with
histamine-induced conjunctivitis. 8 Any underlying condition that
can be identiﬁed should be addressed. Failure of severe

vetexamprep.ir

blepharitis to respond to antimicrobial therapy should prompt
specimen collection for culture and susceptibility testing.

Canine juvenile pyoderma or cellulitis, which typically
develops in puppies aged 3 to 16 weeks, often involves the
conjunctiva and eyelids (Fig. 128.2). Four of the 102 dogs in the
German study had juvenile cellulitis as the underlying cause of
blepharitis. 6 Although the cause is unknown, the response to
treatment suggests it to be immune-mediated. Pustules and
pyogranulomatous inﬂammation develop in the eyelids, face, and
ears.

lymphadenomegaly is common. Puppies may be febrile and have
generalized malaise. Swelling of joints or metaphyses may also be
observed. Diagnosis is based on age, history, and clinical signs.
Prednisolone (1 mg/kg PO q12h) should be administered for 2 to 3
weeks. An oral antibiotic may be used if skin infection is
suspected. A topical preparation such as neomycin-polymyxin Bdexamethasone q6-8h is indicated for conjunctivitis. Lesions
typically improve within a few days of beginning therapy and
resolve completely within 3 weeks.
Cats
Cats appear relatively resistant to bacterial blepharitis, except
when they have a traumatic injury and resulting bacterial
invasion. This type of injury most commonly occurs in cat ﬁghts
and can involve the head and eyelids. Abscesses near the eyelids
should be drained and appropriate systemic antibiotics
administered. Leishmania infantum can cause blepharitis in cats in
endemic areas. 9

Conjunctivitis
Dogs
Bacterial conjunctivitis can be a primary condition or secondary to
another ocular condition such as KCS, entropion or trichiasis,
CDV infection, parasites (e.g., Thelazia spp.), trauma, or foreign
bodies. Primary bacterial conjunctivitis typically occurs for
unknown reasons and in some cases is secondary to an insult that

vetexamprep.ir

is no longer apparent or is merely an overgrowth of resident
conjunctival microﬂora. Clinical signs are purulent discharge and
conjunctival hyperemia with mild to moderate discomfort.
Diagnosis should be based on cytologic examination of the
exudate and identiﬁcation of bacteria and neutrophilic
inﬂammation. Because bacterial overgrowth occurs when tear
production is low, KCS should be ruled out based on a normal
Schirmer tear test result. Culture and susceptibility testing should
be performed, especially if the response to therapy is poor or the
problem is recurrent. A complete ocular exam, including a
Schirmer tear test, ﬂuorescein staining of the cornea, ﬂuorescein
evaluation of NL duct patency, and a search for a foreign body in
the conjunctival sac and behind the third eyelid, should be
performed. Therapy should include a broad-spectrum topical
antibiotic such as bacitracin-neomycin-polymyxin B or
tobramycin q6h until resolution.

Viral conjunctivitis in dogs has been associated most often with
CDV infection (see Chapter 22). The ﬁrst sign of distemper is often
a bilateral conjunctivitis with a serous to mucopurulent ocular
discharge. Lacrimal adenitis may result in reduced tear
production, which in turn results in more profound signs of
conjunctivitis, corneal ulceration, and pain. The KCS typically
resolves over several weeks in dogs that recover. Treatment
should include regular cleaning of the eye, application of a broadspectrum topical antibiotic to help prevent secondary bacterial
infection, and, if KCS is present, topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus
along with artiﬁcial tears.
CHV has been documented as a cause of severe conjunctivitis
and ulcerative keratitis in a group of 3- to 4-month-old laboratory
dogs following recovery from uncharacterized upper respiratory
tract disease. 10 In a study of adult dogs experimentally infected
with CHV using an ocular route, only self-limiting mild
conjunctivitis was noted. 11 In client-owned dogs with and
without idiopathic conjunctivitis, CHV or CAdV-2 were found in
23.3% of aﬀected dogs and 0% of clinically healthy dogs. 12
Topically applied 1% prednisolone acetate solution did not
reactivate latent herpes virus infection; 13 however, systemic
administration of prednisolone at immunosuppressive doses
resulted in reactivation of ocular illness and shedding of virus. 14
If CHV is suspected or documented as a cause of conjunctivitis, a
topical antiviral agent should be used (see Table 9.5) (see also
Chapter 24). Topical 1% triﬂuridine, topical 0.5% cidofovir, and
topical 0.15% ganciclovir gel have been shown to be eﬀective. 15–17
Cats
Neonatal conjunctivitis can occur in cats secondary to bacterial or
viral infection. If infection occurs before the opening of the
eyelids, at approximately 10 days of age, purulent material
accumulates, causing a characteristic distended appearance to the
adherent eyelids. In such cases, the eyelids should be opened by
inserting a small scissor blade at the medial canthus and gently
sliding it along the lid margins. Copious purulent discharge
usually follows (Fig. 128.3). The exudate can be submi ed for
cytologic examination as well as bacterial culture and PCR assays
for respiratory pathogens to aid in identiﬁcation of pathogens that

vetexamprep.ir

may be present. A broad-spectrum topical antibiotic should be
used several times daily. A topical antiviral agent should also be
used in cases suspected to be caused by FHV-1 (see Chapters 9
and 34 and Table 9.5).

FHV-1 is a frequent cause of ocular disease in cats. Young cats
with respiratory tract disease generally have conjunctivitis with
marked conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, and serous to purulent
ocular discharge (Fig. 128.4). Cats typically recover in 2 to 3
weeks. In severe cases of FHV-1 conjunctivitis, the risk of
symblepharon, or adhesions of the conjunctiva to itself or the
cornea, is high (Fig. 128.5). Symblepharon occurs when areas of
conjunctival and corneal epithelial ulceration are present as a
result of the cytopathic nature of FHV-1. Symblepharon may lead
to permanent visual impairment, and an a empt to break these
adhesions early should be made. After application of topical
anesthesia, a co on-tip swab or small forceps can be used to break
adhesions and strip oﬀ cellular debris and ﬁbrin. This process
may need to be repeated frequently until the conjunctivitis has
resolved. A topical or oral antiherpesvirus drug should be
administered (see Table 9.5). In addition to general supportive
care, the eyes should be cleansed frequently and a broadspectrum topical antibiotic applied to minimize secondary

vetexamprep.ir

bacterial infection as the conjunctival surface sloughs. Once
infected, cats become latent carriers of FHV-1 and may have
recurrences of ocular disease, including conjunctivitis and corneal
ulcers. Many cats have transient episodes of conjunctivitis, with
conjunctival hyperemia, serous or purulent ocular discharge, and
blepharospasm. Mild cases that are self-limiting may not require
treatment. If the conjunctivitis is painful or lasts more than a few
days, antiviral therapy should be instituted.

Severe conjunctivitis in a cat
associated with feline calicivirus infection.
FIG. 128.6

Cats can develop chronic conjunctivitis associated with FHV-1
infection. 18 When conjunctivitis becomes chronic, the
inﬂammation needs to be treated. Glucocorticoids should not be
used because of the potential to exacerbate an underlying FHV-1
infection. A topical NSAID such as diclofenac used concurrently
with a topical antiviral drug such as cidofovir appears to be both
eﬀective and safe.
IFN-α and IFN-ω have signiﬁcant inhibitory eﬀects on FHV-1
in vitro at relatively high doses (see Chapter 9). 19 , 20 High doses
of topical IFNs have been used with some success in human
ocular herpetic infections. 21 , 22 However, in a study of naturally

vetexamprep.ir

occurring viral keratoconjunctivitis in cats, treatment with high
dose (106 U/mL) IFNs-α and -ω q12h for 14 days failed to lessen
severity or duration of clinical signs. 23 In general, studies to date
have not supported a beneﬁcial eﬀect of IFNs for treatment of
feline herpesvirus infections. 24
The use of oral famciclovir for treating FHV-1 in cats has
become more common. The drug appears to be safe at least for a
short course (2 to 3 weeks), although the optimum dose remains
unclear, and safety in ki ens has not been determined. A
retrospective study compared the clinical eﬀects of dosing at
either 40 or 90 mg/kg q8h in cats naturally infected with FHV-1. 25
While both groups showed improvement, cats in the high-dose
group had greater improvement in a shorter period of time.
Reduced shedding of FHV-1, but no diﬀerence in reduction in
clinical signs, was noted in shelter cats treated with either 30
mg/kg or 90 mg/kg PO q12h for 7 days when compared with
untreated cats. 26 Treatment of FHV-1 infections is described in
detail in Chapter 34.
Feline calicivirus (FCV) is also a common cause of conjunctivitis
in cats, particularly those in shelter or multicat environments.
Conjunctivitis caused by FCV is indistinguishable from that
caused by FHV-1 and may be severe in some cats (Fig. 128.6) (see
Chapter 35). No antiviral drugs are available, so supportive care is
required.
Chlamydia felis typically causes conjunctivitis in young adult
cats (see Chapter 49) (Fig. 128.7). The clinical appearance of
chlamydiosis is indistinguishable from conjunctivitis caused by
FHV-1, and the two organisms may be present simultaneously.
Chlamydial conjunctivitis can sometimes be successfully treated
with topical tetracycline ointment applied to both eyes q6h until a
week after resolution of clinical signs. Oral doxycycline may be
preferred to clear the organism from extraocular tissues such as
the intestinal tract, reproductive tract, and visceral organs. Results
of one study indicated that oral doxycycline at 10 mg/kg per day
for at least 28 days was necessary to ensure elimination of the
organism from tissues. 27 Hartmannella vermiformis, an amebic
endosymbiont that contains the Chlamydia-like agent Neochlamydia
hartmannellae, has been isolated in greater prevalence from the
ocular surfaces of cats with keratitis or conjunctivitis than from

vetexamprep.ir

those of clinically healthy cats. 28 However, in another study, the
prevalence of the organism did not diﬀer between similar groups
of cats. 29 The clinical signiﬁcance of this organism is unknown
(see Chapters 49 and 105).

Mycoplasma felis has been variably implicated as a cause of
conjunctivitis in cats. Some studies have recovered Mycoplasma
species as resident microﬂora from feline conjunctiva, whereas
others have not. Similarly, experimental infections of clinically
healthy, young cats have produced conjunctivitis in some studies
30 and not in others. Mycoplasma organisms may require a stressor
such as co-infection with FHV-1 to cause disease. One study
reported a slightly higher percentage of cats with conjunctivitis to
have positive PCR results for Mycoplasma spp. DNA (9.6%) as
compared to FHV-1 (6.7%) or C. felis (3.2%) DNA. 31 Suspected
mycoplasma conjunctivitis should be treated as for chlamydiosis.

Keratitis
Dogs
Viral keratitis in dogs can be caused by CHV (see above) and
CAdV-1. Bacterial keratitis in dogs develops after corneal
ulceration or a traumatic wound. Resident bacterial ﬂora
inhabiting the ocular surface are those most likely to invade a
corneal wound. This can lead to ulcerative keratitis or a corneal
abscess. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus spp. are especially
common, although infections with gram-negative bacteria may
also develop. In one study of 476 dogs with ulcerative keratitis
from the USA, bacteria isolated were Staphylococcus spp. (32%,
primarily S. pseudintermedius), Streptococcus spp. (19%, primarily
Streptococcus canis), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (8%); MDR
bacteria comprised 20% of the isolates and increased in prevalence
from 2016 to 2020 from 5% to 34%. 32
Bacterial keratitis usually incites a visible neutrophilic response,
characterized by a yellow-to-white cellular inﬁltrate within the
cornea. Vascular growth into the cornea also occurs but usually
does not begin for several days after injury and infection. Blood
vessels originate from the limbus and grow at a rate of
approximately 1 mm/day toward the site of infection. Rapid
corneal destruction can occur. Invading bacteria and neutrophils
can release proteases and collagenases, which contribute to
corneal melting (Fig. 128.8). Increased cyclo-oxygenase-2
expression has been documented in all corneal layers of aﬀected
dogs, suggesting a possible role for antiprostaglandin therapy as a
treatment for inﬂammatory keratitis. 33 Fungal keratitis, which
can have a similar clinical appearance, is less common but can be
caused by penetrating injuries with plant material or prolonged
topical treatment with antibiotic or glucocorticoid therapy.
Candida spp., Aspergillus spp., and a variety of other molds have
been implicated 34 , 35 ; in one case report, infection with
Malassezia pachydermatis was described. 36 Both bacterial and
fungal infections can lead to corneal perforation.

Diagnosis of infectious keratitis is based on clinical ﬁndings,
cytology, and culture. Fluorescein staining is used to detect
epithelial loss. All corneal ulcers that are progressive or involve
the stroma should be cultured. For specimen collection, a mini-tip

vetexamprep.ir

Culture e swab with a sterile saline-moistened tip should be used
to gently swab the ulcer bed. After application of topical
proparacaine, a ﬂa ened spatula, the blunt end of a scalpel blade,
or a cytology brush should be used to gently scrape the ulcer edge
in order to obtain a specimen for cytologic examination. With
bacterial keratitis, neutrophils are the predominant cell type, and
bacteria can be numerous, few, or not visible. Initial antimicrobial
drug selection can be based on whether cocci or rods are present.
Until culture results are known, broad-spectrum antibacterial
drugs should be used. A combination of chloramphenicol and a
ﬂuoroquinolone has been recommended for infected corneal
ulcers. 32 To achieve broad-spectrum bactericidal activity,
compounding may be required (Tables 128.3 and 128.4).
Frequency of application is critical. In a rapidly progressive
corneal ulcer, topical antibiotics should be applied q1-2h. To
reduce the likelihood of corneal melting, serum or plasma
(autologous, homologous, or heterologous) should be applied
topically q1-2h for anti-collagenolytic eﬀect. 37 , 38 These blood
products should be maintained in a sterile fashion and kept
refrigerated. Systemic antibiotics are usually not indicated unless
the cornea has a penetrating wound. Topical atropine can be used
q12-24h daily if miosis is present, although it should not be used
in dogs with KCS or glaucoma.

If fungal keratitis is documented or suspected, it should be
treated with the application of a topical antifungal agent q2-3h.
Topical 1 to 2% miconazole, 1% itraconazole, or 1% voriconazole
solutions have been eﬀective in treatment of keratomycosis in
dogs (see Chapter 86). 35 , 36 , 39 , 40 Deep corneal ulcers in danger
of perforating respond best to surgical therapy, such as placement
of a conjunctival ﬂap.
Ocular surfaces should be cleaned of discharges frequently to
remove neutrophils and their proteolytic enzymes. If tear
production is inadequate, topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus q12h
and artiﬁcial tears several times daily should be administered to
supplement and stimulate lacrimation. Closing the lids or placing
a third eyelid ﬂap should be avoided. These procedures limit drug
contact with the cornea, impair discharge drainage, and increase
the temperature of the environment, thus promoting bacterial
growth, fungal growth, or both. They also prevent monitoring of
the healing process. Systemic NSAIDs can provide analgesia and
aid in the treatment of uveitis associated with deep corneal ulcers.

Bacterial keratitis in cats may develop secondary to corneal
ulceration (including that initiated by FHV-1) or traumatic
wounds. Appearance, diagnosis, and treatment are the same as
for the dog. Fungal keratitis in cats is rare but can be treated in the
same way as fungal keratitis in dogs. 41

Corneal ulceration and keratitis that occur in association with
FHV-1 infection are very common and begin with invasion of the
corneal epithelium by the virus. 42 The most common corneal
abnormality is punctate or linear (dendritic) epithelial ulcers (Fig.
128.9), which may quickly enlarge to form geographic superﬁcial
ulcers. Conjunctivitis usually accompanies corneal ulceration. 18

vetexamprep.ir

Mechanical debridement of any loose corneal epithelium with a
co on-tipped swab and treatment with a topical or oral antiviral
agent are recommended. A topical antibiotic should also be used
for bacterial prophylaxis. Grid keratotomies should not be
performed in cats because this allows the virus greater access to
the corneal stroma and appears to increase the risk of corneal
sequestration. 43
FHV-1 infection may also be associated with stromal keratitis in
cats, which may occur with or without corneal ulceration. 44
Corneal vascularization and cellular inﬁltrate, often accompanied
by chronic discomfort, are typical signs (Fig. 128.10). Antiviral
agents alone may not improve the keratitis. Topical antiinﬂammatory agents may be needed, although glucocorticoids
should be avoided. Nonsteroidal topical agents such as diclofenac,
and/or 0.2% cyclosporine ointment, can be used in conjunction
with an antiviral agent such as cidofovir. Topical glucocorticoids
predispose cats to the development of corneal ulceration and
sequestration when FHV-1 is present. Topical IFN has been used
in humans with herpetic keratitis and can also be considered (see
Conjunctivitis in cats).
Corneal sequestration can follow chronic corneal ulcers or
keratitis caused by FHV-1 in any breed of cat, but Persian and
Himalayan cats are predisposed (Fig. 128.11). Corneal
sequestration has occurred in cats experimentally infected with
FHV-1 after topical glucocorticoid treatment, and in cats treated
with grid keratotomy. 43 , 45 The condition is characterized by an
area of corneal degeneration with a brown to black discoloration.
Lesions vary from pinpoint sequestra to those that occupy more
than half the cornea. Vascularization and ocular pain may be
intense or absent. Like stromal keratitis, sequestra can be one of
the most serious and potentially blinding sequelae of FHV-1
infection. Most ophthalmologists recommend keratectomy
followed by a graft (corneal or conjunctival) as treatment for
sequestra.
Dacryocystitis
Dacryocystitis, or inﬂammation of the NL system, is usually
associated with bacterial infection (Fig. 128.12). Nasolacrimal
foreign bodies such as plant material are frequently the inciting
cause. Dacryocystitis is less common in cats than in dogs. Clinical

vetexamprep.ir

manifestations of dacryocystitis include conjunctival hyperemia,
especially of the ventral conjunctival sac; purulent ocular
discharge; and epiphora. Blepharospasm may or may not be
present. Palpation of the skin near the medial canthus may elicit
pain and exudation of pus from the lacrimal puncta. Swelling or
draining tracts in the skin near the medial canthus may also be
identiﬁed.

Dacryocystorhinography may be necessary to identify foreign

After NL ﬂushing, a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic solution

also be stented to establish and maintain patency. Stricture of the
NL duct can occur with dacryocystitis, leading to chronic
epiphora.
Orbital Infections
Bacterial infection of the orbit is common, especially in dogs.
Fungal infections have also been reported in both dogs and cats
(see Systemic Mycoses). Bacterial infection of the orbit generally

vetexamprep.ir

has a fairly rapid onset compared with the slow progression of
clinical signs seen with orbital neoplasia. Typical clinical signs of
orbital abscess and cellulitis include periorbital swelling,
exophthalmos, elevation of the nictitating membrane, conjunctival
hyperemia, and pain on palpation of periorbita or when opening
the mouth (Fig. 128.13). Swelling of the oral mucosa behind the
last molar tooth is evident in some animals. Corneal ulceration
and blindness due to exposure keratopathy and optic nerve
damage, respectively, can also occur. 48

Dacryocystitis in a dog. Purulent
ocular discharge is present, particularly at the
medial canthus.
FIG. 128.12

Infectious agents may gain access to the orbit by several routes,
including through the oral mucosa behind the last molar tooth,
from the frontal sinus through breakdown of the medial orbital
bone, by extension from tooth root abscesses, from penetrating
wounds or foreign bodies of the skin or oral cavity, and through
hematogenous spread from distant sites of infection.
Orbital bacterial abscesses are best diagnosed with
ultrasonography. Abscesses appear as a hypoechoic area posterior

vetexamprep.ir

to the globe (Fig. 128.14). Foreign bodies are often best visualized
using ultrasonographic examination. Fungal granulomas appear
hyperechoic and are not readily diﬀerentiated from neoplasia. CT
or MRI may be helpful for determining the extent of infection;
MRI was most often used in one retrospective study of retrobulbar
cellulitis or abscesses in dogs. 48
Drainage of orbital abscesses should be established when
possible. Because only soft tissue separates the oral cavity from
the ventral orbit in the dog and cat, an incision through the tissue
behind the last molar can be used to access the orbit. A sterile
small mosquito forceps or blunt probe should be advanced into
the orbit, using gentle probing—not grasping—to a empt to enter
the abscess cavity. Any purulent material should be submi ed for
cytologic evaluation and cultured for aerobic and anaerobic
bacteria. Pending culture results, broad-spectrum systemic
antibacterial therapy should be instituted. Escherichia coli was the
most frequently isolated bacterial species in the retrospective
study described earlier (9/14 isolates). 48 In other studies,
anaerobes were more often isolated. Nonsteroidal agents should
also be administered for analgesia and to reduce inﬂammation.
The prognosis for bacterial orbital abscesses is generally good,
whereas the prognosis for orbital fungal infections is more
guarded. Occasionally, increased intraocular pressure may be so
severe it can lead to irreversible blindness. 49

Diagnosis
The decision to culture the ocular surface should be made early in
the examination before eye medications have been administered
and manipulations performed. The use of a moist or calcium
alginate swab can increase sensitivity. 50 , 51

Cytologic examination of conjunctival and corneal scrapings is
an important and rapid diagnostic aid. Excessive ocular
discharges should be removed before scraping. Topical
proparacaine should then be applied and the appropriate surface
scraped with a small, ﬂat spatula or the blunt end of a scalpel
blade. Collected material should be gently spread onto glass slides
and air dried. The slides can be stained with modiﬁed Giemsa or
Wright stain for cytologic evaluation and Gram staining to
evaluate the type of bacteria that might be present. Slides can also
be made for direct IFA staining for CDV, FHV-1, and C. felis.
An alternate technique is to roll a small, nylon bristle brush
applicator (Microbrush, Microbrush International, Grafton, WI)

vetexamprep.ir

over the appropriate surface and then onto a slide (Fig. 128.15).
Preparations made with this method have fewer cells that are
dispersed be er on the slide and have less crushing artifact. 52 , 53
This method is less traumatic and easier to perform on cats and
small dogs with tight lid-globe conformations.
Small snip biopsy specimens of the conjunctiva can be readily
obtained after using co on-tipped swabs soaked in a topical
anesthetic and holding it on the area to be excised for a minimum
of 60 seconds. These small pieces of tissue should be spread out
on a piece of paper before they are placed in ﬁxative. Tissue
should also be collected for testing using nucleic acid–based
assays such as PCR; this can be submi ed immediately or frozen
pending the results of histopathology.

Intraocular Infections
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Intraocular bacterial infections may be exogenous or endogenous
in origin. The source of an exogenous infection from a penetrating
ocular injury may be obvious from the history and appearance of
the eye, but injury may also be inapparent, such as a self-sealing
cat claw injury through the conjunctiva and sclera. Infections that
arise from exogenous sources are usually unilateral, whereas
endogenous infections may be bilateral or unilateral.
Local Injury
All recent penetrating ocular injuries should be considered
infected and treated aggressively with broad-spectrum antibiotics
and anti-inﬂammatory drugs, topically and systemically, until
susceptibility data are obtained. Topical ﬂuoroquinolones,
especially oﬂoxacin, moxiﬂoxacin, and gatiﬂoxacin, have excellent
corneal penetration and achieve therapeutic levels in the anterior
segment against a wide variety of bacteria. 54 In suspected or
conﬁrmed bacterial endophthalmitis, a topical ﬂuoroquinolone
should be used every 1 to 2 hours.
Aqueous humor centesis in order to obtain specimens for
cytologic examination and culture is safe when performed
properly and can yield speciﬁc information to guide future
therapy (see section on Diagnosis). Aqueous centesis is not as

vetexamprep.ir

sensitive as vitreous centesis for detection of bacteria in
endophthalmitis; consequently, a negative culture result from an
aqueous specimen does not rule out infection. 55 The ﬁnding of
nondegenerate neutrophils may indicate a sterile purulent
inﬂammation such as that occurring with phacoclastic uveitis
caused by lens capsule rupture. The prognosis for eyes with
endophthalmitis is guarded. Many such eyes develop glaucoma,
and enucleation is a common outcome.
Systemic Diseases
The eye is often a target organ in systemic infections. In some
cases, ocular disease can be the primary owner complaint or the
only sign evident in a systemic disease process. Recognition of
systemic involvement is essential for prognostication and
adequate therapy. Conversely, thorough ocular examination is
indicated in any animals with systemic disease, because it may
provide rapid diagnostic clues and prognostic information. If
infectious agents access the eye, it is usually via the uveal or
vascular tract. Typically, infectious agents or immune complexes
become established in the uvea, producing chorioretinitis, anterior
uveitis, or panuveitis.

Canine Distemper
In addition to conjunctivitis and lacrimal adenitis, CDV often
produces multifocal, nongranulomatous chorioretinitis that does
not usually cause blindness (see Chapter 22). As with CNS signs,
whether chorioretinitis develops likely depends on the viral strain
and immune competency of the host. In one study, dogs with all
neurologic forms of distemper had an overall prevalence of
chorioretinal lesions of 41%, but 83% of the dogs with chronic
leukoencephalopathy syndromes had chorioretinal lesions. 56
Acute focal lesions in the tapetum or nontapetum have gray to
white, hazy or ill-deﬁned borders (Fig. 128.16). 40 Chorioretinal
scars resulting from distemper virus infection have sharply
demarcated borders, are hyperreﬂective in the tapetum (“gold
medallion lesions”), and are depigmented in the nontapetum.
Histologically, retinal changes are characterized by degeneration
of the retina with perivascular cuﬃng in some instances. Lesions
may include focal or diﬀuse degeneration of ganglion cells,
proliferation of retinal pigment epithelium, atrophy of
photoreceptors, disorganization of retinal layers, focal gliosis, and

vetexamprep.ir

distemper inclusion bodies in glial cells. The most serious clinical
ocular problem associated with CDV infection is optic neuritis,
which results in acute onset of bilateral blindness and mydriasis.
57 If inﬂammation extends rostrally to the optic disc,
ophthalmoscopic signs of peripapillary hemorrhages and edema,
retinal vascular congestion, and elevation of the disc are observed
(Fig. 128.17). If the neuritis remains retrobulbar, the diagnosis is
made by exclusion (e.g., blind eyes with mydriasis and normal
retinal function as tested by electroretinography). The optic
neuritis can be isolated, prodromal, or occur in conjunction with
other CNS signs. Distemper-associated blindness also may occur
with inﬂammation of the occipital cortex or optic radiations, but
pupillary light reﬂexes are normal under such circumstances.
Canine Adenovirus-1 Infection
CAdV-1 infection (see Chapter 23) has been estimated to produce
ocular lesions in approximately 20% of dogs recovering from
natural infections. The condition is bilateral in 12 to 28% of
aﬀected dogs. The most visible ocular lesion is stromal corneal
edema (“blue eye”) resulting from immune-complex deposition
and associated inﬂammatory damage to the corneal endothelium
(see Fig. 23.4). Fluid distention of the cornea can cause bullae to
form. If the bullae rupture, corneal ulceration occurs.
Occasionally, a dog has signs of uveitis (blepharospasm, miosis,
hypotony, and aqueous ﬂare) 1 to 2 days before the corneal edema
is evident, although most dogs do not demonstrate discomfort.
Corneal edema may be focal or generalized and is usually
transient. In some instances, the edema is permanent or may
require several months to clear. A marked hypotony combined
with altered corneal rigidity may result in a keratoconus. Other
causes of corneal edema, such as congenital persistent pupillary
membranes, glaucoma, corneal ulceration, and uveitis from other
causes, should be ruled out.

CHV infection has been associated with a bilateral panuveitis with
keratitis, synechiae, cataracts, retinal necrosis and disorganization,
retinal atrophy and dysplasia, and optic neuritis and atrophy. 58

Feline Infectious Peritonitis
The most common ocular manifestation of infection with FIP virus
is bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, often accompanied by
chorioretinitis (see Chapter 31). Frequently, large keratic
precipitates and a ﬁbrinous exudate are found in the anterior
chamber (Fig. 128.18). Pyogranulomatous vasculitis, the hallmark
of the disease’s pathogenesis, may be evident on examination of
retinal vessels (Fig. 128.19). Retinal hemorrhages and detachments
may also develop. Ocular disease is more common with
noneﬀusive FIP and may be the only sign. The use of PCR for
feline coronavirus RNA on aqueous humor specimens may be
helpful for diagnosis of uveitis due to FIP when positive, but
sensitivity was only 36% in one study. 59 Immunocytochemistry
for detection of viral antigens in aqueous humor macrophages
was not recommended because of the potential for false-positive

vetexamprep.ir

results. Topical treatment of ocular disease with glucocorticoids is
supportive, and new antiviral drugs (GS441524 and remdesivir)
oﬀer promise for improved outcomes. Ocular disease may be
temporarily ameliorated, but it usually recurs if the systemic
disease worsens.
Feline Leukemia Virus Infection
Ocular disease in FeLV infection primarily results from FeLVassociated lymphoma (see Chapter 32). Neoplastic lymphocytes
can often be found in the uveal tract as a result of hematogenous
spread. Cats with ocular lymphoma may initially show signs of
mild uveitis, including miosis, aqueous ﬂare, and keratic
precipitates. As the disease progresses, the iris becomes greatly
thickened and distorted with the inﬁltration of tumor cells.
Lymphoma may also initially appear as a mass within the iris in
the absence of clinical signs of uveitis (Fig. 128.20). Glaucoma is a
common sequela because tumor cells inﬁltrate the iridocorneal
angle. Aqueous centesis may be helpful for diagnosis, because
neoplastic lymphocytes readily exfoliate into the aqueous humor.
Aggressive treatment of cats with ocular lymphoma with topical
(e.g., prednisolone acetate) and systemic glucocorticoids, as well
as systemic therapy with chemotherapy can result in
improvement. Lymphoma may also manifest as orbital masses,
with associated exophthalmos and an elevated third eyelid.
Treatment for this form of lymphoma should include
chemotherapy and possibly orbital radiation therapy. Pupillary
abnormalities, including dynamic anisocoria, have been noted in
some cats with FeLV infection, as have retinal hemorrhages
associated with thrombocytopenia. 60

Feline Panleukopenia
Although cerebellar hypoplasia is the most common clinically
apparent abnormality in cats with feline panleukopenia, ki ens
infected in the prenatal or neonatal period may also have retinal
dysplasia and optic nerve hypoplasia or dysplasia (see Chapter
30).
Feline Immunodeficiency Virus Infection

vetexamprep.ir

Ocular inﬂammation has been associated with FIV infection in
both experimentally and naturally infected cats. Anterior uveitis is
most commonly reported, but conjunctivitis, pars planitis, and
chorioretinitis have also been described. Ocular inﬂammation
may result from direct viral damage, secondary immunemediated phenomena, or opportunistic infection. In a
histopathologic study of the eyes of 19 infected cats, 16 cats had
lymphoplasmacytic inﬂammation of the iris and ciliary body. 63
Secondary opportunistic infections with FHV-1, C. felis, and T.
gondii should always be considered in FIV-positive cats with
ocular disease. In an experimental study of chlamydial
conjunctivitis, co-infection with FIV markedly prolonged the
duration of clinical signs and led to chronic conjunctivitis. 64
If another infectious disease can be identiﬁed in an FIV-positive
cat, it should be treated as speciﬁcally as possible. Uveitis that is
associated with FIV infection can be a chronic problem that
requires symptomatic treatment. For long-term use, a topical
NSAID is preferred for treatment because use of glucocorticoids
risks exacerbation of ocular FHV-1 infections. However, oral
prednisolone may be required for treatment of chorioretinitis.
Ehrlichiosis
Ocular lesions occur frequently in dogs with canine monocytic
ehrlichiosis (see Chapter 44). The most common lesions include
unilateral or bilateral anterior uveitis characterized by
conjunctival and episcleral hyperemia or hemorrhage, miosis,
aqueous ﬂare, hypopyon, keratic precipitates, hyphema,
synechiae, and/or hypotony. Glaucoma can occur secondary to
chronic anterior uveitis (Fig. 128.21). Signs of posterior segment
inﬂammation can include chorioretinitis, serous retinal
detachment, retinal hemorrhage, and optic neuritis. Evidence of a
swollen optic disc and peripapillary hemorrhages on fundic
examination suggests optic neuritis (see Fig. 128.17). In a
retrospective study of 90 dogs, bilateral uveitis was the most
common ocular abnormality. 65 In 30 of the 90 dogs, ocular disease
was the only clinical ﬁnding; 60 dogs had systemic signs.
Anterior uveitis has also been seen in dogs naturally infected
with Ehrlichia chaﬀeensis. 66 In an experimental study of dogs
infected with E. canis, E. chaﬀeensis, or Ehrlichia ewingii, histologic
examination of the eyes showed uveitis only in dogs infected with

Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
Ocular lesions are frequently associated with Ricke sia ricke sii
infection and primarily arise as a consequence of vasculitis (see
Chapter 46). Lesions include conjunctival hyperemia,
subconjunctival hemorrhage, hyphema, anterior uveitis, iris
hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhage, retinal edema, and retinal
perivascular inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrate (Fig. 128.22). 68 Lesions
tend to be bilateral in aﬀected dogs but may not be symmetrical.
Fluorescein angiography in experimentally infected dogs
demonstrated increased retinal vascular permeability beginning
on day 6 after infection and 2 days after the onset of pyrexia. 69
Venules were aﬀected twice as frequently as arterioles, and
smaller vessels were aﬀected more frequently than larger primary
vessels. Retinal vascular lesions in this study paralleled the
progression of fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and
prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time during the
second week after infection.
The ocular signs of RMSF resemble those of canine ehrlichiosis.
Although ocular hemorrhages are the most common ophthalmic
sign of RMSF, hemorrhage can also occur with ehrlichiosis.
Although exceptions occur, intraocular hemorrhages and
inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrates tend to be less dramatic in RMSF than
ehrlichiosis. 70

Brucellosis
Brucella canis infection has been associated with unilateral or
bilateral anterior uveitis or panuveitis, endophthalmitis, retinal
detachment, and intraocular hemorrhage (see Chapter 71). Ocular
involvement is often severe and blinding. A retrospective study of
the prevalence of ocular lesions among dogs examined for
brucellosis at veterinary schools in the United States and Canada
found that 38 of 313 (14.2%) dogs had ocular involvement. 71
Testing for B. canis should be performed in dogs with unexplained
uveitis or ocular hemorrhage. The prognosis for resolution of
uveitis associated with brucellosis with treatment is guarded. A
report of three dogs with brucellosis described resolution of
unilateral endophthalmitis in each and apparent systemic clearing
of the organism with a long-term multidrug treatment protocol

vetexamprep.ir

(mean of 96 weeks) that included enroﬂoxacin, doxycycline,
streptomycin, and rifampin. 72
Lyme Borreliosis
In humans, ocular lesions associated with B. burgdorferi infection
have been well described. 73 , 74 Uveitis is the primary
manifestation, but neuro-ophthalmic disorders and surface
inﬂammations such as episcleritis and keratitis have also been
reported. Ocular manifestations are more likely to be seen in latestage disease. A clear association between ocular disease in dogs
and B. burgdorferi infection has not been made.
Leptospirosis
Leptospires incite vasculitis, making the eyes a potential target
organ (Chapter 68). Although leptospires have been found in the
eyes of infected dogs, the paucity of reports of uveitis associated
with canine leptospirosis in the literature probably does not reﬂect
the true prevalence of disease. 75 In horses and humans, the
development of uveitis often occurs months after acute infection.
This likely represents a delayed hypersensitivity reaction between
cell-bound antibodies and persistent leptospiral antigens in the
eye. Bilateral panuveitis and retinal detachments were described
as the only sign of infection in a dog in association with a serovar
Canicola infection. 76 Testing for leptospirosis should be included
in a workup for a canine uveitis even if systemic signs are not
present.
Bacteremia
Bacteremia that occurs in association with conditions such as
infective endocarditis, discospondylitis, UTI, or pyometra may be
associated with uveitis as a result of hematogenous spread of
bacteria to the eye. If endophthalmitis secondary to bacteremia is
suspected, a ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic should be used topically
several times daily in addition to systemic antibiotic therapy.
Fluoroquinolones will penetrate a normal cornea and reach
therapeutic levels in the anterior segment of the eye. In addition, a
topical glucocorticoid such as prednisolone acetate should be used
several times daily to suppress inﬂammation.

vetexamprep.ir

Tetanus and Botulism
Ocular signs are among the most common early clinical
manifestations of tetanus in the dog (Chapter 72) and were among
the ﬁrst signs noticed by the owner in 45% of dogs in one study. 77
Abnormalities included enophthalmos, third-eyelid protrusion,
squinting, swollen eyelids, or a “strange facial expression.” Miosis
is the most common pupillary abnormality on physical
examination. However, mydriasis may also occur (Fig. 128.23).
In botulism, autonomic nervous system dysfunction accounts
for ocular abnormalities. These include mydriasis with sluggish
pupillary light reﬂexes and a decreased palpebral reﬂex. Ocular
surface disease such as conjunctivitis and corneal ulceration may
occur if the palpebral reﬂex is absent, leading to lagophthalmos.
Decreased tear production may also occur secondary to
diminished parasympathetic nerve function to the lacrimal
glands. In animals with lagophthalmos and/or tear deﬁciency,
generous use of artiﬁcial tear products should be incorporated
with other treatments to avoid ocular surface drying.

Bartonellosis
Ocular complications in humans infected with Bartonella henselae
include Parinaud’s oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, and
retinochoroiditis (Chapter 70). 78 In both naturally and
experimentally infected cats, B. henselae DNA and a speciﬁc
antibody have been detected in the aqueous humor, and a role of
Bartonella in anterior uveitis has been hypothesized. 79 In a study
of 366 cats with and without uveitis, the prevalence and
magnitude of serum antibody titers to B. henselae were not higher
in cats with uveitis, suggesting that serum antibody testing cannot
determine whether uveitis in a cat is caused by B. henselae. 80 A
similar lack of correlation was found between B. henselae isolation
from blood or positive serum antibody titer results in cats with
uveitis. 81 A review of our current understanding of the role of
bartonellosis in feline uveitis indicates li le evidence to date that
this disorder is a signiﬁcant cause of uveitis in cats, although
further study is needed. 82 Bartonella vinsonii subsp. berkhoﬃi was
suspected as a cause of uveitis and choroiditis in one dog, 83 but
whether Bartonella spp. can cause ocular disease in dogs remains
unknown.
Mycobacteriosis and Nocardiosis
Granulomatous to pyogranulomatous chorioretinitis, optic
neuritis, and anterior uveitis may occur in disseminated
mycobacterial 84-86 and nocardial infections (Sykes, unpublished
observations) (Chapters 60 and 61). Granulomatous lesions have
also been noted in the conjunctivae and corneas of infected cats. 87
, 88

Systemic Mycoses
Systemic mycoses caused by fungi endemic to North America are
frequently associated with a pyogranulomatous to granulomatous
posterior uveitis. Anterior uveitis accompanies chorioretinitis in
many cases. Ocular involvement occurs in up to 52% of
blastomycosis cases. 89 Ocular lesions always include
chorioretinitis, which may vary from a focal granuloma in the
fundus to widespread subretinal inﬁltrates of organisms and
granulomatous inﬂammation with retinal detachment (Fig.
128.24A). 90 Anterior uveitis is common with extensive posterior

vetexamprep.ir

segment disease, although the organism is not usually found in
these tissues or in aqueous humor aspirates. Secondary glaucoma
is a frequent complication (Fig. 128.24B). Ocular involvement with
histoplasmosis is relatively uncommon in dogs, 91 but is often
recognized in cats and includes granulomatous chorioretinitis,
retinal detachment, anterior uveitis, and secondary glaucoma. 92
Ocular adnexal structures, such as the nictating membrane and
conjunctiva, may also be involved in histoplasmosis. 93 Antigen
testing may be negative in animals with localized ocular disease.
94 In coccidioidomycosis, ocular lesions are similar to those of
blastomycosis (granulomatous chorioretinitis, retinal detachment,
anterior uveitis, and secondary glaucoma). Organisms are found
predominantly in the choroid. Limited data exist regarding the
prevalence of ocular lesions in dogs and cats with
coccidioidomycosis; they appear to be less common than with the
other endemic mycoses described here.

Chorioretinitis with granulomatous inﬂammation and retinal

in color, in contrast to the whitish appearance of most fungal
granulomas (Fig. 128.25). Optic neuritis may also develop, and
ocular disease is often recognized in association with cryptococcal
meningitis.
Clinical signs in cats with sino-orbital aspergillosis (see Chapter
86) include exophthalmos, corneal drying with possible ulceration
secondary to lagophthalmos, ocular discharge, oral cavity
ulceration, pain on opening of the mouth, and nasal discharge if
the infection involves the nasal cavity or sinuses. 95
Brachycephalic cats (especially Persians) appear to be
predisposed. Surgical therapy alone, including orbital
exenteration, has not typically been successful. In one report, a cat
was successfully treated with posaconazole after surgery and
treatment with itraconazole (ITZ) and amphotericin B failed. 96 In
dogs (especially German shepherd dogs), disseminated
aspergillosis may also cause fungal endophthalmitis. In such
cases, chorioretinitis, retinal detachment, and anterior uveitis are
common (Fig. 128.26).

Enucleation of blind eyes has been proposed as a means of
eliminating a nidus of fungal infection that may cause relapse.
Although it is justiﬁable to remove a blind, painful eye (such as
one with intractable glaucoma), enucleation is not indicated in an
animal that has been eﬀectively treated for fungal disease and has
a comfortable but blind eye.
Protothecosis
More than 50% of dogs with protothecosis have ocular
involvement, 98 whereas ocular lesions have not been reported in
cats (Chapter 90). Most dogs with ocular lesions also have
systemic signs such as diarrhea, but in some instances systemic
signs are not evident. Lesions include a granulomatous
chorioretinitis, often with retinal detachment, that is similar in

vetexamprep.ir

appearance to those associated with systemic mycoses. 99 Anterior
uveitis is often present as well. Diagnosis is often possible by
cytologic examination of specimens collected by vitreous centesis.
Toxoplasmosis
The most prominent ocular lesion in dogs and cats with
toxoplasmosis is choroiditis with extension into the retina
(Chapter 93). 100 These lesions typically appear as multifocal dark
gray inﬁltrates in the tapetal fundus and ﬂuﬀy white inﬁltrates in
the nontapetal fundus. Anterior uveitis also occurs, and T. gondii
bradyzoites
and
tachyzoites
have
been
identiﬁed
histopathologically in the irides and ciliary bodies of systemically
aﬀected cats. 101
It is possible that T. gondii may incite immune-mediated uveitis
in the absence of systemic disease. Several mechanisms have been
proposed, including homing of activated immune cells to ocular
tissues, molecular mimicry, circulating antigens or immune
complexes from nonocular sites of parasite replication, and a
nonspeciﬁc increase in immune response. 100 , 102 In ki ens
experimentally infected in utero or in the early neonatal period,
chorioretinitis and anterior uveitis developed without other
evidence of clinical illness. 103

Neosporosis
Although puppies with neosporosis typically die or are
euthanized because of neuromuscular signs, ocular lesions are
present in some dogs (Chapter 94). Retinitis is the primary ocular
lesion with extension into the choroid (retinochoroiditis). A mild
anterior uveitis was also reported. 106
Encephalitozoonosis
In many animals, including rabbits, blue fox, and mink, cataract
formation with uveitis is the most common clinical problem that
results from Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection (Chapter 92). 107-109
Vertical transmission allows the parasite to enter the lens during
fetal development. 110 In one report of 11 domestic cats with
cataract and uveitis, E. cuniculi infection was documented by
serology, cytology, and PCR on aqueous humor and lens material
111 (Fig. 128.27). All cats were successfully treated with oral
fenbendazole for 3 weeks in addition to undergoing
phacoemulsiﬁcation to remove the lens and anti-inﬂammatory
therapy for uveitis.
Leishmaniosis
Ocular and periocular lesions associated with leishmaniosis were
reported in 25% of 105 infected dogs in one study. 112 In 15% of
the dogs in the study, ocular lesions were the only clinical sign.
Ocular signs may include anterior uveitis, conjunctivitis,
keratoconjunctivitis, periocular alopecia, diﬀuse blepharitis,
posterior uveitis, orbital cellulitis, and optic neuritis (Fig. 128.28).
In a study of 127 shelter dogs and 132 client-owned dogs in an
endemic area of Italy, blepharitis predominated in shelter dogs,
whereas anterior uveitis was more common in client-owned dogs.

Diagnosis
Aqueous Centesis
Aqueous centesis can be performed using heavy sedation or
general anesthesia. A 27- to 30-gauge needle on a tuberculin
syringe should be used with the “seal” broken so that movement
of the plunger is smooth. Topical proparacaine should be used
even with sedation. A co on-tip swab soaked in proparacaine
should be held at the site of centesis for 60 seconds before
insertion of the needle. Typically the easiest location to access is
the lateral limbus. Small forceps should be used to hold the
conjunctiva close to the limbus to ﬁxate the globe and apply
counterpressure to the needle. The needle should enter the cornea
just rostral to the limbus and parallel to the plane of the iris (Fig.
128.29). The iris, lens, and corneal endothelium should be
avoided. Unless the anterior chamber is collapsed, the volume
that can be removed from the dog is about 0.3 mL and from the
cat is about 0.5 mL. The needle should be withdrawn slowly and a
sterile co on-tipped swab held over the site, because aqueous will

vetexamprep.ir

leak for a brief time. An aliquot of the aspirated aqueous should
be submi ed in a plain tube for culture and susceptibility testing,
and the remaining aliquot placed in a small EDTA tube to be
centrifuged for cytologic examination. If ﬁbrin is present or iris
adhesions of less than a few days’ duration are present, 25 µg of
tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) may be injected to dissolve
clots and break synechiae. 115
Vitreous Centesis
Centesis of the vitreous cavity has more potential complications
than aqueous centesis and is usually reserved for eyes that have
lost considerable visual function. Choroidal hemorrhage and
retinal tears are the two most likely complications. Topical
proparacaine is not completely eﬀective in anesthetizing the
sclera; thus general anesthesia is recommended. A 22-gauge
needle with a 3-mL syringe should be used. The site of entry
should be 6 mm caudal to the limbus in the dorsolateral quadrant.
Forceps are used to apply counter pressure, and the needle point
is aimed posteriorly away from the lens and toward the center of
the vitreous cavity (Fig. 128.30). The needle should be short (0.5
inch) so that it does not inadvertently pass completely across the
vitreous humor and tear the opposite retina. Approximately 0.5
mL of vitreous humor can be removed for culture and cytologic
examination.

posterior to the limbus and is directed slightly
posterior and toward the center of the globe.

Treatment
Ocular infection and inﬂammation can be treated using topical,
subconjunctival, intraocular, or systemic medications. The route of
administration selected depends on the location, severity of the
infection, and the drug being administered. The eye has three
barriers to drug penetration: the intact cornea for topical
penetration and the blood-aqueous and blood-retinal barriers for
systemic drug penetration. In general, drugs with a diﬀerential
solubility in water and lipids and small molecular size are be er
able to penetrate these barriers. Inﬂammation or ulceration
weaken these barriers to variable degrees and allow be er
penetration. The ability of antibiotics to penetrate the normal eye
varies by drug and route (Table 128.5). The vitreous humor is a
large, rather inert structure, resulting in low drug levels by any
route of drug administration except direct intravitreal injection, in
which the vitreous humor acts as a depot for the relatively slow
release of the drug.

vetexamprep.ir

Topical Administration
Depending on the drug and whether the cornea is ulcerated,
topical therapy may provide adequate drug concentrations only
on the surface or as deep as the iris and ciliary body. Epithelial
defects of 25 to 50% of the surface area increase drug penetration
into the corneal stroma and aqueous humor nine-fold, but larger
defects do not produce an additional increase. 116 Other variables
that
inﬂuence
drug
concentrations
following
topical
administration are the frequency of application, drug contact
time, drug concentration, and formulation. Solutions are generally
easier to apply to a painful eye than ointment and, therefore, are
preferred in terms of compliance. Although medications with
high drug concentrations may have improved absorption, they
can also increase reﬂex lacrimation and become diluted by
osmotic inﬂux of ﬂuid from tissues.
When solutions are used, one drop (about 30 to 50 µL) of a
preparation in the aﬀected eye(s) is adequate. Multiple or rapidly
repeated instillations of the same or diﬀerent preparations simply
increase the rate of loss through the NL system or mutually dilute
each preparation, thereby reducing the availability of each drug.
Waiting an interval of at least 5 minutes between instillation of
diﬀerent drugs is required to allow reﬂex tearing to subside and
prevent dilution of the previous drop.
Treatment of routine surface infections of the conjunctiva or
prophylactic antibacterial therapy of corneal ulcers should include
topical broad-spectrum antibiotics such as neomycin-polymyxin
B-gramicidin that are not used systemically. This rationale
reduces exposure of bacteria to drugs that may be beneﬁcial for
systemic therapy (and hence reduces selection for resistant
bacteria) and avoids sensitization of a patient to a topical
antibiotic that might have potential in systemic therapy. Some
animals develop an allergic reaction to topical neomycin,
particularly when used chronically. Anaphylactic reactions in cats
after administration of topical bacitracin-neomycin-polymyxin B
preparations have been reported. 117 Most cases have been fatal,
so this product is not recommended in cats.
Regardless of cause, treatment of uveitis requires antiinﬂammatory therapy. Topical potent glucocorticoids such as 1%
prednisolone acetate and 0.1% dexamethasone alcohol (the form
present in neomycin-polymixin B-dexamethasone suspension)

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
p y
p
penetrate the corneal barrier well and achieve therapeutic levels in
the anterior segment. Prednisolone and dexamethasone in the
phosphate forms do not penetrate the cornea as well and should
not be used for the treatment of uveitis. Topical NSAIDs such as
diclofenac and ﬂurbiprofen penetrate an intact cornea well and
can also be used for treating uveitis. Topical NSAIDs have less
potent anti-inﬂammatory eﬀects and thus are be er suited for
treatment of mild uveitis. They can also be used in conjunction
with a topical glucocorticoid for an additive eﬀect. The frequency
of use of a topical anti-inﬂammatory agent is dictated by the
severity of the uveitis, ranging from 2 to 6 or more times daily for
mild and severe uveitis, respectively.
Subconjunctival Administration
Subconjunctival administration of antibiotics or anti-inﬂammatory
drugs is used primarily for anterior segment disease and can
achieve therapeutic intraocular levels of medication. The major
limitations of subconjunctival injections are drug irritation and
ocular manipulation. The means by which a subconjunctivally
injected drug reaches the interior of the eye are controversial, but
direct diﬀusion through the sclera, which has no epithelial barrier
as the cornea does, and leakage through the needle hole with
topical absorption have been demonstrated. Except for long-acting
drugs, most others must be re-administered at 12- to 24-hour
intervals to maintain therapeutic levels. Typically, a single
injection of a subconjunctival drug is administered, followed by
topical agents, systemic agents, or both.
