Drugs should be injected under the bulbar conjunctiva, not the
palpebral conjunctiva. The dorsal 12 o’clock position is easiest to
access. Adequate topical anesthesia is required. A proparacainesoaked co on-tip swab should be held at the injection site for at
least 60 seconds. The conjunctiva should be lifted with a small
forceps to allow for proper needle placement. A 25-gauge needle
should be used to slowly inject the drug. In many animals, this
can be accomplished without sedation. In both dogs and cats a
volume of 0.2 to 0.5 mL can be administered, creating a bleb that
resolves in a few hours.
While signiﬁcant posterior segment drug concentrations can be
obtained when injecting near the equator of the globe, the
subconjunctival route achieves inadequate concentrations for
bacterial infections of the vitreous. Subconjunctival dosages vary
by agent (Table 128.6).
Systemic Administration
The systemic route of therapy is indicated in cases of
chorioretinitis and optic neuritis, because topical or

vetexamprep.ir

subconjunctival application does not result in therapeutic drug
concentrations in these tissues. Many drugs are unable to cross the
blood-retinal or blood-aqueous barrier, although some agents
have good ocular penetration (see Table 128.5). However, most
drugs administered systemically do penetrate the eye when it is
inﬂamed and the normal ocular barriers are disrupted. Of the
systemically administered antifungal azole compounds,
ﬂuconazole has optimal penetration of the eye and CNS, but also
is the least active azole. Itraconazole has also been eﬀective in
many animals for treating systemic mycoses such as
blastomycosis with ocular involvement, and may be eﬀective
when treatment with ﬂuconazole fails.
Some systemically administered medications may be associated
with ocular adverse eﬀects. Some cats receiving systemic
enroﬂoxacin (oral or injectable) have developed acute retinal
degeneration and permanent blindness. 118 , 119 This has been
most notable in cats receiving greater than the recommended dose
of 5 mg/kg per day. However, even lower doses may cause retinal
degeneration in some cats, particularly older or debilitated
animals with compromised renal function, and all systemically
administered ﬂuoroquinolones should be viewed as potentially
retinotoxic in cats. However, pradoﬂoxacin was shown to have no
retinal toxicity in young healthy cats at 6 and 10 times the
therapeutic dose. 120 This drug is preferred for cats when
treatment with ﬂuoroquinolones is indicated.
Treatment of moderate to severe anterior uveitis or posterior
uveitis should include the use of an oral anti-inﬂammatory drug.
Prednisone or prednisolone has the most potent eﬀect and should
be used in cases of optic neuritis, moderate to severe
chorioretinitis, or retinal detachment caused by posterior uveitis.
In cases of anterior uveitis without posterior segment
involvement, an oral NSAID may be adequate and will also
provide an analgesic eﬀect.
Adjunctive Treatments
In addition to speciﬁc therapy, standard nursing care involves
cleansing the ocular surface and lids with warm, moist wipes.
Systemic analgesic drugs such as the synthetic opioid tramadol
can be beneﬁcial in treating ocular pain and can be safely used in
conjunction with an oral glucocorticoid or NSAID. Topical

vetexamprep.ir

atropine minimizes ocular pain from ciliary and iridal muscle
spasm and helps prevent synechiae; however, atropine should not
be used if KCS, glaucoma, or iridocorneal angle compromise are
present. Injection of 25 µg of tPA into the anterior chamber is an
eﬀective and dramatic means of breaking down adhesions and
dissolving ﬁbrin clots if given within 3 to 7 days of formation.
Once the clot is organized, drug eﬃcacy is lost. If active or recent
bleeding has occurred in the eye, intraocular rebleeding may
occur after injection of tPA. Injections may be repeated if
necessary. Injection of tPA into the vitreous humor is not as safe
because of retinal toxicity.
Intraocular Administration
Intracameral or intraocular injection of antibacterial drugs is a
heroic and eﬀective means of obtaining high levels of intraocular
antibiotics for the treatment of bacterial endophthalmitis. If vision
is to be preserved, the decision to use the intracameral route must
be made early to avoid rapidly devastating inﬂammation to
delicate intraocular structures. Because culture and susceptibility
testing results are not available for a few days, a broad-spectrum
bactericidal antibiotic is usually selected. The use of intravitreal
vancomycin has been common in human medicine for the
treatment of bacterial endophthalmitis after injury or intraocular
surgery. Prudent use of vancomycin is recommended to reduce
selection for vancomycin-resistant enterococci, which represent a
signiﬁcant threat to human and animal health.

Case Example
Signalment

“Max,” a 10-year-old male neutered bichon frise from northern
California.

History

Max was evaluated by the University of California-Davis
Veterinary Ophthalmology Service for a ﬂeshy pink mass that
had been noticed by his groomer on the outer corner of his left
eye a week before the time of evaluation. The mass did not
appear to be painful or pruritic, and Max had otherwise been

vetexamprep.ir

eating well and was bright and alert. Max had been diagnosed a
year previously with small B-cell lymphoma, which at that time
had been detected in the right conjunctiva, peripheral lymph
nodes, and GI tract. The lymphoma was treated with a
combination chemotherapy protocol (cyclophosphamide,
doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). A month later he
developed a left-sided superﬁcial corneal ulcer that was initially
treated with neosporin-polymixin-bacitracin ointment, but
subsequently ruptured and was treated with a conjunctival
pedical ﬂap. Topical cyclosporine and ocular lubricant were
also prescribed for decreased tear production in the left eye, but
because of persistently decreased tear production at a 3-month
recheck, topical tacrolimus was also added. Since then, he had
done well and was considered to be in complete remission. Max
was up to date on vaccinations and was receiving monthly
heartworm and ectoparasite prophylaxis medications.

Current Medications

Topical cyclosporine (2%, 1 drop q12h OS), tacrolimus (0.03%, 1
drop q12h OS), ocular lubricant (q6-8h OD), prednisone 1
mg/kg PO q24h.

Ophthalmic Examination

Body weight: 4.5 kg.
Eyes were open and appeared comfortable. There was
moderate mucoid discharge OS. Face symmetrical, globe
position and movements were normal OU. Pupil size was
midrange OD. There were anterior synechia OS and the
pupil could not be fully assessed due to large conjunctival
ﬂap and corneal opacity. Pupillary light reﬂexes (direct
and consensual) were intact. The menace response was
intact OU, there was a dazzle reﬂex, and palpebral
reﬂexes were complete OU. Patient behaved as if sighted.
OD: Iris atrophy and nuclear sclerosis were present. All
other ﬁndings were within normal limits.
OS (Fig. 128.31A): There was mild to moderate hyperemia
of the third eyelid with mild diﬀuse thickening of the
third eyelid. Mild diﬀuse conjunctival hyperemia and
chemosis was present. There was a 7 mm × 3 mm × 3 mm
smooth raised pink conjunctival mass arising from the

vetexamprep.ir

temporal bulbar conjunctiva just posterior to the
ventrotemporal limbus. The conjunctival pedicle ﬂap was
integrated into axial cornea. It appeared to be well
perfused, densely pigmented, and ﬁbrotic with extension
of melanin and ﬁbrosis forming a 2- to 3-mm rim around
the incorporated ﬂap. The anterior chamber was clear.
There was a focal anterior synechia temporally. The
visible iris and limited fundoscopic examination
appeared normal.
STT (mm/min): OD-15, OS-5
Intraocular pressures (mmHg-rebound): OD-14, OS-10
Fluorescein stain: OU-no retention
Biopsy Procedure: Tetracaine was applied to the ocular
surface OS and lidocaine 2% gel was applied to the
aﬀected conjunctiva. The conjunctiva adjacent to the mass
was grasped with forceps and scissors were used to excise
the conjunctival mass. Light pressure with a 4 × 4 gauze
over closed lids was applied for hemostasis.
Erythromycin ointment was applied OS at the conclusion
of the procedure. The tissue was cut in half and submi ed
for histopathology and aerobic/anaerobic bacterial
culture.

Histopathology Findings

The submucosa was markedly expanded by an abundant
population of predominantly large foamy macrophages and
plasma cells admixed with fewer neutrophils and Mo cells.
Macrophages often contained phagocytosed cells, karyorrhectic
debris, and occasional coccobacilli. Vascular proﬁles were
cuﬀed by moderate numbers of lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Gram staining revealed small numbers of gram-positive cocci
and rare gram-negative rods sca ered within histiocytes and
occasionally extracellularly. Acid-fast staining revealed
intrahistiocytic bundles of ﬁbrillar to rod-shaped bacteria that
were strongly acid-fast-positive. These organisms were also
visible using Warthin-Starry silver stain.

Aerobic and Anaerobic Bacterial Culture

Very small numbers of mixed growth including methicillinresistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (susceptible only to
aminoglycosides, chloramphenicol, rifampin, vancomycin) and
E. coli (susceptible to aminoglycosides, amoxicillin-clavulanic
acid, ceftazidime, chloramphenicol, tetracyclines, imipenem,
ﬂuoroquinolones).

Diagnosis

Mycobacterial conjunctivitis.

Treatment

Doxycycline, 10 mg/kg PO q24h, topical gentamicin ophthalmic
ointment OS q8h, and oﬂoxacin (0.3% ophthalmic solution, 1
drop OU q8h) in addition to continuing the other medications.
At a recheck examination 1 month later, conjunctivitis had
resolved and there was no evidence of mass recurrence (Fig.
128.31B). Antimicrobial treatment was discontinued. At an
examination 4 months later there was still no evidence of
recurrence, although the owners reported a brief period of
inappetence a week before that visit. However, a month after

vetexamprep.ir

that, Max stopped eating and began to lose weight, and the
owners elected euthanasia. Necropsy was not performed.

Comments

This dog developed mycobacterial conjunctivitis, a rare
infection of the ocular adnexal structures, which was likely
secondary to immunosuppressive disease or medications. The
lack of mycobacterial growth in culture suggests that a slowgrowing or unculturable mycobacterial species was responsible,
such as Mycobacterium avium. Bacteria cultured were likely
secondary invaders and should have been inactivated with the
topical antibacterial medications.
The owner was oﬀered additional diagnostic tests to identify
the Mycobacterium species present and determine whether there
was evidence of more widespread infection, but declined. Such
tests could include mycobacterial culture at a mycobacterial
reference laboratory, species-speciﬁc PCR assays on paraﬃnembedded biopsy tissue, and a minimum database with
thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound examination.
Possible reasons for the decline of this dog after treatment
were recurrence of lymphoma, systemic mycobacterial disease,
or another unrelated illness.

129: Miscellaneous Infections
and Inﬂammatory Disorders of
the Central Nervous System
Andrea Tipold, Marc Vandevelde, Renee Barber, and Jane E. Sykes

KEY POINTS
Prion Diseases and Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy
• First Described: Feline spongiform encephalopathy was first
recognized in 1990, but prion diseases of sheep and goats
have been recognized since the 1700s and 1800s.
• Cause: Prions are small infectious agents that are resistant to
inactivation by heat, formalin, glutaraldehyde, alcohol, and
radiation. Infectivity is associated with a host-encoded protein,
the prion protein (PrP). The mechanism of transmissible
spongiform encephalopathy (TSE) involves a misfolding of the
normal prion protein (PrPc) to a new heat-resistant protein.
• Affected Hosts: Cats, humans, and a variety of other
mammalian species.
• Geographic Distribution: Primarily Europe, but cases have
occurred sporadically worldwide.
• Mode of transmission: The TSEs are transmissible to other
animals, at least under experimental conditions. Routes of
natural transmission of TSEs involve oral ingestion, skin
scarification, or congenital transmission. For example, scrapie
has been consistently found in the placentas of ewes. Infection
has spread iatrogenically through contaminated biologic
products and likely through other veterinary procedures or
feeding practices.
• Major Clinical Signs: Adult cats, slowly progressive neurologic
signs, behavioral changes, gait abnormalities, hypersensitivity.

vetexamprep.ir

• Differential Diagnoses: Degenerative diseases, neoplasia, other
infectious and inflammatory diseases of the CNS.
• Human Health Significance: During the outbreak of bovine
spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in the United Kingdom, a
new variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) occurred in
humans. The disease has also been reported in other countries.
vCJD affected primarily young adults and was suspected of
being caused by ingestion of contaminated cattle products. Not
all humans are equally susceptible to the development of
spongiform encephalopathy. Transmission of the agent through
blood transfusions or organ donation remains a concern.
Bacterial Meningitis and Meningoencephalomyelitis
• Cause: Bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis is caused by a
variety of pyogenic bacteria that enter the CSF spaces or the
CNS parenchyma. Organisms are usually opportunistic
microflora or enter tissues as a result of environmental
contamination of penetrating objects or spread of an infection
from other organs.
• Affected Hosts: Dogs and cats of all ages are affected.
• Geographic Distribution: Worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Bacteria can spread to the meninges
from: (1) sites of infection in the nasal sinuses, retrobulbar
tissues, or middle or inner ear when host immune defenses are
compromised; (2) sites of traumatic focal penetration; (3) sites
of infection in adjacent venous sinuses or bony structures; or
(4) via hematogenous arterial dissemination.
• Major Clinical Signs: Meningitis: fever, reluctance to move, stiff
gait, and muscle spasms are the most common clinical signs.
Paraspinal hyperesthesia and progressive neurologic
dysfunction are progressive features.
Meningoencephalomyelitis: additional signs of brain and/or
spinal cord lesions.
• Differential Diagnoses: Meningoencephalomyelitis caused by
nonbacterial microorganisms and immune-mediated causes
should be considered. Myeloid or lymphoid neoplasias may
cause similar focal, multifocal, or diffuse signs of inflammation.
• Human Health Significance: None. The organisms that cause
bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis are indigenous microflora
or environmental contaminants. Precautions should always be

vetexamprep.ir

taken in collecting or handling CSF potentially laden with
microorganisms during diagnostic medical procedures.
Inflammatory Neurologic Diseases Previously of
Suspected Infectious Origin
• First Described: Granulomatous meningoencephalitis,
necrotizing encephalitis, and feline poliomyelitis were first
described in the 1950s–1980s. Nonsuppurative encephalitis
was reported in Ireland in 2002 and steroid-responsive
meningitis-arteritis was described in 1981.
• Cause: Unknown, but uncultivable infectious agents have been
suspected.
• Affected Hosts: Granulomatous meningoencephalitis,
necrotizing encephalitis, greyhound nonsuppurative
encephalitis and steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis all occur
exclusively in dogs. Feline poliomyelitis has been reported in
domestic and wild felids.
• Geographic Distribution: Some conditions have limited
distributions, whereas others can be found worldwide.
• Mode of Transmission: Mostly unknown.
• Major Clinical Signs: Depending on the localization of the lesion
—spinal cord or intracranial signs, or signs may be multifocal.
Cervical rigidity, and in some diseases fever can occur.
• Differential Diagnoses: The main differential diagnoses are
neoplasia and a variety of infectious diseases of the CNS (viral,
bacterial, fungal, protozoal, and parasitic).
• Human Health Significance: None.

Prion Diseases and Feline Spongiform
Encephalopathy
Etiology, Epidemiology and Pathogenesis
Feline spongiform encephalopathy (FSE) belongs to the
transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs; Table 129.1), 1 a
group of neurodegenerative diseases in humans and animals
characterized by a very long incubation time and degeneration of
the CNS with vacuolation of the neuropil and nerve cells. 2 The

vetexamprep.ir

infectious agent is small and resistant to inactivation by heat,
formalin, glutaraldehyde, alcohol, and radiation. Infectivity is
associated with a host-encoded protein, the so-called prion protein
(PrP). PrP is widely distributed in the CNS, peripheral nerve,
neuroendocrine and lymphatic tissues, and many other organs. 3 It
is involved in neuronal development and function and in the
prevention of cell death. The mechanism of TSE involves a
misfolding of the normal prion protein (PrPc) to a new heatresistant protein known as PrPSc or PrPres (Sc stands for scrapie, the
oldest known spongiform encephalopathy [SE] in small ruminants;
res stands for resistant to protease digestion). In its new
conformation, the PrPSc is protease resistant and hence accumulates
in the tissue. Misfolding of the PrP can also occur spontaneously
and sporadically through genetic mutations in the PrP gene,
leading to hereditary SEs, which are exceedingly rare in humans.
Once formed, the modiﬁed, abnormal PrP is thought to induce
additional copies of itself by interacting with normal PrP. Thus, the
belief holds that this misfolded protein itself becomes an infectious
agent, the prion. 3 , 4 The prion theory is a revolutionary concept in
biology, and many questions remain. Prions are unique because
they can be both inherited and infectious.
The PrPc gene is highly conserved among diﬀerent animals;
however, knockout mice devoid of the protein develop normally
with mild neuronal abnormalities. The presence of an abnormal PrP
in the CNS is devastating. PrPSc is insoluble and aggregates as
amyloid ﬁbrils in infected brain tissue where deposits (amyloid
plaques) can be observed in some SEs. Accumulation of aberrantly
folded PrPSc ﬁbrils is central in the pathogenesis of these diseases. 3
Accumulation leads to astrocytic proliferation, microglial cell
activation, loss of synapses, and ﬁnally to neuronal cell death by
apoptosis. 2 However, PrPc also appears to play an important role
in neurotoxicity. 5

vetexamprep.ir

TABLE 129.1

SE, spongiform encephalopathy.
a Geographic location in parentheses when restricted to a specific area.

The TSEs are transmissible to other animals, at least under
experimental conditions (intracerebral inoculation), even from
sheep to pigs. 6 , 7 Routes of natural transmission of TSEs involve
oral ingestion, skin scariﬁcation, or congenital transmission. For
example, scrapie has been consistently found in the placentas of
ewes, 8 and in a cheetah maternal transmission was suspected. 9
Infection has spread iatrogenically through contaminated biologic
products and likely through other veterinary procedures or feeding
practices. 6
During the incubation period (following mucosal exposure),
which has been studied in small rodents, PrPSc accumulates on the
membranes of follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) in local lymphoid
tissue. 2 A crucial phase of neuronal invasion likely occurs at the
interface of FDC and nerve endings in secondary lymphoid organs.
10 From the lymphoreticular tissues at the site of experimental
inoculation, the prion is thought to gain access to the peripheral
nervous system through local nerve endings, although the exact
mechanism of transfer is unclear. 10 From there, the prion migrates
to the CNS. Following exposure by ingestion, PrPSc may enter the
gut-associated lymphoid tissue, then enter nerve endings in the
intestinal tract, and migrate to the CNS by means of the vagus
nerve. In bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), there seems to

vetexamprep.ir

be some replication in tonsils, 11 but spread appears to occur by
way of the autonomic nervous system of the gut, speciﬁcally the
vagus nerve to the medulla oblongata. 10 , 12
Scrapie, the classic TSE of small ruminants, has been recognized
for approximately 275 years. Since that time, other SEs have been
recognized in humans and animals. TSEs became notorious in the
late 1980s as a result of the BSE outbreak in the United Kingdom, 13
where scrapie has been endemic for centuries. BSE was spread by
animal protein concentrates including scrapie-infected sheep in
ca le feed. The agent present in these meats was no longer being
properly inactivated because of changes in the production
procedures. As a result, the scrapie agent probably became adapted
to a new host and established BSE in bovines with major epidemic
consequences. 14 However, BSE was not restricted to the United
Kingdom. Recycling of imported live animals, processed beef, or
livestock food supplements from the United Kingdom sparked new
small-scale epidemics in most European countries. The United
States had no reported indigenous cases because it banned the
importation of beef from the United Kingdom beginning in the
mid-1980s, and minimal sheep-derived products have been
processed for use in feed for other animals. 15 However, cases in
ca le have occurred in Canada, and two of these ca le were
exported to the United States. Some infected ca le have been
detected in Japan. The incidence of BSE is approaching zero in all
European countries as a result of measures taken by the European
Union.
FSE was ﬁrst recognized during the BSE epidemic in the United
Kingdom. 1 Based on strain-typing experiments, FSE is
undoubtedly caused by the BSE agent. 16 Cats were probably
infected by ingesting BSE-contaminated feed. 17 Cats cannot be
experimentally infected by the scrapie agent directly as they can by
BSE and Creu feldt-Jakob disease (CJD) agents, which indicates an
adaptation to the new hosts. 18 The ﬁrst cases of FSE were
diagnosed in the early 1990s. 17 , 19 The outbreak was a ributed to
consumption of beef products contaminated by CNS tissues from
infected animals.
In addition to the United Kingdom, single cases of FSE have been
described in several European countries, and also worldwide. 20–23
Captive wild species of Felidae such as lions (Panthera leo), tigers
(Panthera tigris), cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus), and pumas (Felis

vetexamprep.ir

concolor) that were fed bovine tissues have also been aﬀected with
BSE. 24 , 25 The number of aﬀected cats being reported annually has
sharply decreased. TSE has not been documented in the dog, most
probably because of a few changes in the sequence of endogenous
PrP. 26 , 27

Clinical Features
Because of the long incubation time of TSEs, the signs of FSE are
observed only in adult cats (peak incidence at age 5 years). The
neurologic signs develop progressively over several weeks to
months and are characterized by behavioral changes such as
aggressiveness and fear. Gait abnormalities include ataxia and
inaccurate landing while jumping. Aﬀected cats are hypersensitive
to tactile stimulation. No focalization of the neurologic signs occurs.
The disease is invariably progressive and fatal.

Diagnosis
The suspicion for FSE is based on geographic location, the age of
the animal, and the clinical signs. From a diagnostic standpoint, a
variety of neurologic conditions have to be considered. No speciﬁc
laboratory ﬁndings are present in cats with FSE. Laboratory
diagnosis of TSE is based on immunohistochemical detection of the
protease-resistant PrPSc in tissues obtained by biopsy or at
necropsy. Tissue is subjected to proteinase K digestion to destroy
PrP and selectively retain PrPSc. Several monoclonal and polyclonal
antibody commercial test kits are available. 28 , 29 Species
diﬀerences exist in reactions to these commercially available tests.
In scrapie, PrPSc can be demonstrated in lymphoid tissues such as
the tonsils or third eyelid. 30 Given that no replication of the BSE
agent occurs in lymphatic tissues, laboratory diagnosis is possible
only on brain material after slaughter. In cats, extraneural PrPSc
accumulation appears to be inconsistent so that obtaining CNS
tissue at necropsy has been the only absolute means of conﬁrmation
when other test results are negative. 31 , 32 A protein misfolding
cyclic ampliﬁcation technique was highly sensitive in detecting
PrPSc in a cheetah. 33 Deposition was found throughout the CNS,
lymphoreticular, and other tissues suggesting widespread spread of
the agent throughout the body. In recent years, new assays have
been developed that are based on conversion of recombinant PrP to

vetexamprep.ir

p

PrPSc by PcPSc in body ﬂuids or tissue homogenates (known as real-

time quaking-induced conversion assays) (Fig. 129.1). 34
Application of these assays to CSF specimens has been useful for
antemortem diagnosis of Creu feld-Jacob disease in humans.
Pathologic Findings
As in all other TSEs, the pathologic ﬁndings in FSE are highly
characteristic. The changes consist of vacuolation in the neuropil
and neurons in a bilaterally symmetric distribution, especially in
the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex (Fig. 129.2A).
Immunocytochemistry for PrPSc reveals accumulation of PrP in
aﬀected areas (Fig. 129.2B). Advanced cases have neuronal loss and
gliosis. Advanced lesions are more commonly observed in human
patients because aﬀected animals are often euthanized in early
stages of the neurologic disease. No inﬂammation is present. The
neuropathologic proﬁle varies after experimental chronic wasting
disease infection. 35 , 36

Treatment
Treatments used for TSEs must be able to cross the blood-brain
barrier. A variety of compounds have been used including polyene
antimicrobials, 37 analogues of Congo red, quinacrine,
chlorpromazine, and inhibitors of peptide synthesis. Eﬀorts are
underway to discover more eﬀective compounds, but to date,
treatment of human SEs is largely supportive. 38 Active and passive
immunization using recombinant PrPc and antibodies to PrPc could
have some merit. TSEs are similar to Alzheimer’s disease in which
neurodegeneration is accompanied by massive deposition of
amyloid-β-protein, and some reduction in progression occurs when
immunotherapy is used. Because the incidence of TSE in humans
has not risen at all as a result of the BSE epidemic that is now at its
end, TSEs remain exceedingly rare diseases. Vaccine development is
therefore unlikely.

Prevention
All TSEs are fatal diseases. Prevention of exposure is the most
important control measure. Although transmi ing an SE from one
species to another orally is generally diﬃcult, nonbovine species
were found to be infected with BSE in the United Kingdom. 16 BSE

vetexamprep.ir

in these other species undoubtedly resulted from oral exposure.
Scrapie-infected sheep were processed into meat and bone meal
supplements being fed to ca le, and tissue from sick animals was
recycled through the animal food supply. However, further spread
in the bovine population in Europe has been prevented by banning
the feeding of animal proteins to ruminant species, and ﬁnally to all
farm animals. The BSE epidemic has ended and FSE has therefore
largely disappeared. Although BSE has been nearly eradicated,
scrapie remains a challenge because it is a transmissible disease.
Because susceptibility to scrapie is genetically controlled, PCR has
been used to detect alleles of scrapie-susceptible sheep to assist
selection for breeding of scrapie-resistant animals. 39

Public Health Aspects
In 1996, during the outbreak of BSE in the United Kingdom, a new
variant of CJD (vCJD) arose in humans there. 40 , 41 The disease has
also been reported in other countries, including the United States,
often in association with a history of residence in the United
Kingdom. A total of 232 cases have been reported worldwide, and
although the epidemic is nearing its end, surveillance eﬀorts
continue. 40 In contrast to classical (“sporadic”) CJD, vCJD aﬀected
primarily young adults and was suspected of being caused by
ingestion of contaminated ca le products. Molecular typing eﬀorts
suggest that the vCJD agent is similar to the BSE agent. 42 , 43 Not all
humans are equally susceptible to the development of SE. A higher
prevalence of disease is associated with homozygosity for a
polymorphism at codon 129 of the PrP gene. 3
Transmission of the agent through blood transfusions or organ
donation remains a concern. Although BSE is the only zoonotic
prion disease that has been recognized to date, concerns remain
about the possibility of new prion strains arising that may be
capable of crossing the species barrier. 44

Bacterial Meningitis and
Meningoencephalomyelitis
Etiology and Epidemiology
Bacterial infections can spread into the meningeal spaces and
subsequently the parenchyma of the CNS from natural oriﬁces such

vetexamprep.ir

as the nasal sinuses, retrobulbar tissues, 45–47 and middle or inner
ear. 48 , 49 Bacteria that proliferate in middle or inner ear infections
can enter the cranial vault and produce cranial meningitis or
subdural abscess formation (empyema) and, frequently, with brain
parenchymal involvement, central vestibular dysfunction. 50–53
Bacteria can also enter the meningeal spaces through traumatic
focal penetration (foreign bodies or bite wounds), 54 , 55 spread from
sites of infection in adjacent venous sinuses or bony or cartilaginous
structures, or spread via hematogenous arterial dissemination. 56 , 57
Vascular spread, a common pathway of entry, can result in
lodgment of bacteria in the endothelial cells of capillaries or the
choroid plexus, which results in bacterial invasion of the
parenchyma of the CNS or colonization of the CSF, respectively.
Associated vascular necrosis may be followed by hemorrhagic
necrosis. In the CSF, bacteria have adequate nutrients and a paucity
of phagocytes and immunoglobulin, and they can proliferate,
which produces a progressive inﬂammatory process that can
readily spread along CSF pathways.

Bacteria that cause meningoencephalomyelitis in dogs or cats are
varied and can include aerobic, microaerophilic, and anaerobic
species. Staphylococci, streptococci, Salmonella spp., Pasteurella spp.,
Actinomyces spp., Nocardia spp., and a variety of anaerobic bacteria
have been isolated. 50 , 58–62

Clinical Features
Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
On entry into the CSF, bacteria can replicate to a moderate degree
before they trigger a host protective response, because the immune
response in this area is slow. The immune response of the host,
rather than virulence of the pathogen, is usually responsible for
most of the subsequent pathologic events. TLRs, which are present
on astrocytes, neurons, microglia, and oligodendrocytes, initiate
innate recognition of the microorganisms. TLR signals initiate the
release of a wide variety of proinﬂammatory mediators including
reactive intermediates, cytokines, and chemokines within the CNS
tissues and CSF spaces. 63 Within the nervous tissue, inﬂammatory
processes lead to increased expression of inﬂammatory cytokines
such as TNF-α; thus, higher CSF concentrations of TNF-α and IL-12
have been used to distinguish bacterial from aseptic meningitis in
humans. 64–66 Immunologic damage to bacteria leads to the release
of breakdown products into the CSF and local CNS tissue. This
further stimulates the release of cytokines and prostaglandins,
which are chemotactic for leukocytes and contribute to meningeal
and ependymal inﬂammation. Subsequent inﬂammation leads to
vascular injury and vascular thrombosis; tissue inﬂammation,
edema, hemorrhage, and necrosis; and increased CNS pressure
within the conﬁnes of the dura mater and bony spaces.
Inﬂammatory processes may also lead to adhesions and obstruction
to CSF ﬂow, resulting in obstructive internal or external
hydrocephalus. 67
In the rare situation of pure meningitis, hyperesthesia from nerve
root irritation is an important clinical sign. The gait of animals with
meningitis is often choppy and stiﬀ. With progression or direct
parenchymal destruction of the spinal cord and brain parenchyma,
focal, multifocal, or diﬀuse neurologic deﬁcits can occur.

vetexamprep.ir

Manifestations of intracranial deﬁcits include gait abnormalities,
central vestibular signs, abnormal placing reactions, seizures,
behavioral abnormalities, and progressive decline in mental status
until coma occurs.
Physical Examination Findings
Elevated rectal temperature may be found on examination because
of fever, as well as excessive muscular exertional activity.
Extraneural signs may occur and depend on the site of primary
infection. Animals with meningitis may walk with a short stiﬀ or
cautious stride. Often the back of aﬀected dogs is arched and the
neck is outstretched with low head carriage. Paraspinal and
extremity hyperesthesia is present with limb and spinal
manipulation. When inﬂammation is conﬁned to the meninges,
postural reactions that involve motor responses are often stilted. As
the inﬂammation involves the CNS parenchyma, deﬁcits in sensory
and motor responses such as delayed placing reactions, paresis, and
ataxia can be observed. Cranial nerve deﬁcits are often seen on
neurologic examination. Further signs of cerebral dysfunction
include signs such as altered mentation (depression, aggression) or
seizures. Myotatic and ﬂexor reﬂexes may be diﬃcult to elicit
because of increased muscle tone from the animal’s extreme
tenderness and unwillingness to relax. Loss of reﬂex function
occurs if spinal nerves or gray ma er become damaged in the
inﬂammatory process.

Diagnosis
The diﬀerential diagnosis for bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis
includes noninfectious CNS disease such as neoplasia, or other
infectious diseases caused by viruses, ricke siae, fungi, protozoa,
algae, and helminths (Table 129.2). 68 , 69 FIP is probably the most
common cause of meningoencephalomyelitis in cats. 70 , 71 When
parenchymal neurologic dysfunction is apparent, then protozoal
meningoencephalomyelitis and meningoencephalomyelitis of
unknown origin (MUO) should be considered. Frequently, more
localized hyperesthesia associated with upper or lower motor
neuron deﬁcits can be observed with epidural empyema,
discospondylitis, or paraspinal osteomyelitis. Steroid-responsive
meningitis-arteritis (SRMA) in dogs can mimic all the signs of
bacterial meningitis. 72 Diseases associated with myositis (such as

vetexamprep.ir

American canine hepatozoonosis and leptospirosis) can also
produce clinical signs that resemble those of meningitis.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Although there are no hematologic or biochemical abnormalities
that are speciﬁc for bacterial meningitis, the CBC may reveal
leukocytosis, often with a left shift, especially if the process that
leads to the meningitis resulted from hematogenous spread;
however, an absence of neutrophilic leukocytosis is common in
dogs or cats with meningitis. 60 Serum chemistry abnormalities are
variable and nonspeciﬁc and can include increased ALT and ALP
activities, hyperglycemia, and variable changes in serum
electrolytes.

Deﬁnitive diagnosis of bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis
requires evaluation of the CSF. Precautions should be taken not to
remove too much ﬂuid if CSF pressures could be increased. If
imaging capabilities are available, they should be performed and
evaluated before CSF removal since they may reveal evidence of
increased intracranial pressure. However, ﬁndings on medical
imaging should not be used to eliminate CNS inﬂammatory
disease, because CSF ﬁndings have a high sensitivity for its
detection. 73 Abnormalities found on CSF analysis in animals with
bacterial meningitis usually consist of marked neutrophilic
pleocytosis (Fig. 129.3), and CSF protein concentration is increased.
CSF protein concentration (often > 100 mg/dL) and leukocyte

vetexamprep.ir

numbers (usually > 100 cells/µL) tend to be greatest in suppurative
meningitis (especially of infectious origin) as compared with other
CNS diseases; however, the electrophoretic pa erns of the proteins
are not speciﬁc for a diagnosis. 74 Neutrophils generally
predominate; however, especially in chronicity or with concurrent
antimicrobial use, monocytes, lymphocytes, or eosinophils may be
observed. In human bacterial meningitis, glucose levels in the CSF
are reduced because of bacterial and inﬂammatory cell utilization,
and lactic acid levels may be increased. In dogs, CSF glucose
concentrations cannot be used as a distinct marker to diﬀerentiate
bacterial meningitis from other inﬂammatory CNS diseases,
especially from SRMA (which is usually accompanied by severe
pleocytosis). In dogs, low CSF glucose concentrations seem to be
associated with elevated CSF cell counts, rather than bacterial
metabolism. 75 Finding organisms in the CSF on cytologic
examination is exceedingly rare, and isolation of organisms in
culture is also uncommon despite their visible presence on
histopathologic examination.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography

vetexamprep.ir

Plain radiographic ﬁndings are unremarkable in dogs or cats with
bacterial meningitis unless a bacterial osteomyelitis of paraspinal or
cranial bones or discospondylitis are part of the infectious process.
Bulla radiography is a valuable procedure for animals with
suspected otogenic sources for their CNS infection; however,
advanced imaging procedures are preferred when available.
Computed Tomography
CT of the brain or spinal cord in dogs or cats with bacterial
meningitis may reveal contrast-enhancing lesions on the meningeal
or ependymal surfaces. Focal areas of enhancement in areas of
abscess formation or edema may also be present. In one puppy with
suspected staphylococcal meningitis, CT imaging revealed external
hydrocephalus. 67
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Purulent exudates that cover the CNS tissue may be visualized by
MRI in animals with meningitis using T2-weighted (T2W)
sequences while suppressing the signal from CSF (high ﬂuida enuated inversion recovery [FLAIR]) (Fig. 129.4A). This method
results in enhancement of signal intensity found in the meninges. 76
In more advanced cases, using postcontrast T1-weighted images,
meningeal or parenchymal enhancement (signal hyperintensity)
may be evident. 77 Occasionally, plaque-like densities are found
that compress nervous tissue, which represent abscesses.
Lentiform-shaped extra-axial collections of ﬂuid have been
described in cases of empyema. 78
Microbiologic Tests
The main microbiologic assays used for diagnosis of bacterial
meningitis in dogs and cats are aerobic bacterial culture and PCR
assay of CSF. False-negative results occur because organism
numbers in the CSF of dogs and cats are often low. Depending on
the sensitivity of the PCR assay used and the viability of the
bacteria in the specimen, culture may be positive when PCR results
are negative, and vice versa.

Bacterial Isolation and Identification
Bacteria may be isolated using routine aerobic and anaerobic
bacterial culture media and conditions. At least 0.5 mL of CSF
should be submi ed for aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture if
possible. Organisms are uncommonly cultured from CSF because of
their low number and the small amounts of ﬂuid that are typically
available; however, when successful, subsequent susceptibility
testing assists in appropriate antimicrobial drug selection. Because
of the infrequency of positive culture results despite the
histopathologic presence of organisms at necropsy, 60 empiric
antibacterial therapy should be employed based on a suspected site
of origin of infection (see Antimicrobial Treatment, later).
Molecular Diagnosis Using Nucleic Acid–Based Testing
Sensitive and speciﬁc real-time PCR assays for detection of bacteria
in the CSF have been described. 79 However, as with culture
methods, their sensitivity is low. Broad-spectrum bacterial PCR
assays have been used to document bacterial infection of the CSF in
human medicine, 80 as well as multiplex PCR panels that are
designed to simultaneously test for a number of diﬀerent pathogens
capable of causing meningitis or encephalitis. 81 Real-time PCR
panels are widely available from commercial veterinary diagnostic
laboratories for detection of CNS pathogens in CSF specimens from
dogs and cats; however, the clinical sensitivity and speciﬁcity of
many of the individual assays in these panels have not always been
well studied. Results should always be interpreted in light of other
clinical ﬁndings and diagnostic tests.
Pathologic Findings
Gross Pathologic Findings
At necropsy, sites of infection in animals with bacterial
meningoencephalomyelitis may be found in organs outside the
CNS, such as the skin or mucous membranes, respiratory tract,
internal organs, external or middle or inner ear, or ocular tissues.
Gross pathologic ﬁndings in the CNS are generally minimal in dogs
or cats with early inﬂammatory changes. As the infection
progresses in the parenchyma, the meninges may appear congested
and nervous tissue parenchyma may be discolored or opaque (Fig.

vetexamprep.ir

129.4B). Focal accumulations of pus may occasionally be observed
in the meningeal spaces or adjacent nervous tissue. In late stages,
ischemic infarction of CNS tissue may occur as a result of severe
vascular inﬂammation and necrosis. Because of vascular damage,
necrosis is often hemorrhagic. Occasionally, obstructive
hydrocephalus occurs if the inﬂammatory process occludes the
mesencephalic aqueduct.
Histopathologic Findings
Microscopic ﬁndings in bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis consist
of a suppurative inﬂammatory response that is prominent in the
meningeal spaces and the penetrating sulci that contain blood
vessels (Virchow-Robin spaces), with or without brain parenchymal
involvement (Fig. 129.4C). With tissue Gram stains, bacteria may be
observed within inﬂammatory cells, blood vessels, or neural tissues,
in association with inﬂammation of the meninges and adjacent
neural parenchyma.

Treatment
Antimicrobial Treatment
Because of the low sensitivity of culture and/or PCR assays in
bacterial meningitis and the turnaround time involved, treatment
must be instituted following the neurologic examination and
availability of the results of CSF analysis (Table 129.3). The earlier
appropriate antimicrobial therapy is administered, the be er the
chance that parenchymal damage will be minimized. Antiinﬂammatory agents have been recommended, with some caution
and on a temporary basis, to reduce intracranial pressure. Almost
all drugs, either ionic or lipid-soluble, penetrate acutely inﬂamed
meninges. However, as the inﬂammation subsides, only lipidsoluble drugs are eﬀective. Where parenchymal abscesses are
present, antibacterial drugs may not eﬀectively penetrate aﬀected
tissue. In these cases, neurosurgical drainage is required in addition
to systemic antibacterial therapy. One case report described the use
of CT to guide drainage of a brainstem abscess in a cat on an
emergency basis. 82
Anti-Inflammatory Therapy
In addition to antimicrobial therapy, control of the immune
response and resultant inﬂammation in CNS tissues is critical when

vetexamprep.ir

intracranial or intraspinal pressures are elevated. Control of CNS
edema is usually achieved with targeted dosages of glucocorticoids;
however, therapy must be judicious since these medications are
immunosuppressive and nonspeciﬁc in their eﬀect on the host. 83
Other Supportive Care Measures
Dogs with severe hyperesthesia may beneﬁt from pain
management and NSAIDs. Anticonvulsant medications may be
needed for animals with seizures. Other supportive care measures,
such as those required for hydration and nutrition, should also be
considered.

Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs with early acute bacterial
meningoencephalomyelitis is good if minimal CNS parenchymal
tissue is damaged. With severe parenchymal damage, long-term
treatment might be necessary; prognosis varies depending on
clinical signs and the extent of tissue destruction.

Prevention
Bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis is a result of exogenous or
endogenous factors that allow bacterial organisms to gain access to
the CNS. Although these insults cannot be completely prevented,
injuries or lesions that occur close to the cranial or paraspinal
spaces potentially predispose to CNS infection. Animals with
wounds or infections in these areas or with systemic bacteremia
should be treated appropriately, then monitored closely for CNS
signs, and placed on judicious antimicrobial therapy if
meningoencephalomyelitis is highly suspected or documented.
Although the signs of bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis are
confused with those of immune-mediated CNS disease, continued
use of immunosuppressive drugs may lead to detrimental
progression of a bacterial disease process.

Public Health Aspects
There are minimal, if any, public health risks associated with
bacterial meningitis in dogs or cats—that is, unless veterinary staﬀ
inadvertently inoculate themselves with organisms being collected
for culture or PCR assays. Haemophilus inﬂuenzae, Streptococcus
pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis, which cause contagious
respiratory disease and subsequent complicating hematogenousorigin meningitis in humans, do not readily infect dogs or cats.

Neurologic Diseases of Suspected Infectious
Origin
The conditions described below are suspected to be caused by
insidious infectious agents or immune aberrations in response to
one or more stealth pathogens. The CNS is a frequent site of
localization of pathogens evading host immune responses. In
clinical practice, a diagnosis of MUO may be used for some of the
described diseases since histologic features cannot be identiﬁed
during routine clinical testing. 84–87 Unfortunately, a variety of
terms
have
been
used
in
the
literature
including
“meningoencephalitis of unknown etiology” and “noninfectious
inﬂammatory diseases of the CNS,” so a common language is still
missing.

vetexamprep.ir

Granulomatous Meningoencephalomyelitis and
Necrotizing Encephalitis
Granulomatous Meningoencephalomyelitis
Granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis (GME) has been
reported in dogs in the United States, 69 , 88–90 Australia, 91 New
Zealand, 92 Japan, 93 and several European countries (Vandevelde
M, unpublished observations). It is a relatively common condition
and is an angiocentric, nonsuppurative, mixed monocytic/lymphoid
inﬂammatory process, predominately aﬀecting the white ma er of
the brain and spinal cord. 89 , 90 Three forms of the disease have
been described—disseminated, ocular, and focal; the disseminated
form is the most common.
Despite its recognition as a clinical entity for over 40 years, the
underlying cause and mechanism of disease production remains
unclear. Genetic, autoimmune, infectious, neoplastic, and even toxic
causes have been theorized. In some studies, female dogs were at
greater risk for GME than male dogs; this ﬁnding is similar to other
autoimmune demyelinating diseases including multiple sclerosis
and experimental autoimmune encephalitis. 94 However, in another
more recent study from Wisconsin, although more females than
males were aﬀected, this diﬀerence was not signiﬁcant when
compared to a control dog population. 95 Young to middle-aged
dogs are often aﬀected, and GME is uncommon before the age of 2
years. Smaller breeds, especially poodles, small terriers, Pekingese,
and Maltese, appear to be predisposed, 88 , 96 although one casecontrol study found no breed predisposition. 95 In the la er study,
more cases occurred in the spring.
GME has been proposed by some to be a DTH reaction with an
autoimmune basis, supported by a predominance of major
histocompatibility complex class 2 and CD3+ T cells. 97 Other
investigators also noted a predominance of CD3+ T cells and a
complete absence of the CD79 (B-cell marker) immunoreactivity in
four cases of GME. 98 Positive immunoreactivity to IL-17 on T cells,
macrophages, and microglia also has suggested an autoimmune
pathogenesis, as this cytokine is often involved in the pathogenesis
of other autoimmune disorders. 99 Anti-astrocytic antibodies and
anti-transglutaminase 2 antibodies also have been identiﬁed in the
CSF of dogs with GME. 100 , 101 The complete immunologic proﬁle

vetexamprep.ir

of GME and whether CNS autoantibodies are the cause or
consequence of inﬂammation remain to be elucidated.
Despite the conventional view that GME is a disorder of immune
dysregulation, some veterinary neuropathologists suggest that at
least some cases of GME may be lymphoproliferative disorders,
with features of both inﬂammation and neoplasia. 102 Focal GME is
particularly similar to neoplasia, because lymphocytes within the
perivascular cuﬀs often have variable degrees of pleomorphism and
mitotic indices. 103 It is unclear whether the abnormal lymphocytes
within brain lesions (and sometimes also CSF) are reactive
inﬂammatory cells or representative of a true neoplastic population.
Potential viral, bacterial, and protozoal infectious triggers for
GME have also been studied using PCR-based methods. 104–106
Borna disease virus was reported in dogs with meningoencephalitis
in Japan and Swi erland and has been proposed as a causative
agent for GME. 107 , 108 Borna disease virus, however, is unlikely to
be a common etiology for GME given its predilection for CNS gray
ma er. Other investigators have demonstrated positive IHC for
West Nile, CPIV, and encephalomyocarditis viruses in severe
lesions of dogs with meningoencephalitides of presumed unknown
origin. 109 The signiﬁcance of these observations is unclear because
the positive IHC may be caused by antibody cross-reactivity with
endogenous proteins, as has been described with measles infections
and in dogs with West Nile virus infection. 110 , 111 GME is most
likely a nonspeciﬁc immunologic response, and multiple
environmental triggers (including microbial antigens) and genetic
factors are likely to play roles in the etiopathogenesis.
Necrotizing Encephalitis
Necrotizing
encephalitis
(NE)
includes
necrotizing
meningoencephalitis (NME) and necrotizing leukoencephalitis
(NLE). Historically referred to as “pug dog encephalitis” and
“necrotizing encephalitis of Yorkshire terriers” respectively, these
conditions have now been reported in various toy breeds including
the pug, Maltese, Chihuahua, Yorkshire terrier, Pekingese, West
Highland white terrier, Boston terrier, Japanese spi , and miniature
pinscher. 112
Pedigree information on a large cohort of pug dogs is suggestive
of a strong familial inheritance pa ern for NME. 113 Disease in pugs
and Maltese terriers has been strongly associated with the dog

vetexamprep.ir

leukocyte antigen (DLA) II complex on chromosome 12 (the canine
equivalent of MHCII); associations with loci on other chromosomes
have also been found. 114 This association with DLAII supports an
aberrant immune response as the underlying cause of disease. 115
Although it is tempting to consider NME and NLE as distinct
entities, these disorders may represent a spectrum of CNS injury
with similar pathogeneses. Histopathologic diﬀerences among the
NEs may result from minor genetic diﬀerences among dog breeds,
modifying genes, and/or variations in antigenic exposures.
In general, a empts at virus isolation from dogs with NME have
been unsuccessful. PCR screening of NME-aﬀected brains for an
extremely diverse group of DNA and RNA viruses has failed to
identify viral nucleic acids. 106 , 113 A viral trigger for NE via
molecular mimicry or the possibility that a pathogen is present in
the CNS (but at undetectable levels) in the presence of a selfperpetuating immune response remain possible.

Clinical Features
Granulomatous Meningoencephalomyelitis
In acute GME, clinical signs develop rapidly over the course of 1 to
10 days, and without treatment, it is rapidly progressive and fatal.
Clinical signs also may develop more slowly over a period of 1 to 4
months. Signs are associated with the site of most extensive
damage, or may be multifocal. Signs can include ataxia, dysmetria,
paresis, and paralysis, and changes in mental status, with
confusion, lethargy, and coma. Cranial nerve dysfunction may also
be observed.
In the acute stage of the disease, more than 50% of animals have
fever, and many exhibit paraspinal discomfort on palpation or signs
of cervical pain. 90 , 116 Central vestibular signs are common, and
seizures also may be observed. Clinical signs alternatively may
suggest a space-occupying mass referring to a single site of
involvement, most frequently the posterior fossa, with brainstem
and cerebellar signs. Cerebral or spinal signs sometimes
predominate. An ocular form of GME, previously called ocular
reticulosis, occurs with acute unilateral or bilateral blindness and
ophthalmoscopic evidence of optic neuritis. 88 , 117
Necrotizing Encephalitis

vetexamprep.ir

The onset of neurologic signs associated with NME varies from 6
months to 7 years of age and most commonly occurs in young dogs,
with a mean age of 29 months. 118 In comparison, NLE typically
manifests between 4 months and 10 years of age, with a mean age
of onset of 4.5 years. 119 In general, signs associated with NE
typically are rapidly progressive and most commonly include
seizures, depression, circling, vestibulocerebellar signs, visual
deﬁcits, and ultimately death.

Diagnosis
Because histologic conﬁrmation is required for deﬁnitive diagnosis
of GME and NE, “MUO” is typically used in the list of diﬀerential
diagnoses after further examinations as described here. The
diagnostic approach should include consideration of potential
infectious causes of inﬂammatory brain disease, and appropriate
serologic or nucleic acid–based assays. Testing for pathogens listed
in Table 129.2 should be considered based on the history,
geographic location, and clinical signs. PCR assays can be used on
CSF or brain biopsies in an a empt to determine an underlying
infectious cause of inﬂammatory brain disease before starting
treatment.
Laboratory Abnormalities
Laboratory abnormalities in GME and NE are nonspeciﬁc.
Neutrophilia may be present in the acute phase of GME. 116 In the
CSF, marked pleocytosis with cell counts of 100 to several thousand
leukocytes/µL is usual. Mononuclear cells predominate, but a
mixed pleocytosis can also be observed with varying numbers of
neutrophils. 120 Cytologic examination of the CSF may reveal large
anaplastic mononuclear cells with abundant lacy cytoplasm, 88 and
up to 20% macrophages. Protein concentrations as high as 1,119
mg/dL have been reported (mean 163.2 ± 25 mg/dL). 120 CSF
analysis results are abnormal in most dogs with NE, with a
predominantly mononuclear pleocytosis (usually 90–600 cells/µL)
and an increased protein concentration (usually 50–200 mg/dL). 121
Diagnostic Imaging
MRI is the preferred imaging technique for dogs with suspected
inﬂammatory brain disease. Lesions in both GME and NE are

vetexamprep.ir

hyperintense on T2W and FLAIR images, and variably isointense to
hypointense on T1W images, and have irregular margins (Fig.
129.5). Both gray and white ma er may be aﬀected. 102 Contrast
enhancement on T1W images is variable. In some cases of GME,
MR images may not reveal any abnormalities. 122 In the uncommon
focal form of GME, mass lesions can be detected with CT and MRI.
102 Lesions associated with NME include asymmetric, multifocal
prosencephalic lesions aﬀecting the gray and white ma er. 123 Loss
of gray and white ma er demarcation also may be discernible. 123
In NLE, multiple, asymmetric bilateral prosencephalic lesions
mainly aﬀecting the subcortical white ma er have been described
on MRI. 124 NLE lesions often include multiple cystic areas of
necrosis. Among the most commonly aﬀected breeds (Yorkshire
terrier, French bulldog, pug dog, and Chihuahua), even breedspeciﬁc MRI characteristics of NE in dogs have been described. 125
Digital analysis of MRI images (texture analysis/radiomics) may be
helpful for diﬀerentiating neoplastic and inﬂammatory brain
lesions in dogs. 126 PET has been used on a limited basis in an
a empt to distinguish NME from other inﬂammatory brain
diseases. 127 , 128
Pathologic Findings
Lesions seen on advanced imaging do not diﬀerentiate MUO from
neoplasia or infectious encephalitis, so deﬁnitive antemortem
diagnosis requires histopathologic examination of brain tissue.
Brain biopsies can be collected using stereotactic methods that are
guided by advanced imaging or an open (free-hand) technique. 129 ,
130 Brain biopsy is associated with some risk, with one study
estimating a 6% mortality and 29% with an MRI-guided free-hand
technique. 129 In some cases, deﬁnitive diagnosis is made at
necropsy.
In GME, lesions are found in the meninges, brain, and spinal
cord, especially in the cervical segments. White ma er often is more
severely aﬀected than gray ma er. Although the lesions are
disseminated, the cerebral hemispheres, the midbrain, and the
region around the fourth ventricle are most frequently involved.
The lesions, which are strictly associated with the vasculature,
consist of perivascular cuﬃng of monocytes, lymphocytes, plasma
cells, and sometimes a few neutrophils and mast cells (see Fig.
129.5). The formation of eccentrically situated nodular foci of

vetexamprep.ir

macrophages within these cuﬀs is a characteristic ﬁnding in GME.
The cuﬀs can be distinguished in three degrees of severity: small
disseminated perivascular lesions, small granulomas resulting from
the conﬂuence of several perivascular cuﬀs, and large focal
coalescing granulomas. Additionally, necrosis of the neuropil,
mitosis in the perivascular cuﬀs, and edema may be observed.
Tryptase-positive mast cells can be found in perivascular cuﬀs.
Dogs with the acute disease have signiﬁcantly more mast cells than
dogs with chronic disease. 131 Special stains can be applied to help
rule out potential infectious agents, and unﬁxed tissue should also
be submi ed for nucleic acid–based testing.
Histologic ﬁndings in NE are characteristic and include diﬀuse
meningitis,
choroiditis,
and
encephalitis,
with
lesions
predominating in the cerebrum (Fig. 129.6). Perivascular and
meningeal inﬂammatory inﬁltrates consisting of lymphocytes,
plasma cells, histiocytes, and macrophages have a strong tendency
to invade the adjacent parenchyma. Extensive compact subpial and
subventricular lesions are present and may extend deep into the
underlying brain tissue, with unusually intense microglial
proliferation and destruction of tissue. In some areas, frank
cerebrocortical necrosis occurs. The cerebral white ma er also is
severely aﬀected, with marked perivascular cuﬃng and gliosis. In
some areas, leukomalacia with liquefaction and cavitation of the
tissue is noted.

Treatment
No speciﬁc therapy for GME or NE exists, although improvement
frequently has been observed in GME cases after administration of
glucocorticoids with or without additional immunosuppressive
agents. Because glucocorticoid therapy provides only temporary
improvement in many cases, a second immunosuppressive drug
may also be required. Options include procarbazine, cytosine
arabinoside, leﬂunomide, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, and
lomustine. 102 In a study using prednisolone alone, or in
combination with lomustine, the response to both regimens was no
diﬀerent. 132 Use of a combination of an immunosuppressive dose
of prednisone and cytosine arabinoside is often used; the cytosine
arabinoside is given for 2 consecutive days every 3–6 weeks on an
outpatient basis. The reader is referred to the Suggested Reading
list for detailed protocols.

Anticonvulsants may be needed to control seizures associated
with inﬂammatory forebrain lesions. Glucocorticoid monotherapy
does not alter the course of this NE in conﬁrmed cases, and seizures
may be refractory to anticonvulsants. However, use of
anticonvulsant drugs may still prolong survival time. 118

Prognosis
The prognosis for dogs with GME is generally guarded given that
many dogs develop progressive neurologic signs despite treatment,
but some dogs may survive for several months. 94 , 122 Treatment
should be a empted if possible because treated dogs have a
signiﬁcantly increased survival time than untreated dogs. Dogs that
survive the ﬁrst month appear to have an increased chance of
surviving longer than a year. MRI features seem to help in
establishing prognosis: loss of cerebral sulci and brain herniation
were associated with a guarded prognosis. 133

Public Health Aspects
There is no public health signiﬁcance of these conditions.

Greyhound Nonsuppurative
Meningoencephalitis
Greyhound nonsuppurative meningoencephalitis was initially
described in dogs from three diﬀerent kennels in southern Ireland
in 2002, 134 and cases continue to be reported from throughout the
British Isles and predominantly from Ireland. 135 The disease aﬀects
young greyhounds, usually less than 12 months of age, and
frequently several li ermates are aﬀected. No evidence of
underlying infectious causes has been found, but gene expression
studies suggested that viral infection or autoimmunity may be
involved in the pathogenesis. 136 Neurologic signs may be acute or
chronic and progressive in onset and include altered mentation,
head tilt, ataxia, recumbency, circling, and blindness. On MRI,

Feline Poliomyelitis
Poliomyelitis in domestic cats was ﬁrst reported in North Africa
and Ceylon in the 1950s. Additional cases have since been described
in North America and Europe. 138–140 A clinically and pathologically
similar condition occurs in large Felidae (lions and tigers) held in
captivity. 141 , 142 The disease occurs sporadically in domestic cats,
but outbreaks have occurred among captive lions and tigers. 141 , 142

vetexamprep.ir

Pathologic ﬁndings indicate that poliomyelitis in cats is caused by a
virus, but a search for known viruses has been unsuccessful. 142
Borna disease in cats is morphologically and clinically distinct from
feline poliomyelitis, and has a diﬀerent geographic distribution, so
Borna virus is unlikely to be the cause.
Feline poliomyelitis has a slow onset and clinical signs progress
over weeks to months. In many instances, the neurologic signs
stabilize, and some animals may recover. Immature and adult cats
appear to be susceptible. The predominant signs are defects in
locomotion, including paresis, ataxia, and depressed placement
reactions. Lower motor neuron involvement is characterized by
muscle atrophy and decreased reﬂexes. Hyperesthesia in the
thoracic and lumbar areas is apparent in some cases. Rarely,
seizures, cerebellar signs, and pupillary abnormalities occur.
On histopathology, disseminated inﬂammatory lesions are found
in the brain and spinal cord. The spinal cord and medulla oblongata
are most severely aﬀected. The lesions consist of perivascular
mononuclear cuﬃng, gliosis, and neuronal degeneration, with the
la er being most obvious in the ventral horns of the spinal cord. In
chronic cases, there is minimal inﬂammation but substantial
neuronal loss and intense astrogliosis in the cord. As a result of
neuronal damage, marked diﬀuse Wallerian degeneration of the
lateral and ventral columns also occurs, resembling a primary
degenerative disorder.
Treatment is supportive. Contact between unaﬀected cats and
those suspected to have the disease should be avoided. The
prognosis is not always unfavorable because large Felidae have
been known to recover. 141

Steroid-Responsive Meningitis-Arteritis
SRMA is an immune-mediated condition of young dogs (usually <
2 years of age) that primarily involves arteries and meninges of the
CNS, and one of the most common inﬂammatory disorders of the
CNS in dogs. It has also been referred to as “beagle pain
syndrome,” “necrotizing vasculitis,” and “sterile suppurative
meningitis.” In some cases, the disease occurs in combination with
polyarthritis. A breed predisposition has been noted in Bernese
mountain dogs, boxers, beagles, Nova Scotia duck tolling retrievers,
golden retrievers, wire-haired pointing griﬀons, and basset hounds.

vetexamprep.ir

143 However, other medium- to large-breed dogs may be aﬀected.

There is no apparent sex predisposition.
A variety of studies have supported an immune-mediated
pathogenesis for SRMA. Findings have included inﬁltration of the
meninges by B cells and plasma cells, and the presence of T cells in
vessel walls. Markedly increased IgA concentrations have been
detected in CSF and serum, and there is an increased B cell to T cell
ratio in the blood. A large portion of T cells are activated,
suggesting the presence of a superantigen. 144 , 145 A Th2 response
predominates based on an increased expression of IL-4 and reduced
Th1 cytokines (IL-2 and INF-γ); other cytokines that predominate
are IL-17 over a Th17-skewed immune response, 146 vascular
endothelial growth factor, transforming growth factor 1, and IL-6.
147 All a empts to identify a causative infectious agent have failed.
Invasion of neutrophils is facilitated through upregulation of
lymphocyte antigen CD11a and matrix metalloproteinases. 148 , 149
Uncontrolled IgA synthesis may be the result of immune
dysregulation.
Classically, clinical signs are episodic and recurrent and include
cervical pain of acute onset, reluctance to move, stiﬀ gait, resistance
to neck manipulation, paraspinal hyperesthesia, and high rectal
temperature. Chronically aﬀected animals develop neurologic
deﬁcits consistent with a multifocal or spinal cord lesion; paresis,
ataxia, strabismus, and anisocoria have been described. In some
cases, spontaneous bleeding in the subarachnoidal space may
occur; in one dog, this led to acute nonambulatory tetraparesis. 150
Hematologic ﬁndings include a predominantly neutrophilic
leukocytosis, often with a left shift. 144 The CSF may be turbid,
blood tinged, or xanthochromic from hemorrhage occurring in the
subarachnoidal space. Neutrophilic pleocytosis (up to several
thousand cells per microliter), a high CSF protein concentration,
and erythrophagocytosis are apparent in acute cases. With
chronicity, mononuclear cells may predominate in the CSF.
Simultaneous demonstration of high IgA levels in serum and CSF
supports the diagnosis with a high sensitivity (approximately 90%),
but low speciﬁcity. 151 In addition, acute-phase proteins, including
CRP, have been shown to be elevated in the serum and CSF of dogs
with SRMA. 152 , 153
CT or MRI may reveal contrast enhancement of the meninges;
evidence of extramedullary hemorrhage has also been reported. 150

vetexamprep.ir

In a few instances at necropsy, subarachnoid hemorrhages may be
found extending over the entire length of the meninges of the spinal
cord and brainstem. In chronic disease, ﬁbrous thickening of the
spinal meninges may be noted grossly. Histopathologic changes
consist of necrotizing arteritis of medium- and small-sized arteries
and associated leptomeningitis, predominantly in the spinal cord
and to a lesser degree in the brainstem (Fig. 129.7). Chronic lesions
include proliferative changes of the vascular intima with stenosis
and adventitial ﬁbrosis. Occasional vessels may be thrombosed.
Extraneural arteritis is more frequently noted in aﬀected beagles,
particularly in the extramural coronary arteries and myocardium.
Spontaneous remission has been observed in some dogs. In
contrast to GME and NE, the response to glucocorticoid treatment
is usually dramatic. Prednisone is given as a long-term treatment
starting at an immunosuppressive dose (1–2 mg/kg, PO, q12h), then
tapering. Response to treatment and follow-up examinations
determine the treatment protocol. The use of second
immunosuppressive agents such as azathioprine 143 or cytosine
arabinoside 154 may allow reduction in the prednisone dose in order
to minimize glucocorticoid adverse eﬀects. Older dogs that have
experienced frequent relapses that were insuﬃciently treated with
glucocorticoids and that have high concentrations of IgA in the CSF
seem to require a longer duration of therapy and have a less
favorable prognosis. Long-term treatment studies have shown
relapse rates of 60% to 16%; the relapse rate with a prednisoneazathioprine protocol was 19%. 143 One study identiﬁed pathogenic
involvement of the endocannabinoid system in SRMA, a potential
target for new treatment strategies. 155

vetexamprep.ir

Case Example 1
Signalment

vetexamprep.ir

“Maxie,” a 6-year-old female Birman cat from Bern, Swi erland.

History

Maxie was evaluated by the neurology service at the University
of Bern in Swi erland in June 2001. Several weeks before
examination, the cat started to drink large quantities of milk, but
refused water. Two weeks before examination, Maxie became
progressively reluctant to have her head touched, became easily
startled, and exhibited short episodes of walking in circles, ataxia,
and hypersalivation. The cat had been purchased as a ki en from
a local Swiss breeder, and was fed commercial cat food as well as
fresh bovine and turkey meat supplemented with vitamins and
minerals. The cat had traveled to other countries including
England in order to participate in cat shows. She had had regular
contact with other cats and a dog. The cat had had several
healthy li ers. Vaccinations were up to date and she was FeLV
antigen negative. Treatment with glucocorticoids and vitamin B
by the referring veterinarian did not improve the cat’s condition.

Physical and Neurologic Examination Findings

Routine physical examination revealed no abnormalities. The cat
was excited and disoriented. There was a continuous ﬁne head
and ear tremor. The cat exhibited bilateral vestibular ataxia with
frequent episodes of walking in circles while hypersalivating. All
postural reactions were delayed. Pupils were dilated but
responsive. Menace response was strongly diminished
bilaterally. There was a pronounced hyperesthesia of the head
region and the cat reacted strongly to sound. Spinal reﬂexes were
normal. A diﬀuse cerebral lesion with partial involvement of the
brainstem was suspected. The diﬀerential diagnoses included
toxic metabolic and infectious diseases.

Laboratory ﬁndings

A CBC, serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis did not reveal any
abnormalities.
Occipital CSF puncture was performed under general
anesthesia. Cell count and protein content were within the
normal range.

Electroencephalography

EEG was performed under general anesthesia. EEG tracings
revealed a generalized iso-electrical course as well as sporadic
spindles of medium amplitude and episodes of slower activity.

vetexamprep.ir

Treatment and Outcome

The cat was hospitalized and treated with 2 mg/kg phenobarbital
IV q12h. The seizures were suppressed but the cat became
increasingly obtunded. The owner requested euthanasia.

Neuropathologic and Microbiologic Examination

Histopathologic examination revealed marked vacuolization of
the neuropil particularly in the cerebral cortex, thalamus, and
brainstem. Spongiform change was most intense in the basal
nuclei. In several gray ma er areas, there was intracytoplasmic
neuronal
vacuolation
and
diﬀuse
astrogliosis.
Immunocytochemical staining with anti-PrP antibodies revealed
accumulations of PrP in aﬀected areas.

Diagnosis

Feline spongiform encephalopathy.

Comments

The clinical ﬁndings in this case were similar to those in cats
described in the literature. However, although rapid onset of
neurologic signs is typical, rapid progression as seen in this cat is
unusual. Metabolic causes were unlikely based on the normal
laboratory ﬁndings, and the normal CSF was not consistent with
viral, bacterial, protozoal, or fungal infection. Against the
background of the BSE epidemic in Europe and the much smaller
FSE epidemic in its wake at the time this case was evaluated, the
history and all clinical ﬁndings raised suspicion for FSE. MRI
may have been helpful for antemortem diagnosis, but this
imaging technique was not yet widely used in veterinary clinics
at the time of the FSE epidemic.
The most likely source of infection in this case was ingestion of
contaminated feed. It is possible that the cat may have been
exposed to contaminated cat feed while in the United Kingdom,
but in view of the long incubation time (5 years or more) the cat
could have been exposed at home to speciﬁed bovine risk
materials, which were ﬁrst banned from animal consumption in
April 1996 in Swi erland. FSE is no longer diagnosed in Europe.
However, the disease may one day reemerge, as SEs continue to
occur in other animal species.

Case Example 2
Signalment

“Jake,” a 10-month-old male Weimaraner from north Georgia,
USA.

History

Jake was evaluated for a 2-week history of reluctance to move, in
association with anorexia and fever. He had been treated with
oral enroﬂoxacin and clindamycin for 2 days; however, the signs
of discomfort returned 2 days after medication was discontinued.
Jake also had a history of external ear inﬂammation and pruritic
skin disease for the previous month. The dog was up to date on
routine vaccinations, lived indoors and outdoors, and traveled
outdoors locally with the owner.

Physical Examination

The dog was alert, but held his head down with his neck
extended. He was reluctant to stand or walk, and appeared
painful when his head was elevated or lifted; however, no further
discomfort could be elicited by more caudal paraspinal
palpation. T = 103.5°F (39.7°C), HR = 110 beats/minute, RR = 30
breaths/minute, with shallow breathing. BCS was 3/9 and body
weight was 31 kg. Mild erythema of the external ear canals was
present and small amount of yellow-colored exudate was noted
in the ear canals bilaterally. With the exception of the neurologic
examination, no other abnormalities were detected.

Neurologic Examination

The dog held its neck extended and head down and walked with
a short, stiﬀ gait. Placing reactions were present in all limbs, but
initiation and follow-through were stilted. In lateral recumbency,
the dog did not relax, and myotatic reﬂexes were diﬃcult to elicit
because of excessive muscle tone. Discomfort was elicited by
paraspinal palpation and application of traction on the
extremities or with deep muscle palpation. No deﬁcits in cranial
nerve responses or reﬂexes were observed.

Imaging Findings

Cervical spinal radiographs without anesthesia showed no
detectable abnormalities.

Laboratory Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Hematologic and biochemical ﬁndings: The only
abnormality of the CBC was a low MCV (65.5 fL; reference
range 66–77 fL) and mild leukocytosis (13,200 cells/µL;
reference range 5,100–13,000 cells/µL). Serum ALP activity
was increased (267 IU/L; reference range 13–122 IU/L). No
abnormalities were found on urinalysis.
Arthrocentesis: Synovial ﬂuid was pink and hazy.
Nucleated cell count was slightly increased (3.2 × 103 cells/
µL in the stiﬂe joint). Nondegenerate neutrophils
predominated; no intracellular inclusions or LE cells
observed. Impressions: Mild purulent inﬂammation.
CSF analysis ﬁndings (specimen collected from cisterna
magna): Clear, RBC = 26 cells/µL, WBC = 462 cells/µL
(reference range, <5 cells/µL), total protein 72.6 mg/dL
(reference range, 15–35 mg/dL). Diﬀerential cell count:
Lymphocytes 4%, macrophages 18%, neutrophils 78%,
occasional RBC, no bacteria observed in this specimen.
Impressions: Marked purulent inﬂammation.

Microbiologic Testing

Aerobic bacterial culture (CSF): Negative. Anaerobic culture was
not done.

Outcome

The dog was treated with chloramphenicol (35 mg/kg, IV, q8h)
for 5 days and was then discharged on oral therapy for 3 weeks.
The dog made a complete recovery from the signs when
monitored for over 1 year.

Diagnosis

Meningitis (antibacterial-responsive)
unidentiﬁed bacterial organisms.

Comments

caused

by

suspected

Bacterial meningitis was suspected in this dog based on the
history, clinical signs, laboratory ﬁndings, and response to
chloramphenicol. Systemic spread of infection from a
hematogenous route was suspected based on some of the
inﬂammatory indicators in the hematologic and biochemical
proﬁle and evidence of mild suppurative polyarthritis that was
found. The original treatment with enroﬂoxacin and clindamycin
may have been subtherapeutic since it was short-lived and may
not have penetrated the CNS tissues and ﬂuids as well as

vetexamprep.ir

p
chloramphenicol. Furthermore, IV dosing with chloramphenicol
for the ﬁrst days of therapy allowed for very high levels of drug
in the CNS (although the use of chloramphenicol is controversial
because of the potential for adverse eﬀects in humans). Although
an organism was not observed or isolated, bacterial infection was
suspected based on the dramatic response to antibacterial
therapy alone. In bacterial meningitis of dogs and cats, organisms
are not often identiﬁed by cytologic or cultural examination of
CSF. Response to antibacterial therapy should be considered
presumptive evidence of bacterial infection.
