130: Hereditary and Acquired
Immunodeﬁciencies
Urs Giger, and Krystle L. Reagan

KEY POINTS
• Immunodeficiencies are a large heterogeneous group of
hereditary (primary immunodeficiencies) and acquired
(secondary immunodeficiencies) disorders of host immunity
that are associated with an increased risk of infection.
• Immunodeficiencies can arise through disturbances in
antigen-specific defense mechanisms mediated by
lymphocytes, the nonspecific defense system (which includes
phagocytes, plasma proteins, and physical barriers), or both.
• The exact pathogenesis of many canine and feline
immunodeficiencies remains unknown, but the molecular
defects for several hereditary immunodeficiencies have been
elucidated.
• A few hereditary immunodeficiency disorders are prevalent
within certain breeds of dogs and cats, whereas others have
been described once and may exist only in research animal
colonies. Some appear transiently in the dog population, then
disappear because of screening and informed breeding.
• A definitive diagnosis of immunodeficiency often requires
specific immune testing in addition to routine laboratory tests,
and therapeutic interventions are limited.

Introduction
Immunodeﬁciencies can be divided into primary and secondary
forms depending on whether they are inherited or acquired (Table

vetexamprep.ir

1–3
130.1).
Certain
clinical
features
can
suggest
immunocompromise (Box 130.1). Speciﬁc organisms and medical
conditions often implicated in immunocompromised hosts are
listed in Box 130.2. A deﬁnitive diagnosis often requires speciﬁc
immune testing in addition to routine laboratory tests, and
therapeutic interventions are limited.

Hereditary Or Primary Immunodeficiencies
Many genetically determined immune defects have been
described in dogs, whereas only a few are known in cats. With
few exceptions, they occur rarely and are summarized in Table
130.2; some are discussed later in this chapter in more detail. They
can be broadly classiﬁed according to defects of the speciﬁc or
nonspeciﬁc immune system as well as combinations thereof. The
innate immune system should be functional at birth and available
on short notice to protect the host from invasion by all sorts of
organisms. It includes physicochemical barriers, phagocytes,
complement and other plasma proteins, and natural killer cells.
Congenital barrier defects particularly involve the skin and
mucous membrane surfaces and are associated with infections of
speciﬁc organs; such infections can become systemic. A variety of
hereditary skin diseases are being further deﬁned and other
immunodeﬁciencies are being recognized. Ehlers-Danlos
syndrome, which leads to fragile, hyperextendable skin in many
dogs and cats as well as the myxedematous skin and
immunodeﬁciencies of sharpeis, predispose to pyoderma,
whereas ciliary dyskinesia in dogs increases susceptibility to
rhinosinusitis and pneumonia. Similarly, X-chromosomal and
other ectodermal dysplasias are associated with skin problems as
well as mild immunodeﬁciencies.
Disorders of the phagocytic system involve defects of
neutrophils and monocytes as well as the complement system and
can lead to pyogenic and granulomatous infections. The
granulomatous reaction can occur when neutrophils malfunction
and mononuclear cells are recruited. A wide variety of bacteria
(e.g., staphylococci, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) are
usually involved, most of which represent resident microﬂora or
pathogens of relatively low virulence. Recurrent infections of the
skin, respiratory tract, and oral cavity are common, and

vetexamprep.ir

intermi ent bacteremia and overwhelming sepsis are also seen.
Multisystemic amyloidosis, vasculitis, and immune-complex
diseases are complications that can occur as a result of chronic
recurrent or persistent infections. Cyclic hematopoiesis and
leukocyte adhesion deﬁciency (LAD) are examples of serious
quantitative and qualitative phagocytic defects, respectively.
The speciﬁc immune system can be divided into humoral and
CMI systems and includes lymphocytes, immunoglobulins, and
cytokines. Deﬁciencies of B cells or humoral immunity aﬀect the
production of immunoglobulins and lead to increased
susceptibility to pyogenic bacterial infections. Deﬁciencies of T
cells or CMI are associated with viral and fungal infections, but
intracellular bacterial infections may also occur. Animals with
cellular immunodeﬁciencies may have smaller thymic and
tonsillar tissues as well as intestinal and peripheral lymph nodes
and decreased numbers of circulating lymphocytes.
The severity of immunodeﬁciency varies among defects.
Infections may be systemic or restricted to a particular organ
system such as the skin or respiratory tract. Some
immunodeﬁciencies in neonates lead to overwhelming infections
and death within the ﬁrst few days to weeks of life, whereas
others, such as morphologic leukocyte changes, are not
consistently associated with any noticeable predisposition to
infection. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome in smoke-colored Persian
cats is characterized by abnormally large eosinophilic granules in
polymorphonuclear leukocytes. It causes no immunodeﬁciencies,
but leads to a bleeding tendency resulting from a platelet storage
pool disease. 4 Similarly, Birman cats with acidophilic granulation
of neutrophils and dogs and cats with various lysosomal storage
diseases
(e.g.,
mucopolysaccharidosis,
gangliosidosis,
mannosidosis) have granulation or vacuolation of leukocytes
without being immunocompromised; frequently they also exhibit
a lymphocytosis. The Pelger-Huët anomaly, which is
characterized by hyposegmentation of granulocytes, causes no
immunodeﬁciency in animals despite the fact that the leukograms
of aﬀected dogs and cats reveal the most severe left shift with a
normal leukocyte count and no toxic changes. In foxhounds,
in vitro chemotactic response of these neutrophils was mildly
diminished, whereas in basenjis no functional abnormalities have
been found. 5–7

Although an increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections
develops, the type of infection varies depending on the immune
system defect present. A few immunodeﬁciency disorders
predispose animals to unusual infectious agents. Miniature
dachshunds appear to be predisposed to Pneumocystis pneumonia
(see Chapter 89), and German shepherd dogs and Hungarian
vizslas may be prone to systemic aspergillosis and other systemic
mold infections. 8 , 9 Golden and Labrador retrievers that had high
serum antibody titers to Borrelia (Borreliella) burgdorferi were more
likely to have glomerulonephritis. 10 Miniature schnauzers and
basset hounds have an increased susceptibility to systemic avian
mycobacteriosis, and possibly other speciﬁc infections like
candidiasis. 11 Boxer dogs and German shepherds have been the
predominant breeds reported with the cutaneous mycobacterial
disease known as canine leproid granuloma syndrome. 12 , 13
Great Danes, boxers, border collies, German shepherds,
Dalmatians, and Doberman pinschers (Australia) 14 and American
cocker spaniels (United States) 15 have been overrepresented in
retrospective studies of cryptococcosis. Boxers and French
bulldogs are predisposed to granulomatous colitis secondary to
adherent and invasive E. coli. 16 A genetic predisposition to
demodicosis has been proposed in various canine breeds and
families within breeds. The predisposition to develop FIP has also
been suggested to have a genetic basis, more commonly in some
purebred cats like Birmans. Mechanisms that predispose diﬀerent

vetexamprep.ir

breeds to speciﬁc infections remain unknown, but have been
elucidated for some, such as miniature schnauzers and systemic
Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection caused by a
CARD9 variant. 11
The mode of inheritance of primary immunodeﬁciencies has not
yet been determined in all cases. Autosomal recessive
transmission, with aﬀected males and females born to healthy
parents is usual, but a few exceptions exist. The Pelger-Huët
anomaly is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Ectodermal
dysplasia of German shepherds (but not other ectodermal
dysplasias) caused by a ectodysplasin (ED) 1 gene defect, and
severe combined immunodeﬁciency (SCID) caused by two
diﬀerent mutations in the common γ-chain of the IL-2 receptor in
basset hounds and Cardigan Welsh corgis, are X-chromosomal
recessive disorders. Thus, only males are aﬀected, and the dams
and one half of the dam’s female li ermates are carriers.
Granulomatous colitis of boxer dogs appears to result from
mutations in the gene that encodes neutrophil cytosolic factor
(NCF) 2, which encodes the cytosolic subunit, p67phox of NAPDH
oxidase. 16 Thus, the breed, sex, age of onset, type of infections,
and other special characteristics can suggest a particular
immunodeﬁciency. Furthermore, it follows that within a breed,
the immunodeﬁciency is typically caused by the same defect and
mutation, whereas diﬀerent breeds can have mutations in the
same or diﬀerent genes.

Diagnosis
Suggestive signs of infection (see Box 130.1) develop in animals
with a primary immunodeﬁciency generally early in life. Despite
receiving colostrum during the ﬁrst day of life, clinically aﬀected
animals can have illness during the neonatal to juvenile period
and can develop recurrent and overwhelming infections that lead
to severe debilitation and death before 1 year of age. Some
animals, but typically not all, in a li er may be aﬀected, whereas
the parents are usually clinically healthy. A genetic predisposition
to infection is less commonly noted after 1 year of age (e.g.,
leishmaniosis in foxhounds and MAC in miniature schnauzers
and basset hounds). Furthermore, animals with hereditary
immunodeﬁciencies
may
have
other
special
clinical

vetexamprep.ir

manifestations. Hypersensitivity reactions can occur and reﬂect an
overall dysregulation of the immune system caused by a lack of
one or more components or a chronic antigen stimulation from
inadequate clearance of infections. Chronic systemic infections
may also impair growth. Characteristic coat color dilutions and
increased tendency for surface bleeding are seen, for example, in
collies with cyclic hematopoiesis, Persian cats with ChédiakHigashi syndrome, and Weimaraners with an incompletely
deﬁned immunodeﬁciency. Nude Birman ki ens and ectodermal
dysplasia are associated with a complete lack or loss of hair and
either severe or minimal predisposition to infection, respectively.

In addition to the listed syndromes, bone marrow dyscrasias have
been described in miniature and toy poodles and transient
hypogammaglobulinemia in Samoyeds, but less is known of these
disorders.
Results of a CBC, serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis can
suggest a speciﬁc immunodeﬁciency. Results of diﬀerential
leukocyte count and microscopic evaluation of a blood smear are
most important. Some breeds, such as greyhounds, have low
reference values for blood leukocyte counts. Neutropenia can be
transient (e.g., cyclic hematopoiesis, parvovirus infection), or can
be persistent (e.g., cobalamin malabsorption defects or sepsis).
Lymphopenia may be observed in dogs with T-cell disorders or
SCID. Although leukocytosis often accompanies infection, defects
in leukocyte adhesion and egress from blood circulation at sites of
infection can be associated with disproportionately high
leukocytosis for the degree of infection as seen with hereditary
LAD or with concurrent glucocorticoid usage. Careful review of a
blood smear can reveal leukocyte abnormalities such as
granulation and vacuolation resulting from lysosomal storage
diseases or Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, 17 acidophilic granulation
of leukocytes in Birmans, 18 phagocytized microorganisms, or
toxic leukocyte changes that suggest overwhelming bacterial
infections.
Serum globulin concentrations are generally increased with
chronic infections. Low or normal globulin levels in infected
animals can suggest major external losses or diminished
production from a humoral immune defect. Indeed, speciﬁc
immunoglobulin deﬁciencies have been recognized in dogs.
Serum protein electrophoresis may identify a γ-globulin
deﬁciency, but immunoelectrophoresis is required to detect the
class and degree of immunoglobulin deﬁciency. Maternally
derived antibodies can only be absorbed during the ﬁrst day of
life and inﬂuence the serum values during the ﬁrst few weeks.
Only IgM can be synthesized very early in life (neonatal period),
whereas the development of IgA can be delayed for months. Thus,
it is important to compare values with data from age-matched
controls. Serum titers against speciﬁc antigens can be measured,
followed by evaluation of the antibody response to vaccination

vetexamprep.ir

against particular agents. However, despite the antibody titer,
cellular immunity is not being assessed. Biopsy specimens of
lymph nodes can reveal disorganization with loss of germinal
centers and normal paracortical lymphocytes. Decreases in
plasma cell populations can also be evident.
T-cell or combined immunodeﬁciencies cause defective CMI
responses, which may be manifested as prolonged allograft
rejection times and decreased delayed-type hypersensitivity
(DTH) reactions to skin testing. 19 Reduced in vitro lymphocyte
stimulation results can also be caused by a primary lymphocyte
defect or by infection.
The identiﬁcation of the nature of microbes that infect an
animal is important for diagnostic as well as therapeutic reasons.
Antibody titers can be used to assess response to vaccines and
humoral immunity. Histopathology and cytology can assist in
characterization of the architecture, morphology, maturation, and
function of the immune system, including barrier systems. In
ciliary dyskinesia, morphologic abnormalities of cilia may be
identiﬁed by electron microscopy. Functional studies using
nuclear imaging or on respiratory epithelial biopsy specimens are
also indicated.
Characterization of immunodeﬁciencies may require special
leukocyte studies. Flow cytometry can be used to diﬀerentiate
between T and B cells, determine T and B cell ratios, “bacterial
killing reaction,” and the presence or absence of leukocyte
adhesion proteins (CD11/18) or IL-2 receptors. Lymphocyte
function studies include lymphocyte stimulation and plaqueforming assays that assess immunoglobulin production.
Phagocyte function studies assess leukocyte adhesion, migration,
chemotaxis, phagocytosis, “respiratory burst,” and bactericidal
activity. Functional assays must generally be performed on fresh
(collected within 24 hours) blood cells and compared
simultaneously with a preferably age- and breed-matched control.
Infection can impair in vitro lymphocyte function and enhance
phagocyte function. Therefore, control of infection before
studying leukocyte function is preferred.
A variety of hereditary immunodeﬁciencies have been
characterized at the molecular genetic level. This permits simple
screening of aﬀected animals or those potentially at risk. Because
genetic variants (mutations) are typically breed speciﬁc, these

vetexamprep.ir

DNA screening tests may be applied within a breed not only for
detection of infected immunodeﬁcient animals but also those
potentially at risk to infection and carriers.

Treatment And Prevention
Successful control of infection in immunodeﬁcient animals
depends on the type of infection as well as the type and severity
of the immune defect. In immunocompromised patients, early
and aggressive antimicrobial therapy is indicated even for mild
infections with agents that are considered nonpathogenic in
immunocompetent hosts. Because of the immunodeﬁcient host’s
potential inability to kill infectious organisms, cidal antimicrobials
are recommended for treatment if available.
Few practical treatments exist for animals with hereditary
immunodeﬁciencies.
Dogs
with
hereditary
cobalamin
malabsorption can be successfully administered parenteral
cobalamin every 2–4 weeks. 20 In experimental studies, bone
marrow transplantation and gene therapy corrected several
canine leukocyte defects and dogs with cyclic neutropenia. 21–23
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) has been used to
increase neutrophil numbers in dogs with cyclic neutropenia and
G-CSF deﬁciency. Fresh whole blood can be transfused repeatedly
to animals with overwhelming infections and neutropenia or
neutrophil dysfunction, but the eﬀect is very transient. Plasma
transfusions or immunoglobulin (hyperimmune serum) injections
can
temporarily
support
animals
with
humoral
immunodeﬁciencies. However, these products should not be used
in animals with complete IgA deﬁciency, because they can
experience anaphylactic reactions to the foreign IgA protein. No
commercial canine or feline γ-globulin is available, and the
human γ-globulin preparations do not target animal-speciﬁc
infections and can cause allergic reactions on repeated use.
If an acquired immunodeﬁciency is present and can be
corrected, the infection is often easily controlled. Administration
of immunosuppressive agents should be withheld during
treatment of infection, and any underlying disorder should be
treated if possible. Immunocompromised animals with an
infection, where the cause of immunosuppression cannot be
corrected, generally have a guarded to poor prognosis. Despite

vetexamprep.ir

aggressive antimicrobial therapy, their infections can be diﬃcult
to control, leading to overwhelming infections, protracted courses,
and recurrences.

Specific Hereditary or Primary
Immunodeficiencies in Dogs
Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
Primary ciliary dyskinesia, also known as immotile cilia
syndrome, is caused by various functional and ultrastructural
ciliary abnormalities that include lack of outer or inner dynein
arms, abnormal microtubular pa ern, random ciliary orientation,
and electron-dense cores in the basal body. Because of impaired
mucociliary clearance, aﬀected animals have recurrent bacterial
rhinitis, sinusitis, and bronchopneumonia with bronchiectasis.
Poorly motile or immotile live sperm results in male infertility.
Although evidence is lacking, dysfunction of ependymal cilia can
cause hydrocephalus and otitis media. The lack of coordinated
cilia motility during embryogenesis is responsible for a 50%
prevalence of concurrent situs inversus in some forms of primary
ciliary dyskinesia. The clinical triad of rhinosinusitis,
bronchiectasis, and situs inversus is known as Kartagener’s
syndrome. 24–26
Primary ciliary dyskinesia is inherited by an autosomal
recessive trait. It represents a heterogeneous group of defects that
have been described in more than a dozen breeds. 27 Clinical signs
typically begin at a young age, and recurrent respiratory
infections lead to death or euthanasia before 1 year of age.
However, a few dogs appear clinically healthy for months to
years. 28
A diagnosis of ciliary dyskinesia is reached through
documentation of absent ciliary clearance of technetium-99mlabeled microaggregated albumin that is placed through a
catheter into the nasal cavity or the tracheal bifurcation; biopsy of
ciliated mucosae with ultrastructural analysis using electron
microscopy; and in vitro motility studies. 29 , 30 Induction of
ciliogenesis can also be determined by use of in vitro cell culture.
30 A likely causative mutation in the NME5 gene encoding a
sparsely characterized protein associated with ciliary function has

vetexamprep.ir

recently been found in Alaskan malamutes with ciliary
dyskinesia. 31 A deletion was found in the AKNA gene, encoding
the AT-hook transcription factor, of rough collies with recurrent
inﬂammatory pulmonary disease similar to ciliary dyskinesia. A
mutation in the CCDC39 gene has been found in Old English
sheepdogs with axonemal disorganization and abnormal ciliary
beating. 32
Chronic recurrent respiratory infections have been observed in
related Irish wol ounds. 33 , 34 In wol ound puppies, the disease
begins with a serous rhinitis that later becomes catarrhal to
hemorrhagic with turbinate ulceration and destruction.
Pneumonia and generalized lymphadenomegaly are apparent in
later stages. Although the disease is responsive to antimicrobial
treatment, it can progress in intervening periods. Ciliary
dyskinesia has been identiﬁed in some wol ounds but has not
been a consistent feature of the disease. Serum IgA levels were
reduced in some dogs, but bronchoalveolar lavage ﬂuid had high
IgA concentrations in tested dogs, which can relate to their
inﬂammatory response to infection. 33
Cyclic Hematopoiesis
Cyclic hematopoiesis is characterized by a periodic production
and maturation defect of hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow.
35 In human patients, the cycle is 21 days, but in dogs, severe
neutropenia (<1,000 cells/µL) occurs every 12 to 14 days and lasts
for 3 to 4 days (cyclic neutropenia syndrome). Serial blood counts
are used to make a deﬁnitive diagnosis unless a molecular test is
performed. During periods of neutropenia, dogs are very
susceptible to bacterial infection. Clinical illness appears at 6 to 8
weeks of age with regular recurrence of bacterial infections. The
condition culminates in sepsis or systemic amyloidosis and death
from organ failure before 1 year of age. The condition may be
accompanied by gingival bleeding from an associated platelet
storage pool disease. Aﬀected collies have a silver gray or light
beige to tan coat color, and secondary hormonal cycling has been
observed. 36
Cyclic hematopoiesis was the ﬁrst reported canine
immunodeﬁciency observed and has only been described in
hypopigmented collies, hence the term gray collie syndrome. It is

vetexamprep.ir

inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, but no case has been
reported since the 1970s outside of the research colony in this
breed. Experimentally, bone marrow transplantation corrects this
syndrome, including the coat color dilution. Injections of G-CSF
also abolish the cycling. The defect in collie dogs is associated
with a homozygous mutation of the gene encoding the dog
adaptor protein complex 3 β-subunit that directs trans-Golgi
export of transmembrane cargo proteins to lysosomes. 37 , 38
Mutations in a leukocyte elastase have been identiﬁed in humans
with a similar syndrome. 35
Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency
LAD, originally described as canine granulocytopathy syndrome
in Irish se ers and ca le and more recently (2017) a cat, 51 is
referred to as canine, feline or bovine LAD (or CLAD, FLAD, or
BLAD). 39 It results from the absence of a family of three leukocyte
integrins. 40–43 These proteins are heterodimers (CD11a-d/CD18)
with a speciﬁc α-chain (CD11a-d) and a common β-chain (CD18).
In LAD, the β2-subunit is missing (CD18 deﬁciency), resulting in a
lack of surface expression and function of all leukocyte integrins.
CD11b/18 (CR3) is the most critical integrin because it is the
receptor that binds leukocytes to C3bi and ICAM-1 on activated
endothelium, thereby mediating tight adhesion of leukocytes (Fig.
130.1). When this is deﬁcient, granulocytes are unable to
marginate and destroy microorganisms, which is associated with
an impaired inﬂammatory response despite marked leukocytosis
(Fig. 130.2A). Furthermore, the in vitro lymphocyte stimulation
response is reduced. A missense ITGB2 mutation substituting a
cystine with a serine has been identiﬁed in aﬀected Irish se ers
and red and white se ers. 40 , 44–48
Dogs with LAD have a severely increased susceptibility to
bacterial infections. Signs of pyogenic infections develop during
the ﬁrst weeks to months of life, are often recurring, and are
poorly responsive to antibacterials. Omphalophlebitis and
gingivitis are often the ﬁrst infections and might be followed by
pyoderma, pododermatitis, thrombophlebitis, pneumonia,
pyometra, osteomyelitis (especially craniomandibular and
metaphyseal), and fatal sepsis. Pups are often stunted or have
poor body condition. 49 , 50 Infection sites exhibit minimal

vetexamprep.ir

inﬂammation and pus formation despite a most severe persistent
leukocytosis of 25,000 to 500,000/µL (Fig. 130.2B). Regional
lymphadenomegaly and poor wound healing are commonly
noted. Long-term therapy with bactericidal antibacterials is
required.
LAD has been reported in Irish and red and white se ers
worldwide and is autosomal recessive. LAD due to other CD18
mutations also has been documented in Holstein ca le, humans,
and one cat. 51 The diagnosis in dogs is currently made by
mutation-speciﬁc DNA testing. 44 , 47 , 48 , 52 Carrier dogs also can
be detected by genetic testing which helped to practically
eliminate the disease in the aﬀecteed breed populations. 40 In the
past, demonstration of neutrophil adherence defects and
deﬁciency of leukocyte glycoproteins CD11/CD18 by ﬂow
cytometry analysis were used (Fig. 130.2C,D). If LAD is suspected
in another dog breed, leukocyte ﬂow cytometry for CD18 is still a
broad and simple screening test.
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation of CD18+ donor cells
and gene therapy can reverse the defect. 12 Mixed chimeric
hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from a histocompatible
li ermate reversed clinical signs in an aﬀected dog. 53
Complement C3 Deficiency
Complement factor C3 deﬁciency was found in a colony of
Bri any spaniels with spinal muscular atrophy. 54–56 Aﬀected
dogs have defective chemotaxis and bacterial phagocytosis from a
complete deﬁciency of C3 (0.1%) and less than 1% plasma
complement activity. The immunodeﬁciency is generally mild and
animals live until adulthood, but serious infections can occur,
including pneumonia, pyoderma, sepsis, pyometra, and septic
arthritis. Aﬀected dogs can develop renal failure with
amyloidosis. This is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder,
and a diagnosis can be reached by documenting a lack of serum
complement activity or mutation test. However, this defect has
not been noted outside the research colony.

Selective Cobalamin Malabsorption
Chronic neutropenia and megaloblastic anemia have been
described in giant schnauzers, beagles, Australian shepherds,
Komondors, and border collie pups. 57–59 Aﬀected animals fail to
thrive and often show lethargy, inappetence, and cachexia but are
only rarely predisposed to infection accompanied by fever,
lameness, or diarrhea. Blood smears show neutropenia with
hypersegmented neutrophils. Aﬀected animals have very low
serum cobalamin concentrations and marked methylmalonic
aciduria. A cobalamin ileal receptor defect was documented in the
CUBAM complex, either due to a mutation in amnionless or
cubulin. 20 , 59 Treatment with parenteral administration of
cobalamin once or twice monthly is highly eﬀective, 20 , 58 but
does not resolve the very mild proteinuria.
Trapped Neutrophil Syndrome—Hereditary Neutropenia in
Border Collies

vetexamprep.ir

Chronic neutropenia and recurrent bacterial infections have been
found in certain lines of border collies in Australia and New
Zealand. 60 This autosomal recessive trait (trapped neutrophil
syndrome) is associated with stunted growth by 2 weeks of age
and fever, anorexia, diarrhea, and lameness by 2 months of age.
Metaphyseal osteomyelitis is seen radiographically, and
neutropenia (<3 × 103 cells/µL) is consistently found. Bone marrow
cytologic abnormalities include granulocytic hyperplasia with a
shift to the right, suggesting that the developing cells cannot enter
the systemic circulation. A DNA test has been oﬀered to screen
border collies. 61 , 62 Puppies respond poorly to antimicrobial
therapy and eventually succumb to systemic infections.
X-Linked Severe Combined Immunodeficiency
X-linked SCID (X-SCID) is characterized by a failure of humoral
immunity and CMI. 63–65 It develops in various animal species
when lymphocyte precursors fail to diﬀerentiate into mature
lymphocytes. In dogs, defects in the γc chain lead to deﬁciency of
several cytokine receptors (IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21).
66 Although profound deﬁciencies are found in T-cell function,
some B-cell activities are preserved. 67 For example, canine XSCID B cells are capable of producing IgM but do not class-switch
to the production of IgG after mitogen stimulation. The shared
usage of a γc chain by these cytokines explains the profound
immunologic abnormalities and the impaired IgG response. 68 The
ability of lymphocytes to bind to IL-2 and proliferate is severely
impaired, and the development of thymocytes is drastically
reduced, with an increased proportion of CD4-/CD8-thymocytes.
69 , 70 Serum IgG and IgA concentrations are low, but IgM values
are normal. 71 Because of the X-chromosomal recessive mode of
inheritance, male dogs are aﬀected, whereas females (the dams
and some li ermates of those aﬀected) are carriers. The Cardigan
Welsh corgi and the basset hound have diﬀerent mutations in the
gene encoding the γ-chain that is common to the IL receptors in
aﬀected male basset hounds and Cardigan Welsh corgis, but both
are restricted to a research colony. 63 , 72–74

After the decline of maternal immunity, aﬀected male dogs

Puppies fail to thrive and generally die within a few months. The
most characteristic clinical features are a lack of lymph nodes,
tonsils, Peyer’s patches, and thymus. Aﬀected basset hounds can
develop vaccine-induced distemper. If they survive, aﬀected
puppies are poor doers and die by 5–6 months of age. They can
survive in germ-free environments. 3 A diagnosis is reached by
histopathology, immunologic testing, or molecular genetic testing
(bassets and corgis); however, these mutations appear to have
been eliminated from breeding populations other than those in
research colonies. Bone marrow transplantation from unaﬀected
li ermates and gene therapy were experimentally eﬀective in reestablishing normal T- and B-cell function in aﬀected dogs. 21 , 67 ,

Autosomal Recessive Severe Combined Immunodeficiency
SCID has been identiﬁed in Jack Russell terriers that has an
autosomal recessive mode of inheritance, similar to that in CB-17
mice and Arabian foals. 76 A faulty V(D)J recombination and
complete deﬁciency of DNA-PKcs activity result from reduced
expression of the DNA-PK catalytic subunit. 76 , 77 Aﬀected dogs
experience severe lymphopenia, agammaglobulinemia, thymic
dysplasia, and peripheral lymphoid aplasia. They typically
succumb to opportunistic and vaccine-induced infections by 2–4
months of age. 76
Autosomal recessive SCID has also been identiﬁed in Frisian
water dogs in South Africa and the Netherlands. A nonsense
mutation alters the RAG1 protein which is important in antigen
recognition by humoral and cellular mechanisms. Aﬀected pups
have
severe
lymphopenia
and
undetectable
serum
immunoglobulin concentrations, and die or are euthanized due to
infections at 8 to 12 weeks of age. 77 Dogs develop diarrhea at 7–8

vetexamprep.ir

weeks of age that responds to antibacterial therapy. However,
progressive neurologic signs including seizures, vestibular ataxia,
and blindness ensue. Histiocytic myocarditis and hepatitis was
identiﬁed in some dogs at necropsy.
Selective IgA Deficiency
Various forms of selective IgA deﬁciency have been described in
several breeds, including beagles, 63 , 78 sharpeis, 79 German
shepherds, 80 and others, 81 but the mode of inheritance remains
unknown. The defect may be either an inherited primary defect or
may arise secondary to pathologic changes within the intestinal
mucosa. Serum IgA concentrations may be completely absent or
markedly reduced and only very slowly developing over the ﬁrst
year of life. Complete deﬁciencies are found in sharpeis, and
partial deﬁciencies have been found in beagles and German
shepherds. 82 For diagnosis, serum IgA concentrations need to be
compared with those of age-matched controls. Reduced
concentrations of IgA have been found in duodenal explant
cultures of some German shepherd dogs that had serum IgA
values within reference limits. 83 Such assays may be more reliable
than serum concentrations but are not as available for routine
diagnostic purposes. Reduced secretory IgA concentrations have
also been found in bronchial secretions of aﬀected dogs. 81 IgAdeﬁcient dogs can have positive rheumatoid factor, anti-IgA
antibodies, or both, and can be predisposed to hypersensitivity
and autoimmune diseases. IgA deﬁciency in German shepherds is
not linked to their predisposition to disseminated aspergillosis,
which may relate to a cell-mediated defect. 84 Although aﬀected
dogs have large polyclonal increases in serum IgG concentration,
it is not directed against Aspergillus terreus.
Lethal Acrodermatitis in Bull Terriers
Also known as “zincers” among bull terrier breeders, the lesions
of lethal acrodermatitis are similar to those of zinc deﬁciency in
dogs, but do not respond to zinc supplementation. Aﬀected dogs
have lower plasma IgA concentrations than clinically healthy
dogs. 85 The syndrome is characterized by hyperkeratosis and
parakeratosis and thymus and lymph node hypoplasia, which is
associated with increased susceptibility to infection, failure to

vetexamprep.ir

thrive, and abnormal hepatic proteomic pa erns. 85–87 Growth
retardation, hard and cracked footpads, pyoderma around body
oriﬁces, and aggressive to unresponsive behavior are hallmark
features and become apparent at a few weeks of age. Aﬀected
dogs die or are euthanized before 6 months of age. A MKLN1
splicing defect has been recently identiﬁed and serves as
screening test for this common trait in bull terriers. 88
Susceptibility to Mycobacterium avium Complex Infections in
Miniature Schnauzers and Basset Hounds
Increased susceptibility to Mycobacterium avium infection has been
recognized in miniature schnauzers and basset hounds (see
Chapter 61). A CARD9 deletion has been identiﬁed in miniature
schnauzers but not yet in bassets. Miniature schnauzers related to
a sire born in 1986 developed progressive disseminated MAC
infections at young adult age that were unresponsive to multidrug
antimicrobial therapy, which led to death or euthanasia. All
MAC-infected miniature schnauzers worldwide are homozygous
for the mutant CARD9 allele which results in a defective
intracellular signaling pathway. 11 Occasionally, these miniature
schnauzers may also develop candidiasis which is typically seen
in humans with CARD9 variants. Bassets do not seem to have a
CARD9 mutation.
Uncharacterized Breed-Associated Immunodeficiencies
Apparent breed predispositions to speciﬁc infectious diseases also
have the potential to reﬂect underlying hereditary
immunodeﬁciency. However, other factors also have the potential
to result in breed-associated infections. For example,
leishmaniosis has been identiﬁed in English and American
foxhounds in the United States (see Chapter 96), 6 , 89 babesiosis
occurs in lines of pit bulls and greyhounds (see Chapter 97), and
boxers and Rhodesian ridgebacks appear to be more susceptible
to neosporosis. In these cases, although a genetic susceptibility
may play a role, transplacental transmission and use of these
breeds for hunting or ﬁghting practices (babesiosis) also
contribute to the apparent breed predisposition.
Doberman Pinschers

vetexamprep.ir

Neutrophil dysfunction has been described in a family of
Doberman pinschers; one young dog had chronic recurrent
respiratory tract infections. 33 Oxygen radical formation and
bactericidal activity of neutrophils were reduced despite normal
phagocytosis of bacteria. The speciﬁc defect was not identiﬁed,
and although ciliary morphology appeared normal, functional
studies were not performed, so ciliary dyskinesia was not ruled
out. Aﬀected Doberman pinschers develop clinical signs of
respiratory tract infections at a few weeks of age that respond to
antibacterials, but prognosis is guarded.
German Shepherds
An apparent increase in susceptibility to ehrlichiosis, RMSF,
pythiosis, aspergillosis, other invasive mycoses, and deep
pyoderma has been described in German shepherds. 8 , 90 , 91
These predispositions likely involve diﬀerent immune defects that
have yet to be deﬁned. Aﬀected dogs with deep pyoderma have
pruritus with lesions distributed primarily over the lumbosacral
region. 92 Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is most commonly
cultured from the lesions. Proposed mechanisms for this
susceptibility include cell-mediated immunodeﬁciency associated
with serum inhibitors or defective helper T cells, and
hypersensitivity reactions to staphylococci. 90 , 91 , 93 , 94
Miniature Dachshunds
Certain lines of miniature dachshunds are predisposed to
Pneumocystis pneumonia by 1 year of age (see Chapter 89).
Aﬀected miniature dachshunds have hypogammaglobulinemia,
with decreased serum IgA, IgG, and IgM concentrations;
decreased lymphocyte transformation to phytohemagglutinin and
pokeweed mitogens; and absence of B cells and presence of T cells
in lymphoid tissues (stained by CD3 and CD79a cell markers). 95
The molecular defect remains unknown. This predisposition also
occurs in cavalier King Charles spaniels that seem to have lower
serum IgG concentrations 27 ; however, additional genetic and
immunologic studies in those dogs are not available.
Sharpeis

vetexamprep.ir

In addition to the severely abnormal skin structure, which leads to
a barrier failure, two distinct syndromes have been characterized
in the sharpei—one involving combined antibody and CMI
defects and the other involving renal amyloidosis and swollen
joints.
The combined immunodeﬁciency syndrome may have been
confused with the selective IgA deﬁciency described in this breed.
Juvenile to adult dogs develop recurrent infections involving
respiratory, skin, and gastrointestinal asystems. 96 Chronic
bronchitis, gastroduodenal or colonic ulceration, diarrhea and
vomiting, adult-onset pyoderma, demodicosis, and bacterial and
fungal otitis may occur. In addition, dogs are predisposed to GI
neoplasia, lymphoma, and other malignancies. Single or multiple
immunoglobulin class deﬁciencies are observed in dogs, with IgM
deﬁciency and decreased IL-2 synthesis predominating. Dogs
with GI signs or malignancy typically have had reduced serum
IgM concentrations. Decreased lymphocyte stimulation test
results were found in most of the dogs, suggesting a combined Tand B-cell defect. 96 In addition, peripheral blood mononuclear
cells (PBMCs) had reduced expression of IL-6.
Recurrent fever of unknown origin and swelling of the
tibiotarsal joints are the clinical signs of another immune-based
syndrome in sharpeis, known as “sharpei fever” or “sharpei
hock.” 97–100 Sharpeis have been strongly selected for thick and
heavily folded skin. Altered sequences within the hyaluronic acid
synthase gene have been found in aﬀected dogs. 101
Fragmentation of hyaluronan following its accumulation in the
thickened skin is thought to trigger an inﬂammatory reaction. The
lameness can be monoarticular or involve multiple joints, usually
aﬀecting the tibiotarsal joints and occasionally the carpus.
Predominant mononuclear cell polyarteritis and cellulitis, with or
without synovial inﬂammation, can develop. Clinical signs of
renal failure—a result of amyloid deposition in the kidney—and
nephrotic syndrome eventually develop. A majority of aﬀected
dogs have amyloid deposition in the renal medulla; 60% to 80%
have glomerular amyloidosis or membranous glomerulitis. 100
Polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss, dehydration, ascites, and
peripheral edema can occur. Thromboembolism can be a sudden
complication in some dogs with the nephrotic syndrome.
Radiographic changes are soft tissue swelling with periarticular

vetexamprep.ir

g p
g
g
p
bone erosion and bone production. Recurrent fever, joint pain,
and swelling often resolve within 24 hours. 99 Postpartum metritis
has developed in intact females and can be another inﬂammatory
feature of this illness. 100 Hyperglobulinemia and increased serum
IL-6 concentrations are found in aﬀected dogs. 102 The syndrome
resembles familial Mediterranean fever, a human hereditary
disorder characterized by polyserositis and reactive amyloidosis.
Treatment with colchicine early in the course of disease can
reduce amyloid deposition in humans and has been proposed for
aﬀected dogs.
Rottweilers
In one report, a li er of ro weiler pups either died before 6
months of age from systemic inﬂammatory disease or
subsequently developed chronic inﬂammatory skin disease. 103
Serum IgA and IgG concentrations were low. Secondary
lymphoid tissues had reduced numbers of CD3+ T cells, although
some were found within foci of B-cell follicles. Irregularities were
found in plasma cell development, and plasma cells were absent
from all mucosal and cutaneous sites. In inﬂammatory lesions,
macrophages expressing major histocompatibility complex
(MHC) class II molecules were present. Related unaﬀected dogs
had reduced serum IgA concentrations; however, the spectrum of
the defect in aﬀected dogs suggests a more complex underlying
defect. Ro weilers have also been considered more susceptible to
parvovirus infection, oral papillomatosis, and nasal and systemic
fungal infections; however, it is uncertain whether these
abnormalities are interrelated.
Weimaraners
At least two distinct immunodeﬁciency syndromes have been
observed in Weimaraners. One syndrome was reported only once,
and was associated with growth hormone deﬁciency with
dwarﬁsm, wasting, and thymic hypoplasia. 104 , 105
The second syndrome, which is similar to the common variable
immunodeﬁciency syndromes described in humans, involves
recurrent bacterial infections and inﬂammatory conditions in
young Weimaraners, which often become systemic. 2 , 106–109 Some
dogs outgrow their condition and do not show signs later in life.

vetexamprep.ir

Clinical signs of those with recurrent disease start at a few months
to young adult and are characterized by lethargy, anorexia,
intermi ent fever, lymphadenomegaly, pyogranulomatous
disease, large abscesses in muscle, stomatitis, osteomyelitis,
surface bleeding, and coat color dilution. Some dogs have
diarrhea or vomiting. Hyperesthesia of long bones or joints (Fig.
130.4), a predisposition to local injection site reactions, and
recurrent urinary infections or pyoderma have also been
observed. Some dogs later develop polyarthritis or meningitis.
Although dogs may respond favorably to select antibacterial
therapy and/or immunosuppressive drug therapy, recurrence of
systemic inﬂammatory disease can occur. While an immunologic
deﬁciency is suspected, inconsistencies exist in the immunologic
studies performed on these dogs. Neutrophilia, which is often
marked with a left shift, has been observed. Decreased neutrophil
phagocytosis of opsonized bacteria and chemiluminescence as
well as slightly low serum IgG and IgM concentrations have been
reported in some dogs with increased amounts of circulating
immune complexes (CICs). 110 In other reports, reduced serum
IgG, IgA, and IgM have been observed with no increase in CICs.
109 The lack of CICs in most reports suggests that primary
decreased production rather than secondary immunoglobulin
consumption is responsible for the defect. No speciﬁc diagnostic
tests are available. Despite antibacterial and supportive therapy,
prognosis is guarded. Some Weimaraners also appear to have an
increased tendency to develop hypertrophic osteodystrophy
(HOD), which has been associated with a postvaccination
reaction. Whether this predisposition is only associated with this
immunodeﬁciency syndrome is uncertain. 109 Dogs that develop
HOD respond most favorably to anti-inﬂammatory doses of
glucocorticoids, and the syndrome may be triggered by
a enuated live distemper vaccination (see Chapter 20). 111

Specific Hereditary or Primary
Immunodeficiencies in Cats
Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency
LAD (see dogs earlier for more details) was described in an adult
domestic medium-haired cat with severe leukocytosis and milder

vetexamprep.ir

signs of infection and inﬂammation. The disorder was associated
with a β2-integrin mutation, but not in any other cats. 51 If LAD is
suspected in a cat, leukocyte ﬂow cytometry for CD18 expression
can be used for diagnosis; the gene mutation may be diﬀerent and
thus genetic testing is not useful.
Hypotrichosis Congenita with Thymic Aplasia
Hypotrichosis congenita with thymic aplasia is a defect that is
characterized by the birth of nude athymic ki ens with severe
immunodeﬁciencies, ki ens that are similar to nude research
mice. This lethal syndrome has been recognized in Birmans and is
autosomal recessively inherited. A deletion in FOXN1 has been
identiﬁed and can be used to screen the breed (Fig. 130.5). 112 , 113
Other Defects
Abyssinians are predisposed to systemic reactive AA amyloidosis,
but clinical signs are caused by renal dysfunction. A genetic basis
is suspected. This syndrome is similar to amyloidosis in sharpeis
and familial Mediterranean fever in humans. Splenic
inﬂammatory diseases, often related to secondary infections from
immunodeﬁciencies, are responsible for the amyloid deposition in
reactive amyloidosis. However, in some aﬀected cats, concurrent
inﬂammatory disease is not detected. 114 Generalized amyloidosis
has also been observed in Siamese and Oriental cats, but clinical
features and amyloid protein composition diﬀer (mostly hepatic
involvement). 115 , 116
A syndrome of unknown cause in ragdoll ki ens is
characterized by fatal infections in the neonatal to weaning
period. 117 Vaccination with a enuated live feline panleukopenia
vaccine may have accelerated their death. Some ki ens died of
panleukopenia at a younger age. By weaning, others developed
numerous systemic fatal infections. Thymic, splenic, and
lymphoid hypoplasia were observed in these aﬀected ki ens.

Acquired Or Secondary Immunodeficiencies
Acquired or secondary immunodeﬁciencies encompass states of a
transiently or permanently impaired immune system during or
after an underlying disease condition or exposure to toxic agents.
Secondary immunodeﬁciencies occur more commonly than
primary immunodeﬁciencies, and, depending on the type and

vetexamprep.ir

severity of the immunosuppression, opportunistic infections may
result in localized or systemic disease.
Secondary immunodeﬁciencies can impact the innate or
adaptive immune systems. Anatomic barrier disturbances, such as
desquamation of skin or damage to the mucociliary escalator of
respiratory epithelium, are types of acquired immunodeﬁciencies.
These can also result from administration of immunosuppressive
agents, exposure to toxins, nutritional deﬁciencies, and speciﬁc
disease processes, including metabolic disorders, neoplasia, and
some infectious diseases (Box 130.3). Certain infections,
particularly retroviral diseases in cats, directly impair the immune
system, predisposing the animals to secondary bacterial, fungal,
or protozoal infections. For example, cats infected with FIV harbor
more diverse fungal microﬂora on the hair and mucosal surfaces
than noninfected cats. 122 FeLV-infected cats are also more likely
to have clinical illness with hemotropic mycoplasma infections
than noninfected cats. 123
Puppies and ki ens are particularly vulnerable to infections
because of their incompletely developed immune systems.
Transfer of maternally-derived antibody (MDA) from colostrum
takes place in the ﬁrst day of life and provides humoral protection
during the initial weeks of life in small animals. 124 , 125 Failure of
this transfer can lead to immunodeﬁciency and susceptibility to
some infections. A transient hypoglobulinemia occurs after the
decline of MDAs in the plasma and before immunocompetency,
and this increases susceptibility to various infections. 126

Specific Secondary or Acquired
Immunodeficiencies
Acquired or secondary immunodeﬁciencies can develop at any
time as a result of an interference with host defense mechanisms.
127 , 128 Immune defects secondary to infectious diseases,
metabolic disturbances, intoxications, nutritional deﬁciencies, and
drug therapies 129 , 130 have been reported (Table 130.3 and see
Box 130.3).
Infectious Diseases
Canine Distemper

vetexamprep.ir

CDV infection causes a chronic and profound inhibition and
impairment of cellular and humoral immune functions
characterized by lymphopenia and immunosuppression,
rendering animals susceptible to opportunistic infection (see also
Chapter 22). Immunosuppression is due to early virus-mediated
lymphocytolysis in the spleen, lymph nodes, thymus, bone
marrow, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), tonsils, and
hepatic Kupﬀer cells. 128 CD4+ T cells are preferentially depleted
during the acute phase, followed by CD8+ T-cell depletion. 131 In
addition, CDV aﬀects antigen presentation and lymphocyte
maturation by a poorly understood mechanism. 132 , 133
CDV infects cells of the immune system via viral H protein
binding to CD150 (signaling lymphocyte activation molecule), a
molecule expressed on B and T cells, monocytes, and mature
dendritic cells. 134 The viral V protein is essential for rapid viral
replication in T cells and antagonizes IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-γ,
and IL-2 in the acute phase of infection. 134 Furthermore, viral
infection leads to a diminished antigen presentation and altered
dendritic cell and B-cell maturation within germinal centers.
Subsequent plasma cell formation and immunoglobulin formation
are reduced. 132 Thus, long-lasting immunologic abnormalities
persist after viral clearance from the peripheral blood leukocytes.
Persistent suppression of CMI in neonatal puppies infected with
CDV can be detected by decreased lymphocyte stimulation test
results and decreased synthesis of T-cell–dependent antibodies
(IgG and IgA). If thymic hypoplasia results from in utero infection,
IgM levels may be reduced during the postnatal period. Transient
depression of CMI has been reported in puppies that are infected
with virulent CDV.

Canine Parvovirus Infection and Feline Panleukopenia Virus
Infection
CPV and FPV have an aﬃnity for replicating in rapidly dividing
cells, including crypt cells of the GI tract and lymphoid tissue,
resulting in severe lymphopenia and immunosuppression (see
Chapters 29 and 30). This combination of anatomic barrier
destruction of the GI tract and leukopenia in immunologically
naïve hosts leads to an increased risk of secondary bacterial
infections.
In addition to virus-induced destruction of WBC precursors in
the bone marrow, massive sequestration of neutrophils within the
inﬂamed GI tract occurs resulting in both a lymphopenia and
granulocytopenia. Mild depression of lymphocyte function has
also been observed as a result of parvoviral infection. 135
Parvovirus-infected dogs and cats are at increased risk for
bacterial translocation from the GI tract and bacteremia, leading to
overwhelming sepsis.

vetexamprep.ir

In utero infection can lead to permanent suppression of CMI
and thymic atrophy. Dogs that recover from CPV infections have
had a higher prevalence of UTIs than age-matched control pups.
Disseminated candidiasis has been reported in animals with
parvovirus. 136 Infection with CPV has also been associated with
development of postvaccinal canine distemper encephalitis. 137
There is li le known about immunodeﬁciency that develops in
cats with FPV infection, other than that associated with
panleukopenia.
Canine and Feline Coronavirus Infection
Opportunistic infections are rarely reported with either enteric
FCoV or FIPV infection. However, FIPV is associated with a
profound,
virus-induced
panlymphopenia
and
hypergammaglobulinemia (see Chapter 31). The virus does not
infect lymphocytes, so the mechanism of lymphocyte depletion is
unclear, although it may be related directly to TNF-α–induced
apoptosis or indirectly to the infection of antigen-presenting cells,
speciﬁcally dendritic cells. 138 , 139
A highly virulent strain of CCoV has been reported to cause
severe systemic illness and induce a lymphopenia. 140 Depletion
of the CD4+ T-cell population was observed 1 month PI in an
experimental model. 141
Feline Leukemia Virus Infection
FeLV is associated with antiproliferative (myelosuppressive) and
proliferative (neoplastic) diseases of the lymphohematopoietic
system, and both forms are associated with immunodeﬁciencies
primarily due to reduced CMI competence (see Chapter 32). A
reduction in CD4+/CD8+ T-cell subset ratios has been shown to
develop in FeLV-infected cats. 142 FeLV-infected cats have
impaired T-cell–mediated immunity as characterized by reduced
in vitro lymphocyte stimulation, prolonged retention of cutaneous
allografts, and impaired response to delayed hypersensitivity skin
testing. 143–145 Lymphopenia and thymic atrophy can be observed
in infected cats. 128 Secondary hyperglobulinemia and
complement depletion have also been recognized. 146 , 147
Persistent neutropenia and decreased neutrophil microbicidal
activity can also be observed as the disease progresses. 148 A

vetexamprep.ir

panleukopenia-like syndrome can develop in cats that are coinfected with FeLV and FIV. 149
The transmembrane viral envelope peptide p15E can mediate
some of the immunosuppression. 150 This viral protein inhibits Band T-cell function, alters monocyte morphology and distribution,
and has been associated with impaired cytokine production and
responsiveness. 143–145 FeLV-infected cats have increased
susceptibility to concurrent infection with other organisms and
severity of disease caused by those organisms, such as commensal
bacteria, pathogenic fungi, hemotropic Mycoplasma spp., and FIP.
Feline Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
Cats naturally infected with FIV may develop fever, variable
neutropenia, and chronic infections of the skin and mucosal
surfaces (see Chapter 33). Experimentally inoculated cats develop
generalized peripheral lymphadenopathy and transient
neutropenia followed by a disease-free period that may last years.
FIV infection of the bone marrow can cause blood leukopenias
and myelodysplasia even in cats without clinical signs. 151 Studies
of FIV infection have identiﬁed several mechanisms of innate and
adaptive immune dysfunction. Defective natural killer cell
proliferation and cytotoxic function occurs in chronically FIVinfected cats, and this may be due to low levels of key cytokines
such as IL-2 and IL-15. 152 , 153 Neutropenia due to apoptosis, 154
dendritic cell dysfunction, and dysregulation of multiple
cytokines have been described (e.g., decreased TNFα, IL-1, IL-2,
IL-6, and IL-12 and increased IL-10 and TGF-β). 155–157 Depletion
of CD4+ T cells is characteristic of the adaptive immune defect
and occurs by several mechanisms including apoptosis, anergy,
and thymic atrophy. Further adaptive immune dysregulation
occurs due to inappropriate activation of regulatory CD4+/CD25+
T cells which in turn downregulate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. 158–160
Alterations in the phenotype of CD8+ and other lymphocytes
eventually lead to immunodeﬁciency. 161
Opportunistic infections eventually occur as immunodeﬁciency
progresses, and can include bacterial infections of the oral cavity,
chronic skin infections, FCV infection, toxoplasmosis, hemotropic
mycoplasma infection, and systemic fungal infections. 162–167
Aﬀected cats tend to have increased severity of disease caused by

vetexamprep.ir

these pathogens. Compared with noninfected cats, Cryptococcus
spp. and Candida albicans are isolated more frequently from the
oropharyngeal mucosa of FIV-infected cats, and Microsporum canis
are isolated more frequently from the skin. 168
Canine Monocytic Ehrlichiosis
Infection with Ehrlichia canis can be divided into acute and chronic
stages (see Chapter 44). No secondary immunosuppression has
been associated with acute canine ehrlichiosis. 169 Dogs with
chronic ehrlichiosis can develop a marked lymphocytosis and
hyperglobulinemia with antibody titers to E. canis occasionally
exceeding 1:1,000,000. Some dogs develop pancytopenia due to
bone marrow failure, and secondary bacterial infections can be
a ributed to neutropenia in those cases. Alternatively, some dogs
can develop opportunistic infections in the absence of
neutropenia; the mechanism underlying this has not been fully
elucidated. These opportunistic infections, all of which rely on a
robust CMI, include leishmaniosis, viral papillomatosis,
generalized demodicosis, neosporosis, and opportunistic fungal
infections, implying alterations in the CMI occur during chronic
ehrlichiosis. 128 , 170 , 171
In vitro studies demonstrate
downregulation of MHC class II molecules in cells infected with
E. canis. 171 German shepherd dogs are over-represented in cases
of ehrlichiosis 172 and appear to experience a greater degree of
suppression of CMI during infection than other breeds. 173
Evaluation of blood lymphocytes from dogs naturally infected
with E. canis demonstrate higher numbers of cytotoxic T cells and
lower numbers of B cells compared with healthy control dogs;
however, their potential immunosuppressive eﬀects remain
unknown. 174 In fact, one study failed to demonstrate the
suppression of CMI or humoral immunity in experimentally
infected dogs up to 4 months PI. 169
Canine Leishmaniosis
Dogs with leishmaniosis are prone to secondary infections and
occasionally neoplasia, especially hematopoietic tumors. 175 The
Leishmania surface protein gp63 mediates entry into macrophages
and promotes survival of the parasite through inhibition of the
respiratory burst and apoptosis. Leishmania can also decrease

vetexamprep.ir

macrophage function and antigen presentation by inhibition of
MHC class I and II molecule expression, inhibition of chemotaxis,
and interference with IL-12 transcription. 176
Leishmania
organisms promote tolerance upon infection of in vitro cultivated
hepatic macrophages, which is reversed with leishmanicidal drug
application. 177 Generalized demodicosis has been described in
dogs with leishmaniosis and was associated with an absence of
CD3+ cells in dermal lesions suggesting a CMI deﬁciency. 178
Fungal Infections
Fungal pathogens including Aspergillus, Candida, and Cryptococcus
spp. are capable of causing immunosuppression. 179–181
Cryptococcus possesses several virulent factors that suppress or
orchestrate the immune response to favor fungal growth and
persistence. The capsular polysaccharide inhibits phagocytosis
and can interfere with leukocyte transmigration by causing these
cells to shed selectin. 182 Cryptococcal urease shifts the CMI to a
nonprotective Th2 immune response and promotes immature
dendritic cell accumulation within the lung tissue by upregulating
IL-10 production and regulatory T-cell accumulation. 183–185
Hemophagocytic Syndrome
Pathologic proliferation of the mononuclear phagocyte system can
either result from infectious diseases or contribute to
immunologic dysfunction and signs of debilitation, weight loss
with anorexia, splenohepatomegaly, and relapsing fever in dogs
or cats. 186–188 In dogs with hemophagocytic syndrome,
parvovirus infection or lymphoid or myelomonocytic leukemia
and lymphoma have been described; however, the association is
189
not
understood.
Dogs
with
infection-associated
hemophagocytic syndrome appeared to have be er 1-month
survival rates than dogs with immune-associated and idiopathic
hemophagocytic syndrome. 190
Metabolic Disturbances
Many biochemical processes that occur in noninfectious disease
states interfere with normal immune mechanisms. Failure of
neonates to ingest colostrum, and dysproteinemias such as
multiple myeloma, are both associated with impaired humoral

vetexamprep.ir

immune system function. Decreased complement concentration
has been noted with endotoxemia and malnutrition.
Newborn puppies and ki ens experience a hypothermic state
during the ﬁrst week of life that suppresses T-cell function. A
decline in CMI in older animals may increase their susceptibility
to infectious and neoplastic disorders. 191 This decline in CMI is
characterized by decrease in B-cell percentages and depressed
lymphocyte stimulation by various mitogens in vitro, with male
dogs more profoundly aﬀected than females. 192
Protein and caloric restriction has resulted in premature thymic
atrophy and decreased cell-mediated, humoral, and phagocytic
responses in animals. In contrast, overfed, obese dogs have
impaired T-cell function and upregulated inﬂammatory cytokine
expression. 193 , 194 Ingestion of organohalogenated compounds in
contaminated environments caused a reduction of serum
antibody titer responses of puppies to various inoculated
antigens. 195
Vitamin E and selenium deﬁciencies in dogs have been
associated with decreased in vitro lymphocyte responsiveness,
decreased serologic response to vaccination, and increased
susceptibility to infection with opportunistic pathogens. 196 , 197
The deﬁcit can be accentuated by excessive intake of
polyunsaturated fats (strong oxidants that counteract the eﬀects of
vitamin E). Vitamin E deﬁciency causes the animal to produce a
suppressor serum factor capable of decreasing lymphocyte
responsiveness to antigenic stimulation. Vitamin A deﬁciency can
cause immunosuppression and opportunistic infections similar to
those associated with vitamin E deﬁciency. 198 Vitamin D is
important in the regulation of the innate and adaptive immune
systems, and deﬁciency has been noted with some infections
including atypical mycobacterial infection in cats. 199 Zinc
deﬁciency during prenatal and neonatal periods can result in
impaired CMI responses and thymic atrophy.
Poorly regulated or untreated diabetes mellitus in dogs is
associated with weaker neutrophil adherence than in controlled
diabetic and nondiabetic dogs. 200 Diabetic dogs have an increased
prevalence of UTIs 201–203 and hepatic abscesses. 204 Intestinal
lymphangiectasia is associated with depressed CMI because of
205
lymphopenia.

hyperadrenocorticism is associated with a high prevalence of
bacteriuria, and mechanisms have been proposed including
decreased neutrophilic chemotaxis or enhanced bacterial growth
in urine due to glucosuria or decreased urine osmolality. 206
Splenectomized dogs and cats are prone to clinical babesiosis,
hemotropic mycoplasma infections, and bacteremia. 207
Neutropenia
Severe neutropenia increases the risk of bacterial infection, and
several infectious agents can result in neutropenia. Broadly,
neutropenia can result from decreased production or increased
demand with several speciﬁc causes (Box 130.4), and can range
from mild to severe. 208–210

Immune-Mediated
• Immune-mediated neutropenia

Primary immune-mediated neutropenia, associated with
circulating antineutrophil antibodies, has also been observed in
dogs and cats. 210–212 Despite the circulating neutropenia, animals
have adequate or high numbers of proliferating neutrophil
precursors in the bone marrow. Circulating neutrophils are
typically nondegenerate and lack toxic change (which might be
seen with other causes of neutropenia, such as sepsis), unless
secondary bacterial infection has occurred. Rapid increases in
neutrophil numbers, usually within a few days, are observed after
glucocorticoids are administered. Secondary bacterial infections
appear to be uncommon in animals with primary immunemediated neutropenia when compared with neutropenias
associated with other causes, such as myelosuppressive drugs.
Immunosuppressive and Myelosuppressive Therapy
Immunosuppression can be induced during treatment for
immune-mediated diseases, neoplasia, or organ transplantation.
Use of glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, or
leﬂunomide has been associated with an increased risk of
opportunistic infections. Glucocorticoid administration increases
the risk of UTI in dogs treated chronically (more than 6 months).
213 , 214 In one case series of 169 feline renal transplant patients
being treated with cyclosporine, infection was the second most
common cause of death after acute rejection of the transplant. 215

vetexamprep.ir

Bacterial infections were the most common, followed by viral,
fungal,
and
then
protozoal
infections.
Disseminated
toxoplasmosis and opportunistic cutaneous fungal infections have
also been reported in animals administered cyclosporine. 216–218
Recovery of T-cell function occurred within 4 days of
discontinuation of cyclosporine in healthy research dogs treated
for 1 week at 10 mg/kg q12h. 219

131: Fever
Amy E. DeClue

KEY POINTS
• Fever may be associated with infectious, inflammatory, immunemediated, and neoplastic disease.
• True fever is associated with a rise in the hypothalamic set point,
and body temperature is increased by enhanced heat production
and conservation.
• Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is defined as persistent or
recurrent fever which is not responsive to treatment and for
which a cause is not easily determined.
• Major endogenous pyrogens are cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6,
and TNF-α. These act to increase synthesis of prostaglandin E2
which acts on thermoregulatory neurons to raise the
hypothalamic set point.
• The diagnostic approach to FUO requires consideration of a
large number of differential diagnoses and a staged diagnostic
investigation with thorough and repeated physical examinations.
• Therapeutic trials should be a last resort as they have the
potential to mask underlying disease, contribute to adverse
outcomes, and result in unnecessary expense.

Fever is a common clinical ﬁnding in patients with infectious,
inﬂammatory, immune-mediated, or neoplastic disease. In many of
these patients, fever is accompanied by other more speciﬁc or
localizing clinical signs, and the cause of the fever is determined with
simple diagnostic tests. In some cases, the cause of the fever is not
readily apparent, but it resolves spontaneously or in response to
empiric therapy, often with antibacterial drugs. In a further small
subset of animals, the cause of fever is not easily determined and not
therapeutically responsive, and the problem becomes persistent or

vetexamprep.ir

p
y
p
p
p
recurrent. Such cases of fever of unknown origin (FUO) present a
particular diagnostic challenge in both human and veterinary
medicine. 1-5 This chapter outlines the pathophysiology of fever and
presents an approach to the small animal patient with FUO.

Etiology of Fever of Unknown Origin
Although fever is frequently associated with infectious diseases, the
same response can be elicited by many inﬂammatory, immunemediated, or neoplastic disorders, some medications and several
miscellaneous disorders. Because the list of diﬀerential causes for
FUO is extensive, grouping these causes into broad categories based
on the underlying disease process is useful. Table 131.1 shows the
causes of FUO divided into infectious and parasitic diseases, Table
131.2 summarizes inﬂammatory and immune-mediated causes of
FUO, and neoplastic and miscellaneous causes are listed in Table
131.3. Similar tables are used in the diagnostic approach to FUO in
humans. In the human medical literature, the causes of FUO are
typically distributed as follows: 17% to 35% are infectious, 10% to
20% are neoplastic, 24% to 36% are inﬂammatory, 3% to 15% are
miscellaneous, and up to 51% are undiagnosed. 5 In general, bacterial
infections are not the most common cause of fever in dogs or in cats. In cats,
fever often results from viral infection (FeLV, FIV, feline respiratory
viruses, FCoV). In dogs, neoplasia and immune-mediated disease are
the more common causes of fever than infectious causes. In a study
of 101 dogs with fever, 22% of dogs had immune-mediated disease,
22% had primary bone marrow abnormalities (usually hemic
neoplasia, but many had myelodysplasia), 16% had infectious
diseases, 10% had neoplasia outside the bone marrow, 12% had
miscellaneous inﬂammatory conditions, and 20% had pyrexia of
unknown origin, where the underlying disease was never identiﬁed.
6 Variation among case series may reﬂect referral bias and
geographic location of the study. Published case series are also
exclusively or predominantly canine. 6 , 7 Fever needs to be
distinguished from hyperthermia and dysthermia; dysthermia
results from damage to the brain (hypothalamus) and is usually
accompanied by other CNS signs.

Pathogenesis
Body temperature is determined by the set-point of the hypothalamic
thermoregulatory center. Thermoregulation depends on sensory

vetexamprep.ir

information from external and internal thermoreceptors and on
physiologic and behavioral eﬀector mechanisms that control heat
production and heat loss. Body heat is lost through the skin and the
respiratory tract and can be gained by transfer from the environment
or generated by muscle activity or body fat catabolism. Body
temperature is decreased by panting, cutaneous vasodilation,
seeking shelter, and remaining inactive. In a cold environment, body
temperature is maintained by shivering, postural changes,
piloerection, and cutaneous vasoconstriction. In a normal animal,
these mechanisms balance heat loss and heat gain and keep the body
temperature as close as possible to the normal hypothalamic setpoint.
In true fever, the hypothalamic set-point increases, and body
temperature is increased by enhanced heat production and
conservation. Heat gain and heat loss mechanisms now act to
maintain body temperature at the new set-point. In nonfebrile
hyperthermic conditions, the hypothalamic set-point is not altered,
and increased body temperature is the result of increased and
unregulated heat gain or heat production or impaired heat loss.
Examples of nonfebrile causes of hyperthermia include heat stroke,
exercise-induced hyperthermia, malignant hyperthermia, seizure
activity, and hypermetabolic disorders. Hyperthermia of this type
can progress to multiorgan-dysfunction syndrome caused by an
interplay among circulatory disturbances, hypoxia, increased
metabolic demand, cytotoxicity of high temperature, and activation
of inﬂammatory and coagulation cascades. 8

Fever is mediated by the action of pyrogens (Fig. 131.1).
Exogenous pyrogens (infectious agents and their products such as
LPS, tumors, drugs, and toxins) stimulate inﬂammatory cells to
release endogenous pyrogens (cytokines such as interferons, IL-1β
and IL-6, and TNF-α), and this leads to induction of cyclooxygenase
2 activation of the arachidonic acid cascade, with enhanced synthesis
of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). PGE2 is synthesized by hypothalamic
vascular endothelial cells and acts on thermoregulatory neurons to
raise the hypothalamic set-point. The cytokine RANKL (receptor
activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand), which is a member of the
TNF superfamily, may also be involved in thermoregulation. 9 The
thermoregulatory set-point is located in a rich vascular network
called the organum vasculosum laminae terminalis in the preoptic
rostral hypothalamus, which possesses li le if any blood-brain
barrier. Endothelial cells within this region are thought to release
arachidonic metabolites themselves, and then metabolites of
cyclooxygenase such as PGE2 are thought to diﬀuse the short
distance to the hypothalamic neurons and induce fever. PGE2, which
itself is not neurally active, can induce production of cyclic adenosine
monophosphate or other neurotransmi ers, which, in turn, raises the
temperature set-point of the body. Additional evidence suggests that
the thermoregulatory center may also be stimulated via vagal ﬁbers
that respond to release of cytokines locally released in tissues. 10
PGE2 may also be released peripherally by hematopoietic cells in
response to activation of TLR4 by bacterial LPS. 9 The increase in setpoint is thought to protect the body from infection. Febrile-range

vetexamprep.ir

temperatures have been shown to enhance the neutrophil respiratory
burst; the release of neutrophils from the bone marrow; the
recruitment of neutrophils to tissues; natural killer cell cytolytic
activity; and the activity of macrophages and dendritic cells, with
upregulation of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) Class I and
MHC Class II molecules.
Cats are especially sensitive to drug-induced hyperthermia, which
can result from drugs such as opioids (including buprenorphine,
oxymorphone, hydromorphone) or ketamine. 11 In some cases, rectal
temperatures may exceed 107°F (41.7°C). The mechanism of opioidinduced fever in cats is not fully understood. Another example of
drug-induced hyperthermia is serotonin syndrome, which in
humans is triggered by medications such as certain migraine
medications, antidepressants, and ecstasy. It has also been reported
in dogs with 5-hydroxytryptophan toxicosis. 12 These medications
cause hyperthermia through both neuromuscular eﬀects (muscle
cramping) and a direct eﬀect on the hypothalamus. A number of
molecules can inﬂuence the hypothalamic neurons, including
serotonin,
norepinephrine,
dopamine,
acetylcholine,
and
prostaglandins.

vetexamprep.ir

Pathogenesis of fever. The recognition
of damage-associated molecular patterns
(DAMPs) or pathogen-associated molecular
patterns (PAMPs), such as LPS, by TLRs and
other pattern recognition receptors drives the
activation of dendritic cells (DCs) and
macrophages. These innate immune cells release
prostaglandin E2 (PGE2 ) as well as pyogenic
cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, and TNF) that act
systemically to induce fever. IL-6 acts
downstream of IL-1 in the median preoptic
nucleus region in the hypothalamus to induce the
synthesis of cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2), the
enzyme responsible for production of additional
PGE2. PGE2 is the major pyogenic mediator of
fever. Receptor activation of NF-κB (RANK)
expressed by astrocytes also acts via the COX2PGE2 pathway to induce fever. It is not known
exactly how this pathway interacts with the IL-6
pathway. Neurons that express PGE2 receptor 3
(EP3) trigger the sympathetic nervous system to
trigger norepinephrine release, which raises body
temperature by increasing thermogenesis in
brown adipose tissue and inducing
vasoconstriction, which reduces heat loss.

Factors That Modify Fever
In some cases, fever may be masked by factors such as extremes of
age, immunosuppression (e.g., immunosuppressive drugs,
hyperadrenocorticism, severe malnutrition), or NSAID treatment.
Renal failure can also mask a fever, because uremic toxins are
considered to be endogenous cryogens; they are thought to act on the
hypothalamus to reduce the set-point, although the true
pathogenesis is unclear. Research into this phenomenon was
stimulated by the ﬁnding that human patients that underwent
dialysis often experienced an increase in rectal temperature. 13
Uremic hypothermia has been documented in dogs and cats
undergoing intermi ent hemodialysis, and appears to be more
common in cats. 14 In this study, for dogs post dialysis, rectal
temperature decreased by 0.05°F for every 1 mg/dL unit increase in
serum creatinine concentration.

Clinical Signs
Rectal temperatures of 103°F to 105.5°F (39.5°C to 40.8°C) are
typically identiﬁed in FUO patients and can be associated with
nonspeciﬁc signs such as anorexia, lethargy, arthralgia, and
dehydration.
Body temperatures above 106°F (41.1°C) can rapidly lead to CNS
damage and subsequent CNS signs, disseminated intravascular
coagulation and evidence of bleeding diathesis, metabolic
derangements, and death. Such temperatures are typically associated
with hyperthermia, rather than fever. When the rectal temperature is
mildly increased (< 104°F), animals that appear otherwise
systemically well and active are more likely to be hyperthermic than
febrile, especially if the weather is warm or the animal has a history
consistent with hyperthermia (e.g., traveled in a hot car). The rectal
temperature should be retaken after 20 to 30 minutes of being
indoors in a cool, quiet environment to determine if the high rectal

vetexamprep.ir

temperature is clinically relevant. In contrast to fever, hyperthermia
is not responsive to treatment with antipyretics.

Diagnosis
Fever (pyrexia) is deﬁned as an increase in body temperature above
102.5°F (39.1°C) in dogs and cats, although fever is typically
associated with body temperature above 103°F (39.4°C). Rarely does
body temperature exceed 106°F (41.1°C). In human medicine, the
following criteria are used to deﬁne FUO:
1. Prolonged fever of > 3 weeks’ duration associated with vague,
nonspeciﬁc signs of illness.
2. Temperature more than 1.5°F above normal on several
occasions.
3. Diagnosis uncertain after 1 week of hospitalization involving
repeated physical exams and routine laboratory tests.
With the availability of faster and more accurate diagnostic tests,
and changing models of care (more outpatient care), this deﬁnition
has changed and the requirement for a week of hospitalization is no
longer considered essential. 5
In veterinary medicine, some practitioners are quick to assign the
term “FUO.” Multiple deﬁnitions of FUO have been used in
veterinary medicine without a clear consensus deﬁnition. FUO in
both human and veterinary medicine can be most usefully deﬁned as
fever that does not resolve spontaneously in the period expected for
self-limited infection and the cause of which cannot be ascertained

vetexamprep.ir

despite considerable diagnostic eﬀort. 1 In veterinary medicine, this
diagnostic eﬀort typically includes a complete history and physical
examination, CBC, chemistry, urinalysis, aerobic bacterial urine
culture, plain radiographs of the thorax and abdomen, and
abdominal ultrasound examination.

Development of a Diagnostic Plan for FUO
Although some patients with FUO may have uncommon infectious,
inﬂammatory, adverse drug reaction or neoplastic diseases, many
patients are ultimately found to have an unusual or early
manifestation of a common disorder. Therefore cases must be
approached in a systematic fashion that allows for the detection of
any potential cause of fever while avoiding unnecessary testing and
minimizing invasive testing. A diagnostic plan for FUO may be
based on consideration of the disease process, as outlined in Tables
131.1, 131.2, and 131.3. Similar tables are used for the approach to
diagnosis of FUO in people. 5 , 15 A complementary approach is
summarized in Table 131.4, in which the causes of FUO are grouped
according to anatomic or body system location. Fever may also be
classiﬁed as “high-grade” (> 104°F) or “low-grade” (≤ 104°F). The
presence of a high-grade fever can raise suspicion for viral infections,
gram-negative and some gram-positive (e.g., Streptococcus spp.)
infections, and diseases such as salmon poisoning disease, plague,
and tularemia. High-grade fevers are uncommon for pathogens that
replicate slowly, such as mycobacteria or fungi; or those that evade
the immune system (“stealth” pathogens), such as Bartonella spp.
