By combining a disease process and anatomic approach, the
clinician can develop a comprehensive diagnostic plan for any FUO
patient. In addition to including appropriate diagnostic tests, the
diagnostic plan should follow a sequence that is both logical and
ﬂexible. The typical diagnostic plan will begin with tests that are
safe, simple, inexpensive, easy to interpret, and high yield. Every
abnormal result has to be carefully considered; the more tests that
are done, the greater the number of false leads that can appear.
“Good practice points” for approach to diagnosis of FUO in humans
have been outlined, 5 and these can be adopted for FUO in dogs and
cats (Box 131.1). A staged approach can be used to guide the
selection of diagnostic tests, and examples are outlined in Box 131.2.
The results of stage 1 tests in the FUO patient will determine the
tests to be performed at the next stage. If the fever has not been
localized, more specialized procedures can also be introduced. Stages
2 and 3 require the repetition of earlier tests and introduce the need
for advanced imaging and more invasive procedures. Ideally, the
selection of the tests used in stage 3 will be based on abnormalities
detected in stages 1 and 2.
An important aspect of staged testing in the FUO patient is the
need to repeat the early, less invasive, and less expensive tests
frequently enough to detect new changes. In animals with acute
illness, fever may develop a day or two before the appearance of
lesions, so withholding extensive diagnostic testing and simply
repeating physical examinations should be considered in animals
with a recent onset of fever to avoid wasting client ﬁnancial
resources and creating undue stress for the patient.
The key is not to rigidly follow a predetermined and ﬁxed
diagnostic plan but rather to review and modify the plan as new

vetexamprep.ir

results become available. For example, if repeated CBCs demonstrate
developing pancytopenia, a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy should
be performed early in the diagnostic plan and not reserved for stage
3.
Client Communication
The management of the FUO patient demands ﬂexibility, dedication,
and patience from both the clinician and the client. By deﬁnition,
patients with FUO will already have undergone several basic
diagnostic tests, and some may have received one or more courses of
antimicrobial therapy. Clients may be frustrated by the failure to
reach a diagnosis or the continuation of the patient’s clinical signs.
Good client communication is vital to the successful resolution of the
FUO case. The clinician should explain that many diagnostic tests,
including repeated tests, may be necessary to reach a diagnosis, that
test results often change over time to become more revealing, and
that the process can be time-consuming and expensive. However,
clients should also be reassured that a diagnosis is reached in most
cases, that many causes of FUO may be treatable or even curable,
and that the fever itself is rarely harmful to the patient.

History
The patient history should include details of geographic location, any
travel history, environment and lifestyle (e.g., indoor vs. outdoor,
history of wildlife exposure or ingestion, boarding, plant awn
exposure, digging behavior), recent adoption from a shelter or rescue
environment, other animals in the household and when they were
introduced, and the possibility of exposure to ticks or other vectors.
All of these factors will inﬂuence exposure to speciﬁc
microorganisms. The medical history should cover diet (especially
whether raw food diets are fed), vaccinations (antigens and timing),
heartworm and other parasite treatment and prevention, the
administration of any other medications, previous medical problems,
trauma, and previous surgeries (including whether implants may be
present). The response to past therapies used for the fever problem
should be noted. A failure to respond to antibacterial drugs can help
to narrow the diﬀerential diagnosis list (Box 131.3), and a previous
response to antibacterials may suggest an underlying, inadequately

vetexamprep.ir

treated bacterial infection or bacterial infection in association with a
foreign body. Clients should be carefully questioned about the
patient’s urination and defecation habits and the presence of clinical
signs such as lameness; neck, back, or abdominal pain; skin lesions;
masses, or swellings; weakness; exercise intolerance; coughing; nasal
discharge; and dyspnea. Any previous medical records should be
thoroughly reviewed as the client may not be aware of or recall
prescribed medications, vaccines, or procedures.

Physical Examination
All body systems should be examined in detail, and a complete
physical examination should be repeated at each hospital visit for
outpatients. Repeated and thorough physical examinations are one of
the simplest and most rewarding things that can be done to localize
the problem. Asking another clinician in the practice to perform a
second physical examination may also be helpful. Inpatients should
be examined twice daily. The physical examination should include
careful cardiac and lung auscultation and regular and thorough
examination of the oral cavity and rectum, bones and joints, lymph
nodes, and skin. Thorough palpation of the entire surface of the skin,
including examination of the foot pads and interdigital spaces
should be performed, in an eﬀort to identify skin lesions or painful
regions of the body. Detection of a cat bite abscess or cellulitis by
means of a thorough physical examination can avoid unnecessary
diagnostic tests. An eﬀort should be made to visualize as much of the
oral cavity as possible. This is especially important in cats, because
oral ulcerations due to viral respiratory pathogens may be located
only at the base of the tongue. Musculoskeletal and neurologic
examinations may reveal spinal pain or subtle neurologic deﬁcits in
dogs with discospondylitis. Repeated ocular examinations, including
a fundoscopic examination, should not be overlooked because they
may provide evidence of infectious, inﬂammatory, or neoplastic
disease. Given that fever can often wax and wane in FUO, the pa ern
of fever in an individual patient should be determined by serial
measurement of body temperature. In veterinary medicine, this
measure is not of any value in elucidating the underlying cause, but
it is important in monitoring the response to any subsequent
therapy.

Laboratory Findings

vetexamprep.ir

Complete Blood Count and Serum Chemistry Panel
Fever is often accompanied by neutrophilia or a stress leukogram,
and serum chemistry tests are frequently nonlocalizing in FUO
patients. However, any abnormalities detected on these tests should
be used to direct further testing. The CBC should always be
accompanied by examination of a blood smear so as to determine
blood cell morphology and look for microorganisms. Automated
CBCs should be veriﬁed by manual counts. Thrombocytopenia may
be a clue to an underlying vector-borne disease or immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia. Neutropenia may be: (1) secondary to bacterial
infection, in which case it is usually accompanied by toxic changes
and bandemia, (2) an underlying cause of secondary bacterial
infection and fever (e.g., because of marrow disease), or (3) an
immune-mediated problem (i.e., immune-mediated neutropenia,
which is uncommon to rare). 16 , 17 When neutropenia exists and
neutrophils appear mature and nontoxic, marrow disease or
immune-mediated neutropenia should be considered. For unclear
reasons, dogs with immune-mediated neutropenia rarely seem to
develop secondary bacterial infections.
Urinalysis and Urine Culture
Because FUO may be associated with focal urogenital infections (e.g.,
prostatitis, pyelonephritis), urinalysis and aerobic bacterial urine
culture are mandatory in the evaluation of fever patients. Urine
specimens should be obtained by cystocentesis and submi ed for
bacterial culture and susceptibility testing, regardless of the
appearance of the urine sediment. However, because subclinical
bacteriuria may be unrelated to the problem causing fever, at the
same time, care should be taken not to overinterpret the ﬁnding of a
positive urine culture (see Chapter 127). With the exception of
Candida, which can cause infections localized to the urinary tract,
funguria generally indicates a systemic fungal infection. However,
candiduria in the presence of fever is suggestive of disseminated
candidiasis.

Diagnostic Imaging
Plain Radiography
Thoracic and abdominal radiographs should be obtained during the
ﬁrst stage of evaluation of the FUO patient. These radiographs may
provide early evidence of neoplastic disease or suggest infectious

vetexamprep.ir

disease such as viral, bacterial, or fungal pneumonia. A ention
should also be paid to each rib and the vertebral column on thoracic
and abdominal radiographs for evidence of osteomyelitis or
discospondylitis. In the second or third stages of diagnosis, complete
spinal, long bone, joint, and dental radiographs should be
considered.
Ultrasonographic Examination
A complete abdominal ultrasound examination should include
examination of the liver, gall bladder, bile duct, gastrointestinal tract,
spleen, pancreas, kidney, urinary bladder, prostate, uterus,
abdominal lymph nodes, and adrenal glands. When lesions are
present, other regions that can be investigated by ultrasonography
include the thorax (particularly in the presence of eﬀusions or
masses), the retrobulbar area, and any other peripheral mass lesion
or swelling. Ultrasonography can also facilitate minimally invasive
acquisition of ﬁne-needle aspirates or biopsies.
Echocardiography
Ultrasonographic examination of the pericardium, myocardium,
endocardium, heart valves, and great vessels is essential in the
evaluation of the patient with FUO and a heart murmur, particularly
if the murmur is of recent onset, which might suggest infective
endocarditis (IE) (see Chapter 122). Because IE can occur in the
absence of a murmur, should other a empts to localize a cause of
fever fail, echocardiography could be considered even in dogs that
do not have a murmur. The results of echocardiography should be
interpreted in light of the patient’s signalment, clinical signs, and
blood culture results. Echocardiographic evaluation is especially
important in medium to large breed dogs because these breeds are
overrepresented and IE is more common in dogs than in cats. 18 , 19
Advanced Imaging
Advanced imaging modalities should be regarded as third-stage tests
in the evaluation of the FUO patient and used when clinical signs
have been localized to a particular body system. For example, CT is
useful for detecting certain pulmonary lesions and for examining the
nasal cavity, tympanic bullae, and pharynx. MRI is often used in
evaluation of the CNS.
Nuclear medicine has provided several techniques that can be
used to visualize infection or inﬂammation in human patients. 20

vetexamprep.ir

Scintigraphic imaging can demonstrate many of the steps involved in
the inﬂammatory process and can, therefore, potentially localize
some causes of FUO. For example, leukocyte inﬁltration of tissues
can be visualized with indium-111 or technetium-99m–labeled
neutrophils. 21 Other techniques in nuclear medicine include the use
of radiolabeled human immunoglobulin, or gallium-67, which binds
to transferrin in the blood, to nonspeciﬁcally demonstrate areas of
increased ﬂuid extravasation associated with enhanced vascular
permeability in inﬂammation. Positron emission tomography (PET)
with ﬂuorine-18 ﬂuorodeoxyglucose is an imaging technique used to
identify areas of increased glucose metabolism such as tumors and
infectious or inﬂammatory lesions. The combination of PET with
computed tomography (PET/CT) allows for anatomic localization of
the lesion which enhances diagnostic value of this technique in
patients with FUO. 22 , 23
Cytologic and Histopathologic Examination
Fine-needle aspirates are usually simple and safe to obtain, and
touch preparations or impression smears can also be made from
ulcerated lesions or discharge material. Cytologic examination of
these specimens is relatively inexpensive and, depending on the skill
of the clinician, can sometimes be performed in-house. For example,
if blastomycosis is suspected, repeated aspirates from lymph nodes
or skin nodules can be examined for Blastomyces organisms because
they are relatively easy to identify (see Chapter 80). Ultrasound,
ﬂuoroscopy, or CT can be used to facilitate guidance. Aspirates of
ﬂuids such as pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal eﬀusions; CSF;
synovial ﬂuid; or bile should also be submi ed for bacterial and
other cultures. Aspiration of peripheral lymph nodes, even if
palpably normal, is recommended in the second stage of diagnostic
testing if the source of the fever has not been localized.
Cisternal or lumbar puncture, bronchoalveolar lavage,
transtracheal or endotracheal lavage, prostatic wash and ejaculation,
and bone marrow aspiration may also be used to obtain specimens
for cytologic examination and culture. Biopsy specimens may also be
obtained with techniques such as thoracoscopy, laparoscopy,
endoscopy, or arthroscopy, or they can be obtained percutaneously,
sometimes with guidance from ultrasound or radiography.
Bone Marrow Cytology and Histology

vetexamprep.ir

Bone marrow disease is a relatively common cause of FUO. Reported
examples include myelodysplasia, lymphoid leukemia, myeloma,
hemophagocytic syndrome, and disseminated adenocarcinoma. 6 , 24
, 25 Bone marrow aspiration is indicated in the early stages of
diagnostic testing if CBCs show unexplained, persistent cytopenias.
Investigation of pancytopenia requires the evaluation of both
cytology of a bone marrow aspirate and histopathology of a core
biopsy. In cats, additional unstained bone marrow cytology smears
should also be reserved for FeLV FA testing. Bone marrow aspiration
is indicated in the third stage of the diagnostic plan if the FUO has
not yet been localized.
Arthrocentesis
Immune-mediated polyarthritis is a common cause of FUO in dogs, 6
, 7 , 26 although only 3 of 79 dogs with polyarthritis in one study were
examined because of intermi ent fever. 26 The condition can be
idiopathic (nondeforming and nonerosive), or it can be caused by
rheumatoid arthritis or associated with other immune-mediated
disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus or steroidresponsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA; see Chapter 129).
Occasionally, nonerosive immune-mediated polyarthritis can be
secondary to infection, drug therapy, or neoplasia. 27 Immunemediated polyarthritis is rare in cats. 28
Lameness, joint swelling, and periarticular pain can wax and wane
or be inapparent in patients with immune-mediated polyarthritis.
Therefore arthrocentesis should be performed in the second stage of
evaluation of canine patients with FUO. Because dogs with immunemediated polyarthritis may have fever as their only clinical sign,
collection of synovial ﬂuid by arthrocentesis should be considered.
Synovial ﬂuid specimens should be obtained from both carpi and
both tarsi if possible. The ﬂuid should be examined for color, clarity,
and viscosity and submi ed for cytologic examination including a
diﬀerential cell count and cytologic description. The cells in synovial
ﬂuid can degrade and undergo apoptosis, quickly altering the
cytologic evaluation. Ideally, joint ﬂuid should be submi ed as
cytologic slide preparations; if additional ﬂuid is available after slide
preparation, that can be submi ed as well. Aerobic bacterial and
mycoplasma culture or mycoplasma PCR should also be performed
if specimen volume is large enough. Bacterial recovery from joint
ﬂuid will be enhanced if the joint ﬂuid is incubated in blood culture

vetexamprep.ir

bo les immediately after collection for 24 hours before bacterial
plating.
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
In a retrospective study of fever in dogs, 10 of 66 patients were found
to have inﬂammatory CNS disease. 29 This included seven dogs with
SRMA (see Chapter 129). Dogs with FUO and evidence of spinal pain
can also have concurrent immune-mediated polyarthritis and SRMA.
30 Therefore arthrocentesis should be considered in dogs in which
this form of meningitis is suspected. If joint ﬂuid analysis is
unremarkable, CSF analysis should be performed.
Blood Culture
Blood cultures are indicated in all patients with FUO and should be
especially considered where there is the presence of a cardiac
murmur; spinal, long bone, or joint pain; neutropenia; or a history of
immunosuppressive drug administration.
Few prospective studies have been done of blood culture
techniques in veterinary patients, although this subject has been
extensively reviewed in the human literature. 31 In human medicine,
the likelihood of obtaining a positive culture result is directly
correlated with the volume of blood drawn, regardless of whether
the blood is obtained as a single blood culture set or divided into
several sets over a 24-hour period. In one study, the yield from a 30mL blood sample was found to be 62% more than that from a 10-mL
sample. However, the sensitivity of blood cultures is also improved
by obtaining more than one set. For example, in a study of
bacteremic humans, 91.5% of bacteremic episodes were detected by
the ﬁrst blood culture set, and 99.3% were detected by the ﬁrst two
sets. Increasing the number of blood culture sets will also increase
the speciﬁcity of the test because contaminants are unlikely to be
present in all sets.
In dogs and cats, blood culture techniques should focus on the
collection of adequately large volumes of blood, with less emphasis
on the timing or periodicity of the collections. The total volume of
blood that can safely be obtained will depend on patient size. If size
allows, more than one blood culture set should be obtained to
increase the sensitivity and speciﬁcity of the test. Detailed
information on blood culture technique can be found in Chapter 3.
Serologic Testing

vetexamprep.ir

Tests available for the diagnosis of infectious disease include assays
for speciﬁc antibodies or antigens, as well as molecular tools such as
PCR-based assays. Many of these tests are performed on blood
specimens; however, other body ﬂuids can be used for detection of
certain organisms. For example, urine antigen detection appears to
be sensitive for the detection of some fungal diseases. 32
Consideration of the signalment, clinical signs, geographic location,
and possible vector exposure of the patient should direct selection of
the most appropriate tests. Vaccination history, local disease
prevalence, sensitivity, speciﬁcity, etiologic predictive value, and
positive and negative predictive values must be considered when
interpreting the results of any diagnostic test (see Chapter 7).
Ensuring that tests are only conducted when there is a reasonable
likelihood of the disease in question being present will help to
minimize problems associated with poor positive predictive value.
Serologic tests are also available for the diagnosis of certain
immune-mediated diseases. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) can be
detected in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. However,
diagnosis of this uncommon multisystem disorder requires the
demonstration of multiple clinical and immunologic abnormalities
and should never be based on a positive ANA assay alone. 33 , 34 In
addition, ANA can be positive in some clinically healthy dogs and in
association with other medical conditions. This disorder is more
appropriately diagnosed by a combination of radiographic changes
indicating an erosive polyarthritis together with joint ﬂuid analysis
and possibly synovial membrane biopsy.
In summary, extensive arrays of wide-ranging serodiagnostic tests
are not recommended in the investigation of FUO, and the use of
panels should be avoided if possible or each result in a panel should
be interpreted with care and a ention to the meaning of a positive or
negative result. Ideally, serologic tests should be used to investigate a
diagnosis that is suspected based on other ﬁndings.

Treatment
The goals of FUO therapy are to treat the underlying cause of the
fever and provide supportive care to the patient. Dogs and cats with
fever have the potential to develop dehydration as a result of
reduced water intake and increased sensible and insensible losses.
Intravenous ﬂuid therapy can correct these conditions. While cooling
measures (e.g., fans, cool water baths, colonic or gastric irritation) are
indicated when body temperature is increased as a result of

vetexamprep.ir

nonfebrile factors such as heat stroke or prolonged seizure activity,
these methods should not be used for true fever unless body
temperature exceeds 41.1°C (106°F) and there is concern for CNS
damage, and then they should only be used to reduce body
temperature suﬃciently to avoid CNS damage. Fever is a regulated
increase in body temperature; therefore any a empts to physically
cool the patient will be working against the body’s own
thermoregulatory mechanisms. Fever is also a protective adaptive
response to the eﬀects of infection and can have beneﬁcial eﬀects.
External cooling is the treatment of choice for hyperthermia in which
core temperature exceeds the thermoregulatory set-point. Thus,
when external cooling is used to treat hyperthermia, no opposition of
regulatory process takes place in an a empt to increase heat gain, as
is the case with fever.
Antipyretic therapies inhibit cyclooxygenase and therefore act
centrally to reduce the hypothalamic set-point. However, it is
extremely rare that antipyretic medications are needed for dogs or
cats with FUO and like steroids, antipyretic medications have many
risks such as masking disease, inducing secondary complications and
preventing treatment with disease-speciﬁc appropriate therapy.
In the editor’s experience, the most common cause of true FUO in
dogs is immune-mediated disease. Usually, fever in cats resolves
spontaneously or an underlying cause is identiﬁed.

Trial Therapy
In many cases, the investigation of the FUO patient will achieve a
deﬁnitive diagnosis, and treatment of the underlying cause will lead
to resolution of fever and other clinical signs. However, in some
cases of true FUO, a diagnosis is not reached, and in other cases,
diagnostic testing is discontinued because of client or patient factors.
In these cases, therapeutic trials are undertaken in the absence of a
deﬁnitive diagnosis. Antibacterial, antifungal, or glucocorticoid
therapies are often used in therapeutic trials.
The goals of a therapeutic trial should be to conﬁrm a presumptive
diagnosis indirectly, control or cure the underlying disease, and
resolve the patient’s clinical signs, without inducing intolerable
adverse eﬀects or exacerbating an undiagnosed disease.
A therapeutic trial should be planned and monitored as rigorously
as the diagnostic plan. It is important to begin with a tentative
diagnosis, select safe and appropriate therapies, and implement a
careful monitoring program, using predetermined criteria for success

vetexamprep.ir

or failure of the therapeutic trial. Medication should be used at
appropriate doses, and the duration of therapy should be suﬃcient
to detect both the presence and absence of a response, particularly
because fever can wax and wane independent of therapy.
Good client communication is essential in developing and
monitoring a therapeutic trial, and clients should understand the
risks of such an approach. Such risks include the continued
progression of an undiagnosed disease if an ineﬀective therapy is
used, development of medication adverse eﬀects or toxicities, and
the possibility of exacerbating an underlying infectious disease if
immunosuppressive therapy is used. Clients should also understand
that some medications, such as antifungals, can be expensive, and
that initiating treatment without a diagnosis for diseases that require
a long course of therapy may make a empts to make a diagnosis
more diﬃcult in the future. The risks and beneﬁts of trial therapy
should be carefully considered if the patient is likely to be referred
for further diagnostic testing. 29 A therapeutic trial is unlikely to be
helpful if the client abandons the plan because of expense, adverse
eﬀects, or lack of immediate response to treatment.
Many causes of FUO are inﬂammatory or immune mediated;
therefore glucocorticoids are commonly used in patients with FUO in
the absence of a speciﬁc diagnosis. Because this approach can be
dangerous if infectious disease has not been ruled out ﬁrst, the
patient should be monitored closely for exacerbation or development
of new clinical signs. The indiscriminate use of glucocorticoids can
also interfere with future diagnostic testing and future more speciﬁc
therapies, or worsen prognosis. This practice is a particular concern
for patients with neoplasia such as lymphoma or fungal disease.
Glucocorticoids can also have nonspeciﬁc antiinﬂammatory eﬀects
and may improve the patient’s clinical signs without addressing the
primary cause of the fever allowing progression of disease to go
unnoticed.
Empiric antibacterial therapy is commonly used in small animal
patients with fever, often with a successful outcome. Ideally, such
therapy should be based on culture and susceptibility testing,
although this is not always feasible. In trial therapy for FUO patients,
antibacterials should be chosen based on a tentative but speciﬁc
diagnosis, with consideration of spectrum of activity and an
understanding of pharmacokinetics. For example, doxycycline is a
reasonable choice if salmon poisoning disease, leptospirosis, or a
ricke sial disease is suspected. A signiﬁcant risk of indiscriminate
antibacterial therapy is that it contributes to antibacterial resistance

vetexamprep.ir

in bacterial populations. Treatment with antibiotics without
a empting basic diagnostics should be avoided if possible, because
serious abnormalities (especially renal failure) may be present, and if
undetected and untreated, these may be life-threatening.
Trial therapy for fungal infections with antifungal drugs is rarely
indicated without strong support for an underlying fungal disease.
Fungal lesions respond slowly to treatment, antifungal drugs are
often expensive, and prolonged treatment is typically required.
Therefore the importance of investing client funds to obtain a
diagnosis ﬁrst cannot be overemphasized. Fortunately the advent of
fungal antigen tests has facilitated diagnosis because they are
relatively inexpensive and can be performed on specimens collected
in a minimally invasive manner.

Case Example
Signalment
“Grover,” a 2-year-old male neutered Shetland sheepdog
from northern California.

History
Grover was evaluated by the University of California-Davis
veterinary emergency and critical care service for fever. Six
days previously, Grover vomited four to six times, and
vomited up a plant awn. He was seen at a local veterinary
clinic and a physical examination was unremarkable. He was
treated with subcutaneous ﬂuids and maropitant on an
outpatient basis. Two days later, the owners found him
shivering and reluctant to move. He was again evaluated at
the local veterinary clinic and his temperature was 104.9°C
(40.5°F). A CBC, serum chemistry panel, urinalysis, and
thoracic radiographs were unremarkable. He was
hospitalized and given IV ﬂuids and ampicillin-sulbactam,
and discharged the following day. For the following 2 days,
the owners reported that he was eating normally but was
quiet and still reluctant to move about the house. The
owners took his temperature at home and it was 104.4°C
(40.2°F).

vetexamprep.ir

Current Medications
Phenobarbital 60 mg in the morning and 90 mg in the
evening; levetiracetam 740 mg q 12h for previously
diagnosed epilepsy. Monthly endoparasite prophylaxis
(milbemycin oxime and praziquantel).

Other Medical History
Acquired from a breeder at 9 months of age. Diagnosed with
suspected idiopathic epilepsy 1 year ago. Last seizure was a
week before the onset of fever.

Physical Examination
Body weight: 13.6 kg.
General: Bright, alert, responsive, hydrated. T = 102.9°C
(39.4°F), HR 132 beats/min, RR 60 bpm, BCS 5/9, CRT 1–2 s,
mucous membranes pink and moist.
GI and genitourinary: Tense abdomen but no apparent pain,
organomegaly, or masses. No other clinically signiﬁcant
ﬁndings.

Laboratory Findings
CBC:

HCT 40.1% (40–55%), MCV 71 fL (65–75 fL), MCHC 33.9 g/dL (33–
36 g/dL), WBC 19,660 cells/µL (6000–13,000 cells/µL), neutrophils
14,015 cells/µL (3000–10,500 cells/µL), lymphocytes 2350 cells/µL
(1000–4000 cells/µL), monocytes 1752 cells/µL (150–1200 cells/µL),
platelets 231,000 platelets/µL (150,000–400,000 platelets/µL).

Serum chemistry proﬁle:

Sodium 143 mmol/L (143–151 mmol/L), potassium 4.3 mmol/L
(3.6–4.8 mmol/L), chloride 105 mmol/L (108–118 mmol/L),
bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (20–29 mmol/L), phosphorus 4.9 mg/dL
(2.6–6.2 mg/dL), calcium 10.3 mg/dL (9.6–11.2 mg/dl), BUN 19
mg/dL (11–33 mg/dL), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.8–1.5 mg/dL),
glucose 83 mg/dL (86–188 mg/dL), total protein 6.3 g/dL (5.4–6.9
g/dL), albumin 3.4 g/dL (3.4–4.3 g/dL), globulin 2.9 g/dL (1.7–3.1
g/dL), ALT 98 U/L (21–72 U/L), AST 72 U/L (20–49 U/L), ALP 236

vetexamprep.ir

U/L (14–91 U/L), creatine kinase 103 U/L (55–257 U/L), GGT 4 U/L
(0–5 U/L), cholesterol 426 mg/dL (139–353 mg/dL), total bilirubin <
0.2 mg/dL (0–0.2 mg/dL), magnesium 2.2 mg/dL (1.9–2.5 mg/dL).
SNAP 4Dx Plus (IDEXX Laboratories, ME, USA): negative for
antibody to Ehrlichia canis, Anaplasma platys, Anaplasma
phagocytophilum, and Borrelia burgdorferi. Negative for antigen to
Diroﬁlaria immitis.

Imaging Findings

Abdominal ultrasound: Abdominal ultrasound examination of the
liver, spleen, pancreas, GI tract, urinary tract, and adrenal glands
was unremarkable. However, within the dorsal right abdominal
wall, adjacent to the kidney and just deep to the last ribs, there was
a gas- and ﬂuid-containing structure. Within this structure there
were one to two foreign bodies visualized that appeared to be
plant awns.

Diagnosis

Suspected plant awn foreign body abscess.

Treatment

Exploratory surgery was performed using a ventral abdominal
approach. This revealed signiﬁcant swelling on the right side of
the body wall under the last rib. The swelling was explored and
purulent material as well as three plant awns were found. The area
was lavaged and a drain placed to allow continuous suction.
Aerobic and anaerobic cultures yielded mixed growth that
included a broadly susceptible Escherichia coli, small numbers of a
viridans streptococcus, and small numbers of Cutibacterium acnes
(formerly Propionibacterium acnes). Grover was discharged on
treatment with clavulanic acid-amoxicillin and carprofen. He
recovered uneventfully.

Comments

This dog had fever that was associated with systemic plant awn
migration. The case illustrates the value of a thorough history (as
the dog had recently vomited up a plant awn) and meticulous
ultrasound examination for detection of migrating foreign bodies.
Plant awns often migrate to sites in the retroperitoneal region and
caudal ribs, which warrants careful scanning of these regions in
dogs with FUO.

Vaccination Schedules for Dogs
and Cats
Jane E. Sykes
The schedules provided below are guidelines for immunization of
dogs and cats against major viral and bacterial agents. These
assume the availability of client resources and suitable products
for immunization. The schedules are based on guidelines wri en
by the WSAVA, AAHA, AAFP and ABCD, 1–11 and information
available at the time of writing. These are general guidelines,
because the vaccine types recommended and the frequency of
immunization vary depending on the lifestyle of the pet being
immunized, i.e., indoor versus outdoor pets, shelter animals,
travel plans, kennel/boarding plans, and underlying disease
conditions such as immune-mediated diseases or preexisting
infections such as FIV infection. Because these factors may change
over time, the vaccination plan for individual pet animals should
be decided by the owner at routine annual examinations, after a
discussion between the veterinarian and the client regarding the
animal’s lifestyle in the year ahead and the advantages and
disadvantages of vaccination. This discussion should be
documented in the medical record. A previous history of vaccine
reactions in an individual pet will also aﬀect recommendations for
immunization. More research is required to generate optimal
recommendations for vaccination of dogs and cats.

vaccines; annual vaccination is recommended for cats that have predominantly
outdoor activities and have aggressive interactions with other cats.

Guidelines for Vaccination of Individual Pet
Dogs and Cats
Guidelines for Vaccination of Dogs and Cats in
Shelter Environments
For shelter animals, a enuated live core vaccines apart from
rabies should be given before or immediately on entry to the
shelter. Optimally, vaccination for CPV and CDV should occur at
least 3 days before entry to a shelter environment, but vaccination
even hours before entry has the potential to make a diﬀerence.
When outbreaks of known parvovirus disease or canine
distemper are present, vaccines can be administered as early as 4–
5 weeks of age, but should not be administered earlier than this
because of the possibility of vaccine-induced disease and
immunosuppression. In the absence of an outbreak situation,
vaccination for these pathogens should be performed no earlier
than 6 weeks of age. In a shelter situation, the beneﬁts and risks of
vaccination of individual pregnant animals with a enuated live
vaccines must be carefully assessed. Vaccination with an

vetexamprep.ir

inactivated vaccine is probably be er than no vaccine for pregnant
animals that enter a shelter, but inactivated vaccines should not be
administered to other animals in the shelter environment, because
the onset of immunity is slower than with a enuated live
vaccines. A enuated live vaccines should be administered if
ovariohysterectomy is to be performed during pregnancy. If
pregnant animals are not vaccinated, they should be strictly
isolated from the rest of the shelter animal population. The use of
rapid in-house serologic tests that assess for protective antibody
titers may be helpful in this situation (see Chapter 20).
Revaccination should be performed no more frequently than at
intervals of 2 to 3 weeks, because administration of an a enuated
live vaccine within 3 to 14 days of another immunization a empt
can interfere with development of immune responses.
Revaccination is most important for pups and ki ens younger
than 16 weeks of age, and is performed to maximize the chance of
immunization as soon as possible after the disappearance of
maternal antibody interference. Puppies and ki ens should also
be physically separated from the rest of the shelter animal
population and handled with strict a ention to quarantine
protocols.
Where aﬀordable, vaccination for respiratory pathogens and
leptospirosis is strongly recommended in shelter environments.
Intranasal vaccines for respiratory pathogens are advantageous in
shelter environments because of the potential for improved local
immunity, the possibility of administration to very young
animals, more rapid onset of protection, and improved protection
in the face of maternal antibody. However, they also have been
associated with vaccine-induced upper respiratory disease, which
may be more severe in debilitated animals and can be diﬃcult to
distinguish from natural infection. In addition, ﬁeld studies have
yet not shown beneﬁt of intranasal over parenteral vaccines for
respiratory disease. Mucosal Bordetella bronchiseptica vaccines
should never be given parenterally. This is an emergency situation
that requires immediate treatment. See Chapter 20 for speciﬁc
instructions on how to manage accidental parenteral
administration of these vaccines. Leptospirosis vaccines are
bacterins and so require 2 doses, 3-4 weeks apart, to provide
protection, with annual re-vaccination. Because leptospires can be

vetexamprep.ir

shed subclinically in the urine of dogs in shelters, vaccination
should nevertheless be considered in an eﬀort to minimize
zoonotic transmission.
In endemic areas, if possible, a rabies vaccine could be
administered at the time of discharge from the facility. 1
Administration of a 3-year product is preferred, but regardless of
the product used, booster immunization must be performed no
later than 1 year after the initial immunization. Rabies
immunization must be properly documented and a veterinarian
must usually be present at the time of immunization. Otherwise,
the number of vaccines should be limited to those that can assist
control of disease that is conﬁrmed to exist within the shelter. This
will avoid excessive immune suppression that may worsen the
severity of illness due to other pathogens in the shelter for which
vaccines are nonexistent.
